Morgan Aspen Client Insights Series focused on China's role in the global economy, featuring interviews with Ronnie Chan, Chairman of Hang Lung Group, and Lee Kuan Yew, former Prime Minister of Singapore. The central argument is that China's contemporary rise is not an aggressive expansion but rather a reassertion of the dominant global position it held for centuries prior to the industrial revolution. To highlight China's massive economic influence, the text notes an IMF statistic predicting that China would likely generate 75% of the world's GDP growth for the three years ending in 2010. 

A bar chart titled "The 20th century was a growth anomaly for China" displays China's share of world GDP from Year 1 through 2003, using data from Angus Maddison. The chart shows that China historically accounted for 25% to over 30% of global GDP for nearly two millennia, peaking around 1820. Its share collapsed during the 20th century, bottoming out below 5% between 1950 and 1975, before climbing back to approximately 15% by 2003. 

To address international apprehensions about China's growing power, the page analyzes defense expenditures. A dual-axis chart titled "Chinese military spending (constant 2005 dollars)" tracks spending from 1989 to 2007 using data from the Stockholm International Peace Institute. It shows absolute military spending on the left axis rising from roughly $12 billion in 1989 to over $60 billion in 2007, while per capita military spending on the right axis rose in tandem from $10 to about $45. 

Another chart, "Global distribution of military expenditure" in 2007, puts this spending into perspective. It shows that the United States dominated global defense spending at roughly 43%, while China's share was only about 5%. The remaining global spending was distributed among Japan, France, and the UK (each at very low single digits), the next ten countries combined (around 17%), and the rest of the world. Despite China's military budget representing only about 10% of U.S. levels, the text notes that its rise is still viewed warily by neighbors, with favorability ratings toward China remaining below 50% in South Korea and Japan.

A biographical sidebar introduces Ronnie C. Chan, detailing his leadership of the Hong Kong-listed Hang Lung Group Limited. It highlights his company's plan to invest $5 billion in eighteen commercial complexes in mainland China between 2005 and 2009, his frequent international speaking engagements, and his leadership of a project to restore the Imperial Gardens in Beijing's Forbidden City.

This page assesses the potential return of capital for the 2006-2007 vintage leveraged buyout (LBO) transactions by modeling three key components: earnings, exit multiples, and debt paydown. 

Before introducing the model, the author notes that improved credit access is being supported by approximately $25 billion in year-to-date inflows into high-yield bond funds, which were mostly funded from money market funds. An accompanying chart showing high-yield mutual fund weekly flows as a four-week rolling average from 1993 through late 2008 highlights a highly volatile historical range between negative $1,200 million and positive $1,500 million. In addition to these inflows, companies are buying time to repay principal, with Standard and Poor's reporting $14 billion in loans restructured through "amend-to-extend" agreements, while other LBO companies are repurchasing their own discounted debt to defer taxable income.

The first part of the valuation model focuses on earnings. From the first quarter of 2008 to the first quarter of 2009, the LBO Composite’s EBITDA fell by 21 percent, performing nearly identically to the S&P 500's decline of 21.9 percent. This outcome was better than feared because the Composite’s concentration in consumer discretionary holdings was nearly 2.5 times that of the S&P 500. A bar chart of the portfolio sector breakdown as of March 2009 illustrates this exposure, showing the LBO Composite with roughly 22 percent exposure to consumer discretionary compared to the S&P 500's exposure of approximately 9 percent. The chart also breaks down allocations across consumer staples, info tech, industrials, financials, utilities, healthcare, materials, telecom, and energy. The portfolio's relative resilience is attributed to its exposure to stable, low-price-point retail, food service, medical devices, healthcare, and cost-cutting measures. For its forward-looking projections, the model assumes the EBITDA decline carries through 2009, followed by an 8 percent recovery growth rate in 2010 and 5 percent growth thereafter. For context, this is compared to the S&P Industrials Index, which averaged 7.2 percent EBITDA growth from 1967 through 2008.

The second part of the model addresses exit multiples. The analysis assumes exit multiples will be 1x to 2x lower than their respective entry multiples, based on 5-to-10-year sector averages, and projects that all companies will exit six years from their initial investment when large amounts of debt begin to mature. The author observes signs that multiples are holding up, pointing to a recent semiconductor IPO executed at 12.5x EBITDA and ten major strategic U.S. mergers and acquisitions executed at a median purchase multiple of 8.5x EBITDA. However, a major risk remains for large-cap transactions, which are less likely to find strategic buyers and must rely heavily on public IPO markets for exit strategies.

The third and final part of the model addresses debt paydown. While LBO sponsors in normal economic cycles typically use excess cash flow to pay down 35 percent to 45 percent of their high-cost debt within the first five to six years, the current model must account for severe downward pressure on cash flows.

This page analyzes the historical context and subsequent economic trajectory of China’s modern growth, arguing that the severe traumas of the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution created a societal willingness to undergo immense sacrifice, which ultimately propelled the Deng Xiaoping reforms. A footnote highlights that the combined death toll from these historical episodes is estimated at thirty to forty million, while another footnote notes a pivotal November 1978 meeting between Deng Xiaoping and Lee Kuan Yew that closely coincided with the onset of these reforms. 

The economic impacts of the Deng reforms are visualized through four charts. The first, titled "China's trade openness begins with Deng reforms," measures total trade as a percentage of GDP from 1952 to 2007, showing both nominal and real trade to GDP. Prior to the late 1970s, both measures sat below ten percent, but following the start of the reforms, they climbed steadily to peak at approximately seventy percent by 2007. The second chart, "China's catch-up the fastest so far," compares per capita GDP trajectories using a normalized x-axis showing the number of years since each country’s per capita GDP was equal to Japan’s in 1950. Comparing China from 1994 to 2007 against postwar Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, and India, the data reveals that China's catch-up curve is the steepest of all, rapidly ascending from a baseline of two thousand to nearly nine thousand over a fourteen-year period.

The page also details how China fostered the growth of private enterprise and reduced state support for failing government entities. The "Entrepreneur explosion" chart tracks the number of enterprises by ownership type in millions from 1992 to 2006. While state-owned and collective enterprises shrank or remained flat, private enterprises exploded from a negligible sliver in 1992 to the dominant share of the total by 2006, when total enterprises approached nine million. Concurrently, the "Government subsidies to loss-making SOEs" chart tracks subsidies in billions of RMB and as a percentage of government expenditures from 1985 to 2006. Subsidies peaked in 1989 and 1990 at nearly sixty billion RMB, which accounted for over twenty percent of total government expenditure. By 2006, these subsidies fell to around twenty billion RMB, representing less than one percent of government spending. A footnote cautions that this chart only tracks support for loss-making state-owned enterprises; citing HKMA research, the author notes that if profitable state-owned enterprises were forced to pay market credit rates comparable to private firms, their profits would entirely disappear. The page concludes by noting that China's combination of inexpensive labor and foreign direct investment successfully moved the country up the high-tech export food chain, positioning it as a top global trading partner.

This page from the publication discusses the sharp rebound in Chinese economic indicators, focusing on the massive stimulus required to achieve this growth and the long-term productivity implications of China's heavy capital investment. The author, Michael Cembalest, notes that China is relying heavily on capital formation to generate GDP and jobs because global trade contributions are low. While this strategy risks creating deflationary excess capacity, it serves immediate job creation needs and promises long-term productivity benefits, similar to historical U.S. infrastructure achievements like rural electrification and the interstate highway system.

Several charts support these observations. The first, located at the top right, is titled Chinese loan growth per unit improvement in real GDP. It displays a ratio from June 1998 through December 2008. The ratio historically fluctuated between 0.5 and 2.5, but spiked dramatically at the end of 2008 to over 4.0, illustrating the colossal amount of monetary stimulus required to spur economic growth.

Below this, a pair of charts contrasts China's domestic investment with global capacity. The chart on the left, Capital formation contribution to GDP growing, illustrates the share of GDP growth from 2000 to the first half of 2009, divided among consumption, capital formation, and net trade. In the first half of 2009, net trade dragged growth down by negative 2.9 percent, while consumption contributed 3.8 percent, and capital formation dominated at 6.2 percent. The companion chart on the right, titled ...just when the world doesn't need it, plots the global operating rate from 1973 to 2009 in standard deviations from its 1991 to 2007 average. By 2009, this rate plummeted to nearly negative 5 standard deviations, emphasizing the severe global overcapacity environment in which China is expanding its production.

The final chart at the bottom, Fixed asset investment by industry, shows the year-over-year percentage change of cumulative fixed asset investment from January to June across several sectors. Railway transport shows an extraordinary expansion, growing by more than 120 percent. This massive railway growth dwarfs other industrial sectors shown, such as coal, electricity and heat, non-metal products, and various metals, all of which grew at rates under 40 percent. The author, referencing insights from an expert named Ronnie and ISI research, explains that this investment is addressing a 50-year stagnation in per-capita rail kilometers. Additionally, the text notes that Chinese agriculture presents another major opportunity for productivity gains, as Chinese corn yields remain far below those of the United States and Europe.

This page from J.P. Morgan's China series outlines the key twenty-first-century challenges facing China. These hurdles include falling U.S. consumer debt, an aging demographic shift over the next decade, rising U.S. political protectionism, growing carbon emissions, and the delicate geopolitical status of Taiwan. The text reflects on a client Q&A session featuring Lee Kuan Yew and Ronnie, which explored how foreign businesses must adapt to unique Chinese business norms, such as the unilateral renegotiation of contracts and the inherent risks of dealing with state-owned companies. 

A callout box discusses bilateral tensions surrounding industrial espionage, noting that China-related FBI cases in Silicon Valley have been rising by 20% to 30% per year, while German and Canadian counter-intelligence estimate that their respective companies lose billions monthly to Chinese espionage. It cites a 2007 report to Congress stating that Chinese espionage represents the single greatest threat to U.S. technology. The page also touches on corporate acquisitions, comparing Western blocks on Chinese acquisitions, such as 3Com, Unocal, and Maytag, with China's decision to block Coca-Cola's proposed acquisition of Huiyuan Juice Group, highlighting China's protectionist stance toward domestic competitors.

A bar chart on the page, titled "China ranks high on one measure of corruption" and sourced from Transparency International in 2008, illustrates the percentage of respondents reporting frequent corrupt practices across twenty-two countries. The data is broken down into three series: bribery to high-ranking politicians (blue), bribery to low-level public officials to speed things up (red), and the use of personal and familiar relationships on public contracting (green). Russia, Mexico, India, and China rank highest on these measures. For China, approximately 30% of respondents report the frequent use of personal relationships, around 25% cite low-level bribery, and nearly 18% report bribery of high-ranking politicians. These figures are significantly higher than those of Western nations like the United States, the United Kingdom, and Germany, which show very low levels of reported corruption across all three categories. Lee Kuan Yew observes that if mainland China were to adopt a more consistent rule of law, Beijing and Shanghai could eventually displace Hong Kong and Singapore as regional financial hubs.

Footnotes add further geopolitical context, suggesting that the U.S. administration's protectionist stance may give China an eight-year free reign to solidify relationships across Asia, Latin America, and Africa. Additionally, relations with Taiwan are noted as improving under President Hu Jintao, underscored by recent multi-billion-dollar procurements of Taiwanese goods by the Chinese government and Lenovo.

This page serves as a concluding reference and notes section for an issue of J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market," which addresses topics such as post-stimulus disorder, credit market returns, private equity bankruptcies, China, and climate change. In an introductory notes section, author Michael Cembalest addresses the base erosion effects of higher tax rates, citing economic studies by Emmanuel Saez, Joel Slemrod, Matthew Eichner, and Todd Sinai. While noting that base erosion is a controversial topic related to the Laffer curve, he explains that J.P. Morgan's models assume it reduces taxable income and capital gains by a modest 3.5% to 5.0%. 

The core of the page features two scatter plot charts analyzing capital spending and employment severities across US recessions since 1953. Both charts demonstrate that the current recession has been exceptionally severe relative to the overall decline in economic output. The first chart, "Business investment vs. GDP in recessions," plots business capital spending declines against GDP declines. It reveals that the current recession has seen capital spending plunge by nearly 18% against a GDP decline of roughly 3.5%, placing it far below the historical trendline. The second chart, "Private sector employment vs. GDP in recessions," compares private employment declines to GDP declines. It shows a similar outlier trend for the current recession, where private employment has fallen by about 5.5%—significantly worse than the historical norm for a 3.5% GDP contraction. 

Additionally, the page provides a list of acronym definitions commonly used in macroeconomic analysis, including OMB, CBO, LBO, BEA, DIP, SOE, FHA, FNMA, and VAT, and concludes with contact information for Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer at J.P. Morgan Global Wealth Management.

This page from the publication discusses "G-FORCE," the powerful positive impact of global fiscal stimulus on Q3 2009 economic recovery, while raising serious concerns about the sustainability of this growth once government support fades. The author notes that world GDP growth is tracking at 4% to 5% for Q3, led by a 12% expansion in Asia during Q2. While manufacturing demand and inventory gaps point to a strong near-term recovery, the text questions the long-term consequences of these massive fiscal and monetary programs. 

An upper right-hand chart titled "Since the recession began, growth been has been stimulus-dependent" maps the connection between fiscal stimulus and GDP. The chart uses two axes from 2007 through projections into 2011. The left-hand scale measures the contribution of fiscal stimulus to GDP growth, which peaks at approximately 3% in mid-2009. The right-hand scale shows the annualized quarter-over-quarter percentage change in real GDP, which hits a trough of roughly negative 6% in late 2008 before surging to a J.P. Morgan Securities Q3 2009 estimate of 4%. This rebound is highly correlated with the peaking stimulus contribution, which is projected to decline sharply through 2010 and turn slightly negative in 2011.

To illustrate the risk of stimulus withdrawal, the author highlights the housing and auto sectors. A bottom-left chart titled "Before and after: California New Home Tax Credit and monthly building permits issued" plots monthly permits from January 2007 to July 2009 on a scale of 1,000 to 8,000. It shows that California building permits, which fell from over 7,000 in early 2007, received a brief boost in early-to-mid 2009 from the state tax credit. However, immediately after the credit expired, July 2009 permits plunged by 29%. Additionally, the author warns that solvency issues at the Federal Housing Administration, such as its tight 2% capital cushion, could soon tighten mortgage credit.

A bottom-right chart titled "Before and after: Cash for Clunkers and Edmunds' car buying intent" shows an index of car-buying intent from June to late August 2009, based on a January 31, 2009 level of 100. The line chart demonstrates a massive spike exceeding an index level of 220 when the "Cash for Clunkers" program launched on July 27, followed by another peak when the program was extended on August 6, before dropping precipitously back to nearly 110 by the time the program officially ended on August 24. A parallel trend is observed in Germany, where the 7-billion-dollar Abwrackprämie program ran out of money on September 2.

Looking ahead to fiscal exit strategies, the text challenges the idea that higher taxes on the wealthy can close the U.S. budget gap. The author argues that taxing the highest two marginal brackets and capital gains would yield about 1.5 trillion dollars, making little impact on the Office of Management and Budget's 9 trillion dollar, 10-year deficit. Consequently, the author predicts that the future for countries like the United States, United Kingdom, Spain, and Japan will inevitably require spending cuts, higher middle-class taxes, value-added taxes, and permanently higher national debt.

This page discusses the macroeconomic transformation of Brazil, analyzing its domestic credit markets, equity valuations, and the key commodity-linked companies that dominate its market index. The author begins by contrasting Brazil's current financial strength with the high budget deficits of the mid-1990s. Today, Brazilian public debt is on a stable path, unemployment is near record lows, and consumer confidence is booming. 

A primary driver of this success has been credit expansion. In a chart titled "Brazil's publicly-owned banks doing the heavy lifting," which tracks year-over-year percentage changes in bank lending from January 2003 to January 2009, the author illustrates a divergence in the financial sector. While private sector bank lending collapsed from its late 2007 peak to about 15% by early 2009, public sector lending—driven by institutions like Banco do Brasil and Caixa Economica—steeply accelerated, rising from roughly 15% in late 2007 to over 40% by early 2009. This state-directed lending, paired with a 40% cut in bank reserve requirements, cushioned the domestic economy.

Regarding equity markets, Brazilian stocks trade at roughly 18 times 2010 earnings. However, the market is highly concentrated, with Petrobras and Vale/CVRD making up 42% of the MSCI Brazil Country Index. On Petrobras, the author cautions that the market is pricing in an ambitious 10% to 12% production growth rate, whereas historical growth from 2001 to 2009 was only 4.7%. Petrobras frequently missed its forward production targets from 2004 to 2007, and its new sub-salt drilling projects—lying kilometers beneath the ocean floor and thick layers of salt—present unprecedented geological and engineering challenges akin to putting someone on the moon.

Vale/CVRD is heavily dependent on Chinese commodity demand, which shows signs of softening. A second chart, "Iron ore supply/demand worsening with Chinese stock building," plots China's iron ore spot price against inventory levels from June 2006 to June 2009. It shows that Chinese iron ore inventories (measured on the left axis in ten thousand tons) steadily marched upward from approximately 4,000 ten thousand tons in late 2006 to over 7,000 ten thousand tons by mid-2009. Over the same period, the China iron ore spot price (measured on the right axis in RMB per metric ton) peaked in mid-2008 at over 1,400 RMB before crashing down toward 700 RMB.

In terms of asset allocation, the author maintains a 2% to 4% holding in Brazilian equities within diversified portfolios but stands ready to sell if valuations become too optimistic. The firm also holds Reais outright and in World Bank bonds. Ultimately, the author warns that while global stimulus is driving a pleasant market ride for now, mounting concerns about asset bubbles and inflation could prompt policymakers to rein in liquidity, evoking a bittersweet sentiment regarding how this credit-fueled story might end.

The author questions why investors would hold European equities given the exceptionally weak domestic rebound following the global financial crisis. Despite some leading indicators turning positive, the underlying economic recovery in Europe lags significantly behind other regions, burdened by high debt, unfavorable labor costs, demographic headwinds, and high energy dependence. 

The page features three tables detailing the percentage recovery of peak-to-trough declines across retail sales, industrial production, and employment for various countries. In retail sales, European nations show weak progress, with Germany at 0 percent, France at 5 percent, and Italy at 16 percent, though the United Kingdom is a notable exception at 89 percent. For industrial production, recovery is similarly sluggish: the United Kingdom, Sweden, and Ireland sit at 0 percent, Spain is at 3 percent, and Germany and France stand at 21 percent and 23 percent respectively, trailing far behind emerging giants like China at 156 percent and India at 182 percent. In terms of employment recovery, the United States and several European nations including France, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Ireland sit at 0 percent, while Germany stands out with a 77 percent recovery, illustrating the resilience of its labor market safety net.

The text is supported by two line charts. The first chart, depicting Euro area government debt as a percentage of nominal GDP from 1991 to 2012, shows debt levels skyrocketing from roughly 66 percent in 2007 to an estimated peak approaching 100 percent by 2012. The second chart details unit labor costs from 2002 to 2009, indexed to 100 in the first quarter of 2002, comparing Germany, the United States, and Japan. It shows German unit labor costs rising sharply to 106.3 by the second quarter of 2009, compared to 108.8 for the United States and a much lower 92.4 for Japan.

Beyond labor and debt, the author highlights structural headwinds, citing Eurostat data that shows European birth rates at 1.5 children per woman, well below the 2.1 replacement rate, with France leading at 2.0 and Italy trailing at 1.3. Furthermore, the European Union's energy vulnerability is acute, currently importing 50 percent of its energy needs with forecasts predicting a rise to 70 percent by 2030, compared to the United States which imports only 30 percent. 

The primary reason to still own European equities, according to the author, is that European companies are highly diversified outside of their stagnant domestic markets. Over the last decade, the share of revenue earned by European companies outside of Europe has increased from 27 percent to 40 percent, significantly reducing their reliance on the local European economic recovery, with exposure to emerging markets providing a crucial boost.

Michael Cembalest discusses the ongoing pressure on consumer spending and leverage, exacerbated by U.S. legislation like the Credit Card Accountability, Responsibility, and Disclosure Act. This law restricts banks from using risk-based pricing on non-delinquent accounts, prompting them to raise rates on delinquent accounts and tighten overall lending standards. Cembalest warns that with organic disposable income growth remaining low, these regulatory shifts could drag consumer spending and leverage down even further.

This argument is illustrated by a line chart tracking mortgage and consumer debt payments as a percentage of disposable income (excluding government transfers) from 1977 to 2009. The chart compares a series representing interest payments only against a series that includes interest plus a 1.5 percent annual amortization of mortgage and consumer balances. Both metrics demonstrate that household debt service remains near historic highs. The combined interest and amortization line peaked near 13 percent in 2007 and remained elevated near 12.5 percent into 2009, indicating that consumer de-leveraging is far from complete.

The commentary then shifts to the performance of defensive equity strategies implemented during the market bottom. A second line chart tracks the one-year forward implied volatility of S&P 500 options from October 2007 through October 2009. Volatility surged from approximately 20 percent in late 2007 to a peak of nearly 48 percent during the height of the financial crisis in late 2008. During Spring 2009, volatility remained highly elevated between 30 percent and 43 percent. Cembalest highlights this period as an ideal time to sell volatility, as high option prices allowed investors to sacrifice upside potential in exchange for robust downside protection.

Following a subsequent 40 percent to 50 percent rally in global equities from their early 2009 lows, many of these structured, defensive investments have begun to exceed their performance caps. Cembalest advises that portfolios containing too many capped investments may no longer provide sufficient equity market exposure and will require rebalancing to restore target allocations. He concludes that while the rapid market rally has capped some gains, the decision to prioritize downside protection was the correct trade-off given the severe systemic bank nationalization risks feared in early 2009.

This page explores the disconnect between domestic European economic difficulties and the performance of European equities, highlighting how corporate exposure to high-growth emerging markets has insulated major companies. 

The first chart, "Revenue exposure of European companies," illustrates this shift by tracking the percentage of total revenues from 1997 to 2009. It shows that revenue exposure to emerging markets rose steadily from approximately 11% in 1997 to 23% in 2009. Meanwhile, exposure to North America peaked at around 21% in 2003 before declining to roughly 16% in 2009. This corporate pivot aligns with the rising global dominance of emerging market economies shown in the second chart, "% of Global GDP represented by EM economies" from 1980 to 2008. Measured by market exchange rates, emerging markets represented 35% of global GDP by 2008. When adjusted for purchasing power parity (PPP) exchange rates to account for currency interventions, emerging market economies accounted for more than 50% of total world output by 2008.

Spain is presented as a key case study of this trend. Despite facing a severe domestic fiscal and housing crisis, Spanish equities outperformed benchmarks in Europe, the United States, and Japan in 2009. This outperformance is driven by the five largest companies on the Spanish IBEX index—Santander, Telefonica, BBVA, Iberdrola, and Repsol—which constitute 70% of the index's market capitalization. These multinational firms generate between one-third and two-thirds of their revenues outside Europe, following a massive expansion period where Spain's outward direct investment rose from 3% of GDP in the 1990–2000 period to a record 44% in 2007.

Finally, the page evaluates overall European equity valuations, suggesting they are currently resting near long-term historical averages. The bottom-left chart, "Price/Earnings ratios in 'fair' territory," tracks price to 1-year forward earnings for the MSCI Europe ex-UK index from 1988 to 2009. It shows the 2009 ratio sitting directly on its 20-year average of approximately 14, down from past peaks of over 22. The bottom-right chart, "Same for Price/Book," presents the price-to-book value for the same index from 1980 to 2009, tracking both the overall index and an "ex-financials" series to control for distorted bank book values. Both price-to-book series have declined from peaks near 3.5 in the late 1990s to sit between 1.5 and 2.0 by late 2009.

This page focuses on two distinct themes: the divergence in global industrial production and corporate earnings, and the debunking of myths surrounding U.S. consumer de-leveraging. 

In the first section, the author argues that stronger-than-expected corporate profits for the first and second quarters of 2009 were driven by corporate cost controls and robust international demand, particularly from markets that are recovering rapidly from the financial crisis. While domestic recoveries remain sluggish, large-cap companies in the United States and Europe source over 30% of their sales internationally, sheltering them from local weakness. 

This global economic divergence is illustrated in a table showing the recovery of peak-to-trough industrial production decline through August 2009. The data reveals that while Sweden, Canada, and the United Kingdom have seen 0% recovery, and the United States and the Euro Area show weak recoveries of 10% and 3%, other regions have surged. China and India are leading the pack, having recovered 156% and 176% of their declines, respectively, placing them well above pre-crisis levels. 

Two charts support the discussion on corporate earnings. The first chart, tracking S&P quarterly 2009 earnings per share expectations from December 2008 through December 2009, asks if third-quarter expectations are too low. It shows actual results beating expectations, with the first quarter actualizing at $12.83 and the second quarter at $16.00, while the third and fourth quarters are projected to bottom out at estimates of $14.83 and $16.62. The second chart, measuring the 13-week average of upward earnings revisions relative to total revisions from 1990 to late 2008, shows a sharp rebound from a post-crisis low of 20% up to approximately 45%, suggesting corporate profits may continue to beat expectations.

In the second section, titled after the urban legend of sewer alligator sightings to emphasize how rare the phenomenon actually is, the author challenges the narrative that U.S. households are successfully de-leveraging. Although some commentators point to contracting consumer credit and lower mortgage interest obligations as signs of progress, the author shows that overall household debt remains high. This is illustrated by a long-term line chart plotting mortgage and consumer debt balances as a percentage of disposable income from 1959 through 2008. The chart depicts a steady, multi-decade climb from 40% in 1959 to a peak of nearly 120% around 2008. By June 2009, this ratio had barely budged from its historic peak, indicating that actual debt reduction has been negligible. The author suggests that to understand the true burden, analysts must look at debt service coverage while excluding temporary government transfers and accounting for principal amortization, which is explored further on the subsequent page.

This page examines European banking recapitalization, equity valuation timing, and the structural challenges of the DESERTEC Sahara solar initiative. 

First, the author notes that European banks require EUR 27 billion to achieve an 8% core Tier 1 capital ratio and an additional EUR 28 billion to repay government equity injections. This recapitalization is a necessary precursor for banks to begin unloading a massive EUR 500 billion pool of non-performing loans, which distressed debt managers are currently purchasing at under 50 cents on the Euro. 

The relationship between earnings cycles and market bottoms is illustrated in a chart titled "When do asset prices bottom? Peak-to-trough decline in European earnings." Spanning from 1969 to 2008, the chart plots the percentage peak-to-trough decline of European earnings on a vertical axis from 0% down to -50%. Thick black vertical lines mark the historical bottoms of the MSCI European equity market. The visual demonstrates that equity markets consistently bottom out prior to, or precisely at, the absolute trough of corporate earnings. Based on this pattern, the author supports owning European equities slightly below long-term targets, arguing that the region's macroeconomic headwinds were already priced in following a 57% market decline. Looking ahead, the critical question for 2010 is how demand will fare as economic stimulus is withdrawn.

The second half of the page evaluates the DESERTEC project, a joint plan backed by major entities like Munich Re, ABB, E.ON, Siemens, and Deutsche Bank to supply 15% of Europe's electricity via Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) in the Sahara. While promising, the author outlines severe practical hurdles. First, the Sahara’s daily temperature swings from -10°C to 60°C threaten sensitive equipment. Second, Vattenfall’s CEO estimates the total cost at EUR 400 billion to EUR 500 billion, posing massive financial and terrorism risks. Additionally, 80% of the optimal locations lie in the Libyan desert or near Mecca, raising expropriation and geopolitical concerns. Economically, CSP estimates of 12 to 15 cents per kilowatt-hour make solar 30% to 40% more expensive than coal or natural gas, even assuming a carbon tax of $30 per ton. Lower capacity factors mean that replacing 1 GW of coal requires building 1.5 to 3.0 GW of CSP, and desert sites lack the water necessary for turbine cooling. 

Despite these concerns, the author acknowledges that CSP is a functional technology currently operating in Spain, California, and Australia, and under construction in Algeria, Morocco, and Israel. Transitioning to zero-emission energy remains crucial for the European Union, as a six-meter rise in sea level would submerge key cities like Barcelona, Venice, Amsterdam, London, Stockholm, and Lisbon. Ultimately, as installed CSP capacity doubles, costs are expected to drop by 10% to 15%, suggesting the technology could eventually achieve cost parity with traditional fossil fuels.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses corporate earnings expectations and analyzes U.S. household leverage in response to a query from J.P. Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon. 

Regarding corporate earnings, Cembalest anticipates that earnings will meet or exceed expectations over the next several quarters. This positive outlook is supported by high corporate operating leverage, where companies have cut 88 cents of expenses for every dollar of revenue decline. Additionally, U.S. growth is experiencing the maximum impact of economic stimulus, Chinese money supply and loan growth continue to rise at a high rate of 30% to 35% per year, and a 50-year high in corporate cash balances is driving a modest recovery in mergers and acquisitions. 

The potential for a technology upgrade cycle is also noted, supported by a line chart showing the percentage of the PC installed base by operating system from 1998 to 2008. The chart tracks the decline of older operating systems like Windows 95 and Windows 98, the moderate peak of Windows 2000 near 30%, and the massive dominance of Windows XP, which peaked near 75% in 2006 and remained above 60% in 2008. With Windows Vista seeing slower adoption, the aging PC base suggests a imminent upgrade cycle.

In the second section, Cembalest addresses household leverage. In response to Jamie Dimon's question about how future defaults might reduce overall leverage, Cembalest notes that currently delinquent mortgage and consumer loans total $900 billion and $145 billion, respectively. An accompanying chart displays mortgage and consumer debt balances as a percentage of disposable income from 1959 through 2008, showing a long-term rise from 50% to a peak of roughly 125%. The chart features two data points comparing the unadjusted leverage figure of approximately 125% to an adjusted figure of roughly 115%, which assumes that all $1.0 trillion in delinquent loans are fully repudiated rather than restructured. Cembalest notes that while this complete write-off would help household finances, it would raise serious questions about bank capital ratios, and the actual outcome is likely to fall somewhere between these two points.

This J.P. Morgan report from October 21, 2009, analyzes third-quarter earnings, economic updates, and the mechanics of the market rally following the 2008 financial crisis. The author begins with a market and economic update, noting that Q3 earnings confirm operating leverage from cost-cutting. With nearly one-fifth of companies reporting, 82% are beating earnings forecasts and 68% are beating revenue estimates. General Electric is highlighted as a bellwether: its industrial business cash flow has returned to trend with record order backlogs, though GE Capital earnings are down 93% year-over-year. The broader economic recovery remains fragile; jobless claims show second-derivative improvements, but small business conditions remain poor, and nearly 60% of the decline in continuing claims is attributed to exhausted unemployment benefits. Furthermore, J.P. Morgan remains cautious about the U.S. housing outlook, anticipating that pending foreclosures will swamp improving price trends.

The report then transitions to analyzing the global equity market rally, which has seen a 67% gain since March 2009. The author argues that markets typically bottom well before improvements in employment, delinquencies, defaults, earnings, and GDP growth. This pattern is illustrated in a chart tracking the peak-to-trough decline in European earnings versus equity market troughs from 1969 to 2008. The chart, sourced from MSCI and Morgan Stanley, shows that MSCI European equities bottomed in March 2009 and subsequently rose about 50% even as sequential monthly earnings continued to decline. 

To support the argument that U.S. equities bottom before recessions end, a table details ten U.S. recessions from 1953 through 2009. This table lists the number of months between the equity market bottom and the recession's end, along with the subsequent S&P 500 rally. For example, during the 1953–1954 recession, the market bottomed nine months before the end of the recession, resulting in a 29% S&P 500 rally. For the recession spanning December 2007 to July 2009, the market bottomed four months prior to the recession's end, sparking a 46% S&P 500 rally. 

Finally, the page presents three comparative charts illustrating the relationship between bank stock bottoms and cumulative bank failures during major financial crises. Each chart tracks the bank stock index level against cumulative bank failures. In the Great Depression from 1929 to 1934, bank stocks (represented by the Dow Jones Industrial Average) bottomed when cumulative bank failures reached 48% of the total cycle failures. During the Savings and Loan Crisis from 1988 to 1994, the S&P 500 Bank Index bottomed when cumulative failures reached 63%. In the financial crisis of 2008 to 2009, bank stocks bottomed remarkably early, when cumulative bank failures were only 34% of the way through the total failure cycle. These charts utilize data from the FDIC and Bloomberg to demonstrate that financial markets consistently anticipate the end of bank failure cycles.

This page explores the concept of network effects in technology, comparing sectors where network effects are powerful against those where they are weaker, and ultimately applying these lessons to the future of Skype. The author argues that in businesses like search engines and communication platforms, every incremental user makes the service more valuable for others. To illustrate this, the page includes a chart titled "Online search engines" showing search volume according to Experian Hitwise and StatCounter. Google overwhelmingly dominates the market with roughly 75% to over 80% share, followed distantly by Yahoo! at around 15%, with Bing, Ask, and AOL holding negligible shares. This is contrasted with a chart titled "U.S. web email service usage," which tracks unique monthly visitors for December 2008 and July 2009. Here, market share is more distributed: Yahoo! Mail leads with around 100 million unique visitors, followed by Hotmail at roughly 45 million, Gmail at 35 million, and AOL at 35 million. The author notes that email does not have strong network effects, as more users on a platform do not inherently improve the experience for others.

The discussion extends to hardware and software applications where dominant players have resisted strong, well-funded competitors by combining network effects with continuous innovation. A chart on "Rich Internet Application software" displays installation rates on computers for the trailing 30 days ending October 26, 2009. Adobe Flash is the clear leader, installed on over 90% of computers (with alternate estimates suggesting up to 99%), followed by Sun Java at approximately 65% and Microsoft Silverlight at roughly 25%. Similarly, a chart on "Portable Music Players" shows market share from the first quarter of 2008, where Apple's iPod commands a massive 70% of the market, leaving competitors like SanDisk Sansa, Microsoft Zune, and Creative Zen with minor single-digit shares.

A dedicated callout box highlights Skype’s expansion into cellular networks, noting that its launch on the iPhone resulted in 1 million downloads in just two days, and that AT&T recently permitted Skype usage over its 3G network. The author raises the open question of whether Skype can pair its current network effect advantage with sufficient innovation to ward off upcoming competitors. Footnotes cite academic research from the Journal of Marketing Research indicating that quality ultimately wins over first-mover advantages, and that network effects alone cannot permanently shield market leaders from competitors who offer a superior product.

This page analyzes the rapid financial market recovery in late 2009, detailing J.P. Morgan's asset allocation decisions, the timing of credit market recoveries relative to fundamentals, and the long-term sovereign debt challenges resulting from government intervention. The author notes that while their balanced portfolios maintained a steady 30% to 38% equity allocation alongside hedge fund and credit holdings, with hindsight, they could have allocated more. Instead, they actively purchased credit, noting that high-yield bond spreads rallied much earlier in this cycle compared to historical precedents.

To support this credit thesis, a series of three charts titled "Credit markets: 1987 to 1993," "Credit markets: 1999 to 2004," and "Credit markets: 2006 to present" plot high yield (HY) spread-to-worst against cumulative issuer defaults. The left axes show spreads (up to 1,200 basis points for the first two cycles and up to 2,000 basis points for the latest cycle), while the right axes show the number of issuers. Across all three cycles, peak spreads occurred well before the majority of defaults materialized. Specifically, cumulative defaults at the time of peak spreads were at 55% in the 1987–1993 cycle, 76% in the 1999–2004 cycle, and just 42% in the 2006 to present cycle, indicating that credit markets priced in the worst of the cycle exceptionally early.

The author points to securitized commercial real estate as the prime example of markets anticipating recovery before fundamental improvements occurred. A chart titled "CMBS: 2006 to present" tracks the AAA CMBS spread (left axis, ranging from 0 to 1,600 basis points) and the 60+ delinquency rate (right axis, from 0.0% to 3.5%). The data shows that AAA CMBS spreads peaked near 1,400 basis points in late 2008 and early 2009, long before the 60+ delinquency rate surged past 3.0% in mid-2009. 

The commentary attributes this disconnect to massive, unprecedented public sector interventions. While these actions stabilized markets, the author warns they could turn into "the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse" for public finances, presenting daunting fiscal challenges for OECD nations. This issue is illustrated by the chart "U.S. and European debt: the end of an era," which plots gross government debt as a percentage of GDP from 1991 through estimated projections to 2012. Both the U.S. and the Euro area show sharp upward trajectories starting in 2008, with Euro area debt projected to reach roughly 85% of GDP and U.S. debt projected to exceed 100% of GDP by 2012, compared to pre-crisis levels of around 70% and 65% respectively. 

The author concludes that resolving these debt levels will be far more difficult than in historical post-war periods because current debts are driven by domestic entitlements and financed abroad rather than being easily cut defense expenditures. To cope, U.S. banks may need to increase their holdings of Treasury and Agency debt from 13% to a historical peak of 22% of assets, which would provide about $1 trillion in incremental demand but displace other productive assets from bank balance sheets.

This J.P. Morgan report examines the potential value and limitations of network effects, arguing that while they can lead to market dominance, they do not guarantee permanent leadership. The author first points to video sharing and online movie retailing as sectors where network effects established dominant leaders despite low product differentiation. A bar chart of monthly video sharing visitors for October 2009 shows YouTube commanding a massive lead of over 80 million visitors, leaving competitors like Metacafe, tv.com, and dailymotion far behind with fewer than 15 million visitors each. Another bar chart on online movie retailing compares 2007 annual revenues, showing Netflix dominating with roughly $1.2 billion in revenue compared to Blockbuster at around $500 million. 

However, the report cautions that network effects can fade, using social networking and internet browsers as key examples of disrupted leadership. A bar chart comparing unique US monthly visitors in October 2008 versus September 2009 shows Facebook dramatically overtaking MySpace, skyrocketing from about 50 million to nearly 120 million visitors, while MySpace slid from approximately 60 million to 55 million. Meanwhile, smaller platforms like Twitter, Classmates, and LinkedIn show modest growth but remain far behind. 

This market volatility is further illustrated by a line chart tracking internet browser market share from 1994 to 2009. It shows the rapid rise and fall of Mosaic, Netscape, and Internet Explorer. Mosaic held nearly 100% share in 1994 before crashing to 9% by 1995 as Netscape rose to peak at over 80%. Netscape then crashed to near-zero as Microsoft's Internet Explorer climbed to over 90% share in the early 2000s, before Internet Explorer itself began a steady decline down to around 65% as Mozilla Firefox rose to around 25% share, alongside emerging gains from Safari and Google Chrome. The accompanying text details this browser war, explaining that while Microsoft's operating system bundling played a role, Netscape ultimately succumbed because its products became crash-prone, slow, and difficult to install compared to Internet Explorer.

This J.P. Morgan report examines three major post-financial crisis dynamics: unprecedented credit expansion in China, the massive expansion of the U.S. monetary base, and the widening global government safety net through expanded deposit insurance. 

First, the author characterizes the monumental scale of China's economic intervention as potentially unstable. Backed by 35% year-over-year loan growth and a total debt-to-GDP ratio exceeding 100%, China's GDP growth is heading back toward 9%. However, most of these loans flow to public sector entities, and capital investment represents close to 50% of GDP—significantly higher than the 30% to 35% seen during the industrial peaks of South Korea, Germany, or Japan. This policy has led to booming asset prices, with the Shenzhen equity market surging 130% since March 2009 and home sales values rising 73% year-over-year, despite household incomes not supporting these prices. This massive excess capacity is resulting in deteriorating returns on invested capital, making China's growth an unstable foundation for the global economy. An accompanying line chart titled Chinese loan growth (YoY % change) from 1998 to 2008 illustrates this dramatic credit surge, showing the year-over-year growth rate spiking vertically from under 15% in late 2008 to 35% by 2009.

Second, the report analyzes the explosion of the U.S. monetary base. While the Federal Reserve's massive liquidity injection has not yet leaked into broader monetary aggregates like M2, the author warns that historically, such easy money has bypassed traditional goods and services to fuel financial asset speculation. A line chart titled Explosion of U.S. monetary base shows Fed purchases of Treasury, Agency debt, and mortgage-backed securities climbing from near zero in late 2008 to estimates of nearly $1.8 trillion by March 2010.

Third, the author discusses the significant expansion of the global government safety net, arguing that taxpayers are being exposed to substantial risks and banks are being given distorted incentives. Notably, the FDIC now guarantees 84% of all bank deposits in the United States. In addition, governments have provided hundreds of billions in asset protection to institutions like Citigroup, Bank of America, RBS, and Lloyd’s, while China guarantees over $600 billion in bonds for state-run Asset Management Companies like DongFang, Cinda, Huarong, and Great Wall. An accompanying table titled Expanded bank deposit insurance highlights the change in deposit limits across several nations. It shows the United States increasing its guarantee from 100,000 USD to 250,000 USD; the United Kingdom increasing from 35,000 GBP to 50,000 GBP; Germany increasing from 20,000 EUR to 50,000 EUR; Spain increasing from 20,000 EUR to 100,000 EUR; Switzerland increasing from 30,000 CHK to 100,000 CHK; Sweden increasing from 250,000 SEK to 500,000 SEK; and both Ireland and Denmark offering unlimited guarantees, with Ireland's set to expire in September 2010.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" covers key investment opportunities in non-performing loans (NPLs) across the United States and Europe, alongside positive signals in global macroeconomic market outlooks. In the first section, the author outlines a strategy to invest in NPLs, noting that the United States presents opportunities primarily through FDIC-restructured failed banks, while Europe’s more consolidated banking sector requires buying directly from ongoing concern banks. The author highlights that the NPL volume across the United Kingdom, Spain, Germany, and Portugal totals roughly 390 billion euros.

This section is supported by two key charts. The first, a line graph titled "Number of failed U.S. banks, 2008 to present," shows a dramatic rise in bank failures, starting near zero in early 2008 and climbing past 120 failures by October 2009. Footnotes add that the FDIC Watch List grew to include 420 banks as of June 2009, with other rating services indicating even higher numbers of troubled institutions. The second chart, a bar graph titled "Non-performing loans - Select European countries," compares NPL levels in billions of euros from the fourth quarter of 2008 to the second quarter of 2009. It shows significant double-digit percentage increases across all four featured countries: the United Kingdom rose 46 percent to nearly 150 billion euros, Spain grew 49 percent to around 45 billion euros, Germany increased 71 percent, and Portugal grew 42 percent.

In the second section, titled "Market outlook: Round up the Usual Suspects," the author notes improving conditions typically tied to rising asset prices following a visit to clients in Louisiana. The discussion highlights stabilizing and improving markers across multiple macroeconomic sectors. Global manufacturing orders are strong relative to low inventories, and U.S. employment metrics show signs of stabilization. The author notes that the United States has experienced its largest inventory collapse in 60 years, which historically precedes growth from replenishment. Additionally, equity valuations remain reasonable at 12.8 times in Europe and 15.3 times in the United States. Massive capital movements are underway, with over 400 billion dollars fleeing U.S. money market funds and corporate cash balances reaching a 50-year high. Global investment activity is also picking up, with sovereign wealth funds like the 280 billion dollar China Investment Corporation and Abu Dhabi's Mubadala increasing overseas investments. Finally, the author points to stabilization in the housing market and strong third-quarter S&P 500 earnings, with 84 percent of reporting companies beating earnings estimates and 58 percent beating revenue estimates.

Michael Cembalest discusses the debate over fiscal stimulus and government spending, evaluating both successful historical precedents and the cautionary tale of Hurricane Katrina recovery in New Orleans. While expressing skepticism about the United States administration's deficit reduction goals, he notes that historical federally funded projects have occasionally yielded immense productivity benefits. 

Three charts illustrate these successful historical projects. The first chart, titled Percent of farms with electricity, shows a sharp upward trajectory from about ten percent in 1935 to over forty-five percent by 1945, demonstrating the massive impact of the Rural Electrification Administration. The second chart, Interstate highway benefits, contrasts the roughly four hundred billion dollar cost of the interstate highway system in 1995 dollars with more than two trillion dollars in total benefits, driven by lower product prices, time and operating cost savings, and reduced accidents and fatalities. The third chart, Thermal efficiency - Power gen facilities, tracks efficiency from 1970 to 2010, demonstrating how the establishment of the Department of Energy Advanced Turbine Systems Project in the early 1990s helped push power generation efficiency from around forty percent to nearly sixty percent, culminating in the General Electric H-System Turbine.

Turning to New Orleans, the author argues for the immense power of preventive spending over reactive recovery spending. For instance, a ten million dollar investment in subsurface testing by the Army Corps of Engineers could have prevented the canal wall failures that ultimately led to eighty percent of the damage from Hurricane Katrina, which required one hundred twenty billion dollars in recovery spending. While post-disaster stimulus spending has kept New Orleans unemployment and job losses remarkably low compared to the national average, the efficiency of this spending has been poor, with half of the contracts awarded non-competitively and thirty to fifty percent of homes in Orleans and St. Bernard parishes still vacant or blighted years later. Ultimately, the author warns that as global players like the United States, China, and Brazil adopt stimulus-driven growth, productivity must keep pace with extra capacity to make the long-term cost of these deficits affordable.

This page of the publication focuses on why the author is advising against taking above-average risk in investment portfolios despite several seemingly positive macroeconomic signals. While third-quarter 2009 earnings are beating expectations, the author cautions that this is primarily because starting estimates were exceptionally low. Other headwinds include a looming wave of delinquent mortgages and consumer loans, and the fact that recent employment gains are largely confined to temporary hiring. 

The top of the page features eight small charts illustrating various economic and valuation trends leading up to late 2008 and 2009. The first chart, JPM Global Manufacturing PMI, shows a steep plunge and a sharp V-shaped recovery. The second, ISM Mfg - Employment, shows a similar steep decline and partial rebound. The third, Real business inventories, plots highly volatile quarter-over-quarter annualized rates of change from 1947 through 2007. The fourth, 12-month forward P/E, compares U.S. and European valuation multiples from 1987 through 2008. The fifth chart shows money market fund assets surging to nearly 3.8 trillion dollars by late 2008. The sixth chart is a pie graph of the China Investment Corporation, indicating a highly liquid asset allocation of 87 percent cash and 13 percent non-cash. The seventh chart, U.S. housing inventory, compares new home inventory against existing home inventory, revealing a sharp drop in new inventory down toward 0.2 million units while existing inventory remains elevated around 4 million units. The final small bar chart, S&P 500: 3Q 2009 "beats," shows that while earnings per share beats were high, revenue beats were much weaker, suggesting cost-cutting rather than demand-driven growth.

Two larger charts in the middle of the page expand on these themes. The chart on S&P 500 quarterly EPS estimates shows how expectations for the third quarter of 2009 bottomed out at 14.72 dollars at the start of the reporting cycle before rising to a current estimate of 16.41 dollars, with a forecast of 19.90 dollars for the third quarter of 2010. The second large chart tracks securitized non-agency mortgages from 1997 through 2009, showing a dramatic spike in distress; by 2009, the share of loans 60 or more days delinquent surged past 25 percent, while loans in the foreclosure process exceeded 10 percent, and bank-owned properties reached roughly 5 percent.

Given these massive housing distress figures and the unprecedented nature of global policy stimulus, the author explains that portfolios are focusing on remnants of the prior cycle, such as bank non-performing loans, rather than over-weighting equities. 

In a section titled "The gospels according to Paul," the author discusses the negative outlook for the U.S. dollar, referencing warnings from economists Paul Samuelson and Paul Volcker. J.P. Morgan has positioned portfolios for a weaker dollar, noting that the Federal Reserve's trade-weighted U.S. dollar index is hovering just 5 to 7 percent above its all-time post-gold standard low set in 2008. A detailed footnote adds context to Samuelson's criticisms of former policy figures like Alan Greenspan, Milton Friedman, Friedrich Von Hayek, and the Bush administration, including his warning of a potential run against the U.S. dollar over the coming decade.

This commentary page, written by Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Global Wealth Management, analyzes the investment implications of the pending 2009 U.S. healthcare reform bill. Cembalest notes that while J.P. Morgan’s active equity managers are generally overweight healthcare, they remain underweight in large-cap pharmaceuticals, preferring health care equipment and life sciences. The text highlights several positive legislative signals for early-stage healthcare and biotechnology investments, such as a potential 12-year data exclusivity period for biologics and the absence of price-limiting boards like those proposed in the 1993–1994 Clinton health care plan. Additionally, Senate negotiations halved a proposed medical device tax to $20 billion over ten years. 

A dedicated callout box defines biologics as therapies derived from living tissue rather than inert chemicals and details their rapid growth. Biologic sales are expanding three to four times faster than traditional drugs, and they represented a quarter of U.S. and European drug approvals from 2003 to 2006. Top-selling examples include Avastin, Rituxan, Humira, Enbrel, and Lantus. Industry forecasts from EvaluatePharma predict that seven of the top ten global drugs will be biologics by 2014, up from five in 2008 and only one in 2000. Highlighting investment potential, the text notes that Talecris, the largest biotech IPO in three years, returned 23 times Cerberus’ investment, helping offset its losses in Chrysler. 

The page also discusses broader market dynamics, noting that looming patent expirations—representing 30% of global large-cap pharma revenues by 2011—have driven major acquisitions by companies like Roche, Abbott, and Wyeth, supported by $70 billion in debt issued in 2009 to finance these transactions. Private equity opportunities are identified in drug development for Hepatitis C, oncology, and Alzheimer's. In his concluding thoughts, Cembalest notes that while the final bill will likely increase overall coverage and costs, the current legislative path is far less damaging to research and development incentives than past efforts. He poses open questions about whether the trillion-dollar bill can deliver enough promised efficiencies to pay for itself, while reassuring investors that a restrictive regulatory framework like the United Kingdom's National Institute for Clinical Excellence (NICE)—which rejects expensive treatments like Bayer's Nexavar or Roche's Avastin based on cost-per-quality-adjusted life years—does not seem imminent in the United States.

This page of "Eye on the Market" addresses the topic of job creation and the Obama administration's frame of reference by examining the historical private sector experience of U.S. Presidential Cabinets from 1900 to 2009. The author compiles data on 432 cabinet members in key economic and infrastructure positions—including Secretaries of State, Commerce, Treasury, Agriculture, Interior, Labor, Transportation, Energy, and Housing and Urban Development—to measure how many had prior business experience in running companies, managing employees, and navigating recessions. 

The central visual on the page is a bar chart titled "Cabinet Appointments: Prior Private Sector Experience, 1900-2009," which plots the percentage of experienced cabinet members for each president from Theodore Roosevelt to Barack Obama. The chart illustrates that most administrations historically maintained a balance of public and private sector experience, with percentages typically hovering between 30% and 55%. For example, Dwight Eisenhower, Ronald Reagan, and George W. Bush had some of the highest proportions of cabinet members with private sector backgrounds, all exceeding 50%. In contrast, the Obama administration represents a stark historical outlier, with prior private sector experience among its cabinet members falling below 10%. 

The author explains that this shift reflects a prevailing cynicism toward private sector involvement following the late-2000s financial crisis. He highlights quotes from Congressman Barney Frank and a deputy of Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner expressing the sentiment that the private sector caused the economic crisis and therefore should not be consulted on how to resolve it. Footnotes on the page further contextualize the discussion by noting that, at the time of publication in late 2009, the probability of finding a job and the Conference Board’s Help Wanted Index were at their lowest levels in 60 years.

This page analyzes developments in the commercial real estate securitization (CMBS) markets and the historical performance and structural issues of Statistical Arbitrage investing.

In the first section, the author highlights a small but notable re-opening of the CMBS market, exemplified by Developers Diversified Realty borrowing $400 million at an all-in cost of 5%. This comes after a massive collapse in overall securitization from $500 billion per quarter in 2007 to just $50 billion as of September 2009. Although this transaction is highly restrictive—featuring a maximum loan-to-value ratio of 52%, conservative rating agency cap rates, and a prohibition on subordinate financing below the A-rated paper—it signals demand from cash buyers seeking 9% to 10% equity returns without relying on the Federal Reserve's Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility (TALF). The collateral portfolio is exceptionally high quality, consisting of shopping centers that are 92% leased with strong tenants like Wal-Mart, Home Depot, and Lowe's, meaning this transaction may offer little relief for over-leveraged property owners with declining rent rolls.

The second section addresses Statistical Arbitrage, explaining why a key multi-strategy manager on J.P. Morgan’s platform maintains a 25% allocation to this strategy despite well-publicized struggles. The author traces the strategy's vulnerability back to August 2007, when it acted as a "canary in the coal mine" for leveraged investing. As a market-neutral strategy isolating stock valuation and momentum, its initial success attracted enormous capital inflows, which in turn compressed returns and prompted managers to deploy leverage as high as 10x. 

Two charts illustrate these dynamics leading up to the 2007 crisis. The first chart, showing annualized six-month rolling returns for Statistical Arbitrage from 1990 through July 2007, displays a clear downward trend from volatile highs of 15% to 20% in the early 1990s to compressed single-digit returns by 2006. The second chart, tracking Equity Market Neutral and Long/Short assets under management from 1995 to 2007, visualizes the explosive growth of capital in these strategies, with total assets surging from under $20 billion in 1995 to roughly $170 billion by 2007.

The text concludes by describing the systematic unwinding in July and August of 2007. Triggered by the collapse of Bear Stearns' subprime mortgage hedge funds, widespread de-leveraging and redemptions forced quantitative funds to liquidate shared holdings. Because many funds used similar valuation and momentum models, selling long positions and covering short positions created a destructive feedback loop that drove long assets down, squeezed short assets higher, and ultimately forced numerous funds to close.

Michael Cembalest presents a case for the indispensable role of private sector innovation in revolutionizing healthcare and lowering long-run expenditures. He describes a meeting at the Mary Crowley Cancer Research Center in Dallas, noting that promising biologic drugs for gene and immune therapies could replace incredibly expensive palliative care, which can cost up to one million dollars per month for a single chemotherapy patient. In contrast, successful immune therapy offers a permanent cure by training the body to fight off recurrence. 

This clinical success is illustrated by a set of before-and-after PET scans tracking the fourteen-month outpatient results of a patient suffering from Stage IV metastatic melanoma. The scan on the left displays several circled cancerous legions, while the scan on the right reveals a complete response with a negative biopsy and no remaining signs of cancer. This outcome was achieved using an oncology vaccine developed by the private firm Gradalis, with the patient's entire post-surgery care costing less than fifty thousand dollars.

Cembalest argues that these breakthroughs require a strong profit motive because developing gene therapies takes one to two decades and carries a high risk of failure, with a Congressional Budget Office study indicating that it takes thousands of compounds to yield a single FDA-approved drug. Highlighting American innovation, he notes that seventy-five percent of drugs approved worldwide from 2005 to 2007 were introduced in the United States, which holds an even larger lead in biologics. Despite the National Cancer Institute spending one hundred and five billion dollars since 1970, survival rates for advanced cancer patients have remained largely unchanged. Cembalest expresses skepticism about the pending healthcare bill's ability to curb costs because it fails to address actual consumption, concluding that society must trust the private sector to develop the very innovations that will ultimately improve lives and lower the long-term cost of treating devastating diseases.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the resilience and performance of J.P. Morgan’s statistical arbitrage (Stat Arb) manager, explaining how a major industry shakeout ultimately created a more favorable environment for their strategy. 

To illustrate the extreme market conditions that prompted this shakeout, the first chart, titled "Out (under)-performance of the cheapest stocks, 1962-2007," displays the five-day relative performance of the cheapest versus the most expensive stock deciles. Measured using price-to-free-cash-flow (Price/FCF) shown as blue squares and price-to-book (Price/Book) shown as red diamonds, the chart’s vertical axis ranges from negative six percent to positive one percent. It highlights a circled region in 2007 where the relative underperformance of cheap stocks plunged to historic extremes between negative two percent and negative four percent. The data shows that such extreme underperformance has occurred only a handful of times over a forty-five-year period, such as in the late 1960s and the late 1990s. 

The second chart, "Market value of 15 institutional quant managers," depicts the resulting contraction in quantitative investment capital. Measuring long market value in billions of dollars from the second quarter of 2007 through the second quarter of 2009, the bar chart shows that assets peaked above three hundred billion dollars in mid-2007 before steadily declining. A sharp drop occurred in late 2008, with assets bottoming out near one hundred twenty-five billion dollars in the fourth quarter of 2008 and the first quarter of 2009, demonstrating that a massive volume of capital left the sector and did not return.

Cembalest argues that this dramatic reduction in assets and competitors ultimately benefited their manager by reducing cross-fund correlations and competitive overlap. The manager adjusted risk models to incorporate the behavioral dynamics of competitors and the "madness of crowds," allowing them to make quicker sell decisions on modest-value positions and avoid crowded trades. Consequently, while the broader hedge fund redemptions of 2008 and early 2009 could have been highly disruptive, a smaller and de-leveraged Stat Arb universe faced far less selling pressure than in 2007. Their manager capitalized on scarce liquidity during this period, making Stat Arb one of the best-performing strategies in the fund. Cembalest concludes by noting that these positive results were not shared industry-wide, as many other Stat Arb managers continued to struggle with a 2009 rally that was heavily led by lower-quality stocks.

This page, titled "The private sector after the fall," analyzes the reputational damage suffered by the private sector during the financial crisis and evaluates potential policy responses to drive job growth. The author argues that despite public perceptions of private sector greed and ineptitude, the private sector must remain the primary engine of employment recovery. 

To illustrate the severity of the corporate collapse, a scatter plot displays "Companies that lost more than their book value," plotting the ratio of total losses to 2007 tangible book value against total losses in billions of dollars. Extreme cases like E*Trade show ratios of losses to book value exceeding twelve, while government-sponsored enterprises Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae suffered colossal absolute losses of roughly $110 billion and $130 billion, representing multiple times their tangible book values. Other massive institutions like Citigroup, Bank of America, and AIG also show substantial losses relative to their capital. 

A second chart, "Public sector employment % of nonfarm payrolls," traces the historical percentage of public sector workers from 1945 to 2005. The data demonstrates that public employment has consistently hovered in a narrow range between 15% and 19%, highlighting that the public sector cannot realistically serve as the primary source of job creation. Furthermore, the text notes that state and local government employees make up 12% of the total U.S. workforce but represent a staggering 64% of all unfunded pension liabilities.

The author critiques proposed solutions like a "hiring tax credit," citing Princeton economist Alan Blinder’s warning that such credits are highly vulnerable to corporate abuse and gaming. Instead, the author emphasizes the importance of entrepreneurial incentives, pointing out that new firms under five years old accounted for all net job creation from 1980 to 2005. Additionally, a survey by the National Federation of Small Business reveals that small businesses are primarily worried about weak sales, high taxes, and government regulation rather than credit availability. 

Finally, a column chart contrasts the total fiscal and monetary stimulus across all prior post-World War II recessions—which averaged less than 10% of nominal GDP—against the colossal scale of the current 2007–current stimulus, which approaches 35% of nominal GDP. The author concludes with an open caution, asserting that any debates over introducing further stimulus must be carefully weighed against the massive financial burden of paying for what is already in motion.

This page discusses the improving earnings outlook in Europe, arguing that while the region's equity market has rallied significantly, the recovery is driven primarily by corporate cost cuts and emerging market demand rather than robust local economic conditions. Despite a thirty-one percent year-to-date rally in the MSCI Europe Equity Index, forward price-to-earnings multiples remain around fourteen times. European earnings, which peaked at one hundred sixty-nine dollars in 2008, are projected to rise to one hundred seventeen dollars in 2010 and one hundred forty-one dollars in 2011, aided by consumer spending outside of Europe. 

The first chart, titled Euro industrial production and manufacturing survey, spans 1997 to 2009 and plots the Euroland PMI manufacturing survey on the left axis against Euroland industrial production indexed to 2005 on the right axis. It highlights that while PMI sentiment has rebounded sharply in 2009, actual industrial production remains in a deep, albeit stabilizing, decline near an index level of ninety-five. The second chart, Global consumption share, shows percentage shares of global consumer spending from 1990 to 2008. It illustrates that the U.S. share peaked at around thirty-six percent in 2002 before falling to thirty percent in 2008, while the emerging market share rose steadily from twenty-two percent to thirty-two percent over the same period, eclipsing the U.S. share and explaining European exporters' reliance on non-domestic demand.

A major headwind to Europe’s operating leverage is its labor market structure, particularly in Germany. While European unemployment has not spiked as dramatically as in the U.S., German figures are distorted by the Kurzarbeit program, where the government subsidizes sixty to seventy percent of wages for employees working reduced hours. The German short-time workers chart shows that the number of workers in this program spiked to one and a half million during the 2009 recession. If one-third of these subsidized workers were laid off, Germany's unemployment rate would stand at eleven percent instead of eight percent. The U.S. and Euro area unemployment chart tracks unemployment rates from 1977 to 2009, showing both regions converging near ten percent in 2009, though the Euro area’s underlying labor hoarding leaves its corporate earnings with less operating leverage to a recovery compared to the U.S. 

In light of these dynamics, the publication notes that its portfolios retain a preference for U.S. equities over Europe and Japan due to superior U.S. productivity and stronger third-quarter earnings. To manage foreign exchange risk, the firm is hedging U.S. dollar exposure through dollar-Euro hedges, short positions in the dollar against commodity currencies such as those of Canada, Australia, and Norway, and direct investments in gold and oil.

This publication explores the challenges of transitioning from coal to renewable energy and the precarious state of US municipal finances. Following announcements by Exelon and Progress Energy to shut down 15 coal plants, representing 2,500 megawatts of generation over the next decade, the author assesses whether renewables can realistically fill the gap. While solar panel prices have plummeted 60 percent due to massive polysilicon expansion in China and wind is increasingly cost-competitive with natural gas, the author notes that Europe remains a more favorable regulatory environment for producers due to stable, 25-year sovereign contracts. Similarly, Brazilian sugarcane-based biofuels far outshine US corn ethanol in efficiency and infrastructure integration. Ultimately, because renewables excluding hydro account for only 4 percent of US electricity generation, and the targeted coal shutdowns represent about 15 percent of total existing US wind and solar capacity, the author argues that natural gas capacity must expand to meet the shortfall, making natural gas a key area to watch for entry points.

The analysis then turns to US municipal debt, noting that the recent rally in municipal bonds is driven by investors fleeing zero percent cash yields rather than strong credit fundamentals. State budget deficits are currently masked by a temporary 170 billion dollar federal stimulus injection. Once these federal funds run out in 2010, the author predicts a very difficult 2011 characterized by widespread tax hikes and spending cuts. 

Two charts illustrate these municipal budget pressures using data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis. The first chart, titled State government receipts and expenditures, spans 1989 to 2009 in billions of dollars. It compares a relatively stable blue line representing total receipts minus expenditures, which hovers near zero, against a plunging brown line representing receipts excluding federal transfers minus expenditures. Stripping out federal transfers reveals a massive deficit expansion post-2007, dropping to nearly negative 650 billion dollars by 2009.
