The second chart, titled Total benefits per full-time employee, covers 1998 to 2008 in dollars. It shows state and local government benefits climbing steeply from roughly 8,500 dollars to over 15,000 dollars, significantly outstripping private industry benefits, which grew much slower from approximately 5,500 dollars to under 10,000 dollars, highlighting a structural driver of municipal financial strain.

This page presents the author’s first New Year’s resolution for 2010, which is to spend more time thinking about Latin America. The author acknowledges a long-held reluctance to deploy capital in the region, shaped by the volatility of the 1990s when Latin American equity returns were only 70% of S&P 500 levels with double the volatility. Historical deterrents included property rights issues, balance of payments crises, poorly conceived currency pegs, corruption, and Argentina's decline from a per capita GDP of 1.5 times Italy's in 1900 to 0.4 times Italy's a century later. However, the author argues that the macroeconomic and structural landscape of Latin America has dramatically improved. 

To demonstrate this macro turnaround, the page features four charts. The first chart shows Latin American year-over-year inflation, which fell from hyperinflationary levels of 200% to 700% in the 1991–1994 period to single digits by the mid-2000s. The second chart traces the region's fiscal balance as a percentage of GDP, showing a recovery from deep deficits of nearly 30% in 1989 to stable levels between 0% and negative 5% by 2009. The third chart displays the difference in real GDP growth between Latin America and the United States, illustrating that the region frequently outperformed the U.S. during the 2000s. The fourth chart displays Latin American foreign exchange reserves excluding gold, which skyrocketed from under $100 billion in the late 1990s to over $500 billion by 2009.

Beyond macroeconomic indicators, the author highlights structural transformations in local capital markets, illustrated by four additional charts. The first shows the history of the Mexican yield curve, illustrating how Mexico went from only being able to issue domestic debt up to 364 days in January 1999 at rates near 30%, to extending its curve out to 30 years with yields under 10% by December 2009. The second chart shows Brazil’s real interest rates—measured as the nominal SELIC rate minus year-over-year inflation—which steadily fell from over 36% in the late 1990s to single digits by 2008. The third chart shows Brazil's sovereign credit risk via 1-year CDS spreads in basis points, highlighting a massive risk premium spike near 4,000 basis points around the time President Lula da Silva was elected in 2002, which subsequently collapsed to negligible levels as his administration governed from the center.

Despite these positive developments, the author notes that high market concentration remains a key reason to keep investment exposures relatively small. A final chart measures the market capitalization of the top three stocks as a percentage of their respective MSCI country index. This comparison reveals that Brazil ranks third globally in market concentration, trailing only Spain and Switzerland, with its top three stocks making up nearly half of the index. In Brazil's case, CVRD and Petrobras alone make up 40% of the MSCI Brazil index. The author concludes with a cautionary footnote on corruption, noting that according to Transparency International's 2008 analysis, Mexico still ranks closely behind Russia regarding bribery and corruption among public officials.

In this opening page of J.P. Morgan’s 2010 Outlook, the author reflects on the global economic recovery following the 2008 financial crisis, arguing that while a modest rebound in manufacturing, trade, consumer spending, and housing is underway, the return per unit of stimulus remains disappointingly low. To illustrate this, the author notes that third-quarter U.S. gross domestic product remained below three percent, even though monetary and fiscal expansion was four times greater than the combined total of all post-World War II recessions. While Asia is currently booming, economic recoveries in Europe and Japan remain muted. 

The central visual on the page, titled Figure 1, Anatomy of the Recovery, is a humorous diagram of an ox mapped out like a butcher's cuts of meat to visualize the sheer variety of global government interventions. These cuts and labels include U.S. and U.K. bank asset guarantee programs, government guarantees of bank bonds, Federal Reserve non-recourse term loans for AAA-rated paper, the Mortgage Forgiveness Debt Relief Act, eased pension funding rules, Chinese reserve accumulation of U.S. dollars, central bank swap lines, massive monetary and fiscal expansion, relaxed mark-to-market accounting rules in the U.S. and Europe, expansion of state-owned bank balance sheets in Brazil, and near-zero interest rates worldwide. The diagram also points to external measures such as International Monetary Fund loans to Eastern and Central Europe, and the European Central Bank lowering its collateral eligibility requirements down to triple-B minus. Moving into 2010, the author suggests that the best investment opportunities will come from exploring the remaining assets and mistakes left over from the prior economic cycle.

Michael Cembalest argues that the United States has entered an era of intense political polarization, comparable to the highly partisan Reconstruction period and Civil War aftermath of the late 19th century. This extreme partisanship has led to legislative dysfunction, which is particularly evident in Congress's long-running failure to resolve estate tax legislation. 

To demonstrate this historical shift, the page features a line chart titled "Party polarization (1879-2009)," which plots the "Distance Between the Parties" on a vertical scale from 0.3 to 1.0, using data from Congressional roll calls. The chart shows parallel paths for the House, depicted in red, and the Senate, in blue, which share a strong correlation of 0.91. Polarization peaked near 0.8 to 0.9 in the late 1800s, declined to a low point between 0.3 and 0.4 during the mid-20th century from the 1930s through the 1970s, and has since surged back to near-historic highs of around 0.9 by 2009.

A second visual, titled "Increasing polarization of the U.S. House," illustrates the literal disappearance of political moderates by comparing the liberal-conservative distribution of representatives in 1973–74 against 2003–04. Plotted on a scale from -1.0 (liberal) to 1.0 (conservative) with density on the vertical axis, the top panel for 1973–74 shows overlapping curves for Democrats (red) and Republicans (blue), with significant concentration near the moderate center and peaks represented by figures like Albert O'Neill and Gerald Ford. In contrast, the bottom panel for 2003–04, during the era of Nancy Pelosi, Tom DeLay, and Dennis Hastert, reveals two entirely separate curves with a stark void at the center zero-point, showing that moderates have become virtually extinct. 

Cembalest points to the gridlock surrounding the estate tax as a prime example of this dysfunction. Under the Economic Growth Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001 (EGTRRA), the estate tax is scheduled for a brief repeal in 2010, after which pre-EGTRRA rates of 55% and $1 million exemptions will automatically reinstate on January 1, 2011, unless Congress acts. Cembalest notes that Congress could still pass last-minute legislation before the end of 2009 or even pass retroactive estate tax legislation in early 2010, highlighting the absurdity of the legislature failing to reach a compromise despite having eight years to address the issue.

In this portion of the J.P. Morgan 2010 Outlook, the author argues that while vital economic signs are improving globally due to unprecedented policy "transfusions," this has created a delicate set of contradictory economic conditions that rely heavily on not withdrawing stimulus too quickly. 

To support the narrative of a global production rebound, the page presents four charts. Chart c.13 illustrates Asia’s industrial production, highlighting a strong recovery to pre-crisis levels for both Emerging Asia excluding China on the left axis and China on the right axis. Chart c.14 shows global motor vehicle sales in millions, showing that developed markets remain depressed while emerging markets experienced a sharp rebound from about 12 million to over 18 million. Chart c.15 tracks the global retail sales volume index, which dipped in late 2008 before rebounding to nearly 130 by late 2009. Chart c.16 depicts the global manufacturing inventory survey PMI, showing a sharp V-shaped recovery from a low of around 39 back toward 50. 

A second set of four charts focuses on earnings, wages, and market multiples. Chart c.17 shows the year-over-year change in U.S. private wage and salary disbursements, which plunged to a historic low of nearly negative 5% in 2009. Charts c.18 and c.19 illustrate earnings revisions for the U.S. (13-week average) and Europe (3-month average), showing both rebounded from deep lows to over 50% by late 2009. Chart c.20 displays one-year forward P/E ratios for the U.S. and Europe, which recovered from single digits to the mid-teens, ending 2009 around 14 to 16. 

The author highlights a bizarre, contradictory "peaceful co-existence" in the U.S. in 2009. On one hand, the country suffered its worst labor market in 70 years, the sharpest decline in private sector wages since 1960, and the fastest decline in top-line non-financial corporate revenues in 50 years. On the other hand, corporate operating margins climbed close to their highest levels of the last 50 years, and consumer spending stabilized. 

Looking ahead, S&P 500 earnings are expected to reach their prior peak by 2011. The consensus 2010 S&P 500 profit expectation of $77 represents a 27% growth rate over 2009, which the author views as achievable, though they advise against applying a forward multiple higher than 15x to 16x. Finally, the author cautions policymakers against withdrawing stimulus too soon, warning against repeating historical mistakes such as FDR in 1937, Japan in the 1990s, or China in 2008. Footnotes clarify that China’s 2009 GDP growth of 7.7% was driven primarily by capital formation at 13%, contrasting with weaker consumption and net trade, signifying a major shift from China’s growth pattern of the previous 15 years.

In this J.P. Morgan investment outlook for 2010, Michael Cembalest weighs positive economic leading indicators against the uncertainties of a post-stimulus world. While G3 monetary policy is expected to remain easy and the U.S. House has approved another $150 billion in spending, the report suggests the most significant stimulus measures have already passed. Consequently, asset returns in early 2010 are projected to be lower than in 2009, prompting the firm to hold equity exposure in balanced portfolios to 38%–42% and add cycle-insulated assets like distressed debt and long-short hedge funds. In fixed income, J.P. Morgan reduced overall durations to 2.5 to 3 years and cut municipal bond durations from 6 to below 4, citing deteriorating state and local fundamentals. 

Regionally, the portfolio maintains a tilt toward the U.S. over Europe and Japan, while holding emerging market equities at a 12% weight, heavily tilted toward Asia. The text notes that emerging markets now make up 50% of global output at purchasing power parity (or 35% at market exchange rates), a shift supported by rising consumption and trade agreements. Chart c.29, "Global consumption share, % consumer spending," shows a "changing of the guard" from 1990 to 2008, as the U.S. share of global consumption fell from roughly 35% to under 30% while the emerging market share rose from around 21% to nearly 27%. Chart c.30, "Number of free trade agreements in East Asia," displays a sharp climb in local trade pacts from near zero in the late 1990s to nearly 100 by 2008, contrasting with stalled global trade rounds. State stimulus has also driven emerging market growth; chart c.31, "Brazil private and public bank lending, YoY % change," illustrates how public sector bank lending YoY growth surged from under 10% in late 2008 to nearly 40% in 2009 to offset a sharp drop in private sector lending, which fell from 35% to roughly 12%.

For equities, the firm continues to favor active management. Chart c.32, "U.S. valuation spreads, cheapest vs. market average," displays historical valuation spreads from 1952 to 2009, highlighting how J.P. Morgan moved to active management in early 2009 when disparities spiked above 2.8, signaling prime conditions for stock-picking. Lastly, the report highlights a massive 2009 credit rally where the share of high-yield bonds trading under 50 cents on the dollar fell from 27.5% to just 1%. Because of this compression, credit will play a smaller role in portfolios for 2010, with selective investments focusing on leveraged loans seeking spreads of 690 basis points and heavily discounted non-agency residential mortgage-backed securities.

This page discusses the macroeconomic and systemic risks heading into 2010, focusing on sovereign debt, China's capital spending, currency values, the U.S. housing market, and oil capacity. 

The author begins by analyzing the risks of deteriorating public sector finances across the OECD. If fiscal adjustments like tax hikes and spending cuts are not made soon, public debt will rise dramatically. Chart c.21 illustrates the projected multiple increase in government debt by 2050 without fiscal adjustments, showing that Ireland faces the largest projected increase at nearly twenty times, while the U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio could quadruple. The author explains that this rise in public debt has been necessary to offset the collapse in private debt, as shown in chart c.22, where the U.S. securitization of real estate, consumer, and corporate loans collapsed from a peak of nearly 500 billion dollars in 2006 to near zero by 2009.

Another critical risk is China's heavy reliance on capital spending to drive growth, which creates profit-deflating overcapacity. Chart c.23 shows gross fixed capital formation as a percentage of GDP at its historical troughs and peaks for Japan, Germany, South Korea, and China. China’s peak capital formation reached approximately 45 percent, dwarfing the peaks of the other countries during their respective industrial booms. This capital expansion has been accompanied by unprecedented foreign exchange intervention to suppress the Chinese yuan. Chart c.24 tracks foreign currency reserves as a percentage of U.S. GDP over a 21-year period, showing China’s reserves skyrocketing exponentially to nearly 12 percent, compared to the much flatter historical paths of Japan and Germany. The author notes that if China’s interventions slow, global inflation and interest rates could become highly volatile, and expects emerging market central banks to tighten monetary policy in 2010.

Turning to the U.S. dollar, the author observes that it is close to its post-gold standard low, as shown in the trade-weighted dollar trend from 1975 to 2009 in chart c.25. However, monetary expansion in Europe has been just as severe. Chart c.26 shows the change in the Federal Reserve and ECB balance sheets since June 2007, indicating that the Fed expanded its balance sheet by over 1.1 trillion dollars and the ECB by over 1.3 trillion dollars. 

In the U.S. housing market, the author warns that pent-up supply from defaulted borrowers will continue to weigh on the resale market. Chart c.27 shows U.S. securitized non-agency mortgages, where both 60-plus day delinquencies and foreclosures surged dramatically by 2009, with delinquencies approaching 30 percent and foreclosures climbing near 10 percent. Despite loan modifications, many delinquent borrowers continue to re-default. 

Additionally, oil spare capacity represents a major constraint as global demand recovers. Chart c.28 displays oil spare capacity as a percentage of demand from 1970 to a 2010 estimate, showing that spare capacity is projected to fall below 5 percent. 

The page concludes by arguing that relaxed mark-to-market accounting rules under FASB and IFRS, as well as eased funding rules for defined-benefit plans, are merely delaying a reckoning for mispriced assets. The author expresses skepticism toward suggestions that high inflation can resolve these debt issues, advising readers that such proposals should give everyone pause.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2010 Outlook, authored by Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest, outlines long-term views on commodities, energy transitions, currency cycles, and political polarization, concluding with advice for families to prioritize generational savings amid rising global instability. 

On commodities, the author highlights that while gold is highly sought after, it is historically expensive against almost all traditional measures. A relative valuation table shows that compared to historical trends, gold is very expensive relative to inflation since 1915, T-bills since 1935, government bonds since 1974, and U.S. home prices since 1968. It is also expensive relative to silver and U.S. equities. The only metric against which gold remains cheap is the U.S. monetary base, making gold a direct bet on whether recent monetary expansion will trigger future inflation. Because of this, the author is hedging gold exposure. For oil, the author expects a fifteen to twenty dollar price increase over the next two years due to limited spare capacity and production challenges in Atlantic sub-salt fields. Conversely, industrial commodities command caution due to overbuilding in aluminum and steel, alongside massive Chinese iron ore inventory stockpiles, which a line chart shows rising steadily from 2006 to a peak of around 7.5 million tons in late 2009.

Addressing the energy sector, the author notes that progress on renewable energy and carbon sequestration remains far behind schedule. A pie chart of 2008 U.S. power generation by fuel source emphasizes the country's deep reliance on traditional fuels, with coal accounting for 49%, natural gas for 21%, nuclear power for 20%, hydro for 6%, and other sources making up just 4%. 

Looking at broader structural risks, the publication discusses the inevitable end of the U.S. dollar's reign as the world's sole reserve currency. A timeline chart of global reserve currencies since 1400 illustrates that dominance does not last forever, showing successive cycles of hegemony held by Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands, France, and Great Britain, with each period typically lasting roughly a century before transitioning to the next. 

This global instability is compounded by extreme political divisions in the United States. A final chart measures U.S. party polarization from 1879 to 2009 using Congressional roll-call data. The distance between the parties follows a sharp U-shaped curve, falling from high post-Civil War levels to a mid-20th-century low point before climbing back to near-historic highs by 2009, where polarization distance approaches 0.9 for the House and 0.8 for the Senate. Footnotes further criticize U.S. congressional policy, arguing that instead of implementing meaningful long-term solutions like alternative energy subsidies, tighter fuel standards, or nuclear expansion, policymakers have engaged in unproductive posturing, comparing the political climate to the final days of the Romanov dynasty.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2010 Outlook analyzes the unprecedented scale of public sector interventions—characterized as "public sector transfusions"—used to stabilize the global economy, the mechanisms for financing these massive deficits, and their downstream market impacts. 

The author begins by illustrating the sheer scale of the U.S. monetary and fiscal expansion. Chart c.1 shows that the cumulative U.S. expansion from 2007 through late 2009 was approximately four times larger than all prior post-World War II recessions combined, approaching 40% of nominal GDP. This aggressive response was mirrored globally. Chart c.2 highlights a dramatic surge in year-over-year Chinese loan growth, peaking near 35% in 2009, with an accompanying footnote noting that Chinese M2 was growing at 30% annually—a rate unprecedented even during the high-growth era of the post-Civil War United States. Chart c.3 details fiscal stimulus as a percentage of GDP for 2009 and 2010 across major regions, indicating that Japan and Emerging Market Asia led with stimulus spending exceeding 3.5% of GDP in 2009, while the Eurozone and Latin America lagged. This massive intervention heavily supported private incomes; Chart c.4 shows that U.S. government transfers spiked to nearly 20% of disposable income in 2009, a level far exceeding any historical point since 1959.

To address how today's mega-deficits are financed, the author points to foreign reserve accumulation, central bank balance sheet expansion, and a dramatic contraction in corporate credit demand. Chart c.5 displays emerging market foreign exchange reserves from 1995 to 2009, which exploded to nearly $6 trillion by 2009, led heavily by Emerging Market Asia as these countries printed local currency to prevent appreciation and purchased Western government debt. Simultaneously, the Federal Reserve purchased $1.4 trillion of Treasury and Agency paper, while the European Central Bank lent heavily to European banks. This government debt was easily absorbed because corporate borrowing collapsed. Chart c.6 shows U.S. non-financial corporate borrowing plunging to negative territory, around negative 3% of GDP, in 2009, creating a vacuum for government issuance. These government funds directly cushioned local states and supported housing; Chart c.7 shows that U.S. state deficits would have plunged to nearly negative $700 billion without federal transfers, but were stabilized at roughly negative $100 billion with them. Meanwhile, Chart c.8 illustrates that the Government National Mortgage Association, or GNMA, mortgage balance nearly doubled to $800 billion by 2009, stepping in to finance 55% of new home purchases with an average loan-to-value ratio of 95% as Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac faltered.

Finally, the author explains how massive excess capacity and low inflation allow central banks to maintain near-zero rates, driving a reallocation of cash. Chart c.9 shows that capacity utilization in developed markets plummeted to historical lows of nearly five standard deviations below the long-term average in 2009, keeping inflation at bay. This easy money policy steepened yield curves, helping banks earn their way out of trouble, while corporations amassed huge cash reserves. Chart c.10 shows U.S. corporate cash balances spiking to over 12% of tangible assets, setting the stage for strategic mergers and acquisitions. Concurrently, individual investors began fleeing low-yielding cash havens; Chart c.11 shows U.S. money market assets under management retreating from a peak of $4.0 trillion down toward $3.2 trillion in late 2009 as $700 billion rotated into riskier assets. To maintain system stability during this transition, nations globally enacted deposit guarantees, detailed in visual c.12, which notes expanded or unlimited deposit guarantees across the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and with unlimited guarantees specifically in Ireland and Denmark.

In this page of the J.P. Morgan 2010 Outlook, the author addresses the critical question of whether the U.S. consumer has successfully de-leveraged, concluding that the answer is a definitive no. This argument is supported by three charts analyzing consumer debt from different perspectives using data from the Federal Reserve Board and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The first chart, titled Mortgage and Consumer Debt Balances as a Percentage of Disposable Income, shows a historical trend from 1959 to 2009. Debt balances rose steadily from around 45 percent of disposable income in the late 1950s to a peak of nearly 120 percent during the 2007–2008 financial crisis, with only a marginal tick downward by late 2009, indicating that very little actual de-leveraging has occurred.

The second chart, Mortgage and Consumer Debt Payments as a Percentage of Disposable Income, covers 1977 to 2009 and features three data series to reveal the true burden of debt servicing. While interest payments alone stood at roughly 8 percent in late 2009, down from a peak of over 10 percent, adding a 1.5 percent annual amortization assumption pushes the payment burden to around 10 percent. Furthermore, when stripping out government transfers from disposable income, the debt payment ratio peaks even higher, ending 2009 at approximately 11 percent.

The third chart, Mortgage and Consumer Debt Interest Payments as a Percentage of Household Net Worth, tracks the period from 1977 to 2009. It shows that although this ratio had declined to around 1.4 percent in the mid-2000s, it spiked sharply back to nearly 1.8 percent by 2009, driven by the severe contraction in household net worth during the recession.

The author concludes with two major caveats regarding these trends. First, because spending is heavily skewed toward higher-income households where leverage is less concentrated, aggregate consumer spending may not suffer as permanent a blow as the leverage charts suggest. Second, the charts do not capture the approximately 1 trillion dollars in delinquent consumer and mortgage loans that remain unresolved. While repudiating or writing off these loans would technically lower household leverage, doing so would likely unleash troublesome second-order economic consequences.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market newsletter from early January 2010 focuses on distressed commercial real estate investment opportunities and the unrealistic expectations surrounding Iraq's future oil production capacity. Michael Cembalest begins with a brief macro overview, noting strong production rebounds in China and expectations for solid U.S. GDP growth, though he cautions about the sustainability of the economic bounce given the weak state of OECD public sector finances and the Chinese regulatory response to inflationary pressures.

In the commercial real estate sector, Cembalest reflects on the post-bubble recovery, detailing how the firm navigated rent declines of up to 40 percent through proactive debt restructuring, avoiding leverage at both the fund and property levels, and taking advantage of early 2009 pricing declines in collateralized mortgage-backed securities. The commentary highlights the dramatic collapse in industry financing with an accompanying stacked bar chart titled "Commercial real estate debt origination." This chart displays debt origination in billions of dollars from 2000 to 2009 across three primary sources: CMBS, Bank, and Insurance. Origination peaked in 2007 at over $400 billion, driven heavily by CMBS, before crashing abruptly in 2008 and falling to negligible levels in 2009. Despite this freeze in credit, Cembalest highlights that real estate investors with cash are finding excellent opportunities in distressed debt, residential land at 15 to 30 percent of peak values, hotels, and over-leveraged companies. He shares three examples of recent transactions executed by a partner manager, including purchasing FDIC condominium loans at 60 cents on the dollar with zero-percent seller financing, buying a London office tower at 60 percent of replacement cost for a 12 percent cash flow yield, and purchasing senior-secured casino debt at 50 cents on the dollar. He expects a steady drumbeat of similar transactions over the next two to three years.

Moving to energy markets, the author challenges the optimistic consensus that Iraq will easily add 10 million barrels of oil per day following recent international auctions, where bidding companies collectively proposed extracting 11 to 12 million barrels per day. While acknowledging Iraq's vast geological potential, Cembalest expresses skepticism regarding its ability to secure and transport this oil due to severe constraints, including inadequate pipeline and highway infrastructure, worker safety issues, terrorism, and political tensions in Kurdistan. To put this in perspective, he contrasts the chaotic situation in Iraq with Saudi Arabia's stable, virtually threat-free environment during the 1970s, where the Saudis, despite having uninterrupted Western expertise and accessing the massive Ghawar field, managed to add only 6 million barrels per day over an entire decade.

This page examines two distinct financial issues: the market for rescue financing for small-to-mid-market companies and a critique of the U.S. government's accounting of its national debt. In the first section, the author highlights that while high-yield markets have recovered for larger corporations, smaller mid-market firms remain shut out of credit. This point is supported by a bar chart showing the quarterly number of debt issuance deals by firms with EBITDA under $50 million from 1997 to 2009. The chart reveals that quarterly deals peaked in late 2007 at over 120 but plummeted during 2008 and 2009, falling to fewer than 20 deals by the end of 2009. Major lenders like regional banks, GE Capital, and CIT Group have drastically reduced their lending, creating lucrative, high-premium rescue financing opportunities for private investors in 2010.

The second half of the page disputes an argument by Peter Orszag of the Office of Management and Budget. Orszag suggested that analysts should focus on "net" debt rather than "gross" debt, thereby ignoring $4.5 trillion in Treasuries held by internal government entities like the Social Security Trust Fund, classifying it as debt the government merely owes to itself. The author strongly rebuts this view, arguing that these non-tradable Treasuries represent binding future entitlement obligations that must eventually be funded as these trust funds run deficits. Furthermore, Social Security holds only half of this $4.5 trillion; the rest belongs to other politically untouchable funds, such as the Military Retirement and Federal Hospital Insurance Trust Funds. 

While Japan adjusted its entitlement system in 2004 to build in flexibility for falling contributor numbers and rising life expectancies, the U.S. has failed to index payments or implement means-testing. A small table provides International Monetary Fund data for FYE 2009 debt-to-GDP ratios to illustrate the massive difference between gross and net metrics. Japan is shown with a massive 218% gross debt compared to a 105% net debt, while the U.S. holds a 91% gross debt versus a 60% net debt. The author concludes that gross debt ratios are vital for forecasting long-term economic growth, interest rate pressures, and future tax hikes, warning that pushing government debt too far can lead to sudden crises, as evidenced by Iceland's public rejection of the "Icesave" repayment plan.

This page from Eye on the Market discusses the challenges of expanding Iraqi oil production, global oil supply limits, and the dynamics of the high yield bond market.

In the first section, the author expresses skepticism about claims that Iraq can easily double its oil production in a few years, noting that the country has historically pumped between one and three million barrels per day. This argument is illustrated by a bar chart titled Untapped Iraqi oil potential, which measures millions of barrels per day on the vertical axis from zero to twelve. It shows that current production from ten major fields—including Najmah, Qayyara, Badrah, Gharaf, Halfaya, Zubair, East Baghdad, West Qurna 1 and 2, Majnoon, and Rumaila—is below 100,000 barrels per day. This stands in stark contrast to the Iraqi oil ministry's target of approximately three million barrels per day and the proposed international oil company output of over eleven million barrels per day. To provide historical context, an adjacent area chart titled Saudi Arabian oil production by field, 1968-1984, displays production volume in millions of barrels per day. It shows total production peaking near ten million barrels per day around 1980, heavily dominated by the Ghawar field alongside Safaniya and Abqaiq, before dropping sharply to around four million barrels per day by 1984. Looking forward, the author anticipates modestly higher oil prices due to falling production expectations, citing Total SA's CEO lowering global peak estimates to under 90 million barrels per day, and notes a willingness to sell oil positions closer to $100 a barrel.

The second section shifts to the high yield bond market, where the author justifies maintaining a three percent to ten percent portfolio allocation despite a massive rally. To explain how high yield spreads stabilized even as media reports pointed to record-high debt issuance in 2009, the author includes a stacked bar chart titled Important distinction between gross and net HY issuance. Spanning the years 2000 to 2009, with a vertical axis in billions of dollars ranging from negative 25 to 200, the chart breaks gross issuance down into net issuance and tendered debt. It reveals that out of more than $170 billion in gross issuance in 2009, roughly $120 billion was simply tendered to replace existing debt, leaving net new supply at only $50 billion.

Despite these positive technicals, the author warns of inherent risks by referencing a 1999 Salomon Smith Barney presentation on wireline telecom companies. A dedicated epilogue box reveals that out of thirteen high-yield recommendations, ten went bankrupt—including Global Crossing, Metromedia, Williams, McLeod, Adelphia, Nextlink, Worldwide Fiber, Winstar, Allegiance, and Focal—while Colt was tendered at sixty cents on the dollar, and only Level 3 and Verio survived. Although the high yield market has since diversified away from telecom into healthcare, utility, energy, and financial sectors, the author warns that animal spirits are returning. They point to European single-B issuers like Heidelberg Cement and Wind Telecom upsizing their deals, with Wind Telecom re-introducing pay-in-kind features, and identify an upcoming 500 million euro unrated Manchester United deal as a key barometer of aggressive investor demand.

Michael Cembalest presents a bifurcated outlook, starting with an optimistic view of corporate profits followed by a sobering analysis of public sector deficits. On the private side, he argues that corporate profits are poised for a massive rebound, driven by the historic inverse relationship between labor costs and profits as well as strength in emerging markets. Cash on corporate balance sheets is at a 50-year high while capital spending is at its lowest level in 40 years, suggesting that a recovery in profits will eventually translate into hiring, stock buybacks, and capital expenditures. 

To support the profit outlook, two charts show model forecasts from ISI Group. The first chart, tracking global corporate profits as a Year-over-Year percentage change from 1989 through 2009, shows actual profits bottoming at -25.6% in the fourth quarter of 2009. The dotted model forecast projects a rapid, sharp rebound to 52.2% by the third quarter of 2010. The second chart shows U.S. corporate profits on a similar Year-over-Year basis from 1993 through 2009, where actual profits hit a low of -6.6% in the third quarter of 2009, but the model projects a rise to 35.5% by the second quarter of 2010. A footnote explains that the reliable ISI model relies on unit labor costs, the yield curve slope, credit spreads, and the OECD Broad Leading Indicator.

The second half of the page shifts to the public sector, arguing that the massive public cost of initiating the economic recovery has created deep fiscal "sinkholes" that could spark political conflicts. To illustrate this, the third chart displays Spain's public sector imbalances by plotting financial positions as a percentage of GDP using four-quarter moving sums from 2000 to 2010. The chart shows that while Spain's household sector has returned to a surplus of about 6% of GDP and the corporate sector has improved to nearly balance at -1%, the Spanish government's financial position has cratered from a surplus in 2007 to a deficit of approximately -10% of GDP by 2010. 

Similarly, the fourth chart illustrates the U.S. state and local fiscal crisis by plotting the Year-over-Year percentage change in real state and local taxes as a four-quarter average from 2004 to 2009. While local tax revenues held relatively steady near 0% by late 2009 because property taxes decline slowly, real state taxes plummeted to nearly -12% due to rapid drops in income and sales taxes. Although U.S. employment, income, and corporate tax receipts showed minor improvements at the end of 2009, Cembalest warns that a full recovery will be a very long road.

This page focuses on key macroeconomic headwinds weighing on global financial markets in early 2010, specifically the sluggish recovery of the United States housing market, monetary tightening in China, shifting US political dynamics, and defensive investment strategies. 

On housing, the author argues that despite improved inventory-to-sales ratios, a bearish outlook remains justified due to a massive overhang of shadow inventory, tightening Federal Housing Administration lending standards, falling apartment rents, and the expiration of Federal Reserve purchases of mortgage-backed securities. This argument is supported by a chart titled "Shadow inventory exacerbates housing supply issues," which plots months of housing supply from January 1999 to July 2009. The line representing standard existing homes peaks around eleven months of supply in late 2008 and declines to roughly nine months by mid-2009. However, the line that factors in seriously delinquent loans and foreclosures tells a far worse story, spiking dramatically to nearly eighteen months of supply by mid-2009, illustrating the severe pressure of shadow inventory.

Turning to Asia, the text highlights China’s rapid post-recessionary growth, noting that it has become the world’s largest exporter, the second-largest economy and stock market, and the largest automobile market. However, much of this growth was driven by massive public sector stimulus, raising concerns of economic overheating. A second chart, titled "Asia exhausts non-inflationary growth potential," plots output gaps (actual GDP relative to potential GDP) from 2006 to 2010 across developed markets, Emerging Market Asia, Latin America, and the Central and Eastern Europe, Middle East, and Africa region. While developed markets and other regions suffered severe, prolonged negative output gaps of negative four to negative five percent in 2009, Emerging Market Asia experienced a shallower dip to negative two percent and is projected to rise back to positive territory in 2010. This indicates that Asia has rapidly absorbed its idle capacity, creating inflationary pressures that have prompted the Chinese government to implement tightening measures such as higher policy rates and monthly lending quotas. Consequently, the author warns that the stimulus-driven market rally of 2009 is over, and investors should expect lower returns in 2010.

In US politics, the election of Massachusetts Senator-elect Scott Brown is expected to complicate legislative negotiations, particularly regarding the extension of the Bush tax cuts and the reinstatement of the estate tax. Despite Democrats maintaining an eighteen-seat Senate majority, historically high partisanship has eroded the political middle ground. This political shift also impacts President Obama's proposed financial sector reforms, which seek to ban proprietary trading and bank ownership of hedge funds or private equity, while placing tighter limits on bank consolidation. The author expresses skepticism toward these proposals, noting that these specific activities were not the primary cause of the financial crisis.

Finally, the page addresses investment strategy, advocating for a shift toward high-dividend stocks to build defensive equity portfolios. By screening for large and mid-cap stocks with stable earnings, consistent dividend growth, and minimal downward revisions, the authors narrowed down a list of thirty candidates to ten preferred stocks. These select stocks carry an average annual dividend yield of 3.9 percent, which matches the ten-year US Treasury yield and doubles the yield of the S&P 500. To weather anticipated market volatility, the author recommends defensive positioning and overlaying twenty to thirty percent of balanced equity portfolios with downside protection.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues against the political tendency to treat the banking sector as a homogeneous entity, specifically criticizing rhetoric from President Obama's administration that paints all bankers with the same brush. Drawing an analogy to the collective punishment in Samuel Coleridge’s "Rime of the Ancient Mariner," he asserts that banks differ dramatically in their leverage, risk management, compensation structures, and public program participation. 

To demonstrate these institutional differences, the page features a bubble chart from February 2009 titled "Compensation, Leverage and Losses." The chart’s horizontal axis measures the change in leverage from December 2003 to June 2007 (ranging from -30% to +60%), while the vertical axis tracks writedowns as a percentage of June 2007 tangible book value (ranging from 0% to over 350%). The size of each bubble corresponds to the institution's total compensation as a percentage of operating profits from 2004 to 2008. The visual mapping reveals clear disparities among major institutions. Failed or distressed commercial banks like National City, Wachovia, and WaMu cluster in the upper-left quadrant, showing leverage reductions but massive writedowns exceeding 300% of tangible book value. Investment banks like Merrill Lynch, Citigroup, and UBS occupy the far-right, showing high leverage increases (up to 55% for Merrill) alongside massive compensation bubbles and high writedowns. Conversely, conservative players like J.P. Morgan, PNC, and Wells Fargo cluster in the bottom-left with negative-to-moderate leverage growth and minimal writedowns under 50%.

Addressing systemic financial sector reform, Cembalest supports initiatives like increased capital targets, OTC derivative clearinghouses, a Government Systemic Risk function, and stronger consumer protections. However, he warns that political pressure risks turning reform into a "morality play" that avoids addressing critical systemic failures. He highlights several overlooked contributors to the crisis: the SEC’s 2004 abandonment of the Net Capital Rule under Bill Donaldson, which allowed the five largest broker-dealers to drastically expand leverage; the role of speculative buyers, noting that second-home and investment-property mortgages tripled to make up nearly 40% of home sales at the peak; and the looming, unaddressed $400 billion taxpayer loss originating from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. 

The commentary is highly detailed, leveraging extensive footnotes to contrast J.P. Morgan’s practices with those of its peers and the broader market. For example, under the "Making Home Affordable" program, J.P. Morgan executed two to three times more trial loan modifications than Wells Fargo, Bank of America, and Wachovia combined. J.P. Morgan also managed counterparty risk tightly, maintaining only $400 million in exposure to AIG collateral calls, compared to several billion dollars each at Goldman Sachs, Merrill Lynch, and European banks like Societe Generale, Deutsche Bank, and Calyon. Furthermore, Cembalest contrasts high-risk Option ARM broker commissions (which reached 3.5% to 4.0%) with traditional loan commissions (1.0% to 1.5%), and notes that ultimate GSE losses will likely dwarf TARP losses, with the largest TARP shortfalls tied to AIG and the auto industry rather than the banking sector.

This page analyzes the prevailing macroeconomic climate, highlighting a dichotomy between strong corporate earnings and weak labor market indicators. It begins by identifying the key drivers behind recent market sell-offs, including lackluster job and economic growth relative to stimulus spending, rising concerns over European Union and United States public sector debt, and monetary tightening in China. 

Despite these macro headwinds, S&P 500 corporate profits are characterized as a distinct bright spot. The publication notes that nearly 80 percent of S&P 500 companies are beating earnings forecasts, while 70 percent are exceeding revenue expectations. Based on 2010 consensus profit expectations of $78.80 and a 15x price-to-earnings multiple, the author estimates fair value for the index to be in the high 1100s, pointing to single-digit equity returns for the year. This valuation landscape underpins J.P. Morgan’s stated tactical preference for U.S. equities over European and Asian alternatives.

The discussion then shifts to the private equity landscape, specifically focusing on the recovery potential of 2005 to 2007 vintage funds. To demonstrate how "peace with honor" might be achieved by returning original capital over time, the author highlights the 2006 leveraged buyout of HCA. Management’s performance is praised for increasing top-line revenues by 18 percent and reducing costs relative to sales, driving a 22 percent improvement in cash flow and allowing leverage to fall from 6.4x to 4.7x. With a planned capital return of $1.75 billion, representing about 35 percent of the initial investment, the total value of HCA is estimated at 2.5 times the original investment.

The final section explores weak U.S. job growth and payrolls, suggesting the auto sector could help trigger a recovery through inventory rebuilding. Two line charts track these trends from January 2002 through July 2009. The first chart, showing the production gap versus sales, displays U.S. sales of domestically produced vehicles alongside U.S. production in millions of annualized units. It illustrates that while sales plummeted during the recession, domestic production fell even faster to a low of approximately 4 million units, only recently starting to rise to close the gap with sales. The second chart shows that auto inventories fell precipitously from historical levels above 3.5 million units down to cycle lows near 1.0 million units in mid-2009. The author notes that because inventories are so depleted, their restocking typically contributes about 2 percent to GDP for four to five quarters in a typical recovery. While manufacturing and temporary hiring show minor improvements, the high real minimum wage—at its highest level in 30 years due to a 2007 bill—is identified as a potential drag on broader employment.

This page addresses the challenges and opportunities in distressed credit and real estate markets, focusing on the high cost of capital for middle-market firms and the investment potential of FDIC loan sales. The author begins by examining how cash-starved companies are accepting highly unfavorable terms to restructure their balance sheets, citing an air transport company that agreed to a second-lien loan yielding up to twenty percent. 

To illustrate the broader financing landscape, a bar chart titled "Debt issuance by mid-market firms (EBITDA < $50mm)" tracks the quarterly number of deals from 1997 through 2009. The chart highlights a severe credit crunch, showing that quarterly transactions peaked near one hundred twenty in both 1999 and 2007 before collapsing to fewer than twenty deals per quarter by late 2009. Next to this, a chart titled "U.S. hotel performance during recent recessions" compares the average annual change in net operating income (NOI) across the 1991, 2001, and 2009 downturns. It demonstrates that the decline eight quarters before inflection was far more severe in 2009, with NOI falling over twenty percent compared to drops of roughly twelve percent in 2001 and three percent in 1991. However, the chart also shows a strong projected recovery eight quarters post-inflection, with NOI rising by approximately sixteen percent for the 2009 recovery, outperforming the prior two cycles.

The main commentary connects these market dynamics to historic real estate workouts, specifically referencing the Resolution Trust Corporation (RTC) during the Savings and Loan crisis of the early 1990s. The author notes that in recent distressed sales, such as Florida condominiums, prices could fall an additional forty to forty-five percent before eroding buyer equity. Recalling the principles of former RTC head Bill Seidman, the text argues that successful asset disposition requires quick sales at low prices to prevent active asset degradation under government management. The author highlights the success of 1993 "retained interest" partnerships, such as Brazos Partners and Mountain AMD, which generated a twenty-five percent internal rate of return on taxpayer equity. This structure was academically validated by Cyrus Gardner and Roger Kormendi as more effective than bulk sales or securitizations. 

Looking forward, the publication estimates that the market is only twenty to thirty percent of the way through the bank failure process, making early-stage FDIC loan sales an attractive, low-competition opportunity for 2010. This lack of competition is illustrated by the Corus Bank portfolio transaction, which drew only eight bidders. The author concludes by noting that investment managers are also identifying value in deeply impaired but cheap sectors, specifically hotels and un-built residential land.

This page of the publication analyzes several global economic developments, beginning with legislative efforts in the U.S. Congress to lower FIRPTA tax rates on foreign investors to stimulate capital inflows into commercial real estate. The author notes that recent valuation climbs in real estate likely stem from compressing capitalization rates on recent transactions rather than improvements in underlying property fundamentals like cash flows, absorption, or rental rates. 

Next, the author critiques the sovereign debt situation in Greece, noting that its aggressive plan to slash its budget deficit by ten percent of GDP over three years is historically unlikely to succeed and is already facing heavy domestic strike action. The author argues that Eurozone nations will likely end up bailing out Greece, causing the Euro to weaken relative to the U.S. dollar. This argument is supported by a line chart titled "Fiscal issues weighing on EUR" spanning January 2009 to January 2010. It plots the inverted U.S. dollar per Euro exchange rate on the left axis against the five-year Greek Credit Default Swap spread in basis points on the right axis. The chart demonstrates that as Greece's five-year CDS spread surged from around 100 basis points to nearly 400 basis points by early 2010, the Euro depreciated significantly against the dollar, moving from around 1.50 USD/EUR down toward 1.35 USD/EUR.

Turning to Asia, the commentary addresses the dominant investor narrative of China’s economic invincibility, cautioning that excessively loose monetary policy has fueled labor tightening and asset speculation. This has driven up producer input prices and property values, forcing Chinese authorities to implement cooling measures. The discussion is illustrated by two charts using data from the National Bureau of Statistics of China. The first, "China PMI Manufacturing - Prices paid," shows the index bouncing back to near 70 by late 2009 after a steep drop in late 2008. The second, "Chinese asset price indices" from 2000 to 2009, displays a sharp late-2009 rebound in both the month-on-month real estate sales price index and the highly volatile land transaction price index. Recalling historical instances of extreme optimism that preceded crises in Indonesia and Russia, the author notes that J.P. Morgan reduced its exposure to Asian equity in September and is waiting for lower valuation entry points, anticipating a market adjustment to a more sustainable growth expectation of eight to nine percent with four percent inflation.

Finally, the piece debunks the narrative that rising lumber prices indicate a recovery in the domestic housing market. Instead, the author explains that the price increase is driven by temporary supply disruptions from wet weather in the Southeast alongside falling international shipping rates, which make exporting lumber to destinations like China more lucrative than domestic shipping.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication analyzes the sustainability of the European Monetary Union amid the emerging sovereign debt issues in Greece. Although Greece represented only two percent of EU GDP at the time, the author compares its potential systemic impact to the fall of Bear Stearns, which similarly constituted only two percent of the broker-dealer market but triggered a wider global financial crisis. The commentary questions whether a durable monetary union can truly exist among regions with highly divergent economic and cultural characteristics, noting that prominent economists like Milton Friedman and Martin Feldstein questioned the Euro's viability years prior. The author warns that the structural problems of the Eurozone will be difficult to resolve regardless of any bailouts or subsidies offered to Greece, leading to major implications for European government bonds, the Euro, and equity markets.

The historical analysis traces the vulnerabilities of European currency integration back to the collapse of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992, when Germany's tight monetary policy proved too painful for recession-hit countries like the United Kingdom, Italy, Spain, and Portugal. Despite this failure, the Euro was launched under a framework that allowed member nations to lock in their exchange rates at elevated levels. The author critiques this setup as a political compromise that ignored vast differences in productivity and income, creating a short-term win-win by inflating the purchasing power of weaker economies while establishing a captive export market for German manufacturing. A sidebar details a discussion with Bernard Connolly, the former Head of Monetary and FX Policy for the EU Commission who was fired in 1995 after publishing a highly critical book about the monetary union's structural shortcomings, titled "Rotten Heart of Europe."

An accompanying line chart, titled "GIPSI currencies vs. Deutsche mark," illustrates the performance of the currencies of Greece, Italy, Portugal, Spain, and Ireland indexed to January 1990. The chart tracks how these currencies weakened relative to the Deutsche mark following the ERM failure in 1992, with Greece suffering the steepest decline, falling from an index level of 100 in 1990 to nearly 50 by 1999. In contrast, the Irish Pound and Italian Lira experienced notable rallies during the Euro convergence period between 1996 and 1997. A red dashed vertical line highlights the period around 1999 when the Euro exchange rates were permanently fixed, locking these disparate valuation levels into place and sowing the seeds for subsequent systemic imbalances.

In this commentary on the long-term U.S. budget outlook, Michael Cembalest argues that the federal government is facing a structural, persistently large deficit driven by unprecedented spending levels rather than below-average revenues. 

To support this, the first chart illustrates U.S. government receipts and outlays as a percentage of GDP from 1950 projected through 2020. The chart shows that while tax revenues consistently hover around their historical average of 18 percent of GDP, expenditures spiked dramatically around 2010 to nearly 25 percent of GDP and are projected to remain elevated above 22 percent through 2020, leaving a permanent fiscal gap. 

The second graphic, a pie chart showing the projected allocation of 2016 government expenditures, emphasizes that discretionary non-defense spending is not the primary driver of this deficit. It accounts for only 10 percent of total outlays, while defense accounts for 19 percent, and the remaining 71 percent consists of mandatory entitlement spending and interest. Cembalest asserts that addressing this mandatory spending is politically daunting because Americans are accustomed to entitlement safeguards like Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security, alongside generous public sector pensions. Footnote data highlights that public sector workers are twice as likely to receive a pension compared to private-sector counterparts, with unfunded federal civil servant and military liabilities reaching approximately 4.6 trillion dollars as of 2007.

Looking ahead, the author warns that massive deficits may make key policy priorities, such as healthcare reform and climate change initiatives, impossible to achieve. Furthermore, the Quadrennial Defense Review and requests by Defense Secretary Robert Gates for advanced military assets indicate that defense obligations will remain heavy in an era of unending conflict. Cembalest poses the open question of how mandatory obligations can be restructured, predicting that global bond market capacity will eventually force difficult choices: raising taxes substantially, cutting entitlements, or letting federal debt continuously expand at whatever rate buyers like China will tolerate. Ultimately, Cembalest forecasts that instead of facing these mathematical realities, the government is likely to cycle through denial and marginal tinkering, leaving citizens to prepare for higher effective tax rates, deep political polarization, and persistent economic uncertainty.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication analyze the fundamental imbalances within the European monetary union, arguing that initial currency conversion rates set the European Union on a course where the peripheral GIPSI countries—Greece, Ireland, Italy, Portugal, and Spain—became uncompetitive consumers while Germany became the primary subsidizer of their debt. The author notes that right from the adoption of the common currency, the GIPSI nations lost competitiveness relative to Germany.

To support this argument, the first two charts track relative competitiveness using two measures of real effective exchange rates from 2000 to 2010, indexed to January 2000. In both charts, a rising line indicates a loss of competitiveness. The first chart, based on labor costs from the EU Commission, shows Germany’s line declining steadily to an index level of approximately 83 by 2010, indicating it became highly competitive. Meanwhile, the GIPSI nations grew increasingly uncompetitive; Ireland’s index peaked near 123 in 2008 before correcting downward, while Italy, Portugal, Spain, and Greece all rose significantly to finish between 108 and 115. France remained relatively flat, hovering around the 100 mark. 

The second chart, which measures goods prices using OECD data, displays a similar dynamic. Germany's price competitiveness remained stable, ending just below 100, while France and the GIPSI group lost ground. Ireland's goods price index spiked spectacularly to nearly 140 in 2008 before dropping back to roughly 128 by 2010. Spain, Greece, Italy, and Portugal steadily rose to index levels between 110 and 120.

Despite this loss of competitiveness, lower interest rates set by the European Central Bank and funded by external capital fueled a major consumption boom in the peripheral states. This is illustrated in the third chart, which measures household consumer credit growth indexed to December 2002. Greece’s credit growth rose so rapidly that it went off the chart, exceeding an index value of 230 by 2005. Spain and Ireland also saw massive consumer credit expansions, ending near 200 by 2009. Portugal and Italy saw moderate increases, and France grew to about 130. In stark contrast, Germany's consumer credit growth remained completely flat, near the 100 index level, for the entire period. 

This consumer credit expansion is directly mirrored in the fourth chart, which tracks the current account balance as a percentage of GDP from 1992 to 2010. While Germany transitioned from a mild deficit in the late 1990s to a substantial surplus that peaked at nearly 8% of GDP in 2007, the GIPSI countries sank deep into deficit. By 2008, Greece's current account deficit approached -15% of GDP, while Portugal and Spain both reached deficits near -10%. Ireland fell to nearly -6%, while France and Italy also dipped into minor deficits of around -2% to -3%. 

A footnote highlights the scale of this external burden by citing 2009 Fitch ratings for net external debt relative to foreign currency receipts. Greece stood at 291%, Spain at 275%, and Portugal at 209%, compared to France at 94%, the United Kingdom at 82%, and Germany in a net creditor position of -4%. 

Ultimately, the author asserts that the arrival of the global recession ended this consumption party, testing the historical concerns raised by economists Milton Friedman and Martin Feldstein regarding the viability of a monetary union. As economic activity collapses and GIPSI budget deficits soar, Europe’s lack of fiscal ammunition is laid bare, as several member states have consistently run debt-to-GDP ratios well in excess of agreed-upon European limits.

This page analyzes the brewing European sovereign debt crisis in early 2010, focusing on the acute challenges faced by Greece and the broader implications for the Eurozone's monetary union. The author highlights stagnant Eurozone growth and the rising cost of sovereign debt protection for the "GIPSI" nations (Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, and Italy). 

Two primary charts illustrate this financial strain. The first, detailing gross sovereign debt as a percentage of GDP from 1992 to 2010, shows Greece and Italy leading the group with debt-to-GDP ratios exceeding 110% by 2010, while Spain, Ireland, and Portugal show sharp upward trajectories in the final years. The second chart traces the cost of five-year default protection spreads in basis points from September 2008 to January 2010. It shows Greece's spreads skyrocketing to nearly 400 basis points by early 2010, dwarfing the spreads of Portugal, Ireland, Spain, Italy, France, and Germany.

The text addresses the skepticism surrounding the Greek "adjustment," noting that Greece’s plan to contract its fiscal deficit by 10% of GDP over three years is historically unprecedented and faces severe domestic resistance, including strikes by civil servants and clinicians. While policymakers insist Greece will not default or be expelled, the nation needs to borrow 50 billion euros in 2010. The situation is further complicated by transparency issues; Greece revised its 2009 budget deficit to three times prior estimates, and it ranks lowest in the EU on corruption indexes. A horizontal bar chart of the shadow economy as a percentage of GDP for OECD countries shows Greece at the very bottom with the largest underground economy, sitting at nearly 28% of GDP, followed closely by Italy at over 25% and Spain at over 20%, which compromises tax collection.

These economic pressures are fueling a debate over European federalism. The author points to proposals by EU President Van Rompuy and ALDE President Guy Verhofstadt advocating for centralized economic enforcement and pan-European bond issuance. However, this federalist push faces significant political roadblocks, particularly in Germany. Chancellor Angela Merkel and her administration face a public strongly opposed to bailouts, with a poll indicating that 70% of Germans oppose bailing out Greece or Ireland. This opposition is shared by prominent financial figures like Otmar Issing, Karl Otto Pohl, and Jürgen Stark. A footnote highlights that the annual transfers required from Germany to offset regional EU disparities could reach 7% of German GDP, a burden compared to post-World War I Versailles reparations.

This publication highlights the stark contrast between strong private sector corporate profits and looming public sector debt issues. The author notes that despite a strong manufacturing rebound, the public sector is bogged down by high debt, weak housing, and slow labor recovery. Two line charts illustrate the corporate strength. The first chart, depicting U.S. equity free cash flow yields for large-capitalization stocks excluding financials and utilities from 1953 to 2009, shows the yield climbing sharply toward eight percent at the end of 2009. The second chart shows U.S. non-financial corporate free cash flow as a percentage of GDP from 1970 to 2010, which reached a 40-year high of over four percent. A footnote highlights an uptick in large merger and acquisition activity in early 2010, citing major deals involving companies like Coca-Cola, Schlumberger, Smith International, Prudential, AIG, Merck, and Millipore.

The author warns of unsustainable public debt across G3 nations, presenting a text box of drastic measures calculated by Martin Sullivan to reduce the deficit to three percent by 2015. These painful choices include raising all tax rates by fifteen percent, cutting Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security by twenty-five percent, or introducing a seven-point-seven percent value-added tax. Similar debt pressures are observed in the United Kingdom, Spain, Ireland, Japan, and Germany, where fourth-quarter GDP growth flatlined at zero percent. Due to these risks, J.P. Morgan reports being slightly underweight in equities, shifting allocation to hedge funds and credit.

The second half of the page addresses the discrepancy in U.S. municipal default data, reconciling Moody’s count of fifty-four defaults since 1970 with the Distressed Debt Newsletter’s count of three hundred forty-seven defaults in 2008 and 2009 alone. The difference is explained by unrated California and Florida dirt bonds—specifically special assessment bonds—and industrial development or multifamily housing bonds, which together make up seventy percent of the newsletter's defaults. The author notes that J.P. Morgan largely avoids these categories, holding risks primarily in general obligation and essential service revenue bonds. The author predicts a critical pressure point for municipal entities in late 2010 when two hundred thirty billion dollars in federal stimulus transfers run out.

This page examines credit investing opportunities following the 2009 market rally, drawing on insights from a major non-municipal fixed income strategy manager who has shifted his portfolio to sixty percent cash. The manager argues that many credit opportunities have been exhausted and good news is fully priced in, prompting him to start shorting overvalued sectors. 

To illustrate these overvalued areas, the page features two charts. The first chart, titled Hartford/Berkshire risk differential evaporates, plots the five-year credit default swap spread differential in basis points from December 2008 to December 2009. This differential, which measures the spread between BBB-rated Hartford—notable for having the largest and lowest quality commercial mortgage-backed securities exposure—and AA+-rated Berkshire, spiked to nearly seven hundred basis points in March 2009 before collapsing to near zero by December 2009. This dramatic convergence demonstrates that differentiation of credit risk in the insurance sector has practically vanished. The second chart, titled Retailer credit risk back to pre-crisis levels, tracks five-year credit default swap spreads in basis points from January 2006 to January 2010 for three retailers: RadioShack, GAP, and T.J. Maxx. Spreads for all three spiked dramatically in late 2008 and early 2009, with RadioShack peaking above three hundred and fifty basis points. However, by January 2010, spreads for GAP and T.J. Maxx had compressed back to around fifty basis points, and RadioShack to around one hundred and fifty basis points, returning to their pre-crisis levels despite ongoing consumer pressures and tight credit. The author also notes that junior investment-grade commercial mortgage-backed securities are trading well above fair value, despite having as little as eight percent subordination at their peak, with projected losses now expected to exceed those levels.

The second half of the page shifts to buying power and distressed debt. While the author expresses concern over the aftermath of the recession—including state and local insolvencies and a severe housing foreclosure overhang where average mortgage loan-to-values stood at ninety-two percent in the third quarter of 2009—he emphasizes the massive amount of capital sitting on the sidelines. This sideline cash is evident in corporate cash holdings reaching a fifty-year high as a percentage of tangible assets, elevated money market fund balances, and cash-rich sovereign wealth funds, such as the China Investment Corporation, which held eighty-seven percent cash in December 2008. Finally, the author highlights a significant spike in U.S. private savings relative to private investment, driven by a collapse in real estate, capital spending, and inventories, with capital equipment and software investment suffering its worst decline in fifty years.

This page from the report features two distinct sections written by Michael Cembalest: an analysis of current trends in savings, investment, and distressed debt markets, and a personal commentary on the negative impacts of video games on children.

In the first section, Cembalest discusses how rising savings are being utilized to pay down debt accumulated during the prior credit boom. This increase in savings highlights the significant buying power available to corporations for financing capital spending, stock buybacks, mergers and acquisitions, and inventory growth. To illustrate the underlying imbalance of the previous cycle, a line chart displays the historical ratio of private saving to private investment from 1947 through roughly 2009. The chart reveals that during the pre-2007 credit boom, the ratio dropped well below the neutral 1.0 mark, indicating savings ran far below investment levels, before spiking sharply higher to over 1.4 by the end of the timeline.

Cembalest notes that because the U.S. high-yield and leveraged loan markets have rebounded strongly—with high-yield bonds trading under 50 cents on the dollar dropping from 27.5 percent to just 1 percent of the market over the prior year—investors are shifting their distressed debt focus to Europe. The European market, totaling around 1 trillion dollars in high-yield bonds and leveraged loans, presents opportunities due to weak industrial production and retail sales. Furthermore, J.P. Morgan Securities estimates that European high-yield defaults in 2010 will double those of the United States, exacerbated by sovereign debt pressures in countries like Spain, Ireland, and Portugal, which face heavy financing needs between April and July.

In the second section, titled Still Holding Out Against the Game Console Invasion, the author discusses his strict family policy banning video game consoles like Xbox, PlayStation, and Wii, as well as violent video games. Cembalest cites several academic and professional studies to argue that video games lead to socially maladaptive behaviors, short-term aggressiveness, lower grades, and physical conflicts, particularly among children under ten. He highlights Massively Multiplayer Online Role-Playing Games (MMORPGs) as being especially problematic for socially isolated children. A reference box on the page highlights studies from the American Medical Association, the Journal of Adolescence, and the Minnesota School of Professional Psychology supporting these claims.

This publication reviews the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy maneuvers and analyzes the investment landscape for acquiring distressed regional banks. 

The author characterizes the Federal Reserve’s 25 basis point hike of the Discount Rate as a mere dress rehearsal rather than the start of actual monetary tightening. This rate adjustment only impacts $15 billion to $30 billion of the Federal Reserve's massive $2 trillion balance sheet and was telegraphed well in advance. The author argues that real tightening is highly unlikely given that two-thirds of the United States economy is operating below 70 percent capacity utilization, inflation is non-existent, and housing and labor markets remain stagnant. This perspective is supported by a line chart titled "Substantial tightening seems unimaginable now," which plots the percentage of sectors with less than 70 percent capacity utilization from 1972 through 2008. The chart displays a historic spike at the end of 2008, peaking near 70 percent, which is dramatically higher than previous recessionary peaks in 1975, 1982, and 2002.

The discussion then turns to the market for acquiring failed or failing regional banks, noting that according to FDIC data, the financial sector is only one-third of the way through the bank default cycle. Regional banks are currently being acquired at valuations substantially below historical norms. In 2009, there were 25 acquisitions of banks with assets over $150 million that were purchased for under $1 billion. The median price-to-tangible book value for these transactions was 1.15x, which is a steep discount compared to the 2.0x to 3.0x multiples paid during most business cycles and the 2.4x average seen from 2002 to 2008. Due to looming regulatory changes affecting consumer and mortgage credit, future acquisition multiples are expected to remain compressed between 1.7x and 2.0x. 

An accompanying scatter plot, titled "2009 regional bank acquisitions at ~ 1x book value," illustrates this valuation trend by plotting the price-to-tangible book value of various transactions over the course of 2009. The size of each circle on the chart represents the size of the acquired bank's asset base, highlighting transactions such as a massive $5.6 billion acquisition priced around 1.3x book value and a smaller $154 million acquisition near 1.6x book value. Nearly all of these 2009 acquisitions cluster well below the red dashed horizontal line that marks the average nationwide acquisition multiple of approximately 2.4x from January 2002 through June 2008.

The author cautions that successful bank acquisitions require sophisticated expertise in evaluating deposit franchises rather than just valuing physical or loan assets. Distressed banks often rely heavily on highly volatile brokered deposits to circumvent FDIC insurance limits. For failed banks over the prior two years, brokered deposits were four times the national norm, making up over 37 percent of total deposits at IndyMac. These deposits can flee rapidly, and even insured, non-brokered deposits present a significant flight risk. An FDIC study revealed that failing banks paying 50 to 100 basis points above national rates still suffered massive deposit outflows. Consequently, management teams vying for these banks must understand the behavior of stranded depositors and predict how many will depart once above-market rates are discontinued.

This page from the publication addresses three distinct issues: U.S. energy policy and coal investing, political bipartisanship regarding entitlements, and the unfolding European sovereign debt crisis. 

In the first section, the author outlines the struggles of the United States to establish a cohesive energy policy, pointing to inconsistent alternative energy subsidies, regulatory barriers to nuclear energy, and political blocks on wind and solar projects. The piece highlights that the Environmental Protection Agency appears poised to enforce the Clean Air Act by potentially capping carbon emissions at 0.4 metric tons per megawatt-hour. Because this level is less than half the emissions rate of a typical coal plant, it would effectively block new coal capacity and create decommissioning risks for existing plants, acting as a back-door carbon tax on utilities that rely on coal for half of the nation's electricity. The author notes that this shift will benefit natural gas and renewable energy sectors, where J.P. Morgan has focused its investments, predicting a gradual but inevitable transition away from coal despite its abundance. A footnote highlights that Germany's installed solar power base per capita is 17 times that of the U.S., despite Germany having cloud cover comparable to Seattle.

The second section examines bipartisanship in entitlement reform, presenting two historical examples accompanied by archival photographs. The first photograph shows President Lyndon B. Johnson signing the 1965 Medicare act alongside former President Harry Truman; the bill passed with substantial Republican support. The second photograph depicts President Ronald Reagan signing the 1983 Social Security reforms alongside Democratic House Speaker Tip O'Neill and Representative Claude Pepper. The author argues that major national policies have historically required bipartisan cooperation rather than back-door reconciliation, expressing concern that the current healthcare debate is distracting from the nation's severe fiscal deficits.

In the final section, the author provides an update on the European sovereign debt crisis, noting that Berlin may support a 25-billion-euro rescue package for Greece because German banks have 522 billion euros of exposure to government bonds in Portugal, Italy, Ireland, Greece, and Spain. The commentary highlights a growing, radical debate within the French establishment, where some are calling for a return to national currencies or for Germany to exit the European Monetary Union to avoid economic depression. The author concludes by introducing a retrospective look at past sovereign debt crises, cautioning that while Greece's situation will likely begin with a bailout, markets and politicians consistently underestimate the true depth of sovereign and currency crises as they transition from "unthinkable" to "patently obvious."

This page functions as a sovereign default time capsule, demonstrating how consensus market commentary remains stubbornly optimistic right up to the brink of historic debt and currency crises. Through three detailed case studies of Argentina, Mexico, and Russia, the author contrasts contemporaneous expert predictions with the reality of sudden financial collapses.

The first section focuses on Argentina and features a line chart plotting the price of the Argentina 11 3/8 2017 sovereign bond from January 1998 to January 2004. The bond price, which hovered near 100 in late 2000, plummeted to around 30 by 2002. Annotations on the chart highlight the prevailing optimism of the era, such as the International Monetary Fund’s Managing Director praising a $40 billion aid package in December 2000, a Bear Stearns economist declaring in January 2001 that the pressure had come off the country, and Bloomberg reports in mid-2001 anticipating billions in bond swap savings and additional IMF financing. The accompanying text notes that Argentina was once the darling of global bond investors, holding a massive 25% weight in the Emerging Markets Bond Index. Despite Templeton Asset Management asserting in 1998 that the central bank had ample reserves to back the one-to-one peso-dollar peg, high fiscal deficits and painful deflation ultimately caused the convertibility program to collapse. The peso fell by 75%, resulting in Argentina's fifth default since the 1820s.
