The second section examines Mexico’s currency crisis through a line chart of the Peso/USD exchange rate from April 1993 to March 1996. The exchange rate remained stable around 3 pesos per dollar before skyrocketing past 7 in late 1994. Chart annotations capture the misplaced confidence of the period, including a Fidelity portfolio manager in April 1993 claiming the risk of a major overnight devaluation was extremely small, and a Bear Stearns research head in August 1993 calling the peso rock solid. Even as emergency measures were enacted—such as a $6.7 billion credit line from the U.S. and Canada in April 1994 and a $20 billion Exchange Stabilization Fund in February 1995—U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin later characterized the crash as a low-probability event that few could have anticipated. The text explains that international investors, believing in the "crawling peg" exchange rate system established in 1989, poured $50 billion into short-term government bonds like Cetes and Tesebonos. When the peg broke, the lack of underlying competitiveness and export growth caused the peso to collapse by more than 50%.

The final section details the Russian financial collapse of 1998, featuring a line chart of Russia's GKO sovereign debt price from March to July 1998. The price experienced a sharp decline, a brief IMF-loan-fueled spike back above 80 in July, and a terminal crash. Quotes on the chart show ANZ Research in June 1998 arguing that Russia did not need a bailout and had no balance of payments problem, while Hermitage Russia Fund and Troika Dialog Fund celebrated a $22.6 billion IMF-led loan package in July 1998 as a massive boost to confidence. The commentary explains that foreign capital had aggressively flooded Russian domestic debt, pouring $30 billion into GKOs, another $30 billion into restructured Soviet-era debt, and buying up Eurobonds. Like the other nations, Russia suffered from a fixed exchange rate and deteriorating terms of trade, leading to a 75% fall in the Ruble. Highlighting the extreme market delusion of the time, the author shares the bizarre anecdote of a Deutsche Bank strategist who publically stated he was confident enough in the GKO market to invest his own daughter’s education savings right before the collapse.

This commentary focuses on the economic and social challenges accompanying China's rapid rise, alongside updates on US fiscal policy, EPA environmental regulations, and European debt. Despite China's position as the world's largest exporter and its projection of over eight percent GDP growth, growing pains are increasingly apparent. The author points to a sharp rise in the loan-to-GDP ratio, which jumped from below 1.0x to 1.25x, prompting large capital raises by major banks including China Merchants Bank, Bank of Communications, Bank of China, and Huaxia Bank. Real estate speculation has also drawn concern, with Premier Wen Jiabao describing the market as a "wild horse" that may require tighter monetary policy.

These domestic pressures are illustrated in two charts. The first chart, titled "Renewable water resources in China" and sourced from the World Bank World Development Indicators, plots cubic meters per capita from 1962 to 2007. It shows a steep, uninterrupted decline from approximately 4,100 cubic meters per capita down to just under 2,200, underscoring severe environmental degradation where Chinese agencies estimate half of all lakes and rivers are contaminated. The second chart, titled "'Mass incidents' (disturbances) in China," compiles data from Gavekal, the China Academy of Social Sciences, and the China Labor Bulletin from 1993 to 2008. It depicts a dramatic rise in social friction, with the annual number of disturbances escalating from under 10,000 in 1993 to roughly 120,000 by 2008. Citing these tightening monetary conditions and capacity risks, J.P. Morgan notes it reduced its Asian equity positions in favor of the S&P 500.

In other global updates, the author clarifies that the options previously discussed to reduce the US budget deficit to three percent by 2015—such as raising all tax rates by 15 percent or cutting entitlement spending by 25 percent—are mutually exclusive rather than additive, meaning the fiscal outlook is "only terrible" rather than catastrophic. In the energy sector, the EPA's enforcement of the Clean Air Act is expected to severely impact coal plants. By tightening emissions standards for mercury and sulfur dioxide, the EPA is driving a shift toward natural gas, with a forecast from Sanford Bernstein suggesting these regulations could accelerate the retirement of up to 24 percent of current coal-fired electricity capacity by 2015. Lastly, the page addresses European sovereign debt, highlighting a proposal by the Centre for European Policy Studies for a "European Monetary Fund" and quoting Eurogroup head Jean-Claude Juncker, who warned currency speculators that Eurozone policymakers possess "instruments of torture in the basement" to stop financial market speculation if necessary.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest, presents a sovereign default time capsule. It explores what market participants were saying in real time as historical debt and currency crises unfolded, moving from initial disbelief to sudden, inevitable default. Through three distinct historical case studies—Dubai, Indonesia, and China—Cembalest highlights how investor complacency, assumptions of government bailouts, and structural vulnerabilities repeatedly lead to sudden market collapses.

The first section focuses on Dubai and the debt price of Nakheel Develop 2 Ltd from June 2007 to December 2009. The chart shows the debt price, scaled on a y-axis from 20 to 100, staying near par at 100 during a massive real estate boom. Early optimism is captured by a June 2007 quote from the Middle East Economic Digest claiming property demand would outstrip supply through the end of the decade. Even as late as September 2009, the price remained elevated after the Ruler of Dubai expressed lack of worry over the emirate’s debt burden, and reports in October 2009 suggested Dubai World was close to a deal to ease its twenty-billion-dollar debt burden. However, the price collapsed precipitously to nearly 50 by late 2009. Cembalest explains that Dubai’s construction boom was larger than Shanghai’s Pudong boom on both a per capita and absolute basis. Investors operated under a moral hazard assumption that Abu Dhabi would step in to bail out the region. Ultimately, this proved false. Cembalest characterizes this as a sovereign event rather than a corporate one, noting that Nakheel’s parent company, Dubai World, represented more than two-thirds of Dubai's eighty-billion-dollar external debt.

The second section examines Indonesia's sovereign debt price from December 1995 to June 1998. The chart, with a y-axis ranging from 30 to 120, shows the price holding above 100 before experiencing a dramatic collapse to around 40 by early 1998. Annotations show that in December 1995, a Morgan Stanley strategist in Fortune Magazine assured investors they did not need to worry about currency risk due to dollar pegs, even advising putting half of a portfolio into emerging Asian equities. In October 1996, an IMF Director expressed great optimism for Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand. Even as the crisis took hold in early 1998, positive quotes regarding IMF lending packages and negotiations with the new Cabinet continued. Cembalest references Paul Krugman's 1993 essay on the myth of Asian growth, noting that overvalued currencies, fixed exchange rates that encouraged unhedged dollar borrowing, and capital diversion into commercial property fueled the crisis. Drawing parallels to Greece and Spain, he notes that Asian equities eventually fell by 66 percent and the Indonesian Rupiah fell by 80 percent in 1998.

The final section looks at China's Guangdong International Trust and Investment Corp, or GITIC, debt price from December 1997 to March 2003. The chart features a y-axis from 0 to 100 and shows a vertical drop from 100 in late 1997 to near zero by mid-1999, where it remained flatlined. Annotations highlight that investors initially relied on comfort letters indicating state support for loans. However, by Spring 2003, the Chinese Supreme Court determined that governmental organizations had issued these loan guarantees illegally. Cembalest compares this to the situations in Dubai and Abu Dhabi, explaining that foreign capital rushed in under the assumption that China would never jeopardize foreign inflows by letting a state-owned enterprise fail. In reality, GITIC defaulted on three billion dollars in Eurobonds, Yankee bonds, and Samurai bonds. The bankruptcy process was highly opaque, and many assets disappeared because they were in sectors off-limits to unlicensed foreign investors.

This page focuses on the positive outlook for commercial real estate and the rapid economic recovery of emerging markets like Brazil and China. 

The author begins by defending a bullish case for commercial real estate, arguing that the market faces a much smaller oversupply issue than in past recessions and is correcting prices much faster. Three charts support this view. The first chart, which displays the percentage change in office stock over the previous three years across various cycles, compares a composite of thirteen European cities alongside Paris, Frankfurt, London, and New York during the peak periods of 1991, 2001, and 2008. The data shows a significantly smaller expansion in office space prior to the 2008 cycle compared to previous ones. For instance, the composite European stock grew by nearly 10% leading up to 1991 and over 8% in 2001, but increased by less than 4% in 2008. Similarly, London's growth was around 13% in 1991 compared to roughly 3.5% in 2008, and New York dropped from over 4% growth to about 1%.

The second chart details the office supply pipeline as a percentage of total stock for the years 2009, 2010, and 2011 across London, Paris, Munich, Frankfurt, Madrid, and New York. This pipeline remains very low overall, with New York reaching 0% by 2011 and London declining from over 3% in 2009 to 2% in 2011. Madrid is the sole exception, with its pipeline projected to expand from roughly 1% in 2009 to over 3% in 2011. 

The third chart illustrates the speed of price corrections, plotting the percentage change in U.S. commercial property prices from cyclical peaks. It compares the trajectory of the 1989 peak with the 2008 peak over successive quarters. The 1989 peak experienced a slow decline, taking 24 quarters to reach its bottom of roughly negative 33%. In contrast, the 2008 peak shows a dramatic and rapid plunge, dropping nearly 43% in just 9 quarters, reflecting a much faster valuation adjustment.

Historical context is provided to explain these supply differences. In the early 1990s, U.S. oversupply was driven by the 1981 Economic and Tax Recovery Act, which allowed accelerated depreciation and passive loss offsets. This created a building glut that was subsequently undercut by the 1986 Tax Reform Act. Because these tax-driven incentives were not present in the run-up to 2008, today’s market is not burdened by a similar supply overhang. This dynamic, combined with the fact that the vast majority of maturing commercial real estate loans were rolled over in 2009 without requiring new equity, supports adding commercial real estate exposure to portfolios.

The page concludes with a discussion of emerging markets, referencing a panel at the Council on Foreign Relations moderated by the author, featuring Ronnie Chan of Hang Lung Group and Arminio Fraga, the former Central Bank Governor of Brazil. Both panelists highlight that Brazil and China are growing faster than the G3 nations, benefit from healthier government and private debt dynamics, and are actively pulling developed economies out of recession. While Brazil faces modest inflationary pressures that might require monetary tightening, its overall economic outlook remains highly positive, driven by booming industrial production.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" publication, authored by Michael Cembalest, evaluates the firm's 2010 market outlook, specifically analyzing the driving forces behind better-than-expected U.S. consumer spending. Cembalest begins by reiterating the firm’s projections of rising earnings, single-digit equity returns, transitioning debt markets, a brewing M&A boom, falling gold prices, and a stabilizing U.S. dollar, noting that there is no need to adjust these forecasts. He highlights that market expectations for Federal Reserve policy rates have finally converged with J.P. Morgan’s expectation of minimal tightening in 2010. 

This interest rate convergence is shown in the top-right line chart, "Market expectations for 3-month Libor in December 2010," which tracks the yield on the 3-month Eurodollar forward rate from June 2009 to February 2010. The yield expectations steadily declined from nearly 3.0% in mid-2009 to approximately 1.0% by February 2010. Cembalest also contrasts differing government deficit forecasts, noting that the Congressional Budget Office estimates 2020 debt-to-GDP at 90%, significantly higher than the Office of Management and Budget’s estimate of 77%.

The main body of the page addresses the surprising resilience of the U.S. consumer compared to European and Japanese counterparts. Beyond improving labor markets, Cembalest attributes this to three main drivers illustrated by a trio of charts. The first bar chart, "Wealthiest 10% account for more than 40% of total consumption," highlights that the highest income bracket accounts for roughly 40% of total consumption, while the lowest 40% accounts for only about 12%, and the middle tiers (40%-80% and 80%-90%) account for roughly 31% and 13% respectively. This underscores how rising equity markets, which bolster wealthy households, disproportionately drive overall spending. The second line chart, "Government transfers as a percentage of disposable income," details a steady rise in government assistance from 1960 to 2010, peaking at a 50-year high of nearly 21% of disposable income in 2010. The third chart, "Sources of squatters income - Delinquent loan balances by type, bn," details nearly $1 trillion in delinquent loan balances as of late 2009. This delinquent debt—comprising non-agency securitized mortgages, bank-owned mortgages, agency securitized mortgages, and consumer loans—acts as "squatters income," freeing up substantial cash flow that consumers can spend elsewhere rather than servicing their loans.

In the final section, Cembalest reflects on observations from J.P. Morgan's annual CEO conference and spending data from Chase Card Services, which confirm that year-over-year spending growth is positive only among wealthier cohorts. He uses Las Vegas tourism as a real-time proxy for discretionary retail sales, displaying a line chart titled "Las Vegas strip gaming revenue & average room rate" measuring year-over-year percentage changes from December 2003 to December 2009. The chart reveals that while year-over-year gaming revenue has started to rebound from its nadir of -15% up to roughly -10%, hotel room rates remain severely depressed at nearly -20% due to ongoing overbuilding, leverage, and aggressive discounting. Cembalest concludes that while overall spending trends are slightly better than businesses had anticipated, they are recovering from highly depressed levels and remain well below historical peaks.

This page analyzes the investment case for emerging market local currency bonds and discusses shifts in hedge fund strategy toward merger arbitrage as corporate cash levels rise. 

The author begins by outlining the long-term benefits of emerging market local bonds, which generally yield more than G3 bonds and feature favorable structural dynamics compared to the United States. While J.P. Morgan remained on the sidelines during the speculative credit bubble, they are now increasing exposure following a sharp 25% correction in late 2008 when FX spot rate declines overwhelmed interest carry. The J.P. Morgan GBI-EM Global Diversified Index currently yields around 7%. The 13 member countries of the index possess stronger fundamentals than the United States, including higher growth, higher interest rates, less public debt, and smaller trade deficits. Highlighting this regional transformation, over 30% of global M&A volumes now target emerging market entities, compared to just 10% from 2000 to 2007. The author expects EM currency risks to be lower than in 2008, naming Brazil as a potential exception due to its rising external financing needs and political election risks. 

This argument is supported by a line chart tracking the returns on EM local currency bonds using the GBI-EM Global Diversified Index from January 2003 through early 2010, with January 2003 indexed to 100. The chart decomposes total returns into Spot FX and the carry/yield curve. The total return series reached a peak of nearly 240 in 2008 before dropping to about 180 during the financial crisis and subsequently recovering back toward 240. The Spot FX series shows a volatile trajectory that fell below 100 in late 2008, while the carry and yield curve components show a steady, non-volatile upward path.

In the second section, the author evaluates corporate cash balances and merger activity. Corporate balance sheets are holding the highest level of cash relative to tangible assets seen in 50 years. This excess cash is expected to drive dividends, stock buybacks, and capital spending, with a primary acceleration in M&A. Already, the first two months of 2010 have seen more announced deals over $5 billion than any year since 2000, and European mid-market M&A has risen 36% year-over-year. To capture this trend, the author's multi-strategy hedge funds have rotated out of credit positions and into merger and statistical arbitrage. 

Two charts support this discussion. The first, a stacked area chart of representative hedge fund strategy allocations from January 2008 to January 2010, illustrates a clear shift: allocations to US and European convertibles, credit, and volatility strategies decreased from around 45% in late 2008 to roughly 25% by January 2010. Concurrently, merger arbitrage and statistical arbitrage allocations both expanded to roughly 15% each, while long/short equities remained stable at approximately 20%. The final chart displays monthly global M&A volume in billions of dollars from 1999 to 2010. The data illustrates a peak of over $600 billion in monthly volume during 2007, a subsequent collapse to near the $100 billion level in 2008 and 2009, and a minor recovery trend beginning in early 2010.

This page analyzes the post-financial crisis economic recovery and evaluates political narratives surrounding the United States federal deficit. In a section titled "Praying for Time," the author argues that while trillions of dollars in monetary and fiscal stimulus have successfully generated a sharp rebound in global exports, manufacturing, and tax receipts, this recovery acts like a steroid-treated patient who must heal quickly before prolonged treatment yields severe side effects. Although retail sales and credit quality at regional banks like Comerica and Fifth Third are improving, February saw a record monthly U.S. budget deficit of $221 billion. Treasury yields remain low for now because households and businesses are actively de-leveraging, resulting in the lowest overall debt growth since 1952, but Treasury funding risks will rise once stimulus is withdrawn. 

To illustrate the macroeconomic rebound, three charts are presented. The first chart, "Global real exports," plots the annualized six-month percentage change from 1991 through 2009, showing a dramatic collapse below negative 30 percent during the crisis followed by a swift rebound back above 30 percent. The second chart, "Global manufacturing PMI," details a seasonally adjusted index from 2000 to 2010, where activity plunged to a low of 35 before recovering to over 55. The third chart, "Federal tax receipts, billions," uses a three-month moving average to display seasonally adjusted annualized rates from 2003 to 2009. This chart plots corporate taxes on the left axis, showing a drop from over $350 billion to under $100 billion before turning upward, alongside individual income and payroll taxes on the right axis, which fell from a peak near $1,750 billion to approximately $1,400 billion. 

In the second section, titled "Whose Deficit is it?", the author challenges the label of the "2010 Obama Deficit" by demonstrating that the deficit impacts of President Obama and President Bush are almost a dead heat. A diagram titled "Components of FY 2010 U.S. fiscal budget" breaks down the $3.7 trillion in total expenditures. Base spending includes $1.9 trillion for core defense, mandatory programs, discretionary spending, and net interest, and $1.3 trillion for entitlements like Social Security and Medicare/Medicaid. The remaining discretionary policy impacts of the two administrations are compared side-by-side using colored bars. President Obama’s estimated impact is $462 billion, consisting of $265 billion in expenditures (principally the ARRA Stimulus and the Extenders bill) and $198 billion in tax cuts. President Bush’s estimated impact is $468 billion, comprising $228 billion in expenditures (the Iraq and Afghanistan wars and Medicare Part D) and $239 billion in tax cuts from 2001 and 2003. 

The author closes with several cautious forecasts, predicting single-digit developed market equity returns for the year due to risks associated with stimulus withdrawal. Additionally, the author notes impending funding shortfalls at Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, rising costs for FDIC deposit insurance from failing banks, a possible downgrade of the U.S. outlook by Moody's, and a bearish outlook on home prices given that delinquent homes outnumber homes currently for sale.

In this commentary, Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest explores two distinct topics: the future of plant-based vaccines to curb healthcare costs and the long-term investment implications of climate-induced sea-level rise. 

First, Cembalest outlines the promise of plant-based vaccines, highlighting a client’s consortium that recently received Department of Defense funding to develop vaccines for viruses like H1N1. He contrasts traditional vaccine production—which relies on breeding viruses inside chicken eggs over twenty to twenty-five weeks—with a novel plant-based approach. This newer method involves identifying a viral antigen, introducing its DNA into bacteria to infect tobacco plants, and harvesting the generated antigens directly from the plant tissue. This process is much quicker and cheaper, avoids animal-based allergen risks, and holds promise for cancer gene therapies. Phase I clinical trials using personalized plant-based vaccines for non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma have shown strong immune responses. If successfully scaled, this could significantly lower the seventy billion dollars spent annually on cancer care in the United States and make vital treatments accessible to the one billion people globally living on less than one dollar a day who cannot afford expensive, cold-chain-dependent traditional vaccines.

Second, Cembalest reflects on a presentation at the Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory concerning the melting of the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, which could hypothetically raise sea levels by six meters and inundate areas like Florida and Manhattan. He notes that while the current historical rate of sea-level rise—averaging two to three millimeters per year—implies that a six-meter rise would take about two thousand years, historical data presents a more urgent warning. Approximately one hundred and twenty thousand years ago, during the peak of the last interglacial period, sea levels rose ten times faster without any human influence. Cembalest poses the open question of whether human activity will accelerate the natural climate cycle, prompting him to caution clients against holding long-dated Qualified Personal Residence Trusts on waterfront real estate.

An accompanying line chart from the Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory, titled "Sea level rise as measured by tidal gauges and satellite: 2mm-3mm per year," supports this discussion. The chart tracks global sea level change in millimeters on the vertical axis, ranging from negative two hundred to one hundred, against a timeline on the horizontal axis spanning from 1880 to 2000. The data series, depicted with red error bars representing tidal gauge measurements and a blue line representing modern satellite data, shows a clear and steady upward trajectory. The sea level rises from about negative one hundred and fifty millimeters in 1880 to nearly fifty millimeters by the year 2000, visually reinforcing the steady annual increase of two to three millimeters.

This page explores whether rising government debt risks are poised to derail the current economic expansion, framing the situation with a geological metaphor of living near major fault lines where daily life improves despite looming systemic threats. The author notes that while the United States is experiencing self-reinforcing improvements across production, consumption, profits, inventories, and employment, these gains sit precariously close to fiscal "fault lines," which include massive U.S. Treasury funding needs, the conclusion of Federal Reserve asset purchases, potential crowding out of private sector demand, and rumors of a sovereign credit rating downgrade. 

An illustrative map of California, titled "The Recovery and its Fault Lines, Reimagined," visualizes this tension. It traces the San Andreas Fault using lines representing Treasury debt and state/local debt, surrounded by callouts pointing to positive economic developments. These indicators include rising industrial activity like steel production and railcar loadings, positive labor market surveys with declining jobless claims, surging CEO confidence and share buybacks, improving retail and vehicle sales, reasonable S&P valuations at fourteen times consensus earnings, stabilizing home prices that outperform the Federal Reserve's worst-case stress-test assumptions, improving delinquency trends, and six consecutive weeks of retail inflows into equity mutual funds. 

Despite these positive signs, the author highlights the unprecedented scale of the U.S. budget deficit, which represents the largest peacetime deficit and debt-to-GDP ratio in history. Reducing the deficit is complicated by the growing share of mandatory spending, such as entitlements and interest, which are projected to consume seventy-one percent of government expenditures by 2015. To reduce the deficit to three percent by 2015, the author outlines stark hypothetical policy options: raising all taxes by fifteen percent, raising individual taxes by thirty percent, increasing the top tax brackets to seventy percent, or implementing a seven point seven percent value-added tax. The piece emphasizes that these deficits are directly keeping the recovery alive, as massive government transfers have offset the largest collapse in private income in sixty years to keep consumer spending stable.

The analysis also examines the ownership of the eight point two trillion dollars in publicly tradable U.S. Federal debt. Foreign entities and central banks hold half of this outstanding debt, led by China with eight hundred ninety billion dollars and Japan with seven hundred sixty-five billion dollars. The remaining debt is held by domestic entities, with households, state and local governments, and the Federal Reserve each owning between seven and ten percent, money market funds holding five percent, and pension funds, banks, broker-dealers, and life insurance companies holding two to three percent each. 

Finally, the author addresses foreign demand for Treasuries, asserting that demand remains stable primarily because Asian nations purchase U.S. debt out of mercantile self-interest to prevent their own currencies from appreciating. This symbiotic relationship is described as the largest macroeconomic imbalance of our times, and the author warns that it remains highly vulnerable to domestic inflation and political shifts in buying countries, meaning any break in this demand could cause substantial economic damage.

This page analyzes macroeconomic tensions in the Eurozone and outlines two distinct investment opportunities in Asian currencies and natural gas exploration and production stocks. 

The author begins with a critical view of the European political landscape, focusing on the tensions surrounding a potential Greek default and bailout. Key entities discussed include the European Central Bank, the Bundesbank, the German Finance Ministry, the German Constitutional Court, the IMF, and the French government. Highlighting German Finance Minister Wolfgang Schäuble’s stance that EU aid to Greece would be expensive and restricted only to cases of imminent default, the commentary suggests that markets are misreading Germany's resolve, drawing a historical parallel to the 1993 Exchange Rate Mechanism crisis. With regional elections in Westphalia fueling anti-bailout sentiment, the author predicts that temporary IMF intervention will be necessary. The core structural issue is framed not merely as a budget deficit crisis but as a fundamental crisis of unsustainable consumption, private-sector wages, and competitiveness across the Eurozone, which is likely to trigger deflationary pressures and heightens the risk of a Greek debt event.

In response to these European headwinds, the publication recommends going long on a basket of three Asian currencies—the Korean won, the Indonesian rupiah, and the Singapore dollar—while shorting the Euro. The first chart, "Asian basket vs the Euro," plots an index from 1999 to 2010 (with 1999 base 100) showing a long-term downward trend representing Euro appreciation, which peaked near 130 in 2001 before dropping to approximately 75 by 2010. The author argues this trend is ripe for reversal. This thesis is supported by a second bar chart comparing 2010 fundamental forecasts between the Euro Zone and the Asian basket. The data demonstrates the Asian basket's superior economic strength, with current account balances at over 4% of GDP compared to 0% for the Euro Zone, policy rates at 3% versus 1%, GDP growth at a robust 6% versus roughly 1%, and year-over-year inflation at 3.5% versus 1.5%. These strong fundamentals are expected to force higher policy rates or currency appreciation in Asia.

The second investment thesis focuses on opportunities in North American Exploration and Production (E&P) stocks with heavy exposure to natural gas. Driven by EPA enforcement of the Clean Air Act, the author notes that Sanford Bernstein expects the decommissioning of 290 million megawatt-hours of coal capacity—about 15% of total coal capacity—which could drive a 10% to 15% increase in natural gas demand. A bar chart titled "E&P stocks currently trade at a discount to NAV" shows that these stocks currently trade at just 60% of their net asset value, a deep discount compared to the broader industry average of roughly 72% and the ten-year historical average of 85%. Additionally, a line chart tracking the steep natural gas futures curve from April 2010 to April 2015 shows prices rising from under $5.00 per million BTU to over $7.00 per million BTU in a cyclical pattern. Based on these favorable valuations and rising demand, the author favors E&P companies with more than half of their reserves in natural gas.

This page begins by discussing the natural gas sector and corporate mergers, noting that five large oil majors—Exxon, Chevron, BP, Shell, and Total—hold a combined fifty-five billion dollars in cash, which represents a significant portion of the market capitalization of the stocks being monitored. The publication highlights major acquisitions in this sector, including Exxon’s forty-one billion dollar purchase of XTO and Consol Energy’s three and a half billion dollar purchase of Dominion Resource’s natural gas assets. 

Next, the author addresses the debate over "hermetic" portfolios, which are characterized by defensive positioning, such as holding fifteen percent in equities compared to normal weights of thirty-five to forty percent. While acknowledging severe macroeconomic headwinds—such as an IMF estimate from John Lipsky that advanced economy debt-to-GDP will rise from sixty percent to one hundred and ten percent by 2014—the author argues against retreating to such conservative allocations. He lists several supportive factors for maintaining near-normal U.S. equity exposure, including corporate cash balances at sixty-year highs, reasonable twelve-to-fourteen times forward price-earnings multiples on U.S. and European equities, a necessary post-recession inventory restocking cycle in the United States and Japan, and the redeployment of two hundred and forty billion dollars year-to-date from cash into credit.

Two charts illustrate these arguments. The first, titled "Core inflation back at lowest level since 1965," plots the six-month annualized percent change in core inflation using Bureau of Labor Statistics data from 1960 to 2010. It shows inflation dropping below two percent in 2010 to its lowest point in forty-five years, allowing the Federal Reserve to maintain an accommodative policy. The second chart, "Lowest debt growth since 1952," plots the year-over-year percentage change in domestic non-financial sector debt, combining federal, state, local, corporate, and individual debt based on Federal Reserve Flow of Funds data from 1954 to 2009. This chart shows debt growth plunging to roughly three percent in 2009, its lowest level since 1952, demonstrating that private sector deleveraging is temporarily buffering the rise in public sector deficits.

The page concludes with a discussion of "Hotel California and squatter’s income," which examines the unintended economic boost of delinquent mortgages. The author explains that one trillion dollars in delinquent consumer and mortgage loans effectively functions as "squatter's income" because delinquent borrowers who choose not to leave their homes are freed from making housing payments, creating extra disposable income. An anecdote of a homebuyer in Irvine, California, illustrates this dynamic, showing how an owner took out multiple mortgages, refinanced into an Option ARM, extracted capital, went delinquent in late 2006, and has lived rent-free ever since despite failed loan modifications. A footnote notes that "Hotel California" also describes the Volcker rule proposal, which would subject Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley to Federal Reserve oversight even if they shed their bank holding company status.

This page discusses the macroeconomic impacts of delinquent mortgage behavior, the length of the foreclosure process, and the implications of the newly passed U.S. healthcare reform bill. Michael Cembalest argues that "squatter’s income"—the disposable income consumers retain by living in their homes without paying their mortgages—temporarily boosts U.S. retail sales, but is ultimately an unsustainable source of economic support in a system tilted too far in favor of delinquent homeowners. 

To support this, the page features multiple visuals. A stacked bar chart displays delinquent loan balances by type, totaling nearly one trillion dollars as of late 2009. This balance is composed of non-agency securitized mortgages, bank-owned mortgages, agency securitized mortgages, and consumer loans. Additionally, a detailed table outlines a real-world example from Irvine, California, where a home buyer with zero downpayment extracted eighty-eight thousand five hundred dollars in capital through refinancing and home equity loans, ultimately accruing over eighty-three thousand dollars in unpaid interest over a timeline spanning from October 2006 to February 2010. Below this table, a horizontal bar chart illustrates foreclosure timelines in days, showing that judicial states like New York, Florida, and Illinois take over seven hundred days to complete a foreclosure, while non-judicial states like California, Nevada, and Michigan take more than six hundred days. A supporting footnote highlights that borrowers in foreclosure have, on average, gone four hundred ten days without making a payment.

Cembalest warns that current proposals allowing individual states to enforce their own foreclosure rules inject local politics into the financial system, arguing instead for clear national rules set at the federal level, akin to the Pecora Commission of the 1930s. He references a warning from the head of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency that some reforms overly prioritize consumer protection at the expense of bank stability. 

The page also lists J.P. Morgan's active investment themes, which include middle-market private lending, bank roll-up strategies involving FDIC dispositions, local-currency emerging markets bonds, merger arbitrage, and companies targeting Asian consumers.

In the final section, Cembalest reviews the passage of the landmark healthcare reform bill. He notes that the bill moves the United States into alignment with thirty-two other developed nations that provide universal healthcare. While the bill expands coverage by applying highly progressive Medicare tax increases to joint filers earning over two hundred fifty thousand dollars, the author expresses concern that the bill fails to control healthcare cost growth. Although the Congressional Budget Office projects the bill to be deficit-neutral, Cembalest warns that historically underestimated entitlement costs could destabilize the broader federal debt outlook. He concludes by presenting the counter-argument from the bill's supporters, who claim that the economic benefits of insuring the uninsured—including reduced mortality and fewer bankruptcies—will double the overall cost of the program.

This analysis assesses whether government debt risks will derail the economic expansion, focusing on global demand for U.S. Treasuries and the shifting mechanics of U.S. debt issuance. The author notes that despite concerns, Treasury demand remains strong. To measure this, the page compares two datasets. The first chart, showing non-U.S. demand for Treasuries via Federal Reserve custody holdings from March 2000 to March 2010, illustrates a steady rise in holdings from approximately 700 billion dollars to over 2.4 trillion dollars. The second chart details Chinese Treasury and Agency purchases using Treasury International Capital data, which rose from near zero in 2000 to about 1.3 trillion dollars by late 2009. The author suggests China’s true ownership may be even higher, approaching 1 trillion dollars, because the State Administration of Foreign Exchange likely places orders through United Kingdom intermediaries, where holdings surged from 130 billion dollars in 2008 to 300 billion dollars in 2009.

The publication warns against misinterpreting the low yields of 2009 as a sign of long-term stability in the Treasury market, arguing that two key tailwinds are fading. The first tailwind was the Treasury's initial reliance on short-term T-bills rather than long-term debt. A chart of net U.S. Treasury issuance, plotted as an annualized 26-week average from 2000 to 2010, shows that while total net issuance spiked to nearly 2.5 trillion dollars in late 2008, issuance of paper with maturities over one year and over five years did not catch up in bulk until late 2009. This transition is critical because, as shown in another chart comparing the average maturity of federal debt across various OECD nations, the United States has one of the shortest average maturities at roughly four years, whereas countries like Greece, Austria, and the United Kingdom have much longer debt profiles, with the United Kingdom exceeding 13 years. The author predicts that the Treasury will have to issue a large volume of longer-dated paper to push the U.S. average maturity back to five or six years.

The second fading tailwind is the massive intervention by the Federal Reserve. In 2009, net issuance of fixed income across Treasury, municipal, housing, asset-backed, and corporate entities totaled 1.75 trillion dollars, while Federal Reserve purchases of Treasuries and Agencies reached 1.6 trillion dollars. This means the central bank effectively absorbed 90 percent of all net dollar-denominated fixed income issuance. The author concludes that these supportive conditions will not persist into 2010 and 2011, and that upcoming longer-tenor Treasury issuance, coupled with the withdrawal of Federal Reserve support, means the market is only beginning to face the real challenge of absorbing massive government debt supply.

Michael Cembalest discusses the significance of ten-year interest rate swap spreads turning negative against U.S. Treasuries for the first time, exploring whether this development signals a fundamental government debt risk or merely technical market noise. He details the scale of this fourteen trillion dollar interest rate swap market before laying out several technical explanations. These arguments suggest the negative spread is just noise, driven by corporate demands to swap fixed exposure to floating to lower interest expenses, pension funds and cash-strapped endowments using swaps to add duration, reduced mortgage hedging due to lost convexity, and hedge funds covering failed short-spread positions that they used to bet on higher rates with positive carry. On the other hand, a more bearish interpretation suggests that a massive supply of U.S. Treasuries is overwhelming demand, a concern highlighted by the fact that high-quality corporate bonds from Procter and Gamble, Johnson and Johnson, and Lowe's have recently traded tighter than Treasuries.

An accompanying line chart, titled "10 year swap spreads have turned negative," plots the ten-year swap spread in basis points from 1989 to early 2010 using data from the U.S. Treasury and Bloomberg. The chart shows that while these spreads typically fluctuated between forty and one hundred basis points—peaking near one hundred and forty basis points around 2000—they collapsed precipitously after 2008, dropping below zero into negative territory by 2010. 

Cembalest leans toward a technical explanation rather than a fundamental systemic collapse. Nevertheless, he warns that while rising long-term rates can reflect a healthy economic recovery, the combination of massive U.S. budget deficits, changing supply-demand dynamics, and the tense economic relationship between the United States and China could cause major problems if ten-year Treasury rates climb significantly above five percent. He concludes by noting that J.P. Morgan Private Banking is maintaining short fixed-income durations and holding cash reserves. Lastly, a yellow summary box highlights several ongoing J.P. Morgan investment themes from early 2010, including middle-market private lending, bank roll-up strategies, emerging markets bonds, merger arbitrage, natural gas stocks, a normal weighting to U.S. equities, and investments targeting the Asian consumer.

This page of the publication covers two main topics: a strengthening global market outlook and the dynamics of private lending within the credit space. The author begins by highlighting positive global manufacturing data, noting that the J.P. Morgan Global Purchasing Manager Survey has reached a cyclical high, accompanied by a 26 percent rise in Brazilian vehicle sales and a 23 percent rise in Korean semiconductor sales. In the United States, the Supplier Delivery Index is highly elevated, historically indicating the early stages of economic expansion. An accompanying line chart titled "Supplier deliveries: a bullish indicator" plots this seasonally adjusted index from 1980 to early 2010. It shows the index historically fluctuating between 35 and 65, with recent levels rising sharply toward 60, nearing previous cyclical peaks marked by a horizontal red dashed line at approximately 64.

The discussion then shifts to corporate profits, supported by two line charts plotting data from 1988 to late 2009 in billions of dollars at a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR). The first, "U.S. fin. corporate profits," shows financial sector profits surging back to near 400 billion dollars, close to their 2006 peak of 450 billion dollars after a severe crisis-era dip. The second, "U.S. non-fin. corporate profits," displays non-financial profits recovering toward the 750 billion dollar level after falling from a 2006 high near 900 billion dollars. The author points out that because this Bureau of Economic Analysis data excludes loan write-offs, it provides a cleaner operational view, revealing that a steep yield curve has driven financial sector profits back near historical highs.

Despite these positive indicators, the author expresses concern over fiscal deficits, drawing historical parallels to the United States in 1937 and Japan in 1997 when deficits led to tax hikes and subsequent equity declines. Rising long-term interest rates are also a worry, with 10-year Treasuries approaching 4 percent. These pressures, along with potential shifts in emerging market reserve accumulation policies, pose risks of a short-lived recovery. Consequently, J.P. Morgan's portfolios maintain normal overall risk levels but with defensive adjustments, including more hedge funds, fewer directional equities, a preference for U.S. large-cap stocks, and shorter fixed-income durations. 

The second half of the page addresses private lending opportunities. Although credit markets have improved, mid-sized companies face tighter underwriting standards, with credit availability dropping from 5.5 times cash flow pre-crisis to about 3.0 times today. This financing gap creates private lending opportunities yielding 10 percent to 14 percent cash coupons, with lenders targeting an additional 5 percent to 7 percent from equity warrants. However, the author cautions that achieving yields near 12 percent requires lending to highly risky, CCC-rated issuers in structural decline, such as print media, telephone directories, check printing, and analog switching, or high-fixed-cost commodity producers like airlines. Investors looking for these high returns must accept risks comparable to those found in economically distressed nations like Venezuela and Ecuador, or distressed 2007-vintage subprime debt.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication analyses global credit markets and commercial real estate trends. The main argument regarding credit is that markets have tightened substantially following three hundred and eighty billion dollars of inflows into fixed-income mutual funds in 2009, which represented a twenty-five percent increase in industry assets under management. While the author does not anticipate significant credit spread widening due to strong fundamental and technical factors, J.P. Morgan is slowing its investments in more expensive credit segments and exiting others. Instead, the firm views private lending as an attractive alternative with a better risk-reward profile than many of the higher-yielding credits.

To illustrate the current credit constellation, the page features a scatter plot titled Global Fixed Income Monitor (US Dollars). The chart plots pre-tax yield on the vertical axis, ranging from zero to thirteen percent, against maturity in years on the horizontal axis, spanning one to fourteen years. The data is color-coded by asset class, including high yield bonds, leveraged loans, sovereign debt, trust preferreds, asset-backed securities, and municipals. High-yield credits yield the most, with names like JPM CCC HY Index, Venezuela, Hexion, Dynegy, and MGM Mirage clustered between ten and thirteen percent. Other entities such as Ford, GMAC, and Sallie Mae sit at much lower yields under five percent with maturities under three years. Sovereign issues like South Africa, Pakistan, and Ukraine, alongside municipal bonds like the Sacramento Revenue, Massachusetts General Obligation, and New York MTA pre-refunded bonds, are also mapped across various maturities, showing how municipal and government-backed debt clusters in the lower yield ranges below six percent. 

The text outlines these yield tranches in detail. In the eight to nine percent range, investors can find the J.P. Morgan High Yield Index, Pakistan, Ukraine, highly leveraged casinos, retailers, and an Iraq bond maturing in 2028 that yields around eight percent. The six to eight percent tier holds cheaper leveraged loans, AAA-rated commercial mortgage-backed securities, BB and B-rated high-yield bonds, long-dated bank trust preferreds, and certain municipal bonds. Below six percent lies the safer investment-grade universe, including Build America Bonds, sovereign debt from the Dominican Republic, South Africa, Turkey, and Indonesia, alongside U.S. Treasuries and agencies.

The bottom portion of the page transitions to commercial real estate, specifically examining sublet space and property debt. The author notes that supply-demand imbalances in the supply-constrained New York City market are stabilizing. Although sublet space remains elevated, it represents a lower percentage of total vacant space than during the prior recession and is currently shrinking. This trend is bolstered by the relatively mild decline in New York City private sector payrolls during this crisis, which fell by one hundred and fifty-seven thousand compared to a loss of two hundred and twenty-six thousand in the 2001 to 2002 recession. Ultimately, while highly leveraged property owners with aggressive rental growth projections have suffered, owners with moderate leverage and low-cost debt are successfully weathering property value declines.

This publication by Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Private Banking, covers two primary topics: the sovereign debt crisis in Greece and the growth of the Chinese consumer market. 

Addressing Greece, the author argues that historical precedents of large fiscal adjustments in post-war Europe were almost always accompanied by substantial currency devaluations, typically ranging from 30% to 50%, to soften the economic blow. Without currency devaluation, wages and prices must bear the brunt of the adjustment, which is deflationary and socially destabilizing. The author compares Greece trying to achieve fiscal adjustment within the Eurozone without devaluation to the fairy tale of Rumpelstiltskin spinning gold from straw, accompanied by an illustration of Rumpelstiltskin from Andrew Lang's 1889 Blue Fairy Book. A column chart titled "Currency devaluations during fiscal adjustments" shows the percentage of currency depreciation against the USD for past European fiscal adjustments, listing countries and time periods such as Italy, Denmark, Ireland, Spain, Belgium, Greece, the United Kingdom, Finland, Sweden, Austria, and France, with depreciations clustered between 30% and 50%, and Portugal reaching 80%. Additionally, the author notes that if private lenders view government and IMF bailout loans merely as a way to exit their exposure, the Greek crisis will reemerge the following year. 

The second section focuses on targeting the Chinese consumer. While the capital-intensive nature of China’s growth has caused household consumption as a percentage of GDP to decline, the absolute level of consumption is rising rapidly. This trend is illustrated in a dual-axis chart titled "Household consumption and retail sales per capita" from 1993 to 2008. The chart shows household consumption as a share of GDP (measured on the left axis) peaking near 47% in 1999–2001 before dropping to roughly 36% by 2008. Meanwhile, Chinese retail sales per capita in Yuan (measured on the right axis) rise steadily from around 100 Yuan in 1993 to over 700 Yuan by 2008. The author highlights projections indicating that by 2016, the size of both the Chinese and U.S. middle classes will reach parity at approximately 300 million people. Consequently, J.P. Morgan’s investment strategy focuses on growth equity in private companies expanding their retail presence in the region. Lastly, the author notes that rising inflation in China could prompt policy makers to allow a faster appreciation of the Renminbi, which would further accelerate household wealth and consumption growth. However, the author characterizes the currently priced-in 3% annual Renminbi appreciation as insignificant given that the currency remains undervalued by 25% or more according to estimates from the Peterson Institute.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest analyzes the severe economic adjustments facing southern European nations, specifically Spain and Greece, in the aftermath of the financial crisis. Spain is enduring a grueling seven-quarter recession with 20% unemployment following a collapse in its private construction sector, which at one point accounted for 45% of all construction activity in Europe. Meanwhile, Greece faces the second toughest fiscal adjustment in modern European history, made far more difficult because it cannot devalue its currency or rely on high GDP growth. Cembalest argues that the European Monetary Union’s structural flaws—combining disparate levels of productivity and wages without robust regional fiscal transfers—create intense deflationary pressures. He notes that Germany has increasingly resisted a more federalist European Union, leaving austerity as the primary tool, which he compares to medieval medical practices like bloodletting or "economic anorexia." 

To illustrate how currency devaluation historically assisted in economic recoveries, the page includes a line chart titled "Swedish krona decline was a critical component of the 1990s recovery." Plotting the dollar value per Swedish krona from 1990 to 1995, the chart shows the currency peaking near $0.19 in late 1992 before experiencing a sharp depreciation down to roughly $0.12 by late 1993, which helped catalyze Sweden's recovery. 

A second visual, a scatter plot titled "Can Greece pull off one of the largest adjustments in recent European history?", compares historical European fiscal adjustments against real GDP growth during those periods. The vertical axis measures real GDP growth from 0.0% to 4.0%, while the horizontal axis tracks the annual fiscal adjustment from 0.0% to 3.0%. Successful historical adjustments, such as Denmark's from 1982 to 1986 and Finland's from 1993 to 2000, achieved high annual fiscal adjustments of over 2.0% while maintaining robust GDP growth above 3.0%. In contrast, Greece's projected trajectory for 2010 to 2014—using its announced austerity plan and IMF growth estimates—is highlighted as an outlier at the bottom right. It requires an aggressive annual fiscal adjustment of approximately 2.6% while suffering from depressed real GDP growth of well under 1.0%.

The page ends on a lighter, personal note accompanied by a photograph from a fishing trip in Boca Paila, Quintana Roo, Mexico, showing a group holding a freshly caught barracuda.

This page from the publication addresses commercial real estate allocations, the cyclical nature of Japanese equities, and the potential pitfalls of European fiscal austerity. It opens with a brief update on commercial property, noting that lower rental growth, higher vacancies, and higher cap rates are bringing allocations back to normal after J.P. Morgan reduced them in mid-2007. This is accompanied by a bar chart showing Midtown NYC sublet availability as a percentage of total office vacancy from 1995 to 2009. The data shows sublet availability peaking in 2001 at over 40% and rising again in 2009 to nearly 30% from a low of around 20% in 2007.

The commentary then shifts to a detailed critique of Japanese equities, termed the "Pete Townshend strategy" in reference to the lyric "we won’t get fooled again." While Japan is showing short-term signs of economic life—such as JP Morgan Securities upwardly revising its Q1 GDP forecast from 1.8% to 3.5%, strong earnings momentum, and consecutive monthly gains in industrial production—the author remains skeptical of long-term investments. A line graph titled "Japanese exports linked to Asian rebound" plots export demand by country from January 2007 to January 2010 as a percentage of their pre-crisis peaks. The chart reveals that while exports to Korea and China have rebounded significantly to nearly 90% and 100% of pre-crisis levels respectively, demand from the U.S., EU, and U.K. remains depressed, hovering between 40% and 60%. 

Furthermore, structural problems like demographic decline, deflation, and poor corporate governance persist, and local households hold only 6% to 8% of their net worth in equities. Consequently, domestic stock performance relies heavily on foreign demand, which eventually rolls over when fundamental weakness reasserts itself. This pattern is demonstrated in the bar chart "Land of the frequently setting sun," which displays the quarterly Topix total return minus the S&P 500 total return from 1994 to 2010. The chart illustrates persistent, deep periods of Japanese underperformance relative to the U.S. This leads the author to recommend short-term, liquid, non-Yen-exposed positions over long-term allocations.

The final section, "Europe and economic anorexia," expresses concern over the austerity measures being adopted across Europe. While Ireland has successfully enacted a 7.5% fiscal tightening over five years—including cutting public sector wages by 5% to 8%—the author worries that requiring European nations to absorb all adjustments domestically without the help of a weaker currency is dangerous. To highlight this, the text cites the Scandinavian banking crisis of the early 1990s, when Sweden's recovery was heavily aided by a 30% to 40% devaluation of the Swedish Krona against both the U.S. dollar and the Deutsche Mark. Under the current structure of the European Monetary Union, countries like Greece, Spain, and Portugal are forced to absorb these severe economic adjustments entirely through domestic price and wage declines, lacking the option of currency devaluation.

This page analyzes two distinct financial topics: the relative value of investing in collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) and the severe fiscal adjustments required of Greece within the Eurozone. 

In the first section, the author argues that the structured corporate loan market offers a highly compelling discount compared to buying individual credit. Specifically, acquiring senior-secured loans through the CLO market is about ten points cheaper than purchasing individual loans directly. This pricing discrepancy is equivalent to buying senior-secured loans at a spread of L+875 basis points, compared to the L+515 basis points average of the S&P/LSTA Performing Loan index. To illustrate this arbitrage opportunity, the page includes a line chart titled "CLOs still trading at a relative discount" that tracks prices as a percentage of par from April 2005 to March 2010 using Barclays Capital data. The chart compares leveraged loans with the CLO implied price. Both series remained near 100% of par until 2007, crashed during the financial crisis with the CLO implied price bottoming out near 55% in early 2009, and then staged a recovery. By March 2010, a significant gap remained, with leveraged loans trading at roughly 88% of par and CLO implied prices at approximately 78% of par. JP Morgan forecasts improving credit trends, predicting a 4% default rate for leveraged loans in 2010, down from peak levels of 15%, which makes CLOs an appealing vehicle for investing in the loan market despite lower liquidity and complexity.

The second section addresses the Greek debt crisis. The author points out that although EUR 45 billion in potential Eurozone and IMF loans could buy Greece time to cover maturities of EUR 30 billion in 2010 and EUR 43 billion in 2011, the nation must embark on one of the largest post-war European fiscal adjustments in history. Greece suffers from an overvalued currency dating back to its EMU entry, rapid household credit growth, and uncompetitive labor costs that are 15% to 20% out of line. The IMF is insisting on structural reforms, including greater hiring and firing flexibility, part-time work, wage caps, and utility privatization. 

These deep imbalances are captured in a line chart titled "Current account balance as % of GDP" spanning 1992 to 2010 based on OECD data. The chart tracks Germany, France, Italy, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, and Greece. It contrasts Germany’s rising current account surplus, which grew from a slight deficit in the early 1990s to over 5% of GDP by the mid-2000s, with the ballooning deficits of peripheral European nations. Greece displays the most severe trajectory, declining steadily from near 0% in 1992 to a massive deficit of nearly 15% of GDP around 2008, before recovering slightly to a deficit of over 10% in 2010. Spain and Portugal also show deep deficits peaking near 10% of GDP in the late 2000s, while France and Italy remained closer to balance.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market explores global macroeconomic risks, potential economic potholes for 2010, and the daunting prospects of Greece's proposed fiscal adjustment within the Eurozone. 

To set the stage, the author presents two top charts. The first shows the OECD Broad Leading Indicator from 1980 to 2008, highlighting a sharp cyclical decline toward the index level of 90 by late 2008. The second chart details select emerging market inflation indicators—specifically the three-month annualized rates for China CPI, Brazil CPI, and India WPI from May 2005 to November 2009—revealing significant inflation pressures, particularly a sharp spike in India's WPI and Brazil's CPI toward the end of the timeframe. 

These inflationary trends underpin the author's discussion of 2010 "potential potholes." Chief among these is Asian inflation and subsequent monetary tightening, highlighted by China's aggressive actions to cool its property market, including higher home down-payment requirements, new property taxes, home purchase restrictions, and regulator pressure on banks to reduce non-collateralized lending to local governments. Other listed risks include the maturity profile of US Treasury debt, fading inventory and stimulus contributions to growth, and the expiration of federal aid to US states and Greece. To navigate these challenges, J.P. Morgan highlights several active investment strategies, such as middle-market private lending, bank roll-up opportunities, local-currency emerging market bonds, merger arbitrage, and leveraged loans.

The core of the commentary focuses on the European sovereign debt crisis, arguing that while a Eurozone-IMF package provides temporary breathing room, Greece's proposed fiscal belt-tightening is uniquely difficult. The author warns that "austerity by itself has a poor track record" and point to rising Greek bond yields as a sign that the market anticipates a debt rescheduling. In a footnote, the author reflects on how Greece might handle a debt swap, recalling Argentina's controversial strategy of utilizing sympathetic local bondholders to strip foreign investors of their rights as a warning of what might happen. 

This skepticism is visualized in two final charts. The first asks whether Greece can achieve one of the largest fiscal adjustments in recent European history by plotting real GDP growth against annual fiscal adjustments. It highlights that Greece's projected 2010–2014 path, which demands an annual fiscal adjustment of roughly 2.5% amid nearly flat GDP growth, is an extreme outlier compared to historical adjustments made by Denmark, Sweden, Finland, and Ireland, which typically enjoyed higher growth. The final chart, showing currency devaluations during fiscal adjustments, underscores that previous European adjustments were accompanied by significant currency depreciations against the USD—such as Ireland's 80% depreciation from 1980 to 1985, and Spain's depreciation of over 50% from 1981 to 1985. Because Greece is in the Eurozone, it cannot devalue its currency, making its planned adjustment unprecedentedly difficult.

In this commentary, the author provides a macroeconomic market outlook alongside an analysis of a rising global merger wave. Looking at global risk, the author addresses the headlines surrounding EUR 40-45 billion in Eurozone and IMF loans to Greece. While the author characterizes Greece as a potential time bomb for markets in about a year, the immediate crisis has been deferred by Germany, France, and the IMF. Furthermore, the combined GDP of Spain, Portugal, Ireland, and Greece, which totals 2.3 trillion dollars, is dwarfed by the combined 23 trillion dollar GDP of the United States and China. Global economic momentum is heavily dominated by these two giants, where a broad recovery is successfully transitioning from manufacturing to services. The author notes that a robust recovery is essential to generate government tax revenues; otherwise, significant tax hikes—such as Paul Volcker’s suggested VAT tax or steep marginal tax rates in New York City reaching 49.5 percent to 51 percent—will follow. 

Supporting this positive economic outlook are two visual charts. The first, titled Global manufacturing and services activity, displays seasonally adjusted indices from 2000 to 2010. It shows both manufacturing and services indices plunging to extreme lows during the 2008 financial crisis before sharply rebounding above the critical expansion threshold of 50 by 2010. The second chart, CEO optimism continues to increase, tracks index data from December 2002 to November 2009 across CEO Sales Outlook, CEO Capex Outlook, and CEO Employment Outlook. All three measures show a severe, coordinated drop during the recession followed by a sharp V-shaped recovery by late 2009, signaling that business sentiment is returning to levels consistent with prior expansions. This global health is further reflected in OECD home prices rising in over 70 percent of member countries, and private equity managers holding half a trillion dollars in uncalled capital. Consequently, J.P. Morgan maintains larger holdings in U.S. equities than European equities, has purged Greek bonds from its bond funds, and maintains a portfolio comprising roughly 40 percent equities and 20 percent hedge funds.

The second half of the page details why the global merger wave is picking up steam, pointing to recent transactions such as Reliant Energy/Mirant, Sinopec/Syncrude, and Cerberus/DynCorp. To illustrate the underlying driver of this M&A activity, the chart titled Corporate cash balances at their highest levels plots nonfinancial corporate liquid assets as a percentage of tangible assets from 1951 to 2009. The ratio hit a historic low of under 4 percent in 1980 but steadily climbed over the next three decades, spiking dramatically in 2009 to reach an all-time high of approximately 14.5 percent. This cash abundance has driven increased allocations to event-driven mutual funds, M&A targets, and restructuring credit. This tactical shift is shown in the final chart, Representative event driven hedge fund strategy, which plots portfolio allocations from 2005 to 2010 among credit strategies, special situations, and merger strategies. The chart reveals that managers heavily rotated into credit strategies and away from merger strategies during the market collapse of late 2008. By 2010, however, managers are taking profits on those credit holdings and rebuilding their allocations back into merger arbitrage strategies to capture the new wave of corporate activity.

This page of the publication explores the structural vulnerabilities of the European Monetary Union by comparing its current challenges to the historical development of the United States as a successful monetary union. The author argues that for monetary unions to function properly, they require four essential pillars: capital mobility, a lender of last resort, labor flexibility, and substantial regional transfers to smooth out economic imbalances. While Europe has established capital mobility and a lender of last resort, it significantly lacks labor flexibility and regional transfer mechanisms, threatening its long-term stability in the wake of the Greek debt crisis.

To address labor flexibility, the page contrasts historical wage convergence in the United States with diverging labor competitiveness in Europe. A chart showing real effective exchange rates based on labor costs, indexed to January 2000, tracks various European nations from 2000 to 2010. This visual highlights a widening competitiveness gap: Germany's relative labor cost index steadily declined to around 82, indicating increased competitiveness, while peripheral nations like Ireland, Italy, Portugal, Spain, and Greece saw their indexes climb well above 100, peaking near 110 to 120. In contrast, a historical chart tracking Midwest real wages relative to the Northeast from 1820 to 1920 illustrates how US regional labor markets converged over time, with Midwest wages declining from a high of nearly 135 percent of Northeast wages down to around 105 to 110 percent by the early 1900s.

The author identifies regional fiscal transfers as the weakest link within the European Monetary Union, highlighting the intense German domestic debate over the bailout of Greece. In contrast, the United States relies heavily on federal transfers to stabilize regional downturns, as shown by three charts detailing net private sector receipts versus Treasury transfers from 1929 to 1938. In Minneapolis, representing a depressed agricultural region during the Great Depression, net private sector receipts fell deep into negative territory, dropping to around negative 300 million dollars, which was mitigated by positive federal Treasury transfers that peaked above 200 million dollars. Meanwhile, economically stronger regions like New York and Boston saw positive private sector receipts—with New York peaking above 1 billion dollars—which were offset by substantial negative Treasury transfers of corresponding magnitudes, demonstrating an active, balancing redistribution of wealth.

In conclusion, the author emphasizes that the United States only resolved its own historic regional and monetary disputes after establishing federally funded transfer programs and integrated labor markets. Footnotes highlight that historical US tensions included political battles over national bank charters, the gold standard, and even secession threats. By contrast, the European Monetary Union currently lacks a comparable system of fiscal transfers, leaving peripheral countries like Greece, Ireland, and Belgium highly dependent on the European Central Bank as a lender of last resort to support their banking systems and finance sovereign deficits.

This J.P. Morgan publication focuses on the economic recovery in the United States, presenting a positive outlook characterized by manufacturing strength, robust technology spending, and rising corporate earnings. The author notes that J.P. Morgan portfolios are heavily tilted toward U.S. large- and mid-cap equities, credit-oriented hedge funds, emerging market currencies, and select corporate credit, while remaining underweight on European assets, long-duration bonds, buyouts, and the U.S. housing sector. 

To support the narrative of a strong U.S. manufacturing rebound, the page features a chart showing ISM manufacturing activity versus customers' inventories from April 2007 to April 2010. The ISM manufacturing index shows a sharp V-shaped recovery, rising from a low of about 33 in late 2008 to near 60 by April 2010. Meanwhile, the index for customers' inventories remains low, hovering under 40, which suggests lean supply chains and the potential for future production and employment gains. Alongside this, a chart on information processing equipment and software spending, measured in billions of chained 2005 dollars from March 2007 to late 2009, highlights a strong tech replacement cycle. This spending series bottomed at $540 billion in early 2009 before surging past its previous peak to exceed $610 billion by the end of the year.

The publication also discusses U.S. corporate profits, noting that earnings and revenues have broadly exceeded expectations. A bar chart illustrating positive earnings and sales surprises by sector shows that across the S&P 500, over 80% of reporting companies beat their earnings-per-share estimates and roughly 70% beat sales estimates. The information technology sector led these surprises, with nearly 90% of companies beating earnings estimates and over 80% beating sales. This widespread outperformance has prompted analysts to revise their corporate outlooks upward. 

A final dual-axis chart tracks these rising forward S&P 500 earnings estimates from January to May 2010. The blue line representing 2010 estimates, plotted on the left axis, rose from $78 per share to over $80 per share. Concurrently, the brown line representing 2011 estimates, plotted on the right axis, climbed from $94 per share to approximately $100 per share. The author notes that these revised expectations place U.S. equities at a reasonable 14.5 P/E multiple given low inflation, though they curb their enthusiasm due to the unknown future impact of monetary and fiscal stimulus withdrawal. The page concludes with a brief note postponing further discussion of housing indicators, Fannie Mae, and mortgage debt to a later date.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s financial commentary critiques the planned Eurozone-IMF austerity program for Greece, comparing the severity of the measures to the myth of Prometheus. The author argues that Greece is embarking on the most austere fiscal adjustment seen in an OECD country in 50 years, made exceptionally difficult because it lacks the typical relief valves of a devaluing currency, robust GDP growth, or a highly open economy. 

To illustrate this, a three-dimensional scatter plot titled "2010 Greece Fiscal Adjustment: No Man's Land" maps historical national adjustments across four distinct dimensions. The vertical axis measures the average annual fiscal adjustment as a percentage of GDP; the diagonal left-to-right axis tracks GDP growth; the diagonal right-to-left axis plots currency devaluation; and the color of the data points represents the size of the tradables sector as a percentage of GDP, with red representing under 45%, yellow between 45% and 75%, and blue over 75%. Greece’s projected 2010–2014 adjustment is highlighted as a red sphere at the extreme top-left of the chart, signifying a massive annual fiscal adjustment of approximately 2.5% with 0% GDP growth, 0% devaluation, and a relatively closed economy. This positioning isolates Greece in "No Man’s Land" compared to historical precedents. For instance, Greece’s previous 1989–1994 adjustment (represented by a blue sphere) was aided by a 50% devaluation of the Drachma. Other historical comparison points mapped on the chart include Denmark from 1982 to 1986, Sweden, Finland, Belgium, Ireland, Portugal, Italy, the United Kingdom, Australia, Spain, France, and the Netherlands, almost all of which relied on devaluation, positive GDP growth, or highly open economies to absorb fiscal consolidation.

The commentary presents several pessimistic observations regarding the €110 billion bailout package. First, the author asserts that Greece’s plan to absorb the fiscal adjustment purely through internal devaluation—specifically 15% to 20% declines in wages and prices—is untested and implausible. While structural changes to retirement ages and privatization are logical, they are unlikely to improve competitiveness in the short run. The author points out that during the Great Depression, countries that abandoned gold as a monetary anchor to regain control of their monetary policy recovered much faster, citing historical examples like the United Kingdom’s 20% devaluation in 1931 and the U.S. dollar’s 30% decline from 1985 to 1995. Additionally, a footnote warns that the targeted 0% GDP growth for Greece might be overly optimistic, pointing to Latvia’s recent 20% GDP contraction and doubling of unemployment in the absence of a currency adjustment. Finally, the author poses open questions about whether this bailout will successfully shield other peripheral European nations like Ireland, Spain, and Portugal. While these nations have lower public debt burdens than Greece, they suffer from similar productivity gaps relative to core Europe and face heavy corporate debt burdens.

This page outlines J.P. Morgan's core portfolio positions, which remain unchanged from previous months. Recommended allocations include underweighting European equities overall while favoring mid-cap German exporters over the rest of the region, and shorting the Euro against long positions in Asian currencies. In fixed income portfolios, the firm advises holding little to no exposure to Portugal, Greece, Ireland, and Spain. Total equity weights are targeted at 35% to 40% with a significant overweight in US large-cap equities and downside protection on European equities, underpinned by a projected S&P 500 target of 1175 to 1225 for the year. Additionally, the strategy calls for gradually reducing credit investments made in 2009, maintaining gold positions with plans to hedge against falling prices starting at $1,250 to $1,300, and target oil at $90. Investors are also advised to shift into merger arbitrage hedge funds as cash-rich corporations face extended periods of near-zero interest rates from a paused Federal Reserve and European Central Bank.

Below the portfolio update, a client quiz section features a colorful classic illustration from the German fairy tale "Die Geschichte vom fliegenden Robert" (The Story of Flying Robert) from Heinrich Hoffman’s Struwwelpeter, depicting a boy being swept into the sky by a heavy wind while holding a red umbrella over a countryside landscape with a church. 

The page concludes with a personal inquiry from Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest, who requests first- or second-hand insights from readers regarding pediatric scoliosis surgery. A brief notes section at the bottom provides details on accessing a conference call replay and lists economic acronym definitions.

This publication, authored by Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Private Banking, argues that investors should not rely solely on rising corporate profits when making equity portfolio allocations. The author notes that historical market corrections often take place while corporate earnings are still rising. To illustrate this point, the page displays three historical charts of the S&P 500 twelve-month trailing earnings per share (EPS). The first chart shows that before the Savings and Loan collapse, EPS steadily rose from around $17 in late 1987 to nearly $27 in late 1989. The second chart shows that prior to the tech collapse, EPS rose consistently from $25 in 1994 to nearly $60 in 2000. Similarly, the third chart shows that before the 2007-2008 credit crisis, EPS climbed from $45 in 2002 to over $90 by late 2006.

Turning to the economic climate of mid-2010, the author observes a positive U.S. payroll report, strong productivity, and high profit margins.
