A global manufacturing boom is also evident, highlighted by a 5% rise in German factory orders in March and a 4% increase in German industrial production, alongside improving manufacturing surveys in Spain, Ireland, and Italy. To depict this economic recovery, a line chart of the seasonally adjusted J.P. Morgan Global PMI output index from 2000 to 2010 tracks both manufacturing and services. The index reveals that while both sectors collapsed below the neutral 50-level threshold during the 2008 recession—with manufacturing dropping near 30 and services falling to around 38—both have rebounded strongly above 55 by 2010.

Despite this cyclical recovery, the author warns that structural problems in the public sector limit these improvements, making many sell-side forecasts for 2010 equity market returns too optimistic. A bar chart comparing 2010 S&P 500 year-end projections across major financial institutions demonstrates that J.P. Morgan Private Banking’s forecast of 1,175 to 1,225 is among the most conservative. This projection sits alongside Citi at 1,175, Morgan Stanley at 1,200, Barclays at 1,210, and higher estimates from Goldman Sachs at 1,250, Credit Suisse at 1,270, and Bank of America at 1,300, leading up to Deutsche Bank’s peak target of 1,375. 

Cembalest projects moderate 2010 U.S. equity returns of +7% to +9% with high volatility. Because of these structural headwinds, J.P. Morgan Private Banking maintains a relatively defensive position, recommending limited equity allocations of 35% to 40% in balanced portfolios, with downside protection on large positions. The remainder of the portfolio is directed toward commodities, credit, and low-exposure hedge funds to guard against potential market shocks.

In this appendix update focusing on the spread of the European contagion, the author argues that relying solely on austerity is a highly difficult and historically unproven path for Greece. Highlighting market skepticism, the text notes that prices for March 2012 Greek government bonds are falling, even though they mature within the Eurozone-IMF rescue window, because investors do not believe Greece will deliver on its austerity promises. The author asserts that achieving these targets under current conditions would be a miracle, using historical precedents to back up this claim.

The core visual of the page is a three-dimensional bubble chart titled 2010 Greece Fiscal Adjustment: No Man's Land. The chart plots historical fiscal consolidation episodes across four distinct dimensions. The vertical axis measures the average annual fiscal adjustment as a percentage of GDP, ranging from 0.5 percent to 2.5 percent. The depth axis on the bottom-left tracks GDP growth during the adjustment period, from 0 percent to 3 percent. The horizontal axis on the bottom-right measures currency devaluation, ranging from 20 percent to 100 percent. Finally, the bubble colors represent the size of the country's tradables sector relative to GDP at the start of the period, with red indicating less than 45 percent, yellow between 45 percent and 75 percent, and blue greater than 75 percent.

The chart dramatically highlights the unique position of Greece's projected 2010 to 2014 adjustment path. Represented by a red bubble at the top left, Greece is isolated in No Man's Land with an extremely high annual fiscal adjustment target of 2.5 percent, zero currency devaluation, nearly zero GDP growth, and a small tradables sector of under 45 percent. 

To demonstrate why this combination is historically unprecedented, the chart maps several other international adjustment episodes. It shows that countries achieving high annual fiscal adjustments of 1.5 percent to 2.5 percent either utilized significant currency devaluation or benefited from solid economic growth. For instance, Denmark (1982-1986) achieved a high fiscal adjustment of over 2 percent per year with a moderate devaluation and solid GDP growth, while Sweden (1993-1998) combined an adjustment of nearly 2 percent with solid growth and devaluation. In this version of the chart, the author added 1980s Latin American crises to strengthen the conclusion; Mexico (1981-1988) and Brazil (1982-1990) achieved high annual fiscal adjustments with small tradable sectors, but relied on massive currency devaluations of roughly 80 percent to 100 percent. Other comparative historical episodes plotted on the chart include past adjustments in Belgium, Portugal, Finland, Ireland, the United Kingdom, Italy, Australia, Spain, France, and the Netherlands, almost all of which enjoyed far better growth, currency devaluation cushions, or larger export sectors than Greece.

This page, titled "Leaner Pastures," discusses the global market and portfolio outlook in light of the inevitable consequences of the massive stimulus programs initiated in 2009. Michael Cembalest notes that global equities are down five percent year-to-date, validating his firm's cautious 2010 outlook, which warned that the recovery's heavy reliance on government support would soon exact a heavy toll. To illustrate these risks, the page features a diagram of an ox with several sections highlighted in red, representing specific stimulus measures that are now weighing heavily on global markets.

The author details four key areas of concern. First, China's massive 2009 stimulus, measured by money supply and bank lending, has forced aggressive policy tightening in 2010. Even with newly instituted loan quotas and mortgage down-payment hikes, M2 growth is on track to exceed twenty percent, and China's national property price index rose twelve point eight percent in April, contributing to a volatile boom-bust cycle in Asian equity markets. Second, the relaxation of European Central Bank collateral rules sparked concerns about a sovereign domino effect, particularly regarding a potential failure in Greece. European banks are three to four times larger relative to GDP than their U.S. counterparts and hold six to eight times more of their own sovereign debt, creating a fragile web that the International Monetary Fund and European taxpayers are only beginning to dismantle.

Third, record peacetime deficits in the United States are prompting expectations of post-midterm election tax hikes, especially given that entitlement spending is projected to make up seventy percent of government expenditures by 2015. This threat of higher taxes on multinationals, carbon, or value-added taxes is depressing price-to-earnings multiples. A parallel debate in the United Kingdom could see capital gains tax rates surge from eighteen percent to between forty and fifty percent. Fourth, while government guarantees temporarily stabilized credit markets in the U.S., UK, and Europe, they brought severe regulatory consequences. An accompanying sidebar list titled Strings Attached details these burdens, which include too-big-to-fail taxes, derivatives restrictions, credit card interest caps, limits on proprietary trading, and higher capital ratios. Cembalest reports that these cumulative provisions could shrink pre-provision bank earnings by twenty to thirty percent. He concludes that these consequences are the natural by-products of the previous year's stimulus machine, which prepared investment managers should have anticipated.

This page analyzes the deep political and economic tensions within the Eurozone in the wake of the Greek bailout, focusing on the domestic political backlash in Germany and the economic hurdles of imposing strict austerity. The author highlights how the European Central Bank’s sudden reversal on its "no bail-out" clause has shocked German political figures and voters. This backlash is illustrated by a line chart showing the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) electoral results in North Rhine-Westphalia from 1947 to 2010. Popular support for Chancellor Angela Merkel’s CDU in Germany's largest state fell to a historic low of just over 30% in 2010, down from peaks above 50% in the late 1950s and 1970s. This voter anger reflects widespread concern that the bailout represents a breach of European Union treaty law and threatens long-term euro stability.

The author argues that Europe is embarking on a program of severe austerity, which historically has a very low success rate when not accompanied by currency devaluation. He cites the 2008 Latvian experience as a warning, where maintaining a currency peg under austerity caused unemployment to rise from 5% to 22% and GDP to plummet by 20%. 

While forward-looking manufacturing and service indicators show signs of recovery across most of Europe, Southern Europe remains deeply troubled. This divergence is depicted in the Euro Manufacturing PMI chart from December 2009 to April 2010, where Germany and France show robust recovery with indexes near 60 and 58, respectively, while Greece's manufacturing PMI plunges sharply to around 43. Similarly, the European GDP Recovery Index (benchmarked at 100 in Q4 2006) reveals that by late 2009, Germany and France had stabilized around 98, whereas Spain, Greece, and especially Ireland—which fell to approximately 92—were still suffering from contraction.

Although Germany is currently experiencing an export-led boom, the author warns that it is highly vulnerable to a downturn in the rest of Europe. A line chart tracking German trade exports from 2004 to 2009 shows exports peaking near 90 billion euros in 2008 before dropping to 60 billion euros in 2009. According to a pie chart of German export destinations, the Eurozone is by far Germany's largest customer, accounting for 43.3% of all exports, with another 24.4% going to non-Eurozone European nations. 

Finally, the page examines employment conditions using a bar chart of the Employment PMI Index by country, distinguishing between Eurozone and non-Eurozone countries. Non-Eurozone nations like the United States and Sweden lead global employment trends with index scores well above 50, while Eurozone nations consistently lag behind. At the very bottom of the global list are Greece, Spain, and Ireland, all with employment PMI indexes deeply in contraction territory below 45. The author concludes with an open warning that if competitiveness differences across member states are not addressed through fundamental structural reforms, maintaining the monetary union will require continuous, politically unpopular financial transfers in the future.

This page analyzes the European sovereign debt crisis, exploring whether the newly announced "Kitchen Sink" rescue package is large enough to stem contagion and assessing the potential financial burden on Germany. 

The author, writing alongside Dr. Jacob Frenkel, argues that sovereign debt cannot be evaluated in isolation from private sector debt because austerity-driven deflations inevitably transfer household and corporate liabilities to the government. This dynamic is illustrated in a stacked bar chart titled "Total country debt" as a percentage of GDP in Q4 2009. While Greece’s government debt is the highest among the selected nations at 114% of GDP (with 52% household and 69% non-financial corporate debt), Ireland, Portugal, and Spain exhibit significantly larger private debt burdens. Ireland's government debt of 64% is coupled with 122% household and 104% corporate debt; Portugal has 73% government, 98% household, and 142% corporate debt; and Spain has 54% government, 87% household, and 141% corporate debt. 

To address whether the rescue packages are sufficient, a column chart compares "Gross financing needs vs. approved and announced packages" in billions of Euros. It shows that the 860 billion Euros in approved and announced packages is sufficient to cover the 745 billion Euros in gross financing needs (maturities and deficits) for Greece, Ireland, Portugal, and Spain from 2010 to 2012. However, the package would not suffice if extended to 2013 (an additional 167 billion Euros) or if Italy’s massive 2010–2013 financing needs of 892 billion Euros are factored in, which would bring the total required financing to 1.805 trillion Euros. The author posits that Italy’s risks are lower due to its smaller primary deficit and domestic debt ownership, meaning the announced packages and ECB bond purchases should buy enough time for the other four nations to implement fiscal adjustments.

A key open question is whether the largest component of the bailout, the 440 billion Euro Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV), will be approved, given the substantial commitment required from stronger nations like Germany. A bar chart titled "Total potential German contributions" as a percent of GDP illustrates Germany's escalating exposure. Under its standard ECB capital weight share, Germany's commitment would be just under 6% of GDP. However, if non-EMU members do not participate, this rises to nearly 8%, and if the burden falls solely on Germany, France, and the Benelux countries, it could exceed 10%. To put this in perspective, the chart compares these potential liabilities to historical precedents: the annual cost of German Unification since 1991 (roughly 4% of GDP) and the peak Versailles reparations paid in 1929 (around 3.2% of GDP).

Finally, a summary table outlines the core initiatives of the rescue plan and their intended results. The fiscal measures include 440 billion Euros in government-backed loan guarantees from Eurozone countries, a 60 billion Euro EU Balance of Payments facility, and 220 to 250 billion Euros from the IMF, all aimed at allowing sovereigns to finance deficits at reasonable rates. The monetary initiatives consist of ECB uncapped repo lines with relaxed collateral rules, the expansion of Federal Reserve US dollar swap lines to the ECB to ease banking sector funding, and ECB secondary market bond purchases to stabilize European debt markets.

This page presents J.P. Morgan's market and portfolio outlook, explaining why the firm is maintaining its current portfolio risk levels and presenting a constructive yet tempered view on U.S. corporate profits. The author argues that while corporate profits are recovering strongly, Wall Street’s overall S&P 500 projections for 2010 are overly optimistic because they overlook the challenges posed by public sector problems. Consequently, the firm expects single-digit returns on developed market equities for the year. The firm's proxy Balanced portfolio has maintained volatility below 10%, comparable to a 60% fixed-income portfolio, by using credit, commodities, currencies, hedge funds, and principal-protected equity structures rather than relying heavily on bonds.

Five charts illustrate these dynamics. The first chart, depicting trailing 12-month S&P 500 earnings from 2000 to 2010, shows that J.P. Morgan does not expect a "double dip" in corporate profits. Instead, operating and reported earnings are shown recovering sharply, with both top-down and bottom-up estimates converging toward $90 per share by mid-2010. The second chart compares actual year-over-year corporate profit growth to a model forecast from 1993 through 2010. The model indicates a strong profit rebound, projecting year-over-year profit growth to peak at 37.7% in the third quarter of 2010, up from an actual growth rate of 30.6% in the fourth quarter of 2009. 

The third chart demonstrates the high operating leverage supporting this corporate profit recovery by comparing pre-tax margins. Although flat Q4 2009 margins were low, the incremental margins relative to Q4 2008 were exceptionally high, exceeding 100% for both consumer durables and economically sensitive sectors like commodities, capital goods, consumer cyclicals, and technology. 

The fourth chart compares various financial institutions' 2010 S&P 500 projections to argue that market expectations are too high. J.P. Morgan Private Bank’s projection of 1,175 to 1,225 sits at the conservative end of the spectrum, alongside Citi and Morgan Stanley. In contrast, peer institutions such as Goldman Sachs, Credit Suisse, Bank of America, HSBC, and UBS project targets ranging from 1,250 to 1,350, with Deutsche Bank presenting the most aggressive forecast at 1,375. 

Finally, the fifth chart shows that the global economic rebound remains on track, displaying the seasonally adjusted J.P. Morgan Global PMI output index from 2000 to 2010. Both the manufacturing and services indices show a sharp V-shaped recovery from their late-2008 lows of under 40, rising back to levels between 55 and 60 by early 2010.

This page analyzes the financial stability of Italy relative to other highly indebted European nations, arguing that immediate contagion risks for the country are subdued despite its high debt levels. The author separates Italy, whose gross domestic product equals that of Spain, Portugal, Ireland, and Greece combined, from these peripheral nations due to several key structural advantages. First, Italy has a much smaller budget deficit problem, with its 2009 primary deficit standing at less than 1 percent compared to 9 percent for Greece. Second, while Italy’s sovereign debt is very high, 45 percent of it is owned by domestic residents, which is far higher than Greece’s 25 percent or Ireland’s 14 percent. Third, Italy relies much less on foreign capital, carrying a modest 3 percent current account deficit compared to the double-digit deficits of Portugal and Greece. Finally, Italy’s banking sector is exceptionally well-funded, with deposits exceeding 100 percent of loans.

Four charts support this analysis. The first chart, titled Gross financing needs vs. approved and announced packages in billions of Euros, shows that approved bailout packages of 860 billion Euros are sufficient to cover the combined 2010–2012 funding needs of Greece, Ireland, Portugal, and Spain, which total 745 billion Euros, as well as their 2013 needs of 167 billion Euros. However, Italy’s individual financing needs for 2010–2013 are a massive 892 billion Euros, bringing the total gross financing needs for all five countries to 1.805 trillion Euros. 

The second chart, Gross sovereign debt as a percentage of GDP from 1992 to 2010, shows that Greece and Italy have the highest debt ratios in Europe, both tracking above 110 percent of GDP in 2010, while countries like Spain, Ireland, France, Portugal, and Germany sit lower but show varying upward trajectories. 

The third chart, Current account balance as a percentage of GDP from 1992 to 2010, tracks the deep deficits of Greece and Portugal, which reached close to 15 percent at their worst, while Italy’s deficit remained stable and comparatively modest at around 3 percent in 2010. 

The fourth chart, Total borrowing from the European Central Bank as a percentage of bank assets, compares peak and current borrowing across ten European countries. While Ireland and Greece rely heavily on the ECB at approximately 12 percent of bank assets, Italy has the lowest reliance in Europe, with both peak and current borrowing at roughly 1 percent of bank assets.

Despite these near-term strengths, the author concludes with a warning that Italy faces significant long-term structural risks. In particular, Italy’s shadow economy is exceptionally large, second only to Greece in Europe, which impairs long-term productivity, growth, and per capita economic indicators.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" focuses on global portfolio strategies, the outlook for gold and U.S. debt inflation, and the diverging economic realities facing members of the Eurozone. The author begins by highlighting how equity markets have been reversed by three major forces: the withdrawal of Chinese monetary stimulus, financial reforms in the U.S. and Eurozone, and austerity triggered by the unraveling of the EMU periphery. Against a backdrop of global equity markets falling 8% year-to-date, the publication outlines several defensive moves made in their Balanced Portfolios in late 2009. These include keeping equity weights low at 35% to 40%, favoring U.S. large and mid-caps over Europe, and hedging European equity and Euro currency exposure. They also trimmed Asian positions due to rising property prices in China, allocated 17% to 22% of portfolios to risk-reducing hedge funds, and maintained exposure to high-yield credit and real estate securities.

The author notes missed opportunities in gold and long-duration Treasuries. While gold was trading around $1,200 per ounce, the author suggests selling it at slightly higher levels, arguing that the U.S. is unlikely to inflate away its public debt. Unlike the post-World War II era of 1946, when U.S. debt was held entirely domestically and carried an average maturity of nine years, modern U.S. debt is shorter-term (averaging 4.3 years) and widely held internationally, making inflation a much more dangerous strategy. Instead, the Federal Reserve is expected to rein in its balance sheet, a normalization process that St. Louis Fed President James Bullard estimated could take five years.

The final section explores the "right" value of the Euro through a chart titled "Equilibrium Euro by country: solvency without deflation." The chart displays the implied USD/EUR exchange rate necessary for individual Eurozone countries to resolve external imbalances without forcing domestic deflation. Horizontal lines on the chart mark the exchange rate in December 2009 (approximately $1.48) and the then-current rate (approximately $1.23). The vertical bars illustrate a severe divergence across member states: Germany’s equilibrium rate is near $1.90, while France and Italy are closer to parity with current rates at roughly $1.10 and $1.05, respectively. In stark contrast, highly indebted peripheral nations require a much weaker currency to balance their accounts; Spain's equilibrium rate is around $0.60, while Portugal and Greece are estimated at around $0.30. Because German inflation concerns would prevent the Euro from falling to such low levels, the author concludes that these peripheral nations will have to rely on painful domestic austerity to resolve their imbalances.

This page from Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Private Banking, analyzes the structural, political, and economic headwinds facing Italy in comparison to its European peers, while advocating for a long-term investment shift toward Asian consumption. 

Cembalest first points out that Italy's institutional framework resembles Greece's much more than it does the rest of Europe. To support this, he presents a chart of the World Bank Governance Indicators from 2008, which measures percent rank across six categories: accountability, political stability, government effectiveness, regulatory quality, rule of law, and corruption. The data includes Germany, the UK, Ireland, France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, and Greece. Across almost all categories, Italy and Greece trail the rest of the pack, scoring lowest on political stability, government effectiveness, and corruption. 

In addition to governance, Italy faces severe structural economic hurdles, illustrated by two tables comparing annualized research and development expenditure as a percentage of GDP and average firm size by number of people. In R&D expenditure, Italy ranks last among its peers at just 1.10% of GDP, well below Sweden at 3.89%, Germany at 2.48%, and the EU 27 average of 1.84%. Similarly, in average firm size, Italy sits at the bottom with only 2.7 people per firm, compared to Germany’s 11.4 and the U.K.’s 10.6. Cembalest argues that Italy’s low growth is a function of these small-scale firms, low R&D, and an economy still heavily reliant on easily outsourced sectors like textiles. 

Despite these issues and Italy's high government debt, the author notes a current cyclical bounce in industrial production and states that Italy is not expected to become a weak link requiring further additions to the existing EUR 750 billion bilateral EMU and IMF loan and guarantee package. Footnotes clarify political tensions in Germany, where FDP head Frank Schaeffler stepped down over disputes regarding the European Stabilization Mechanism, though Cembalest predicts the legislation will still pass the Bundestag and Bundesrat with simple majorities. 

Ultimately, the author recommends seeking growth in regions with rising incomes and low debt burdens, specifically pointing to Asia. This regional economic divergence is visualized in a chart of annualized auto sales as a percentage of the population from 2000 to 2010. The chart plots World sales on the left-hand scale and World ex-China sales on the right-hand scale. The visual shows a dramatic divergence starting in 2008: while total global sales rebounded strongly to nearly 0.9%, the global series excluding China lagged significantly, remaining depressed near 0.7%. This serves as a proxy for how Chinese consumption is driving global wealth creation. The page concludes with a brief, humorous reflection on the author's recent experience with jury duty and the nature of hearsay.

This page analyzes the risks of political overreach in both the Eurozone’s crisis response and domestic financial regulatory reforms. The author begins by examining the push toward European federalism, quoting former EU Commission President Romano Prodi, who argued that the Eurozone crisis represents an opportunity to force economic governance that was impossible at the Euro's inception. This "Revolution from Above" carries significant risk, suppressing European risk-taking; year-to-date European capital markets and merger activity are down 17%, whereas activity is up 53% in the United States and 68% in Asia. The author cautions that European asset prices must cheapen further before investors should return. 

This European economic divergence is illustrated in an accompanying line chart titled "Something's rotten near Denmark," which plots current account deficits as a percentage of GDP from 1975 to 2008. The chart displays two distinct paths: a relatively stable, slightly positive trend for France, Germany, and the United Kingdom, and a sharply declining trend for the southern European nations of Greece, Italy, Ireland, Portugal, and Spain. Following the fixing of the Euro exchange rate in 1999, the current account balances of this latter group plunged from near parity to a deficit of nearly 8% of GDP by 2008, visualizing the structural imbalances that Prodi noted the Euro’s designers anticipated.

The discussion then shifts to domestic financial reform. While acknowledging necessary post-bailout objectives—such as ending "too big to fail," establishing a systemic regulator, ensuring securitizers retain "skin in the game," and increasing derivative oversight—the author questions where regulation begins to yield diminishing economic returns. This tension is highlighted by former Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker’s opposition to Section 716, which would counterproductively push swaps activity out of regulated bank entities. 

This theme of regulatory overreach is explored at the state level in a detailed sidebar titled "Das Eigene Nest Beschmutzen" ("To Soil One's Own Nest"), which reviews a report by the Public Policy Institute of New York. The author criticizes New York politicians for failing to protect their state's primary economic engine. Currently, 94 bills before the New York State Legislature seek to tax, restrict, or penalize financial services, carrying a potential cost to the industry of up to $12 billion annually. This legislative hostility is particularly risky because the financial sector constitutes $187 billion of New York's $318 billion economy, represents 39% of state wage income, and pays 40% of personal income taxes. The author warns that because technological advances in networking and telecommuting make physical concentration in New York less necessary, these punitive measures could drive the industry away. This threat is compounded by the state’s fiscal situation; New York has the second-highest per capita state debt in the nation, driven by a spending growth rate from 1999 to 2010 that outpaced personal income growth by 20% and inflation by 30%.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication begins by introducing a primary theme: rising Chinese consumption as a resilient, secular trend driven by urbanization, modernization, rising wages, and domestic economic openness, contrasting it against intensifying credit market stresses in Europe, particularly Spain. To illustrate China's economic evolution, the page features an image of Chinese Renminbi banknotes alongside two famous quotes: one from Mao Zedong in 1964 predicting that the socialist system would eventually replace capitalism, and another from Deng Xiaoping in 1992 declaring that poverty is not socialism and getting rich is glorious.

The commentary then pivots to the contemporary oil spill disaster in the Gulf of Mexico and the resulting six-month federal moratorium on offshore drilling. Noting that offshore oil represents thirty percent of total United States production, the author emphasizes the extreme difficulty of deep-sea drilling, citing a Schlumberger geologist who compared sub-salt drilling to putting a man on the moon. This frames an analysis of whether alternative energy powering electric vehicles could replace offshore oil.

A bar chart titled "Incremental MW by alternative energy source needed to replace all U.S. federal and state offshore oil production powering vehicles" compares current installed capacity against the required incremental megawatts for five energy sources: hydro, solar, wind, biomass, and geothermal. Hydro shows a substantial base of around seventy-eight thousand megawatts but requires nearly forty thousand more. Wind has roughly twenty-five thousand megawatts installed but needs an additional seventy-eight thousand megawatts. Solar and geothermal have almost no current installed capacity shown on the scale, requiring massive jumps of over one hundred and ten thousand megawatts and eighteen thousand megawatts respectively to fill the gap.

Focusing on the wind power scenario, the author calculates that while matching raw energy output would require a fifteen-fold increase in wind capacity, adjusting for the higher efficiency of electric vehicles over internal combustion engines reduces this to a quadrupling of wind capacity. Even this smaller increase, however, presents severe challenges. It would require seven thousand square miles of new wind farms, an area roughly the size of New Jersey, calculated using a space requirement of sixty acres per megawatt. Additionally, the author notes a host of associated hurdles, including high upfront capital costs, the need for upgraded high-voltage direct current transmission lines, grid stability issues, eminent domain conflicts, consistent subsidies, backup natural gas facilities to handle wind's intermittency, battery and lithium supply constraints, political NIMBYism, and environmental impacts. The page concludes with a warning that while the nation needs alternative energy, it desperately requires an open discussion about the actual sacrifices and costs involved in achieving it.

This page focuses on the shifting spending patterns of Chinese consumers and the corresponding hurdles and opportunities for global investors trying to capture this rapidly growing market. 

The first chart, "What Chinese people buy when they get wealthier," maps consumption across five income levels from poor to affluent. It reveals that while automobile purchases skyrocket the most, peaking at a consumption index over 100 for affluent buyers, categories like home decoration and prestige/luxury goods also show steep rises, climbing to indexes of approximately 25 and 18 respectively. To illustrate current luxury preferences, a second horizontal bar chart titled "Chinese luxury purchases: survey results" presents data from a September 2009 sample of 627 shoppers in major Chinese cities. Louis Vuitton dominates the brand landscape, claimed by roughly 34% of shoppers, followed by Gucci at approximately 26%, while Chanel, Prada, Hugo Boss, Ferragamo, Armani, and Dior all hover around 7% to 8%, and Burberry and Max Mara pull up the rear at under 5% each.

The author highlights that reaching these wealthy consumers requires increasingly broader geographic coverage. While Shanghai and Beijing rival New York and Chicago in luxury retail locations, the market is rapidly decentralizing. In 2005, a consumer company could reach 70% of China's middle and affluent classes via just 70 locations, but by 2010, reaching that same percentage required 240 locations. This geographic shift is depicted in two side-by-side maps showing the expected dramatic expansion of locations with significant affluent populations between 2010 and 2020. The 2010 map shows wealth concentrated heavily along the eastern seaboard, whereas the 2020 map projects a dense, sprawling network of affluent hubs extending deep into the interior of mainland China.

The text cautions that foreign brands do not hold an automatic advantage, citing studies on consumer ethnocentrism and a reluctance to buy foreign goods, particularly those from Japan and the United States. This sentiment is stronger among older, male, and rural demographics. However, some trusted foreign brands, especially in western China, are actually perceived by locals as Chinese simply because they are highly regarded. The author warns that cultural insensitivity in marketing has previously provoked boycotts for prominent brands like McDonald's, KFC, Toyota, and Nike, the latter due to a LeBron James advertisement, pointing to the need for highly nuanced local marketing strategies.

Finally, the page addresses the regulatory and operational realities for foreign businesses. Citing an April 2010 survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in China, the author notes that while US companies are largely successful—71% are profitable, 75% match or exceed their worldwide margins, and 91% are optimistic about their five-year outlook—they face severe operational hurdles. Key challenges include inconsistent enforcement of intellectual property laws, licensing difficulties, regulatory rollbacks on open sectors, and China's Indigenous Innovation Policy which favors domestic firms. The author concludes that foreign firms face tougher environmental and labor standards, noting that navigating Chinese business remains historically complex, drawing parallels to the historical experiences of Marco Polo, 18th-century Britain, and modern-day Google.

This page highlights how US Congressional discussions have largely ignored the rapidly declining costs of the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), the profitability of the Federal Reserve’s Maiden Lane facilities, and the near-complete repayment of Fed emergency credit facilities. The author contrasts this lack of recognition with the massive, ongoing potential losses from Government-Sponsored Enterprises (GSEs) like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which have faced far less political scrutiny despite remaining consistently high.

To illustrate this disparity, a bar chart titled "Potential losses, TARP vs GSEs" compares loss estimates in billions of dollars across various institutions and dates. It shows that as of May 2010, the U.S. Treasury estimated TARP losses—comprising the Home Affordable Modification Program (HAMP), automotive industry assistance, and AIG—at well under $150 billion. This figure excludes $16.7 billion in offsetting gains from other programs. In contrast, estimates of potential GSE losses are significantly larger, ranging from around $300 billion by the Congressional Budget Office in August 2009 and $400 billion by Wallison of the American Enterprise Institute in December 2009, to a peak estimate of $806 billion by Bridgewater in April 2009. The author notes that some GSE losses will be absorbed by private bank putbacks, mortgage insurers like PMI and Radian, and GSE fee income, rather than direct Treasury contributions.

Two line charts support the argument that government intervention programs have performed better than politically acknowledged. The first, titled "Maiden Lane I, II and III: in the black," tracks billions of dollars from July 2008 to April 2010. It shows that net portfolio holdings have consistently stayed above the principal loan amount since early 2009, remaining in the $65 billion to $75 billion range while the principal has hovered around $60 billion. The second chart, "Federal Reserve emergency credit facilities," illustrates the dramatic rise and fall of emergency credit outstanding from October 2007 to April 2010. Outstanding credit peaked near $2.0 trillion in late 2008 before tumbling to roughly $300 billion by April 2010, with 86% of the remaining balance comprised of FX swaps, AIG support, and the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility (TALF).

In the "Odds and Ends" section, the commentary covers broader market developments and geopolitical tensions. S&P’s slow response to the Financial Sector Reform Bill is noted to have reduced immediate downgrade risks for major banks like Citigroup, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo, stabilizing the triparty repo system. In Europe, the author questions the fragility of a market that views the Fed's unlimited dollar lending rate of 1.22% (Libor plus 70 basis points) as "too expensive," especially given reports that BBVA was unable to renew $1 billion in commercial paper. Regarding equity markets, South Korea is highlighted as an attractive entry point, trading at a forward price-to-earnings multiple below ten, assuming conflict is avoided. Finally, the author poses a geopolitical question about how China's $800 billion holdings of US Treasuries might affect how the US manages relations with North Korea, pointing out that Chinese military officials have recommended using this financial leverage to advance broader policy goals.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues that buying Chinese equities is a highly ineffective way to capitalize on China's economic growth and consumer expansion, noting that despite strong GDP growth, its stock market has yielded some of the worst returns globally. 

To support this claim, the page presents two scatter plot charts comparing equity market performance against nominal GDP growth. The first chart, covering the period from the fourth quarter of 2007 to mid-2010, plots cumulative nominal USD GDP growth against cumulative USD equity market performance. It highlights China at the extreme bottom right, with stellar cumulative GDP growth of approximately 60% but a dismal cumulative equity market return of nearly negative 50%, vastly underperforming peers like Colombia, Indonesia, and Brazil. The second chart shows annualized performance from 2003 to mid-2010. Here, China is again a clear outlier at the bottom right, with high annualized nominal GDP growth of around 20% but annualized equity returns of only about 10%, trailing far behind most other emerging markets. 

Cembalest explains this disconnect by analyzing the structure of China's stock market, which is illustrated in a pie chart showing the sector breakdown of the Shanghai Composite Index. The market is dominated by state-owned enterprises that prioritize non-profit objectives, with Financials accounting for 32.3% and Energy making up 21.9%. The rest of the index is composed of Industrials at 16.8%, Materials at 9.9%, Consumer Discretionary at 5.9%, Utilities at 4.0%, Consumer Staples at 3.2%, Health Care at 2.9%, Information Technology at 2.3%, and Telecommunications at 0.8%. Because of this composition, the equity market functions more as a reflection of monetary liquidity and stimulus than of entrepreneurial corporate profits.

The text also highlights a severe funding imbalance in the Chinese economy. While China has experienced massive loan expansion, domestic banks primarily channel capital to state-owned enterprises, which represent just 5% of all firms but receive 75% of all bank loans. Meanwhile, small and medium-sized enterprises received less than 5% of the loans extended in 2009, forcing private entrepreneurs to look offshore for growth capital. 

Concluding with a historical perspective, Cembalest recounts a 1978 conversation where Singapore’s former Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew encouraged Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping to initiate market reforms, leading to the establishment of Special Economic Zones in Xiamen, Shantou, Zhuhai, and Shenzhen. Cembalest notes that while Chinese financial markets are currently correcting due to stimulus withdrawal and property overheating, the long-term trend of rising per capita wealth and consumption remains intact. Consequently, he advises investors to seek direct exposure to Chinese consumption rather than broad public equities.

This page analyzes California's fiscal health, arguing that the state is not insolvent but rather suffering from political gridlock and structural spending issues. To illustrate the deep division hindering a legislative budget agreement, the first line chart, titled "Party polarization at an all-time high," plots the distance between political parties in Congress from 1879 to 2009 based on Congressional roll-call analysis. Both the House (red line) and Senate (blue line) series track closely with a correlation of R = 0.91, showing that political polarization plunged to a low point around the mid-20th century of around 0.3 to 0.4 but climbed back to near-historic highs above 0.8 by 2009. The author compares California’s $22 billion budget gap to Greece's sovereign crisis, noting that California’s situation is far more manageable, requiring only a tenth of the fiscal adjustments that Greece needs. However, a footnote cautions that when adding California's state debt to its pro-rata share of U.S. federal debt, the total burden is roughly 70% of state GNP, which is similar to Eurozone levels, though still well below Greece's 115%.

A second bar chart, titled "California: Annual population plus inflation growth vs. annual spending growth, 1991 - 2009," demonstrates that across three consecutive gubernatorial administrations, state spending consistently outpaced the rate of population growth plus inflation. Under Pete Wilson (R), annual spending growth of approximately 5.2% exceeded the combined population and inflation benchmark of about 4%. Under Gray Davis (D), spending growth rose to nearly 6.5% compared to a population and inflation rate of 5%. This trend continued under Arnold Schwarzenegger (R), with spending remaining near 6.5% against a benchmark of just over 5%. The text attributes these structural imbalances to generous public benefits, including the state paying 100% of retiree healthcare costs, state and local employment growing 33% faster than the population since 1990, public sector salaries averaging 44% higher than the private sector, and a highly volatile tax base where 1% of Californians paid 81% of capital gains taxes in 2007. 

Looking ahead, the author warns that if California attempts to bridge its budget gap using revenue anticipation notes, municipal markets may balk, and rating agencies could downgrade the state's debt to BBB- or lower. While the author does not expect severe defaults on California general obligation bonds, they advise municipal bond investors to remain diversified. Specifically, they recommend keeping California municipal exposure 5% to 10% below its 16% weight in national benchmarks, noting that the state's credit risk pricing of 100 basis points over top-tier states like Virginia and Georgia does not warrant a larger position.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Private Banking, contextualizes the environmental impact of the BP Deepwater Horizon oil spill by examining various historical risk and failure rates. He references data from Gavekal Securities showing that 27 million barrels of oil were spilled out of 800 billion barrels produced between 1978 and 2010. While this highlights a statistically low failure rate for oil extraction, Cembalest argues that comparing oil spills to other industrial failures is ultimately unconvincing because ecological disasters carry prolonged, severe aftershocks that typical mechanical or medical failures do not. 

The main visual on the page is a table titled "The Gulf spill and an index of unwelcome events," which ranks various risk occurrences alongside their sources. The table starts with high-probability failures, such as salmonella-contaminated chickens at 1 in 7 according to Consumer Reports, medical prescription errors at 1 in 9, cluster bomb failures at 1 in 20, and public well water contamination from man-made substances at 1 in 22. Mid-tier risks include vasectomy failures at 1 in 150, U.S. bridge collapses between 1966 and 2005 at 1 in 400, and the failure rate of recalled Firestone Wilderness AT tires in 2001 at 1 in 5,000. 

The table places oil extraction risks toward the lower end of the probability spectrum. Prior to the Gulf incident, the rate of barrels of oil spilled per barrel produced from 1978 to 2009 stood at 1 in 30,000. When incorporating the estimated 4 million barrels lost in the 2010 Gulf spill, this hazard ratio worsened to 1 in 25,000. For comparison, the table lists even lower-probability events, such as pacemaker malfunction fatalities at 1 in 43,000, recalled Sony laptop lithium battery failures in 2006 at 1 in 200,000, contaminated blood transfusions resulting in Hepatitis C at 1 in 2 million, and fatal airline accidents per departure between 1990 and 2007 at 1 in 4.5 million. 

Cembalest concludes by reflecting on the historical link between energy access and human longevity, noting that U.S. life expectancy rose from 39.5 years in 1850—when kerosene began replacing whale oil—to 77.4 years today. While acknowledging that fossil-fuel-driven productivity has always suffered intermittent and severe failures, he poses open questions about how the BP spill will shape future energy policy and supplies, warning that replacing offshore drilling with alternative energy sources presents complex challenges with no easy answers.

In this report, Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Private Banking, argues against the prevailing view that a return to more affordable housing will automatically trigger a US housing market recovery. He highlights that while theoretical affordability has climbed, actual market conditions remain weak due to tighter underwriting criteria and higher down-payment requirements that offset the benefits of lower prices and mortgage rates. This is illustrated by two charts. The first, titled "Theoretical home affordability close to all-time highs," plots the ability of renters to qualify for a mortgage on a starter home from 1981 to 2009. This index surged from around 100 in 2005 to nearly 180 by 2009, indicating historically high theoretical affordability. However, the companion chart, "...but the housing recovery is a weak one," indexed to January 2000, demonstrates a very tepid actual recovery. It tracks the Case Shiller 20 city composite, the FHFA house price index, and the NAR median sales price of existing homes sold through 2010. Despite massive federal interventions—including over $1 trillion in Federal Reserve mortgage and agency purchases, modification programs, FHA refinancing, and homebuyer tax credits—the Case Shiller composite and FHFA indices both remained depressed near 145, down from peaks of approximately 206 and 180 respectively, indicating no imminent housing recovery.

Cembalest then shifts focus to investment strategies, recommending a 20% weight to hedge funds in Balanced Portfolios and advocating for increased exposure to macro hedge funds to navigate volatile market conditions. He notes that macro funds have historically outperformed a 60/40 World Equity/Fixed Income blend with lower volatility. To address the inherent risk and high dispersion of individual macro funds, he presents two scatter plots of annualized return versus annualized volatility based on five-year performance data from Hedge Fund Research Inc. The first plot, "5 year performance of individual macro funds," shows a massive dispersion of returns ranging from below -15% to over 30%, with annualized volatility extending past 70%. The second plot, "Portfolios of 5 randomly selected macro funds," demonstrates how combining just five randomly selected funds collapses this dispersion risk, clustering the portfolios tightly at a much safer 5% to 15% return and 5% to 15% volatility. Cembalest asserts that this reduction in dispersion risk through diversification is far more pronounced in macro strategies than in other approaches such as long-short, distressed, merger arbitrage, or statistical arbitrage.

In this commentary, the author expresses caution regarding global equity market outlooks, anticipating single-digit returns and addressing specific market perceptions he disagrees with, focusing first on European sovereign debt and second on S&P 500 earnings valuations.

Addressing the view that European sovereign debt auctions are proceeding successfully, the author argues that these auctions have relied heavily on ECB intervention rather than pure market demand. A table titled "ECB support for sovereign debt issuance" detailing May and June 2010 data in billions of euros illustrates this point. While Italy appears stable with 21.7 billion euros of issued debt and 3.9 billion euros in ECB repo funding, other nations show deeper dependence. Ireland and Portugal issued 3.3 billion and 3.9 billion euros of debt, respectively, while drawing much larger repo funding from the ECB of 14.5 billion and 23.3 billion euros, alongside participating in a broader 51 billion euro ECB debt purchasing scheme. Spain issued 14.0 billion euros in debt, which was offset by an identical 14.0 billion euros in ECB repo funding, suggesting hidden support. Additionally, a line chart titled "Banking system reliance on short term funding" plots the funding gap as a percentage of assets from 1998 to 2010. It shows that while the United States successfully reduced its short-term funding gap to near zero percent after the 2008 financial crisis, Europe's gap remains elevated at around 20%, unchanged from its peak 2007 levels.

The author also challenges the belief that the S&P 500 is exceptionally cheap at an 11.5x price-to-earnings multiple, which relies on a consensus 2011 earnings estimate of 95 dollars. He suggests a more realistic target of 85 dollars, yielding a less dramatic 12.9x multiple. To support this skepticism, a bar chart shows the percentage change in "Beginning of year vs. End of year earnings estimates" for the S&P 500 universe from 1986 to 2010. This historical data demonstrates that analysts routinely overestimate earnings, with year-end revisions frequently dropping by 10% to over 20%. This persistent optimism is underscored by another line chart displaying the "Percent of S&P 500 stocks with mean analyst rating of 'Sell' or 'Hold/Sell'" from 1996 to 2010. Despite the enactment of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, the proportion of stocks with negative analyst ratings remained consistently low, hovering near zero to five percent, indicating a systemic reluctance among analysts to issue sell ratings.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses China's recent currency policy announcement regarding the resumption of its crawling peg for the renminbi (RMB). He argues that this move, driven largely by G-20 political considerations, is unlikely to lead to aggressive appreciation, projecting a modest 3% annual appreciation which is lower than the rate seen between 2005 and 2008. He notes that China's slowing economic growth and a shrinking trade surplus—which fell from 11% of GDP in 2007 to 3% in the first quarter of 2010—limit the likelihood of further aggressive action. 

Two supporting charts illustrate China's economic context. The first chart, titled "Chinese reserve accumulation: unprecedented," plots reserve accumulation as a percentage of GDP over a 21-year period, comparing China from 1990 to 2009 against historical periods for Germany and Japan from 1955 to 1975. The data highlights how China's accumulation skyrocketed to nearly 12% of GDP, whereas Germany and Japan remained flat, never exceeding 2%. The second chart, "Chinese renminbi spot price," tracks the renminbi per dollar from October 2004 through late 2009, illustrating a 2.0% one-time appreciation in mid-2005 followed by a 5.7% annualized appreciation until a flat peg was re-established in late 2008.

The commentary then transitions to the impact of low interest rates on global asset flows. While low rates historically drove investors into riskier assets, Cembalest warns of a shift toward risk aversion, termed "zerophobia," where low yields fail to attract capital. He references a San Francisco Fed study by Glenn D. Rudebusch suggesting that macroeconomic conditions do not justify interest rate hikes until 2012, with the theoretical Fed Funds rate hitting negative 2.9%. If further quantitative easing (QE2) occurs, Cembalest notes it would likely drive gold prices higher, admitting that J.P. Morgan has shelved its upper price targets for gold due to the lack of opportunity cost in holding the metal.

Two charts support this monetary policy discussion. The first, "Funds rate rule adjusted for unconventional policy," charts the actual and suggested Fed target rates from 2002 to 2012. It shows the suggested target rate from a simple rule dropping below negative 4% and the suggested rate adjusting for unconventional policy bottoming near negative 6% in 2010 before projecting a recovery toward negative 1% by 2012. The final chart, "Flows into global equity and bond funds," compares average monthly flows in billions over the last 12 months against the 2010 year-to-date figures. It shows a dramatic decline in equity inflows from around $4.5 billion over the last 12 months to nearly zero in the 2010 YTD period, while average monthly credit inflows fell from roughly $16 billion to around $11 billion, illustrating that investment flows have slowed markedly despite low interest rates.

Michael Cembalest discusses the outlook for Chinese unit labor costs and productivity, arguing that the era of negative unit labor cost growth, which persisted from 1991 to 2004, has ended. He forecasts low single-digit unit labor cost growth going forward as the Chinese economy gradually shifts from production to consumption. This analysis is supported by a line chart titled China labor productivity - manufacturing and construction, which plots the year-over-year percentage change from 1981 to 2009. The productivity data shows significant historical volatility, dipping to nearly negative 10 percent around 1989, surging to a peak of roughly 35 percent in 1993, and ultimately slowing to about 3 percent by 2009.

To address whether rising wages pose a threat to corporate profits or U.S. inflation, the page presents a scatter plot titled China: Labor is a much smaller percent of goods and services than in the U.S. This chart plots labor compensation per unit of output against sector size as a percentage of total output for 42 economic sectors. While the United States average labor compensation across all sectors sits near the top of the chart at roughly 66 percent, almost all Chinese sectors sit far below this threshold. Agriculture is the highest outlier in China, with labor compensation making up around 55 percent of output for a sector that comprises 5.5 percent of the economy. Other services like Social Organizations and Education have labor components around 40 to 45 percent. Crucially, the vast majority of China's manufacturing and energy sectors, depicted as red and blue dots, show labor components well below 10 percent, indicating substantial room for wage growth before U.S. import prices or corporate profits are materially impacted. Cembalest concludes with a currency prediction, stating that the firm expects modest Renminbi appreciation of no more than 3 percent to 4 percent annually, viewing the policy move as political but supportive of existing long positions in other Asian currencies funded against the Euro.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses why mediocre economic data is insufficient given the massive fiscal stimulus deployed during the recession. The author argues that the return on stimulus has been weak, and the U.S. economy has failed to reach escape velocity. 

To illustrate the unique and unprecedented cost of this recovery, Figure 1, titled "Recoveries used to bloom on their own," contrasts the increase in the ISM manufacturing survey in points against the increase in Federal Debt as a percentage of GDP across recovery periods from 1952 to 2008–2010. While prior recoveries required very little or even negative federal debt expansion to achieve solid manufacturing rebounds—often under four percent debt-to-GDP increase—the 2008–2010 recovery, projected through year-end 2010, is accompanied by a massive surge in federal debt of around sixteen percent of GDP, making it the most expensive recovery in modern history. 

Figure 2, titled "Lower follow-through from production to growth in Q1 2010 (not annualized)," is a scatter plot mapping historical GDP growth on the vertical axis against industrial production growth on the horizontal axis from 1948 to 2010. It highlights that in the first quarter of 2010, despite industrial production growing by nearly six percent, GDP growth languished around just one percent. This data point is a significant outlier, falling well below the historical trend where six percent industrial production growth typically yielded two and a half to three and a half percent GDP growth.

The author asserts that for equity markets to realize gains, the economy needs consistent U.S. capital spending, monthly payroll gains closer to 200,000, credible European bank stress tests, and easier monetary policy in China. He expresses skepticism regarding European regulatory efforts, noting that previous stress tests by the Committee of European Banking Supervisors in May 2009 appeared designed to avoid demanding more capital, particularly from politically sensitive state-owned regional banks. 

To explain why this financial cycle is uniquely complex, the author points to systemic risks such as European wholesale funding, Chinese money supply expansion, and the collapse of structured credit. Figure 3, "Non-agency securitization quadruples," displays a line chart of total quarterly issuance in billions from 2000 to 2007. This issuance, which encompasses subprime loans, HELOCs, Alt-A, option ARMs, prime jumbo, commercial real estate, autos, and other assets, skyrocketed from under 100 billion dollars in 2000 to a peak of over 450 billion dollars in late 2005 and early 2006, highlighting the massive expansion of structured credit that preceded the crisis.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s financial publication addresses the aftermath of the May 6, 2010, Flash Crash, arguing that while electronic trading represents financial innovation, adjustments are necessary to ensure market stability and confidence. The author notes that innovation is not always synonymous with progress, comparing unregulated high-frequency trading (HFT) to other problematic innovations like overused antibiotics or complex derivatives. The commentary focuses on three key positive developments arising from the crash.

The first development is the implementation of stock-specific circuit breakers. While Asia utilizes daily trading bands of up to 15% and Europe’s Deutsche Bourse pauses trading for five minutes after moves of 3% to 10%, the U.S. has historically relied on retrospective trade cancellations. In the wake of the Flash Crash, a pilot program applying 10% circuit breakers was introduced and has already been triggered on stocks like Citigroup, Anadarko, and the Washington Post Company. Additionally, the SEC is debating whether to eliminate high-frequency traders' unfiltered, naked access to exchanges to prevent rapid, compounded losses, a risk previously highlighted by the Chicago Fed.

Second, the Flash Crash has prompted a more balanced discussion regarding high-frequency trading and its relationship with market liquidity. The author notes that while trading volumes have tripled, volume does not equal true liquidity. According to a May survey by the Tabb Group, only about half of industry participants felt confident in the U.S. equity market structure, and 73% did not believe it was orderly. This has fueled proposals to force HFTs to register as broker-dealers, establishing minimum quote durations to bring them more in line with legacy specialist systems.

Third, regulators are considering proposals to make HFTs behave more like traditional floor specialists, particularly by curbing the practice of placing and immediately canceling orders. Currently, 97% of HFT orders are canceled, resulting in a ratio of 30 cancellations for every single executed order. An accompanying line chart, titled "HFTs driving order cancellations higher," illustrates this trend. Using NASDAQ ITCH data provided by Knight Capital Group, the chart plots the ratio of cancelled to executed orders from 2002 to 2009. The ratio climbs steadily from a low of around 11 in early 2002 to peak above 30 by late 2009. To curb what an Ameritrade representative labeled "opportunistic liquidity"—where quotes are pulled within a nanosecond of being posted—some market participants recommend imposing fees on high-frequency traders who generate excessive cancellations.

On this page, J.P. Morgan's Michael Cembalest argues that to successfully navigate global markets, investors must scrutinize highly granular data—the "lower intestines" of markets—to spot systemic risks before they trigger crises. 

To support this thesis, the page features five historical charts. Figure 4, "Loss protection for AAA CMBS investors," tracks subordination levels from 1995 to 2008. It shows that the "Below AAA" credit enhancement buffer protecting senior commercial mortgage-backed securities shrank dramatically over this period, dropping from more than 30% in 1995 to around 11% by 2007 and 2008, revealing how unprotected AAA investors became right before the subprime collapse. 

Figure 5, titled "Flightless birds, circa 1999," illustrates the tech bubble by plotting the aggregate market capitalization of Cisco, EMC, Oracle, and Qualcomm alongside their average analysts' long-term EPS growth forecasts from 1995 to 2000. While the combined market cap of these companies exploded from under $100 billion to nearly $1 trillion by 2000, analysts' average long-term EPS forecasts remained completely flat, hovering between 30% and 35%, showing a major mismatch between valuation and projected fundamentals.

Moving to macro-economic imbalances, Figure 6, "Signs of stress - Korea, Thailand & Indonesia," displays a three-country average from 1990 to 1997 to show the build-up to the Asian Financial Crisis. Bank lending to the private sector rose from 50% to over 80% of GDP, and short-term debt escalated from around 90% to nearly 170% of foreign exchange reserves, while inward foreign direct investment relative to the current account deficit fell. 

Figure 7, "Mexican exchange rate peg and consumption," tracks the Mexican peso and year-over-year consumption growth from 1989 to 1995. During the exchange rate peg of 1989 to 1993, average consumption growth surged to 4.5%, compared to just 1% during the pre-peg period of 1981 to 1988. The author notes this unproductive consumption boom mirrors the contemporary issues facing Greece, Spain, Portugal, and Ireland, where currency pegs combined with rising labor costs and consumption booms often lead to severe crises.

Finally, Figure 8, "Commercial property boom a consequence of 1981 bill," tracks the net new supply of commercial real estate and occupied space in millions of square feet from 1980 to 1990. Following the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981, net new supply shot up to nearly 140 million square feet by 1985, far exceeding occupied space and creating empty properties built solely for tax purposes. This tax-incentivized bubble burst following the Tax Reform Act of 1986, leading to the Savings and Loan crisis and a recession, proving that deep analysis of tax policies and bank property exposure was vital to predicting bank survival.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Private Banking, discusses the challenges and opportunities of investing during what he terms the largest fiscal and monetary experiment of the last century. He focuses on wholesale funding risks in Europe, corporate earnings valuations, and the compelling risk-reward profile of credit relative to equities. Cembalest notes that European wholesale funding risks remain unchanged since the financial crisis began, with 3.3 trillion Euros of wholesale debt, half of which matures within two years. Consequently, J.P. Morgan remains underweight in Europe unless equity valuations drop significantly relative to the U.S. and Asia. Meanwhile, in China, some companies are trading more cheaply in Shenzhen and Shanghai than in Hong Kong, indicating that the decline in Asian risk appetite may be bottoming out.

This European risk is illustrated in Figure 9, a line chart sourced from Bridgewater Associates showing the banking system's reliance on short-term funding, represented as the funding gap as a percentage of assets, from 1998 to 2010. The chart compares Europe and the U.S. While the U.S. funding gap sharply declined from around 15% in 2008 to nearly 0% by 2010, the European funding gap remained persistently high, fluctuating between 20% and 25% over the same period, underscoring Europe's ongoing vulnerability.

Cembalest argues that investing in equities is difficult, pointing out that J.P. Morgan discounts consensus earnings because analyst forecasts are historically overoptimistic. This point is supported by Figure 10, a bar chart sourced from First Call titled "Beginning of year vs end of year earnings estimates" showing the percentage change in earnings for the S&P 500 universe from 1986 to 2010. The chart reveals that in almost every year, analysts' initial earnings estimates are revised downward by the end of the year, often by 5% to over 20%, with only a handful of years in the late 1980s, mid-1990s, and mid-2000s showing positive adjustments. Based on J.P. Morgan's realistic expectations, which discount consensus earnings, equities are valued at 12.5-13x for 2010. This leads J.P. Morgan to hold existing equities but shift portfolio reliance toward macro hedge funds and credit.

In the credit markets, first lien exposures to commercial and residential property, as well as high-yield companies, offer yields of 6% to 11%. Cembalest highlights newly underwritten mezzanine loans to commercial property owners as a prime opportunity. Under current conservative market conditions, these loans require owners to contribute 30% to 35% equity—underwritten on price declines of 40% to 50%—and pay cash yields of 11% to 13%. Cembalest concludes that if the markets continue to trade sideways over the next few years, credit may deliver the best risk-adjusted returns.

This page provides a comprehensive market and merger & acquisition update, focusing on the upcoming European bank stress tests, macroeconomic growth expectations, and tactical asset allocation strategies. Discussing the upcoming July 23 release of European stress tests, the author notes that J.P. Morgan Securities estimates capital needs at roughly 80 billion euros. Compared to the U.S. SCAP stress tests in May 2009, which required 75 billion dollars of capital against a 523 billion dollar equity base, Europe's 81 billion euro requirement is backed by a much larger existing equity base of 1,014 billion euros. A bar chart titled "On paper, stress tests should be less stressful for Europe" illustrates these figures in billions of local currency. However, the author raises several critical, unresolved questions: whether a 3% adverse-case GDP assumption is too mild, whether non-profit Spanish Cajas and German Landesbanken can recapitalize, if loss assumptions are realistic given low assumed default rates (such as 5.2% for German commercial real estate and 3.6% for Spanish residential mortgages), and whether losses will apply to hold-to-maturity sovereign debt. J.P. Morgan argues that Tier 1 capital expansion does not resolve the structural issues of wholesale funding reliance and sovereign bailout credibility.

Turning to the macroeconomic outlook, while U.S. corporate profits are healthy, the author highlights a broad slowdown in spending, housing, manufacturing, and exports starting in June, prompting a downgrade in consensus GDP forecasts for the remainder of 2010. The global economy may slow, as evidenced by semiconductor sales hitting a 25-year high relative to GDP. For recovery to resume, employment must follow business spending. A line chart titled "Capital spending leads employment" traces year-over-year percentage changes from 1955 to 2010, demonstrating that business equipment and software spending (measured on the left axis from negative 20% to positive 25%) serves as a reliable leading indicator for seasonally adjusted non-farm payrolls (measured on the right axis from negative 5% to positive 5%).

Consequently, J.P. Morgan is shifting allocations away from directional equities toward credit and hedge funds, particularly merger arbitrage. With corporate cash balances near 50-year highs, transaction activity and premiums are robust, with average deal premiums exceeding 30% in the preceding two weeks. A combined bar and line chart titled "Rising M&A premiums and transaction volumes" from 2000 to Q2 2010 plots the rising average premium percentage on the left axis (spanning 10% to 35%) alongside the rising volume of deals in thousands on the right axis (spanning 4.0 to 9.0). Recent deals highlighting this trend include Aon-Hewitt, United Financial-LSB-Smithtown, Carlyle-NBTY, J&J-Micrus Endovascular, Tyco Electronics-ADC, Honam Petrochemicals-Titan, and TPG-Healthscope.

In this publication, Michael Cembalest, Chief Investment Officer of J.P. Morgan Private Banking, discusses strategies for managing downside risk in venture capital portfolios, focusing heavily on biotechnology, international markets, and post-crisis IPO recovery. 

Cembalest argues that while early-stage drug discovery is highly risky—with only 5,000 to 10,000 initial compounds narrowing down to 250 preclinical compounds, and only 5 compounds entering clinical trials—investing in later-stage Phase 3 trials significantly lowers the expected failure rate. Although this stage yields lower expected returns, it aligns better with J.P. Morgan's risk-return objectives. This drug pipeline is illustrated in an infographic titled Improving the odds in VC investing, sourced from the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America. The visual traces the timeline from drug discovery and preclinical testing (taking 3 to 6 years), through Phase 1, 2, and 3 clinical trials (taking 6 to 7 years), and FDA review (taking 0.5 to 2 years) before resulting in a single approved drug. A list of specific areas of interest highlights medical technologies such as digital imaging, ingestible cameras, cryosurgery, and treatments for Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, multiple sclerosis, cancer, macular degeneration, leukemia, and lymphoma.

Beyond biotechnology, Cembalest notes the firm's successful exposure to later-stage alternative energy investments. When seeking venture opportunities outside the United States, the firm targets regions characterized by a high ratio of R&D to GDP, deep scientific talent pools near universities, supportive government seeding programs, active IPO markets, a relative shortage of local venture capital, and private companies trading at discounts to public peers.

The monetization of these investments is analyzed in a bar chart titled Average monthly IPO issuance, measured in billions of USD and sourced from Bloomberg. The chart compares the U.S., Western Europe, and Developed Asia Pacific across three distinct timeframes. From January 2000 to August 2008, average monthly volumes stood at roughly 5.0 billion USD for the U.S., 4.3 billion USD for Western Europe, and 2.9 billion USD for Asia Pacific. During the financial crisis trough from September 2008 to June 2009, issuance dried up globally, falling to near-zero levels. In the recovery period of July 2009 to July 2010, U.S. volumes rebounded to 2.8 billion USD, representing about 50% of pre-crisis levels. Western Europe recovered to 1.6 billion USD, or roughly 35% of its prior baseline, while Developed Asia Pacific surged to 4.5 billion USD, significantly exceeding its pre-crisis average.

This page presents a detailed critique of the European banking stress tests released by the Committee of European Bank Supervisors (CEBS). Michael Cembalest argues that the results reflect significant "grade inflation," pointing out that the announced 3.5 billion euro capital shortfall for all of Europe was far below the expected 60 to 90 billion euros. He jokes that this small sum seemed more appropriate for the tiny nation of Andorra, which is highlighted in a small inset map of Western Europe showing France, Spain, and Andorra. 

Cembalest highlights several flaws in the CEBS stress tests. While European banks raised 220 billion euros in capital beforehand, boosting Tier 1 capital ratios to 10.2%, the test itself failed to apply a sufficiently grim economic outlook. By comparison, the U.S. May 2009 stress tests assumed losses two to three times higher. The European adverse case GDP growth scenario was only 0.8% below current levels, and its assumed 560 billion euros in losses were conveniently offset by projected pre-provision income that remained only 5.5% below 2009 results—an unrealistic projection for a region starting fiscal austerity. Additionally, sovereign stress was only applied to trading books, completely ignoring the much larger hold-to-maturity books. Cembalest suggests these tests were designed to show minimal capital shortfalls to avoid triggering the politically sensitive European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF) borrowing mechanism. 

Looking at the broader market, Cembalest notes modest signs of receding fear, citing shrinking sovereign bond purchases by the European Central Bank (ECB) and successful short-term debt issuances by Greece, Spain, and Portugal. However, he cautions that Europe still needs to prove it can survive major fiscal adjustments without triggering low-growth loops. Since robust growth in Germany and the United Kingdom is heavily export-driven rather than consumer-driven, it does not benefit peripheral Europe. Consequently, J.P. Morgan plans to maintain its investment strategy of a "barbell" of U.S. and Asian equity exposures.

The commentary concludes with observations from Cesar Perez, European Private Bank Strategist. Perez emphasizes that the CEBS test failed to address critical liquidity challenges facing European banks. Although near-term pressures might ease due to a softening of Basel III liquidity requirements by a G-20 committee chaired by ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet, European banks face structural headwinds. Having relied far less on customer deposits as their balance sheets grew over the previous decade, banks must now seek costly deposits, decrease leverage, or issue expensive long-term debt, all of which will depress the sector's Return on Equity (ROE) in the coming years.

This page of the publication analyzes municipal fiscal health, specifically challenging the optimistic narrative that US state and local budgets returned to a surplus as of the first quarter of 2010. The author outlines three primary objections to this view: the misleading inclusion of temporary federal transfers in aggregate budget data, the highly preliminary nature of Bureau of Economic Analysis data which is prone to large revisions, and the widespread use of borrowing and non-accrual accounting gimmicks to artificially balance state budgets. 

To illustrate the impact of federal aid, two side-by-side line charts cover the years 2000 to 2010, measuring budgets in billions of dollars on a seasonally adjusted annual rate from negative 90 billion to positive 70 billion. The first chart, showing state and local budgets apparently returning to a surplus in early 2010, is contrasted with the second chart, which strips out federal transfers. The second chart reveals that without 58.3 billion dollars in emergency federal aid, state and local budgets would actually remain in a deep deficit of approximately negative 25 billion dollars, as indicated by a prominent red dot.

The text discusses how individual states are managing their fiscal gaps. While some states like Georgia, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Florida, Utah, and South Carolina cut expenditures by more than 15 percent since 2008, others have turned to accounting maneuvers. Illinois is highlighted for using implicit debt financing by delaying payments to vendors and school districts, a strategy criticized by Fitch Ratings. New York is also singled out; despite Lieutenant Governor Richard Ravitch's failed proposal to directly finance the state's deficit in bond markets, New York's budget still relied on more than 2 billion dollars in deferred tax credits to local businesses and deferred pension fund contributions to create paper savings.

A final scatter plot, titled Escape from New York, compares states by plotting per capita personal taxes (sales, property, and income) on the y-axis from 2,000 to 7,000 dollars against per capita spending on the x-axis from 6,000 to 14,000 dollars using 2008 U.S. Census Bureau data. The plot shows New York as a severe outlier, with per capita spending near 13,000 dollars and per capita taxes exceeding 6,000 dollars. Other labeled states include Connecticut, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Hawaii, California, Delaware, and Wyoming, the latter of which has the highest per capita spending on the chart but lower per capita taxes than New York. The author concludes by noting that New York's corporate taxes per capita are also 25 percent higher than those of the next highest state, New Hampshire.

This analysis argues that the U.S. payroll report is significantly weaker than consensus estimates suggest, reinforcing the view that the economy is entering a prolonged "sideways" market transition rather than a standard recession-to-recovery phase. The author critiques the optimistic mid-2010 forecasts of rival firms and highlights structural weaknesses in income, manufacturing, and labor participation. 

The first chart, titled "Private sector payrolls hit a speed bump," displays the month-over-month net change in private payrolls from August 2009 through mid-2010. It contrasts actual net changes, which peaked in April 2010 before falling sharply, with the much higher May 2010 consensus estimates of 225,000 to 250,000 monthly gains through year-end projected by Bank of America/Merrill Lynch, JPMorgan, Deutsche Bank, Barclays, and ISI. 

The second chart, "Government transfers and tax cuts mitigate the decline in earned income," tracks income as a percentage of GDP from June 2000 to June 2010. It plots Earned Income—defined as employee compensation, proprietor's and rental income, and dividend and interest income—against Disposable Income, which adds government transfers and subtracts personal taxes and social insurance contributions.
