The data shows that while Disposable Income hovered around 78% to 80% by mid-2010, Earned Income plummeted from over 93% in 2000 to around 85% by 2010, underscoring that consumer spending has been heavily dependent on temporary fiscal policy rather than organic earnings.

A third chart, "A slowdown in manufacturing orders," illustrates a decline in economic momentum from July 2007 to July 2010. It compares "New Orders minus Production" against the "Orders/Inventory" ratio. Both indicators peaked in late 2009 and rolled over sharply by July 2010, pointing to slower production ahead and making aggressive payroll additions unlikely. 

To provide historical context for this sluggishness, the fourth chart, "Sideways: 1970s equity market wilderness," displays the real returns of the S&P 500 and the German DAX from 1972 to 1982, indexed to 100 in January 1972. During a decade-long "period of extreme monetary and fiscal uncertainty," both indices fluctuated wildly without making net gains—with the S&P 500 dipping as low as 60 in late 1974—before a sustained bull market finally commenced in 1982. Because of this parallel, the author advises investors to look to credit markets and long-short hedge funds rather than directional equity investments.

Finally, the page outlines the deeper problems within the payroll report. It details that temporary employment is on a downward trend, and labor income growth has faded from 5.3% in the first quarter of 2010 to just 2.3% in the third quarter. The college graduate labor participation rate has hit its lowest point since 1992, and the employment-to-population ratio stands at a near-cycle low of 58.4%. Crucially, the author asserts that if the labor participation rate were normalized, the true unemployment rate would sit between 12% and 13%, rather than the officially reported 9.5%. Additional weaknesses include anemic service sector growth, sharp state and local government job cuts, and three consecutive monthly drops in the household employment survey.

This page discusses the nature of the global profit recovery and evaluates economic conditions in both the United States and China. The author begins by arguing that the current corporate profit recovery is exceptionally reliant on declining labor costs, characterized by high productivity and low real wage growth, which should prevent equities from commanding high price-to-earnings multiples. 

To illustrate this, two charts based on data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis and the Bureau of Labor Statistics are featured at the top. The first chart shows the year-over-year percentage change of nominal GDP less unit labor costs from 1950 to 2010, with recessions shaded. The adjacent scatter plot, titled "A profit recovery exceptionally reliant on labor," maps nominal GDP growth against unit labor costs. It highlights the three most recent quarters as significant outliers, showing negative unit labor costs between negative four percent and negative six percent alongside positive nominal GDP growth, sitting well below the historical trend line for five percent profit combinations. 

Based on these observations, the author details implications for investment portfolios, recommending a defensive posture with an underweight position in equities, particularly in Europe. Conversely, they advise overweighting high-grade and high-yield credit, alongside macro and long-short hedge funds. Additionally, the author flags an upcoming discussion regarding European banks buying back hybrid securities that no longer qualify as Tier 1 Capital under Basel III regulations.

The second half of the page focuses on China under the header "China: slowing but not stumbling." The author argues that China is not overheating, which mitigates the risk of aggressive monetary tightening. While consumer prices have risen to 3.3 percent, this is attributed mainly to food prices, as ex-food consumer price index inflation remains below two percent. Property sector risks are also described as manageable; property sector lending accounts for only 19 percent of total bank loans, far below the 36 percent in Korea and 58 percent in the United States. Additionally, the aggregate loan-to-value ratio for 2010 Chinese home mortgages was a conservative 45 percent. 

This cooling trend is visualized in a chart titled "Inflationary pressures easing in China," spanning 2005 through 2010. The chart plots manufacturing input prices on the left axis using the purchasing managers' index, and the quarter-over-quarter percentage change of the Producer Price Index on the right axis. Both lines show a clear downward turn starting in early 2010, with manufacturing input prices falling from near 80 down toward 50, and the PPI rolling over from its six percent peak toward zero. The page concludes by highlighting that despite this deceleration, China continues to show strong growth in industrial production, capital spending, net exports, and retail sales, with overall output remaining well above pre-crisis levels.

This page analyzes whether Japanese Government Bonds (JGBs) are the short of a lifetime, concluding that while pressure is building, the moment has not yet arrived due to domestic demand dynamics. The author explains that falling private sector loan demand has left banks with excess deposits, which they use to purchase JGBs, mitigating the decline in direct household purchasing. This phenomenon is illustrated in the first chart, Excess deposits in the Japanese banking system, which plots deposit growth minus loan growth on a twelve-month rolling sum in trillion yen from June 2008 to June 2010. The chart shows excess deposits rising dramatically from negative ten trillion yen in late 2008 to nearly twenty-five trillion yen by mid-2010. 

Addressing whether the Japanese government has begun to direct-monetize its debt, the author notes that Bank of Japan holdings have risen only modestly in recent years. This is supported by the second chart, Bank of Japan holdings of government securities, which displays holdings from 1998 to 2010 in trillions of yen. The chart breaks down holdings into Japanese Government Bonds and Financing Bills plus Treasury Bills, showing combined holdings peaked around one hundred trillion yen in the early 2000s and have since plateaued at a lower level. However, quasi-sovereign entities like the Public Pension Fund (GPIF), Japan Post Bank, and Japan Post Insurance have heavily absorbed JGBs. This trend is captured in the third chart, Assets owned by three public institutions, which tracks assets from 1980 through late 2009. The stacked area chart reveals that these institutions hold over six hundred trillion yen in total assets, including a massive three hundred and ten trillion yen in JGBs and one hundred and sixty-two trillion yen in Fiscal Investment and Loan Program (FILP) investments. This forced mobilization of domestic savings has helped suppress bond yields.

Finally, the author questions the true scale of Japan’s debt, arguing that the country's reported net debt is a misleading measure of its real burden. The final chart, Net vs. gross debt as a percentage of GDP as of June 2010, compares ten countries: Japan, Italy, Belgium, the United States, France, Portugal, the United Kingdom, Canada, Germany, and Spain. While Japan's gross debt is the highest in the group at nearly two hundred percent of GDP, its net debt is reported at a much lower level of around one hundred and ten percent. The author argues this net figure is artificially low because the three hundred trillion yen in JGBs held by public entities offset actual obligations to private pensioners and depositors. Unless these entities renege on their obligations, these bonds must be factored into the net debt, meaning Japan's true fiscal burden is far more severe than official net figures indicate.

This page analyzes two major macroeconomic trends: the shifting balance of economic power from Japan to China, and the dichotomy in the United States between strong corporate earnings and weak GDP growth. 

Addressing the Asian markets, the author argues that Japan’s structural problems and deflation—with the latest measure around negative four percent—make any equity market rallies short-lived. In contrast, China has surpassed Japan to become the world’s second-largest economy. This shift is supported by two charts. The first, titled Land of the frequently setting sun, displays the quarterly total return of the Japan Topix index minus the S&P 500 total return from 1994 to 2010. The bar chart shows that periods of Japanese outperformance are brief, while periods of underperformance are deep and frequent, often dropping fifteen to twenty-five percent below the S&P 500. The second chart, titled The Sino-Eclipse, plots nominal GDP in USD billions from 1995 to 2010. It shows Japan's nominal GDP stagnating between four thousand and five thousand billion dollars, while China's nominal GDP rises steadily from under one thousand billion dollars to eclipse Japan's curve near the five thousand billion dollar mark around 2009. Consequently, J.P. Morgan maintains low exposure to Japan while adding to Asia-ex Japan exposures.

The second half of the page examines U.S. corporate profits versus broader economic growth. The author notes that U.S. equity markets are struggling with the contrast between six consecutive quarters of earnings exceeding expectations and a weakening outlook for GDP growth. This trend is illustrated by a chart titled Six quarters of positive earnings surprises, which compares estimated versus actual quarterly S&P 500 earnings per share from Q1 2009 to Q2 2010. In each quarter, actual corporate earnings, represented by brown bars, consistently beat estimates, represented by blue bars, climbing to over twenty dollars per share by the second quarter of 2010. 

A final chart, titled Evolution of Q2 2010 GDP estimates vs actual, tracks how economic forecasts deteriorated between October 2009 and August 2010. The consensus sixty-nine-firm composite estimate peaked at over three percent in early 2010 before falling to around two and a half percent at the first release. This is contrasted with J.P. Morgan's much lower current estimate of around one percent. An embedded table shows that major research providers held far more optimistic Q2 GDP estimates, led by Barclays Capital and Capital Economics at four point five percent, Deutsche Bank and MF Global at four percent, Credit Suisse and Morgan Stanley at three point eight percent, and State Street, Bank of America/Merrill Lynch, and the US Chamber of Commerce at three point seven percent. 

The author concludes that this corporate earnings recovery is uniquely reliant on low real wages and declining unit labor costs rather than robust economic expansion, as nominal GDP growth remains below four percent. Because this dynamic suppresses consumer spending to just over one percent, the author forecasts modest single-digit returns for equities, maintaining that while equities should outperform bonds, it represents a relatively low hurdle.

This J.P. Morgan commentary, written by Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest, argues that fiscal stimulus has failed to spark a durable private sector recovery, as positive growth spikes in 2009 and 2010 merely coincided with peaks in stimulus programs. With GDP growth rates hovering at or below two percent, developed economies face headwinds from consumer de-leveraging and historically high public debt. Cembalest expresses concern over this unscripted recovery, anticipating a prolonged sideways equity market. As a result, J.P. Morgan has shifted assets away from directional equities toward income-oriented corporate and commercial property strategies, as well as targeted hedge funds such as merger arbitrage and macro.

This sideways market thesis is supported by two comparative charts. The first chart, titled "Sideways, 1970's version," tracks the real returns of the S&P 500 and Germany's DAX from 1972 to 1982, using January 1972 as a base value of 100. It highlights a prolonged period of extreme monetary and fiscal uncertainty between late 1975 and late 1981, during which both indices stagnated or declined before a new bull market finally began in 1982. The second chart, "Sideways, 2010 version," compares the levels of the S&P 500 on the left axis (from 600 to 1,300) and the MSCI Europe/Far East (EAFE) index on the right axis (from 650 to 1,850) between September 2008 and September 2010. It illustrates that after a sharp rebound from early 2009 lows, both indices began trading in a horizontal, range-bound pattern starting in early 2010, validating J.P. Morgan's previously published sideways outlook.

Cembalest also reports on global policy confusion, characterizing the recent Jackson Hole central bank gathering as directionless. He criticizes China's announced exchange rate flexibility as political theater, pointing out that the Chinese renminbi has only appreciated 1.8 percent on an annualized basis since the announcement, and warns that competitive devaluations across the G3 nations could have negative consequences. 

Further detail is provided regarding contradictions in the ISM manufacturing survey, noting the largest discrepancy in 25 years between the strong top-line survey and weaker regional surveys. Although the ratio of corporate profits to employee hours is at a 50-year high and the ISM employment component is at its highest since 1983, actual payroll gains are only half of what economists expected six months prior. Lastly, he observes that unlike past post-war recessions where private debt grew or held steady, current consumers are actively de-leveraging with no sign of embarking on a re-leveraging phase. This page serves as an introduction to a broader summer 2010 review covering the Flash Crash, commodities, fixed income, and private equity.

This J.P. Morgan market commentary, titled "Summer Stock 2010," argues that the post-crisis economic recovery is structurally fragile, artificially supported by unprecedented government debt, and facing severe headwinds in housing and labor markets. The author cautions against relying on traditional cyclical recovery indicators and historical stock market patterns, such as the presidential election cycle, because current fiscal conditions are fundamentally unique. 

The analysis begins with the ongoing deleveraging of the private sector. A line chart tracking the year-over-year percentage change in non-financial credit shows that, for the first time since 1960, private credit growth collapsed into negative territory in 2009 and 2010, dropping to nearly negative four percent. The author notes that as household and corporate credit decline, the Fed will likely need to introduce more stimulus to combat deflation. 

To illustrate why normal cyclical dynamics do not apply, a bar chart compares the current recovery to historical periods since 1952. While the increase in the ISM manufacturing survey (at roughly 24 points) is comparable to past cycles, this recovery is unique due to its immense fiscal cost. The increase in Federal Debt to GDP through the end of 2010 is projected to rise by nearly 18 percent, whereas previous manufacturing recoveries bloom on their own with little to no federal debt accumulation. 

The report is highly skeptical of a housing recovery, pointing to a stacked bar chart of potential homes for sale. While existing inventory hovers around four million homes, it is doubled by an equivalent "shadow inventory" of foreclosures in process and homes that are over 90 days delinquent, pushing potential supply past seven million. With rental vacancies at their highest levels since 1956, the author expects housing prices to remain stagnant for a long time. 

Similarly, the corporate profit recovery is described as highly reliant on labor-cost cutting rather than top-line growth. A scatter plot of profit combinations since 1948 shows the last three quarters of 2010 clustered far from historical norms, characterized by very low nominal GDP growth of two to four percent paired with steeply negative unit labor costs of minus two to minus four percent. This trend of low real wages boosts profits but weakens consumer spending. 

Finally, the publication addresses the third year of the presidential election cycle, historically a period of strong equity gains. A bar chart of S&P 500 returns shows that the 12-month period following midterm elections has consistently produced positive returns, often exceeding 20 percent. However, a final bar chart shows that no other presidency since 1948 has faced fiscal headwinds like the Obama administration, where the federal debt-to-GDP ratio surged by nearly 20 percent from the inception of the presidency. Consequently, the author warns against trusting historical election-cycle parallels. The page concludes by noting that prominent calls for more fiscal stimulus by economists Paul Krugman and Joseph Stiglitz have faced substantial political opposition.

This page presents a series of six financial analyses and macroeconomic observations under the theme of "Summer Stock 2010." 

The first topic reviews equity valuations, noting that while equities seem inexpensive at a 12.4x price-to-earnings ratio based on consensus earnings, historical data indicates analysts are consistently over-optimistic outside of the 2004–2007 window. The author adjusts the realistic multiple closer to 14x. This argument is supported by a bar chart plotting the percentage change in analyst earnings estimates from the beginning to the end of the year for the S&P 500 universe from 1986 to 2010, which reveals that downward earnings estimate revisions—reaching nearly negative 25% in 2008—are much more common than positive revisions.

Turning to corporate health, the author argues that robust corporate cash flow supports credit portfolios despite lower GDP growth raising questions about equity multiples. A dual-axis line chart tracking the non-financial corporate sector from 1970 to 2010 depicts a high return on tangible assets on the left axis alongside an exceptionally strong free cash flow yield on the right axis, which spiked to around 9% in late 2008 and remained elevated near 7% through 2010.

The third analysis focuses on capital expenditures, observing that in 2009, US capital spending on equipment and software fell below the depreciation rate for the first time in the post-WWII era, indicating significant pent-up demand. This trend is shown via a line chart of year-over-year percentage changes in US capital stock from 1950 to 2010. The chart illustrates a historic plunge to negative year-over-year rates of about negative 1% in late 2009, with a partial recovery estimated for 2010.

Next, the publication advocates for maintaining a small allocation in venture capital, pointing out that innovation and patent filings are historically resilient to recessions. A chart spanning 1963 to 2008 plots US patent filings against gray recession bars. The line representing patent filings climbs steadily from around 100,000 in the early 1960s to nearly 500,000 by 2008, moving upward virtually uninterrupted by economic contractions.

The analysis then shifts to municipal credit, warning that spending in New York has been out of control since the second George Pataki administration, prompting a massive population exodus. Investors are advised to diversify away from concentrated New York municipal bond portfolios. This fiscal stress is illustrated in a scatter plot comparing state personal taxes per capita against spending per capita as of 2008. New York stands out near the top right, combining exceptionally high per capita spending of over $11,000 with high per capita taxes of over $6,000, contrasted against states like Connecticut, New Jersey, and Wyoming.

Finally, the author addresses the federal budget debate, asserting that proposed tax increases on wealthy individuals will not significantly close the fiscal gap, and that more fundamental tax changes like a value-added tax (VAT) will be necessary. A bar chart comparing cumulative projections for 2010 to 2019 shows that the cumulative 10-year Office of Management and Budget deficit is projected at nearly $9 trillion, while a hypothetical 5% tax increase on high earners would generate less than $1 trillion in cumulative revenues over the same period.

This J.P. Morgan research report focuses on market structure vulnerabilities following the Flash Crash, corporate cash accumulation driving mergers and acquisitions, and the divergence between Chinese economic growth and its equity market performance. 

The first section addresses market stability, noting that high-frequency traders account for seventy percent of all trades and ninety-seven percent of all orders are cancelled rather than executed. A bar chart based on TABB Group data shows that confidence in competition among exchanges supporting a liquid and orderly market dropped from around forty-seven percent in September 2009 to twenty-seven percent in May 2010. Accompanying this is a line chart plotting the ratio of cancelled to executed orders from 2002 to 2009, demonstrating a steep rise from around ten in 2002 to over thirty by late 2009, illustrating how high-frequency trading drives cancellations.

The second section highlights that corporations are holding significant cash reserves, which are beginning to be redeployed into capital expenditures, dividends, and mergers. A historical line chart tracking nonfinancial corporate liquid assets to tangible assets from 1950 to 2010 reveals that cash balances as a percentage of tangible assets peaked near thirteen percent in 2010, matching levels last seen in the low-rate environment of the 1950s. Concurrently, a dual-axis chart shows rising merger and acquisition activity from 2000 to 2010. This chart tracks the average premium on the left-hand scale, which fluctuated between twenty percent and thirty-five percent, alongside the number of deals on the right-hand scale, which bottomed near four thousand five hundred in late 2009 before rising.

The final section explores the rise of the Chinese middle class. A bar chart comparing total middle-class consumption in USD billions on a 2005 purchasing power parity basis shows that while Chinese middle-class consumption was a fraction of the United States' four point three trillion dollar level in 2009, it is projected to reach parity with the United States by 2020. Despite this massive growth, the author cautions that Chinese equities are a poor proxy for this expansion due to the heavy index weights of banks, utilities, and state-owned enterprises. This disconnect is illustrated in a scatter plot comparing annualized nominal GDP growth against annualized equity market performance from 2003 to 2010 for various emerging markets. China is circled as an outlier, experiencing stellar GDP growth of approximately twenty percent but yielding a comparatively weak equity market return of only ten percent. By contrast, countries like Peru, Colombia, and Brazil produced equity returns between thirty-five and forty percent despite having lower annualized GDP growth rates between ten and fifteen percent.

This page, titled "Summer Stock 2010" by Michael Cembalest, presents a diverse collection of brief market commentaries, economic charts, and a personal update. 

On the top left, the author focuses on fiscal sustainability, asserting that the present value of future unfunded entitlement obligations is ten times the size of current public debt and larger than the real-term cost of all American wars combined since the Revolution. An accompanying bar chart titled "Unfunded entitlement obligations dwarf existing public debt in the U.S...." contrasts these figures in trillions of USD. The chart shows current public debt at approximately 10 trillion USD, while the present value of future entitlement shortfalls looms far higher at roughly 60 trillion USD. The graphic features a classic quote from the comic strip character Pogo: "We have met the enemy, and he is us."

On the top right, the author analyzes the investment appeal of gold. He argues that gold’s valuation remains low relative to other financial assets when compared to prior historical periods of high monetary and fiscal anxiety, predicting that gold will continue to rise as the Federal Reserve approaches its second round of quantitative easing (QE2). A chart titled "Value of investible gold relative to global financial assets" plots this metric as a percentage. In 1982, investible gold accounted for roughly 16.5% of global financial assets, whereas in 2009, it stood at only about 4.5%, highlighting significant potential room for growth.

On the bottom left, the commentary shifts to corporate credit, noting that favorable credit markets have allowed private equity-backed leveraged buyout (LBO) companies to extend their debt maturities and avoid near-term defaults. The column chart, "Improving debt profile for '06-'07 vintage private equity," displays the percentage change in debt maturity by year compared to a March 2009 baseline for a composite of 43 companies. The data reveals a substantial reduction in immediate refinancing risks, with near-term maturities declining by nearly 40% for 2011, 28% for 2012, and 18% for 2013. Correspondingly, long-term maturities pushed out to 2017 and 2018+ increased by approximately 42% and 48% respectively, showing how companies successfully pushed their debt maturities further into the future.

Finally, the bottom right contains a personal update and note of thanks from the author. He shares that his oldest son underwent successful spinal surgery in July, reducing his spinal curvature from 60 degrees to 20.7 degrees to lower the risk of future pulmonary complications. He expresses gratitude to J.P. Morgan clients who shared their own advice and experiences. Two X-ray images are displayed side-by-side to visually demonstrate the before-and-after correction of the spine using corrective rods and screws.

This visual-heavy page from J.P. Morgan's Summer Stock 2010 publication features six charts and accompanying commentary examining global macroeconomic imbalances, European fiscal adjustments, bank funding, and historical monetary regimes. 

The first section analyzes the rise of China as it overtakes Japan to become the world's second-largest economy. A chart titled The Sino-Eclipse plots nominal GDP in USD billions from March 1995 to March 2009, illustrating China's steep upward trajectory as it catches up to Japan's stagnant GDP line around the five thousand billion dollar level. To highlight the scale of global imbalances, a second chart, Chinese reserve accumulation: unprecedented, tracks FX reserves as a percentage of GDP over a twenty-one-year horizon. It compares China from 1990 to 2009 against post-war Germany and Japan from 1955 to 1975. While the European and Japanese historical precedents peaked below two percent of GDP, China's reserve accumulation is shown skyrocketing to over eleven percent of GDP.

The middle portion of the page shifts focus to Europe and fiscal discipline. The author notes that the G-I-P-S countries (Greece, Ireland, Portugal, and Spain) are attempting a difficult adjustment of fiscal tightening during low growth without the cushion of currency devaluation. This challenge is visualized in the chart Fiscal adjustments, then and now, which plots GDP growth against currency devaluation percentage. Prior adjustments from 1975 to 2000 are represented by yellow bubbles, showing they frequently benefited from currency devaluations or higher baseline growth. In contrast, the 2010 EMU fiscal adjustments are represented by orange bubbles concentrated in a zone of zero devaluation and low-to-negative GDP growth. Next to this, a chart titled German GDP growth, best since reunification plots quarter-over-quarter seasonally adjusted annual rate growth from 1991 to 2010. It highlights a sharp rebound to nine percent in the second quarter of 2010, though the commentary cautions that this export-led growth provides limited benefits to the rest of the European Monetary Union.

The bottom section of the page addresses banking sector health and historical monetary lessons. A chart showing the Loan-to-deposit ratio of banks by region illustrates the median, lower, and upper quartiles for Western Europe, the United States, and Japan. Western Europe is shown to have a significantly higher median ratio of approximately 1.3, highlighting its vulnerability and heavy reliance on wholesale funding markets compared to the United States and Japan. Finally, the page draws a parallel between modern currency constraints and the Great Depression in a chart titled The earlier a country exited the gold standard, the higher its industrial production. Using an index where 1929 equals 100, the chart plots industrial production from 1929 to 1937 for Japan, the United Kingdom, Germany, the United States, and France, marking each nation's year of gold standard exit. The data shows that early exiters in 1931, like Japan, experienced the strongest industrial recoveries, climbing to nearly 170 on the index by 1937, while late exiters like France in 1936 lagged severely.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, titled "By Any Means Necessary," evaluates the rumors and potential consequences of aggressive government intervention through monetary and fiscal policies. The commentary analyzes the prospect of further quantitative easing by the Federal Reserve, with potential programs ranging from $100 billion per month to a total of $1.5 trillion. While the Fed's goal in lowering Treasury rates is to spur equity investing and allow mortgage refinancing, the author notes that around 40% of mortgages are already underwater, a figure expected to rise as home prices decline by an estimated 5% to 8% in the coming months. To maximize QE, policymakers might try to extend credit to these underwater borrowers. Footnotes emphasize that investors have not yet embraced equities, noting that institutional pension funds hold their lowest equity weights since the mid-1990s, and retail investors have pulled money from US equity mutual funds in 19 of the past 20 weeks. Furthermore, if the Fed purchases another $1 trillion in bonds, central banks would own over 60% of all outstanding U.S. Treasuries. 

In terms of fiscal policy, the author discusses a potential compromise on the Bush tax cuts that permanently extends middle-class tax cuts while extending the top two brackets for one to two years, preventing a $100 billion annual drag on disposable income in 2011. Although durable goods orders remain strong, the author cautions that the U.S. is experiencing its lowest private sector money supply growth since the 1930s, at just 1% to 2%, signaling very low nominal GDP growth. 

Addressing the market and portfolio outlook, the author compares the rumored "All-In" intervention strategies to a risky game of Texas Hold 'Em. While a stimulus-driven rally could support J.P. Morgan's high-single-digit return view for global equities, the author warns that such actions debase cash, the dollar, and government bonds. To illustrate the global scale of currency intervention, the page lists the massive sums printed by central banks since January 2008 to purchase government bonds and prevent exchange rate adjustments, including 1.2 trillion U.S. dollars, 132 billion British pounds, 183 billion Swiss francs, 6.6 trillion Chinese RMB, 7.6 trillion Japanese yen, 115 billion Brazilian reais, 825 billion Hong Kong dollars, 486 billion Saudi riyals, 3.2 trillion Taiwan dollars, and 1.9 trillion Thai baht. This monetary expansion is linked to comments by Brazilian Finance Minister Guido Mantega, who described the situation as an "international currency war" featuring "Weapons of Mass Devaluation" to preserve the "Chimerica" relationship first detailed by Niall Ferguson and Moritz Schularick. 

The page features a historical black-and-white political cartoon from the Civil War era titled "RUNNING THE 'MACHINE'." It depicts President Abraham Lincoln and his cabinet members actively running a printing press to crank out greenback paper money, satirizing the government's historical recourse to inflation and money printing during times of crisis.

This page explores investment opportunities in bank consolidation, focusing on the historical and modern role of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) in managing failed institutions. It opens with insights from Bill Seidman, the former Chairman of the Resolution Trust Corporation (RTC) during the 1990 savings and loan crisis, who emphasized that failed bank assets lose value under government management, large inventories depress market prices, and low upfront pricing is crucial to attract private buyers. The success of this philosophy is demonstrated by the 1993 Brazos Partners and Mountain AMD partnerships, which managed $4 billion in distressed assets and generated a 25% internal rate of return on taxpayer equity. 

In the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, the page analyzes BankUnited, which underwent FDIC intervention in the spring of 2009. Acquirers purchased its $12.8 billion in assets and $8.3 billion in deposits at an estimated 23% purchase discount, supported by an FDIC loss-sharing arrangement covering 80% to 95% of losses. This structure helped BankUnited quickly improve its Tier 1 capital ratio to 10% and generate net income equal to 33% of the buyer's investment.

The narrative notes a clear shift toward less generous FDIC terms as the banking sector stabilized. According to Keefe, Bruyette & Woods (KBW), average purchase discounts on assets fell to approximately 10% by late 2010, down from the 23% level seen with IndyMac and BankUnited, and down from a 14% average in calendar year 2009. In some cases, optimistic acquirers like First Merit and Toronto Dominion paid no discount at all due to perceived franchise expansion potential. 

This trend is illustrated in a chart titled "Premium/discount paid for FDIC asset dispositions as a percent of assets, December 2008 - September 2010." The chart features a horizontal time axis from January 2009 to August 2010 and a vertical axis measuring the premium or discount from negative 50% to positive 10%. Individual blue diamonds represent 211 disclosed FDIC dispositions with assets over $100 million, while a red trend line traces the monthly average. The visualization highlights IndyMac and BankUnited near the negative 23% mark in early 2009, demonstrating how monthly average discounts peaked in mid-to-late 2009 before steadily rising and stabilizing near the negative 10% level by late 2010.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" argues for a structural overweight in Asian equities relative to European equities, while explaining why private equity is often a superior vehicle to public markets for capturing Chinese economic growth. The author points to stronger growth, lower public debt, lower corporate taxes, and superior innovation in Asia—noting that patent filings in China and Japan are five times higher than in Europe. 

The first chart, "Price to book ratios, Developed vs Emerging Markets," covers the years 2000 through 2010. It shows that developed market price-to-book valuations have fallen from a peak of around 4.0 in 2000 to approximately 1.8 in 2010, converging with emerging markets, which fluctuated between roughly 1.2 and 2.8 over the decade and ended in the 1.8 to 2.0 range. This valuation convergence suggests emerging markets are not overbought. The second chart, "Portfolio allocations to Emerging markets equities," highlights that while emerging markets represent roughly 26% of total global equities by MSCI market capitalization and 13% by free float, institutional and retail surveys from Goldman Sachs, Bank of America Merrill Lynch, Pensions & Investments, and Morningstar show actual portfolio allocations are significantly underweight, ranging from just 5% to 8%.

The page then transitions to China, explaining that Chinese public equity markets have been a poor proxy for the nation's economic expansion. The scatter plot "Equity markets vs. GDP growth - 2003 to the present" compares annualized USD equity market performance on the vertical axis against annualized nominal USD GDP growth on the horizontal axis. China is a clear outlier, achieving a high annualized nominal GDP growth of around 18% but yielding a relatively modest annualized equity market return of about 15%. This underperformance lags far behind countries like Peru, Colombia, and Brazil, which delivered much higher equity returns despite lower nominal GDP growth. The author attributes this to the heavy concentration of financials, energy, and state-owned enterprises in public Chinese indices, which leaves the most entrepreneurial and consumer-driven aspects of the economy underrepresented.

A second bottom chart, "Chinese capital formation eclipses prior industrializations," plots capital formation as a percentage of GDP. It shows that China’s capital formation rate from 1981 to 2009 soared to nearly 45%, far exceeding the historic investment peaks of other industrializing nations, including Japan from 1960 to 1988, Korea from 1978 to 2006, and Germany from 1954 to 1982. This massive capital deployment is characterized as a "mixed blessing" that may not translate directly to equity shareholder profits.

To bypass these limitations, J.P. Morgan advocates for Asian private equity, a sector they began investing in during 2006. The investment strategy focuses heavily on the rapid rise of the Chinese middle class. Because consumer-related stocks make up only about 5% of the MSCI China index, private equity managers target privately held companies in sectors that consumers need but currently lack, such as high-end retail, consumer staples, food safety and certification, healthcare, medical equipment, and water treatment. Furthermore, instead of focusing on saturated tier-one cities like Beijing and Shanghai, these private equity investments target fast-growing middle-tier cities with average populations of 6 million and rising disposable incomes, specifically highlighting regions such as Guizhou, Hunan, Henan, Sichuan, and Hubei.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication, titled "AEIOU: Asia, Equities, Intervention, Opium and Unsustainability," discusses the mechanics and geopolitical debates surrounding China's currency intervention and reserve accumulation strategy. The author examines the argument posited by economists Niall Ferguson and Morris Schularick, who suggest that China's willingness to fund American debt suppressed US long-term interest rates and ultimately fueled the mid-2000s housing bubble. The author counters this theory by pointing out that China's trade surplus with the US did not accelerate significantly until after 2004, following the Federal Reserve’s decision to lower interest rates to 1%. Furthermore, the author argues that the trade imbalance is primarily a reflection of US consumption habits rather than systemic currency manipulation.

Two charts at the top of the page illustrate these dynamics. The left chart, "Foreign exchange reserve accumulation," plots an index from December 2007 through June 2010 for several Asian nations, setting the baseline at 100. It demonstrates that reserve accumulation was widespread across the region, with Thailand, Hong Kong, and China leading the trend by reaching index levels between 165 and 175 by mid-2010. Other nations, including Singapore, Indonesia, Taiwan, and the Philippines, also accumulated reserves steadily, while Korea experienced a sharp drop in late 2008 before recovering. The right chart, "China trade balance with the US and rest of world," shows China's trade surplus in billions of USD from 1995 to 2009. The data reveals that China's trade surplus with the US grew exponentially after 2001, climbing from roughly $50 billion to over $250 billion in 2008, whereas its trade surplus with the rest of the world remained comparatively modest, peaking near $100 billion before declining.

The text then addresses the prospects of Chinese currency revaluation. Highlighting quotes from domestic media, the author explains that China is reluctant to rapidly appreciate the renminbi (RMB) due to fears of harming export competitiveness and risking millions of manufacturing jobs. Additionally, Chinese leadership views the appreciation of the Japanese Yen following the 1985 Plaza Accord as the catalyst for Japan’s subsequent multi-decade economic stagnation. While the RMB appreciated by 2.3% against the US dollar after China announced greater exchange rate flexibility in June 2010, it remained down on a trade-weighted basis against all currencies. 

At the bottom of the page, a third chart titled "Germany & Japan: cumulative currency valuation vs USD" tracks historical currency appreciations from 1957 to 1980. The data shows Germany’s cumulative appreciation rising to nearly 60% and Japan's exceeding 40% during the 1970s. An accompanying callout box notes that the RMB's 20% appreciation against the US dollar since 2005 puts China approximately halfway to the historical appreciation levels experienced by Germany and Japan. Footnotes provide additional context, detailing how Japan's policymakers incorrectly assumed a stronger Yen would safely stimulate domestic consumption, which instead triggered a devastating asset bubble and long-term economic decline.

This page analyzes current global market conditions, focusing on the U.S. equity rally, policy signals from China, and a deep-dive historical perspective on India's growth. The author opens by discussing the U.S. equity market, which is heading toward J.P. Morgan's 2010 year-end target of 1175 to 1225 on the S&P 500. While corporate profits are beating expectations, the author attributes the rally to expectations surrounding the Federal Reserve's second round of quantitative easing, noting that the rally was catalyzed by Ben Bernanke's Jackson Hole speech in August. To illustrate this relationship, a dual-axis line chart tracks the 10-year Treasury rate against the S&P 500 from November 2009 to September 2010, demonstrating how the Treasury rally coincided with a falling equity market until the speech, after which weak economic data fueled both falling yields and rising stock prices. A secondary bar chart shows year-end S&P 500 projections from various financial institutions as of May 2010, placing J.P. Morgan Private Bank's conservative forecast of 1,175 to 1,225 on the lower end of the industry spectrum, with other firms like Deutsche Bank projecting as high as 1,375. 

Turning to China, the author highlights a shift in policy rhetoric, where a recent Party communiqué emphasized "economic development" thirteen times while mentioning "economic growth" only twice. This shift, along with the exclusion of real estate and autos from listed leading industries, signals a gradual transition toward domestic consumption and a smaller trade surplus. 

The lower half of the page details J.P. Morgan's positive stance on India, noting that ten out of thirteen emerging market managers on their platform are overweight the country. Although China has shown superior growth dynamics, the author argues that India offers attractive long-term potential, especially regarding corporate profitability. This argument is supported by a line chart of India's real per capita GDP in constant 2000 USD from 1960 to 2008. The chart reveals a distinct turning point: under the Nehru/Gandhi economic model from 1960 to 1991, per capita GDP grew slowly at a 2.7% compound annual growth rate, whereas the subsequent Rao reforms accelerated growth to a 4.7% compound annual growth rate. An accompanying text box details the restrictive features of the Nehru/Gandhi model from 1947 to 1991, which was characterized by heavy central economic planning where state-owned enterprises made up 39% of gross investment but only 14% of GDP, high import tariffs averaging 87% in 1990, strict industrial licensing requiring 80 separate permits to start a firm, the nationalization of banks in 1970, and severe restrictions on foreign ownership.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" provides a comparative analysis of India and China, focusing on India's efforts to catch up on infrastructure and trade, as well as the reasons behind the superior performance of Indian equity markets. The author notes that while India suffers from low agricultural productivity (one third of China’s) and high electricity losses (such as a 25% loss in 2006 and a 34% un-monetized power rate in 2007 due to theft or leakage), it is aggressively working to close its infrastructure gap. The Indian government projected a $1 trillion infrastructure spend for its 2012–2017 Plan, though it faces a steep 55% average cost overrun rate that it must address to keep private capital engaged. 

The first chart, titled "India has been closing the infrastructure gap," plots fixed investment as a percentage of GDP from 1990 to 2010. The y-axis ranges from 20% to 45%. It illustrates China’s sustained high investment, hovering between 35% and 44%, while India’s investment rate rose steadily from approximately 23% in 2002 to nearly 38% by 2007 before slightly easing, demonstrating a significant narrowing of the gap. 

The second chart, "Progress on trade and capital account," displays a bar chart of the percent of GDP from 2000 to 2008. Blue bars represent "Exports and imports," which steadily climbed from roughly 25% to over 45% of GDP. Brown bars show "Capital inflows and outflows," which spiked dramatically from single-digit percentages in the early 2000s to nearly 60% of GDP by 2008, indicating India's growing integration into global financial markets. 

The second half of the page shifts to Indian equity markets and investments, arguing that GDP growth does not always translate directly into equity gains, as shown by India’s outperformance of China over most timeframes. This divergence is attributed to India’s market reforms, including deregulating petrol prices, lifting licensing constraints, encouraging foreign direct investment (FDI), and permitting up to 74% foreign ownership in telecommunications. 

A table titled "China & India equity returns" details annualized percentage returns for China's Shenzhen index versus India’s Sensex index as of September 30, 2010. India consistently outperformed China across almost all listed horizons: year-to-date (22% for India vs. -3% for China), 3 years (6% vs. -8%), 7 years (26% vs. 19%), 10 years (19% vs. 7%), and since 1993 (12% vs. 9%). The sole exception was the 5-year period, where China led with 34% compared to India's 20%. 

A primary catalyst for this outperformance was a massive tariff reduction, illustrated in the line chart titled "Customs duty collection." This chart tracks collections as a percentage of imports on a y-axis from 0% to 60% between 1970 and 2006. It shows India's tariff rates peaking above 50% in the late 1980s before dropping precipitously to under 10% by 2006, converging toward China’s historically lower tariff levels. The author concludes that India's market-exposed corporate sector enjoys superior profitability and margins, yielding an average return on equity of approximately 18% over the preceding 15 years.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the surprising strength of corporate profits and profit margins in the United States despite weak economic growth. He argues that while quantitative easing (QE2) and midterm election results were anticipated, the resilience of corporate earnings in a weak-GDP environment is unexpected. This profitability is being supported by international revenues—which account for 30% of S&P revenues—aggressive cost control, particularly labor cost reductions, and government transfer payments that are supporting household consumption. 

A scatter plot titled "Profit growth outpacing GDP growth" maps year-over-year S&P 500 profit growth against year-over-year nominal GDP growth from 1978 to 2010. While profits typically decline when GDP growth is weak, the highlighted red data points for 2010 show an anomaly: corporate profit growth is surging between 30% and 50% even as nominal GDP growth languishes between 0% and 3%. Meanwhile, a line chart titled "Profit margins near historical highs" displays S&P 500 Net Operating Margins from 1979 to 2010. Combining historical data for S&P Industrials and S&P 500 margins, the visual shows a range of 3% to 9%, with the 2010 full-year estimate pointing to margins nearing a peak of approximately 9%. Rising commodity prices pose a threat to some low-margin sectors like apparel, consumer staples, furniture, machinery, airlines, and waste management, though energy and industrial commodities represent only 7% of total input costs for the median industry. 

The underlying support for consumer spending is examined in a line chart titled "Government transfers to households," which tracks these transfers as a percentage of disposable income from 1960 to 2010. The chart illustrates a dramatic, unprecedented spike beginning around 2008, reaching an all-time high of nearly 18% in 2010. Cembalest notes that these transfers are temporarily propping up middle-class consumer demand but warns that such fiscal support is unsustainable. To sustain growth, the recovery must shift to corporate investment. A line chart titled "Corporate cash balances at their highest levels" shows the ratio of nonfinancial corporate liquid assets to tangible assets from 1950 to 2010. Liquid assets have surged from a low of roughly 4.5% in the early 1980s to nearly 15% by 2010, indicating that corporations have ample cash to fund capital expenditure. 

Unlike the last three recessions, housing and commercial property construction will not lead the economic recovery due to severe oversupply in both sectors. While corporations have the cash to drive a stronger economic recovery, Cembalest poses the open question of whether CEOs will choose to deploy it. He suggests that weak consumer demand—rather than political headwinds like EPA regulations, healthcare reform, cap-and-trade, or unionization rules—is holding them back, and he doubts the Republican takeover of the House will serve as an economic inflection point. Despite these concerns, J.P. Morgan remains comfortable with its equity holdings, spread across active managers, exchange-traded funds, private equity, and hedge funds, due to low valuations, such as a 13x price-to-earnings ratio, though portfolios remain modestly less equity-reliant than in previous recoveries.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest analyzes the rhetoric of the 2010 midterms and evaluates what "ending big government" would actually require, given the structural realities of the federal budget and extreme political polarization. To contextualize federal spending, a pie chart titled "United States government expenditures, 2010" illustrates that mandatory commitments and defense consume three-quarters of the budget. Specifically, Social Security accounts for 20%, Medicare and Medicaid 19%, defense 21%, interest payments 12%, and unemployment benefits 4%. The remaining 24%, labeled as "Other," comprises discretionary spending and the administrative costs of mandatory programs. Cembalest argues that even if this entire "Other" category were completely eliminated, the nation would still run a budget deficit of 3.5% of GDP. Consequently, "ending big government" must mean either deep cuts to narrow discretionary programs, substantial reductions in defense or entitlement spending, a highly unlikely bipartisan strategy to achieve 4% to 5% real GDP growth, or a politically symbolic but economically insignificant $100 billion spending cut, which aligns with the actual Republican pledge.

Bipartisan solutions are rendered highly improbable by a historic rise in political division, which is depicted in a line graph titled "Party polarization at an all-time high." This graph measures the degree of partisanship and distance between the parties based on Congressional roll calls from 1879 to 2009. Both the House (red line) and the Senate (blue line) show party polarization returning to near-record heights last observed in the late 19th century, following a mid-20th-century low point around the 1950s and 1960s.

Finally, Cembalest examines the 2010 midterm results, in which the House experienced a massive swing. A line graph tracks the rolling five-year volatility of US GDP from 1900 to 2010, overlaid with historical House of Representatives seat shifts of greater than 60 seats. Red squares denote Republican gains, while blue circles indicate Democratic gains. The chart shows that such dramatic swings were common during the economically volatile pre-war era, including a 62-seat Republican gain in 1914 following the party's reunification, a 62-seat Republican gain in 1920 in reaction to Woodrow Wilson's international policies, a 76-seat Democratic swing in 1922 following the Teapot Dome scandal, a 97-seat Democratic landslide in 1932 amid the Great Depression, and an 81-seat Republican gain in 1938 driven by New Deal fatigue. After 1948, when Harry Truman's coattails helped Democrats gain 75 seats, such massive shifts ceased until 2010, where early estimates pointed to a 64-seat Republican gain. Cembalest posits that as economic volatility persists, these major political swings may once again become a regular feature of American politics.

This page analyzes two major regional developments: the severe economic and military imbalances of North Korea and signs of economic overheating in China, along with a brief note on the United States consumer outlook.

The author argues that North Korea operates outside conventional logic as a heavily militarized, totalitarian state that remains a persistent drag on South Korean and regional equity valuations. Despite frequent predictions of an unavoidable collapse, the regime has demonstrated surprising staying power, making accidental military escalation a distinct risk. 

Three charts illustrate North Korea’s extreme situation. First, a chart on per capita GDP from 1950 to 2008 shows a massive divergence: while North Korea's per capita GDP stagnated near zero, South Korea's soared to nearly $20,000. Second, a comparison of military expenditures as a percentage of GDP reveals North Korea spends an estimated 30% to 35% of its GDP on its military, compared to roughly 4% or less for China, the United States, Russia, South Korea, Germany, and Japan. Third, the troop-to-population ratio among the four largest armies shows North Korea’s ratio is near 4.5%, while China, the United States, and India are all well below 1%.

Turning to China, the author observes that the economy is heating up, making its currency peg increasingly difficult to defend, especially in the wake of the Federal Reserve's QE2 stimulus. Inflation and real estate activity are rising rapidly, with consumer price satisfaction surveys indicating that citizens view inflation as a more severe issue than official CPI figures suggest. 

Two charts depict this Chinese overheating. A chart on year-over-year Chinese CPI from 2005 to 2010 reveals that inflation is predominantly driven by food prices, which reached a growth rate of over 20% in late 2007 and are climbing back toward 10% in 2010, while non-food inflation remains flat, just above 0%. A second chart tracking China’s property market via a 5-day moving average of residential units sold from October 2009 to October 2010 shows that sales in Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen are heating up again. In Shanghai, sales rebounded from a low of about 200 units in mid-2010 back toward 800 units by October.

Because food constitutes 32% of Chinese CPI, the government is responding with historical tactics, such as releasing food reserves, cracking down on hoarding, reducing industrial power and rail costs, increasing oil production, and hiking commodity futures margin requirements. 

In a brief footnote on the United States, the author notes that while private payroll gains are expected to range from 150,000 to 200,000 per month, overall holiday sales are anticipated to rise 2% to 3% compared to 2009, even though Black Friday sales grew by only 0.3%.

This page analyzes the divergence between a reviving "Core Europe," led by Germany, and the struggling Eurozone periphery, highlighting the fundamental monetary policy dilemma this creates for the European Central Bank. The author argues that setting a single monetary policy is exceptionally difficult when Germany is overheating while peripheral nations are trapped in severe economic downturns. 

To support the assertion of Germany's economic strength, the top of the page features two charts. The first, "German unemployment rate: lowest in 20 years," plots the unemployment rate as a percentage of the labor force from 1992 to 2010. It shows unemployment peaking near 11.5% in 2005 before steadily declining to a 20-year low below 8% in 2010. The second chart, "German manufacturers reporting labor shortages," shows the percentage of firms listing labor shortages as a production-limiting factor from 1985 to late 2009. This measure spiked sharply toward 6% in 2010, underscoring tight labor market conditions.

The commentary contrasts Germany's boom with the periphery, drawing a historical parallel to the 1992 collapse of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM). This historical precedent is illustrated in the chart "1992 collapse of prior monetary union (ERM)," which indexes the currencies of Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Italy, and Greece from 1990 to 1996 (January 1990 = 100). The chart shows that following the 1992 ERM collapse—triggered when the UK needed weaker monetary policy than an overheating, post-unification Germany—the currencies of the periphery weakened significantly, dropping to index values between 50 and 80 by 1996, with Greece experiencing the steepest devaluation.

The page then focuses on the difficulty of imposing fiscal austerity without the cushion of currency devaluation. The bubble chart "Fiscal adjustments, then and now" plots GDP growth (y-axis, -1.0% to 4.0%) against currency devaluation (x-axis, 0% to 100%). Yellow bubbles represent historical European and Latin American adjustments between 1975 and 2000, most of which benefited from significant currency devaluations and positive GDP growth. In contrast, the orange bubbles representing the 2010 EMU fiscal adjustments sit at 0% devaluation with negative or near-zero growth. The author emphasizes that large fiscal adjustments in such a low-growth, no-devaluation environment are nearly unprecedented. 

The final section examines Ireland's compounding troubles. The line chart "Irish austerity chasing its tail" plots Irish government expenditures and tax receipts in billions of euros from 1999 to 2010. While expenditures climbed steadily from €25 billion to over €70 billion, tax receipts peaked at approximately €68 billion in 2007 before plummeting to around €53 billion by 2010, widening the deficit. The author asserts that Irish austerity measures have triggered a vicious cycle of lower growth and lower tax revenues. Furthermore, the Irish bank bailout is projected to cost 8 to 10 times more relative to its economy than the US TARP program, leading the author to conclude that the "Irish Bailout" is functionally a rescue of European banks and the ECB at the expense of Irish taxpayers.

This page serves as an introductory letter and foreword from Mary Callahan Erdoes, the Chief Executive Officer of J.P. Morgan Asset Management, welcoming readers to the outlook publication. Erdoes reflects on the mixed macroeconomic signals of the past year, contrasting negative headwinds like the European sovereign debt crisis, contracting housing markets, and high unemployment against positive indicators such as record corporate profits and strong growth in emerging markets. Looking ahead, she introduces Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest, noting his recent work collaborating with investment leaders worldwide to construct a comprehensive view of the global macroeconomic landscape for 2011. The introductory note, which concludes with Erdoes's signature, emphasizes the firm's commitment to guiding clients through both exciting investment opportunities and areas requiring caution.

This page presents a 2010 year-end market wrap-up analyzing the accuracy of J.P. Morgan's prior outlook, the performance of various asset classes, and the current asset allocation of their model portfolios. The author notes that while many of their 2010 predictions proved correct—including rising US equities, emerging markets outperforming the US, lagging European equities, and positive returns for commodities like gold, copper, and oil—they missed key inflection points on the Euro/USD exchange rate and underestimated the Bank of Japan's intervention to weaken the Yen. Their biggest missed trend was the massive rally in long-duration government bonds, which was bolstered by QE2 and $1.7 trillion in foreign exchange reserve accumulations by emerging market central banks during 2009 and 2010. Additionally, the author notes that while macro, event-driven, and credit hedge funds performed well, statistical arbitrage and general market-neutral strategies continued to struggle.

Two charts illustrate these market dynamics. The first, a bar chart titled "From May EoTM: Most 2010 S&P forecasts too high given public sector problems," displays S&P 500 forecasts across major Wall Street firms. It shows that J.P. Morgan Private Bank's conservative forecast of 1,175 to 1,225 (represented by a bar at 1,200) was highly accurate compared to peers like Citi at 1,175, Goldman Sachs at 1,270, and Deutsche Bank at a much higher 1,375. The second line chart, titled "Market-neutral hedge fund strategies continue to struggle, even against a zero benchmark, Percent," compares the HFRI market-neutral index to 3-month Treasury Bills from December 2004 to December 2010. The chart shows that after peaking in late 2007 near 122%, the market-neutral index declined sharply in 2008 and has since flatlined, failing to show recovery and barely keeping pace with near-zero T-bill returns by late 2010.

The bottom of the page outlines J.P. Morgan Private Bank's model portfolio allocations as of December 2, 2010, using two detailed pie charts. "Our Balanced Portfolio" allocates 34% to public equity, 19% to single-strategy hedge funds, 12% to high yield, leveraged loans, and structured credit, 8% to core bonds, 6% to diversified hedge funds, 5% to private equity, 4% to hard assets, 4% to real estate, 3% to emerging market FX, 3% to cash, and 2% to inflation. "Our Growth Portfolio" shifts toward higher-risk assets, allocating 42% to public equity, 20% to single-strategy hedge funds, 9% to high yield, leveraged loans, and structured credit, 8% to private equity, 6% to diversified hedge funds, 5% to hard assets, 4% to real estate, 3% to emerging market FX, 2% to core bonds, and 1% to cash. The commentary notes that these allocations are highly skewed toward the US and Asia over Europe and Japan, and that the firm feels they currently hold an appropriate level of risk given the status of the global recovery.

This page examines the year-end economic outlook for the United States and Asia, focusing particularly on growth trends, leading indicators, and inflation-control policies. The author argues that both the US and China are showing resilient signs of growth after experiencing mid-year slowdowns, supported by manufacturing sectors that are expanding and experiencing a pickup in new orders. 

To support this observation, the page features two line charts. The first, tracking US and China manufacturing output surveys from January 2008 to late 2010 on a seasonal diffusion index, shows that both nations rebounded from severe contractions in late 2008 to levels well above the neutral fifty-mark threshold. By late 2010, both countries hover in expansion territory around the fifty-five to fifty-seven range. The second chart depicts new orders surveys for both nations over the same period, illustrating a similar trajectory. Following deep troughs in late 2008 where the US dipped below thirty and China fell below thirty-five, both countries have rebounded strongly into expansion, with the US rising to nearly sixty and China positioned around fifty-five.

For the US, the text describes a mixed but generally improving set of leading indicators. A vertical checklist categorizes twenty-two indicators using color-coded arrows. Three indicators are declining: the ISM order backlog, supplier deliveries index, and SIA semiconductor shipments to North America. Seven are stabilizing, including analyst earnings upgrades, the UCLA Pulse of Commerce Index, factory orders, job openings, and average hourly earnings. Twelve indicators are listed as improving, such as ISM new orders, temporary employment, initial unemployment claims, M2 money supply, and business equipment spending. Despite these improvements, the author forecasts a weak recovery with 2.5% US GDP growth for 2011, noting that a sustained 4% growth rate is necessary to bring the budget deficit down to 3% by 2015 without resorting to austerity measures.

The discussion on China highlights the government's aggressive strategies to combat inflation, mapping their actions to historical parallels in a structured table. The table compares China's release of food reserves to biblical times under Joseph, its crackdown on hoarding to Lenin’s prosecution of speculators, and its commodity margin hikes and cost-reduction policies to Richard Nixon’s price controls. Additionally, China’s plan to construct fifteen million low-end housing units by 2012 is compared to Robert Moses's development of public housing, while its hikes in bank reserve requirements are compared to Marriner Eccles’s actions in the 1930s.

The author concludes that Asia is undergoing a classic business cycle adjustment, where policymakers must utilize currency appreciation and higher interest rates to cool inflation. Even with these policies, the region is expected to lead global growth. To illustrate this strength, the text highlights robust income growth in China of 7% to 9%, alongside exceptional regional growth rates: Singapore at 15%, Taiwan at 9% in the third quarter, and Thailand at 6%. Despite anticipated volatility in Asian equities, the author maintains confidence in the region's strong fiscal health relative to the West.

This page analyzes the outlook for the United States economy in 2011, presenting a narrative where a modest private sector recovery temporarily overshadows growing fiscal imbalances. The author highlights that while global demand relies heavily on US consumers, household balance sheets are improving as debt service burdens decline. 

Seven charts support this analysis. Chart c16 shows a recovery in a labor income proxy outpacing employment growth. Chart c17 displays the household financial obligations ratio, illustrating that the excess debt accumulated over the prior decade has begun to unwind, dropping back toward seventeen percent of disposable income. Chart c18 shows US retail sales growth rebounding sharply after the financial crisis, while chart c19 depicts a recovery in business equipment and software spending. Chart c20 tracks long-term nonfarm business productivity trends. To illustrate the cost of this recovery, chart c21 compares various historical expansions, demonstrating that the 2008 to 2010 period required an unprecedented increase in Federal Debt relative to the expansion of the ISM manufacturing index. Chart c22 projects short- and long-term fiscal pressures from government spending as a percentage of GDP through 2034, driven primarily by rising healthcare and social security costs. 

The author forecasts payroll gains of approximately 200,000 per month and GDP growth between 3.0% and 3.5% for 2011, but warns of massive impending deficits and the eventually unavoidable need for fiscal tightening. The commentary references international perspectives, citing a Peking University paper on US decline, and notes the rejection of the Bowles-Simpson deficit commission's proposals. Finally, the author questions the efficacy of the Federal Reserve’s portfolio rebalancing channel, noting it may distort commodity and financial markets rather than generating sustainable employment.

This page discusses global equity allocations and fixed-income strategies. The author favors emerging markets, particularly Asia and Brazil, over Europe and Japan. A table on global equity returns shows MSCI EM Asia leading one-year returns at 19 percent in USD terms, while MSCI Europe lagged at 5 percent. Regarding Brazil, a bar chart depicts the dramatic expansion of its middle class, which is projected to exceed 100 million people by 2014. An adjacent analysis of Brazil notes structural strengths like low household credit and a 50 percent decline in poverty since 2000, balanced against risks like wage inflation and high real interest rates.

In fixed income, the text outlines a supply-demand imbalance supporting bond prices due to negative net issuance of US credit instruments. A table on credit instruments shows a net contraction of 195 billion dollars, driven by massive mortgage and bank loan contractions despite over 1.4 trillion dollars in new Treasury issuance. Highlighting corporate credit health, a line chart shows a steep decline in US corporate bond and loan default rates from their 2009 peaks down to low single digits. Finally, the author discusses structured credit, utilizing a chart of CMBS subordination cushions to show that protection for AAA investors has recovered to nearly 30 percent after bottoming near 5 percent in 2007, making the asset class attractive once more.

This page of the Outlook report, written by Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest, outlines the global economic backdrop heading into 2011, characterizing the environment as an era of massive monetary experimentation labeled "The Printing Press." Globally, corporate profits are rising, U.S. household balance sheets are showing signs of improvement, and manufacturing is expanding. This expansion is demonstrated in chart c1, which plots U.S. and China manufacturing output survey index levels from 2008 through 2010. The index shows both countries dipping deeply into contraction territory below 50 in late 2008, with China recovering first in early 2009 and the U.S. following in mid-2009, with both ending 2010 firmly in expansion territory above 55.

However, the justification for continued monetary easing differs significantly by region, as shown in chart c2, which tracks excess capacity using the output gap between GDP and potential output from 2003 to 2010. While the U.S. has significant excess capacity with an output gap hovering around negative four to five percent, Emerging Market Asia has recovered completely, showing no excess capacity and a positive output gap of nearly three percent by 2010. This regional disparity is reflected in emerging market inflation, illustrated in chart c3. This chart displays headline, core, and food inflation year-over-year change for Asia ex-Japan and Latin America from 2005 to 2010, demonstrating a sharp rise in 2010 headline inflation to about 4.5 percent, driven primarily by food inflation spiking toward 5 percent, while core inflation remains more stable around 2.5 percent.

A major concern for the author is the persistent scale of global imbalances, measured in chart c4 as an index of current account and fiscal deficits and surpluses as a percentage of global GDP from 1970 to 2010. This index rose from under two percent in the early 1970s to a historic peak of over eleven percent in 2006, and remained near eleven percent in 2010, indicating elevated systemic risks. Despite these imbalances, global equity valuations remain historically attractive, as shown in chart c5, which compares the current forward price-to-earnings multiples to their averages since 1988. MSCI Europe's current multiple of 10.5x is well below its 14.5x average, MSCI USA is at 13.0x compared to its 16.0x average, and MSCI EM is at 11.5x compared to its 14.0x average. Asset prices are further supported by immense cash reserves: U.S. corporate cash as a share of tangible assets is at record highs, and Sovereign Wealth Fund balances have expanded from one trillion to four trillion dollars since 2005. 

Finally, chart c6 displays the inflation-adjusted cost of money from 1981 to 2010. Real policy rates for developed countries plunged below zero to roughly negative one percent by 2010, while emerging market real rates fell to near zero percent, making cash savings practically useless as a store of value. Given this backdrop, the author expects 2011 to resemble 2010, characterized by volatile but rising equity markets and modest returns on a balanced portfolio. J.P. Morgan's client portfolios are positioned globally across public and private equity, credit, hedge funds, commodities, and real estate, operating under the belief that the global economy will avoid a major relapse.

This page analyzes the structural challenges and deep economic divisions facing Europe in 2011, questioning whether the divergence between Germany and peripheral nations is irreconcilable. The author outlines a five-point summary of the situation. First, Germany is experiencing an impressive export-driven recovery, but this performance is not successfully pulling the other European Monetary Union nations along. Second, while peripheral European nations remain trapped in severe austerity to receive European Union and International Monetary Fund assistance, Iceland has managed a post-default recovery with rising real wages and tourism. Third, historical lessons from Latin America and Asia show that financial crises are difficult to ring-fence. Fourth, Spain represents a critical vulnerability; despite potentially manageable banking fixes, its private sector non-financial debt remains exceptionally high. Lastly, the author poses the open question of whether Germany and France will ultimately agree to direct subsidies or joint European Union government bonds, testing whether Europe will move toward a federal identity.

To illustrate these points, the author provides three charts and a comprehensive risk scorecard table. The first chart shows German retail and manufacturing surveys from 1991 through 2009. It highlights a massive divergence where manufacturing has rebounded sharply to an index level over 105, while retail remains depressed below 90. The second chart details the percent contribution to German GDP in Q2 and Q3 of 2010, confirming that growth was overwhelmingly driven by exports, which contributed roughly 3.5% in Q2 and over 1% in Q3, while household spending and government consumption made negligible or negative contributions. The third chart indexes core versus periphery GDP from 2007 to 2010. While core countries rebounded to an index level of approximately 101 by 2010, the periphery continued its steady decline down to 96.

The Sovereign Risk Scorecard table quantifies the intense pressure on Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece, and Spain across dozens of metrics. Spain stands out with a staggering 20.7% unemployment rate as of October 2010, alongside a 2010 fiscal deficit of 9.3%. Greece and Italy face the highest projected 2012 gross debt-to-GDP ratios at 142% and 133% respectively. External vulnerabilities are also severe, with net international investment positions showing massive net liabilities, particularly in Portugal at negative 114% of GDP and Ireland at negative 102% of GDP. Required fiscal adjustments for the 2010–2020 decade are high across the board, peaking at 10% for Ireland and Spain. The table also includes lighter, unconventional metrics, listing the number of World Cup and Euro Cup victories for each country and the ancient eras during which their respective empires held the world's reserve currency, such as Rome from 200 BC to 275 AD. Ultimately, the author concludes that the concentration of high-risk indicators across the peripheral Eurozone will continue to overshadow Germany's strong recovery until these structural differences are resolved.

This page of the J.P. Morgan report details the firm's outlook on equity portfolios, arguing that equity markets have priced in a substantial amount of pessimism, making them attractive relative to other assets. The author notes that J.P. Morgan is comfortable holding a 35% to 45% allocation to equities in Balanced and Growth portfolios because forward P/E multiples across major regions are low and growth stocks look particularly cheap. 

To support this, the first group of charts displays valuation and asset trends. Chart 26 shows that forward P/E equity multiples for the US, Europe, and Emerging Markets have clumped together between 10x and 13x in 2010, down from peaks of 16x to 18x in the mid-2000s. Chart 27 shows that the P/E of the top decile of growth stocks relative to the overall market is near a historic low of 1.3x, down from a late-1990s peak of 2.5x. Chart 28 focuses on mega-cap technology stocks—including Microsoft, IBM, Apple, Intel, Hewlett-Packard, Cisco, Oracle, Google, Qualcomm, and Corning—revealing a dramatic divergence where their average P/E multiple compressed from 70x in 2000 to nearly 10x in 2010, while their cash and cash equivalents surged from roughly $70 billion to over $200 billion. 

The author explains that the United States is J.P. Morgan's largest regional equity allocation because US corporate profit growth and margins are strong. This strength is partly driven by international exposure; S&P 500 revenues are more closely linked to global economic growth than to US domestic growth. Chart 29 demonstrates that from 1996 to 2010, S&P 500 core revenue growth averaged over 6%, aligning closely with world GDP growth rather than the lower US GDP growth. Chart 30 traces US corporate profits from the rest of the world, showing they have risen from under 0.5% of GDP in the late 1940s to nearly 3.0% by 2010, now accounting for 35% of total US profits. Chart 31 illustrates the breakdown of S&P 500 earnings by end-market, showing a diverse mix led by Business at 21%, Consumer Staples at 18%, Energy & Commodities at 17%, Financials at 16%, and Consumer Discretionary and Medical at 14% each. 

Looking ahead, J.P. Morgan forecasts S&P 500 returns of roughly 10% in 2011, driven by 8% to 10% earnings growth and stock buybacks running at 2% of market cap. The author observes that analysts have underestimated S&P 500 earnings by roughly 10% per quarter since January 2009 because companies successfully cut costs during the recession, leading to high incremental margins as demand recovers. However, the author poses a cautionary note regarding the sustainability of these margins, using Chart 32 to show how US profit drivers co-exist. The chart reveals that US corporate sales as a percentage of GDP are at a 50-year low of approximately 46%, but profit margins remain high because labor costs as a percentage of sales have fallen to a historic low of around 61%, a level unseen by some measures since 1929. Because corporate earnings are so heavily reliant on low real wages, J.P. Morgan remains reluctant to forecast higher valuation multiples.

This page of the publication analyzes the shifting dynamics of global growth, focusing on the robust expansion and emerging inflation pressures in Asia and other emerging markets (EM).
