The absolute best-case scenario, which assumes a 20% EFSF guarantee, IMF assistance, and coverage through 2013 only, projects a coverage ratio of 2.4x.

This page presents a critical, biological metaphor comparing the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) to its flightless, awkward namesake, the emu. The author argues that Europe’s upcoming sovereign and bank bailout package faces a series of severe structural flaws that may weigh it down and prevent a successful resolution to the debt crisis. 

The center of the page features a detailed, annotated illustration of an emu bird, with callouts pointing to different parts of its body to symbolize the various vulnerabilities in the Eurozone bailout plan. These annotations, cross-referenced with detailed footnotes, cover critical areas of banking, fiscal health, and monetary policy. 

Regarding banking capitalization and stress tests, the author notes that the EU is avoiding a stringent stress test in favor of a mark-to-market exercise on sovereign bonds, resulting in reported recapitalization needs of only 75 to 100 billion Euros. Footnotes clarify that using prior European Banking Authority (EBA) stress tests and a 9% Tier 1 ratio would actually reveal a capital shortfall of 150 billion Euros. The author criticizes prior tests for assuming a low 1.3% household and corporate loan loss rate over two years, compared to current market-implied rates of 3.4% and the 9% loss rate assumed in the 2009 US stress tests. This is particularly problematic given that German banks hold substantial non-sovereign GIPSI debt. Additionally, the author notes a warning from Deutsche Bank CEO Josef Ackermann that raising capital ratios too quickly could force EU banks to shrink their loan books by 1 trillion Euros, exacerbating a looming recession.

On sovereign debt and guarantees, the graphic questions the unproven demand for Italian and Spanish bonds even with a first-loss guarantee from the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF). A 20% first-loss guarantee may be insufficient given historical Moody's sovereign recovery rates of 53%. Direct EFSF guarantees also risk violating Article 125 of the Lisbon Treaty, which prohibits member states from being liable for other states' commitments. These guarantee commitments present a significant risk to France’s AAA rating; France is already highly taxed, has an 84% debt-to-GDP ratio, and faces EFSF commitments equal to 8.4% of its GDP. Spain is also highlighted as an example of fiscal slippage, with flow of funds data indicating a 2011 budget deficit of 8.6% against a 6% target. 

Finally, the page outlines macroeconomic and regulatory complications. For Greece, attempting to keep debt forgiveness under 50% to avoid triggering credit default swap (CDS) contracts could destroy the credibility of the restructuring. To manage these pressures, the European Central Bank (ECB) may be forced to print hundreds of billions of Euros to purchase secondary market debt, potentially exceeding the public and Bundesbank's tolerance for monetary expansion. The author concludes by critiquing "Orwellian" EU regulatory draft proposals to restrict credit rating agencies from publishing sovereign ratings during sensitive moments, comparing such censorship to Soviet-era state media.

This page addresses global macroeconomic dynamics, focusing on stabilizing indicators in China and a proposed repo-market mechanism to resolve the sovereign debt crisis in Southern Europe. 

The commentary begins with a positive assessment of China's economy, noting that it does not appear to be tilting into a recession. Industrial value-added, cement production, and steel demand all picked up in late summer, while urban household consumption rose in the third quarter. Additionally, the manufacturing business survey climbed back above the expansionary threshold of 50 after three months in contraction territory. While Chinese monetary policy is expected to remain steady, any eventual shift would likely lean toward easing due to decelerating core inflation and below-target money supply growth.

The primary focus of the page is the "Jackrabbit solution," which explores using repo markets to leverage the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF). With Spain and Italy requiring funding that far exceeds the EFSF's remaining uncommitted capital, alternative solutions like Special Purpose Vehicles remain highly fragile, relying on France maintaining its AAA rating and the market's appetite for unorthodox sovereign bonds. The author proposes instead tapping into massive global pools of sidelined cash looking for low-risk, short-term homes. 

To illustrate these vast reserves of capital, a quartet of charts is presented. The first chart, tracking foreign exchange reserves in trillions of USD from 1970 to 2011, shows emerging market reserves climbing exponentially to nearly eight trillion dollars, while Japan's reserves remain comparatively flat at just over one trillion dollars. The second chart, tracking US commercial banks in trillions of USD from 2000 to 2011, displays a significant post-2008 divergence where bank deposits surged to approximately nine trillion dollars while total loans plateaued around six and a half trillion dollars. The third chart shows the European Central Bank (ECB) deposit facility in billions of EUR from 2008 to 2011, illustrating extreme volatility with massive spikes exceeding three hundred billion Euros in both 2009 and late 2011. The fourth chart displays US institutional money market fund assets in trillions of USD from 2001 to 2011, showing assets peaking at nearly two and a half trillion dollars in 2009 before settling to around one point nine trillion dollars in late 2011. 

In theory, these pools of capital could participate in Europe's six-trillion-Euro short-term collateralized repo market. The EFSF could utilize this market to buy Italian and Spanish government bonds, pledge them, and buy more. Even with highly conservative lending haircuts of thirty percent, the EFSF could theoretically build a one-trillion-Euro backstop. This structure would offer cash providers higher yields than the ECB's zero point seventy-five percent deposit rate or the zero point ninety percent overnight interbank rate. 

However, the author points out a critical flaw: repo market lenders behave like "jackrabbits" that flee at the first sign of trouble. Because these lenders prioritize capital preservation over yield, sudden withdrawals can accelerate a systemic crisis. The author highlights historical precedents of this behavior, noting that haircuts on AA and AAA asset-backed securities rose from one point eight percent to eighteen percent during the 2008 financial crisis, and haircuts on Irish debt skyrocketed to eighty percent in the summer of 2011. Ultimately, the author concludes that a repo-market rescue plan for Europe cannot succeed without upfront reassurance that the ECB will act as a backstop in the event of a sudden, collective financing meltdown.

This page examines the critical intersection of politics and economics in Europe, focusing on the systemic struggles facing Italy and Greece. Author Michael Cembalest outlines several structural vulnerabilities for Italy, including its national debt reaching post-reunification highs outside of the World Wars, poor labor competitiveness, a reversal of interest expenditure benefits from the late-1990s European Monetary Union convergence, and weak bank loan loss provisions that are only fifteen to twenty-five percent of United States levels. 

To illustrate Italy's immediate economic headwinds, a line chart titled "Plunge in Italian manufacturing survey points to recession" tracks the country's purchasing managers' index output index from June 1997 to June 2011. The chart shows a steep contraction in late 2011, with the index falling toward forty, nearing the historic lows of approximately thirty to thirty-two seen during the 2008 financial crisis. This plunge underscores J.P. Morgan's projection that even with a three percent primary surplus, a modest one and a half percent GDP contraction in 2012 paired with five percent interest rates would cause Italy's debt to rise rather than fall over the next three years.

Cembalest awards "Chart of the Year" to a visualization titled "Industrial production in Germany and Italy," which indexes production levels from 1982 to 2010, with December 31, 1998, set to one hundred. The line chart demonstrates how Germany and Italy’s industrial output tracked closely historically, but diverged dramatically after the Euro exchange rate was fixed at the end of 1998. While Germany's industrial production index soared to nearly one hundred thirty by 2008 and recovered strongly post-recession, Italy's production stagnated and ultimately fell to around ninety by 2010. The author argues this divergence highlights the damaging consequences of a shared fixed-currency model on a structurally weaker economy that holds more absolute debt than Germany.

Turning to Greece, the commentary warns against European market desires to bypass early elections or public referendums on fiscal austerity. Cembalest asserts that trying to enforce IMF-approved austerity measures without public consent is dangerous, arguing that a national unity government formed solely to secure European Union disbursements will lack political legitimacy and ignore the shredded social fabric of the country.

This page analyzes the ideological composition and potential for compromise within the U.S. congressional Deficit Reduction Committee, often referred to as the "Super Committee." Michael Cembalest introduces "trading cards" for the twelve committee members, colored blue for Democrats and red for Republicans. The cards feature each member's Political Ideology Indicator (PII) score, which is based on historical voting records compiled by the University of Georgia, where a score of -1 is highly liberal and +1 is highly conservative.

The six Democratic members listed with their PII scores are Xavier Becerra of California (-0.554), James Clyburn of South Carolina (-0.495), Chris Van Hollen of Maryland (-0.435), John Kerry of Massachusetts (-0.396), Patty Murray of Washington (-0.378), and Max Baucus of Montana (-0.226). The six Republican members are Fred Upton of Michigan (0.306), Dave Camp of Michigan (0.383), Rob Portman of Ohio (0.393), Jon Kyl of Arizona (0.563), Pat Toomey of Pennsylvania (0.699), and Jeb Hensarling of Texas (0.755).

A visual spectrum chart at the bottom of the page plots these individual scores on a scale from -0.8 to +0.8. This chart illustrates a stark ideological polarization, leaving a significant void in the political center. Cembalest points out that Max Baucus is the only member who comes close to being a "moderate"—defined as within +/- 0.2 of the center—while the rest of the members sit firmly within their respective party wings. Consequently, Cembalest argues that a bipartisan compromise is highly unlikely, as members face pressure from party leadership not to cross party lines. He concludes that the committee's makeup reflects the deep polarization of the broader Congress, ultimately leading to a lack of progress on deficit reduction.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest, analyzes the critical intersections of politics and economics in the Eurozone, focusing on the potential exit of Greece from the Euro and contrasting it with Iceland's post-devaluation economic recovery. 

The first chart, titled "Fiscal adjustments, then and now," plots GDP growth against currency devaluation. It shows that the 2010 European Economic and Monetary Union fiscal adjustments, represented by orange circles clustered at 0% currency devaluation, have resulted in depressed GDP growth ranging from negative 1.0% to positive 2.0%. In contrast, prior European and Latin adjustments from 1975 to 2000, represented by yellow circles, achieved higher GDP growth of 1.5% to 3.5% by utilizing currency devaluations ranging from 20% to nearly 100%. This comparison highlights the historical benefit of currency devaluation in aiding fiscal recovery.

The second chart, "Iceland took the normal route, and is now recovering," tracks sovereign credit default swap spreads in basis points from June 2007 to June 2011. It depicts Iceland’s spreads spiking sharply above 1,000 basis points in late 2008 before steadily declining to around 300 basis points by mid-2011. Italy's spreads remained comparatively low but began to rise toward the end of the period, while Greece's spreads skyrocketed completely off the chart, rising toward 5,700 basis points.

In the text, Cembalest discusses the severe potential consequences of a Greek default and Euro exit, including high inflation, damaged central bank credibility, and trade finance disruptions. However, he posits that Greece must weigh these severe costs against the alternative of certain economic failure if it remains within the Euro. 

The second portion of the commentary, titled "The Sun Also Rises: Iceland’s post-devaluation recovery," details how Iceland successfully recovered from its financial crisis by following a traditional formula. This path included fiscal austerity, a massive currency devaluation, an IMF loan, and a refusal to absorb the debts of its failing banks. Despite its debt-to-GDP ratio rising from 40% to 100% and unemployment reaching 9%, Iceland's economy has rebounded. By 2011, inflation dropped from an 18% peak in 2009 back to 2%, the budget deficit sat at 4.5% of GDP, and economic growth was projected to reach 3.5% to 4.0%. A small photograph of Skálafell farm in Iceland accompanies this section, reinforcing the theme of renewal.

This page focuses on the challenges facing a new Italian government, the historical limitations of International Monetary Fund interventions, and the critical role of the European Central Bank as a lender of last resort. The author argues that IMF and other bilateral loans historically have not marked the end of sovereign debt problems, illustrating this with four historical charts from J.P. Morgan's "Sovereign Default Time Capsule." 

The first chart tracks Argentina's sovereign debt price from 1998 to 2004, showing a collapse in bond prices in 2001 despite a $40 billion aid promise from the IMF, Spain, and others in late 2000 and subsequent optimistic bond swaps. The second chart shows the Mexican Peso/USD exchange rate from 1993 to 1995, highlighting a severe currency devaluation starting in late 1994 that occurred despite a $6.7 billion credit line from the US and Canada and a subsequent $20 billion Exchange Stabilization Fund. The third chart details Russia's GKO sovereign debt price in 1998, which plummeted in August 1998 right after a $22.6 billion loan promise led by the IMF in July 1998, demonstrating how quickly market optimism can evaporate. The fourth chart tracks Indonesia's sovereign debt price from 1996 to 1998, showing a severe drop through late 1997 and early 1998, even as the IMF resumed lending under a $40 billion package in April 1998. 

The author points out that the key difference in the modern European crisis is the presence of the ECB as a potential lender and buyer of last resort, which these historical default countries lacked. A stacked area chart titled "Total public support to European banks and sovereigns" from 2000 to late 2011 shows that public support surged from negligible levels before 2008 to nearly 1.0 trillion EUR by late 2011. This support is broken down into repo to core banks, repo to periphery banks, purchases of periphery bonds via the Securities Markets Programme, and purchases of collateralized bank bonds. The author poses the open question of whether the ECB will continue to expand this balance sheet, noting that the increasing risk of these holdings—rather than their size—is likely what troubles the German Bundesbank.

The text concludes with a skeptical analysis of Italy's capacity to resolve its debt through its extensive household wealth and €1.8 trillion in state-owned assets. The author notes that Italy's tax evasion is estimated to be the highest in the OECD and has been rising since the late 1980s. Furthermore, the sale of state-owned assets has historically been slow and complex, with Italy only selling non-financial assets worth 2% of GDP over the entire decade from 1997 to 2006. Most concerningly, the author cites an analysis showing that Italy's debt ratio improvements during that decade were almost entirely driven by temporary measures, leaving its structural deficit largely unimproved.

This page from Eye on the Market discusses the challenges and potential solutions in the search for viable energy alternatives, focusing heavily on natural gas reserves, energy efficiency, and the critical bottleneck of commercial-scale electricity storage. The author notes that US shale gas production has increased 14-fold over the last decade, leading the Energy Information Administration to project that the US will stop importing gas by 2035. This is despite volatile reserve estimates, such as the Energy Department slashing Marcellus Basin estimates from 410 trillion cubic feet to 84 trillion cubic feet. While shale gas is vital to offset other declining gas categories, the author highlights that efficiency remains a highly practical near-term solution. Examples of impactful efficiency measures include natural gas furnaces that are 95 percent efficient, LED or fluorescent lighting, and diagnostic devices in residential and commercial buildings to manage HVAC systems, as highlighted by a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report.

The core of the page addresses the need for a commercial-scale energy storage breakthrough, which would drastically improve the cost-effectiveness of intermittent solar and wind, reduce required peak capacity for urban power grids, and defer expensive transmission grid upgrades. Currently, the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation reports that only 27 percent of grid upgrades relate to integrating renewables, with nearly half designed to manage fluctuating loads. The author points out that battery storage progress is incredibly slow compared to semiconductors, with solar cell efficiency doubling over 15 to 18 years and commercial battery storage advancing even slower. Companies like A123 offer commercial-scale lithium-ion batteries, but these are limited to brief grid-smoothing operations rather than long-term storage.

A pie-style diagram on the page illustrates just how dominant pumped hydro is in the global energy storage landscape, representing over 99 percent of total storage capacity. According to 2010 data from the Fraunhofer Institute and EPRI, pumped hydro accounts for 127,000 megawatts of electric capacity. All other storage methods are negligible by comparison, including compressed air energy storage at 440 megawatts, sodium-sulfur batteries at 316 megawatts, lead-acid batteries at approximately 35 megawatts, nickel-cadmium batteries at 27 megawatts, flywheels at less than 25 megawatts, lithium-ion batteries at roughly 20 megawatts, and redox-flow batteries at under 3 megawatts. Although pumped hydro is the only viable large-scale technology, the author notes it suffers from a 10 to 20 percent energy loss due to evaporation and conversion. Furthermore, even with 127 gigawatts of installed capacity, running these systems for 10 hours would yield only 1,270 gigawatt-hours, representing a minuscule 0.0064 percent of annual global electricity generation. This stands in stark contrast to crude oil, where inventory storage typically represents 10 to 12 percent of annual production.

This page, titled "Topic: The quixotic search for energy solutions," analyzes the logistical, physical, and economic limits of carbon sequestration, biofuels, and wind power. The author presents four analytical questions to frame these challenges, accompanied by two detailed charts illustrating the critical issue of wind power intermittency. 

The first analysis addresses the scale of burying 15% of global carbon dioxide emissions. The calculations show that burying 5.0 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide requires compressing it to a volume of 6.2 billion cubic meters, which is significantly larger than the annual global crude oil extraction volume of 4.6 billion cubic meters. The implication is that carbon capture and sequestration would require an infrastructure larger than the oil industry, raising coal plant capital costs by 40% to 75% and increasing their internal electricity consumption by 30% to 40%.

The second analysis evaluates the potential of repurposing the entire unused 2010 U.S. corn harvest of 160 million tonnes into ethanol. This would yield 63.8 billion liters of ethanol, equivalent to 42.7 billion liters of gasoline, which represents only an 8% reduction in total U.S. gasoline consumption. The author points out that corn ethanol’s energy return on investment is extremely low, ranging from 0.8:1 to 1.6:1, compared to traditional oil at 10 to 20 or wind at 15 to 20. 

The third analysis considers alternative biofuels, calculating that converting U.S. corn stover would reduce gasoline needs by only 2.74%, and gathering all the world's spent coffee grounds to make biodiesel would offset a negligible 0.16% of global diesel production. This highlights that biofuels are severely limited by low energy densities and high aggregation and extraction costs.

The fourth analysis estimates the land required for wind to generate a quarter of U.S. electricity. Meeting a 23% target wind generation would require an incremental 387,312 megawatts of capacity. At an energy density of 2 watts per square meter, this requires 193,656 square kilometers of land—roughly the size of Nebraska. Furthermore, the analysis highlights a major geographic mismatch: only about 30 million Americans out of a total population of 309 million live in the prime wind and solar states of the Great Plains and Southwest.

The final section focuses on wind's reliability, presenting two charts. The first line chart, "Day-to-day variability in wind generation in April 2005," measures hourly output in megawatts at a wind farm in Tehachapi, California. It shows extreme daily volatility across the 24-hour cycle, where output on a day like Day 29 peaks near 600 megawatts, while on Day 5 it remains below 100 megawatts, resulting in a low, flat hourly average of under 300 megawatts. 

The second chart, "California energy demand vs. total wind - summer 2006," compares hourly California energy demand on the left axis against total wind generation on the right axis over a 24-hour period. The data reveals an inverse relationship: consumer demand peaks sharply in the late afternoon between hours 15 and 18, reaching nearly 38,000 megawatts, precisely when total wind generation dips to its daily low of approximately 300 megawatts. This gap underscores wind's fundamental unreliability during peak demand periods.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication "Eye on the Market" explores the realities of United States electricity generation and the practical limitations of transitioning to renewable energy and electric vehicles. The author argues that despite enthusiasm for renewables, they face deep thermodynamic, structural, and practical challenges. 

A detailed table compiled from Energy Information Agency data presents the status of US electricity generation in 2010. Coal remains the dominant source, accounting for 45.4 percent of total generation with a 67 percent capacity factor and a levelized cost of ninety-five to one hundred ten dollars per megawatt-hour. Natural gas follows at 24.3 percent of generation, possessing a lower capacity factor of 28 percent (reflecting its use as a peaking source) and a cheap levelized cost of sixty to seventy dollars. Nuclear power provides 19.8 percent of generation with a highly reliable 91 percent capacity factor, though its levelized cost is high at one hundred fourteen dollars. Hydroelectric power represents 6.4 percent of generation, while non-hydroelectric renewables make up less than five percent combined. Specifically, wind contributes 2.3 percent with a 28 percent capacity factor and a ninety-seven dollar levelized cost, while solar photovoltaics and concentrated solar power represent a negligible 0.0 percent of total generation due to high costs ranging from two hundred ten to three hundred twelve dollars and a low capacity factor of 15 percent. 

The lower half of the page features a section titled "Energy Conversions 101," which uses two hypothetical questions to analyze the feasibility of electric cars. The first question asks how much more electricity the US would need if it switched entirely to electric passenger vehicles. Assuming two hundred forty-five million cars driving twenty thousand kilometers annually at an average consumption of two hundred watt-hours per kilometer, and factoring in a 10 percent increase for battery self-discharge, the US would require an additional one thousand seventy-eight terawatt-hours of electricity. This represents a substantial 25 percent incremental increase over the nation's total electricity generation of four thousand three hundred twenty-five terawatt-hours. The author notes this would severely strain what they describe as one of the worst electrical grids in the OECD, even before factoring in transmission losses, battery degradation, and the cost of rare earth metals.

The second question analyzes whether electric cars require less primary energy than gasoline-powered cars. When accounting for a 60 percent efficiency loss in fossil-fuel power generation and 10 percent transmission losses, the primary energy required to power an electric car is 12.2 megawatt-hours annually. This converts to approximately 37.4 miles per gallon in gasoline equivalents. The implication is that electric vehicles do not offer a major energy efficiency advantage over existing high-mileage gasoline cars. While electric vehicles would successfully reduce dependence on foreign oil, the author concludes that a high-mileage gasoline fleet might achieve similar benefits with far less societal disruption, unless power plant conversion efficiencies improve from 60 percent to 50 percent.

This analysis explores the challenges and potential breakthroughs in electricity grid storage, framing it as a critical but historically difficult pursuit. The author highlights that current inexpensive storage options like pumped hydro and compressed air energy storage (CAES) are geographically constrained and expensive to construct, while existing battery technologies are plagued by high costs, short cycle lives, and safety issues. 

A potential disruptor is introduced in the form of Eos Energy Storage, which is working on a zinc-air battery solution aiming to deliver capital costs of around $160 per kilowatt-hour. This technology is evaluated in the first chart, "The cost of electricity storage options," which plots the range of levelized costs in dollars per kilowatt-hour across multiple storage types. The data reveals that while pumped hydro and below-ground CAES are the cheapest existing options at roughly $0.12 to $0.15 per kilowatt-hour, advanced lead-acid is the most expensive, spanning $0.40 to $0.60. The "Proposed Zinc-Air Solution" is projected to cost between $0.12 and $0.17 per kilowatt-hour. This projection places it below the cost of traditional natural gas peaking plants, which range from $0.20 to $0.29 per kilowatt-hour. Since utilities heavily rely on gas peaking plants to handle daily peak demands and compensate for intermittent renewable energy, a successful, cheap battery storage alternative could render many of these peaking facilities obsolete.

The urgent need for grid storage is demonstrated in a second chart, "Texas electricity demand vs. actual wind output," which tracks hourly grid data from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) in early August 2011. The chart plots electricity demand (on a scale from 20,000 to 70,000 megawatts) alongside wind output (on a scale from 0 to 7,400 megawatts). The data shows a stark, nearly 100% inverse correlation: wind generation peaks at night when demand is lowest, and drops to near zero during the heat of the day when electricity demand peaks. Without large-scale storage solutions or connections to the national grid, a significant portion of wind energy remains underutilized.

This lack of storage, combined with aging grid infrastructure—where 70% of transmission lines, transformers, and circuit breakers are 25 to 30 years old—is leading to rising congestion. This trend is captured in the final chart, "Transmission loading relief requests," which shows the number of grid incidents from 2002 to 2008. The stacked bar chart shows incidents rising from under 10 in 2002 to over 80 in 2008. This congestion is driven heavily by issues in the Southwest Power Pool, the Midwest Independent Transmission System Operator, and the PJM Interconnection. The author suggests that grid storage has the potential to alleviate these mounting congestion problems by absorbing and releasing power strategically.

In this commentary, the author examines why European nations are struggling to act decisively to rescue the European Monetary Union (EMU). Despite historical precedents for massive national sacrifice—such as Germany spending two trillion dollars in real terms on reunification—the author questions whether Europe possesses a true unified consciousness that is ready for statehood. Pointing to the work of anthropologists Christian Welzel and Geert Hofstede, the commentary notes that cultural differences between European nations are as vast as those between non-unified Asian or Latin American nations, a reality that influenced the decision to avoid European equity and credit during the debt crisis.

To illustrate these deep-seated regional divisions, the page features a scatter plot titled "The search for a 'European consciousness' vs. the contours of history," which displays regional population clusters based on DNA sequence data. The vertical axis represents the primary genome sequence (ranging from -0.08 to 0.04), while the horizontal axis represents the secondary genome sequence (ranging from -0.05 to 0.05). The resulting clusters map almost precisely onto the actual geography of Europe, with distinct genetic groupings labeled for nations such as the United Kingdom, Ireland, Norway, Denmark, Sweden, Poland, Germany, the Netherlands, the Czech Republic, Switzerland, Austria, Hungary, France, Yugoslavia, Romania, Greece, Spain, Portugal, and Italy. The author argues that these patterns reflect hundreds of years of localized shared experiences and values. The lack of genetic and cultural overlap between Northern Europe and Southern European nations like Greece and Italy explains why Northern Europe is hesitant to mortgage its financial future to save the South.

Turning to the immediate financial crisis, the author details the growing market alarm. It has been six months since backstop legislation for Southern Europe was passed, yet it remains non-operational. In response, US money market funds have slashed their exposure to Europe from 55% of total assets in 2009 to 35%. The crisis is also spreading to Belgium, whose debt levels are approaching those of Italy. Highlighting the pressure on Italian yields, Italy recently had to pay 6.5% for T-bills, which is nearly double the rate paid just a month prior. In terms of forward-looking policy, the author poses an open question regarding potential European Central Bank intervention. While a massive one-trillion-Euro bond-buying program by the ECB would likely trigger a major global relief rally, the author questions what will happen in the long run if global investors simply use the opportunity to dump their Southern European bonds onto the ECB at inflated prices.

This page examines the United States residential housing outlook, arguing that the market remains flat to downward-bound and that popular indicators of a housing recovery may be misleading. The author first addresses the bullish argument based on housing affordability and pent-up demand. The first chart, depicting the National Association of Realtors' Housing Affordability Index from 1995 to 2011, shows the index rising sharply after 2008 to over 180, though the text cautions that tightening underwriting standards and exhausted demand limit this metric's relevance. The next two charts analyze pent-up demand from 1990 to 2010 using Census Bureau and J.P. Morgan Private Bank data. The first of these shows a gap emerging between actual household formations and a higher projected trend line, while the residual chart shows household formation falling significantly below trend to a deficit of nearly 1.5 million households around 2008 before starting a slight recovery, suggesting a substantial pool of eventual demand once conditions normalize.

The core of the page's argument focuses on the massive threat of shadow inventory and underwater mortgages, illustrated by three progressive stacked-area charts tracking housing inventory from 2003 to 2011. The first chart shows only US existing housing inventory, which sits at roughly 3.5 million units. The second chart layer adds shadow inventory, including properties that are ninety-plus days delinquent, in foreclosure, or bank-owned real estate. The third chart adds an estimate for mortgages that are current but underwater, meaning their loan-to-value ratio is above one hundred percent. This final adjustment pushes the total potential inventory of units near ten million, understating the potential selling pressure facing the market, especially considering that modified mortgages are re-defaulting at a forty to fifty percent pace. 

The author notes that this distress is highly concentrated in six states: Nevada, Arizona, Florida, Michigan, Georgia, and California, while CoreLogic ranks New York as the best state regarding underwater mortgages. The text suggests that regional selling pressure will depend heavily on government policies such as the Home Affordable Refinance Program, or HARP 2.0. This policy aims to assist underwater homeowners with mortgages guaranteed by government-sponsored enterprises by removing loan-to-value caps, lowering refinancing fees, and relaxing credit score and income requirements. While the Federal Housing Finance Agency hopes to double refinancings from their current level of nine hundred thousand by the end of 2013, the author cites a Macroeconomic Advisers estimate that the resulting twenty-billion-dollar consumption gain will not significantly boost overall economic growth.

This page analyzes the European sovereign debt and banking crisis ahead of the December 2011 EU summit, arguing that any resulting fiscal agreements will likely be weak and unenforceable "Maastricht 2.0" commitments. The author, Michael Cembalest, predicts that the European Central Bank (ECB), led by Mario Draghi, will nevertheless use these agreements as a "fig leaf" to justify aggressive debt monetization, such as purchasing peripheral sovereign debt or lending to the IMF to support Italy and Spain. 

The first chart, titled "Italian sovereign debt maturities and 10-year yields," shows quarterly Italian debt maturities in billions of euros alongside 10-year yields from July 2011 through mid-2012. It highlights that Italy's sovereign borrowing needs are set to surge from around 70 billion euros in late 2011 to roughly 120 billion euros in Q1 2012. Meanwhile, Italian 10-year yields have climbed sharply to over 7.0%, illustrating the pressing need for a non-market funding alternative. 

The second chart, "How would France cope with a 3% deficit constraint?," tracks the French budget deficit as a percentage of GDP from 1980 to 2010 against a proposed Maastricht 2.0 deficit limit of negative 3%. The historical data reveals that France has repeatedly run deficits far exceeding this limit, bottoming out near negative 8% around 2010, which suggests France is unlikely to adhere to strict new deficit caps given its reliance on counter-cyclical fiscal policy. 

The third chart, "Central bank balance sheet size," measures central bank assets as a percentage of GDP from 2007 to 2011 for the US, ECB, UK, and Japan. The chart includes a cartoon of the German folk character "Suppen-Kaspar" to represent German ECB members' futile tantrums over debt monetization. It plots a projected trajectory where the ECB's balance sheet would balloon to nearly 35% of GDP if it adds an extra 1 trillion euros, as rumored by the London Times. 

The fourth chart, "More signs of inter-bank distress in Europe," plots the one-month moving average of the ECB deposit facility in billions of euros from January 2008 to late 2011. It shows a stark spike up to approximately 250 billion euros by December 1, 2011, illustrating that European banks are increasingly parking their excess cash with the central bank rather than lending to each other. 

The author concludes by noting that sovereign debt is only part of the issue, as banking sector funding challenges persist with rising retail bank deposit outflows in Spain. A footnote, citing insights from Joyce Chang, raises the open question of who will ultimately bear the risk of ECB loans to the IMF that are on-lent to Italy—the IMF as a preferred creditor, or the ECB itself.

In this market commentary, Chief Investment Officer Michael Cembalest discusses the challenges of the post-stimulus economy, highlighting that while some risks are being managed, long-term debt questions in the West remain unresolved. He draws a historical parallel to the 1970s and early 1980s, pointing out that markets struggled through a sideways "wilderness" of monetary and fiscal uncertainty until a clear path forward emerged in 1982. 

To support this historical comparison, the page features six charts. The first chart, c1, titled "1970s post-recovery equity market wilderness," plots the S&P 500 level on the left y-axis (ranging from 20 to 180) and the Germany DAX level on the right y-axis (ranging from 300 to 800) from 1972 to 1982. It highlights a prolonged decade-long period of extreme monetary and fiscal uncertainty where markets moved sideways before a sustained bull market finally began in late 1982. 

The next two charts illustrate the structural fiscal issues facing Western economies from 1970 to 2012. Chart c2, "OECD debt levels," tracks gross OECD debt as a percent of GDP, illustrating a continuous climb from approximately 40% in 1970 to over 100% by 2012. Chart c3, "OECD budget deficits," tracks public expenditure against public revenues as a percent of GDP. Expenditure peaked near 46% of GDP in the early 1980s and again around 2010, consistently outpacing revenues which fluctuated between 34% and 38% of GDP.

Chart c4, "Global manufacturing surveys," shows the seasonally adjusted Purchasing Managers Index (PMI) from 2007 to 2011 for the US, Asia, and the Euro area. The chart illustrates a sharp divergence in late 2011: while the US manufacturing sector showed resilience by staying above the expansion threshold of 50, the Euro area fell back below 50, and Asia faced a moderate slowdown. 

Chart c5, "Fiscal adjustments, then & now," plots annual GDP growth against currency devaluation. Historical adjustments in Europe and Latin America between 1975 and 2000 are shown as yellow bubbles, cluster in a region of high devaluation (between 35% and 95%) and robust GDP growth (2.0% to 4.0%). In contrast, Europe today is represented as a single bubble positioned at the bottom-left corner, suffering from very low growth (around 1.2%) and virtually no currency devaluation (around 5%), highlighting Europe’s difficult path of austerity without growth or devaluation.

Chart c6, "Real S&P 500 earnings yield," displays the trailing earnings yield less core CPI from 1956 to late 2011. As of December 16, 2011, the yield sat at an elevated level of nearly 6%. Even assuming a 15% decline in corporate earnings, the yield remains cheap by historical standards, sitting at roughly 5%. 

Looking forward into 2012, Cembalest notes that a primary concern is the depth of the impending European recession. He suggests that while the immediate risk of a catastrophic European meltdown has diminished due to the European Central Bank and member central banks stepping in to support bank assets, the region faces a slow-burning recession and credit contraction. Consequently, J.P. Morgan maintains a modestly lower-than-normal equity weighting, keeping the US as its largest regional position while remaining heavily underweight Europe. A concluding footnote points out that negative S&P 500 earnings pre-announcements in the fourth quarter of 2011 matched the peaks seen in the 2001 and 2008 recessions, and companies reporting before Alcoa missed consensus estimates by 2%.

This page analyzes the economic crisis in Europe as it enters a recession, arguing that the structural flaws of the Euro have created severe North-South disparities and necessitated a mid-flight redesign of the currency union due to a loss of market confidence. The author highlights that the crisis is multi-faceted, involving sovereign refinancing pressures, under-capitalized banks, bloated corporate debt, and the painful process of internal devaluation. 

The first chart, titled "Death in Venice," plots the seasonally adjusted Industrial Production Index for Germany and Italy from 1982 to 2010. It shows that while the two nations tracked closely for decades, their paths diverged dramatically after the Euro exchange rate was fixed in 1999; Germany's industrial production index rose toward 130 by 2008, while Italy's fell below 90 by 2010. This divergence is mirrored by a loss of market confidence shown in the sovereign ten-year yields chart, where yields for Belgium, Spain, Italy, and France spiked during 2011, with Spain and Italy both climbing toward 7%. Refinancing needs are immense, as shown in a chart detailing maturing debt, interest due, and primary deficits for 2012. France faces €355 billion in obligations, Italy €327 billion, and Spain €203 billion, representing substantial portions of their respective GDPs. 

To address these pressures, a chart on central bank balance sheets from 2007 to 2011 indicates that the European Central Bank's balance sheet, which stood at roughly 20% to 25% of GDP in 2011, may need to expand by an additional €1 trillion to support sovereigns and banks, pushing it past 30% of GDP. Sovereign risk is exemplified by Italy's total gross general government debt-to-GDP ratio, charted from 1861 to 2011, which shows modern debt levels climbing back toward 120%, near historical peaks seen during World War I and World War II. 

The banking sector's vulnerabilities are illustrated in a chart displaying bank liabilities as a multiple of GDP across several nations. Ireland is the most extreme case, with bank liabilities reaching seven times its GDP, followed by the United Kingdom at five times GDP. Meanwhile, a chart comparing loan loss provisions on performing credit loans shows that US banks have maintained much higher provisions, often between 1% and 5%, while EU banks have kept provisions consistently below 1%, suggesting European financial institutions are severely under-reserved. 

Beyond sovereigns and banks, the corporate sector is heavily leveraged. A chart on the change in non-financial corporate debt from 2000 to 2010 shows that corporate debt as a percentage of GDP rose by nearly 60% in Spain and over 40% in Portugal. Finally, the long road to convergence is charted using unit labor costs from 2000 to 2011. While Germany successfully kept its unit labor costs flat near an index level of 95, competitors like Spain, Italy, and Ireland saw theirs climb above 130. Ireland is the only country showing progress in internal devaluation, with its unit labor cost index dropping back to around 120, though the author notes that Ireland's recovery remains crippled by a 140% debt-to-GNP ratio resulting from its decision to bail out EU depositors in Irish banks.

This page analyzes the European sovereign debt crisis, focusing on whether "Maastricht 2.0" structural reforms and austerity measures can stabilize the economies of Italy, Spain, and France, or if the region is headed toward prolonged recession. 

The author begins by highlighting the irony of Italy's fiscal situation: despite consistently running a primary budget surplus since 1991, Italy remains burdened by a 1.9 trillion Euro debt legacy from its 1980s crisis. A chart of the Italian primary balance from 1970 to 2012 shows both reported and cyclically adjusted balances staying positive for most of the period post-1991, peaking near 6% in the late 1990s. This prolonged austerity, combined with low productivity, has suppressed economic expansion. A comparison of 20-year growth rates from 1991 to 2011 shows Italy's GDP growth near the very bottom of the OECD at roughly 1%, just ahead of Japan. Looking forward, a debt stabilization projection through 2014 offers two scenarios. Under a pessimistic case (real GDP growth of -1.5% to -0.5% and a primary balance of 1.3% to 2.2%), Italy's government debt as a percentage of GDP rises steadily from 116% in 2009 to over 131% by 2014. Under an optimistic case (real GDP of 0.5% and a primary balance of 2.6% to 4.1%), debt peaks near 124% before slowly declining. The author doubts Italy can achieve solvency under these conditions.

The broader Eurozone faces a combined sovereign and financial debt burden of 20 trillion Euros. A chart tracking outstanding Euro Area debt from 2001 to 2011 shows that financial corporation debt climbed rapidly to peak near 13 trillion Euros around 2009, while general government debt grew steadily to about 9 trillion Euros by 2011. To address this, European policymakers are pushing structural reforms, but a chart modeling the growth response to these reforms shows that they carry immediate economic pain. Over a twelve-year horizon, trade and tax reforms steadily boost cumulative real GDP per capita, but labor reforms trigger a sharp short-term economic contraction, dragging GDP per capita down to nearly -3% by year four before recovering back to flat by year twelve. 

Furthermore, a significant competitiveness gap separates Germany from other major European economies. A chart measuring French real exports as a percentage of German real exports from 1970 to 2010 illustrates a severe decline, dropping from over 60% in the late 1990s to below 40% by 2010. The author argues that France is highly unlikely to stick to a proposed 0.5% structural budget deficit limit, pointing out that debt-to-GDP levels for both France (85%) and Germany (81%) are already elevated. Once pro rata shares of bilateral guarantees, central bank SMP purchase guarantees, and risks of deficit slippage are included, both nations' debt-to-GDP ratios are projected to exceed 90%. 

Concurrently, private investors are retreating from the Eurozone. In 2011, US money market funds cut their exposure to European banks in half, and dollar bond issuance by EU banks fell by 70%, amid concerns over bank leverage ratios of 26:1. The author concludes that bilateral and European Central Bank funding facilities do not solve the region's underlying current account deficits. Ultimately, J.P. Morgan doubts that Germany and other AAA-rated countries will possess the political will to shoulder the massive fiscal costs of backing their European peers.

The author discusses the pressing issue of US government debt, which he terms the elephant in the room. He argues that the failure of the Super Committee to establish a deficit reduction plan leaves the government debt burden unstabilized. To reach sustainable debt levels projected by the Congressional Budget Office, an additional five trillion dollars in deficit reduction is required over the next decade. This challenge is compounded by the fact that almost all government revenues are pre-committed to mandatory spending programs or interest payments, leaving very little fiscal democracy or room for discretionary congressional action. 

This dynamic is illustrated across eight charts. Chart c31 displays three long-term net-debt-to-GDP scenarios from 2004 to 2019, contrasting the CBO August Baseline, which projects debt stabilizing near 60 percent of GDP, against the CBO June Alternative case, where debt climbs past 100 percent of GDP, highlighting a five-trillion-dollar gap. Chart c32 charts the historical decline in the percentage of government revenue not committed to mandatory spending from 1962 to 2016; this figure fell from roughly 70 percent in the early 1960s to near zero, illustrating the lack of budgetary flexibility. Chart c33 shows gross US debt to GDP from 1900 to 2010, highlighting that the debt-to-GDP ratio has passed 100 percent for only the second time in history, with the first occurrence being during World War War II.

Chart c34 shows the fiscal adjustment in 2012 as a percentage of GDP from 1963 to 2011, indicating that extending payroll tax cuts and unemployment benefits cushions the immediate fiscal tightening but defers the debt challenge. This survival of the US Treasury is attributed to the kindness of strangers, as shown in Chart c35 and Chart c36. Chart c35 traces foreign holdings of US debt from 1994 to 2010, demonstrating that holdings by the foreign official sector surged from under 10 percent to over 30 percent of total net debt, while private sector holdings hovered around 13 percent. Concurrently, Chart c36 shows Federal Reserve holdings of US debt as a percentage of total net debt, which dipped to 8 percent in 2008 before spiking back up to over 16 percent by 2010. 

Chart c37, titled reserve currency status does not last forever, visualizes the historical lifecycle of global reserve currencies since the 15th century, showing how nations like Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands, France, and Britain each held dominant reserve status for roughly 80 to 110 years before the US assumed the role in the early 20th century. Finally, Chart c38 looks at quarterly state tax revenue growth on a year-over-year basis from 1999 to 2011, which rebounded sharply to positive 8 percent in 2011 after bottoming out near negative 16 percent in 2009. The author notes this revenue recovery, combined with spending cuts, supports municipal bond credit risk, though it carries a broader economic cost. The author closes with a quote from MIT economist Rudiger Dornbusch, warning that while fiscal crises take a long time to arrive, they happen much faster than expected once they begin.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2012 outlook focuses on investment strategies for putting idle capital to work despite widespread market pessimism. The author observes that concerns over global imbalances have created unprecedented levels of sideline cash, including retail bank deposits, central bank reserves, corporate balance sheets, and seven hundred billion dollars in unspent private equity commitments. In response, J.P. Morgan's 2012 strategy targets global and European multinational equities, technology stocks, and specific high-yield, low-payout equity income funds, even while overall portfolio equity weightings remain below normal.

The page features several charts illustrating cash accumulation. The first, chart forty-eight, displays US commercial bank excess deposits in trillions of USD from 2000 to 2010, showing deposits rising sharply to over eight trillion dollars while loans flatten at around six and a half trillion dollars after 2008. Chart forty-nine tracks foreign exchange reserves in trillions of USD from 1970 to 2010, highlighting a massive exponential surge in emerging markets reserves to nearly eight trillion dollars, dwarfing Japan's steady rise to around one trillion. Chart fifty plots US corporate cash balances as a percentage of cash and equivalents to tangible assets from 1952 to 2010, showing that corporate cash dipped from fourteen percent in the 1950s to a low of four percent in the late 1970s before surging back to nearly twelve percent by 2010.

A comparative analysis of multinational equities is presented across two tables and a chart. Table fifty-one details global multinationals, which boast average characteristics of a one hundred thirty-one point five billion dollar market capitalization, an eleven-times forward price-to-earnings ratio, a three point two percent dividend yield, and sixty-nine percent revenue exposure outside their home country. Table fifty-two covers oversold European multinationals, which average a ninety-three point three billion dollar market cap, a nine point eight times forward price-to-earnings ratio, a four point eight percent dividend yield, twenty-nine percent return on equity, and fifty-one percent revenue exposure outside of Europe. Chart fifty-three shows the forward price-to-earnings multiples of the S&P 500 and S&P 500 Tech Index from 1995 to 2010. It highlights that the technology index, which traded at an extreme multiple near seventy in 2000, has converged with the broader S&P 500 at around eleven to thirteen times earnings, making technology a compellingly cheap growth option.

The final section focuses on equity income strategies. Chart fifty-four displays the scope for dividend increases from 1988 to 2008 by plotting the payout ratio on the left-hand scale against cash to tangible assets on the right-hand scale. The payout ratio dropped from nearly sixty percent to below thirty percent, while corporate cash to tangible assets climbed from five percent to over twelve percent, indicating significant room for companies to increase dividends. Chart fifty-five tracks the total return from 1990 to 2010 for companies that can afford high dividends. It demonstrates that portfolios consisting of high dividend yield, low payout companies significantly outperformed the broad S&P 500 and vastly outperformed high dividend yield, high payout companies, which generated the lowest cumulative returns over the twenty-year period.

This page from J.P. Morgan's market outlook analyzes the performance of the United States economy, proposing that it is decoupling from Europe and Asia. The author explores how better-than-expected manufacturing, light truck sales, and consumer spending are sustaining growth, even as disposable income remains weak and housing provides little economic support. 

The first series of charts examines consumer and household trends. Chart c22, which tracks manufacturing surveys, shows that both new orders and the total manufacturing index have stabilized well above their late-recessionary lows. Chart c23 displays credit card delinquencies of ninety days or more, illustrating a sharp decline from a peak above three percent in late 2009 to approximately one point five percent in late 2011, signaling healing household balance sheets. Chart c24 presents household debt and debt service as a percent of disposable income. While total household debt peaked near one hundred thirty-five percent around 2008 and has declined only moderately, the actual debt service ratio has plunged from nearly fourteen percent to eleven point five percent, explaining why consumers have more cash to spend. Chart c25 tracks shadow housing inventory in millions of units, illustrating a massive burden of seven to eight million units by 2011 across existing listings, ninety-day delinquencies, foreclosures, bank-owned real estate, and underwater homes, which explains why housing is not boosting the economy. Chart c26 tracks quarter-over-quarter annualized change in real spending versus disposable income, showing that consumption remains resilient despite weak disposable income growth that relies heavily on government transfers. This spending may be driven by the wealthiest ten percent of households who account for thirty to forty percent of overall spending. Chart c27 highlights a bipolar labor market in millions of workers. Employment in construction, government, and finance has languished around thirty-four point five million, while total employment excluding those three struggling sectors has recovered sharply from its trough of ninety-four million to nearly ninety-eight million.

The second half of the page covers business activity and capital spending. Chart c28 tracks the recovery of capital spending, which rebounded by eight percent from under nine billion dollars in 2009 to over eleven billion dollars in 2005 USD by late 2011. Chart c29 shows year-over-year percent change in capital stock, highlighting that 2009 was the first year since 1932 in which net capital stock declined, falling to nearly negative one percent, making the recent capex bounce a necessary catch-up after severe underinvestment; estimates for 2011 show a recovery back to around two percent. Looking forward, despite mixed capital expenditure surveys from Citi and the Institute for Supply Management, J.P. Morgan forecasts a positive contribution from the business sector and an economy-wide growth rate of approximately two point twenty-five percent. This outlook is supported by chart c30, which shows year-over-year commercial and industrial loan growth accelerating from a bottom of negative eighteen percent in 2010 to nearly ten percent by late 2011, helping offset weak residential loan demand.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2012 Outlook, titled "ASIA: finding out what growth looks like without all the stimulus," analyzes the economic challenges and long-term potential of the Asian market as policy stimulus fades. 

The author begins by noting that while Asia generated the best combination of real GDP and corporate profit growth in 2011, Asian equities underperformed. This underperformance was driven by two main issues. First, the region over-stimulated, pushing real interest rates to zero and driving up inflation. Chart c39 shows that in 2011, Asia ex-Japan’s real GDP growth led at around 8% compared to the US at 2% and Europe at 1.5%, though US earnings growth led at 14% compared to Asia's 5%. Chart c40 depicts this over-stimulation by tracing Real GDP and Headline CPI from 2001 to 2011, illustrating a V-shaped growth recovery accompanied by rising CPI inflation that peaked near 7%. To rein in inflation, aggressive policy tightening was implemented. Chart c41 shows how China cooled inflation by halving its M2 money supply growth from 30% in late 2009 to roughly 13% by 2011, which successfully brought CPI inflation down toward 4%. 

The second major problem is European bank deleveraging, which poses a credit contraction risk for Asia. Chart c42, titled "Bankenstein's Monster," shows that European bank claims on Asia ex-Japan ballooned from roughly $400 billion in 2005 to nearly $900 billion in 2011, vastly exceeding US bank claims, which remained flat near $150 billion. Concurrently, Asian growth has become increasingly dependent on credit expansion. Chart c43 illustrates this by showing China’s society-wide credit as a percentage of nominal GDP surging from 120% in 2002 to 220% in 2011. This credit tightening and weaker European demand have slowed Chinese manufacturing and exports, as seen in chart c44, where year-over-year export growth declined alongside the purchasing managers' index (PMI), which fell back toward the neutral 50 level in late 2011.

Despite these headwinds, the author remains optimistic about Asia’s long-term outlook. This optimism is supported by strong domestic consumption in China and robust external positions. Chart c45 argues that observers should focus on the absolute level of Chinese consumer spending rather than its share of GDP; while household consumption as a percentage of GDP fell from 45% in 1993 to 34% in 2008, annual retail sales per capita surged exponentially from 1,300 Yuan to over 11,300 Yuan. Additionally, chart c46 highlights that Asia ex-China/Japan has consistently run current account surpluses between 2% and 6% of GDP since the late 1990s, reducing its vulnerability to external shocks. Looking ahead to 2012, chart c47 outlines real GDP growth rate forecasts for Asia ex-Japan. Although growth is projected to slow from its historical peaks, the IMF forecast of approximately 7.5% and the Consensus forecast of roughly 7.0% still point to a healthy, self-sustaining expansion that should make 2012 an improvement over 2011.

This page from Eye on the Market discusses global equity valuations and the investment outlook for 2012, focusing on the imbalances of the current US economic recovery and the ongoing banking crisis in Europe. The author argues that while equity valuations have fallen sharply on a price-to-book and price-to-earnings basis, multiple expansion is unlikely because US corporate profits have been artificially boosted by depressed labor compensation. To support this, three charts are presented. Chart c56, titled "The men who fell to earth," plots price-to-forward-earnings against price-to-book ratios for major countries. It shows that current valuations for the US, Japan, France, Germany, Spain, the United Kingdom, Korea, Australia, China, and Hong Kong are significantly below their long-term averages; for example, the US stands at a price-to-book ratio of roughly 1.8x and a price-to-forward-earnings ratio of about 12x, compared to a much higher historical average. Charts c57 and c58 compare the past five recoveries to the current recovery in billions of 2005 US dollars over eleven quarters since the trough. In past recoveries, labor compensation closely tracked sales growth while profits rose moderately. In contrast, the current recovery shows a decoupling where corporate profits surged to nearly 800 billion dollars by quarter eleven, while labor compensation remained negative near minus 100 billion dollars and sales reached 500 billion dollars. 

The author also cautions against making a contrarian overweight call on European equities, preferring to remain underweight Europe and overweight the US. Instead of buying European equities, the focus is on purchasing discounted loans from deleveraging European banks. Examples of recent transactions include performing consumer loans in Spain bought at a 50 percent discount, consumer loans in the Netherlands at 64 cents on the Euro, 2 billion Euros of non-performing commercial mortgage loans in the United Kingdom, Germany, and other countries at a 58 percent discount, and UK residential mortgage loans at a 36 percent discount to par. 

Three European-focused charts contextualize this banking distress. Chart c59 shows the price-to-book ratio of the Eurostoxx Banks Index from 2007 to 2011, which collapsed from above 2.0 to around 0.4. Chart c60, titled "How bad can banks get in a crisis?", compares trough price-to-tangible-book ratios across past crises. While Europe in 2009 had a trough of about 0.4 and the historic average sits at 0.5, severe past crises like Korea in 1997 and Sweden in 1991 saw troughs fall as low as 0.2. Chart c61 displays the G-3 banking sector loan-to-deposit ratios, showing that Western Europe has a median ratio of 1.3 and a weighted average of nearly 1.6, reflecting an extreme reliance on volatile wholesale funding compared to the US, which has a median of 1.1 and weighted average of 0.85, and Japan, which sits at 0.8 for both metrics. A footnote cites a Bridgewater Associates report estimating that European banks hold about 4 trillion dollars in US dollar-denominated assets, 90 percent of which are funded on a wholesale basis. Ultimately, the author remains neutral on potential changes to the Eurozone constituency, Germany's breaking point, and the US dollar to Euro exchange rate, but expects European equities and sovereign credit to continue underperforming.

This page analyzes investment opportunities and risks across private credit, high-yield debt, leveraged loans, and US commercial real estate. The author argues that while post-recession spreads rallied, many mid-sized companies still face restricted capital access, driving them to private mezzanine credit. 

A table detailing private credit fund characteristics shows that corporate mezzanine debt offers enticing yields to maturity of 13.1% to 14.2% and cash coupons of 8.6% to 10.4%, paired with an estimated equity cushion of 23% to 42%. Commercial real estate private credit offers a 12.6% yield to maturity and a 33% equity cushion. The trade-off for these yields is portfolio illiquidity and sector concentration. 

The publication then addresses the broader high-yield market, which experienced a sharp sell-off following the S&P credit downgrade of the United States. A line chart tracking high-yield versus US government bonds illustrates this divergence: while five-to-seven-year Treasuries rose to a total return index value of 110 by late 2011, US High Yield plummeted to below 100. This market distress pushed the market-implied five-year cumulative default rate to roughly 44%. While this rate is below the March 2009 peak of nearly 70%, it remains higher than the worst default rates experienced during the historical cycles of 1989–1994 and 1999–2004, which peaked at approximately 33%. 

Two main caveats are highlighted for credit markets. First, a maturity wall is looming. A stacked bar chart of high-yield loan and bond maturities shows manageable refinancing needs of about $50 billion annually through 2013, which then surge to over $250 billion per year between 2016 and 2018. Second, liquidity has deteriorated. A chart tracking primary dealer corporate bond positions reveals that dealer inventories collapsed from a peak of nearly $250 billion in 2007 to virtually zero by 2011, a consequence of post-crisis regulatory changes that have increased market volatility.

Finally, the discussion turns to US commercial real estate, where a divergence has emerged between core and distressed assets. A line chart tracking price declines from the 2007 peak shows that "major properties in major markets" have recovered significantly, sitting at just a 15% discount to peak pricing. In contrast, overall properties remain down by 40%, and distressed properties languish at a 55% decline from their peak. The author suggests the best value lies in the distressed sector, where buyers can leverage motivated sellers like undercapitalized regional banks or downsizing REITs. Cited examples include a portfolio of sixty suburban offices purchased at a 9.3% cap rate at a 40% discount to replacement cost, and a half-vacant Boston office building acquired at a 50% discount to replacement cost.

This page serves as a comprehensive reference index for the chart sources used throughout the publication, cataloging entries from c1 to c86. The citations cover a vast array of global financial, governmental, and academic institutions. Prominent sources include major international bodies like the International Monetary Fund, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, and the Bank for International Settlements. National statistical and financial agencies are heavily represented, including the Federal Reserve Board, the Bureau of Economic Analysis, Eurostat, the Bank of Japan, the Bank of England, and the China National Bureau of Statistics. Private financial sector data is sourced from Bloomberg, J.P. Morgan Securities, Barclays Capital, Credit Suisse, Markit, and Moody's. Additionally, the index references specific academic papers, such as Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff's work on debt crises, and Jacopo Ponticelli and Hans-Joachim Voth's research on austerity and social unrest. The listed data points are primarily current up to late 2011, underpinning the timely economic analyses presented in the outlook.

This page from the report discusses investment opportunities across energy markets, gold, and macro hedge funds, highlighting the growing reliance on non-conventional energy sources and tactical asset allocation strategies for 2012. 

In the oil and gas sector, the author notes that future projections for both global liquids and US dry gas production depend heavily on non-conventional sources. Even with low natural gas prices, large oil and gas majors are actively acquiring proven reserves for the long term. On the crude oil side, investments are focused on "renaissance" plays in older, depleted fields, as well as oil service companies specializing in fracking, wastewater management, and technically challenging deep-water projects, such as the sub-salt fields located seven kilometers beneath the ocean surface off the coast of Brazil. 

Three energy charts illustrate these trends. Chart c68 shows the historical US natural gas spot price in USD per mmBtu from 1999 to 2011, detailing its rise from under four dollars to peaks near 14 dollars in 2005 and 2008, before falling back below four dollars by late 2011. Chart c69 depicts global liquids production history and projections from 1990 to 2030, showing total daily production rising from roughly 85 million barrels to nearly 110 million barrels, with unconventional sources representing a substantial portion of the future mix alongside OPEC and Non-OPEC conventional sources. Chart c70 details US dry gas production history and projections from 1990 to 2030 in trillion cubic feet per year, showcasing a dramatic projected expansion of shale gas that is expected to displace net imports and push total production toward 30 trillion cubic feet.

The text also addresses gold, describing it as highly correlated with European sovereign credit spreads and liquid money supply, and inversely correlated with 10-year TIPS yields. This is illustrated in Chart c71, which tracks the close relationship between gold prices, inverted ten-year TIPS yields, the liquid money supply, and Western Europe sovereign five-year CDS spreads from January 2009 to October 2011. The author predicts that gold will remain volatile but will end 2012 higher, advising investors not to sell yet. 

To complement underweight equity positions, the author recommends macro hedge funds. Chart c72 plots five-year annualized returns against volatility to demonstrate the power of diversification. While individual macro hedge funds (shown as blue diamonds) display highly dispersed performance and volatility stretching up to 75%, randomly grouped five-fund pods (shown as brown squares) cluster tightly together, significantly reducing volatility to under 25% while maintaining positive returns.

Finally, the author projects below-trend growth in oil demand for 2012 due to economic slowdowns in Europe and Asia, though overall demand is still expected to rise. Potential supply increases from Libya and Iraq may be offset by major Gulf producers—including Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE, which have increased output by two million barrels per day since July 2010. Iran's ongoing uranium enrichment is flagged as the primary geopolitical wild card for oil markets, and the author concludes that any price decline of 10% or more represents an attractive buying opportunity.

This page discusses the severe economic downturn in Spain and explores the historical relationship between austerity policies and social unrest in Europe. The author argues that Spain is currently testing the socioeconomic limits of how much austerity a nation can endure while remaining in a currency union, citing an overall unemployment rate of 23% and a youth unemployment rate exceeding 40%. Highlighting research on 32 European countries since 1919, the author notes that spending cuts have historically led to an increase in demonstrations, riots, and strikes, especially in nations that began with high levels of government debt. 

Six charts track Spain's economic decline and one positive outlier. Chart c73, showing the Spanish services activity survey from 2000 to 2010, details the seasonally adjusted Purchasing Managers Index crashing from above 60 to below 30 in late 2008, followed by a weak recovery and subsequent drop below 45. Chart c74 displays the Spanish unemployment rate from 1983 to late 2011, illustrating a dramatic surge starting around 2008 that pushes the rate back toward historical highs near 22%. Chart c75 tracks Spanish industrial production indexed to January 2007, which precipitously declines from 100 down to roughly 75 by 2009 and falls further by late 2011. Chart c76 demonstrates the dramatic collapse of the country's building boom, showing cement consumption in millions of tons dropping from a peak near 55 million tons in the mid-2000s to around 20 million tons in 2008. Chart c77 displays Spanish retail sales indexed to January 2003, which peaked above 110 in 2007 before entering a steady multi-year decline to below 90 in late 2011. The sole bright spot is featured in chart c78, representing year-over-year percent change in Spanish exports; after plunging to nearly negative 16% in 2009, export growth rebounded to over 12% in 2010.

Chart c79 addresses the broader relationship between budget cuts and social instability, showing the number of annual incidents per country for demonstrations, riots, and general strikes from 1919 to 2008. The data is divided into five policy types: expenditure increases, and expenditure reductions exceeding 1%, 2%, 3%, and 5%. The chart demonstrates a clear upward trend in all forms of unrest as spending cuts deepen; for instance, the rate of riots escalates from near zero during spending increases to over 1.2 incidents per country per year when budget cuts exceed 5%. 

The author questions whether Europe can maintain political and social cohesion along its current path, pointing to a growing democratic deficit at the European Union level that has been criticized by Germany's Constitutional Court. This lack of solidarity is highlighted by a defensive statement from Bank of France head Christian Noyer, who argued that rating agencies should downgrade Britain instead of France because Britain possesses larger deficits, comparable debt, higher inflation, lower growth, and declining credit.

This page from the publication discusses sovereign debt restructurings, the unequal treatment of creditors, and the historical failure of official sector rescue packages to prevent market meltdowns. The author argues that official entities like the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, along with favored local entities like Greek Social Security Funds, receive preferred treatment during restructurings, concentrating losses on the remaining bondholders. Unlike corporate credit, which features legal mechanisms to enforce equal treatment, sovereign debt lacks practical enforcement remedies. A rare exception occurred in 2000 when a hedge fund successfully blocked Peruvian payments on its Brady bonds through New York and Belgian courts to enforce a pari-passu clause, but the author notes that such successes are now highly unusual and that pari-passu clauses hold little weight today. Ultimately, the history of sovereign crises suggest that investors must demand substantial yields to justify taking on sovereign debt risk, as official bailouts have historically failed to halt market declines. In some cases, like Argentina and Russia, these asset price declines were permanent, while in Mexico and Indonesia, recovery only occurred after massive currency devaluations of 50% to 70% re-established economic equilibrium.

To support this argument, the page features four charts tracking sovereign debt prices during historical crises, illustrating how official aid packages failed to prevent immediate price collapses. The first chart displays Argentina's sovereign debt price for its 11 3/8 2017 bond from January 1998 to January 2004. In December 2000, when the debt price was hovering around 90, the IMF, Inter-American Development Bank, Spain, and private banks promised a $40 billion aid package, which the IMF Managing Director claimed would lay the groundwork for sustained growth. Instead, the price collapsed precipitously over the next year, bottoming out near 20 in 2002 before stabilizing at a fraction of its pre-crisis value.

The second chart shows Mexico's Sovereign Brady Bond price for its 6 1/4 2019 bond from December 1993 to March 1995. Despite the creation of a permanent $6.7 billion line of credit from the United States and Canada in April 1994 when the bond price was around 65, prices continued to decline. Even after the subsequent creation of a $20 billion Exchange Stabilization Fund in February 1995, the bond price fell further to near 45 before eventually finding a floor and beginning a temporary recovery.

The third chart tracks Russian sovereign GKO T-bill prices maturing March 10, 1999, over a compressed timeline from January 1998 to July 1998. In January 1998, IMF Managing Director Stanley Fischer expressed strong optimism that the Russian economy would outperform pessimistic expectations. In July 1998, Russian stocks and bonds soared briefly as the IMF led a promise of $22.6 billion in loans, and the IMF Executive Board completed a review to disburse a $700 million tranche. However, immediately after these announcements, the debt price crashed from near 80 to 40.

The fourth chart illustrates Indonesia's sovereign debt price for its 7 3/4 2006 bond from July 1996 to July 1998. In April 1998, when the bond price was around 80, the IMF expressed positive sentiment regarding negotiations with the new Cabinet and signaled it would resume lending under a $40 billion package. Rather than stabilizing the market, this optimism preceded a sharp sell-off, with the bond price falling to nearly 50 by July 1998.

This page of the publication explores two main themes: the challenging environment for active equity managers due to low stock dispersion, and the escalating sovereign debt crisis in Europe. 

In the first section, the author examines stock return dispersion in 2011, characterizing it as "slim pickins." A detailed table shows that the calendar year stock return dispersion for the S&P 500 in 2011 was only 23 percent, significantly below its 20-year average of 34 percent and closer to its 20-year minimum of 21 percent. Sectors like Information Technology saw a dispersion of 26 percent in 2011 compared to a historical average of 46 percent, while Utilities sat at 14 percent compared to a 23 percent average. This relationship is further contextualized by an accompanying line chart, "Stock dispersion and active equity management," which plots S&P 500 stock dispersion alongside the percentage of Large Cap Core managers beating their benchmark from 1991 to 2011. The visual comparison reveals that periods of lower stock dispersion generally coincide with a lower percentage of managers outperforming their benchmarks, illustrating why active management struggled in 2011.

The second half of the page, titled "The latest from Europe: strange days," details the critical credit and capital flow strains in the Eurozone. The author argues that without substantial European Central Bank intervention, countries in the Periphery—namely Italy and Spain—would likely have abandoned the Euro already. The first supporting chart plots the year-over-year percent changes of M2 money supply from 2003 to 2011 as a proxy for intra-European capital flight. It shows a stark divergence starting around 2010: while the Core nations (Germany, France, Netherlands, and Finland) saw M2 growth climb to nearly 10 percent, the Periphery nations (Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece, and Spain) saw their M2 growth plummet to roughly negative 4 percent by late 2011.
