It shows farm income plummeting to a low of about 85 around 1866, before steeply recovering to over 100 by 1870. The second chart, "Post World War II recovery in the Axis Powers," plots two data series: Japanese industrial production on the left-hand axis and German exports on the right-hand axis. It shows Japanese industrial production rebounding from a low index value of under 50 in 1946 to over 200 by 1956, while German exports surged from near zero in 1948 to over seven billion dollars by 1956. 

The bottom half of the page features a prominent, long-term chart titled "Dow Jones Industrial Average, May 1896 to April 2012," plotted on a logarithmic price scale. The chart highlights alternating market cycles colored in red (representing periods of crisis and consolidation) and blue (representing mega-bull markets). The first period, in red, is characterized as an under-regulated world plagued by frequent recessions, bank failures, and the Great Depression. This is followed by a blue-coded post-war bull market of prosperity and productivity associated with rebuilding the Axis Powers. The chart then enters a red-coded phase marked by Vietnam, Nixon, OPEC, and inflation, which is eventually broken by a blue-coded bull market set in motion by Paul Volcker destroying inflation as interest rates tumbled. The final period on the chart, colored in red, captures the inflating and bursting of the credit, housing, and European debt bubbles. Cembalest uses this historical progression to suggest that equity markets are currently in a sideways, volatile consolidation channel, and cautions investors that it may take some time before a sustained new bull market emerges.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" analyzes global economic and financial trends through an illustrative "alien's" perspective, focusing on why stock valuations remain historically cheap despite solid earnings. Cembalest attributes this cheapness to structural headwinds, notably the massive buildup of household, corporate, and government debt across OECD countries, which nearly quadrupled in real terms between 1980 and 2010. Although some deleveraging has occurred—such as US household debt falling from a peak of 99% of GDP to 86%—overall debt remains a significant drag on Western economies. While central banks have injected unprecedented liquidity to cushion this deleveraging, boosting assets like gold and equities, real economic growth still lags. Cembalest warns that governments might address these high debt levels and deficits through taxation rather than spending cuts, which historically dampens future growth. However, because equity valuations already discount much of this bad news, he recommends a portfolio strategy of caution rather than panic.

The page features five visual aids to support this analysis. The first chart, showing actual S&P 500 EPS versus estimates (excluding financial firms) from September 2008 to March 2012, illustrates that earnings outperformance peaked at nearly 10% in late 2009 before normalizing to a still-positive 4% to 5% range by early 2012. The second chart on global earnings revisions displays the ratio of upgrades minus downgrades over total revisions from 2008 through early 2012. This chart highlights a severe contraction in late 2008 where revisions fell to negative 0.7, a subsequent post-crisis rebound peaking near positive 0.3 in early 2010, and a return to net-negative territory throughout late 2011.

Two charts track OECD non-financial sector debt from 1980 to 2010. The first displays debt as a percentage of GDP, averaged across 18 OECD economies, showing total debt rising from about 165% to over 300% of GDP. This growth was led by private sector debt, which climbed from 120% to around 220%, and government debt, which rose from 40% to roughly 90%. The second OECD debt chart measures real debt levels deflated by consumer prices, indexed to 1980. This chart reveals that by 2010, total real debt levels had quadrupled to an index value of 400, led dramatically by household debt growth, which soared to an index value exceeding 600. 

The final chart tracks cumulative mutual fund net flows in billions of US dollars from 2007 to 2012, highlighting a stark divergence in investor sentiment. While US bond funds and global bond funds experienced massive cumulative inflows reaching nearly $1,000 billion and $750 billion respectively, US equity funds faced relentless net redemptions, losing nearly $300 billion cumulatively over the same five-year period.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the systemic instability of the Eurozone, framing the struggles of the single currency through the mythological lens of the "Fall of Icarus" depicted in an included 1650 painting by Jacob Pieter Gowy. The author argues that a single central bank and currency without a unified state has proved inherently unstable. In Greece, extreme austerity has led to youth unemployment exceeding 50%, rising political extremism, and a bleak outlook where potential economic output has been permanently damaged. 

To illustrate Greece’s unsustainable position, a chart titled "Greece's debtor's prison" compares Greek post-restructuring debt-to-GDP projections from 2009 to 2020 against historical precedents. While Mexico’s 1990 post-restructuring debt hovered around 45% and Argentina’s 2001 restructuring sat around 80%, J.P. Morgan’s central scenario projects Greece’s debt-to-GDP ratio to peak above 170% and remain around 170% by 2020. Even the more optimistic IMF/ECB/EU baseline scenario only projects a decline to roughly 120% of GDP by 2020. The author highlights that 70% to 80% of Greek bailout funds were recycled to facilitate capital flight and repay foreign bondholders rather than helping the domestic economy, leaving Greece effectively trapped in a debtor's prison.

Regarding France, the commentary explores the political outlook under newly elected President François Hollande. A chart titled "France's twin deficits may constrain Hollande" plots the nation’s current account and budget deficit as a percent of GDP from 1960 to 2010. It shows that by 2010, France’s budget deficit had widened near -8% of GDP and the current account was running at a deficit of roughly -2% of GDP. This historically deep twin deficit, the author poses, is highly likely to constrain Hollande’s ability to enact expansive socialist reforms, forcing him to remain aligned with market expectations.

The author also analyzes the escalating risks in Spain, where the recapitalization of Bankia is deemed insufficient. With Spain's sovereign debt approaching 90% of GDP in a low-productivity, service-based economy, the author warns that emergency ECB funding provided to Italy and Spain could run out by the end of 2012. Finally, Germany is described as being in good economic shape. The author suggests Germany might tolerate higher domestic inflation to prevent an exchange rate mechanism collapse similar to the early 1990s, which would postpone tighter monetary policies and marginally assist Southern European economies.

This page addresses questions regarding US equity valuation methods, specifically analyzing how Graham-Dodd and Shiller price-to-earnings (P/E) models work and examining their underlying assumptions. The author explains that these models use a smoothed, 10-year backward-looking earnings average to capture underlying market earning power and reduce cyclical noise. While these models currently indicate that the S&P 500 is historically expensive, the author argues that this perspective changes significantly when accounting for the prevailing inflation environment.

To illustrate these concepts, the page presents four charts based on data from Robert J. Shiller, Standard & Poor's, and Empirical Research Partners. Chart I, a line chart tracking the S&P 500 Price-to-10 year average reported earnings from 1901 to 2011, plots J.P. Morgan's version of the Graham-Dodd model on a scale of 0x to 35x. It classifies multiples above roughly 25x as expensive and those below 10x as cheap. Chart II covers the same time frame and scale, overlaying J.P. Morgan's model with the Shiller P/E ratio to show that both methodologies yield nearly identical historical results, with major peaks near 30x or higher around 1929 and 2000. 

The author questions the validity of comparing valuation multiples across vastly different historical inflation regimes, noting that the lowest post-war multiples occurred during the high-inflation 1970s, when earnings stream values were eroded. To adjust for inflation, the author inverts the P/E ratio into an earnings yield. Chart III plots the Nominal S&P 500 10-year trailing earnings yield from 1945 to past 2005 on a scale of 2% to 10%, where low yields (such as the 2% reached around 2000) represent expensive valuations and high yields (such as the 10% yield around 1980) signify cheap valuations. 

Chart IV adjusts these figures by subtracting headline CPI inflation to show the Real S&P 500 10-year trailing earnings yield from 1945 onward, with a scale ranging from -2% to 5%. This real yield represents the actual required return for investing in equities. In this adjusted view, the high-inflation period of the late 1970s and early 1980s shifts from looking "cheap" to looking very "expensive," dipping below -1%. Conversely, the valuation at the time of publication (rising toward a real yield of 2%) does not appear nearly as expensive as shown in the nominal charts. Ultimately, the author concludes that factoring in how inflation alters required equity returns reshapes the historical perspective on market valuations.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication addresses the contemporary "German question," reframing the historical concept of German economic dominance from a source of European conflict into a modern economic inquiry: will Germany spend its accumulated national wealth to save the Eurozone, and what would it cost? 

To establish the historical precedent of Germany's economic power outpacing its neighbors, the author presents three line charts based on Angus Maddison's historical database. The first chart, tracking the period before the Franco-Prussian War from 1850 to 1871, shows German GDP relative to France rising from a base of 100 in 1850 to approximately 120 by 1871. The second chart, focused on the years before World War I (1890 to 1913), shows German GDP relative to France and England combined growing from 100 to nearly 135. The third chart shows the period before World War II (1924 to 1942), with German GDP relative to France and England climbing from 100 to over 160.

Moving to the present crisis, the author poses the question of how much it would cost Germany to single-handedly backstop the Eurozone periphery over a five-year period (2012–2016) without assistance from France or the IMF, and without resorting to inflationary ECB solutions. J.P. Morgan estimates this cost to be approximately 1 trillion Euros. 

A central table details this five-year projection in billions of Euros across five periphery nations: Portugal, Ireland, Italy, Greece, and Spain. Under public capital account support (Column A), the total required is 584 billion Euros, with Spain needing the most at 305 billion, followed by Italy at 166 billion, Ireland at 45 billion, Greece at 43 billion, and Portugal at 26 billion. Private capital account outflows (Column B) total negative 692 billion Euros, driven by Spain at negative 479 billion and Italy at negative 168 billion; Greece and Ireland are projected at zero capital flight due to previous outflows or stabilization. Current account balances (Column C) total negative 313 billion Euros, with Spain at negative 111 billion and Italy at negative 106 billion. This results in a total balance of payments deficit support (Column D) of 420 billion Euros periphery-wide. Combining public support and balance of payments deficits, the total support required over five years (Column E) is projected at 1,005 billion Euros, consisting of 589 billion for Spain, 273 billion for Italy, 90 billion for Greece, 52 billion for Portugal, and 1 billion for Ireland.

The model is built on several key assumptions, including a gradual improvement in current accounts due to depressed periphery import demand, and an assumption that foreign private investors will withdraw 60% of their accumulated investments since the inception of the Euro. Crucially, the authors note that this 1 trillion Euro estimate omits potential bank recapitalization costs, meaning the actual required rescue sum could be significantly higher.

Michael Cembalest discusses the policy measures needed to unleash the substantial mountains of corporate cash currently held by businesses, arguing against further Federal Reserve intervention such as a third round of quantitative easing. Since policy rates are already at zero and 10-year Treasury yields are below 2%, he suggests instead looking to the pro-growth policies of the 1950s under President Dwight Eisenhower. During that decade, US federal debt declined from 80% to 46% of GDP through real GDP growth exceeding 4%, rather than through inflation or austerity. He highlights that Eisenhower-era policies championed easing tax burdens on small businesses, introducing Subchapter S to eliminate double taxation, and removing wage and price controls, which allowed the private sector to account for a post-war peak of 86% of all employment.

To support his assessment of positive US recovery signals alongside corporate cash accumulation, the page presents five distinct charts. The first chart, US small business optimism, plots an index from 2000 to 2012, showing index values dropping from over 100 down to a low of nearly 80 during the 2008 recession, with a partial recovery to around 95 by 2012. The second chart, US job openings rising, shows job openings in millions from 2001 to 2011, dropping from a peak near 4.5 million in 2007 to a low of 2.5 million in 2009 before rising back to around 4 million. The third chart, Railroad carloads recovering, graphs a 4-week moving average of railcars in thousands, excluding coal, from 2000 to 2012, illustrating a steep drop from pre-recession levels of roughly 190,000 to a low of 130,000, followed by a steady climb back toward 170,000. 

The fourth chart, Company sales surveys upbeat, covers airlines, homebuilders, and trucking companies on a scale from 0 to 100 from 1998 to 2012. It shows that while all three sectors suffered steep declines during the financial crisis—with homebuilders plummeting from a peak near 70 down to under 10—all three sectors show notable rebounds by 2012, led by airlines and trucking. The final chart, What will it take to unleash corporate cash, tracks cash and equivalents as a percentage of tangible assets from 1952 to 2008/2012. This ratio declined from a high of 12% in the 1950s to under 5% in the late 1970s, but has since steadily risen to nearly 14% by 2012, illustrating the massive corporate cash buildup.

In wrapping up, Cembalest notes that global economic growth is highly interdependent and fragile, with China, Europe, and the US all relying on one another. He highlights an unusual market anomaly in which 98% of the S&P 500's cumulative 27% return since January 2010 occurred during corporate earnings seasons or immediately following QE announcements, leaving the market flat during other periods. Consequently, J.P. Morgan Asset Management recommends taking modestly less risk than normal, favoring allocations to distressed residential and commercial real estate, long-term energy projects, and private lending. Geographically, they see the best opportunities in public and private equity in the US and the Pacific Rim, specifically excluding China and Japan.

This page addresses the critical question of whether a projected one-trillion-Euro cost for a five-year fix of the Eurozone is economically feasible, arguing that saving the Euro is fundamentally a political decision rather than an economic one. The author notes that Germany's capacity to absorb more debt is highly constrained after twenty years of funding its own reunification. 

To illustrate the scale of the proposed rescue package, the top-left bar chart compares various historical estimates of the cost of German reunification to the estimated one-trillion-Euro cost to save Europe. The historical estimates, gathered from multiple economic institutes, range from roughly 500 billion to nearly 1.6 trillion Euros, placing the trillion-Euro cost to save Europe on par with these massive historical expenditures. To the right, a line chart plots German gross general government debt as a percentage of GDP from 1991 to 2016. This chart shows debt rising gradually from around 40% of GDP in 1991 to over 80% in 2011, and it projects that adding the estimated one-trillion-Euro rescue cost would drive Germany's debt ratio past 105% of GDP.

The bottom portion of the page focus on market dynamics and analyst behavior during the crisis. The bottom-left line chart plots the foreign private sector investment position as a percentage of GDP from 1999 to 2011 for Greece, Italy, Spain, and Portugal. This chart visualizes severe capital flight from the European periphery, with sharp, downward trajectories in private investment across all four nations. To the right, a timeline chart from December 2011 to May 2012 compares the S&P 500 index level against changes in strategist forecasts. The S&P 500 line shows a temporary early-year rally peaking near 1,400 before declining. Step-line overlays show that major Wall Street firms, including Credit Suisse, UBS, Citi, HSBC, and Bank of America, raised their S&P 500 forecasts during this surge, while Deutsche Bank, J.P. Morgan Securities, Barclays, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley left their forecasts unchanged. The author characterizes this rally as a temporary "Prague Spring" sparked by the European Central Bank's liquidity injections, which may only carry Italian and Spanish government funding through the end of 2012.

The analysis concludes by reiterating a highly skeptical, underweight stance on Europe, noting that European equities have underperformed the United States by 36% over the prior three years. Observing a lack of concrete agreement at the summit between François Hollande and Angela Merkel, the author warns that while extreme pressure might eventually force policies like Euro T-bills, a pan-European deposit guarantee, direct bank funding by the European Stabilization Mechanism, or a broader IMF-led rescue, investors should not treat these possibilities as an investment strategy. The author calls for extreme caution regarding European assets due to Europe's ongoing potential to disrupt global markets.

This analysis frames the global market landscape as a struggle between massive macroeconomic imbalances, termed "The Squid," and strong corporate fundamentals, termed "The Whale." This tension underpins the recommendation to maintain an underweight position in equities, as the temporary boosts from monetary stimulus consistently fade. 

Two comparative charts illustrate this conflict from the 1980s through 2012. The first chart, depicting the "Squid," tracks a series of worsening macroeconomic imbalances. These metrics include rising OECD government debt relative to GDP, a widening gap between peripheral European unemployment and Germany's unemployment, an increasing Spanish reliance on foreign capital, high Chinese capital spending as a share of GDP, a large US fiscal deficit, and a stark divergence in industrial production between Germany and Italy. Conversely, the second chart, representing the "Whale," highlights highly supportive corporate metrics, showing historically elevated levels for the S&P earnings yield, economy-wide profits to GDP, and corporate cash relative to tangible assets. 

A third chart, titled "Another Prague Spring," tracks the Global Composite Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) from 2007 to 2012 on a scale from 35 to 60, where 50 represents the threshold for economic expansion. Shaded areas denote periods of monetary stimulus, which correspond directly to temporary peaks in economic activity labeled "PS" (Prague Springs) in 2010, 2011, and 2012. The chart demonstrates that as soon as these periods of monetary stimulus fade, global economic activity drops back down.

The commentary concludes with a focus on Europe's highly indebted monetary union. The author highlights that approximately one-third of all OECD banking system assets are held by banks currently in distress, which is defined as having credit spreads of more than 3%. Crucially, the vast majority of the banks contributing to this high-risk category are European, reinforcing why European sovereign and banking stability remains a central concern for global portfolios.

This page presents a satirical 16-panel comic strip that critiques the handling of the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis, complemented by a closing commentary on the structural differences between European and American fiscal unions. 

The comic strip features a back-and-forth dialogue between two cartoon figures debating various policy responses and political realities in Europe. The figures discuss the limitations of European Central Bank interventions, such as buying Spanish bonds or lending to EU banks, noting that credit spreads continue to widen and foreign interbank funding is fleeing. They poke fun at former French President Nicolas Sarkozy's premature declaration that the crisis was over, as well as the transition to François Hollande, depicted metaphorically by an artist wrapping an austerity belt around France. The debate shifts to Eurobonds, which are favored by Italian politicians like Mario Monti and Giulio Tremonti but strongly resisted by Germany, whose own debt already exceeds 80% of GDP following reunification. 

A central point of structural critique in the comic is the comparison of tax systems: while the United States sees 66% of its taxes paid federally to Washington, D.C., only 2% of European taxes are earmarked for EU-level activities, undermining Jean-Claude Trichet's assertion that there is no design flaw in the Euro. The characters also mock the proposed Redemption Fund, noting that for quasi-Eurobonds to work, countries like Italy would have to maintain an unrealistic 4% primary surplus for 25 years and comply with debt brakes that would have been breached 70% of the time since Italian unification in 1861. The comic ends in a repetitive loop, with the characters in unison asking once again if the ECB can just keep lending to EU banks to buy sovereign bonds, concluding with a resigned "We cannot go on like this."

In the text commentary below the comic, the author asks how long this policy cycle can continue, pointing out that Spain's economic outlook is particularly grim and that current policy options are unlikely to be decisive. To provide historical context on monetary unions, the author references an influential 1949 paper from the US Quarterly Journal of Economics on how the United States survived the Great Depression. The author highlights that a critical factor in the success of the US monetary union was unilateral regional transfers by the US Treasury, which acted as gifts or capital movements to enable weaker states to sustain growth and consumption—a level of fiscal integration that the Eurozone currently lacks.

This page features an introductory commentary by Michael Cembalest regarding his current investment outlook, followed by a satirical 16-panel comic strip titled "Waiting for Godot, 2012." 

In the introduction, Cembalest outlines his views on global economic conditions, noting that the US recovery is stable but weak at around 2%, Chinese growth is slowing to 7% to 8% with further stimulus anticipated, and the European economy is struggling significantly. He highlights Europe's 38.6% equity underperformance relative to the US since the Eurozone crisis began in November 2009. Cembalest lists several investment areas J.P. Morgan favors, including distressed US real estate, oil and gas, high yield, Asian private equity, US tech stocks, European bank loan sales, mezzanine debt, and macro hedge funds. However, due to the ongoing European crisis, he describes his state as one of "suspended animation, waiting."

The rest of the page consists of a comic strip set "at a bar in Madrid, or Milan," featuring two silhouetted figures, Vladimir and Estragon. Through their dialogue, the characters humorously analyze and dismiss various proposed policy solutions to the Eurozone crisis. 

First, they discuss the European Central Bank buying Spanish bonds again, but worry that German members will resign in protest. Next, they propose jointly and severally guaranteed Eurobonds (punningly called "EuroBunds"), but note that Maastricht Article 125 prevents this, dryly pointing out that "Maastricht" is an anagram for "Chasm Trait." A pan-European Deposit Guarantee is suggested to address EU insurance coverage ratios that fall far short of the US FDIC, prompting one character to confess they have already moved their euros to Deutsche Bank. 

The conversation then turns to legal and institutional barriers, citing the 2011 German Federal Constitutional Court ruling that declared large, unquantifiable financial risks enforced by permanent international treaties to be unconstitutional. When one character dreams of a 360 billion euro IMF bailout for Europe, the other points out this represents the IMF's entire global capacity, though they joke that the IMF might ignore this since it is run by a European. 

Ultimately, the characters conclude that "nothing is to be done" because there is 10 trillion euros of economy-wide peripheral debt in existence. They note that direct bank recapitalization via the EU Stabilization Fund is rejected by Finland, Austria, the Netherlands, and Germany—coining the acronym "FANG" for this bloc of opposing nations. The strip ends with a sarcastic critique of European bank stress tests, noting that Dexia and BFA-Bankia both passed official stress tests just before being nationalized, which they mockingly dismiss as mere exceptions, "just like Greece."

This page from the publication features a detailed commentary on "The Greek Question" by Michael Cembalest, who argues that politicians and economists are wrong to believe Greece should not be compared to Argentina or that Greece would be worse off leaving the Eurozone. While Greece's recovery would likely be slower than other historical examples due to Eurozone and austerity damage, Cembalest asserts that leaving the Euro and pursuing a structural devaluation supported by the IMF is Greece's only viable path forward. To support this thesis, the page presents fifteen charts detailing Argentina’s macroeconomic, social, and financial recovery before and after its 2001 default and devaluation, denoted on each chart by a vertical dashed line.

The first group of charts examines immediate monetary and macroeconomic shocks. The Peso overnight interbank interest rate chart shows rates spiking from roughly ten percent up to nearly one hundred percent during the 2001 crisis, before rapidly stabilizing back down to around ten percent by 2005. The YoY inflation chart illustrates a brief, sharp rise in price levels, peaking at around forty percent post-devaluation before declining back toward ten percent, though the text notes that Argentina underreports inflation by at least half. Real GDP growth YoY percent change fell precipitously to a low of negative fifteen percent in 2002 but staged a dramatic V-shaped recovery to average around nine percent growth between 2003 and 2005. Real GDP per capita in thousands of 1993 pesos demonstrates a similar trajectory, bottoming out at six point five in 2002 before rising back to nearly seven point eight by 2005. 

External balances and investments also showed dramatic post-crisis adjustments. The current account balance as a percent of GDP shifted from a deficit of negative three percent prior to the crisis to a massive surplus of nine percent by 2002, before normalizing to around three percent by 2005. Gross investment as a percent of GDP dropped from roughly twenty percent down to a low of twelve percent in 2002, followed by a strong rebound back to over twenty-two percent by 2005. 

Social and labor indicators highlight the temporary severity of the crisis followed by steady improvement. The poverty index, measuring the percent of the population living below one dollar and twenty-five cents per day, spiked to twelve percent in 2002 but steadily fell to about four percent by 2005. Inequality, measured by the Gini coefficient, peaked at over fifty-three percent in 2002 before steadily declining to under forty-eight percent by 2005. The unemployment rate spiked to over twenty percent in 2002 but steadily dropped to around eleven percent by 2005. Real wages indexed to Q1 1996 fell from over one hundred and five down to a low of eighty-five in 2002, then rose sharply to nearly one hundred and twenty by 2005.

Business and market health indicators also show a pronounced V-shaped pattern. The Merval equity index in USD crashed to nearly one hundred during the default, followed by a major bull run that carried the index close to eight hundred by 2005. Industrial production, seasonally adjusted and indexed to January 1996, dropped to eighty-five in 2002 before climbing steadily to nearly one hundred and thirty-five by 2005. The number of companies filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy peaked at nearly one hundred and ninety in 2001 before dropping to under fifty by 2005. Consumer confidence bottomed out around thirty-two in 2002, subsequently recovering to index levels between fifty and sixty. Finally, the public sector fiscal balance as a percent of GDP saw its primary balance rise from negative two percent to a surplus of nearly four percent, while the headline balance including interest payments rose from negative four percent to a surplus of two percent. 

Cembalest highlights that similar "morning after" recoveries occurred in the United Kingdom after 1992, Southeast Asia after 1998, and Iceland after 2009, posing the open policy question of whether the IMF will pivot to support a Greek devaluation rather than continuing to finance rescues for German and French banks.

This page discusses the challenges faced by non-investment grade companies when they must resort to "Plan C," which refers to private credit markets, after being shut out of traditional bank loans (Plan A) and public bond markets (Plan B). The author argues that while high yield spreads recovered after spiking during the Great Recession, broad indices obscure the limited credit access for small and medium-sized firms. 

The top-left chart, titled "US high yield spreads," tracks the spread to worst in basis points from 1987 to 2012, showing a massive spike near 2,000 basis points in late 2008 followed by a sharp recovery to around 600 to 800 basis points. To the right, a bar chart titled "J.P. Morgan US high yield index" shows the distribution of the number of companies across various spread-to-worst intervals as of June 6, 2012. With the current index spread to worst standing at 709 basis points, the chart highlights a wide dispersion among high-yield borrowers, with some companies enjoying spreads as low as 250 basis points, while a substantial number face spreads exceeding 1,550 basis points.

The text attributes this bifurcation of credit access to a sharp decline in collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) and new post-crisis regulations that restricted proprietary trading and primary dealer positions. This dynamic is illustrated in two additional charts. The bottom-left chart, "US CLO quarterly gross issuance," shows quarterly volumes in billions of USD from 2000 to 2012. Issuance peaked at over $30 billion per quarter in 2006 and 2007 before collapsing to near-zero levels during the crisis, showing only a modest recovery to under $5 billion by 2012. Beside it, the chart "Debt issuance by mid-market firms (EBITDA <=$50mm)" tracks the quarterly number of deals from 1997 to 2012. Mid-market deal activity fell dramatically from peaks of over 120 deals per quarter in 2007 to fewer than 20 deals per quarter by 2012. 

As a consequence of this credit squeeze, smaller and mid-sized companies have turned to private lending and mezzanine debt. The author notes that since 2009, investment conditions in private lending have been highly favorable, featuring substantial equity subordination of 30% to 40% below mezzanine debt, cash coupons of 10% to 12%, discounted pricing relative to Par, and pro-forma debt service coverage ratios of 2.4x to 2.7x. The author cautions that these favorable terms are only available to relatively healthy high-yield companies, whereas severely challenged entities—much like the sovereign nation of Spain—are forced to seek "rescue financing," a topic explored in the succeeding sections.

This page, titled "What could go right in the world, surpassing the low expectations for just about everything? A postscript on Beijing," discusses the historical context of China's relations with the West and its modern implications for US-China relations, featuring insights from Henry Kissinger. The author argues that China's current political consciousness is heavily influenced by its 19th-century trauma during the Opium Wars, when British opium imports addicted up to twenty-five percent of China's adult population, drained its silver, and decimated its trade surplus. Despite imperial bans, British pressure and eventual military victory in 1840 forced the unequal Treaty of Nanking, doubling the opium trade and eventually contributing to the collapse of the Qing Dynasty. 

To illustrate this historical impact, the page features two charts sourced from Man-houng Lin's work via the Harvard University Asia Center. The first chart, "Opium imported into China," tracks the number of imported chests between 1801 and 1857. It depicts imports rising from near zero in 1801 to about thirty thousand chests around 1836, where a red marker denotes the re-instatement of the Imperial opium ban. Following a brief dip during the first Opium War around 1840, imports spiked dramatically, reaching nearly eighty thousand chests by the late 1850s. The second chart, "Chinese silver outflows to England and India," displays a five-year rolling average in millions of silver dollars from 1818 to 1854. A red marker around 1820 highlights when China's balance of payments shifted from a surplus to a deficit at roughly five million silver dollars. Outflows subsequently climbed, reaching a peak of over twenty-five million silver dollars by the early 1850s.

In the modern context, Kissinger suggests that the West must view China's interests in global energy security, North Korea, climate change, and currency through this historical lens. Although ideological factions in the United States advocate for confronting non-democratic nations—as highlighted in a footnote quoting Aaron Friedberg on the ultimate US strategy to hasten a peaceful revolution to replace China's one-party state—Kissinger argues that mutual economic dependence incentivizes both nations to maintain the status quo. He maintains that conflict is not inevitable, as both sides have too much to lose, suggesting that successful diplomatic compromises could defy pessimistic global expectations. The page concludes with a list of miscellaneous source materials and common economic abbreviations.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the persistent macroeconomic challenges in Europe and the United States, contrasting rising profits and low equity valuations with unresolved structural sovereign and banking crises. The author is highly skeptical of Eurozone policy solutions, particularly those proposed by German policymakers, and highlights the ongoing weakness in both European banking systems and the broader US economy.

A key focus is the European Redemption Fund proposal, which would require Eurozone members to meet constitutional debt brakes and primary surplus targets to reduce debt to 60 percent of GDP over 25 years. The author argues this is completely unrealistic for Italy, as shown in a chart of Italy's primary fiscal balance as a percentage of GDP from 1960 to 2010. The chart shows Italy's primary fiscal balance has historically been deep in negative territory, reaching its lowest points around negative six percent in the mid-1970s and 1980s. The balance only briefly surpassed the European Redemption Fund's proposed four percent primary surplus target in the late 1990s. The author points out that Italy would have breached this proposed debt brake 70 percent of the time since Italian unification in 1861.

Beside the Italian fiscal chart, another chart tracks the percentage of OECD banking system assets in distressed banks, where distress is defined as credit spreads exceeding three percent, from October 2007 to late 2011. This metric peaked near 17 percent during the 2008 financial crisis before climbing even higher, past 40 percent, in late 2011, illustrating the recurring and intensifying nature of the banking crisis. 

The exhaustion of European Central Bank rescue funds is detailed in a table showing what Spanish and Italian banks did with their Long-Term Refinancing Operation funding from December 2011 to February 2012. Out of 195 billion euros in funding received by Spanish banks, 102 billion went to purchasing government bonds or loans, 48 billion to pay down interbank liabilities, and 25 billion to pay down bonds, leaving only 20 billion euros. Italian banks received 114 billion euros, spending 73 billion on government bonds, 26 billion on other bonds, 45 billion on interbank liabilities, and 18 billion on bond paydowns, resulting in a deficit of 48 billion euros. The author uses this data to show that rescue money has already been spent, questioning the capacity and political will of countries like Germany to fund further bailouts.

To illustrate the fragility of the European banking sector, the page includes a timeline of Bankia, Spain's third-largest bank. Despite receiving a clean bill of health in July 2010 stress tests and raising three billion euros in a July 2011 IPO, the bank rapidly deteriorated. By May 2012, the Spanish government had to convert 4.5 billion euros of preferred shares into voting stock and announce another 19 billion euros was needed to cover provisions, with Bankia shares falling 72 percent since its IPO. 

Finally, the commentary addresses the United States, noting a disappointing payroll report and weakening disposable income growth. Most economists are revising 2012 US GDP growth projections down toward two percent. While lower gasoline prices and reduced debt service costs have supported consumer cash flow, the author concludes that the US economy lacks the escape velocity to act as a stabilizing force for global markets.

This page from "Eye on the Market" discusses the impending European Union summit and the broader structural and political crises plaguing the Eurozone. The author begins by highlighting Europe’s critical role in the global economy, noting that one-third of OECD banks are in distress—most of which are European—and that Europe accounts for 15% of S&P 500 revenues, 23% of S&P industrial revenues, and roughly 30% of technology revenues. 

As European policymakers prepare to discuss bank recapitalizations, Greek repayment timetables, and deposit guarantees, the author cautions that Periphery nations like Italy, Spain, Greece, and Portugal are contracting at a 2% to 5% annualized pace. This severe economic contraction is visualized in the first chart, "Spanish and Greek unemployment," which plots unemployment percentages from 1985 to 2012. The chart shows both nations' unemployment rates skyrocketing past historical norms to exceed 20% by 2012, with Spain approaching 25% and Greece surpassing 20%. 

To emphasize the grave political risks of these levels, the author provides a second chart, "Unemployment and the end of liberal capitalism, 1930's." This chart tracks German unemployment (depicted as a red area) and Reichstag seats by party (in percentages from 0 to over 40) from 1922 to 1934. It illustrates that when German unemployment surged past 20% in the early 1930s, the seat share of the totalitarian National Socialists (shown in brown bars) exploded, while the seat share of liberal parties, such as the German People's Party and German Democratic Party (shown in green bars), collapsed. The author warns that if the jobs picture in the European Periphery does not improve, fringe political parties may gain substantial traction, risking the viability of the entire European project.

The publication also criticizes recent regulatory steps, specifically a draft Rating Agency Reform passed by the EU's Economic and Monetary Committee. The author argues that forcing financial institutions to develop internal rating systems and holding external agencies liable for "methodological mistakes" is a confidence-damaging move that suggests EU policymakers simply want to silence dissenting opinions—drawing a tongue-in-cheek parallel to Galileo Galilei's house arrest for his scientific theories. 

Ultimately, the author asserts that Europe's crisis is much broader than a simple sovereign debt or banking issue. Although Spanish banks are borrowing over €300 billion from the European Central Bank, this massive sum represents a mere 12% of total Spanish bank liabilities. Combined with the observation that cyclically adjusted current account deficits in the Periphery remain nearly unchanged from three years prior despite severe austerity measures, the author concludes that Europe's private sector economies remain incompatible within a single monetary union and still have a long way to go toward recovery.

This page presents a mid-year self-assessment scorecard of the major market, economic, and investment views published in J.P. Morgan’s 2012 Outlook. The author evaluates nine specific January predictions, detailing their outcomes and assigning color-coded grades—green for correct, yellow for mixed or partially correct, and red for incorrect. 

Several views received a positive green grade. J.P. Morgan correctly anticipated that OECD private sector economies would have to rely less on fiscal stimulus and that the European Central Bank’s balance sheet would expand dramatically, growing by €620 billion. Their regional equity positioning was also highly successful, yielding strong returns by favoring the US and Asia over Europe and Japan; US equities rose 9.0%, Asia ex-Japan grew 7.9%, and European equities gained only 1.1%. Additionally, their optimism regarding slowing US corporate profit growth proved correct as S&P earnings decelerated toward 10% growth. In Europe, Germany's continued resistance to fiscal commingling and Eurobonds was correctly predicted, though the possibility of the European Stability Mechanism directly recapitalizing banks introduced new burden-sharing. J.P. Morgan’s deep concerns about Italy’s contracting GDP and high credit spreads, as well as their warning that Spain would be the epicenter of the Eurozone crisis, were fully vindicated, with Spain suffering severe capital flight and a 19.5% equity market decline.

Two views were graded yellow or red. The view on US GDP and payroll growth was deemed slightly too optimistic and graded yellow; GDP growth was lower than expected, at 1.9% in the first quarter and an estimated 1.5% in the second quarter, while nonfarm payroll gains averaged 150,000 to 159,000 per month rather than the predicted 200,000. Red grades were assigned to their failed views on US economic resilience relative to Europe and Asia—as US new orders and export orders collapsed in June to their lowest levels since 2009—and their nervousness over long-duration US government bonds, which performed well due to heavy buying from foreign central banks and the Federal Reserve, which purchased 66% of all Treasury issuance in 2011.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s “Eye on the Market” analyzes a unique historical aspect of the 2012 US Presidential election, arguing that the race between Barack Obama and Mitt Romney offered voters the least amount of prior high-level public service experience in many decades. The author notes that the two candidates possessed a combined total of only 12 years of high-level public sector experience, which represents a modern-era anomaly. To find another election with similarly low levels of experience, one has to look back to the 1952 election between Dwight Eisenhower and Adlai Stevenson, or more accurately to the 1924 election between Calvin Coolidge and John W. Davis, because the 1952 candidates possessed substantial uncounted public sector heft in military and diplomatic roles.

The central visual is a line chart titled “US Presidential Elections: prior years of high level public sector experience of both candidates combined, 1912-2012.” The vertical axis tracks the combined years of experience from 0 to 60, while the horizontal axis tracks election years from 1912 to 2012. The chart displays two data series. The first is a green line representing Category 1 experience, which includes service as a Governor, US Senator, US House Representative, Vice President, or President. The second is a brown line representing Category 1 plus Category 2 experience, which adds service in the Supreme Court, Cabinet posts, and major military positions, such as the Supreme Commander of NATO or CIA Director. 

The chart highlights a peak in combined experience in 1996 at approximately 51 years, followed by a sharp decline leading to the 2012 low point of 12 years, where both lines converge. Specific annotations point to historical comparison points, including the 1924 election of Coolidge vs. Davis, where combined experience fell below 10 years for Category 1, and the 1952 election of Eisenhower vs. Stevenson. 

The author connects this low-experience trend to multi-decade lows in public confidence across major institutions, which has fueled a public desire for political outsiders. However, he poses an open, disconcerting question about whether politicians who have not previously wielded substantial power are prone to underestimating the consequences of making policy errors. Additionally, a detailed footnote explains that state legislative experience was excluded from the analysis because power has increasingly shifted from state legislatures to the federal level. To support this exclusion, the author cites the Brennan Center for Justice at NYU School of Law, which characterized the New York State legislature as the most dysfunctional and least deliberative in the nation.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the limitations of Federal Reserve policies to boost growth and the critical need to address long-term US fiscal imbalances. He notes that global economic data is weakening, with the world economy growing at only 1.5 percent to 2.0 percent compared to 5.0 percent during post-stimulus periods in 2009 and 2010, and 80 percent of the world seeing slower growth rates. He questions the effectiveness of further quantitative easing when 10-year Treasury rates are already at 1.6 percent, noting that the Fed's logic of lowering capital costs to spur investment closely resembles supply-side economics. While US corporate profits have outrun GDP growth by the widest margin in decades, Cembalest argues that stock multiple expansion is unlikely without real growth and employment. Additionally, he addresses the impending fiscal cliff, stating that the US cannot permanently sustain a libertarian tax policy alongside a Scandinavian welfare state. He raises the question of whether a bipartisan compromise like the Bowles-Simpson plan can realistically pass after the upcoming presidential election.

To support these points, the page includes four charts. The first chart, titled "Another Prague Spring (PS)," tracks the Global Composite Purchasing Manager’s Index from 2007 through mid-2012 on a vertical axis ranging from 35 to 60, where 50 indicates expansion. Shaded grey areas mark periods of monetary stimulus, and red dots labeled "PS" highlight brief spring-time economic recoveries that subsequently faded, showing the index declining toward 50 in 2012. 

The second chart, "Earnings still outperforming the economy," displays the ratio of 2-year earnings growth to 2-year nominal GDP growth from 1952 through 2008 on a vertical scale from negative 10x to 15x. The chart shows that the historical average peak ratio was 2.1x, which grew to a later average peak of 4.2x. It highlights a massive spike to a peak of 14.3x before dropping to a recent level of 5.4x, underscoring how corporate earnings have historically outstripped overall economic growth. 

The third chart, "The Squid," visualizes multiple "tentacles of macroeconomic imbalances" from 1980 to 2010. It maps six highly volatile indicators: the unemployment rate of the European periphery less Germany, OECD government debt as a percentage of GDP, China's capital spending to GDP, Spanish reliance on foreign capital, US fiscal deficits, and the differential in industrial production between Germany and Italy. These lines show sharp, chaotic divergence by 2010, highlighting severe systemic imbalances. 

The final chart, "The Whale," details the cheapness of corporate profits and substantial cash holdings from 1985 to 2012. It plots three upward-trending series: the S&P earnings yield, economy-wide profits to GDP, and corporate cash relative to tangible assets, all of which remain at historically elevated levels by 2012, reflecting high equity yields and massive corporate cash piles.

In this commentary, the author reflects on the highly tense political dynamics of the June 2012 EU summit, questioning whether the practice of strong-arming Germany—the primary country expected to fund the Euro's survival—is how monetary unions are ultimately made or broken. While Germany is inclined to prevent sovereign or banking system failures in the Periphery, the lack of a clear roadmap leaves the future form of this assistance uncertain. The author hopes that Europe can stay out of the headlines long enough for markets to refocus on private-sector recoveries in the United States and China, alongside the potential benefits of further monetary stimulus and lower oil prices.

A cartoon-style map titled "June 2012 EU Summit Maneuvers" visualizes these political shifts, using colored arrows and icons to map out the positions of various countries. The map and its accompanying key detail how France and Italy teamed up to challenge German austerity. French President Hollande started the resistance by threatening to let the summit fail unless Germany compromised, ultimately securing a growth compact. Italian Prime Minister Monti defected from Germany's camp to join Hollande, threatening to tank the talks and blame Chancellor Merkel. Spain allied with Italy to push for EU purchases of sovereign bonds with minimal strings attached to aid its struggling banking sector.

These coordinated efforts left an isolated Germany retreating on its European Stability Mechanism lending stance, receiving only vague language regarding region-wide ECB banking oversight in return. This concession dealt a blow to Germany’s fiscally conservative allies—Austria, Finland, and the Netherlands. Meanwhile, Ireland emerged as a major winner of this revolt, hoping the EU will directly recapitalize its major banks with 15 billion Euros to prevent its debt-to-GNP ratio from soaring past 140%. Elsewhere on the map, Great Britain is shown in "Splendid Isolation" after vetoing the fiscal compact, a position the author views as favorable given the Eurozone's turmoil. Switzerland is depicted as under siege from capital inflows, with Swiss National Bank foreign exchange reserves growing by an enormous 40% of GDP since 2009. Finally, Poland is shown waiting on the sidelines, still desiring to join the Eurozone but waiting for Germany to resolve the crisis and for the Periphery to adopt strict fiscal rules.

This page presents an assessment of global market and economic conditions, explaining why US equities have remained resilient despite disappointing domestic economic data, and analyzing the limitations of the recent European Union summit. The author argues that the disconnect between subpar US economic data and strong stock performance is driven by resilient corporate profits and massive global liquidity. 

To illustrate this, a scatter plot compares the six-month change of the S&P 500 against the six-month change of the Citi US Economic Surprise Index from 2003 through mid-2012. A highlighted data point from June 29, 2012, shows the S&P 500 posting a gain of roughly 15% even as the economic surprise index plunged to nearly negative 100, demonstrating that US equities have performed significantly better than historical trends would suggest. 

Three subsequent charts underscore the abundance of liquidity in the financial system. The first chart, tracking US commercial bank excess deposits in trillions of dollars from 2000 to 2012, reveals a massive divergence post-2008; bank deposits surged to approximately $8.5 trillion while loans stagnated at around $7.2 trillion. The second chart shows global foreign exchange reserves from 1970 to 2012, highlighting emerging market reserves climbing exponentially to nearly $8 trillion, while Japan's reserves remained flat at around $1 trillion. The third chart shows US corporate cash balances as a percentage of tangible assets from 1952 onwards, indicating that cash holdings rebounded from a late-1990s low of about 5.5% to nearly 10% by the late 2000s.

In the section titled "European Subjunctivitis," the author analyzes the June EU summit, where Germany, under pressure from Italy, Spain, and France, agreed to allow the European Stability Mechanism to directly recapitalize banks and purchase periphery bonds. While this initially boosted markets, the author urges caution and lists five critical uncertainties, or "ifs." These include whether the ESM will be fully ratified by all governments, whether it will transition to direct bank recapitalization rather than sovereign lending, whether member states will reject proposed protocols, whether future losses will deter investment—noting that Ireland’s National Reserve Pension Fund lost 80% on its bank recaps, presenting a clear warning for Spain—and whether the German Constitutional Court will raise legal objections. 

Ultimately, the author asserts that the Eurozone crisis is fundamentally a structural issue of external imbalances between private-sector economies in the core and the periphery, which the summit failed to resolve. Highlighting a worrisome trend, the author points out that loan creation in Italy has turned negative for the first time in 20 years, threatening a nation that already has the lowest growth rate in the OECD, saving only Japan.

This page presents J.P. Morgan's self-assessment of its 2012 market, economic, and investment views as of mid-year. The assessments are presented in a structured scorecard with color-coded performance indicators, where green denotes views that are on track, yellow indicates mixed results, red shows underperformance or incorrect views, and "N.A." is used for long-term investments that are too early to evaluate.

The firm's macroeconomic expectations for China received a mixed yellow assessment. While headline and core inflation fell as expected, allowing for reserve requirement easing, and the RMB depreciated by 1.1% compared to a 5% appreciation in 2011, the slowdown in the Chinese economy was more severe than anticipated, settling into a 6% to 7% growth range. Nonetheless, Chinese consumption as a share of GDP growth reached its highest level since the late 1990s. 

Equity market recommendations generally performed well and were marked in green. The general view to deploy capital into equities saw the MSCI World Equity Index rise by 5.8% year-to-date, while the preferred strategy of MSCI World ex-Europe rose by 7.6%. Specific equity sector calls were also successful: technology stocks outperformed, with the S&P 500 Info Tech sector rising 12.8% compared to the broader S&P 500's 9.0% return. Large-cap multinationals also outperformed, as the Morgan Stanley Multinational Nifty Fifty Index gained 10.7%. However, the focus on high-dividend and equity-income stocks yielded mixed yellow results, as the S&P Dividend Aristocrats Index rose 8.4% year-to-date, lagging slightly behind the S&P 500.

Equity valuations remained low as predicted, keeping this view green. Driven by macroeconomic imbalances and low labor compensation, the MSCI World Index trailing price-to-earnings multiple started the year at 13x, rose above 15x in March, and fell back to 14x.

In credit markets, the call to find value in high yield and leveraged loans was correct, with the Barclays High Yield Index up 7.9% year-to-date and the S&P/LSTA Leveraged Loan Index up 4.8%. This was supported by the Federal Reserve's zero-interest-rate policy, which stimulated a high demand for yield. Meanwhile, distressed and illiquid opportunities in European bank loan portfolios, distressed real estate, and mezzanine debt were labeled N.A., as they represent long-term holdings that require years to evaluate.

The call on macro hedge funds was the primary underperformer, receiving a red designation. The HFRI Macro Hedge Fund Index rose only 1.0% through May, underperforming the broader HFRI Fund of Funds Diversified Index and the HFRI Fund Weighted Composite, both of which rose 1.6%. Macro managers struggled by exiting long-duration trades too early, being whipsawed by the rallying Japanese Yen, and failing to profit from oil or gold. Lastly, gold's performance was mixed, marked by high volatility that saw prices start the year at $1,563, rise close to $1,800 in February, and fall back to $1,584.

This page from the publication addresses the resilience of global equity markets in the face of sluggish economic data and analyzes the underlying mechanics of the weak post-war U.S. economic recovery. The author notes that despite extensive monetary and fiscal stimulus, recent indicators such as retail sales, payrolls, small business surveys, and GDP have been weak across the United States, China, and Europe. Even so, equity markets have held up reasonably well, with U.S. equities up 7% and Asia ex-Japan up 5%. The author suggests that low valuations and reduced equity positions among investors have kept markets stable, leaving the market in a state of neutral wait-and-see.

The first major section focuses on the sluggish U.S. recovery, which is described as the weakest post-war recovery on record, struggling to maintain a 2% growth rate. A chart titled "US real GDP growth following post-war recessions" indexes GDP growth (with the trough quarter set to 100) against quarters since the GDP trough. The line representing the current recovery is marked in red and shows a flatter, lower trajectory than any other post-war recession, barely climbing above 105 index points by quarter 12, whereas historical recoveries typically reached between 115 and 125 index points over the same timeframe. 

The author explains that corporate profits have managed to outpace overall GDP growth due to demand from emerging markets and a shift in compensation from labor to capital. A second chart, titled "Earnings still outperforming the economy," plots the ratio of 2-year earnings growth to 2-year nominal GDP growth from 1952 to 2012. It shows that while historical average peaks for this ratio were 2.1x and later 4.2x, the ratio surged to an extreme peak of 14.3x in the post-2008 period and remains elevated at 5.4x.

The final section examines how extremely weak labor compensation has been the primary driver behind these elevated profit margins. The author warns that while high profit margins may persist for a while, their consequences—such as weak consumer spending, high government transfers to households, and political tension—will likely suppress price-to-earnings (P/E) multiples. Nominally, the employment cost index and average hourly earnings are growing at only 2% year-over-year.

To illustrate this structural shift, the page displays two comparative charts showing the change in billions of 2005 dollars over 13 quarters since the profit trough. The first, "Corporate profit cycle - past 5 US recoveries" (representing average trends from 1958, 1974, 1982, 1990, and 2001), shows sales rising to nearly $900 billion, followed by labor compensation at around $500 billion, and corporate profits trailing at roughly $300 billion. The adjacent chart, "Corporate profit cycle - current US recovery," shows a dramatic inversion of this historical relationship. Here, corporate profits lead the cycle, soaring to over $800 billion by quarter 13, while sales growth reaches roughly $600 billion, and labor compensation remains severely depressed, dipping as low as negative $100 billion in the initial quarters and barely returning to zero by the thirteenth quarter.

This page, titled "Report card charts," compiles key global economic and financial indicators to provide a mid-2012 self-assessment of macroeconomic and investment views, focusing on the US, the Euro area, Asia, and global monetary policy. A sidebar defines key regional and financial acronyms including the OECD, ECB, RMB, MSCI, HFRI, EU, and ESM. 

The first chart tracks central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP from January 2011 to May 2012. It highlights a massive expansion by the European Central Bank, which surged from around 20% to over 31% of GDP by early 2012, overtaking Japan, which hovered around 28% to 30%. Meanwhile, the Bank of England's balance sheet increased steadily to about 24%, while the US Federal Reserve's balance sheet remained flat around 19%.

The second chart tracks global manufacturing surveys using the seasonally adjusted Purchasing Managers Index from January 2010 to January 2012. It shows diverging economic fortunes, with the US index remaining in expansion territory above 50, ending around 53, while Asia slid slightly below 50, and the Euro area contracted sharply to approximately 46. This slowdown is reflected in the third chart, which shows annualized US real GDP growth falling from a late 2011 peak of around 3% to an estimated 1.8% by the second quarter of 2012.

Regional equity markets during the first half of 2012 showed the US leading with total USD returns peaking near 13% in March and settling around 8% by July. This outperformed Asia, which hovered around 3%, and Europe, which hit a low of -7% in June before recovering to -2%. This trend correlates with the deceleration of trailing four-quarter S&P 500 operating EPS growth, which fell from nearly 48% in late 2010 to an estimated 12% in early 2012.

Highlighting Eurozone sovereign debt stress, the sixth chart shows Italian 10-year government bond yields exhibiting extreme volatility, falling from above 7% in January 2012 down to under 5% in March, before climbing steadily back to about 6% by July. In the US, capital expenditure showed a resilient recovery from the financial crisis, with equipment and software spending contributions to real GDP growth rising from a low of over -2% in 2009 to contribute about 1% to growth by late 2011.

Looking at emerging markets, China's central bank began easing monetary policy as year-over-year headline inflation cooled from over 6% in mid-2011 to around 3% in early 2012, allowing the reserve requirement ratio to be cut from 21.5% to 20.5%. Globally, equity valuations compressed, with the MSCI World trailing price-to-earnings multiple contracting significantly from its post-crisis spike of over 30 down to a historical valuation of approximately 13 to 14 by late 2011.

This page of the publication, written by Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management, focuses on the cognitive impacts of aging and retirement in a section titled "No Country for Old Men (2007): what happens after you turn 50?" Cembalest humorously references cultural touchstones like H.R. Haldeman and Ursula Andress before presenting research from a 2012 study titled "Ageing, cognitive abilities and retirement" by Fabrizio Mazzonna and Franco Peracchi of the Munich Center for the Economics of Aging. The main argument posits that while mental capabilities generally decline after age fifty, continuing to work rather than retiring helps preserve cognitive function. 

Two series of line charts support this observation. The first series, "Age-profiles of average test scores by gender," tracks normalized average test scores on a vertical axis from negative 0.5 to 0.5 against ages fifty to seventy on the horizontal axis. Across five cognitive domains—Orientation, Immediate recall, Delayed recall, Fluency, and Numeracy—the charts show a general decline with age. Women, represented by an orange line, consistently outperform men, shown in grey, in all categories except numeracy, where men maintain a clear lead. 

The second series, "Age-profiles of average test scores by employment status," utilizes the same metrics and axes to compare retired individuals, shown in orange, with employed individuals, shown in grey. In every category, those who remain employed exhibit significantly higher average cognitive scores than their retired peers across the entire fifty-to-seventy age span. Cembalest concludes that these cognitive benefits, combined with the financial realities of zero interest rates, make delayed retirement the superior option.

This page addresses two major themes: the historical lessons of how the United States managed its post-World War II debt in the 1950s, and the escalating contemporary sovereign debt crisis in the Eurozone.

In the first section, the author challenges the common narrative that the U.S. halved its post-WWII debt through sharp spending cuts or tax hikes. A historical data table from 1950 to 1960 shows that net debt as a percentage of GDP fell dramatically from 80% in 1950 to 46% in 1960. However, absolute net debt actually rose slightly from $219 billion to $237 billion. The reduction in the debt ratio was driven by robust economic expansion, with real GDP growing at a 4.3% compound annual rate. Federal outlays remained stable, ranging between 14% and 21% of GDP, while receipts hovered between 14% and 19%. This growth was supported by positive real interest rates—averaging 1.3% in 1950 and rising to 2.7% by 1960—rather than engineered negative rates. 

An accompanying sidebar, titled "1950’s time capsule," highlights that President Eisenhower championed pro-business tax relief, such as the elimination of double taxation through Subchapter S, and dismantled wage and price controls. During this era, private sector employment peaked at 86% of all jobs. The author poses an open question about how the United States will manage its modern debt burden, which has returned to 80% of GDP for only the second time in history, given that similar pro-growth policies are not currently being utilized. A brief cultural detour referencing the 1971 film "Sometimes a Great Notion" explores a general cinematic hostility toward capitalism, citing theories by Joseph Schumpeter and Larry Ribstein.

The second half of the page shifts to the unfolding "European Credit Divorce," where Eurozone and global banks are rapidly withdrawing capital from the European periphery. This trend is visualized in a line chart titled "Flight of the Bumblebee," spanning 2004 to 2011. The chart shows cross-border lending within the Eurozone peaking at nearly 6.5 trillion USD in 2008 before dropping toward 4.5 trillion USD by late 2011. Similarly, non-Eurozone lending to the periphery peaked near 1.0 trillion USD and fell to around 0.7 trillion USD. 

The scale of this crisis is further illustrated in an area chart titled "Peripheral sovereign and financial debt" from 2002 to 2011. This chart shows total outstanding debt in the European periphery climbing steadily from under 3 trillion Euros in 2002 to nearly 7 trillion Euros by 2011. This total is comprised of roughly 3 trillion Euros in sovereign debt and nearly 4 trillion Euros in financial sector debt. The author notes that while the European Central Bank is acting as a crucial stop-gap to prevent a full-scale depression, serious questions remain regarding how the ECB and the European Union will ultimately finance these trillions of Euros in maturing debt as private investors refuse to hold them.

This page addresses three major economic and financial themes: the relative impact of labor versus energy costs in US manufacturing, the reset of corporate profit expectations, and the generational conflict presented by "dueling" US fiscal cliffs. 

The first section analyzes labor and energy intensity across US manufacturing sectors. A bar chart titled "Labor and energy intensity in US manufacturing" illustrates the share of total expenses for various sectors, including food, machinery, technology, semiconductors, autos, paper, chemicals, plastics, metals, and iron and steel. The data shows that labor costs consistently dwarf energy costs, representing over 30% of expenses in technology and around 20% to 25% in machinery, autos, and chemicals. In contrast, energy costs make up less than 5% of total expenses for almost all listed sectors. The author observes that while high unemployment keeps labor margin pressures low, the minimal share of energy expenses means investors should temper their optimism regarding the bottom-line benefits of cheap US natural gas.

The second section evaluates corporate earnings estimates. A line chart titled "S&P 500 operating earnings per share estimates" tracks the downward revision of US dollar EPS estimates for Q2 and Q4 of 2012 from August 2010 to April 2012. The blue line for Q2 2012 estimates fell from a peak near $28.00 down to under $26.00, representing a very low year-over-year growth hurdle of just +0.9%. Conversely, the brown line for Q4 2012 estimates fell from $30.00 to around $28.50, which still reflects a much higher year-over-year growth hurdle of +16.3%. The author argues that because Q2 expectations have been revised so low, corporate profits will not need to do much to beat consensus, potentially supporting equities.

The third section outlines a generational battle between two distinct fiscal crises, visualised through two charts. The first, "Fiscal cliff #1: 2013," shows the historical change in the cyclically-adjusted federal deficit as a percentage of potential GDP from 1963 to 2013. The chart features bars indicating fiscal stimulus (positive values) and fiscal drag (negative values). The 2013 estimate, assuming then-current law, reveals an unprecedented fiscal drag of nearly -4% of potential GDP. The second chart, "Fiscal cliff #2: 2013 and beyond," presents net debt to GDP from 2004 to 2022 on an inverted scale, where a downward trajectory denotes rising debt. It plots three scenarios: the CBO Baseline (showing debt leveling off near 65% of GDP), the Post-BCA case, and the CBO Alternative Case, where net debt ballooning toward 95% of GDP by 2022 represents the long-term generational cliff. The author posits that while the immediate 2013 fiscal cliff of austerity is painful, completely avoiding it simply passes the escalating debt burden to the next generation. The author poses the open question of whether the US will continue to avoid paying a price for this debt expansion, noting that financial markets would react positively to any progress on long-term debt reduction despite the prevailing political gridlock.

This page, titled "A Bug’s Life: Investment opportunities in Big Data," explores the technological drivers and commercial applications of the rapid growth in data generation and processing. The author highlights several factors powering the Big Data boom, including the deployment of approximately 30 million sensor nodes in the internet of things (growing at 30 percent annually), massive healthcare databases, and corporate databases that logged 71 billion credit and debit card transactions in the US and 135 billion globally in 2011. This growth has been supported by over 600 million global broadband subscribers in late 2011, along with dramatic shifts in hardware capabilities illustrated in two log-scale charts.

The first chart, "Cost of a gigabyte of storage," shows a spectacular decline in storage costs per gigabyte from 1980 to 2008. The logarithmic y-axis spans from $0.01 to $1,000,000, tracing the drop from around $1,000,000 per gigabyte in 1980 (associated with manufacturers like VR Data Corp.) to under $0.10 by 2008 (with Hitachi), through intermediate milestones involving Percom, Western Digital, Seagate, Maxtor, Quantum, and Fujitsu. The second chart, "Processing power," tracks transistor count per processor from 1971 to 2011 using data from Intel, AMD, Sony, IBM, and Sun Microsystems. The logarithmic y-axis spans from 1,000 to 10,000,000,000, showing a steady rise in processing power from around 1,000 transistors in 1971 to nearly several billion by 2011. These combined trends are exemplified by the ability to store 32 GB of data on a tiny camera chip for under $100, which is millions of times lighter and 30,000 times cheaper than three decades prior.

The bottom section of the page outlines existing and emerging Big Data products and services across four key sectors. In Government, Big Data is applied to combat tax and Medicare fraud, support defense and security agencies analyzing satellite and signal intelligence, and help municipalities manage toll collection and identify road potholes via smartphone data. In Healthcare, digitization efforts funded by the $20 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 helped raise US hospital adoption of electronic health records from 16% in 2009 to 35% in 2011; other applications include clinical decision support systems to prevent prescription errors and remote patient monitoring. In the Pharmaceutical sector, data analysis evaluates drug efficacy and safety, with the author noting that historical analysis of Vioxx might have led to earlier detection of adverse side effects. Finally, the Automotive sector features examples from GM and BMW integrating traffic, maintenance, and mobile phone location data to optimize travel, map traffic patterns, and reduce fuel consumption.

This page explores the rapid rise of Big Data and its expanding investment and operational opportunities across multiple sectors, emphasizing the shift toward unstructured data. In retailing, businesses utilize technologies like radio frequency identification (RFID) tags to track shopping cart movements, customize real-time recommendations, and deploy geo-targeted advertisements. Retailers face intense pressure from online price-comparison applications like RedLaser, especially as web-influenced purchases are projected by McKinsey and Forrester to soon represent over 50% of total US sales. Furthermore, retailers' share of operating profits on consumer goods has dropped from over 50% in 1999 to just 30% today. In the financial sector, brokerage firms rely on speed of execution to address information asymmetry, and insurance companies use satellite imagery to assess property risks. According to Nilson, the transition away from cash and checks (which made up 84% of transactions in 1990) toward debit and credit card purchases is expected to reach 67% of transactions by 2015, adding to the data surge. Other sectors leverage Big Data for customer retention analysis in telecommunications, complex supply chain modeling in aerospace and semiconductors, and route optimization to lower delivery and energy costs.

The page explains that the vast majority of newly generated data is unstructured, including text messages, social media feeds, images, and video, which require advanced non-relational storage technologies such as Hadoop, Splunk, and NoSQL. Citing Carnegie Mellon, the text notes a severe talent shortage in machine learning to analyze these trends. To translate complex findings for human operators, sophisticated visual tools are required. 

This transformation is illustrated by two graphics. The first, a bar chart titled "Unstructured data takes over" from the Enterprise Strategy Group, projects worldwide total archived capacity by content type in exabytes from 2008 through 2015. The chart demonstrates that archived capacity is set to balloon from less than 50 exabytes in 2008 to more than 300 exabytes by 2015, with the growth driven entirely by unstructured data, while capacity for email and relational databases remains comparatively flat. The second graphic, "An example of data visualization from GE and MIT," showcases a medical network map from the MIT Senseable City Lab Health Infoscape project. Based on an analysis of 217 million medical records, the clustergram visualizes the co-occurrence of various health conditions, connecting nodes such as depression, tobacco abuse, high blood cholesterol, diabetes, and heart disease to help clinicians recognize unexpected relationships between illnesses.

This page analyzes the surprising 13% year-to-date rally in US equity markets in the face of weak economic indicators, proposing that extremely low expectations have turned mediocre news into positive market catalysts. The author argues that this rally is primarily driven by anticipation of central bank intervention rather than expectations of an imminent private-sector recovery. 

This dependency is highlighted in the first chart, which tracks the Global PMI survey of manufacturing activity and sentiment from 2007 to 2012. The index fluctuates between values of 35 and 60, with shaded regions marking periods of intense monetary intervention that boosted sentiment. These include the Federal Reserve and Bank of England's first and second rounds of quantitative easing, the Fed's Operation Twist, the European Central Bank's Long-Term Refinancing Operations, interest rate cuts, and Securities Markets Programme hints. 

The second chart illustrates the "low expectations" phenomenon by looking at historical instances from 1966 to 2012 where the S&P 500 rallied by more than 2% on a payroll release day. It displays thirteen dates, measuring normalized job gains. Historically, such massive single-day market gains were reserved for periods of robust job growth, such as the 427,000 jobs added in August 1984 or the 351,000 added in December 1973. By contrast, the rally on August 3, 2012, was triggered by a mediocre gain of just 163,000 jobs, making it one of the lowest historical catalysts on record. The only lower instances occurred during the 1999 dot-com bubble (such as June 1999 with 11,000 jobs or September 1999 with 128,000 jobs) and in July 2002 when post-holiday trading dynamics overshadowed the employment data.

The author advises maintaining normal allocations to US equities rather than capitulating, pointing out that stocks began the year at a low valuation of 11.5x price-to-earnings, which already discounted significant economic trouble. Looking ahead, J.P. Morgan forecasts a stable but mediocre economic trend, predicting average payrolls around 150,000 and roughly 2% GDP growth. The durability of this trend relies heavily on the upcoming US election and the resolution of the fiscal cliff. Currently, markets appear to assume that the legislated 4.5% tax drag on GDP will eventually be negotiated down to a more manageable 1.5%.
