On a global scale, the author highlights the loss of US manufacturing jobs using a chart that plots the ten-year rolling percentage decline in US manufacturing jobs alongside China's foreign exchange reserve accumulation as a percentage of its GDP from 1958 to 2013. The chart marks China's accession to the World Trade Organization in 2001, illustrating a visual correlation where US job losses sharply accelerated, peaking near a 40 percent decline around 2009, while Chinese reserve accumulation concurrently surged to nearly 40 percent of its GDP. The author poses the open question of whether there is a direct causal link between these events, suggesting that the ultimate test of US democracy will be its ability to achieve fiscal solvency through compromise.

The second half of the page explores the relationship between economic complexity, credit, and financial regulation. The author presents a line chart showing the finance and insurance share of private industry value-added from 1947 to 2012. This metric rose steadily from just under 3 percent in 1947 to peak near 9 percent in the early 2000s, reflecting US businesses' growing reliance on financial services to navigate a service-oriented, leveraged economy. This rising economic complexity is further illustrated by a bar chart comparing the degree of vertical specialization—measured as imports per unit of export—across five sectors between 1995 and 2005. Every sector saw an increase, with the most dramatic jumps occurring in office, accounting, and computing machinery, which rose from roughly 0.2 to 0.45, and electrical machinery, which surged from 0.2 to over 0.9. 

The page concludes with a critique of the massive scale of regulatory reform. Although supporting core goals like higher bank capital and stronger consumer protections, the author voices concern over the unknowable impacts of Dodd-Frank. Citing a July 2012 progress report, the author notes that while the act was only 30 percent complete, it had already generated 8,800 pages of regulations from 10 regulatory entities, leaving swap dealers with 3,700 new operational and legal tasks. The author leaves readers with the question of how these heavy regulatory burdens will alter the creation and pricing of credit, especially since large businesses currently rely on capital markets for 75 percent of their credit, compared to only 25 percent from traditional bank lines.

This page discusses the emerging compromise to avoid the full force of the 2013 United States fiscal cliff, noting that the expected deal will likely reduce legislated austerity from 4.3 percent of GDP to roughly 1.5 percent of GDP. While markets are expected to welcome this reprieve, the author cautions that deferring these tax hikes and spending cuts will ultimately worsen the nation's long-term debt outlook. 

A detailed table titled "Fiscal cliff options, in billions and percentage of GDP" compares the legislated baseline against the estimated compromise package. The legislated path demands a total fiscal adjustment of 667 billion dollars, or 4.3 percent of GDP, comprising 535 billion dollars in revenue increases and 132 billion dollars in spending cuts. Under the estimated compromise, the total fiscal adjustment shrinks to 231 billion dollars, or 1.5 percent of GDP. This compromise keeps the 115 billion dollar expiring payroll tax holiday and 24 billion dollars in new healthcare taxes intact but slashes expiring personal tax provisions, business tax provisions, and upper-income tax relief. Notably, it completely zeroes out the legislated 40 billion dollar Alternative Minimum Tax adjustments and the 171 billion dollar remaining 2001/2003 tax relief. On the spending side, expenditure reductions fall from 132 billion dollars to just 17 billion dollars, which comes solely from ending the extension of unemployment benefits while entirely deferring the 85 billion dollar Budget Control Act sequester and 14 billion dollars in Medicare physician reimbursement cuts.

The long-term consequences of these choices are illustrated in a line chart tracking US net debt to GDP from 2004 to 2022 under three scenarios. The CBO Baseline, humorously marked with a unicorn to emphasize its improbability, shows net debt declining to 60 percent of GDP by 2022 under the assumption that all scheduled tax increases and spending cuts take effect. In contrast, the CBO Alternative Case, which assumes all tax cuts and subsidies are extended with no sequester, shows net debt rising steadily to 90 percent of GDP by 2022. The President's budget proposal represents a middle path, showing debt leveling off near 80 percent of GDP.

The page concludes with a debate over whether the trillion-dollar deficit is cyclical or structural. A final bar chart, "Varying estimates of how the cycle is impacting US deficits," compares estimates from the IMF, OECD, CBO, Paul Krugman’s blog, and a recent Krugman New York Times op-ed. The IMF, OECD, and CBO consistently attribute the vast majority—roughly 80 to 85 percent—of the deficit to structural factors, meaning a simple economic recovery will not solve the problem. While Krugman's blog estimates the structural portion at 60 percent, his New York Times op-ed asserts that the cyclical deficit is actually the larger contributor, a claim the author disputes as being out of step with professional consensus.

This page outlines the state of the US economic recovery, arguing that while the consumer and housing sectors are steadily improving, the looming "fiscal cliff" and long-term budget deficits present significant headwinds. 

The first set of charts illustrates signs of life in the consumer sector. Chart c22 shows that credit card delinquency rates (90+ days) and first-time mortgage default rates have fallen back to pre-crisis levels by late 2012, dropping to roughly 1.5% and 0.7% respectively. Chart c23 tracks household debt and debt service as a percent of disposable income, showing household debt declining from a 130% peak to around 105%, while low interest rates have pushed debt service down to under 11%. Chart c24 demonstrates a cyclical recovery in payrolls (excluding construction, government, and finance) from a bottom of 93 million in 2010 to nearly 98 million by 2012. Chart c25 shows University of Michigan consumer sentiment stabilizing near 75. Chart c26 plots US consumer trends, showing real personal consumption growth stabilizing near 2.0% and auto sales recovering strongly from a 9-million annualized trough in 2009 to nearly 15 million in late 2012. 

The primary risk to this recovery is a slowdown in business capital spending. Chart c27 illustrates this caution, showing that non-defense capital goods orders have plateaued near $65 billion, while the small business survey index remains depressed below 90. This stagnation is driven by global weakness and concerns over the looming "fiscal cliff." Chart c28 highlights the magnitude of this threat, showing that legislated austerity under current law would impose a massive fiscal drag of roughly 3.5% of potential GDP in 2013, the largest in decades. Chart c29 contextualizes this by showing the structural mismatch between US tax receipts (about 16% of GDP in 2012) and expenditures (exceeding 22% of GDP). Looking forward, chart c30 presents various net-debt-to-GDP scenarios through 2022. Under the CBO Alternative Case, net debt rises toward 95% of GDP, whereas the CBO Baseline shows it falling to roughly 65%. Other compromise proposals, such as the Obama budget with sequesters, point to stabilizing debt around 70% of GDP, though this would require an estimated $4 trillion in deficit reduction over ten years. 

Ultimately, the author predicts that political compromises will reduce the fiscal cliff's impact to 1.5% of GDP in 2013. This compromise is expected to pave the way for payroll growth of 200,000 per month, a rebound in business investment, and overall US GDP growth of roughly 2.5% by autumn 2013.

This page of the publication, titled "The Ship," presents a highly positive outlook for global markets and the US economy in 2013, using nautical metaphors to describe nine key structural supports. The author argues that powerful drivers, ranging from aggressive central bank monetary policy to strong corporate cash positions, are steering the economy forward.

The first driver, or "foresail," is central bank balance sheet expansion. Chart c13, titled "To infinity...and beyond!!", plots central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP from 2008 to 2013 for the European Central Bank, Bank of Japan, Federal Reserve, and Bank of England. The data shows all four banks expanding their balance sheets aggressively, rising from around 10% to 15% of GDP in 2008 to between 25% and 35% by 2013. The author points out that this monetary easing has not sparked inflation because of a massive output gap. Chart c14 shows the output gap of advanced economies as a percentage of potential GDP from 1970 to 2010; unlike the positive output gap of the 1970s that triggered inflation, the post-2008 gap remained deeply negative at around negative 4%, leaving plenty of room to expand without inflation. Consequently, government debt remains cheap to service, as illustrated in Chart c15, which shows OECD government net interest expense as a percentage of GDP declining from a peak of nearly 3.5% in the mid-1990s to under 2.0% in 2012.

The recovery of US housing serves as another key driver. Chart c16 shows the US housing "shadow inventory" in millions of units from 2000 to 2012, broken down by 60+ days delinquent loans, foreclosures, and real estate owned. This inventory steadily declined from a peak of nearly 6 million units in 2010 to around 4.5 million in late 2012. Meanwhile, consumption in emerging markets remains a vital support; Chart c17 shows emerging markets year-over-year retail sales volume growth from 2001 to 2011, which stayed robust and hovered around 8% to 10% despite a broader manufacturing slowdown. 

Corporate health and attractive stock valuations further bolster the positive outlook. Chart c18 tracks the free cash flow to assets of US large-cap growth stocks from 1970 to 2010, which rose to a historically high level of nearly 10%. Chart c19 shows the S&P 500 trailing earnings yield minus 10-year interest rates from 1952 to 2012. This spread sat at a highly attractive level of over 5% in late 2012, indicating that equities are cheap and historically poised for positive returns.

The final two supports are energy and liquid cash reserves. Chart c20 illustrates the global natural gas boom, showing that the global production index for natural gas (based on a 1970 value of 100) soared to nearly 350 by 2010, far outstripping crude oil's rise to 170. Lastly, Chart c21, "The Walls of Cash," tracks corporate cash-to-assets and household cash-to-GDP from 1960 to 2010. Household cash to GDP peaked near 12% and corporate cash to assets remained elevated above 6% post-crisis, representing massive, untapped buying power. The author concludes by noting that as 2012 ended, these deep cash reserves were finally being deployed into consumer spending, higher dividends, and corporate acquisitions.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2013 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, introduces a collection of macroeconomic and geopolitical concerns metaphorically referred to as "The Squid," symbolizing sprawling global challenges. The primary commentary details concerns ranging from Europe's structural economic divide and Japan's high debt to weak US labor compensation and China's dependence on credit expansion. The text also details the geopolitical threat of Iran's nuclear enrichment, predicting that 2013 will be the year Iran amasses enough enriched uranium to develop a weapon.

Several charts are presented to support these observations. Chart four, illustrating the periphery employment crisis, tracks the unemployment gap between peripheral Europe and Germany from 1980 to 2012. It shows that after the Euro exchange rate was fixed in 1999, the gap eventually spiked to nearly ten percent by 2012. Chart five visualizes Spanish net foreign liabilities as a percentage of GDP from 1999 to 2011, illustrating how official financing from the European Central Bank and EMU central banks surged to replace foreign private sector funding after 2010, with total liabilities nearing one hundred percent of GDP. Chart six highlights the growing Franco-German gap, charting how Germany’s export lead over France widened to nearly eight hundred billion euros by 2010, while France’s unemployment rate relative to Germany’s climbed to roughly three percent.

In chart seven, the difficult OECD fiscal situation is detailed, showing gross debt rising toward one hundred ten percent of GDP by 2010, alongside a plunging fiscal balance that hit negative eight percent. Chart eight highlights weak US labor compensation during the recovery; while the previous five economic recoveries saw labor compensation rise to over six hundred billion dollars by quarter fourteen, the current recovery remained near zero, signaling potential headwind risks for consumer spending. 

For Asia, chart nine tracks China's capital spending and credit overhang from 1980 to 2010, showing gross fixed capital formation nearing forty-eight percent of GDP while total non-financial sector debt surged close to one hundred ninety percent. Chart ten plots Japan’s nominal versus real GDP growth from 1991 to 2011 against peer IMF advanced economies, showing Japan isolated with a stagnant one percent real GDP growth and negative one percent nominal GDP growth. Chart eleven illustrates the fading global growth benefits of post-crisis stimulus, showing the Global Manufacturing PMI peaking near sixty in 2010 before steadily sliding back down toward the expansion-contraction threshold of fifty by late 2012. 

Finally, chart twelve tracks Iran's 19.75 percent enriched uranium stockpile from February 2010 to a projected peak in February 2013. The chart illustrates how additional capacity from the Fordow and Natanz facilities has driven stockpiles upward, overcoming a mid-2012 drawdown for reactor fuel, to cross the red-lined minimum threshold of roughly one hundred twenty to one hundred forty kilograms required for nuclear weapon production, with projections pushing past one hundred sixty kilograms by early 2013.

This page analyzes the Eurozone crisis in late 2012 and early 2013, arguing that while aggressive policy interventions have stabilized financial markets, severe underlying economic and social stresses persist. The author notes that Eurozone growth is projected at zero percent for 2013, with periphery unemployment at eighteen percent, driving a rise in support for extremist political parties. 

The narrative is supported by nine distinct charts. Chart forty-seven illustrates that fiscal tightening peaked in 2012 for Germany, Italy, and Spain. Chart forty-eight depicts the sharp contraction of German and French bank claims on peripheral European nations from their 2008 peaks of nearly nine hundred billion dollars. Chart forty-nine presents the potential capacity of public support programs, showing trillions of Euros in committed and uncommitted funding across the ESM, IMF, EFSF, and ECB. 

Charts fifty through fifty-four illustrate the dramatic market stabilization that followed ECB President Mario Draghi’s supportive rhetoric and policy actions. These charts track falling Spanish credit spreads, stabilizing peripheral bank deposits, a leveling off of private foreign holdings of Spanish and Italian sovereign debt, a recovery in periphery bank net debt issuance, and a peak in ECB lending to Spanish banks at roughly eleven percent of liabilities. Finally, chart fifty-five tracks the rising electoral success of right-wing extremist parties in countries such as Austria, France, Greece, and Norway. The author concludes that the region remains a high-stakes economic experiment, with competitiveness gains depending on painful adjustments in relative wages and productivity.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication examines the potential contribution of the US housing recovery to overall economic growth in 2013. The author argues that while housing indicators show a robust rebound, the total direct contribution to 2013 GDP growth will be a modest 0.75%. Positive multiplier effects should bring total GDP growth to around 2.5% after accounting for the drag of fiscal austerity. The recovery's moderate impact is attributed to housing starting from an exceptionally low base post-collapse and a lack of credit expansion. The author notes that average FICO scores have risen due to tight refinancing criteria, while purchase mortgages remain flat. To close, he raises a warning flag regarding purchase loans from 2009 to 2011, noting that almost half of the volume was underwritten by the Federal Housing Administration, Veterans Affairs, and the Department of Agriculture with average down-payments of only 3%. 

To support this outlook, the page features nine charts. Chart c31 displays an estimate of pent-up demand for housing in millions of units from 2004 to 2012, showing demand recovering from a bottom of negative 1.5 million units up to positive levels by 2012. Chart c32 illustrates the percentage of metropolitan statistical areas where buying is cheaper than renting, which surged from a flat 10% in the mid-2000s to over 50% by 2012. Chart c33 tracks the net percentage of banks reporting more or less demand for residential mortgages from 1991 to 2012, highlighting a return to positive demand by late 2012 after deep negative readings during the financial crisis. Chart c34 utilizes a six-month moving average to show the percentage of consumers planning to buy a home within six months, which fell from a peak near 9% down to 4% before ticking back up toward 5.5% in 2012. 

Chart c35 presents two metrics of improving demand: the traffic of prospective buyers index and the average of housing starts and permits as a percentage of households, both of which bottomed around 2009 and have since turned upward. Chart c36 highlights the "sand states" of Arizona, Nevada, Florida, and California, plotting building permits and real estate-related employment year-over-year percent changes; it reveals a dramatic rebound in building permits from nearly negative 80% to positive 40% growth. Chart c37 places the current market in historical context, plotting the construction share of employment and the residential investment share of GDP from 1939 to 2009, revealing that both metrics collapsed to historic lows of roughly 3.5% and 1% respectively. Chart c38 shows why credit is not yet driving this expansion, contrasting a flat index of mortgage applications for purchase with a surging average FICO score that climbed from under 700 to roughly 750 between 2001 and 2012. Finally, Chart c39 provides the long-term context of residential investment's contribution to real GDP growth in percentage points from 1930 to 2010, confirming that the projected 0.75% contribution for 2013 is far smaller than the post-war peaks of over 2.0% in the late 1940s or the recovery of 1982.

This page argues that Chinese economic growth will be a positive force in 2013, supported by a broader rebound in Emerging Asia. While the quality of Chinese growth is debatable due to its reliance on government stimulus and credit, the consensus forecast of approximately 8% growth seems attainable. This outlook is supported by a series of nine charts and tables illustrating regional economic conditions. Chart c56 shows Chinese real GDP growth, which spiked near 14% in 2007 and fell below 8% in 2012, with the 2013 consensus forecast expecting a recovery back toward 8%. To support this, Table c57 presents high-frequency indicators for China, noting steady trend growth in cement and container throughput, and strong rebounds in electricity consumption, freight (highway, rail, waterway), and steel production, despite weaker exports. Chart c58 demonstrates that Emerging Asian countries, including China, have substantial fiscal room to spend compared to developed markets; the chart plots 2012 estimates of general government fiscal balance against debt as a percentage of GDP, showing developed markets crowded in the high-debt, high-deficit quadrant, while EM Asia remains well-positioned with low debt and manageable deficits. Chart c59 highlights the role of government stimulus by tracking Chinese fixed asset investment, showing infrastructure spending rebounding to nearly 20% in late 2012 after dipping to zero, while manufacturing investment remains around 20% to 30%. Despite China's strength, Chart c60 reveals a divergence in manufacturing output, where China's index rose steadily from 100 in early 2011 to nearly 120 in late 2012, while EM Asia ex-China remained stagnant below 100. Chart c61 tracks exports for Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore, illustrating that while they have stabilized slightly above 0% after a steep drop from their 2010 peaks, they remain weak. 

Looking ahead, the author expects improved economic data in emerging Asia, driven partly by declining interest rate expectations. Chart c62 plots the emerging market interest rate swap curve, comparing the elevated forward rate expected in mid-2011 to the significantly lower spot and forward rates starting in December 2012, signaling supportive monetary policy. Similar stabilization is anticipated in Brazil, where Chart c63 displays year-over-year industrial production and export growth stabilizing near 0% in late 2012 after sharp declines from 2010 peaks. However, the author notes that European demand is unlikely to assist, as Chart c64 shows a sharp contraction in Euro area imports from Latin America and Asia, falling to negative year-over-year rates in late 2012. The primary risk highlighted for the region is a potential resurgence in inflation, which could force central banks to raise policy rates, especially since the output gap for Asia ex-Japan has turned positive.

This page from the publication addresses the discrepancy between the Eurozone capital market rescue and the lack of real economic improvement on the ground. The author structures this analysis as a hypothetical road trip across Europe on behalf of Chancellor Angela Merkel to assess local economic conditions, starting in Berlin and traveling through Paris, Madrid, Rome, and Athens. 

The journey begins in Germany, where growth is slowing to approximately one percent. This slowdown is illustrated in chart c40, which tracks the decline in German business surveys and manufacturing orders. The chart compares the year-over-year percent change in manufacturing orders against the IFO survey of non-financial businesses, showing both metrics falling sharply toward the end of 2011 and into 2012. 

The road trip then moves southwest to France, where economic progress has stalled. Chart c41 shows French growth stalling, with real GDP growth hovering near zero percent and the business climate survey dropping well below its long-term average index value of 100 down to around 90 by late 2011. This economic stagnation is exacerbated by structural rigidities, as demonstrated in chart c42. This chart ranks countries by how favorable their policies are to workers across nine factors, placing France at the far left as the premier worker’s utopia, well ahead of other nations like Germany, the United States, and Singapore, which sits at the far right as the least favorable. 

Continuing south to Spain, the author notes that the nation's current economic decline is historic. Chart c43 tracks the five-year percent change in real Spanish GDP since 1850, showing that outside of the Spanish Civil War in the 1930s, the current Euro-era boom-bust cycle represents the worst economic decline in modern Spanish history, surpassing previous shocks like the Pan-European banking crisis and the revolution that exiled Queen Isabella. Additionally, chart c44 argues that Spain's apparent current account improvement is a cyclical mirage. While the actual current account has risen from a deficit of over ten percent of GDP in 2008 to near zero percent in 2012, the cyclically-adjusted current account remains deeply negative at around minus six percent, revealing that the improvement is driven by a deep recession and twenty-five percent unemployment rather than improved fundamental competitiveness.

The next stop is Italy, where the focus shifts to government debt. Chart c45 displays Italy's gross general government debt as a percentage of GDP since its unification in 1861. The data shows that outside of World War I and World War II, when debt peaked between 140 percent and 160 percent of GDP, Italy's debt-to-GDP ratio has reached its highest level in history, exceeding 120 percent. This high debt burden requires constant primary budget surpluses to manage. 

The final destination of the road trip is Greece, where the GDP contraction is characterized as one of the worst in the post-war era. Table c46 lists the largest post-war GDP declines globally over five-year periods, showing that Greece’s 20.8 percent contraction through December 2013 ranks alongside catastrophic events like the collapse of the Soviet Union (which caused declines in Ukraine, Russia, and Kazakhstan), the post-revolution isolation of Iran, and severe crises in Venezuela and Peru. The author concludes by noting that Greece's debt ratio remains unsustainable at 170 percent of GDP even after private sector debt relief, far exceeding the forty percent to sixty percent debt levels yielded by similar restructuring exercises in Argentina and Mexico.

This section on US equities argues that slow economic growth does not preclude strong stock market performance, particularly right after a recession ends when valuations are depressed and investor pessimism is high. For example, US equities began 2012 at a forward multiple below twelve times due to European sovereign debt concerns, rising to twelve point seven times by the end of the year. The author asserts that US equities appear fairly valued at twelve to thirteen times 2013 earnings estimates, balancing the debate between the Graham-Dodd/Shiller valuation model, which suggests stocks are expensive, and the Federal Reserve's favored model comparing S&P 500 earnings yields to ten-year bond yields, which suggests they are very cheap. 

The accompanying charts illustrate these divergent perspectives. Chart c65, plotting global equity returns against global GDP growth from 1970 to 2012, highlights a cluster of years—including 2012—where low global GDP growth of roughly one to three percent still yielded positive equity returns of up to twenty-five percent. Chart c66 tracks the Graham-Dodd/Shiller valuation approach from 1901 to 2012, showing the price-to-ten-year average earnings ratio approaching twenty-five times, which historically indicates expensive valuations. Conversely, Chart c67 presents the S&P 500 trailing earnings yield minus ten-year interest rates over the same century-long period, showing a spread of roughly five percent which places equities in cheap territory. 

The page also highlights strong corporate profitability. Chart c68 shows that the S&P 500 ex-financials net profit margin recovered robustly from its 1977-2012 lows of under four percent to approximately nine percent by late 2012, driven by manufacturing productivity. However, Chart c69 reveals that the ratio of US earnings growth to nominal GDP growth recently spiked to an extreme peak of sixteen point six times, far higher than previous average peaks of two point one times and four point two times, before reverting to trend. Chart c70 tracks the 2012 and 2013 year-over-year S&P 500 earnings growth estimates as they evolved throughout 2012; while 2012 expectations fell to around six percent, 2013 growth estimates stabilized near a healthy ten percent by October 2012. 

A detailed breakdown at the bottom outlines reservations about the Graham-Dodd model. The author notes that anchoring expectations on a trailing ten-year window unfairly penalizes current valuations because of the anomalous 2008 financial crisis, during which reported earnings plummeted seventy percent. Additionally, two hundred and forty of the S&P 500 companies have changed since 2000, meaning a decade of historical data is a poor proxy for the current index's performance. Looking forward, the author predicts that S&P 500 returns of eight to ten percent are achievable in 2013, with further upside potential if policymakers in Washington DC secure a long-term grand bargain fiscal deal to push price-to-earnings multiples higher.

This page of the outlook assesses equity valuations and investment opportunities across the United States, Europe, and emerging markets, specifically highlighting cyclical versus defensive sectors, banking capitalization, and geographic valuation discounts. 

In the US market, the author argues that cyclical stocks trade at a substantial discount to defensive stocks due to a multi-year rush for dividend-paying equities, presenting an investment opportunity as pent-up consumer and business demand for durable goods builds. This trend is illustrated by chart c71, "Cyclicals trading cheaply vs. Defensives," which tracks the cyclicals-to-defensives trailing P/E ratio from 1974 to 2010, showing the ratio hitting a deep historical trough near 0.6. Chart c72 supports this view by tracking "Durable goods spending by consumers and businesses as a percent of GDP" from 1947 to 2007, showing spending cycling down to a low of 13% to 14%. Furthermore, US banks have successfully recapitalized, as demonstrated in chart c73, "US bank Tier 1 capital ratio." This chart shows the capital ratio of banks with assets between 1 billion and 10 billion rising from roughly 12% in 2009 to over 15% by 2012, while banks with assets over 10 billion increased their ratio from 8% to nearly 13%. Valuation-wise, healthcare is highlighted as the deepest value sector relative to consumer staples.

Turning to Europe, the author addresses "The Sick Men of Europe," noting that European equities recently traded at a historical 40-year discount to the US. Chart c74, "European equity discount to US," plots a composite of P/E, P/B, and P/Dividend from 1975 to 2010, demonstrating that the discount dipped to a historic low of approximately 30% to 40% before stabilizing. The author suggests that because so much bad news is priced in, investors should no longer hold radically underweight European positions, though fundamental growth concerns persist in Eurozone countries like Spain.

Lastly, the page discusses emerging markets, noting that earnings revisions are declining as profit growth slows in nations like China, Taiwan, Brazil, Chile, and Indonesia. This contraction is visualized in chart c75, "EM earnings revisions," which charts the six-month percent change in earnings revisions from 1995 to 2011, showing a slide from positive territory down to roughly -10%. Focusing on China, chart c76, "Chinese equity valuations," compares price-to-trailing-earnings from 2001 to 2012 for the Shanghai Composite Index (which fell from a 2007 peak of nearly 50x down to around 11x) and the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index H-shares (which dropped below 10x). While the author remains skeptical of Chinese growth data, H-shares under 10x forward P/E are deemed interesting, and the rest of Asia ex-Japan, trading at 12x to 15x multiples with fewer structural issues, is positioned as a favored region for 2013.

This page from the Outlook 2013 report analyzes global credit markets, the potential of precious metals amid monetary expansion, and the investment thesis surrounding Japan's economic stagnation. 

The first section discusses credit markets and argues that the Federal Reserve's portfolio rebalancing channel is clearly at work. High-yield spreads have rallied but are not yet back to historical lows of the late 1980s, 1990s, or 2007. This is illustrated in a chart of global USD high-yield spreads, showing the spread to worst in basis points from 1987 to 2011, where spreads spiked past 1,800 basis points in 2008 and have since declined toward 600 basis points. Underwriting standards have loosened, as shown in another chart detailing underwriting standards from 1997 to 2012. This chart tracks high-yield B- and lower issuance as a percentage of total issuance on the left axis, which is rising back toward 40%, alongside senior leveraged buyout debt-to-cash-flow multiples on the right axis, which have climbed back above 5x. Despite these looser standards, the author expects no US recession in 2013, noting that corporate default rates remain low. A chart of issuer-weighted corporate default rates for US high-yield bonds, global high-yield bonds, and US leveraged loans from 1981 to 2009 demonstrates that defaults have plummeted from their 2009 peaks of over 10% down to very low single digits. Additionally, a chart of US high-yield bonds and loans trading at or below 80% of face value highlights that distressed debt opportunities have dried up; after peaking in late 2008 at 77% for bonds and 81% for loans, the share has collapsed to near zero, making it harder for distressed debt managers to find cheaply priced assets. 

The second section focuses on commodities, specifically precious metals, as the author does not expect much from industrial metals or energy due to sluggish global growth. Even though inflation is currently low, precious metals performed well in 2012 and have returned 15% to 16% annualized since late 2007. The author attributes this performance to the massive expansion of base money. This dynamic is illustrated by a chart of year-over-year core consumer price index changes from 2004 to 2012, which shows developed markets core CPI hovering around 1.5% while emerging markets sit near 3%. Meanwhile, a chart of excess reserves held at major central banks shows an explosion from near zero prior to 2008 to nearly $3.5 trillion by 2012. The author argues that if private sector banks deploy these inert reserves as the output gap closes, it could fuel significant inflation. The author agrees with market bets that central bankers will allow inflation to exceed target levels to support growth, predicting another positive year for precious metals in 2013.

The final section addresses Japan, where some investors advocate adding Japanese equities while shorting both the Yen and Japanese Government Bonds. This thesis relies on the idea that Japan's weak economy will force unlimited monetary printing to reach a 2% inflation target. Gloomy indicators support this view: Japan's growth is exceptionally low, its current account surplus is near zero, its trade balance is in a sustained deficit for the first time since 1965, and corporate profits have stagnated at 2004 levels. A comparative chart of US versus Japan corporate profits from 1999 to 2011 highlights this divergence, showing US profits climbing toward $2 trillion while Japanese profits remain depressed around 10 to 12 trillion Yen. However, the author ends with a cautionary note, reminding investors that many have lost money over the last twenty years betting on a reflationary "Japocalypse" that never materialized, and warning that Japan must still compete with other inflating global central banks.

This page of the publication outlines several key themes for investors looking toward the year 2013, spanning Japanese equities, emerging market private equity, private credit, commercial real estate, and energy sectors. The author first counsels caution regarding the reflation trade in Japan. Although short-term money-printing may pressure the Yen and boost equities temporarily, the author expects any such gains to be unsustainable. This skepticism is driven by fundamental weaknesses, including Japanese bank holdings of Japanese Government Bonds being nine times their capital and an average return on equity that is less than one-third of the levels seen in the United States and Europe. Supporting this cautious view is the historical fact that Japanese equities have produced a negative one point five percent annualized return since 1993, accompanied by massive booms and busts.

Turning to alternatives, the publication suggests that private equity is an excellent way to capture the growing middle class in emerging markets like China and Brazil. While urban household consumption in China grows by ten to twelve percent annually and the service sector accounts for over half of both nations' GDPs, their public equity markets do not reflect this reality. In China, banks, energy, industrials, and basic materials dominate eighty-one percent of the Shanghai Composite. Similarly, in Brazil, the non-financial services, telecom, and transport sectors comprise only fifteen percent of the Bovespa. This mismatch makes private equity a superior investment vehicle for emerging consumption. Chart eighty-four supports this, showing five-year annualized returns through the first quarter of 2012, where the Asia PE and VC Index returned about ten percent and the Asia EM PE and VC Index reached eleven percent, both handily beating the negative three percent return of the MSCI Pacific and the five and a half percent return of the MSCI Asia ex-Japan. Similarly, the Latin America and Caribbean PE and VC Index outperformed public markets with a ten and a half percent return compared to eight percent for MSCI EM Latin America.

The page also details the state of credit markets and commercial real estate. While public debt markets have healed, smaller middle-market companies face restricted access to capital. Chart eighty-five illustrates quarterly debt issuance by mid-market firms with EBITDA under fifty million dollars, revealing that the number of deals plummeted from pre-crisis peaks of over one hundred per quarter down to only about twenty deals quarterly by 2012. Chart eighty-eight tracks monthly global M&A volume from late 2010 to late 2012, showing a relatively flat but volatile trend that mostly fluctuated between one hundred fifty billion and two hundred fifty billion dollars. For commercial real estate, low interest rates have driven demand for prime locations, but non-prime locations continue to trade at heavy discounts. This divergence is captured in chart eighty-six, which indexes real estate values to late 2000. Major market central business district offices experienced a powerful rebound, climbing to an index level of roughly one hundred seventy-five by 2011, while non-major market suburban offices stagnated at index values below one hundred. 

Finally, the author contrasts investments in traditional exploration and production of oil and gas with renewables, arguing that traditional energy remains more compelling due to the high costs of green energy. Chart eighty-seven demonstrates the levelized cost of electricity production in Germany, measured in USD per megawatt-hour. Traditional sources are significantly cheaper, with nuclear at fifty dollars, coal at seventy dollars, and natural gas at ninety dollars, compared to onshore wind at one hundred twenty dollars, offshore wind at one hundred seventy dollars, and solar at a substantial four hundred twenty dollars. This high cost structure makes renewable energy heavily dependent on volatile political subsidies.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Outlook 2013, authored by Michael Cembalest, focuses on the structural fiscal challenges facing the United States, specifically the threat that rising entitlement spending poses to discretionary investments and the long-term status of the U.S. dollar as the world's reserve currency. 

Cembalest argues that political debates focusing on cutting discretionary budgets, such as proposals to curtail the Environmental Protection Agency, miss the larger issue. Following the Budget Control Act, non-defense discretionary spending is already projected to hit its lowest level relative to GDP in decades. The true driver of the U.S. fiscal challenge is the boiling frog problem of mandatory entitlement spending—encompassing Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid—which is crowding out crucial investments in energy, education, infrastructure, and worker retraining. The author highlights that when Medicare was created, the House Ways and Means Committee estimated its expenses would grow sevenfold by 1990, but they actually grew sixty-one-fold.

To illustrate this crowding out, the page includes three visual exhibits. The first chart, titled The Boiling Frog, tracks U.S. expenditures and government receipts as a percentage of GDP from 1972 with projections through 2022. It demonstrates how growing entitlement programs and interest payments are squeezing discretionary and defense spending, while government receipts remain relatively flat. An adjacent table highlights this displacement by comparing estimated 2017 spending levels for critical public sectors against their historical peaks. It shows that energy spending is projected to drop to 33 percent of its historical peak, education to 69 percent, teacher and worker retraining to 86 percent, ground transportation to 4 percent, and air transportation to 9 percent.

The second chart displays non-defense discretionary spending as a percentage of GDP from 1962 projected to 2017. It illustrates a clear downward trend, peaking at over 5 percent in the late 1970s and falling toward approximately 2.5 percent by 2017 under the caps of the Budget Control Act, even without factoring in the sequester.

Finally, Cembalest warns that mismanagement of fiscal, military, and political policies has historically led to the collapse of reserve currency eras. The final chart timeline tracks the dominant reserve currencies and superpowers since 1400, detailing the successive cycles of global dominance by Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands, France, Great Britain, and finally the United States. The author concludes that achieving energy independence and resolving entitlement policies are critical to preventing the United States from suffering a similar loss of its global reserve currency status.

This page from the Outlook 2013 publication begins with a brief overview of hedge fund positioning, focusing on event-driven strategies, long/short strategies based on fundamental research, emerging market credit, and reinsurance. The core of the page then transitions to a deeper analysis of long-term US growth prospects, arguing that further progress on entitlements and energy independence is crucial. The author poses the question of whether the US will adopt a more aggressive pro-growth agenda, drawing a historical parallel to the 1950s when the nation successfully reduced its high debt load through economic expansion rather than austerity, high inflation, or tax increases.

A detailed table titled "(c89) 1950's Federal debt reduction relied on growth..." displays annual financial metrics from 1950 to 1960. It shows that net debt-to-GDP fell from 80% in 1950 to 46% in 1960. This reduction was driven by a robust real GDP compound annual growth rate of 4.3%, while federal outlays and receipts remained relatively stable as a percentage of GDP, and the real 10-year US Treasury rate averaged positive returns for most of the decade despite a sharp dip to negative 5.3% in 1951.

The commentary then shifts to US energy independence, defining it as relying only on Western Hemisphere partners (excluding Venezuela) for crude oil and maintaining a competitive domestic electricity cost advantage. To visualize this, a bar chart titled "(c90) What US energy independence might look like" compares US net crude oil imports in 2012 with a 2025 projection. Net imports are projected to drop from roughly 7.5 million barrels per day in 2012 to around 2.5 million barrels per day by 2025. The chart attributes this decline primarily to a net increase in domestic production, alongside reduced consumption from CAFE standards, displacement by natural gas vehicles, and oil imported for refined product exports. The projected 2.5 million barrels per day matches current imports from Canada, Mexico, and Colombia/Brazil.

The author emphasizes that the substantial US electricity cost advantage is driven by cheap domestic natural gas, contrasted against costly nuclear phase-outs and renewable energy transitions in Germany and Japan. This advantage is illustrated by three charts at the bottom of the page. The first, "(c91) Wholesale electricity prices," tracks prices in USD/MWh from 2006 to 2012, showing US prices declining to around $40/MWh, while prices in Europe hovered around $65/MWh and prices in China rose to approximately $80/MWh. The second chart, "(c92) US electricity from natural gas," shows that natural gas's share of net electricity generation steadily climbed from a low of about 9% in the late 1980s to 24% by 2012. The final bar chart, "(c93) Global natural gas prices," shows US natural gas prices sitting at an extremely low level of around $2.50/MMBtu, compared to significantly higher prices in peer nations, rising from about $5.00/MMBtu in Brazil to nearly $14.00/MMBtu in Japan. The author concludes by citing energy analyst Vaclav Smil, who contextualizes hydraulic fracking as an extension of established secondary recovery techniques.

This page analyzes Chinese consumption trends, the expansion of luxury retail, and the historical divergence between China's economic growth and its stock market returns. The author highlights that while luxury points of sale are traditionally concentrated in major hubs like Beijing and Shanghai, reaching China’s growing affluent class increasingly requires moving inland. To illustrate this geographic dispersion, a set of maps shows the dramatic expansion of locations with significant affluent populations between 2010 and 2020. A related bar chart details the massive scale of luxury retail expansion from 2008 through November 2011, led by brands like Armani with nearly 80 new stores, Dunhill with approximately 60, and Hugo Boss and Coach with over 50 stores each. Despite this consumer potential, the text cautions that international businesses continue to face operational hurdles, including inconsistent intellectual property laws, cyber security threats, and unequal regulatory treatment compared to domestic firms.

The commentary then shifts to the challenges of investing in Chinese public equities. The author points out that onshore Chinese equities listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen have historically performed poorly relative to the country's economic expansion. A scatter plot comparing annualized equity market returns to nominal GDP growth from 2003 through early 2013 demonstrates that the Shanghai Index delivered an annualized USD return of only about 10% despite nominal GDP growth of around 16%—underperforming virtually all other depicted emerging markets, including Colombia, Peru, and Indonesia, which generated far higher equity returns with lower GDP growth. Offshore Hong Kong-listed H-shares performed better, returning roughly 18% annualized. 

To show the resulting valuation compression, a trailing price-to-earnings line chart from 2001 to 2012 tracks the severe de-rating of both the Shanghai Composite Index and the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index. The Shanghai Composite's price-to-earnings ratio fell from peaks above 50x in 2001 and 2007 to near 10x by 2012, while H-shares fell below 10x. The author attributes this downward trend to investor anxieties regarding corporate governance, state-oriented business objectives, and slowing growth. However, the commentary concludes on a slightly positive note, suggesting that these cheapened valuations and signs of economic stabilization had recently made the firm more constructive on Chinese equities.

This page provides an analysis of Chinese consumer spending patterns, the limitations of official economic statistics, and the scale of investment opportunities linked to the country’s growing wealth. The author argues that despite statistical challenges, examining specific retail categories reveals robust, long-term consumer demand that offers unique scale compared to other Asian markets. 

The first chart, "Retail sales growth rate by country," shows the year-over-year percentage change using a six-month moving average from 1996 to 2012 for China, the United States, Japan, and the United Kingdom. This visual highlights China's dramatic outperformance; while the U.S., UK, and Japan dipped deep into negative growth during the 2008 to 2009 financial crisis, China's retail sales growth consistently remained above 10%, hovering around 15% in late 2012. 

To bypass the flaws of aggregate national statistics, the second chart, "Retail sales growth for 4 top categories at 200 largest retail enterprises," tracks year-over-year three-month moving averages from 2009 to 2012. It details highly volatile spending patterns across key sectors. The "Gold, Silver and Jewelry" category saw growth peak near 60% in early 2011 before falling back to roughly 10% by late 2012. "Garments" and "Articles for daily use" maintained steadier trends, while "Household electric appliances" fell below zero percent growth in late 2011 before making a mild recovery in 2012. 

Addressing China’s scale, the chart titled "Total investable wealth of high net worth individuals" compares wealth in billions of dollars across eight Asian territories. China completely dominates the region with approximately $2.6 trillion in investable wealth, leaving runner-up nations like India, Singapore, Hong Kong, Korea, Thailand, Taiwan, and Indonesia far behind, with none of them exceeding $400 billion. 

The subsequent index chart, "What Chinese people buy when they get wealthier," tracks how consumption priorities shift from poor to affluent wealth tiers. It reveals that automobile purchases accelerate fastest as households climb the income ladder, with the index for cars rising toward 100 for the affluent class. Purchases of prestige and luxury goods, alongside home decoration, also climb noticeably as consumers enter the middle and affluent classes. 

In the commentary, the author notes that although car purchases have historically benefited from government subsidies, emerging and middle-class consumers are increasingly prioritizing luxury goods and home furnishings. Even though a cooling economy, declining corporate profits, and political restrictions on official gift-giving slowed luxury spending growth to 7% in 2012, firms like Bain expect a partial rebound. Looking forward, Chinese consumers are projected to account for 35% of global luxury consumption by 2015, up from 27% in 2012. This positive outlook is underpinned by strong consumer optimism, with 74% of Chinese households believing their income will rise significantly over the next five years, compared to less than 50% of households in the United States. 

Finally, a detailed footnote explains that official Chinese urban household consumption statistics are structurally flawed and likely understate actual consumption. This underestimation occurs because the statistics rely on a limited survey of 66,000 households, fail to capture China's large underground cash economy, omit corporate subsidies that disguise personal consumption as business expenses, and systematically underestimate the imputed rent of owned homes.

In this final segment on Chinese consumption, Michael Cembalest argues that sustained increases in Chinese spending are underpinned by genuine growth in household wealth and income, countering the views of many China skeptics. To support this, a line chart titled "Chinese real wage growth" displays year-over-year percent changes from 2008 through 2012. It tracks two metrics deflated by rural and urban consumer price indexes: cash wage per capita in rural households and average income per capita in urban households. The rural series demonstrates robust growth, hovering between 11% and 19% year-over-year, peaking in late 2011, and remaining at a strong 15% by late 2012. The urban series exhibits more volatility, spiking over 20% in late 2008 before stabilizing between 10% and 12% in 2011 and 2012. This data underscores that wage gains have stayed strong even as overall GDP growth slowed, rising faster than the broader economy itself. Additionally, the text notes that the ratio of job opportunities to job seekers reached a ten-year high of 1.08, according to the Ministry of Human Resources.

Beside the chart is a historical black-and-white photograph from the Associated Press showing Singapore's former Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew and Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping shaking hands in 1978. Cembalest recounts a personal conversation with Lee Kuan Yew, who detailed how he encouraged Deng Xiaoping to reform China's economy by pointing out Singapore's success with descendants of landless peasants, suggesting China could do even better with its own thinkers and writers. This meeting preceded the establishment of China's first four Special Economic Zones in Xiamen, Shantou, Zhuhai, and Shenzhen, launching the country's economic transformation. Cembalest concludes that consumption remains one of the most promising frontiers for investors in this ongoing economic shift. A comprehensive list of references at the bottom of the page cites various studies on China's middle class, luxury markets, high-speed rail, housing, and savings rates from major institutions including the Brookings Institution, OECD, McKinsey, Bain, Boston Consulting Group, and J.P. Morgan Securities.

This page provides an update on Chinese consumption and private equity investment opportunities, highlighting the rapid growth and massive scale of potential target companies in China. By the end of 2011, China accounted for 25% of all private equity activity in emerging markets. The first chart, a log-scale scatter plot comparing purchasing-power-parity GDP to the number of large companies with revenues exceeding 250 million dollars, shows China's immense scale. Positioned high up on both axes, China is second only to the United States and has roughly ten times the number of large potential target companies as peers like Mexico, Turkey, and Indonesia. Highlighting this growth, the author notes that China is now 3.5 times larger than Germany on a purchasing-power basis and that McKinsey projects 29% of global growth from 2007 to 2025 will originate in 225 Chinese cities.

To evaluate whether private equity returns justify the risks in emerging Asia, the second chart displays five-year annualized returns through the second quarter of 2012. It reveals that private equity and venture capital have significantly outperformed public equity markets in the region. While the MSCI Pacific index returned approximately negative 3% and the MSCI Asia ex-Japan index returned about 1%, both the Asia PE & VC Index and the Asia EM PE & VC Index delivered robust returns of roughly 8%. 

The page then focuses on the critical importance of exit strategies, pointing out that Greater China dominates the exit landscape. The third chart, a stacked column chart, illustrates that while Greater China represents less than half of private equity-backed investments in emerging Asia, it accounts for a disproportionate share of exits at approximately 80%. In contrast, India secures a significant portion of investments but yields very few exits. The final set of visuals breaks down these exits, showing that IPOs are the primary exit strategy, making up about 70% of exit value compared to strategic sales and sponsor-to-sponsor transactions. A companion pie chart shows that Greater China almost entirely dominates these Asian IPO exits, with India and Southeast Asia making up only tiny fractions.

Despite this dominance, the author notes that 2012 was a difficult year for Chinese listings, with global Chinese IPO proceeds falling from over 400 billion RMB in 2011 to 168 billion RMB in 2012 due to poor IPO performance, accounting controversies, and regulatory interventions. The text explains that local RMB-denominated funds, which operate with shorter terms and higher purchase multiples than dollar-denominated funds, have contributed to a significant IPO backlog. In response, the Chinese government is screening applicants with the goal of shortening the IPO queue from five years to just one or two years.

This page details J.P. Morgan's update on Chinese consumption and related investment opportunities, arguing that China's public equity markets offer surprisingly limited options for investors wishing to focus on the consumer. The primary reason is that Chinese equity markets are heavily dominated by financials, energy, and industrials, which together make up about 71 percent of the market. Furthermore, the author notes that contacts in China report sharply rising, underreported non-performing and special mention loans, signaling a potential brewing banking crisis after the massive emergency stimulus of 2008 and 2009. 

Two charts support these points. The first is a pie chart showing the Chinese stock market breakdown by sector, using the Shanghai Composite Index. Financials dominate at 37.4 percent, followed by energy at 18.0 percent, industrials at 15.3 percent, and materials at 9.7 percent. By comparison, consumer discretionary accounts for only 6.7 percent, consumer staples make up 3.8 percent, utilities are at 3.7 percent, health care stands at 3.0 percent, information technology is at 1.9 percent, and telecommunications sits at 0.5 percent. The second chart, a bar chart comparing index weights for consumer discretionary and staples across various nations, shows that China has one of the lowest consumer-sector weights at around 10 percent, ranking only ahead of Canada and Poland. This stands in stark contrast to markets like Mexico, Japan, and France, which boast consumer sector weights of approximately 37 percent, 27 percent, and 25 percent respectively.

To assess the available consumer options, a dual-part table lists the valuation metrics of the largest consumer discretionary stocks in the MSCI China Index as of February 2013. The table details trailing P/E ratios, next-twelve-month P/E ratios, long-term earnings growth forecasts, and PEG ratios. Featured companies include Belle International Holdings with a trailing P/E of 27 and a forward P/E of 22, and China ZhengTong Auto Service, which shows a trailing P/E of 21.6, a forward P/E of 11.3, and an expected long-term earnings growth rate of 40.8 percent, resulting in a low PEG ratio of 0.3. Other major holdings listed include automotive companies such as Dongfeng Motor Group, Great Wall Motor Company, Guangzhou Automobile Group, and Geely Automobile Holdings, alongside retail and consumer goods firms like Golden Eagle Retail Group, Intime Department Store, Daphne International Holding, Haier Electronics Group, Parkson Retail Group, Dah Chong Hong, Zhongsheng Group Holdings, Anta Sports Products, Bosideng International Holdings, and Hengdeli Holdings. While these consumer names have historically been highly valued compared to their US counterparts, recent declines have somewhat lowered these multiples.

Given these public market limitations, the author proposes two alternative investment strategies. The first is investing in global companies with high sales exposure to BRIC countries. Over the prior three years, a basket of such companies outperformed emerging market equities, the MSCI global all-country index, Asia ex-Japan, and both onshore and H-share Chinese equities. The second strategy centers on Chinese and Asian private equity, which acts as growth equity rather than traditional leveraged buyouts. In China, bank loans are disproportionately directed to state-owned enterprises, which make up only 5 percent of all companies by number but receive 75 percent of all loans. Meanwhile, small and medium-sized enterprises received less than 5 percent of bank loans in 2009 and only 20 percent in 2012. As a result, Chinese entrepreneurs must rely heavily on private equity as their primary source of growth capital rather than bank loans.

This page from the publication addresses the complex state of the credit markets, balancing near-term positive technical factors against growing structural risks. Framed around the theme of "Fifty Trades of Grey," the author discusses the consequences of Quantitative Easing and low interest rates, invoking Vladimir Lenin’s definition of a "rentier capitalist" to describe savers forced into "reach for yield" behavior. On the positive side, corporations possess strong cash flows, the Fed is expected to keep rates low until 2015 based on unemployment thresholds, and net new supply is extremely tight. However, the author cautions that underwriting standards are deteriorating, dealer liquidity has fallen to just 20% of 2007 levels, and credit yields are historically low. Citing Federal Reserve Governor Jeremy Stein’s concerns over overheating, the author warns that a period of diminishing credit returns is beginning and advises investors to trim overweighted credit positions. 

Four charts support this analysis. The first, "Global USD high yield markets," plots yields and spreads in basis points from 1987 to 2012. It demonstrates that while credit spreads are not at historic tights, nominal yields have plummeted near record lows, highlighting the distortion caused by riskless rate manipulation. The second chart, "Emerging markets US$ debt and high grade bonds," plots EMBI Global Diversified sovereign spreads (left scale, 0 to 1,600 basis points) and US High Grade spreads (right scale, 0 to 600 basis points) from 1998 to 2013. Both series illustrate a massive post-financial crisis compression, with spreads returning near their pre-crisis lows. 

The third chart, "Maturity extension by high yield borrowers," shows the volume of US high yield bonds maturing (in billions of USD) from 2012 to "2020 or later," comparing expectations from December 2008 against October 2012. This chart visualizes how companies successfully pushed out their imminent refinancing risks; the substantial maturities once scheduled for 2012 through 2015 were pushed into the future, culminating in a spike of nearly $450 billion maturing in 2020 or later. Finally, the fourth chart, "Underwriting standards softening, but below prior peaks," tracks credit quality from 1997 to 2012 using two metrics: high yield issues rated B- and lower as a percentage of total issuance (left axis, 0% to 70%) and the LBO senior debt to cash flow multiple (right axis, 2x to 6x). This visual demonstrates that by late 2012, highly speculative B- or lower issuance had surged past 40%, and LBO leverage multiples had climbed back to approximately 5x, showing that while standards remain below 2007 peaks, significant softening is underway.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest assesses the state of global equity market valuations, arguing that while specific dividend-paying sectors have become expensive, overall equity markets remain reasonably valued. Since credit tightening began, investors have favored defensive, dividend-paying stocks, pushing cyclical sectors to historically cheap levels. This trend is shown in the chart "Cyclical stocks still looking cheap to defensive ones," which tracks the ratio of cyclical stock P/Es to defensive ones from 1973 to 2013. The ratio plummeted from a post-2000 peak of around 1.5 to near-record lows of roughly 0.6 by 2013, highlighting the steep discount of cyclicals. Conversely, yield-seeking behavior has elevated other sectors, as illustrated in the chart "Valuations of REITs and Timber companies" from 1997 to 2013. Here, REIT valuations measured by price to forward Adjusted Funds From Operations have recovered from a 2009 low of 10x back to over 20x, while the P/E ratio for Plum Creek Timber Company has surged back to high levels between 35x and 40x.

To evaluate the broader market, Cembalest presents the chart "S&P 500 price to 3 and 5-year trailing average earnings." Tracking multiples from 1900 to 2010, the chart shows that the 3-year trailing multiple is currently reasonable and close to its long-term median around 16x. While the 5-year trailing multiple looks more expensive, Cembalest notes that this is due to the distortion of the 2008 earnings collapse. Another valuation metric, shown in the chart "Tobin's Q: not at extremes, and therefore less interesting," plots the ratio of market value to replacement cost for US non-financial companies from 1900 to 2009. Unlike its dot-com peak near 1.8, the ratio currently hovers around a moderate 0.8, indicating the market is not at a dangerous valuation extreme. A footnote adds that modern Tobin's Q calculations may be slightly overstated due to high proportions of intangible assets in sectors like pharmaceuticals and technology.

Looking ahead, Cembalest predicts that reasonable valuations coupled with a modest economic recovery in the United States, China, and the developing world should sustain the equity market. Although eventual inflation and Federal Reserve tightening will pose risks, the current large US output gap provides a buffer. He notes comments from Federal Reserve figures Ben Bernanke, Charles Evans, and Janet Yellen suggesting the Fed will tolerate inflation drifting above its long-term target to secure the recovery, thereby postponing monetary tightening for as long as possible.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues that Spains economic adjustment process is unsustainable and likely destined to fail because it relies on painful internal devaluation—slashing wages and enduring high unemployment—rather than the historical method of currency devaluation. 

The first chart, titled Trade improvement, courtesy of Tomas de Torquemada, illustrates this dynamic by plotting Spains trade balance as a percentage of GDP against the year-over-year percentage change in total nominal employee compensation from 2006 to 2012. It shows that Spains trade balance improved from a deficit of roughly 10 percent of GDP in 2008 to near 0 percent in 2012, but this recovery directly mirrored a collapse in employee compensation growth, which plummeted from an 8 percent year-over-year increase in 2008 to negative 6 percent by late 2012. 

A table titled The road less travelled contrasts Spains current predicament with past balance-of-payments crises. Historically, countries adjusted through currency devaluation: Mexico in 1994 saw a 56 percent decline in the trade-weighted Peso; Thailand in 1997 saw a 22 percent decline in the Baht; Korea in 1997 saw a 20 percent decline in the Won; Italy experienced devaluations of 26 percent in 1975 and 10 percent in 1981; and Spain itself saw a 20 percent decline in the Peseta in 1981. In contrast, Spains 2008 episode achieved external adjustment without currency flexibility, resulting in an 11 percent decline in total compensation and a devastating 26 percent unemployment rate.

Three side-by-side charts compare Spains current trajectory (ESP 08) against these historical episodes, with data indexed to quarter zero, representing the quarter before devaluation or crisis. The Trade balance chart shows that Spains trade balance as a percent of GDP climbed from negative 10 percent to positive territory over 20 quarters, but did so much more slowly than historical comparison cases. The Real exports index chart shows that while Spains exports grew to an index level of roughly 110 after 18 quarters, this is the weakest export recovery of the entire group, lagging far behind Mexico 1994, which surged to an index level of nearly 220. The Real GDP index chart is described as the smoking gun; while all other historical episodes saw real GDP bounce back sharply after a brief post-devaluation dip, Spains real GDP steadily contracted, languishing at an index level of about 92 after 18 quarters.

Cembalest concludes that Spains apparent trade balance improvement is driven by an import collapse and severe domestic pain rather than a healthy, export-led recovery. With only half of the competitiveness gap closed relative to Germany, he predicts this adjustment cannot be sustained indefinitely. He warns investors that despite temporary rallies in Spanish sovereign and bank spreads, they should exercise caution across the European Periphery unless asset prices drop significantly.

This page presents an analysis of Venezuela's economic and social state, characterizing the country as a place of severe contradictions. The author highlights that while Venezuela has achieved notable milestones in income equality, these gains are undermined by rampant inflation, high crime, failing institutions, and stagnant economic growth. 

A series of four tables at the top of the page illustrates these contrasts using international metrics. The first table shows improvement in the UN Human Development Index ranking from 2006 to 2011; Venezuela achieved the third-highest improvement in this group, jumping 7 spots from 75 to 68, trailing only Hong Kong and Cuba. The second table shows the number of intentional homicides per 100,000 people in 2008, where Venezuela ranks among the worst with 52 homicides, just behind countries like Honduras at 82 and El Salvador at 71. The third table shows income equality as measured by the Gini coefficient, with Venezuela leading the region with the lowest inequality score of 0.397, ahead of Uruguay at 0.402. However, the fourth table on headline inflation reveals that Venezuela has the highest five-year trailing annualized inflation rate in the world at 25%, followed by Ethiopia at 23% and Iran at 21%. The author suggests that this high inflation means Venezuelans have partially been made more equal by having their incomes inflated away.

A middle table displays World Economic Forum rankings from 2012 across 144 countries, where a rank of 1 is the best and 144 is the worst. This table demonstrates that Venezuela ranks at or near the absolute bottom in several foundational pillars. It ranks dead last at 144th in both legal and judicial systems and goods market efficiency, placing behind countries like Haiti, Burundi, Algeria, and Chad. Additionally, Venezuela ranks 143rd in labor market efficiency, just behind Argentina and Iran; 131st in innovation, behind Bangladesh and Libya; and 120th in infrastructure, behind Ethiopia and Tajikistan.

At the bottom of the page, two line charts compare Venezuela to a universe of 17 Latin American countries using data from The Conference Board. The left chart tracks the level of per capita GDP in real constant dollars from 1980 to 2012. It shows that Venezuela, represented by a bold red line, has historically been one of the richest countries in the region, consistently tracking near the top of the group. The right chart indexes growth in per capita GDP from 2008 to 2012, setting 2008 as 100. This chart shows that since oil prices stopped rising, Venezuela's wealth has stagnated. Its red line dips to the absolute bottom of the 17-country comparison, falling below 95 in 2010 and recovering only to around 97 by 2012, while almost all other regional peers experienced positive growth, reaching index values between 105 and 122. 

Ultimately, the author concludes that Venezuela continues to underutilize its oil wealth. While its level of per capita GDP remains high due to historical resources, its growth has stagnated near the bottom of the region, suggesting that a chaotic redistribution of wealth has prevented the broader economic pie from growing.

This page discusses the potential economic and investment impacts of Japan's aggressive new monetary and fiscal policies under the Shinzo Abe administration, often referred to as Abenomics. The author argues that while Japan faces deep structural issues, these policy actions could temporarily boost Japanese equities, making them an attractive short-term trade for investors who hedge their Yen exposure. To support this view, the page presents five visual elements illustrating the long-term stagnation of the Japanese economy. 

The first chart, titled Japan growth, 1991-2012, plots nominal GDP growth against real GDP growth for IMF advanced economies. While most peer nations lie along a positive trendline with healthy nominal growth, Japan is highlighted as a stark outlier, showing real growth of around one percent and nominal growth near zero percent. 

The second chart compares United States and Japanese corporate profits from 1999 to 2011. While US corporate profits, measured in billions of USD on the left axis, rebounded sharply after the 2008 financial crisis, Japanese corporate profits, measured in trillions of JPY on the right axis, have remained stagnant and failed to recover to their pre-crisis peaks. 

The third chart tracks total cash earnings per employee in Japan from 1990 to 2011, using an index where 2011 equals 100. It shows that cash earnings peaked in the late 1990s and have since collapsed back to 1990 levels, showcasing the erosion of Japanese household purchasing power. 

The fourth chart displays Japanese current account and trade balances as a percentage of GDP from 1968 to 2012. Japan’s historically solid trade and current account surpluses, which have persisted since 1980, have sharply deteriorated, with the trade account dipping into negative territory near negative two percent of GDP by 2012. 

Finally, a table details Japanese general government debt as a percentage of GDP from 1990 to 2012. It reveals that actual government debt escalated from 67 percent of GDP in 1990 to 237 percent in 2012. The table features a counterfactual scenario showing that if Japan's nominal GDP had grown at a modest three percent instead of zero percent over this period, its debt-to-GDP ratio in 2012 would have been controlled at a far more manageable 130 percent instead of the actual 237 percent. The author concludes that the pressure for political and economic change is likely coming from the struggling corporate sector rather than aging households.

This page discusses the chaotic and inconsistent nature of European Union policymaking, comparing the investment and political landscape to a high-stakes game of "Eurozone Roulette." Spurred by the thirteen-billion-dollar bailout of Cyprus, the author argues that bondholders, equity investors, bank depositors, and European citizens are exposed to highly unpredictable policy swings. 

The center of the page features a graphic of a roulette wheel, with its pockets representing various erratic policy outcomes. The accompanying text elaborates on each of these outcomes. Under depositor confiscation and subordination, the author details the shocking initial proposal in Cyprus to tax depositors while sparing senior bond-holders, despite uninsured deposits making up forty-five percent of bank deposits in Spain and Germany and up to eighty percent in the United Kingdom and Italy. Conversely, under zero risk weight rules, EU banks are still permitted to apply zero-percent risk weights to sovereign debt regardless of credit ratings, even after Greek bonds suffered massive losses. 

The author also points out double standards within the EU. Regarding fiscal discipline, Southern Europe is currently heavily pressured to meet Maastricht debt and deficit targets, even though France and Germany failed to simultaneously comply with these targets in any single year from 1992 to 2008. In terms of tax rates, Cyprus was forced to raise its corporate tax rate from ten percent, while Ireland was allowed to keep its twelve-point-five percent rate. Furthermore, while Cyprus was politically targeted as a tax haven, a Congressional Research Service report shows that Luxembourg's foreign-sourced profits represent eighteen percent of its GDP—double that of Cyprus and six times higher than Switzerland, Singapore, and Panama.

Other arbitrary policy shifts on the roulette wheel include changing protections for senior bank bondholders, who were protected in Ireland's bailout but left vulnerable in Cyprus. Additionally, the European Central Bank unilaterally asserted preferred creditor status to exempt fifty billion Euros of its own Greek debt holdings from restructuring. The author also notes the EU's attempt to impose arbitrary bonus caps on stand-alone asset management firms and UCITS funds, despite a lack of evidence that they contributed to the sovereign debt crisis. Lastly, the author highlights the political toll of EU pressure, colorfully termed the "defenestration" of Prime Ministers, which forced the resignations of Silvio Berlusconi in Italy, George Papandreou in Greece, and José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero in Spain to make way for EU-approved reforms.

This page analyzes improving US business conditions and rising equity markets, which have rallied despite declining corporate earnings growth. The main argument is that the US private sector has regained its footing after pausing during the late 2012 elections and fiscal cliff debates. This positive economic shift is validating the market’s prior advance rather than driving a new one. The author notes that the recession predicted for 2012 by the Economic Cycle Research Institute never occurred, and the S&P 500 has hit new highs in an anomalous period where equity markets are outperforming what growth conditions alone would imply. 

The commentary is supported by eight charts. A group of six charts highlights key economic indicators showing recovery. The first shows US business spending on equipment and software in billions of real 2005 USD, reflecting a strong post-recession rebound from a low of around $800 billion up toward $1,100 billion. The second chart tracks durable goods orders in billions of USD (non-defense, excluding aircraft) from 2006 to 2013, showing a recovery from under $50 billion in 2009 to nearly $65 billion. The third chart shows US production capacity utilization for total industry rising from its 2009 low of around 67% to nearly 78% by 2013. The fourth chart displays the year-over-year percent change in the number of private establishments, showing a rebound from a contraction of nearly negative 1.0% in 2009 to over 1.5% growth by 2012. The fifth chart illustrates commercial real estate transaction volume recovering from its 2009 trough to around $60 billion in 2012. The sixth chart shows a modest revival in gross CLO and CMBS issuance by 2012, though still far below the 2007 peaks of over $200 billion for CMBS and nearly $100 billion for CLOs.

The bottom of the page features two larger charts illustrating the market disconnect and cash reserves. The first of these plots the forward P/E ratio against expected 2013 earnings growth from January 2012 to January 2013. It depicts a clear divergence where the forward P/E expanded from roughly 11.5x to nearly 13.5x while year-over-year expected earnings growth collapsed from 13.0% to 8.0%. The final chart plots household and corporate cash balances as a percentage of tangible assets from 1952 to 2012, showing that cash holdings rose to nearly 26%, which is close to historical highs. The author concludes by suggesting that improving economic conditions may eventually prompt households and corporations to reduce these cash holdings, especially since the Federal Reserve is projected to keep short-term policy rates low until 2015 or 2016.

This page analyzes the potential economic and investment implications of Japan's aggressive monetary and fiscal policies, often referred to as a "bazooka," and how these actions are challenging the long-standing investment strategy of underweighting Japanese equities. Historically, avoiding Japanese equities was a highly effective strategy during Japan's prolonged period of deflation.
