This historical context is illustrated in the chart titled "The benefit of being underweight Japanese equities," which shows the rolling two-year cumulative outperformance of the MSCI World ex-Japan index versus the MSCI World index from 1988 to 2012. The data shows a persistent outperformance of the ex-Japan portfolio, peaking near 30 percent in the early 1990s and dipping below zero only briefly around 1999 to 2000, which is noted as the last major period of Japanese equity outperformance. The underlying reason for this persistent underweighting is shown in the "Return on Equity" line chart from 1995 to 2013. This chart compares the return on equity of the United States, Europe, Emerging Markets, and Japan, revealing that Japanese corporate margins and ROE have consistently lagged behind, rarely rising above 8 percent, while the United States and Emerging Markets frequently achieved ROEs between 10 percent and 18 percent.

The author notes a dramatic shift starting in late 2012, as the Nikkei index surged in anticipation of easier financial conditions. A table titled "US Dollar and Local currency total returns by region" compares Year-to-Date returns as of March 15, 2013, with cumulative returns from 2007 through 2012. The table highlights that while MSCI Japan and the Nikkei posted stellar Year-to-Date local currency returns of 22.6 percent and 20.9 percent respectively, their returns in US Dollar terms were much lower, at 11.5 percent and 9.0 percent. This is a sharp reversal from the 2007–2012 period, when MSCI Japan fell 44 percent in local terms but only 22 percent in US Dollar terms. This divergence demonstrates how rapid Yen depreciation has eroded returns for unhedged foreign investors, leading the author to suggest that hedging Yen exposure is the most sensible strategy for purchasing Japanese equities.

The close relationship between the equity market's rise and the currency's decline is detailed in the chart "Japanese equities & the Yen since last September." Tracking daily data from September 2012 to March 2013, the chart plots the Nikkei 225 index on the left axis against the USD/JPY exchange rate on the right axis. The two lines move in near-perfect lockstep, with the Nikkei rising from around 9,000 to over 12,500 while the USD/JPY rate rose from approximately 78 to 95, indicating a weakening Yen. The chart highlights several key political turning points that drove these trends, including September 26, when Shinzo Abe became head of the LDP; November 16, the dissolution of the Lower House; December 16, the Lower House election; and January 15, the introduction of a supplementary budget. 

Looking forward, the author suggests that if Japan continues to pressure the Yen downward, its export-reliant economy stands to benefit significantly. Citing a 2007 Federal Reserve paper, the text explains that Japanese export prices have an unusually high sensitivity to exchange rates. While a 10 percent depreciation of EU currencies, the Canadian dollar, or Asian emerging currencies would raise export prices from those regions by 3 percent, a similar 10 percent decline in the Yen would boost the Yen price of Japanese exports by 5 percent. This higher sensitivity means Japanese companies stand to benefit more from currency devaluation than competitors in other regions.

This page from the publication discusses how the United States is running easier monetary and fiscal policies than Europe, playing what the author terms a game of American Roulette by betting that eventual stimulus withdrawals will occur during a period of higher economic growth. On the fiscal side, the author notes that cyclical tax receipt increases and declining unemployment insurance are projected to bring the US fiscal deficit to approximately 5.5 percent by the end of 2013. The Congressional Budget Office projects the deficit will drop further to 3.7 percent in 2014 and 2.5 percent in 2015, assuming the sequester remains in place and interest rates remain low, though mandatory entitlement spending and interest are set to accelerate starting in 2015. On the private sector side, easy monetary policy is helping fuel a recovery. The author expects US GDP growth of approximately 2.5 percent by the end of 2013, supported by improving household debt, rising auto sales, consumer spending, and a healing housing market. 

A series of nine charts provides data on these consumer, employment, housing, and policy trends. The first chart, tracking US household debt service as a percent of disposable income, shows a sharp decline from its peak of 14.0 percent in late 2007 down to 10.5 percent by 2012, returning to levels last seen in 1990. Alongside this, the percent of consumers increasing debt balances, excluding student loans, shows signs of stabilizing and rising slightly to around 31 percent after hitting a bottom of 30 percent in 2010, down from a pre-crisis level of 44 percent. Employment trends show a stark divergence in the chart comparing US versus European quarter-over-quarter annualized employment growth. While both regions collapsed in 2008 and 2009, with the US bottoming near negative 8 percent, the US rebounded to positive territory of around 2 percent by 2013, whereas the Euro area remains mired in negative territory at roughly negative 1 percent. 

Further labor and consumer trends are illustrated in charts for initial jobless claims, auto sales, and real personal consumption. US initial jobless claims, measured as a four-week moving average in thousands, have steadily declined from a peak of over 650,000 in 2009 to approximately 350,000 by early 2013. US auto sales, in millions of seasonally adjusted annualized units, have climbed back from a low of 9 million units in 2009 to nearly 16 million units in 2013. Real personal consumption expenditures, measured as a three-month annualized percent change, shows highly volatile growth that collapsed to negative 5 percent during the crisis but has since rebounded to fluctuate mostly between 1 percent and 4 percent through early 2013. 

The housing market recovery is detailed in two charts focusing on inventory and hard-hit states. A stacked area chart of US housing inventory in millions of units from 2000 to 2011 shows a steady decline in overall inventory, which includes homes for sale, properties sixty or more days delinquent, foreclosures, and real estate owned, after total inventory peaked near 8 million units around 2008. In the major crisis states of Arizona, Nevada, Florida, and California, a chart titled Phoenix Rising shows year-over-year percent changes in building permits and real estate-related employment. Both metrics crashed severely in 2008 with building permits dropping nearly 80 percent, but both have shown a strong rebound into positive territory by late 2011. 

Finally, a chart titled Fifty Trades of Grey shows the scale of Federal Reserve interventions, plotting Fed purchases of Treasuries and Agencies as a percentage of total net supply issued. Measured in ten-year equivalents using a six-month moving average, the chart shows that the Fed’s purchases have frequently absorbed between 40 percent and over 60 percent of net supply from 2009 through early 2013. This massive intervention program highlights that despite gradual improvements, the Fed does not yet see the substantial labor market gains needed to halt its asset purchases.

This page presents an academic exercise called "Countrymatch.com," which explores which countries would be the most suitable partners for an economic and political union with Germany based on shared practices, values, and institutions, rather than geographic proximity. The analysis evaluates countries across twenty-two factors sourced from the World Economic Forum’s 2012–2013 Global Competitiveness Report and the Economist Intelligence Unit’s Democracy Index. These variables encompass civil liberties, political culture, primary and secondary educational enrollment and quality, local market competition intensity, wage flexibility, hiring and firing practices, and technological and scientific innovation capacity.

The main visual is a color-coded world map titled "The German Monetary Union re-imagined: inclusion based on economic, political and judicial similarities," which groups countries by their average ranking differential versus Germany. The closest matches, with an average ranking differential of 15% or less, are colored blue and include Australia, Norway, the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Ireland, Belgium, and Luxembourg. The next closest tier, colored green with a differential of 25% or less, includes France, Finland, Denmark, Japan, Cyprus, Israel, Taiwan, Malta, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, and Iceland. Countries colored orange have a differential of 30% or less, including Canada, Spain, Costa Rica, Estonia, the United States, Mauritius, Portugal, Switzerland, and Uruguay. The rest of the world is largely shaded red, indicating a ranking differential of greater than 30%, with grey indicating areas where no data is available. 

The author uses this analysis to argue that the structural differences between Germany and Southern European nations like Spain, Italy, Greece, and Portugal make them poor economic and political matches. Pointing to comments by Benoit Coeure of the European Central Bank regarding "structural rigidities" that impede monetary policy, the author explains that these fundamental structural disparities in the Eurozone have historically contributed to over-consumption, balance of payments problems, and capital flight, making the central bank's efforts to reignite a recovery far more difficult.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues that the long-term economic growth conditions in France, Italy, and Spain are currently at their weakest levels in over a century outside of wartime. Despite a rally in European sovereign debt spreads, bank lending to businesses and households is declining, and the cost of small business loans in Italy and Spain remains higher than both real and nominal growth. This dynamic explains why European equity markets continue to trail their US counterparts. In contrast, Japanese equity markets are rising on expectations of a seismic shift in monetary and fiscal policy designed to combat worsening deflation, even though domestic economic data remains weak. Emerging market equities have started the year with disappointing returns, despite showing superior performance over longer-term horizons. 

A supporting table outlines equity market returns by region, comparing year-to-date performance in early 2013 against cumulative returns from 2007 to 2012 in both US dollars and local currencies. The S&P 500 posted a year-to-date return of 10.6% in both US dollars and local currency, contrasting sharply with the Eurozone, where the MSCI EMU fell 0.6% in US dollars and the Euro Stoxx fell 2.8% in US dollars. Over the 2007 to 2012 period, the S&P 500 rose 15%, while both the MSCI EMU and Euro Stoxx fell by 17%. Meanwhile, Japan's markets surged year-to-date, with the MSCI Japan rising 11.8% in US dollars and 21.6% in local currency. Emerging Markets lagged year-to-date with a loss of 1.8% in US dollars, though they gained 36% from 2007 to 2012. Cembalest clarifies in a footnote that the Eurostoxx 50 and the MSCI Europe index have only a 26% overlap, with the latter carrying heavy exposure to non-Eurozone countries like the United Kingdom and Switzerland, making the Eurostoxx or MSCI EMU index a superior measure for Eurozone-specific performance.

The primary visual is a historical line chart titled "Current long-term growth rates in France, Italy and Spain: That 19th Century Feeling," which plots the rolling seven-year real GDP growth rate for France, Italy, and Spain from 1826 through 2006, excluding major conflicts like the World Wars and the Spanish Civil War. The chart demonstrates that current growth rates for all three nations have plunged toward 0%, a level of weakness not seen since the 19th and early 20th centuries. Shaded grey areas mark the World Wars' periods of mobilization, destruction, and rebuilding. The chart identifies several historic economic shocks to put the current downturn in perspective: France's growth drops are linked to the Franco-Prussian War tariff reductions and the Great Depression, which was worsened by a delayed exit from the gold standard; Italy’s historical troughs highlight the 10-year Franco-Italian tariff war that cut bilateral trade by 60%; Spain’s historic volatility is tied to the overthrow of Queen Isabella II, the railway boom collapse, a late-19th-century banking crisis following the Argentine sovereign default and the failure of Baring Brothers, and the phylloxera agricultural epidemic.

This page examines the shifting value and curriculum of higher education, sparked by a critical report on Bowdoin College released by the National Association of Scholars. While author Michael Cembalest critiques the report's politically conservative agenda and its dated perspectives, he finds merit in its central question: how does a costly, non-specialized liberal arts education prepare graduates for a highly specialized global economy? Highlighting specific concerns from the report, Cembalest questions Bowdoin's lack of a coherent curriculum, the rise of niche topical courses, grade inflation, and minimal requirements in natural sciences. He raises open questions about how average students fare with self-selected degrees, how prospective employers view non-rigorous transcripts, and how the United States—which ranks 47th in math and science knowledge—can compete globally with a lack of core curricula.

To provide empirical context, the author presents two scatter plots of data from the Georgetown Center of Education displaying median 2010 earnings against unemployment rates by academic major. The first chart analyzes recent college graduates, showing that technical majors like Electrical Engineering yield high median earnings near $55,000 with roughly 7.5% unemployment, while Nursing stands out with low unemployment under 4.5% and a solid $48,000 in earnings. Conversely, Liberal Arts and Philosophy graduates see much lower median earnings around $30,000 with unemployment rates hovering near 9.5% and 11%, respectively, while Film Video & Photography sits at the high-unemployment extreme of 13% with earnings around $30,000.

The second chart illustrates the financial returns for graduate degree holders, where median earnings rise significantly but stark disparities persist. Graduate degree holders in Electrical Engineering and Economics earn more than $100,000 with relatively low unemployment rates around 3.5% to 4.5%. At the lower-paying end of the graduate spectrum, General Education offers high employment security with only 2% unemployment but lower median earnings near $60,000, while Film graduate degree holders face a persistent 13% unemployment rate. Ultimately, the author advises buyers to beware, pointing out that earnings power and job security remain highly dependent on the chosen field of study.

This page discusses the impact of massive, coordinated central bank stimulus on global equity returns and analyzes the current health of the US economic recovery. The author argues that regional equity returns correspond closely to the aggressiveness of local central banks, noting that the Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan have been much more active than the European Central Bank and the People’s Bank of China. Globally, central bank expansion has been massive since 2007, with the four largest central banks engaging in 6.5 trillion dollars of domestic bond purchases and lending, while China’s balance sheet expanded by 3 trillion dollars in foreign assets. To illustrate this colossal expansion, the author compares the aggregate effect to a stellar planetary nebula, accompanied by a telescope image of the Helix Nebula, NGC 7293, from the California Institute of Technology.

A table titled Equity Market Returns by Region illustrates this trend, showing year-to-date and 2007 to 2012 returns in both US dollars and local currencies. The data, current as of April 15, 2013, highlights the outperformance of the US and Japan. The S&P 500 gained 9.5 percent year-to-date, following a 15 percent return from 2007 to 2012. MSCI Japan surged 33.9 percent in local currency and 18.2 percent in US dollars year-to-date, marking a sharp reversal from its 2007 to 2012 losses. In contrast, European indices show weak or negative returns, such as Euro Stoxx at negative 0.7 percent in US dollars year-to-date, while Emerging Markets fell, with the MSCI EM down 4.4 percent in US dollars year-to-date despite its 36 percent gains during the 2007 to 2012 period.

Turning to the US economy, the author observes growth hovering around 2 percent. Although fiscal drag from the sequester and higher tax rates is weighing on retail sales, the author predicts this income loss will not trigger a recession. Labor markets are healing slowly, and the Federal Reserve is projected to hold interest rates near zero until 2015 or 2016. Meanwhile, private sector demand and durable goods spending remain stable, though Basel III capital standards have restricted revolving credit card lending relative to auto and student loans, prompting stronger auto sales over home appliances.

Two historical line charts support this US analysis, tracking year-over-year percentage changes from 2002 to late 2012. The first chart, showing real consumer and business investment as a proxy for cars, homes, and business equipment, illustrates a deep plunge to negative 17 percent during the 2009 recession, followed by a recovery to around 4 percent by late 2012. The second chart, tracking private sector demand via real private final sales of domestic product, shows a similar trajectory, dropping to negative 5 percent in 2009 before stabilizing between 2 percent and 3 percent growth through 2012. Ultimately, the author views the US private sector as on a slow but correct track, raising concerns only about the sheer volume of monetary stimulus required to achieve this stability and the potential risks of its eventual withdrawal.

This page addresses two primary topics: evaluating hedge fund of funds as an alternative to low-yielding corporate bonds, and analyzing the economic conditions and public assets in Italy and France. 

In the first section, the author discusses whether hedge fund of funds portfolios could serve as a bond substitute given the shrinking real yields on high-grade credit. To demonstrate this, a scatter plot chart titled "Randomly generated portfolios of 5 hedge fund of funds" plots annualized returns against the annualized volatility of monthly returns, using HFRI data from January 2000 to February 2013. The chart illustrates a dense cloud of data points representing portfolios of five managers, with different colors indicating observation frequency. The data reveals that 90% of the portfolio outcomes fall within a volatility range of 4% to 7%, with annualized returns mostly clustered between 3% and 7%. A vertical dashed line marks the volatility of BBB corporate bonds at approximately 6%, showing that the epicenter of the hedge fund of funds cloud lies to the left of this line. While a 5% return with 5% volatility is typically unremarkable, the author suggests this risk-return profile might merit consideration under current market conditions, though he cautions that they are not suitable for hedging long-duration defined benefit liabilities.

In the second section, the commentary turns to Europe's weak economic data despite stable equity and debt markets. Focusing first on Italy, which plans to issue debt to repay 100 billion Euros in private-sector arrears, the author references a public asset report from the Ministry of Economy and Finance. A supporting table titled "Italy: central government, local government, social security plus public" outlines estimated values in millions of Euros. It lists total public sector assets of 1,771,427 million Euros—which includes 970,473 million in tangible fixed assets (comprising 465,407 million in infrastructure and 169,420 million in natural resources) and 254,752 million in liquid funds—against total liabilities of 1,381,394 million Euros. Although these figures suggest Italy owns tangible assets worth up to 70% of its debt, the author points out that with debt already exceeding 100% of GDP, these assets are far harder to monetize in practice than on paper. Finally, the author highlights an economic malaise in France, where private equity activity collapsed from $36 billion in 2006 to just $430 million in the first quarter of 2013, accompanied by an expanding current account deficit and rising unemployment. This leads to open questions about whether President Hollande will be forced to make significant policy changes to restore growth.

This page discusses the clear winners and losers resulting from the Federal Reserve's strategy of maintaining zero percent interest rates and driving real rates below zero. The author argues that this environment has created a sharp divide: "haves" include luxury retailers and consumer staples, while "have-nots" include traditional retailers, life insurers facing asset-liability challenges from guaranteed annuities, and savers reliant on fixed-income portfolios. 

Three top charts illustrate these dynamics from 2003 through mid-2013. The first chart, an equal-weighted index starting in January 2003, shows luxury retailers like Tiffany, Coach, and LVMH surging to nearly 600 by 2013, while traditional retailers such as Macy's, Kohl's, and J.C. Penney stagnate below 200. The second chart tracks price-to-book valuations from 2006 to 2013, highlighting a stark divergence where consumer staples rose to a price-to-book ratio of over 4.3 while life insurers languished around 0.8. The third chart shows annualized returns net of inflation across four historical periods, illustrating that from 2008 to 2012, a capital preservation portfolio consisting of fifteen percent equity, forty-five percent five-year US Treasuries, and forty percent cash yielded negative real returns of nearly negative two percent, while a balanced portfolio containing seventy percent equity returned almost ten percent. This represents the widest performance gap between the two styles across all compared periods.

The second half of the page addresses the sustainability of the equity market rally by looking at global economic imbalances. A bottom chart from Bridgewater Associates aggregates global current account deficits, fiscal deficits, and private sector debt accumulation from 1979 to 2013. This metric peaks dramatically during major historical disruptions, including the Latin American debt crisis and Mexican defaults in the early 1980s, Black Monday in 1987, the Asian financial crisis and Thai devaluation in 1997, and finally the global financial crisis around 2008. By 2013, this measure of imbalance had fallen substantially, indicating that the raw materials for an immediate systemic shock had diminished. 

However, the author cautions that this improvement is partially flattered by an unappealing economic collapse in Southern Europe, where trade deficits fell primarily because high unemployment crushed domestic consumption and imports. Despite a spike in peripheral non-performing bank loans to approximately 500 billion Euros, the author expects Europe's woes to remain a slow-burning issue rather than an imminent market disruptor in 2013, pointing to Spain's ability to easily issue seven billion Euros of debt at tight spreads. In a concluding footnote, the author notes that only a full European fiscal transfer union with centralized federal taxation could change his bleak outlook for the European periphery, an option that a German public sector official dismissed as "never going to happen."

This page of the publication examines the outlook for future market returns and the U.S. fiscal situation, cautioning that future savers may face tougher conditions than those experienced in previous decades. The author argues that real median income growth over the next 35 years is unlikely to accelerate and that future investment returns will probably be lower than historical averages.

To illustrate historical income trends, Exhibit 8 tracks the annual growth of median household wage and salary income from 1977 to 2012 using a three-year moving average. The chart displays two series: one unadjusted for inflation and one adjusted for inflation. Unadjusted growth peaked near 8% in the late 1970s and steadily declined to around 2% by 2012. Meanwhile, inflation-adjusted growth frequently fluctuated near or below 0%, peaking only briefly around 3% in the late 1980s and late 1990s. This sluggish performance supports the author’s bottom line that real median income growth is unlikely to differ much from its historical pace.

Exhibit 9 displays the long-term 35-year annualized returns on the S&P 500 from 1905 to 2005, illustrating nominal returns and real returns. While nominal returns peaked near 14% around 1970 and 2000, real returns have historically fluctuated within a post-war channel of 5% to 9%, averaging approximately 7% above inflation for the 35-year period ending in 2012. The author suggests a conservative downside projection for future real equity returns of 5%, which sits at the lower end of this historical range. 

This projected decline in returns is attributed to the end of the long-term interest rate decline that began in 1982, alongside the end of the great disinflation period that previously boosted government and corporate bonds. If future returns remain lower, savers will need to increase their savings rates or adopt a higher risk tolerance to meet their financial goals. Lastly, the page addresses the U.S. fiscal situation, explaining that growing entitlement spending is steadily crowding out other government investments such as infrastructure, energy R&D, and worker retraining. The author notes that by 2017, the first phase of the Budget Control Act will push non-defense discretionary spending well below the lowest levels seen in the last 40 years, leaving little room for further discretionary cuts.

This page of the publication outlines key global risks, focusing heavily on the geopolitical implications of Iran's nuclear capabilities and their potential impact on financial markets. The author notes that while US inflation and a structural slowdown in China below seven percent are risks, the most complex and immediate threat comes from Iran. 

To illustrate the difficulty of a military strike on Iran's nuclear infrastructure, the author includes a chart detailing the estimated penetration depth of massive ordnance penetration weapons. This chart plots the cumulative meters penetrated on the vertical axis against the number of missiles fired in the same location, from one to seven, on the horizontal axis. It compares a base case with a scenario involving denser soil and gravel collapse, relative to a horizontal reference line representing the estimated ninety-meter depth of the Fordow mission space. In the base case, four successive missiles are required to exceed the ninety-meter threshold, whereas in the denser soil scenario, even seven missiles barely reach ninety meters. The text emphasizes that firing multiple massive weapons in precise succession is exceptionally difficult, and recent weapon design improvements have improved guidance and fuses rather than physical penetration capability.

The discussion then frames the Iranian nuclear situation within the broader history of global warfare and the theory of nuclear deterrence. Two historical charts accompany this section. The first, illustrating war deaths as a percentage of the world population from 2500 BC to 2000 AD, shows that conflict in the first half of the twentieth century drove war deaths to a historic peak of nearly four and a half percent of the global population, far exceeding any prior century. The second chart, detailing annual battle deaths from 1946 to 2008, shows a dramatic, though volatile, downward trend from a peak of over five hundred thousand deaths in the early 1950s to below one hundred thousand by the mid-2000s. The author poses the open question of whether nuclear deterrence played a role in this post-war decline, though he cautions that this stabilizing logic may not apply to a nuclear-armed Iran, making it a premier geopolitical risk.

The page concludes with a market summary, noting that global equity markets have enjoyed an uninterrupted year-to-date rally of eleven percent, or thirteen percent when excluding emerging markets. This performance has outpaced underlying GDP and profit growth, fueled by a cautious international stance on Iran and a widespread investor aversion to traditionally safe assets. The author poses an open question about what 2014 will hold for these risk-on market dynamics.

This page presents a collection of twelve financial and economic charts, labeled "Recipe Exhibits," that provide a comprehensive visual overview of macroeconomic trends, monetary policy impacts, and corporate health supporting J.P. Morgan's assessment of equity markets at all-time highs. 

The first chart shows the year-over-year percentage change in US private sector demand for all goods and services, measured by real private final sales of domestic product from 2002 to 2012. It highlights a massive contraction of below negative four percent in 2009, followed by a recovery to positive growth of around two percent by 2012. Beside it, a chart of the US output gap from 1965 to 2010 displays actual output relative to potential output, showing that the post-2008 output gap fell to near-historic lows of around negative six percent, comparable only to the early 1980s recession. The third chart details the US budget balance as a percentage of GDP under the Congressional Budget Office's baseline case from 2006 with projections through 2021. It reveals that the deficit peaked near ten percent of GDP in 2009 and is projected to steadily narrow, though interest payments are expected to start consuming a larger share of the budget after 2015.

A middle row of charts focuses on interest rates and central bank actions. One chart highlights that real yields reached their lowest levels in thirty years by 2012, tracking real yields for emerging market sovereigns, BBB corporates, and ten-year US Treasuries; the real yield on ten-year Treasuries plunged below zero percent in 2011 and 2012. This drop coincides with the Federal Reserve's massive accumulation of high-duration US Treasuries with over ten years of maturity, which rose from an average of ten to fifteen percent of marketable Treasuries to nearly forty-five percent by 2011. A third chart in this row visualizes the massive global monetary expansion, showing that the combined balance sheets of the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Bank of England, Bank of Japan, and the People's Bank of China expanded by nearly nine trillion US dollars between 2007 and 2013.

The next row tracks corporate and household liquidity. US household and corporate cash balances as a percentage of tangible assets are shown from 1952 to 2012, revealing a steady increase from a low of eighteen percent in the late 1990s to over twenty-four percent by 2012. This high liquidity is mirrored by rising investor leverage, as shown in the NYSE margin debt chart, which rose from a post-crisis low of under two hundred billion dollars in 2009 to nearly four hundred billion dollars in early 2013, close to its 2007 peak. Corporate confidence is further illustrated by a chart showing announced share buybacks as a percentage of potential GDP from 1995 to 2013; buybacks rebounded from under one percent in 2009 to over two percent in 2013, highlighted by a massive Apple buyback. 

The bottom row showcases domestic recovery and labor trends. A chart depicting housing improvements tracks the value of US home inventories listed for sale as a percentage of GDP alongside foreclosures started in thousands from 1999 to 2013. Home inventories peaked at over seven percent of GDP in 2007 but fell to under three point five percent by 2013, while foreclosures started sharply declined from a peak of over three hundred thousand in 2009 to near one hundred thousand by 2013. Finally, two charts track non-financial labor compensation from 1947 to 2012. Whether measured as a percentage of sales or as a percentage of nominal GDP, labor compensation has experienced a multi-decade decline, hitting historic lows of approximately sixty-one percent of sales and thirty percent of nominal GDP by 2012, pointing to a long-term structural shift of income from labor to corporate profits.

This page analyzes how the ongoing federal budget and fiscal debates could affect retirement security, particularly for median-income retirees in the United States. The author argues that while some proposed policy changes could negatively impact retirees, most reforms currently being debated are targeted at higher-income families and would spare the average household. Specifically, the analysis notes that proposals such as the Bowles-Simpson limits on pre-tax 401(k) contributions, means-testing for Social Security benefits, tighter limits on itemized deductions, and higher Medicare co-pays would have zero impact on median-income families. In contrast, altering Social Security's cost-of-living adjustments to lag behind inflation for the elderly, or returning to pre-2001 tax rates across all brackets, would have a moderate impact.

Three visual exhibits support these points. At the top of the page, Exhibit 10 charts historical and projected federal government spending by category as a percentage of GDP from 1972 to 2023, comparing total spending against government receipts. The chart shows that while defense and discretionary spending have generally shrunk or stabilized as a percentage of GDP, mandatory programs—specifically Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid—have grown significantly and are projected to dominate future outlays alongside rising interest payments on national debt, while revenues consistently lag behind.

At the bottom left, Exhibit 11 demonstrates the high progressivity of retiree tax rates by plotting effective tax rates against gross income up to one million dollars. The resulting curve shows that median-income retirees face an effective tax rate near the single digits, while tax rates rise steeply for wealthier retirees, flattening out near thirty percent for those making one million dollars. Finally, at the bottom right, Exhibit 12 projects the future value of financial assets for a median-income household through 2032. It compares a status-quo baseline, under which assets grow to over $400,000, to a future baseline that incorporates the proposed policy changes under discussion. Under the latter scenario, accumulated retirement assets are projected to plateau at approximately $300,000, demonstrating a noticeable but overall modest long-term impact on average retirees.

This page, titled "The Affluent Family: On the Importance of Being Earnest," highlights how disciplined saving and strategic financial planning can secure a stable retirement. The author uses a hypothetical affluent couple, "the Browns," who retire in 2013 at age 65, to demonstrate how factors within a family's control, such as consumption versus savings and portfolio risk, can offset elements they cannot control. 

The Browns are characterized as having one working spouse who consistently earned six times the median income from 1972 through 2012, reaching $340,000 in 2012. They maintained a lifetime savings rate of 22%, consisting of a 6% pre-tax 401(k) contribution matched by 3% from their employer, alongside an additional 4.5% in after-tax savings. They also owned their home free of any mortgage by retirement and managed a balanced investment portfolio that transitioned from 65% equities at age 25 to 45% equities by age 65. Upon retirement, their target cash flow is set at 80% of their pre-retirement, after-tax living expenses, equating to $190,000 in 2013, which is then adjusted annually for inflation.

Exhibit 1, a line chart tracking the value of financial assets from 1972 to 2037, shows that the Browns accumulate over $3 million by their retirement in 2012. Following retirement, the baseline asset trajectory steadily declines as funds are withdrawn to support their lifestyle. 

Exhibit 2, a stacked bar chart mapping retirement cash flows against their rising income target from 2013 to 2037, illustrates how the Browns fund their retirement. To maximize tax efficiency, they deplete their after-tax savings first, which allows their 401(k) to continue compounding pre-tax and keeps their effective Federal tax rate low, at 0% to 3%, for the first four years. Once those after-tax savings are exhausted, they meet their escalating income target—which rises past $300,000 by 2037—using a combination of Social Security benefits, mandatory 401(k) distributions, and discretionary 401(k) withdrawals. This transition increases their effective Federal tax rate to 18%. The analysis concludes that consistent, earnest saving and investing can successfully carry a family to age 90, serving as a warning that those who do not save as aggressively will face much steeper challenges in retirement.

This page addresses the critical impact of retirement timing on the financial security of median-income families, represented by a hypothetical family named the Smiths. The author argues that while modest policy changes like Social Security cost-of-living adjustment lags have minor consequences, the true risk to median-income families lies in the decision of when to retire. If economic circumstances, health issues, or job losses force an individual to retire early at age 62 rather than the standard age of 65, the financial consequences are severe due to three fewer years of saving, a longer retirement horizon, and a substantial 22 percent discount on accelerated Social Security benefits.

To illustrate this vulnerability, the first chart, Exhibit 13, compares the standard retirement scenario of retiring at age 65 in 2012 against an early retirement scenario at age 62 in 2009. The vertical axis measures the value of financial assets from zero to 450,000 dollars, while the horizontal axis spans from 1972 to 2032. Under the standard retirement path, the Smiths' financial assets steadily grow post-retirement, climbing toward 400,000 dollars by 2032. In contrast, the early retirement path shows financial assets peaking near 250,000 dollars before steadily depleting to zero by around 2029, interrupted only by a brief spike in the late 2020s.

The second chart, Exhibit 14, explains this asset depletion by displaying how the early retirement household meets its annual cash flow needs. Spanning from 2010 to 2032, the chart tracks an orange line representing an escalating income target that starts at roughly 55,000 dollars in 2010 and reaches about 75,000 dollars by 2032. Stacked bars detail the shifting mix of funding sources used to meet this target. While baseline Social Security benefits provide a steady foundation, the household is forced to rapidly exhaust its after-tax savings by around 2015. To compensate, they rely heavily on discretionary and mandatory 401(k) distributions. When these assets are ultimately depleted, the household must resort to a home sale in 2029—represented by a distinct brown block—to temporarily inject cash back into their portfolio before assets decline once again. The analysis relies on data compiled from the Tax Policy Center, Bureau of Economic Analysis, National Association of Realtors, Bureau of Labor Statistics, Census Bureau, Bloomberg, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page analyzes central bank monetary policy, equity market volatility, and anomalies in Spanish macroeconomic data. The author argues that cheap money solutions have inherent trade-offs and that investors should prepare for increased volatility as discussions of Federal Reserve tightening emerge. The author forecasts that 2013 is a year of economic improvement but not strong enough to trigger global policy tightening, pushing the likely "day of reckoning" to 2014 or 2015. 

Two visuals support the discussion of global markets at the top of the page. First, a table titled "The volatility of equity markets by period and by Fed era" presents historical Dow Jones volatility across various eras and Fed chairs. It highlights that the Greenspan and Bernanke cheap money era (1987–2013) averaged 18.8% volatility, compared to just 11.8% under tight money chairs like Paul Volcker and William McChesney Martin. The second visual is a chart titled "World Equities vs Major Economy Economic Surprises," showing the MSCI World Index level against the Economic Surprise Index for Major Economies from 2010 to 2012.

The lower half of the page details a "Spanish Madriddle," calling into question the reliability of Spain's official economic reporting. The author points out that while Spanish unemployment soared from 10% to 25% between 2008 and mid-2012, Spanish banks reported suspiciously stable residential mortgage non-performing loans of just 3%. 

To further illustrate this data discrepancy, the page compares corporate earnings data from Spain and the United States using two side-by-side charts tracking 2001 to 2013. The chart "Spain: economy-wide profits vs. public company profits" shows a severe divergence: while MSCI Spain Earnings collapsed from a peak of over 70 EUR per share in 2007 down to under 30 EUR by 2012, the country's non-financial corporations gross operating surplus steadily climbed from under 30 billion EUR to over 60 billion EUR. Because this gross operating surplus is a key input for calculating GDP, this divergence casts doubt on Spain's reported GDP strength. In contrast, the chart "US: economy-wide profits vs. public company profits" shows that S&P 500 Earnings and US non-financial corporations gross operating surplus closely correlate and trend together over the same period. The author concludes by questioning whether Spain can survive the painful process of declining wages and asset prices to eventually attract foreign capital again.

On this page, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management examines the risks that lower market returns and policy changes pose to retirement security. While historical returns on US equities from 1977 to 2012 were highly favorable—averaging roughly 7% above inflation on the S&P 500—this outperformance was supported by a structural decline in interest rates beginning in 1982, a trend that has now run its course. Real returns on 5-year Treasuries also averaged a generous 3.5% during this period. Cembalest argues that future retirees must plan for a less accommodating environment where real equity returns fall to 5% and real fixed-income returns decline to 2.0%. 

This argument is supported by a line chart tracking the 35-year annualized returns on the S&P 500 from 1905 to 2005. It contrasts a volatile nominal return series against a more stable real return series, illustrating that the post-war channel of real equity returns has historically remained tightly bounded between 5% and 7%. 

A second chart simulates the projected value of financial assets for a hypothetical, diligent saving family called "the Browns" from 1972 out to 2032. The "Original Baseline" projection shows assets peaking near $7 million around 2012 and gradually declining but remaining above $4 million by 2032. However, when factoring in adverse "Policy changes," the asset curve drops significantly. When further combined with "Lower market returns," the family's assets deplete entirely, crashing to zero by approximately 2022. Cembalest notes that under these combined pressures, even disciplined savers will run out of assets before the end of their retirement, necessitating major spending reductions to remain solvent. 

Connecting these issues to broader American habits, the author points out that US public policy—such as low sales, VAT, excise, and import duties relative to other countries, alongside housing tax treatments that encourage suburban sprawl—actively promotes a high-consumption lifestyle. He references the classic fable of "The Ant and the Grasshopper," accompanied by a 1919 Milo Winter illustration, to caution against prioritizing immediate consumption over long-term planning. To help clients navigate these challenges, he announces the upcoming release of demographic-specific retirement studies.

This appendix page presents six distinct charts illustrating key financial baselines, including median household incomes, home prices, inflation metrics, savings rates, real yields, and retirement equity allocations over time. The page begins by explaining that the working spouse in J.P. Morgan's model is assumed to earn six times the age-adjusted median income. It also notes that while various consumer price indexes behave similarly, minor divergences in inflation measures compound significantly over time, and that the national savings rate mask massive disparities across income percentiles.

The first chart, titled Median Household Income and Age Adjustments, tracks three income series in current dollars from 1977 to 2009. Median household income starts near $13,000 in 1977 and climbs to approximately $50,000 in 2009. When looking strictly at the prime working-age cohort of 25 to 64, the average median household income rises higher, reaching nearly $60,000. The age-adjusted median household income used in the model peaks during the middle-aged years and falls below the overall median for younger and older workers. 

The second chart, Median One-Family Home Price, spans 1977 to 2012, plotting both the median single-family home price in US dollars and its rolling three-year annualized percent change. The median home price rose from about $50,000 in 1977 to a peak of roughly $225,000 around 2007, before sliding during the housing bust. The rolling three-year annualized change peaked above 12% in the late 1970s and again in the mid-2000s, before plummeting to nearly negative 8% by 2010, eventually recovering to around 0% in 2012.

The third chart, Measures of Inflation, shows the year-over-year percentage change for four consumer price indexes from 2000 to 2012. While all four track closely, their average annualized rates differ over this period: Chained CPI averaged 2.18%, CPI-U averaged 2.42%, CPI-W averaged 2.45%, and the elderly-focused CPI-E averaged 2.53%. 

The fourth chart, Savings Rates by Income Percentile, uses a bar graph to display the active savings of current income as a percentage of income. The lowest 20% of earners save less than 1% of their income, while the 20-40% cohort saves roughly 3%. Middle-income groups between the 40th and 80th percentiles save around 6%. Savings rates jump to approximately 13% for the highest 20% of earners, and reach an estimated 20% for the top 5%.

The fifth chart, The War on Savers Returns, plots the three-year annualized percent change in inflation-adjusted Treasury Bill returns from 1957 to 2012. This real rate of return peaked near 5% in the mid-1980s but went sharply negative during periods of high inflation or low nominal rates, dropping below negative 2% by 2012.

The final chart, Allocation to Equities Within 401(k) Over Time, shows how equity exposure is modeled to decline over a forty-year investment horizon from 1972 to 2012. A baseline investor's equity allocation starts at 65% and gradually steps down to 41% by the end of the period. A more conservative investor starts at 52% equity exposure and finishes with 22% in equities. 

Data throughout the page is sourced from J.P. Morgan Asset Management, the U.S. Census Bureau, the National Association of Realtors, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the U.S. Treasury, and academic research by Dynan, Skinner, and Zeldes.

In this analysis, the author examines the economic divide between the "haves"—owners of corporate profits and real estate—and the "have-nots," consisting of bondholders and labor, arguing that recent equity market corrections stem from a widening disconnect between these groups. To illustrate the unique nature of the current US profit cycle, the page presents four charts tracking economic indicators over sixteen quarters since the profit trough, measured in billions of 2005 USD. Chart A shows that the current revenue recovery, highlighted in red, is the weakest of six post-war recoveries, barely rising above the baseline. In contrast, Chart B shows that the corporate profits recovery is by far the strongest, climbing rapidly toward 700 billion USD. The author explains this disparity using Chart C, which depicts an anemic, negative trajectory for labor compensation that hovers around negative 100 billion USD, and Chart D, which shows a dramatic plunge in interest expenses to below negative 150 billion USD due to Federal Reserve intervention.

The commentary points out that while profit margins remain high, sequential profit growth is slowing, interest rates are rising, and US GDP growth is projected to reach only 2.5% rather than the historical recovery average of 4.2%. Much of the recent consumer strength is attributed to declining savings rates rather than rising earned income. Nonetheless, J.P. Morgan expects US equities to outperform general economic conditions and other global regions. 

Addressing concerns over rising interest rates triggered by Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke's comments, the author notes that equity markets historically perform well during periods of rising yields. This is illustrated in a bar chart showing S&P 500 total returns during periods of rising long-term interest rates from 1949 to 2011; almost all periods yielded positive returns, with the sole exception of a minor negative return of roughly 3% between December 1980 and April 1981. However, the author cautions that the current situation is unprecedented due to the unwinding of the Fed's massive bond market intervention. This intervention is detailed in the final bar chart, which measures Fed purchases of Treasury and Agency securities as a percentage of total net supply issued from January 2009 to January 2013, showing that the Fed frequently purchased between 50% and 60% of the net supply. The author concludes by questioning whether Bernanke can achieve a graceful exit from these orthodox bond market relationships to secure his legacy.

This page explores the stark contrast between winners and losers within the S&P 500 technology sector, arguing that high revenue dispersion makes sector-level valuations far less informative than looking at individual companies. 

The first chart, titled "S&P 500 Technology sector: companies with best and worst revenue growth," indexes rolling annual revenue growth from December 2009 to December 2012, setting the initial index level at 100. High-growth "haves" plotted in blue are led by Apple, which reaches an index level near 250, followed closely by Cognizant, KLA-Tencor, Salesforce.com, Akamai, Amphenol, Ciena, Google, Qualcomm, and SunEdison. In contrast, the underperforming "have-nots" in red fall below the baseline to between 70 and 90, featuring companies such as Advanced Micro Devices, Autodesk, Computer Sciences Corporation, Convergys, Dell, Electronic Arts, Lexmark, QLogic, Yahoo!, and Tellabs. Bellwethers HP, IBM, and Microsoft are colored green and track near the broader tech sector index, which climbs to about 130. 

A second chart, "S&P 500 intrasector revenue growth dispersion," measures the difference between the fastest- and slowest-growing companies from 2009 to 2013 across various sectors. The technology sector exhibits the widest revenue growth dispersion, spanning from roughly 125% at the top end to -25% at the bottom. This vast spread is similar only to the Energy sector, whereas defensive sectors like Consumer Staples show a highly concentrated, narrow dispersion band. Given this divergence, the author suggests that investment strategies like long-short technology funds or concentrated tech funds are particularly worth considering.

To address how to value individual stocks under such dispersion, a third visual titled "On an intrasector basis, tech valuations seem to reflect company-specific fundamentals" presents a scatter plot of estimated versus current trailing P/E ratios. Using nine independent variables—revenue growth since 2009, dividend yield, market cap, operating margin, estimated long-term growth rate, return on assets, return on equity, earnings growth, and gross margin—the model achieves a strong fit with an R-squared of 62.5%. This indicates that tech P/E multiples are not necessarily mispriced relative to one another, as lower multiples generally align with larger companies that have lower gross margins and slower earnings growth. 

In closing, the author points out that today's megacap tech giants are twice as large relative to the overall economy as they were in the 1990s. This raises an open question of whether these massive companies can continue to grow at the same pace, either organically or through acquisitions. Ultimately, the author suggests that while tech stocks are not universally cheap, they may offer better long-term value than the popular, highly bid-up defensive dividend-paying sectors.

In this introductory commentary, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management frames his annual review of private equity around a major structural shift: the massive migration of institutional capital away from public equities and into alternative investments over the prior decade. To establish this context, the page features two charts illustrating exit activity and asset allocation trends. 

The first chart displays the "Global number of private equity-backed exits by type and aggregate exit value" quarterly from the first quarter of 2006 to the second quarter of 2013. This stacked bar and line chart shows that overall exit volume—comprising trade sales, sales to other private equity firms, initial public offerings, and other transactions—rebounded strongly after the 2008–2009 recession. During the depths of the financial crisis in early 2009, quarterly exits fell below 100 and aggregate values plummeted below twenty billion dollars. By 2011 and 2012, quarterly exits recovered to the 250 to 350 range, and aggregate exit values regularly surpassed eighty billion dollars, peaking near one hundred and twenty billion dollars. 

The second chart, "US institutional investors: asset allocation to equities, fixed income, and alternatives, 2001 vs. 2011," illustrates why private equity has become so vital to institutional portfolios. It compares the asset mix of corporate pension plans, state and local plans, and endowments and foundations. Across all three categories, equity allocations shrank significantly; for instance, endowment and foundation equity allocations fell from roughly fifty percent in 2001 to thirty percent in 2011. Over the same period, alternative allocations surged. Endowments and foundations saw their alternative investments double to over forty percent of their portfolio, while corporate plans and state and local plans saw their alternative allocations roughly triple to approximately fifteen percent.

Given the increasing reliance of underfunded state pension plans on these non-public assets, Cembalest argues that investors must look past anecdotes and review empirical, academic literature. He introduces a series of twelve open questions that the remainder of the report will address. These topics include how private equity performs relative to public markets, the influence of fund size and manager consistency, potential database reporting errors, whether managers artificially adjust net asset values during fundraising, the impact of high fees, operating improvements in leveraged buyouts, adjusting for stale pricing in portfolio models, the industry-wide impact of private equity on public competitors, secondary buyouts, bondholder impacts, and the potential performance drag of localized in-state investment mandates.

This page evaluates whether the struggling economies of the European Periphery—specifically Spain, Italy, Portugal, and Greece—are poised for a genuine economic recovery. While their current account deficits have successfully closed to near-zero or positive levels, the author argues that this milestone is deceptive. Instead of being driven by healthy, export-led growth as seen in previous global crises, this improvement is primarily the result of a severe collapse in imports, reflecting deep economic pain, falling demand, and high unemployment.

To support this analysis, the page features five charts. The first line chart illustrates current account balances as a percentage of GDP from 2007 to 2013. It tracks how Spain, Greece, and Portugal climbed out of massive deficits of 10% to 16% of GDP in 2008 and 2009 to reach balanced positions by 2013. The next three charts look for signs of domestic recovery but find only minimal, depressed improvements. A chart of manufacturing and services composite PMIs from 2006 to 2013 compares the Core (France and Germany) with the Periphery, showing the Periphery ticking up but remaining below the expansion threshold of 50. A historical chart of car sales from 1990 to 2013 shows new car registrations in the Periphery collapsing from peak levels of over 600,000 units in the mid-2000s to around 470,000 units, with a minuscule upward bend at the very end. Similarly, a consumer confidence chart from 2000 to 2013 shows periphery confidence languishing at an extremely low negative 40% balance, far below the Core.

The core of the argument is visualized in a final bar chart showing the percentage of current account improvement driven by collapsing imports. In Greece, import collapse accounts for approximately 80% of the adjustment, followed by roughly 50% in Portugal, 35% in Italy, and 30% in Spain. This stands in stark contrast to past balance of payment resolutions, such as Italy in 1974, Mexico in 1994, and Thailand in 1995, where the contribution of import collapse was 0% because export growth successfully outpaced rising imports.

The author emphasizes these points with a custom-written sonnet titled "A Matter of Import in Portugal, Spain, Italy and Greece." The poem warns that celebrating these balanced accounts as a resolved crisis is a delusion, explaining that this adjustment is merely a forced tightening of the belt rather than a sign of economic health. Ultimately, the author poses an open question regarding Europe's ability to endure such intense, ongoing economic stress.

This page continues an annual review of private equity, focusing on manager performance consistency, data quality in academic research, valuation practices during fundraising, and the impact of fees and ownership structures. 

The author first addresses performance consistency, noting that while buyout and venture capital manager performance was consistent prior to 2000, buyout performance since then is no longer reliably linked to the performance of a manager's prior funds. The text then challenges widely cited research by scholar Ludovic Phalippou, which used the Venture Economics database to argue that private equity underperforms public equity. The author details severe anomalies in this database, noting that over 40% of its funds stopped being updated during their active lifetimes and incomplete funds were missing over 60% of their cash distributions. Correcting these errors and excluding incomplete records reverses the findings, turning a previously estimated 3% to 6% underperformance against the S&P 500 into a 4% per annum outperformance. 

The middle section of the page examines whether private equity managers manipulate net asset values (NAVs) to attract investors during fundraising. Research indicates this behavior is mostly limited to unsuccessful firms that fail to raise a subsequent fund. This dynamic is illustrated by three charts tracking the index trajectory of buyout fund NAVs (scaled from 1.0 to 1.8) across a timeline from 12 periods before to 12 periods after subsequent fund inception. In the first two charts—representing situations where the next fund was raised "early" or "late"—the NAV trajectory continues steadily upward with no material trend changes following the subsequent fund's inception at point zero. In contrast, the third chart, representing unsuccessful fundraising, shows a pronounced flattening of the NAV curve around the mark of "4 years before existing fund resolution." Across all three charts, solid lines represent typical periods, while dotted lines represent funds raised during declining or bear markets. 

The final section explores whether higher management fees or lower general partner (GP) ownership levels ("skin in the game") lead to underperformance for limited partners (LPs). Referencing a June 2013 study of 837 funds from 1984 to 2010, regression analysis showed no identifiable relationship between higher fees or lower GP ownership and worse net LP performance. The authors of that study concluded that higher-fee managers tend to generate higher gross returns, which ultimately results in similar net returns for LPs.

This page, titled "Faith, hope and charity: active equity managers and excess returns, your relatives and your money," explores the motivations behind investor adherence to actively managed equity funds. Michael Cembalest poses the question of whether active management is chosen based on faith, hope, or experience. To address this, he distinguishes between actual investor experience, which is heavily affected by transaction timing, and the specific skill of picking active managers who can beat their benchmarks. 

The page features two charts and a table to illustrate these points. The first line chart, titled "Long-term return on the S&P 500, highlighting the post-war channel of real returns, 35-year annualized return," plots nominal and real returns from 1905 through 2013 using Robert J. Shiller data. It highlights that the 35-year annualized real returns on US equities have remained remarkably stable within a 5% to 7% channel over the last 60 years. 

The second visual is a stacked bar chart titled "Active vs. passive management in US equities," which presents the percent of total mutual fund and ETF assets from 1996 to 2012. It shows that while passive options like index funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) have steadily grown over the fifteen-year period, actively managed products still represent the vast majority of investor holdings. 

The table at the bottom of the page, titled "The behavior gap: timing decisions by investors have in aggregate been negative," displays Morningstar asset-weighted performance data over the 10 years ending December 31, 2010. The table compares Investor Return to Total Return to reveal the "Gap" caused by poor buy and sell timing. Across every single fund group, investor returns are lower than total fund returns. For example, US Diversified Funds achieved a total return of 3.30% but yielded an investor return of only 2.32% (a gap of -0.98%). More severe performance drags are found in US Sector Funds (a gap of -2.19%), International Regional Funds (-2.40%), and Alternative assets (-3.13%). Across All Funds, the investor return of 3.38% trailed the total return of 4.71% by -1.33%. Cembalest concludes that because these investor timing decisions create such a significant behavior gap, actual investor returns are an inaccurate measure of active manager skill. He asserts that the focus should instead be on the likelihood of a manager outperforming their stated benchmark.

This page explores how active equity managers' outperformance statistics change under different analytical assumptions, arguing that standard metrics often understate active management's value. The author posits that adjusting benchmarks to reflect actual investible options and filtering out extremely small funds reveals that active managers perform much better than typically reported, which explains why both institutional and individual investors retain significant active exposure. 

The central table on the page, titled "Percentage of active equity vehicles that outperform benchmarks under different assumptions," presents seven years of trailing Lipper data through June 2013 across fifteen investment styles. It shows that comparing funds against actual investible ETFs rather than stated benchmarks, and excluding the smallest two to five percent of funds by asset size, consistently raises outperformance rates. For instance, Large Cap Core fund outperformance rises from 27% against stated benchmarks to 38% against investible ETFs when excluding the smallest five percent of funds, and hits 39% when looking exclusively at institutional share classes. Similarly, Large Cap Growth outperformance climbs from a meager 15% to 28% after the five percent size filter is applied, and reaches 30% for institutional classes. Small Cap Value funds demonstrate the highest overall success, with outperformance starting at 75% and rising to 87% for institutional share classes. The author suggests that if these size and benchmark adjustments remain consistent over time, the center of gravity for Large Cap Core funds would shift above the 50% outperformance mark. Looking ahead, the author notes that as stock-to-stock correlations continue to decline, industry alpha measures should improve from their low levels at the end of 2012. 

The bottom portion of the page provides a follow-up on private equity performance, focusing on historical database limitations. The author discusses how researchers such as Phalippou of Oxford, Kaplan of Chicago, Schoar of MIT, and Rhodes-Kropf of Harvard originally relied on the Venture Economics database, which led to papers showing that private equity underperformed the S&P 500. However, newer academic research using superior, more recent datasets has reached the opposite conclusion, showing that private equity has actually outperformed the S&P 500. The author emphasizes that their previous critiques of these older papers were intended to highlight the flaws of the Venture Economics database itself, rather than to question the academic integrity of the individual researchers.

This page serves as an appendix discussing municipal bankruptcy, the U.S. Constitution, and state rights, using Detroit's financial distress as a backdrop. It outlines how only about half of U.S. states authorize municipal bankruptcy under Chapter 9 and explains how Michigan’s municipal distress statute allows for an emergency manager to override local decision-makers to address financial emergencies. The core tension addressed is how federal bankruptcy law, which mandates equal treatment of creditors, clashes with state laws that often shield retiree pensions from being altered.

To illustrate this active legal debate, the page features a side-by-side comparison table. On one side, the "Federalist" argument asserts that the U.S. Constitution, specifically Article I, Section 8, Clause 4, and U.S. bankruptcy law under Chapter 9, empower Congress to establish uniform bankruptcy laws requiring fair, non-discriminatory treatment of impaired creditor classes. On the other side, the "State's Rights" argument cites the 10th Amendment and state-specific provisions, like Article IX, Section 24 of the Michigan State Constitution, which protect pension benefits as contractual obligations that cannot be diminished or impaired.

The author highlights several ongoing municipal bankruptcies that exemplify this unresolved legal tension. In Central Falls, Rhode Island, pension restructuring was mutually agreed upon, though Rhode Island legislatively upgraded unsecured general obligation bonds to secured status just before bankruptcy. Stockton, California, took the opposite approach by prioritizing retirees over bondholders, with CalPERS insisting retiree obligations cannot be altered, leaving the bankruptcy court to decide if impairing bondholders while leaving pensions untouched is legally equitable. Conversely, in Vallejo, California, the court ruled that federal law trumps state law, forcing both retirees and bondholders to make sacrifices. Lastly, in San Bernardino, California, a federal judge opted for mediation rather than ruling directly on the city's petition. The page draws from legal research by David A. Skeel, Jr. and C. Scott Pryor to emphasize these ongoing constitutional questions.

In this analysis of Detroit's fiscal crisis, the author examines the city's proposed Chapter 9 bankruptcy plan, which features aggressive 80% to 90% writedowns on general obligation bonds alongside deep cuts to retiree pension and healthcare benefits. The author raises a critical question for municipal investors: is Detroit an outlier shaped by unique industrial decline, or is it a paradigm for other struggling US cities? To address this, the page evaluates Detroit's long-term credit slide and its underlying economic fundamentals.

To illustrate the credit decay, a table lists ratings on Detroit's uninsured general obligation bonds from June 1998 through July 2013. The data from Moody’s, Standard & Poor’s, and Fitch show a steady slide from comfortable investment-grade ratings in 1998, such as Baa1 and A-, down to speculative junk status by 2009 (Ba2/BB), and ultimately collapsing to near-default levels of Ca and C by July 2013. This rating deterioration closely mirrors a line chart tracking the sales of the "Big 3" automakers—General Motors, Ford, and Chrysler—as a percentage of total US auto sales from 1980 to 2012. This three-month moving average reveals a dramatic decline in domestic market share, falling from nearly 80% in the early 1980s to around 45% by 2012, highlighting how the city's credit profile was tethered to its primary manufacturing sector.

The page further analyzes Detroit's economic fundamentals relative to 381 other US Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs) using two percentile-ranked charts. The first chart plots the growth in Gross Metropolitan Product from 2001 to 2011, indexed to 2001. While the nation's top-performing metros in the 95th percentile neared an index level of 190, Detroit's output line fell below the 5th percentile mark, stagnating near its baseline. The second chart measures labor force growth from 2000 to 2012, indexed to January 2000. While median and high-growth MSAs saw their workforces expand, Detroit's labor pool steadily contracted, ending at an index value below 90 by 2012, which placed it well below the 5th percentile and anchored the city in the bottom 1st or 2nd percentile nationally. 

In footnotes, the author provides additional context on the restructuring, noting that while unsecured general obligation bondholders face the heaviest losses, essential service agency debt, such as water and sewer system bonds, is expected to avoid substantial impairment due to its dedicated net revenues. The commentary also refers to the historical shift in the US auto market, referencing Ralph Nader’s 1965 book, "Unsafe at Any Speed," as a milestone marking the beginning of the domestic industry's long-term market share decline. Data sources cited include Moody’s, Standard & Poor’s, Fitch, J.P. Morgan Securities, the Bureau of Economic Analysis, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

This page, titled "How Different is Detroit: A story in pictures," outlines the severe demographic and economic challenges facing the city of Detroit, contrasting its trajectory with other major American cities. The author argues that Detroit’s declining labor force and population have created unsustainable pension and fiscal dynamics. To illustrate this, the text cites the 2012 annual report of the Detroit Police & Fire Pension, which shows a stark imbalance of 3,200 active workers supporting 9,300 beneficiaries, compared to a much healthier ratio in Chicago of 12,000 active workers to 13,000 beneficiaries. Additionally, a Brookings study is cited, noting that only 30% of jobs within Detroit are held by city residents, with the rest commuting from outside.

The page features six charts that benchmark Detroit against other major U.S. metropolitan areas and cities. The first chart, "Growth in personal income per capita" (indexed to 1990 = 100), shows that Detroit’s income growth from 1990 to 2008 lagged near the bottom 5th percentile of metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs), ending well below most peer cities. The second chart, "MSA-level population growth" (indexed to 1970 = 100), shows that Detroit’s broader metropolitan population stagnated and slightly declined between 1970 and 2010, tracking along the 5th percentile line, while top-performing MSAs grew by nearly 300%. 

The author points out that metropolitan statistical area definitions often obscure the deeper difficulties of the city proper, which excludes healthier suburbs like Warren and Livonia. The next two charts focus on city-proper statistics for 30 major cities. The "Median household income" bar chart shows Detroit at the very bottom, with a median household income under $30,000, compared to high-income cities like San Francisco, which exceeds $60,000. The chart "Change in city-proper population from 1960 to 2010" illustrates that Detroit’s population shrank by nearly 60% over those fifty years, a decline matched only by St. Louis, while sunbelt cities like Phoenix grew by over 200%. 

The final two charts cement Detroit's position as one of the nation's most troubled urban centers regarding education and poverty. In "Percent of population over 25 years old with bachelor's degree or higher," Detroit ranks last among the 30 cities with a rate of roughly 10%, while Seattle leads at nearly 60%. Conversely, the chart measuring the "Percent of individuals below poverty line" shows Detroit with the highest rate of poverty at approximately 36%, with Cleveland close behind and Seattle at the lowest end at under 10%.

This page presents a visual comparison illustrating how Detroit is a severe outlier compared to other major municipal General Obligation (GO) bond issuers. To evaluate municipal credit risk, the author maps J.P. Morgan's 70 largest city GO issuers—which make up approximately 70% of their portfolios' city GO exposure—into their respective Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs). These holdings, represented by blue lines on multiple charts, consistently display far stronger economic and social dynamics than Detroit, which is highlighted by a stark black line. 

The first chart displays 2011 FBI data for violent crime per 100,000 inhabitants across various MSAs. Detroit sits at the far left of the chart as the highest-crime city, approaching 1,200 violent crimes per 100,000 residents, followed by Chicago and Miami, while Provo sits at the far right with the lowest rate. 

The subsequent four charts track economic fundamentals using index values alongside percentile bands from the 5th to the 95th percentiles of the portfolio MSAs. In the growth of Gross Metropolitan Product chart, which is indexed to 2001, Detroit’s growth trends downward after 2005, dropping below the 5th percentile by 2007 and ending near 100 in 2011, while the 95th percentile of the J.P. Morgan portfolio MSAs rises toward 200. 

A similar underperformance is visible in labor force growth, indexed to January 2000. Detroit's labor force contracted steadily over the decade, falling to an index value of approximately 85 by 2012, well below the 5th percentile line which remained near 100, while the 95th percentile exceeded 130. 

In terms of growth in personal income per capita, indexed to 1990, Detroit tracked closely with the bottom 5th percentile, ending near an index level of 180 in 2008, whereas the strongest-performing MSAs in the portfolio neared 240. 

Lastly, MSA-level population growth indexed to 1970 highlights Detroit's long-term demographic decline. Detroit's index value hovered flatly around 100 for forty years, sitting below the 5th percentile by 2010. In contrast, the comparison MSAs showed robust population gains, with the 80th percentile surpassing 230 and the 95th percentile nearing 370. Together, these metrics demonstrate that the underlying credit and economic profiles of typical municipal holdings are vastly superior to Detroit's.

In this page of the publication, the author evaluates the global economic and profit cycle, presenting a cautiously optimistic outlook. Written in a narrative, pseudo-biblical style, the text argues that while S&P 500 valuations are roughly average on a long-term basis, corporate profit margins are high primarily due to historically low labor compensation. However, the author highlights a broad-based improvement in the primary drivers of the US economy, alongside stabilizing manufacturing conditions in Europe and Asia, which could catalyze stronger revenue and profit growth if sustained into 2014.

The analysis is supported by five charts. The first, "S&P 500 trailing price to earnings ratio," plots the index's trailing multiple from 1926 through mid-2013. It shows that although multiples have risen recently, the ratio remains near its historical median—hovering around 15x to 17x—well below the peak of over 30x seen in the late 1990s. 

The second chart, "US growth firing modestly on all cylinders," displays three-month annualized rates of change for four key economic indicators. Utilizing a dual-axis format, the chart shows that as of mid-2013, production is expanding at approximately 4%, consumption is growing at 2%, and employment is steady at around 2% (all on the left axis). Meanwhile, housing, measured on the right axis, shows robust growth of around 15% after peaking near 25% in late 2012. 

The third chart, "A summer rebound in European manufacturing surveys," tracks Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) levels from 2010 to 2013 for major European economies. It illustrates a summer 2013 recovery across most of the region: the United Kingdom's index spikes to over 55, Germany's rises above the expansion threshold of 50, and the European Periphery climbs toward 50. In contrast, France lags behind, remaining in contraction territory below 50. 

The fourth chart, "China and Japan manufacturing surveys," tracks PMI levels in Asia, demonstrating stabilization by mid-2013. Japan's PMI has recovered to around 52, while China's index has stabilized right around the neutral 50 level. 

The final chart, "Ratio of global manufacturing orders to inventory," presents a leading indicator for global industrial production. The ratio bottomed out near 1.00 in late 2012 and early 2013 but has since rebounded to approximately 1.12 by mid-2013, suggesting an imminent acceleration in global industrial production. Ultimately, the author poses the open question of whether these synchronized positive trends will endure into 2014, potentially lifting corporate earnings out of their current stagnation.

This page examines the historical bipartisanship of major, nationally impactful United States domestic legislation over the last century, contrasting it with the highly partisan passage of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, commonly known as Obamacare, in 2010. The author argues that major and controversial laws of the 20th century—concerning civil rights, entitlement creation, welfare reform, labor, and financial controls—typically secured some level of participation and consent from both political parties in both chambers of Congress.
