To expand this observation across all styles, Exhibit 15 presents a bar chart detailing the percentage of managers who underperformed in at least two out of five individual years but still outperformed overall on a cumulative five-year basis. The vertical axis runs from 0% to 80% and the horizontal axis spans nineteen different styles and regions: Large Cap Core, Value, and Growth; Mid Cap Core, Value, and Growth; Small Cap Core, Value, and Growth; Multi-Cap Core, Value, and Growth; EAFE; Emerging Markets; Global; All Country ex-U.S.; Europe; Japan; and Asia ex-Japan. The data shows high percentages of interim underperformance across the board. The bars consistently exceed 50% for most categories, peaking above 70% for Large Cap Value, Mid Cap Value, and Mid Cap Growth. Even the lowest category, Global, shows that roughly 40% of five-year outperforming managers underperformed in at least two individual years.

The accompanying text argues that these findings prove that even high-quality managers go through extended periods of poor relative returns. To explain why this happens, the author references an academic study of over 100 million individual active equity transactions from 1999 to 2009 by Chakrabarty of St. Louis, Moulton of Cornell, and Trzcinka of Indiana. This study revealed that the vast majority of active managers' excess return was earned on positions held between two and three years. The author concludes that because these necessary holding periods require multiple years to bear fruit, portfolio outperformance must be evaluated over longer, multi-year time frames rather than short-term periods.

This page from J.P. Morgan Asset Management addresses the question of manager consistency, arguing that analysis at the industry level suggests only modest levels of repeat outperformance by investment managers from one period to the next. The core visual is Exhibit 16, which tables the manager consistency ratio—defined as the percentage of managers outperforming in an initial five-year period (Period 1) who also managed to outperform in a subsequent five-year period (Period 2). The data, sourced from J.P. Morgan and eVestment as of June 2013, highlights several five-year interval comparisons across a variety of investment styles. 

For the comparison between the five-year periods ending June 30, 2008, and June 30, 2013, manager consistency is notably low, starting at just 26% for Mid Cap Value and 32% for Small Cap Growth, and peaking at only 45% for Asia ex-Japan. In the comparison between periods ending June 30, 2006, and June 30, 2011, consistency ratios improve slightly, ranging from 47% for Large Cap Core up to 60% for Asia ex-Japan, with Mid Cap Growth and All Country ex-U.S. both sitting at 53%, and Europe at 57%. The comparison between periods ending June 30, 2004, and June 30, 2009, shows even higher repeat outperformance, led by Large Cap Core at 63%, alongside Small Cap Value and Europe both at 61%, and Large Cap Value at 52%. Lastly, the single style tracked for the periods ending June 30, 2002, and June 30, 2007, Small Cap Value, registered a 62% consistency ratio. 

The analysis maintains specific criteria for inclusion: each category must contain at least 60 active managers in both five-year periods, and the difference in overall manager outperformance between the two periods must be within a +/- 10% range to control for stable outperformance trends and isolate actual manager rotation.

This page addresses whether active equity managers took on excess risk to achieve outperformance by comparing manager volatility to the volatility of respective ETFs on an ex-post basis over a trailing five-year period. The author argues that for most investment styles, risk-adjusted outperformance measures are higher than nominal outperformance. This suggests that positive active manager performance was not simply a byproduct of higher risk exposures than the market.

The main visual on the page is Exhibit 17, a table titled "Frequency of Manager Outperformance vs. ETF on a Nominal and Risk-Adjusted Basis, Trailing 5 Years," based on September 2013 data from J.P. Morgan and eVestment for $25 million segregated accounts. The table breaks down the percentage of managers outperforming their respective ETFs on both a nominal and risk-adjusted basis across twenty investment styles, calculating the difference between the two metrics.

According to the data, the Equity Income style exhibits the most significant positive shift, with its outperformance rising 20 percentage points from 68% on a nominal basis to 89% on a risk-adjusted basis, a trend attributed to its typical focus on safer, dividend-paying stocks. Other styles showing strong risk-adjusted improvements include Mid Cap Value, which increases by 11 percentage points to reach 78% risk-adjusted outperformance, and Multi Cap Core, which rises 10 percentage points to 55%. Several categories maintain extremely high levels of outperformance under both measures, such as Japan (95% nominal and 96% risk-adjusted), Small Cap Value (holding steady at 94% under both), and All Country ex-U.S. (92% risk-adjusted, up from 89% nominal).

Conversely, a few styles saw their outperformance rates drop when adjusted for risk. Multi Cap Growth suffered the largest decline, dropping 8 percentage points from 45% nominal to 37% risk-adjusted. Multi Cap Value decreased by 5 percentage points to 74%, while Large Cap Growth fell by 4 percentage points to 26%. Europe also fell slightly, dropping 2 percentage points to 77% risk-adjusted outperformance. Overall, the findings reinforce the idea that manager outperformance trends remain generally positive even when controlling for volatility.

This page discusses the impact of survivorship bias on investment manager performance databases, specifically focusing on the eVestment database. The text explains that survivorship bias arises when a database fails to include the full historical record of all active and inactive managers. While the eVestment database relies on self-reported data rather than public regulatory or SEC filings, it mitigates survivorship bias by retaining the historical performance of inactive or "dead" managers and prohibiting the retroactive withdrawal of reported performance. The author notes that a start date of 1996 was chosen for their rolling outperformance analysis to ensure a statistically significant sample size of managers across various categories. A general decline in the number of reporting managers since 2006 is attributed to industry consolidation and the discontinuation of unsuccessful strategies, matching trends observed among active mutual funds by the Investment Company Institute.

The page features four line charts displaying the historical count of managers reporting monthly performance to eVestment from 1975 through mid-2013, with a vertical dashed line marking the 1996 analysis start date. 

Exhibit A3 focuses on U.S. Large and Mid Cap managers, showing that Large Cap Value, Growth, and Core counts all grew rapidly starting in the 1990s, peaking near 450 managers around 2006 before declining, while Mid Cap strategies remained much less populated, peaking under 150 managers. 

Exhibit A4 presents U.S. Small Cap, Multi Cap, and Equity Income managers, where Small Cap Value and Small Cap Growth peaked highest at approximately 250 to 270 managers in the mid-2000s, while Equity Income stayed consistently below 100. 

Exhibit A5 covers Multi-Country managers, showing a dramatic rise in Global managers from fewer than 100 in 1996 to a peak of over 550 around 2008, dwarfing Emerging Markets and All Country ex-U.S. strategies, which both peaked under 200. 

Exhibit A6 details Regional managers, showing that Europe-Australasia-Far East strategies peaked highest at over 300 managers, followed by Europe and Asia ex-Japan peaking between 200 and 250, while Japan-focused strategies remained the lowest, peaking near 150.

This appendix section of J.P. Morgan's publication on active equity management discusses the rationale and methodology for comparing active fund managers against exchange-traded funds (ETFs) rather than theoretical indices. Because ETFs represent actual, investible alternatives, they provide a more realistic performance baseline, although their returns can diverge from underlying benchmarks due to management fees and tracking error. While fees explain most differences in domestic markets, tracking error is highly impactful in international and emerging markets. The author notes that ETFs covering these complex regions significantly underperformed their underlying indices, indicating substantial replication challenges. To address historical gaps where an ETF did not yet exist, the author applies the historical average return difference between the benchmark and the ETF to the benchmark for the earlier periods.

The page features Exhibit A1, a table displaying five-year annualized returns for the period ending September 30, 2013, comparing benchmark indices to corresponding ETFs. The table tracks various investment styles, index returns, ETF returns, the tracking difference, and ETF fees. Domestic styles generally show tight alignments; for instance, Large Cap Core (S&P 500) benchmark returns were 10.02% compared to 10.04% for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF, a difference of just negative 0.02% against a 0.09% fee. Similarly, Large Cap Value (Russell 1000 Value) showed a small 0.12% gap with a 0.21% fee. 

Conversely, international and emerging markets reveal dramatic performance gaps. The MSCI Emerging Markets benchmark returned 7.22% while its corresponding iShares ETF returned 5.37%, showing a substantial 1.85% underperformance gap that far exceeds its 0.67% fee. For Asia ex-Japan, the MSCI benchmark returned 10.26% compared to 8.79% for the iShares ETF, a gap of 1.47% against a 0.67% fee. The All Country ex-U.S. category likewise experienced a 1.27% underperformance gap (6.26% benchmark versus 4.98% ETF) against a 0.34% fee. MSCI Japan lagged by 1.22% (5.16% benchmark versus 3.94% ETF) with a 0.49% fee. The source data comes from Bloomberg and ETF factsheets as of October 2013, with fund classifications mapped via the eVestment database.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, authored by Michael Cembalest, transitions from a brief market outlook to a personal year-end reflection addressed to his college-bound son. Cembalest begins by previewing the upcoming annual outlook, noting a divergence between booming financial markets and more modest economic growth, though leading indicators suggest improvement. He references previous publications covering topics like private equity, energy notes with Vaclav Smil, the Detroit municipal bankruptcy, retirement dynamics, and the housing crisis using Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac data. 

To support the assertion that global economic growth is picking up, a line chart titled Rising number of countries in expansion mode tracks the percentage of a thirty-five country purchasing managers index leading indicator universe that is expanding. This metric spiked near ninety percent in 2006, plunged to near zero percent during the 2008 global financial crisis, recovered back to around ninety percent in late 2009, dropped again to approximately thirty percent in 2012, and rebounded close to ninety percent by late 2013.

The main essay, titled De Omnibus Dubitandum, advises the author's son to practice intellectual skepticism, warning him about the profound political asymmetry he will encounter in higher education. This argument is illustrated by a table detailing the ratio of Democrat to Republican professors across US universities, drawing on studies from California universities, thirty-two elite colleges, and a five-school aggregate including Dartmouth and Duke. The data reveals that academic departments skew overwhelmingly Democratic. For instance, in sociology, the ratio of Democrats to Republicans ranges from thirty point four to one in elite universities to forty-four to one in California, and is listed as infinite in the five-study aggregate. Anthropology similarly shows an infinite ratio in the aggregate study. History exhibits a ratio as high as seventy-five to one in the aggregate. Even more quantitative fields show notable disparities, with political science ratios ranging from six point five to one to seven point nine to one, while economics remains the most politically balanced, though still skewed, with ratios between one point six to one and four point three to one. 

Cembalest concludes this section by questioning the value of tenure-track professors for introductory courses, citing a September 2013 study from Northwestern University published by the National Bureau of Economic Research. The study, co-authored by Figlio, Schapiro, and Soter, found that non-tenure-track faculty actually encourage greater student interest and lead to higher subsequent grades in those subjects compared to their tenure-track peers.

This J.P. Morgan "Eye on the Market" page, published by Michael Cembalest, offers guidance for college students and recent graduates, focusing first on the academic impact of college drinking habits and second on the threat of technological automation in future careers. 

The first section discusses the negative influence of heavy-drinking roommates on college male GPAs, citing studies from Harvard and Mathematica Policy Research. It notes that while a roommate's high school grades or family background do not affect a student's GPA, their drinking habits do. A circular diagram illustrates a negative feedback loop: heavier drinking leads to later bedtimes, daytime drowsiness, fewer study hours, and missing 8:00 AM classes. Drawing from research at a Northeastern liberal arts university with an average SAT score of 1260, the author notes that the average college student consumes five drinks on a weekend night. Every additional drink beyond that threshold declines a student's GPA by 0.17 points directly, with sleep disruption subtracting another 0.07 points, leading to a substantial total GPA reduction of 0.24 points on a 4.0 scale.

The second half of the page shifts to career advice, advising students to prepare for technological change. While engineering, math, physics, and economics majors tend to enjoy low unemployment and high salaries, a broader long-term risk is job computerization. The author highlights an Oxford University study by Frey and Osborne showing that a staggering 47% of the US workforce faces a high probability of being computerized. 

This risk is illustrated in an area chart titled "Probability of computerization by occupation," which plots US employment in thousands against a computerization probability scale from 0 to 1. The chart divides the labor market into three risk categories: a low-probability category (0.0 to 0.3 probability) containing 33% of employment, a medium-probability category (0.3 to 0.7 probability) representing 19% of employment, and a high-probability category (0.7 to 1.0 probability) representing 47% of employment. The visual breakdown uses color-coded stacks for various sectors. On the low-probability side, occupations like Management, Business, Financial, Computer, Engineering, Science, and Healthcare predominate. Conversely, the high-probability side is heavily dominated by sectors such as Office and Administrative Support, Sales and Related, Production, and Transportation and Material Moving. 

To conclude, the author references the classic film *The Man in the White Suit*, starring Alec Guinness, where an invention that never wears out threatens tailors and dry cleaners. This allegory underscores the warning that technological productivity improvements can shift too much power from labor to capital, and students must choose careers where computers cannot easily reduce their economic value.

This page, titled Life away from home, offers a lighthearted yet data-backed argument that popular music has objectively declined in quality and variety since the classic rock and R&B era of 1965 to 1978. To support this claim, the author references a May 2012 study published in Scientific Reports by Serra et al., which analyzed the Million Song Dataset covering western popular music from 1955 to 2010. The researchers tracked three variables: timbre, which measures texture and tone quality; pitch, which indicates chord progression and transition diversity; and loudness.

The first chart illustrates that western popular music has become progressively blander since the 1960s. On the left axis, a measure of timbral variety plotted in brown diamonds peaks in the mid-1960s near a value of 9 before steadily declining to about 4 by 2005, indicating a loss of instrumentation richness. Conversely, the narrowness of chord transitions, plotted in blue diamonds on the right axis, climbs from around 2.90 in 1955 to roughly 3.20 by 2005, demonstrating that chord structures have become narrower and more predictable. 

The second chart shows that popular music has also gotten significantly louder. Plotting the median loudness value in full-scale decibels, the data reveals a steady increase from roughly -22 decibels in the mid-1950s to approximately -13 decibels by 2005. The text cites a Rolling Stone report regarding Metallica fans in 2008 complaining that the CD version of their album sounded worse than the Guitar Hero video game version because the CD had been remastered at an excessively high decibel level—a prime example of the ongoing Loudness Wars. 

Ultimately, the researchers concluded that popular music is undergoing a progressive homogenization of musical discourse, making it both blander and louder over time. The author concludes the note with a personal recommendation for a Method Man and Mary J. Blige duet and well-wishes to a college-bound student, encouraging them in their future endeavors.

This page focuses on the transition from a policy-driven market to one dependent on fundamental economic and corporate profit growth. The author argues that while easy monetary policy and low central bank interest rates successfully accelerated asset prices after the recession, cheap money alone will no longer suffice to drive equity markets higher in 2014. Instead, investors must look to concrete improvements in economic indicators, particularly manufacturing surveys, to forecast future earnings growth.

Two charts at the top of the page address interest rates. The first chart, titled "Central Bank policy rates expected to remain low...", compares policy rates in percent from 2000 to 2013 for emerging and developed markets. Developed market rates fell from around 5% in 2000 to near 0% after the 2008 financial crisis, where they remain flat, while emerging market rates trended down from roughly 12% in 2000 to approximately 6% in 2013. The second chart, titled "...while longer term rates rise modestly higher," plots 10-year real government bond yields (less core inflation, in percent) from 1998 to late 2013 across eight nations: Australia, Canada, France, the United Kingdom, the United States, Switzerland, Japan, and Germany. This visual shows a broad historical decline in real yields, which fell from a range of 3% to 5% in the late 1990s down to a clustered range of -1% to 2% by late 2013.

The bottom half of the page highlights manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) surveys as the key forecasting tool. The third chart, titled "Rising U.S. business surveys point to rebound in earnings," plots the U.S. PMI business activity survey on a scale of 30 to 65 against year-over-year U.S. corporate earnings growth with a four-month lag (ranging from -50% to 50%) from 1989 to 2013. The tight correlation between the two lines shows that a recent uptick in U.S. PMI surveys underpins J.P. Morgan's forecast of an 8% to 10% rebound in U.S. corporate profits for 2014. 

The fourth chart, titled "Similar but more muted outcome in the Eurozone," maps the Eurozone PMI business activity survey against Eurozone earnings growth with a two-month lag from 1998 to 2012. Although leading indicators have risen, signaling that the Eurozone is emerging from recession with sequential profit growth, the gains are visibly smaller than those in the United States. The author forecasts that a sharp Eurozone profit rebound is unlikely, characterizing the dramatic profit spike seen between 2003 and 2007 as a temporary, non-repeatable consequence of a Southern European consumption boom.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Outlook 2014 argues that the Federal Reserve will likely proceed slowly with interest rate hikes because the post-2008 economic recovery has been disproportionately driven by interest-rate-sensitive sectors. Michael Cembalest points out that this reliance makes premature rate hikes particularly risky, especially given that real hourly earnings have stagnated since 2008, leaving weak wage growth as the primary driver behind the corporate profits boom while GDP growth remains stuck in the 1.5% to 2.0% range. 

Despite these concerns, the author expresses optimism for 2014, predicting that the U.S. economy will accelerate after moving past the severe fiscal drag of 2013. This drag—the third-largest in fifty years—was caused by tax increases related to payroll, income, and Obamacare, along with spending cuts and a federal government shutdown. With these hurdles cleared, and with the 10-year deficit outlook stabilized following the 2011 Budget Control Act and the 2013 tax act, growth is expected to improve. Furthermore, U.S. household and corporate balance sheets have undergone significant healing, characterized by a slowing deleveraging trend and a sharp decline in household debt service relative to disposable income. 

Four charts support these assertions. The first chart, titled "The importance of low interest rates to the recovery," indexes GDP contributions starting in Q2 2009 at 100. It shows that by Q3 2013, interest-rate-sensitive sectors (defined as durable goods consumption plus structures) climbed significantly to nearly 114, whereas "everything else" grew much more slowly, ending near 108. 

The second chart, "The pillars of U.S. economic growth," plots the three-month annualized rate of change for various indicators. While consumption and production fluctuate actively, housing (measured on the right axis) experienced volatile but explosive growth, peaking near a 25% annualized rate in late 2012 and early 2013 before cooling slightly by mid-2013. Employment growth, also tracked on the right axis, remained stable but low in comparison. 

The third chart, "U.S. deleveraging appears to be slowing," compares the debt of households and nonfinancial corporations as a percentage of GDP for both the U.S. and the Eurozone. The U.S. debt level (left axis) peaked at approximately 140% in 2009 and fell to about 128% by mid-2013, indicating a flattening trend. By comparison, the Eurozone debt level (right axis) peaked later, near 215% around 2101, and has since only marginally declined to roughly 210%. 

The final chart, "Debt service declining more sharply than debt levels," tracks indicators as a percentage of household disposable income from 1980 to 2013. It demonstrates that while total outstanding household debt (left axis) surged from 60% in 1980 to a peak of 130% in 2007 and then fell to about 105% by 2013, the household debt service ratio (right axis) plunged much faster. Driven down by low interest rates, debt service fell from its peak of 14.0% in 2007 to 10.0% in 2013, successfully returning to levels last seen in the early 1990s.

This page analyzes Japan's aggressive monetary policy experiment launched at the end of 2012, highlighting that while the stimulus dwarfs that of the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, its actual positive impact on the real economy seems limited to a temporary weakening of the Yen. The author questions the efficacy of the program, noting that while the Japanese stock market rallied, key economic indicators rolled over once the Yen's depreciation stalled. Specific limitations of the experiment include a fifty percent increase in the monetary base paired with a less than five percent increase in the money supply, rising inflation driven by energy costs rather than wages, corporate capital spending concentrated outside of Japan, and job growth dominated by part-time workers.

The first chart, titled "Japan's massive money experiment," tracks central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP from 2000 projected out to 2020. It illustrates that the Bank of Japan's balance sheet is on track to shoot past one hundred percent of GDP under committed and contingent paths, far eclipsing the Federal Reserve and European Central Bank, which both remained below thirty percent of GDP. 

The second chart, "The end of Japanese deflation in the 1930's," shows year-over-year percentage changes in Real GNP, Nominal GNP, and the GNP deflator from 1920 to 1938. It marks a period of severe deflation between 1926 and 1931, followed by the launch of Finance Minister Takahashi's expansionary financial policy, which successfully drove nominal GNP and deflation indicators back into positive territory, peaking over twenty percent. 

The final pair of charts links the temporary summer 2013 economic uptick to the weakening currency. The chart "The temporary summer 2013 improvement in Japan..." tracks the three-month percent changes in exports, machinery orders, consumer spending, and the index level for consumer confidence from January 2011 to July 2013. This visual shows a synchronized spike and subsequent rollover in mid-2013. The companion chart, "...coincided with a weaker Yen," maps the Japanese Yen per US Dollar over the same timeframe, showing the exchange rate rising from approximately seventy-five JPY per USD in 2011 to over one hundred by mid-2013, aligning perfectly with the temporary boost in economic activity.

This page highlights signs of economic improvement across the Eurozone, framing the current period as a positive intermission characterized by rising manufacturing surveys and returning foreign capital, particularly in distressed real estate and bank acquisitions in Spain. 

The analysis is supported by four key charts. The first chart, titled "Eurozone rebound: everywhere but France," plots the Purchasing Managers' Composite Index from 2010 to 2013 on a scale of 40 to 65. It demonstrates that while Germany, the United Kingdom, and peripheral European nations show rebounding composite indices toward the end of 2013, France lags behind and remains in a downward trend. The second chart, "'Non-Eurozone Europe' doing better," plots the Purchasing Managers' Manufacturing Index over the same period. It illustrates that non-Eurozone countries—including Denmark, Poland, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom—have performed significantly better than Germany and the rest of the Eurozone, supported by their independent monetary policies. 

The commentary outlines several other positive indicators. Consumer confidence is rising, hiring indicators are picking up, and massive current account deficits in Southern Europe have balanced out after reaching gaps of 10% to 14% of GDP in 2008. Fiscal drag from austerity measures is also projected to ease, declining from 1.7% of GDP in 2012 to an estimated 0.7% in 2014. Additionally, low-cost European Central Bank lending has mitigated short-term default risks, with Spanish and Italian banks purchasing 50% to 60% of government debt since 2008.

The bottom-left chart, titled "Germany goes for growth; Eurozone job outlook improves," compares the Eurozone employment PMI (ranging from 34 to 58) against the German IFO Business Climate Index (ranging from 80 to 120) from 1997 to 2013. Both indices show a sharp, synchronized recovery in late 2013, coinciding with Germany's newly adopted pro-growth agenda of higher minimum wages and increased spending. The final chart details "Competitiveness improvements in Portugal, Spain and Greece," tracking unit labor costs relative to Germany from 2000 to late 2012, indexed to Q4 2000. This visual demonstrates that while unit labor cost gaps have peaked and declined significantly in Greece, Spain, and Portugal—dropping from over 125 down toward 110—labor markets in Italy and France have failed to improve their competitiveness relative to Germany, leaving them structurally disadvantaged.

This page analyzes the relative stability of emerging market economies and details the shifting economic environment in China. The author argues that today's emerging markets are better positioned to weather capital flight than during past crises, such as those in the 1980s and late 1990s. This resilience is attributed to significantly higher foreign exchange reserves and flexible exchange rates. A comparative table of emerging market external account measures contrasts the 1980s (featuring Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, and Venezuela), 1996 (featuring Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia, and Thailand), and Today, referring to late 2013 (featuring Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey). The table highlights key improvements, particularly those circled in red: reserves as a percentage of external debt have grown to 61.6% compared to 28.8% in 1996 and 7.7% in the 1980s; recent exchange rate declines against the US dollar are far shallower at negative 13.7% compared to historic drops of negative 61.1% and negative 97.5%; and exchange rate frameworks have shifted from managed to floating. While the author notes that 2014 will be a difficult year of adjustment, these structural cushions are expected to limit broader economic fallout.

Turning to China, the commentary notes recent positive indicators, with gross domestic product growth at eight to nine percent and stable fixed investment growth. Two charts illustrate this recovery. The first, tracking Chinese manufacturing surveys from 2005 through late 2013, displays the Purchasing Managers' Index through the China NBS PMI and the Markit PMI. Both series dipped sharply during the 2008–2009 global financial crisis before recovering, with both indexes hovering around the modest expansion mark of fifty by late 2013. The second chart measures the year-over-year percentage change in electricity production from 2005 to late 2013, showing a plunge below negative five percent in late 2008, a strong rebound peaking above twenty percent in 2010, and a stabilization around ten percent in late 2013, confirming positive industrial momentum.

Despite these positive signs, the author highlights significant credit risks in China stemming from post-recession credit expansion and loose fiscal policy, which have masked lower underlying real growth. Tensions like rising real estate prices, rising wages, and a tight labor market are driving interest rates up. Consequently, the author forecasts that tighter monetary policy aimed at deleveraging and capacity reduction, orchestrated by China’s Central Bank, will likely cool economic growth down to around seven percent in the near future. This planned transition seeks to prioritize market mechanisms and curb inefficient state-owned enterprises, but it portends near-term challenges.

This page of the publication, titled "Tracking performance trends in active equity management," explores the relationship between stock market correlations and the success of active investment managers. The author argues that while analyzing active management is notoriously difficult due to varying mutual fund fees and share classes, examining a cleaner database of seven trillion dollars in institutional assets reveals a key trend: a decline in pair-wise stock correlations generally signals a period of more consistent manager outperformance.

To support this claim, the page presents two charts. The first chart, titled "Pair-wise stock correlations falling...", tracks the percentage of one-year average cap-weighted return correlations from 1964 to 2012 across three asset classes: U.S. Large Cap, U.S. Small Cap, and International. This graph shows that after peaking significantly around 2008 to 2011—with large cap and international correlations reaching near 45%—correlations have begun a steep downward trend, with U.S. Small Cap dropping toward 10% and the other categories falling below 30%. 

The second chart, titled "... which in the past coincided with higher outperformance," is a scatter plot comparing U.S. stocks' pair-wise return correlations on the horizontal axis (ranging from 5% to 55%) against the percentage of active managers outperforming their benchmark ETFs on a one-year basis from 1996 to 2013 on the vertical axis (ranging from 0% to 100%). A downward-sloping regression line clearly illustrates that lower stock correlations correlate with higher active manager success rates. When correlations are low, near 15%, many active managers achieve outperformance rates above 60% to 80%, whereas high correlation periods drag these success rates down. 

Additional key findings listed at the bottom of the page outline several observations on active management dynamics. The author states that a full five years is necessary to accurately evaluate a manager's skill through different market cycles. Over the five-to-seven-year period leading up to the report, active outperformance was strongest in U.S. value styles and non-U.S. categories such as Emerging Markets, Europe, Japan, and Asia ex-Japan, while U.S. growth categories proved to be the weakest. Furthermore, the frequency of outperformance serves as a strong proxy for net excess returns, and there is no meaningful connection between a fund's size and its performance. Crucially, the author notes that consistency is rare, as even the most successful active managers who outperform over a five-year period typically underperform in two or three of those years. Finally, these outperformance trends remain consistent even when evaluated on a risk-adjusted basis.

This page, titled "Risk and opportunity in credit markets," examines how five years of the Federal Reserve’s zero interest rate policy have driven a search for yield, prompting a rise in looser underwriting standards even as core credit fundamentals remain positive. The author cautions that while default rates are low and cash flow coverage is strong, investors should ensure their portfolios are not overallocated to credit priced for perfection in 2014.

To support this perspective, the page features four charts tracking credit trends. The first chart, showing the percent of total annual issuance from 2002 to 2013, highlights a dramatic surge in covenant-lite leveraged loans. By 2013, these loans represented nearly 50% of annual issuance, a substantial increase from their previous peak of approximately 30% in 2007, while high-yield bonds with PIK/Toggle features remained low. 

A second chart tracks underwriting quality through dual indicators from 1998 to 2013: high-yield issues rated CCC and lower as a percentage of total high-yield issuance, alongside the senior debt-to-cash flow multiple for leveraged buyouts. Both metrics reflect rising risk tolerance: lower-rated CCC issuance rose back toward 30% to 35% in 2013, while LBO senior debt-to-cash flow multiples rebounded from a post-crisis low of 3x to approach 5x.

The third chart demonstrates the shrinkage of distressed debt by tracking the percentage of outstanding U.S. high-yield bonds and loans trading at or below 80% of face value from 1994 to 2012. After peaking dramatically in November 2008—with bonds at 77% and loans at 81%—the share of discounted debt fell to near-zero levels by 2012, indicating a highly compressed credit environment.

The final chart details quarterly debt issuance by mid-market firms with EBITDA of $50 million or less from 1997 to 2013. In contrast to the booming public credit markets, quarterly deal counts for these smaller firms collapsed from over 100 in the mid-2000s to consistently run below 40 deals per quarter post-crisis. The text explains that because smaller and mid-sized companies are finding public market access much more difficult, they are turning to private credit and mezzanine debt markets. Although these private credit portfolios offer less liquidity and diversification, they provide lenders with higher rates and protective covenants often absent in public markets.

Lastly, the page discusses European credit, noting that bank loan sales in Europe are accelerating across various countries as rising earnings help banks absorb losses. European institutions like Lloyd's, Unicredit, BBVA, Commerzbank, and Société Générale took significant asset charges in 2012. PricewaterhouseCoopers reports bank loan sales going for 10 to 40 cents on the Euro in Ireland, and UK and German real estate loan sales clearing at 40 to 50 cents. Given that European bank loan-to-deposit ratios remain high, the author projects that bank loan sales will continue for an extended period.

This page presents visual evidence of several key financial and economic indicators that have returned to their pre-crisis levels of 2007, highlighting areas where valuations or market behaviors have fully normalized. The author notes that because of direct and indirect central bank interventions in government bonds, credit yields are currently a better measure of value than corporate bond credit spreads over Treasuries. Six charts illustrate this return to pre-crisis norms. First, a chart on global and U.S. trailing price-to-earnings ratios from 1970 to late 2013 shows that multiples for both the S&P 500 and the MSCI World index have climbed back into the 15x to 20x range, matching their 2007 valuations. Second, speculative stock-bond positions, measured by the net CFTC stock-bond futures position from 1993 to late 2013, have spiked to around 10%, a highly bullish level last seen just before the 2008 crash. Third, U.S. and European volatility indices tracking the S&P 500 and EuroStoxx 50 from 1990 to late 2013 have dropped back down to the quiet 10 to 15 range, similar to the calm pre-crisis period of 2005 to 2007. Fourth, a housing indicator shows the number of homes resold within six months of purchase in California from 2001 to 2013; this quick-flip volume collapsed from nearly 2,000 units in 2005 to around 400 in 2008, but has since surged back to roughly 1,600 units. Fifth, U.S. corporate investment-grade and high-yield bond yields from 2002 to late 2013 show that yield-to-worst has compressed to historic lows—around 3% for investment-grade and 5% to 6% for high-yield bonds—fully matching or exceeding pre-crisis depths. Finally, discount rates for newly underwritten core U.S. real estate transactions have fallen from nearly 10% in 2009 back down to approximately 6.5%, matching the low unlevered real estate discount rates seen in 2007.

This page of the publication addresses the municipal bond market's concerns surrounding Detroit, exploring whether the city's financial crisis is an isolated incident or indicative of a broader trend across the city-level municipal market. The author argues that Detroit is a clear outlier rather than a paradigm. This discussion is framed by the actions of Detroit's state-appointed emergency manager, who proposed write-downs of 80% to 90% on unsecured general obligation bonds alongside significant reductions to retiree pension and healthcare obligations, which are two to three times larger than the bond debt. 

To support the argument that Detroit is a unique case, the page presents four charts comparing Detroit’s economic indicators against percentile bands and J.P. Morgan’s largest general obligation holdings, represented by blue lines. In all four charts, Detroit's performance, marked by a black line, sits at or well below the bottom 5th percentile, while the firm's holdings are positioned in much healthier percentiles. 

The first chart, mapping Growth in Gross Metropolitan Product from 2001 to 2011 with a base index of 100, shows Detroit's economic output sliding below the 100 mark by 2009, while other municipal holdings grew substantially. The second chart measures Growth in Personal Income per Capita from 1990 to 2008 with a base index of 100, illustrating Detroit tracking right along the bottom 5th percentile line, far below the clustered blue lines of J.P. Morgan's municipal holdings. The third chart displays Labor Force Growth from 2000 to 2012, where Detroit's index fell below 90 by 2010, indicating a shrinking workforce compared to the growth seen in other major municipalities. The final chart presents MSA-level Population Growth from 1970 to 2010 with a base index of 100, showing Detroit's population remaining flat to declining, barely hovering at the 5th percentile index of roughly 100, while the 95th percentile exceeded an index of 350. 

In conclusion, the author notes that while other midwestern cities like Cleveland, Youngstown, Dayton, and Toledo share some of Detroit’s structural problems, Detroit's struggles are uniquely severe. Looking ahead, the publication forecasts that while more municipal bankruptcies may occur in the coming years, the visibility of Detroit's problems and those of similarly positioned cities should allow defensive-minded municipal portfolio managers to easily identify and avoid large exposures to the nation's most troubled municipal issuers.

This analysis examines the dual headwinds facing developing economies: a mild growth deceleration in China and severe balance of payments issues in emerging market debtor nations. The author argues that China's transition is orderly, with real GDP growth slowing from 9 percent quarter-over-quarter in the third quarter of 2013 to 7.5 percent in the fourth quarter. This slowdown is characterized as a deliberate policy outcome driven by monetary tightening and slowing credit growth rather than a catastrophic event. In contrast, emerging market debtor nations face more severe systemic challenges due to slowing growth, rising interest rates, depreciating currencies, and reversing capital flows. The author cautions that while trade balances in these debtor nations are stabilizing, valuations remain elevated, and weakening commodity prices will continue to exert downward pressure.

Four charts illustrate these economic dynamics. The first chart, titled "China slowdown mild so far," displays the Markit manufacturing PMI level on the left axis and the year-over-year percentage change in real GDP on the right axis from 2005 through 2013. It reveals that China's real GDP growth peaked near 14 percent in 2007, fell to about 6 percent during the 2008 financial crisis, rebounded to over 10 percent in 2010, and has since stabilized in the 7.5 percent range. The PMI business activity survey tracks this trend closely, dipping below 45 in late 2008 before stabilizing near 50 by 2013. 

The second chart, "EM debtor nations coming off 7 years of plenty," shows net capital inflows and current account deficits as a percent of GDP for Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey from 2002 to 2013. Net capital inflows peaked near 6.5 percent in 2007 and again near 4.5 percent in 2010. Meanwhile, the aggregate current account deficit for these nations steadily widened from a surplus of over 0.5 percent in the mid-2000s to a deficit of nearly 5.5 percent of GDP by 2013, highlighting a growing reliance on external financing.

The third chart, "Balance of payments pressures result in FX declines," tracks the trade-weighted exchange rate index from April 2011 to October 2013, with April 27, 2011, indexed to 100. While China's exchange rate appreciated steadily to nearly 120, other emerging markets saw significant declines. Mexico and Russia fell to indices of roughly 90 to 95, while India, Brazil, Turkey, and South Africa depreciated sharply, falling to indices between 70 and 80 by late 2013.

The fourth chart, "EM debtor nation trade balances stabilizing," displays trade balances as a percent of GDP from 2005 to 2013 for Indonesia, Brazil, Turkey, and India. Brazil and Indonesia saw their trade surpluses, which peaked between 4 percent and 8 percent of GDP in the mid-2000s, decline toward 0 percent by 2013. Turkey’s trade balance hovered between negative 4 percent and negative 8 percent. India experienced the most severe deficit, bottoming near negative 12 percent in 2012 before recovering slightly to negative 8 percent by late 2013. 

Looking forward, the author projects a medium-term outlook for stable Chinese growth in the 7 percent range. Because Chinese consumption accounts for 50 percent to 60 percent of base metals and 25 percent to 50 percent of many agricultural commodities, this moderate growth rate, combined with a global exploration boom, is expected to weigh heavily on commodity prices. Investors are advised to approach emerging markets with caution, as equity price-to-earnings ratios for these debtor nations are currently around 12x and have not yet reached rock-bottom valuations.

This page features a mix of personal travel observation and macroeconomic analysis. It begins with Michael Cembalest describing a trip to Chilean Patagonia, where he observes the successful integration of non-native Chinook salmon into local waters since escaping fish farms in the 1970s. This success in South America stands in contrast to the species' decline in the Northern Pacific due to habitat destruction, over-harvesting, and hydropower. The discussion is illustrated by a photograph of Cembalest holding an 18-kilogram (40-pound) Chinook salmon caught in Rio Serrano in December 2013, alongside a scatter plot of Patagonian Chinook salmon observations. The plot maps weight in kilograms against length in centimeters, marking Cembalest's catch with a red diamond at approximately 18 kilograms and 115 centimeters, illustrating how it aligns with historical length-weight characteristics published in the Chilean Magazine of Natural History.

The second half of the page transition to a market appendix analyzing European equities, specifically focusing on France, Spain, and Italy. Cembalest argues that while price-to-earnings (P/E) multiples in France and Spain have climbed back to pre-crisis levels, their actual corporate earnings remain deeply depressed. This stands in stark contrast to the United States, where corporate earnings have already exceeded pre-crisis peaks. He warns that the 2003–2007 economic boom in Southern Europe was a leverage- and consumption-fueled bubble that will not recur, and forecasts a modest 8% to 10% growth in European earnings for 2014, reflecting a slow Eurozone GDP recovery of closer to 1% than 3%. 

This economic analysis is supported by two charts. Chart A1 displays the forward P/E multiples on the MSCI equity indexes for Spain and France from 2006 to 2014, showing that valuations for both countries have rebounded from their post-crisis lows of around 7x to 8x to sit between 13x and 14x by early 2014. Chart A2 tracks indexed earnings per share from 1999 to 2013, with December 31, 1998, as the baseline of 100. It shows that while the S&P 500 has rebounded past 200, Spain’s indexed earnings have collapsed from a 2007 peak of over 300 down to roughly 100. Similarly, Italy's indexed earnings sit below 100, and France's index languishes near 180, highlighting the massive earnings gap that European equities have yet to recover.

This page examines the long-term impact of activist investor involvement on corporate financial performance and stock returns, specifically analyzing whether outside investors can successfully "piggy-back" on activist announcements. Drawing on data from Empirical Research Partners spanning 1994 through 2013 and analyzing approximately 4,200 activist events, the analysis suggests that while activism generally improves operational metrics, subsequent stock performance is highly varied and skewed.

The first set of charts tracks three key financial metrics from the year prior to activist involvement through three years after. The median free cash flow to enterprise value shows steady improvement, rising from approximately 4.0% prior to activism to 4.4% in the first year, 4.7% in the second, and 4.9% by the third year. Earnings quality also rises, with the percentage of firms in the best quintile of earnings quality jumping from 20% before activism to roughly 26% after two years before settling at 25.5% in the third year. A major driver of these improved cash flows is a significant reduction in capital spending, as median capital expenditures relative to net property, plant, and equipment drop from 22% prior to activism to 18.5% by the third year.

The second section evaluates stock returns for investors who purchase these targeted U.S. stocks after the activist announcement, excluding the performance of the first month. A bar chart details relative stock returns across five periods: the year before the event and the four subsequent years. This chart plots the average return, median return, and the interquartile range from the 25th to 75th percentiles. In the year before the event, the targeted stocks underperformed heavily, with a median relative return of roughly negative 20% and an average near negative 15%. In the four years following the activist event, the average relative return is consistently positive, hovering around 5% to 7% annually. However, the median relative return remains near zero, fluctuating between negative 2% and positive 2%. 

This divergence is explained by a very wide 25th-to-75th percentile range, which consistently spans from roughly negative 25% to positive 20% in the post-event years. Because a small subset of highly positive performers pulls up the overall average, the typical or median investor experiences flat performance. The author concludes that piggy-backing on activist announcements yields mixed results, and investors would require broad diversification and consistent purchasing rather than selective buying to reliably benefit from activist-driven corporate improvements.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication analyzes the drivers behind the corporate profit recovery and the potential role of shareholder activists. The author argues that activists are increasingly focusing on return on equity, targeting companies with a median RoE of around 4.5 percent compared to the long-term average of 15 percent. Although corporate profits have seen a historic recovery, a closer look reveals that this was not driven by top-line revenue growth, but rather by shrinking labor and interest costs. Since these cost-reduction trends have likely run their course, future earnings growth may slow, making the operational changes proposed by activists more compelling to shareholders.

To support this argument, four charts compare the current economic recovery, represented by a red line, against five past U.S. recoveries from 1958, 1974, 1982, 1990, and 2001, represented by blue lines, over 19 quarters since their respective profit troughs. All values are measured in billions of 2005 USD. 

The first chart, titled Profits, reveals that the current profit recovery has been exceptionally strong, peaking near 900 billion dollars by quarter 19, which is significantly higher than any of the past five cycles. 

In contrast, the second chart, titled Revenue, shows that top-line revenue growth during this same period has been weak, reaching only about 1.1 trillion dollars by quarter 19, whereas past recoveries often saw revenue growth reach between 1.4 trillion and nearly 1.9 trillion dollars. 

The third chart, titled Labor compensation, demonstrates how these profits were sustained; labor costs in the current cycle remained severely suppressed, actually dipping below the initial trough level and only recovering to around 100 billion dollars by quarter 19, while past recoveries experienced labor cost increases ranging from 400 billion to over 1.1 trillion dollars. 

Finally, the fourth chart, titled Interest expense, shows a deep contraction in borrowing costs, with interest expenses dropping by over 110 billion dollars in the current recovery, compared to past cycles where interest costs remained relatively flat or even increased. 

The data for these charts is sourced from the Bureau of Economic Analysis and J.P. Morgan Asset Management as of the third quarter of 2013.

This page from the publication addresses corporate cash holdings and the spread between equity and debt. The main text discusses the rising cash-to-assets ratios of US companies since 1980, attributing it almost entirely to research and development-intensive firms, while non-R&D firms cash levels have remained flat. A few massive firms hold a vast majority of this cash, with five companies—Apple, Microsoft, GE, Cisco, and Google—accounting for 25% of the total, and 22 companies accounting for half. Many of these cash balances are held offshore to benefit from lower tax rates, sometimes representing 70% to 90% of a company’s total cash. For example, Apple issued $17 billion in debt while holding over $100 billion offshore in March 2013, and SEC filings show that 93% of Microsoft's corporate cash is invested in US government and corporate bonds.

The page features three charts and one comprehensive table. The first chart, titled Cash holdings of R&D and Non-R&D intensive firms, displays cash-to-assets ratios from 1980 to 2012. It shows the mean and median for R&D-intensive firms climbing significantly over time, with the mean rising from roughly 10% to around 25%, while the mean and median for non-R&D intensive firms remain flat between 5% and 10%. The second chart, titled Cash to assets of R&D intensive industries, shows cash as a percentage of total assets from 1993 to 2011 across sectors such as Info Tech, Tech & Hardware, Building materials, Pharma, Industrials, and Energy. Info Tech and Tech & Hardware lead the group, climbing to peak levels near 30%.

The middle table, titled Large foreign cash balances in billions of dollars, compiles cash statistics for major corporations. Apple tops the list with $110 billion in total cash ($74 billion foreign, or 67%), followed by GE with $84 billion total ($42 billion foreign, or 50%), Microsoft with $60 billion total ($50 billion foreign, or 84%), and Google with $49 billion total ($26 billion foreign, or 52%). Other companies shown include Cisco, Oracle, J&J, Pfizer, Amgen, Qualcomm, Coca-Cola, Dell, Merck, Medtronic, HP, eBay, and Wal-Mart, with J&J and HP notable for holding 100% of their cash balances abroad.

Finally, the bottom section discusses the spread between equity and debt, noting that activists view market conditions as highly favorable for raising debt to fund mergers, acquisitions, buybacks, and dividends. The accompanying chart, titled Spread between equity and debt, measures the S&P 500 Earnings Yield minus the Barclays US Aggregate Corporate Yield from 1973 to 2013. The line graph illustrates that the spread has historically fluctuated, dipping into negative territory throughout the 1980s and 1990s, but spiked sharply positive following the 2008 financial crisis and remained high at around 3% to 4% by 2013, indicating that many companies can easily afford to adjust their capital structures.

This J.P. Morgan "Eye on the Market" page presents visual and textual analysis concerning US small businesses, global market sentiment, Brazil's structural current account deficit, and political shifts in Argentina, concluding with a financial glossary and a list of references.

The first chart, labeled A3, tracks US small business activity using National Federation of Independent Business survey data from 2000 through late 2013. It compares the percentage of firms planning to raise worker compensation, which fluctuates between roughly 5% and 20% on the left axis, against the percentage of firms making capital expenditures during the last six months, plotted on a right axis ranging from 40% to 70%. Both metrics fell sharply during the 2008 financial crisis, bottoming out around 2009 to 2010. By late 2013, both series show a partial recovery, with about 15% of firms planning to raise compensation and 55% making capital expenditures, though both remain below their pre-crisis peaks.

The second chart, labeled A4, is titled "The price of fear almost back to pre-crisis levels." It measures market anxiety from 2004 to early 2014 by plotting the price of a 5% out-of-the-money put option as a percentage of the index level, smoothed using a three-month moving average. The chart tracks indices for Europe, Japan, the UK, Germany, Hong Kong, and the S&P 500. Option prices across all regions spiked dramatically during the 2008–2009 financial crisis, peaking between 6% and 10% of index values. By early 2014, these prices declined back to historical lows of between 1% and 3%, indicating that downside protection costs have returned to pre-crisis levels.

The third chart, A5, decomposes Brazil's current account deficit as a percentage of GDP from 2005 through 2013. The accompanying text explains that despite Brazil’s trade balance showing a modest surplus of around 0.5% of GDP in late 2013, the country still relies heavily on foreign capital. This reliance stems from structural deficits in its services balance, which sits around -2% of GDP due to costs like tourism and financial services, and its income balance, which sits near -2.5% of GDP due to interest and dividend payments on foreign investments. Together, these factors drag the overall current account balance down to a deficit of approximately -3.5% of GDP, leading the author to project potential future weakness for the Brazilian Real, which remains overvalued in real terms.

Additionally, the page notes a significant political shift in Argentina, where the ruling Frente para la Victoria party suffered a decline, receiving only 32.5% of the national vote in recent elections—a roughly 20% drop from 2011. The party lost in all major provinces, including Buenos Aires, Córdoba, Santa Fe, and Mendoza. 

The bottom of the page includes brief definitions of MSCI and FTSE benchmarks, a glossary of terms including the Bank for International Settlements, the Governmental Accounting Standards Board, the International Monetary Fund, the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, the National Federation of Independent Business, and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Finally, a list of referenced reports from late 2012 to early 2014 covers topics such as US pension gains, public pension funding, the commodity investment cycle, and country classification reviews.

This page analyzes the geopolitical situation in Ukraine and Crimea following the Russian occupation, focusing on demographics, energy leverage, and the implications for global markets. 

To illustrate the region's demographic makeup, the page features two maps of Ukraine based on the 2001 Ukrainian census. The first map displays linguistic and ethnic distribution, highlighting that while Western Ukraine is predominantly Ukrainian-speaking, Eastern and Southern Ukraine are mostly Russian-speaking, with Crimea unique in having an ethnic Russian majority. The second map shows the precise percentage of ethnic Russians by region, revealing that Crimea's population is 58.3 percent ethnic Russian and the city of Sevastopol is 71.6 percent ethnic Russian, contrasting sharply with the city of Kiev at 13.1 percent and western regions that show single-digit percentages. 

A supporting table compares the percentage of Russian ethnicity against active Russian language usage across fourteen former Soviet Republics. The data shows that while Russian language usage is high in many of these countries—such as 78 percent in Belarus, 67 percent in Kazakhstan, and 61 percent in Ukraine—the actual size of the ethnic Russian diaspora is much smaller, standing at 11 percent in Belarus, 26 percent in Kazakhstan, and 17 percent in Ukraine. Other countries like Latvia and Estonia also show high language usage (58 percent and 39 percent) relative to their ethnic Russian populations (27 percent and 24 percent). This comparison underscores that Crimea represents a unique case of a high-density Russian diaspora.

The author provides historical context, noting that Crimea’s high concentration of ethnic Russians is partly due to the Red Army's deportation of Crimean Tatars after World War II, and that the transfer of Crimea to Ukraine in the 1950s was likely seen as a minor bookkeeping entry under the Soviet Union. Crimea is also strategically important as the host of the Russian Black Sea fleet in Sevastopol, leased through 2042.

Regarding future outlooks, the author indicates that while comparisons to Germany's 1938 annexation of the Sudetenland are being made, defense contacts suggest the probability of US or European military support for Ukraine is very low. Instead, the US is contemplating economic sanctions and asset freezes. For investors, this crisis is expected to pressure emerging market asset pricing, increase recession risks in Russia where economic growth is just over 1 percent, and raise geopolitical risks for neighboring countries like Turkey. Furthermore, because Russia controls the natural gas pipelines crossing Ukraine, Europe's leverage is heavily restricted. The author notes this dynamic could prompt the US to accelerate approvals for domestic liquefied natural gas (LNG) export projects to help European customers reduce their reliance on Russian energy.

This appendix examines the performance and governance trends of corporate actions frequently targeted by activist investors, specifically spinoffs, share buybacks, poison pills, and board structures. 

The first section analyzes the cumulative performance of spinoffs and share buyback programs since June 30, 2008. The chart S&P 500 vs. Bloomberg Spin-Off index illustrates that corporate spinoffs have generated significant outperformance relative to the benchmark. By late 2013, the Bloomberg Spin-Off index achieved a cumulative return of over 120%, while the S&P 500 reached roughly 55%. Similarly, the chart S&P 500 vs. S&P 500 Buyback index compares the benchmark to an index representing the 100 companies with the highest share buyback ratios. This buyback index also outperformed the broader market, finishing near 100% cumulative return by the end of 2013. The author notes that while these figures do not measure activist-specific returns, they highlight the historically positive outcomes associated with these specific corporate actions.

The second section focuses on corporate governance changes, observing that shareholder activism is driving companies to dismantle traditional defensive measures. The chart Companies with a poison pill demonstrates a sharp decline in poison pill usage from 1998 to 2012. For both S&P 500 and S&P 600 mid-cap companies, the prevalence of poison pills dropped from peak levels of roughly 60% in the early 2000s to around 11% and 15% respectively by 2012. The author adds a caveat that many companies utilize standby arrangements to deploy a pill quickly if needed. Additionally, modern poison pills increasingly employ a lower ownership threshold of 10% instead of the traditional 20% to deter activists. 

Finally, the chart Companies with classified board of directors tracks the percentage of companies where directors serve staggered terms rather than facing annual elections. Between 1998 and 2012, S&P 500 companies steadily declassified their boards, with the percentage dropping from approximately 60% to less than 15%. In contrast, mid-cap companies in the S&P 600 maintained classified boards at a much higher rate, declining only slightly from 60% to roughly 50% by 2012.

This page of the commentary analyzes the challenges facing Bitcoin and warns of the broader systemic risks should it or a competing virtual currency succeed. The author characterizes Bitcoin as the "Esperanto of currencies"—an elegant concept that has attracted passionate followers but failed to achieve broad acceptance, with low transaction growth compared to trading activity. The analysis highlights three main hurdles: the transactional costs of converting Bitcoin to cash through platforms like Bitpay and Coinbase, which charge fees around 1.0% that may not be sustainable; regulatory crackdowns, such as China banning financial institutions from processing Bitcoin transactions; and safety vulnerabilities, epitomized by the collapse of the Mt Gox exchange and the theft of 6% of outstanding Bitcoins due to algorithm clearing delays and vulnerable online wallets. Additionally, resolving issues like lost passwords and irreversible transactions will likely raise transaction costs, eroding any arbitrage advantage over fiat currency.

Ultimately, the author's deepest concern is that a successful, untraceable cryptocurrency would push economic activity into the shadow economy, unfairly shifting the tax burden onto the remaining regulated sector. To illustrate the danger of a dominant underground sector, the page includes a scatter plot titled "Large shadow economies coincide with less wealth." This chart plots the size of the shadow economy as a percentage of GDP against per capita GDP in real constant thousands of dollars, using 2009 data from the Conference Board, Buehn, and Schneider. The chart's red trendline depicts a strong inverse relationship, showing that countries with high per capita GDP near $30,000 to $40,000 generally maintain small shadow economies under 20% of GDP, whereas poorer countries with per capita GDP under $10,000 often suffer from shadow economies that consume 30% to over 60% of GDP. This visual data supports the author's final point that libertarian tax-avoidance ideals can ultimately lead to collective economic suffering.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses whether US equity markets are currently too expensive to own. Michael Cembalest argues that while they are not yet prohibitively expensive, they are no longer cheap, and small-cap stocks are becoming increasingly pricey. With US large-cap price-to-earnings multiples edging toward the high end of mid-cycle valuations, future investor returns will likely depend on actual earnings growth, which is expected to be in the high single digits, rather than further multiple expansion. The author notes that recent US economic weakness is partly weather-related due to a severe winter, but some soft data, such as housing’s response to higher interest rates, pre-dated the cold. Consequently, the market is depicted as taking a temporary pit-stop to wait for further fundamental proof of the growth already priced in.

To support this analysis, the page features two valuation charts. The first, titled S&P 500 forward price to earnings ratio, tracks the index’s forward P/E multiple from 1985 to early 2014 on a scale from 6x to 30x. The data series shows a major peak near 25x during the late 1990s dot-com boom, followed by a decline, with the ratio rising back to approximately 15x by early 2014, as indicated by a red marker. An accompanying footnote explains that these large-cap valuations appear even higher if the technology sector is excluded, as tech currently trades at a discount to its historical average. This discount is partly because today’s dominant tech giants are twice as large relative to the overall economy as they were in the 1990s, making their growth profiles different.

The second chart, titled Small cap valuations, tracks the forward P/E multiple of the Russell 2000 index from 1986 to early 2014 on a scale of 9x to 24x. The chart highlights previous valuation spikes in early 2000 and late 2001, which occurred due to price surges amid stable earnings and post-9/11 relief rallies amid falling earnings, respectively. For the current period, the chart plots two scenario markers for early 2014: one assuming a 20% consensus earnings-per-share growth rate, which keeps the valuation around 18x, and another assuming a more conservative 10% EPS growth rate, which pushes the valuation up to nearly 20x. A stylized graphic in the upper-right corner depicts race cars labeled with various indices, including the S&P 500, Russell 2000, and Hedge Funds, visually reinforcing the author’s market pit-stop metaphor.

This page offers an analysis of Puerto Rico’s debt situation alongside a detailed evaluation of Bitcoin’s utility, particularly for populations facing severe capital controls. 

Addressing Puerto Rico's financial landscape, the author suggests that if an upcoming March debt offering succeeds, investors should use any resulting relief rally to reduce exposure to uninsured general obligation bonds and weaker revenue bond issuers. This recommendation is supported by two charts. The first chart illustrates Puerto Rico’s persistent labor force decline, showing that the index of employees on nonfarm payrolls (indexed to 100 in March 2006) has steadily fallen to around 87 by 2014, while the overall United States index has rebounded to over 100. The second chart details Puerto Rico's debt term structure, showing a massive concentration of long-term debt maturing in the future, with over $20 billion in the 10-to-20-year range and more than $22 billion in the 20-to-30-year range.

The page then pivots to Bitcoin, exploring whether it is a viable electronic currency. Citing J.P. Morgan research, the author notes that while Bitcoin replicates the supply limitations of gold, it fails as a traditional "store of value" due to extreme illiquidity, lack of yield, and massive volatility—being twenty times more volatile than the Japanese Yen, with historical single-day drops of 38%, 36%, and 33%. 

Despite these drawbacks, the author suggests that Bitcoin provides a lifeline for the "financially oppressed"—businesses and individuals in nations characterized by strict capital controls, dual exchange rates, and persistently negative real deposit rates, such as Venezuela, which has seen negative real interest rates for 25 years. A supporting table identifies countries with severe capital account restrictions. The "Most restrictive" category, including nations like Venezuela, Ukraine, Angola, and Myanmar, represents a combined population of 260 million and a GDP of $1.238 trillion. The "Next 10" category, which includes massive economies like China, India, Thailand, and South Africa, accounts for a population of over 3.2 billion and a GDP of $22.012 trillion. Together, these restrictive regimes represent around half of the global population and 28% of world GDP.

The final chart tracks Bitcoin's daily transaction volume and USD price from June 2012 to December 2013. It highlights a massive spike in Bitcoin's price to over $1,000 in late 2013. However, this price surge contrasts with relatively low growth in daily transactions, which peaked at approximately 60,000 transactions per day (on a rolling 30-day average) in early 2013 before declining and fluctuating between 40,000 and 50,000 transactions per day.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication examines the persistent issue of overly optimistic transportation forecasting, focusing on why toll road economics consistently fail to accurately estimate drivers' willingness to pay for convenience. 

On the left, Exhibit 3 displays a chart showing the distribution of actual traffic volumes as a percentage of the initial forecast, using data from a 2009 study by Robert Bain at the University of Leeds. The chart displays two bell curves: one for countries without prior toll roads, which peaks at a mere 58% of the forecast, and another for countries with prior toll roads, which peaks slightly higher at 81%. Both curves highlight that even experienced nations fall well short of the 100% forecast line. 

On the right, Exhibit 4 illustrates the performance of U.S. toll roads opened between 1986 and 2004, charting actual revenue as a percentage of projected results from operations over five years. Using 2006 data from the National Cooperative Highway Research Program, the scatter plot maps individual projects as colored dots across Years 1 through 5. The vast majority of these projects lie far below the 100% dashed threshold line, with a heavy concentration of projects generating only 20% to 80% of their projected revenue. The text notes that this forecasting issue is global, citing a 2010 study by David Hensher and Zheng Li of the University of Sydney, which found that first-year traffic volumes for 14 Australian toll roads averaged only 55% of forecast levels.

At the bottom of the page, a detailed discussion box titled "Estimating the Value of Time (VoT)" explains the methodology behind these forecasting errors. The text outlines how traditional macro-level demand models, while popular due to low costs, fail because they forecast on a regional level and poorly estimate the price points drivers are willing to pay. To address this, academic researchers are turning to micro-level models that attempt to capture individual variations in the Value of Time by analyzing household-level data, smartphone GPS activity, and mail-in surveys. The author leaves open the question of whether these newer micro-level models will successfully improve forecasting accuracy in the future.

This page, titled "Executive Summary: A Quick Snapshot of Infrastructure Investing," provides an overview of infrastructure as an investment asset class, explaining its appeal, its sectoral composition, global deal volumes, and regional distribution. The text explains that institutional investors are drawn to infrastructure for its diversification benefits, inflation protection, and stable, long-term yields derived from tolling, regulated utility models, and long-term contracts. While Europe has led in utilizing public-private partnerships (PPPs)—financing 20% to 30% of infrastructure this way in countries like the United Kingdom and Portugal—the United States has historically relied more on municipal bonds, though US PPPs are growing from a low base. 

An "Infrastructure Overview" table categorizes the asset class into six major sectors and their respective subsectors: regulated assets (covering water, wastewater, electricity transmission, and natural gas/power distribution); transportation (covering toll roads, airports, seaports, rail, and parking); power generation (covering conventional coal and natural gas as well as renewables); midstream (including pipelines, storage, and gathering/processing); communications (such as cell towers, cable networks, and satellite systems); and social infrastructure (such as hospitals, schools, and courts/prisons). 

A bar chart tracks the "Estimated Aggregate Value of Infrastructure Deals Completed Globally by Private Funds" from 2007 through 2013 in USD billions, using data from the Preqin Infrastructure Group. The chart show that global deal values stood at approximately $260 billion in 2007 and fell to a recessionary trough of about $150 billion in 2009. From there, deal activity recovered strongly, rising to around $280 billion in 2011 and peaking at roughly $310 billion in both 2012 and 2013. 

An adjacent 100% stacked bar chart, also sourced from Preqin, shows the "Breakdown of Infrastructure Deals by Region" from 2008 to 2013. The regions represented are Europe, North America, Asia, Australasia, Latin America, and Other. Throughout this period, Europe and North America consistently dominate global deal activity. Europe represents the largest share, fluctuating between approximately 40% and 55% of the total, while North America holds the second-largest share, generally ranging between 20% and 30%. Asia, Australasia, and Latin America consistently make up much smaller, single-digit to low double-digit shares of the overall deal breakdown.

Looking ahead, the page discusses pension fund trends, noting that current allocations to infrastructure stand at just 1% to 2%, with two-thirds of plans remaining below their long-term targets. Preqin surveys indicate that underweight pension plans intend to increase these allocations. Additionally, Bain & Company projects that while the majority of institutional investors allocate less than 5% to infrastructure today, they are expected to increase their allocations to 5% or more in the coming years.

In this page, Michael Cembalest addresses the pressing question of whether emerging market equities have finally become cheap enough to buy. His short answer is no, advising investors who want to build a position to dollar-cost average slowly rather than trying to time the bottom of the market. 

To support this view, Cembalest highlights that while equities in the four major emerging market debtor nations—Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey—have fallen by roughly 15% in U.S. dollar terms since December 2012, their forward price-to-earnings multiples have only seen a modest decline. This is because earnings expectations have fallen almost as fast as equity prices. The chart titled "EM debtor nations trade at higher multiples than surplus nations" tracks 12-month forward P/E multiples from 2011 to 2014, showing that the group of Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey has consistently traded at a higher valuation multiple (ending near 11.5x in early 2014) than the rest of the emerging markets (which sat around 10.5x).

From a technical perspective, a second chart, "Sectors trading below their 2-year moving averages," monitors the percentage of 62 MSCI emerging market sectors trading below this trendline. Cembalest points out that while historical capitulation and market distress typically see 80% to 90% of sectors trading below their moving averages, the current reading is only at 55%. This indicates that the market has not yet reached a capitulation phase.

The commentary also contrasts the improving return on equity trends in the United States with weakening trends in emerging markets. The "Return on equity" chart compares S&P 500 and MSCI EM ROEs from 2002 to 2014. While the S&P 500 ROE has steadily recovered to around 15% in 2014, the MSCI EM ROE has trended downward to approximately 12%. Cembalest notes that this divergence might be structural rather than cyclical, citing research by Chief Economist Michael Vaknin suggesting that the U.S. outsourcing cycle may have reached its limit.

Additionally, rising interest rates in debtor nations are weighing on retail sales, employment, and capital expenditures. The final chart, "EM debtors experience rising rates," shows the average 1-year and 5-year interest rates for Brazil, India, Indonesia, and Turkey from 2011 to early 2014. Both yields spiked sharply from their late-2012 lows, with average 5-year interest rates climbing back toward 10% and 1-year rates rising above 9.0%. 

While India’s current account has improved due to a sharp drop in gold imports, Cembalest warns that other debtor nations still have a long way to go, estimating that economic stabilization is at least a few months away. In a footnote, he expresses particular concern over rapid private sector debt growth since 2008 in Turkey and Brazil. He specifically mentions Petrobras, the highly leveraged Brazilian state-owned oil company, noting that it would need to borrow $20 billion per year to sustain its current cash flow and capital expenditure plans.

This page from J.P. Morgan's infrastructure investment report analyzes the financial risks of building new infrastructure versus acquiring existing capacity, focusing on Panda Energy's 2010 power plant project in Texas. In 2010, Panda Energy secured financing to construct three natural gas-fired combined-cycle power plants at a projected cost of $1,000 per kilowatt (kW) for completion in 2014.
