The author suggests that Panda Energy likely paid this high cost under the assumption that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) would shift from a "production pricing" model to a "capacity pricing" model, which would have allowed the company to easily recoup construction costs. However, ERCOT maintained its production pricing system, leaving the new plants to compete in merchant power markets with a very high cost base. S&P subsequently raised concerns regarding high future cash flow volatility due to this lack of regulatory shift. The author concludes that it is risky to assume Texas power markets will align with regulatory practices in the rest of the United States without convincing evidence.

To illustrate how expensive new builds are compared to buying existing capacity, the page features a table titled "Exhibit 10: Select Combined Cycle Natural Gas Plant Transactions in Texas, 2010-2013." The table lists Panda Energy's 2010 plant construction with an 1,800 megawatt (MW) capacity and a deal size of $1.8 billion, representing a cost of $1,000/kW. In contrast, existing asset transactions during this period were significantly cheaper. For instance, in April 2010, the Colorado Bend Energy Center and Quail Run transaction represented 1,124 MW of capacity at $325/kW. Other notable transactions include the Oyster Creek Unit VIII in October 2010 at $233/kW, the Odessa-Ector asset in June 2011 at $295/kW, and the Rio Nogales plant in March 2012 at $600/kW. Even the highest-priced transaction for an existing asset, the Freestone Energy Center in October 2010, came in at $836/kW, which is still lower than the Panda Energy new build cost. The data is sourced from UBS, SEC filings, FactSet, Bloomberg, and Sparkspread.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s infrastructure report focuses on a second major pitfall: projects whose success is overly dependent on subsequent development or the completion of other, related public or private sector assets. If these related assets are delayed or never built, the entire value of the infrastructure investment is put at risk. 

The first case study illustrating this risk is the Northwest Parkway in Denver, Colorado. In 2007, local authorities signed a 99-year, $603 million concession agreement to operate this nine-mile stretch of highway. Investors paid an exceptionally high valuation—amounting to 90 times the road's 2006 revenues—because they expected the regional beltway to be completed. The deal structured contingent payouts, including $40 million for completing the rest of the beltway and an additional $60 million if finished by 2020. Exhibit 6 presents a map of the Denver metropolitan area showing the Northwest Parkway, the E-470 tollway, and the unbuilt beltway portion, marked as a red dotted line. Despite political assurances that this missing link would be completed, the beltway has faced significant design and financial hurdles, and its completion remains in doubt. As a result, current traffic levels on the Northwest Parkway sit at just 17% of total capacity. The author concludes that investors should heavily discount political promises regarding developments they cannot control.

The second case study examines the South Bay Expressway in San Diego, California. Detailed in Exhibit 7, this 10-mile express toll road was designed through a public-private partnership to connect San Diego with the Mexican border. Completed in 2007, the project suffered a 13-month construction delay. Daily traffic volumes in 2009 reached only 23,000 to 29,000 vehicles, falling far short of the projected 60,000. This shortfall occurred because the projections relied on overly optimistic expectations for suburban development outside San Diego and underestimated the competition from nearby free-to-use roads. Following a $40 million litigation dispute with contractors and dismal toll revenues, the expressway filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. This resulted in a complete write-down of equity and a 30% haircut for lenders. The map in Exhibit 7 highlights the expressway’s location relative to major local interstates and the Mexican border. The author warns that there is a stark difference between investing in infrastructure that connects established areas and investing in projects that depend on subsequent, unbuilt development.

This page, titled "Pitfall #4: Too much financial engineering and/or leverage," examines infrastructure projects whose operational performance aligned with expectations but whose highly structured or aggressive financing caused severe issues. 

The first case study focuses on the Indiana Toll Road, which was awarded as a 75-year concession in 2006. The financing package included a nine-year, interest-only bullet loan combined with a 20-year accreting interest rate swap. While the underlying business performed well, declining interest rates caused substantial mark-to-market losses on the swap, nearly doubling the total project debt from $3.4 billion at acquisition to $6.0 billion by 2011. This increase in leverage prevented early refinancing and kept debt-to-cash-flow multiples elevated at 40x. 

This case is illustrated by two charts. Exhibit 13, a bar and line chart titled "Revenues and gross margins have grown as expected," shows Indiana Toll Road annual revenue from 2007 to 2012. Total revenues grew from approximately $150 million to around $190 million, while EBITDA steadily increased and the EBITDA margin expanded from roughly 73% to over 81%. Exhibit 14, a stacked bar and line chart titled "The negative impact from an accreting swap," displays the annual debt metrics from 2006 to 2011. While long-term debt remained relatively stable between $3.3 billion and $3.8 billion, the swap liability expanded significantly starting in 2008, pushing total liabilities toward $6.0 billion by 2011. The debt-to-cash-flow multiple, shown on the right axis, started near 58x in 2006, dipped to around 35x in 2007, and fluctuated back up to end at 40x by 2011. 

The second case study highlights a diversified global marine and rail terminal operating company. In this deal, an infrastructure manager purchased a 49% minority stake in a global company owning 210 terminal facilities for 20x cash flow, with debt at 13x cash flow. Between 2006 and 2012, revenues fell by 7% annually. Because the financing terms required increased interest payments if leverage multiples rose, the project faced rising capital costs just as revenues declined. The asset was eventually refinanced under more conservative terms. 

This shift toward conservative structures is shown in Exhibit 15, a table titled "Comparison of Financing Approaches" comparing terms from 2007 to 2014. Loan-to-value ratios decreased from 65%–75% in 2007 to 55%–60% in 2014, while equity contributions rose from 25%–35% to 40%–45%. The cost of financing shifted from LIBOR plus 130 basis points with a step-up based on EBITDA multiples to a flat LIBOR plus 220–250 basis points. Additionally, the minimum debt coverage ratio required before default tightened from 1.0x–1.1x in 2007 to 1.4x in 2014. The page concludes that while geographic diversification is valuable, globalization has increased the correlation of country growth patterns, meaning highly leveraged global infrastructure portfolios must be managed with caution.

This page, titled Appendix III: Natural gas peaker plants and the dispatch curve, examines the investment dynamics of natural gas peaking facilities, contrasting them with baseload power plants. Peaker plants are brought online to meet peak demand, especially on hot summer days. While they command very high compensation rates when active, their revenue profile is highly variable and risky due to unpredictable usage.

A line chart, Exhibit A3.1, displays monthly capacity factors from January 2011 to July 2013 across different energy sources. It shows that baseload sources maintain high capacity factors: nuclear runs consistently between 75 percent and 95 percent, geothermal stays around 70 to 75 percent, and coal fluctuates between 50 and 75 percent. Meanwhile, natural gas peaker plants hover near zero for most of the year, spiking up to roughly 15 to 20 percent only during summer months, illustrating their extreme seasonality and variable demand.

To explain pricing dynamics, Exhibit A3.2 presents a hypothetical dispatch curve for the United States, showing variable operating cost in dollars per megawatt-hour on the y-axis against available capacity in gigawatts on the x-axis. The curve illustrates the order in which electricity sources are brought online based on marginal cost. Renewables, nuclear, hydro, and coal are called first at low variable costs under 30 dollars per megawatt-hour. Natural gas combined-cycle plants sit at about 40 to 50 dollars per megawatt-hour and typically satisfy early-morning demand at roughly 65 gigawatts of capacity. As demand rises toward peak capacity near 112 gigawatts, less efficient natural gas single-cycle plants, natural gas peakers, and finally petroleum are called into service, with variable costs spiking sharply from 100 dollars to over 250 dollars per megawatt-hour. 

The accompanying text explains that all active providers are paid the marginal rate set by the last needed unit of capacity. It details the grid's balancing act, noting that supply and demand must remain within 5 to 10 percent of each other to avoid brownouts or equipment damage. This challenge is highlighted by a reference to Czech grid operators taking defensive measures against wind-power surges originating in Germany. The text also explains the differences between efficient combined-cycle gas plants used for baseload and fast-starting combustion turbines used as peakers. It concludes by noting that while wind and solar are low-cost price-takers, excess renewable generation on sunny or windy days can force grid operators to curtail renewable energy or costly scale back coal, hydro, and gas generation.

This appendix addresses the financial risks associated with using accreting swaps to finance infrastructure projects. Because infrastructure revenues, such as those from toll roads, are bond-like and tend to rise over time, project owners often use accreting swaps—where the fixed interest rate starts low and rises over time—to match debt payments with rising cash flows. However, this structure creates a substantial risk if interest rates fall. A mark-to-market loss on a long-term swap adds to the project's total debt, which can severely jeopardize its ability to refinance when the underlying bank loan matures, even if the project's cash flows are performing as expected.

To illustrate this, the page presents a model simulation of an infrastructure project financed by a nine-year bank loan overlaid with a 20-year accreting swap. The underlying assumptions for the simulation include a total deal size of 10,000, financed with 80% leverage (8,000 debt and 2,000 equity). The project assumes a free cash flow purchase multiple of 20, a required internal rate of return of 12%, an implied annual cash flow growth rate of 4.09%, and a bank loan credit spread of 1% with refinancing occurring in Year 8. The 20-year swap coupon schedule starts at a low rate of 3.13% for the first four years, steadily steps up to 4.90% by Year 10, and eventually rises to a peak of 11.29% in Years 18 through 20.

The primary visual component is a matrix, labeled Exhibit A4.1, which details the time-weighted net present value (NPV) gain or loss on the USD 2 billion equity investment across different scenarios. The vertical axis represents annual cash flow growth relative to original underwriting, ranging from negative 5.0% to positive 5.0%. The horizontal axis represents changes in the long-term interest rate swap curve, ranging from negative 2.5% to positive 2.5%. 

The table highlights three specific scenarios to prove the author's points. In Scenario 1, where cash flows match the original underwriting but interest rates drop by 1.0%, the project suffers a loss of 328 due to the mark-to-market swap hit. Scenario 2 demonstrates a situation where cash flows outperform underwriting by 1.0%, but a 1.5% drop in interest rates still results in a net loss of 55 because the swap's mark-to-market losses outweigh the positive cash flow. Scenario 3 represents the worst-case combination, where cash flow underperforms by 3.0% and interest rates fall by 1.0%, resulting in a steep loss of 1,507. Extreme underperformance combined with severe interest rate declines, such as a 5.0% cash flow drop and a 2.5% drop in interest rates, can lead to losses as high as 2,685, completely wiping out the initial 2,000 equity investment.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, titled "The US: bottom-feeding in the aftermath of bank/financial crises," argues that during major banking crises, equity markets and bank stocks bottom out and begin to recover long before bank failures have peaked. The author cautions "bottom-feeders" against waiting for banks to stop failing before reinvesting, as historical data shows markets bottom while the failure process is far from over. 

To support this observation, the page features three charts comparing stock indices with cumulative bank failures across different eras. The first chart, "The Great Depression: Equity market vs. bank failures," covers January 1929 to December 1933. It plots the Dow Jones Industrial Average against cumulative bank failures, showing that equities bottomed in mid-1932 when only 48% of the eventual bank failures had occurred. 

The second chart, "Savings and Loan Crisis: Bank stocks vs. bank failures," tracks the S&P 500 Bank Index against cumulative bank failures from March 1988 to October 1994. In this crisis, bank stocks bottomed in late 1990 when cumulative bank failures were at 63% of their ultimate total. 

The third chart, "Financial crisis: Bank stocks vs. bank failures," covers January 2008 to January 2014, comparing the S&P 500 Bank Index with cumulative failures during the Great Recession. This chart highlights that when equities and bank stocks bottomed in March 2009, a mere 8% of the banks that would eventually fail had done so. The author notes that policy actions, specifically the Supervisory Capital Assessment Program stress tests announced by the US Treasury in May 2009 and the Federal Reserve's expansion of discount window operations, were much more effective indicators of a market bottom than tracking bank defaults.

This page addresses "Pitfall #5" in infrastructure investing: overly optimistic renewable energy projections, using wind energy as a primary example. The author argues that wind farm economics are highly complex and sensitive to government subsidies, raw material pricing such as neodymium for magnets, operational degradation, maintenance costs, curtailment due to grid congestion, and the high volatility of wind itself. While wind has significant momentum—representing 40 percent of all U.S. capacity additions in 2012, with newer GE turbines and Danish offshore wind farms targeting 40 to 50 percent capacity factors—actual performance frequently underdelivers relative to consultant forecasts. 

To demonstrate this gap, Exhibit 16 displays projected versus actual wind capacity factors, measured as actual generation as a percentage of potential nameplate capacity, at locations in Ohio and New York. For the Blue Creek Wind project in Ohio, the projected capacity factor was 34.7 percent, but the actual realized capacity factor was 29.8 percent in 2013 and 26.7 percent in 2012. For Class 3–4 wind in New York, the projected capacity factor was 31 percent, whereas actual figures fell to a range of 25 percent to 29 percent. A footnote explains that because wind power is a function of wind velocity cubed, a small 10 percent reduction in wind speed causes a roughly 30 percent reduction in electricity generation, which has historically depressed returns for large portfolios, such as German closed-end wind funds.

Exhibit 17 illustrates how individual wind project performance differs substantially from industry averages. This chart plots actual generation as a percentage of potential on the y-axis against the installation vintage year on the x-axis, spanning from 1998–99 to 2011. While the power generation-weighted average capacity factor consistently clusters between 30 percent and 35 percent across all vintages, the performance of individual projects shows immense dispersion. In the 2011 vintage, which includes 63 projects totaling 5,854 megawatts, individual project capacity factors range from under 20 percent to nearly 50 percent. This dispersion underscores the author's warning that investors cannot assume the stable averages of a massive nationwide portfolio of 446 wind farms will be consistently realized in smaller subsets. Additionally, the U.S. Department of Energy notes that while modern projects benefit from larger rotor diameters and taller towers, these technological improvements are being partially offset because newer wind farms are increasingly built in less optimal wind locations.

This page presents Appendix II on infrastructure performance based on a study from the Center for Private Equity Research (CEPRES) conducted by professors Florian Bitsch, Axel Buchner, and Christoph Kaserer at Technische Universität in Munich. The study examines 363 infrastructure deals from 1971 to 2009 to evaluate returns and risks. The main observation is that while infrastructure investment returns significantly exceeded those of venture capital and private equity during similar vintage years, there was exceptionally high dispersion among the returns, meaning there were many high-performing assets alongside some very poor performers. The dataset is heavily dominated by U.S. and European telecommunication privatizations from the late 1990s, and the author cautions that future privatizations may not mirror this historical performance. 

By sector, telecommunication investments made up 59% of the analyzed deals, followed by natural resources and energy at 25%, transportation at 13%, and alternative energy at 3%. Geographically, the deals were concentrated in Europe and North America, which each accounted for 43% of the total, while Asia represented 8% and the rest of the world made up 6%. 

The page includes two exhibits to illustrate these findings. Exhibit A2.1 is a bar chart showing the distribution of infrastructure deals by year from 1971 to 2007. It reveals that deal activity was minimal before the mid-1990s, surged dramatically in the late 1990s, and peaked around 1998 and 2001—where annual deals represented up to 12% of the overall dataset—before tapering off after 2002. 

Exhibit A2.2 is a performance comparison table tracking internal rate of return (IRR) and investment multiples across different private asset classes from 1971 to 2007. The data shows that overall infrastructure delivered an average IRR of 67% and a median IRR of 19%, compared to non-infrastructure's average of 20% and median of 6%. However, infrastructure showed a high standard deviation of 300%. When broken down by development stage, early-stage greenfield infrastructure achieved an average IRR of 46% and a median IRR of 5%, strongly outperforming venture capital, which saw an average IRR of 6% and a median IRR of negative 22%. Established brownfield infrastructure outperformed late-stage private equity across all metrics, posting an average IRR of 91% and a median IRR of 36%, compared to late-stage private equity's average IRR of 40% and median IRR of 25%. In terms of valuation multiples, brownfield infrastructure led all categories with an average multiple of 3.3x and a median of 2.5x, compared to late-stage private equity's average of 2.9x and median of 2.0x.

The key qualitative findings from this data highlight that infrastructure investing carried a lower risk of total capital loss, with only 5.26% of brownfield infrastructure deals ending in complete write-offs compared to 9% for late-stage private equity. Additionally, European infrastructure investments outperformed other regions. The study's authors suggest this European outperformance was driven by governments failing to prioritize the maximization of asset sales prices, which allowed private sector buyers to acquire assets at favorable valuations and subsequently realize substantial gains by correcting operational inefficiencies.

This page from JP Morgan’s Eye on the Market argues that an upturn in the Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) serves as the most reliable "buy" signal for US equities following major market downturns since the end of the Gold Standard. 

To support this claim, the page presents four charts comparing the 30-day moving average of the S&P 500 index level on the left axis against the Manufacturing PMI index level on the right axis across four distinct historical crises. The first chart, depicting the 1970s stagflation crisis from 1973 to 1978, illustrates that the S&P 500 bottomed in late 1974 just as the PMI reached its trough of around 35 and began to turn upward. The second chart focuses on the 1980s inflation and housing crisis between 1981 and 1984, showing that the S&P 500's bottom in late 1982 coincided closely with the PMI's upturn from its low of approximately 35. The third chart covers the tech collapse from 1999 to 2006, highlighting that the Manufacturing PMI bottomed earlier in late 2001 at roughly 43, acting as a leading indicator before the S&P 500 finally bottomed in late 2002 and early 2003. The fourth chart displays the Global Financial Crisis from 2007 to 2013, showing the S&P 500 bottoming in early 2009 alongside a sharp recovery in the PMI, which had plunged to a low of nearly 33. 

The page also includes an informational summary explaining the mechanics of the PMI. It contrasts the surveys compiled by Markit Group and the Institute for Supply Management (ISM), noting that the ISM version has a much longer US history dating back to 1948. The ISM PMI is constructed by surveying approximately 400 companies across 20 industries, with responses weighted by each industry’s relative share of US GDP. Designed as a diffusion index, a reading above 50 indicates that manufacturing activity is expanding, while a reading below 50 indicates contraction. The headline index is a weighted average of five core components: employment, new orders, inventories, production, and business activity.

This page explores the timing and drivers of the European equity market recovery in the early 2010s, emphasizing how markets often turn around well before economic indicators fully recover or the financial press gives the signal to reinvest. The author argues that the durable portion of the European equity recovery was closely tied to two key catalysts: the European Central Bank’s implicit guarantee, marked by Mario Draghi’s famous "whatever it takes" speech in the summer of 2012, and the inflection point in the manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index, even when the PMI remained in contractionary territory below 50. 

To support this argument, a chart titled "Equity recovery more closely aligned with ECB..." compares the STOXX European Broad equity index, measured on the left axis from 225 to 350, against the Spanish and Italian 5-Year Credit Default Swap spreads in basis points, measured on the right axis from 0 to 600, between 2010 and 2014. It highlights Draghi’s speech in mid-2012 as a clear turning point, showing how the STOXX index rebounded from a low near 225 just as the Spanish and Italian CDS spreads peaked near 600 basis points and subsequently plummeted, signaling restored market confidence. 

An adjacent chart, titled "...and the turn in leading indicators", tracks the STOXX European Broad equity index alongside the Manufacturing PMI from 2010 to 2013. The PMI, plotted on the right axis ranging from 44 to 60, bottomed out at approximately 44 in late 2011 before turning upward. The author points out that this upward turn in momentum, rather than the absolute level of the PMI, was the critical indicator for bottom-feeding investors, as the equity index steadily climbed from its lows in lockstep with the improving, though still contractionary, PMI. 

The page also notes that overall market valuations can be misleading during crises. While European equities as a whole traded at approximately 11 times trailing earnings in the summer of 2011, this average obscured massive dispersion across specific countries and sectors. A table titled "Trailing price-to-earnings ratios across countries and sectors in September 2011" details these valuations across Germany, France, Italy, and Spain. During the market bottom, French financials traded at a remarkably low trailing P/E ratio of 5.2x, and German consumer discretionary stocks stood at 5.9x. Conversely, defensive consumer staples in Spain commanded a P/E of 38.3x, and French staples were at 21.5x. Industrials in Spain were exceptionally depressed at 5.6x, while German industrials sat at 10.6x. The author concludes that these single-digit P/Es in substantial market segments demonstrated that investors had already priced in an immense amount of negative news, creating a compelling entry point for risk-tolerant investors well before mainstream market research recommended re-investing.

This page analyzes the effectiveness of the European Purchasing Managers' Index as a leading indicator for stock market performance, arguing that the PMI does nearly as good of a job marking equity bottoms in Europe as it does in the United States. The author notes that while the signals are not flawless, they consistently serve as a reliable cue for investors to put capital back at risk before actual economic conditions have fully improved.

To demonstrate this relationship, the page features four separate line charts plotting the STOXX European Broad equity index on the left axis against the Manufacturing PMI on the right axis across different historical crises. The first chart covers the Asia, Russia, and LTCM Crisis from December 1997 to June 2000. It shows the STOXX index, measured from 225 to 385, and the Manufacturing PMI, measured from 46 to 60, both bottoming in late 1998. The PMI troughed just above 48, closely matching the equity index bottoming near 245, after which both indicators steadily climbed.

The second chart illustrates the Tech Collapse from 2000 to 2006, with the STOXX index scaled from 170 to 380 and the PMI from 42 to 60. During this period, the PMI found its initial bottom near 44 in late 2001, serving as an early indicator before the equity index finished carving out its double bottom near 205 in early 2003. 

The third chart displays the Financial Crisis from 2006 to 2009, with the STOXX index scale spanning 150 to 400 and the PMI index level spanning 32 to 59. Here, the PMI fell precipitously to a bottom near 35 in early 2009, which coincided almost perfectly with the bottoming of the STOXX index near 170 before a sharp recovery ensued. 

The final chart details the Eurozone sovereign debt crisis from 2010 to 2013, with the STOXX index scaled from 220 to 340 and the PMI scaled from 42 to 60. During this crisis, the PMI hit a low point near 44 in late 2011 and early 2012, flagging the bottoming out of the STOXX index around 230 to 240, after which both lines steadily rose throughout 2013. Collectively, these charts reinforce the observation that tracking PMI turnarounds is a highly useful tactical tool for European equity investors.

This page from the April 2014 issue of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market presents a historical case study of Brazil between 1997 and 2000 to illustrate the timing of market rallies relative to macroeconomic indicators following a currency devaluation. The author argues that Brazil's 1998 currency devaluation coincided almost immediately with a recovery in the Bovespa equity index. Waiting for lagging indicators like industrial production or export growth to turn around, or waiting for inflation to peak and subside, would have caused an investor to miss the majority of the stock market rally. 

To support this observation, the page features four comparative line charts, all tracking the Bovespa equity index level on their primary left axis (ranging from 6,000 to 18,000) from 1997 to 2000. 

The first chart shows that the Bovespa rise coincided with the Real devaluation. It plots the Bovespa index against the currency exchange rate in BRL per USD on the right axis (ranging from 1.00 to 2.00). In early 1999, the sharp devaluation of the Real, where the currency level jumped from approximately 1.21 to nearly 2.00 BRL per USD, directly aligned with the bottoming out and subsequent rapid ascent of the equity index. 

The second chart demonstrates how the Bovespa recovery preceded the rise in industrial production. Plotting industrial production on the right axis (indexed to 2002 equals 100, ranging from 84 to 104), the data shows that industrial production did not bottom out until later in 1999, around a level of 88, lagging the stock market’s initial rebound. However, the author notes that industrial production still serves as an effective investment signal.

The third chart illustrates how the equity market recovery preceded the export recovery by about a year. It tracks nominal exports in billions of USD on a three-month moving average on the right axis (ranging from $3.7 billion to $4.9 billion). Nominal exports bottomed out at roughly $3.8 billion in early 1999 and did not show a sustained upward trajectory until late 1999 and into 2000, long after the equity market had already surged. 

The fourth chart displays how the market upturn preceded the downturn in inflation by about one and a half years. Measuring Year-over-Year inflation on the right axis (from 0% to 10%), the chart shows that inflation rose steadily after the devaluation, peaking at nearly 9% in late 1999 before starting to decline in 2000. This reinforces the author's point that waiting for inflation to cool would have meant missing the bulk of the equity rally. Data for these charts is sourced from the Financial Times, Banco Central do Brasil, IBGE, and the IMF.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses historical patterns in credit markets, highlighting that for high-yield credit investors, the absolute bottom in credit markets—coinciding with the peak in credit spreads—occurs long before corporate defaults peak. Furthermore, this bottom aligns closely with turning points in Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index indicators. The author argues that credit spreads peak and begin to recover even as bad news and actual corporate failures continue to rise, meaning bottom-feeding investors who wait for defaults to peak will miss the ideal entry point. 

The first chart, titled "Peak credit spreads coincide with bottom in PMI," plots high-yield credit spreads measured as spread-to-worst on the left axis from 500 to 1,300, against the Manufacturing PMI index level on the right axis from 37 to 57. The horizontal axis measures months from the cyclical trough in PMI, ranging from negative 12 to positive 24 months. Based on data from the 1991, 2001, and 2008 cycles, the chart illustrates that high-yield credit spreads peaked precisely at month zero, coinciding exactly with the bottoming out of the Manufacturing PMI.

Three subsequent charts analyze the lag between peak high-yield spreads and cumulative defaults during major crises, measuring the spread-to-worst on the left vertical axis and the cumulative number of defaulting issuers on the right vertical axis. The first of these, titled "Savings and Loan Crisis," spans 1987 to 1993 and shows that high-yield credit spreads peaked when cumulative defaults had reached only 55% of their ultimate cycle total. The second, titled "Tech collapse," spans 1999 to 2004 and shows that high-yield credit spreads peaked when cumulative defaults stood at 76% of their eventual total. The final chart, titled "Financial crisis," spans 2006 to 2013 and shows that high-yield spreads peaked when only 30% of eventual defaults had occurred. This visual data underscores that seventy percent of defaults in the most recent crisis took place after high-yield spreads had already peaked, rewarding diversified investors who put capital to work in 2009 despite prevailing negative headlines.

This appendix page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market publication examines the relationship between equity market performance and the unemployment rate, illustrating that unemployment is a lagging market indicator. The central argument is that by the time a durable and convincing decline in the unemployment rate is underway, equity markets have typically already bottomed out roughly a year earlier. 

To support this observation, the page displays four historical comparison charts, each plotting the S&P 500 index level as a 30-day moving average against the US unemployment rate using data sourced from Bloomberg and the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The first chart, covering the 1970s stagflation crisis from 1973 to 1978, shows the S&P 500 bottoming around late 1974 near an index level of 70, while the unemployment rate did not peak at 9.0% and begin to reliably decline until late 1975. The second chart, focused on the 1980s inflation and housing crisis between 1981 and 1984, shows the stock index finding its low point near 105 in mid-1982, whereas the unemployment rate peaked near 10.8% in late 1982 before starting its downward path in 1983. 

The third chart illustrates the tech collapse era from 1999 to 2006, where the S&P 500 bottomed around 800 in late 2002 to early 2003, while the unemployment rate peaked at approximately 6.3% in mid-2003. Lastly, the fourth chart shows the Great Financial Crisis period from 2007 to 2013, with the stock market bottoming in early 2009 near an index level of 700, while the national unemployment rate did not peak at 10% and begin its durable decline until late 2009 or early 2010. Across all four historical crises, the visual evidence consistently demonstrates that waiting for unemployment to improve before buying equities would cause investors to miss the initial year of stock market recovery.

This page analyzes how US states share responsibility for pension Annual Required Contributions (ARCs) with local entities, highlighting that states with the highest debt service ratios tend to carry a disproportionate burden for local teacher pension plans. 

The first table categorizes states by their aggregate share of state-run pension plan ARCs in 2012. States with a low share (0% to 25%), such as Arizona, Florida, and Ohio, rely heavily on local entities to cover these liabilities and consequently enjoy lower state-level debt ratios. In contrast, states in the highest tier (75% to 100%), including Connecticut, Illinois, Kentucky, Maryland, and Massachusetts, assume nearly all of the pension burden at the state level. 

The second table examines the ten states with the highest debt service ratios, displaying the percentage of their 2012 pension ARC devoted to the state-run teacher plan and their share of responsibility for employer contributions into that plan. For nearly all of these highly indebted states, the state assumes 100% responsibility for the teacher plan contributions. For instance, New Jersey devotes 60% of its pension ARC to its teacher plan, Illinois devotes 52%, West Virginia devotes 74%, and Maryland devotes 63%, all with 100% state responsibility. Hawaii and Delaware are exceptions because they do not have distinct pension plans for teachers, while Louisiana is a unique outlier in this group, devoting only 6% of its pension ARC to its teacher plan with a mere 4% state responsibility. The author notes that even when cities make offsetting payments to the state, discussions with Moody's suggest these payments do not substantially reduce the state's net obligation.

This analysis examines state-level debt service ratios when recomputed based on Annual Required Contributions (ARC) for pensions and Other Post-Employment Benefits (OPEB) rather than actual current payments. The author points out that several states, most notably New Jersey, face dramatic increases under this recomputation due to historically low actual contributions relative to their ARCs and more conservative actuarial determinations. 

The first stacked bar chart displays the percentage of state revenue collections required to cover interest on bonded debt, defined benefit plan contributions, retiree healthcare, and defined contribution expenses. Sorted from highest to lowest burden, the chart compares actual current payments to the state actuarial assumptions for accruals. New Jersey leads the country, with its ratio jumping from roughly 10% under current payments to over 30% when applying actuarial assumptions. Connecticut is the second highest, hovering around 25%, followed by Hawaii, Illinois, and West Virginia, all of which exceed a 15% threshold marked by a green horizontal line. A red horizontal line highlights a 25% warning threshold, which only New Jersey and Connecticut exceed or reach under accrual assumptions.

The second chart uses the same y-axis and state-by-state ordering to break down these ARC-based debt service ratios into four cost components: interest on bonds, pension contributions, OPEB contributions, and defined contribution plan expenses. The narrative highlights that the composition of these liabilities varies significantly by state, which has major implications for potential cost mitigation because states have historically been more active and successful in restructuring OPEB than pensions. For instance, Hawaii and Delaware show a much larger burden from OPEB than pensions, whereas Illinois has a significantly larger pension burden. In Connecticut, New Jersey, and West Virginia, the financial burden is split roughly equally between pension and OPEB liabilities. Bond interest also represents a notable share of the total for states like Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Illinois, while defined contribution plan expenses make up a negligible fraction of the overall state liabilities across the board.

This analysis examines whether Russian and broader Emerging Markets (EM) equities have become cheap enough to attract investors. The author notes that Russia is the least expensive of the major EM equity markets, trading at a sector-neutral forward P/E discount compared to peers. If not normalized for Russia’s heavy concentration in oil companies, which typically trade at lower multiples, its forward P/E sits at a historically low 4.5x. While Russian equities historically kept pace with overall emerging markets, they decoupled and significantly underperformed following the escalation of the Ukraine crisis in early 2014.

Six charts support these observations on valuation and performance. The first chart, showing sector-neutral 12-month forward P/E multiples from 2006 to 2014, compares Russia against Taiwan, South Africa, Brazil, Korea, and China. Russia consistently sits at the bottom of this group, with its multiple hovering below 7x by 2014. The second chart details this underperformance by plotting total returns indexed to January 2013 for the MSCI Russia and MSCI Emerging Markets indices. The two series closely tracked each other until early February 2014, when MSCI Russia plummeted to an index value near 75 while MSCI EM stabilized around 95. 

On an aggregate level, the discount of EM equities relative to developed markets continues to widen due to a lack of an earnings catalyst. Two comparative charts show price-to-book and sector-neutral forward P/E ratios from 2008 to 2014 across the US, Europe, the World, and Emerging Markets. On a price-to-book basis, EM is the cheapest region at approximately 1.4x, compared to the US at over 2.6x. On a forward P/E basis, EM trades near 10.5x, well below the US at nearly 16x and Europe at 13x. 

The historical trajectory of this valuation gap is illustrated in a fifth chart, which tracks the EM price-to-book ratio divided by the Developed World price-to-book ratio from 2004 to 2014. This ratio went from a peak premium of nearly 20% in late 2009 to a discount of nearly -30% by early 2014. Finally, the lack of an earnings catalyst is highlighted in a comparison of forward 12-month earnings per share from 2003 to 2014 for the S&P 500 and MSCI Emerging Markets. While S&P 500 earnings expectations have risen steadily to over $110, EM earnings expectations have flatlined and trended slightly downward since 2011, explaining why lower share prices are required to draw investors back to emerging markets.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market addresses the economic complexity of imposing sanctions on Russia, comparing European and American business ties with Russia and exploring Europe's deep reliance on Russian natural gas. The author argues that European-Russian business interests are far larger than US-Russian trade, making the sanctions discussion highly complex for Europe. Specifically, Europe is Russia’s main trading partner, accounting for 45 percent of Russian imports and 55 percent of its exports, with 65 percent of those imports being energy-related. Additionally, the European Union represents 80 percent of cumulative foreign investment in Russia, prompting major companies like BP, which holds a 20 percent stake in Rosneft, to warn of negative consequences from severe sanctions.

To visualize these economic links, the first chart, titled "Russia-EU ties are 10x Russia-US ties," displays exports and imports combined as a percentage of GDP to illustrate the importance of these bilateral trading relationships. On the left side of the chart, representing the importance of Russia to developed market economies, Russia-EU trade accounts for 2.2 percent of the European Union's GDP, whereas Russia-US trade accounts for only 0.2 percent of the United States GDP. On the right side, showing the importance of developed market economies to Russia, trade with the European Union represents a substantial 18.7 percent of Russia's GDP, while trade with the United States represents just 1.6 percent.

The second section of the page assesses Europe’s reliance on Russian natural gas and evaluates whether United States liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports could realistically offset this dependence. A detailed table, titled "Russia's share of natural gas imports across Europe," outlines the percentage of total natural gas imports coming from Russia for various European nations. The data highlights extreme dependence in Eastern and Northern Europe: Finland relies on Russia for 100 percent of its imports, followed closely by Slovakia at 93 percent, Poland at 82 percent, Hungary at 81 percent, Greece at 78 percent, the Czech Republic at 66 percent, Austria at 62 percent, and Turkey at 57 percent. Larger Western European economies show lower but still significant dependence, including Germany at 35 percent, Belgium at 24 percent, Italy at 20 percent, France at 16 percent, and the Netherlands at 14 percent. The text notes that this exposure could rise as Gazprom co-invests in natural gas projects in Algeria, which is currently the third-largest gas exporter to Europe.

Regarding the feasibility of US LNG exports replacing Russian gas, the author explains that while the math looks simple on paper—given that the United States produces 723 billion cubic meters of natural gas annually compared to Europe’s 130 billion cubic meters of imports from Russia—the physical and economic realities are highly challenging. First, US export facilities are slow to receive approval, expensive, and time-consuming to construct, with the earliest completions scheduled for 2015 and 2018. Additionally, European nations would need to construct substantial LNG import infrastructure. Crucially, the author points out that private sector dynamics, rather than government mandates, will dictate where US LNG is sold. Asian markets, such as South Korea, India, and Japan, are likely to outbid European buyers, meaning US exports might not redirect to Europe at all. Finally, because of geographic proximity and its possession of the world's largest proven natural gas reserves, Russia could easily undercut US LNG pricing, raising an open question of how much premium Europe would actually pay for more reliable American energy.

This page analyzed the significant cumulative impact on US state budgets when applying a conservative 6% pension investment return assumption combined with 30-year level amortization payments. While shifting the return assumption to 6% has a modest incremental effect on its own, the overall transition to level payments would severely strain the revenues of several states, particularly those currently underfunding their obligations. 

The first chart illustrates the percentage of state revenue collections required to cover interest on bonded debt, defined benefit plan contributions, retiree health care costs, and defined contribution plan expenses across all fifty states. It contrasts a model of 30-year level payments for unfunded liabilities, represented by blue bars, with the incremental impact of adopting a 6% pension investment return, shown in gold. Green and red horizontal threshold lines are set at 15% and 25%, respectively. For the most fiscally stressed states on the left—Illinois, Connecticut, Hawaii, New Jersey, and Kentucky—the combined retirement cost burden exceeds 30%, with Illinois approaching 40% of its total revenue collections. 

The second chart uses the same axes to compare actual current state payments, in blue, against the total projected costs of a 30-year level-payment model with a 6% return, in gold. This comparison highlights a stark funding gap. While Illinois currently spends roughly 18% of its revenue on these costs, a transition to currently funding its liabilities under the revised assumptions would require nearly 40% of its revenue, indicating an acute budgetary challenge. 

The text at the bottom clarifies that these charts do not revise discount rate assumptions for Other Post-Employment Benefits (OPEB), such as retiree health care. Because most states have not substantially prefunded OPEB liabilities, they already use lower discount rates to value them. The median OPEB discount rate across states is 4.5%, and only five states use a rate above 6%. Consequently, OPEB liabilities and annual required contribution payments remain unchanged in the visual calculations.

This page contains Appendix B from a J.P. Morgan report, focusing on "Debt supported by tax and other general revenues." The section details the methodology used to calculate "net tax-supported debt" for US states as of the end of 2012. An inset box defines the Debt Service Ratio (DSR) formula as DSR equals the sum of I, P, O, and D, divided by R. To align the debt service numerator with a denominator that represents state tax and general revenue collections, the analysis only includes bonds whose repayment is sourced from those specific collections.

A comprehensive table, titled "Description of Net Tax-Supported Debt" and sourced from Moody's, contrasts the types of debt that are included in this metric versus those that are excluded. Included debt types comprise general obligation (G.O.) debt paid from statewide taxes and fees, appropriation-backed bonds, lease revenue bonds, special tax bonds secured by statewide taxes and fees, highway bonds secured by gas taxes and DMV fees, GARVEE highway bonds, lottery bonds, moral obligation debt paid from statewide taxes and fees, capital leases, public-private partnerships (P3s) with state concession obligations, and pension obligation bonds. Excluded debt categories consist of self-supporting G.O. debt and moral obligation debt with an established history of being paid from non-tax or non-general revenues, tobacco securitization bonds with no state backup, unemployment insurance obligation bonds, debt guaranteed but not paid by the state, special assessment bonds, and revenue bonds of state enterprises such as toll roads.

The text also highlights that some states run large negative balances in their General Funds. If these negative balances were factored in as additional bonded debt, the debt service ratios for states with particularly large negative balances relative to their bonds—specifically California, West Virginia, and Illinois—would increase by one percentage point.

This page presents a scenario analysis focusing on public pension amortization terms and the potential fiscal impact of a future market correction on U.S. states. It addresses recommendations by the Society of Actuaries to shorten amortization terms from the typical thirty years down to fifteen or twenty years. The author notes that while shorter terms are structurally healthier, they disproportionately increase the immediate debt service burden on states that are already heavily underfunded, raising ratios by an additional seven to ten percent for the five worst-performing states.

The first chart, titled "Comparison of amortization terms," illustrates the percentage of state revenue collections required to cover interest on bonded debt, alongside state shares of defined benefit plan contributions, retiree health care costs, and defined contribution plan expenses. It contrasts a baseline thirty-year term, shown in blue, with a fifteen-year term, shown as a gold increment. A red reference line is set at twenty-five percent and a green reference line is set at fifteen percent. The chart reveals that for the most distressed states—specifically Hawaii, Illinois, Connecticut, and New Jersey—shifting to a fifteen-year term pushes their revenue requirement well above thirty-five percent, with Hawaii and Illinois exceeding forty percent. Conversely, the majority of states remain below the fifteen percent threshold.

The second chart, titled "Impact of a bear market correction," models the consequences of a bear market correction where pension assets remain flat over a three-year period while liabilities continue to grow at five percent per year. This chart compares the baseline level payment of unfunded liabilities under a thirty-year term (blue bars) to the incremental impact of the bear market scenario (gold bars). In this scenario, Illinois, Connecticut, Hawaii, New Jersey, and Kentucky face the highest overall revenue requirements, though the incremental impact of the bear market remains modest because the resulting asset-liability gap is amortized over a long thirty-year horizon.

This page analyzes the systemic risks of traditional market-cap weighted investing, arguing that it naturally leads to dangerous concentrations of risk and overvaluation. The author highlights historical precedents within the S&P 500, such as the US tech sector rising from a 6% index weight in 1990 to 29% in 1999, and the US financials sector growing from 7.5% in 1990 to 22% in 2006. 

To demonstrate this pattern globally, the analysis segments equities into 40 region-sector buckets from 1995 to 2011. Two scatter plots illustrate the subsequent performance of these buckets relative to the MSCI World Total Return Index. The first chart plots the percentage increase in a region-sector's weight over a 24-month period against its relative return over the subsequent 18 months. The distribution demonstrates that when region-sector weights balloon, they subsequently underperform the market. The second scatter plot evaluates relative volatility over a 36-month period against subsequent 18-month returns, revealing a similar pattern of underperformance for highly volatile sectors. The author notes that a circled group of outliers on this chart, representing Asia ex-Japan tech stocks in the late 1990s, also went on to underperform shortly after the analyzed time horizon ended.

To counter these risks, the author proposes an active investment strategy designed to limit exposure to overvalued and highly volatile region-sectors. This framework can be enhanced by integrating classic stock-picking factors, as illustrated in the bottom bar chart, which measures excess returns versus the MSCI World Index from December 1995 to December 2012. The chart breaks down performance across five quintiles for Value, Size, Momentum, and Low Volatility. The first quintile, representing the most favorable exposures, shows consistent outperformance, led by Momentum at approximately 5% excess return, followed by Value and Size at roughly 3.5%, and Low Volatility at nearly 2%. In contrast, the fifth quintile represents significant underperformance, particularly for Momentum, which drags returns down by more than 5%. The author suggests that combining sector-limiting rules with these long-standing factors offers substantial benefits over a standard market-cap weighted approach.

This page examines the historical relationship between global geopolitical conflicts and US equity market performance, arguing that military confrontations generally have limited medium-term impacts on the S&P 500. A small table highlights that while conflict-ridden countries represent 11.7% of the global population and 9.0% of oil production, they account for less than 4% of foreign direct investment, GDP, and trade, and under 1% of global corporate profits and equity market capitalization, which explains their minimal footprint on global financial markets. 

Two charts trace the S&P 500 index from twelve months before to twenty-four months after major military events. The first chart, covering 1950 to 1968, plots index trajectories for the Korean War, the Soviet invasion of Hungary, the Six-Day War, and the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia, demonstrating that these events did not trigger severe market downturns. The second chart, tracking 1973 to 1983, shows that the 1973 Arab-Israeli War was a major exception, causing a sharp equity decline to around 60% of its initial value due to the subsequent Saudi oil embargo and resulting US energy crisis. In contrast, other events of this era—such as the Soviet war in Afghanistan, martial law in Poland, the Falklands War, and the US invasion of Grenada—had negligible market impacts, with the market decline in 1981 driven instead by a domestic recession and the Volcker Fed's anti-inflation policies. Overall, the author emphasizes that the business cycle remains a far more critical factor for investors than geopolitical conflicts.

In this section of the publication, Michael Cembalest from J.P. Morgan Asset Management shifts focus from investments to medical innovation, exploring how mining DNA patterns could help cure childhood diseases. He discusses his conversations with Stephen Friend of the non-profit Sage Bionetworks, who previously led cancer research efforts at Merck, regarding an initiative called The Resilience Project. The core premise is to identify EX-Men, which refers to individuals over the age of forty who remained healthy during childhood despite carrying genetic mutations that normally cause severe, single-gene diseases like cystic fibrosis, Tay-Sachs, or ataxia. If scientists can isolate the genetic or environmental factors that blocked these diseases, they could develop breakthrough preventive therapies.

To explain the underlying biological concept, the page includes a diagram titled DNA Mutations: some can be beneficial, which illustrates how a mutation can result in a beneficial copy rather than the original disease-causing sequence. A supporting table titled The Resilience Project: snapshot of potential EX-Men so far highlights nine potential EX-Men identified in preliminary sampling. The table lists two individuals carrying mutations normally associated with Cystic Fibrosis (c.1558G to c.1558T), two with Smith-Lemli-Opitz Syndrome mutations (c.964-1G to c.964-1C), and single individuals with mutations associated with Familial Dysautonomia, Sanfilippo Syndrome, Epidermolysis Bullosa, Pfeiffer Syndrome, and APECED. 

Looking to the future, Sage Bionetworks seeks to analyze over one million DNA samples collected via swab. Recent advances allow these samples to be analyzed for under one hundred dollars each, a cost that should fall further with scale. To reach this goal, Sage hopes to incorporate the project into the wellness programs of large corporations and institutions. They plan to use an open-source approach to keep findings in the public domain and accelerate the global discovery of new treatments.

This page, titled "Appendix: a petro-sectarian map of the Middle East," argues that global energy markets are highly sensitive to Middle Eastern sectarian conflicts because the region's primary oil and gas deposits are heavily concentrated near sectarian fault lines. It highlights that while Iraqi oil fields in the south near Basra are secure and generate seventy-five percent of the country's production, northern exports from Kirkuk remain low due to pipeline attacks in areas outside Kurdish control.

The visual focus of the page is a detailed map from the Columbia University Gulf2000 Project showing the distribution of primary oil and gas deposits overlaid with the religious demographics of the Middle East, Caucasus, and Central Asia. The map colors denote various Islamic groups, specifically highlighting Shiite-majority areas in blue, Sunni-majority areas in green, and Wahhabi/Salafi areas in pale green. Major oil fields, super-giant oil fields, and major gas fields are marked, demonstrating a clear geographical overlap between energy reserves and Shiite-populated regions. Annotations on the map point out that this correlation is especially strong from Azerbaijan down through the Persian Gulf, noting that three-quarters of Saudi Arabia's oil deposits lie within its eastern, Shia-inhabited districts such as Hasa, Qatif, and Hofuf, as well as the adjoining continental shelf.

A horizontal bar chart in the lower-left corner displays proven developed combined oil and gas reserves in billions of barrels of oil equivalent as of the end of 2004, sourced from PFC Energy and The Economist. The data compares five key nations, showing Russia with the largest reserves at approximately two hundred eighty billion barrels of oil equivalent, followed closely by Iran and Saudi Arabia at around two hundred sixty billion barrels each. Qatar holds about one hundred sixty billion barrels of oil equivalent, and Iraq rounds out the group with roughly one hundred twenty billion barrels.

This page focuses on the European Central Bank's highly accommodative monetary policy and explores why Germany has unexpectedly acquiesced to these easy-money initiatives. The author argues that part of the answer lies in low inflation across the continent. Although the first chart, "Germany: house prices," shows year-over-year home price growth surging from flat or negative levels before 2010 to around 5% by 2012, the second chart on "Germany: wage inflation" reveals that industrial and construction wages remain controlled, trending between 2% and 3% in 2013, far below the pre-recession high of nearly 6% in 2008. Furthermore, the "Euro area core inflation" chart shows that from 2008 to 2013, core inflation across Germany, Core Europe excluding Germany, and the Periphery has persistently run below the ECB’s 2.0% target. By late 2013, Periphery inflation approached 0%, while German core inflation hovered under 1.5%, mitigating German fears of immediate runaway inflation. 

The author also posits that Germany's acquiescence may stem from a need to support a struggling France. The fourth chart, "France: Vive la Difference," illustrates a divergence between rising valuations and stagnant economic activity from 2004 to 2014. While the forward price-to-earnings multiple has expanded significantly from under 10 in 2011 to approximately 14 by 2014, year-over-year earnings growth has languished in negative or near-zero territory, and industrial production has flatlined near a reading of 100. This economic stagnation draws parallels to French President François Mitterrand's policy volte-face in 1982, prompting questions about whether François Hollande’s current corporate tax cuts and pension reforms will trigger a similar market rally. Ultimately, the author concludes that European valuation expansion has likely run its course, leaving future market progress dependent on genuine earnings growth.

This page argues that the Federal Reserve is facing mounting pressure to abandon its zero-percent interest rate policy, as various economic indicators suggest the U.S. economy has progressed to a mid-cycle phase where emergency monetary policy is no longer justified. 

To illustrate this tension, the page features a prominent graphic of a boiling pot labeled "United States Federal Reserve" sitting atop rising flames. Inside the pot are frogs labeled with the names of dovish Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) members: Charles Evans, Eric Rosengren, Janet Yellen, Narayana Kocherlakota, and William Dudley. A footnote explains that these dovish members represent those who would be the last to "jump out" of the zero-percent interest rate pot. 

The heat sources beneath the pot are detailed in a list of twenty economic indicators, color-coded by how much they pressure the Fed to hike rates. The hottest indicators prompting policy normalization include the job opening rate reaching prior-cycle highs, a rapid decline in the unemployment rate, elevated risk-taking in credit markets, a structural decline in credit market liquidity, and key inflation measures rising toward 2%. Additionally, capacity utilization, durable goods orders, and business capex have returned to normal levels, while ISM prices paid signals for both manufacturing and services are expansionary at 60. Other hot metrics include rising small business plans to raise worker compensation, high M&A deal volumes, and rising M&A purchase multiples. 

Medium-heat indicators include healthy growth in corporate loans, a modest uptick in the employment cost index to 2%, and early signs of rising industrial metals prices. Conversely, several cooler indicators still support lower rates, such as inflation expectations in TIPS markets remaining below 1.5%, weak residential mortgage demand, flat import prices, high underemployment, and average hourly earnings growth stagnant at 2%.

Ultimately, the author concludes that even if the Fed does not explicitly target credit market distortions, a broader recovery in growth, shrinking excess capacity, and rising inflation make it difficult to defend current zero-rate policies. Consequently, future monthly wage and consumer price inflation reports will be closely watched, introducing heightened volatility to U.S. equity markets.

This executive summary page introduces an analysis titled "The Agony and the Ecstasy: The Risks and Rewards of a Concentrated Stock Position," authored by Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The text argues that despite the celebrated success of certain entrepreneurs, holding a concentrated stock position carries severe risks, and the odds of long-term success are heavily stacked against the average concentrated holder. 

To support this claim, the author shares several key findings from a historical analysis of Russell 3000 companies since 1980. First, roughly 40% of all stocks in this universe suffered a permanent decline of 70% or more from their peak value, with even worse rates of impairment occurring within the Technology, Biotech, and Metals & Mining sectors. Second, the median stock experienced a lifetime return of negative 54% relative to an investment in the Russell 3000 Index, with two-thirds of all individual stocks underperforming the index and 40% posting negative absolute returns. Third, when accounting for single-stock volatility, 75% of concentrated stockholders would have benefited from some degree of diversification. 

The author also notes that since 1980, over 320 companies have been removed from the S&P 500 due to business distress, illustrating the forces of creative destruction and competition. He points out that while globalization—specifically China’s acceptance into the World Trade Organization in 2001—expanded market opportunities, it also heightened operational, regulatory, and competitive risks for individual businesses. A whimsical illustration on the right side of the page depicts a grand piano falling from the sky toward a person holding a small, inadequate umbrella, metaphorically warning of the sudden, devastating risks associated with a lack of diversification.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest addresses the "prophet warnings" issued by central banks, specifically the Federal Reserve and the Bank for International Settlements, which have cautioned against a puzzling disconnect between buoyant markets and underlying economic developments. He highlights the irony of central banks expressing concern over aggressive risk-taking that was directly encouraged by their own post-2008 monetary policies. 

To put geopolitical and valuation concerns into perspective, the page features four detailed charts. The first chart, titled S&P 500 Index around military invasions and conflicts from 1991 to today, indexes the S&P 500 to 100 at the month of invasion and tracks performance from twelve months before to twenty-four months after. It maps the market’s resilient path during the 1991 US invasion of Kuwait, the 1998 Serbian invasion of Kosovo, the September 11 attacks and subsequent invasion of Afghanistan in 2001, the 2003 US invasion of Iraq, and the 2010 sinking of a South Korean navy vessel by North Korea. The visual demonstrates that equity market reactions to these events were generally mild and temporary, with indexes often recovering within weeks or months. For instance, the steep drop after September 11 reversed quickly, and the subsequent 2002 market downturn is characterized as an unraveling of the technology bust rather than an direct aftermath of geopolitical conflict.

Turning to current valuation concerns, the second chart, Equity valuations across regions, tracks forward price-to-earnings ratios from 2008 to 2014. It reveals that P/E multiples have risen across the board, with the US leading at roughly 15.5x, followed by the World index at 14.5x, Europe at 14x, and Emerging Markets lagging but still rising to approximately 11x. 

The third chart zooms in on the sectors flagged by the Federal Reserve: Internet and Biotech stocks: the secular growth stories, plotted by their price-to-sales ratios from January 2011 to July 2014. This chart shows that a basket of seventy-five secular growth stocks peaked at an elevated price-to-sales ratio near 11x in late 2013 before pulling back to around 8x. Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 Biotechnology Index and the S&P 500 Internet Software and Services Index rose dramatically from around 4x in 2011 to peaks between 7x and 8x in early 2014, while the benchmark Russell 1000 Index remained flat and conservative, hovering between 1.5x and 2x. 

The final chart, S&P 500 P/Es: Forward and median trailing, contextualizes current valuations by comparing forward price-to-earnings ratios against median trailing ratios from 1985 through mid-2014. It illustrates that while multiples have risen significantly since their post-crisis lows in 2009—with the forward P/E climbing to roughly 15x and the median trailing P/E rising to around 17x—they still remain well below the extreme peaks of 22x to 24x seen during the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s.

This page explores how equity markets historically react to Federal Reserve interest rate hikes and assesses the state of the United States economy in 2014. The main argument is that initial Fed rate hikes tend to introduce market volatility rather than trigger bear markets, with equity markets ultimately rebounding once it becomes clear that rate hikes are accompanied by sufficient economic growth and controlled inflation.

A historical table supports this argument by analyzing five tightening cycles between 1987 and 2006. Across all five cycles, the initial market reaction to the first rate hike was negative, with S&P 500 price returns dropping between 5% and 9%. However, subsequent reactions to the remaining hikes were consistently positive, ranging from 7% in the 1994–1995 cycle to 32% in 1987. Consequently, the total market reaction to the entire hiking cycle was positive in four out of five periods, with the 1994–1995 cycle being the sole exception at a minor decline of 2%. The table also tracks the two-year Treasury change in yield, showing substantial increases in yields across all cycles, culminating in total yield increases as high as 361 basis points in 2004–2006.

The second half of the page discusses how the US economic recovery in 2014 is playing out as expected, characterized by rebounding business capital spending, durable goods, and steady improvements in consumer indicators. The author forecasts a reasonable profit growth expectation of 8% to 10% for 2015, noting that higher revenue growth will likely be offset by rising labor and interest costs. 

Three charts illustrate these positive economic trends. The first chart displays light vehicle sales and pending home sales from 2004 to 2014. It shows that light vehicle sales recovered from a low of around 9 million units in 2009 to near 17 million units by 2014, while pending home sales rebounded from a low index value of 75 in 2010 to around 105 in 2014. The second chart depicts consumer confidence and consumer credit per household from 2006 to 2014. Consumer confidence steadily rose from its post-recession trough of under 30 to around 90 by mid-2014, while consumer credit expanded to over 27,000 USD per household. The final chart presents S&P 500 year-over-year earnings and revenue growth, excluding financials, from Q1 2010 to Q2 2014. While both metrics slowed from their post-recession peaks in 2010, earnings growth stabilized around 10% and revenue growth hovered near 5% by mid-2014, showing modest yet positive momentum.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market presents the final step of an empirical analysis on risk factors for concentrated stock holdings between 1980 and 2014. It weaves together three primary risks: catastrophic loss, underperforming the Russell 3000 index, and experiencing heightened volatility that would prompt an optimal portfolio model to allocate no more than twenty percent to the stock. The author argues that, with the benefit of hindsight, some amount of diversification would have been beneficial in approximately three-quarters of all cases to help sustain family wealth.

The page features a single table titled "Percent of stocks whose concentrated holders would have benefited from diversification, 1980-2014." Across all sectors combined, seventy-four percent of stocks would have benefited from diversification. By specific sector, Utilities presents the highest percentage of stocks benefiting from diversification at eighty-seven percent, followed closely by Information Technology at eighty-two percent and Energy at eighty-one percent. Other sectors with high percentages include Materials and Industrials both at seventy-five percent, Consumer Discretionary and Telecommunication Services both at seventy-four percent, and Health Care at seventy-two percent. The sectors with the lowest percentages, though still representing a clear majority, are Financials at sixty-three percent and Consumer Staples at fifty-eight percent. The data presented in the table is sourced from FactSet and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market analyzes the historical prevalence of "catastrophic loss" among individual US stocks, expanding the discussion beyond S&P 500 deletions to include small and mid-cap companies. Analyzing approximately 13,000 stocks that were members of the Russell 3000 Index between 1980 and 2014, the author defines a catastrophic loss as a decline of 70% or more from a stock's peak value with minimal recovery, leaving an eventual permanent loss of at least 60%.

An included table reveals that 40% of all Russell 3000 stocks suffered such permanent declines during this period. The risk of catastrophic loss varied significantly by sector. Information Technology experienced the highest rate at 57%, followed by Telecommunication Services at 51%, Energy at 47%, Consumer Discretionary at 43%, and Health Care at 42%. Conversely, the lowest catastrophic loss rates were found in Financials at 25% and Utilities at 13%. Other sectors sat in the middle, with Industrials at 35%, Materials at 34%, and Consumer Staples at 26%. The text highlights that specific subsectors, such as Biotech within Health Care and Metals & Mining within Materials, suffered catastrophic loss rates exceeding 50%.

A corresponding line chart tracks the catastrophic loss rates on Russell 3000 companies over time, plotting the percentage of companies in the process of suffering these unrecovered losses from 1980 through 2012. The chart demonstrates that while distress rates spike during recessions—peaking at nearly 20% during the early-2000s tech bust and climbing above 12% during the 2008 financial crisis—there is a steady baseline of distress around 10% even during economic expansions. 

Addressing the sharp drop in loss rates down to under 5% between 2010 and 2013, the author cautions against assuming a permanent shift in market health. This decline is attributed to a massive Federal Reserve monetary experiment that kept the real cost of money negative for more than five years, alongside the natural mathematical lag that gives newer companies less time to fail. Ultimately, the high historical rate of permanent decline is used to argue that diversification must remain a cornerstone of wealth management planning for concentrated stock holders.

This page analyzes the lifetime returns of individual stocks by sector from 1980 through 2014 to demonstrate that the distribution of success and failure is remarkably similar across almost all industries. The central argument is that individual stock returns are heavily skewed, with a high frequency of catastrophic declines, making diversification an essential strategy for wealth planning, particularly for entrepreneurs holding concentrated stock positions.

A key table, titled "Analysis of lifetime returns by sector, 1980-2014," compiled from FactSet and J.P. Morgan Asset Management, shows that across all sectors combined, the median excess return versus the Russell 3000 was negative 54 percent. Furthermore, 64 percent of all stocks generated negative excess returns, 40 percent generated negative absolute returns, and only 7 percent qualified as extreme winners. Looking at specific sectors, Consumer Staples was the strongest performer, with a median excess return of negative 3 percent, 51 percent negative excess returns, 26 percent negative absolute returns, and 15 percent extreme winners. Conversely, Utilities had the worst median excess return at negative 141 percent, with 85 percent of utility stocks producing negative excess returns, although only 14 percent produced negative absolute returns and none achieved extreme winner status. Other major sectors detailed include Information Technology, which had a median excess return of negative 63 percent and a negative absolute return rate of 53 percent, alongside Consumer Discretionary, Energy, Materials, Industrials, Health Care, Financials, and Telecommunication Services.

To address the counterargument that concentrated holders of some volatile tech stocks still benefit in the long run, the page includes a line chart tracking the stock price of Cisco Systems from 1990 to 2014. The chart shows that despite Cisco surviving the tech collapse, it suffered a maximum loss from its peak of negative 86 percent, and an eventual loss from its peak of negative 67 percent by 2014. Even with this extreme volatility and partial recovery, Cisco generated an annual stock price return of 27 percent from its inception compared to general market returns of 8 percent. The author points out that while Cisco is a positive life-cycle example of a stock surviving a massive decline, the negative skew of the overall market indicates that the vast majority of collapsing stocks do not replicate this success. 

The page concludes with a prominent callout box warning that the combination of frequent catastrophic stock declines and negative skew compounds the risk of holding concentrated stock, highlighting the vital role of diversification for wealth management. An explanatory footnote adds that the low frequency of negative absolute returns in Utilities is a function of the sector's lower catastrophic loss rate, which is offset by lower overall returns that lead to a high rate of negative excess returns.

This page from the publication discusses why volatility—specifically downside volatility, or semi-deviation—matters when determining the optimal size of a concentrated stock holding. The author argues that because investors are generally only concerned with falling stock prices, semi-deviation is a highly practical proxy for risk. 

To illustrate the relationship between risk and return, the page features a scatter plot titled "Higher volatility usually associated with lower stock price returns," analyzing Russell 3000 stocks with at least three years of returns between 1980 and 2014. The horizontal axis measures downside volatility (semi-deviation) from 0% to 140%, and the vertical axis shows annualized stock price returns from -100% to 200%. The data shows a clear negative correlation: as downside volatility increases, the dispersion of returns shifts downward, and higher-volatility stocks increasingly cluster in negative return territory. This indicates that rising downside volatility is strongly linked to falling returns.

Next, the author presents a historical analysis of the optimal risk-adjusted combination of an individual stock and the Russell 3000 index, using hindsight to find the weight that would have delivered the best risk-adjusted performance. The results are displayed in a bar chart titled "Optimal mix of a concentrated stock position with the Russell 3000, 1980-2014, number of observations." The vertical axis tracks the number of observations from 0 to 3,500, while the horizontal axis displays the optimal concentrated stock weight from 0% to 100% in 10% increments. 

The bar chart reveals that holding 0% of the individual concentrated stock—and 100% of the Russell 3000—was the most common optimal outcome, occurring nearly 3,400 times. The optimal allocation drops off rapidly at higher weights, with a 10% allocation appearing around 2,600 times, a 20% allocation around 1,900 times, and a 30% allocation around 1,100 times. While there is a small uptick at the 100% weight bar, showing that holding the concentrated stock exclusively was optimal about 6% of the time (representing approximately 500 observations), the majority of cases suggest holding 30% or less. This aligns with the broader reality that two-thirds of individual stocks historically underperform the Russell 3000, making a diversified index allocation the preferred risk-adjusted choice for most investors.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market analyzes the historical timing and magnitude of catastrophic loss rates—defined as companies suffering sharp, unrecovered price declines—by sector compared to the broader Russell 3000 index from 1980 through approximately 2012.
