This contraction is comparable to the collapse of Soviet-satellite economies, such as Ukraine's 50.8 percent decline and Russia's 26.4 percent decline, as well as major crises in Venezuela and Peru. Despite this depression, the author notes that markets did not suffer, partly because the vast majority of aid sent to Greece was immediately round-tripped back to European creditors.

Two charts tracking data from 2008 to 2015 illustrate how Spain and Italy have separated themselves from Greece's financial trajectory. The first chart displays the 10-year government bond yield spreads over Germany. While Greece's spread spiked drastically to nearly 35 percent in 2012 and remained highly elevated near 15 percent in 2015, the spreads for Spain and Italy peaked around 5 percent in 2012 before successfully recovering to under 2 percent by 2015. The second chart displays equity markets indexed to January 2008. It shows that while Greek equities collapsed to a fraction of their former value, bottoming out near 10, Spanish and Italian equities stabilized and rallied, with Spain recovering to an index level of nearly 80 and Italy to around 60 by mid-2015.

This analysis examines first-quarter US corporate earnings, arguing that S&P 500 performance was surprisingly resilient despite a contraction in real US GDP. While US equities face several headwinds—including anticipated Federal Reserve tightening, a rising dollar, high valuations, and record fund flows moving out of US equities (with forty billion dollars in outflows) and into international equities (with one hundred and five billion dollars in inflows) since the start of the year—robust core earnings and healthy profit margins have kept US equity returns from turning negative.

To support this view, the discussion presents several charts and a table. The first chart details the year-over-year percent change in revenues and earnings for core sectors, which exclude the financial, energy, and utility sectors. It shows that estimated core earnings growth in the first quarter of 2015 remained resilient at roughly eight percent, which is fairly consistent with 2014 performance, whereas core revenue growth hovered near three percent. The second chart focuses on S&P 500 core revenue growth from 2010 to early 2015, highlighting a downward trend since late 2011. Notably, it illustrates that while reported revenue growth in the first quarter of 2015 was low at around three percent, currency-adjusted revenue growth would have been significantly higher at approximately six percent, proving that the advancing dollar has heavily weighed on sales.

The third chart plots the percentage of large-capitalization stocks with rising profit margins from 1984 to 2014. The data demonstrates that despite historical volatility, the proportion of companies with expanding margins has risen above the fifty percent threshold and is continuing to trend upward. 

Finally, a detailed table compares S&P profit margins in the first quarter of 2015 against their historical averages from 1995 to 2014. Overall, the S&P 500 margin reached ten point five percent, notably higher than the historical average of eight point seven percent. Excluding financials, the margin was nine point five percent compared to an eight point one percent average, and excluding both financials and energy, the margin was ten point zero percent compared to an eight point two percent average. On a sector level, Information Technology boasted the highest margin at nineteen point three percent (well above its fourteen point one percent average), followed by Financials at seventeen point zero percent (above its twelve point six percent average). In contrast, Energy margins fell to five point eight percent, down from a seven point five percent average, and Telecommunication Services slipped to nine point eight percent from a ten point six percent average. Most other sectors, including Health Care, Industrials, Materials, and Utilities, posted margins that exceeded their long-term averages.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, argues that slower global economic growth and muted equity market gains in 2015 are driven by major structural headwinds rather than geopolitical conflicts in war-torn regions. To prove that geopolitical hotspots are not the proximate cause of market weakness, a table titled "War zone countries as a % of total world..." highlights that while these conflict areas account for 11.7% of the global population, their actual global economic and financial footprints are minuscule. Specifically, they represent only 9.0% of oil production, 3.8% of foreign direct investment, 3.0% of GDP, 2.6% of trade, 0.7% of equity market capitalization, and a mere 0.4% of portfolio investment inflows.

Instead of geopolitical crises, the author identifies four key factors restraining markets, illustrated through a series of charts and tables. The first factor is the surge in the US dollar, driven by super-easy monetary policy in Europe, Japan, and China. An accompanying line chart titled "The surge in the dollar" plots the USD real broad effective exchange rate index from 1980 to 2015, showing a rapid spike starting around 2014 that pushed the index value well past 110, near levels last seen in the early 2000s.

The second factor is the end of the global fixed investment boom linked to Chinese infrastructure and commodity consumption. A line chart depicting global business fixed investment as a percentage of GDP from 1970 to 2014 shows historical peaks, labeling the late-1970s "EM and commodity boom," the late-1980s "Japanese boom," and the recent "China and commodity boom" which peaked near 16% in the early 2010s before turning downward.

The third headwind is high aggregate debt. A line chart titled "Despite a painful recession, overall economy-wide debt levels did not decline" displays non-financial total debt as a percentage of GDP from 2001 to 2013. The data reveals that debt has continually expanded post-crisis rather than deleveraging, with developed market debt rising from roughly 200% to 260% of GDP, global debt rising from 160% to over 200% of GDP, and emerging market debt climbing to approximately 150% of GDP.

The fourth factor is highly stretched investor positioning heading into 2015. A table titled "Market sentiment and positioning elevated heading into 2015" measures various sentiment indicators as of December 2014 against their historical percentiles. The AAII bull/bear ratio was at the 91st percentile (since 1987), Investors Intelligence Advisory Sentiment was at the 94th percentile (since 1963), NAAIM Active Managers Sentiment was at the 98th percentile (since 2006), net long stock-bond futures positioning was at the 98th percentile (since 1993), and Bank of America hedge fund net exposure was at the 99th percentile (since 2005). 

The author concludes with the prediction that most of the year's equity market gains have already been achieved, particularly with the Federal Reserve poised to raise interest rates.

This page analyzes the structural economic challenges facing Italy, arguing that while the country possesses notable strengths compared to Greece—including Europe's second-largest manufacturing sector, a more diversified economy, a higher savings rate, and a more favorable net international investment position—it suffers from deep structural weaknesses that make its economy look more like Greece than Germany. The author suggests these structural weaknesses explain why Italy has registered the lowest real GDP growth rate among twenty-eight advanced economies since 1991, performing worse than both Greece and Japan. 

To support this comparison, a scatter plot displays the 2014 World Economic Forum competitiveness rankings across 144 countries, with 1 being the best rank and 144 the worst. The chart plots individual sub-pillar scores for Germany in blue, Greece in brown, and Italy in green across seven major categories: property rights and legal frameworks; infrastructure; education; competition, taxation, and starting a business; labor flexibility and productivity; competitive advantage and value chain breadth; and innovation and patents. Across nearly all categories, Italy’s green data points cluster closely with Greece’s low rankings—frequently scoring between 80 and 140—while Germany's blue points consistently rank near the top, between 0 and 40. This gap is especially wide in categories concerning judicial independence, investor protections, labor flexibility, and the tax and regulatory environment required to start a business.

The text discusses how Matteo Renzi’s government has proposed an ambitious structural reform program to address these poor rankings. The author highlights the political difficulty and danger of such reforms in Italy, noting that a decade earlier, government adviser Marco Biagi was assassinated by a Red Brigades offshoot while drafting legislation to end guaranteed lifetime employment. The author poses that the success of these reforms and Italy’s ability to manage their short-term growth consequences may be the most critical trend currently shaping Europe.

A detailed table lists the key components of the Italian structural reform program. The proposed changes focus on reducing employment protections for permanent employees to eliminate labor market dualism, reforming unemployment benefits, and liberalizing several key sectors, including banking, pharmaceuticals, energy, telecommunications, and auto insurance. The program also aims to curb tax evasion through agreements with Switzerland, raise 0.7 percent of GDP annually through privatization, enact corporate tax cuts, and reduce regional government oversight on infrastructure and educational reforms. To clean up the financial sector, the plan proposes creating a bad bank to purchase approximately 190 billion Euros of non-performing loans, which represent 9.5 percent of Italy's GDP, to restart lending by private banks. 

A footnote adds context regarding the net international investment position, which measures liabilities to foreigners divided by GDP. As of 2014, Italy's position stood at negative 27 percent, which is significantly healthier than Spain's negative 90 percent and Portugal's negative 110 percent.

This page discusses global equity performance, focusing on the supportive central bank policies in Europe and Japan versus the downturn in Emerging Markets, specifically China. The author argues that positive returns in globally diversified portfolios this year have been driven by unprecedented interventions from European and Japanese central banks. While Europe shows improving leading indicators and Japan shows signs of corporate cash distribution and rising earnings growth, Emerging Markets are struggling due to the end of the Chinese commodity and capital spending boom. The author asserts that the recent, short-lived surge in Chinese equities was driven entirely by margin debt rather than fundamental strength or state coordination, and notes that Chinese equity valuations remain relatively expensive despite recent market corrections. 

Four charts support these observations. The first, titled "China: margin debt vs. onshore equity prices," tracks January 2014 through July 2015. It shows a near-perfect correlation between the CSI 300 index of onshore equity prices and outstanding margin debt as a percentage of GDP. Both series peaked sharply in mid-2015, with the CSI 300 index reaching over 5,000 and margin debt spiking to nearly 4.0% of GDP, before both experienced a steep reversal. 

The second chart, "The end of the China/commodity capital spending supercycle," displays global business fixed investment as a percentage of GDP from 1970 to 2014. It highlights three historical investment peaks: the EM and commodity boom of the late 1970s reaching over 16%, the Japanese boom around 1990 at approximately 16%, and the China and commodity boom peaking above 16% around 2012 before declining toward 15% by 2014. 

The third chart, "China: onshore equity P/E multiples," shows forward P/E ratios for CSI 300 A-share companies from 2010 to 2015. It contrasts the market-cap-weighted valuation, which rose from a low of roughly 8x to peak around 14x in 2015, with the equal-weighted sector valuation, which spiked dramatically from 12x up to over 22x in 2015, indicating that average sector valuations became highly stretched. 

The final chart, "China: offshore equity P/E multiples," presents forward P/E ratios for HK-listed H-share companies from 2004 to 2015. This chart displays three series: market-cap-weighted, equal-weighted by sector, and market-cap-weighted ex-financials. While these valuations peaked dramatically near 18x to 20x in 2007, by mid-2015 they sat at more moderate levels, with the market-cap-weighted ex-financials series trading around 15x, and the equal-weighted and market-cap-weighted series hovering between 10x and 12x.

This page analyzes the proposed 2015 nuclear agreement with Iran, examining the efficacy of economic sanctions and the physical capabilities of Iran's nuclear centrifuge infrastructure. The author argues that while sanctions severely impacted Iran's economy, they failed to deter its nuclear program or foster regime change. 

To support this, the first chart, "Iran centrifuge growth not affected by sanction misery," tracks the country's misery index against its centrifuge count from 2007 to 2014. Despite Iran’s misery index spiking from around 40 in 2007 to nearly 90 in 2012, its centrifuge count climbed relentlessly from roughly 3,000 to approximately 20,000. This indicates that economic hardship did not stall nuclear ambitions.

The second chart, "Sanctions more successful on Personalist Regimes and Monarchies than on Single-Party or Military Regimes," utilizes historical data from 1946 to 2000 to show the probability of autocratic regimes losing power when targeted by sanctions. For personalist or monarchic regimes, sanctions are effective, increasing the probability of collapse from about 6% to 15%. For single-party regimes like Iran, sanctions have no impact, with the probability remaining flat at roughly 8%. For military regimes, sanctions are counterproductive, actually decreasing the probability of the regime losing power from 18% to 13%. 

The final chart, "Iran's centrifuges and what they could be used for," contrasts civilian and military centrifuge requirements to highlight the strategic reality of the nuclear deal. The horizontal bar chart shows that to generate one year's worth of low-enriched uranium fuel for the civilian Bushehr 1GW reactor, Iran would need 200,000 centrifuges. Iran's actual stockpile of roughly 20,000 is far short of this civilian requirement but is more than enough to manufacture weapons. The proposed US-Iran deal would reduce Iran's allowed centrifuges to 6,000. The chart demonstrates that 6,000 centrifuges are virtually useless for commercial power generation—representing only 3% of the Bushehr reactor's annual fuel needs—but are the precise amount needed to produce enough 90% highly enriched uranium for one nuclear weapon per year. 

The author shares the reservations of experienced negotiators, noting that the deal grants Iran front-loaded sanctions relief in exchange for compliance measures. Because the remaining 6,000 centrifuges serve no practical civilian energy purpose but can produce one bomb's worth of highly enriched uranium annually, the deal's ultimate success hinges entirely on rigorous nuclear oversight.

This analysis by Michael Cembalest discusses the macroeconomic ramifications of Chinese currency depreciation on neighboring Asian export nations and global monetary policy. Countries with tight trading relationships or high export-to-GDP ratios like Thailand, Taiwan, Malaysia, Korea, and Vietnam are expected to feel the greatest impact. Turkey is also highlighted as highly vulnerable due to poor business surveys, weak trade, and substantial debt refinancing needs. Furthermore, the author notes that China’s actions present disinflationary challenges for Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen. 

The commentary is supported by six charts addressing what is labeled "The China Syndrome." The first chart illustrates the Chinese Renminbi real effective exchange rate index from 1994 to 2015, showing a long-term strengthening trend that saw the index rise from roughly 80 in 2005 to nearly 130 by mid-2015. Accompanying this is a chart tracking capital flows through the change in foreign exchange reserves minus the current account balance. This metric shows a stark shift from positive net capital inflows into deep net capital outflows, plummeting past negative 150 billion USD by mid-2015 as the central bank defended the exchange rate.

Domestically, China faces growing economic headwinds. An index of Chinese labor market conditions—which incorporates wage growth, labor supply-demand, employment growth, and PMI surveys—reveals sharp deterioration, dropping from a positive score of nearly 1.0 in 2011 to below negative 1.0 by mid-2015. Concurrently, non-financial corporate debt as a percentage of GDP has surged. After hovering below 110% from 1992 through 2008, corporate debt spiked post-financial crisis to exceed 150% of GDP by the end of 2014.

Lastly, the page compares onshore and offshore Chinese equity valuations. Onshore forward price-to-earnings multiples for CSI 300 A-share companies show a widening disparity by 2015, where the equal-weighted-by-sector multiple spiked to over 26x while the market-cap-weighted multiple remained much lower around 14x. Offshore, HK-listed H-share companies display similar divergence from 2004 to 2015; market-cap-weighted valuations hovered near a relatively low 8x to 10x in 2015, whereas the equal-weighted-by-sector and market-cap-weighted ex-financials multiples sat higher, between 11x and 14x.

This page, titled Appendix II: on stock buybacks and shareholder value, analyzes the surge in stock buybacks and questions whether they truly build long-term shareholder value. The author notes that buyback announcements are on pace for a record year, surpassing the previous high-water mark set in 2007. To illustrate this trend, an accompanying bar chart titled Buyback announcements on pace for record year displays S&P 500 buybacks in billions of US dollars from 1997 through an annualized estimate. The chart shows a major peak in 2007 at around seven hundred billion dollars, a sharp drop during the financial crisis in 2009 to under two hundred billion dollars, and a steady climb back up, with the annualized bar indicating that the total is approaching eight hundred billion dollars. The author highlights that the ten largest buyback programs make up more than half of all buyback dollar value, specifically citing Apple and General Electric at fifty billion dollars each, Home Depot at eighteen billion, Gilead and Qualcomm at fifteen billion each, PepsiCo and American Express at twelve billion each, Merck at ten billion, and PNC at nine point seven billion.

The central argument is that boosting earnings per share through share repurchases does not inherently increase shareholder value and can even destroy it if executed poorly. The author supports this perspective with several expert citations. A quote from McKinsey warns that buybacks can help managers hit short-term EPS targets at the expense of long-term corporate health and capital investment. Oaktree Research suggests that buybacks reduce a firm's financial slack, meaning companies must face greater shareholder scrutiny to raise new capital when new opportunities arise. Comments from Warren Buffett of Berkshire Hathaway emphasize that buybacks only make sense when a company has plenty of operational cash and its stock is trading at a material discount to its intrinsic value, a principle also championed by JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. Finally, the author points to a University of Illinois study showing that companies close to missing their EPS targets are highly likely to use buybacks to close the gap, but subsequently tend to cut employment, capital spending, and research and development in the year that follows.

This page analyzes the underlying causes of the late summer 2015 financial market correction, arguing that while the proximate trigger was emerging markets contagion sparked by a modest 2% devaluation of the Chinese RMB, the deeper vulnerability is a global economy stuck in a slow-growth "2% world." Despite six years of global monetary and fiscal stimulus, both developed and developing markets are experiencing tepid growth, making elevated asset valuations highly sensitive to disruption. A cartoon illustration in the top right visualizes this fragility, depicting a massive "China" semi-truck careening off a highway and colliding with a "Japan" vehicle, sending shockwaves toward a high-performance US race car labeled with major indices like the S&P 500 and Russell 2000 that has run off the road, alongside disrupted cars from the Eurozone and Emerging Markets.

The centerpiece of the page is a horizontal bar chart titled "The Terrible Twos: market and economic data growing in the neighborhood of 2%," which compares 21 distinct market and economic metrics, showing how they all cluster around the 2% mark. Market data series reveal very weak top-line corporate performance, including Euro Stoxx 50 revenue per share growth at approximately 1.0% and S&P 500 ex-energy revenue growth at 1.5%. Economic indicators show a similar slowdown; Eurozone industrial production and household credit growth are struggling below 1.5%, while German real GDP growth sits at 1.6%, showing the drag from China's slowdown. In the United States, retail sales growth is soft at 2.3%, first-half 2015 real GDP growth has averaged 2.2%, and five-year forward inflation expectations are stuck at 2.1%, signaling that bond markets are skeptical of a strong rebound. Furthermore, the Congressional Budget Office revised its 2015 US GDP growth forecast down to 2.0% from an initial 2.9%, while five-year cumulative US labor force growth is weak at 2.5%, less than half of its historical average.

In emerging and other global markets, the data is equally constrained. The growth premium spread between emerging markets and developed markets has fallen to 2.0%, the lowest level since 2001. China’s electricity consumption growth has plummeted to 2.1% (compared to typical 7% to 8% growth since 2009), and its real estate fixed investment growth of 3.3% is at its lowest level since 2000, far below its ten-year average of 24%. South Korea's real GDP growth has slowed to 2.2% with the Won hitting a five-year low, and EM Asia ex-China annualized GDP growth of 3.5% is weak compared to its 6% average since 2009. The chart also tracks bond yields, showing that a 2.1% rise in dollar-denominated emerging market bond yields has been driven by weakness in Brazil, Turkey, Russia, and Indonesia. 

Looking ahead, the author notes that the initial Chinese RMB devaluation of 2.0% could be followed by another 6% to 8% decline in the RMB in 2016. In a footnote, the author provides historical context for the correction, noting that the average intra-year S&P 500 correction since 1980 is 14%, and that calendar year returns remained positive in 27 of those 35 years. Prior to this recent 10% pullback, the S&P 500 had gone through its third-longest period in 90 years without a correction. Finally, the author observes that ETF volume during this selloff reached 45% of total market volume, the highest share since early 2009, suggesting a high degree of indiscriminate, program-driven selling.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, titled Appendix I, explores three main themes: the state of US equities characterized by low revenue and earnings growth alongside high margins, the powerful economic pull of China on the emerging market world, and the increasingly divergent economic conditions between developed and emerging countries. 

The first section analyzes S&P 500 performance. A chart showing year-over-year percent changes in S&P core revenues and earnings versus nominal global GDP from Q1 2014 to Q2 2015 demonstrates a softening environment. S&P 500 core revenues—excluding financial, energy, and utility sectors—saw growth drop from around 4% in early 2014 to less than 2% by mid-2015, while core earnings growth fell from a peak of nearly 14% down to an estimated 6%. This trend mirrored a decline in nominal global GDP growth from 4.5% to 3%. Despite this deceleration, a historical chart of S&P 500 GAAP profit margins from 1965 to 2015 shows that margins remained near record highs of around 9% to 10% in 2015, well above the 4% to 6% historical norms of the late twentieth century.

The second section focuses on the growing systemic influence of China. A chart detailing the 10-year rolling correlation of Chinese GDP growth with other emerging market nations illustrates that this relationship has risen from near zero in the mid-1990s to approximately 0.45 by 2014. As a result, the estimated impact of a China growth shock is highly concentrated in the emerging world. According to a chart analyzing the cumulative impact of a 1% change in Chinese growth, developed markets and the United States are insulated, suffering growth drag of less than 0.2% and 0.1%, respectively. In contrast, emerging regions suffer severe consequences, with real GDP growth impacts of roughly 1.1% in Latin America, 1.1% in emerging Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, and 0.9% in emerging Asia excluding China. 

The final section highlights the stark divergence between developed and emerging economies. A dual-axis chart tracking year-over-year global domestic bank credit growth from 2009 to 2015 shows that credit growth in developed markets steadily recovered from a trough of -3% in 2010 to around 3% by mid-2015. Conversely, emerging market credit growth has been in a structural slowdown, falling from nearly 20% in 2009 to roughly 11% in 2015. This divergence is reinforced by manufacturing output trends measured by the Purchasing Managers Index from January 2014 to July 2015. While developed markets maintained healthy, expansionary manufacturing activity around the 54 level, emerging markets contracted, falling below the 50-threshold to about 49. This emerging market weakness was led by China, whose manufacturing PMI experienced a sharp decline to approximately 47 by July 2015.

This page outlines a summary of findings concerning the financial challenges facing millennials and offers pathways to secure their retirements despite structural headwinds. Millennials must contend with high student debt, wage stagnation, rising pressure on federal entitlements, and longer life expectancies. Furthermore, late-career disruptions such as layoffs or illness often interrupt savings plans. To counter these challenges, J.P. Morgan suggests that millennials must save early, beginning at age 25, utilizing pre-tax and after-tax savings along with employer matches.

The first chart, titled "Recommended annual pre-tax contribution to savings by each working spouse to offset impact of adverse events," shows the necessary annual savings percentage of pre-tax income. For median-income households, the recommended range is roughly 4% to 8%; for affluent households, it rises to 10% to 14%; and for high-net-worth households, it reaches 14% to 18%. This model assumes a 2% after-tax savings rate and a 50% employer match capped at 3%. 

If households fail to make these savings adjustments, they risk sharp declines in their retirement standard of living, as detailed in the top-right chart, "Income replacement ratios if no savings adjustments take place to offset adverse events." The chart compares original target ratios to those achieved after negative life events. For median-income households, the ratio of retiree spending relative to pre-retirement income falls from a 100% target to 90%. For affluent households, the ratio drops from an 85% target to about 78%, while high-net-worth households see their ratio fall from an 83% target to around 75%. 

The final chart, at the bottom right, demonstrates why millennials cannot simply rely on strong market returns to rescue their retirements if they retire three years earlier than planned. Titled "Required annual real return on equity to offset the impact of a single individual retiring 3 years early," it compares the required annualized real return on equity against historical annualized S&P 500 real returns over rolling 35-year periods from 1935 to 2015. To bridge the retirement gap, a median-income individual would need a real return of approximately 10.5%, an affluent individual would need about 9.2%, and a high-net-worth individual would need roughly 8.2%. These figures are exceptionally high compared to historical S&P 500 performance, where the median real return was 6.8%, the 75th percentile was 7.0%, and even the peak historical return was only 8.5%. This indicates that relying on investment outperformance to offset early retirement is highly unrealistic, underscoring the critical importance of early and disciplined savings.

This page analyzes a slow-growth global economic environment characterized by flat-lining manufacturing output and exports, a narrowing growth premium for emerging markets, and the severe deflationary impact of China's economic slowdown. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that the resulting market correction has pulled S&P 500 valuations down from their peak levels in early 2015, bringing them closer to historical mid-cycle averages, with European multiples following a similar pattern. 

The core of the argument centers on the erosion of the emerging market growth premium, primarily driven by the end of China's massive capital spending boom. This shift is captured in the chart titled "Falling emerging markets growth premium," which plots year-over-year real GDP growth for emerging and developed markets from 1997 to 2015. While emerging markets once held a massive growth advantage—frequently growing at 7% to 9% in the mid-2000s compared to developed markets' 2% to 3%—by 2015, EM growth had slipped to around 4% while developed markets hovered around 1.5% to 2%. Cembalest highlights that China's slowdown is highly consequential because China's share of world GDP is now more than twice as large as Asia ex-Japan's share was in 1997. Furthermore, there is an 80% or greater correlation between manufacturing surveys in China and Asia ex-China, resulting in a nearly 1:1 pass-through of Chinese economic weakness to the broader emerging market universe.

To illustrate these trends, the page features several highly detailed charts. The top-left chart, "Global manufacturing and exports: stagnating," tracks quarter-over-quarter annual rate changes from 2010 to 2015. It shows that both global manufacturing output and exports have fluctuated wildly but ultimately stagnated, dropping from expansion peaks of 10% to 15% in 2010-2011 to nearly 0% by mid-2015. The top-right chart, "S&P 500 valuation declines from peak levels," plots the median trailing 12-month price-to-earnings ratio from 1980 to 2015. It marks a point in February 2015 as the 91st percentile of historical expensiveness before showing a subsequent downward correction toward the 15x to 18x range.

The bottom portion of the page links global investment to commodity pricing trends. The bottom-left chart, "Global business fixed investment leveling off," displays business investment as a percentage of global GDP from 1970 to 2014. It highlights three historical investment waves: the EM and commodity boom of the late 1970s, the Japanese boom of the late 1980s, and the most recent China-driven commodity boom, which peaked near 16.5% of global GDP in 2011 before starting to decline. The bottom-right chart, "Decline in commodity prices since their 2011 peak," indexes prices for agriculture, industrial metals, and energy from a January 2011 base of 100 through late 2015. All three sectors show steep, persistent declines: by late 2015, agriculture and industrial metals indices had fallen to approximately 60, while energy plunged even lower to around 40. Cembalest warns that because of the long lead times required to bring new industrial metals and energy projects online or adjust production, the downslope of these commodity super-cycles can drag on for 10 to 20 years.

This page introduces a demographic framework called "The Millennials," which tracks a hypothetical cohort of eight University of Colorado graduates entering the workforce at age 25 to monitor their lifetime career trajectories and financial wealth. The text outlines key economic and educational characteristics defining this generation. Although millennials are the most highly educated generation of young adults in U.S. history—with 47 percent of 25-to-34-year-olds holding a postsecondary degree in 2013—they carry significant financial burdens. Approximately 60 percent of bachelor's degree recipients in 2012–2013 graduated with an average debt of $27,300, which helped push the average student loan balance as a percentage of median income from 20 percent in the late 1990s to 50 percent by 2014. Furthermore, U.S. millennials face a global skills gap, ranking 21st out of 22 OECD nations in numeracy, underperforming in literacy, and lagging in problem-solving. They are also less likely than previous generations to major in business, healthcare, or STEM fields, instead favoring social sciences, communications, and criminal justice, while computer science majors have actually declined over time, particularly among women. 

These factors, combined with slow real income growth and delayed household formation, have dramatically impacted homeownership. A line chart titled "Probability of homeownership: 18 to 34 year olds" illustrates this trend from 1980 through roughly 2013. The chart plots a steadily declining "Long-run trend" line, which starts near 16 percent in 1980 and declines to approximately 14 percent. This is compared against the "Actual" probability of homeownership, which displays significant volatility. Starting high at roughly 18 percent in 1980, the actual rate dipped below 14 percent in the early 1990s before climbing to a peak of nearly 17 percent around 2005. Following the financial crisis, the actual probability plummeted sharply, ending near 13 percent in 2013, well below the long-run trend. The text notes that this decline prevents young renters from building long-term equity to draw upon in the future.

This page serves as an introduction to the "Season Summaries" section, which outlines Seasons 1, 2, and 3 of a simulated financial series titled "The Millennials." The project models how changing personal choices and macroeconomic conditions affect the savings rate required from age 25 onward to sustain financial assets throughout retirement. The author lists the specific financial, personal, and policy variables—referred to as "plot devices"—used to construct these scenarios. These variables include pre-tax and after-tax savings, employer matching, stock-and-bond asset allocation, market returns, retirement spending goals and age-based adjustments, income levels and growth, unemployment, family emergencies, long-term care expenses, home down payments, student debt, children's college tuition, inflation, interest rates, tax rates, and government entitlement policies. Additionally, a styled grey callout box playfully mimics television production credits, stating that all characters are fictitious and no animals were harmed in the filming of the show.

This page, titled "Retirement Insights: Backstory," argues that millennials are likely to face more job and wage uncertainty than prior generations due to long-term secular forces, particularly automation and weak income growth, which may disrupt their long-term savings goals. 

The first chart, "Real median household income growth," tracks the six-year rolling average of annual percentage changes from 1975 to 2010 using U.S. Census Bureau data. It illustrates a downward secular trend where income growth peaked near 2.0% in the late 1980s and 2.2% in the late 1990s, but steadily deteriorated after 2000, eventually falling below 0% after 2005 and reaching roughly -1.2% by 2012. 

The second chart, "Manufacturing output vs. hours worked," indexes performance to March 31, 1980, using data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Federal Reserve Board through the first quarter of 2015. It highlights a stark decoupling of productivity from labor: while real manufacturing output grew steadily from an index level of 100 in 1980 to over 200 by 2015, the actual hours worked declined over the same period, falling from an index level near 100 down to approximately 65. 

The third chart, "Probability of computerization by occupation," visualizes data from a 2013 study by Oxford professors Frey and Osborne. It plots millions of U.S. jobs across a probability scale of 0.0 to 1.0 to show how susceptible different fields are to computerization. The chart categorizes employment into three risk zones: "Low" (32% of employment, under 0.3 probability), "Medium" (17% of employment, 0.3 to 0.7 probability), and "High" (51% of employment, over 0.7 probability). Low-probability occupations are dominated by management, business, financial, computer, engineering, and science roles. Conversely, the high-probability zone features a massive spike in employment volume, heavily driven by office and administrative support, sales and related roles, service, and production jobs. 

The accompanying text and footnotes note that although college graduates maintain a strong advantage—experiencing half the unemployment rate of high school graduates (2.7% versus 5.4%) and enjoying a college wage premium of about 75%—they are still highly exposed to the threat of computerization. Ultimately, the author emphasizes that about half of all U.S. jobs in both services and manufacturing face a high risk of automation over the next one to two decades, threatening to interrupt millennials' lifetime savings goals through periods of under-employment.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Backstory" section addresses the dual financial challenges facing Millennials: increasing lifespans and the corresponding rising fiscal pressures on public entitlements like Medicare and Social Security. The author argues that Millennials must save more for longer retirements, especially as government entitlement spending is projected to crowd out non-defense discretionary spending—items crucial for long-term economic growth.

The first chart, titled "Increasing median life expectancy for retirees," uses U.S. Census Bureau data to display life expectancy at age 65 by birth cohort, ranging from 1940 to 2000. The chart reveals a steady upward trend for both genders. For men, median life expectancy at age 65 rises from approximately 81.5 years for the 1940 cohort to over 85 years for the 2000 cohort. For women, it increases from around 84 years to nearly 87.5 years across the same span. To highlight the longevity risk, the second chart, "Probability at least one millennial spouse lives to various ages," demonstrates that if both spouses reach age 65, there is nearly a 100% chance at least one lives to 75, an 80% chance at least one lives to 85, a 50% chance of reaching 90, and a small but notable 5% chance of reaching age 100.

On the right, the third chart, "Federal debt held by the public," plots U.S. federal debt as a percentage of GDP from 1970 with a Congressional Budget Office extended baseline projection through 2030. The debt shows a dramatic climb after 2008, stabilizing near 80% of GDP through 2020 before rising again toward 100% by 2030. The final chart, "Entitlement and non-defense discretionary spending," shows how these two spending categories have diverged as a percentage of GDP. From 1970 to 2025, entitlement spending rises from roughly 5% of GDP to a CBO-projected peak of nearly 12% of GDP. In contrast, non-defense discretionary spending steadily declines from over 4% of GDP in the 1970s to a projected low of under 3% by 2025. The author highlights that due to policies like the Budget Control Act of 2011, the ratio of entitlement-to-discretionary spending is projected to shift from 1:1 in the early 1970s to 4:1 by 2020, likely forcing a curtailment of these benefits at the expense of Millennials.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s "Backstory" series explores the unique demographic, psychological, and institutional challenges that millennials face regarding retirement and long-term financial security. The author argues that millennials are structurally and behaviorally disadvantaged compared to previous generations due to lower marriage rates, a deep-seated skepticism of the stock market, and the widespread disappearance of traditional defined-benefit pensions. 

The first section addresses how millennials are less likely to marry, which deprives them of dual-income advantages, shared expenses, and dual Social Security benefits. This trend is illustrated in a chart titled "One in four of today's young adults may never marry," which tracks the percentage of unmarried individuals across different generational cohorts from 1960 to 2030. The data, sourced from Pew Research, shows that older cohorts (born mid-century) had never-married rates of only around 6% by the time they reached ages 45–54. In contrast, the millennial cohort—which had a never-married rate of roughly 35% at ages 25–34 in 2010—is projected to still have a never-married rate of over 20% by the time they reach ages 45–54 in 2030.

The second section explains why millennials are highly skeptical of financial markets, noting that their formative years coincided with two separate 40% plus equity market declines. A Brookings Institution study cited on the page shows that 52% of millennials aged 21 to 36 keep their savings in cash, compared to only 23% of older savers. This dynamic is illustrated in a log-scale chart of the S&P 500 total return index from 1975 to 2015, using data from Robert Shiller. A bracket highlighting the period when "Millennials join labor force" (roughly 2000 to 2010) visually emphasizes that this generation entered the workforce during a decade defined by the dot-com bust and the 2008 financial crisis. The author points out that this aversion to stocks, coupled with high cash allocations, poses a major risk to retirement goals, especially during a period of Federal Reserve interest rate suppression.

Finally, the page details how millennials are increasingly forced to finance their own retirements. Citing the Employee Benefit Research Institute, the author notes that only 51% of workers have employers who sponsor retirement plans, and those plans have shifted overwhelmingly toward defined contribution schemes. A line chart tracks the percent of private-sector workers participating in employer-sponsored retirement plans by type from 1979 to 2011. The chart reveals a dramatic inversion: participation in "Defined benefit plan only" plummeted from nearly 30% in 1979 to under 5% in 2011. Conversely, participation in "Defined contribution plan only" rose from roughly 7% to over 30% during the same timeframe, while the share of workers with "Both types" of plans hovered between 10% and 15%. This structural shift means about 85% of private-sector workers must now individually fund and manage their own retirement assets.

This page from JP Morgan’s Retirement Insights series presents a summary of retirement savings requirements for median-income millennial households, framed through various simulated life scenarios or "episodes." The primary goal for these households is to maintain their final working-years spending level throughout retirement, leaving a small financial cushion. While Social Security is projected to cover the majority of retirement spending, the analysis warns that the common 3% employer auto-enrollment rate is only sufficient if everything goes perfectly according to plan. Because unpredictable real-life events like unemployment, forced early retirement, market downturns, or policy changes can severely disrupt savings, the author argues that a resilient financial plan should target annual pre-tax savings of 4% to 9%, plus an additional 2% in after-tax savings.

The core visual is a bar chart detailing the annual pre-tax savings rate required by each median earner for their financial wealth to last through retirement, starting at age 25. The chart assumes a 2% after-tax savings rate and a 50% employer match capped at 3%. The data is split into three household structures: couples with a single-income lifestyle, couples with a dual-income lifestyle, and single earners. 

For single-income couples, if everything goes to plan, the required pre-tax contribution is roughly 1%, resulting in a 4% total lifetime savings rate. However, extreme events like early spouse death or involuntary retirement can increase the required pre-tax contribution to 3% or 4%, corresponding to total lifetime savings rates of 12% to 13%. 

For dual-income couples, the ideal scenario requires a 3% pre-tax contribution (11% total savings rate). Common disruptions increase this need; for instance, lacking an employer match raises the pre-tax requirement to 4% (11% total), while retiring early at age 62 raises it to 9% (24% total). In the worst-case scenario, labeled "The perfect storm," where multiple negative events hit at once, the required pre-tax contribution climbs to approximately 13%, which demands a 28% total lifetime savings rate. 

For single individuals, going according to plan requires a 3% pre-tax contribution (13% total savings rate). This requirement rises to 5% (15% total) for lower market returns and life events, and to 6% (17% total) under conservative investing and policy changes. 

A footnote highlights data from Vanguard showing that half of the retirement plans they oversee feature a 3% auto-enrollment rate, while 12% are at a 2% rate, 12% are at a 4% rate, and approximately 20% have auto-enrollment rates of 5% to 6% or higher.

This page from J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Season Summaries series addresses several crucial questions regarding retirement savings for median-income millennials and the strategies they might use to offset low savings rates. 

First, the author explains that if median-income millennials fail to save enough by retirement and encounter adverse circumstances, they may have to reduce their retirement spending by twenty-five percent to forty percent in real terms, pushing them close to subsistence living. Second, the text considers whether working longer can offset inadequate savings, noting that working three to four more years, until age seventy or seventy-one, could allow millennials to accumulate more savings, defer drawdowns, and increase Social Security payments, though physical health and job availability remain key risks. Third, the author addresses whether millennials can invest their way out of low savings rates, citing a scenario where an individual named Ken retires early and attempts to do so. This approach would require a highly unrealistic ten-point-five percent real annual return on equity throughout his entire working and retirement life, a rate far exceeding historical post-war equity market index returns.

Finally, the page examines the impact of starting a savings journey later in life. A detailed table presents the required pre-tax contributions by each spouse in median-income households across twenty different hypothetical episodes, comparing the rates needed if savings begin at age twenty-five versus age thirty-five. Across all scenarios, delaying savings by a decade significantly increases the necessary pre-tax contribution rate. For example, in Episode one, the required contribution rises from one-point-zero percent to one-point-seven percent. In more demanding scenarios, such as Episode eleven, the required savings rate jumps from eight-point-eight percent at age twenty-five to thirteen-point-three percent at age thirty-five. In the most extreme scenario shown, Episode fourteen, the rate increases from fifteen-point-four percent to nineteen-point-one percent. Other representative scenarios include Episode two, which rises from three-point-five percent to five-point-nine percent, and Episode seventeen, which increases from nine-point-six percent to fourteen-point-five percent. This comparison underscores the substantial cost of delaying retirement planning and the power of compounding early in life.

This page analyzes retirement readiness for affluent millennials, raising critical questions about savings shortfalls, delayed planning, and mitigating factors. The author notes that if affluent millennials fail to save enough and face adverse market events, they may have to slash their retirement spending by 35% to 45% in real terms, bringing their lifestyle down close to median-income living. To offset inadequate savings, working three to four more years until age 70 or 71 is an option, though physical limitations and job availability may make this impractical. Relying solely on superior investment performance is also depicted as unrealistic, as a millennial would need to generate an unprecedented 9% real annual compound rate of return on their equity portfolio for life. In contrast, receiving an inheritance can be a powerful counterweight; a model shows that a $400,000 windfall at age 35 allows a couple to withstand adverse policy and market events without raising their savings rate. In support of this, a footnote references a Boston College study projecting a $59 trillion wealth transfer over the next decade.

The page features a detailed table titled "Affluent households: Required pre-tax contribution by each spouse if savings begin at:" which compares required savings rates across 22 distinct modeled episodes, contrasting starting at age 25 with starting at age 35. Across all episodes, delaying retirement savings by ten years systematically increases the required contribution rate. For example, in the baseline scenario of Episode 1, the required rate increases from 7.5% to 8.2% when delaying savings. In more challenging scenarios, such as Episode 10, the required pre-tax savings rate rises from 14.0% at age 25 to 15.0% at age 35. In Episode 15, the rate increases from 8.3% to 9.9%, while Episode 21 climbs from 13.0% to 15.2%. For the most savings-intensive scenario, Episode 23, the required pre-tax contribution reaches 14.6% if savings start at age 25 and jumps to 16.4% if delayed until age 35. This data highlights the compounding cost of waiting to save for retirement.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Retirement Insights" series provides a summary of "The Millennials, Season 2," focusing specifically on affluent households, defined as families with household incomes in the top five percent according to 2015 U.S. Census Bureau data. The retirement goal for this cohort is to retire in their mid-60s, spend 15% less in retirement than during their final working years, ensure their financial assets last to the end of their lives, and keep their family homes. 

The main argument is that while a modest 7.5% to 8.0% pre-tax annual contribution is sufficient when everything goes perfectly, real-world events out of their control—such as repayment of student debt, redundancy, family emergencies, policy changes, and lower market returns—require a more robust strategy. To survive these unpredictable events, affluent millennials must target annual allocations of 9% to 14% of pre-tax income into diversified retirement accounts, assuming a 50% employer match capped at 3%, plus an additional 2% saved annually out of after-tax income. 

The page contains a detailed bar chart, titled "The Millennials: Summary of Season 2," which displays the annual pre-tax savings rate required by each affluent earner, starting at age 25, for their financial wealth to last through retirement. The vertical axis shows the pre-tax contribution as a percentage of income, ranging from 0% to 15%, while the horizontal axis breaks down different hypothetical "episodes" for single earners (represented by gold bars) and dual-income couples (represented by gray bars). Beneath each episode, the chart lists the corresponding household lifetime total savings rate, which combines active and passive savings. 

For single earners, the required pre-tax contribution starts at roughly 7.5% under Episode 1, where "everything goes according to plan" (with a 21% lifetime savings rate). This requirement rises steadily as negative scenarios are introduced. For instance, Parent elder-care costs under Episode 4 require over 9% pre-tax savings, and retiring early at age 62 under Episode 2 requires nearly 12% pre-tax savings (with a 27% lifetime savings rate). The most extreme case for singles, Episode 10, represents "the perfect storm" where multiple negative events hit at once, pushing the necessary pre-tax contribution rate to nearly 14% and the lifetime total savings rate to 28%.

For dual-income couples, a parallel trend is shown. Under the ideal scenario in Episode 15, the required pre-tax contribution is approximately 8% (with a 23% lifetime savings rate). This increases to about 9.5% if a spouse loses their job or market returns are low, and reaches approximately 12% if they face policy changes and early retirement at age 60 under Episode 21. The most demanding scenario for couples is Episode 23, "conservative investing and family emergencies," which pushes the required pre-tax savings rate to 14%, resulting in a 25% lifetime savings rate. Through these scenarios, the author demonstrates that a higher, disciplined savings rate acts as a necessary buffer against life's unpredictable disruptions.

This page, titled "The Millennials, Season 3 Summary: High Net Worth Households," discusses retirement planning goals and strategies for high-net-worth millennial families, defined as households with incomes in the top 1% based on 2015 U.S. Census Bureau data. The primary retirement goal for these families is to retire in their early to mid-60s, reduce spending by 15% in retirement compared to their final working years, ensure financial assets last through their lifetimes with a modest safety cushion, and avoid selling the family home. 

The commentary notes that under ideal circumstances where everything goes according to plan, a 12% pre-tax contribution rate is sufficient, as illustrated in Episodes 1 and 13. Social Security plays a minimal role here, financing only 25% of retirement spending. However, real-life events such as family emergencies, early retirement, long-term care needs, private college tuition, lower market returns, conservative investing, or policy changes to Social Security and 401(k) plans can hinder wealth accumulation. To weather these events, the authors argue that a robust financial plan requires annual pre-tax allocations of 14% to 18% into diversified retirement accounts, assuming a 50% employer match capped at 3%, alongside saving an additional 2% of after-tax income annually starting at age 25.

This analysis is supported by a bar chart displaying the annual pre-tax savings contribution required by each high-net-worth earner for financial wealth to last through retirement. The chart is split into two series: "Single" and "Couple; dual-income lifestyle" (where rates apply to both spouses). 

For single individuals, the required pre-tax contribution rate rises from 12% in the ideal scenario (Episode 1) up to approximately 20% for an ultra-conservative investor (Episode 7). Intermediate single scenarios include parent elder-care costs at 14% (Episode 4), lower market returns at 15% (Episode 5), family emergencies with lower market returns at 16% (Episode 10), and "the perfect storm" where multiple events hit at once at 19% (Episode 8). Below each bar, the corresponding lifetime total active and passive savings rate is shown, ranging from 27% to 31% for singles.

For couples with a dual-income lifestyle, the ideal scenario also starts at 12% (Episode 13) and rises to 18% for conservative investing combined with family emergencies (Episode 20). Other couple scenarios include the cost of long-term care insurance at 12.5% (Episode 17), a long-term care event at 13% (Episode 16), private college tuitions at 13.5% (Episode 15), and no access to a 401(k) plan at 17.5% (Episode 14). The corresponding lifetime total savings rate for couples ranges from 24% (in the scenario with no 401(k) access) to 31%. The chart demonstrates how external shocks and conservative asset allocation elevate the necessary baseline savings rate well above the ideal 12% mark.

This page from J.P. Morgan Asset Management discusses the financial realities and retirement planning challenges faced by high net worth millennials across various hypothetical scenarios, referred to as episodes. 

The text addresses several critical questions about retirement preparation. First, it notes that if high net worth millennials fail to save enough by retirement and encounter adverse circumstances, they would have to slash their real retirement spending by 35% to 45% compared to their pre-retirement levels to avoid insolvency. Second, the author addresses whether they can compensate for low savings rates with aggressive investing, concluding that this strategy is highly unrealistic, as it would require generating an 8% real annual compound rate of return on equities over their entire lives, a rate near historical peak post-war equity market returns. Third, high savers face the hurdle of exhausting tax-advantaged allowances, such as 401(k) and IRA contribution caps. Concerns about creditor exposure in non-qualified deferred compensation plans often force these individuals to save in tax-inefficient accounts, raising the overall savings needed per dollar of retirement spending. Lastly, the author highlights the powerful impact of inheritances; for example, receiving a $700,000 inheritance at age 35 can entirely offset adverse policy changes, lower market returns, and negative life events, allowing retirees to maintain their ideal spending plan without increasing their baseline savings rate.

A central element of the page is a table detailing the required pre-tax contribution by each spouse in high net worth households under two scenarios: starting to save at age 25 versus delaying until age 35. Across all nineteen episodes listed, starting late consistently requires a significantly higher contribution rate. For example, in the baseline scenario of Episode 1, the required rate rises from 12.3% at age 25 to 13.8% at age 35. In Episode 7, one of the more demanding scenarios, the required rate climbs from 19.2% to 21.8%. In Episode 13, the required rate increases from 11.9% if started at age 25 to 13.8% at age 35. Under the most extreme scenario, Episode 20, the required pre-tax savings rate jumps from 19.5% at age 25 to 22.6% at age 35. Other notable scenarios include Episode 8, where rates rise from 18.9% to 21.3%, and Episode 14, which moves from 17.1% to 19.4%. The data underscores that waiting a decade to begin saving requires couples to commit several additional percentage points of their pre-tax income to remain on track.

This page serves as an introduction to individual retirement case studies, or "episodes," followed by a detailed profile of Season 1, Episode 6, titled "Chad and Jane Selphy when everything goes according to plan." The introductory text explains that each episode brief includes a narrative, charts tracking financial and total assets, an analysis of how retirement is financed, a table detailing savings and breakeven rates, and a list of underlying assumptions. 

The narrative for Episode 6 introduces Chad and Jane, two music teachers who work until age 67. They are active savers who each contribute 3% of pre-tax income to their retirement, receive a 1.5% employer match, and save an additional 2% of after-tax income, achieving an 11.1% lifetime savings rate. Due to $54,000 in early student debt, they never purchase a home. However, by working until age 67, they accumulate enough assets to sustain their retirement lifestyle. Chad passes away at age 90, and Jane successfully draws down their remaining savings until age 95. 

Three charts illustrate this successful scenario. The first, "Financial Assets," shows USD millions from age 25 to 95, with assets rising steadily to a peak of approximately $0.8 million around age 67 before declining to near zero by age 95. The second chart, "Total Asset Composition, Episode 6," shows net worth alongside 401(k) assets, after-tax savings, and debt. It illustrates a negative net worth in their mid-20s due to student debt, which is steadily paid off, allowing net worth to align with total assets and peak at retirement. The third chart, "Sources of Funds for Retirement Spending, Episode 6," details annual retirement income in USD thousands from age 68 to 95. It shows that spending, which ranges from roughly $150,000 to over $200,000, is funded by a combination of Social Security, mandatory 401(k) withdrawals, and supplementary savings account drawdowns. 

A "Savings" table details the breakeven analysis, showing that the actual 3.0% pre-tax contribution rate by both spouses perfectly matches the 3.0% required to reach their financial asset target by age 95. The alternative of maintaining 100% retirement income replacement implies a minor real spending reduction of 12%. 

Finally, the "Other assumptions" table lists the baseline parameters for this model: both spouses earn median incomes, retire at age 67, do not buy a home, and model a 5.5% real equity return and a 1.0% real fixed-income return. Spending is projected at 100% of pre-retirement disposable income, with a 20% reduction in spending applied after the death of the first spouse at age 90.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" presents a hypothetical financial case study of a median-income couple, Meri and Evan Ablaste, to illustrate the vulnerability of a low-savings retirement plan, even when "everything goes according to plan." In this scenario, the couple prioritizes lifestyle experiences, saving only 1% of pre-tax income and 2% of after-tax income, while allocating early savings to clear $54,000 in debt. Meri retires at 45 and Evan retires at 67. Because everything goes perfectly—Evan works uninterrupted to age 67, and they live to age 90—their reliance on the Social Security safety net successfully funds their retirement, with payments rising faster than spending. However, the author cautions that relying on such a flawless sequence of events makes them massive gamblers.

The financial narrative is supported by three charts and two detailed tables of assumptions and metrics. The first chart, titled Financial Assets, shows total wealth in millions of US dollars from age 25 to 95. It demonstrates that the couple's assets remain virtually flat and near zero until age 55, after which they rise sharply to peak at nearly $0.5 million around age 90, before dipping slightly by age 95. 

The second chart, Total Asset Composition, breaks down this wealth trajectory into 401(k) assets, after-tax savings, debt, and net worth from age 25 to 95. It highlights a negative net worth in their early years, represented by a red debt bar of roughly $50,000 that persists until age 50. Once debt is retired, after-tax savings, depicted in blue, grow exponentially to over $0.4 million by age 90, while the grey-shaded 401(k) assets remain a negligible sliver. 

The third chart, Sources of Funds for Retirement Spending, details the couple’s income sources against an orange spending line from age 68 to 95. The spending line begins at approximately $110,000, climbs to nearly $160,000 by age 90, and then drops to roughly $120,000 after the death of the first spouse. Green bars representing Social Security provide almost all the necessary funding, eventually exceeding spending requirements in their later years, which allows them to accumulate modest after-tax savings, visible in blue, starting at age 91.

A pair of tables outlines the underlying data and assumptions. The savings table shows that both Meri and Evan make a 1.0% pre-tax contribution with a 0.5% employer match. Combined with a 2.0% additional household savings rate and 0.6% portfolio returns, their lifetime savings rate is 3.7%. A breakeven analysis notes that their actual 1.0% pre-tax contribution matches the exact amount required to reach their financial target by age 95, yielding a 121% retirement income replacement and a 7% real increase in spending. The assumptions table details that they do not purchase a home due to insufficient down payment, assume a real equity return of 5.5% and a real fixed income return of 1.0%, and project a 20% spending reduction after the death of a spouse, with Social Security taken at age 68 at 108% of age 67 benefits.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Retirement Insights series, titled Season 1, Episode 2, presents a case study of a hypothetical couple, Meri and Evan Ablaste, to demonstrate the financial dangers of relying solely on government safety nets when unexpected life events occur. The scenario models the compounding negative effects of Evan’s involuntary early retirement at age 62 due to health reasons, followed by Meri’s early death at age 73. 

Because of Evan's early retirement, the couple is forced to take Social Security payments early at age 63, reducing their benefits by 25% compared to what they would have received at age 67. When Meri passes away at age 73, her Social Security benefit is lost, leaving Evan with an extreme income shortfall. Even with an assumed 20% drop in spending after his wife's death, Evan is forced to cut his spending by 40% to 45% in real terms relative to pre-retirement levels starting at age 68. The author points out that to avoid this outcome and have assets last until Evan is 95, both would have needed to save 3.5% of their respective incomes in a 401(k) annually, supplemented by an employer match.

The page features three charts and two data tables. The top-left chart, titled Financial Assets, plots USD millions against age from 25 to 95. It compares a scenario where everything goes according to plan, where assets steadily climb after age 55 to peak near $0.5 million at age 85, against the actual scenario of early death and involuntary retirement, where financial assets flatline at zero starting in their mid-50s. 

The top-right chart, Sources of Funds for Retirement Spending, shows annual funding in USD thousands from age 63 to 95. The chart displays Social Security as green bars and a rising orange line representing spending. At age 73, Social Security funding drops abruptly from nearly $80,000 to approximately $50,000, leaving a massive gap below the spending line, which continues to rise toward $120,000 by age 95.

The bottom-left chart, Total Asset Composition, shows the couple’s balance sheet from age 25 to 95. It reveals that the couple carried significant debt, shown in red, which peaked at approximately -$0.06 million around age 35. Their net worth, shown as an orange line, peaks briefly near $0.02 million in their late 50s before crashing to zero at age 62 and remaining there.

A table on savings rates shows that the couple’s actual pre-tax savings rate was only 1.0% each, with a 0.5% employer match, contributing to a total lifetime savings rate of 3.6%. The breakeven analysis notes that to reach their financial target by age 95, pre-tax contributions would need to be 3.5% for both spouses. Alternatively, they would have to accept a retirement income replacement rate of 68%, implying a real spending cut of 44%. Other assumptions listed in the final table include a median income for both spouses, no home purchase due to insufficient down payment, a real equity return of 5.5%, a real fixed-income return of 1.0%, and an initial debt of $54,000.

This page presents a retirement case study from J.P. Morgan Asset Management featuring Chad and Jane Selphy, two hypothetical music teachers whose financial lives are modeled under a scenario where everything goes according to plan. The couple, both earning median incomes, save actively throughout their careers, retiring at age 67. They never buy a home due to prioritizing the payoff of fifty-four thousand dollars in student debt during their youth. In retirement, Chad passes away at age ninety, and Jane lives to age ninety-five. The analysis demonstrates how their assets successfully sustain them through the end of Jane's life, though the author notes this happy ending serves as a baseline before less ideal scenarios are explored in future sections.

The first chart on the page, titled Financial Assets, shows the trajectory of the couple's total wealth from age twenty-five to ninety-five in millions of US dollars. Their assets grow slowly at first, accelerate after age forty-five, and peak at nearly eight hundred thousand dollars around age eighty-five, before drawing down to about four hundred and fifty thousand dollars by age ninety-five. 

A second chart, titled Total Asset Composition, provides more detail on this wealth accumulation by showing 401k holdings, after-tax savings, debt, and overall net worth. The chart illustrates how their initial fifty-four thousand dollars of debt is fully extinguished by their mid-thirties. From there, their 401k accounts, shown in grey, make up the vast majority of their wealth, supplemented by a smaller portion of after-tax savings shown in blue. Net worth closely tracks the top of these combined asset pools, peaking at age eighty-five.

The third chart, Sources of Funds for Retirement Spending, breaks down the couple's income and spending from age sixty-eight to ninety-five in thousands of US dollars. Annual spending, depicted as an orange line, begins at approximately one hundred and seventy thousand dollars at age sixty-eight and rises steadily to around two hundred and forty thousand dollars by age ninety. Following Chad's death at ninety, spending drops by twenty percent to roughly two hundred thousand dollars. The chart shows that Social Security benefits, represented in green, serve as their primary source of retirement income. This is supplemented by mandatory 401k withdrawals, in grey, and savings account withdrawals, in blue. Notably, after Chad passes away and their Social Security income drops, they rely much more heavily on their savings accounts to cover their spending.

Two tables detail the specific parameters and assumptions underlying this case study. The savings table shows that both Chad and Jane make three percent pre-tax contributions to their savings, which are met with a one point five percent employer match. They also save an additional two percent of their after-tax income. Combined with a five point five percent contribution from portfolio returns, their lifetime active and passive savings rate is eleven point one percent. A breakeven analysis confirms that their actual three percent pre-tax savings rate is exactly the amount required to reach their financial target at age ninety-five. This achieves a one hundred percent retirement income replacement, which implies a twelve percent real reduction in spending. 

Other key assumptions listed on the page include a two-income median lifestyle, a real equity return of five point five percent, a real fixed income return of one percent, and Social Security taken at age sixty-eight at one hundred and eight percent of age sixty-seven benefits. Their asset allocation transition is also noted, with after-tax savings starting at fifty percent fixed income at age twenty-five and remaining at fifty percent at retirement, while their retirement plan starts with twenty percent fixed income at age twenty-five and shifts to sixty percent by retirement.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication, titled Season 1, Episode 7 of the Retirement Insights series, focuses on the financial outlook for a hypothetical couple, Chad and Jane Selphy, under a scenario of lower financial market returns. The author argues that even if the couple sticks to their savings plan, structural macroeconomic factors can derail their retirement security. Specifically, worsening demographics across OECD nations limit overall trend growth, and U.S. productivity remains sluggish compared to high-growth historical eras driven by electrification, the interstate highway system, and the early internet. Current innovations like driverless cars and 3D printing have not matched those past productivity booms. Consequently, real equity and fixed income returns are projected to be 0.75% lower on an annual basis than in previous, more optimistic scenarios, leading the couple to completely exhaust their retirement assets by age 95.

A line chart comparing financial assets illustrates this dynamic. Under the previous scenario where everything goes according to plan, the couple's assets peak above $0.8 million near age 85 and leave a cushion of roughly $0.45 million at age 95. Under the lower-return scenario of Episode 7, their financial assets peak earlier, at about $0.7 million around retirement age 67, and steadily decline to zero by age 95. A second area chart detailing total asset composition shows that the couple begins with $54,000 in debt at age 25, which they pay off by age 40. From there, their net worth is driven by after-tax savings and 401(k) accumulation, peaking at age 67 before depleting rapidly in their post-work years.

The sources of funds for retirement spending are detailed in a bar chart. From retirement at age 68 through age 89, spending—which grows from roughly $160,000 to over $220,000—is covered by Social Security and mandatory 401(k) withdrawals. At age 90, when the second spouse is assumed to die, retirement spending drops by 20%. Despite this reduction, their discretionary 401(k) and savings accounts are entirely depleted over the subsequent five years, leaving only Social Security to cover expenses, which falls short of their spending needs by age 95.

A data table outlines the savings metrics and a breakeven analysis. Chad and Jane each make 3.0% pre-tax contributions to savings, receiving a 1.5% employer match, alongside additional household savings of 2.0% of after-tax income. Combined with a 4.4% contribution from portfolio returns, this yields a lifetime active and passive savings rate of 10.1%. To avoid running out of money, the breakeven analysis suggests the couple could have increased their pre-tax contributions from 3.0% to 3.6% throughout their working lives. Alternatively, they could target a 95% retirement income replacement rate, which would require a 16% real reduction in retirement spending. Other underlying assumptions for this episode include a two-income median lifestyle, no home purchase due to insufficient downpayment, retirement at age 67, real equity returns of 4.8%, and real fixed income returns of 0.3%.

Because a family bankruptcy during the 2001 tech collapse left them deeply suspicious of financial markets, Chad and Jane hold the majority of their savings in cash and fixed income. This conservative stance, coupled with low policy rates from the Federal Reserve, results in their retirement savings depleting much faster than they would under a standard plan.

A line chart titled "Financial assets" compares their wealth trajectory under this conservative scenario to a baseline scenario where everything goes according to plan. In the baseline scenario, represented by a blue dotted line, financial assets peak at approximately $0.8 million around age 85. Under the conservative scenario, shown by a solid grey line, assets peak much lower at roughly $0.6 million at age 67 and plummet to zero by age 92. 

The "Total asset composition" chart breaks down their net worth from age 25 to 95. The consequences of this depletion are illustrated in the bar chart "Sources of funds for retirement spending." This chart compares projected annual spending, which starts around $160,000 at age 68 and rises to over $220,000 by age 95, against their funding sources. While Social Security and discretionary and mandatory 401(k) withdrawals cover their expenses initially, their personal savings and 401(k) accounts are fully depleted by age 91. From that point on, Jane, who survives Chad, is left solely with Social Security payments of approximately $100,000, leaving a massive funding gap relative to her spending needs.
