This page from J.P. Morgan’s Retirement Insights series examines the severe financial strain of early retirement at age 62 for a hypothetical median-income couple, Chad and Jane Selphy. The central argument is that early retirement is highly challenging for median earners because it simultaneously reduces working-years savings contributions, lowers the accumulation of portfolio returns, and permanently decreases Social Security benefits due to the early-retirement acceleration discount. Under their baseline scenario, in which Chad and Jane contribute 3.0% of their pre-tax income to savings, they face near-immediate insolvency upon retiring at age 62 if they maintain their planned retirement spending at 100% of their pre-retirement disposable income.

To visualize this outcome, a line chart titled Financial Assets compares two trajectories. In the baseline trajectory, where everything goes according to plan, the couple's financial assets peak at nearly 0.8 million dollars around age 85 and remain above 0.5 million dollars by age 95. In contrast, the early retirement trajectory shows assets peaking at roughly 0.5 million dollars at age 58 before plummeting steeply to zero by age 67.

A secondary chart, Sources of funds for retirement spending, Episode 11, shows why this insolvency occurs. It plots annual spending against sources of income in thousands of US dollars from age 63 to 95. The orange spending line starts near 175,000 dollars, rises to about 240,000 dollars by age 90, and then drops slightly to 225,000 dollars after the death of the first spouse. To fund this, Chad and Jane must draw down their savings accounts and discretionary 401(k) assets. These assets are completely exhausted by age 68, leaving only Social Security—represented by green bars holding steady around 100,000 to 125,000 dollars—as their sole source of income, creating a massive annual funding gap.

An asset composition area chart, Total asset composition, Episode 11, tracks the progression of their 401(k) accounts, after-tax savings, debt, and net worth from age 25 to 95. It displays initial debt of 54,000 dollars in their early years, with net worth peaking near 0.5 million dollars at age 58 before rapidly flatlining to zero by age 68 as all 401(k) and after-tax savings are depleted.

The tables on the page lay out the underlying savings metrics, breakeven analysis, and other modeling assumptions. Under the baseline, both Chad and Jane contribute 3.0% of pre-tax income to savings with a 1.5% employer match, bringing their lifetime active and passive savings rate to 9.7% when including after-tax household savings and portfolio returns. To avoid running out of money by age 95, a breakeven analysis calculates that the couple would have to raise their pre-tax contributions to 8.8% during their working years. Alternatively, if they keep their savings rate at 3.0%, they would have to accept a retirement income replacement rate of just 66%, which equates to a real spending reduction of 46%.

Other key assumptions for this analysis include a two-income median lifestyle where no home is purchased due to insufficient downpayment accumulation. The model assumes a 5.5% real return on equities and a 1.0% real return on fixed income. Social Security is assumed to be taken at age 63 at 75% of the full benefit level available at age 67. The second spouse is projected to die at age 90, triggering a 20% reduction in household spending thereafter. Asset allocations glide from age 25 to retirement, shifting fixed-income exposure in after-tax savings from 50% to 50%, and in retirement plans from 20% to 60%.

The chart "Sources of funds for retirement spending, Episode 10" shows the annual breakdown of retirement income from age 68 to 95. The analysis follows a hypothetical single individual named Ken Ebbis who experiences several real-life disruptions, including three years of unemployment—spurred by a temporary job loss at a medical marijuana distribution center due to a theft eventually traced to the Alpha Kappa Cheeba sorority—and two years of family emergencies.

Two tables provide the quantitative basis and assumptions for this scenario. This page from J.P. Morgan's "Retirement Insights" publication presents Season 1, Episode 22 of a hypothetical retirement case study featuring an individual named Ken Ebbis. The core argument is that individuals do not necessarily have to increase savings preemptively to protect against unfortunate events if they are prepared to make other sacrifices, such as working longer. In this scenario, Ken faces several compounding challenges—specifically a family emergency, lower market returns, and adverse policy changes. Rather than slashing his retirement spending by 25% to 30%, Ken maintains his 3.3% pre-tax savings contribution rate and decides to work longer, delaying his retirement from age 67 to age 70. This delay increases his savings contributions, boosts his portfolio income, and raises his Social Security benefit to 124% of what it would have been at age 67. The author cautions that while this strategy works well for Ken, not everyone possesses the physical or mental capacity to work uninterrupted until age 70.

The page includes several charts and tables that detail this financial projection. A chart titled "Financial assets" tracks Ken's accumulated assets in USD millions from age 25 to 95, comparing the Episode 22 scenario (working longer to offset headwinds) to the Episode 20 baseline (where everything goes according to plan). Under both scenarios, assets grow starting around age 35, peak near $0.48 million around age 85, and decline to near zero by age 95, demonstrating that delaying retirement to age 70 effectively offsets the severe headwinds Ken faced. 

A stacked area chart titled "Total asset composition, Episode 22" breaks down Ken's net worth from age 25 to 95. This visual shows that Ken starts with $27,000 in debt, which is cleared by his early 40s. Finally, the page lists the background assumptions for this case study. Ken is modeled as a single individual with a median income who does not purchase a home due to an insufficient down payment. This page of the publication focuses on a hypothetical case study titled "Season 2, Episode 3: Ima Narcissus wants to retire at 62 and invest her way out." The narrative analyzes the feasibility of retiring early at age 62 while maintaining a modest 7.5% pre-tax contribution rate by attempting to achieve superior portfolio returns. The author argues that this strategy is highly unrealistic, as it would require the individual, Ima, to beat the market by 3.6% annually for over 50 years. This translates to an unprecedented 9.1% real long-term equity return, which is higher than any post-war historical period, including the tech boom of the late 1990s. The author concludes that increasing savings is a far more reliable method for funding early retirement.

To illustrate this, a line chart titled "Financial assets (excl. home sale and related proceeds)" tracks assets from age 25 to 95 in USD millions. It compares three paths: a base scenario where "everything goes according to plan" and assets peak near $2.0 million around age 65 before ending at $1.0 million; a second scenario of retiring at age 62 without higher returns, which causes assets to completely deplete by age 82; and the third "invest her way out" scenario, which matches the successful asset trajectory of the base case but relies entirely on the assumed 9.1% real equity return. 

Another visual, "Total asset composition, Episode 3," shows net worth peaking at nearly $3.0 million around age 65 and stabilizing around $2.5 million by age 95. This asset mix is broken down into 401(k) savings, after-tax savings, home equity, and an initial $27,000 of debt that is paid off early in life. 

The cash flows required to sustain this plan are detailed in the stacked bar chart "Sources of funds for retirement spending, Episode 3." From age 63 to 95, annual retirement spending in USD thousands rises from approximately $175,000 to $230,000. These expenditures are funded by a combination of Social Security, which provides about $80,000 to $100,000 annually, alongside mandatory and discretionary 401(k) distributions, and a small, short-lived savings account balance.

Key metrics are organized in the "Season 2, Episode 3: Savings" table, which notes Ima's 7.5% pre-tax contribution rate, a 3.0% employer match, and additional household savings of 2.0% of after-tax income, culminating in a lifetime active and passive savings rate of 23.8%. Under the high-return breakeven analysis, her actual 7.5% contribution matches what is required to reach her target assets by age 95. Alternatively, achieving an 85% retirement income replacement ratio would instead force her to make a steep 32% real reduction in spending. The underlying modeling assumptions listed at the bottom of the page specify a single, affluent individual, taking Social Security at age 63 at 75% of full benefits, purchasing a home at age 36, and shifting fixed-income investment allocations from 20% to 60% in her retirement plan as she ages.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s retirement analysis explores how unexpected life events can disrupt long-term financial plans, using a hypothetical scenario titled "Season 2, Episode 4: Ima Narcissus deals with parent elder-care costs." In this narrative, a single, affluent individual named Ima must unexpectedly contribute $40,000 per year in 2015 dollars over a five-year period to fund her parents' assisted living facility. Because her siblings offer minimal assistance, Ima is forced to pause her retirement savings contributions. This temporary disruption has a severe compounding effect on her retirement security, causing her nest egg to draw down much faster than anticipated and run out completely before she reaches age 95.

The financial impact of this disruption is illustrated across several charts. The first chart, tracking financial assets excluding home sale proceeds from age 25 to 95, compares her original plan against the elder-care scenario. Under her initial plan, where everything goes according to design, Ima's financial assets peak at approximately $1.8 million at age 65 and remain around $1.0 million by age 95. Under the parent elder-care scenario, her financial assets peak at a lower level of roughly $1.5 million at age 65 and are completely depleted by age 92. 

A second chart shows the sources of funds for her retirement spending from age 66 to 93. While her spending line steadily rises from about $170,000 to over $230,000, her discretionary and mandatory 401(k) balances run out around age 90. This shortfall forces her to draw heavily from savings accounts and ultimately fund her final years through a home sale. This is further detailed in a chart tracking total asset composition and net worth, which shows her total net worth peaking at roughly $2.3 million at age 65, followed by a steep decline and a liquidation of home equity between ages 90 and 95.

Key assumptions for this analysis include retirement at age 65, retirement spending at 85% of pre-retirement disposable income, Social Security taken at age 66 at 93% of the age 67 benefit, and an initial debt of $27,000. Real investment returns are assumed at 5.5% for equities and 1.0% for fixed income. Under normal conditions, Ima has a pre-tax savings contribution rate of 7.5%, an employer match of 3.0%, and additional household savings of 2.0% of after-tax income, leading to a lifetime savings rate of 17.9%. 

The breakeven analysis concludes that to absorb the $40,000 annual elder-care costs and still reach her financial target by age 95, Ima would have needed to increase her pre-tax savings contributions from 7.5% to 9.5%. If she is unable to increase her savings, her alternative is to accept a lower retirement income replacement rate of 77%, which would require a significant 34% reduction in her real retirement spending.

This page, titled "Season 2, Episode 5: Ima Narcissus and lower market returns," analyzes how lower financial market returns impact the retirement security of an affluent single individual named Ima. The author argues that worsening demographics in the OECD, alongside weak U.S. productivity compared to peak eras like the 1930s, 1950s, and 1990s, will lead to lower trend growth. Specifically, over Ima's lifetime, annual equity and fixed income returns are projected to be 0.75% lower than in previous models, with real equity returns at 4.8% and real fixed income returns at 0.3%. A key axiom highlighted is that lower market returns have a disproportionately large impact on affluent retirees who rely heavily on investment portfolios rather than Social Security. While a median-income retiree can offset this decline with a minor 0.6% increase in annual contributions, Ima must raise her pre-tax savings from 7.5% to 9.7% to maintain her financial target, or face a 35% reduction in real spending. 

An accompanying table outlines Ima’s savings profile and assumptions. Under normal assumptions, she retires at age 65 with a 7.5% pre-tax contribution rate, a 3% employer match, 2% in additional household savings, and an overall lifetime active and passive savings rate of 19.4%. Her retirement spending is modeled at 85% of her pre-retirement disposable income, with Social Security initiated at age 66. If she does not increase her contribution rate to the breakeven target of 9.7%, her retirement income replacement drops to 76%, representing a 35% reduction in real spending. 

Three charts illustrate these dynamics over time. The first line chart, "Financial assets (excl. home sale and related proceeds)," plots financial assets from age 25 to 95 in millions of USD. Under a baseline scenario where everything goes according to plan, assets peak near $1.8 million at age 65 and decline to roughly $0.9 million by age 95. In the lower market returns scenario, assets peak at about $1.7 million and deplete entirely to zero by age 93. 

The second chart, "Sources of funds for retirement spending, Episode 5," is a stacked bar chart showing annual income sources against a rising retirement spending curve from age 66 to 95. Annual spending grows from $175,000 to $240,000. Up to age 85, spending is funded by Social Security, mandatory 401(k) withdrawals, and discretionary 401(k) withdrawals. At age 86, discretionary 401(k) funds run dry, and spending must be supported by savings account balances and proceeds from a home sale. 

The final area chart, "Total asset composition, Episode 5," tracks net worth and asset breakdown from age 25 to 95. Net worth peaks at approximately $2.3 million at age 65, supported by 401(k) balances, after-tax savings, and home equity from a home purchased at age 36. At age 86, the home is sold to transition home equity into liquid after-tax savings, which are then steadily drawn down to fund her remaining years.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Retirement Insights series, titled "Season 2, Episode 6," examines the potential impact of proposed Social Security, tax, and 401(k) policy changes on a fictional single, affluent individual named Ima Narcissus. The premise assumes a political shift in Washington where moderates implement entitlement and tax reforms to curb long-term deficits. Because these policy changes—such as Social Security means-testing, limits on 401(k) contributions, and reduced itemized deductions—are designed to target individuals earning over $250,000, Ima faces a much greater impact than lower-income earners. 

A summary table details Ima’s savings profile under these assumptions. Her baseline scenario includes pre-tax contributions to savings of 7.5%, an employer match of 3.0%, additional household savings equal to 2.0% of after-tax income, and a 10.6% contribution from portfolio returns, yielding a lifetime active and passive savings rate of 21.2%. A breakeven analysis shows that to offset the proposed policy changes and successfully reach her financial asset target by age 95, Ima must increase her pre-tax savings contribution rate from 7.5% to 8.9%, representing a 1.4% increase. Alternatively, if she keeps her contribution rate at 7.5%, she must accept a retirement income replacement of 78%, which implies a real 34% reduction in retirement spending.

The page features three charts to illustrate these dynamics. The first chart, "Financial assets (excl. home sale and related proceeds)," plots financial assets in USD millions from age 25 to 95, contrasting a baseline where everything goes according to plan with the policy change scenario. Under the baseline plan, Ima's assets peak around age 65 at nearly $1.8 million and remain around $1.0 million by age 95. Under the policy changes, her financial assets are completely depleted to $0 by age 95.

The second chart, "Sources of funds for retirement spending, Episode 6," shows a breakdown of how Ima's annual retirement spending of approximately $170,000 to $230,000 is funded from age 66 to 94. The stacked bar chart shows that her spending is met primarily through Social Security, which provides a steady base of around $100,000 annually, alongside discretionary 401(k) withdrawals, minor mandatory 401(k) payouts, and savings account draws. At age 95, a home sale is utilized to bridge the remaining spending gap. 

The third chart, "Total asset composition, Episode 6," tracks Ima's overall net worth in USD millions from age 25 to 95. Her net worth peaks at roughly $2.4 million around age 65, comprised of 401(k) assets, after-tax savings, and home equity, offset by a modest initial debt of $27,000 in her youth. By age 95, the chart highlights the liquidation of her home, which converts her home equity into after-tax savings to sustain her.

Additional assumptions for this model include retiring at age 65, purchasing a home at age 36, and taking Social Security at age 66 at 93% of her age 67 benefit. The model applies a real equity return of 5.5% and a real fixed income return of 1.0%. It also assumes the use of the Consumer Price Index for Social Security earnings compounding, a lower Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA) for benefit growth, and further reductions in itemized deductions.

This page, titled "Season 2, Episode 7: Ima Narcissus is made redundant," examines the financial consequences of late-career job loss and the necessity of proactive retirement planning. The narrative focuses on Ima, a healthcare consultant who is laid off in her 50s when her employer automates her role. At age 58, she takes a lower-paying job in meal procurement at a local hospital, permanently shifting her from an affluent income to a median income. To maintain her planned affluent retirement despite this setback, Ima would have needed to save 9.1% of her income annually instead of her actual 7.5%. Lacking that, she must face a median-income retirement, necessitating a 34% reduction in retirement spending to achieve a 78% income replacement rate.

The analysis is supported by several charts and tables. A line chart comparing financial assets (excluding home sale proceeds) from age 25 to 95 shows two trajectories. Under the ideal plan, assets peak near $1.8 million at age 65 and decline gradually to about $0.9 million by age 95. In the redundancy scenario, assets peak around $1.7 million but deplete entirely by age 93.

A second chart shows total asset composition and net worth over time. Net worth peaks at approximately $2.4 million at age 65, supported by 401(k) holdings, after-tax savings, and home equity, before declining until age 95, when a home sale provides a final liquidity boost. 

A third chart displays the annual sources of funds for retirement spending from age 66 to 95. Annual spending rises from approximately $170,000 to $230,000 over this period, funded by a combination of Social Security, mandatory and discretionary 401(k) withdrawals, after-tax savings, and eventually, the home sale.

A savings table shows that Ima has a 7.5% pre-tax contribution rate, a 3.0% employer match, a 2.0% additional household savings rate, and a 12.0% return contribution, resulting in a 22.5% lifetime savings rate. Other model assumptions include retiring at age 65, taking Social Security at age 66 at 93% of age 67 benefits, starting with $27,000 of debt, purchasing a home at age 36, and achieving real returns of 5.5% on equities and 1.0% on fixed income.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication "Eye on the Market" analyzes the case of "Ima Narcissus," a hypothetical ultra-conservative investor. Although Ima is a consistently high saver, she is paralyzed by apocalyptic economic theories and keeps her wealth primarily in cash and fixed income. The central argument is that affluent retirees who invest too conservatively risk failing to meet their wealth accumulation goals unless they compensate with substantially higher savings rates. In successful retirement scenarios, portfolio returns typically account for over half of total lifetime savings; however, for a highly conservative investor like Ima, returns account for only about one-third of that total, requiring her to adjust her contribution rate upward.

The page features three charts and two detailed tables. The first chart, "Financial assets (excl. home sale and related proceeds)," plots assets in millions of US dollars against age from 25 to 95. It contrasts a successful baseline scenario ("Everything goes according to plan," shown as a blue dotted line peaking at $1.8 million at age 65 and ending near $0.8 million at age 95) with the ultra-conservative path (shown as a solid grey line peaking at $1.4 million at age 65 and falling to $0 by age 85). 

The second chart, "Total asset composition," tracks asset types and overall net worth from age 25 to 95 in USD millions. Net worth peaks near $2.2 million at age 65. Because of her conservative portfolio, her 401(k) and after-tax savings are depleted by age 85, forcing a home sale to fund the remaining decade of her life. 

The third chart, "Sources of funds for retirement spending," tracks annual funding sources in USD thousands from age 66 to 95 against a rising spending curve that starts at roughly $175,000 and approaches $240,000. This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market discusses a severe financial scenario titled Season 2, Episode 10: Ima Narcissus and the perfect storm, where multiple adverse events occur simultaneously. In this scenario, Ima is forced to retire early at age 63, faces lower market returns, and experiences policy changes that negatively impact her retirement benefits, 401(k) contributions, and effective tax rate. The primary argument is that under these conditions, a standard savings strategy is highly vulnerable, requiring a doubling of pre-tax savings to avoid running out of money. 

The analysis is supported by several charts and tables. A table outlining the savings assumptions shows that while Ima’s actual pre-tax savings rate is 7.5% with a 3.0% employer match, she would actually need a 14.0% pre-tax contribution rate to reach her financial target by age 95. Alternatively, achieving retirement security would require a 59% income replacement rate, which implies a real spending reduction of 52%. Other model assumptions include an affluent single individual, Social Security taken early at age 64 at 80% of benefits, an initial debt of $27,000, and conservative real asset returns of 4.8% for equities and 0.3% for fixed income. Policy assumptions include a lower COLA for Social Security, a higher Social Security income cap with means-testing, and further reductions in itemized deductions.

The chart detailing financial assets over time compares the baseline scenario where everything goes according to plan against the perfect storm scenario. Under the baseline, financial assets peak at nearly $1.8 million around age 65 and remain above $0.8 million at age 95. In contrast, under the perfect storm, financial assets peak at $1.5 million and are entirely depleted by age 78. 

The total asset composition chart displays a stacked view of Ima’s net worth, debt, home equity, after-tax savings, and 401(k) assets from age 25 to 95. This visual highlights a critical juncture at age 78, where Ima is forced to liquidate her home. Her net worth, represented by an orange line, flatlines to zero by age 88. 

The sources of funds chart provides a year-by-year breakdown of how Ima funds her retirement spending from age 64 to 94. Up to age 77, her spending is covered by a mix of Social Security, mandatory and discretionary 401(k) withdrawals, and after-tax savings. From age 78 to 87, she relies heavily on the proceeds from her home sale alongside Social Security. By age 88, both her financial assets and home equity proceeds are entirely gone, leaving her to live solely on Social Security, which falls far short of her projected spending needs. The author poses an open question for the next episode, noting that this scenario assumes the housing market appreciates, and asks what would happen to Ima's financial security if the housing market fails to grow.

This page of Retirement Insights details Season 2, Episode 11, titled "Ima Narcissus, the perfect storm and the lower home price." Her funding sources—including Social Security, mandatory and discretionary 401(k)s, and savings accounts—fail to meet this curve after age 78. Although the home sale proceeds cover the spending gap from ages 78 to 83, they run out completely by age 84, leaving her with only Social Security to cover a massive spending deficit.

An area chart tracking total asset composition, including debt, home equity, after-tax savings, and 401(k) values, shows that Ima's net worth peaks at roughly $1.8 million around age 63 but drops to zero by age 84, immediately after the home sale proceeds are fully exhausted. 

Two tables outline the baseline savings assumptions and a breakeven analysis. Ima's actual pre-tax savings contribution is 7.5%, with a 3% employer match, contributing to a lifetime savings rate of 18.7%. To survive this localized real estate underperformance and reach her financial asset target by age 95, her required pre-tax contribution rate would need to jump to 13.7%. Alternatively, she would face a retirement income replacement rate of only 59%, forcing a painful 52% real reduction in retirement spending. Other modeling assumptions include a single, affluent individual retiring at age 63, taking Social Security at age 64 at 80% of full benefits, and real investment returns of 4.8% on equities and 0.3% on fixed income.

The third chart, "Total asset composition, Episode 15," displays their net worth and underlying components in millions of USD from age 25 to 95. This page provides a key to the "plot devices" used in a series of scenario analyses about millennial retirement savings. It defines four primary variables. First, pre-tax contribution to savings measures the percentage of pre-tax income saved in tax-efficient vehicles like 401(k) plans, IRAs, and non-qualified deferred compensation, incorporating any employer matching; a footnote adds that tax efficiency comes from tax-free compounding, though distributions are taxed if funded pre-tax. Second, additional savings as a percentage of after-tax income accounts for money held in brokerage or money management accounts. Third, asset allocation outlines the mix of equities and fixed income starting at age 25, which linearly shifts along a "glide path" to retirement age. Standard target-date fund assumptions are used, typically starting with an 80 percent equity and 20 percent fixed-income allocation and shifting to a 40 percent equity and 60 percent fixed-income/cash split at retirement. Finally, financial market returns refers to the assumed investment returns on these savings, pointing readers to page 62 for more details.

This page, titled "Plot Devices," serves as a conceptual guide and methodology glossary for a J.P. Morgan Asset Management analysis tracking millennial retirement scenarios. It outlines five key variables used to model these projections. 

First, the concept of the "Retirement smile" explains that post-retirement spending does not rise linearly; instead, data from JPMorgan Chase’s Consumer and Community Bank shows that for some income categories, real spending tends to fall before rising again later in retirement. 

Second, "Retirement spending projections" are determined by initial income replacement goals, the spending smile, and inflation. For median-income households, the replacement goal is set at 100% of terminal pre-retirement cash flow due to limited budget flexibility during their working years. For affluent and high-net-worth households, the goal is set at 85%, reflecting typical reductions in commuting, clothing, dining out, and mortgage expenses. 

Third, the distinction between "Financial assets and total assets" is tracked over working and retirement years, emphasizing that a successful retirement is one where retirees can fund their spending entirely via financial assets rather than having to sell their home. 

Fourth, "Breakeven savings rates" calculate how much both spouses would have to save as a percentage of pre-tax income to regain solvency (ensuring financial assets last through age 95 with a modest cushion) after facing unfortunate life events or costly lifestyle choices. 

Finally, "Policy changes" warns of future government spending pressures that could impact retirement by limiting contributions to tax-efficient savings plans, reducing Social Security benefits, or reducing deductions for state and local taxes, mortgage interest, and charitable contributions.

This page analyzes the financial impact on a fictional millennial couple, Anita and Chip Oatley, who must fund half of their two children’s private college tuitions over four years because student loans are unavailable due to high default rates. Rather than lowering their lifestyle spending to pay for college, the Oatleys temporarily halt their retirement savings contributions. This choice significantly diminishes their retirement nest egg. To offset this interruption and avoid retirement spending cuts, the couple would need to increase their pre-tax savings rate from 8.3% to 9.7% during their active savings years. 

The consequences of this strategy are illustrated across three financial charts. The first chart compares the Oatleys' financial assets under this private college scenario against a baseline where everything goes according to plan. In the college tuition scenario, their financial assets peak at roughly $3.2 million near age 60 and hit zero by age 91, whereas the baseline scenario peaks near $4.0 million and maintains a substantial cushion through age 95. A second chart displays total asset composition from age 25 to 95, tracing a net worth curve built from 401(k) assets, after-tax savings, and home equity, offset early on by a small debt. It also highlights a critical home sale at age 90 that injects cash into their portfolio. 

The sources of retirement funds are detailed in a stacked bar chart showing annual retirement spending of over $300,000 from age 64 to 94. The Oatleys fund this spending using Social Security, mandatory and discretionary 401(k)s, and savings accounts. However, because of the savings interruption, their 401(k) accounts are fully depleted by age 91, leaving them reliant solely on Social Security and the proceeds of their home sale to get through their remaining years. 

The data tables clarify the couple's savings metrics and modeling assumptions. Anita and Chip each have actual pre-tax contributions of 8.3% and a 3.0% employer match, which, combined with additional after-tax savings and portfolio returns, yield a lifetime savings rate of 20.3%. A breakeven analysis warns that if they keep their savings rate at 8.3% instead of rising to the required 9.7%, they will miss their age 95 asset target, resulting in an alternative retirement income replacement rate of 78% and forcing a painful 36% real reduction in retirement spending. This analysis assumes an affluent couple retiring at age 63 with a retirement spending target of 85% of pre-retirement disposable income, a 20% spending reduction after the first spouse dies at age 90, real equity returns of 5.5%, and real fixed income returns of 1.0%.

This page from J.P. Morgan's retirement analysis focuses on Season 2, Episode 16 of a case study featuring Anita and Chip Oatley, an affluent millennial couple. Under the ideal conditions of Episode 15, the couple's financial assets would have peaked at approximately $4.0 million around age 65. A stacked area chart details the couple's total asset composition over time. The savings table outlines that both Anita and Chip currently save 8.3% of their pre-tax income with a 0% employer match. Due to IRA contribution limits, 42% of their intended tax-efficient savings are diverted to less efficient, non-tax-advantaged accounts. The accompanying assumptions note that both spouses retire at age 63, the home is purchased at age 36, and the second spouse passes away at age 90, which triggers a 20% reduction in retirement spending. This page from J.P. Morgan Asset Management's "Eye on the Market" focuses on Season 2, Episode 19 of a financial planning case study, examining the financial impact of long-term care insurance for an affluent couple, Anita and Chip Oatley. Worried about a hereditary risk of Alzheimer's disease, Chip and Anita purchase long-term care insurance starting at age 55, paying premiums until Anita develops a covered condition at age 79 and lives to age 82. The analysis highlights that because this insurance is highly expensive—costing nearly $10,000 annually in 2015 dollars—their final financial position is only marginally better than in a previous scenario where they paid for care out of pocket. To offset the high cost of premiums and avoid depleting their assets, the couple would need to raise their annual pre-tax savings rate from 8.3% to 9.8%.

The first chart, "Financial assets (excl. home sale and related proceeds)" in USD millions from ages 25 to 95, compares three scenarios. In Episode 15, where everything goes according to plan, assets peak near $4.0 million around age 63 and slowly decline to just under $1.0 million by age 95. In Episode 18, which features an uninsured long-term care event, assets plummet to zero by age 85. In the current Episode 19, despite having insurance, the high cost of premiums causes their assets to deplete to zero at virtually the same point, around age 85, demonstrating the severe financial drag of the insurance premiums.

The second chart, "Sources of funds for retirement spending, Episode 19," displays annual retirement cash flows in USD thousands from ages 64 to 94. Spending starts around $350,000, then drops to about $250,000 at age 82 following the death of one spouse, which triggers an assumed 20% spending reduction, before climbing slightly. Funding is initially sourced from Social Security, discretionary 401(k) funds, and mandatory 401(k) funds. At age 85, a home sale provides a liquid influx of funds, which is subsequently drawn down from a savings account to sustain the remaining spouse.

The third chart, "Total asset composition, Episode 19," shows the couple's net worth from ages 25 to 95. Net worth peaks near $4.0 million in their early 60s, comprised of home equity, after-tax savings, and 401(k) balances, offset by a small initial debt of $27,000. At age 85, the home is sold, converting home equity into after-tax savings to cover remaining life expenses.

Additional tables detail the savings and model assumptions. For savings, both Anita and Chip contribute 8.3% pre-tax with a 3.0% employer match, yielding a 22.7% lifetime savings rate when accounting for investment returns. A breakeven analysis shows that to avoid running out of money by age 95, they must either raise pre-tax contributions to 9.8% or reduce their retirement income replacement rate to 77%, which would require a 37% real reduction in spending. Key underlying assumptions include a home purchase at age 36, retirement at age 63, real equity returns of 5.5%, real fixed income returns of 1.0%, and taking Social Security benefits at age 64 at 80% of the age 67 benefit level.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication "Eye on the Market" focuses on the financial implications of long-term care, specifically using a scenario where a spouse is diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. The author highlights that as millennial lifespans increase, the prevalence of Alzheimer's is projected to rise, noting Alzheimer's Association data showing that 11 percent of Americans over age 65 and 32 percent of those over age 85 suffer from the disease. Because traditional insurance rarely covers round-the-clock care, these medical events can rapidly deplete family savings.

To illustrate this risk, a case study analysis follows a hypothetical affluent couple, Anita and Chip Oatley, in an scenario designated as "Season 2, Episode 18." In this scenario, Anita is diagnosed with Alzheimer's at age 79 and lives until age 82. The accompanying financial asset chart compares a baseline scenario where everything goes according to plan against this long-term care event. While the baseline scenario shows financial assets peaking near 4.0 million dollars at age 65 and remaining solvent past age 95, the long-term care event causes assets to crash to zero by age 83. 

To fund this period of care, a chart detailing the sources of retirement funds shows spending spiking from a baseline of roughly 350,000 dollars to nearly 800,000 dollars annually between ages 79 and 82. This surge is funded by rapidly draining discretionary and mandatory 401(k) accounts, and eventually forces the sale of the family home around age 82 to sustain Chip’s subsequent retirement years. This transition is also visualized in a total asset composition chart, which tracks net worth peaking near 5.0 million dollars at age 65 and declining sharply until the home sale is finalized, leaving Chip with a net worth that approaches zero by age 95.

A savings table and breakeven analysis show that both Anita and Chip originally contributed 8.3 percent pre-tax to their savings, which, combined with a 3.0 percent employer match and other savings, resulted in a 22.9 percent lifetime savings rate. To have successfully absorbed the costs of Anita's long-term care without depleting their assets, they would have needed to increase their pre-tax savings rate to 10.4 percent during their working years. Alternatively, they would have had to accept a 74 percent retirement income replacement rate, representing a real spending reduction of 40 percent. 

The analysis is built on several key assumptions detailed at the bottom of the page, including retirement for both spouses at age 63, a home purchase at age 36, and retirement spending set at 85 percent of pre-retirement disposable income. Following the death of a spouse, spending is assumed to drop by 20 percent. Social Security benefits are claimed at age 64 at 80 percent of the age 67 benefit level. The investment portfolio assumes real returns of 5.5 percent for equities and 1.0 percent for fixed income, with asset allocations gradually shifting toward higher fixed income concentrations as the couple ages.

This page, titled "The retirement 'spending smile'", argues that the common practice of estimating retirement spending by growing a fixed target at the rate of inflation fails to reflect real-world retiree behavior. Drawing on data from JPMorgan Chase's Consumer and Community Bank and the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Expenditure Survey, the analysis explores how spending patterns evolve by age and wealth level in real, inflation-adjusted terms. For median-income households, spending declines through age eighty due to lower costs for housing, transportation, and food, but eventually ticks upward later in life as healthcare costs accelerate and double as a share of total expenditures. This trajectory forms a u-shape known as the "spending smile." A footnote emphasizes the burden of these healthcare expenses, noting that medical bills contributed to half of American bankruptcy filings in 2001, with three-quarters of those individuals having health insurance at the onset of their illness.

Conversely, affluent and high-net-worth households do not exhibit this late-life spending rebound; their rising healthcare costs are fully offset by ongoing spending reductions in food, apparel, and housing. These distinct paths are illustrated in a line chart titled "Real retirement spending paths differ by wealth level," which indexes spending at age sixty to one hundred. The chart tracks spending from age sixty to ninety-five, showing the median curve bottoming out near seventy-five at age eighty before rising to over eighty by age ninety-five. Meanwhile, the curve for affluent and high-net-worth households declines steadily to about sixty-five by age ninety-five.

Finally, the text outlines a three-step methodology for constructing realistic retirement spending curves: establishing an initial income replacement goal based on pre-retirement cash flow, growing that level annually using the real change of the spending smile, and adjusting for nominal inflation. For couples, the analysis assumes spending drops by twenty percent following the death of a spouse, reflecting the inelastic nature of major household expenses like housing, utilities, and transportation.

This page serves as a reference and appendix for the publication, listing the sources and acronyms used throughout the report. The sources section references numerous academic studies, institutional reports, and media articles from organizations such as the Council of Economic Advisers, Wells Fargo, Boston College, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Stanford University, Georgetown University, Oxford, Goldman Sachs, and the Pew Research Center. The cited works focus on key themes like millennial economic trends, student loan debt, the financial impact of health issues and marital status changes on retirement, wealth transfer, and defined contribution plans. Below the sources, an acronym guide defines essential terminology used across the report. These definitions include standard economic agencies and metrics like the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Congressional Budget Office, Cost-of-living adjustments, Consumer Price Index, Federal Housing Finance Agency, and the Social Security Administration. It also defines terms specific to retirement and finance, including Employee Benefit Research Institute, Fixed income asset allocation, Individual Retirement Account, J.P. Morgan Asset Management, Long-term care, and STEM.

This page outlines four distinct working income vectors for millennials, operating under the assumption that all protagonists hold bachelor's degrees. The four prototypes developed to represent different career paths are the Median earner, the Median late bloomer, the Affluent earner (representing the 5th percentile of earners), and the High net worth earner (representing the 1st percentile of earners). 

The first chart, titled "Real income curves by millennial type," shows annual income in thousands of 2013 USD for the Median and Late bloomer prototypes from ages 25 to 70. The median path starts at around $30,000 at age 25, climbs to a peak of approximately $55,000 at age 50, and then tapers off to about $36,000 by age 70. The late bloomer curve begins at about $15,000, which represents 45% of the median, and gradually converges to match the median trajectory by age 45. These curves are sourced from U.S. Census Bureau data and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

The second chart, also titled "Real income curves by millennial type," tracks the higher-earning cohorts using a scale up to $400,000. The Affluent curve starts around $35,000 at age 25, rises to a peak of roughly $130,000 near age 55, and ends at about $100,000 by age 70. The High net worth trajectory starts at approximately $100,000 at age 25, peaks at around $350,000 between ages 50 and 55, and declines to about $240,000 by age 70. The data for these upper-percentile curves is derived from the U.S. Census and a joint study by the University of Minnesota, the Minneapolis Federal Reserve, Princeton University, and the Social Security Administration. All income curves are inflation-adjusted based on assumed wage inflation to reflect a full working career.

This page analyzes the idiosyncratic price risk of individual homes compared to nationwide real estate indexes, arguing that relying on a single home as a retirement asset is risky because it is a non-diversifiable asset tied to one location. The author illustrates this with a hypothetical retiree whose home sale proceeds would support them to age 88 under average historical appreciation rates. However, if annual home price appreciation is just 1.25 percent lower than the national average, the home would sell for about half as much, depleting the retiree's savings five years earlier.

To demonstrate how common such underperformance is, the page highlights geographical return dispersion. At the metropolitan statistical area level, the standard deviation of home price returns was slightly over 1 percent from 1975 to 2015. When zooming in to the neighborhood level from 2004 to 2015, the standard deviation rose to 2.4 percent, proving that smaller geographical units suffer from greater return dispersion relative to nationwide indexes like Case-Shiller or FHFA.

This dispersion is visualized in a bar chart titled Real home price returns by MSA, 1975-2015, which plots the number of metropolitan statistical areas, from zero to fifty, against real annual return intervals ranging from less than negative 2.00 percent to over 4.25 percent. The distribution is roughly bell-shaped, with the median and mean lines marked near the center-left. A designated bracket highlights a substantial number of metropolitan statistical areas whose returns fell between 1.0 percent and 1.5 percent below the median, underlining how easily an individual property can underperform the national average over long horizons. The chart's data is sourced from CoreLogic Case-Shiller, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management as of the first quarter of 2015.

This page, titled "Financial market returns," establishes long-term financial market assumptions for stocks, bonds, and cash, which are crucial for projecting retirement income. The author emphasizes that portfolio returns often make up half or more of a person's total lifetime savings by retirement. 

For equities, the author sets a base-case real return expectation of 5.5% for millennial investors. This estimate is positioned near the bottom of the historical post-war range of 5% to 7% due to headwinds like slower potential U.S. economic growth, an aging population, and anticipated mean reversion. This analysis is supported by a line chart titled "S&P 500 total real return," which plots 35-year rolling periods from 1905 to 2010. The chart shows that while post-war real returns have historically remained steady within a 5% to 7% corridor, they recently spiked toward 8% to 9%. The author notes this recent spike is anomalous because it measures from the cyclical low of 1980 to the low-rate-driven equity recovery of 2015.

The discussion then turns to the bond market, explaining that real returns are highly directional and correspond to major economic regimes, spanning from Great Depression deflation to post-financial crisis policy era under Federal Reserve Chairs Alan Greenspan and Ben Bernanke. A line chart titled "U.S. bond market real return" tracks 35-year rolling periods from 1965 to 2015 for both intermediate U.S. Treasuries and long corporate bonds. It illustrates how real returns bottomed near -1.5% around 1980 and rose steadily to peak between 4% and 5% by 2015. 

To project future bond performance, a scatter plot titled "U.S. bond market returns vs. inception yields" maps 35-year rolling total real returns for intermediate U.S. Treasuries (1926–2015) against their yields at the start of each period. The plot reveals a strong positive correlation: starting yields of 12% to 14% in 1980 produced high subsequent returns, whereas starting yields of 1% to 2% historically limit subsequent 35-year real returns to a range of -1% to +2%. Consequently, the author forecasts a conservative +1% real return on government bonds for millennial investors, warning that today's low-yield environment structurally caps future real returns.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, published by Michael Cembalest, focuses on the deep de-carbonization of electricity grids, spurred by policies like President Obama's Clean Power Plan. The analysis specifically compares Germany’s Energiewende plan, which targets an 80 percent renewable grid, with a simulated California counterpart referred to as Caliwende. Both plans are evaluated against current electricity mixes and balanced systems that combine renewable and nuclear energy.

Two main scatter charts illustrate these electricity grid options by plotting system cost in USD per megawatt-hour consumed on the vertical axis against carbon dioxide emissions in metric tonnes per gigawatt-hour on the horizontal axis. Each chart incorporates three pricing scenarios: current costs, future cost assumptions incorporating cheaper renewables and storage but higher nuclear and gas costs, and a second future cost scenario with lower nuclear costs.

The first chart illustrates Germany's electricity grid options. The current German system, which is 48 percent coal, has a cost of around 110 dollars per megawatt-hour and emissions of 410 tonnes per gigawatt-hour. Implementing the 80 percent renewable Energiewende system successfully lowers emissions to approximately 160 tonnes but increases system costs to 190 dollars per megawatt-hour, which decreases to 170 dollars under future cost assumptions. Adding battery storage to this system elevates costs further to 210 dollars per megawatt-hour. In comparison, a balanced German system composed of 40 percent renewable and 35 percent nuclear energy achieves similar low emissions of 160 tonnes for a significantly lower cost of 125 to 140 dollars per megawatt-hour. 

The second chart illustrates California's electricity grid options. The current California system, dominated by 56 percent natural gas, costs roughly 95 dollars per megawatt-hour with emissions around 190 tonnes per gigawatt-hour. Transitioning to the Caliwende system reduces emissions to about 85 tonnes but raises current costs to 140 dollars per megawatt-hour, which drops to 125 dollars under future cost assumptions. Adding battery storage to Caliwende increases current costs to 150 dollars per megawatt-hour. California’s balanced system option of 40 percent renewable and 35 percent nuclear energy achieves low emissions of about 80 tonnes for a cost between 110 and 120 dollars per megawatt-hour.

The author draws several primary conclusions from this comparison. First, high-renewable systems incur substantial costs for backup thermal power and storage during periods of low renewable generation, meaning that the standalone levelized costs of wind and solar do not accurately represent the true cost of these grids. High-renewable systems reduce emissions by 65 to 70 percent in Germany and 55 to 60 percent in California, but they currently cost 1.9 times the current system in Germany and 1.5 times in California. Although future cost declines could reduce these premiums to 1.6 times and 1.2 times respectively, adding battery storage still inflates costs due to intermittent utilization and energy loss. While balanced systems with nuclear power offer the lowest estimated costs and emissions, high capital cost uncertainties in the US and Europe make these assessments less certain than in Asia, where nuclear plant costs are 20 to 30 percent lower. Finally, geographic advantages play a major role, as California’s superior natural wind and solar capacity factors make the Caliwende system more cost-effective than Germany's Energiewende.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market analyzes the real-world feasibility of Germany’s "Energiewende" energy transition policy by modeling hourly electricity generation and demand under a projected 2050 scenario. The author argues that despite scaling up wind and solar capacity, Germany will still face a substantial need for backup thermal power because annual renewable supply surpluses are much smaller than deficits, meaning energy storage can only partially solve the grid's intermittency issues.

The top two charts illustrate modeled hourly electricity generation in gigawatts across January and June under the 2050 policy scenario, using historical weather profiles from German grid operators. In both charts, hydro and biomass power are assumed to run at a constant baseline rate of roughly 5 gigawatts, while wind and solar generation are scaled by three and two times their baseline capacities, respectively. The January chart shows a winter profile dominated by highly volatile wind power peaking up to 80 gigawatts, paired with negligible solar generation. In contrast, the June chart shows a summer profile characterized by lower, more stable wind generation offset by massive, regular daily spikes of solar power that also peak near 80 gigawatts.

The bottom two charts superimpose a brown "Load" line onto these generation profiles, representing German electricity demand based on 2014 data that has been reduced by 25% in accordance with Energiewende targets. The January chart highlights extended, multi-day periods of wind variability—most notably between January 16 and January 21—where renewable generation collapses, leaving large gaps of unmet demand that must be filled by natural gas and coal generation. In the June chart, the supply-demand gaps are short but occur daily, driven by the nightly absence of solar power, which requires thermal backup to step in as soon as the sun goes down, even though midday solar generation frequently creates a surplus.

In terms of broader projections, the author notes that while these charts only show two representative months, the mismatch persists year-round. Over an entire year, the simulated renewable surpluses would amount to 47 terawatt-hours, whereas the deficits would reach 107 terawatt-hours. Because the total annual deficit is more than double the surplus, Cembalest concludes that Germany cannot rely on storing excess renewable energy alone to achieve grid stability and will require a permanent, substantial fleet of backup thermal power plants.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market analyzes the economic and environmental impacts of integrating energy storage into Germany's Energiewende energy transition. The author models hypothetical scenarios where grid operators use pumped storage, zinc hybrid battery storage, or hydrogen storage, adjusting power and reservoir sizes to mitigate the largest annual renewable generation demand gaps. The analysis reveals that the best energy storage outcomes reduce emissions by only eight percent while increasing system costs by six percent. System costs rise because the capital and operating expenses of storage exceed the fuel costs of foregone natural gas, and thermal capacity remains online. 

An accompanying scatter plot visualizes these tradeoffs by mapping system cost in USD per MWh consumed on the y-axis against annual CO2 emissions in million metric tonnes on the x-axis. The baseline Energiewende scenario without storage is plotted as a green circle at approximately seventy million metric tonnes of CO2 and two hundred dollars per MWh. Alternative scenarios involving battery storage, shown as red circles, and pumped storage, shown as blue diamonds, succeed in lowering emissions to between fifty-eight and sixty-three million metric tonnes, but drive system costs up to between two hundred ten and two hundred thirty dollars per MWh. A diagonal dashed line indicates a cost-emissions preference curve, suggesting that choosing to implement storage at these higher costs remains a subjective valuation of carbon reduction.

The page also features a perspective from the International Energy Agency's 2014 Technology Perspectives Factsheet, which warns that energy storage is unlikely to be a transformative force on its own. The agency notes that, at current costs and performance levels, storage falls short of the flexibility provided by competing options like dispatchable natural gas, especially in high-power and high-energy applications. Finally, the author notes that hydrogen is generally impractical for utility-scale storage due to a low round-trip efficiency of around forty percent, and that short-term technologies like flywheels are omitted from the discussion because they cannot handle large amounts of excess renewable generation.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, titled Appendix II, discusses the ongoing need for backup thermal capacity in high-renewable electricity systems. The main argument is that the total thermal capacity required by a grid depends on the single largest supply-demand gap of the year, which occurs when renewable generation falls short of electricity load. Even under high-renewable scenarios, the peak unmet load is very close to the capacity of the current system. Consequently, while backup thermal plants in high-renewable systems would run less frequently—reducing variable fuel costs and carbon dioxide emissions—the upfront capital costs and annual fixed operations and maintenance costs would remain roughly the same as they are today. 

Two charts illustrate this dynamic by modeling hourly electricity demand gaps over a full calendar year. The first chart analyzes Germany's 2050 electricity demand gap under its Energiewende targets, plotting the projected hourly load not met by wind, solar, hydro, and biomass in gigawatts. It shows a highly volatile demand gap that frequently spikes throughout the year. The thermal capacity of Germany's current electricity mix sits at approximately 45 gigawatts, while the thermal capacity required under the 2050 Energiewende targets is slightly higher, at roughly 47 gigawatts, with the highest demand gaps occurring during the winter months of November and December. 

The second chart presents a similar analysis for California, referred to as Caliwende, showing the projected hourly load not met by wind, solar, hydro, biogas, biomass, and geothermal sources. In California's case, the thermal capacity of the current electricity mix is just under 27 gigawatts, while the backup capacity required under Caliwende is approximately 28 gigawatts. The largest supply-demand gaps for California are concentrated in the late summer and early autumn, particularly around September and October. 

Ultimately, both the German and Californian case studies demonstrate that transitioning to a high-renewable grid does not significantly reduce the peak thermal backup capacity needed to ensure reliability, as the maximum potential gap between renewable supply and total demand remains virtually unchanged.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the relevance of Germany and California as templates for global renewable energy transition. The author argues that while both regions have abundant natural resources to draw upon, their specific energy profiles are not universal. Germany’s wind and solar patterns are comparable to certain US Midwestern states, such as Illinois, Ohio, Michigan, Indiana, and Minnesota. Meanwhile, California’s solar-heavy footprint is similar to much of the Mediterranean and the Middle East. The text notes a critical distinction between potential energy and deliverable electricity, citing Germany's low wind capacity factors despite its good wind resource, and emphasizes that low population densities allow renewable resources to go much farther.

The main visual on the page is a scatter bubble chart titled Wind and Solar potential energy resources, and population: Countries and US States. The x-axis represents the percentile of solar resource energy potential, measured in kilowatt-hours per square meter per day based on direct normal irradiance, ranging from zero to one hundred. The y-axis represents the percentile of onshore wind resource energy potential, measured in kilowatt-hours per square meter per year based on wind speed, also scaled from zero to one hundred. The bubble sizes represent population, covering eighty-five percent of the world's population. 

Germany is highlighted with a red box in the upper-left quadrant of the chart, positioned near the twenty-fifth percentile for solar and the seventy-fifth percentile for wind, indicating a high-wind, low-solar profile. It is plotted near Poland, New Zealand, and the state of Michigan. California, labeled as CA, is highlighted in a red box in the bottom-right quadrant, sitting near the ninetieth percentile for solar and the tenth percentile for wind. This solar-dominant, low-wind profile groups California with states like Arizona and Nevada, as well as nations like Egypt and Yemen. 

The top-right quadrant of the chart is marked as having the best solar and wind combinations, featuring places like Texas, Kuwait, Argentina, and Somalia. Large population bubbles like China and India are plotted in the lower-left and lower-middle sections of the chart, indicating relatively modest percentiles for both wind and solar resources compared to top-tier resource areas. 

An extensive footnote details the resource methodology, explaining that solar potential is calculated based on direct normal irradiance to incorporate the benefits of dual-axis tracking systems. Harvard's wind analysis restricts sites to those with capacity factors of at least twenty percent and excludes urban, forested, and water- or ice-covered areas. Additionally, the National Renewable Energy Laboratory applies stricter land-use exclusions, omitting national parks, military lands, and slopes over twenty percent, which ultimately excludes nearly thirty percent of windy US lands and lowers the estimated US onshore wind potential by thirty-five percent compared to the Harvard study.

This page presents an analysis comparing a high-renewable electricity grid system in California—referred to as "Caliwende"—to both California’s current power grid and a hypothetical balanced system that meets 35% of its electricity demand with nuclear energy and 40% with renewables. The author notes that Caliwende’s cost premium of 1.5 times the current system is lower than the 1.9 times premium observed in Germany. However, under current costs, the balanced system remains the more cost-effective transitional option, costing only 1.2 times the current system. 

A detailed data table outlines installed capacity, thermal generation, system costs, and carbon emissions for five scenarios based on current costs. The current grid operates on 77 gigawatts (GW) of capacity, generating 129 terawatt-hours (TWh) of thermal energy and emitting 44 million metric tonnes (MMT) of carbon dioxide at a system cost of $97 per megawatt-hour (MWh). The balanced system with no storage runs on 84 GW of capacity, utilizing 10 GW of nuclear power alongside 24 GW of wind and solar. This balanced option reduces CO2 emissions by 56% to 20 MMT, costing $116 per MWh, which yields a carbon reduction cost of $174 per metric tonne. 

In comparison, the three Caliwende scenarios—no storage, pumped storage, and battery storage—all require 128 GW of capacity. They succeed in reducing emissions to 23 MMT, 17 MMT, and 18 MMT respectively, but do so at higher system costs of $142, $149, and $151 per MWh. These options result in very high carbon reduction costs, ranging from $436 to $477 per metric tonne. 

Two scatter plots illustrate these dynamics by charting system costs against annual CO2 emissions. The first chart, representing current costs, visually depicts how Caliwende scenarios cluster at high costs, while the balanced system sits in a more favorable position. The second chart explores future cost projections under two cases. In the "FUT COST 1" scenario—which assumes solar and wind costs decline by 47% and 10%, battery storage costs decline by 40% to 50%, nuclear costs rise by 25%, and natural gas rises to $8 per MMBtu—the cost of Caliwende with storage falls to around $116 per MWh, converging with the balanced system's cost of $113 per MWh. In the "FUT COST 2" scenario, which models a 20% decline in nuclear costs relative to current estimates, the balanced system once again becomes the preferred choice, offering less than half of California’s current emissions at roughly the same cost of $96 per MWh.

This page analyzes whether incorporating nuclear power into a balanced energy system is a cheaper way to reduce carbon emissions than Germany's Energiewende policy. The author examines a scenario where Germany maintains its existing wind, solar, hydro, and biomass capacity, uses nuclear power to meet 35% of electricity demand by turning back on idle plants, and relies on a half-and-half mix of natural gas and coal for the remaining generation. 

A central table compares Germany's current system, various Energiewende scenarios with different storage solutions, and the balanced nuclear scenario across capacity, generation, cost, and carbon dioxide emissions. The table shows that the current system operates at a consumer cost of $108 per megawatt-hour with 188 million metric tonnes of carbon emissions. Under the balanced system with no storage, total capacity would rise to 149 gigawatts, including 16 gigawatts of nuclear power. This balanced system reduces carbon emissions by 67% down to 62 million metric tonnes, matching the highest emission reductions achieved under the Energiewende scenarios. However, it does so at a consumer cost of $136 per megawatt-hour and a carbon reduction cost of just $84 per metric tonne. In contrast, the Energiewende scenarios achieve similar 63% to 67% emission reductions but at much higher consumer costs ranging from $203 to $212 per megawatt-hour and carbon reduction costs exceeding $300 per metric tonne.

A scatter plot on the bottom right visualizes these findings by mapping system cost in dollars per megawatt-hour against annual carbon emissions. The chart clearly positions the balanced system as a far more cost-effective option for low-carbon generation than any of the Energiewende pathways, which cluster near the top left of the chart with high system costs around $210 per megawatt-hour. 

The viability of this balanced system, however, depends entirely on the accuracy of nuclear cost projections. To address this, a chart on the bottom left plots capital cost estimates of large nuclear plants in dollars per kilowatt from a 2013 Carnegie Mellon University survey of 16 industry experts. The experts' median cost estimates mostly cluster around the current Energy Information Administration estimate of roughly $5,300 per kilowatt, sitting between a lower future cost estimate of $4,000 and a higher estimate of $6,800. 

Despite this alignment, the author cautions that real-world nuclear construction costs in the OECD have historically risen rather than followed these projections. In the United States, real costs per megawatt-hour for nuclear power have increased by 19% annually since the 1970s. Even France, which has historically relied heavily on nuclear energy, is experiencing rising costs and shifting priorities toward renewables, aiming to reduce nuclear’s share of its electricity mix from 70% to 50%. The author points to massive cost overruns and multi-year delays at new European nuclear plants, specifically Flamanville in France and Olkiluoto in Finland, as evidence of these financial risks. The Finnish utility ultimately abandoned plans for a second reactor after facing a 50% cost overrun and a nine-year delay, while the French developer Areva requested a suspension of US design certifications. Reflecting these challenges, nuclear power's global share of electricity generation has declined from an 18% peak in 1995 to 11% today.

This page, titled Appendix VI: Energy learning curves, explains how capital costs for various energy technologies fall as cumulative production capacity rises. The page displays four charts illustrating these dynamics for wind, solar, storage, and power generation technologies.

The first of three smaller charts at the top displays the wind learning curve, plotting capital cost in 2005 USD per watt against cumulative capacity in megawatts, both on log scales. The data tracks the United States and Denmark from 1981 to 2014. While both nations saw capital costs fall from around two to four dollars down to near one dollar per watt, both experienced an interruption starting in 2004 where costs rose temporarily due to higher prices for labor, energy, and raw materials like steel and copper, before resuming their downward trend. The second chart depicts the solar photovoltaic learning curve, showing crystalline silicon module prices in 2011 USD per watt against cumulative capacity in megawatts on log scales from 1976 to 2014. This curve illustrates a consistent, steep decline from roughly one hundred dollars per watt to under one dollar per watt as cumulative capacity approached one million megawatts. The third chart shows the lithium-ion battery pack learning curve, comparing the whole industry against market leaders in 2014 USD per kilowatt-hour against cumulative megawatt-hours. Both cohorts show steep cost reductions as production scale grew, though market leaders maintained a clear cost advantage, dropping towards two hundred dollars per kilowatt-hour.

The bottom half of the page features a historical chart produced in 2003 for the European Commission’s 2030 World Energy, Technology and Climate Outlook report. It illustrates how analysts projected learning curves into the future using pre-2000 data. The chart plots total investment cost in 1999 EUR per kilowatt against cumulative installed capacity in megawatts, both on log scales, with solid lines representing historical data before 2000 and dotted lines representing projections up to 2030. It tracks a wide array of power generation technologies, including PV, solar thermal, new nuclear, biogas turbines, hydro, nuclear, conventional lignite, conventional coal, small hydro, SFC and PEM fuel cells, direct coal, biomass CHP, wind, conventional gas, coal gasification, supercritical coal, and gas combined cycle. This comprehensive projection shows rapid expected cost declines for emerging technologies like photovoltaics and fuel cells, contrasted against flatter trajectories for more mature technologies like conventional gas and nuclear.

This appendix explores the concept and challenges of energy demand management, which aims to reconfigure electricity demand to better align with renewable power generation. This alignment theoretically reduces the need for expensive energy storage by shifting consumption to periods of high solar and wind output. To test the potential of this strategy, the author models a scenario in which electricity load is reconfigured within every 72-hour period to match renewable output in California.

A line chart at the top of the page, titled "Our magical implementation of demand management may not be possible in the real world," shows hourly load and generation in gigawatts from late May to mid-June. It plots a highly volatile blue line of renewable generation alongside a solid gold line representing the flatter original load. A dotted gold line shows the reconfigured load, illustrating how demand management forces consumption to mimic the peaks and troughs of renewable energy. However, the author cautions that real-world demand management operates on timescales of hours rather than days, making this model an optimistic best-case scenario.

Two scatter plots at the bottom of the page compare the system costs and CO2 emissions of different grid configurations for Germany and California, assuming demand management incurs no cost. In both cases, demand management is shown as a highly attractive theoretical alternative to physical energy storage. In the Germany chart, which maps system cost per MWh against CO2 emissions, the demand management option under the "Energiewende" framework achieves the lowest system cost of roughly 190 USD per MWh and the lowest emissions at about 60 million metric tonnes per year. This outperforms the "No storage" option and physical storage options—including battery, pumped, and hydrogen storage—which cluster at higher costs between 210 and 225 USD per MWh and higher emissions of 70 to 80 million metric tonnes.

In the California chart, mapped under the "Caliwende" target, demand management similarly leads the pack, achieving a system cost of about 135 USD per MWh and emissions of roughly 16 million metric tonnes per year. By comparison, physical storage methods cost between 150 and 155 USD per MWh, and the "No storage" scenario costs roughly 145 USD per MWh with 24 million metric tonnes of emissions. Despite these favorable theoretical results, the author concludes that the cost-emission benefits are significantly overstated because implementing such drastic changes in consumer behavior would require costly incentives, meaning the true costs of demand management remain unquantified and speculative.

Michael Cembalest reflects on the decline of bipartisanship in the United States Senate by comparing historical voting patterns with modern political polarization. He notes that while past Democratic senators such as Pat Moynihan, John Glenn, Sam Ervin, Hubert Humphrey, Henry Jackson, Claude Pepper, and Harry Truman championed liberal causes, they frequently voted across party lines. Cembalest contrasts this historical willingness to compromise with the extreme ideological purity of contemporary senators like Elizabeth Warren and Jesse Helms. He warns that this rise in political polarization makes the political climate hostile for economists and academics who present differing views.

To support this argument, the page features two charts based on data from Keith T. Poole of the University of Georgia, using the DW-Nominate algorithm to measure political voting consistency from 1937 to 2014. The first chart, titled "Ideological uniformity of Senate Democrats, 1937-2014," plots individual senators on a scale where 1.0 represents the most liberal voting pattern. The chart shows Bernie Sanders near 0.9 and Elizabeth Warren near 0.8. In contrast, historical figures show much lower ideological uniformity scores: Hubert Humphrey is near 0.45, John Glenn is near 0.35, Pat Moynihan is near 0.30, and Sam Ervin is below zero at approximately -0.1.

The second chart, titled "Ideological uniformity in the US Senate, 1937-2014," compares the distribution of voting patterns for all Democrats and Republicans, where 1.0 represents the most polarized voting behavior. The curves show that while both parties have highly polarized wings, the Republican curve sits slightly higher than the Democratic curve, illustrating a high level of ideological uniformity across the entire party. Cembalest notes that contemporary Republican senators like Mike Lee, Jim DeMint, and Tom Coburn occupy the same highly polarized territory on the right as Senator Warren does on the left. On both curves, political moderates who vote more consistently with the opposing party are indicated by values below zero.

This page explores the relationship between increasing US federal regulation, stagnant productivity, and declining business dynamism. The author notes that despite rising private research and development spending, non-farm productivity growth in the US has stalled. 

This productivity puzzle is illustrated in the first chart, titled "Why isn't R&D growth helping productivity?", which plots data from 1980 to 2015. It compares the two-year annualized change in non-farm productivity against private R&D spending as a percentage of GDP. While private R&D spending steadily climbed from roughly 1.35% of GDP in 1980 to over 1.75% by 2015, non-farm productivity showed a volatile downward trend, dropping from peaks near 4% in the early 2000s to around 0% by 2015.

To highlight potential regulatory hurdles, an accompanying table presents selected observations from the 2015 World Bank "Starting a Business" rankings, where a lower number indicates a better environment. While peer nations like Canada rank 3rd, Hong Kong ranks 4th, and Singapore ranks 10th, the United States sits at a dismal 49th place, just ahead of Italy at 50th and Greece at 54th. 

This friction is further illustrated in the chart "The ever expanding Code of Federal Regulations," which tracks data from 1975 to 2011. It shows a parallel rise in both the total number of pages in the Code, which grew from around 70,000 to over 175,000, and the actual number of specific restrictions, which climbed from 350,000 to over one million.

The consequences of this expanding regulatory burden on the economy are shown in the chart "A decline in business dynamism," spanning 1977 to 2013. This chart shows a steady downward trend in the job reallocation rate, which fell from around 36% of total jobs in the late 1970s to about 26% in 2013. Similarly, the net firm entry rate plummeted from 4% of US firms to negative territory during the Great Recession, recovering to only about 0% by 2013.

The page concludes with a narrative regarding Bob Litan, a researcher who co-authored work on business dynamism. The author details Litan's resignation from his 40-year affiliation with the Brookings Institution following his congressional testimony about the potential adverse impacts of proposed changes to financial advisor disclosures. Litan's independent testimony, financed by a mutual fund company, clashed with the positions of the White House and Senator Elizabeth Warren, leading to controversy despite full disclosure of his funding sources.

In this analysis, the author evaluates the plausibility of corporate earnings projections for 2016, offering a mixed outlook across sectors. The first major argument addresses profit margins, with the author agreeing that confidence in margins is justified. While overall S&P 500 profit margins have declined recently, a historical comparison reveals this is primarily driven by the energy sector collapse rather than systemic economic weakness, mimicking a similar trend from the mid-1980s. This is supported by the chart "US net profit margin decline mostly an energy story," which plots margins from 1973 to 2015 on a 2% to 10% scale. The data demonstrates that while the "Total market" margin line has dipped significantly, the "Ex-energy" line remains robust and near peak historical levels.

The author also expresses confidence in a consumer discretionary earnings recovery in 2016, fueled by low inflation, an improving labor market, lower energy prices, and rising home values. However, skepticism is directed toward projected technology sector earnings. This doubt is visualized in the chart "Tech revenues declining, after excluding AAPL & GOOG," which shows year-over-year sales growth from 1Q 2006 to 1Q 2015 ranging from -16% to 24%. While aggregate tech revenue looks stable, stripping out Apple and Google reveals that year-over-year sales growth has fallen to near-zero levels, mirroring the weakness seen in the "Industrials ex-Defense" series, which is deeply negative. The author attributes this weakness to Tech's high foreign sales exposure and a strong US dollar.
