To illustrate the currency headwind, two charts depict the greenback's trajectory. "The rise of the dollar" tracks the real effective exchange rate from 1980 to 2015 on an index scale of 80 to 140, comparing the dollar against a basket of currencies with and without the Chinese RMB; both series show a steep appreciation starting around 2011. A companion chart, "After a rapid climb, the Dollar has stabilized despite Chinese devaluation," plots the trade-weighted USD index from 2010 to 2015 on a scale of 65 to 95, showing that while the dollar's appreciation has stabilized recently, a major decline is unlikely. Coupled with stagnant growth projections for Brazil, China, Europe, Japan, and the Far East, international headwinds are expected to persist.

Lastly, the author details mounting pressures on domestic small businesses, illustrated in the chart "Proxy for small business operating margin trends." This metric, plotting the net percentage of businesses planning to raise prices less the net percentage planning to raise wages from 1987 to 2015 on a -5% to 15% scale, shows a sharp decline toward 0% in 2015. This compression indicates that rising wages are outpacing pricing power, signaling flat or only modestly better earnings for 2016. Consequently, the author forecasts that 2016 will likely yield single-digit returns for US equities.

This page presents a historical perspective on the tension between political ideology and business reality, focusing on the retrospective insights of George McGovern, a prominent progressive politician of the 20th century. 

An accompanying chart measures the "Degree of liberalism based on Senate voting records, 1937-2014" on a scale from negative 0.1 to 1.0, where 1 represents the most liberal. Using the DW-Nominate algorithm developed by Keith T. Poole at the University of Georgia, the chart illustrates the ideological positions of dozens of notable senators. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts score at the very top of the scale, above 0.8. George McGovern of South Dakota is shown closely behind them with a score of approximately 0.75, validating his reputation as a paragon of 20th-century liberalism. The remaining data points slope downward across various historical figures, landing near or below 0.0 for conservative-leaning Democrats like John Stennis of Mississippi and Sam Ervin of North Carolina.

The narrative text focuses on McGovern's experiences after retiring from the Senate, when he used his lecture earnings to purchase a leasehold interest in a New England hotel. Following the business's subsequent bankruptcy during a recession, McGovern authored a 1992 op-ed titled "A Politician's Dream Is a Businessman's Nightmare." In the featured excerpts, McGovern admits that firsthand experience with the daily hardships of running a business would have made him a better senator and a more understanding presidential candidate. He notes that while Democrats like Bill Clinton, Paul Tsongas, and Bob Kerrey helped shift their party's debate toward encouraging business growth, public policy too often chokes off entrepreneurial opportunities. Specifically, he critiques "one-size-fits-all" regulations, explaining that rigid thresholds—such as those triggered at 50 employees or $500,000 in sales—fail to account for local market economics, profit margins, or whether a business is capital- or labor-intensive. He concludes with an open question for legislators on how to set regulatory standards without creating barriers that are too high for businesses to clear. A brief footnote references a past publication concerning a Massachusetts senator and the Brookings Institution.

This J.P. Morgan publication explores how US equities have managed to erase their August correction despite persistent weakness in emerging markets and soft domestic fundamentals. The author argues that while developed banks have limited exposure to emerging market crises, it is surprising that US equities are ignoring a domestic economy operating on one leg—namely services, but not manufacturing—coupled with high inventories and a disappointing third-quarter earnings season. Rather than tracking easily cleared earnings beats, the analysis focuses on underlying earnings and sales growth, noting that even excluding energy, third-quarter growth was a weak four percent year-over-year, and full-year 2015 is projected to yield only three percent sales growth and seven percent earnings-per-share growth for the S&P 500 ex-energy. Expectations for 2016 are higher, driven by projected doublings in consumer discretionary and tech earnings, alongside the assumption that energy and materials have finally bottomed out.

To illustrate the impact of global developments, the first chart plots the S&P 500 and the MSCI EM index levels from January through November 2015. It shows both indices declining dramatically following the initial Chinese Renminbi devaluation in August, but by November, the S&P 500 had recovered almost all of its losses, whereas emerging market equities lagged significantly. The second chart focuses on the domestic economic split, showing US business survey Purchasing Managers Index levels from 1995 to 2015. The three-month average shows the service sector expanding strongly at around fifty-seven, while manufacturing has slid down toward fifty, emphasizing the stark divergence between the two sectors.

A detailed table breaks down year-over-year earnings-per-share and sales-per-share growth across major sectors for Q2 2015, Q3 2015 estimates, full-year 2015 estimates, and projected full-year 2016. The aggregate S&P 500 earnings growth is estimated to be negative seven percent in Q3 2015 and negative three percent for the full year 2015, but is projected to experience a strong sixteen percent rebound in 2016. This 2016 turnaround relies heavily on specific sectors rebounding: materials earnings are projected to bounce back sixty percent in 2016 after a twenty-nine percent decline in 2015, and energy is projected to surge three hundred and sixty-four percent after a ninety-one percent contraction. Information technology and consumer discretionary earnings are both projected to rise fourteen percent in 2016. Sales growth projections for 2016 are much more modest, with the total S&P 500 expected to grow six percent, indicating that the market is banking on corporate profit margins remaining very high.

This page analyzes how the decline of US manufacturing employment has disproportionately harmed African American workers and contributed to a widening racial wealth gap. The author argues that both job loss and earned income consequences have been more severe for African American workers than for white workers due to a faster and deeper drop in manufacturing employment over the fifteen-year period starting in 2000. 

The first chart, titled US manufacturing employment by race, plots the employment-to-population ratio indexed to 100 in January 2000 as a three-month average through 2015. The chart compares three groups: White, African American, and Hispanic workers. While all three groups experienced major declines, the index for African American and Hispanic workers fell faster and deeper than that of White workers. By 2010, the index for African American manufacturing employment had bottomed out near the 50 mark, compared to the White index which hovered around 60. By 2015, the African American index showed only a modest recovery to just under 60, remaining well below the level for White workers.

The second chart, titled The racial wealth gap, illustrates the median net worth of households in constant 2013 US dollars on a logarithmic scale from 1983 to 2013. It tracks the wealth divergence between White and African American households, annotating the ratio of difference between them over time. The wealth gap was widest in 1989 at 17x, before narrowing to 6x in 1998 and 2001. However, following the 2008 financial crisis, the gap widened again to 10x in 2007 and ultimately reached 13x by 2013, as the median net worth of African American households fell back toward $10,000 while White household median net worth remained robust at over $130,000. The author connects these two visual trends, suggesting that the deeper manufacturing job losses for African American workers explain a substantial portion of this renewed wealth gap expansion. Data sources cited include the Bureau of Labor Statistics, J.P. Morgan Asset Management, and the Pew Research Center.

This page analyzes the actual impact of tort reform, arguing that punitive damage caps and medical malpractice reforms often have a much smaller effect on lowering systemic costs than their proponents claim. 

To illustrate this, the page includes three scatter plot charts based on research by Theodore Eisenberg of Cornell University. The charts map punitive awards against compensatory awards in millions of US dollars on log scales ranging from $0.0 to $100.0 million, using regression lines to show the best fit of individual case results. The first chart analyzes the impact of the landmark 1996 Supreme Court case *BMW v. Gore*, which aimed to limit punitive damages. It compares the relationship between punitive and compensatory awards one year before and one year after the decision, showing that the regression lines for both periods are nearly identical, meaning the ruling had almost no noticeable impact. The second and third charts analyze the 2005 Supreme Court case *State Farm Mutual Auto v. Campbell* across bench trials and jury trials respectively. In both cases, the regression lines tracking awards before and after the ruling remain tightly aligned, indicating that the decision had very little impact on relative punitive damages regardless of whether they were decided by a judge or a jury.

The text also addresses medical malpractice tort reform, referencing a 2014 study conducted by the University of Illinois and Northwestern University Schools of Medicine and Law. This research looked at nine states that implemented damage caps between 2002 and 2005 to see if tort reform successfully reduced defensive medicine and lowered healthcare spending. Contrary to expectations, the study found no significant reduction in Medicare Part A and Part B spending, and actually observed a small post-reform rise in spending on physician services. The author notes that defensive medicine is practiced for multiple reasons, and reducing liability only addresses one of them. The page concludes with a quote from David Hyman, a professor of law and medicine at the University of Illinois, who summarizes tort reform as a very small idea that is unlikely to have the major impact proponents claim.

This page addresses the historical necessity and overall effectiveness of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), challenging the popular political argument for abolishing the agency due to regulatory overreach. While acknowledging modern complaints—such as heavy fines levied on landowners or broad federal definitions of protected waterways—the author argues that leaving environmental regulation to the states prior to 1970 was highly ineffective. To support this, the text highlights that as late as 1968, 70% of industrial discharges went untreated, and in 1972, 15 million gallons of raw sewage entered the Potomac River daily. A historical footnote adds political context, noting that the EPA was proposed by Senator Ed Muskie and created by President Richard Nixon via executive order in 1970, and that Congress overrode Nixon's veto of the Clean Water Act in 1972.

The success of federal environmental legislation is illustrated through two line charts and a water quality status table. The first chart, tracking a history of air pollutants and federal legislation from 1970 to 2013, uses an emissions index where 1970 equals 100. It shows that following key regulatory milestones—such as the Clean Air Act, the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, the Clean Air Act Amendments, and the Clean Air Interstate Rule—pollutant levels dropped dramatically. By 2013, sulfur dioxide emissions fell to approximately 20% of 1970 levels, carbon monoxide dropped to around 30%, and nitrogen oxide decreased to roughly 50%. 

The second line chart displays the history of national ambient lead levels from 1980 to 2012, measuring lead concentration in micrograms per cubic meter. Ambient lead concentrations plummeted from about 1.6 micrograms per cubic meter in 1980 to near zero by 2012. The chart attributes this success to specific policy actions: the introduction of unleaded gasoline in the 1980s, emission reductions at smelters and battery plants, and the elimination of lead compounds in paints and coatings.

Finally, a table titled "Plenty of work still to do" details the status of US waters assessed by states and interstate commissions, using EPA data from 2004 and 2010/2012. It shows that despite major progress, pollution remains widespread. Out of 3.5 million miles of rivers, 54% are classified as polluted, 46% as good, and 1% as threatened. For lakes, covering 41.7 million acres, 68% are polluted, 31% are good, and 1% are threatened. Estuaries, covering 87,000 square miles, are 78% polluted and 22% good. Lastly, of the 1,300 wadeable stream sites assessed, 42% are in poor condition, 25% are fair, and 28% are good. The primary pollutants cited include bacteria, PCBs, sediment, metals, siltation, sewage, and pesticides.

This page argues that the implementation of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) in 2002 has coincided with a substantial, steady improvement in the quality of corporate financial statements. Although criticized for high compliance costs, the legislation—designed to reduce fraud and bolster investor confidence—appears to have achieved its goals. To address the cost debate, the author cites a 2015 survey by Protiviti finding that 95% of small companies spend less than $500,000 annually on SOX compliance, while large companies with over $10 billion in revenue spend between $1 million and $2 million. Regulatory changes in 2007 and the 2012 JOBS Act (which exempted companies with under $1 billion in revenue from SOX section 404(b)) further mitigated these burdens. Although international companies cross-listing in the US declined after SOX was passed, the author suggests this is a reasonable price to pay for increased financial reporting integrity.

A series of nine charts illustrates these improvements across various metrics. SEC Accounting and Audit Enforcement Releases declined from a peak of around 240 in 2003 to about 100 by 2014. General 4.02 restatements, which occur when prior statements are declared unreliable, fell from roughly 1,000 in 2005 to 400 in 2014, while those for "accelerated filers" (corporations with market capitalizations of $75 million or more) dropped from nearly 400 to below 100 over the same period. 

The financial impact of these errors has also lessened: the average net income adjustment per restatement shrank from roughly negative $22 million in 2005 to around negative $3 million in 2014, and the share of restatements impacting the income statement fell from over 70% to about 45%. Additionally, the largest single restatements shrunk from a peak of over negative $6 billion in 2005 to near zero by 2014. Finally, internal control health has shown major progress: the number of companies filing 4.02 forms with material internal control weaknesses fell from approximately 130 in 2005 to under 40 in 2012. During a similar timeframe, restatements involving more than one issue declined from 65% to 35%, and those affecting core earnings fell from over 65% in 2003 to roughly 42% in 2012.

This page examines the economic slowdown in emerging markets and assesses its potential to impact the broader global economy. The central argument is that while emerging markets face significant headwinds, contagion to developed economies is expected to be limited. This resilience in the developed world is attributed to stable domestic conditions, strong service sector activity, and a massive five hundred fifty billion dollar annual wealth transfer from oil-producing nations to oil-consuming nations. The author highlights that the United States is a primary beneficiary of this transfer due to its low gasoline taxes, which allowed consumer-facing gasoline prices to fall thirty to thirty-five percent from June 2014 to September 2015, compared to a mere five to ten percent decline in emerging markets outside of China.

Four charts illustrate these diverging economic paths. The first chart, titled "Falling emerging markets growth premium," tracks year-over-year real GDP growth from 1997 through 2015 for emerging and developed markets. It shows that the historical growth premium for emerging markets has been shrinking since 2010, with emerging market GDP growth falling from approximately eight percent in 2010 to around four percent in 2015, while developed markets stabilized at around two percent.

The second chart, "Advanced economies stable despite EM weakness," plots a three-month average of manufacturing and services Purchasing Managers' Index surveys from 2010 to late 2015. It tracks China, broader emerging markets, and a combined index for the United States, Eurozone, and Japan. While the China and emerging market series steadily declined toward the contraction threshold of fifty by late 2015, the developed economies series remained robustly in expansion territory, holding steady near fifty-four.

The third chart, "A divergence in bank credit growth...", displays year-over-year percentage changes from 2009 to 2015 using dual axes. The developed markets series, measured on the left axis, rose from a low of negative three percent in 2010 to nearly four percent by 2015. In contrast, the emerging markets series, measured on the right axis, fell from a peak of nearly twenty percent in 2011 to roughly eleven percent in 2015.

The final chart, "...and in real retail sales," presents year-over-year percentage changes from January 2013 to July 2015, also on dual axes. It depicts developed markets retail sales growth rising from one percent to over three percent on the left axis, while emerging markets retail sales growth on the right axis steadily declined from eight percent down to around four and a half percent over the same period.

In the executive summary of the Outlook 2016 report, titled "Planet of the Aches," Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan outlines a slow-growth environment characterized by mid-single-digit returns for diversified portfolios in 2016. This projection is slightly higher than 2015, where a typical 60/40 stock and bond portfolio yielded flat 0% returns for US dollar investors and 3.5% returns for Euro-based investors. Cembalest argues that while robust consumer spending—demonstrated by 3% to 4% real growth in global retail sales annually since 2012—prevents a global recession, other vital economic engines are lagging. Specifically, manufacturing, trade, and corporate capital spending are stagnating despite unprecedented monetary stimulus from major central banks. Declines in the energy and mining sectors have further weighed on global profits, contributing to diminishing returns on global equities.

The stagnation of industrial activity is illustrated in the first chart, which tracks year-over-year percentage changes in global manufacturing output, export volumes, and equipment capital expenditures (excluding China) from 2010 to 2015. All three metrics show a sharp downshift from post-recession peaks. Equipment capex plummeted from nearly 15% growth in 2010 to roughly 0% by late 2015, while export volume and manufacturing output growth leveled off to low single digits, averaging between 1% and 3% in 2015. 

To emphasize the extent of global monetary intervention, the second chart tracks developed world central bank assets alongside GDP-weighted policy rates from 2005 to 2015 across major economies like the US, Eurozone, Japan, and the UK. Central bank assets grew dramatically from approximately $4 trillion in 2007 to nearly $13 trillion by late 2015. Meanwhile, the GDP-weighted policy rate plunged from a peak of over 4.0% in 2007 to a historical low of around 0.5% in 2015. Cembalest forecasts that central bank assets are likely to increase by another $2 trillion to $3 trillion over the next two years, driven by the Federal Reserve’s reinvestment policy, the European Central Bank's 60 billion Euros per month asset purchase program, and expected increases in asset purchases by the Bank of Japan. 

The third chart illustrates how this monetary stimulus has failed to revive corporate profits, plotting the slowdown in trailing 12-month earnings per share for the MSCI World Equity Index from 2010 to 2015. Earnings per share excluding emerging markets grew steadily from 30 in 2010 to peak near 71 in late 2014, but flatlined and dipped to roughly 68 by late 2015. Earnings per share including emerging markets followed a similar path, peaking at 26 in late 2014 before deteriorating to 24 by late 2015, reflecting the deeper economic stress in developing nations.

This profit stagnation directly translates to diminishing equity performance, as shown in the final chart. This visual tracks the rolling one-year total return in local currency for the MSCI World Equity Index, comparing performance with and without emerging markets. While rolling returns fluctuated and peaked near 25% to 30% in both 2010 and 2013, they steadily declined throughout 2014 and 2015, converging near 0% by late 2015. This trend underscores Cembalest's core argument that aggressive central bank policies are yielding diminishing returns for equity markets.

This page from the publication addresses the outlook for US corporate earnings and sales in 2016, questioning whether consensus growth projections make sense. The author argues that consensus estimates are likely 1% to 2% too high, establishing a J.P. Morgan base case that S&P 500 earnings and sales will instead rise in the mid-single digits for 2016. 

The accompanying table displays Year-over-Year Earnings and Sales Growth by sector for Q2 2015, Q3 2015, and estimates for FY 2015 and FY 2016. The data highlights a projected turnaround: overall S&P 500 earnings growth is expected to bounce from negative 2% in FY 2015 to positive 8% in FY 2016, while S&P 500 sales growth is projected to recover from negative 4% in FY 2015 to positive 5% in FY 2016. Key drivers of this expected rebound include Consumer Discretionary, where earnings are projected to rise from 8% in FY 2015 to 14% in FY 2016, and Information Technology, which is projected to rise from 4% to 9%. Meanwhile, the hard-hit Energy sector is expected to see its severe earnings decline of negative 59% in FY 2015 moderate to negative 10% in FY 2016.

In evaluating these projections, the author agrees with the Consumer Discretionary bounce due to low energy prices, labor market improvements, rising home prices, and low inflation, but warns that stock valuations are elevated and hedge fund positioning is crowded. The author is highly skeptical of the projected Tech earnings bounce, noting that when Apple and Google are excluded, Tech revenues look as weak as those of Industrials. Tech is heavily vulnerable due to its high foreign sales exposure, and economic outlooks for Brazil, China, Europe, and Japan remain flat compared to 2015. Additionally, the author believes an Energy sector rebound will not occur until 2017 due to expiring oil hedges. 

The page concludes with a detailed warning about late-cycle market behavior, using Amazon as an example of overvaluation in the Consumer Discretionary sector. Amazon’s market capitalization has risen to equal the combined value of Wal-Mart, Costco, and Target, even though its revenues and free cash flows are only 15% to 25% as high. Furthermore, a basket of five major growth stocks—Google, Facebook, Amazon, Netflix, and Salesforce.com—is trading at relative P/E ratios 3.3 times that of the overall market. This level of concentration and valuation, alongside a trailing three-year correlation of daily excess returns reaching 45% in December 2015, closely mirrors the late-1990s tech bubble behavior observed in Microsoft, Intel, Cisco, and Dell.

This page of the publication argues that the August market correction in US equities was driven not just by China's two percent currency devaluation, but also by a domestic slowdown in US core revenue and earnings growth. The author points out that even after stripping out declines in the energy sector, core growth has remained in the single digits, with overcrowding in high-performing areas like healthcare ultimately precipitating a subsequent correction in that sector.

To illustrate the relationship between foreign exchange policy and global markets, the first chart plots the impact of the Chinese renminbi devaluation on US and emerging market equities from January to November 2015. This dual-axis chart compares the S&P 500, ranging from 1,800 to 2,150, with the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, ranging from 700 to 1,100. A vertical line marks the initial renminbi devaluation in August, showing a sharp simultaneous drop in both indices, after which emerging market equities remained depressed while the S&P 500 experienced a partial recovery.

Beside this, a three-panel chart details the year-over-year percentage change from Q1 2014 to Q3 2015 for key growth metrics. The first panel shows S&P 500 core revenues, which exclude financials, energy, and utilities, falling from over four percent growth in 2014 to under two percent in late 2015. The middle panel tracks S&P 500 core earnings, which peaked near eleven percent in 2014 before dropping to around four percent. The final panel shows nominal global GDP growth similarly sliding from a peak of four percent down to approximately two percent. 

The author transitions to discussing how currency strength and weak earnings have damaged expectations for the coming years. A chart tracking consensus earnings per share estimates for the S&P 500 shows that expectations for 2015 fell by twelve percent from their peak to below $120, while 2016 expectations fell fifteen percent from their peak of roughly $144 to around $125. Another chart provides a proxy for small business operating margin trends from 1987 to 2015, defined as the net percentage of businesses planning to raise prices minus those planning to raise wages. This volatile index rose to nearly ten percent in 2014 but slid sharply toward zero percent by late 2015, signaling building margin pressures. 

In terms of market outlook, the author suggests that these weak trends justify lower, average-level price-to-earnings multiples rather than the peak multiples some investors advocate for based on low inflation and interest rates. A footnote notes that during the healthcare sector's correction, stock correlations spiked to sixty percent, which is double the average historical level since the mid-1970s. This correction drove forward price-to-earnings multiples below market parity for the first time in twenty years, drawing parallels to the regulatory threats the sector faced in the mid-1990s.

This page analyzed the slowdown in equity and credit returns in 2015, arguing that this cooling was a predictable response to the excessively high market expectations that peaked around late 2013 and 2014. To demonstrate this shift, the page presents the Market and Investor Optimism Barometer, which tracks various valuation and sentiment indicators as historical percentiles where the 99th percentile represents extreme optimism. Comparing December 2013 to December 2015, the table shows a dramatic deflation in bullishness. For example, individual investor bull/bear sentiment collapsed from the 93rd percentile down to the 8th, portfolio manager optimism fell from the 99th to the 57th percentile, high-grade bond spreads fell from 99th to 24th, and high-yield bond spreads fell from 98th to 29th. Meanwhile, some valuation metrics remained elevated, such as the large-cap forward P/E ratio, which rose slightly from the 75th to the 78th percentile, and the futures market long-short indicator, which held steady at the 95th percentile.

An accompanying line chart tracks the cumulative total return of a simplified portfolio of risky assets from 2005 through late 2015, rebalanced quarterly with a mix of 30 percent S&P 500, 30 percent MSCI Europe, 20 percent US high yield, and 20 percent Europe high yield. The chart highlights that after J.P. Morgan published its Optimism Barometer in October 2014, the portfolio's upward trajectory stalled and trended sideways, reflecting the realization of these elevated risks.

The publication further notes that the Federal Reserve was also overly optimistic during this post-recession period. A chart titled "Federal Reserve growth expectations too high" compares actual real US GDP year-over-year percentage growth against FOMC projections made between 2010 and 2014. While the Fed regularly projected growth rates of 3 percent to 4 percent for the upcoming years, actual real GDP growth consistently lagged, remaining mostly in the 1.5 percent to 2.5 percent range from 2010 to 2014. 

Finally, the page discusses the post-recession shift of debt from households to governments in much of the developed world. This shift is projected to limit the political and fiscal ammunition available to boost future growth, leading the author to project a neutral, rather than stimulative, fiscal impact for 2016. A final line chart illustrates that overall global debt did not decrease despite the painful recession. Plotting total non-financial debt as a percentage of GDP from 2000 to 2015, the chart shows that developed market debt climbed from roughly 200 percent to over 250 percent of GDP. Global debt similarly rose to around 225 percent, while emerging market debt, which sat near 100 percent in 2008, climbed steadily to about 160 percent by 2015.

This page analyzes how the rising US dollar has negatively impacted corporate revenue, profit growth, and exports, while domestic demand and the service sector remain robust. A humorous cartoon map of the United States at the top highlights several geographic economic pain points, labeling them as Dollar Altitude Sickness in the North, Shale Gas Acid Reflux in the South, Earnings Anemia in the Midwest, and Toxic Political Sclerosis on the East Coast. The author notes that the trade-weighted dollar's rise from 2011 to March 2015 was one of the fastest on record, though it has since remained range-bound. Looking forward, the publication predicts that the majority of the dollar's appreciation against the Euro and Yen is likely over.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, titled Fast and furious: the rise of the dollar, plots the real effective exchange rate index from 1980 to 2015 against a foreign exchange basket both including and excluding the Chinese RMB. Both indices rose sharply from a low near 90 in 2011 to approximately 120 in 2015. The second chart, Domestic demand strong, exports weak, displays contributions to GDP growth from 2012 to 2015. It reveals that while domestic final demand consistently contributed between 1.5 percent and 3.5 percent to GDP, net exports turned into a significant drag, detracting over 1 percent from growth by early 2015. 

The commentary also points out a growing divergence between domestic services and global manufacturing. Business capital spending is rising by 10 to 15 percent for domestic-facing firms, while falling at a similar rate for global and energy-focused companies. Additionally, Chinese capital outflows are targeting commercial real estate in rule-of-law nations like the US, UK, Canada, and Australia, inflating property prices and lowering capitalization rates. 

The final two charts illustrate this gap in the domestic economy. The third chart, Unusually large gap between services and manufacturing, tracks PMI survey levels from 1998 to 2015. In late 2015, the services PMI hovered comfortably in expansion territory near 56, whereas the manufacturing PMI plummeted close to the neutral 50 level. The fourth chart, Domestically oriented labor markets holding up, compares the six-month average change in payrolls from 2010 to 2015. It shows that services and construction payroll additions remained strong, averaging over 200,000 jobs, while manufacturing and mining payrolls fell from a positive 30,000 average to nearly negative 30,000 by the end of 2015.

This page focuses on the credit markets, analyzing how rising energy bond yields, driven by high default expectations, are widening spreads and pointing toward greater volatility. The author highlights a J.P. Morgan Securities report projecting a 30% default rate in the high-yield energy market by 2017 if oil remains at $45 and natural gas at $2.75. Crucially, the widening of credit spreads is not confined to energy but is broadening out, mirroring trends from the late 1990s and 2007 that foreshadowed broader equity market downturns. This trend is driven by a prolonged period of central bank financial repression that has pushed investors into high-yield, emerging markets, and municipal debt. This frantic search for yield has led to loose credit terms, evidenced by covenant-lite loans ballooning to 70% of US loan issuance in 2015 compared to just 10% in 2009. The author warns that these conditions are paired with severely reduced market liquidity, meaning that if redemption demands rise, mutual funds’ typical 5% to 7% cash buffers will quickly deplete, forcing the sale of highly illiquid assets and exacerbating price discovery problems—a situation already demonstrated by the forced gating of withdrawals at Third Avenue's distressed credit fund in late 2015.

Four supporting charts illustrate these dynamics. The first chart, tracking US high-yield corporate bond spreads over 10-year Treasuries from 1995 to 2015, shows a dramatic split in 2015: energy-sector spreads spiked towards 14%, while ex-energy spreads remained significantly lower near 6%, though both showed an upward trajectory similar to past cycle peaks in 2000 and 2008. The second chart details the growing footprint of energy firms in the high-yield market from 1996 to 2014, showing that high-yield issuance by energy companies surged to nearly $60 billion by 2014, representing roughly 15% to 18% of the total annual high-yield market. The third chart shows the rapid expansion of total mutual fund and ETF debt holdings from 2005 to 2015, where total assets ballooned from approximately $0.5 trillion to nearly $1.8 trillion, led by a massive influx into emerging markets, municipal bonds, and high-yield debt. Finally, the fourth chart demonstrates declining liquidity in high-grade corporate bonds from 2006 to 2015 by measuring the days required to trade the entire market on a five-quarter average. This metric steadily climbed from around 200 days in 2010 to over 300 days in late 2015, signaling a much less liquid market environment.

This page focuses on the economic and equity market outlook for the United States in 2016, presenting an optimistic view of domestic growth driven by improving labor markets, falling energy costs, and strengthening consumer credit. The author forecasts that the US economy will grow between 2.5% and 3.0% in 2016, outpacing its performance in 2015. This expansion is supported by rising credit card, auto loan, and consumer credit balances, alongside an end to federal and local fiscal drags. While overall corporate profit margins have declined, the analysis attributes this entirely to the energy sector, drawing parallels to a similar non-recessionary energy-driven dip in 1985. Consequently, the central scenario for 2016 is a single-digit positive return for the US equity market.

To support this outlook, the page features six charts. The first, tracking year-over-year steady employment growth from 1990 to 2015, illustrates that after falling to nearly negative 5% during the Great Financial Crisis, employment growth stabilized and held steady at approximately 2% through 2015. The adjacent chart for consumer credit growth shows a similar recovery from 1980 to 2015, where credit growth rebounded from a historic low of roughly negative 4% in 2010 to a healthy positive rate of around 7% by late 2015. 

Wage and spending trends are explored in two additional charts. The chart on private wages normalizing shows wages as a percentage of GDP from 1980 to 2015; after hitting a multi-decade low of about 34% following the 2008 recession, wages normalized back toward 37% by late 2015. Meanwhile, the chart showing home and auto sales trends tracks light vehicle sales and home sales from 2000 to 2015. It shows that light vehicle sales rose steadily from their post-crisis trough of under 3.5% of the population to over 5.5% in 2015, while new and existing home sales recovered more modestly from a low of 3.5% of households to about 4.3%.

The bottom of the page features two final charts addressing consumer activity and corporate health. A chart comparing bank loans to consumers with nominal consumer spending from 2013 to 2015 reveals that both indicators expanded over the period, with bank loan growth rising from 3% to peak near 7% before settling around 6% in late 2015, while consumer spending hovered between 2% and 6%. Finally, a long-term historical chart from 1973 to 2015 details US profit margins, noting that the overall market profit margin decline to around 7% in 2015 is misleading. When excluding the energy sector, corporate profit margins remained near record highs of 9%, mirroring the divergence seen during the mid-1985 oil shock when a sharp drop in energy margins did not result in a broader economic recession.

This page from the United States section of the Outlook publication discusses the Federal Reserve's trajectory for interest rate tightening, arguing that market expectations are likely underestimating how quickly the Fed will have to raise rates. Although markets expect the weakest tightening cycle on record, predicting a rate of only 1.35% two years out, the author identifies labor market tightening and subsequent wage inflation as the single biggest risk for global markets in the upcoming year.

Four charts support this analysis. The first chart, "Current expectations vs. historical Fed tightening cycles," plots the change in the policy rate over twenty-four months. It shows previous tightening cycles as grey lines, many of which rose by three to five percentage points, while current market expectations, represented by a blue line, show a remarkably flat path ending well below any historical precedent since 1964.

The second chart, "Labor market dropouts by category since 2008," displays the decline in the labor force participation rate from 66.0% in 2008 to roughly 62.5% by late 2015. This decline is broken down into three shaded categories: retirees, who make up nearly half of the dropouts, self-diagnosed disabled individuals, and other leavers. This contraction in the labor supply is highlighted as a primary driver for potential wage pressure.

The third chart, "Three measures of wage growth," tracks the year-over-year percentage change from 1997 through 2015 using a three-month average. It displays median wages, average hourly earnings, and wages and salaries from the Employment Cost Index. While these measures hit historical lows around 2010, they have since rebounded, with median wages reaching around 3.5% and the other measures rising to between 2.0% and 2.5% by late 2015.

The fourth chart, "Net percentage of small businesses planning to raise worker compensation," shows a three-month average from 1987 to 2015 based on National Federation of Independent Business data. The series shows a sharp post-recession drop to nearly zero percent, followed by a steady recovery back up toward 15% by late 2015, marking the highest reading for expected wage gains since 2007.

Ultimately, the author warns that even in an environment with low core goods price inflation, a tight labor supply could cause wage inflation to surge, forcing the Fed to raise rates faster than current low market projections suggest.

This page analyzes Japan's macroeconomic landscape, corporate sector cash dynamics, and the Bank of Japan's unprecedented monetary policies heading into 2016. The author argues that despite the Bank of Japan holding back on further anticipated monetary easing in October 2015, several positive tailwinds support Japanese equities. Key factors include rising corporate profits, nominal gross domestic product growth averaging three percent compared to a zero percent average from 1991 to 2013, and massive government-backed equity purchasing. Notably, the Government Pension Investment Fund doubled its equity allocation from twelve percent to twenty-five percent, while recently privatized massive financial conglomerates like Japan Post Bank and Japan Post Insurance hold three hundred trillion yen in assets that may shift toward equity risk.

A set of bar charts contrasts the financial behavior of Japanese and American companies to show that Japanese companies hold significantly more cash but distribute far less of it to shareholders. In the first panel, Japan's corporate cash as a percentage of market cap stands at nearly fifty percent compared to under ten percent for the United States, and Japan's cash as a percentage of gross domestic product is near forty percent compared to under ten percent for the United States. Conversely, the second panel shows that Japan's dividend payout ratio is only about thirty-two percent compared to fifty percent in the United States, and Japanese buybacks represent only about point five percent of gross domestic product compared to over three percent in the United States. The author points out that newly introduced corporate governance reforms aim to resolve this disparity by pushing cash-rich Japanese companies to increase shareholder distributions.

The second half of the page details the unprecedented nature of Japan’s monetary expansion, which the author describes as a "Japanese experiment" with few historical precedents. The text warns that the Bank of Japan's aggressive purchasing of Japanese Government Bonds could cause private sector banks to run out of bonds by the end of 2016, forcing the central bank to buy directly from the non-bank private sector, an outcome with highly uncertain consequences. 

An accompanying line chart, titled "A professor I once had told me this was impossible," illustrates the long-term trends of Japanese money velocity and central bank expansion from 1970 to 2015. The blue line, representing the velocity of money measured as gross domestic product divided by money supply, shows a continuous downward trend from over one point zero in 1970 to less than point four by 2015. Meanwhile, the brown line tracking Central Bank assets as a percentage of gross domestic product shows a massive spike starting after 2010, surging from roughly thirty percent to over seventy percent of gross domestic product by late 2015. The diverging lines illustrate a stark economic paradox of skyrocketing central bank balance sheets occurring alongside a historic collapse in the velocity of money.

This page analyzes the cyclical economic recovery taking place across Europe, arguing that while improvements are visible across a wide range of indicators, the true test of this recovery will arrive in 2017. The author observes positive momentum in employment, business confidence, bank lending, retail sales, and credit demand, even in peripheral economies like Spain and Italy that are recovering from a very low base. This broader expansion is supported by six charts illustrating these trends. 

The first chart displays Eurozone employment and total hours worked from 2001 to 2015 as a year-over-year percentage change. Both series show a clear recovery from the negative territory of the European sovereign debt crisis, with employment growth approaching 1% and total hours worked rebounding to positive territory by late 2015. The second chart traces the Composite PMI survey indices for Germany, France, and the average of Italy and Spain from 2010 to 2015. While Germany consistently leads with index values above 53, the average for Italy and Spain has rebounded sharply from a low of nearly 43 in 2012 to match or exceed Germany's strength in late 2015, leaving France trailing near the 50 expansion-contraction threshold. 

The third chart overlays Eurozone bank lending in billions of euros on a three-month average against a net balance of consumer confidence responses. Both metrics show a synchronized rebound, with consumer confidence recovering from below negative 30% in 2013 to around negative 5% in 2015, and bank lending returning to positive territory at approximately 10 billion euros. Similarly, the fourth chart shows a strong recovery in consumer spending, plotting Eurozone retail sales and new car registrations on a year-over-year three-month average. Retail sales growth rebounded to nearly 3% by late 2015, while new car registrations climbed to around 10% growth. 

The final two charts depict the net percentage of banks reporting higher credit demand over a two-quarter average for Spain and Italy from 2003 to 2015, broken down by corporate, consumer, and mortgage demand. In Spain, corporate and consumer credit demand have moved firmly into positive territory, reaching around 25% to 50%, while mortgage demand has dramatically improved from its historic lows near negative 100%. In Italy, mortgage credit demand shows a particularly sharp spike to nearly 50% net positive, with consumer demand also positive, though corporate credit demand remains weaker. 

The author concludes with a focused commentary on Italy, noting that while the country has entered an expansion mode marked by rising exports, falling unemployment, and stronger consumer spending, long-term risks remain. To maintain this momentum, Italy will require years of accommodative monetary policy from the European Central Bank, alongside leniency from the European Commission regarding fiscal tightening and debt reduction. Furthermore, the rising stock of Italian bank non-performing loans continues to act as a significant constraint on the banking sector's lending capacity.

This page discusses the macroeconomic situation in Japan, focusing on how government interventions and currency devaluation have failed to support the Japanese consumer despite aiding corporate profits. The central argument is that while corporate profits in both the United States and Japan rebounded strongly after the global financial crisis, household incomes in the two nations diverged. In the United States, rising profits accompanied a recovery in household income, but in Japan, corporate profits and household incomes moved in opposite directions.

Two side-by-side charts at the top of the page illustrate this divergence from 2007 through 2015. The first chart shows the rebound in trailing 12-month earnings per share for the S&P 500 and MSCI Japan, both of which recovered dramatically after bottoming in 2009. The second chart shows real household earnings indexed over the same period, revealing that while US household earnings rose after 2013, Japan's real household earnings steadily declined, accompanied by a small illustrative cartoon map warning of "consumercury poisoning." 

The author explains that the benefits of a weaker Yen are concentrated among large corporations that realize translation gains on offshore income. In contrast, smaller companies and households suffer from imported inflation. Consumer spending has not rebounded to pre-2014 levels following the imposition of a Value Added Tax. Looking ahead, the author notes that Japanese GDP growth was volatile and averaged 1.5% in 2015, and projects a similar outcome for 2016. 

A chart at the bottom left traces Japan's real GDP and its components from 2008 to 2015, indexed to the first quarter of 2008. It shows that exports fell precipitously to an index level of 63 in the first quarter of 2009, recovered, and remained volatile through 2015. Meanwhile, real GDP and consumer spending remained relatively flat, with consumer spending dipping after 2014.

An accompanying table, titled "The incredible, shrinking benefits of massive Japanese money printing," highlights the diminishing returns of Japan's monetary policy since 2012. It shows that while the Bank of Japan's balance sheet expanded by 144% and the Yen experienced a real devaluation of 27% as of November 2015, these massive interventions translated into minimal economic expansion. Annualized monetary growth was 3.9%, bank loan growth was 2.4%, nominal GDP growth was 1.9%, core inflation was 1.3%, and annualized real GDP growth was a mere 0.8% as of September 2015.

A detailed footnote highlights another structural burden on the Japanese consumer: Japan's high agricultural "OECD producer protection ratio" of 1.9, which indicates that Japanese agricultural producers benefit from domestic prices nearly double those of international markets. This ratio is significantly higher than those of the European Union at 1.05 and the United States at 1.02, with only South Korea having a higher ratio. The author expresses skepticism that the Trans-Pacific Partnership will successfully dismantle these protective barriers.

This page argues that emerging markets have evolved from exotic, niche options into mainstream economic powerhouses that merit greater investor attention today than during past crises like the 1998 Asian financial crisis. A central theme is the overwhelming influence of China, which has created a massive economic gravity well that leaves many other emerging market nations deeply overexposed to its domestic demand for commodities and intermediate manufacturing goods. 

A data table titled "The increasing importance and footprint of emerging markets" spans the years 1980 to 2015 to illustrate this shift. It shows that inflows into emerging markets grew from 1.0% of world GDP in 1980 to 17.5% in 2015, while developed world asset allocations to emerging markets rose from under 0.5% to 5.75% over the same period. Concurrently, the emerging market share of global output expanded from 27% to 47%. Annual emerging market corporate bond issuance swelled from just $2 billion in 1990 to $931 billion in 2015, with China's share of that issuance skyrocketing from 0% to 72%. Furthermore, China's share of global fixed investment jumped from 3% in 1980 to 27% in 2015, far outstripping the rest of emerging Asia, which only grew from 2% to 8%.

To emphasize China's outsized influence, a bar chart titled "China's growing share of the global economy" compares data from 2000 and 2014 across several categories. Over this fourteen-year period, China's share of steel consumption rose from roughly 16% to nearly 46%, while its commodity consumption jumped from approximately 12% to 42%. China's share of global growth went from 18% to 37%, and its share of global fixed investment grew from about 6% to 33%.

A second chart, "China's impact on the copper market," tracks copper consumption from 1900 to 2010 in millions of metric tons. It shows global consumption rising to nearly 18 million metric tons, with China's consumption remaining barely visible for most of the twentieth century before exploding after 2000 to represent nearly half of the entire world's demand by 2010. 

A third chart, "The gravitational pull of China," plots the rolling 10-year correlation between Chinese GDP growth and the GDP growth of all other emerging market countries on a GDP-weighted basis. This correlation climbed from a low of about 0.1 in the early 1990s to peak near 0.45 around 2010, illustrating how tightly bound other emerging economies have become to China's business cycle. 

Finally, a hand-drawn cartoon map visualizes these vulnerabilities. It labels the Southeast Asian region as suffering from "Asian Tigers Sinoverexposure" and "Balance Sheet Inflammation," while depicting Chile as a long chili pepper afflicted with "Copperiodontitis" to symbolize its extreme dependence on copper exports to China.

This page analyzes the ongoing ramifications of China’s economic slowdown on global commodity prices and emerging market debt vulnerability. The author argues that while most commodity prices have fallen sharply from their 2011 peaks, several remain higher than their levels in the year 2000. Additionally, the author references projections from Barclays indicating that the copper market is expected to endure excess supply until 2020.

To support this analysis, the page features two commodity-related charts. The first, titled "Oil, coal and copper prices still above year-2000 levels," indexes January 2000 prices to 100 and tracks copper, coal, oil, aluminum, natural gas, and agriculture through late 2015. It shows that although prices have dropped significantly from peaks near 500 to 800 on the index, major components like copper, coal, and oil remain above the baseline index of 100. The second chart, "Iron ore prices," tracks the price per metric tonne delivered to Qingdao, China, from 2008 to 2015. This line graph illustrates a dramatic price decline, falling from a peak of nearly $190 per metric tonne in 2011 to approximately $40 per metric tonne by late 2015.

The discussion then shifts to the regional GDP impact of a potential Chinese growth shock and the rising systemic risks in emerging markets. J.P. Morgan Securities estimates that a 1% decline in China's growth rate has a minor impact on developed economies, which is visualized in the bar chart titled "Estimated impact of China growth shock on GDP by region." This chart shows the cumulative real growth impact to be roughly 0.1% for the United States, 0.2% for developed markets overall, and around 0.5% for Japan and the Euro Area. In contrast, emerging markets face a much higher growth impact, exceeding 1.0% for EM ex-China, Latin America, and EM EMEA.

A major concern raised is the expansion of emerging market non-financial corporate debt, which doubled from $9 trillion in 2008 to $18 trillion in 2014, with much of it tied to commodities and real estate in China. This risk is depicted in the stacked bar chart "External debt vulnerability by country," which plots external debt as a percentage of exports as of the second quarter of 2015 across categories including government and central banks, banks, intercompany loans, and other sectors. This visual highlights that while China’s vulnerability remains relatively low at roughly 60% of exports, countries like Turkey and Brazil are highly exposed, with external debt exceeding 200% of their exports, driven heavily by corporate and bank debt.

This page analyzes which emerging market countries are experiencing the greatest economic pain, focusing primarily on Brazil and Turkey, with additional commentary on Russia, Chile, and South Africa. 

Brazil is described as entering the commodity price decline from a weak position, now grappling with rising domestic debt, growing fiscal deficits, double-digit inflation, falling growth and wages, and an unemployment surge from 4.6% in the second quarter of 2014 to 8% by the third quarter of 2015. Despite these pressures, a default on external debt is deemed unlikely due to the country's $350 billion in foreign exchange reserves. To illustrate this distress, a humorous medical-themed map cartoon labels Brazil with ailments such as Iron Ore Deficiency, Dilma-cular Degeneration, Inflation Outbreak, and Petrobranchitis. Below the cartoon, a line chart titled "Brazil: if you forgot what stagflation looks like, this is it" tracks year-over-year real GDP growth alongside inflation from 1990 to 2015. The chart highlights historical inflation peaks of 4,922% in June 1994 and 17% in May 2003, and shows a stark divergence in late 2015 where inflation rises sharply toward 10% while GDP growth plunges past negative 3%.

Turkey is characterized as one of the most capital-reliant countries in the world, suffering from capital flight, a falling Lira, declining central bank reserves, rising inflation, and bank currency mismatches, all exacerbated by political instability. A companion medical-themed cartoon depicts the region suffering from Erdogangrene, International Capital Addiction, and Greece's Conjunctivdebtivitis. A line chart titled "Turkey net international investment position" tracks the country's net international investment position in billions of US dollars from 1997 to 2015. The metric, which measures household, corporate, and sovereign liabilities to foreigners less domestic holdings of foreign assets, shows a steady, volatile decline from near zero in the late 1990s to approximately negative $400 billion by 2015, illustrating a negative position second only to Greece among major emerging markets.

The page concludes with a brief look at Russia, which faces flat growth prospects for 2016 after a 4% decline in 2015. However, financial markets have largely priced in this distress; the Russian equity market is trading at the lowest price-to-earnings ratio in the emerging market world, and its currency has fallen by 60% from its 2011 peak. Russia is depicted in a final cartoon suffering from Pu-tinnitus, Petronucleosis, and Labor Syndrome. Finally, the author notes that, aside from Brazil, commodity exporters Chile and South Africa possessed the worst economic momentum heading into the end of 2015.

This page focuses on emerging markets, posing the question of whether emerging market equities have corrected enough and if they are nearing a bottom. The author argues that markets typically rise before economies do, and while timing a bottom is difficult, emerging market asset prices are likely to bottom out over the next 12 to 18 months. This bottom is expected to form before peak distress metrics—like loan defaults, unemployment, and bank failures—are fully realized and before exports begin to recover. 

To support this outlook, the page features one table and three charts detailing emerging market valuations, investor positioning, currency values, and macroeconomic pressures.

A table titled "Balance of payments pressures in the emerging world" presents data for Malaysia, Brazil, Colombia, Turkey, Indonesia, and South Africa. It compares their worst current account since 2010 to current levels and tracks percentage changes in imports, exports, currency, and unit labor costs relative to their peaks since 2010. For instance, Brazil's current account improved from a worst-of -4.8 percent of GDP to -3.2 percent, while its currency depreciated 47 percent and unit labor costs declined 29 percent. Colombia shows a severe 44 percent drop in exports, while Turkey improved its current account from a worst of -10.2 percent of GDP to -4.3 percent. Overall, significant import compressions (ranging from -18 percent in Colombia to -35 percent in Brazil) and currency depreciations (up to -47 percent in Brazil and -44 percent in South Africa) indicate that significant adjustment is underway across these nations.

A line chart on the upper right, "On a P/B basis, EM getting closer to 1998 levels," tracks the relative price-to-book value of emerging markets from 1990 through late 2015 against both the United States and Europe, Australasia, and the Far East, or EAFE. Both lines show emerging market valuations on a steady downward trajectory since 2010. The emerging market versus US price-to-book ratio is down to roughly 0.5x, nearing the historic lows of around 0.4x set in 1998 and 2001, while the emerging market versus EAFE ratio stands at approximately 0.7x, nearing its late-1990s low of around 0.5x.

On the bottom left, a chart titled "Global fund managers underweight EM vs. DM" displays fund manager relative positioning from 2001 to late 2015. The data shows that positioning has swung sharply from an emerging market overweight peak of nearly 60 percent in late 2009 to a deep underweight of approximately -50 percent in late 2015, reflecting exceptionally bearish sentiment that exceeds any prior period in the last fifteen years.

Finally, a line chart on the bottom right, "Emerging markets: real effective exchange rates," tracks GDP-weighted broad real effective exchange rates from 1995 to late 2015, comparing China with emerging markets excluding China. While China's real effective exchange rate has appreciated dramatically to nearly 130 in 2015, the emerging markets excluding China index has depreciated back down to around 90, matching the low valuation levels observed during the Asian Financial Crisis around 1998 to 2002.

This page analyzes China's slowing economic momentum and structural challenges heading into 2016, predicting that the nation is on its way to a lower 4% annual GDP growth rate by 2020. The author argues that a massive overhang of housing inventory will prevent any meaningful rebound in residential construction, while the recent margin-debt-fueled equity bubble and subsequent crash have severely damaged the inner workings of onshore Chinese financial markets, resulting in a 90% decline in index futures open interest and trading volumes.

To support these points, the page features six charts. The first row focus on the consumer. The China Real Consumer Activity Index chart, measuring year-over-year percentage change from 2004 to 2016, shows a long-term decline from peaks near 38% in late 2009 to under 5% by the end of 2015. Next to it, a chart of China Retail Sales from 2012 to late 2015 shows nominal year-over-year sales growth decelerating from 16% to roughly 11%, while real retail sales growth fluctuated slightly but remained relatively flat near the 9.5% mark.

The middle row highlights structural headwinds in housing and the workforce. A bar chart comparing housing inventories as a percent of 2010 levels reveals that smaller Tier 3 cities suffer from a massive overhang at approximately 330% of 2010 levels, whereas Tier 2 cities stand at roughly 210% and Tier 1 cities are at 150%. Beside this, a labor market conditions index—which aggregates wage growth, labor supply-demand, employment growth, manpower surveys, and PMI surveys—indicates a steady deterioration from 2011 through late 2015, with the index sliding from around 0.5 to -1.0.

The bottom row explores the financial markets. One chart tracks the CSI 300 index of onshore equity prices against outstanding margin debt as a percentage of GDP from January 2014 to July 2015, illustrating how the rapid rise and sudden crash of onshore stock prices almost perfectly mirrored the spike and collapse in margin debt, which peaked at about 3.5% of GDP. Finally, a chart of China price-to-earnings multiples from 2004 to late 2015 displays forward P/E ratios equal-weighted by sector, showing that expensive Onshore A-shares spiked to over 22x in 2015 before dropping, while cheaper Offshore H-shares traded at a much lower multiple of around 10x, starting to reflect the reality of slower underlying economic growth.

This page details the structural economic slowdown of China heading into 2016, illustrating how its competitive edge has diminished due to stagnant industrial profits, currency headwinds from a 50 percent rise in the RMB, excess capacity, and severe environmental issues. An illustrative map graphic in the upper-right represents these systemic challenges with satirical medical labels like Cirrhosis of the River, SOE-Coli Infection, and Compulsive Building Disorder. 

The first chart compares Chinese capital formation with historical industrializations, showing gross fixed capital formation as a percentage of GDP. From 1981 to 2012, China’s capital formation reached an unprecedented peak near 45 percent of GDP, eclipsing the historical peak investment periods of Japan (1960–1988, peaking near 35 percent), Korea (1978–2006, peaking near 40 percent), and Germany (1954–1982, peaking under 30 percent). 

The second chart contrasts the Chinese service and manufacturing sectors using the Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) on a three-month average from 2010 to 2015. The services index remained stable in expansion territory above 50, ending late 2015 at approximately 54, whereas the manufacturing index fell into contractionary territory below 50, ending near 48. 

The third chart tracks China's fixed asset investment year-over-year percentage change by sector from 2008 to 2015. It shows a dramatic decline in the real estate and construction sector, which fell from a peak growth rate of 35 percent in 2010 to nearly 0 percent in 2015. During the same period, industrial fixed asset investment fell to about 10 percent, other service sectors moderated to around 20 percent, and infrastructure investment stabilized between 15 percent and 20 percent. 

The fourth chart plots the year-over-year percentage change in electricity consumption and railway traffic from 2010 to 2015. Railway traffic growth plunged deeply into negative territory, hitting approximately negative 15 percent in late 2015, while electricity consumption growth ground down from peaks over 20 percent in 2010 to near 0 percent in 2015. 

The fifth chart shows a steep rise in non-financial corporate debt as a percentage of GDP from 1994 to 2015. After remaining relatively stable near 100 percent of GDP from 2003 to 2008, corporate debt ballooned rapidly to over 150 percent of GDP by mid-2015. 

The sixth and final chart documents China’s industrial profits from 2011 to 2015 using a three-month average of year-over-year percentage changes. Industrial profit growth collapsed from rates above 25 percent in 2011 to contractionary territory, hovering around negative 5 percent by the end of 2015.

This page from the publication discusses the peaking impact of stock buybacks, share count reductions, and rising corporate leverage as late-stage market signals. The author argues that stock buybacks, which have been adding roughly two percent per year to earnings per share growth, may see their contribution fall by half by 2017 due to rising credit spreads and elevated debt balances. Additionally, relative stock market returns for acquiring companies turned negative in the fourth quarter of 2015, ending a positive run that began in 2010. 

To support these observations, the page features four charts. The first chart, titled "Another strong year for buybacks," displays S&P 500 buyback announcements in billions of US dollars from 1997 to 2015. The bar chart shows buybacks surging from around one hundred billion dollars in the late 1990s to a peak of over seven hundred billion dollars in 2007, dropping sharply in 2009, and rising back up to nearly six hundred billion dollars annualized in 2015. The second chart, "S&P 500 M&A transactions and buybacks," tracks these activities as a percentage of earnings before interest, taxes, and intangibles using a four-quarter average from 1999 to 2015. This line chart reveals that M&A and buybacks now surpass 2007 levels, rising to over twenty percent of earnings by late 2015.

The third chart, titled "Rising S&P 500 leverage, particularly ex-tech," displays net debt to EBITDA ratios from 2000 to 2015. It compares a line for "Ex-financials" with a line for "Ex-financials & technology" to demonstrate how the cash-rich technology sector masks leverage across the rest of the corporate universe. While the ex-financials ratio rose moderately to around 1.3 by 2015, the ratio excluding both financials and technology surged dramatically starting in 2012, climbing to nearly 2.1 by 2015, which is close to its post-dot-com peak. 

The final chart, "Remembrance of things past: low percentage of technology company IPOs with profits," displays a bar chart from 1980 to 2015 showing the percentage of technology companies with positive net income at the time of their IPO. Profitability peaked at around eighty percent in the late 1980s before plunging to below twenty percent during the dot-com bubble of 1999 and 2000. After recovering to around seventy percent in 2009, the share of profitable tech IPOs fell back below twenty percent in 2014 and 2015. Although the author notes that longer pre-IPO lifespans and lower price-to-sales ratios mean the tech IPO market is structurally healthier than it was in 1999, the current low profitability metrics still indicate a high appetite for risk.

This page details the improved resilience of global banking systems since the financial crisis of 2008. The central argument is that banks are now in a much stronger position to absorb potential write-downs from energy-related investments and emerging markets because they have dramatically increased their capital ratios and reduced their reliance on volatile wholesale inter-bank funding. Furthermore, the risk from these sectors is now spread across a wider variety of less-leveraged non-bank entities, such as pension funds, corporate, and individual investors, meaning that future market corrections may be less systemic and severe than in past cycles where banks held the bulk of the risk.

The analysis is supported by four charts. The top-left chart displays Tier 1 capital ratios for banks in the United Kingdom, Eurozone, United States, and Japan from 2000 to 2015. Prior to the financial crisis, these ratios sat primarily between 7.5% and 10.0%. Following the crisis, they rose sharply across all four regions, climbing to between 12.5% and 15.0% by late 2015. 

The top-right chart illustrates loan-to-deposit ratios for the same four regions over the same period, showing a clear reduction in reliance on wholesale funding. In the Eurozone and the United Kingdom, loan-to-deposit ratios peaked at roughly 140% in 2008 before steadily declining to about 110% to 115% by 2015. Over the same timeframe, the United States ratio dropped from nearly 100% to approximately 85%, and Japan's ratio declined from around 90% to below 70%.

The bottom-left chart breaks down foreign funding to emerging markets by creditor type in a stacked bar format from 1985 to 2015. In 1985, banks provided nearly 90% of the foreign funding to emerging markets. By 2015, the share held by banks had plummeted to approximately 30%, while the remaining shares were absorbed by non-bank institutional investors and corporates, reducing direct bank exposure to emerging market defaults.

The bottom-right chart highlights US energy debt as a percentage of shareholders' equity from 2001 to 2015. It shows that although total energy debt climbed rapidly to nearly 80% of shareholders' equity by 2015, the vast majority of this rise was driven by non-bank debt, such as high-yield bonds and commercial paper, which reached nearly 70%. In contrast, direct energy bank loans remained low and exceptionally flat throughout the entire period, hovering at roughly 10% to 15% of shareholders' equity. This proves that the bank-held portion of energy debt is minimal, further insulating the banking sector from energy-related defaults.

This page outlines a multi-part market narrative arguing that global oil prices are likely to remain rangebound and could temporarily drop to around thirty dollars in the near term before recovering modestly in 2017 and 2018. The current market environment is characterized by significant oversupply, structural demand shifts, and altered producer dynamics. 

The narrative begins by showing that the world is currently oversupplied, with global storage capacities nearing their limits. A chart of the world oil supply balance, which measures production minus consumption as a percentage of trailing twelve-month production, illustrates a sharp rise in oversupply to nearly two percent in 2015, reaching levels not seen since the late 1990s. This supply imbalance is mirrored in global floating crude oil storage, which surged dramatically in 2015 to nearly one hundred eighty million barrels, a stark increase from its typical range of sixty to one hundred ten million barrels seen between 2010 and 2014.

On the demand side, structural shifts have contributed heavily to this oversupply. Annual growth in Chinese crude oil demand has decelerated sharply from peaks of over one thousand thousand barrels per day in 2010—driven by strategic reserve accumulation and post-2009 stimulus programs—to roughly two hundred to three hundred thousand barrels per day in 2015. Furthermore, major economies are experiencing a long-term decline in energy intensity, measured as barrels of crude oil demand per unit of real GDP indexed to 2005. China’s intensity index dropped the most, falling to nearly sixty by 2015, followed by declines to the high seventies and eighties for India, Japan, Europe, and the United States. Russia is the sole major exception, showing very little efficiency gain and remaining above an index value of ninety.

Supply-side headwinds are further exacerbated by impending geopolitical developments and shifting OPEC strategies. A chart of Iranian crude oil production shows that output declined from nearly four million barrels per day in 2010 to a trough of around two point seven million barrels per day under sanctions. Assuming the implementation of the nuclear deal, J.P. Morgan forecasts Iranian production to climb back to three point twenty-five million barrels per day by late 2016. At the same time, Saudi Arabia has refused to act as a swing producer to prop up prices. A historical table contrasts previous oil price declines with the 2014 to 2015 crash. In past downturns, such as the 2008 to 2009 price crash of nearly seventy-five percent, Saudi Arabia and OPEC cut their output by eighteen point one percent and fifteen point six percent, respectively. In contrast, during the 2014 to 2015 price drop of nearly sixty-three percent, Saudi Arabia actually boosted production by five point four percent, and total OPEC output grew by five point nine percent. Meanwhile, many United States shale producers remain resilient, with shut-in incentives only occurring at prices below forty dollars.

This page explores the multi-faceted impact of the 2015–2016 oil price bust on the energy sector, focusing on supply chain deflation, projected price paths, earnings resilience, widening credit spreads, historically low valuations, and modeled default scenarios. 

The author begins by noting that oil price downturns historically trigger severe deflation across the exploration and production supply chain, significantly lowering marginal costs and causing financial distress among suppliers. As a real-world example, the text mentions that per-well development costs have fallen from $4.0 million to $2.2 million in some locations. An accompanying chart plotting nominal and real well costs from 1975 to 1985 (indexed to 1975 = 100) illustrates that the massive cost run-up of the late 1970s and early 1980s completely reversed in real terms by 1984. These tracked expenses include site preparation, drilling, casing, and completion. Adjacent to this, a commodity futures chart shows a modest projected price rebound for both Brent and WTI crude over a 36-month horizon, rising from approximately $35 per barrel at month zero to around $50 to $53 per barrel by month 36.

Turning to corporate fundamentals and credit, the text explains that while the oil crash has decimated energy earnings and driven up credit spreads, systemic operational impacts may be contained because investment-grade producers represent 75% of US oil output, while those rated B or lower make up just 8%. This divergence is visualized in a bar chart of S&P 500 sector earnings indexed to 2014, showing energy earnings plummeting 59% in 2015 and an additional 10% in 2016, while non-energy earnings steadily grow by 5% and 8% over the same years. Consequently, a chart of US high-yield corporate bond spreads over 10-year Treasuries from 1995 to 2015 reveals a dramatic spike in energy-sector spreads to nearly 12% in late 2015, even as non-energy spreads remained comparatively flat.

Finally, the page details the historic collapse in energy equity valuations and potential credit defaults. A long-term chart tracking the price-to-book ratio of large-cap energy stocks relative to the broader large-cap universe from 1925 to 2015 demonstrates that relative valuations have fallen below 0.6x, marking their lowest levels in nearly a century. The author cautions that if oil prices remain depressed, up to 30% of energy high-yield issues could default by 2017. This risk is modeled in a bottom-up energy default rate table across three scenarios, all assuming a natural gas price of $2.75. In a modest recovery scenario of $55 oil, the total energy default rate from 2015 through 2017 is estimated at 20.0%. At a spot market scenario of $45 oil, the total default rate rises to 29.6%, peak-loaded in 2017 at 18.6%. In an unsustainably low scenario of $35 oil, the total default rate climbs to 35.3%, with a massive front-loaded spike of 20.0% defaulting in 2016 alone.

This page from the publication addresses what could eventually drive oil prices higher, focusing on the supply-side adjustments of key US shale oil plays, global oil majors, and Saudi Arabia's fiscal pressures. The author's central prediction is that while oil prices may remain below forty dollars per barrel for a few months in 2016, a gradual supply-demand adjustment—including the absorption of idle storage—will be well underway by early 2017, at which point oil prices will likely start rising again. 

To illustrate the supply-side shifts, a chart titled "Key US shale oil plays: Bakken, Eagle Ford, Permian" compares the US oil rig count with oil production from 2007 to 2015. It shows that although oil production, measured in millions of barrels per day on the right axis, surged from under one million to over four and a half million by late 2015, the corresponding oil rig count on the left axis plummeted sharply in 2015 from a peak of over one thousand rigs to below four hundred, signaling a forthcoming drop in production. 

A second chart, "The eventual supply adjustment is underway," plots the annualized capital expenditure and annualized cash from operations in billions of 2015 US dollars for ninety-seven major global oil companies from 2011 to 2016. It shows that cash from operations peaked near five hundred forty billion dollars in 2014 before dropping below four hundred twenty-five billion dollars in 2015. In response, annualized capital expenditure declined from a peak of over five hundred billion dollars to under four hundred fifty billion dollars in 2015, with a 2016 capex estimate dropping even further toward three hundred fifty billion dollars, reflecting significant global capex cuts.

The page then shifts to Saudi Arabia, noting that declining oil prices led to significant drops in Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency, or SAMA, balances in 2015. A stacked area chart titled "Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency balance sheet" shows SAMA assets in billions of Saudi Riyals from 2000 to 2015. Government deposits and banking sector reserves reached a peak combined value of over two thousand five hundred billion Riyals around 2014 before noticeably contracting in 2015, which is critical given that oil accounts for ninety percent of government revenues and eighty-five percent of exports. 

The potential future impact of these trends is explored in a chart titled "Impact of government spending and oil prices on government deposits at SAMA," showing projections from 2013 to 2019 under different scenarios. With ninety-dollar oil and a three percent fiscal adjustment, deposits stay healthy near one thousand five hundred billion Riyals.
