However, with sixty-five-dollar oil and no adjustment, SAMA deposits are projected to collapse entirely and enter negative territory by late 2018, while a three percent fiscal adjustment at sixty-five-dollar oil still results in a massive decline to roughly five hundred billion Riyals by 2019. 

Finally, a chart titled "Saudi Arabian government debt and Brent crude oil price" displays government debt as a percentage of GDP alongside the Brent crude oil price from 1991 to 2015. It shows that Brent crude prices crashed from over one hundred dollars per barrel down to around forty dollars in 2015. While Saudi government debt was virtually zero in 2015, the chart highlights that debt previously reached over one hundred percent of GDP in the late 1990s, indicating that Saudi Arabia has substantial fiscal runway before rising debt forces them to aggressively tighten oil supply.

This page, titled "Act IV: A chorus of concern emerges," counters assertions by Paul Volcker and Federal Reserve officials that increased regulation has not significantly harmed credit market liquidity. The author argues that sponsors of legislation are rarely unbiased critics of their own policies, comparing the situation to a lack of accountability from the Federal Reserve and the Department of Housing and Urban Development regarding their contributions to the 2008 housing crisis. To build his case against the Volcker Rule and market transparency mandates, the author presents a compilation of critical statements from prominent academic and financial experts warning of adverse consequences dating back to 2012. 

Anjan Thakor of Washington University in St. Louis warns that the Volcker Rule will force banks to retrench from market-making, particularly in smaller and riskier securities where unexpected supply-demand shocks are common and where market-making is most vital. Darrell Duffie of the Stanford Graduate School of Business similarly argues that the rule increases the cost of borrowing, raising capital, hedging, and obtaining liquidity, and warns that relying on non-bank entities to fill this gap could threaten the safety and soundness of the financial system. Charles Calomiris of Columbia University notes that proprietary trading and market-making are transactionally similar and hard to separate by intent, and he references concerns from Central Bank of Mexico Governor Agustin Carstens regarding global liquidity impacts. Calomiris compares eliminating proprietary trading to a "Volcker lobotomy" that strips banks of their most knowledgeable human capital. Paul Asquith of MIT provides empirical data showing that mandated transparency causes a significant decrease in trading activity, including a 41.3 percent decline in trading activity and a 24.7 percent decrease in daily price standard deviation for high-yield bonds. Finally, Howard Marks of Oaktree Capital Management cautions that restricting banks from proprietary buying during crises will severely reduce liquidity at the exact moment it is most desperately needed.

This page analyzes Brazil's fiscal and corporate vulnerabilities in 2016, comparing its current state to historical crises and assessing the specific threat of "Petrobranchitis" stemming from the state-controlled oil company Petrobras. The author argues that while Brazil faces deep structural problems due to wage and price indexation to inflation—reversing progress from the 1990s and resulting in collective bargaining covering 60% of labor contracts—the risk of sovereign default on external debt is lower than in 2002. This improvement is because sovereign financing has shifted heavily from external to domestic debt, with public sector external debt falling from 18% of GDP in 2002 to just 5% in 2015. 

To support this view, a table titled "Indicators of external vulnerability: 2002 and today" compares various debt metrics across percent of GDP, percent of exports, and percent of international reserves. Notably, gross external debt dropped from 44% of GDP and 598% of international reserves in 2002 to 34% of GDP and 151% of reserves in 2015, while the non-bank public sector share of gross external debt shrank from 18% of GDP to 5% of GDP.

A line chart titled "Brazil credit spread on external sovereign debt" tracks 5-year credit default swaps in basis points from 2001 to 2015. It shows that while spreads rose toward 500 basis points in 2015 due to junk downgrades by S&P and Fitch, they remained vastly lower than their October 2002 peak of 3,950 basis points. A second line chart, "Foreign financial exposure to Brazil," measures foreign exposure as a percentage of world GDP (excluding Brazil) on a 4-quarter average from 1980 to 2015. This chart shows a steady rise in exposure from about 0.5% in the mid-1990s to a peak of over 2.0% in 2011, before leveling off near 1.8% in 2015, underscoring the global relevance of Brazil's financial health.

The author concludes with a warning regarding Petrobras, whose debt quintupled between 2009 and 2014 without generating free cash flow since 2008. Facing US$ 24 billion of debt maturities over the next two years, the company is predicted to burn through its remaining cash by the end of 2016. The author outlines four potential avenues to resolve this: asset sales, extraordinary government support, local bank expansion to replace international bondholders, or a highly dilutive equity offering. Although rating agencies believe government support is highly probable, the author urges caution for investors despite bond yields in the 12% to 14% range. Additional entities mentioned in comparative contexts include Argentina, Greece, India, Mexico, Thailand, and Malaysia.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest addresses the recent market correction driven by weak sales, disappointing earnings growth, soft US manufacturing, and uncertainty regarding China. He examines whether the current profits recession will transition into a broader US GDP recession. Cembalest forecasts that US GDP growth for 2016 will remain low, in the range of 1.5% to 2.0%, avoiding a full-blown recession. Consequently, he expects equity markets to remain range-bound due to stagnant earnings and valuations that are not yet exceptionally cheap. Looking ahead, he anticipates that US and European consumer spending will benefit from payroll growth and low oil prices. Conversely, he expresses skepticism about China's ability to maintain its currency peg or basket, predicting that weak growth and capital outflows will force China to devalue its currency further. 

To support these assertions, the page presents four charts. The first chart, titled "Manufacturing surveys are in territory that has coincided with combined profit/GDP recessions in the past," plots the ISM Manufacturing index from 1960 to 2015. Shaded bars indicate periods of economic recession and profit recession. The line demonstrates that ISM levels dropping below the expansion threshold of 50 historically correspond with dual recessions, though the author notes that other economic indicators currently remain stronger. 

The second chart, "When services hold up better than manufacturing, GDP recessions can be avoided," shows the three-month average PMI survey levels for Services and Manufacturing from 1998 to 2015. This visual highlights a divergence where the services index has remained solidly in expansionary territory above 50, even as the manufacturing index dipped below 50, bolstering the argument that a full economic recession may be avoided. 

The third chart displays the "China real effective exchange rate" using the CPI-based REER index from 1995 to 2015. The line shows a steady, massive appreciation of the Chinese currency, climbing from around 70 in the mid-1990s to nearly 130 by 2015, illustrating why the currency is creating substantial headwinds for China's economy. 

The final chart, "After correction, stocks cheaper but not that cheap," plots the combined price-to-sales ratio on MSCI US, Europe, and Japan equities, excluding financials and energy, from 2004 to early 2016. It tracks both forward twelve-month and trailing twelve-month ratios. Following the correction, the ratio pulled back to roughly 1.2x, which is cheaper than its recent peak near 1.4x but still significantly higher than the 0.6x low observed during the 2008–2009 financial crisis. A footnote adds that J.P. Morgan expects fourth-quarter 2015 S&P 500 earnings to drop 3% year-over-year but rise 2% excluding energy, with an estimated ex-energy earnings growth of 4% to 6% for 2016.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" argues that efforts to reduce systemic risk may inadvertently increase market risk by making it harder for banks to expand their balance sheets to take risks or facilitate risk-taking during crises. 

To support this argument, the page features a detailed reference table outlining post-crisis regulations impacting credit markets across seven scopes: bank capital, bank liquidity, stress testing, bank structure, money market reform, credit market transparency and buy-ins, and securitization. For bank capital, rules like Basel III, the Basel Fundamental Review of the Trading Book, the Supplementary Leverage Ratio, and the Global Systemically Important Bank Surcharge enforce higher capital requirements against trading inventories and phase out non-core Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital. Bank liquidity rules, specifically the Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio, require banks to hold high-quality liquid assets, reducing the money multiplier in the banking system. Stress testing under the Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review forces economic and market shock analysis, which dampens banks' incentives to participate in certain businesses. Under bank structure, the Volcker Rule and EU Bank Structural Reform prohibit proprietary trading, limiting banks' willingness to hold potentially illiquid inventory. For money market reform, the SEC Money Market Reform requires floating instead of fixed Net Asset Values, with J.P. Morgan Securities Research forecasting that investor outflows and fund conversions could shift $600 billion to $650 billion away from prime money market funds. Credit market transparency rules, such as US TRACE rules and the European Securities and Markets Authority’s MiFID standards slated for 2017, increase reporting requirements for 144a securities and derivatives. Lastly, securitization capital rules impose capital charges on retained positions, changing balance sheet economics.

The page concludes with a footnote citing a November 2015 J.P. Morgan Securities report on credit market transparency. Drawing parallels to mandated equity market transparency in the 1990s and 2000s, the report warns that transparency can cause principal traders to disappear and make large trades harder to execute, forcing institutional investors to use multiple venues and tickets. It cautions that agency-driven and high-frequency traders show less commitment and quickly withdraw from market-making during volatile periods, contributing to "flash crashes" and demonstrating that equity-style transparency is not a cure-all for bond markets.

This page of the publication, titled Act III: Changes to the regulatory landscape, argues that significant post-crisis regulatory changes have successfully reduced systemic risk, making a repeat of the 2008 financial crisis less likely. The author points to several key shifts, including higher risk-based capital ratios, lower loan-to-deposit ratios, enhanced stress testing of bank portfolios, and a mechanism where bondholders, rather than taxpayers, depositors, or the Federal Reserve, would bear the brunt of any future bank failures. 

To support this view, two line charts compare banking metrics across the United Kingdom, Eurozone, United States, and Japan from 2000 to 2015. The first chart, tracking Tier 1 capital ratios, shows a universal post-2008 upward trend, with ratios climbing from a range of 7.5% to 10.0% in the mid-2000s to between 12.5% and 15.0% by 2015. The second chart displays loan-to-deposit ratios, illustrating a reduced reliance on wholesale funding. Eurozone and United Kingdom ratios, which peaked near 140% around 2008, fell to approximately 110% to 115% by 2015. Meanwhile, the United States ratio declined from nearly 100% to roughly 80%, and Japan's ratio consistently remained the lowest, declining further to below 80%.

The narrative provides context on why these dramatic protections were needed in the first place, noting that in 2009, the scale of deposits in failed and assisted US banks as a percentage of GDP was even higher than the peak of the Great Depression in 1933. The text cites a 2014 statement by former Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke, who declared that September and October of 2008 constituted the worst financial crisis in global history, including the Great Depression.

This severity is visually quantified in a bar chart tracking deposits in failed and assisted US banks as a percentage of GDP across three eras: the Great Depression, the Savings and Loan Crisis, and the Great Recession. While the Savings and Loan Crisis saw deposits in failed banks peak at roughly 3% of GDP, the Great Depression peaked at over 6% in 1933. This was surpassed in 2009 during the Great Recession, when deposits in failed and assisted banks spiked to nearly 9% of GDP.

To prevent widespread default during this period, the Federal Reserve took extraordinary intervention measures. An accompanying table details the peak outstanding balances of these emergency facilities in billions of dollars. The largest of these programs was the Term Auction Facility, which peaked at $493 billion, followed by the Commercial Paper Funding Facility at $348 billion and the Term Securities Lending Facility at $236 billion. Other significant interventions included the Asset-Backed Commercial Paper Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility at $152 billion, the Primary Dealer Credit Facility at $147 billion, Term Repurchase Transactions at $80 billion, the AIG Revolving Credit Facility at $72 billion, and the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility at $48 billion.

This page analyzes the valuation of the high yield credit market, examining whether rising spreads offer a sufficient margin of safety for investors. The author notes that implied default rates have reached 18% on energy bonds and 6% on non-energy bonds, both of which are significantly higher than trailing default rates. However, historical data suggests that high yield spreads lead default rates, meaning default rates are likely to rise further.

The primary chart at the top, titled Relationship between high yield default rates and credit spreads, displays rolling 12-month data from 1985 through 2015. It plots default rates on the left vertical axis (up to 18%) and credit spreads on the right vertical axis (up to 20%). The chart shows that spikes in spreads consistently precede peaks in defaults during economic recessions, which are represented by grey vertical bars.

To illustrate when investors should buy high yield credit, the bottom of the page features three historical case studies comparing high yield credit spreads (measured as spread-to-worst) against cumulative defaults and the number of issuers. The first chart, covering the Savings and Loan Crisis from 1987 to 1993, shows that credit spreads peaked when 55% of cumulative defaults had occurred. The second chart, tracking the Tech collapse from 1999 to 2004, shows that spreads peaked when cumulative defaults reached 76%. The third chart, representing the Global Financial Crisis from 2006 to 2013, shows spreads peaking when only 30% of cumulative defaults had taken place. Collectively, these charts argue that while it is beneficial to buy credit before defaults peak, investors should wait until defaults actually begin to rise.

Finally, the author discusses credit valuation methodologies, explaining that investors typically estimate default and recovery rates to determine the minimum spread required to compensate for losses. However, the author cautions that if market liquidity conditions are deteriorating, investors must demand an additional risk premium to compensate for illiquidity, similar to the extra yield required by private equity investors compared to public equity markets.

This page examines how credit hedge fund managers positioned themselves for a more volatile 2016 by analyzing gross, net, and long exposures alongside cash balances. Credit hedge fund managers are categorized into three groups: directional managers who are mostly long; dynamic low net managers with low net exposures; and distressed managers targeting low-dollar-price securities. Based on discussions with managers, J.P. Morgan finds that these groups significantly cut exposures and increased cash cushions in late 2015 to preserve ammunition for emerging market opportunities.

The first chart, titled Directional Credit Hedge Funds, tracks fund exposures throughout 2015. On the left axis, net and long exposures are shown, while gross exposure is plotted on the right axis. The data illustrates a steady retreat in risk-taking: net exposure fell from a peak of over 80% in April to below 60% by December, and long exposure similarly declined from over 70% to around 58%. Gross exposure, which peaked at more than 110% in the spring, fell back to approximately 90% by year-end.

The second chart, Dynamic Low Net Credit Hedge Funds, tracks net exposure on the left axis (5% to 20%) and gross exposure on the right axis (250% to 285%). This category of managers also reduced risk substantially in the second half of 2015. Net exposure sharply declined from nearly 19% in mid-2015 to around 6% by December, while gross exposure declined from a high of over 280% down to roughly 255%.

The third chart, Distressed Credit Hedge Funds, plots net exposure on the left axis (50% to 75%) and long exposure on the right axis (80% to 94%). After peaking mid-year, net exposure fell from 70% to approximately 55% by December, while long exposure retreated from a peak of 92% in the spring to 84% at the end of the year.

The final chart, Cash Balances, highlights cash as a three-month average percentage of assets from 2012 through late 2015, serving as a primary indicator of risk appetite for directional and distressed managers. Both fund categories experienced a sharp defensive rotation at the end of 2015. Directional funds saw cash levels spike from a low of about 5% in mid-2015 to around 17% by late autumn, while distressed funds increased their cash balances from approximately 7% to nearly 13% over the same period.

In this section of the publication, Michael Cembalest assesses the emerging risks and potential opportunities in the credit markets, observing that a significant migration out of credit is underway. This is driven by substantial redemptions from global high-yield mutual funds and ETFs, which he illustrates in a chart titled "The levee is already breaking." This chart tracks cumulative flows into global high-yield bond funds in billions of USD from 2005 through late 2015, showing that flows peaked near $140 billion in 2014 before sharply reversing to around $100 billion. Alongside this, another chart displays US high-yield corporate bond spreads over the 10-year Treasury from 1995 to early 2016. It highlights how the energy sector's spreads spiked dramatically to roughly 16% by early 2016, whereas ex-energy sectors remained much lower, between 6% and 8%. Cembalest notes that credit spreads for most non-energy and non-mining high-yield sectors are currently in the 6% to 8% range, making it difficult to gauge the full scale of potential selling pressure.

Turning to issuer fundamentals, the author argues that tight ex-energy spreads in April 2014 were never justified. Although stable interest coverage and cash flow margins offer some support, leverage has been rising, and sales growth has been weak, averaging just 2% to 3% annually since 2013. He posits that risk related to weak credits is lower than it was in 2000 but comparable to 2007. To illustrate rising leverage, a bar chart titled "Median leverage for US high yield issuers" displays the gross debt-to-EBITDA multiple from 2000 to the third quarter of 2015. This multiple climbed from a low of about 3.3x in the mid-2000s to over 4.0x by late 2015, nearing the previous peaks of 2001 and 2009. 

An additional horizontal bar chart, "Weakest credits in high yield," compares current credit risk metrics to those of 2000 and 2007 as a percentage of the notional amount outstanding in the high-yield index. The data shows that the current environment is significantly healthier than in 2000 but very similar to 2007. For instance, only about 15% of the index currently has interest coverage under 2x, compared to 57% in 2000 and 35% in 2007. However, current leverage exceeding 6x cash flow stands at about 43%, which is close to the 46% level seen in 2007, and the share of issuers with cash-to-debt under 5% is currently at 48%, slightly higher than the 43% seen in 2007.

Regarding refinancing risk, Cembalest notes that while the bulk of high-yield maturities fall after 2020, the share of bonds due within four years is roughly the same as in 2008. He addresses the high-profile decision by a Third Avenue high-yield mutual fund to "gate," or suspend, redemptions, clarifying that this fund is not representative of the broader market because it held over 85% of its assets in CCC and unrated securities as of July 2015. Finally, he flags potential selling pressure from collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), noting that 30% to 35% of the loans they hold are rated B or B-. Because most CLOs cap their exposure to CCC-rated assets at 7.5%, a wave of rating downgrades could trigger widespread forced selling.

This page addresses why US equity markets experienced a downturn in early 2016 despite the US economy's heavy reliance on the service sector. J.P. Morgan's Michael Cembalest argues that while the service industry dominates domestic GDP, manufacturing, capital spending, energy, and international currency exposure have a disproportionately large impact on corporate profits and stock market performance. 

This divergence is illustrated in a detailed table comparing US GDP indicators with S&P 500 metrics. While US exports comprise only 12% of GDP, foreign-sourced profits represent 40% of total S&P profits. Similarly, personal consumption expenditures make up 69% of GDP, but consumer-related services generate only 35% of S&P profits. This imbalance is even more pronounced in manufacturing and goods-producing industries, which account for just 14% of US employment but drive 65% of S&P profits. Furthermore, business capital spending constitutes 13% of GDP compared to 20% of S&P earnings, and the oil and natural gas sector made up only 1% of employment but accounted for 11% of S&P profits in 2014. This high concentration in industrial and global sectors explains why a surging US dollar historically leads to only a modest decline in overall economic growth but frequently triggers stock market corrections or crashes. This relationship is further reinforced by correlation data from 2005 to 2015, showing that manufacturing sector surveys have a 59% correlation with S&P returns, compared to just 39% for service sector surveys. 

Two subsequent line charts support the argument that market participants in 2016 are pricing in very low revenue and earnings growth. The first chart, tracking ISM manufacturing and services PMI survey levels on a three-month average from 1998 to 2016, shows that manufacturing weakness historically drags down services. In early 2016, both indices were trending downward, with manufacturing dipping close to the contractionary threshold of 50. The second chart details global and US earnings revisions from 2008 to 2016, calculated as the number of upgrades minus downgrades divided by total revisions. Since late 2011, revisions for both the S&P 500 and the MSCI All Country World Equity Index ex-US have remained largely negative, dipping sharply to nearly negative 40% by early 2016. This negative trend underscores why consensus S&P 500 sales growth expectations for 2016 dropped to just 2% as analysts reacted to weak corporate guidance.

This page examines whether the US economy was in an earnings recession in 2015, arguing that the answer depends entirely on the accounting definition of earnings. If using a pro-forma definition favored by major brokerage firms like Morgan Stanley, Deutsche Bank, Bank of America Merrill Lynch, Royal Bank of Canada, Citigroup, and J.P. Morgan Securities, earnings growth appeared flat. However, under S&P operating earnings or GAAP reported earnings, the US was already in an earnings recession by the third quarter of 2015. This divergence was primarily driven by energy company write-downs, which pro-forma definitions exclude.

To illustrate these differences, a table and an accompanying line chart outline S&P 500 earnings per share and year-over-year growth. In the fourth quarter of 2015, GAAP reported earnings—the metric favored by Yale's Robert Shiller—stood at $91. Adding back $13 of restructuring charges related to acquisitions, sales, and discontinued operations yields S&P operating earnings of $104, which is preferred by S&P, Goldman Sachs, and Barclays. Adding an additional $14 of items such as asset sales, goodwill impairments, M&A costs, non-cash compensation, and amortization of pension gains yields the pro-forma operating earnings figure of $118. The line chart tracks the year-over-year growth rate from 2011 to late 2015 under these three definitions, revealing that by Q3 2015, the GAAP measure fell sharply below zero percent, S&P operating earnings was flat to slightly negative, and the pro-forma measure remained positive.

Looking forward, the page highlights that projections for the first quarter of 2016 continue to deteriorate, with only three of ten sectors showing projected earnings growth. This decline is detailed in a table showing S&P earnings expectations for Q1 2016 compared between December 31, 2015, and February 5, 2016. The data shows downward revisions across all ten sectors. For example, expectations for Technology fell from 0.2% growth to a 7.4% decline, while Energy plummeted from an expected 43.3% contraction to an 84.0% contraction. Other sectors show mixed results, such as Consumer Discretionary dropping from 16.0% to 13.2% and Healthcare slipping from 5.3% to 4.8%. The table also tracks foreign sales exposure, noting that Tech has the highest exposure at 59%, followed by Energy at 56% and Materials at 55%.

Finally, the page addresses market valuations, noting that despite equity declines and cautious sentiment, valuations are not in deeply oversold territory compared to the 2009–2012 period. A final line chart tracks the S&P 500 enterprise value to operating cash flow ratio before capital spending from 2002 through early 2016 for four key sectors: Healthcare, Staples, Consumer Discretionary, and Technology. This metric is highlighted as crucial for tracking valuations because enterprise value includes both equity and debt, which is important during periods of rising corporate leverage. The chart shows that while Staples and Healthcare trade at relatively high multiples of around 13x to 14x, Consumer Discretionary and Technology trade at lower multiples of around 10x to 11x.

This page addresses the potential tax rates under a hypothetical Bernie Sanders presidential administration, pointing out that implementing such policies would require massive and unlikely Democratic gains of at least 30 seats in the House and 4 in the Senate. The author details the core pillars of Sanders' tax proposals: a 6.2% Social Security tax on earned income over $250,000; a 2.2% premium tax on ordinary income across all brackets; capping itemized deductions to a 28% tax credit for filers making over $250,000; taxing long-term capital gains and qualified dividends as ordinary income above that same threshold; and introducing new marginal brackets up to 52% for high-income earners. The author highlights the critical distinction between marginal and effective tax rates, noting that while the top marginal rate in 1979 was 70%, the actual effective rate paid was just 22% due to deductions and exemptions. 

Four charts demonstrate that the proposals would primarily impact the top 1% of earners—those with incomes above $430,000—by comparing current effective tax rates to proposed rates across a range of incomes from $25,000 to $10 million. For a salaried worker earning 90% of their income from wages, the effective tax rate under Sanders' plan diverges sharply above $250,000, rising to nearly 55% at $10 million compared to about 38% under current law. For a retiree with no wage income, the effective tax rate under Sanders' plan would peak at around 43% at $10 million, compared to roughly 31% currently. A control investor or private equity principal, who receives 80% of their income from long-term capital gains, would see the most dramatic increase because those gains would be taxed as ordinary income; their effective tax rate would spike from a current level of under 30% to roughly 50% at high income brackets. Similarly, a hedge fund manager or active investor receiving 50% ordinary unearned income and 20% capital gains would see their effective rate climb from a current flat level of around 31% to approximately 50% under the Sanders proposal.

Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management addresses the market performance of "unicorn" companies—private startups valued at over $1 billion—after they transition to public markets. He notes that while the number of unicorns has surged to around 150 with a collective valuation of over $500 billion, their performance once public has been generally disappointing. 

The primary visual is a line chart titled "Many unicorns finding it hard to survive in the wilderness," which indexes the stock price performance of 17 public unicorns against their closing price on their IPO date, represented as 100. The horizontal axis shows days post-IPO from 0 to 900, alongside a "Current" section representing the performance of companies public for more than 980 days. The vertical axis measures the price index from 0 to 300. The chart tracks notable companies such as Facebook, LinkedIn, Alibaba, Zynga, Twitter, Square, Groupon, Lending Club, Atlassian, Pure Storage, Box, GoPro, Mobileye, Sunrun, Shopify, Fitbit, and Etsy. A cartoon unicorn with a rainbow mane is depicted on the chart, and a note highlights that stock price weakness typically intensifies around the expiration of the standard 180-day lock-up period. 

The main takeaway from the data is that, relative to first-day closing prices, only Facebook has sustained material gains, while the vast majority of these companies are substantially negative. Even when measured against the initial IPO price rather than the first-day close—which strips out the average first-day pop of 45%—only Facebook, LinkedIn, and Shopify show gains over 15%, while ten of the seventeen remain deeply negative. 

Cembalest explains that early-stage unicorn investors often escape losses because IPO valuations averaged 55% higher than the final private round, which itself was typically 75% to 100% higher than preceding rounds. However, late-stage private investors face significant downside, particularly when IPO valuations fall below final private rounds, as occurred with Zynga, Square, and Box. Looking forward, the author warns that persistent underperformance in the public markets will eventually depress private unicorn valuations, restrict access to capital, and lead to more stringent investment terms. Additionally, the page notes that ten major firms, including Uber, Xiaomi, Airbnb, Palantir, China Internet Plus Holding, Snapchat, Flipkart, Didi Kuaidi, SpaceX, and Pinterest, represent 45% of the aggregate $532 billion unicorn market.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the strict terms and downside protections that late-stage startup investors demand in exchange for high valuations, which can ultimately trap "unicorn" companies. The author warns that many unicorns may be boxed in by complex shareholder provisions such as blocking rights, ratchets, and senior liquidation preferences. These terms, which may have been granted too readily during the optimistic period of 2014 and early 2015, can severely hinder subsequent fundraising or block realistic M&A exits. Consequently, the author foresees a potential industry shake-out over the next one to two years, which could allow strategic and non-venture-capital investors to acquire stakes in surviving unicorns at steep discounts. To illustrate the historical outcomes of private unicorn exits, the text notes that of ten privately acquired unicorns, only WhatsApp and Zulily yielded substantial gains, whereas Good, Better Place, Gilt Groupe, and Fab suffered significant losses, with the remaining four generating modest gains.

The accompanying table, titled "Select Unicorn terms and conditions" and sourced from Fenwick & West, highlights how financing terms tightened as the market cooled between the second quarter of 2014 and the fourth quarter of 2015. The number of financings dropped from 37 in the initial period (second quarter of 2014 through the first quarter of 2015) to just 12 in the fourth quarter of 2015, even as the average percentage of the company purchased in these rounds increased to 11 percent. Over this same timeframe, the median per-share price increase from prior financing rounds fell from 100 percent to 70 percent, while the average price increase from Series A financing collapsed from 7,390 percent in the second quarter of 2015 to 2,081 percent in the final quarter of the year. 

Concurrently, protective terms for new investors surged. Senior liquidation preferences—which prioritize new investors over common stock and earlier preferred stock if a company does not IPO—jumped from 19 percent in the initial period to 42 percent in the fourth quarter of 2015. IPO protection terms also sharpened; blocking rights doubled from 16 percent to 33 percent, ratchets rose from 14 percent to 17 percent, and the prevalence of either a blocking right or ratchet reached 50 percent of deals by late 2015. Other aggressive investor participation features, such as cumulative dividends and liquidation preferences at a multiple greater than 1.0, both spiked to 17 percent in the final quarter of 2015, up from 0 percent and 3 percent respectively in the earlier period.

This page of J.P. Morgan's publication addresses two distinct investment concerns: the disconnect between emerging market economic growth and stock market performance, and the sharp correction in high-growth cloud computing valuations. 

The author begins by addressing why emerging market equities have struggled despite emerging market GDP overtaking developed world GDP. Michael Cembalest argues that economic expansion does not translate directly to equity returns, pointing out that when the IMF first showed emerging markets representing over 50% of world GDP in 2012, McKinsey released a highly optimistic report predicting annual consumption in emerging markets would reach $30 trillion by 2025. Ironically, 2012 marked the peak in emerging market equity outperformance relative to developed markets. Stress points since then have included emerging markets' reliance on US dollar-denominated debt and their sensitivity to slowing Chinese demand for commodities.

To illustrate this, the author includes two side-by-side charts. The first, titled "Emerging market equities hit the wall in 2012...", compares total return indexes for developed and emerging markets from 1995 to 2015, set to a baseline of 100 in December 2012. It shows developed market equities steadily climbing to roughly 140 by late 2015, while emerging market equities languish and drop below 100. The second chart, titled "...just when the EM share of global GDP hit 50%", maps the percentage of world GDP at purchasing power parity from 1980 to 2012. This visual shows the developed market share declining from over 70% to meet the rising emerging market share at the 50% convergence point in 2012.

The second half of the page explains the steep decline in cloud computing stocks. While these companies feature strong gross margins of around 70% and rapid revenue growth near 25%, their valuations had reached unsustainable levels of 7 to 8 times sales, and roughly two-thirds of the companies still had negative operating cash flow. The sector faces headwinds like potential slowdowns in enterprise IT spending and intensifying price competition from major players Google and Amazon. Following the selloff, the cloud sector is priced at a much smaller premium to mature tech giants Microsoft and Oracle. 

This tech analysis is supported by two charts. The first, "Remembrance of things past", is a bar chart showing the percentage of technology companies with positive net income at IPO from 1980 to 2015. It reveals a long-term decline from over 80% profitable IPOs in the early 1980s to under 40% in recent years, approaching the lows of the dot-com era. The final chart, "Valuations and profitability of cloud computing sector", tracks a 45-company Bessemer universe from 2011 to early 2016. It contrasts the average enterprise-value-to-sales ratio, which plummeted from a peak of nearly 11 times in 2013 to around 5 to 6 times in 2016, with the percentage of companies with negative operating cash flow, which grew from roughly 30% in 2011 to over 60% by 2015. A benchmark dot indicates that Microsoft and Oracle trade at a much lower enterprise-value-to-sales ratio of around 3.5 times. Cembalest concludes that the defining task for investors in 2016 will be finding the correct price for growth, regardless of whether a recession occurs.

This page evaluates several global macroeconomic and market indicators, including stock market performance drivers, corporate earnings trends, disposable income, credit downgrades, and the relationship between oil prices and high-yield energy defaults. 

In discussing equity performance, the author argues that short covering played a major role in driving the returns of the best-performing S&P 500 stocks since late January. This is supported by a bar chart showing total return by short-interest decile, where the most heavily shorted decile of S&P 500 members achieved the highest returns of nearly nine percent, whereas the remaining deciles showed more moderate, fluctuating returns.

The commentary highlights slowing consensus earnings growth for 2016, noting that US growth expectations have plummeted from twelve percent last summer to just two percent. A line chart tracing 2016 consensus earnings per share growth estimates shows a steep downward trend from mid-2015 into early 2016 for both the S&P 500 and Europe, while Japan remains relatively stable and emerging markets experience a slight recent uptick. The author suggests that for corporate profits to rebound, rising labor incomes and consumer spending must play a role. To illustrate this, a line chart of year-over-year growth in disposable personal income across the United States, Germany, and France from 2005 to 2016 shows resilient, positive growth heading into 2016, with the US hovering around three percent.

In the credit markets, the author presents a positive outlook for high-yield bonds, noting that the volume of high-grade downgrades falling into the high-yield sector is much smaller than in previous cycles. A bar chart comparing investment-grade downgrades as a percentage of the high-yield market shows that the current forecasted cycle stands at roughly fifteen percent, compared to nearly sixty percent during the 2000 to 2003 tech downturn.

Finally, the page addresses the non-linear impact of oil prices on energy credit defaults. A line chart tracking the WTI crude oil price from January 2014 to January 2016 captures the dramatic decline from over one hundred dollars per barrel down to near thirty dollars. Annotation on this chart outlines the estimated two-year high-yield energy bond default rates at various price thresholds: a price of twenty-five dollars per barrel corresponds to a sixty percent default rate, which declines rapidly to thirty-six percent at thirty-five dollars, twenty-seven percent at forty-five dollars, and eleven percent at fifty-five dollars.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management explores the potential market implications of electing a political novice, drawing comparisons between Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign and historical political uncertainty. Cembalest notes that Trump’s proposed policies, like negotiating Medicare drug prices, could impact healthcare companies, and mentions a Tax Foundation estimate projecting a ten-trillion-dollar budget deficit increase over ten years under Trump’s tax plan, compared to eight hundred billion dollars under Ted Cruz. 

To understand the broader impact of extreme political uncertainty on markets, the author looks back eighty years to the rise of Huey Long in Louisiana. The page features a historical image of a 1928 campaign flier for Huey Long from Tulane University. Biographies detail Long’s authoritarian rule, which included bribery, blackmail, and voter fraud, prompting Franklin D. Roosevelt to label him one of the most dangerous men in America. Despite this corruption, a footnote details Long's extensive public works, such as growing Louisiana's paved roads from just 330 miles in 1928 to thirteen thousand miles. 

Despite Long's radical methods and targeted taxes on oil companies, academic research from American University and the University of Iowa found that Louisiana-domiciled stocks and bonds showed no substantial performance deviations, positive or negative, from national averages between 1924 and 1936. Cembalest concludes that this historical precedent demonstrates how financial markets can remain remarkably stable even during times of deep political uncertainty and transition into the unknown.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, published on March 16, 2016, discusses three primary macroeconomic developments: the ongoing slowdown in China, the sudden end of the momentum stock era, and the resilience of the US non-energy economy. 

Regarding China, the author notes that almost all economic indicators are slowing down, except for those related to property markets. In response, the Chinese government is implementing various capital control measures, such as freezing outbound investment quotas, restricting corporate foreign exchange purchases, and scrutinizing foreign exchange transfers, amidst rising labor unrest. This trend is illustrated in the chart titled "China: The Year Of The Draggin'", which shows a consistent multi-year decline from 2011 to early 2016 across several economic measures: employment surveys, exports, business conditions, GDP, corporate earnings, industrial production, and retail sales.

The second section addresses a sharp correction in momentum stocks in early 2016. From 2011 to January 2016, stocks with the strongest trailing price appreciation had significantly outperformed. However, this trend reversed abruptly as markets stopped overpaying for high earnings growth. The accompanying chart, "Expensive momentum stocks hit a wall in 2016," tracks this relationship from 2013 to 2016. It plots the total return index of "Best" minus "Worst" momentum stocks (measured on the left axis from 18 to 34), showing it peaked near 34 in early 2016 before dropping sharply. Additionally, the forward P/E valuation gap between the best momentum and best value stocks (plotted on the right axis from 2x to 10x) peaked near 9x in late 2015 before falling back toward 8x.

Finally, the author argues that a US recession is unlikely due to the stability of the non-oil economy, specifically in capital spending and payrolls. While default rates in the energy sector spiked to 12% of outstanding issues, non-energy default rates remained stable at 2%, a level held since 2011. Two charts illustrate this divergence. The first, "US business capital spending," tracks the year-over-year percentage change in non-residential fixed investment from 2011 to 2016. It shows that oil and mining capex plummeted to nearly negative 50% by early 2016, whereas all other capex remained stable and positive at around 5%. The second chart, "US jobs: a tale of 2 economies," shows the month-over-month annualized percentage change on a six-month average from 2010 to 2016. In this chart, oil and mining employment growth fell from a peak of 15% in late 2014 to roughly negative 15% in 2016, while employment growth in all other sectors held steady between 1.5% and 2.0%.

This page of the publication analyzes the impact of massive fiscal and monetary stimulus in China and assesses the resilience of global credit markets amid substantial fund outflows. 

The author begins by evaluating China's economic response to aggressive stimulus measures, characterizing the resulting short-term bounce as unconventional, unusual, and unsustainable. He notes that while industrial production has rebounded slightly and capital outflows have moderated, private sector indicators still point to a sub-6% growth rate. This discussion is supported by two charts covering the period from 2011 to early 2016. The first chart, titled "Pump Up the Volume," tracks year-over-year percentage changes in various funding and spending metrics, highlighting a massive surge in mortgage lending that approached 30% alongside a significant uptick in government spending and capital expenditure by state-owned enterprises. In contrast, the second chart, "China: The Year Of The Draggin'," displays a downward convergence of multiple key indicators over the same period, including employment surveys, exports, business conditions, GDP, corporate earnings, industrial production, retail sales, and non-state-owned enterprise fixed asset investment, indicating that massive stimulus is producing only a modest economic response.

The second half of the page focuses on credit markets, noting that they have successfully weathered significant redemption pressures from high yield and emerging market debt funds despite tight liquidity conditions. Two charts tracking cumulative flows in billions of USD from 2005 to early 2016 illustrate the severity of these withdrawals. Cumulative flows for global high yield bond funds experienced a decline of $86 billion from their May 2014 peak, while global emerging market debt funds saw a cumulative drop of $110 billion from their May 2013 peak. Despite these severe outflows, credit spreads have proven resilient and staged a strong recovery starting in February 2016. This turnaround is depicted in the final two charts. The first plots emerging market dollar-denominated debt—both sovereign and corporate—alongside US high yield ex-energy spreads from January 2014 to January 2016, showing spreads peaking in early 2016 before sharply tightening. The last chart displays the total return index level for emerging market local currency government debt, which fell from over 310 in early 2014 to a low of nearly 230 in early 2016, before mounting a sharp recovery toward the 260 level by April 2016.

This page explores investment opportunities in structured credit and assesses the broader economic conditions in Europe, highlighting a divergence between tepid GDP growth and positive micro-level signs. The author begins by discussing structured credit, explaining that underwriting for pools of commercial real estate and corporate loans has become significantly more conservative and investor-friendly compared to the pre-crisis era. Key improvements include higher credit enhancement for BBB- rated investments backed by commercial real estate, which has risen to 8% to 13% from pre-crisis levels of 3.5% to 4.5%. Additionally, loan-to-value ratios are lower, and the prevalence of interest-only loans has dropped from 75% of each pool to 25%. Regulatory changes also offer support, such as a December 2016 rule requiring sponsors of structured credit transactions to retain 5% of the pool. The author argues that a recent price sell-off in these assets represents a compelling investment opportunity relative to expected default rates.

To support this view, two charts illustrate the recent price declines. The first, showing the CMBS price index for structured credit backed by commercial real estate, tracks the BBB- rated 2012, 2013, and 2014 vintages from 2013 through early 2016. All three experienced a sharp drop in late 2015 and early 2016, with the 2014 vintage bottoming out near 72 before initiating a recovery. The second chart presents the CLO price index for corporate-loan-backed structured credit across post-crisis tranches. It highlights a steep drop for the riskier tranches in early 2016, where the B tranche plummeted to around 55 and the BB tranche fell to approximately 75, followed by modest rebounds.

The discussion then turns to the European economy. While Eurozone GDP growth is running at a slow 1.5% to 2.0% pace, and Q1 earnings (excluding energy) are expected to decline by 12% before rebounding by over 20% later in the year, several positive indicators have emerged. These include a rebound in Spanish and Italian credit demand alongside gains in retail sales and car registrations. 

Three subsequent charts illustrate these positive European trends. The first displays Eurozone retail sales and new car registrations as a three-month average year-on-year percentage change from 2006 to 2016. By early 2016, new car registrations were growing at a robust clip of around 10%, while retail sales grew at a stable rate of approximately 2%. The remaining two charts depict credit demand in Spain and Italy, measuring the net percentage of banks reporting higher demand for corporate, consumer, and mortgage loans. In Spain, all three categories rebounded strongly from deep negative territory during the Eurozone debt crisis to positive territory by 2016, with demand generally hovering between 25% and 50%. In Italy, consumer and mortgage credit demand recovered well into positive territory by 2016, though corporate demand lagged behind, remaining slightly negative.

This page analyzes the surging strength of the German economy and how its unique cultural characteristics are driving intense domestic opposition to the European Central Bank's expansionary monetary policies. Michael Cembalest argues that while German core consumer price index is currently low at 1% and wage inflation is moderate at 2% to 3%, a potential rise in German inflation could pressure the ECB to tighten its policies, though he projects this as an issue for 2017 at the earliest. 

Two charts illustrate the current boom in Germany. The first chart, tracking the booming German housing market from 2002 to 2016, shows year-over-year mortgage lending growth alongside indexed levels of house prices and residential investment. By 2016, both residential investment and house prices had surged dramatically, with residential investment rising to an index level of roughly 130 and house prices climbing to about 135, while mortgage lending growth hovered around 2%. The second chart shows surging real retail sales and real household income from 1996 to 2016, indexed to January 1996. By early 2016, real household income had climbed sharply to an index value of nearly 106, and real retail sales had recovered to an index level of about 101. 

The commentary shifts to the controversial steps the ECB is taking, which include acting as an anchor investor to finance European businesses directly, purchasing up to 70% of corporate bond issues rated BBB- or better, and including small companies by setting no minimum issuance volume. Cembalest highlights that this policy, paired with the fact that approximately 40% of European government bonds trade with negative yields, has fueled intense political debate in Germany. German Finance Minister Wolfgang Schäuble went so far as to attribute the rise of the right-wing, Eurosceptic party Alternative for Germany (AfD) to these ECB monetary policies. A footnote additionally notes that while immigration was the primary driver for the rise of the right-wing Freedom Party in Austria, the upcoming elections signal the beginning of a broader, existential election cycle for Europe.

To explain why Germans are uniquely sensitive to these low and negative interest rates, a third scatter plot chart correlates a country's cash and deposits as a percentage of financial assets against its real household disposable income per capita in euros. The chart demonstrates that German households have an exceptionally strong preference for cash relative to their income. At a disposable income level of nearly 28,000 EUR, German households hold almost 40% of their financial assets in cash and deposits. This is vastly higher than other high-income European nations; for instance, France sits at roughly 30% cash, the Netherlands at about 22%, and Sweden and Denmark both hold only around 15% of their financial assets in cash. This disparity explains the deep-seated opposition to the ECB's negative interest rate policies coming from German savers.

This page explores the economic and social factors driving the appeal of outsider political candidates during the 2016 primary elections, suggesting that China’s 2001 entry into the World Trade Organization (WTO) is a primary empirical explanation. The author argues that this event had a massive negative impact on American workers, prompting voters to favor candidates advocating for the renegotiation of trade deals. 

To support this argument, the page features two paired line charts covering the period from 1960 to 2015. The first chart, titled "After China joins the WTO, its FX intervention rises and US manufacturing job losses accelerate," maps the 10-year percentage change in US manufacturing jobs against Chinese foreign exchange intervention as a percentage of GDP on an inverted scale. It shows that following China's entry into the WTO in 2001, Chinese FX intervention surged, peaking near 45% of GDP around 2007, while US manufacturing job losses sharply accelerated, dropping to a 10-year change of nearly negative 35% by 2010. The second chart, titled "...coinciding with a sharp decline in US labor's share of corporate profits," plots the same manufacturing job losses alongside US labor's share of non-financial gross profits. Following the 2001 WTO milestone, labor's share of profits plummeted from approximately 64% down to around 57% by 2012, highlighting a major departure from historical trends.

The page cites prominent academic research to reinforce these charts, including a 2015 paper by Pierce of the Federal Reserve and Schott of Yale, which links the swift decline in US manufacturing to Congress granting Permanent Normal Trade Relations to China in October 2000. Additionally, a paper by David Autor of MIT, Dorn of CEMFI, and Hanson of UC San Diego, titled "The China Syndrome," is cited to show that rising imports from China directly caused higher unemployment, lower labor force participation, and reduced wages in local US labor markets facing direct import competition.

Addressing another prominent campaign topic, the author notes that data on undocumented immigrants do not show similarly sharp recent changes. A line chart titled "Estimates of unauthorized immigrant population relative to total foreign-born population, Millions" tracks data from 2000 to 2014. It shows that while the total foreign-born population rose steadily from around 31 million to over 40 million, the unauthorized immigrant population remained relatively flat, peaking at 32% of the total foreign-born population in 2007 and declining modestly to 27% by 2014.

Despite the flat trend in unauthorized immigration, public anxieties around these economic and social issues have driven high voter engagement. The final line chart, "Primary turnout since 1980 (modern primary era)," tracks primary votes cast as a percentage of eligible voters. It shows Democratic primary turnout peaking near 18% in 2008 before declining to roughly 12% in 2016. Conversely, Republican turnout, which historically hovered around 10% or lower, experienced a notable upward spike through the March 15, 2016 primaries, reflecting the heightened mobilization of GOP primary voters.

This page analyzes the severe fiscal challenges faced by six US states—Illinois, New Jersey, Connecticut, Kentucky, Hawaii, and Massachusetts—whose retirement and debt obligations loom large relative to their revenues. The author utilizes the "IPOD" ratio, which measures the sum of interest on bonds, pension payments, other post-employment benefits (OPEB) payments, and defined contribution payments divided by state revenues. The analysis contrasts the current IPOD ratios with "full accrual" ratios required to service all future accrued obligations, outlining the drastic fiscal policy changes needed to close the gap.

The first table, titled "Mutually exclusive means of raising incremental revenues required to meet full accrual payments to retirees," illustrates the options available to these states over a 30-year period. To transition from current to full accrual IPOD ratios, states must choose between substantial tax hikes, direct spending cuts, or massive hikes in public sector worker contributions. For instance, New Jersey’s IPOD ratio would need to rise from 12% to a full accrual level of 38%. To achieve this, the state would require either a 26% increase in tax revenues, a 24% cut in direct non-retirement spending, or a 471% increase in worker contributions. Similarly, Illinois must move from 22% to 39% IPOD, requiring either a 17% tax increase, a 16% spending cut, or a 400% increase in worker contributions. Connecticut faces the highest required worker contribution increase at 699%, alongside a needed 14% tax increase or 14% spending cut to reach its 35% full accrual ratio. 

The second table demonstrates that these options are politically and mathematically daunting. It details the effective state tax rates on middle-quintile earners and the required annual investment returns if no fiscal policy changes are made. Raising taxes is politically difficult because several of these states already have among the highest tax rates in the nation: Hawaii ranks 3rd highest with an 11.4% effective rate, Illinois ranks 4th at 10.8%, Kentucky ranks 6th at 10.8%, and Connecticut ranks 7th at 10.7%. Alternatively, relying solely on investment returns to close the gap requires historically unrealistic annual returns over the next 30 years, ranging from 10.6% in Massachusetts and 13.8% in Illinois to 16.8% in Kentucky. For New Jersey, solving the shortfall through investment returns alone is deemed "not mathematically solvable."

Additional footnotes clarify that defined contribution plans comprise a negligible portion of the IPOD ratio, averaging just 0.31% of state revenues. Furthermore, the author dismisses pension obligation bonds as a viable savior, noting that even if these states issued bonds equivalent to one-third of their outstanding general obligation debt and earned a consistent 3% spread, it would cover only about 5% of their incremental funding needs.

This page analyzes how state-level retiree healthcare, or Other Post-Employment Benefit, liabilities might be mitigated by the Affordable Care Act and direct policy reforms, and the subsequent impact on state IPOD ratios, which measure the percentage of state revenue required to cover bond interest, unfunded pension and retiree healthcare liabilities, and defined contribution payments. 

The first visual, SM Exhibit 7, is a bar and scatter chart depicting the IPOD ratio across all fifty states for fiscal year 2015. The states are ordered from highest to lowest original ratio. The chart compares an original scenario, represented by blue bars, with an alternative scenario where the OPEB obligation is capped at the 25th percentile with cost-of-living adjustments, represented by brown dots. Reference lines are drawn at 15% in green and 25% in red to mark risk thresholds. The chart illustrates that while states like Hawaii and Delaware would benefit the most from these adjustments, high-debt states like Illinois, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Kentucky remain at or above the 25% threshold even under the capped scenario, indicating that pension burdens, rather than healthcare costs, dominate their financial strain.

The lower half of the page, SM Exhibit 8, outlines real-world examples of OPEB plan changes enacted by individual states, citing a survey showing that two-thirds of state respondents have recently modified retiree healthcare. The narrative describes a variety of cost-cutting measures. For example, Delaware and Pennsylvania extended vesting and service requirements, while Georgia, Indiana, and Maryland increased retiree premiums, copayments, deductibles, or out-of-pocket limits. Idaho stopped covering Medicare-eligible retirees entirely, and New Jersey shifted costs to the federal government by becoming an official Medicare Part D plan. Other states restricted access for future workers: Nevada and Utah closed their retiree healthcare plans to employees hired after 2011 and 2005, respectively, and West Virginia capped subsidy levels while limiting eligibility to those hired before July 2010. Meanwhile, Ohio is actively phasing out spousal coverage and Medicare Part B reimbursements.

This page analyzes US state pension plan discount rates and the financial stress placed on states if they adopt more conservative funding assumptions. The author argues that states' typical assumption of a 7.6% nominal annual return—or a 5.6% real return assuming 2% inflation—is overly optimistic. While historical 30-year rolling returns on a 65/35 stock-bond portfolio have often exceeded this level since 1996, those returns benefited from unique tailwinds, including the post-Volcker fixed-income rally and the 1990s equity boom. Looking forward, pension analysts argue for lower return expectations due to Federal Reserve monetary policy and yield curve suppression. J.P. Morgan models a more conservative real return assumption of 4% (a 6% nominal return), which aligns with the lower boundary of historical trailing 30-year returns since the 1920s.

The first chart, "Historical real returns for hypothetical 65% stock, 35% bond portfolio, 30-year rolling real return," displays a timeline from 1956 to 2016 on the X-axis and real returns from 3% to 8% on the Y-axis. A fluctuating blue line shows the rolling 30-year real returns, which peaked above 7.5% in the early 2010s but bottomed near 3.5% in the early 1980s. A red dotted line marking the average state pension assumption of 5.6% sits well above the historical lows, while a black dotted line represents J.P. Morgan's conservative 4% assumption, sitting near the historical floor.

The text also references a 2014 independent Blue Ribbon panel commissioned by the US Society of Actuaries, which concluded that while current pension assumptions are not entirely inconsistent with historical experience, they should ideally be calculated using a risk-free rate plus explicit forward-looking risk premia. 

The second chart, "IPOD ratio: the impact of a lower discount rate and shorter amortization term," demonstrates how a state’s Interest, Pension, and Other Debt-related (IPOD) ratio—measured as the percentage of state revenue required to cover debt and retirement liabilities—increases under tighter rules. The X-axis ranks all fifty US states from highest to lowest debt burden, and the Y-axis shows the IPOD ratio from 0% to 50%. The chart features two horizontal threshold lines: a green line at 15% and a red line at 25%. The original baseline scenario (a 6% discount rate and 30-year amortization) is represented by blue bars, while the stricter scenario (a 5% discount rate and 20-year amortization) is represented by brown dots. 

The visual shows that while states with low debt burdens experience negligible changes, highly indebted states face severe increases in their IPOD ratios under the stricter scenario. For example, Illinois rises from approximately 38% to nearly 50%, and New Jersey jumps from about 36% to roughly 45%. The author notes that under this stricter scenario, Hawaii, Massachusetts, Texas, and Maryland would all see their debt burdens rise to cross or sit directly on the critical 25% red line threshold.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication features a chart and a detailed list of technical definitions examining state-level financial sustainability across the United States. 

The primary chart, SM Exhibit 9, compares full accrual IPOD ratios against current yields on 30-year general obligation bonds and Moody's credit ratings for each US state. The IPOD ratio measures the percentage of state revenue collections required to pay the sum of bond interest, the state's share of unfunded pension and retiree healthcare liabilities, and defined contribution plan payments. The chart's horizontal axis lists the states from highest IPOD ratio on the left to lowest on the right. The left axis scales the IPOD ratio from 0 percent to 40 percent, shown in blue vertical bars, while the right axis displays the 30-year general obligation yield from 2.00 percent to 4.50 percent. Individual state yield data points are color-coded by credit rating category, ranging from unrated open circles and AAA light blue dots to BBB-plus to BBB-minus red dots. The author notes that for states with the highest IPOD ratios, markets apply a modest yield premium of 0.5 percent to 1.5 percent. This is evident in Illinois, which has the highest IPOD ratio at nearly 35 percent and a BBB-range rating yielding over 4.00 percent, and New Jersey, with an IPOD ratio of over 30 percent and an A-range rating yielding around 3.50 percent. Most other states cluster below a 15 percent IPOD ratio, with credit ratings in the AAA or AA range and yields generally sitting between 2.50 percent and 3.00 percent.

The lower half of the page, SM Exhibit 10, outlines the definitions and assumptions used for these calculations. Revenues include state tax collections, sales taxes, and General Fund items like lottery proceeds and resource royalties. Bonds include tax-supported and general revenue debt, specifically excluding revenue bonds like toll roads. Liabilities are calculated using the entry-age normal method, and unfunded liabilities are amortized over 30 years using level dollar amortization to harmonize data across states. A conservative 6 percent investment return discount rate is assumed; if a state plan already uses a lower rate, it is left unchanged. Spending figures reflect education, public welfare, corrections, and highways. The methodology also accounts for cost-of-living adjustments, noting that in legal challenges across several states, courts allowed pension COLA reductions in 8 out of 9 cases under the premise that COLAs are not contractual rights. Lastly, pension plan durations are set at 11.5 years when disclosures are missing, while retiree healthcare liability durations are assumed at 14.3 years based on California's disclosures.

This page serves as the table of contents and introduction for J.P. Morgan’s research paper on energy, authored by Michael Cembalest. The paper focuses primarily on the promise, potential, and constraints of renewable energy, starting with a brief analysis of the commodity super-cycle and oil market dynamics. 

The first section examines whether the current commodity super-cycle is nearing its end, suggesting that recent price declines indicate we are close to its conclusion, and forecasts that a global oil supply deficit relative to demand could emerge by mid-2017. The second section evaluates electric vehicles and hybrids, arguing that hybrid cars represent a more impactful near-term energy-reducing trend than electric vehicles, for which historical adoption projections have been overly optimistic. The third section analyzes New York State's ambitious energy plan to generate fifty percent of its electricity from renewable sources and reduce building energy consumption by twenty-three percent by 2030, questioning the plan's feasibility given the state's limited solar and wind resources. The fourth section details how changes in utility billing structures across the United States could slow the future growth of distributed residential and commercial solar power. The final section analyzes the modest potential for additional US hydropower, comparing the US to countries like Norway, Switzerland, Canada, Austria, and Brazil, where hydropower contributes more than fifty percent of overall electricity generation.

The page notes that the energy report is overseen by Vaclav Smil, a Distinguished Professor Emeritus at the University of Manitoba, an expert on energy systems, and a recipient of the OPEC award for research. Additionally, a photograph at the bottom depicts winding light trails on Jinshui Road in Taiwan at night, which serves as the cover image of the report. This image symbolizes the report's overarching theme of distinguishing between reality and aspiration in the energy transition.

This page of the publication, titled Sentimental Journey: the long, winding road to a renewable energy future, argues that the transition to renewable energy and electric vehicles is progressing much more slowly than major analysts and agencies historically predicted, even though cost reductions are now driving record-breaking global investments. 

The top-left chart illustrates the share of US primary energy derived from renewable sources from 1960 to 2030, comparing actual data with several notable forecasts. While the actual renewable share has crawled slowly upward, reaching only about 10 percent by 2015, past forecasts depicted far more aggressive trajectories. For example, physicist Bent Sorensen predicted renewables would supply nearly 50 percent of US primary energy by 2005, and Amory Lovins of the Rocky Mountain Institute projected a share of over 30 percent by 2000. Even the Carter Administration's solar-only forecast estimated 20 percent by 2000. Looking ahead, more recent projections by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory and the Google 2030 Clean Energy Plan continue to project steep upward curves toward 2030.

The top-right chart demonstrates a similar gap between expectation and reality for electric vehicles, plotting electric vehicle and plug-in hybrid sales as a percentage of total car sales from 2009 to 2020. While actual US and global sales hovered at just 0.6 percent in 2015, a wide range of forecasts from Deloitte, BCG, Roland Berger, IEA, Bloomberg NEF, Frost & Sullivan, PwC, and Deutsche Bank projected rapid adoption, with some expecting market shares near 10 to 12 percent by 2020.

The bottom-left chart shows annual global investment in renewable energy in USD billions from 2004 to 2015. It tracks a dramatic rise in total investment, peaking at an all-time high of 286 billion dollars in 2015 despite falling fossil fuel prices. The stacked area chart breaks down this investment by region, highlighting a massive expansion of spending in China and Asia, stable contributions from the US, and a notable decline in European investment since its peak in 2011.

The bottom-right chart displays global renewable electricity generation as a percentage of total generation from 1985 to 2015. The chart makes the point that global renewable electricity is still predominantly a hydroelectric story. Out of nearly 25 percent total renewable generation, hydro makes up the vast majority. Wind is shown to be steadily rising, while solar represents a tiny 1 percent sliver of total generation in 2015. Geothermal, biomass, and other sources make up the remaining small fraction. 

The accompanying text and footnotes discuss how dramatic cost declines, particularly in solar module costs which fell from 100 dollars per watt in 1976 to 1 dollar per watt by 2015, have finally allowed non-hydro renewables to represent 54 percent of newly installed capacity in 2015, though they only accounted for 7 percent of actual global electricity generation. The author also critically notes Jacobson and Delucchi’s highly ambitious 2009 proposal for a 100 percent renewable global energy system by 2030, listing its massive physical requirements, such as 3.8 million wind turbines and 1.7 billion rooftop solar installations.

This page explores the environmental comparison between electric vehicles (EVs) and hybrid vehicles, arguing that the true greenhouse gas (GHG) footprint of an EV depends heavily on the energy mix of the power grid used to charge it. In regions where coal usage is high, full hybrid cars like the Prius can actually produce better GHG results than EVs. 

To illustrate this, a stacked bar chart titled "How Green is My Valley: the CO2 footprint of your electric car is heavily dependent on where you live" displays the percentage of total electricity generation by source across various geographies. The y-axis ranges from 0% to 100%, and the generation sources are categorized into renewables (green), nuclear (yellow), natural gas (brown), and coal and oil (black). The chart is divided into three sections: countries with the largest number of EV cars, other select countries, and select US states. 

Among the leading EV countries, Norway and Sweden are shown to have grids dominated by renewables, while France relies heavily on nuclear energy, and China is heavily dependent on coal and oil. In the "other select countries" section, Brazil and Portugal exhibit high shares of renewable energy, whereas India and Poland rely mostly on coal and oil. Among the select US states, Washington is almost entirely powered by renewables, California utilizes a mix of natural gas and renewables, and states like Missouri and Ohio are dominated by coal and oil. 

The author highlights three key nuances to keep in mind regarding this data. First, natural gas is significantly cleaner than coal, as an EV charged on a 100% natural gas grid has roughly half the GHG footprint of one charged on a 100% coal grid. Between 2006 and 2014, only the United States experienced a double-digit decline in coal's share of generation, primarily due to natural gas expansion, while the global share of coal remained unchanged. Second, the "renewable" segment in the chart consists mostly of hydroelectric power, which globally had a share 3.6 times higher than wind and solar combined in 2015. Third, the role of nuclear energy remains a complex debate. While pro-nuclear advocates—including the Clean Air Task Force, climatologist James Hansen of Columbia University, David Mackay of Cambridge, Robert Hargraves of Dartmouth, and 65 biologists who signed an open letter in 2015—support its use, critics point to the severe environmental aftermath of the Fukushima disaster, where radioactive water has leaked into the ground and ocean.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest addresses the sustainability of the 2016 oil price bounce, arguing that the rally is indeed real. Despite a persistent supply glut, a significant 35% to 40% drop in global oil capital spending, alongside a greater than 75% drop in the US rig count, points to future supply constraints. He highlights that non-OPEC field decline rates—which had slowed to 3% to 4% during high-price years as expensive recovery techniques were deployed—are projected by Wood Mackenzie to rise back to 5% by 2017. 

On the demand side, global consumption continues to rise at roughly 1.3% annually. While OECD consumption has fallen by 10% since 2005, non-OECD demand—primarily driven by transportation—has surged by 37%, officially overtaking OECD demand in 2013. He dismisses claims that renewable energy is suppressing oil demand, noting that only 5% to 6% of global oil is used for electricity generation, and electric vehicle adoption remains very slow. Notably, despite declines in heavy industry, Chinese oil demand grew by 5.7% in 2015 and 3% year-over-year in the first quarter of 2016, fueled by rising car sales.

Four charts support this thesis. The first chart, "The wild ride in oil prices in 2016," plots the WTI crude oil futures curve in USD per barrel against months until delivery up to 60 months. It compares curves from January 4, March 31, and June 14, 2016, illustrating how the curve shifted dramatically upward by June, starting near $48 for immediate delivery and rising to over $53, compared to the sub-$40 front-month prices seen earlier in the year. 

The second chart, "World oil supply-demand balance," shows the historical net balance in million barrels per day from 1995 to 2015. It highlights the massive surge in excess supply peaking near 2 million barrels per day in 2015, illustrating the scale of the recent glut. 

The third chart, "World oil capex," tracks upstream capital spending as a share of global GDP from 1985 to 2015, with estimates for 2015 and 2016. It shows capex peaking near 0.8% of GDP in 2014 before sharply contracting to an estimated 0.5% in 2016, representing a historic pullback in infrastructure investment. 

The final chart, "Oil prices, production freeze rumors & positioning," contrasts the spot oil price in USD per barrel on the left axis with the volume of oil short contracts in thousands on the right axis from January 2013 to mid-2016. This visual demonstrates that spot prices fell from around $100 to under $30 by early 2016, just as short positioning surged to near 300,000 contracts. This extreme bearish positioning primed the market for a rapid bounce when the first production freeze rumors hit the press.

Ultimately, Cembalest concludes that compounding demand growth and severely reduced non-OPEC capital spending will likely push the current oil glut into a supply deficit sometime between 2017 and 2018, justifying the sustainability of the oil price rally.

This page analyzes the market adoption of hybrid vehicles versus electric vehicles (EVs), arguing that auto analysts have historically been overly optimistic about EV adoption while the more impactful industry developments have quietly occurred in hybrid vehicles. To illustrate this over-optimism, the first chart compares actual US EV and PHEV sales—which hovered at less than one percent of total sales through 2015—with lofty 2020 market share projections made by various industry forecasters. Deloitte projected 2020 sales at 4%, BCG at 6%, Roland Berger and the IEA at 8%, Bloomberg NEF and Frost & Sullivan at 9%, PwC at 10%, and Deutsche Bank at over 11%.

The author defines the various hybrid types—micro, mild, full, and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs)—noting that while PHEVs and EVs represent only 0.7% of US light vehicle sales, full hybrids have captured 3% of the market. The second chart, tracking US vehicle sales from 1999 to 2015 in thousands of units, displays the steady dominance of full hybrids (such as the Toyota Prius, Ford Fusion, and Hyundai Sonata) which peaked near 500,000 annual units around 2013. By contrast, plug-in hybrids (like the Chevy Volt and BMW i8) and pure electric vehicles (like the Tesla Model S and Nissan LEAF) both remained flat at under 100,000 units each.

Although full hybrids can reduce fuel consumption and carbon emissions by up to 35%, the economic trade-off remains challenging for consumers.
