The author argues that while there is no cyclical reason for fiscal stimulus at this stage of the business cycle—given a large budget deficit at full employment and federal debt projected to hit 90% of GDP by 2027—the bill will deliver meaningful, positive structural benefits for corporations. He projects a minimal growth boost of only 0.3% because the primary beneficiaries, corporations and high-net-worth individuals, have low marginal propensities to spend. 

To support the assertion that tax cuts are an inefficient stimulative tool, a chart titled "Fiscal multipliers are lowest for corporate tax cuts and high income tax cuts" shows the change in economic output per dollar of fiscal policy. It illustrates that corporate tax cuts and one-year tax cuts for higher-income individuals yield the lowest economic multipliers, at roughly 0.3x and 0.4x respectively. In contrast, government spending on the purchase of goods and services yields the highest multiplier, at about 1.6x, followed by federal infrastructure transfers to states at around 1.4x.

Another chart, "Change in Federal taxes paid by income level," projects the absolute change in federal taxes in US dollars from 2019 through 2027. It shows that the $100k-$500k income bracket receives the largest dollar benefit, peaking at more than a $120 billion tax reduction in the early years. However, because individual tax cuts are set to expire, the tax savings for all groups sharply diminish, trending back toward zero by 2027.

Addressing corporate-level impacts, a table titled "Tax scenario analysis: potential impact to S&P 500 EPS" compares the House and Senate versions of the tax plan, assuming a 21% corporate rate. Starting with a baseline 2018 S&P 500 consensus EPS of $146.00, the corporate tax rate reduction adds $12.90 under both plans. Limiting interest expense deductibility subtracts $1.00 under the House plan and $2.80 under the Senate plan, while one-time repatriation taxes subtract $3.80 and $4.00 respectively. After factoring in buybacks induced by cash repatriation, the total benefit from tax reform is estimated at +$10.60 (+7.3% upside) for the House plan and +$8.50 (+5.8% upside) for the Senate plan, leading to revised S&P 500 EPS estimates of $156.60 and $154.50. Factoring in immediate expensing of capital expenditures adds an identical cash flow benefit of $3.80 to both scenarios. A footnote adds that while the interest deductibility cap is a concern for levered companies, only 1% of S&P, 3% of Russell 2000, and 8% of the high-yield market would see free cash flow declines exceeding 10% under the stricter EBIT test scheduled for 2022.

Finally, a bar chart titled "Marginal effective tax rate" displays the effective tax rate on new investments in manufacturing and services. It shows that the tax reform dramatically improves US global competitiveness by lowering its marginal effective rate from a high of 34.6% down to approximately 19%. This shift brings the US in line with Europe (~19%), Canada (~18%), and Mexico (~17%), well below the Asia-Oceania average of roughly 27%, which the author expects will curb the pace of corporate tax inversions.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest argues that despite current optimism regarding the Eurozone's recovery, unresolved structural issues remain a significant risk that will resurface during the next recession, projected for 2020 or later. He points to declining global central bank trust in the Euro, Germany's economic dominance over France, and structural rigidities. While French President Emmanuel Macron has achieved domestic labor reforms—such as decentralizing collective bargaining and lowering wealth and capital gains taxes—broader Eurozone-level integration efforts remain stalled. 

Four charts illustrate these structural challenges. The first, titled Global currency reserves, tracks the percentage of global reserves allocated to the Euro and the US Dollar from 1999 to 2017. Euro allocations peaked near twenty-eight percent around 2009 before declining to roughly nineteen percent in 2015, only recently stabilizing around twenty percent, which signals that central banks are not fully convinced of the Euro's value as a reserve. The second chart, Franco-German wealth gap, displays the ratio of Germany's real per capita GDP to France's from 1850 to 2015. After stabilizing in the late twentieth century, this ratio has risen significantly since 2000, climbing from around 1.05 to over 1.15, highlighting Germany's widening lead. The third chart, titled Death in Venice, displays the Industrial Production Index for Germany, France, and Italy from 1980 to 2017, indexed to December 31, 1999. It shows that economic cycles were highly synchronized before the Euro exchange rate was fixed, but afterward, performance diverged drastically; Germany's industrial production index rose to nearly 130 by 2017, while France stagnated near 100, and Italy fell below 90. Finally, the fourth chart, German banks less willing to lend to periphery banks, tracks German outbound lending to Italy and Spain in billions of US dollars from 2005 to 2017. Lending to Italy plummeted from a peak of over three hundred billion dollars in 2008 to under one hundred billion dollars by 2017, while lending to Spain saw a similar dramatic drop from a peak of nearly two hundred seventy-five billion dollars to around seventy billion dollars, showing that the European Central Bank has had to step in to support these peripheral economies.

The author argues that lower European equity valuations are justified by a systematically lower return on equity (ROE) across European industries compared to those in the US. Furthermore, the apparent benefits of Eurozone investing in 2017 were modest and entirely driven by the rally in the Euro; in local currency terms, the Eurozone underperformed the US. This discussion supports the author's historical preference for a "barbell" strategy that overweights the US and Emerging Markets (EM) while underweighting Europe and Japan. Although this barbell's outperformance was small in 2017, its long-term consistency since 1988 is notable. Looking forward, the author has a neutral view on the barbell and instead recommends a balanced global portfolio. 

The first visual is a bar chart titled "Europe vs. US: return on equity," which displays the difference in ROE by sector (Europe minus US) as of November 2017. It illustrates that nearly all European sectors lag behind their US counterparts. Only communication services, insurance, and energy show positive relative ROE for Europe. In contrast, sectors such as technology hardware and consumer services show severe relative underperformance, falling roughly 20% to 25% below US levels. 

The second visual, a line chart titled "Europe: large P/E discount vs the US, but nowhere near deep value," tracks the Stoxx 600 forward P/E discount relative to the S&P 500 from 2006 to late 2017. It shows that Europe trades at a substantial discount, hovering around negative 20% recently. However, this is not near the deep value levels of negative 30% to 33% seen during the financial crisis and subsequent Eurozone debt crisis between 2008 and 2012. Footnotes clarify that adjusting for sector weight differences yields a similar discount and that pre-2006 data is excluded due to historical accounting rule differences regarding goodwill amortization.

The third visual is an area chart showing the "Benefits of overweighting US/EM, underweighting Europe/Japan" on a three-year rolling outperformance basis from 1991 to 2017. The chart emphasizes the historical reliability of this barbell strategy, which has spent the vast majority of the last 25 years in positive territory (shaded blue), peaking near 9% in the early 1990s and remaining consistently positive over the last decade, except for brief periods of underperformance (shaded red) in the late 1990s and mid-2000s.

The final visual is a performance table titled "Regional equity market performance" that breaks down MSCI weights and returns. Under the barbell strategy, weights are shifted to 67% US and 17% EM, while EUR is reduced to 12% and JPN to 4%. In 2017, Emerging Markets led with a dollar return of 34% (28% in local currency). While Europe showed a strong 25% dollar return, its local currency return was only 14%, confirming that currency strength drove its performance. The US returned 22% in both dollar and local currency terms. Overall, the barbell strategy achieved a modest year-to-date relative outperformance of 0.3%.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" outlines a broad-based economic recovery across emerging markets. The main thesis is that lending conditions are picking up, foreign direct investment is returning, exports have rebounded to pre-2014 levels, and this acceleration in emerging market growth has coincided with a recovery in US oil and gas investment, suggesting the commodity supercycle downturn has concluded.

To support this observation, the page features four charts. The first chart, which monitors emerging market bank lending conditions via a diffusion index from 2009 to 2017, tracks three series: trade finance, demand for loans, and performing loan health. This index demonstrates that all three metrics bottomed out around 2015 to 2016 and have since steadily improved, with trade finance and loan demand both recovering to near or above the key 50-point mark by late 2017.

The second chart displays capital inflows, combining foreign direct investment and portfolio investment, into emerging markets in billions of US dollars from 2000 through estimated figures for 2018. It shows that capital inflows peaked near 1.4 trillion dollars in 2013, plummeted to approximately 350 billion dollars in 2015, and are projected to recover to roughly one trillion dollars by 2018.

The third chart plots emerging Asian exports from 2011 to 2017 as a year-over-year percentage change on a three-month moving average. It illustrates a clear rebound from a low point of nearly negative ten percent in late 2015 and early 2016 back into positive territory, reaching nearly ten percent growth in 2017.

The final chart shows how the end of the commodity supercycle downturn has benefited both emerging markets and the US energy sector. It compares emerging economy real GDP growth, on the left axis, with US oil and gas real investment, on the right axis, from 2012 to 2017. The chart shows a synchronized cycle where emerging market real GDP growth decelerated from over five percent in 2012 to a trough of four percent in 2016, coinciding with a drop in US oil and gas real investment to nearly negative forty-five percent. By 2017, both series show a sharp V-shaped recovery, with US oil and gas investment surging to around seventy-five percent growth and emerging market GDP growth picking up to about 4.6 percent.

Michael Cembalest discusses Japan's cyclical economic upside, noting that while the country is experiencing a solid expansion driven by the global recovery—evidenced by seven straight quarters of real GDP growth and strong exports—its long-term structural outlook remains constrained. The central issue is that while Japanese corporate profits are booming, household incomes have failed to recover. This creates a one-legged recovery that leaves investors hesitant to overweight Japanese equities.

The page features four charts that support this analysis. The first chart, which tracks Japanese business conditions using the Tankan survey diffusion index from 1990 to 2017, shows business sentiment recovering from its financial crisis low of nearly negative fifty percent to its highest level since the early 1990s, reaching nearly twenty percent in late 2017. The second chart, comparing Japanese equities and the Yen from 2010 to 2017, tracks the USD/Yen exchange rate against the MSCI Japan equities index. It illustrates a historical correlation between a weaker Yen and rising stock prices, which recently decoupled as Japanese equities rose toward an index level of over one thousand despite the exchange rate consolidating around one hundred and ten Yen.

The third and fourth charts contrast the corporate and household sectors in Japan and the United States from 2007 to 2017. The third chart shows that both nations enjoyed a massive corporate profits rebound, with S&P 500 trailing twelve-month earnings per share rising from around sixty dollars to over one hundred and twenty dollars, and MSCI Japan earnings recovering from near zero to roughly sixty Yen. However, the fourth chart reveals a stark divergence in real household earnings. While the United States index rose steadily from 2012 to over one hundred, Japan’s real household earnings index fell almost continuously from a peak of one hundred and twenty-two in 2007 to roughly ninety-two by late 2017.

The author raises the question of whether this wage stagnation might finally change given Japan's extremely tight labor market, where job vacancies relative to applicants are at their highest level since 1974. Until this Achilles heel of the recovery is resolved, J.P. Morgan Global Economic Research notes that foreign institutional and retail investors remain neutral on Japanese equities, positioned midway between the pre-Abenomics lows of 2012 and the post-Abenomics peak of 2015.

This page analyzes China's debt situation and its ongoing structural transition toward a consumption-driven economy. The author argues that unlike Western countries, China is not a free-market economy, and its government controls critical financial levers that can prevent a typical banking crisis. Specifically, China’s debt is mostly internally held, with external debt representing only about 15 percent of GDP. Additionally, 55 to 60 percent of corporate debt belongs to state-owned enterprises with government backing, and the majority of bad debt is held by state-owned banks, supported by stable retail deposits that make up 80 percent of liabilities.

Four charts support this analysis. The first chart, titled "Total China economy-wide debt" as a percentage of GDP from 2007 to the third quarter of 2017, illustrates the rapid expansion of Chinese debt. Corporate debt increased from 89 percent of GDP in 2007 to 166 percent in the third quarter of 2017. Over the same period, household debt grew from 18 percent to 48 percent, and government debt rose from 42 percent to 56 percent, pushing total economy-wide debt to roughly 270 percent of GDP.

The second chart, "Pre-crisis household and corporate debt," compares China's combined household and corporate debt to other countries before their respective financial crises, such as Japan, Sweden, Thailand, Spain, Ireland, and the United States. China's trajectory shows a steep rise to over 210 percent of GDP by 2016, which visually resembles the pre-crisis debt surges of Spain and Japan. However, the accompanying text stresses that China's state-controlled system reduces the risk of a disorderly balance of payments crisis.

The third chart, "Slowly switching from investment to consumption," plots gross fixed capital formation against private consumption as a percentage of GDP to show China's macroeconomic rebalancing. Between 2011 and 2016, China's position shifted: gross fixed capital formation fell from nearly 47 percent to around 43 percent, while private consumption climbed from roughly 35 percent to 39 percent. This movement brings China slightly closer to the main cluster of industrial and emerging economies, which typically average 50 to 70 percent private consumption and 15 to 25 percent capital formation.

The fourth chart, "China A-share reported profits" in trillions of RMB from 2008 to 2016, highlights the positive long-term trend of rising profits in new economy sectors like consumer staples, discretionary spending, healthcare, and technology. Total profits climbed from roughly 0.55 trillion RMB in 2008 to over 1.10 trillion RMB in 2016. While old economy profits still represent the largest share, the new economy segment has steadily expanded its share of total profits, while the energy sector's profit contribution, which includes companies like Sinopec and PetroChina, has contracted. This shifts the corporate profit landscape toward higher-efficiency sectors as wage growth in China reduces its reliance on cheap labor.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market examines the varying debt burdens of US cities, counties, and states by evaluating the percentage of municipal revenue required to fully meet future projected obligations. The analysis introduces the IPOD ratio, which calculates the percentage of a municipality's revenues required to pay the sum of interest on net direct debt, its share of unfunded pension and retiree healthcare liabilities, and defined contribution plan payments, assuming a 6% asset return rate and a 30-year level dollar amortization. 

The accompanying chart plots these ratios, color-coding the issuers into three distinct curves: cities in pink, counties in green, and states in brown, ranking them from the highest debt burdens to the lowest based on fiscal year 2015 data. Among cities, Chicago exhibits the heaviest burden, with its IPOD ratio exceeding 60%, followed by other heavily burdened cities including Lubbock, Atlanta, Pittsburgh, Baton Rouge, Austin, Honolulu, and Oakland. For states, Illinois stands out with the highest burden at approximately 45%, followed by New Jersey, Connecticut, Kentucky, Hawaii, and Maine. Within the county category, Prince George's County in Maryland and Shelby County in Tennessee exhibit the highest burdens, both hovering around the 40% mark, followed by King County in Washington and Santa Clara County in California.

Overall, the data demonstrates a highly heterogeneous credit landscape where cities generally carry the most severe burdens relative to their revenues, while states tend to have lower overall IPOD ratios, with a few notable exceptions. The author notes that these high debt burdens are particularly concerning in the wake of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which could drive high-income residents to migrate away from high-tax states and municipalities, thereby eroding their revenue bases. To mitigate this asymmetric risk in fixed-income portfolios, J.P. Morgan actively monitors these liabilities, limiting its municipal bond portfolio exposure to the general obligation bonds of these highest-risk designated cities and counties to roughly 1% of total assets.

This page discusses the changing environment for stock-pickers and hedge funds in 2017, noting that while falling stock correlations have helped performance, the compression of valuations remains a major challenge. The author attributes this valuation compression to massive central bank stimulus distorting equity, corporate, municipal, and real estate markets. He suggests that the lingering impact of this central bank intervention may persist until 2020 or later. Specific sectors mentioned as helpful to hedge fund performance due to growth-oriented preferences include technology and healthcare.

To support these observations, the page features two charts. The first chart, titled S&P 500 and its average stock correlations, plots average pair correlations using 100 daily rate of change data from 1997 through 2017. The visual shows that after peaking near 0.7 around 2011, average correlations plummeted significantly by 2017 to below 0.2, indicating that individual stocks are no longer moving entirely in tandem. 

The second chart, titled Valuation dispersions across stocks: lowest on record, measures the difference between the 90th percentile and 10th percentile of cheapness across five factors: earnings yield, free cash flow yield, dividend yield, book to price, and sales yield. The data is indexed to 100 starting in January 1978 and runs through 2017. The chart reveals that valuation dispersion across all five metrics has compressed to near-historic lows, hovering between 40 and 60 on the index. This represents a substantial decline from historical highs that exceeded 180 during the early 2000s and late 2000s. An accompanying footnote highlights that the gap between cheap and expensive stocks has narrowed by 50% to 75% since the 1980s, making it one of the narrowest valuation gaps on record and severely limiting the potential returns for managers trying to isolate cheap versus expensive stocks.

This page analyzes how Brazil is demonstrating a classic economic recovery cycle, proving that improving macroeconomic fundamentals can override severe domestic political turmoil. Despite persistent negative press and unending political corruption scandals, the author argues that Brazil is undergoing a typical balance of payments adjustment. This process begins with currency depreciation that narrows the current account deficit, followed by slowing growth that cools inflation and allows the central bank to ease policy rates. Eventually, credit, employment, and foreign direct investment recover, supported by privatizations from the federal and state governments and major firms like Vale, Petrobras, and Eletrobras, alongside rising commodity prices. Finally, business and consumer confidence rebound, bolstering equity markets despite the ongoing "Operation Car Wash" investigations.

Six supporting charts illustrate this turnaround. The first chart, tracking Brazil's current account deficit and the USD/BRL exchange rate, shows the current account deficit narrowing from over four percent of GDP in 2015 to roughly one percent of GDP in late 2017, coinciding with the Brazilian Real depreciating from under 2.0 per dollar in 2013 to a peak of 4.0 in late 2015 before stabilizing around 3.2. The second chart shows Brazil's consumer price inflation peaking above ten percent in late 2015 and then plummeting to under three percent by late 2017, which allowed the central bank to aggressively cut its policy rate from over fourteen percent down to around seven percent. The third chart displays business and consumer confidence indexes, which bottomed out in late 2015 near index levels of 70 and 60, respectively, before rebounding back to the mid-80s and 90s by late 2017. 

The remaining three charts focus on employment, commodities, and equities. Brazil's employment growth, measured as a year-over-year percentage change of a three-month moving average, bottomed at nearly negative three percent in 2016 but rebounded sharply back toward zero percent by late 2017. This labor market stabilization was aided by a recovery in global industrial metals prices, which rose from an index low of nearly 60 in early 2016 back to approximately 100 by late 2017. Reflecting these combined improvements, the final chart shows the MSCI Brazil Index plunging from 100 in 2013 to a low of around 35 in early 2016, followed by a strong recovery to roughly 75 by late 2017. Red dots plotted along the equity curve mark major developments in the "Operation Car Wash" scandal, highlighting that the stock market steadily advanced even as the political investigation intensified.

This page analyzes the concentration of US equity market returns in 2017, examining whether the dominance of a few mega-cap stocks was an abnormal market event compared to historical data from 1991 through 2016. In 2017, the top five stocks contributed 5.0% of the S&P 500's total return of 21.9%, supported by strong fundamentals including 21% year-over-year sales growth for the FAAMG stocks (Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google) in the third quarter of 2017. While this absolute contribution of 5.0% is higher than the historical average of 3.4% and median of 2.6% from 1991 to 2016, the top five stocks' relative contribution share of approximately 25% of total market returns is considered roughly average for a positive return year. 

To illustrate these trends, the page features two bar charts tracking annual data from 1991 to 2017. The first chart, titled "Impact of removing top 5 S&P 500 stocks each year," shows the total return foregone if the top five performers were excluded. This impact peaked in 1999 at over 8% and stood at 5.0% in 2017. The second chart, "Share of market returns from top 5 stocks," measures this concentration as a percentage capped at 50%. It shows that the top five stocks regularly represent a massive portion of market returns, reaching the 50% cap in multiple years like 1999, 2007, 2010, and 2015, while 2017 remained more moderate at around 25%.

A concluding table lists the "Top S&P 500 Contributors in 2017" and documents how often these companies have appeared in the top five list between 1991 and 2017. Apple ranked first in 2017 with a 1.62% contribution and has appeared in the top five nine times since 2005. Microsoft ranked second with a 1.04% contribution and has appeared thirteen times overall, marking its fifth straight year in the top five. Amazon ranked third with a 1.02% contribution, followed by Facebook at 0.76% and Alphabet at 0.50%, all of which have made previous top five appearances. The author notes that this repetition is typical of market history, as more companies have repeated as top five contributors than have appeared only once over the analyzed period.

This page explores the shrinking number of US public companies, examining what is referred to as the US "listing gap" where public listings are rising globally but declining in the United States. The author argues that this decline is a troublesome trend driven by both increased de-listings and fewer new listings. 

Two charts illustrate these trends. The first, "The growing listing gap between the US and the world," compares domestic US-listed companies (on the left axis in thousands) against non-US listings (on the right axis in thousands) from 1975 to 2015. The chart shows that while non-US listings grew steadily from around 10,000 to over 40,000, domestic US-listed companies peaked in the late 1990s at around 8,000 before steadily falling to near 4,000 by 2015. The second chart, "Additions and subtractions to listed companies" from 1976 to 2016, displays the total number of listed firms as a black line alongside blue vertical bars representing new listings and red vertical bars representing delistings. This visual shows that the decline in total listed firms from their peak in the late 1990s was initiated by a massive wave of delistings in the late 1990s and early 2000s, followed by a persistent lack of new listings to replace them.

Regarding de-listings, the text attributes them to corporate consolidation and mergers and acquisitions. The average US company has a market cap of $7 billion, which is ten times higher in real terms than in 1976. Furthermore, industry concentration as measured by the Herfindahl index rose 45% from 1995 to 2015, even though the annual pace of de-listings has remained fairly steady at 8% to 10% of listed firms since 2002. 

The decline in new listings is attributed to two major factors: increased regulatory costs and the deregulation of private capital. On regulatory costs, a PwC survey indicates that 45% of firms found the costs of being public exceeded expectations, and US companies spend 166% more on legal services per dollar of revenue than global peers. On private capital deregulation, the author details how private markets have become more accessible, allowing companies to remain private. For instance, the 1982 SEC Regulation D Rule 501 defined accredited investors by thresholds of over $200,000 in income or $1 million in net worth, which have not been updated for inflation and would otherwise be $2.5 million today. Additionally, Congress expanded the accredited investor definition in 2016, and the 2012 JOBS Act further eased private capital rules by lifting bans on general solicitations, creating crowdfunding exemptions, raising the shareholder threshold for public reporting from 500 to 2,000, and introducing Regulation A+ for offerings up to $50 million. Footnotes add that technology and social media companies now have lower capital needs, and tight credit spreads encourage companies to finance via debt rather than equity.

This page argues that the US Administration's decision to end the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) program for individuals from El Salvador, Honduras, and Haiti could inadvertently trigger higher wage inflation and a more aggressive Federal Reserve policy. The author contends that deportations will worsen severe construction labor shortages in states still rebuilding from major natural disasters, specifically California, Texas, and Florida. 

This argument is supported by a color-coded map of the United States showing the concentration of TPS holders by state. The map reveals that the highest concentrations—with more than 50,000 holders per state—are in California, Texas, and Florida. Text callouts on the map highlight the massive rebuilding needs in these areas, noting 15,000 homes damaged or destroyed by wildfires in California, 200,000 homes damaged or destroyed by Hurricane Harvey in Texas, and 800,000 insurance claims filed on residential and commercial buildings after Hurricane Irma in Florida. 

Two supporting charts provide macroeconomic context. The first chart, showing the seasonally adjusted US unemployment rate from 1970 through late 2017, displays a sharp downward trend, with unemployment dropping to near-historic lows of around 4.1%. The second chart tracks US wage inflation versus goods inflation from 1997 to 2017, using a three-month average of year-over-year percentage changes. It demonstrates that wage indicators—including median wages, average hourly earnings, and the Employment Cost Index—are rising faster than goods inflation, represented by Core CPI and Core PCE, which remain low near 1.5%. Together, these charts show a highly tight labor market where further labor reductions could exacerbate wage pressures. The author concludes that ending the TPS program risks worsening construction backlogs, driving up wages, and slowing the broader economic recovery.

In this publication, Michael Cembalest discusses the potential for a Democratic victory in the 2018 midterm elections and its anticipated impact on US equity markets. Polling and political futures indicate a high likelihood of Democrats reclaiming control of the House of Representatives, an outcome that could lead to political gridlock, an increased risk of a constitutional crisis, and a reversal of the positive market sentiment that followed the 2016 election. 

This analysis is supported by four main charts and tables. The first chart, titled "Number of House challengers that have raised >$5,000" from 2003 to 2017, illustrates a massive surge in Democratic enthusiasm. In 2017, the number of Democratic challengers raising over $5,000 spiked to 391, compared to just 71 for Republicans, a stark contrast to previous cycles such as 2009 when there were 184 Republican challengers to 71 Democrats. 

The second chart, "A century of wave elections," tracks the number of House seats gained by a party during major wave elections between 1912 and 2010. A horizontal line marks the number of seats Democrats need to regain control of the House, showing that historical wave elections have frequently surpassed this threshold. 

The third chart, "Capex plans and CEO confidence: the post-election spike," plots CEO confidence on a 1-to-10 scale alongside the percentage of respondents planning capital expenditures from 2010 to 2017. Following the November 2016 election, both indicators saw dramatic spikes, with CEO confidence jumping from approximately 4.5 to over 7.0, and capex plans rising from around 15 percent to over 25 percent. 

The final table, "S&P 500 returns during periods of US political unity & gridlock, 1945-2018," presents historical annualized stock market returns under different Washington leadership scenarios over 74 years, where the overall average return was 11.4 percent. The data reveals that the lowest equity market returns historically occurred under a Republican president with a split Congress (6.2 percent average return over 8 years) or a unified Democratic Congress (6.9 percent average return over 22 years). In contrast, a unified government under a Republican president averaged a 16.0 percent return, suggesting that a Democratic takeover of Congress could pose headwinds for the S&P 500. Additionally, a personal footnote from the author notes a family arrangement to donate some company stock gains attributable to the 2016 presidential election to various global and local non-profit organizations.

This page examines the consequences of private capital deregulation in the United States, pointing to a sharp rise in venture capital investment and a growing delay before technology companies choose to go public. The author notes that venture capital investors funded 2,888 private US companies in 2006, which grew to 4,244 companies in 2015, leaving approximately one trillion dollars in unspent private equity and venture capital funds as of late 2017. This shift creates two distinct issues for US capital markets. First, it hurts the average investor's access to early wealth creation because they must rely on defined contribution retirement plans that lack access to pre-IPO returns. Second, it reduces overall market knowledge while allowing private firms to free-ride on the detailed disclosures of the remaining public companies, a dynamic that Duke Law Professor Elisabeth de Fontenay describes as unsustainable. Expert networks like GLG, which can cost up to one thousand dollars per hour, underscore the high value of this information.

Three charts support these arguments. The first chart, Global venture capital investment by quarter, shows stacked bar data from the first quarter of 2010 through the first quarter of 2017 in billions of US dollars. The data, sourced from KPMG and PitchBook, illustrates a massive growth trend where total quarterly global investment grew from around ten billion dollars in 2010 to peak at over forty billion dollars in late 2015 and early 2016, with the United States consistently comprising a major portion of the total. The second chart, Waiting longer to go public, tracks the median age of technology companies at IPO from 1980 to 2016, using data from Jay Ritter at the University of Florida. It reveals that the median age dipped to a low of four years during the dot-com era around 2000, peaked near fourteen years in 2008, and remained high at around ten to eleven years by 2016. The final chart, Number of participants in pension plans, tracks millions of participants from 1975 to 2011 using Department of Labor data. It shows a clear divergence where defined benefit plans stagnated and declined to around forty million participants, while defined contribution plans steadily climbed from under twenty million to over ninety million participants.

This page addresses whether blockchain is poised to take over the financial world, with the author, Michael Cembalest, concluding "not any time soon" specifically regarding consumer payments. 

To illustrate the current landscape, the page features a table detailing key participants and their roles, which include Retailers selling goods, Merchant Acquirers like Vantiv communicating point-of-sale data, Card Networks like Mastercard and Visa processing bilateral transactions and establishing rules, and Issuing Banks providing consumer credit. A second table displays US consumer payments data from 2016 sourced from the Nilson Report. This data shows that card payments dominate the market: credit cards accounted for $3,153 billion (32% of the total) and debit cards represented $2,561 billion (26%). Cash made up $1,572 billion (16%), followed by checks at $830 billion (8%), preauthorized electronic payments at $790 billion (8%), remote payments at $638 billion (6%), other cards at $322 billion (3%), and other paper at $69 billion (1%).

The author argues that a blockchain solution aiming to eliminate Card Networks would face significant hurdles. Visa and Mastercard only receive about 0.15% out of a total retailer discount of 2.0% to 3.0%, meaning their removal would not drastically alter payment economics. Additionally, displacing established card networks would force Merchant Acquirers and Issuing Banks to assume the complex and costly responsibilities of system governance. Performance is another issue, as Visa can process over 50,000 transactions per second compared to only hundreds of transactions per second on private blockchain networks. 

Lastly, the author explores a more radical hypothetical scenario where a blockchain directly connects retailers and consumers. However, this system would require extending an estimated $3 trillion in annual credit and float, preventing fraud, and providing consumer protections. The author notes that only mega-retailers like Walmart or Amazon would have the scale to try this, though it would rival the complexity of their core businesses. A footnote referencing the American Bankers Association points out that 30% to 35% of credit card users utilize monthly float, while 40% to 45% carry a balance.

This page begins with an analysis of potential practical applications for blockchain technology, discussing wholesale global payments, cost-cutting in settlement and clearing as announced by the Australian Securities Exchange, peer-to-peer business lending, and record-keeping ledger functions. However, the author expresses skepticism about the level of industry disruption, characterizing blockchain startups as temporary service providers with programming skills that will likely become commoditized, which calls their high valuations into question. 

The page then shifts to a lighter advice-style column focusing on how online dating profiles can be optimized. Citing statistics, it notes that by 2010, online dating had surpassed most other ways of meeting a partner, and by 2013, 35 percent of married couples met online. To illustrate this trend, a line graph tracks the percentage of couples meeting from 1940 to 2010 across different categories like friends, family, college, work, and church. It depicts a dramatic surge for the online category starting in the mid-1990s and rising to approximately 22 percent by 2010, while traditional avenues like meeting through friends steadily declined from a peak near 40 percent. 

Accompanying this is a table showing the percent change in inbound messages based on specific food mentions in dating profiles. Guacamole leads with a 144 percent increase in response rate, followed by chocolate at 100 percent, sushi at 93 percent, hamburger at 68 percent, and ice cream at 62 percent. Conversely, mentioning yams results in a severe decline of negative 70 percent. The page concludes with a brief reference list of other publications from the same year, including outlooks on Western centralization and the impact of the Trump administration.

This page addresses the Trump administration's ongoing trade disputes, emphasizing that recent and pending tariffs are concentrated in sectors that represent only a fraction of trade volume. The author notes that early tariff decisions on washing machines, solar panels, steel, and aluminum account for just 0.25 percent of Chinese exports and 0.25 percent of US imports, meaning investors should not overreact to these measures.

A scatter plot titled A general lack of tariff reciprocity illustrates this dynamic by plotting tariffs applied by the US on the vertical axis against tariffs applied to the US on the horizontal axis. A diagonal reciprocity line reveals that almost all nations lie below the diagonal, meaning they charge higher tariffs on US goods than the US charges on theirs. For example, China is positioned at roughly a 4 percent US tariff rate versus a 10 percent rate applied to the US, while Bangladesh is positioned at the far right with a US tariff of around 7 percent against a tariff applied to the US of nearly 14 percent.

The actual drivers of the US trade deficit with China are explored in a second bar chart, which lists the largest contributors to the US-China net goods deficit over a trailing twelve-month period. The sum of the top ten contributors is 384 billion dollars. The single largest contributor is the category for phones, TVs, and radios, which accounts for nearly 90 billion dollars of the deficit. This is followed by toys, jewelry, and building fixtures at around 58 billion dollars, and computers at approximately 50 billion dollars. 

Beyond tariffs, the text discusses the potential implementation of a reciprocal investment regime under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act. This policy would restrict Chinese foreign direct investment in the United States to the same degree that China restricts US investment. This issue is visualized in a final bar chart measuring regulatory restrictions on inbound foreign direct investment on a 0-to-1 scale. China is listed as having the third-worst score globally at approximately 0.33, trailing only the Philippines at 0.38 and Saudi Arabia at 0.34. In contrast, the United States and other developed nations like Italy, Japan, France, the UK, Germany, and Spain maintain highly open FDI policies, with index scores below 0.10. 

Ultimately, the author concludes that the administration faces the delicate challenge of trying to alter historically one-sided trade deals without triggering destructive retaliatory protectionism or boosting domestic inflation.

This page addresses concerns about the stability of the financial system in the event of faster rate hikes by the Federal Reserve. The author argues that the financial system is far better protected today than it was in 2008, citing significant increases in bank and insurance capitalization alongside marked declines in wholesale funding risks, securities lending, asset-backed securities issuance, and money market fund risks.

To support this claim, the author presents seven charts comparing pre-crisis levels to recent years. First, the Bank Risk-Weighted Capital Ratio shows substantial increases from 2007 to 2017 in both the US, rising from around 9% to over 13%, and Europe, rising from about 8% to nearly 16%. Similarly, Bank Liquid Assets as a Percentage of Short-Term Liabilities saw gains over the same decade, climbing from roughly 41% to 48% in the US and from 35% to 41% in Europe. For the insurance sector, life insurance risk-based capital ratios increased from around 400% in 2004 to nearly 490% by 2014, while property and casualty operating leverage declined from over 1.0x to below 0.8x, indicating lower overall leverage.

The page also demonstrates systemic risk reduction through improving liquidity and debt metrics. Bank Loan-to-Deposit Ratios show a significant downward trend since 2008, with Eurozone banks falling from a peak of nearly 140% down to roughly 110% in 2017, and US banks dropping from 100% to around 75%. Outstanding debt supported by securities lending as a percentage of GDP peaked near 15% before the financial crisis and has since collapsed to approximately 4%. The chart on US Asset-Backed Securities shows that total outstanding volume peaked near $6 trillion in 2007–2008, heavily driven by non-agency residential mortgage-backed securities and collateralized debt obligations, but has since fallen to under $3 trillion. Finally, the shift in money market funds highlights a major transition toward safety; following regulatory reforms in 2016, assets under management in higher-risk Prime money market funds plummeted to about $0.5 trillion, while lower-risk Government money market funds surged to over $2.0 trillion. Together, these indicators suggest that despite hidden risks, the visible parts of the financial system are significantly more resilient.

This page presents a detailed summary of the common arguments made by advocates of net neutrality, organized into four primary thematic sections. First, advocates argue that net neutrality is essential to prevent content discrimination and monopolistic practices by internet service providers (ISPs). This concern is highlighted by consolidation, such as Comcast's acquisition of NBC Universal and AT&T's proposed acquisition of Time Warner. Proponents point to historical examples of anti-competitive behavior, such as Madison River blocking Vonage in 2005 to protect its landline business, and note that past Republican FCC chairs have supported open-internet conditions, such as those attached to the 4G spectrum auction in 2008.

Second, the text outlines the FCC's important role in encouraging the growth of the communications network. Beginning with the 1996 Telecom Act, the FCC's regulatory goal has been to spur investment and innovation rather than allow pure rent-seeking. Repealing net neutrality risks harming entrepreneurs who develop applications for mobile streaming, gaming, and smart devices. Net neutrality advocates argue that the FCC never fully utilized its regulatory powers under Title II and that the post-2015 ISP capital spending trends remain inconclusive.

Third, the page discusses how utility-like regulations are needed because the internet functions as a public good. Because ISPs face minimal pressure from "customer outrage" due to their low overall public image—evidenced by a 2017 survey where cable operators and ISPs tied for last place with a 64% satisfaction rating—regulations are needed to ensure universal access. Major platforms like YouTube are now viewed as public goods, and without protections, content creators may face higher pass-through costs. A footnote adds that over 20 states restrict or prohibit local governments from building their own broadband networks, complicating public-utility alternatives.

Finally, advocates highlight that most consumers have limited choices, being forced to deal with a single, expensive ISP. This is supported by data from a June 2015 FCC report showing that 78% of developed census blocks had one or fewer fixed broadband providers offering speeds of at least 25 Mbps, and a 2014 Department of Commerce report showing 67% of the US population had only one option at that speed. The text notes that US broadband penetration rates are among the lowest in the OECD due to high prices, and cable and satellite TV inflation over the last 20 years (3.4%) has consistently outpaced core inflation (2.0%). Additionally, mobile 5G is deemed unlikely to serve as a viable home broadband replacement due to complex infrastructure costs. An explanatory footnote clarifies that while paid prioritization between ISPs and content creators is highly contested, similar speed-optimization practices by Content Delivery Networks and Transit Providers already occur regularly in the broader internet ecosystem.

This page analyzes the macroeconomic pressures mounting on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, arguing that the central bank is currently behind the curve in the face of tightening labor markets and rising budget deficits. Michael Cembalest forecasts that the Fed will implement six rate hikes over the next 18 months, leading to a peak Fed Funds rate of approximately 3.5% in 2019. Consequently, he expects 2018 equity returns to land in the 8% to 10% range as declining price-to-earnings multiples partially offset positive corporate earnings and economic growth.

The argument is supported by four main visuals. The first chart, a bar graph on the top left, displays the lowest five-year average real yields on cash since 1830, calculated as the T-bill or Funds rate minus inflation. It shows that negative real cash yields have historically occurred almost exclusively during major conflicts, specifically the Civil War, World War I, and World War II, as well as the aftermath of the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. Notably, the five-year period ending in 2017 marks a rare peacetime era of negative real yields. To the right, a line chart tracking the period from 1995 through late 2017 compares the negative real Fed Funds rate against a falling unemployment rate, which has dropped toward 4%, and stable, economy-wide inflation. This visual emphasizes that while economic conditions have returned to normal, the real Fed Funds rate has remained stubbornly below zero.

The bottom portion of the page examines market reactions and historical precedents. A line chart on the bottom left plots US bond yields and cash rates from 2014 to early 2018, showing the US current cash rate rising from near 0% in late 2015 to roughly 1.5% by 2018, while the US 10-year bond yield rose from a low of around 1.5% in mid-2016 to nearly 3.0% by early 2018. Beside this, a detailed table lists fifteen historical periods of rising rates between December 1991 and March 2018. Across these periods, the US 10-year bond yield increased on average by 149 basis points, moving from a trough yield of 3.8% to a peak yield of 5.3%. During these rate-hiking cycles, the S&P 500 experienced an average 12-month forward P/E change of 4% and an average 12-month forward EPS growth of 8%, demonstrating that corporate earnings typically rise alongside interest rates as the economy improves.

This page outlines the primary arguments made by opponents of Net Neutrality, presenting a counter-narrative to the regulations established in 2015. 

The first core argument suggests that the 2015 FCC Net Neutrality rule was an unnecessary regulation in search of a problem, pointing out that paid prioritization, content blocking, or throttling were rare before its implementation due to market discipline and mutual economic incentives between content creators and internet service providers. Furthermore, the text argues that consumers enjoy ample choices, noting that over half of the US population had access to more than one fixed broadband provider at speeds over 25 megabits per second as of late 2016. 

An accompanying horizontal bar chart illustrates the peak download rates per second of mobile generations on a log scale from 1G to 5G, ranging from under a bit to over 10 gigabits. The chart demonstrates the massive speed leap of 5G, pointing out that 5G is 20 times faster than 4G and will act as an increasingly viable substitute for wired broadband access. 

Opponents also assert that utility-like regulations stifle innovation and business investment by creating policy uncertainty, citing the FCC's scrutiny of "Zero Rating" streaming plans as an example of overreach. The page characterizes Net Neutrality as a form of regulatory capture that unfairly transfers wealth from ISPs and consumers to dominant tech giants like Netflix and YouTube, which account for approximately half of all downstream peak traffic. It argues that allowing ISPs to charge third-party Content Delivery Networks for interconnect access helps distribute bandwidth costs rather than passing them on to end consumers. 

Rather than relying on FCC Title II classification, opponents recommend that anti-competitive behavior, such as throttling or blocking, should be policed by the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice, as was the norm before 2015. Finally, the page highlights that US internet costs and quality compare very favorably to other developed nations, citing OECD data from early 2018 showing the US has the second-lowest cost per gigabyte among member countries, alongside Bureau of Labor Statistics data showing negative inflation for quality-adjusted broadband services since 1997.

This analysis focuses on the underlying structural drivers of US trade deficits, arguing that while they are partly due to historically one-sided trade agreements, they are primarily driven by domestic structural issues. These include expanding US budget deficits that stimulate imports, persistent oil imports of roughly six million barrels per day, stimulative tax cuts, and an overvalued dollar. The author contends that using tariffs to force trade concessions is an ineffective strategy because unilateral trade policy does not address the worsening budget deficit that structurally expands the trade deficit.

To support this argument, the page features four charts. The first chart displays the large US non-oil goods deficit as a percentage of GDP from 1990 to 2016. This deficit worsened from near 0.0% of GDP in 1990 to an extreme of around negative 4.5% in the mid-2000s, before recovering to negative 2.0% in 2010 and settling around negative 3.0% by 2016.

The second chart traces the historical relationship between the federal budget balance and the current account balance as percentages of GDP from 1960 through projections to 2019. This chart shows that both metrics often move in tandem. The budget balance reached a low of nearly negative 10% around 2010, recovered, and is projected to decline again toward negative 5% by 2019, while the current account deficit is projected to remain relatively flat near negative 3% of GDP.

The third chart tracks the trade-weighted dollar index from 1988 through 2016, with March 1973 set to 100. It highlights a highly volatile dollar, peaking near 105 in 2002, bottoming out below 75 during the global financial crisis, and rebounding back up toward 90 to 95 by 2016, illustrating the author's point that the dollar remains somewhat overvalued.

The fourth chart visualizes a general lack of tariff reciprocity by plotting simple average tariffs applied by the US against tariffs applied to the US for dozens of trading partners. A diagonal reciprocity line represents equal tariffs. Nearly all countries fall below this line, meaning they impose higher tariffs on US goods than the US imposes on theirs. For instance, China faces a US tariff of around 2.5% but applies a tariff of nearly 10% to US goods. Extreme examples of non-reciprocity include Brazil, India, Bangladesh, and Egypt, which apply tariffs between 10% and 14% on US goods while facing US tariffs of 6% or less. This chart highlights the one-sided nature of historical trade deals, even as the author maintains that tariffs are the wrong tool to fix the broader deficit.

Finally, the page notes a previous publication from February 21, 2018, which covered inflation, US equities, hedge funds, and blockchain.

This page, titled "The industrial sector and the slow pace of decarbonization," argues that the industrial sector is exceptionally difficult to decarbonize because electricity currently accounts for only 15% of OECD industrial energy use. The remaining 85% of industrial energy is consumed directly through fossil fuels, which are critical both as raw materials and as sources of sustained, high-temperature process heat. The author notes that while electricity could theoretically provide some process heat, very little progress has been made toward this transition. 

To support this argument, the page features a pie chart detailing OECD industrial sector energy consumption by source based on 2016 data from the Energy Information Administration. It shows that liquid fuels represent the largest share at 37%, followed by natural gas at 29%, electricity at 15%, coal at 11%, and renewables at a mere 8%. 

A companion horizontal bar chart shows OECD industrial sector energy consumption by specific product category as a percentage of the total. Chemicals are by far the largest consumer at approximately 18%, followed by iron and steel at around 12%, oil refining at roughly 10%, and paper at about 8%. Nonmetallic minerals and food each make up around 5%, while nonferrous metals account for approximately 3%. 

The bottom of the page is split into two tables detailing the physical necessity of these fossil fuels. The first table focuses on fossil fuels used as raw materials, illustrating that metallurgical coke is used as a carbon source for smelting pig iron into steel, methane serves as a hydrogen source to synthesize agricultural fertilizer ammonia, methane, naphtha, and ethane are used to synthesize plastics, and heavy petroleum products are processed into carbon black for rubber tires. The second table covers fossil fuels used to generate process heat, highlighting their necessity in manufacturing construction materials like cement, bricks, tiles, glass, and kiln-dried timber, as well as in producing petrochemicals, plastics, food, beverages, and smelting iron ores in blast furnaces.

This page addresses the physical limits of attempting to decarbonize global energy systems through electricity alone, pointing out that fossil fuels serve critical direct roles beyond power generation, such as fueling combustion engines, industrial smelting, heating, and serving as chemical feedstocks. 

The author presents four distinct charts to support this thesis. The first chart, "Global energy consumed by end-user," visualizes global energy consumption in quadrillion BTUs across primary energy inputs for electricity and three major end-use sectors: industrial, transport, and residential/commercial. It illustrates that electricity ultimately represents only 17% of total final energy consumed, with the remainder consisting of direct fuel use. The visual shows the industrial sector as the largest energy user, reliant on direct coal, natural gas, and petroleum, while the transport sector is almost entirely dependent on petroleum. 

To the right, a pie chart titled "Electricity accounts for less than one third of global fossil fuel consumption" reinforces this distribution. Out of total global fossil fuel use, 341 quadrillion BTUs are consumed directly for non-electrical purposes, whereas only 141 quadrillion BTUs are used indirectly to generate electricity. 

At the bottom left, a line graph titled "The world uses fossil fuels for ~85% of its energy" tracks the share of global primary energy derived from coal, oil, and natural gas from 1965 through 2016. The chart illustrates a gradual decline from about 94% in 1965 to roughly 85% in 2016. It highlights two distinct transition periods: the nuclear adoption era of the 1970s and 1980s, which drove a steady downward shift, and the solar/wind era beginning around 2010. 

The final chart, "Living for the city: global urbanization trends," projects the percentage of the population living in urban areas from 1950 to 2050 across various countries and regions, including Japan, the United States, Europe, South America, China, Africa, and India. It shows steep upward urbanization trajectories for all regions. China, for instance, is projected to rise from under 20% urbanized in 1950 to nearly 80% by 2050. The author uses these trends to argue that because global populations are increasingly concentrating in massive urban centers, decentralized or "off-the-grid" energy solutions are increasingly impractical, meaning decarbonization solutions must be engineered to support dense, centralized urban infrastructure.

This page analyzes whether the Republican Party is facing an historically unusual midterm election rejection in the fall of 2018, set against a backdrop of rising stock markets and falling unemployment. The author notes that while the President's party almost always loses House seats in midterm elections—occurring in all but three midterms since 1910—a major defeat during strong economic times would be an extreme anomaly. 

The central visual is a bubble scatter plot mapping midterm elections since 1910, excluding the years 1934, 1998, and 2002 when the President's party actually gained seats. The vertical y-axis measures the trailing two-year change in the unemployment rate, inverted so that falling unemployment is at the top (ranging to negative eight percent) and rising unemployment is at the bottom (up to eight percent). The horizontal x-axis tracks the trailing two-year real equity market return, ranging from negative fifty percent to fifty percent. Each bubble's size indicates the number of House seats lost, and its color denotes the President's party, with blue representing Democrats and red representing Republicans. 

The chart reveals that large losses typically cluster in quadrants representing economic distress, such as rising unemployment and falling stock markets (such as 1930 with 52 seats lost, 1938 with 72, and 1914 with 60) or rising unemployment despite rising markets (such as 1922 with 77 seats lost or 2010 with 63). Conversely, the top-right quadrant, which represents falling unemployment and a rising stock market, historically features very minor losses, such as 1926 with 9 seats, 1986 with 5 seats, and 2014 with 13 seats. 

The chart inserts a projected red bubble for the 2018 midterms in this strong economic top-right quadrant, reflecting an estimated loss of 25 to 40 GOP seats based on a forecast by Seth Masket at the University of Denver. If realized, this loss would represent an historic outlier. The author outlines opposing forces shaping the election. Arguments against a Democratic wave include the lowest unemployment rate in decades and numerous non-competitive, gerrymandered districts. In contrast, arguments favoring a wave include strong Democratic special election performances in Republican-leaning districts, historically low presidential approval ratings, strong Democratic fundraising, and quirky cultural signals like John Oliver's parody book outselling Vice President Mike Pence's book about his rabbit, Marlon Bundo. Ultimately, the author suggests the 2018 midterm may serve more as a referendum on presidential unorthodoxy than on economic or market data.

This page addresses the global transition to electric vehicles (EVs) and examines whether they represent a minor adjustment or a major solution to climate goals. The author points out that although renewable power has grown tenfold since 2004, fossil fuels still supply 85% of primary energy globally. Because road transportation accounts for half of global oil consumption, decarbonization depends heavily on the speed of EV adoption. However, the author posits that this transition is likely to be gradual, despite aggressive projections by futurists. 

To illustrate the scale of energy demand, a stacked bar chart titled "World transportation energy consumption by mode" shows that passenger transport, dominated by light-duty vehicles, uses more than 55 quadrillion Btu of energy, while freight transport, led by heavy trucks, accounts for over 35 quadrillion Btu. This is paired with a table on "Global consumption of oil products" showing that road transportation is by far the largest consumer, representing 50% of the total (1,823 million tons of oil equivalents), followed by feedstocks at 16%, other transportation (air and marine) at 15%, heating and industry both at 8%, and agriculture at 3%.

The bottom half of the page compares public policy and manufacturer targets. The "Government policy goals" table lists country-level EV adoption targets alongside their 2017 light vehicle sales in millions. Notable entries include China, the largest market with 28.3 million sales, which has a pending internal combustion engine (ICE) ban and a cap-and-trade policy targeting 5% EV sales by 2020. In contrast, the United States, representing 17.2 million in sales, has no stated national goal. Other countries have set firm dates to end ICE sales, including Norway and the Netherlands by 2025, Germany and India by 2030, and the United Kingdom and France by 2040. 

Complementing these public policies, the "Company policy goals" table tracks the EV ambitions of global automakers against their 2016 production volumes. Large-volume manufacturers have set substantial targets: Chinese original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) aim for 4.5 million annual EV sales by 2020, Toyota targets 5.5 million EV sales by 2030, and Volkswagen plans for 2 to 3 million annual EV sales by 2025. Meanwhile, specialist manufacturers outline even more rapid shifts, such as Volvo targeting 100% EV sales by approximately 2024, and Tesla aiming to scale up to 1 million EV sales by 2020 from its 2016 production base of 0.1 million vehicles.

This page discusses why the electric vehicle (EV) revolution might progress at a slower pace than many expect, focusing on two key bottlenecks: massive infrastructure costs and the technical limits of reducing battery prices. 

To address the infrastructure challenge, the first chart illustrates the total cumulative investment required through 2030 to meet national EV policy targets. According to data from Bridgewater Associates, the combined investment needed for India, China, and Europe could reach $1.7 trillion. Specifically, assuming 2030 EV sales targets of 100% in India, 25% in China, 50% in Europe, and 12% in the United States, cumulative capital needs are approximately $600 billion for India, $500 billion for China, $450 billion for Europe, and $150 billion for the US. The chart shows that the overwhelming majority of these funds must be spent on power generation and distribution, rather than just charging stations or production facilities. The author notes that these massive expenditures present a difficult fiscal trade-off for aging societies already grappling with rising, unfunded pension and healthcare liabilities.

The second primary challenge is the cost trajectory of lithium-ion batteries. A line chart detailing the capital cost of EV battery packs per kilowatt-hour (kWh) from 2006 to 2020 shows a dramatic decline from roughly $1,300 per kWh to around $200 per kWh, referencing specific cost milestones achieved by Tesla and General Motors (GM). However, achieving the US Department of Energy (DoE) target of $100 per kWh on a cell basis (approximately $130 per pack) is a major hurdle. Reaching this price point is widely considered the threshold for mass-market EVs to achieve cost parity with internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles. The author cites a January 2018 paper by ARPA researchers in Nature Energy warning that current battery designs may struggle to hit this goal without failing to meet other necessary performance standards.

Finally, a table sourced from the US Department of Energy outlines a vehicle energy storage technology overview, comparing three classes of battery tech. Current lithium-ion technology (graphite/NMC) has a current cost of $235 per kWh, a potential future cost of $100 to $160 per kWh, and a cycle life of 1,000 to 5,000 cycles, requiring R&D in high-voltage cathodes, electrolytes, and extreme fast charging. Next-generation lithium-ion batteries based on silicon composite/high-voltage NMC have a current cost of $256 per kWh, a potential cost of $90 to $125 per kWh, and a cycle life of 500 to 700, requiring additional R&D for a durable silicon anode. Long-term lithium metal batteries are the most expensive currently at $320 per kWh, with a potential cost of $70 to $120 per kWh, but suffer from a very low cycle life of only 50 to 100, demanding significant research into lithium protection and highly conductive solid electrolytes.

This page focuses on the speed of electric vehicle (EV) adoption, arguing that current long-term market forecasts are likely overly optimistic. The author points out that although current projections for the global EV fleet size in 2030 vary wildly—ranging from 2% to 20% of a projected 1.4 billion vehicle global fleet—the median forecast is around 125 million EVs. The author favors the "under" on this median projection, noting that forecasters historically let optimism cloud real-world hurdles such as high upfront and maintenance costs, intricate supply chains, infrastructure/refueling requirements, and safety standards. 

To support this skepticism, the first chart, titled "Electric vehicle projections for the year 2030: from 2% to 20% of the global fleet," plots global fleet size in millions of EVs on the left axis and the corresponding 2030 EV penetration as a percentage of the global fleet on the right axis. The projections span from 2016 to 2030. The highest projection, reaching nearly 250 million EVs or roughly an 18% penetration rate, comes from the IMF's "horse-to-car method." The author strongly criticizes this IMF forecast, pointing out that switching from internal combustion engines to EVs does not offer the same dramatic leap in utility that switching from horses to cars did, and that horses in urban transit were historically replaced by electric streetcars and subways before personal vehicles emerged. Below the IMF forecast, the International Energy Agency's high-end projection lands around 14% penetration, and its low-end projection sits near 12%. Bloomberg New Energy Finance projects about 9%, the UN Paris Agreement sits at 8%, and Morgan Stanley, Wood Mackenzie, BP, and Smil regressions cluster around 6% to 7%. The lowest projections come from Goldman Sachs, IHS Automotive, and Exxon, which expect penetration rates between 2% and 4%. 

The second chart, titled "Prior generation of electric car projections out of sync with reality," highlights how past industry forecasters failed to predict real-world outcomes. This chart plots EV and plug-in hybrid EV sales as a percentage of total car sales from 2009 to 2020. A series of dotted projection lines starting around 2009 showcase highly optimistic forecasts for 2020: Deutsche Bank projected sales penetration would reach 11% by 2020, PwC, Frost & Sullivan, and Bloomberg NEF expected 8% to 9%, the IEA and Roland Berger predicted 6% to 7%, BCG projected 5%, and Deloitte projected 3.5%. In reality, actual US EV and plug-in hybrid sales, represented by a solid blue line, remained largely flat, hovering around only 1.1% in 2016. 

Footnotes on the page provide additional context. One note highlights a World Economic Forum forecast which suggests that by electrifying high-use fleets, taxis, and public transport, 35% of US vehicle miles traveled could be electrified by 2030 even if the actual vehicle stock remains 85% internal combustion engine cars. Another footnote indicates that J.P. Morgan assumes a lower light-vehicle growth rate of 2.8% to 2030 (compared to the historical 3.8% rate from 2005 to 2015) due to the potential efficiency gains from autonomous vehicles.

This page highlights China's global leadership in the installation of High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) transmission lines to overcome the geographic distance between its renewable energy production sites and urban centers, which has historically caused high curtailment rates. While China holds 30% of the world’s wind and solar capacity, these resources make up only 5% of its total electricity generation. To achieve its goal of cutting coal’s primary energy contribution from 62% in 2016 to 58% by 2020, China is expanding wind, solar, and hydro power, supported by 20 HVDC projects either currently operating or under construction.

An accompanying map of China illustrates these HVDC transmission lines, depicting hydropower pathways in blue and PV and wind energy lines in red, with solid lines representing operational infrastructure and dotted lines showing those slated for completion by 2020. A supporting table contextualizes this expansion by tracking announced, in-country HVDC projects over 400 kilovolts. To normalize the data, the table introduces a metric calculated as the kilometers of HVDC projects divided by total gigawatts of electricity generation capacity. Mexico tops this ratio at 40.6 (2,740 kilometers of projects against 67 gigawatts of capacity), followed by Brazil at 29.8 (4,640 kilometers against 156 gigawatts). China exhibits a ratio of 18.4, with an extensive 27,953 kilometers of domestic projects and 1,519 gigawatts of capacity. Other nations listed include Indonesia with a ratio of 15.3, the United Kingdom at 12.5, Germany at 12.2, the United States at 7.5 (8,075 kilometers of projects against 1,074 gigawatts of capacity), and India at 6.2.

The author points out that China’s HVDC metric is more than double that of the United States. This discrepancy is presented as a worrisome signal for American energy infrastructure transition, especially given the author's warning that some of the announced US projects may face obstacles and might not ever reach completion.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2018 Annual Energy Paper, written by Michael Cembalest, argues that high voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission lines are highly efficient and economic for long-distance power transmission, highlighting how China leads in this technology while the United States lags. The central issue is that major nations like China, the US, Brazil, India, and Australia must transmit renewable power over long distances from generation sites to population centers. Using standard high voltage alternating current (HVAC) lines over these distances leads to substantial transmission losses and high involuntary curtailment rates for wind and solar power. 

Four distinct graphics illustrate these dynamics. The first chart, a scatter plot on the top left, displays transmission and distribution losses as a percentage of total generation against population density per square kilometer. It shows a clear downward trendline, demonstrating that low-density nations with long transmission distances face the highest losses. For example, Canada and Australia experience losses near 8% and 7% respectively, while the US is around 5%. In contrast, higher-density nations like Germany, Japan, and South Korea exhibit lower transmission losses, clustering around 4% to 5%. 

To the right, a table details involuntary wind and solar curtailment ratios across various countries and regions. The data highlights a severe transmission bottleneck in China, where curtailment rates reached 17.1% in 2012, 10.7% in 2013, and 17.0% in 2016. By comparison, European nations like Denmark and Portugal achieved 0.0% curtailment in 2014, while US regional grids like ERCOT and MISO reported curtailment rates of 0.5% and 5.5% respectively in 2014. 

The text outlines the core economic tradeoffs of HVDC systems, which require higher upfront capital costs for DC voltage conversion terminals but offer lower per-kilometer line costs because they require fewer conductors and smaller towers. Additionally, HVDC systems incur far fewer transmission losses over time. A chart on the bottom left, comparing transmission losses between HVAC and HVDC from 200 km to 400 km, illustrates this. Active power losses for HVAC rise steeply from approximately 82 megawatts at 200 kilometers to 110 megawatts at 400 kilometers. Meanwhile, HVDC active power losses remain remarkably flat, increasing from 80 megawatts to only about 88 megawatts over the same distance.

The final chart on the bottom right compares lifetime system costs for HVAC and HVDC across distances up to 1,400 kilometers. The total AC cost curve starts low but climbs steeply, while the total DC cost curve starts much higher due to terminal expenses but climbs at a gentle slope. The two lines intersect between 600 and 700 kilometers, representing the economic breakeven distance beyond which HVDC becomes the cheaper option. The author notes that major industrial firms Siemens and ABB report similar breakeven distances and are actively working on the world's first 1,100 kV HVDC transformers in Guquan, China. A detailed footnote adds that for underwater or underground systems, the HVDC breakeven point drops significantly to just 50 to 80 kilometers due to high electrical capacitance and reactive power losses in long AC cables.

This page of the publication examines whether the supply of rare earth metals and critical materials can keep pace with growing demand from clean energy technologies and electric vehicles. While general research indicates that lithium and graphite supplies will be sufficient, a 2011 US Department of Energy report highlights potential medium-term supply risks for dysprosium, neodymium, and terbium. These concerns are reinforced by a 2017 study from researchers at the University of Science and Technology in Beijing, which points out that electric vehicle demand is projected to grow from 50 percent of all rare earth demand to 68 percent by 2030. Although 478 megatons of rare earth oxides exist globally—enough to sustain current production for over 100 years—extraction is highly concentrated in China and Australia, and expected spikes in demand for neodymium and dysprosium present acute supply chain risks.

Three charts illustrate these supply and demand dynamics. The first visual is the Medium Term Criticality Matrix from the US Department of Energy. It plots elements across two axes from one to four: importance to clean energy on the vertical axis and supply risk on the horizontal axis. Neodymium and dysprosium are flagged in the highest-risk red zone, scoring highest in both clean energy importance and supply risk. Terbium, europium, and yttrium also sit in this high-risk zone. Lithium and tellurium occupy a yellow medium-risk area, while nickel, cobalt, manganese, and other elements are positioned in the green, low-risk section.

The second chart, from the Beijing study, shows global rare earth production and demand in metric tons from 1950 to 2015. The two series track closely together, showcasing a sharp, parallel rise from negligible levels in the mid-twentieth century to around 120,000 metric tons by 2015. 

The third chart plots EV battery metals prices from 2014 to early 2018, indexed to January 2014 at 100. This Bloomberg data reveals stark differences in price trends: while dysprosium prices dropped below 50, and terbium, copper, and neodymium hovered relatively flat near or below their starting index, cobalt and lithium saw massive price surges starting in 2016, both skyrocketing to nearly 300 by early 2018.

The page concludes with a brief commentary on autonomous vehicle energy consumption. Referencing researchers from the University of Michigan Center for Sustainable Systems, the text explains that the computing power, added weight, and aerodynamic drag of autonomous hardware require extra energy. While driving efficiencies in small self-driving electric vehicles can offset this drag, tests of larger applications, such as Waymo technology installed in a minivan, resulted in higher net energy use. The author notes that they will continue to monitor this emerging trend.

Michael Cembalest discusses the apparent paradox of strong 2018 economic indicators coexisting with flat equity markets, for which he projects single-digit returns. Despite impressive US corporate profits, a 20 percent increase in capital spending, and 32 of 35 major economies expanding (with Korea, Turkey, and Hong Kong as exceptions), markets are restrained by monetary tightening. This theme of declining western centralization is illustrated by an artwork of a central bank liquidity spigot. A list of first-quarter 2018 earnings highlights notes that with 86 percent of the S&P 500 market cap reporting, revenues grew 8 percent, earnings surged 24 percent, and 76 percent of companies beat estimates by an average of 7 percent. The federal tax cut added approximately 7.5 percent to the bottom line, and capital spending grew 20 percent year-over-year, driven significantly by technology companies and Royal Caribbean.

To explain the market headwind, two charts analyze monetary policy and interest rates. The first chart, titled Fed hike expectations, compares the number of 25-basis-point interest rate hikes expected through year-end 2019. It shows a wide range of predictions: HSBC expects around 2 hikes, TS Lombard expects 3.5, Wells Fargo expects 4, Deutsche Bank expects 5, Macroeconomic Advisers and the market expectations futures expect around 4.5, while the median FOMC projection, Goldman Sachs, and J.P. Morgan expect 6 to 6.5 hikes. J.P. Morgan projects that 6 to 7 more hikes will flatten the yield curve, bringing Fed Funds to 3.25 percent to 3.50 percent and 10-year rates to 3.50 percent to 3.75 percent.
