In this J.P. Morgan "Eye on the Market" special edition publication titled "The ARC and the Covenants 4.0: The State of the States, 2018," the fiscal stress facing US states is analyzed. This stress is measured as the percentage of state revenues required to cover interest on general obligation debt alongside all future pension and retiree healthcare obligations. The featured visual is a color-coded map of the United States categorizing states from lowest (green) to highest (red) debt service relative to revenues. The map illustrates that most states, represented in green, have manageable burdens of 15 percent or less. Moderate-burden states colored in yellow include Texas, New York, Washington, Montana, Colorado, Missouri, Louisiana, Alabama, South Carolina, Maryland, Delaware, Vermont, and Maine. Orange-shaded states with higher burdens include California, Alaska, Georgia, Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island. The states under the greatest fiscal stress, colored red, are Hawaii, Illinois, Kentucky, New Jersey, and Connecticut. The commentary explains that the severe burdens in these high-stress states may necessitate politically or economically unfeasible tax increases or spending cuts. To address these potential crises, the author mentions public policy discussions at Harvard’s Kennedy School regarding the use of Puerto Rico's Promesa legislation as a dry run for establishing state-level bankruptcy frameworks. Ultimately, the author acknowledges that the declining funding ratios in several states lead some public policy analysts to advocate for expanding Chapter 9 bankruptcy legislation to encompass US states.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" by Michael Cembalest analyzes Federal Reserve rate hike expectations and the mounting fiscal tensions between Italy and the Eurozone. 

First, the author examines the Fed’s trajectory, noting that J.P. Morgan expects six 25-basis-point rate hikes by the end of 2019 to restore a positive cost of money in real terms. This prediction exceeds the futures market, which prices in only three hikes, setting up a potential mismatch that could disappoint markets. Cembalest notes that even modest interest rate increases have begun dampening demand for housing and autos. He also mentions President Trump's criticism of the Fed, comparing it in a footnote to President Nixon’s aggressive, backchannel pressure on Fed Chairman Arthur Burns during the 1972 presidential campaign.

Two charts illustrate these interest rate dynamics. The first, "Fed hike expectations," shows the number of 25bp hikes expected through year-end 2019 across different institutions as of July 2018. J.P. Morgan and Goldman Sachs expect nearly six hikes, while the median FOMC projection stands at five. In contrast, institutions like HSBC expect only one, and the market expectation implied by futures sits at three. The second chart, "Plans to buy homes and autos rolling over," tracks the percentage of respondents intending to buy a home or auto within the next six months from 2000 to 2018. Both metrics peaked around late 2017 and have rolled over in 2018, with home buying intentions falling to around 5% and auto buying intentions dipping toward 13%.

The second half of the page addresses Italy’s friction with the Eurozone. Italy's new government is pushing for a 6% fiscal expansion, whereas Eurozone rules dictate fiscal contraction due to Italy's heavy debt load. Although the government denies any plan for "Europartenza"—a term coined by the author to describe an Italian exit from the Eurozone—the structural risks are high. Italy has logged the lowest growth rate in the developed world since 1988, and its citizens show the lowest support for the Eurozone at just 58%. Lombard Research also estimates Italy’s fiscal multiplier is only 0.5, capping best-case growth at 1.5% for 2019. 

Two charts highlight the resulting financial anxiety. "Italy: the cost of protecting against Europartenza" tracks the Italian 5-year credit default swap contract price in basis points from 2010 to 2018. It shows a dramatic spike in mid-2018, with the ISDA 2014 contract (which protects against default and value-reducing redenomination) surging toward 300 bps, while the ISDA 2003 contract rose past 200 bps. The final chart, "Foreign investors lose confidence in Italy, again," shows net quarterly debt flows by non-Italian investors in billions of euros from 1997 to 2018. It reveals a severe capital flight in 2018, with outflows spiking past negative 200 billion euros, matching the worst capital flight period of the 2011–2012 Eurozone crisis. Cembalest concludes that while a compromise is the most likely outcome, global investors will get crucial clarity when Italy submits its budget to the European Commission in October.

In this publication, titled "The ARC and the Covenants: The State of the States, 2018," Michael Cembalest discusses the fiscal stress that US states face from unfunded pension and retiree healthcare obligations. Because J.P. Morgan manages billions in municipal bonds, the firm closely tracks these liabilities; historical precedents in municipalities like Central Falls, Vallejo, San Bernardino, Stockton, and Detroit demonstrate that bondholders often suffer worse losses when public employees face pension writedowns. To measure this burden, the author analyzes the Annual Required Contribution divided by municipal revenue across more than 300 plans.

A major bar chart details the cost of unfunded pensions and retiree healthcare as a percentage of state revenues for 50 US states, utilizing fiscal year 2017 data. The chart compares what states are currently paying against what they would have to pay to fully amortize their liabilities over 30 years assuming a 6% plan return. This combined metric includes interest on net direct debt, the state's share of unfunded pension and retiree healthcare liabilities, and defined contribution plan payments. 

The data shows that while most states have manageable required contribution ratios of 15% or less, several states face severe challenges. Illinois is the most extreme case, with required payments approaching 47% of its revenues compared to its current payment of around 26%. Other highly distressed states include New Jersey, Hawaii, and Connecticut, where required payments range from approximately 35% to 40% of revenues, while actual current payments sit much lower at roughly 15% to 21%. Kentucky, Massachusetts, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Delaware, and West Virginia also have required payments above the 15% threshold. Conversely, states like North Dakota, Nebraska, South Dakota, and Idaho have exceptionally low required contributions well below 5%.

In light of these deep fiscal imbalances, Cembalest advocates for the expansion of Chapter 9 bankruptcy legislation to the state level, noting that a Harvard Kennedy School seminar suggested using Puerto Rico's Promesa legislation as a blueprint for state-level bankruptcy rules. The author also references former FDIC Chairman William M. Isaac, who argued that Illinois and the city of Chicago should proactively use restructuring tools to put their fiscal challenges behind them.

This page introduces the supplementary materials for the 2018 "ARC and the Covenants" analysis, which assesses the risks of unfunded pension and retiree healthcare obligations across US states. It outlines twelve specific supplementary documents, labeled SM1 through SM12, that provide deeper data and methodological details. These materials cover topics such as the risks of a six percent investment return assumption and cash flow timing, the impact of special funding situations on state IPOD ratios, and the historical context of state and local pension funding ratios. Additionally, the documents feature a case study on how New Jersey ended up in a severely underfunded position, explain the IPOD ratio methodology, define key terms, and compare level dollar versus level percent amortization methods for unfunded obligations. Projections are also featured, including an analysis of how long it might take deeply underfunded pension plans to run out of money. Finally, the supplements provide extensive state-by-state data tables, including required tax increases, required worker contributions, required asset returns, and detailed pension and OPEB (Other Post-Employment Benefits) statistics such as reported versus revised funding ratios, actual versus revised ARC payments, discount rates, and ten-year projected funding ratios.

This page of J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" commentary by Michael Cembalest discusses why several US states have accumulated massive unfunded pension and Other Post-Employment Benefit (OPEB) obligations relative to their state revenues. The author attributes this to states enacting benefit increases prior to market declines, chronically undercontributing relative to recommended levels, or managing pension systems that are disproportionately large relative to their state economies and tax bases. 

The analysis is centered on Table 2, which outlines key pension and OPEB statistics for eleven of the weaker US states: Illinois, New Jersey, Hawaii, Connecticut, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Delaware, West Virginia, and California. The table presents reported funding ratios alongside J.P. Morgan's revised funding ratios, which utilize a more conservative 6% discount rate. It also shows a projected 10-year pension funding ratio, the actual contributions made in FY 2017 versus both reported and revised Actuarially Required Contributions (ARC), and the pension versus OPEB shares of the combined revised ARC. 

The data highlights severe funding gaps across these states. For pensions, Illinois has a reported funding ratio of 38% (revised to 34%), with a projected 10-year ratio of 52%. New Jersey's pension system is even more stressed over the long term, with a reported funding ratio of 36% (revised to 40%) but a projected 10-year ratio of just 27%, driven by the state contributing only 49% of its reported ARC. Kentucky also reports a very low pension funding ratio of 34% (revised to 40%). Conversely, Delaware and West Virginia show higher reported pension funding ratios of 82% and 79%, respectively. 

On the OPEB side, the table reveals that most of these states do not prefund these benefits, instead using a pay-as-you-go approach. This is reflected in OPEB funding ratios of 0% for Illinois and New Jersey, and a mere 1% for California. Consequently, pensions generally constitute the larger share of the unfunded ARC, accounting for 78% in Illinois and 77% in Kentucky, though Delaware is an exception with OPEBs making up 61% of its unfunded ARC. A footnote contextualizes these figures by noting that the average corporate pension funding ratio was a much healthier 86% in 2017, even though corporate plans use lower discount rates than public plans.

Looking forward, the author poses open questions about the feasibility of long-term funding recovery. While 10-year projections suggest that depletion risks are not imminent, this outlook assumes that states like Illinois, Connecticut, and Hawaii can continue allocating 20% to 25% of their state revenues to underfunded plans. The author warns that this allocation may not be sustainable given competing public needs, such as infrastructure and education, and cautions that these rough estimates remain highly sensitive to future market volatility and political outcomes.

This page analyzes the financial stress of several United States state pension and retiree healthcare systems using J.P. Morgan's "IPOD" ratio, which measures interest, pension, retiree healthcare (OPEB), and defined contribution payments as a percentage of state revenues. Assuming a standard six percent return on assets and amortizing unfunded balances over thirty years, the author explores how states could close their funding gaps through three mutually exclusive options: raising tax revenues, increasing worker contributions, or securing higher investment returns. The author argues that states like Illinois and New Jersey face nearly irreversible declines, noting that required tax hikes would face steep political opposition, worker contribution increases would need to be astronomically high, and double-digit investment returns are practically unachievable.

Table 1 details the states with the largest revised IPOD ratios and the requirements under each of the three funding options. For Illinois, the current IPOD ratio of twenty-six percent would need to rise to a revised fifty-one percent, requiring either a twenty-five percent tax revenue hike, a six-hundred-eighty-nine percent increase in worker contributions, or an eleven point five percent pension investment return alongside no viable return solution for retiree healthcare. New Jersey’s IPOD ratio rises from seventeen percent to thirty-eight percent, but the state has no investment return solution for either pension or healthcare funds, meaning it must rely on a twenty-two percent tax hike or a five-hundred-twenty-one percent worker contribution increase. Hawaii is a notable outlier; its ratio goes from twenty-one percent to thirty-seven percent, which would require an impossible one-hundred-seventeen-thousand-ninety-one percent increase in worker contributions because of an extremely low baseline. 

Other high-stress states shown in the table include Connecticut, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Delaware, West Virginia, and California. For nearly all of these states, the table indicates there is no viable investment return solution for retiree healthcare, and several require double-digit pension investment returns, such as thirteen percent for Pennsylvania and ten point five percent for Connecticut. Footnotes clarify that spending cuts of similar magnitude to tax hikes would have to be even larger because they must target non-pension spending. Additionally, the author notes that historical nominal returns on a seventy-thirty stock-bond portfolio since 1956 only reach nine point six percent at the ninetieth percentile, reinforcing the idea that any required return above this threshold is highly improbable.

This page of the publication explores potential solutions for states dealing with heavy pension and retiree healthcare (OPEB) obligations, noting that while pension obligations are legally protected, retiree healthcare benefits can be altered at a state's discretion. The author details recent OPEB liability reductions across several states, such as Kansas at negative one hundred percent and Nevada at negative seventy-three percent, while noting that unfunded OPEB obligations are typically smaller than unfunded pensions. 

To analyze the impact of OPEB restructuring, the author presents a line chart titled "What if states make large cuts to retiree healthcare and use a much longer amortization period?" The chart measures the IPOD ratio—representing the percentage of state revenues required to fund interest on net direct debt, unfunded pension and retiree healthcare liabilities, and defined contribution payments—across forty-nine US states. It compares two scenarios: a baseline IPOD ratio using reported liabilities and a thirty-year amortization period, depicted by a blue line, versus an alternative scenario assuming a thirty-three percent haircut to OPEB liabilities and a fifty-year amortization period, depicted by a grey line. The y-axis scales from zero to fifty percent. The data reveals that while the alternative scenario reduces ratios across the board, it fails to significantly alter the risk profile for the most vulnerable states on the left side of the chart. Illinois remains the highest risk state, with its baseline ratio near forty-eight percent dropping to around forty-two percent under the alternative model, followed closely by New Jersey, Hawaii, Connecticut, and Kentucky. 

The analysis also discusses "Special Funding" situations in states like Illinois, New Jersey, and Connecticut, where state-level IPOD ratios would fall substantially if local municipalities took over payments made on their behalf, though local governments are deemed financially or politically unable to do so. Finally, the page connects these financial pressures to local politics ahead of the 2018 midterm elections. The author observes that underfunded pensions are highly correlated with Democratic-leaning states, noting that of the eleven states with IPOD ratios exceeding fifteen percent, seven had state legislatures controlled by Democrats for the past twenty years, two were mixed (Kentucky and Delaware), and two were controlled by the Republican Party (Alaska and Pennsylvania).

This page discusses state pension plan investment return assumptions, arguing that a 6% assumption is conservative because it translates to a 4% real return plus 2% inflation. To support this, the author presents two charts analyzing state-level discount rates and historical market returns.

The first chart, titled "Downward migration of state pension plan discount rates," plots individual state pension discount rates for 2014, 2016, and 2017 across all fifty states alphabetically. The vertical axis scales from 3% to 9%. The data shows a clear downward trend in assumptions over time, yet almost all states remain above the 6% mark. Furthermore, state assumptions are vastly higher than the 3.60% average pension discount rate used by the Milliman 100 corporate defined benefit plan universe in fiscal year 2017, which is indicated by a dashed horizontal line. A footnote notes that the average OPEB discount rate used by states is lower, at 4.5% with a standard deviation of 1.4%. 

The second chart, titled "Historical real returns for hypothetical 70% stock, 30% bond portfolio, 30-year rolling real return," tracks 30-year rolling real returns from 1956 to 2016. The vertical axis ranges from 3% to 8%. The chart marks the 90th percentile of real returns at just over 7% and the 10th percentile at roughly 4.2%. The historical trend line shows that 30-year rolling real returns bottomed out near 3.5% in the mid-1980s before rising again. By illustrating that a 4% real return sits near the 10th percentile of historical post-war outcomes, the author demonstrates that a 6% nominal return assumption is a highly conservative expectation for a standard balanced portfolio.

This page examines the concentration of state debt in regions with weak fiscal indicators, specifically analyzing how the highest-debt-issuing states tend to have elevated IPOD ratios, which represent the combined costs of interest, pensions, and other post-employment benefits as a percentage of state revenues. Author Michael Cembalest explains that while many states maintain healthy, low IPOD ratios, they are not the ones issuing the bulk of municipal debt. Because over half of outstanding general obligation debt is issued by states with IPOD ratios exceeding 15 percent, J.P. Morgan asset managers exercise caution regarding general obligation exposures in weaker states. When investing, they prefer issuers with no direct state retirement system exposure, such as Northwestern Memorial Healthcare in Illinois or Princeton University in New Jersey, or separate legal entities like local public utilities that have segregated revenues and better-funded local pensions.

A detailed dual-axis chart titled "Plenty of states have low IPOD ratios, but states with high IPOD ratios issue the most state debt" displays data from Moody's and State Annual Financial Reports for fiscal year 2017. The horizontal axis lists all fifty US states, ordered from left to right by decreasing IPOD ratio. The left vertical axis measures the revised IPOD ratio from 0 percent to 50 percent, represented by blue vertical bars. The right vertical axis measures the state's share of total net direct debt from 0 percent to 20 percent, plotted as orange dots. Illinois shows the highest IPOD ratio at nearly 50 percent, with a corresponding debt share of roughly 10 percent. California and New York, while having more moderate IPOD ratios of around 15 percent and 12 percent respectively, represent a massive share of total net direct debt, with California near 16 percent and New York near 12 percent. 

An inset pie chart on the right side of the visual, titled "Net debt breakdown by IPOD ratio," divides total net debt into three segments. It shows that states with healthy IPOD ratios under 15 percent make up less than half of the total net debt, whereas the combination of states with IPOD ratios between 15 and 20 percent and those with ratios exceeding 20 percent collectively account for more than half of all outstanding net debt.

Before concluding, Cembalest emphasizes the vital societal role of public sector workers, such as safety personnel, educators, and healthcare providers, asserting that they have earned their accrued pension benefits and possess the right to see them fully paid. Finally, the page notes that the publication's supplementary materials provide further analysis on market return timing risks, special funding situations, the pace of asset depletion, and historical funding ratios dating back to the year 2000.

Michael Cembalest discusses the critical importance of the timing of market returns for public pension funding, explaining that low returns early in a 30-year horizon can lead to substantial asset shortfalls even if the overall compound return eventually meets the expected 6% target. To model this sequence-of-returns risk, the analysis references research from Harvard and the Pew Charitable Trusts and recomputes the state IPOD ratios—the percentage of state revenues required to cover interest on net direct debt, unfunded pension and retiree healthcare liabilities, and defined contribution plan payments—using a more conservative 4% plan return assumption as a proxy. 

The page features a line chart comparing state-by-state revenue burdens under a 6% plan return baseline versus a stressed 4% plan return, both utilizing a 30-year level dollar amortization. The y-axis measures the percentage of state revenues required, ranging from 0% to 60%, while the x-axis lists US states from highest burden to lowest. The blue line represents the 6% plan return, showing that under normal conditions, high-burden states like Illinois and New Jersey require roughly 50% and 40% of their revenues, respectively, to cover these obligations. Under the stressed 4% plan return scenario, shown by the grey line, the fiscal burden climbs significantly for weaker states, pushing Illinois above 55% and New Jersey near 50%, while Hawaii and Connecticut rise to between 40% and 50%. A highlighted box on the chart draws attention to a group of states—including West Virginia, California, Alaska, Georgia, Texas, and South Carolina—whose required revenue shares jump toward the 20% mark under the 4% scenario. In contrast, well-funded states on the far right of the chart, such as South Dakota, Nebraska, and North Dakota, remain largely unaffected with burdens staying well under 10% in both scenarios. 

The discussion also incorporates recommendations from a 2014 Society of Actuaries independent Blue Ribbon panel, which concluded that while historical returns are a useful reference, public pension discount rates should ideally be based on a risk-free rate plus forward-looking risk premia, and recommended the disclosure of plan liabilities using this risk-free rate.

This page focuses on how "special funding" arrangements affect state IPOD ratios, which represent the percentage of state revenues needed to pay interest on net direct debt, the state's share of unfunded pension and retiree healthcare liabilities, and defined contribution plan payments. Michael Cembalest explains that many states make pension payments on behalf of local cities and counties, particularly for teacher plans. While standard state IPOD ratios include these costs because states disclose them as permanent obligations, most states also disclose their liabilities without this special funding. 

The accompanying table lists nineteen states and compares their Revised IPOD ratios to their Revised IPOD ratios when excluding special funding situations for the 2017 fiscal year, based on data from J.P. Morgan, state reports, and Moody’s. The data reveals dramatic drops in several states when local obligations are excluded: Illinois drops from fifty percent to twenty-five percent, New Jersey falls from thirty-eight percent to twenty-five percent, Connecticut declines from thirty-five percent to twenty-six percent, Kentucky falls from twenty-nine percent to fifteen percent, and Texas declines from thirteen percent to seven percent. Other states listed show varying degrees of impact, including Alaska declining from fifteen percent to twelve percent, Maryland dropping from twenty percent to twelve percent, Vermont halving from twelve percent to six percent, and West Virginia decreasing from sixteen percent to ten percent. States like Georgia, Kansas, Massachusetts, Montana, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Carolina, Rhode Island, Tennessee, and Washington show minimal or no changes. 

Despite the optical improvement in these ratios when special funding is stripped out, the author warns that these lower numbers should not provide comfort to investors. His assessment is that the local municipalities and counties currently receiving state help are either unwilling or unable to take back these massive funding obligations. Additionally, the author notes that while Indiana and Pennsylvania also have special funding setups, they did not disclose enough data to calculate what their ratios would look like without them.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" provides critical definitions and data sources under the section titled "SM6: Definitions and data sources" to establish the methodology behind the state pension, OPEB, and debt analyses in the report. For data aggregation, the analysis sources information from FY2017 reports, substituting FY2016 data for Alabama where necessary, with net direct debt and revenue figures sourced from Moody’s as of July 31, 2018. The report defines "net direct debt" to include bonds, unconditional general fund obligations, capital leases, pension obligation bonds, lease revenue bonds, and negative operational fund balances, while excluding state enterprise revenue bonds and self-supporting debt. 

Plan liabilities in the model incorporate the state’s share of both the amortization of unfunded liabilities and state-level service costs, which are calculated by subtracting worker contributions and applying the state's share. State revenues are based on Moody’s "Own Source Revenue" series, encompassing taxes and payments to the General Fund and general debt service funds, but excluding non-recurring revenues. For multi-employer plans, the state's portion of obligations, or state shares, is estimated where not disclosed by comparing the state's reported ARC to the plan-level ARC. The methodology also includes special funding situations in the state IPOD ratios, which occur when states make permanent or temporary payments on behalf of local entities, particularly for teacher plans. 

Addressing missing OPEB data, the author explains that a Macaulay duration of 15 was assumed for the roughly one-third of plans lacking duration disclosures, and service costs were estimated for the 20% of plans missing that data. This missing information is attributed to delayed adoption of new GASB rules on OPEB disclosure in states such as Arizona, Arkansas, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Mississippi, Montana, and New York. Finally, the author addresses data uncertainties, noting that while some clarifications from states were sought, remaining uncertainties lie within smaller plans and do not materially impact the overall IPOD results.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the history and measurement of state and local pension funding ratios. The central focus is a significant methodology shift implemented by the Federal Reserve in the second quarter of 2018. The Fed transitioned from the Accumulated Benefit Obligation (ABO) methodology to the Projected Benefit Obligation (PBO) methodology. Because the PBO method includes estimates of future salary growth, it yields higher projected liabilities, which effectively revised downward the entire historical series of national funding ratios.

An accompanying line chart displays the State and Local Government Pensions Funding Ratio from 1991 through 2018, comparing the Q1 2018 ABO series with the Q2 2018 PBO series. The ABO series peaked near 130% around the year 2000 and ended near 75% by 2018. In contrast, the PBO series peaked at just over 80% in 2000 and hovered near 50% in 2018. Both lines show a precipitous decline following 1999, driven by two separate 40% or greater stock market crashes in the decade, and show very little recovery after the 2009 financial crisis.

The author argues that the lack of recovery in public sector funding ratios since 2009 is not due to reduced portfolio risk, but rather to four key factors. First, after the market downturns, states had to pay contractually promised pension distributions from a much smaller asset base, even as they earned high returns on what remained. Second, many states failed to make their full Actuarially Required Contributions (ARC). Third, states have increased their longevity assumptions; a cited study by PGIM Investments warns that adding four to five years to average life expectancy can raise plan liabilities by 15% to 20%. Fourth, Federal Reserve monetary policy lowered fixed-income returns, though this had a smaller impact because public plans hold only 25% in cash and bonds compared to 45% for corporate plans.

Lastly, the text explains the discrepancy between the Fed's 50% PBO funding ratio and the officially reported national state pension funding ratio of 68%. This gap exists because the Fed discounts liabilities using the conservative 4% AAA corporate bond rate, while states discount their liabilities using a much higher average rate of 7.1%.

This page outlines the methodology for calculating the IPOD ratio, a metric designed by J.P. Morgan to evaluate the fiscal burden of state-level liabilities. The IPOD ratio is calculated by dividing the sum of interest on net direct debt, pension costs (comprising amortization of unfunded pension liability and pension service costs), other post-employment benefit (OPEB) costs (comprising amortization of unfunded retiree healthcare obligations and OPEB service costs), and defined contribution payments by total state revenues. 

The calculation relies on several key conservative assumptions, including a 5% interest rate on net direct debt, a 6% investment return on pension and OPEB assets, and a 30-year level-dollar amortization period for unfunded obligations. To ensure comparability, the methodology normalizes state plans by adjusting gross liabilities based on plan duration and the difference between the state’s assumed return and the 6% baseline, re-amortizing net liabilities, and adjusting service costs over a duration extended by five years. 

The publication highlights that these normalized estimates of pension and OPEB costs are typically higher than actual state contributions. This difference exists because states often fail to meet their actuarially required contributions, some legislatures set contribution levels by statute rather than actuarial guidance, many states assume overly optimistic investment returns compared to the 6% baseline, and states frequently use level-percent amortization, which obscures true costs compared to the level-dollar approach used here. Footnotes clarify that defined contribution plans are minor, representing only 2% of combined obligations, and identify Illinois, Hawaii, Connecticut, and Massachusetts as states particularly sensitive to these IPOD ratio stress tests.

This page, titled "SM4: How did New Jersey end up in such bad shape?", analyzes the long-term pension crisis in New Jersey, attributing it to a bipartisan failure by state governors and legislators to fund the retirement system. Author Michael Cembalest explains that state leaders effectively starved the pension plan for fifteen years by making contributions far below the required levels. Additionally, New Jersey failed to disclose its pension issues properly, leading to an SEC enforcement action for twenty-six billion dollars in fraudulent municipal bond offerings. The text notes that New Jersey was the first state to face federal charges of this kind, though Illinois and Kansas later faced similar enforcement actions.

The page features three aligned visual elements tracking the period from 2000 to 2016. The first chart displays New Jersey's ARC versus actual contributions in millions of US dollars. The actuarially required contribution, depicted as a line, climbs from under one thousand million dollars in 2000 to over three thousand five hundred million dollars by 2016. Meanwhile, actual payments, shown as blue bars, remain close to zero for most of the decade, and only reach a fraction of the required amount in the years they are made, peaking at roughly one thousand two hundred million dollars in 2016. Below this chart, two horizontal color bars show the political landscape. The governor affiliation bar indicates Republican leadership at the beginning and end of the period, with Democratic leadership in the middle, while the General Assembly majority party bar shows solid Democratic control from 2002 through 2016. Together, these charts demonstrate that the chronic underfunding occurred under both Republican and Democratic leadership.

This page presents a comprehensive data table titled "SM9: IPOD results and remediation by state," which analyzes the fiscal pressure on US states using the IPOD ratio. The IPOD ratio measures the percentage of state revenues required to cover interest on net direct debt, unfunded pension liabilities, retiree healthcare liabilities (OPEB), and defined contribution plan payments. The table contrasts current IPOD ratios with revised figures and presents mutually exclusive, thirty-year remediation options categorized by who funds the gap: taxpayers via tax revenue increases, public sector workers via increased contributions, or state fund managers through required pension and OPEB investment returns. 

Illinois is shown to have the highest fiscal strain, with its current IPOD of 26 percent rising to a revised 51 percent. To remediate this gap, taxpayers would face a 25 percent increase in tax revenues, or public sector workers would need to increase their contributions by 689 percent; alternatively, fund managers would need an 11.5 percent pension return, though there is no viable investment solution for its OPEB obligations. Other highly stressed states include New Jersey, with its IPOD rising from 17 percent to 38 percent, requiring a 22 percent tax increase, and Connecticut, rising from 22 percent to 35 percent, requiring a 12 percent tax increase. The table reveals that for many states, relying solely on state fund managers is unrealistic, as evidenced by numerous "No solution" entries for required OPEB returns. Extreme public sector contribution hikes are also illustrated, such as Hawaii's astronomical required increase of 117,091 percent to close its gap. At the other end of the spectrum, states like North Dakota show much healthier fiscal standing, with a current IPOD of only 1 percent rising to a revised 2 percent, requiring just a 1 percent tax increase to fund the gap.

This page of the publication, authored by Michael Cembalest, discusses the impact of different amortization methods—specifically level dollar versus level percent—on calculating unfunded public pension obligations. While most public pension plans assume rising payments over time using the level percent approach, J.P. Morgan normalizes across plans using the level dollar approach, which assumes flat payments. Cembalest argues that the level dollar approach offers a more accurate metric for comparing the future cost burdens of different states.

A line chart titled "Level dollar vs. level percent amortization" illustrates the difference in annual required contribution payments for a hypothetical plan with a 70% funding ratio, a $100 million gross pension liability, and a 7.5% discount rate over a 30-year period. Under the level dollar method, payments remain flat at roughly $2.5 million annually. Under the level percent method with a 3.5% annual escalator, payments start lower, at roughly $1.7 million in year one, but rise steadily to nearly $5 million by year 29.

An accompanying table and text present a hypothetical example of how altering these assumptions affects a state's IPOD ratio, which is the percentage of state revenues required to cover interest on net direct debt, unfunded pension and retiree healthcare liabilities, and defined contribution payments. In the base case, which uses a 7.5% discount rate, a $1,000 million pension liability, 70% funding, and $200 million in revenues, the pension amortization with an escalator is $17.7 million, resulting in a 16% IPOD ratio. Removing the escalator under the level dollar approach increases the base pension amortization to $25.4 million. If the discount rate is also lowered to 6%, the total pension liability rises to $1,207 million, and the unescalated pension amortization climbs to $36.8 million, pushing the revised IPOD ratio up to 26%. The author highlights that the shift to the level dollar method accounts for about half of this overall increase, with the more conservative discount rate explaining the rest.

This page addresses the critical question of how long it might take for a deeply underfunded public sector pension plan, starting at a 65% funding level, to run out of money. The analysis, conducted in partnership with J.P. Morgan Asset Management, establishes a set of fixed assumptions: a state discount rate of 7.5%, plan service costs at 3% of total pension liabilities, payroll growth of 4% per year, a liability duration of 13%, and an open amortization approach that re-amortizes net pension liability each year over a subsequent 30 years. Against these baselines, the authors vary three inputs: the realized investment return on assets, the percentage of the actuarially required contribution paid, and the amortization method used.

Two line charts illustrate the projected pension funded status over a 30-year horizon, plotting assets over liabilities as a percentage on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis. The left chart models the level dollar amortization method. Under this method, if a state contributes 100% of its actuarially required contribution and achieves its 7.5% target return, the funding ratio rises from 65% to approximately 85% by year 30. If the state contributes 100% of its required contribution but only earns a 6% return, the funding ratio stays nearly flat, ending around 65%. If the state only contributes 75% of its required contribution and earns a 6% return, the funding ratio deteriorates down to roughly 50%. 

The right chart models the level percent amortization method, which is highly relevant because 80% of state plans, weighted by liabilities, utilize this approach. Because level percent amortization defers larger payments to later years, the dynamics are markedly worse. Under a 7.5% realized return with 100% of the required contribution paid, the funding ratio rises more slowly, reaching only about 80% by year 30. If the return drops to 6% with 100% of the required contribution, the funding ratio drifts downward to about 60%. Most severely, if the state experiences a 6% return and only contributes 75% of its required contribution, the funding ratio drops sharply over the 30-year period, falling to approximately 35% and putting the pension plan on a path toward insolvency.

This page functions as an index or reference appendix titled "SM12: List of reviewed pension and OPEB plans by state." It contains a dense, three-column list of the specific public pension and Other Post-Employment Benefit plans analyzed within the broader report. The list is organized alphabetically by state, covering Alabama through Missouri on this page. Included in the list are numerous state-specific retirement systems, judicial funds, teachers' retirement systems, state police pension funds, and dedicated healthcare or OPEB trusts. Notable entities listed include the California Public Employees' Retirement System, the Colorado Public Employees' Retirement Association, and various state-level programs across Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, and Missouri. There are no charts, tables, or analytical discussions on this page.

This page presents a comprehensive reference table of state-by-state pension statistics for the United States, compiled using fiscal year 2017 data from J.P. Morgan Asset Management, State Annual Financial Reports, and Moody's. The table details various state pension health metrics, highlighting significant discrepancies between reported figures and revised calculations that reflect more conservative accounting assumptions. 

Key columns compare each state's reported funding ratio against its revised funding ratio, alongside the actual contributions made relative to both the reported and revised Annual Required Contributions. For instance, Illinois shows a critical funding gap with a reported funding ratio of 38% that drops to 34% under revised assumptions, coupled with paying only 53% of its revised ARC. New Jersey and Kentucky also exhibit some of the lowest reported funding ratios at 36% and 34%, respectively. In contrast, South Dakota boasts a perfect 100% reported funding ratio, which adjusts to 93% under revised terms, while Wisconsin is close behind with a 99% reported ratio that adjusts to 87%.

The table also provides structural metrics including the pension share of combined pension and other post-employment benefits, liability-weighted discount rates, and liability-weighted durations. Discount rates vary significantly, with Kentucky and Colorado using a low 4.7% liability-weighted discount rate, compared to Alaska’s higher rate of 8.0%. Additionally, the pension portion of total retirement liabilities ranges from a low of 26% in North Carolina to 100% in states like Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Nebraska.

Finally, the chart projects 10-year outlooks for state pension health under two different amortization methodologies: Level Dollar and Level Percent. States with existing funding crises are projected to experience diverging paths; Illinois is projected to reach a 63% funding ratio under the Level Dollar method but only 52% under Level Percent by Year 10, while New Jersey’s funding ratio is projected to languish at 36% under Level Dollar and fall to a critical 27% under Level Percent. Conversely, well-funded states are projected to maintain their stability, with South Dakota estimated to achieve a 98% funding ratio under both methods, and New York projected at 92% under Level Dollar and 90% under Level Percent.

This page consists of a dense, three-column reference directory listing individual state and local public retirement systems, pension funds, and other post-employment benefit (OPEB) plans across the United States. Arranged alphabetically by state, the list begins with the University of Missouri Retirement System and continues through several states, including Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming, concluding with the Wyoming State OPEB plan. There are no charts, tables, or narrative arguments on this page; instead, it serves as a comprehensive index or appendix of the specific public-sector pension and benefit entities analyzed within the broader J.P. Morgan publication.

This page contains a single comprehensive table titled "SM11: OPEB statistics by state," which details various financial metrics related to state-level Other Post-Employment Benefits (OPEB), primarily consisting of retiree healthcare, for fiscal year 2017. The table lists US states by their abbreviations and analyzes several key columns: reported funding ratio, revised funding ratio, actual versus reported Annual Required Contribution (ARC), actual versus revised ARC, the OPEB share of combined pension and OPEB liabilities, liability-weighted discount rates, and liability-weighted duration. 

The data highlights a severe underfunding issue across much of the United States, with numerous states reporting a 0% funding ratio for retiree healthcare, including Illinois, New Jersey, Vermont, New York, Washington, Louisiana, New Hampshire, Mississippi, Nevada, Arkansas, Kansas, Florida, Minnesota, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Iowa, and Wyoming. Even some highly populated states like California and Texas show near-zero reported funding ratios at 1%. Conversely, a small group of states stand out with relatively strong funding levels, led by Arizona with a 104% reported (85% revised) funding ratio, Alaska at 91% reported (70% revised), Oregon at 87% reported (79% revised), and Utah at 70% reported (78% revised). 

The table also illustrates the fiscal pressure that OPEB puts on overall state retiree obligations. The "OPEB share of Pen+OPEB" column shows that for some states, retiree healthcare accounts for more than half of their total combined retirement liabilities, such as North Carolina at 74%, New York at 62%, Delaware at 61%, New Hampshire at 59%, and Michigan at 58%. Liability-weighted discount rates range from a low of 3.0% in Minnesota to a high of 8.0% in Alaska and Arizona. The liability-weighted durations, where available, range from a low of 5% in Utah to a high of 20% in Illinois, New Jersey, and Massachusetts. The source for this statistical compilation is J.P. Morgan Asset Management, State Annual Financial Reports, and Moody's.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest addresses a rising risk for global financial markets: the withdrawal of central bank support, which he describes as a "Lord of the Flies" scenario where markets will be left on their own in 2019 and 2020. The page features a line chart titled "Lord of the Flies: a 20 year period of central bank intervention comes to an end," which plots the rolling 12-month net purchases of G4 financial assets by both developed and emerging economy central banks as a percentage of world GDP from 1975 to 2018. The chart reveals that after decades of hovering mostly between 0% and 2%, net purchases surged post-2000, peaking near 5.5% around the 2008 global financial crisis and again exceeding 4% in late 2016 before experiencing a sharp downturn toward 0% in late 2018. The G4 cohort in this analysis includes the US, Eurozone, UK, Japan, and Switzerland. The visual highlights the end of a two-decade era where developed central banks utilized aggressive quantitative easing and emerging central banks purchased G4 assets to curb currency appreciation and build foreign exchange reserves.

Cembalest notes that while a recent 9.5% correction in the S&P 500 has lowered valuations from 17.0x to 15.5x forward 2019 earnings, this multiple still sits at the 65th percentile of historical valuations since 1985. He warns that a reflexive "buy the dip" strategy, which succeeded in previous corrections since 2009, is now less compelling. Looking ahead, he identifies vulnerable sectors hardest hit by recent corrections, including rate-sensitive industries like homebuilders and high-dividend stocks, companies with high foreign sales impacted by a strong dollar and retreating globalization, and crowded trades like the FANG stocks. Over the medium term, he foresees pressure on corporate earnings arising from rising labor costs, elevated interest and credit expenses, fading globalization, and an eventual decline in share repurchases.

This page analyzes how business cycles end and discusses the implications for investors, focusing on the lead time investors have before asset prices peak relative to economic and earnings peaks. Michael Cembalest argues that while the last two business cycles saw equities, earnings, and economic growth collapse simultaneously, historical cycles prior to those often saw equities peak about a year before economic growth slowed and earnings began to weaken. If the current cycle follows this older pattern, markets may be entering the final stages of one of the strongest bull runs since the Great Depression, even as immediate earnings and growth indicators remain positive.

The page features a data table titled "How cycles end: US equity markets often peak even as profits and the economy keep growing." The table divides historical peaks into two categories. The first category details business cycles when equities peaked a year or more before profits and the economy: January 1966 (next 12-month equity return of -7%, 10 months to economic peak, and 4% earnings growth), November 1968 (equity return of -13%, 9 months to economic peak, and 2% earnings growth), December 1972 (equity return of -19%, 11 months to economic peak, and 27% earnings growth), November 1980 (equity return of -13%, 9 months to economic peak, and 4% earnings growth), and August 1987 (equity return of -18%, 19 months to economic peak, and 41% earnings growth). The second category lists cycles where equities peaked concurrently with earnings and the economy: August 2000 and October 2007, both showing a next 12-month equity return of -25%, with economic peaks occurring within 1 and 4 months, and negative earnings growth of -16% and -23% respectively.

Several detailed forecasts and geopolitical risks are outlined in the footnotes. J.P. Morgan projects 8% to 10% S&P profit growth for 2019, though with downside risks from tariffs. US stock buybacks are projected to reach $800 to $900 billion in 2019, compared to approximately $700 billion in 2018. Regarding international trade, the author notes that the next round of US tariffs on China will target consumer goods in addition to capital and intermediate goods, leading to a larger direct impact on US consumers. In Europe, indicators show weakening, with third-quarter earnings on track for the worst season since late 2008, reinforcing the long-term outperformance of US equities relative to Europe and Japan. Lastly, the author notes that the S&P's roughly 14% annualized price return since March 2009 represents a historic bull run matched only a few times since 1940, such as in the late 1950s, late 1980s, and the late 1990s.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest discusses the outlook for the US stock market following the 2018 midterms, projecting single-digit equity market returns for 2018 and 2019. Despite strong macroeconomic indicators—including third-quarter GDP growth exceeding three percent, robust job and wage growth, and S&P profit growth over twenty percent—Cembalest expects returns to fall below the post-midterm historical average price return of fourteen percent. This conservative stance is driven by fiscal concerns, particularly the massive budget deficit and rising federal debt.

The page features four charts illustrating these dynamics. The first chart, titled The S&P tends to rally following midterms, plots a price index where the midterm election month of November equals 100. It traces historical performance from 1982 to 2014, showing an average post-election rally to over 110 by the following August, and compares this with the path of the 2018 market. The second chart, titled North America hedge fund short positions, displays the z-score of short market value to gross market value from 2015 to late 2018. It shows short positions rising significantly to a z-score near 1.5 by late 2018, which is technically a bullish indicator. 

The narrative then shifts to the rising deficit under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and other Trump administration policies, which the Congressional Budget Office projects will increase US borrowing by 2.7 trillion dollars over a decade, consisting of one trillion dollars in increased spending and 1.7 trillion dollars in lost revenues. The third chart, titled Abnormally high deficit given full employment, plots the unemployment rate against the budget deficit as a percentage of GDP from 1960 to estimated projections in 2025. This chart highlights a historic divergence: while low unemployment typically correlates with a budget surplus or a minimal deficit, the current period of full employment with unemployment near four percent is accompanied by a worsening deficit projected to approach five percent of GDP. The final chart, titled Prior tax cuts coincided with much lower levels of debt, tracks Federal debt as a percentage of GDP from 1970 with projections to 2027. It highlights that previous tax cuts occurred when federal debt was relatively low, between thirty and forty percent of GDP. In contrast, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was enacted when debt was already near eighty percent of GDP, with projections showing it climbing toward the historic World War II peak of over one hundred percent by 2027.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management examines the 2018 midterm election results, arguing that the loss of the House of Representatives by the Republican Party represents the worst House retention relative to economic and market conditions in 100 years. While the GOP expanded its Senate majority, the retaking of the House by Democrats was remarkable because midterm seat losses usually occur during times of poor economic or market performance.

The centerpiece of the analysis is a scatter plot mapping midterm House seat losses since 1910 against prevailing economic and asset market conditions. The vertical axis scores employment and inflation conditions from 0 (worst, representing high inflation, deflation, or rising unemployment) to 100 (best, representing low inflation and falling unemployment). The horizontal axis shows the trailing two-year real return on equities and residential home prices, ranging from -30% to 30%. Individual bubbles represent midterm years, color-coded by the president's political party (blue for Democrats, red for Republicans), with the bubble size and text label indicating the number of House seats lost. 

The 2018 election bubble is positioned near the top right of the chart, indicating highly favorable economic conditions—a high score near 90 for employment and inflation and positive real asset returns of roughly 12%. Despite these optimal conditions, the GOP lost 34 to 36 House seats. In contrast, massive historic losses like 1922 (77 seats lost), 1930 (52 seats lost), and 1938 (72 seats lost) occurred under severe economic contraction, high unemployment, or falling asset markets. Cembalest highlights 2006 as the closest modern parallel to 2018, where the president's party lost 30 seats despite favorable economic conditions due to voter backlash against the Iraq War. He also contrasts 2018 with 1994, where a larger seat loss of 54 occurred under much worse economic conditions, and with 1950 and 1966, where geopolitical tensions and social unrest drove substantial seat losses of 28 and 47 respectively, though the incumbent Democrats still retained control of both legislative chambers in those cases. The top right of the page includes an image of an elephant sitting on a bench looking out at the horizon.

This page analyzes the impact of the Trump administration's deregulatory agenda on the US economy, arguing that while deregulation efforts are substantial, their direct positive effects on capital spending and employment remain difficult to measure and are currently being overshadowed by broader cyclical forces. 

The first chart, tracking the annual number of new pages in the Federal Register of regulations from 1975 to 2017, illustrates a dramatic drop under the Trump administration. After peaking near 95,000 pages in 2016, the page count plummeted to approximately 61,000 pages in 2017, returning to levels not seen since the early 1990s. This reduction is supported by the second chart, which compares the cumulative number of economically significant regulations published by presidents during their terms. In his first year, President Trump added very few regulations, tracking far below the historical first-year trajectories of Presidents Clinton, Bush, and Obama. For context, President Obama’s cumulative count reached nearly 500 such regulations by his eighth year, while Trump’s first year remains near the bottom of the scale.

Despite this regulatory rollback, the charts on capital spending indicate that the post-election boost is losing momentum. The third chart shows the year-over-year percentage change in US nondefense capital goods, excluding aircraft, from 2011 to 2018. Both shipments and new orders peaked near 10% growth in late 2017 and early 2018, but have since rolled over, dropping back toward 5% by late 2018. A similar softening is visible in the fourth chart, which displays the Duke CFO capital spending survey's expected growth in capex over the next 12 months. CFO expectations reached a post-recession high of nearly 10% in early 2018 but have since declined to around 5% by the third quarter of 2018. Ultimately, the author concludes that while finding the right balance of regulation can yield long-term growth benefits, shorter-term cyclical economic forces will likely exert a greater influence over the coming year.

This page discusses US capacity constraints, interest rate forecasts, and the historical market impacts of political crises. The author notes that a proxy for US excess capacity indicates very little slack remains, particularly in labor markets. Consequently, J.P. Morgan forecasts that the Federal Reserve will implement five 25-basis-point interest rate hikes by the end of 2019, bringing the Fed Funds rate to 3.5 percent. The author argues this is a moderate expectation that simply aligns the rate with historical post-war levels of at least 1 percent above inflation.

Two charts support this analysis of monetary policy. The first, showing the US output gap as a percentage of GDP from 1970 to 2018, highlights periods of economic abundance versus capacity shortages, with the late-2018 data firmly in the shortage zone above 0 percent. The second chart compares 2019 Fed hike expectations among various institutions, showing that J.P. Morgan is the most hawkish with five expected hikes, compared to a median FOMC projection of three, and other bank forecasts ranging from HSBC at just over two to Deutsche Bank and Goldman Sachs at over four. 

The second portion of the page examines political risks, warning that the risk of a US constitutional crisis post-midterm is elevated. To analyze how political scandal and macroeconomic stagflation intersect, the author draws parallels to the Nixon and Watergate era, pointing out that the S&P 500 fell 15 percent immediately following the October 1973 Saturday Night Massacre. 

A detailed, annotated dual-axis timeline from September 1972 to December 1974 overlays the S&P 500 price level with the US Misery Index, which combines inflation and unemployment. During this period, the S&P 500 fell from roughly 120 to around 65, while the Misery Index spiked from under 10 percent to over 18 percent. The chart tracks key Watergate milestones—such as the conviction of G. Gordon Liddy and James McCord, the Senate hearings, Nixon's refusal to release tapes, the Saturday Night Massacre, and Nixon's eventual resignation—alongside major economic shocks. These shocks include the end of the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates, the expiration of domestic wage and price controls, and the October 1973 Arab-Israeli War which led to the OPEC oil embargo and quadrupled oil prices to twelve dollars per barrel. The author concludes that it is difficult to isolate whether the presidential crisis or severe stagflation was the primary driver of the S&P 500's weakness during this era.

This page examines the potential for the Trump administration to resort to unilateral executive actions, particularly tariffs, if politically constrained by the House of Representatives. While negotiations with China continue, trade hardliners within the administration remain influential, and there is an active possibility of the US imposing auto tariffs or quotas by the spring of 2019 to close loopholes in the newly negotiated USMCA. Meanwhile, tensions over China's acquisition of US semiconductor intellectual property have escalated, highlighted by the US export ban on Fujian Jinhua.

The tariff conflict is starting to drag on forward-looking sentiment. In the chart tracking developed economy business confidence from 2010 to 2018 measured in standard deviations from the mean, "current conditions" remain robust at around one standard deviation above average. However, "expectations" have fallen sharply in 2018, reflecting the growing negative impact of trade uncertainty on future business outlooks. 

A historical perspective on US trade policy is shown in the chart "A century of globalization: US import tariffs, 1900-2018." After peaking near 30% in the early 1930s, the US tariff rate on total imports steadily declined to near 1% by the 2010s. Recent protective measures have begun to reverse this trend. The chart marks implemented tariffs on washing machines, solar panels, steel, and aluminum, as well as Section 301 tariffs on $50 billion of Chinese imports at a 25% rate. If the administration follows through on potential tariffs spanning $200 billion to $467 billion of Chinese imports and Section 232 tariffs on $290 billion of auto and auto parts imports at 25%, the effective US import tariff rate could spike back up to levels not seen since the mid-20th century.

The commentary also analyzes where the United States derives its unique leverage over China, pointing to the semiconductor industry. A stacked bar chart of China's semiconductor imports by country of origin shows that China imports roughly the same dollar value of chips and equipment from Japan and the US, at approximately $2.4 billion each, followed by Taiwan, South Korea, and Singapore at around $1.3 billion to $1.4 billion each. However, J.P. Morgan sector analyst Harlan Sur argues that these figures are misleading. The true leverage lies in the lack of global substitutes for proprietary US technology. For instance, the US export ban on ZTE crippled the company because it relied entirely on critical networking chips, optical components, and microprocessors from US firms like Broadcom, Inphi, and Intel. 

Ultimately, the author poses an open question regarding the future of trade policy, suggesting that a potential Trump pivot away from trade conflicts could act as a significant positive catalyst for global equity markets after a year dominated by trade-related anxiety.

This introductory page of a Thanksgiving-themed report by Michael Cembalest at J.P. Morgan Asset Management sets the stage for an in-depth analysis of private equity, specifically focusing on the growing amount of committed but unspent capital, often referred to as dry powder, and its implications for investors. Cembalest connects this topic to the broader theme of late-cycle market dynamics, where asset prices peak before the economy or corporate profits do, referencing his prior analysis on the end of the colossal monetary stimulus cycle. The report's table of contents details an eight-part structure covering a historical review of buyout and venture capital performance, methods for measuring dry powder, the drivers behind its rise, whether this accumulation poses a problem for investors, the feasibility of timing private equity commitments, demand-driving factors, and an examination of private equity fees.

In addition to the financial outline, the page features a prominent informational sidebar highlighting the social and developmental benefits of family rituals and shared mealtimes for children. Citing various academic studies and articles, the box explains that regular family dinners promote marital satisfaction, strengthen relationships, and serve as a powerful predictor of academic achievement. Notably, the text highlights that dinnertime conversation boosts vocabulary significantly, exposing young children to 1,000 rare words compared to only 143 from parents reading storybooks aloud. The research also links regular family meals to a lower risk of adolescent depression, school problems, and high-risk behaviors like smoking and substance abuse.

This page from Michael Cembalest's "Eye on the Market" provides a historical review of buyout and venture capital performance, focusing on data sourcing and performance measurement methodologies. The author outlines the persistent challenges of measuring private equity performance relative to public markets, highlighting two key decisions: sourcing reliable fund data and choosing a proper benchmark comparison. 

Historically, data from aggregators like Venture Economics suffered from significant survivorship bias and incomplete reporting, as detailed in a 2013 paper by Rudiger Stucke of Oxford. To address these data quality issues, the author advocates using the Burgiss dataset, which pulls net-of-fee cash flow data directly from 300 institutional limited partners across 1,400 private equity funds, covering roughly 70% of the historical universe. 

For comparing private equity to public markets, the author explains why academics prefer the Public Market Equivalent ratio over traditional measures like Internal Rate of Return or Multiple of Invested Capital. The Public Market Equivalent compares private equity commitments and distributions to public market investments over identical periods, avoiding the unrealistic reinvestment assumptions of Internal Rate of Return and the lack of time-weighting in Multiple of Invested Capital. A Public Market Equivalent ratio of 1.20 corresponds to roughly 3% to 4% in annual excess Internal Rate of Return over the long term. Finally, the author cautions readers to scrutinize assumptions in private equity research, emphasizing the importance of examining net-of-fee performance and vintage years rather than gross-of-fee figures or cherry-picked launch dates.

This page outlines the dominant global position of United States semiconductor companies, the complex nature of US-China trade relations, and the financial implications of US political gridlock following the midterm elections. 

The discussion begins with an assessment of the multi-year lead the United States holds in the semiconductor sector, supported by a table detailing the massive estimated market shares of US firms across critical technology products. For microprocessor chips used in PCs and servers, Intel and AMD control 99 percent of the market. In graphics processors for artificial intelligence and deep learning, NVIDIA and AMD hold a 95 percent share. Broadcom commands 95 percent of the market for networking chips in cloud datacenters, while Qualcomm and Intel together hold a 70 percent share in smartphone cellular processing chips for 4G and 5G. Furthermore, Texas Instruments, Analog, and Maxim hold 90 percent of the electric vehicle power management chip market, and Intel and NVIDIA control 90 percent of next-generation fully autonomous car processors. 

Despite this technological leadership, China maintains significant leverage in trade negotiations. The author notes that Chinese regulatory approval is a critical hurdle for major pending mergers, citing Disney-Fox and United Technologies-Rockwell as examples. Two charts illustrate these trade tensions and corporate dynamics. The first chart displays the cumulative total return from November 2017 to November 2018, demonstrating that US semiconductor chip and equipment stocks heavily underperformed the S&P 500. While the S&P 500 gained roughly 10 percent over this period, semiconductor stocks fell into negative territory, ending down nearly 10 percent. The second chart presents the US-China trade balance in billions of dollars from 2003 to 2017. While the officially reported US-China trade balance shows a deepening deficit that approached negative 350 billion dollars by 2017, an alternative metric that includes the sales of US subsidiaries operating inside China reveals a completely different picture, with the adjusted balance rising to a slightly positive position of around 10 billion dollars. 

The final section of the page shifts to domestic policy, arguing that political gridlock resulting from the midterm elections is likely a positive development for healthcare stocks because it prevents radical policy changes from either political party. For biotechnology and large-cap pharmaceutical companies, gridlock protects them from Democratic efforts to legislate lower prescription drug costs and insurance premiums, as well as Republican efforts to cut Medicaid and Medicare spending. Similarly, for managed care and hospitals, a split government prevents Democrats from advancing "Medicare for All" initiatives that could eliminate health insurance fees, while also blocking Republican attempts to dismantle the Affordable Care Act. The author concludes with an open question regarding what the midterm results portend for the 2020 Presidential election, promising to address this topic in the upcoming December holiday publication.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the historical trends, composition, and relative performance of US buyout investing. Michael Cembalest argues that while buyouts have historically been volatile but rewarding, their outperformance has declined since the 1990s. This decline is attributed to strong S&P 500 returns—specifically a 14% annualized return since January 2009—and increased competition among buyout funds. 

The analysis features four charts and one table to illustrate these dynamics. The first chart displays US buyout fund performance by vintage year from 1984 to 2014, showing the Public Market Equivalent (PME) ratio for the average manager against the S&P 500. Both median and asset-weighted performances historically exceeded a PME of 1.0 (indicating outperformance), with major peaks in the late 1980s and late 1990s, though they have converged closer to 1.0 in more recent vintages. The second chart details the distribution of US leveraged buyouts by transaction volume from 2002 to the first half of 2018. It shows that sponsor-to-sponsor transactions have grown significantly to make up more than half of overall transaction volume in recent years, while public-to-private deals, corporate division divestitures, and other transaction types make up the remainder.

A third chart examines buyout performance against alternative benchmarks from 1984 to 2010, including the Russell 2000, the Russell 2000 Value, and a leveraged S&P 500 with a beta of 1.5. This visual demonstrates that while buyout outperformance is highest compared to the standard S&P 500, it is modestly lower when evaluated against these more leveraged small- and mid-cap indices. An accompanying table compares the underlying characteristics of the Russell 2000 and the S&P 500, showing that the Russell 2000 has a much smaller median market cap of $0.8 billion compared to $21.1 billion for the S&P 500, alongside considerably higher leverage; 24% of the Russell 2000 has a Debt/EBIT ratio greater than 12x, and 21% has negative EBIT. Finally, a fourth chart measures the dispersion of US buyout fund performance by quartile from 1994 to 2010. This chart highlights a significant narrowing of the performance gap over time, as first-quartile performance fell from a PME of around 2.5 in the mid-1990s to just above 1.0 by 2010, while last-quartile performance hovered consistently below 1.0.

This page presents several observations on private equity performance, highlighting that excess returns are not always driven by improved operations, while also discussing issues of illiquidity, secondary market discounts, and overstated risk-adjusted returns.

The author begins by noting that while buyout funds have historically generated excess returns compared to public markets, these gains often stem from financial factors rather than operational improvements. To illustrate this, the first chart shows how, for the 2010-2011 vintage years, multiple expansion made up for a significant shortfall in margin expansion relative to the original deal model. The stacked bar chart, which measures multiple on invested capital improvement or decline, displays a negative margin shortfall extending to about negative 0.3x, which is offset by a very small sliver of positive revenue growth and a massive block of multiple expansion reaching up to around 0.7x. 

Another key observation is the illiquidity of private equity, which requires a premium to compensate investors, particularly when considering the steep discounts seen in the secondary markets. The second chart tracks the average secondary market pricing for private equity limited partner positions as a percentage of net asset value from 2007 through 2016. In 2007, both buyout and venture positions priced near 100% of net asset value. During the 2008–2009 financial crisis, buyout pricing plummeted to nearly 60% before recovering to between 90% and 95% by 2016. Venture pricing fell to around 65% during the downturn and recovered much more slowly, remaining at a persistent discount of around 75% to 80% by 2016. 

Additionally, the text notes that venture capital shows a greater persistence of individual manager outperformance than buyout, and there is minimal dispersion in buyout public market equivalents over time based on fund size. Finally, the author discusses how stale pricing of limited partner net asset values overstates risk-adjusted returns. Applying de-smoothing techniques to estimate actual private equity volatility significantly impacts portfolio construction. Specifically, for a projected 10% absolute return, correcting for stale pricing reduces the optimal private equity allocation in a traditional mean-variance model from 20% down to 14%.

This page analyzes the measurement and composition of global private equity dry powder, noting that estimates range widely from $500 billion (usually representing buyout funds only) to $1.5 trillion (encompassing all private equity categories). The author argues that current dry powder levels exceed those of 2008 and 2009, with the capital heavily concentrated among the largest managers and originating from recent vintage years. However, these figures may be overstated by an estimated $350 to $400 billion in outstanding subscription loans used by managers to temporarily boost internal rates of return (IRRs). While Cambridge Associates estimates that subscription loans can theoretically boost IRRs by 3% per year, data from the Institutional Limited Partners Association points to a median IRR impact of no more than 0.45%. Industry surveys highlight the popularity of these loans, with 87% of respondents at a 2018 CFO and COO forum indicating they use or plan to use them. Conversely, dry powder may be understated because estimates typically exclude separate accounts not invested in commingled limited partnership vehicles.

Three charts illustrate these trends. The first, a stacked bar chart of global dry powder by category from 2003 to 2017 using Bain data, shows total dry powder rising from roughly $0.4 trillion to nearly $1.7 trillion. Buyouts consistently represent the largest share of this capital, followed by real estate, venture capital, private credit, and other categories like infrastructure and distressed private equity. 

The second chart, based on Pitchbook data, depicts US dollar billions of dry powder by vintage year (from 2010 to 2017) and fund size. It illustrates a dramatic concentration of capital in the largest funds, particularly in the 2017 vintage year, where total dry powder approaches $320 billion. In that year, mega-funds of $5 billion or larger account for more than half of the total, with the next largest category being funds sized between $1 billion and $4.99 billion. 

The final chart shows current dry powder stacked by vintage year, totaling around $900 billion. This visualization highlights that the vast majority of current dry powder is concentrated in recent vintages, with the 2017 and 2016 vintages commanding the largest shares of the total outstanding capital, while older vintages from 2010 through 2014 represent only a small fraction of the remaining dry powder.

This page analyzes the historical performance of venture capital (VC) funds relative to public equity markets, observing that while VC experienced massive outperformance in the late 1990s, the average manager has since closely tracked public benchmarks. Additionally, the author highlights the high importance of manager selection in private equity, noting that the performance gap between top-quartile and bottom-quartile managers is particularly pronounced in venture capital compared to buyout funds.

The first chart, titled US Venture Capital fund performance by vintage year, displays the Public Market Equivalent (PME) ratio for the average VC manager against the S&P 500 for vintages from 1984 to 2014. It plots both median and asset-weighted performances, showing a dramatic spike in the late 1990s that reached three to four times the benchmark, after which both measures fell to hover near the 1.0 parity line. The second chart, Venture capital performance vs different benchmarks, presents the PME of the average US VC fund against the S&P 500, a leveraged S&P 500 with a beta of 1.5, the Russell 2000, and the Russell 2000 Growth. Similar to the first chart, a massive spike of three to five times is visible in the late 1990s, but for vintages after 2000, the performance under all benchmarks converges closely to 1.0.

The third chart, US Venture Capital fund performance by quartile, compares the average S&P 500-based PME of first-quartile and last-quartile VC managers from 1994 to 2010. The first-quartile managers experienced a peak of nine to ten times outperformance in the late 1990s and have remained above 1.5 in the subsequent decade, while last-quartile managers remained consistently below the 1.0 parity line. Finally, the fourth chart, The importance of picking the right manager, maps the PME spread between the first and last quartiles for both venture and buyout funds. The spread for venture capital peaked sharply in the late 1990s at nearly 3.0 and has since stabilized between 1.0 and 2.0, while the buyout spread has hovered more steadily between 1.0 and 1.5. The text notes that a PME gap of 1.0 is highly significant, representing the difference between a 2.0x and 0.9x multiple on invested capital, or a 20% versus 0% internal rate of return.

This page explores private equity fundraising dynamics and examines conflicting evidence regarding whether the pace of capital deployment has slowed down. To set the stage, the page highlights strong 2017 fundraising data from Bain & Company, noting that over two-thirds of private equity funds closed that year met or exceeded their targets, and forty percent closed in under a year.
