The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that the clearest example of central bank intervention driving up asset prices is the European Central Bank, whose purchases of sovereign and corporate bonds have exceeded the actual amounts issued by Eurozone governments and companies. This financial repression pushed a significant portion of Eurozone government bonds into negative yield territory and spurred extreme risk-taking. 

This distortion is visualized in a pair of bar charts titled "ECB sovereign and corporate purchases vs issuance" in billions of Euros. The first chart shows that ECB corporate bond purchases under the Corporate Sector Purchase Programme reached approximately 175 billion EUR, surpassing the estimated Eurozone term corporate debt issuance of about 140 billion EUR. The second chart reveals an even larger gap for sovereign bonds under the Public Sector Purchase Programme, where ECB purchases reached roughly 1.8 trillion EUR, far exceeding the Eurozone sovereign issuance of approximately 1.0 trillion EUR.

This heavy intervention led to extreme market pricing, shown in a chart titled "The strange pricing of Italian high yield bonds." This area chart tracks the face value of Italian BB-rated high-yield bonds from 2005 to 2018, showing the portion trading with yields lower than US Treasuries in blue and those with yields higher than US Treasuries in grey. By late 2017 and early 2018, almost the entire outstanding face value of these Italian high-yield bonds, totaling around 30 to 35 billion EUR, was trading at a lower yield than US Treasuries. The author highlights this as one of the single biggest fixed-income distortions of his 31-year career.

As a result of this prolonged financial repression, investor allocations to cash plummeted to historic lows, as illustrated in the line chart "Investor allocations to cash fell to record lows by 2016." Tracking data from 1980 to 2018, the chart shows that household cash allocations dropped from over 50% in 1980 to about 15% in 2016. During the same period, pension fund cash holdings fell to around 8%, and non-US investor cash allocations bottomed out near 4% in 2016. This trend is now reversing as US policy rates rise and investors take profits, resulting in a record 32 billion USD outflow from active US equity mutual funds in the week ending December 18, 2018.

This shift has caused equity valuations to contract sharply. The final chart, "Eurozone multiples collapse as earnings growth slows," compares the 12-month forward P/E ratio and the 12-month forward earnings per share (EPS) in Euros from December 2016 to December 2018. It shows that while Eurozone forward EPS rose steadily from around 230 EUR to a peak of roughly 270 EUR in mid-2018 before dipping slightly to 265 EUR, the forward P/E multiple collapsed from a peak of nearly 14.5x in late 2017 to under 11.5x by December 2018. The author notes that this dramatic decline in P/E multiples despite resilient earnings expectations is a global phenomenon, mirrored in the United States, China, and Japan.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication presents an executive summary analyzing the Trump administration's impact on financial markets by drawing historical parallels with past U.S. presidents. The author argues that while market-positive impacts peaked in 2017, negative policy consequences began in 2018 and will likely persist. High investor anxiety is tied to unprecedented senior-level turnover and policy choices described as disruptive.

A central reference table titled "Elements of Trumpism for Investors" features portraits of six historical presidents, associating specific Trump-era policy elements with their presidencies. Andrew Jackson is linked to anti-globalization and loyalty-based political patronage. Herbert Hoover represents tariffs, trade wars, and the deportation of undocumented workers. John F. Kennedy represents economic re-engineering that triggers bear markets, along with attacks on individual companies. Richard Nixon is associated with the bullying of the Federal Reserve Chairman, political scandals, and constitutional risks. Ronald Reagan represents deregulation, tax cuts, and government shutdowns. Lastly, George W. Bush represents large fiscal deficits outside of a recession and conservative court appointments.

The lower half of the page details these historical parallels. Under anti-globalization, the author compares Trump's foreign policy shift to Jackson's isolationist stance, where the country wants to be left alone but will fight aggressively if attacked. Regarding tariffs, the text warns that if all proposed tariffs are implemented, U.S. tariff rates could surge from 1.5% to 10%—the largest rise in fifty years—encompassing taxes on Chinese imports and automotive imports from Europe and Japan. 

The text also draws a parallel between Trump’s public attacks on private corporations—such as Amazon, Comcast, Boeing, Delta, ESPN, GM, Lockheed Martin, Merck, Nordstrom, Toyota, and the Washington Post—and JFK’s April 1962 intervention against US Steel, which initiated a severe 20% bear market as investor confidence deteriorated. Finally, the author compares Trump's direct questioning of the Federal Reserve's leadership to Nixon's pressure on Arthur Burns. The text warns that undermining central bank independence threatens investor confidence, citing the single-digit price-to-earnings multiples in Turkey and Argentina as modern examples of the damage caused by autocratic interference in monetary policy.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2019 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the Q4 2018 market selloff and its implications for valuations and future returns. Cembalest observes that while the sharp decline in late 2018 pushed valuations below their historical medians, the path forward for 2019 remains constrained by major headwinds, including central bank quantitative tightening, the unorthodox policies of the Trump administration, and ongoing trade tensions with China. Consequently, J.P. Morgan forecasts volatile, single-digit returns for diversified stock and bond portfolios in 2019, noting that any substantial upside is likely contingent on a trade deal with China.

An introductory table details the correction by comparing peak 2018 levels with year-end positions across five asset classes. US equities, represented by the S&P 500 forward P/E, fell from a peak of 18.5 (the 86th historical percentile) to 14.3 (the 42nd percentile). European equities, tracked via the Stoxx 600 forward P/E, dropped from a peak of 15.1 (91st percentile) to 12.0 (34th percentile), while emerging market equities, measured by the MSCI EM forward P/E, decreased from 13.2 (59th percentile) to 10.3 (18th percentile). In credit markets, US High Yield spreads widened from a peak tightness of 305 basis points (the 89th percentile) to 534 basis points (the 35th percentile), and US Investment Grade spreads expanded from 108 basis points (89th percentile) to 182 basis points (35th percentile). 

To contextualize this selloff, the first chart, titled "S&P 500 returns after P/E ratio declines of 20%+", displays the subsequent 12-month returns after twenty historical valuation contractions since the 1920s. Although severe post-contraction declines occurred following November 1929, October 1931, and April 1937, fifteen of the twenty episodes resulted in positive returns over the subsequent year. Since 1950, subsequent 12-month returns have averaged roughly 12%, suggesting that historical precedents favor a market rebound.

The final visual, "Short interest in S&P similar to levels before 2016 correction," comprises two panels showing the relationship between S&P ETF short interest and the S&P 500 index. The first panel, spanning November 2015 to November 2016, shows short interest peaking above 5% as the S&P 500 index bottomed near 1,850 before subsequently rebounding. The second panel, covering June to November 2018, demonstrates a highly similar pattern, with short interest surging back toward 5% as the S&P 500 fell toward 2,400. Cembalest highlights this surge to suggest that thin year-end markets could be ripe for a short-covering rally.

This page presents an executive summary from Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan, analyzing key policy, regulatory, and political dynamics under the Trump administration heading into 2019. It begins by highlighting deregulation efforts, noting that the Federal Register expanded by its lowest number of new pages since 1992 in 2017, a rate 25% below the 2009 to 2016 average. Consequently, the NFIB small business survey showed that "Regulation and Red Tape" dropped from the top concern in 2014 to the third-largest problem, trailing labor quality and taxes. 

In terms of fiscal policy, the author describes the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act as the fourth-largest tax cut relative to GDP since 1950, which successfully brought US corporate marginal effective tax rates from the highest in the OECD to below the median. While highlighting bipartisan interest in territorial tax systems—dating back to President Obama’s 2010 Bipartisan Fiscal Commission—the author notes a lack of consensus on personal tax cuts and remarks that Trump’s campaign pledge to fund infrastructure using taxes on non-repatriated offshore earnings was not realized. Additionally, the summary warns of unusually large fiscal deficits during a period of full employment. The US deficit stood at 3.8% in 2018 and is projected by the Congressional Budget Office to rise to 4.6% in 2019. 

The summary also critiques several administrative actions, citing the proposal of Trump's personal pilot to head the Federal Aviation Administration as an example of loyalty-based political patronage. On immigration, Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests of non-criminal undocumented immigrants surged by 171% in 2017 compared to 2016. The author contrasts this restrictive immigration policy, which exacerbates labor shortages and wage inflation during full employment, with historical deportations under Herbert Hoover in the 1930s when unemployment was far higher. The text suggests that pursuing restrictive immigration while simultaneously criticizing the Federal Reserve for raising interest rates is economically inconsistent. 

Finally, the page addresses historical and institutional precedents. It draws parallels between modern political scandals and Richard Nixon’s 1973 Saturday Night Massacre, which sparked a sudden 15% drop in US equity markets amidst a larger S&P 500 selloff driven by stagflation. It notes that government shutdowns for policy leverage were popularized during Ronald Reagan's presidency, and points out that 80% of Trump’s federal judicial nominees have ties to the conservative Federalist Society, a strategy similar to the judicial appointment patterns of George W. Bush. The page concludes with a recommendation to read J.P. Morgan's 2018 holiday piece regarding the highly polarized political choices facing voters in the upcoming 2020 election.

This J.P. Morgan Eye on the Market page, written by Michael Cembalest as part of the 2019 Outlook, serves as an executive summary that contextualizes the late 2018 market selloff within historical market cycles. Cembalest argues that GDP and corporate profits often continue to grow even after asset prices peak, suggesting that the September 2018 peak will likely mirror historical precedents where economic growth outlasted the equity market top. 

To support this observation, the page features a table titled "Asset prices tend to peak before growth/profits" which details historical market peaks. For the five cycles prior to 2000, equity peaks in January 1966, November 1968, December 1972, November 1980, and August 1987 saw negative S&P 500 returns over the subsequent 12 months, ranging from negative 7% to negative 19%. However, in all five cases, economic data did not peak for another 9 to 19 months, and corporate earnings grew by 2% to 41% over the following year. For the September 2018 peak, the next 12-month S&P 500 return was negative 15%, with the subsequent economic peak and earnings growth figures left as open questions. In contrast, the market peaks of August 2000 and October 2007 were exceptions, where economic peaks occurred within 1 to 4 months and earnings declined by 16% and 23% respectively over the next year.

Looking forward, Cembalest reflects on the historic bull run from March 2009 to December 2018, during which the S&P 500 delivered a 13% annualized price return—a feat matched only three times in the post-war era, specifically in 1959, 1992, and the late 1990s. For 2019, he forecasts modestly positive returns post-correction and advises investors to hold plenty of liquidity, especially since US cash is poised to yield a positive real return. He also suggests looking at Emerging Markets, citing their highly attractive valuations, particularly if there is a cease-fire in the US-China trade war.

The page concludes with a table of contents outlining the rest of the report, highlighting upcoming coverage on the United States, Europe, China, Japan, and a ten-year retrospective on the financial crisis. This retrospective promises to analyze critical points such as the hijacking of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac balance sheets, broker-dealer deregulation, the implosion of bond reinsurers, and systemic risk.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan "2019 Outlook" argues that United States households are in a much stronger financial position than they were a decade prior, though an acute labor shortage in the construction sector poses a risk of wage inflation that could prompt the Federal Reserve to continue raising rates in 2019. 

The first chart, "Homeowners' equity above pre-crisis levels," shows that US household equity in trillions of dollars has fully recovered from the Great Recession. Equity peaked near thirteen trillion dollars in 2006, bottomed out at six trillion dollars during the 2009–2011 period, and has since steadily risen to surpass fifteen trillion dollars by late 2018. 

The second chart, "Household debt," displays two trends as a percentage of disposable income from 1980 through 2018. The household debt line peaked near one hundred and thirty percent in 2008 and has steadily declined to approximately one hundred percent. Concurrently, the debt service ratio, which peaked above thirteen percent before the recession, has fallen to around ten percent, indicating a much lighter debt burden for consumers.

The third chart, "Signs of a healthy US labor market," illustrates a strong job market using a three-month moving average from 2001 to late 2018. The firing rate spiked to two point five percent during the financial crisis but has since dropped to a low of one point three percent. Meanwhile, the voluntary quit rate, which bottomed out at one point one percent during the recession, has risen back to around one point eight percent, reflecting worker confidence in finding alternative employment.

The fourth chart, "Sharp upward revision in US savings rate," tracks the personal savings rate on a three-month moving average from 1990 to 2018. It highlights a massive upward data revision by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). While the pre-revision data suggested that the savings rate had declined to nearly three percent by 2018, the post-revision line reveals that the savings rate actually remained robust at around seven to eight percent.

The final chart shows the "Job openings rate: construction" from 2001 to late 2018. The construction job openings rate has risen dramatically to nearly four percent, marking its highest level in twenty years. An accompanying commentary warns that this shortage could intensify if the Trump administration successfully terminates the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) program in 2019 or 2020. This policy change, though currently blocked in federal courts, would impact three hundred thousand Central American workers. The analysis notes that these workers primarily reside and work in Florida, Texas, and California—three states facing critical rebuilding efforts following recent hurricanes, floods, and wildfires.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2019 Outlook presents a balanced view of the United States economy, highlighting strong late-2018 indicators while cautioning that growth is likely to slow in the coming year. The author outlines several positive economic developments, including expansionary business surveys with PMI readings at their strongest levels since 1978, high holiday retail sales, peak consumer and small business confidence, and rising wages. However, rising interest rates and the fading effects of fiscal tax cuts are expected to act as headwinds. Consequently, J.P. Morgan forecasts that US GDP growth will decelerate from 3.40% in Q3 2018 to 2.25% by the end of 2019, with early estimates for Q4 2018 already cooling to 2.60%. Emerging soft spots are noted in housing, capital spending surveys, and new orders.

The first chart, titled "Small business and consumer confidence surging," plots a three-month moving average of two indices from 1975 to late 2018. On the left axis, small business optimism is tracked from index levels of 60 to 140, while the right axis tracks personal finances sentiment from 75 to 115. Both curves show a dramatic multi-year recovery following the 2008 financial crisis, with both indicators hovering near historic highs by November 2018. 

The next chart, "Wages picking up," details wage acceleration from 2000 to Q3 2018. It measures year-over-year private sector wage growth on the left axis from 1.0% to 4.0% alongside the percentage of companies reporting higher wages on a four-quarter moving average on the right axis from 10% to 50%. The visual displays a steady upward trend, with private sector wage growth climbing past 3.0% and the share of companies reporting higher wages surging toward the 50% mark, indicating strong wage pressure.

The final two charts point to signs of economic moderation. "US core capital goods" displays the rolling three-month percentage change for orders and shipments from 2014 to late 2018. Both indicators peaked in late 2017 with growth rates above 4% but have since trended downward, with both orders and shipments registering around 2% by November 2018. Adjacent to this, the chart "US business surveys rolling over from high levels" tracks expected growth in capital spending over the next 12 months on the left axis from -15% to 15% alongside ISM new orders on the right axis from index levels of 30 to 70. Running from 2000 to late 2018, this visual shows that while ISM new orders remain above the expansionary threshold of 50, both capital spending expectations and new orders have begun to roll over from their cyclical highs. Data sources across these charts include the National Federation of Independent Business, the University of Michigan, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the National Association for Business Economics, the Census Bureau, the Duke CFO Survey, and the Institute for Supply Management.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication, written by Michael Cembalest, outlines two primary macroeconomic headwinds for the United States economy heading into 2019: rising interest rates and escalating trade tariffs. 

The first section addresses interest rates and their cooling effect on the housing market. The author notes that housing is already showing signs of slowing down after a modest half-percent increase in mortgage rates. A major headwind is that the average homeowner no longer has an "in the money" option to move, as prevailing mortgage rates have surpassed the average outstanding mortgage rate owed. While housing and autos are transitioning from positive growth contributors to minor negative ones, the author expects only a modest housing downturn due to excess household formation and pent-up demand from young adults. This is illustrated in a bar chart titled "Housing measures declining as rates rise," which tracks year-over-year percentage changes across eight housing indicators during three periods: 2017, the first half of 2018, and September–November 2018. The chart highlights a sharp deceleration across almost all categories; for instance, housing affordability drops to nearly negative nine percent year-over-year in late 2018, while single-unit building permits flatten to zero percent growth and the Mortgage Bankers Association purchase index edges down to negative 0.1 percent.

The second section addresses the threat of tariffs. The author warns that if the full range of proposed tariffs is implemented, US consumer price inflation could rise faster than anticipated. If a deal is reached, the impact remains small, but further escalations could represent the largest globalization rollback in fifty years. To contextualize this, a line chart titled "A century of globalization: US import tariffs, 1900-2018" tracks the historical US tariff rate on total imports. The chart shows a steep decline from nearly twenty percent in the early twentieth century down to historical lows, but notes a potential upward spike represented by five distinct tariff actions: the first three already imposed (including washing machines, solar, steel/aluminum, and early China Section 301 tariffs) and the final two proposed (a 25 percent tariff on $460 billion of Chinese imports under Section 301, and a 25 percent tariff on $290 billion of automotive imports under Section 232).

To demonstrate who will bear the burden of further escalation, the bar chart "Consumer products would be hit by next round of tariffs" breaks down US imports from China by economic category across three tariff rounds. While Round 1 ($50 billion) and Round 2 ($200 billion) primarily targeted capital and intermediate goods, the proposed Round 3 ($267 billion) consists almost entirely of capital goods (valued at roughly $120 billion) and consumer goods (valued at over $100 billion), pointing to a direct hit on the US consumer.

Finally, the chart "US tariffs on China as a share of selected measures" demonstrates that while total tariffs appear negligible when measured as a share of overall US GDP, consumer spending, or S&P 500 earnings (all registering well below two percent), the impact is highly concentrated. When viewing relevant tariffs as a share of affected companies' earnings by industry, the burden rises dramatically to approximately eleven percent for industrial capital goods and nearly thirteen percent for technology hardware. The page also references White House National Trade Council head Peter Navarro and his book "Death by China: Confronting the Dragon – A global call to action."

This page highlights the growing, longer-dated risks associated with US corporate debt. The author argues that while US household debt remains low by historical standards, corporate debt relative to equity and cash flow is nearing record highs. Although the median debt-to-EBITDA ratio hovers around 2.0x, this median obscures a wide and worrying leverage distribution across the corporate universe. 

The first chart, titled Corporate Debt, tracks the largest 1,500 stocks from 1974 to 2016 to show two rising leverage metrics. On the left axis, the median net debt to equity ratio (ranging from 0.15x to 0.55x) has climbed back toward 0.45x. On the right axis, median net debt to EBITDA (ranging from 0.6x to 2.2x) has spiked to nearly 2.0x, approaching historical highs. 

To reveal the underlying distribution, the second chart, Distribution of Leverage at Small and Large Cap Companies, displays the percentage of equity index market cap across various net debt-to-EBITDA categories for the Russell 2000 (small cap) and S&P 500 (large cap). While over 40% of S&P 500 companies sit comfortably in the 0-to-3 leverage range, a significant portion of the Russell 2000 is heavily leveraged. Nearly 15% of Russell 2000 companies have negative EBITDA, and another substantial portion falls into the extremely high leverage categories of 6-to-12 and 12-plus. The author notes that 50% of US and European BBB-rated issuers now have higher leverage than the BB average.

The third chart, S&P 500 Debt Service Ratio, plots the median company's interest expense as a share of operating income from 1990 to 2018 on a scale from 10% to 30%. Debt service burdens bottomed out near 13% around 2014 but have since ticked up toward 15%. As corporate debt reprices at higher yields, the author projects that rising debt service will gradually pinch highly leveraged sectors like consumer staples, telecommunications, and utilities.

The final chart, High Yield Default Rates Low Despite Sharp Rise in Debt, illustrates an unusual decoupling between corporate leverage and defaults from 1987 to 2018. It overlays debt-to-GDP for non-financial companies (left axis, 38% to 47%) with the high-yield default rate (right axis, 0% to 12%). While non-financial debt-to-GDP has surged to a record high of nearly 47%, the high-yield default rate has remained exceptionally low, hovering between 2% and 3%. The author attributes this disconnect to easy money policies from central banks that have sustained artificial demand for high-yield debt, warning that this protective gap is unlikely to last forever.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes US sectors that appear oversold—specifically technology, banking, and mining—while detailing the regulatory clouds hovering over the healthcare sector. The author argues that tech valuations, bank multiples, and mining stock prices are heavily depressed, pricing in severe macroeconomic risks, whereas Democratic healthcare proposals present significant regulatory uncertainty for pharma and biotech investors in 2019.

The first chart, "FAANG premium to the market," traces the average forward P/E ratio of FAANG stocks (defined as Facebook, Amazon, Apple, Netflix, and Google) relative to the S&P 500 from June 2012 to late December 2018. It shows that FAANG premiums have collapsed from peak levels above 3.4x down to near historical lows around 2.0x.

The second chart, "Tech P/E ratios relative to the market at cycle peaks," uses a bar chart comparing historical peaks from July 1953 to mid-December 2018. It demonstrates that the tech sector traded at only about 1.4x relative to the market in mid-December 2018, which is far below the dot-com bubble peak of 2.4x in March 2000 and lower than almost all other historical cycle peaks.

The third chart, "Bank P/E ratios relative to the market at cycle peaks," compares banking sector valuations across historical cycle peaks. By mid-December 2018, bank valuations relative to the market dropped to approximately 0.5x, which is similar to levels that preceded the financial crisis, though the author notes systemic risks are much lower now. 

The fourth chart, "Metals/Mining: price to sales relative to the market," presents a long-term line chart from 1952 to 2018. It indicates that metals and mining stocks are trading at deeply depressed price-to-sales ratios relative to the market (near 0.4x). The author attributes this to secular and cyclical slowdowns in China, alongside market expectations of a global recession in 2019 and an unfavorable resolution to the US-China trade war.

Lastly, the page discusses political risks within the healthcare sector, listing several Democratic proposals aimed at controlling drug pricing. Although their support in the Senate or White House remains unclear, the author suggests some measures may pass in 2019. These proposed reforms include implementing price controls on drug "gouging," increasing Medicaid rebates, allowing "dual eligible" drugs to be purchased at lower Medicaid pricing, reducing biologic patent exclusivity from 12 years to 7 years, allowing direct government negotiation of drug prices, capping monthly out-of-pocket costs at $250, establishing an independent price-tracking board, reducing Medicare Part B drug prices, limiting tax deductions for advertising, requiring FDA pre-approval for ads, requiring development cost disclosures, and allowing drug re-importation.

This page analyzes US stock market valuations and corporate earnings growth heading into 2019. The main argument is that while US earnings growth is expected to continue in 2019, it will decelerate significantly from the rapid pace of 2018, which was boosted by federal tax cuts and stronger global growth. Additionally, rising interest rates present a headwind for value sectors such as financials, staples, and healthcare. Although a market correction in late 2018 helped compress multiples, many valuation measures remain higher than their historical averages. 

A line chart titled Consensus S&P 500 Earnings Growth tracks the year-over-year percentage change in expected earnings per share for 2018 and 2019, measured from August 2017 to August 2018. It shows that while consensus expectations for 2018 earnings rose dramatically from around 11% to over 20%, expectations for 2019 earnings remained much flatter, tracking near 8% to 10% by late 2018. 

To illustrate how interest rates pressure value equities, a dual-axis chart titled Rising Rates Lead Weaker Value Sector Earnings tracks the percentage of S&P value stocks with positive revisions against the two-year change in the 10-year US Treasury yield, which is advanced 18 months and inverted. Spanning 2006 to 2019, the closely correlated lines show that rising Treasury yields historically precede a contraction in the percentage of value stocks receiving positive earnings revisions. 

A detailed table of S&P 500 Valuation Metrics as of December 21, 2018, compares current valuations to their historical percentiles since 1976. It shows that many metrics remain elevated, with a median metric in the 70th percentile. Specific figures include US market cap to GDP at 164% (88th percentile), Enterprise Value to Sales at 2.0x (87th percentile), Cyclically Adjusted P/E at 24.0x (81st percentile), Price to Book at 2.9x (70th percentile), and Enterprise Value to EBITDA at 10.1x (69th percentile). In contrast, the forward P/E of 14.3x sits closer to the historical average at the 56th percentile, while the free cash flow yield of 5.1% and the S&P earnings yield minus the 10-year US Treasury of 422 basis points sit in the 20th and 18th percentiles, respectively. 

Another chart, US Valuation Measures, displays deviations from long-term averages for three major asset classes from 1950 to late 2018: the S&P 500 forward P/E ratio, home prices, and commercial real estate prices. The data shows that while the equity forward P/E ratio has pulled back toward its historical average, home prices and commercial real estate prices remain significantly elevated relative to their long-term means. 

Footnotes on the page explain that these historical percentiles are sensitive to start dates, noting that shifting the historical baseline from 1976 to 1985 lowers the forward P/E percentile from the 56th to the 42nd. Additionally, the author notes that the low percentile for free cash flow yield is partly due to a structural post-2002 decline in capital spending intensity, with S&P 500 capital expenditures as a percentage of cash flow from operations averaging only 40% to 50% since 2002 compared to 60% to 80% before 2002. Data sources cited include J.P. Morgan Equity Strategy, Cornerstone, Bloomberg, Goldman Sachs Investment Research, the Federal Reserve, Shiller, and Datastream.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, focuses on the rising risks within the United States credit markets. The central argument is that central bank security purchases of fourteen trillion dollars since 2009 drove down interest rates, sparking massive growth in both the issuance and demand for corporate debt. However, this trend coincided with the introduction of the Volcker Rule in the US, which suppressed proprietary trading and market making. Consequently, a massive expansion in fixed-income supply took place alongside a collapse in fixed-income liquidity, creating a fragile environment should investors decide to exit. 

To illustrate the liquidity mismatch, the first chart, titled Debt stock expanding while liquidity shrinks, compares the change in market size and turnover from 2006 to 2017 across various debt categories. It shows that while the debt stock for US Treasuries and Investment Grade corporate bonds expanded by more than 200 percent and approximately 180 percent respectively, their turnover ratios collapsed by roughly 50 percent and 40 percent. High-yield debt stock also expanded by over 100 percent alongside a modest decline in turnover, while mortgage debt stock remained flat but suffered a significant decline in turnover.

The second visual, BBB rated bonds take over post-crisis, demonstrates how lower-rated credit has come to dominate the US investment-grade corporate bond index. Comparing December 2007 to December 2018, the share of lower-tier investment-grade bonds—specifically BBB1, BBB2, and BBB3—grew significantly, with BBB1 rising from around 12 percent to more than 16 percent. Conversely, the shares of higher-quality cohorts like AAA, AA1, AA2, and AA3 all shrank, with AAA bonds falling to less than 2 percent of the index.

The third chart, Highest rated corporate bonds squeezed out by BBBs, measures Single A or better bonds as a percentage of total investment-grade supply. It reveals that in 2017, the share of higher-rated bonds fell to about 48 percent in the US and to just 30 percent in Europe. In both regions, these 2017 levels sat at the absolute bottom or below their historical 2008 to 2017 ranges, indicating a global shift toward lower-quality corporate credit.

The final chart, Rise in US corporate borrowing costs, displays the ratio of US BBB yields to their trailing five-year average from 1925 to late 2018, with shaded grey bars indicating historical recessions. The chart demonstrates that BBB yields spike relative to their five-year trend during periods of economic distress. Recently, BBB yields have widened by their largest margin versus trend since the 1980s, excluding the 2008 financial crisis, indicating a sharp and sudden increase in borrowing costs for US corporates.

In this section of the J.P. Morgan Outlook, Michael Cembalest argues that US equities are poised to continue outperforming European and Japanese equities, as they have done for most of the past three decades. He points out that while European equities rose by 62% since December 2011, largely driven by trillions of Euros in ECB intervention, the S&P 500 outperformed them with a 116% return over the same period. For 2019, Cembalest forecasts that this outperformance streak will likely continue, driven by weakening European earnings revisions and slowing economic growth in France and Italy back to around 1%. 

The first chart, titled "US outperformed for most of the last 30 years," displays the three-year rolling out- or under-performance of an equity portfolio—which is 15% overweighted to the US, 10% underweighted to Europe, and 5% underweighted to Japan—against the MSCI All World Index from 1991 to 2018. The chart illustrates that this US-overweight strategy generated positive returns for almost the entire thirty-year timeframe, climbing as high as 13% in the late 1990s and consistently hovering around 5% in the 2010s. The single major exception was a period of underperformance during the mid-2000s Southern European growth boom, which bottomed out around negative 7% in 2006. 

The second chart, titled "Europe: P/E discount vs the US is par for the course," shows the forward price-to-earnings discount of the Stoxx 600 relative to the S&P 500 from 2006 to 2018. The P/E discount has consistently remained in negative territory, fluctuating between roughly negative 10% and negative 25%. It hit its lowest level of nearly negative 28% during the financial crisis in late 2008 and sat near negative 20% at the end of 2018, illustrating that a deep valuation discount is typical rather than a signal for imminent European outperformance. 

Additional commentary notes that this discount persists even when adjusting for sector weights, refuting the idea that US outperformance is solely a byproduct of its larger technology sector. Instead, US outperformance vs Europe looks identical since 2010 regardless of whether market cap-weighted or sector-neutral indices are used, showing that US firms also outperformed in the financials, consumer discretionary, and energy sectors. Pre-2006 data is noted as being excluded from the valuation comparison due to historical differences in European goodwill amortization rules that distort earlier P/E comparisons.

This page of J.P. Morgan's 2019 Outlook provides an overview of non-US markets, arguing that while global growth was synchronized a year prior, indicators outside the United States have since softened significantly. The author highlights disappointing economic data from Europe and notes that the European Central Bank has very limited capacity to respond to negative growth surprises. This is because Eurozone short-term interest rates are already negative, and the ECB already owns 20% to 30% of many Eurozone government bonds, bringing it close to its self-imposed 33% holding limit. Compounding this challenge, the private sector only owns 20% to 25% of German and Dutch government bonds. These constraints, along with rising wages and home prices in Germany, lead the authors to prefer Emerging Markets over Europe as a deep-value investment option for 2019.

Four charts support this analysis. The first chart, titled US growth holding up better than Rest of World, compares US and Global manufacturing PMI surveys from 2013 to 2018. It reveals that while the US PMI remained robust at around 57 late in 2018, the Global PMI declined steadily from its late 2017 peak of approximately 54.5 down toward 52, confirming weaker external conditions. The second chart, Earnings revisions, tracks the net percentage of positive minus negative revisions for three regions from 2010 to 2018 using a three-month moving average. S&P 500 earnings revisions spiked to nearly 35% in early 2018 before falling sharply, while European revisions dipped below zero to around negative 10%, and China Offshore revisions plunged deeply to nearly negative 30% by late 2018.

The third chart plots Global ex-US and ex-China business confidence as a standard deviation from its long-term average. It shows that after peaking at roughly 1.3 standard deviations above average in late 2017, business confidence fell precipitously in 2018, ending the year near 0.4 standard deviations. The final chart, German home prices and wages starting to heat up, displays year-over-year percentage changes from 2010 to 2018 for German economic metrics. It shows that house prices have experienced high growth, holding near 5% in 2018 after peaking at 6% in 2016. Hourly wages and unit labor costs have also trended upward, reaching approximately 3.5% and 3% respectively by late 2018, even as the GDP deflator and core CPI remained more subdued between 1% and 2%.

In this page from J.P. Morgan's 2019 Outlook, Michael Cembalest examines European economic history, the post-World War II recovery, and the structural challenges facing the modern Eurozone. The commentary begins with a discussion between the author and former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, who lamented a loss of vitality among contemporary European leaders compared to post-war giants like Konrad Adenauer. Cembalest poses an open question about whether the immense political and economic efforts required to maintain the Euro are currently adding to or subtracting from Europe's overall vitality.

To contextualize the scale of post-war reconstruction, the author presents a bar chart illustrating the ratio of 1960 per capita GDP compared to 1946 levels. This chart highlights the rapid economic recovery of devastated nations, led by Germany, where per capita GDP tripled, followed closely by Austria with a ratio over 3.0. Other nations also experienced substantial recoveries, with Taiwan and Japan near 2.7, Italy at approximately 2.4, and France at nearly 2.0.

Cembalest then pivots to the structural issues threatening the Euro today, presenting a second bar chart that compares economic efficiency scores on a scale where 100 is best. This index is based on goods and labor markets, innovation, corruption, legal frameworks, and investor protections. The data reveals a massive divergence within the Eurozone: Germany scores over 90, whereas Italy scores under 50. The author emphasizes that this efficiency gap is strikingly similar to the gap between the United States, which scores over 90, and Mexico, which scores around 36. This comparison suggests that Germany and Italy lack the shared economic foundations typical of a successful monetary union.

The page is anchored by two historical vignettes detailing the absolute devastation of the post-war era, contrasting the rapid recovery with its bleak starting point. The first text box, featuring recollections from historian Margaret MacMillan, describes a ruined Europe and Asia where major cities lay in rubble, millions survived on fewer than 1,000 calories a day, and the "four horsemen of the apocalypse" seemed to return to the modern world. The second text box features a personal letter written in August 1945 by the author's uncle, describing a ruined, starving Vienna under Russian military occupation, providing a stark reminder of the desperate conditions that preceded Europe's economic miracle.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication analyzes the economic challenges and lack of integration within the Eurozone, with a particular focus on the divergence between core and peripheral nations and the specific fiscal pressures facing Italy. 

The author begins by arguing that contrary to expectations, regional economic dispersions in Europe rose following the inception of the Euro, signaling reverse integration. This dynamic is illustrated in a chart titled "Death in Venice," which plots the Industrial Production Index for Germany, France, and Italy from 1980 through late 2018, indexed to December 31, 1999. While national economic cycles were highly synchronous before the Euro exchange rate was fixed, Germany's industrial production diverged sharply upward after 2005, reaching nearly 130 by 2018, whereas France remained flat near 100, and Italy fell significantly to around 80. Another chart, "German banks less willing to lend to periphery banks," tracks German outbound lending to Spain and Italy from 2005 to mid-2018. Lending peaked in 2008 at approximately $325 billion for Spain and $275 billion for Italy, before collapsing to below $100 billion for both countries by 2017, illustrating a severe pullback in regional credit integration.

The commentary then shifts to Italy's fragile economic state. Although a budget deal reached with Brussels eased immediate default concerns, the author warns that Italy's recession risk has actually increased because the deal relies on corporate tax hikes and cuts to infrastructure spending. This is particularly problematic given that Italy's infrastructure quality ranks near the bottom of the OECD, outperforming only Mexico and Poland. To demonstrate the financial market impact, two charts are presented. The first, "Italy: the cost of protecting against default," shows the Italian 5-year CDS contract price in basis points from 2010 through 2018. It compares the ISDA 2014 contract, which protects against default and any redenomination that reduces security value, with the older ISDA 2003 contract. After peaking during the Euro crisis in 2011–2012 at over 500 basis points, CDS prices spiked again in late 2018, with the ISDA 2014 contract rising to around 250 basis points. The second chart, "Foreign investors lose confidence in Italy, again," shows quarterly debt flows by non-Italian investors on an annualized basis in billions of Euros from 1996 to Q2 2018. In mid-2018, non-Italian investor flows plummeted to nearly negative 200 billion Euros, reminiscent of the sharp capital flight seen in 2011–2012.

Finally, the author looks at the broader political landscape, noting that German Chancellor Angela Merkel’s decision not to seek re-election in 2021, combined with disruptive labor strikes in France, severely dampens prospects for future fiscal integration or risk-pooling in the Eurozone. The author concludes that such fiscal integration is a necessary precursor to narrowing the persistent market valuation gap between Europe and the United States.

This page features J.P. Morgan's 2019 Outlook commentary on Brexit, presenting the views of London-based J.P. Morgan economist Malcolm Barr. Barr does not consider a second referendum to be the most likely outcome. Instead, he predicts that while the withdrawal agreement with the European Union will fail to pass the House of Commons on its first attempt in early January, it will eventually pass once other unpalatable options are exhausted. He anticipates another no-confidence vote, likely initiated by the Labour party, which Prime Minister Theresa May is expected to survive. 

Following the eventual passage of the deal, Barr forecasts that PM May will step down in 2019, making way for a more strongly pro-Brexit Conservative leader whose negotiation parameters will still be constrained by the already signed withdrawal agreement and its Irish border backstop. Finally, Barr notes that the current agreement is merely a roadmap for future trade and regulatory negotiations, predicting that the status quo transition period will likely be extended to 2022, with a slight chance of a long-term Norway-style arrangement. Footnotes add context on the historical origin of the House of Commons dating back to Simon de Montfort in 1258.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, discusses the economic rollover in Europe and why ECB interventions have failed to significantly boost Eurozone equities. While early 2018 pointed to a regional revival, growth rolled over later in the year, with Q3 2018 marking one of the weakest quarters for Europe since 2014. For 2019, Cembalest forecasts sub-2% growth in Europe, prompting the ECB to potentially consider more low-cost financing to encourage bank lending, especially in Italy. Despite cumulative ECB asset purchases reaching 2.6 trillion Euros, Eurozone equities have largely returned to their 2014 levels. 

To support these observations, the page features three charts and one comparative table. The first chart, "Tracking Eurozone GDP growth," displays quarter-over-quarter percentage changes from 2010 to 2018, comparing actual growth with business survey predictions. This visual highlights a sharp decline in actual growth starting in early 2018, falling to a low of approximately 0.2% quarter-over-quarter by the end of the year. The second chart, "Eurozone bank lending to non-financial corporations," shows year-over-year percent changes from 2005 to 2018 across Germany, France, Spain, and Italy. While lending has improved relative to the negative growth seen during the 2013–2015 European debt crisis, it remains far below pre-crisis levels, with most countries clustered between 0% and 5% in late 2018. The third chart, "Eurozone equities and ECB asset purchases," plots the MSCI Eurozone index against cumulative ECB purchases from 2014 to late 2018. It illustrates that although ECB purchases steadily scaled up to €2.6 trillion, the equity index fluctuated wildly, ultimately ending in late 2018 near its starting 2014 level of 100.

The underperformance of European equities is further explained by a table titled "Tech sector: US vs Europe," which highlights structural disadvantages in Europe's technology sector compared to the US. In the US, tech represents a heavy index weight of 20% in both the S&P 500 and MSCI US, whereas it represents only 5% of MSCI Europe and 9% of MSCI Eurozone. Furthermore, US tech companies exhibit superior profitability: the S&P 500 tech sector boasts a 24% operating margin, a 16% net income margin, and a 27% return on equity. In comparison, MSCI Europe tech shows a 12% operating margin, a 9% net income margin, and an 11% return on equity. Despite lower profitability, European tech is more expensive, with a 12-month forward P/E ratio of 16.1 for MSCI Europe and 15.9 for MSCI Eurozone, compared to 14.0 for the S&P 500.

Finally, the page includes a detailed footnote analyzing Italian bank reliance on ECB funding, which ranges from 6% of assets at Unicredit to 12% at Monte dei Paschi and Banco BPM. Italian banks currently own 20% of all Italian government bonds, accounting for 15% of their total assets. This concentration creates a complex, potentially unstable interplay between deposit flight risk, rising bank borrowing spreads, and government debt holdings. On a positive note, Cembalest points out that even under stressed liquidation values of 20 to 40 cents on the Euro for Italian non-performing loans, Italy’s two largest banks, Unicredit and Intesa, would still maintain robust Tier 1 Capital ratios above 10%.

This page examines the economic and social drivers behind recent worker strikes in France, arguing that the unrest goes far deeper than a simple propensity for activism. The author observes that while France did not experience the massive unemployment spikes seen in Italy or Spain, the country is grappling with a fifty-year-high wealth gap with Germany and a collapse in growth not seen since the nineteenth century outside of wartime. President Macron’s proposed fuel tax hike, officially framed as a climate initiative, was met with deep skepticism because France already has one of the lowest carbon footprints and highest gasoline prices in the developed world. The author contends that the tax was likely designed to meet Eurozone fiscal targets, a move that is highly painful for French citizens who already bear the heaviest tax burden in Europe. 

Six visual charts support these observations. The first, titled Franco-German wealth gap, plots the ratio of Germany’s real per capita GDP divided by France's from 1850 to 2015. It reveals that the ratio has climbed back toward 1.15, marking the widest wealth disparity between the two nations in half a century. The second chart, Remembrance of things past: low French growth, displays the six-year percent change in real GDP from 1825 to 2015, excluding world wars. It labels key historic growth slowdowns, including the Franco-Prussian War, the Union Generale failure, the Great Depression, and finally the Euro crisis, which shows growth dipping toward 5%, an exceptionally low level by historical standards. 

The third chart, France CO2 emissions versus OECD, ranks countries by tons of CO2 per $1,000 of GDP. France ranks near the very bottom of the forty-six listed nations at approximately 0.1 tons of CO2, illustrating its exceptionally clean energy profile. The fourth chart, France: taxed to the gauls, plots total personal tax revenue as a percentage of GDP, placing France first among thirty-four countries with a tax ratio of nearly 44%. The fifth chart, Gasoline prices per gallon, ranks forty-six countries and shows France near the top of the distribution, with gasoline prices hovering near $6 per gallon. 

Finally, the sixth chart, Average days not worked due to strikes, compares the periods of 2000–2009 and 2010–2017 across twenty-two European countries. France is the ultimate outlier, with the average days lost to strikes rising from roughly 80 in the earlier decade to over 120 days in the 2010–2017 period, vastly outpacing runner-up Belgium and the European average of under 40 days.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2019 Outlook examines the economic and investment risks associated with a "hard" Brexit. The author argues that while Brexit has already dragged UK growth down by 1% relative to the developed world—largely due to depressed business investment—the current deep valuation discount in UK equities could set the stage for a strong performance in 2019 if a disorderly, violent divorce is avoided in favor of a multi-year negotiation.

A table detailing UK exposure to the European Union highlights three critical sectors: production, distribution/transport, and finance/insurance. Together, these sectors account for substantial shares of corporate tax (14%, 20%, and 18% respectively) and employment (9%, 26%, and 3%). Their high exposure to the EU is shown by foreign workforce reliance (ranging from 11% to 14%), high import-to-input ratios (up to 51% for production), and significant EU shares of total exports (51% for production, 49% for distribution, and 37% for finance). Operational risks of a hard Brexit are further illustrated by a sidebar on medical risks, which notes that exiting Euratom could disrupt cancer treatment, as up to 80% of the UK's rapidly decaying, un-stockpilable medical isotopes are imported from the Netherlands, France, and Belgium.

Two charts illustrate the financial toll and the resulting market pricing. The first chart, tracking real business fixed investment as a percentage change since the Brexit referendum, reveals a severe divergence. While business investment in the US and the EU steadily rose to roughly 15% and 10% above pre-referendum levels respectively by late 2018, UK investment stagnated near 0%. The second chart plots the MSCI UK price-to-earnings discount or premium based on forward earnings against Europe and the Eurozone from 2006 to late 2018. This visual shows UK equities trading at a steep discount to broader Europe, hovering around negative 10% by late 2018, and at historically low levels relative to the Eurozone. Finally, the author cautions against sensationalized media narratives, pointing out that a Financial Times report erroneously claimed $1 trillion in UK equity outflows since the Brexit vote, a figure that was revised down to $20 billion after J.P. Morgan pointed out the error.

In this page from the J.P. Morgan 2019 Outlook, Michael Cembalest analyzes the rising risk of a significant depreciation of the Chinese RMB in response to an escalating trade war with the United States. He argues that while China has previously spent reserves to support the currency, several factors now make a large RMB decline of ten to fifteen percent likely to restore competitiveness against US tariffs. This potential shift, however, could heavily destabilize other emerging market countries whose corporate sectors are highly indebted in hard currencies.

To support this outlook, the page features four key charts. The first chart displays the USDCNY exchange rate from 2016 through late 2018 on an inverted axis, where lower values represent a weaker Chinese Yuan. The data reveals that the RMB steadily weakened throughout 2018, falling from approximately 6.3 to nearly 6.9, with a sharp downward acceleration occurring immediately after President Trump announced fifty billion dollars in tariffs on China. 

The second chart illustrates China capital flows from 1998 to 2018, calculated as the change in foreign exchange reserves minus the current account balance. While capital outflows reached massive levels between 2015 and 2016, approaching negative three hundred billion dollars, they have since stabilized near zero by late 2018, reducing some of the immediate flight risk associated with a weaker currency. 

The third chart tracks China’s current account balance as a percentage of GDP from 1998 to 2018. It shows that China's once-massive current account surplus, which peaked at around ten percent of GDP in 2007, has completely evaporated to near zero percent by 2018. A footnote explains that despite a large goods surplus with the US, China runs a substantial global services deficit alongside trade deficits with Taiwan, Korea, Australia, and Brazil. 

The final chart presents the shrinking net interest carry between China and the US, measured as the spread between the twelve-month SHIBOR and LIBOR from 2015 to late 2018. This spread contracted significantly from over four percent in 2015 to roughly half a percent by late 2018, showing that the narrowing interest rate differential naturally pressures the RMB downward. Collectively, these charts suggest that macroeconomic fundamentals and trade policy are converging to make a weaker Chinese currency the path of least resistance.

This J.P. Morgan report page, titled China and the Emerging Markets, argues that China has become so massive that its domestic economic health dictates the outlook for all emerging markets. The author points out that China’s weight in the MSCI Emerging Markets equity index has reached thirty percent and is expected to rise further. This trend is illustrated in the chart Emerging Market equities: China then and now, which tracks index weights from 1998 to 2018. The data shows China's share rising from under five percent in 1998 to about thirty percent by 2018, while Latin America's weight fell from over thirty percent to around twelve percent, and South Korea, Taiwan, India, and other Asian nations saw their shares decline or flatten. A second chart, EM countries becoming more tied to China, shows a GDP-weighted ten-year rolling correlation of GDP growth between nineteen emerging market countries and China. This correlation rose steadily from under twenty percent in the early 1990s to approximately sixty percent by 2016, proving how closely tied these nations are to China's economic trajectory.

The commentary notes that China's 2017 economic recovery is starting to roll over because its recent fiscal and monetary stimulus measures were transient. This slowdown is depicted in the China economy monitor chart, which plots eight domestic variables from 2011 to 2018: employment surveys, exports, business conditions, GDP, corporate earnings, industrial production, retail sales, and non-state owned enterprise fixed asset investment. Nearly all of these lines show a structural downward trend over the decade, with a brief spike in 2017 followed by a renewed decline in 2018. A footnote adds that Chinese car sales fell fifteen percent year-over-year in November 2018, and both retail sales and industrial production grew at their slowest pace in ten years. 

A primary concern is the sustainability of China's debt-fueled growth. The author cites IMF data showing that China’s GDP would have grown by five point five percent instead of seven point twenty-five percent between 2012 and 2016 if debt levels had not increased. Although a balance of payments crisis is unlikely because China's external debt-to-GDP ratio is very low, the threat of lower trend growth is significant. The author reinforces a 2014 Conference Board forecast predicting that Chinese economic growth will slow to four percent by the 2020-2025 period. This leverage dilemma is depicted in the final chart, Chinese credit growth slowing, but from high debt level, which compares annual credit growth against total credit as a percentage of GDP from 2003 to 2017. While annual credit growth has slowed from a peak of over thirty percent during the 2009 financial crisis stimulus down to about ten percent in late 2017, total outstanding credit has relentlessly climbed from around one hundred ten percent of GDP in 2003 to over two hundred ten percent of GDP by late 2017.

This page focuses on tariff risks and the dynamics of semiconductor warfare between the United States and China, arguing that while China has reduced its macro reliance on exports, it remains deeply dependent on US semiconductor technology. The author highlights the US export ban on ZTE as an example of this vulnerability, noting that the company was effectively shut down because it could not find non-US substitutes for critical components from Broadcom, Inphi, and Intel. Huawei similarly depends on core US suppliers like Intel, Qualcomm, Micron, Microsoft, and Oracle. 

To illustrate the commanding position of US companies, the page features a table outlining the estimated market share of US semiconductor firms across key product categories. According to J.P. Morgan's research, Intel and AMD command a ninety-nine percent market share in microprocessor chips for PCs and servers, while NVIDIA and AMD hold ninety-five percent of the market for graphics processors used in artificial intelligence and deep learning. Broadcom has a ninety-five percent share of networking chips for cloud datacenters. In smartphone cellular processing chips for 4G and 5G, Qualcomm and Intel hold seventy percent. For electric vehicle power management, Texas Instruments, Analog, and Maxim capture ninety percent of the market, while Intel and NVIDIA command ninety percent of the market for next-generation fully autonomous car processors.

Four charts support these observations about economic decoupling and market impacts. The first chart, showing China's decreasing reliance on exports as a percentage of GDP from 2000 to 2018, demonstrates that exports fell from a peak of thirty-six percent in 2006 to around twenty percent by 2018. The second chart details China's semiconductor imports in US dollars for 2017, separating chips from equipment. It reveals that Japan is the leading source of imports at nearly two point five billion dollars, mostly consisting of fabrication equipment, while the US also provides significant equipment. In contrast, imports from South Korea, Singapore, and Taiwan are heavily dominated by finished chips.

The bottom two charts focus on the financial market toll of the trade dispute. A performance index chart shows that China has been the primary equity market loser in the tariff war. Tracking index performance throughout 2018 from a base of one hundred, the series for Chinese stocks with US exposure underperformed all other groups, dropping to a level of roughly seventy-five by late November, while US and European exposures fared better. The final valuation chart tracks twelve-month forward price-to-earnings multiples for Chinese onshore and offshore equities from 2005 to 2018. It shows valuations hitting historical lows of approximately ten times earnings, down from a peak of nearly thirty times onshore in 2007. The author warns that front-loaded investments in 2018 could lead to weaker demand in 2019 as companies relocate production out of China to avoid tariffs.

This page from the Emerging Markets section of the J.P. Morgan Outlook publication addresses the future of global tariffs, starting with key lessons from the USMCA trade agreement between the United States, Mexico, and Canada. The author observes that under USMCA, tariffs are being used to extract concessions rather than as a final destination, the agreement remains a rules-based multilateral system, and its net economic impact compared to NAFTA is ultimately quite modest. 

The text then transitions to the more complex trade negotiations between the United States and China. The US is demanding increased market access in non-critical sectors, fewer restrictions on inbound foreign direct investment, stronger enforcement against cyber intrusions targeting intellectual property, and the elimination of industrial subsidies under the Made in China 2025 plan. In response, China has offered concessions including increased purchases of US goods, a temporary reduction in auto tariffs from 40% to 15%, stricter enforcement against IP theft, a ban on fentanyl exports, relaxed restrictions on foreign investment in banking and autos, and a reconsideration of the blocked Qualcomm-NXP merger. 

Reflecting on a meeting with Henry Kissinger, the author notes that while both the US and China have much to gain from a deal, the anniversary of World War I serves as a reminder of how easily unintended consequences can escalate. The author warns of a mixed outcome by March, where a deal with China might prevent Round 2 tariff increases to 25%, but a new tariff conflict could simultaneously emerge with Europe and Japan regarding 300 billion dollars of US auto and auto parts imports. 

An accompanying line chart illustrates how global business sentiment has fallen much faster than current economic activity, hinting at the potential market upside if a comprehensive trade deal is struck. Titled "Expectations declining faster than current conditions, which could reverse with a comprehensive deal," the chart displays J.P. Morgan Economic Research data from 2012 through November 2018. It compares the Current Global Output Survey, indexed on the left axis from 46 to 56, with the Future Global Output Survey, indexed on the right axis from 58 to 68. While the current activity line remains relatively resilient, ending 2018 at approximately 52, the future expectations line has plunged sharply from its late-2017 high of 65 down to about 59 by late 2018. If no deal is reached and further tariffs are imposed, the author expects the resulting costs to be shared via lower margins for Chinese and European producers and higher prices for US consumers, which could prompt global markets to assume the worst.

This J.P. Morgan Outlook page focuses on Chinese and global emerging markets, highlighting how a comprehensive trade deal could spark a market turnaround. Although Chinese corporate profits were recovering in early 2018, the onset of trade tariffs triggered a rollover in profit growth and a subsequent decline in Chinese equities. This market downturn was worsened by high corporate leverage, specifically Chinese CEOs borrowing heavily against their own shares for liquidity or personal investment, which sparked destructive margin calls. 

To illustrate onshore profit trends, the first chart displays EBIT growth as a three-quarter moving average from 2008 to 2018, divided into state-owned, private, and total categories. Onshore profits, particularly for private enterprises, saw a sharp reversal in 2018 after a strong recovery in 2017. The severe impact of share-pledging is detailed in the second chart, which compares the year-over-year change in the Shenzhen Composite Index against the number of firms facing extreme margin pressure. As the Shenzhen index fell toward a 40 percent year-over-year decline by late 2018, the number of firms where CEOs had pledged more than 80 percent of their stock—and saw prices fall by over 40 percent—surged from nearly zero in early 2017 to over 300 firms by late 2018.

Further pressure on the market is reflected in the third chart, which tracks earnings revisions as the percentage of positive minus negative revisions. For both China Offshore and Asia ex-Japan, this metric tumbled deep into negative territory in 2018, reaching levels below negative 20 percent. Finally, the page outlines J.P. Morgan Economic Research projections for China's 2019 earnings outlook in a waterfall chart. While the initial consensus estimate for year-over-year earnings growth stood at approximately 15 percent, and domestic tax cuts are expected to provide a positive boost, these benefits are outweighed by negative forces. Specifically, drag from yuan depreciation, trade tensions, and slower GDP growth are projected to reduce the final adjusted earnings growth outlook to 10 percent.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2019 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest under the Emerging Markets section, argues that Emerging Markets represent a more compelling contrarian deep-value opportunity for 2019 than Europe. The author points out that although European and EM earnings have shared nearly identical trajectories since 2014, Europe trades at a substantial 15 percent to 20 percent price-to-earnings premium compared to EM. Furthermore, valuation spreads indicate a higher prevalence of deep value stocks within EM. Additionally, EM's share of global mutual fund and ETF holdings is near a decade-low, highlighting how under-owned the region is compared to Europe. The author notes that stabilization in the EM currency index, which has declined 40 percent since 2012, would be beneficial, though this remains heavily contingent on China's economic path.

The first chart, titled Europe vs Emerging Markets: 12-month forward earnings, plots indexed earnings from January 2015 to July 2018, with January 1, 2015, equal to 100. The chart tracks both the Stoxx 600 and MSCI Emerging Markets, visually demonstrating their highly correlated paths, with both indexes rising from around 85 to 90 in early 2016 to peak near 110 in late 2017 before trending downward in 2018.

The second chart, titled Europe: P/E premium vs the Emerging Markets, displays the Stoxx 600 P/E discount or premium versus the MSCI EM based on forward earnings from 2006 to 2018. This visual highlights that Europe's P/E premium rose sharply from negative territory, with discounts as low as 10 percent in 2008 and 2010, to a peak of roughly 40 percent around 2014, and still sits at a significant premium of around 15 percent to 20 percent in late 2018.

The third chart, Europe and Emerging Markets valuation spreads, tracks the deviations of the top quintile from the long-term average from 2000 to 2018. The chart indicates whether valuation disparities within each region are wide, shown as positive deviations, or narrow, shown as negative deviations. While Europe's spread has dropped into negative territory near minus 1 as of 2018, indicating narrow disparities, the Emerging Markets spread is elevated above 1, signifying wider disparities and therefore more opportunities to find exceptionally cheap, deep-value stocks in the EM space.

The final chart, EM countries no longer worried about too much FX appreciation, tracks the EM currency index from 2000 to 2018, re-indexed to December 31, 2009, at 100. The index peaked near 110 in 2011 before embarking on a prolonged downward trend, landing near the low 60s by late 2018. This illustrates a severe currency depreciation of approximately 40 percent since 2012, underscoring the potential for EM assets to benefit if local currencies begin to stabilize.

This page examines the Japanese economy, focusing on the divergence between booming corporate profits and stagnant household incomes. The author argues that while Japanese corporate profits have kept pace with those in the United States, and capital spending on fixed assets and software has risen steadily under the "Abenomics" economic policy framework, these profits have failed to benefit workers and consumers, leaving real household incomes stagnant.

Four charts support this analysis. The top-left chart, titled "Both the US and Japan had a profits rebound...", plots trailing 12-month earnings per share from 2007 to late 2018. The S&P 500, measured on the left axis in US dollars from $50 to $155, and the MSCI Japan index, measured on the right axis in yen from ¥0 to ¥80, both display a tightly correlated recovery from their 2009 lows. By late 2018, S&P 500 earnings climb past $140, while MSCI Japan earnings rise above ¥70. 

In contrast, the top-right chart, titled "...but household incomes only rose in the US," demonstrates a stark divergence in worker compensation. This chart plots a real household earnings index from 2007 to late 2018. The US index, plotted on the left axis, rises steadily from a low of around 102 in 2011 to approximately 126 by late 2018. Meanwhile, Japan’s index, plotted on the right axis as a three-month average, falls precipitously from a peak near 122 in 2007, bottoming out around 92 in late 2015, and remains stagnant between 92 and 94 through late 2018.

The bottom two charts illustrate the positive side of Japan's corporate landscape under Abenomics. The bottom-left chart, "Japan capital investments," displays the year-over-year percentage change in capital spending from 2006 to 2018. Capital investments hit a low of nearly negative 25 percent in 2009 but stabilized post-2013—the period marked by a vertical dashed line indicating when Abenomics began—remaining consistently positive and hovering between 0 percent and 10 percent through 2018. Similarly, the bottom-right chart, "Japan software investments," shows year-over-year percentage changes from 2003 to 2018. Software investments, which plunged to nearly negative 10 percent in 2010, stabilized and trended upward following the start of Abenomics, reaching nearly 10 percent growth by late 2018. Taken together, these trends demonstrate that while corporate reforms successfully stimulated business investments, they have yet to trickled down to boost consumer incomes.

This page begins a retrospective on the Global Financial Crisis ten years after the event, arguing that the crisis resulted from a complex set of interactions involving banks, broker-dealers, investors, insurance companies, rating agencies, the Federal Reserve, and policymakers, rather than being caused by banks alone. To illustrate the scale of the banking failures, the author includes a bar chart showing deposits in failed and assisted United States banks as a percentage of GDP across three major banking crises: the Great Depression, the Savings and Loan Crisis, and the Great Recession. This chart reveals that deposits in failed banks in 2009 peaked at nearly eight percent of GDP, which exceeded the peak of approximately six and a half percent of GDP reached in 1933 during the Great Depression, while the Savings and Loan Crisis peak remained much lower, at around three percent of GDP in 1989. 

To show the extent of the subsequent rescue efforts, a supporting table lists the emergency liquidity facilities created by the Federal Reserve during the crisis alongside their peak outstanding balances in billions of dollars. The largest of these emergency programs was the Term Auction Facility with a peak balance of 493 billion dollars, followed by the Commercial Paper Funding Facility at 348 billion dollars, and the Term Securities Lending Facility at 236 billion dollars. Other significant interventions included the Asset-Backed Commercial Paper Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility at 152 billion dollars, the Primary Dealer Credit Facility at 147 billion dollars, Term Repurchase Transactions at 80 billion dollars, the AIG Revolving Credit Facility at 72 billion dollars, and the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility at 48 billion dollars. 

The author outlines the structure of the upcoming sections in the publication, which explore the deeper, systemic causes of the crisis. These include the role of policymakers in hijacking Government-Sponsored Enterprise balance sheets during the housing crisis, the deregulation of broker-dealers, poor underwriting decisions by rating agencies, bond reinsurers, and institutional investors, as well as systemic risk contributions from individual institutions. The section concludes with an assessment of the positive subsequent regulatory changes implemented in capital requirements, liquidity, leverage limits, and the shadow banking sector.

This page focuses on the persistent challenges facing the Japanese economy and equity market, specifically highlighting dormant consumer demand, deflationary mindsets, and significant foreign investor capital outflows despite cheap valuations. 

To illustrate Japan's ongoing struggle with inflation, the first chart, titled "Japan CPI ex food, alcoholic beverages and energy," tracks the year-over-year percentage change from 2005 through late 2018. The data shows that inflation has structurally remained below the Central Bank's target, hovering mostly between negative one percent and one percent. The only substantial exception was a temporary spike up to nearly two and a half percent driven by the April 2014 VAT hike, after which inflation rapidly subsided back toward zero percent. This lack of demand is further reinforced by the second chart, "Japanese consumers spending plans," which measures the net percentage of respondents planning to spend more on services from 1991 through 2018. Spanning categories such as entertainment tickets, housekeeping, eating out, amusement parks, and self-enlightenment, the series have consistently remained deep in negative territory, often fluctuating between negative ten percent and negative forty percent, showing that a deflationary mindset is highly entrenched.

On the market side, the page details how international investors pulled capital out of Japan in 2018 despite favorable corporate earnings. The chart "Non-resident net purchases of Japanese equities" measures rolling six-month flows in trillions of Yen from 2005 to late 2018. It highlights that while the start of Abenomics in late 2012 triggered a massive surge in foreign buying that peaked near eight trillion Yen, subsequent periods saw heavy selling. Notably, outflows in late 2018 plummeted to around negative six trillion Yen, a pace of disinvestment rivaling the major sell-offs of 2008 and 2016. 

This heavy selling pushed Japanese stock valuations down, as shown in the final chart, "Japan P/Es at low end of range." This chart tracks the price-to-forward 12 months earnings from 2005 to late 2018. After the launch of Abenomics, the P/E ratio frequently flirted with a fifteen-times multiple but fell back down each time. By the end of 2018, valuation multiples dropped to nearly twelve-times earnings, placing Japanese equities at the bottom of their historical post-crisis range. 

Looking forward, the author suggests that while these low valuations may attract international value investors, a sustainable recovery in Japanese equities likely depends on a broader global economic recovery taking root in 2019. However, the author notes that if such a recovery occurs, emerging markets would likely benefit more than Japan. Additionally, Japan remains highly exposed to the downside risks of an escalating US-China trade war, particularly if it leads to a depreciation of the Chinese Renminbi.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" report, authored by Michael Cembalest, discusses how deregulation of broker-dealers, rather than commercial banks, played a pivotal role in the scale of the 2008 global financial crisis. The author highlights that the five largest US broker-dealers experienced rapid balance sheet growth after the SEC Uniform Net Capital Rule was changed in 2004. As a stark example, Lehman Brothers held a massive $690 billion balance sheet in 2007, which was larger than the real-term assets of all failed banks during the Great Depression combined, yet it was supported by just $22 billion in equity and funded heavily by short-term repurchase agreements.

To illustrate this, the page features two charts. The first chart, titled "Growth in assets and major financial sector legislation," indexes assets from December 1992 through December 2007, with 1992 set to 100. It shows that while commercial banks with over $1 billion in assets grew to a total of $10 trillion across 513 institutions, their indexed asset growth was relatively modest, reaching around 200. In contrast, the five major broker-dealers experienced astronomical growth, spiking to an index value of nearly 900 and totaling $4.2 trillion in assets. This explosive growth accelerated sharply after the SEC Uniform Net Capital Rule Change in 2004, far outpacing the growth rate seen after the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. The second chart, "Lehman's evolution into a leveraged, risky portfolio accelerated after SEC rule repeal," indexes Lehman's stock price against a highly leveraged portfolio of stocks, high-yield bonds, and high-grade bonds leveraged at 85 percent, from 1994 to roughly 2008. Prior to the end of the SEC Uniform Net Capital Rule in 2004, Lehman's stock and the leveraged portfolio did not correlate closely.
