Afterward, the two tracked each other almost perfectly, peaking near an index level of 2,500 before crashing.

The page concludes with reflections from Eric Rosengren, President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, regarding broker-dealer stability. Rosengren notes that the most dramatic runs of the financial crisis targeted broker-dealers, listing the failures and distress of Lehman Brothers, Bear Stearns, Merrill Lynch, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley. He explains that broker-dealers are structurally prone to runs because they rely on uninsured short-term credit markets. While capital ratios and liquidity have improved since the crisis, Rosengren cautions that broker-dealers remain heavily reliant on wholesale funding, with repo usage as a percentage of liabilities declining only from 70 percent in 2008 to 50 percent by the time of his retrospective analysis.

This page, titled "The role of policymakers in the housing crisis: the hijacking of GSE balance sheets," is part of a series reflecting on the Global Financial Crisis ten years later. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that government policy and political directives, rather than purely private-sector greed, initiated the housing crisis by forcing Government-Sponsored Enterprises (GSEs) like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to systematically lower their underwriting standards. Prior to 1990, the GSEs adhered to conservative loan-to-value and debt-to-income standards, with less than 10% of their loan purchases classified as subprime. However, a 1993 HUD regulation mandated that GSEs meet low- and moderate-income lending targets, which started at 30% and rose to 50% by 2001. This mandate successfully grew the GSE mortgage market share from 35% to 60% and expanded overall mortgage volumes by 2.5 times, but it severely degraded the quality of their balance sheets. Cembalest highlights how policymakers and prominent economists, such as Joseph Stiglitz and Peter Orszag, dangerously underestimated this risk in 2002, predicting the likelihood of a GSE balance sheet shock at less than one in 500,000. Crucially, the author asserts that this government-mandated "blurring of the lines" between conventional and subprime lending paved the way for private-sector banks and brokers to follow suit with their own low-quality, securitized subprime products.

An accompanying line chart visually supports this argument, tracking annual underwriting metrics from 1990 to 2009 as percentages from 0% to 60%. The GSE Low & Moderate Income lending target, represented by a solid blue line, begins at 30% in 1993 and climbs steadily to 50% by 2001. Accompanying this policy mandate, the Fannie/Freddie share of the total mortgage market (a solid green line) rises from 35% in 1990 to peak near 57% in 2001. Concurrently, five different red dashed lines representing Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac underwriting that exceeded traditional standards—including Freddie Mac non-traditional loans, cash-out combined loan-to-value ratios over 75%, and debt-to-income ratios over 38% and 42%—all trend sharply upward throughout the 1990s, peaking in the 2001 to 2003 window. In stark contrast, the solid black line tracking the private sector's subprime and Alt-A loans as a percentage of total origination remains flat and under 10% for the entirety of the 1990s. The private sector's subprime origination only begins to climb after 2002, eventually peaking near 35% in 2006 before crashing back to near 0% by 2009. This clear temporal lag demonstrates that the degradation of GSE underwriting standards preceded, and likely catalyzed, the private sector's subprime expansion.

This page, part of the J.P. Morgan "GFC: Ten Years Later" series, analyzes how individual banks and broker-dealers contributed to systemic risk leading up to and during the Global Financial Crisis. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that the historical record of these contributions is varied and highly revealing of management behavior. 

The primary visual is a bubble chart titled "Changing leverage, pre-crisis compensation and post-crisis writedowns." The horizontal axis measures the change in balance sheet leverage (assets to equity) heading into the crisis from 2003 to 2007, ranging from negative forty percent to one hundred twenty percent. The vertical axis displays writedowns from 2007 through the second quarter of 2011 as a percentage of second-quarter 2007 tangible common equity, ranging from zero to three hundred fifty percent. The size of each bubble corresponds to employee and management compensation as a percentage of operating income from 2004 to 2007. The chart illustrates that institutions in the lower-left quadrant, such as JPMorgan Chase, Banco Santander, and UniCredit, reduced their leverage, suffered fewer post-crisis writedowns, and distributed a greater share of net income to shareholders rather than internal management. In contrast, institutions like Wachovia, Washington Mutual, and National City experienced extreme writedowns exceeding three hundred percent. Merrill Lynch is plotted on the far right with a massive bubble, indicating a substantial increase in leverage alongside very high pre-crisis employee compensation.

The author provides three key qualifying notes on the data. First, he highlights the lingering debate surrounding Goldman Sachs, noting that its low writedowns on the chart must be viewed in the context of the Federal Reserve bailing out its AIG exposure at one hundred cents on the dollar, with Goldman receiving the largest share of AIG bailout funds. Second, the losses shown for Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers are understated because they only reflect realized write-downs through 2008, when both entities were either liquidated or acquired. Third, the chart only captures the first wave of European bank losses (spanning 2007 to 2010), omitting the second wave of losses that hit European financial institutions from 2011 to 2015.

This page examines firm-specific contributions to systemic risk during the Global Financial Crisis by analyzing collateral postings to the Federal Reserve’s emergency Primary Dealer Credit Facility. The primary dealer facility extended nine trillion dollars in cumulative collateralized loans to banks and broker-dealers in 2008 and 2009. Although all loans were ultimately repaid in full with interest before the facility was closed on February 1, 2010, the volume and risk tier of collateral pledged by each firm provides a clear picture of their relative systemic footprint. 

A horizontal stacked bar chart details cumulative collateral postings to this facility in trillions of dollars, broken down by four asset categories: investment grade, non-investment grade, unrated or loans, and equities. Merrill Lynch recorded the highest postings, approaching two point three trillion dollars, with substantial portions consisting of lower-tier assets such as unrated loans, non-investment grade debt, and equities. Citigroup and Morgan Stanley follow closely, both exceeding two trillion dollars in cumulative postings with a large mix of non-investment grade and equity collateral. Bear Stearns ranks fourth at over one trillion dollars, though its postings consisted almost entirely of investment-grade collateral. Other firms with smaller but notable cumulative postings include Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, and Barclays, while firms like Lehman Brothers, Countrywide, and BNP Paribas show relatively minor total postings to this specific facility.

To provide a broader view of government interventions, an accompanying table presents total emergency facility usage across twelve programs, including the Agency Mortgage Backed Securities Program, the Asset Backed Commercial Paper Facility, and Maiden Lane vehicles. This table lists the total usage in billions of dollars and each firm's share of the overall total. Citigroup leads total usage at two thousand eight hundred thirty billion dollars, representing fourteen percent of the total. Merrill Lynch follows at two thousand four hundred forty-nine billion dollars, or twelve point one percent, and Morgan Stanley at two thousand three hundred five billion dollars, or eleven point four percent. Other major users of emergency facilities include Bank of America at one thousand one hundred twenty-nine billion dollars, AIG at one thousand forty-seven billion dollars, Goldman Sachs at one thousand thirty-three billion dollars, Barclays at one thousand thirty billion dollars, and BNP Paribas at one thousand two billion dollars. Smaller amounts were utilized by Bear Stearns, Credit Suisse, Deutsche Bank, Royal Bank of Scotland, JP Morgan Chase, and UBS, while all other participants combined accounted for three thousand three hundred twenty-three billion dollars, or sixteen point five percent of total usage.

In this section of J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" report focusing on the Great Financial Crisis ten years later, Michael Cembalest analyzes the systemic failures in underwriting, rating, and insuring structured credit that precipitated the 2007–2008 collapse. Cembalest argues that the pre-crisis euphoria was facilitated by a combination of banks originating poorly designed loans, rating agencies rubber-stamping low subordination levels, bond reinsurers eagerly backing them, and institutional investors readily buying them. Additionally, monoline insurers unsafely diversified away from stable municipal bonds into risky structured credit, while the Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates at an ultra-low 1% in 2004 poured further fuel on the fire.

The first chart, titled "Property decline cushion for AAA CMBS Investors," tracks AAA CMBS subordination adjusted for rating agency loan-to-value ratios from 2001 to 2018. It illustrates a perilous downward slide from a protective cushion of roughly 35% in 2001 to a mere 5% in 2007. This razor-thin cushion meant that a property write-down of just 5% would directly expose AAA-rated investors to losses. Post-crisis, this cushion spiked back up to nearly 37% by 2010 before leveling off to around 20% by 2018.

To the right, a stacked area chart titled "US asset-backed securities" shows the total outstanding volume of asset-backed debt in billions of US dollars from 1990 to 2016. The chart distinguishes among non-agency residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS), which represent the largest block of debt, non-agency commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS), collateralized debt obligations (CDOs), student loans, equipment, credit cards, auto loans, and other categories. Outstanding volume grew moderately through the 1990s before exploding in the 2000s, peaking at approximately $5.5 trillion in late 2007 before undergoing a steep contraction.

On the bottom left, the chart "Monolines become multi-lines" demonstrates how monoline insurers expanded away from their core business. It plots municipals as a percentage of annual industry net par insured risk from 1991 to 2005 for a universe of insurers including AMBAC, MBIA, American General, CIFG, FGIC, FSA, SCA, ACA, and Radian. The line shows municipal risk plummeting from a peak near 90% in 1992 to below 40% by 2000, illustrating how these insurers aggressively diversified into riskier structured credit instruments.

The final chart at the bottom right, "Structured credit market accelerated in 2004, in the wake of a 1% Fed Funds rate," maps the relationship between monetary policy and leverage from 1990 to 2008. Plotting the Federal Funds rate against structured credit as a percentage of US GDP, the chart shows that structured credit to GDP hovered below 15% for much of the 1990s. However, when the Fed cut interest rates to 1% in 2004, structured credit to GDP accelerated dramatically, climbing from roughly 15% to nearly 40% by 2007, showing how prolonged low rates catalyzed the structured credit boom.

This page, titled Aftermath: substantial improvements in capital, liquidity and shadow banking, is part of J.P. Morgan's 2019 Outlook by Michael Cembalest. It argues that regulatory changes following the Global Financial Crisis have successfully reduced systemic risk. The author highlights four main areas of improvement: increased risk-weighted capital ratios, improved liquid asset availability, declining loan-to-deposit ratios, and a structural shift in the money market fund industry toward lower-risk government funds. 

The first chart, Rising capital ratios since crisis, compares risk-weighted capital ratios from 2007 to 2017 for both the US and Europe. In the US, the ratio rose from roughly 9 percent in 2007 to about 14 percent in 2017. In Europe, the increase was even sharper, jumping from approximately 8 percent to nearly 16 percent over the same decade, indicating much stronger capital buffers in both banking systems. 

The second chart, Improving liquidity ratios since crisis, details liquid assets as a percentage of short-term liabilities. In the US, this liquidity ratio climbed from around 42 percent in 2007 to about 48 percent in 2017. In Europe, the ratio grew from approximately 35 percent in 2007 to around 42 percent in 2017, demonstrating that banks are better prepared to handle short-term funding pressures. 

The third chart, Bank loan-to-deposit ratios, maps trends from 1995 to 2017 for US and Eurozone banks. Eurozone banks reached a peak loan-to-deposit ratio of nearly 140 percent around 2008 but successfully deleveraged down to about 110 percent by 2017. US banks saw their loan-to-deposit ratio decrease from a high of 100 percent in 2008 to roughly 75 percent in 2017, showcasing a healthier reliance on stable deposits rather than wholesale funding. 

The final chart, A shift to lower risk money market funds, tracks assets under management in trillions of US dollars from 2002 to 2018 for prime and government money market funds. The timeline highlights key events such as the Lehman Crash in 2008 and the implementation of Money Market Reform in late 2016. While prime funds previously held a significant share of assets, peaking near 2.0 trillion dollars in 2008, the 2016 regulatory reforms triggered a massive migration of capital. By 2018, government fund assets surged well past 2.0 trillion dollars, while prime fund assets collapsed to under 0.5 trillion dollars, demonstrating a massive reallocation of shadow banking assets into safer government instruments.

Morgan Chase & Co. and its affiliates, outlining regulatory compliance across jurisdictions including Brazil, Mexico, and Australia. It details the company's status with the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission, the Australian Securities and Investment Commission, and the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, with specific guidelines for wholesale clients in Australia under the Corporations Act 2001 and exemptions regulated by the United States SEC, FINRA, and CFTC.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the political economics of wealth and income redistribution. Cembalest addresses modern progressive proposals, such as a 70% top marginal tax rate and Elizabeth Warren’s proposed wealth tax on households with assets exceeding $50 million. He argues that while advocates are free to propose these policies, they should not justify them with the historically inaccurate claim that the wealthy paid significantly higher tax rates in the past. He notes that the effective tax rates paid by the top 1% have remained relatively stable over the decades, and warns that the underlying wealth tax research by Emmanuel Saez, Thomas Piketty, and Gabriel Zucman faces methodology concerns from the US Treasury, the Federal Reserve, the Joint Committee on Taxation, and Columbia University professors.

Two line charts support this analysis. The first chart, titled "What the top 1% pay in Federal taxes hasn't changed much despite the decline in the top statutory rate," compares federal tax rates from 1979 to 2015 using data from the Congressional Budget Office and the Internal Revenue Service. It shows that while the top statutory Federal income tax rate plunged from 70% in 1979 to a low of 28% in the late 1980s before rising back to around 39.6%, the actual effective federal tax rate for the top 1% (which includes income, payroll, and excise taxes) remained nearly flat, fluctuating tightly between approximately 20% and 25%. A footnote adds context to this historical comparison, noting that in 1955, the top tax bracket was only triggered at an income equivalent to $3.5 million in today’s dollars, compared to just $466,000 today.

The second chart, titled "Average effective tax rate on the top 1% including all Federal, state and local taxes," tracks a broader measure of taxation from 1955 to 2015 using data from Piketty, Saez, and Zucman. This chart demonstrates that even when accounting for all federal, state, local, payroll, property, and excise taxes, the average effective tax rate on the top 1% has consistently hovered between 30% and 45%. It began at just over 40% in 1955, dipped to a low of roughly 31% around 1986 and 2009, and ended at approximately 37% in 2015. 

Cembalest concludes that history does not provide a valid precedent for a 70% effective tax rate. Additionally, he highlights a structural shift in government spending since the 1960s: the ratio of entitlement spending to growth-fueling discretionary spending (such as infrastructure and R&D) has dramatically inverted. In the 1960s, the federal government spent $0.60 on entitlements for every dollar of discretionary spending, whereas it currently spends $3.30. According to Congressional Budget Office projections, this entitlement-to-discretionary spending ratio is forecast to reach $4.50 per dollar by 2025.

This page focuses on the debate surrounding wealth taxes and the underlying data used to justify them, specifically critiquing the methodology of economists Emmanuel Saez, Thomas Piketty, and Gabriel Zucman. The author introduces the topic by highlighting Senator Elizabeth Warren's proposal for a two percent annual wealth tax on household assets exceeding fifty million dollars, a plan advised by Saez, Piketty, and Zucman. However, the author presents counterarguments from economists at the Federal Reserve, the US Treasury, and the Joint Committee on Taxation, who argue that the Saez and Piketty methodologies rely on sensitive assumptions and unadjusted tax return data, leading to overstated and improbable trends in both wealth and income inequality.

Two line charts illustrate this critique by comparing alternative data series. The first chart, titled Top 1% wealth share in the US, tracks the percentage share of total wealth held by the top one percent from 1960 to 2010. Under the capitalization method favored by Saez, the top one percent's wealth share rises dramatically from around twenty-five percent in the late 1970s to nearly forty percent by 2010. In contrast, the Survey of Consumer Finances method shows a much flatter trend, fluctuating between roughly twenty-eight percent and thirty-three percent over the same period. Meanwhile, the Estate tax multiplier method indicates that the top one percent's wealth share actually declined from approximately twenty-five percent in the mid-1960s to around twenty percent by 2010. 

The second chart, titled Top 1% income shares in the US, tracks the top one percent's share of total national income from 1960 to 2015. The Saez and Piketty method depicts a massive surge in income inequality, with the top one percent's share rising from around nine percent in the late 1970s to over twenty percent by 2015. Conversely, the Treasury and Joint Committee on Taxation method, which adjusts for changes in tax laws and utilizes a broader definition of income, shows a nearly flat trajectory, rising only slightly from roughly nine percent in 1960 to around ten percent by 2015. The Treasury and Joint Committee on Taxation researchers conclude that the actual rise in income inequality since 1960 is only one-tenth of what Saez and Piketty claim, demonstrating how unadjusted tax return data can present a distorted view of economic trends.

This page, from a section titled "GFC: Ten Years Later," analyzes how the US financial system has restructured its funding and intermediation mechanisms in the decade following the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. The central theme is that US commercial banks have become safer by relying more heavily on stable customer deposits and significantly less on short-term wholesale funding sources like interbank loans and repurchase agreements (repo). 

The introductory text highlights that the overall repo market declined from $4.2 trillion to $2.2 trillion since 2008, driven primarily by broker-dealers shrinking their balance sheets. This trend is illustrated in the first chart, "US commercial banks: deposits and interbank loans" (covering 1990 to 2018), which shows interbank loans falling from over 4% of bank assets before the crisis to approximately 1% by 2018. Concurrently, customer deposits climbed from around 60% of assets to roughly 75%. The adjacent chart, "Repo usage by financial intermediary" (1970 to 2018), displays repo as a percentage of total liabilities. It shows that while US banks and foreign banks in the US maintained low repo reliance, broker-dealers saw their repo usage peak near 80% prior to 2008 before dropping to about 50% by 2018.

The middle portion of the page explains that shadow banking's share of liabilities has retreated to levels last seen in the year 2000. This contraction is partly explained by a drop in securities lending by institutional investors, as depicted in the chart "Securities lending against cash collateral by institutional investors, US$ trillions" (2007 to 2015). This stacked area chart shows total securities lending peaking near $1.2 trillion in 2008 before shrinking to roughly $0.4 trillion by 2015, with declines visible across retirement and pension plans, mutual funds, insurance, and other institutional sectors. 

The bottom of the page features two charts sourced from economists Stephen Cecchetti and Kermit Schoenholtz, illustrating how these shifts have pushed financial intermediation back toward traditional commercial banking. The chart "US: shadow banking and traditional banking" (1960 to 2015) tracks liabilities as a percentage of GDP. It reveals that shadow banking liabilities peaked above 110% of GDP in 2008—briefly overtaking traditional commercial banking—before falling back to around 80% by 2015. Meanwhile, bank holding companies and broker-dealers saw their liabilities drop from about 35% of GDP down to around 20%. Lastly, the "Commercial Bank share of intermediation" chart (1960 to 2015) shows that the traditional banking sector's share of financial intermediation steadily declined from over 90% in 1960 to an all-time low of roughly 35% in 2007, but has since rebounded to nearly 50% by 2015.

This page analyzes the degradation of political discourse, rising polarization, and the constitutional debate surrounding wealth taxes. The author warns that the United States may be entering its most ideologically charged presidential election campaign in a century, advising readers to remain skeptical of political rhetoric from all sides. 

To illustrate the prevalence of political misinformation, the first chart plots the cumulative false or misleading claims made by President Trump, as tracked by the Washington Post Factchecker Database. Covering the period from January 2017 to January 2019, the line graph shows a steep, accelerating curve that starts near zero and climbs to nearly 8,000 claims. Footnotes contextualize this trend, noting that fact-checking often relies on subjective interpretations and pointing out that neither party is immune to falsehoods, citing President Obama’s controversial promise regarding the Affordable Care Act. 

The second chart, titled "Presidential administration ideology and a look at 2020," maps the ideological trajectory of U.S. administrations from 1916 to 2020 using a scale from -0.7 (most liberal) to 0.7 (most conservative). The historical timeline traces the ideological shifts of past presidents, showing George W. Bush at approximately 0.45, Obama at -0.35, and Trump at nearly 0.55. For the 2020 election, the chart categorizes potential Democratic contenders into three ideological camps: moderates like Bennet, Biden, Klobuchar, and O'Rourke at roughly -0.15; progressives like Brown and Gillibrand at -0.3; and ultra-progressives such as Sanders, Warren, Harris, and Booker at nearly -0.45. This creates a stark ideological divide against Trump's conservative positioning.

The bottom half of the page consists of an appendix addressing the constitutionality of wealth taxes. While direct wealth taxes are often considered unconstitutional under the 16th Amendment because they are not apportioned among the states, the text introduces "Wealth Integration Methods" as a viable legal alternative. Rather than taxing assets directly, these methods use wealth as an input to calculate income taxes. The author references a January 2019 paper by Ohio State law professor Ari Glogower, who argues that wealth integration taxes are constitutionally sound and supported by existing precedents, such as provisions in the 2017 tax bill and Section 1202 capital gains rules. The author outlines several potential policy mechanisms for a wealth integration tax, including deduction phase-outs based on wealth, higher marginal tax rates, mark-to-market valuations on liquid assets, and the unification of ordinary income and capital gains tax rates.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest highlights the recent historic performance drought of New York professional sports teams, arguing that the 2017–2018 period represents one of the worst eras for local fans in modern history. 

To support this observation, the page features two historical line charts tracking New York teams—including the Mets, Yankees, Knicks, Nets, Jets, Giants, Bills, Rangers, and Islanders—from 1950 through 2018. The first chart, tracking the average winning percentage of these teams, shows that the average has generally fluctuated between 44% and 58%. However, in 2018, the average plummeted to nearly 42%, a low matched only once before during the 1966–1967 season. A detailed footnote contextualizes that 1966 low, noting the Giants' dismal 1-12 season and a last-place finish for the Yankees that drew an infamous record-low crowd of 413 people to Yankee Stadium. The second line chart, tracking playoff appearances, shows that New York postseason berths collapsed to just one team in 2018, representing the worst playoff drought since the expansion era of the 1950s and 1960s.

Cembalest pairs this performance data with a cost analysis to show how much local fans are paying for subpar results. A stacked bar chart, titled "Daily ticket price package for 4-sport cities," compares the total cost of general seating across major U.S. metropolitan areas for a combined package of NHL, MLB, NBA, and NFL tickets. New York is divided into two combinations. The premium "NYC 1" package—comprising the Giants, Knicks, Yankees, and Rangers—is the most expensive sports market in the country, topping the list at over $350. This is followed by Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles, and San Francisco. Meanwhile, the budget-friendly "NYC 2" package—comprising the Jets, Nets, Mets, and Islanders—offers a more average cost structure, ranking eighth overall at roughly $230. Phoenix ranks as the least expensive 4-sport city, with a package totaling just under $200.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s financial publication analyzes the rapid stock and bond market rebound from the December 2018 lows. Michael Cembalest argues that the sharp recovery was driven primarily by short-covering from "fast money" accounts closing their short positions, rather than long-term "real money" investment inflows. He also notes that supportive Federal Reserve policy has underpinned this rally, but he predicts that one more interest rate hike is still likely in late 2019 if labor markets remain tight. 

The first chart, titled "Mirror images: as the shorts cover, equity market rallies," plots the S&P 500 index against short interest from June 2018 to February 2019. It illustrates a clear inverse relationship: short interest peaked near 6% in late December 2018 as the S&P 500 hit its bottom around 2,350, and then plummeted to around 2% as the S&P 500 quickly rebounded toward 2,750 in early 2019. 

Supporting this, the second chart, "S&P 500 rebound not accompanied by real money flows," shows that while the S&P 500 staged a massive recovery from January 2018 to January 2019, cumulative US equity flows continued to drop sharply, reaching nearly negative $80 billion by early 2019. This demonstrates that institutional or retail "real money" did not participate in the rally.

The third chart, "Valuations for stocks and corporate bonds," displays valuation percentiles versus historical averages for five asset classes (US equities, European equities, EM equities, high yield, and high-grade debt) across three points in time: Peak 2018, December 26, 2018, and Current (as of February 11, 2019). The data shows valuations fell from peak percentiles of 60% to 80% down to depressed levels of 20% to 30% on December 26, before rising back to near-median levels of 50% to 60% today.

The final chart, "Fed models suggest that equilibrium policy rates might only need to be 50-100 bps over inflation," presents two versions of the Holston-Laubach-Williams model from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. It tracks the equilibrium real interest rate from 1980 through 2015, showing a long-term decline from around 3.5% in the early 1980s to between 0.5% and 1.0% recently. Cembalest uses this to explain the Federal Reserve's newfound patience, alongside potential political pressure from President Trump, but cautions that if tightening labor markets persist, the Fed faces difficult choices ahead.

This page argues that de-carbonizing the electricity grid is insufficient to eliminate carbon emissions, as electricity represents only a minor fraction of global energy consumption, and fossil fuels are deeply integrated into other sectors like industry, transport, and heating. 

Four key charts illustrate these points. The first, a stacked bar chart showing global energy consumed by end-user in quadrillion BTUs for 2017, demonstrates that primary energy used for electricity generation feeds into a system where final electricity only represents 17% of total energy consumed. The rest of the energy is directly consumed as fossil fuels: the industrial sector relies heavily on coal, natural gas, and petroleum; the transport sector is nearly entirely reliant on petroleum; and residential and commercial buildings depend on natural gas, coal, petroleum, and direct electricity. A second pie chart reinforces this by showing that fossil fuels used for direct, non-electricity purposes account for 341 quadrillion BTUs, which is more than double the 141 quadrillion BTUs of fossil fuels used indirectly to generate electricity.

A third line chart tracks the world’s reliance on fossil fuels as a percentage of global primary energy consumption from 1965 to 2018, with International Energy Agency estimates extending to 2040. It shows that fossil fuels have consistently accounted for about 85% of global energy. The chart highlights a brief dip during the nuclear adoption era of the 1970s and 1980s, followed by another gradual decline starting around 2010 with the rise of the solar and wind era, which is projected to lower the fossil fuel share to around 76% by 2040. 

A final line chart details global urbanization trends from 1950 to 2050, showing the percentage of total population living in cities across regions like Japan, the United States, Europe, China, South America, Africa, and India. With urbanization rising steeply in places like China, India, and Africa, the author notes that energy solutions must be tailored for dense urban environments rather than off-the-grid scenarios. 

The author concludes that because electricity shares of total energy and fossil fuel shares are similar in major economies like the United States, China, and Europe, countries face steep challenges in meeting aggressive targets, such as Germany's goal of a 40% emissions decline by 2030 or any United States proposals aiming for zero net emissions by the same year.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication analyzes the macro and technical drivers behind the early 2019 market rebound while outlining the firm's broader asset allocation strategy. 

The author begins by highlighting a structural technical support for the market: a shrinking supply of publicly traded equities. This is illustrated in a chart plotting the S&P 500 Index Divisor from 1997 to 2018 as a proxy for US equity supply. The divisor shows a long-term decline from its peak above 9.0 around 2004 down to approximately 8.3 in 2018, driven by primary and secondary issuance, buybacks, mergers and acquisitions, and de-listings. While this shrinking supply does not prevent market declines, it provides a favorable backdrop for recoveries when large institutional investors rebalance. 

Another projected tailwind is Chinese fiscal policy, depicted in a bar chart tracking China's stimulus as a percentage of GDP from 2015 to an estimated 2019. The chart reveals that total stimulus is projected to rise to 3.0% of GDP in 2019, consisting of roughly 2.0% in tax cuts and 1.0% in spending, which is a notable increase from the roughly 1.8% total stimulus in 2018. This stimulus, coupled with any trade agreement that delays or cancels 25% US tariffs on $200 billion to $460 billion of Chinese imports, is expected to provide a positive market bump.

However, the author cautions that the equity rally may pause due to uncertainties over potential US tariffs on European and Japanese auto parts, alongside slowing corporate profit momentum. To support this, two charts track deteriorating earnings metrics. The first compares S&P 500 year-over-year EPS growth with an Earnings Leading Indicator from 1989 to 2019. The leading indicator has plunged to near-zero levels, signaling that corporate earnings growth will likely flatten or become slightly negative in 2019, with a low point in the second quarter. This weakness is corroborated by the second earnings chart, which plots S&P 500 earnings revisions as the percentage of positive minus negative revisions over a three-month moving average. This metric fell precipitously to nearly negative 30% by February 2019, indicating that downward revisions heavily outweigh upward ones.

In the bottom-line investment outlook, the publication advises maintaining normal risk allocations rather than making major portfolio changes, noting that the December selloff was an excellent buying opportunity that reset valuations back to historical medians. While US GDP growth is expected to slow to 2% by the end of 2019—sharply cooling earnings growth—the combination of a dovish Federal Reserve and Chinese stimulus is expected to stave off recession risks and potentially push valuations back toward 2018 highs. Regarding regional preferences, the author favors Emerging Markets over Europe as a deep value opportunity, noting that the recommended overweight position of US and Emerging Market equities versus Europe and Japan is outperforming again, on track for its 10th outperforming year in the last 13 years.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, covers two primary topics: escalating trade controls in the US-China technology rivalry and a critique of political proposals regarding corporate stock buybacks.

In the first section, the author details the United States' moves toward more aggressive export controls aimed at denying Chinese firms access to US technology. Under the Export Control Reform Act, these policies restrict international sales of products containing American components and treat information transfers to foreign nationals as deemed exports. Consequently, Chinese nationals working for US tech firms may face segregation from critical projects in emerging and foundational sectors such as biotechnology, neurotechnology, advanced computing, machine learning, robotics, hypersonics, advanced materials, and surveillance.

The second, larger section addresses a December 2018 assertion by Senator Marco Rubio that corporate stock buybacks come at the expense of investing in workers and products. Rubio proposed taxing buybacks as imputed dividends to incentivize capital expenditure and hiring. Cembalest counters this by questioning where the senator sees weakness in the data, pointing to historically strong labor and investment indicators.

Two charts support this critique. The first shows the US job openings rate from 2000 through late 2018, utilizing Bureau of Labor Statistics data. The rate hit a historic peak of over 4.5 percent in late 2018, recovering steadily from a low of around 1.8 percent in 2009, indicating robust hiring demand. The second chart, displaying US fixed investment from 2011 through the third quarter of 2018 based on Bureau of Economic Analysis data, indexes investment to December 2011. The visual reveals that all five major non-residential categories are on an upward trajectory. Research and development, software, and information processing equipment have led the growth, indexing around 145 to 150 by late 2018, while structures and industrial equipment also grew to indexes of approximately 130 and 120, respectively. Ultimately, the author argues that capital spending and hiring remain exceptionally strong despite ongoing trade conflicts, rendering the proposed tax changes unnecessary.

This page addresses the immense difficulty of decarbonizing the global industrial sector, which is the world's largest energy consumer. The author argues that decarbonization in this sector is remarkably slow because fossil fuels are heavily integrated as both raw materials and sources of intense thermal heat and pressure. Crucially, electricity currently supplies only 15% of global industrial energy, largely because it is three to five times more expensive per unit of energy than natural gas. Furthermore, in countries like Germany and China, where coal dominates power grids, electrifying industrial processes could paradoxically increase overall carbon emissions.

Several visuals support these observations. A pie chart on global industrial energy consumption by source in 2017 shows that liquid fuels lead at 29%, followed by coal at 26%, natural gas at 23%, electricity at 15%, and renewables at just 7%. A horizontal bar chart of global energy consumption by product in 2016 reveals that basic chemicals and iron and steel are the primary energy consumers, each capturing roughly 15% to 16% of the total, followed by refining at around 9%, nonmetallic minerals at 8%, food at 4%, paper at 3%, and nonferrous metals at 2%.

The economic barrier is detailed in a column chart showing the ratio of industrial electricity prices to natural gas prices per megajoule in 2018 across key regions, including Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, France, Japan, China, and major US industrial states like California, Louisiana, Texas, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. The ratio is consistently high, ranging from about 1.5 times in Louisiana to over 5 times in California, Germany, the UK, and Italy.

The technical necessity of fossil fuels is summarized in two reference tables. The first outlines their use as raw materials, showing metallurgical coke used in pig iron smelting for steel; methane used to synthesize ammonia for fertilizers; methane, naphtha, and ethane used for plastic monomers; and heavy petroleum products used to produce carbon black for tires. The second table details the use of fossil fuels to generate process heat for construction materials like cement, glass, and brick, as well as for smelting iron ore and processing petrochemicals. Lastly, the author notes a 2018 Wuppertal Institute study suggesting that while electrifying 100% of German industrial steam is theoretically possible, doing so is highly constrained by cost and grid electricity sources.

This page provides a historical overview of what the author describes as the four industrial pillars of modern society: cement, steel, ammonia, and plastics. While production growth for these materials has recently slowed due to a deceleration in China, the International Energy Agency expects global consumption of all four to rise significantly by 2050, with cement projected to increase by 12 percent, steel by 30 percent, ammonia by 60 percent, and plastics by 150 percent. The author highlights the critical role of ammonia in the global food supply, noting that half of the world’s population could not be sustained without it due to its use in fertilizer. However, a footnote emphasizes that between 40 percent and 70 percent of applied ammonia is lost globally to leaching, erosion, or de-nitrification, making the minimization of usage losses a key target for decarbonization efforts.

The top of the page features two charts tracking the production index of these four pillars since 1950, where 1950 production equals one. The first index chart shows that by 2015, cement (primarily using coal and petroleum coke inputs) and ammonia (using methane inputs) had both grown to index levels above 30, while steel (using metallurgical coke and natural gas inputs) grew more modestly to an index level of around seven. The second index chart tracks plastics (using methane, naphtha, and ethane inputs), demonstrating massive relative growth that reached an index level of approximately 170 by 2015.

The middle of the page contains individual production charts for cement and steel in millions of tonnes from 1950 through the 2010s. The cement chart shows global production rising to over 4,000 million tonnes, with a callout noting that China produced 2,500 million tonnes of cement in 2017—nearly ten times the output of the next largest producer, India—and consumed almost all of it domestically. The steel chart shows global production rising to over 1,600 million tonnes by 2017, driven largely by China, which produced 50 percent of the world's steel in 2017, up from 36 percent in 2007.

The bottom of the page features individual production charts for ammonia and plastics. Global ammonia production increased to nearly 180 million tonnes by 2015, with China producing 33 percent of the global supply, followed by India, Russia, and the United States. Eighty-five percent of this ammonia is used in fertilizer. The final chart illustrates global plastic production, which grew to roughly 400 million tonnes by 2015. This stacked area chart breaks down plastic use by sector, showing that packaging represents the largest share of plastic consumption, followed by building and construction, textiles, consumer and institutional products, transportation, electrical and electronic applications, and other miscellaneous categories.

This page examines the role of forest management, specifically reforestation and afforestation, as low-tech biological solutions for sequestering carbon dioxide in the United States. US forestlands currently cover approximately 750 million acres and capture about 10% of annual domestic greenhouse gas emissions. 

To illustrate these dynamics, a line chart titled "US forests offset 10% of annual GHG emissions" plots data from 1990 to 2014 in million metric tons of CO2 equivalents per year. The chart reveals that total US greenhouse gas emissions hovered between 6,000 and 7,000 million metric tons, with energy-related emissions accounting for the vast majority of this total. Meanwhile, the carbon sink from forests and land-use changes provided a steady offset of around negative 700 to 800 million metric tons annually. A secondary pie chart titled "Cleared US forestland by disturbance source, 2014" highlights that wildfire is the dominant cause of forest loss, accounting for 62% of cleared land. Other contributing disturbances include general natural causes at 12%, grazing at 11%, insects at 5%, timber harvesting at 4%, and drought and disease at 3% each.

The text details the distinct potentials of reforestation and afforestation. Reforestation, which involves replanting cleared areas, could target 20 million acres of land previously disturbed by fires or pests. Doing so could sequester 50 million metric tons of greenhouse gases annually, representing nearly 1% of total US emissions. However, the author notes that this is a monumental task given that the US Forest Service reforested only 122,000 acres in 2017. Reforestation is increasingly vital to offset carbon losses from aging forests, wildfires (which have released 60 to 80 million metric tons of CO2 annually since 2013), and severe weather events like Hurricane Michael, which destroyed 3 million acres of trees in Florida in 2018. 

Afforestation, the practice of planting trees on previously unforested cropland and pastures, presents a separate opportunity. A National Academy of Sciences study suggests that establishing a carbon price of $15 per tonne could incentivize farmers to convert 7 to 10 million acres of land, sequestering an additional 150 million metric tons of CO2 annually. However, such efforts must navigate complex farmer decision-making, land-use competition for food and biofuels, and the loss of agricultural flexibility. 

Ultimately, the author concludes that while reforestation and afforestation are effective, low-tech solutions, expanding them to achieve an additional 3% sequestration of annual US emissions would require unprecedented private sector participation and substantial financial capital. This option receives a moderate rating on the J.P. Morgan feasibility scale, represented by a graphic of three mountain peaks with the middle peak shaded.

This page evaluates the feasibility and scale of carbon capture and storage as an underground de-carbonization solution. While a 2018 Congressional bill spurred interest by establishing tax credits for carbon dioxide sequestration, and studies support the long-term geological integrity of underground reservoirs, the author urges caution. By the end of 2018, active carbon capture facilities processed a mere 0.1 percent of global emissions. This sluggish start is compounded by historical setbacks, including the withdrawal of Department of Energy support for major projects like FutureGen, legal uncertainties regarding leaks, a 30 percent energy drag on coal facilities, and high-profile project failures. A notable example of these failures is the Kemper Clean Coal plant in Mississippi, a joint project of Southern Company and Mississippi Power, which was suspended in 2017 after falling more than two years behind schedule and running more than 4 billion dollars over its initial 2.4 billion dollar budget. 

The primary hurdle for carbon capture is the colossal physical scale required to make a meaningful impact on global emissions. An accompanying chart, titled "To capture 15% of global carbon dioxide emissions, CCS would have to be larger than the global oil ecosystem," compares the scale of a hypothetical 15 percent sequestration target against the actual global oil extraction infrastructure. If the world aimed to sequester 15 percent of annual global carbon dioxide emissions—equivalent to 5 billion metric tons—the resulting volume of compressed, supercritical gas would require handling 6 billion cubic meters of carbon dioxide annually, calculated at a ratio of 1.25 cubic meters per metric ton. By comparison, annual global oil extraction and refining, which has taken a century to develop, processes only about 4.4 billion metric tons in mass and 5 billion cubic meters in volume, calculated at 1.15 cubic meters per metric ton. 

Because building an infrastructure larger than the entire global oil system is a daunting prospect, the author remains highly skeptical of carbon capture as a primary climate solution. While noting that the technology may be useful for specialized applications like enhanced oil recovery, the author forecasts that global carbon capture is unlikely to exceed 5 percent of carbon dioxide emissions by 2030. This skeptical outlook is reflected in a low visual grade assigned to the technology at the bottom of the page. Additionally, the author notes that similar scale bottlenecks apply to other alternative solutions, such as enhanced weathering, which would require mining and distributing billions of tons of silicate rock each year.

In this section, Michael Cembalest presents a highly skeptical analysis of cellulosic ethanol, contrasting media hype with harsh physical and thermodynamic realities. He notes that despite high-profile promotions, such as a segment on the news program 60 Minutes featuring a company using electron-beam accelerators to break down plant cellulose, the sector has a long history of failing to meet aggressive expectations. For instance, venture capitalist Vinod Khosla predicted in 2006 that the United States would produce 24.8 billion gallons of cellulosic ethanol by 2017, yet actual production reached only 10 million gallons, and major plants built by companies like DuPont, Abengoa, INEOS Bio, Range Fuels, and Cello Energy are no longer operational. Cembalest highlights that because corn stover has just 6% of the volumetric density of gasoline, a fully realized cellulosic ethanol storage and transportation infrastructure would need to be 110 times larger than the current gasoline equivalent.

To show the limited potential of the technology even under highly optimistic assumptions, an analytical table details the potential displacement of US gasoline. Assuming all available US corn stover is harvested at a 40% removal rate from 385 million metric tons of corn, and taking a 15% haircut for transportation and harvesting losses, 130.9 billion kilograms of stover would remain. At a conversion ratio of 0.32 liters per kilogram, this yields 41.888 billion liters of ethanol. However, because the energy density of cellulosic ethanol is only 66% of gasoline, this translates to roughly 7.34 billion gasoline-equivalent gallons. Compared against the 142.98 billion gallons of US gasoline consumed in 2017, this maximum potential displacement is only 5%.

Finally, a horizontal bar chart titled "US Energy Return on Investment" compares the energy return on investment (EROI) of various power sources, demonstrating that biofuels are highly inefficient. While hydropower delivers an EROI greater than 100x, and other sources like wind, nuclear, natural gas, solar photovoltaics, and shale oil provide substantial energy returns, corn ethanol products are grouped at the very bottom. Biodiesel, cellulosic iso-butanol, cellulosic ethanol, cellulosic n-butanol, and corn-based ethanol all cluster around a meager 1.0x energy return on investment, meaning they yield barely more energy than is required to produce them.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication contrasts supercapacitors with lithium-ion batteries for utility-scale energy storage. Supercapacitors, which store energy as static charge rather than through electrochemical reactions, offer higher durability, faster charging times, and less lifetime degradation, making them ideal for short-term power reserves and frequency regulation. However, they trail lithium-ion batteries in energy density and upfront costs. The text highlights Tesla's acquisition of Maxwell Technologies as a sign of the technology’s potential, alongside real-world examples such as Northwestern Energy partnering with Kilowatt Labs to deploy supercapacitor storage in South Dakota. On the other hand, real-world lithium-ion deployment has faced degradation issues, as seen in projects by the French utility EDF and US utility AES, which both experienced substantial capacity de-ratings that align with findings from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.

The comparison is detailed in a comprehensive table evaluating utility-scale applications. Supercapacitors outperform lithium-ion batteries in life cycle, boasting one million cycles compared to lithium-ion’s 2,000 to 10,000 cycles, and they offer a constant 99 percent round-trip DC efficiency and useable capacity that does not degrade. Supercapacitors also function in a wider temperature range of -30°C to 85°C, compared to 0°C to 40°C for lithium-ion, and they carry zero risk of thermal runaway. However, lithium-ion batteries currently maintain a significant advantage in upfront capital cost, at $350 per kilowatt-hour compared to $500 per kilowatt-hour for supercapacitors without production scaling, and in energy density, where lithium-ion achieves 150 to 260 watt-hours per kilogram compared to just 5 to 30 for supercapacitors. Regarding disposal, supercapacitors defer waste due to their longer life, and while graphene-based supercapacitors appear less toxic than lithium-ion, studies still note human and environmental impacts from graphene exposure.

The author concludes that utility-scale battery storage remains in its infancy, requiring solved engineering issues and regulatory changes to unlock its full economic value. On J.P. Morgan's proprietary five-peak graphic rating scale, lithium-ion based utility-scale battery storage receives a grade of two out of five, while supercapacitors receive a grade of one out of five. The author suggests these scores could improve by 2025 if scaling succeeds in driving the costs of either technology below $200 per kilowatt-hour.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Annual Energy Paper critiques the hyped media coverage surrounding a joint venture between Alcoa and Rio Tinto, financed by Apple, to develop a carbon-free aluminum smelting method. While the technology is an ingenious development that utilizes an advanced conductive material to release oxygen instead of carbon dioxide during aluminum electrolysis, the author argues that its actual climate impact is marginal. 

To support this conclusion, the page features a stacked bar chart showing greenhouse gas sources across different stages of aluminum production, measured in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per tonne of aluminum produced. The stages evaluated are bauxite mining, alumina production, anode production, electrolysis (smelting), and ingot casting. The data shows that electrolysis is by far the most carbon-intensive stage, generating over twelve tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per tonne of aluminum. However, the vast majority of these emissions—approximately eighty-four percent—stem from electricity generation. The carbon anode itself, which is the target of the joint venture, represents only sixteen percent of electrolysis emissions and just ten percent of emissions across the entire aluminum production lifecycle. 

Consequently, the maximum possible carbon dioxide reduction from eliminating the carbon anode is limited to the small red segment of the electrolysis bar. Even under a best-case scenario of universal adoption across sixty-three million tons of annual global aluminum production, the technology would eliminate an upper bound of one hundred thirty-eight million tons of carbon dioxide annually, reducing global emissions by only about point four percent. Due to this limited overall impact, the author gives the innovation a very low grade, symbolized by a graphic where only the first of five peaks is shaded, concluding that the advancement does not warrant transformational descriptions like carbon-free smelting.

This page evaluates the accomplishments and impacts of Germany's "Energiewende" energy transition policy, focusing on the substitution of solar and wind for traditional thermal and nuclear power generation. The author notes that Germany's renewable generation reached 38% in 2017, a notable achievement given the country's limited 4% hydropower share. Furthermore, despite concerns that high wind and solar penetration rates could compromise grid reliability, Germany's power outages have declined, with its average annual outage figure for 2017 being among the lowest in Europe.

The page features four charts supporting this analysis. The first line chart, titled "Renewables and the decline in thermal and nuclear generation," tracks electricity generation shares in Germany from 1991 to 2017. It shows thermal generation from coal and gas declining from approximately 60% to about 50%, while nuclear power declined from nearly 30% to around 12%. Over the same period, total renewables increased from under 5% to 38%, driven largely by solar and wind, which rose from near-zero to about 20% of the total generation. 

The second line chart, "Germany’s wind and solar capacity build-out now matches its thermal capacity, with more to come," plots capacity in gigawatts from 1991 to 2015. It reveals that while thermal capacity hovered around 80 to 90 GW, solar and wind capacity experienced a steep ascent, matching thermal capacity at roughly 85 GW by 2015.

The third chart is a scatter plot comparing the installed capacity footprint of wind and solar across developed nations, measured in kilowatts per square kilometer against kilowatts per capita. Germany leads the developed world as a clear outlier, boasting more than 1.0 kW per capita and nearly 250 kW per square kilometer. Other countries analyzed include Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands, Japan, the United Kingdom, Italy, Spain, Sweden, Austria, France, the United States, Canada, Finland, and Norway. 

The final bar chart, "Average annual power supply interruption," displays 2016 outage minutes for European countries. It demonstrates that Germany's grid reliability has improved, with average annual outages dropping from about 22 minutes in 2006 to roughly 15 minutes in 2017. This is second only to Switzerland, which has around 10 minutes of interruptions, and is far superior to nations like Spain, Italy, Finland, Sweden, Ireland, and Norway. The author adds that the comparable United States figure was much higher at 128 minutes.

This page examines the major financial and logistical challenges of Germany's Energiewende energy transition policy, focusing on high household electricity costs and projected regional supply-demand imbalances. The author emphasizes that German household electricity costs are already among the highest in Europe, even before accounting for the additional costs of transmission infrastructure expansion, nuclear power substitution, and higher renewable penetration. The author questions whether the political willpower exists to finance these remaining transition expenses. 

The first visual is a stacked bar chart showing electricity prices for household consumers in Euros per kilowatt-hour across dozens of European nations, based on Eurostat data from the second quarter of 2018. The prices are categorized into three components: value-added tax, renewable energy levies and other taxes, and the base price without taxes. Denmark has the highest overall electricity price at over 0.31 EUR per kWh, followed closely by Germany at approximately 0.30 EUR per kWh. A red arrow points to Germany's bar, which features a notably large gray section representing high renewable energy levies and taxes. By comparison, the overall European Union average sits at roughly 0.20 EUR per kWh. The accompanying text notes that while German household incomes are similar to those in France, Ireland, and the United Kingdom, Germany's electricity prices are much higher in relative terms. Conversely, because household incomes in Spain and Italy are lower, their real financial burdens are closer to Germany's than their raw positions on the chart suggest.

The second visual illustrates the expected regional power balance deficits in Germany, comparing a map from 2015 to a projected map for 2030 using data from Amprion GmbH. The maps use a color-coded scale where blue indicates an energy surplus and pinkish-purple indicates a deficit. In 2015, the map of Germany is overwhelmingly blue, showing a healthy power surplus across most of the country. By contrast, the 2030 projection shows a dramatic shift, with massive swaths of deep purple deficit spreading across central and southern Germany. This shift highlights a worsening regional supply-demand gap, where wind energy is primarily generated in the North, but the major population and energy-demand centers are located in the South.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Annual Energy Paper analyzes the feasibility of Germany's Energiewende transition goals, focusing on the steep discrepancy between ambitious policy targets and historical energy use trends. The author points out that while the policy aims for a thirty percent decline in primary energy use from 2015 to 2030, actual German energy use has remained essentially flat since 2000. 

This challenge is visualized in two charts. The first, titled Germany primary energy consumption, Mtoe, displays German energy consumption from 2000 to 2018 fluctuating between 310 and 340 Mtoe. A steep, dotted projection line shows the dramatic reduction required to reach the Energiewende goal of a thirty percent decline by 2030, highlighting how unrealistic this trajectory is compared to historical flat performance. The second chart, Energy intensity, measures Mtoe of primary energy per unit of nominal GDP from 2000 to 2016 across five countries: the United States, Germany, France, Japan, and the United Kingdom. Although all listed nations show declining energy intensity—with Germany dropping from roughly 0.13 to 0.09 and the United States dropping from 0.22 to around 0.13—the author argues that these efficiency gains have been offset by overall economic demand, leaving total energy consumption flat.

The commentary highlights the German Federal Government's Expert Commission self-assessment, which gave its lowest grade of "unlikely to meet 2020 target" to progress in transportation, fuel mix, transmission grid expansion, and primary energy use. Looking ahead, the author addresses three key questions regarding Germany's energy future. First, while reaching sixty-five percent renewable power generation by 2030 is possible, it would demand substantial political will to construct missing grid infrastructure, eighty percent of which is still on the drawing board, and could drive up electricity prices. A footnote adds that if households resist prices above 35 cents per kilowatt-hour, industrial users currently paying 12.5 to 15.5 cents per kilowatt-hour may bear the cost burden instead. Second, cutting greenhouse gas emissions in half by 2040 is deemed highly unlikely due to slow decarbonization outside the power grid. Finally, the page concludes that Germany’s goal of phasing out all coal and lignite by 2038 is completely unrealistic.

This page explores the ongoing risks of investing in utilities located in wildfire-prone regions, arguing that severe wildfire seasons are not anomalous but rather a lasting risk driven by climate change. The author highlights the financial consequences of this hazard by focusing on PG&E, which experienced a catastrophic stock collapse after the 2017 and 2018 wildfire seasons. This decline is illustrated in a chart tracking PG&E's market capitalization in billions of US dollars from January 2017 to January 2019. The company's market cap plummeted from a peak of over $35 billion in mid-2017 to under $5 billion in early 2019, before recovering slightly to around $10 billion.

To address whether this wildfire threat is permanent, the page presents scientific research from a 2016 study by Abatzoglou and Williams, representing Columbia's Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory and the University of Idaho. A cumulative chart tracking millions of hectares of US forest fires from 1984 to 2016 compares the actual forest area burned against a non-anthropogenic baseline of natural causes. While natural causes alone would have resulted in roughly 4 to 5 million cumulative hectares of burned forest by 2016, the actual and total estimated burn area reached nearly 10 million hectares. This gap, which represents the forest area burned due to anthropogenic climate change, demonstrates that human-caused climate factors have effectively doubled the total cumulative burn area over this period, cementing a permanently heightened risk profile for regional utilities.

This page examines the connection between human activity and wildfire severity, focusing on both climate-induced fuel aridity and direct human-caused ignitions. 

The first visual is a line chart depicting the estimated temperature increase in the Western forest region due to human activities from 1900 to 2010 in degrees Celsius. The chart shows that after remaining relatively flat or slightly negative through the mid-20th century, estimated temperature changes rose sharply from the 1970s onward, exceeding 1.0 degree Celsius by 2010. A corresponding scatter plot analyzes U.S. forest fire area in thousands of hectares on a logarithmic scale against fuel aridity relative to a non-anthropogenic baseline from 1984 to 2015. This plot highlights two distinct periods: 1984 to 1999, which experienced lower fuel aridity and fewer hectares burned, and 2000 to 2015, which saw significantly higher fuel aridity levels and a corresponding exponential rise in burned forest area, reaching over one million hectares in peak years. Both of these charts cite research by Abatzoglou and Williams from 2016. A footnote explains that fuel aridity is a composite index built from eight metrics of potential forest fire risk and intensity, such as the Fire Weather Index, vapor pressure deficit, and drought severity indices.

The page also details how humans directly start the vast majority of wildfires and account for nearly half of the total area burned. A data table from Balch et al. at the University of Boulder, spanning 1992 to 2012, shows that across the continental United States, humans started over 1.27 million fires, representing 84% of the total, compared to about 245,000 started by lightning. These human-started fires burned over 16 million hectares, representing 44% of the total area burned, while lightning-caused fires burned over 20 million hectares. The table breaks these figures down across ten geographical regions. Human-caused fires are particularly dominant in areas like Mediterranean California, where they account for 97% of fires and 89% of the area burned, as well as Eastern Temperate Forests, where they represent 95% of fires and 82% of the area burned. In contrast, in the Northwest Forested Mountains, lightning causes the majority of both fires and burned area. 

The author concludes by noting that while humans remain a primary driver of fire starts, overall fire frequency in the United States actually peaked around 1980 and has since declined. This downward trend is attributed to fewer instances of arson, fewer controlled burns getting out of control, and a decrease in cigarette-related ignitions.

In this analysis, titled "Fed Zeppelin," Michael Cembalest discusses the rapid global market rebound in early 2019, which marked the fastest post-war recovery from a December equity bear market. He attributes this rally primarily to the Federal Reserve’s sudden shift toward patience, halting balance sheet reductions and rate hikes. While drawing a comparison to a policy mistake in 1966 when the Fed eased prematurely and triggered inflation, Cembalest argues that current stable wage and price inflation measures provide sufficient breathing room today. He forecasts that the Fed's next move will likely be a hike in early 2020, despite easing pressures from President Trump’s nominees. 

Beyond US monetary policy, China is identified as the other major market driver due to Chinese stimulus, rising leading indicators, and a high probability of a US-China trade deal. Although global growth and corporate earnings are slowing, Cembalest characterizes this as a soft patch centered in European manufacturing rather than the end of the economic cycle. He expects modest appreciation for the rest of 2019, favoring US and Emerging Markets equities, and notes that US and European equity valuations have stretched well above their medians despite consensus 2019 EPS growth projections of just 3% to 5%.

The page features a comprehensive bar chart detailing 2019 year-to-date total returns in US dollars across dozens of global asset classes as of April 5, 2019. The assets are color-coded into eight categories, spanning US growth equities, US equities, US fixed income, European and developed market equities, non-US developed fixed income, emerging market equities, emerging market bonds, and commodities. The chart visually underscores the massive scale of the early 2019 rally, with risk assets dominating. Several top performers exceeded the visual limits of the vertical scale, which spans from negative 15% to positive 20%. Footnoted outliers include Shenzhen equities up 44%, Oil up 36%, Shanghai equities up 33%, S&P Tech up 22%, FANG stocks up 22%, and MSCI China equities up 21%. Major equity benchmarks, such as the Nasdaq, S&P 500, and various European and emerging market indices, posted robust gains generally ranging from 5% to 15%. In contrast, traditional safe havens and select sovereign bonds underperformed, with trade-weighted US dollars, gold, and Japanese local bonds hovering near flat or slightly negative. The worst-performing assets were concentrated in agricultural commodities like corn, natural gas, and highly stressed sovereign debt, with Argentina local bonds losing approximately 15%.

This page focuses on the rapid rebound of global equity markets in early 2019 despite slowing economic growth, attributing the bounce largely to the Federal Reserve’s "pivot" toward patience regarding balance sheet declines and interest rate hikes. The author notes that while global markets have rallied substantially and pushed valuations back above historical medians, economic indicators present a mixed picture. For the United States, the author projects flat to negative year-over-year earnings growth in the first and second quarters of 2019, with modest full-year growth of only 3% to 5%. In Europe, manufacturing is characterized as being in a "black hole," though the service sector shows more resilience.

The analysis is supported by six charts. The first, "Fed Zeppelin: the Fed fuels the bounce," plots the percentage of the S&P 500 bear market recovered against the days after the market bottom. It illustrates that the 2018/2019 recovery curve skyrocketed to nearly 100% within 70 days, vastly outperforming the median post-war recovery, which typically reaches only about 30% in the same timeframe. The acceleration is marked by the Fed’s announcement of patience around day 10. The adjacent chart confirms that the 2018/2019 rebound is tied for the fastest post-war recovery of a bear market decline, placing it at the top of a historical comparison spanning from 1957 to 2018.

A bar chart titled "Valuation percentiles back above median" compares historical percentiles across US equities, European equities, Emerging Market equities, high-yield bonds, and high-grade bonds. Across all categories, valuations have surged from their December lows—which hovered between 15% and 40%—to current levels well above the 50% median, with US and European equities both pushing past the 70% mark. 

To contextualize this growth against economic reality, a chart titled "Global GDP and profits: soft patch not recession" plots nominal GDP alongside corporate profits from 1998 through 2018, with estimates for 2019. This visual suggests that while both metrics are softening, they point to a temporary soft patch rather than an impending recession, with nominal GDP expected to stabilize around 5% to 6%. 

Concurrently, regional divergence is highlighted in "Black hole in European manufacturing," which tracks manufacturing new orders for the US, Eurozone, China, and Japan from 2013 to 2019. The Eurozone line has plunged deeply below the 50-expansion threshold to near 45, whereas the US remains in expansion territory and China and Japan hover near the neutral line. Finally, a chart on capital spending surveys indicates that US corporate capital expenditure is cooling off, as both the Duke CFO survey and the NFIB small business survey show a downward trend in plans to increase capital expenditures and expected growth over the next year.

On this page, Michael Cembalest examines China's role as a major market catalyst, driven by substantial fiscal and monetary stimulus, rebounding economic indicators, and the strong likelihood of a US-China trade deal due to unprecedented economic integration. He argues that despite potential criticisms of a modest trade deal, any progress represents a step forward compared to past administrations, noting that the immense economic linkages between the US and China provide a powerful buffer against catastrophic conflict, defying the historical Thucydides Trap.

To illustrate China's policy support, a bar chart titled "More China fiscal stimulus on the way" shows Chinese tax and spending measures as a percentage of GDP from 2015 through an estimate for 2019. After stimulus dipped to less than negative 0.1 percent of GDP in 2017 and rebounded to roughly 1.8 percent in 2018, the estimate for 2019 projects a massive surge to over 3.0 percent of GDP. This 2019 stimulus is heavily weighted toward tax cuts, represented by a blue bar segment of approximately 2.2 percent of GDP, with spending comprising the remaining 1.0 percent.

Accompanying this is a line chart titled "China business surveys rebounding," which tracks Caixin and Markit business survey levels from 2010 to 2019, where a level above 50 indicates expansion. It depicts both Services PMI and Manufacturing PMI recovering from recent lows in early 2019. The Services PMI historically remains robustly in expansionary territory, hovering around 52 to 54, while the more volatile Manufacturing PMI shows a sharp dip below the 50 expansion threshold in late 2018 before bouncing back up toward 50 by early 2019.

The central thesis of deep economic integration is supported by a stacked bar chart titled "China and the US: much deeper economic linkages than actual and potential adversaries of the last 100 years." This chart measures the sum of bilateral foreign direct investment stock, central bank holdings of each other's government debt, and bilateral annual trade as a percentage of combined GDP for various adversarial country pairs across history. The US and China in 2014 stand out dramatically at over 7 percent of combined GDP—composed of roughly 4.5 percent bilateral central bank debt holdings, 2.5 percent bilateral annual trade, and a small sliver of foreign direct investment. By comparison, historical adversaries like France and Germany in 1930 or the UK and Germany in 1930 peak at roughly 4 percent and 3.5 percent of combined GDP respectively, while Cold War adversaries like the US and Russia in 1983 or regional rivals like India and Pakistan in 2014 show almost negligible economic linkages near 0 percent.

Cembalest notes that while critics might lament the lack of deeper structural changes in a potential US-China trade agreement—such as minor progress on intellectual property, joint ventures, or subsidies—even a modest deal would outpace what the Bush or Obama administrations achieved. He references the high stakes of this relationship, pointing out that China's 2001 entry into the World Trade Organization led to a severe collapse in US manufacturing jobs and between 250 and 600 billion dollars in annual losses from IP theft and counterfeit goods. He also highlights that Europe is similarly contemplating stricter regulations on Chinese foreign direct investment in high-tech, transport, and energy sectors to address these same issues of forced tech transfers and unfair competition.

Michael Cembalest addresses whether the Federal Reserve is making a policy mistake by pausing interest rate hikes, comparing the current economic landscape to the Fed’s policy error of 1966 to 1968, when the central bank lowered rates despite mounting inflation and deficits. He argues that, unlike the late 1960s, current measures of price and wage inflation look remarkably stable despite a highly tight labor market. While corporate labor costs are rising, productivity gains have successfully neutralized this pressure, and core PCE remains anchored around two percent. However, Cembalest notes that the expanding federal budget deficit during a period of falling unemployment remains a significant concern. Ultimately, he concludes that the Fed’s decision to pause rate hikes is justified by the underlying economic data.

To support this perspective, several charts detail labor, inflation, and deficit dynamics. The first chart, which shows that labor costs are rising alongside worker output, plots the year-over-year percentage changes of the Employment Cost Index and Unit Labor Costs from 1995 to late 2018. Although the Employment Cost Index has risen steadily to nearly three percent, Unit Labor Costs remain volatile but low, averaging below two percent due to rebounding productivity. 

Inflation indicators remain firmly anchored according to two subsequent charts. The chart on US core PCE inflation shows year-over-year inflation from 1990 to late 2018, illustrating a long-term decline from around four percent down to a stable channel fluctuating between one and two percent. Directly below, a chart on inflation expectations tracks three separate metrics from 1995 to 2019: the University of Michigan survey of five-year inflation expectations, which has hovered between two and a half and three percent; the Philadelphia Fed survey of ten-year CPI expectations, which remains highly stable at just over two percent; and the New York Fed survey of three-year inflation expectations, which has leveled off near two and a half percent.

Fiscal and employment trends are contrasted in a chart tracking the decoupling of the US unemployment rate and the budget deficit from 1960 to 2019 estimates. Historically, the budget deficit and the unemployment rate have moved in tandem, but they have recently diverged sharply. While the unemployment rate has fallen to its lowest level in forty years, dropping below four percent, the budget deficit has expanded countercyclically to around five percent of GDP.

The final two charts emphasize the robust health of the US job market. The first displays labor market health from 2001 to early 2019 using a three-month moving average of the firing rate and the voluntary quit rate as a percentage of the labor force. The firing rate has fallen to historical lows of around one and a third percent, while the voluntary quit rate has climbed to historical highs near two percent, demonstrating high worker confidence. The last chart tracks job openings in the construction sector alongside corporate mentions of labor costs during earnings calls from 2001 to 2019. Construction job openings have surged toward three and a half percent, while corporate concerns about wages have shot up dramatically, with the labor cost mention index rising from a low of thirty in 2010 to over one hundred and ten by 2017.

This page consists entirely of legal disclaimers and regulatory disclosure text with no financial charts, tables, or market analysis. The disclosures outline compliance requirements for several jurisdictions, focusing heavily on Brazil and Australia.
