For Brazil, the text cautions that public offerings of securities without registration at the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission (CVM) are prohibited. For Australia, it details the regulatory oversight of J.P. Morgan Chase Bank, N.A. by the Australian Securities and Investment Commission and the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, stating that the publication is intended only for wholesale clients as defined under Australian law. Additionally, it highlights that J.P. Morgan Securities LLC is exempt from holding an Australian Financial Services Licence under the Corporations Act of 2001 and is instead regulated by U.S. entities including the SEC, FINRA, and CFTC. It concludes with specific warnings for Australian investors regarding non-Australian dollar references, accounting standards, foreign currency investment risks, and local tax issues.

This page analyzes the systemic risks associated with the Federal Reserve's long-term low interest rate policy, arguing that it creates severe headwinds for pension funds and insurers while fueling excessive investor risk-taking. 

The first section examines the strain on fixed income investors. A stacked bar chart illustrates the percentage of state revenues required to meet future pension and OPEB obligations plus interest on debt across ten states, including Illinois, New Jersey, Connecticut, and California. Under a scenario where portfolio returns drop from 7.5% to 4.5%, the required portion of state revenues spikes dramatically, exceeding 55% for Illinois, 40% for New Jersey, and 35% for Connecticut. In tandem, a line chart tracking insurance company fundamentals from 2005 to 2018 shows a severe post-QE deterioration. Return on equity dropped from near 20% in the mid-2000s to around 10% by 2018, while the average price-to-book value fell from a peak near 2.0 down to approximately 1.0.

The second section focuses on the consequences of heightened market speculation and structural vulnerability. A historical bar chart shows the percentage of tech companies with negative trailing 12-month earnings at their IPO from 1980 to late 2018. The share of unprofitable tech IPOs surged to over 80% by 2018, reaching levels not seen since the peak of the dot-com bubble in 2000. Additionally, a final bar chart compares the change in debt market size against trading turnover from 2006 to 2017 across mortgages, municipals, high yield, investment grade debt, and US Treasuries. While the overall debt stock expanded enormously—by over 150% for investment grade corporate debt and over 200% for US Treasuries—trading turnover plunged across nearly all categories, particularly for treasuries and investment grade bonds. 

The author warns that this combination of speculative issuance and shrinking market liquidity could prove destructive when the economic cycle eventually turns. Consequently, the publication advises investors to maintain normal portfolio allocations and avoid over-weighting risky assets, even though the cycle may not be ending immediately.

This page analyzes shifts in macroeconomic indicators, focusing on the Federal Reserve’s required policy rates and the implications of the recently inverted US yield curve. 

The author begins by connecting structural economic shifts to a long-term decline in labor bargaining power, illustrated in a chart spanning 1947 through 2018. This chart shows a parallel decline in both the labor share of output in the non-farm business sector, which fell from around 65% to under 57%, and private sector union membership, which plummeted from over 35% of the workforce to roughly 7%. These trends, alongside shifting population and productivity dynamics, have resulted in lower required policy rates. 

A second chart displays estimates of the required real policy rate from two Federal Reserve Bank of New York models alongside the actual real Fed policy rate from 1980 through 2018. Both models indicate that the equilibrium policy rate has fallen from around 3.5% in the early 1980s to between 0.5% and 1.0% today, suggesting that the equilibrium rate may only need to exceed inflation by 50 to 100 basis points. The author notes that the current real Fed policy rate is aligned with these estimates, contrary to proposals by former nominee Stephen Moore, who advocated for a 50-basis-point rate cut—a position criticized by economist Greg Mankiw. Cembalest forecasts that the next central bank action will be a rate hike in early 2020, driven by rising healthcare and housing inflation.

The bottom half of the page evaluates the recently inverted US yield curve. Although a 3-month to 10-year yield curve inversion historically preceded recessions in seven out of eight cases with a lag of 1.5 to 2.0 years, the author argues this cycle's inversion may be a less reliable recession signal. First, the 2-year versus 10-year spread remains positive. Second, aggressive quantitative easing by central banks in Europe, Japan, and the UK has depressed yields overseas, driving foreign capital into long-duration US Treasuries and keeping long-term US yields artificially low. Third, the repeal of Regulation Q in 2011 allowed banks to pay interest on demand deposits, pushing short-term yields up. Finally, other key metrics, such as the employment-to-population ratio and private investment as a percentage of GDP, still suggest the economy is in a mid-cycle rather than late-cycle phase.

This page analyzes the Federal Reserve's decision to pause monetary tightening, which represents a gamble that the Phillips Curve—the traditional inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation—remains broken. The author explains that since 2000, the curve has flattened, meaning low US unemployment no longer triggers significant wage or price inflation. Four structural explanations are proposed and supported by data.

The first chart, "Phillips Curve has flattened since the year 2000," plots the responsiveness of inflation to unemployment changes. In the 1980s and 1990s, the responsiveness coefficient hovered between -0.4 and -0.6. Since 2000, it has risen sharply to around -0.2 or higher, indicating a much flatter curve. A footnote addresses a speech by NY Fed President Williams, who argued the curve is active for cyclically sensitive prices; however, the author counters that even this coefficient, at -0.16, is minor compared to pre-2000 levels of -0.50 to -0.65.

The second chart demonstrates that companies are responding to labor cost increases by reducing profit margins rather than raising prices. In the late 1970s and 1980s, a 1% increase in unit labor costs raised core PCE inflation by about 0.8% with minimal impact on profit margins. By 2015, the same labor cost increase had almost zero impact on PCE inflation, while the negative impact on inverted profit margins deepened to around -0.6%. 

The third chart illustrates the role of globalization in reducing price sensitivity to domestic conditions. From 1960 to 2015, world trade as a percentage of GDP rose from roughly 25% to nearly 60%, and world cross-border capital stock surged from under 10% of GDP to over 110%. This indicates that US prices are increasingly tethered to global rather than domestic market forces.

The fourth chart shows how online retailing has increased price transparency and diminished corporate pricing power by reducing the duration of retail price changes. Between 2008 and 2017, the duration of price changes in months collapsed across multiple categories: furnishings and household price durations fell from a peak of nearly 18 months in 2011 to about 6 months; recreation and electronics fell from around 11 months to under 6 months; and food and non-alcoholic beverages experienced a milder decline, ending near 5 months.

This appendix analyzes the Federal Reserve's historical policy mistake between 1966 and 1968, outlining how a premature policy pivot and structural miscalculations initiated a decade of runaway inflation. The narrative begins in 1966 when the Fed tightened policy in response to rising core inflation and falling unemployment. This tightening triggered a sharp equity market correction, with the S&P 500 falling twenty-one percent by October 1966. In response to the market decline, the Fed paused and pivotally cut rates in March 1967, an action illustrated in the federal funds effective rate chart where rates fell from nearly six percent to around four percent.

This policy pivot occurred because the Fed underestimated the non-inflationary rate of unemployment, or NAIRU. The chart showing estimates of the natural rate of unemployment illustrates that real-time estimates placed NAIRU between four percent and four and a half percent during the late 1960s, whereas retrospective Congressional Budget Office estimates later revealed the true natural rate was much higher, between five and a half percent and six percent. Consequently, the Fed eased policy while the labor market was already excessively tight, with the US unemployment rate hovering below four percent. 

At the same time, fiscal policy became highly stimulative due to Vietnam War spending, causing the US fiscal surplus to collapse into a deficit of nearly three percent of GDP by early 1968. With unemployment continuing to fall and core inflation remaining stubborn at three and a half percent, the Fed was forced to reverse course in November 1967. The central bank hiked the federal funds effective rate to six point one percent by May 1968 and continued raising it toward nine percent by 1969. As depicted in the US core inflation chart, both CPI and PCE measures surged, with CPI core inflation approaching six percent by 1969. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 index, which had recovered temporarily after the 1967 pivot, peaked and began to decline again in late 1968, marking the onset of a highly unstable era for both financial markets and monetary policy.

This page consists entirely of standard legal disclosures and regulatory boilerplate for various global jurisdictions, including Spain, Germany, Italy, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Latin America, and Australia. It contains no charts, financial data, or market commentary.

This page analyze the friction in the United States-China trade relationship, explaining the Trump administration's resistance to last-minute Chinese reversals of trade concessions. The author points out that since China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, it has remained highly mercantile, ranking near the bottom in intellectual property protection, receptivity to foreign direct investment, and state-backed domestic favoritism. He references a May 8 Reuters article detailing how Chinese negotiators deleted critical compliance commitments across all seven chapters of a draft agreement. Despite these setbacks, the author places the odds of a final trade agreement in 2019 at 50 percent.

To illustrate the historical context, the page includes a line chart titled "The seismic impact of China joining the WTO," tracking Chinese imports and exports in trillions of US dollars from 1989 to 2017. Following China's WTO entry in 2001, both trends skyrocketed from near-zero levels. By 2017, China's exports reached approximately 2.3 trillion dollars, consistently outstripping its imports, which climbed to around 1.8 trillion dollars. 

A neighboring bar chart, titled "Points of dispute in the US-China trade war," ranks China against developed and emerging economies on a scale of 0 to 100, where 0 is worst and 100 is best. Across all eight categories evaluated—including protection of trade secrets, intellectual property enforcement, software piracy, market access barriers, copyright protections, foreign investment receptivity, state control of the private sector, and the overarching Mercantilism Index—China ranks poorly, with all scores clustered between roughly 5 and 30.

The discussion then turns to equity markets. Despite the trade dispute, European and Japanese equities failed to outperform. Instead, the United States and Emerging Markets equity barbell outperformed Europe and Japan in 2019 through May 10, representing the tenth year of outperformance out of the last thirteen.

The page concludes with a boxed case study on Section 232 washing machine tariffs. The data shows that US imports of washing machines from tariffed nations fell 31 percent from 2017 to 2018, while imports from China rose 24 percent as consumers bypassed the tariffs. Consequently, US washing machine and dryer prices both rose by 12 percent. While domestic production plans by Samsung and LG were projected to create 1,600 US jobs, researchers from the University of Chicago and the Federal Reserve calculated that these jobs cost American consumers a steep 1.2 billion dollars in inflated retail prices.

In this publication of J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market," Michael Cembalest assesses the US-China trade war, evaluating whether the tariff conflict represents a major economic threat or a more modest headwind. Cembalest argues that while the trade dispute is unlikely to match the destructive scale of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley tariffs, the risk to corporate earnings is substantial, particularly for the highly globalized technology and industrial sectors. 

To contextualize the scale of current trade policies, the page features a line chart depicting US tariff history and projections from 1910 through the 2010s, measured as the effective tariff rate. The historical data shows a sharp peak near 20% during the Smoot-Hawley era, followed by a steady multi-decade decline to below 2% by the 2010s. Plotted against this history are six incremental steps of recent and proposed tariffs. These progress from initially imposed Section 232 tariffs on washing machines, solar, steel, and aluminum at under 2%, through various China Section 301 tranches, up to a proposed 25% tariff on the remaining $290 billion of Chinese imports, which would push the effective rate to roughly 5%. The final proposed step, a 25% tariff on automobile and parts imports, would elevate the effective tariff rate to nearly 10%.

The moderate macroeconomic impact is supported by an accompanying table estimating the one-time impact of these tariffs on US inflation. Forecasts from major institutions remain subdued. J.P. Morgan projects a 0.1% to 0.2% increase in inflation from the latest 25% hike on $200 billion of Chinese exports. The Federal Reserve and Bridgewater both project a 0.4% inflation impact from across-the-board or full escalation. Goldman Sachs outlines the widest range, estimating a 0.2% impact from the 2018 tariffs, rising to 0.6% for 25% across-the-board Chinese tariffs, and peaking at 0.9% if a 25% tariff is expanded to include both China and auto imports. 

Despite these modest inflationary figures, Cembalest warns that permanent tariffs threaten to roll back decades of globalization that boosted corporate profit margins by suppressing wage inflation and growing foreign sales. This vulnerability is illustrated in a chart tracking trailing four-quarter free cash flow margins for Tech versus the broader S&P 500 from 1977 to 2016. While both series hovered below 5% for much of the late 20th century, the Tech sector dramatically diverged after 2004, climbing to nearly 20% by 2016, while the broader S&P 500 remained below 10%. Because US tech companies derive 50% to 55% of their sales from foreign markets, they are uniquely exposed to trade friction.

The final bar chart, which measures US tariffs on China against various economic metrics, reinforces this concentrated risk. While tariffs comprise a negligible fraction of overall GDP and consumer spending, they represent a significant burden when compared to corporate earnings. Tariffs as a share of affected companies' earnings are roughly 1% for the overall S&P 500, but they rise dramatically to approximately 11% for industrial capital goods and nearly 13% for technology hardware. This concentration of impact suggests that while the broader US economy may remain resilient, the tariff war poses a severe downside risk to key industrial and technology earnings.

This J.P. Morgan report page discusses the reasons behind recent equity market weakness and identifies structural factors that may provide technical support. The author attributes the market's vulnerability to elevated valuations preceding a breakdown in trade talks. He highlights that the spring 2019 rally was the fastest post-bear market recovery in the post-war era, driven heavily by Federal Reserve policy shifts. This rapid recovery is illustrated in a line chart titled Fed Zeppelin: the Fed fuels the bounce, which plots the percentage of the S&P 500 recovered against the number of days after the market bottom. The 2018/2019 recovery curve dramatically outperforms the historical median recovery curve, surging to nearly 100% within 90 days following the Federal Reserve's announcement of patience and market watching.

A second bar chart, Valuation percentiles back above median, shows valuation percentiles utilizing 12-month forward P/E ratios for US equities, EUR equities, and EM equities, alongside credit spreads for high yield and high-grade bonds across four periods: Peak 2018, Low 2018, Peak 2019, and Current. This data demonstrates that current valuations, such as European equities sitting at the 60th percentile, have rebounded significantly from their late-2018 lows and sit above historical medians, though they are starting to moderate with recent market weakness.

On the supportive side, the author points to an unprecedentedly low level of net equity supply globally and in the US. A bar chart titled Unprecedented low levels of net equity supply measures supply in billions of USD from 1999 to 2019 based on the MSCI All Country World Equity Index. It reveals that massive stock buybacks and merger-and-acquisition activity, particularly in the US, have caused net equity supply to turn deeply negative in recent years, with US net supply dropping to nearly negative 400 billion USD in some periods. An accompanying commentary box explains that even with a recent surge in US IPOs that could match 1999 levels when projected for the full year, the overall net supply remains restricted, offering strong technical support to equity markets.

Finally, the author observes that the market's near-term path is highly binary, with either very good or very bad outcomes on the horizon. He transitions the discussion to two structural topics: the outlook for US prescription drug price legislation and the political ideology of the 2020 Presidential candidates. He notes that the rising influence of progressive candidates is closely tied to the potential enactment of drug price controls, which could happen even before the 2020 election.

This page serves as the reference and glossary endmatter for the publication. It first lists several key academic and media sources used in the issue's analysis, which cover the economic return to protectionism, the inflationary effects of trade disputes with China, the relocation and price impacts of U.S. trade policy on washing machines, Medicare Part B and Part D drug pricing differentials between the U.S. and other countries, and news reporting on U.S.-China trade deal negotiations. Below these citations, the page provides a glossary defining the "Acronyms of the week," which include BSA (Business Software Alliance Trade Group), EM (Emerging Markets), GIPC (Global Innovation Policy Center), HHS (Health and Human Services), IPO (Initial Public Offering), ITIF (Information Technology and Innovation Foundation), NBER (National Bureau of Economic Research), P/E (Price/earnings ratio), S232 (Section 232 trade tariffs related to national security), S301 (Section 301 trade actions against treaty violations), and WTO (World Trade Organization). The lower portion of the page contains standard J.P. Morgan legal disclosures, compliance disclaimers, and regulatory entity information.

This page analyzes the growing political and public pressure to control US prescription drug prices, which has contributed to large-cap pharmaceutical and biotech stocks underperforming the S&P 500 by 12% to 18% in early 2019. The author notes that legislative momentum is building ahead of the 2020 election, supported by studies showing how much higher US drug prices are compared to other industrialized nations. 

To illustrate these price discrepancies, the page features two bar charts. The first chart, based on 2018 Department of Health and Human Services data, compares US discounted prices to average international prices for top Medicare Part B drugs, which are mostly cancer-related. The chart reveals that US premiums of two to four times the international average are common across dozens of drugs, with some medications like Treanda and Lucentis reaching nearly eight and seven times the international average, respectively. 

The second chart focuses on Medicare Part D drugs, showing the ratio of US discounted prices to average international prices. A red bar representing a basket of 79 high-spending Medicare Part D drugs, sourced from a 2019 Johns Hopkins study, shows a US premium ranging from a low estimate of roughly 2.7 times to a high estimate of 3.6 times. Blue bars representing individual drugs from a 2017 Commonwealth Fund study show Crestor, Lantus, Advair, and Januvia all priced at over three times their international averages, while Humira is priced at more than double. The text notes that many of these high-priced Part D drugs are not new innovations and have been on the market for nearly a decade.

The author outlines substantial potential cost savings from drug price convergence. Medicare accounts for 31% of all US drug spending, with 75% going to Part D and 25% to Part B. If US Medicare Part B drug prices were reduced to international averages, annual spending could decline by 50%, yielding eight billion dollars in yearly savings. For Medicare Part D, converging prices to international levels could save between 40 billion and 80 billion dollars annually. However, achieving these Part D savings would require legislation to bypass the "non-interference" clause that currently prevents the federal government from directly negotiating Medicare Part D prices. The author concludes by noting that such legislative reform enjoys overwhelming, bipartisan public support of over 90%.

This page serves as an appendix summarizing the February 2019 US Trade Representative report on China's compliance with World Trade Organization rules. It outlines a comprehensive list of areas where China has reportedly failed to comply, focusing heavily on market access barriers, unfair industrial policies, and intellectual property concerns.

In the automobile sector, the report highlights that foreign manufacturers are forced into joint ventures with Chinese enterprises where they cannot hold majority ownership, effectively forcing them to transfer core new energy vehicle technologies to local partners. Additional barriers include discriminatory taxes in the integrated circuit sector and hundreds of prohibited subsidies across manufacturing sectors such as steel, aluminum, solar panels, and fishing, which create massive excess capacity and disrupt global markets. In the tech and service sectors, the USTR notes severe market access barriers for cloud computing, where foreign companies are prohibited from direct operations and must hand over technology, intellectual property, and branding to partner with domestic license holders. Similarly, online supply of foreign video and entertainment software is highly restricted, and technology licensing regulations remain discriminatory.

The report also details financial and raw material restrictions, specifically highlighting how China blocks major electronic payment providers like Visa and MasterCard from its market to protect the national champion, China Union Pay, despite previous WTO dispute commitments to open up by 2006. Furthermore, China is accused of repeatedly abusing trade remedies through retaliatory antidumping and countervailing duty investigations, such as those targeting US grain-oriented electrical steel, chicken broiler products, and automobiles, while frequently failing to comply with resulting WTO rulings. In agriculture, China is criticized for excessive domestic support and protectionist tariff-rate quotas, notably delaying its tariff schedule updates for the Harmonized System dating back to 2002. Finally, the report asserts that China's legal system is structured to act as an instrument of the ruling Party and government to secure specific economic outcomes and advance national industrial policy.

This analysis from J.P. Morgan Asset Management discusses the rising influence of progressive politicians in Congress and its potential impact on future legislation, such as drug pricing. To illustrate this trend, the author highlights that 44 percent of 2018 House primary candidates identified as progressive, up from 29 percent in 2016, and notes that the Congressional Progressive Caucus has grown to become the largest group in the Democratic Party with 100 members. 

At the center of the page is the "Presidential administration ideology and a look at 2020" chart, which tracks the ideological placement of historical administrations and current presidential candidates based on empirical congressional voting patterns. The horizontal axis measures ideology from negative 0.7, representing the most liberal, to positive 0.7, representing the most conservative. Historically, the chart displays a stark zigzag pattern. Starting in the early twentieth century, the Coolidge and Hoover administrations rate around 0.45 conservative, shifting sharply leftward to FDR and Truman at negative 0.55 liberal. The trend then swings back to Eisenhower at 0.12 conservative, left to JFK and LBJ at negative 0.5 liberal, right to Nixon and Ford at 0.25 conservative, and back left to Carter at negative 0.52 liberal. Moving toward the modern era, Reagan and Bush score around 0.35 conservative, Clinton lands at negative 0.42 liberal, George W. Bush sits at 0.52 conservative, Obama is positioned at negative 0.5 liberal, and Trump marks the conservative peak on the chart at 0.58. 

Along the top of this chart, 2020 presidential candidates are grouped into four ideological categories based on their congressional voting history. Ultra-progressives, including Kamala Harris, Bernie Sanders, and Elizabeth Warren, cluster furthest to the left around negative 0.65. Progressives, including Cory Booker, Kirsten Gillibrand, and Tim Ryan, sit near negative 0.48. Liberals, consisting of Joe Biden, Jay Inslee, Seth Moulton, Beto O'Rourke, and Eric Swalwell, are positioned near negative 0.35, while Centrists, containing Michael Bennet, John Delaney, Tulsi Gabbard, and Amy Klobuchar, sit near negative 0.3. Candidates without congressional voting histories, such as Pete Buttigieg, Julián Castro, John Hickenlooper, Wayne Messam, Bill Weld, Marianne Williamson, and Andrew Yang, are omitted.

An accompanying table, "Administration ideology constituents," lists the prominent legislative and administrative figures used to calculate each historical administration's position. For example, the Trump administration's score is derived from figures like Tom Cotton, Lindsey Graham, Orrin Hatch, and Paul Ryan. Obama's score is calculated using figures like Joe Biden, Dick Durbin, Hillary Clinton, Ted Kennedy, John Kerry, Nancy Pelosi, Harry Reid, and Henry Waxman. George W. Bush is represented by figures such as John Ashcroft, Roy Blunt, Dick Cheney, Tom DeLay, Mitch McConnell, and Rick Santorum, while Clinton's score relies on figures like Lloyd Bentsen, Tom Carper, and Richard Gephardt. 

The author outlines a wide array of progressive policies that are driving this ideological shift, including proposals for a 70 percent tax on incomes over 10 million dollars, financial transaction taxes, a wealth tax on assets over 50 million dollars, the "Accountable Capitalism Act," bans on stock buybacks, employee representation on corporate boards, Medicare-for-All, breaking up large banks and technology firms, free public college, and student debt forgiveness. The key forward-looking question raised is whether and to what extent these ambitious progressive policies will be adopted by the liberal and centrist candidates in the 2020 field.

This introductory commentary page by Michael Cembalest, titled "Listen when people tell you who they are," addresses the escalating global trade war driven by President Donald Trump. Cembalest acknowledges that he underestimated the potential for an escalating tariff war given its severe implications for US businesses, the stock market, and political alliances. He emphasizes that Trump's protectionist views, including a desire for 25% tariffs on China, have been consistently articulated since the 1980s and as recently as a 2011 CPAC speech. Consequently, Cembalest argues that the US equity market no longer deserves premium price-to-earnings multiples of 17x or 18x. J.P. Morgan's optimistic "trade war resolved" outlook expects a 7% to 9% return for the S&P 500 by year-end, though downside risks remain, particularly regarding trade policy and burgeoning tech anti-trust issues.

The author previews the subsequent four pages of charts, which cover weakening global and US economic indicators, historical tariff levels approaching pre-World War II eras, US exposure to Chinese retaliation, negative impacts on consumption and employment, border apprehension trends that prompted proposed tariffs on Mexico, and the relationship between US fertility rates and immigration.

Extensive footnotes elaborate on several key points. Cembalest notes that US tariffs often result in self-inflicted wounds, pointing out that two-thirds of US imports from Mexico come from US-owned companies, and Section 301 tariffs on China primarily harm US and non-Chinese subsidiaries. He highlights that the S&P 500 experienced its second-worst May since the 1960s, falling 6.6% in 2019. He details opposition to the Mexico tariffs from Senate Republicans—including Rob Portman, John Kennedy, Chuck Grassley, Joni Ernst, Pat Toomey, and John Cornyn—and mentions past criticisms of protectionism from Trump advisers Stephen Moore and Larry Kudlow. 

The footnotes also discuss a potential shift in anti-trust philosophy away from the traditional "consumer welfare" price standard, which historically protected tech giants, back toward "overall market dominance," citing the Federal Trade Commission's legal victory against Qualcomm. Trump's immigration and deportation policies are compared to those of President Herbert Hoover during the Great Depression, though under vastly different economic conditions. Finally, Cembalest shares a personal anecdote about a hostile childhood cat named Spiro, named after Vice President Spiro Agnew, to illustrate the core lesson that one must believe people when they show their true nature.

This page consists entirely of legal disclaimers and regulatory disclosures for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication. It details compliance information regarding public offerings in Brazil and Mexico, as well as extensive regulatory notices for Australian investors. Specifically, it notes that J.P. Morgan Chase Bank, N.A. is regulated by the Australian Securities and Investment Commission and the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, clarifies that the materials are intended solely for wholesale clients under the Corporations Act 2001, and states that J.P. Morgan Securities LLC is exempt from holding an Australian Financial Services Licence as it is regulated by U.S. entities such as the SEC, FINRA, and CFTC.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, focuses on US asylum trends and details the complexities of the immigration system. The author highlights that asylum applications are soaring, overwhelming an ill-equipped system. The analysis divides applications into two main types: affirmative and defensive. Affirmative asylum applications have maintained a consistently high approval rate since 2016, whereas defensive asylum applications based on credible fear have seen a modest decline in approval rates, and other defensive applications remain flat at much lower levels. The text notes that these approval statistics only represent decided cases, as roughly half of all applications filed since 2009 remain pending. In terms of policy, a Trump administration memorandum is highlighted for reversing an Obama-era policy by denying work permits to both pending and denied applicants. 

Looking closer at credible fear asylum, the US Citizenship and Immigration Service (USCIS) has determined that about three-quarters of applicants have a credible fear, resulting in their referral to an Immigration Judge. However, only slightly more than half of those approved actually filed for asylum. The author notes that abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) would significantly restrict the US government's ability to prosecute these non-filers, given that the Border Patrol's jurisdiction only extends 100 miles from the border. 

A detailed definition block defines affirmative asylum eligibility as a proactive application made by individuals not in removal proceedings within their first year in the country. Conversely, defensive asylum is sought by those already in removal proceedings to avoid deportation, which can occur after a denied affirmative claim, apprehension without legal documents, or being stopped by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) while claiming credible fear. The section also references the roles of USCIS and the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR).

This page presents a collection of six charts analyzing current and leading indicators to illustrate how the US-China trade war is negatively impacting global, Chinese, and US economic and trade activity. 

The first two charts track global activity surveys through May 2019 using Markit data. Part one shows that both global services and manufacturing, alongside global manufacturing output, peaked in early 2018 and have steadily declined. By mid-2019, the composite services and manufacturing index dropped to approximately 51.5, while manufacturing output fell closer to the 50.0 neutral mark. Part two tracks global services and manufacturing employment alongside new export orders. It reveals a dramatic decline in new export orders, which fell below the expansionary threshold of 50 to around 49 in mid-2019, indicating contraction, while global employment indicators cooled to roughly 51.5. 

The third chart illustrates the toll on world merchandise trade volume from 2007 through March 2019, indexed to a 2010 average of 100. This CPB index shows a steady post-recession rise that peaked around 125 in late 2018 before flattening and starting to decline in early 2019. 

The next two charts examine bilateral trade dynamics between the US and China from 2000 to 2019, utilizing a three-month moving average of year-over-year percentage changes. US exports to China show a severe contraction, plummeting to nearly negative 25% to 30% by 2019, a level of decline comparable to the depths of the 2008–2009 Great Recession. Meanwhile, China's exports to the US also dropped sharply to around negative 15% year-over-year in early 2019, which is the steepest decline for Chinese exports to the US since the global financial crisis. Both of these charts feature grey vertical bars to indicate US recessionary periods.

The final chart compares two major US manufacturing surveys, the Institute for Supply Management (ISM) and Markit, from 2007 through May 2019, with levels above 50 indicating economic expansion. Both surveys show a significant downshift after peaking in 2018; the ISM index fell from around 60 to approximately 52, while the Markit survey dropped from 55 down to nearly the 50 threshold, indicating that US domestic manufacturing is nearing stagnation.

This page serves as the executive summary of an analysis by Michael Cembalest titled "Lost in Space: The Search for Democratic Socialism in the Real World, and how I ended up halfway around the globe from where I began." Cembalest challenges the popular American perception that Nordic nations are models of democratic socialism. He argues instead that these countries are robust market economies with highly capitalistic and pro-business policies, funded by regressive taxation on middle-class consumption and payrolls rather than progressive corporate taxation. To support this view, he quotes Danish Prime Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen, who clarified in 2015 that Denmark is a market economy, not a socialist planned economy.

A scatter-plot chart illustrates that the Nordic approach to the private sector is, on many measures, even more business-friendly than that of the United States. The chart ranks the Nordics (represented by solid blue circles) and the US (represented by hollow red circles) on a 0-to-100 scale across several indices grouped into three categories: business-friendly policies, oligopolies, and state control. In the "Business-friendly policies" category, the Nordics score higher than or equal to the US on business freedoms, starting a business, free-trade policies, receptivity to foreign direct investment, property rights protections, freedom of capital flows, and economic globalization. In the "Oligopolies" category, the Nordics show higher bank asset concentration and lower competition among firms than the US. Under "State control," the US ranks slightly higher on state control of business and government impact on competition. 

To address how these nations fund their extensive social programs, a table titled "Who pays for Nordic entitlement programs? Everyone, particularly the middle class" presents 2018 OECD data. The table shows consumption, Social Security, and payroll taxes as a percentage of GDP. Sweden leads at 27.0%, followed by Finland at 26.3%, the Netherlands at 25.1%, Norway at 22.3%, and Denmark at 14.9%. In contrast, the United States registers significantly lower at 10.6%, highlighting that Nordic social benefits are underpinned by high regressive taxation on the broader population.

This analysis from J.P. Morgan evaluates the multifaceted impacts of the US-China trade war, examining tariff scenarios, their growth and inflation consequences, US corporate vulnerability, and structural trade friction points. 

An initial chart traces the US effective tariff rate from 1910 through proposed 2019 scenarios. Historically, the US effective tariff rate peaked around 20% during the Smoot-Hawley era of the 1930s before steadily declining to under 5%. Projections show that imposing successive waves of Section 301 tariffs on China, Section 232 auto tariffs, and 25% tariffs on Mexico could push the US effective tariff rate back up to nearly 10%. 

The publication characterizes these Section 301 tariffs as an "own goal" because they heavily impact multinational supply chains rather than Chinese firms. A supporting table shows that for goods exported from China to the US, a significant share is produced by US and non-Chinese multinationals located in China. Specifically, non-Chinese firms account for 86% of exported computer products, 68% of miscellaneous manufacturing, 63% of electrical equipment, and 59% of machinery, leaving Chinese firms with minority export shares in these critical sectors.

Economic growth and inflation forecasts from Goldman Sachs project the trade war’s impacts after three years. In terms of real GDP, under a scenario where all threatened tariffs are implemented, China’s GDP is projected to fall by nearly 0.9% and US GDP by about 0.85%, while the global GDP impact sits around 0.5%. Inflation impacts are heavily concentrated in the US; under the total threatened scenario, the US Consumer Price Index is projected to rise by roughly 0.9%, compared to 0.25% in China, while the Euro Area, Japan, and the broader world face negligible CPI impacts of less than 0.05%. 

The analysis also highlights that US corporate interests are highly exposed to retaliation. While the reported US-China trade balance showed a deficit of nearly $350 billion in 2017, this deficit virtually disappears to nearly zero when accounting for the in-country sales of US subsidiaries operating inside China, representing a massive profit center vulnerable to regulatory or consumer backlash. 

Finally, a ranking of US-China trade disputes rates China's policies compared to developed and emerging economies on a scale of 0 to 100, where 100 is best. China scores poorly across the board, particularly on state control of the private sector, receptivity to foreign direct investment, and barriers to market access. Its worst performance is on the Mercantilism Index, which tracks forced local production, export subsidies, intellectual property theft, and currency manipulation.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest of JP Morgan Asset Management argues that Nordic countries are firmly capitalistic market economies rather than democratic socialist ones. To find examples of democratic socialism in practice, he defines a search criteria for countries with high personal and corporate tax rates, high government spending, strict worker protections that limit hiring and firing flexibility, heavy state regulation and product market intervention, and protectionist trade and capital controls. Finding no perfect match, Cembalest identifies Argentina as the closest approximation of these traits. He critiques Argentina's economic history, highlighting that the nation has defaulted seven times since its independence in 1816, suffered the largest relative decline in standard of living in the world since 1900, and remains on the brink of political and economic chaos. He concludes that a real-life proof of concept for a successful democratic socialist society has yet to be found, comparing it to the mythical Lost City of Atlantis. 

A central graphic displays a blue globe with a curved orange arrow tracing a path from Scandinavia down to Argentina, representing the author's analytical journey. The bottom of the page outlines the table of contents for the supporting data in the rest of the report, which includes sections on the basics of Nordic countries, how their market economies are as business-friendly as the United States, their heavy taxation on middle-class wages and spending, their redistribution and worker protection policies, and a historical review of Argentina's decline from 1913 to 2018. Footnoted sources for the upcoming data include the World Bank, OECD, World Economic Forum, Fraser Institute, Swiss KOF Institute, and the Wall Street Journal.

This page focuses on the domestic consequences of US trade policies, cyclical shifts in the global technology supply chain, an unusual divergence in the US consumer credit market, and the resetting of global equity valuations. 

The first section evaluates the impact of tariffs on US employment and consumption. The top-left chart measures US employment, comparing tariff-protected industries—including household appliances, steel and aluminum products, and auto parts—to all other industries using an index where February 2018 equals 100. Following the implementation of the first round of tariffs in early 2018, employment in tariff-protected industries stalled and began a slight decline toward 100, while employment in all other industries grew steadily to nearly 102 by early 2019. Correspondingly, the top-right chart illustrates real consumer spending indexed to February 2018. Following the tariff implementation, consumer spending on tariff-impacted categories like major appliances and auto parts dipped below 100 and stagnated, while spending on all other core goods continued its upward trend, reaching approximately 107 by early 2019.

The second section highlights a cyclical downturn in the global semiconductor market. The middle-left chart depicts days of global semiconductor inventory across producers, distributors, and customers, showing a steady climb from under 160 days in late 2016 to more than 200 days by the fourth quarter of 2018. At the same time, the middle-right chart tracks global semiconductor sales on a three-month moving average in billions of US dollars. This series shows that sales peaked in 2018 at more than 40 billion dollars before suffering a sharp contraction down to roughly 31 billion dollars by early 2019.

The third section poses an open question regarding the US labor market and consumer credit: why auto loan delinquencies are rising despite an all-time low in unemployment. The bottom-left chart plots the unemployment rate alongside 90-day-plus auto loan delinquencies from 2004 to 2019. Historically, these two metrics have moved together, but since 2012, they have diverged sharply. Even as the unemployment rate steadily fell below 4% in 2019, serious auto loan delinquencies climbed from a low of about 3% to nearly 5%.

The final section examines global equity valuation percentiles, comparing 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios against their historical ranges from July 2016 to mid-2019 for the United States, Europe, and Emerging markets. After a synchronized peak in late 2017 and early 2018—where US and European valuations exceeded the 80th percentile of history—multiples compressed significantly. By June 2019, US valuations sat near the 70th percentile, Europe hovered around the 60th percentile, and Emerging markets recovered from a late 2018 low near the 30th percentile to settle near the 55th percentile.

This page analyzes demographic trends in the United States, focusing on the intersection of rising southwest border enforcement actions and asylum applications with declining domestic fertility rates and their combined impact on projected national population growth. 

A chart tracking apprehensions and inadmissibles at the southwest border through the first six months of each fiscal year from 2009 to 2019 shows a dramatic spike at the end of the period. Total apprehensions and inadmissibles surged to nearly 450,000 in 2019, with apprehensions alone rising toward 400,000 after hovering near 200,000 for much of the preceding decade. Alongside this trend, annual asylum applications filed skyrocketed from around 50,000 in 2009 to nearly 300,000 in 2018. However, the volume of applications adjudicated did not keep pace, rising only modestly to just under 100,000 by 2018. Inset data reveals that of the cumulative 1,152,661 asylum applications filed since 2009 (comprising 44% defensive other, 40% affirmative, and 16% defensive credible fear), only 52%, or 598,035, have been adjudicated.

The page further details the steep drop-offs in the credible fear asylum process using cumulative data from 2008 to 2018. Out of all individuals who claimed credible fear, 76% were granted it. Of those, only 55% filed for asylum. Within that group of applicants, 61% of cases remained pending, 29% were rejected, and only 11% were ultimately granted asylum. Meanwhile, a table on Temporary Protected Status (TPS) beneficiaries details Trump Administration efforts to terminate the status for several nations, a move currently tied up in court. Major affected groups include El Salvador with 251,526 beneficiaries, Honduras with 80,633, and Haiti with 56,209, alongside terminations slated for Nepal, Nicaragua, and Sudan. Conversely, extensions were granted to smaller beneficiary populations from Somalia, South Sudan, Syria, and Yemen. 

These immigration dynamics are set against declining domestic demographic indicators. A chart plotting the US total fertility rate from 1920 through the 2010s shows that, following the mid-century baby boom peak of over 3.5 births per woman, the rate fell below the replacement level of 2.1 in the early 1970s. It has remained below replacement level ever since, dipping further below 2.0 in the years following 2010. Consequently, a final chart depicting five-year averages for US annual population growth from the 1960s through 2029 projections shows a steady decline in overall growth from over 1.2% to less than 0.8%. This projection highlights a shrinking share of organic population growth, leaving immigration as an increasingly dominant driver of overall US population growth in the coming decade.

This J.P. Morgan report page, titled "Nordic countries: The Basics," compares the economic and social profiles of Nordic countries—specifically defined here as Sweden, Finland, Norway, Denmark, and the Netherlands—with those of the United States and the OECD average. The author argues that while Nordic nations rank high on prosperity and happiness, they are significantly smaller, more ethnically homogeneous, and less open to immigration than the US. Their relative wealth compared to the US has remained remarkably stable, with Nordic per capita GDP hovering at roughly 90% of US levels in both 1960 and 2018, suggesting that their unique social and economic policies did not dramatically shift their wealth trajectory. The page features nine distinct charts to illustrate these points.

The first three charts focus on basic demographics and scale. The Population chart highlights that the average Nordic country is small, with only 9 million residents, compared to the US population of over 300 million and the OECD average of around 35 million. Similarly, the GDP chart shows that the average Nordic country has an economy of about $500 billion, whereas the US economy stands around $20 trillion and the OECD average is closer to $1.5 trillion. The Ethnic Homogeneity chart uses a scale where 1.00 represents total homogeneity; the average Nordic country scores high at nearly 0.90, whereas the US scores just over 0.50 and the OECD average is around 0.74.

The middle row of charts explores immigration and historical economic performance. The chart on Immigrant Percentage of Total Population reveals that immigrants make up around 12.3% of the average Nordic population, compared to nearly 15% in the US and 13.7% for the OECD average. The 1960 GDP per Capita chart shows the average Nordic nation at roughly $15,500, which was 91% of the US level. Decades later, the 2018 GDP per Capita chart shows the average Nordic nation at approximately $54,000, representing 90% of the US level, while the OECD average stands lower at around $45,000. 

The bottom row of charts highlights key structural and social differences. The Gun Ownership chart demonstrates a massive gap in safety metrics, showing that the average Nordic country has about 15 guns per 100 persons, which is similar to the OECD average but far below the US average of nearly 120. The Defense Spending chart shows that the average Nordic nation spends just under 3% of its total government budget on defense, compared to over 8% in the US, allowing more public funds to be directed toward social programs. Finally, the Renewable and Nuclear Energy chart shows that the average Nordic country relies heavily on clean energy, generating over 70% of its electricity from renewable and nuclear sources and deriving over 40% of its total primary energy from these sources. In contrast, the US and the OECD averages both generate only about 30% to 40% of their electricity and derive under 20% of their primary energy from these clean sources.

This page consists entirely of legal and regulatory disclosures for J.P. Morgan, specifically addressing securities offering restrictions in Latin American jurisdictions, such as Brazil's Securities and Exchange Commission, as well as detailed regulatory compliance notices for Australian wholesale clients under the Corporations Act 2001.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication argues that Nordic countries are market economies that are just as, if not more, business-friendly than the United States. To support this thesis, the author contrasts the Nordic average, the United States, and the average of OECD nations across nine distinct economic indicators using a series of bar charts. 

The first chart, the Business Freedom Index, measures how pro-business a country is on a 100-point scale. The Nordic average leads with a score of approximately 87, followed by the United States at 82 and the OECD average at 78. The second chart, Trading Across Borders, evaluates pro-trade friendliness on a 100-point scale. The Nordic average again leads with a score of roughly 96, while the OECD average and the United States score 90 and 89, respectively. The third chart shows Receptiveness to Foreign Direct Investment on a 100-point scale. The Nordic average scores about 90, outperforming the OECD average of 83 and the United States at 77. 

The fourth chart focuses on the Absence of Capital Controls, with higher scores representing fewer controls. The Nordic average scores roughly 54, whereas the OECD average is at 44 and the United States lags at 38. The fifth chart, protecting physical and intellectual property rights, shows the Nordic average leading at about 84, compared to 81 for the United States and 71 for the OECD average. The sixth chart addresses the negative impact of government regulation on competition, where a higher score indicates greater impact. The United States exhibits the highest negative impact at 2.3, compared to 1.7 for the OECD average and a much lower 1.1 for the Nordic average. 

The final three charts demonstrate that Nordic countries are comparatively friendly to corporate management. The seventh chart, Competition Among All Firms, indicates that the United States is highly competitive with a score of 78, while the Nordic average is 64 and the OECD average is 58, indicating that Nordic systems allow greater market dominance by large firms. The eighth chart shows the Asset Share of the Five Largest Banks, revealing significant banking consolidation in Nordic countries at roughly 86%, compared to 77% for the OECD average and only 42% for the United States. Lastly, the Conflict of Interest Regulation chart shows that the United States maintains the most stringent oversight with a score of 83, while the OECD average is 64 and the Nordic average is 59, reflecting that Nordic corporations operate with fewer regulatory constraints on management misuse of assets.

This page argues that Nordic countries do not adhere to a democratic socialist model, as their levels of state control and government regulation are highly similar to—and in some cases lower than—levels found in the United States. The author asserts that the data on state control demonstrates that Nordic nations operate on free-market principles rather than a model of collective ownership of the means of production. 

To support this, the page features two charts. The first is a bar chart titled State Control of the Economy, which utilizes the Public Ownership components of the OECD’s 2013 Product Market Regulation indicator. In this index, where higher numbers represent more state control, the United States actually registers a higher score, just above 3.0, compared to the Nordic average of approximately 2.8 and the overall OECD average of roughly 2.7. A supporting text box explains that this indicator measures the share of thirty economic sectors with state-owned firms, government ownership in six major network sectors, the presence of special voting rights in private firms, and competitive insulation given to state-owned enterprises.

The second visual is a line chart tracking Competitive Distortion Induced by Government Regulation from 1990 to 2013, based on the OECD's Non-Manufacturing Regulation Indicator. The chart shows that while Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland, and the Netherlands started with high distortion scores between 4.5 and 5.5 in 1990, all of these countries experienced a steady, significant decline over the subsequent two decades. By 2013, their scores had converged to between 2.0 and 2.5, coming very close to the low baseline level of the United States, which remained between 1.5 and 2.0. A second text box explains that this distortion index covers seven network sectors, assessing entry regulations, public ownership, vertical integration, and overall market structure.

Additionally, a footnote on the page explains that higher indicators for these measures are linked to suboptimal profit persistence, lower capital expansion, and lower productivity growth. It notes that the US indicators are measured specifically with respect to New York State, and references research suggesting these indicators may actually overstate the intensity of European Union regulations because they fail to account for the streamlined regulatory benefits of the EU internal market.

This page of the publication explores the characteristics of Nordic healthcare systems, highlighting how higher tax revenues support greater government spending on state-sponsored programs, leading to some of the highest healthcare quality and access indices in the world. However, the author contrasts these systems with proposed "Medicare for All" programs in the United States. Specifically, Nordic systems depend heavily on cost-sharing and containment; all five Nordic National Health Plans require patient co-payments, and the largest Nordic countries require patients to meet deductibles before government coverage kicks in. This reflects a broader trend among OECD public plans of shifting cost burdens to patients. Additionally, Nordic systems enforce strict prescription drug guidelines and volume tracking, which can restrict drug availability compared to US Medicare.

To support these observations, the page includes three bar charts. The first shows non-defense government spending as a percentage of GDP, revealing that the Nordic average sits at approximately 45 percent, compared to around 34 percent in the US and 38 percent for the OECD average. The second chart illustrates that nearly 100 percent of the population is covered by government or social health insurance in the Nordics and about 98 percent in the OECD overall, while the US lags significantly at roughly 35 percent. The third chart plots a Healthcare Access and Quality Index, where the Nordic average scores near 95 out of 100, outperforming the OECD average of 91 and the US score of 89.

Finally, a table compares cost-sharing and containment policies across Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and US Medicare. It shows that while all systems utilize copayments, only Norway bases these copayments on socio-economic conditions. Furthermore, Denmark, the Netherlands, Sweden, and US Medicare require deductibles, while Finland and Norway do not. Regarding prescription policies, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, and Sweden implement strict drug guidelines and track prescription volume patterns, while US Medicare uses neither of these cost-containment strategies.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market analyzes the dramatic economic decline of Argentina relative to the rest of the world over more than a century, spanning 1913 to 2018. The author presents two distinct analytical frameworks to illustrate the scale of this decline.

The first chart, titled "Argentina's per capita GDP has barely doubled in over 100 years," shows the ratio of real per capita GDP in 2018 compared to its 1913 baseline. The y-axis scales from zero to forty-five times. East Asian economies like Taiwan, South Korea, Singapore, and Hong Kong lead the chart with massive growth ratios exceeding thirty to forty times. In stark contrast, Argentina sits at the far right of the chart with the lowest ratio of all countries with available data for both years, having barely doubled its per capita GDP over the 105-year period. 

The second visual, titled "Reversals of fortune: changes in per capita GDP rankings since 1913," is a scatter plot comparing a nation's per capita GDP percentile in 1913 on the x-axis to its percentile in 2018 on the y-axis. A diagonal line divides the chart into two zones: countries above the diagonal improved their relative global rankings, while those below the line saw their rankings fall. The distance from the diagonal represents the magnitude of change. The chart emphasizes that Argentina’s drop from the 83rd percentile in 1913—when it was among the wealthiest nations in the world—to the 40th percentile in 2018 represents the largest decline on the chart. Other countries suffering notable ranking declines include Venezuela, South Africa, and Algeria, which lie well below the diagonal. Conversely, nations like Singapore, Hong Kong, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea lie far above the line, showing significant upward movement. Both charts rely on data sourced from the Conference Board, the University of Groningen, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page analyzes the tax structure of Nordic countries, arguing that their exceptionally high tax burden is not driven by progressive taxes on wealthy households or corporations, but rather by regressive taxes that hit the lower and middle classes. Michael Cembalest emphasizes that the Nordic model relies heavily on consumption, payroll, and social security taxes to fund its spending, while keeping corporate and capital gains taxes relatively low and maintaining much lower estate taxes than the United States. 

To support these assertions, the page presents five distinct bar charts comparing the Nordic average, the United States, and the OECD average using 2017 data. The first chart, which displays the total tax burden as a percentage of GDP, shows that the Nordic average total tax burden stands at roughly 43% of GDP, compared to just 26% in the US and 34% for the OECD average. While income taxes represent around 14% of GDP in the Nordics and 11% in the US, the major difference lies in consumption, social security, and payroll taxes, which make up about 27% of GDP in the Nordics but only 10% in the US. 

The second chart focuses on progressive personal and corporate income taxes. It reveals that corporate income taxes are low across all regions, contributing only 2% to 3% of GDP in both the US and the Nordics. Personal income taxes are about 15% of GDP in the Nordics, 10% in the US, and 8% in the OECD. The third chart details regressive taxes, showing that consumption taxes represent a significant 12% of GDP in the Nordics and 11% in the OECD, compared to a meager 4% in the US. Social security taxes make up another 11% of GDP in the Nordics, compared to 6% in the US. 

The fourth chart examines taxes on earned income and capital gains as a percentage of GDP. It illustrates that individual capital gains taxes are minimal across all three categories, while taxes on earned income account for roughly 14% of GDP in the Nordics, 9% in the US, and 9% in the OECD. The final chart presents estate tax rates on generational transfers, showing that the United States has a high estate tax rate of 40%, whereas the OECD average is 15% and the Nordic average is only 11%, with some Nordic countries charging no estate tax at all. 

Additionally, the commentary notes that certain design elements of Nordic taxes further diminish their progressivity. For instance, social security taxes in Denmark and the Netherlands are flat or capped, making them regressive, while large flat municipal taxes in Sweden and Denmark substantially reduce the overall progressivity of personal income taxes.

This page analyzes the economic and social model of Nordic countries, comparing their labor markets, educational access, redistribution mechanisms, and poverty rates against the United States and the OECD average. The author observes that while Nordic countries feature high worker protections, their income redistribution system is the primary driver of their remarkably low levels of inequality and poverty compared to the US. 

The analysis is supported by nine charts. The first chart, showing the percentage of university students enrolled in public institutions, reveals that about 90% of Nordic students attend public universities, compared to approximately 70% in the US and 80% across the OECD. Labor market flexibility is compared through two World Economic Forum indices where a higher score indicates greater ease or flexibility. On the ease of hiring and firing index, the US scores around 78, significantly higher than the Nordic average of 50 and the OECD average of 48. Similarly, for the flexibility of wage determination, the US scores roughly 78, compared to about 45 for Nordic countries and 65 for the OECD.

Labor protections and representation are explored in three subsequent charts. The unionization rate is over 50% in Nordic countries, compared to only 11% in the US and 25% for the OECD average. This difference is even more pronounced in the collective bargaining coverage rate, which reaches about 84% in Nordic nations but is only 12% in the US. Additionally, on the Workers Rights Index, which measures collective bargaining, striking, and association rights, Nordic nations score above 90, whereas the US scores below 70. Despite these strong protections, the labor share of GDP is actually higher in the US, at roughly 55.5%, compared to 53% in Nordic countries and 52% in the OECD.

The final section of the page details the outcomes of these structural differences on poverty and inequality. The poverty rate, defined as the percentage of families with incomes below 50% of the median, is about 7% in Nordic countries, less than half of the US rate of approximately 18%. The final chart details the Gini coefficient of income before and after taxes and transfers. Before taxes and transfers, market inequality is somewhat similar, with the Nordic average at 0.47 and the US at 0.51. However, after redistributive taxes and transfers are applied, the Nordic Gini coefficient drops dramatically to 0.26, representing one of the lowest inequality levels in the world, while the US post-tax and transfer Gini remains much higher at approximately 0.39.

This page consists entirely of standard legal disclaimers and regulatory disclosures for J.P. Morgan, specifically addressing compliance guidelines for wholesale clients under Australian financial licensing laws and U.S. regulatory bodies.

This page of the publication, written by Michael Cembalest, introduces the thematic conflict between President Donald Trump and Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell. It draws a historical parallel to the 1970s clash between President Richard Nixon and then-Fed Chair Arthur Burns, analyzing the intense political pressure placed on central bank chairs during periods of low unemployment and the threats such actions pose to Federal Reserve independence. 

A side-by-side comparison table contrasts the specific tactics and statements from the Nixon versus Burns era with those of the Trump versus Powell era. For the 1970s conflict, the table outlines how the Nixon administration planted negative press stories, threatened to dilute the Chairman's power by doubling the number of Federal Reserve Board members, directly blamed the Fed for potential economic stagnation, and leaked a false story about Burns demanding a pay raise, culminating in HR Haldeman's crude assertion that they had Burns controlled on the money supply. On the contemporary side, the table documents Trump's public criticisms of Powell, including calling the Fed "crazy" and "loco," tweeting that the Fed is the nation's "most difficult problem," and comparing the institution to a "powerful golfer who can't score." Trump's remarks also show his public desire to trade Powell for European Central Bank head Mario Draghi and his criticism of the Fed's quantitative tightening balance-sheet reduction as "sucking money like from a vacuum cleaner." 

The author reflects on the outcome of the 1970s conflict, noting that Burns ultimately succumbed to political pressure to boost the economy before the 1972 election, which triggered a decade of stagflation. Looking to the future, the author suggests that modern structural deflationary forces—such as globalization, de-unionization, industrial robotics, and internet-driven price discovery—will likely prevent a repeat of 1970s-style inflation. Instead, the author predicts that the primary consequence of Powell's potential monetary easing will be the formation of asset bubbles.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan market commentary discusses how expected Federal Reserve easing is coinciding with a slowing global business cycle, which is bringing down business surveys, sales, global GDP growth, and S&P earnings-per-share growth. Despite these headwinds, the author argues that a global or US recession is unlikely due to a resilient services sector and expected easing from twenty developed and emerging market central banks. To support a durable equity rally past current all-time highs, leading indicators must make a decisive positive turn. Over the near term, markets are expected to be flat after the July Federal Reserve meeting as the economic benefits of easing are largely exhausted, while abnormal monetary dynamics in Europe, such as high-yield bonds trading with negative yields, continue to challenge central bankers.

Six charts support these arguments by illustrating the ongoing slowdown in manufacturing, trade, and corporate fundamentals. The first chart, plotting global business surveys and S&P sales surprises from 2010 to 2019, shows that global manufacturing business surveys, advanced by two quarters, strongly lead S&P positive sales surprises. Both metrics have declined steeply from late 2017 peaks, with the manufacturing survey falling toward the 50-expansion threshold and positive sales surprises dropping toward 45%. The second chart compares S&P earnings per share year-over-year growth against Japanese machine tool orders, advanced by six months, from 1995 to 2020. This historical indicator reveals a deep plunge in Japanese machine tool orders into negative territory (approaching negative 40% to 60%), pointing to a imminent contraction in S&P earnings-per-share growth. 

The next three charts focus on macroeconomic activity and the divergence between sectors. The third chart displays global business surveys and quarter-over-quarter GDP growth from 2011 to 2019, showing that a decline in composite manufacturing and services business surveys closely tracks a deceleration in global GDP growth, which has slipped to around 2.5%. The fourth chart, tracking global output business surveys for services versus manufacturing from 2013 to 2019, highlights that while manufacturing has slipped below the 50 threshold into contraction territory near 49.5, the services sector remains resilient in expansionary territory above 52. This divergence is further underscored by the fifth chart, which shows global manufacturing new orders dropping steadily from a peak of nearly 56 in late 2017 to under 50 by mid-2019. Finally, the sixth chart plots real-time world trade indicators from 2012 to 2019, demonstrating that both the world trade volume proxy and the world trade indicator have deteriorated from growth rates of 5% to 6% in 2017 down to near 0% growth, with the June 2019 estimate for the world trade indicator dipping to roughly negative 1%.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, examines the growing controversies surrounding the $1.2 trillion US leveraged loan market, focusing on the prevalence of "covenant-lite" loans. The author highlights a dual conflict: while investors are aggressively buying these loans—which offer 5% annualized returns with low volatility since 2010—the structural protections for these investments have degraded significantly. Easy Federal Reserve monetary policy and aggressive underwriting standards are driving covenant protections to record lows, which the author predicts will lead to materially lower loan recovery rates in the next recession. 

The analysis is supported by three charts. The first, a dual-axis chart titled "Cov-lite loans dominate a growing leveraged loan market" spanning 1999 to 2018, plots total loans outstanding in billions of US dollars alongside the percentage share of covenant-lite loans. The data shows total outstanding loans swelling to roughly $1.2 trillion by 2018, represented by blue columns, while the covenant-lite share of these loans, represented by a gold line, climbs from near-zero percent prior to 2007 to approximately 80% by late 2018. 

The second chart, "Leveraged loan and high yield returns," tracks cumulative total returns from January 1, 2010, through mid-2019. It compares the S&P/LSTA Leveraged Loan Index with US High Yield bonds. The high yield index, shown in gold, displays higher volatility but reaches a superior cumulative return of nearly 95%, while the leveraged loan index, shown in blue, shows steadier, less volatile growth to a cumulative return of around 60%.

The third chart is titled "Loan investors waving the white flag: Moody's loan covenant quality score is the weakest on record" and tracks quarterly scores from 2012 to 2018. On a scale where 5.0 represents the weakest covenant quality, the blue line climbs from around 3.2 in late 2012 to nearly 4.2 by late 2018, highlighting the historic erosion of lender safeguards. 

An accompanying text block titled "Moody’s: the last bastion of creditor protection is fading away" details how modern borrowers are increasingly allowed to make restricted payments, investments, and incur new debt even after a default, effectively removing traditional safeguards that historically prevented "Hail Mary" transactions at the eleventh hour. Footnotes elaborate on the specific protections investors are surrendering, which are monitored by Moody’s and Fitch, including interest coverage maintenance tests, limitations on asset leakage from collateral pools, EBITDA adjustments, and restrictions on transferring assets to unrestricted subsidiaries.

This page explores how financial sponsors are raising the risk profiles of leveraged loans through the practice of "collateral stripping," in which sponsors exploit loose covenants to move valuable collateral out of the reach of senior creditors. The author details three high-profile examples of this trend. First, during J.Crew's near-bankruptcy in 2016, sponsors TPG and Leonard Green transferred the brand's intellectual property to a separate entity, subsequently pledging it as collateral to secure three hundred million dollars in new funding, which dilutes original creditors' claims if the company fails. Second, in 2017, PetSmart’s sponsor, BC Partners, transferred its stake in Chewy.com, valued at three point four billion dollars, to a subsidiary that shielded it from bondholders, and none of the proceeds from Chewy’s subsequent public offering were used to pay down PetSmart's eight billion dollars of debt. Third, in September 2018, Neiman Marcus moved its luxury e-commerce platform, MyTheresa, to a holding company owned by sponsors Ares and the Canadian Pension Board, shielding the asset from creditors of the heavily indebted retailer.

These practices have drawn official concern, notably in an October 2018 speech by Todd Vermilyea at the Federal Reserve. However, regulatory bodies are sending mixed signals; while the Fed highlights risks, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency has weakened its 2013 EBITDA leverage guidelines, making highly leveraged loans with debt-to-EBITDA ratios of six to seven times commonplace. The author also notes the conflict of interest inherent in "sponsor-designated counsel," a practice where financial sponsors dictate which law firms the lending banks must use to draft loan agreements.

Looking forward, the author predicts that while these structural changes will not necessarily drive up default rates, which will be dictated by a recession that the author expects to be much milder than the 2008 crisis, they will severely hurt recovery rates when defaults do occur. While historical loan recoveries have averaged seventy percent compared to forty percent for high-yield bonds, the author forecasts that recovery rates for loans may fall to a midpoint of fifty-five percent in the next downturn. The author concludes that in the ongoing negotiation battles over credit protections, issuers are firmly defeating lenders.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication analyzed by Michael Cembalest assesses growing risks within the leveraged loan market, specifically detailing how strong-looking interest coverage ratios mask rising average leverage and the widespread, artificial inflation of earnings through "EBITDA add-backs." These add-backs, which let companies factor in non-recurring expenses and projected merger synergies, now appear in roughly 30% of all deals, up from 10% historically. While these adjustments typically represent 10% to 15% of unadjusted EBITDA, some deals allow up to 30% or lack caps entirely. Highlighting the unreliability of these assumptions, a Moody’s analysis of European issuers reveals that only 45% of projected add-backs were actually realized, and nearly 20% of issuers failed to achieve any of their targets. 

Two charts support this analysis. The first line chart, "Rising interest coverage, but rising leverage as well," tracks trends from 2002 to 2018. It shows debt-to-EBITDA on new loans rising back toward 5.0x (on the right vertical axis, ranging from 3.5 to 5.5), even as interest coverage on outstanding loans remains elevated around 4.0x to 4.5x (on the left vertical axis, ranging from 2.5x to 5.0x). The second graphic, a stacked bar chart titled "M&A loan leverage trends using unadjusted EBITDA," demonstrates that when the hypothetical benefits of merger synergies are excluded, leverage multiples have expanded significantly between 2006 and 2018. By 2018, loans leveraged at over 6x (encompassing the 6x–6.9x and greater-than-7x buckets) made up over half of the market, while loans leveraged under 5x shrank to approximately 30%.

Cembalest also challenges the argument that the surge in "cov-lite" (covenant-lite) loans is acceptable because the market is now dominated by larger, more recognizable issuers. Although smaller loans under $300 million have plummeted from 50% of the loan market in 2000 to just 10% today, the author emphasizes that these larger borrowers are still non-investment grade. Furthermore, the overall market credit quality has deteriorated, with the share of loans rated below split BB rising from 50% to 60% since 2016. Finally, he warns about potential losses when defaults eventually occur. Since 2010, only 13 cov-lite loans have defaulted during this low-default cycle, but their average recovery rate was just 56%, significantly lower than the historical 80% to 85% recovery rate typical for standard bank loans and senior secured bonds.

Michael Cembalest challenges the common argument that financial sponsors, or private equity firms, will step in to support their loans during times of economic stress. He argues that sponsor-backed loan default rates are not actually superior to non-sponsor defaults once debt exchanges—which often result in heavy losses for lenders—are factored into the equation. To support this, he references several high-profile debt exchanges from the 2009 and 2010 period, including TXU, Harrah’s, Freescale, Realogy, Intelsat, and Hexion. 

This argument is visually backed by a chart tracking sponsored versus non-sponsored default rates from 2000 to 2012. The chart reveals that while sponsor-backed defaults excluding debt exchanges peaked at a modest 8% in 2009–2010, the rate spiked to a much higher peak of approximately 22% when debt exchanges were included.
