This is slightly worse than the peak default rate of around 18% seen in non-sponsored loans during the same cycle.

Cembalest also highlights a critical gap between market pricing and ultimate realized losses during downturns. During a recession, market panic and falling dealer liquidity drive down pricing across the entire loan sector, meaning loan investors often experience paper losses that far exceed actual credit losses. A chart illustrating leveraged loan market pricing versus estimated realized losses index from 2006 to 2010 demonstrates this divergence. During the Great Financial Crisis, the S&P/LSTA Leveraged Loan Index collapsed from a baseline of 100 down to a low near 70 in late 2008 and early 2009—a drop of 25% to 30%. In contrast, J.P. Morgan's estimates of actual peak realized losses, shown as a data point in late 2008, sat much higher at around 90 on the index scale, reflecting a loss of only 6% to 8% based on peak default rates of 20% to 22% and average recovery rates of 65% to 70%. For future cycles, Cembalest projects that a milder recession with lower loan recovery rates could still trigger a 7% to 10% decline in the loan total return index.

Finally, the page reviews the current environment via a chart of leveraged loan default rates from 2012 to 2019. It shows that default rates have generally hovered at a low and manageable 1% to 2%, with the notable exception of a wave of energy-sector defaults that pushed the overall default rate above 4% between late 2014 and 2016. By mid-2019, default rates had subsided once again to around 1.5%.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, titled "So Long Yellow Brick Road: Trumpism shows its true colors to investors," argues that the initial market optimism surrounding the Trump administration's pro-business domestic policies has been derailed by its protectionist trade policies. The author explains that while conservative organizations like the Heritage Foundation and the American Enterprise Institute initially welcomed Trump’s deregulation, corporate tax cuts, and judicial appointments, the subsequent trade war has stalled economic and manufacturing dynamism. Cembalest lists several negative global indicators resulting from this shift, including US tariffs reaching 40-year highs, global trade volumes hitting their lowest levels since 2010, declining German production orders, contracting global manufacturing surveys, and falling US manufacturing hours. Looking forward, the author predicts that this volatile, sideways environment is unlikely to change before the next election, advising investors to range-trade equities within the boundaries established since early 2018.

The core visual on the page is a line chart tracking the S&P 500 Index level from January 2015 to September 2019, with the vertical axis running from 1,800 to 3,200. The chart marks the November 2016 election, after which a rising line highlighted in yellow bricks represents the market's positive run-up from around 2,100 to nearly 2,900. An annotation explains that this "yellow brick road" represents the market rise driven by deregulation, tax cuts, incentives for business investment, and pro-business court appointments. This upward trend abruptly halts on January 22, 2018, marked as the beginning of the trade war when tariffs were imposed on washing machines and solar panels. Following this date, the chart details a highly volatile, sideways trajectory fluctuating between approximately 2,400 and 3,000, which is bracketed and labeled as the "Trumpism trading range."

This page outlines multiple structural headwinds that are dampening inflation in the United States and globally. Michael Cembalest presents six charts to illustrate the key drivers behind this trend, which include declining labor bargaining power, online retail transparency, globalization, altered corporate margin behavior, automation, and a broader global shift toward low inflation.

The first chart, focusing on the decline in labor bargaining power, contrasts the labor share of non-farm business sector output against private sector union membership from 1947 to 2017. It shows the labor share of output falling from around 65% in the mid-1950s to roughly 57% by 2017, while private sector union membership experienced a steady, steep decline from over 35% in the mid-1950s to approximately 7% by 2017.

The second chart demonstrates how online retailing increases price transparency and reduces corporate pricing power by tracking the duration of price changes in months from 2008 to 2017. The duration of price changes for recreation and electronics, as well as furnishings and household items, both dropped from peaks of 12 to 17 months around 2011 down to roughly 5 to 6 months by 2017, meaning prices are changing much more rapidly. 

The third chart depicts the rise of globalization, showing that world trade as a percentage of GDP rose from under 30% in 1960 to nearly 60% by 2015. Concurrently, world cross-border capital stock as a percentage of GDP surged from around 30% in the 1990s to over 110% by 2015, indicating that US prices are increasingly sensitive to global rather than domestic conditions.

The fourth chart examines how companies respond to labor cost changes. It compares the change in core PCE inflation from a 1% increase in unit labor costs against the change in profit margins from that same labor cost increase from 1975 to 2015. The impact of labor costs on core PCE inflation has dropped from about 0.8% to nearly 0.0%, while the negative impact on corporate profit margins has widened to roughly -0.6%, proving that companies are now absorbing labor costs through compressed margins rather than passing them on via price hikes.

The fifth chart shows the steady rise of US automation, plotting industrial robots per thousand workers from 1993 to 2018 using data from Acemoglu at MIT, the Institute for Employment Research, and the Bruegel Institute in Belgium. All three sources show an increase from about 0.4 robots per thousand workers in 1993 to between 1.8 and 2.2 by 2018.

The final chart illustrates that these deflationary forces are global. It tracks the percentage of world GDP with low, positive headline inflation between 0% and 4% from 1960 to 2015. This metric fell close to 0% during the high-inflation period of 1980 but steadily climbed over the subsequent decades, with roughly 80% to 90% of global GDP experiencing low and stable inflation by 2015.

This text-only commentary analyzes the negative impacts of the US-China trade war on corporate profits and household income, while arguing that a US recession is unlikely in 2019 or 2020. Although S&P 500 earnings growth has slowed to just two to three percent and organic growth is near zero without buybacks, the author highlights the strength of the US consumer, supported by low unemployment and wage growth above three percent. 

While the page contains no visual charts or tables, the text references a series of external figures (labeled c11 through c24) to support various observations. These points include a downward restatement of economy-wide profits, indicating the lack of a substantial Trump profits boom, and an estimated trade-war profit hit of three to five percent that could offset corporate tax cuts, hitting tech hardware by up to twenty-two percent and capital goods by ten percent. Additionally, J.P. Morgan Equity Research estimates that tariffs will cost US households six hundred to one thousand dollars, neutralizing individual tax cut benefits. 

To adapt, multinationals like Qualcomm, Micron, Broadcom, Texas Instruments, AMD, Intel, Apple, Nike, and Boeing are navigating these headwinds, with some shifting US-bound assembly lines to Vietnam. Despite concerns over deteriorating leveraged loan underwriting standards and an inverted yield curve—which the author discounts due to negative European and Japanese government bond yields—the outlook is bolstered by strong mortgage refinancing, rising home purchases, a tentative trade deal with Japan, potential central bank easing from the Federal Reserve and European Central Bank, and favorable equity supply and demand dynamics from mergers, acquisitions, and buybacks.

In this J.P. Morgan publication, Michael Cembalest argues that central banks are unlikely to eliminate the market volatility stemming from the ongoing trade war with China. He points out that while the broader United States economy is seventy percent reliant on consumption, the US equity market is heavily dependent on production and global trade, making corporate profit margins highly vulnerable to de-globalization. Cembalest predicts that without a substantial rollback of the trade war—which seems unlikely from either President Trump or potential Democratic successors—the US equity market is likely to remain stuck in the trading range established since January 2018.

To support this outlook, the page features four charts tracking long-term structural and cyclical trends. Chart one shows the percentile rank of the United States regarding the ease of starting a new business from 2005 to 2017. Relative to the world, the US percentile rank dropped from roughly ninety-five to seventy-five, while its rank relative to OECD peers fell even more sharply, from eighty to below fifty, indicating that starting a new business in the US has become relatively harder. Chart two tracks US manufacturing sector labor dynamism in thousands of workers from 2000 to 2018. This chart illustrates a cyclical pattern where new hires and voluntary quits fell dramatically during the 2001 and 2008 recessions, while layoffs surged, followed by a gradual post-crisis recovery in hiring and quits alongside declining layoffs.

Chart three visualizes the history and projections of the effective US tariff rate, measured as tariffs collected as a percentage of all imported goods, from 1910 to 2019. The graph highlights the historic Smoot-Hawley peak near twenty percent in the early 1930s, followed by a multi-decade decline to under two percent by the 2010s. However, recent and proposed actions—labeled one through seven—project a sharp reversal. These actions include tariffs on steel and aluminum, Section 301 tariffs on hundreds of billions of dollars of Chinese imports, and proposed fifteen percent tariffs on remaining goods, which collectively threaten to push the effective tariff rate back up to over six percent by late 2019. Finally, chart four plots the six-month over six-month percentage change in global industrial production and world trade volume from 2004 to 2019. Both metrics plummeted below negative six percent during the 2008 financial crisis, recovered, and have most recently trended downward, approaching zero percent growth by mid-2019 as global trade slows.

This page consists entirely of standard legal disclosures and regulatory disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market publication. It outlines regulatory exemptions and licensing information for wholesale clients in Australia under the Corporations Act 2001, noting that J.P. Morgan Securities LLC is regulated by the United States SEC, FINRA, and CFTC rather than Australian authorities. Additionally, the text details distribution restrictions and private offering guidelines for jurisdictions in Latin America, specifically highlighting compliance requirements for Brazil's Securities and Exchange Commission and Mexican platforms, alongside general copyright and personal-use restrictions for the publication.

This page presents six charts analyzing US corporate profit trends, the targeted pressure of Chinese import tariffs on specific sectors and households, and the positive consumer response to falling interest rates in the housing market. 

Looking first at corporate earnings health, Chart 11 shows that S&P 500 12-month forward earnings per share year-over-year growth peaked at over 20% in 2018 before decelerating dramatically to nearly flat levels by mid-2019. This slowdown aligns with major government revisions to macroeconomic data illustrated in Chart 12, where US economy-wide after-tax non-financial corporate profits were revised downward significantly, showing that profits were closer to $1.0 trillion rather than the previously reported $1.2 trillion peak. This divergence is contextualized in Chart 13, which tracks the long-term ratio of S&P 500 reported EPS to economy-wide NIPA profits from 1969 to 2019. Historically, peaks in this ratio have often preceded or coincided with economic recessions, and by 2019, the ratio had risen back toward an elevated level of approximately 140. 

The next two charts address the headwinds of the US-China trade war. Chart 14 measures tariffs on Chinese imports as a share of key economic metrics, highlighting that the impact is highly uneven. While tariffs account for less than 1% of US GDP and roughly 3% of overall S&P 500 earnings, they represent over 11% of industrial capital goods earnings and a substantial 23% of technology hardware earnings. Chart 15 illustrates how these tariffs threaten to wipe out consumer benefits from the 2017 tax reform. Against an estimated average tax cut benefit of $1,350 per household, the combined costs of Phase I and II tariffs already offset over half of that gain. If Phase III is fully implemented, both Federal Reserve and consensus estimates—which aggregate forecasts from the Peterson Institute, Oxford Economics, and UC Davis—project household tariff costs to reach between $1,400 and over $1,600, entirely neutralizing the tax reform’s positive impact. 

Finally, Chart 16 offers a brighter economic signal from the housing sector, plotting the US home refinancing and purchase indices from 2014 to 2019. Driven by declining interest rates, the seasonally adjusted refinancing index experienced a massive spike in 2019, surging from under 1,000 to over 2,000, while the home purchase index steadily climbed toward a multi-year high near 260.

This page presents six charts assessing a broad downturn in global manufacturing alongside the specific domestic impacts of US tariff policies on consumer spending and employment. Together, the data argue that global economic momentum is slowing, and that US protectionist measures are failing to produce their intended benefits.

The first two charts illustrate a broad cooling trend in global industrial activity. Chart 5, which tracks German manufacturing production against an order-to-inventory survey, shows that the declining ratio of orders to inventories reliably predicts lower industrial production; by mid-2019, both measures had fallen sharply into negative territory, with production around -5% year-over-year. Globally, Chart 6 shows that manufacturing and employment business surveys have deteriorated from their late 2017 peaks. The global manufacturing PMI index dropped below the 50 expansion threshold in mid-2019, closely trailed by a declining employment sub-index that sits just above 50, pointing to stagnant hiring.

This weakness is explored regionally in the next two charts. Chart 7 plots regional manufacturing business surveys for the US, China, the Eurozone, and Japan. The Eurozone displays the most severe contraction, hovering around 47 in mid-2019, while Japan and China also sit below the 50 line. The US manufacturing PMI has also suffered a steep decline throughout 2018 and 2019, landing near 50 in preliminary August 2019 data. This slowing US momentum is reinforced in Chart 8, which plots the year-over-year change in aggregate weekly hours of US manufacturing employees. Growth in hours plummeted from a peak of nearly 2.5% in early 2018 to negative territory of roughly -0.2% by mid-2019.

The final two charts evaluate the domestic consequences of US trade policy, revealing that protectionist tariffs have had counterproductive results. Chart 9 indexes real consumer spending from 2015 to mid-2019, setting February 2018 equal to 100. Following the implementation of the first round of tariffs in mid-2018, spending on tariff-impacted categories—such as housekeeping supplies, major appliances, and auto parts—decoupled from other core goods, flattening and falling to around 100 while non-tariffed core goods spending climbed steadily to nearly 107. Similarly, Chart 10 indexes US employment over the same period. It shows that employment in tariff-protected industries, including steel, aluminum, and household appliances, actually peaked shortly after the mid-2018 tariff implementation and fell below 100 by mid-2019, whereas employment in all other industries steadily marched upward to nearly 103. This indicates that trade protections failed to safeguard jobs in the very sectors they aimed to defend.

This page outlines the policy proposals of select Democratic presidential candidates for the 2020 election and discusses the potential regulatory and tax consequences of a Democratic Sweep, noting that Democrats would need to gain only three seats to regain effective control of the Senate. The author highlights that funding massive progressive programs, including Medicare-for-All, free college tuition, student debt forgiveness, infrastructure spending, affordable housing, universal pre-K, and the Green New Deal, would require substantial new funding sources. 

To explore these potential sources, the page details several key policy categories. Under higher taxes on income and capital gains, Joe Biden has suggested doubling the capital gains tax rate on those earning over one million dollars and eliminating the step-up in basis for heirs, while Ron Wyden has proposed taxing unrealized capital gains. Bernie Sanders would treat capital gains and dividends as ordinary income, implement a seventy-seven percent top estate tax rate, and apply a twelve point four percent payroll tax on incomes over two hundred and fifty thousand dollars. Elizabeth Warren supports an annual wealth tax of two percent on assets over fifty million dollars. 

Regarding corporate income taxes, most candidates favor raising corporate tax rates or repealing the 2017 tax law, with Warren proposing an additional tax on corporate profits over one hundred million dollars to raise nine hundred billion dollars in tax revenue. On stock buybacks, Sanders and Chuck Schumer propose restricting share repurchases unless companies meet requirements like a fifteen-dollar minimum wage and sick leave. Warren, Sanders, and Kirsten Gillibrand co-sponsored the Reward Work Act to prohibit open-market buybacks and require employee representation on boards, while Sherrod Brown introduced legislation tying buybacks to direct worker payouts. 

For the financial sector, Sanders’ Inclusive Prosperity Act proposes a financial transaction tax on stocks, bonds, and derivatives that could raise four hundred to eight hundred billion dollars over a decade. Kamala Harris proposes a bank tax modeled on Barack Obama’s proposed bank liability fee, Amy Klobuchar proposes taxing banks to fund infrastructure, and both Warren and Sanders advocate retroactively breaking up big bank and big tech mergers. Finally, Warren’s plan for private equity would require firms to guarantee the debt and pensions of companies they take over, while limiting dividends and monitoring fees.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" analysis explores themes of equity supply, banking sector divergence, geopolitical linkages, global trade, and globalization metrics. 

The first chart, Chart 23, shows unprecedented low levels of net equity supply from 1999 to 2019, measured in billions of US dollars using the MSCI All Country World Equity Index. The chart splits net supply into US and non-US components, with a dot representing the total. It highlights that global net equity supply has plummeted over the two decades, turning negative in 2016, 2018, and 2019, which indicates that share retirements through buybacks and mergers and acquisitions have significantly outpaced new stock issuance.

Chart 24 compares the total return performance of US and European banks from 2009 through 2019, indexed to 100 in January 2009. The line chart reveals a massive divergence between the two regions: the S&P 500 banks index steadily climbed to peak above 300 in 2018, while the Euro STOXX banks index stagnated, spending most of the decade fluctuating around or below its initial 100 level.

Chart 25 illustrates that economic linkages between China and the US are much deeper than those of actual and potential adversaries of the last 100 years. It plots bilateral economic linkages as a percentage of the nations' combined GDP for various historical pairings. The US and China in 2014 registered near 8% of combined GDP, consisting of bilateral annual trade, bilateral central bank holdings of each other's government debt, and bilateral foreign direct investment stock. In contrast, historical rivalries, such as France and Germany in 1930, the US and Russia in 1983, or the US and Japan in 1940, rarely surpassed 4% of combined GDP and relied almost exclusively on trade without the deep investment and debt ties seen today. A footnote highlights additional dimensions of this relationship, including $450 billion in sales by US affiliates operating in China, high enrollment of Chinese college students in the US, and extensive co-authored scientific research papers.

Chart 26 outlines the historical relationship between global profit margins and global trade to GDP from 1995 to 2017. The two metrics historically tracked closely together: both rose through the late 1990s and mid-2000s, with global profit margins peaking near 8.5% and global trade to GDP peaking around 31% in 2007, before experiencing a sharp contraction during the financial crisis and subsequently recovering. 

The final chart, Chart 27, demonstrates that US globalization measures are among the world's highest despite a lower direct contribution of trade to GDP. Comparing twelve nations, the bar chart contrasts each country's KOF globalization index against its imports plus exports as a percentage of GDP. While the US trade-to-GDP ratio is very low at around 27%, its KOF globalization index stands exceptionally high at over 80%, matching highly open European nations like Sweden, Germany, and France. An accompanying text block notes that the KOF index accounts for both de jure elements, like trade regulations and investment restrictions, and de facto elements, such as foreign direct investment, portfolio investments, embassies, and international patents.

This visual compendium from J.P. Morgan features six economic and financial charts monitoring consumer health, international capital flows, trade dynamics, global monetary policy, and corporate behavior. 

The first chart tracks year-over-year US same-store retail sales growth on an eight-week average from 2005 to mid-2019. The data highlights a robust recovery in consumer spending, where sales growth rebounded from a financial crisis low of nearly negative five percent in 2009 to a strong peak of over six percent by 2019. This consumer resilience is further explored in the second chart, which illustrates transition rates into ninety-day-plus loan delinquencies from 2005 to 2019. It tracks first mortgages, second mortgages, credit cards, and auto loans. While first mortgages peaked dramatically near the ten percent mark during the housing crisis, they have since normalized. Currently, delinquency rates for second mortgages remain exceptionally low, auto loans hover steadily under two percent, and credit card delinquencies show a mild upward trajectory toward four percent.

Shifting to international capital flows, the third chart displays cumulative net purchases of foreign bonds by Japanese and Euro area residents in trillions of dollars since March 2015. Euro area residents have been aggressive buyers, with cumulative purchases climbing steeply to over one point four trillion dollars by mid-2019, whereas purchases by Japanese residents grew at a more measured pace to about zero point six trillion dollars. Global trade shifts are detailed in the fourth chart, which plots the share of total US imports by country as a six-month average from 2010 to 2019. China’s share, which peaked near twenty-two percent around 2017 to 2018, shows a noticeable decline down to approximately eighteen percent in 2019. Conversely, Mexico's import share has steadily increased toward fifteen percent, followed by Canada around twelve percent, and smaller, stable shares from Japan, Korea, and Vietnam.

The fifth chart analyzes how central bank rate cuts lead global manufacturing activity using data from 1998 to 2019. It overlays the global manufacturing survey PMI, where a reading above fifty indicates expansion, against the net number of central banks easing policy or maintaining negative rates, plotted with an eight-month lead. Historically, a rise in central bank easing strongly correlates with subsequent rebounds in manufacturing, suggesting that recent central bank interventions could act as a leading indicator for manufacturing stabilization. Finally, the sixth chart traces S&P 500 buybacks in billions of dollars from 1998 to 2019. Corporate buybacks show sharp cyclicality, peaking near one hundred seventy-five billion dollars in 2007 before plummeting to near-zero during the Great Recession, and then climbing steadily to historical highs of nearly two hundred twenty-five billion dollars by 2019.

On this page, Michael Cembalest argues against an outright ban on hydraulic fracturing, suggesting that associated environmental and operational risks can be managed through regulatory oversight instead. He highlights that fracking and wastewater handling are far less complex than crude oil refining or nuclear power operations. With the US aiming to decommission aging coal and nuclear plants while reducing foreign oil dependence, Cembalest asserts that renewable energy is not growing fast enough to replace natural gas and oil. Natural gas remains essential to balance intermittent renewables, particularly given the lack of a nationwide electricity grid and affordable energy storage options. He questions whether advocates for an immediate ban on these energy sources, which account for roughly forty percent of the US energy supply, have fully considered the severe impacts on economic growth, employment, energy prices, independence, the US dollar, and national security.

To support his points, Cembalest includes a line chart illustrating the shares of US primary energy consumption by source from 1965 to 2018. The data shows that oil consistently holds the largest share, starting near forty-five percent in 1965 and declining slightly to around forty percent by 2018. Natural gas has maintained a significant share, fluctuating between twenty-three percent and thirty percent over the decades. Meanwhile, coal usage has dropped sharply from its peak of twenty-five percent to around thirteen percent. Nuclear energy remains steady at approximately eight percent, while hydroelectric power stays low at around two to three percent. Crucially, modern renewables, despite recent growth, still account for only about four percent of primary energy consumption by the end of the period, demonstrating the nation’s continued reliance on fossil fuels. 

The commentary is further detailed in two footnotes. The first details the local opposition that often stalls clean energy infrastructure, referencing the canceled Northern Pass transmission line. This project, which aimed to bring one gigawatt of Canadian hydropower from Hydro-Quebec to Southern New England, was rejected by New Hampshire regulators and ultimately killed by the state’s Supreme Court in July 2019 due to concerns over tourism and local disruptions. This decision stood despite warnings from grid operator ISO New England that the region could face rolling blackouts without such capacity upgrades. The second footnote underscores the scale of the energy storage challenge, noting that while the US generates over four billion megawatt-hours of electricity annually, it possesses only about fifteen hundred megawatt-hours of utility-scale storage, ninety-five percent of which is limited to pumped-storage hydropower.

This page features a commentary by Michael Cembalest on the potential consequences of a proposed immediate, nationwide ban on hydraulic fracturing (fracking) in the United States. Cembalest argues that while the environmental and health concerns associated with fracking are significant, an immediate ban would severely disrupt the US energy landscape because fracking has successfully eliminated the nation's long-standing energy deficit. 

The author supports this argument with four charts detailing US energy dynamics. The first chart, "US net energy deficit, in dollar terms," plots energy imports minus energy exports as a percentage of GDP from 1978 to 2018. It shows the deficit fluctuating and peaking near 3.3% in the late 1970s and again in the late 2000s, before rapidly dropping to nearly 0.0% by 2018. The second chart, "US net energy deficit, in energy terms," measures net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal in million tonnes of oil equivalent from 1972 to 2016. This physical deficit peaked at over 700 million tonnes around 2005 to 2008 before dropping sharply to less than 100 million tonnes by 2016. 

The third chart, "Percentage of US oil and gas production derived from hydraulic fracturing," tracks the growth of unconventional extraction from 1995 to 2019. It shows that by 2019, fracking accounted for approximately 80% of natural gas production, over 60% of crude oil production, and over 60% of natural gas liquids (such as ethane, propane, and butane). The fourth chart, a stacked column titled "Hydraulic fracturing accounts for 40% of all US primary energy consumption," breaks down total US energy consumption using 2018 data. It reveals that unconventional oil, gas, and NGLs extracted via hydraulic fracturing make up the single largest share of US energy consumption at 40%. This is followed by conventional oil, gas, and NGLs at roughly 20%, coal at approximately 15%, nuclear energy at around 8%, and smaller single-digit shares for biomass, hydro, wind, and solar/geothermal power.

In addition to demonstrating fracking's economic importance, the commentary addresses its environmental and regulatory challenges. Cembalest points out that the US is practically the only country heavily engaged in hydraulic fracturing, with only minor activity occurring in Canada, China, and Argentina. He outlines several key environmental risks, including aquifer contamination from shallow wells drilled between 1,000 and 2,000 feet, exponential water usage in the Permian Basin, and toxic flowback water containing hazardous materials such as lead, arsenic, barium, chromium, uranium, radium, radon, and benzene. He also notes that the EPA's Advisory Board has questioned the agency's 2016 report, which found little evidence of systemic impacts on drinking water. A concluding footnote connects these environmental concerns to broader regulatory trends, noting alarm over the Trump administration's rollbacks of federal oversight of US waterways.

This page from Michael Cembalest J.P. Morgan publication explores the performance of active equity managers during a period of market distortions driven by central bank quantitative easing. By analyzing 6,700 institutional equity managers across 23 style categories using data going back to 1996, the analysis evaluates what percentage of managers outperformed their respective benchmarks or tracking ETFs on a net-of-fees basis. The central observation is that while manager outperformance was generally weaker in the 2014 to 2019 period compared to 2010 to 2014, a significant portion of non-US and small-cap categories still saw more than 50% of managers beat their benchmarks.

The core visual is a bar chart titled Active equity manager outperformance trends, which displays the percentage of managers outperforming their respective ETF on a one-year basis using monthly data. The vertical axis ranges from 30% to 70%, with a dashed horizontal reference line at 50%. The horizontal axis covers 23 distinct style categories, comparing performance across three time horizons: January 1996 to December 2009 in grey, January 2010 to June 2019 in gold, and January 2014 to June 2019 in red. The chart illustrates a clear divergence between US and international categories. For instance, US large-cap core and large-cap growth managers struggled, with less than 45% outperforming in the 2014 to 2019 period. Conversely, non-US and global categories such as Europe, Japan, EAFE, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Emerging Markets consistently show stronger active management results, with over 50% of managers outperforming during the same recent timeframe.

To summarize these findings, the author groups the style categories into three performance tiers based on average outperformance since 2014. Grade A categories, which averaged above 50% outperformance, include small-cap growth, small-cap value, Global, ACWI ex-US, Europe, Asia ex-Japan, Japan, EAFE, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Emerging Markets. Grade B categories, ranging from 45% to 50% outperformance, consist of large-cap value, mid-cap core, mid-cap growth, mid-cap value, small-cap core, all-cap growth, and Australia. Finally, Grade C categories, averaging below 45%, comprise large-cap core, large-cap growth, all-cap core, all-cap value, and US double focus. The methodology notes that managers were assessed against their individual stated benchmarks and representative ETFs, accounting for a simulated fifty-million-dollar separate account fee structure to ensure realistic net-of-fee comparisons.

This page analyzes active investment manager performance post-2010, focusing on the relationship between how frequently managers outperform their benchmarks and the magnitude of that outperformance. The author argues that a direct correlation exists: when managers succeed more frequently, the magnitude of their successful outperformance also tends to greatly exceed the losses of underperforming managers, creating a net positive alpha boost. Conversely, in categories where fewer than 50% of managers outperform, the unsuccessful managers lose more alpha than the successful ones gain, creating an alpha drag that worsens the outcome of active management. Overall, the data demonstrates that the performance boost from successful active categories is significantly larger than the drag from unsuccessful ones.

These findings are illustrated with a scatter plot titled "Outperformance frequency vs outperformance magnitude, 2010 - 2019." The chart plots the frequency of manager outperformance on the x-axis, ranging from 40% to 70%, against net alpha on the y-axis, ranging from -1.0% to 3.0%. Net alpha is calculated as the average annual successful manager alpha minus the average annual unsuccessful manager alpha. The upward-sloping distribution of data points shows that regions like Australia, Japan, Asia ex JPN, and Emerging Markets occupy the upper right, representing high frequency and high net magnitude of outperformance. Meanwhile, US large-cap and mid-cap style categories, such as Large Cap Core and Mid Cap Value, cluster in the lower left, depicting lower frequencies of outperformance and negative net alpha values.

To provide precise figures, an adjacent table titled "Magnitude of out/underperformance" details the average positive alpha of successful managers, the average negative alpha of unsuccessful managers, and the resulting net alpha for 23 style categories. For example, ACWI ex-US managers show a high outperformance frequency with an average positive alpha of 4.7% and average negative alpha of -3.2%, yielding a net positive alpha of 1.5%. Australia boasts the highest net alpha at 2.8%, derived from a 6.1% positive alpha versus a -3.3% negative alpha. On the opposite end, Large Cap Core has a net negative alpha of -0.4%, consisting of a 2.8% positive alpha versus a -3.2% negative alpha, while US Dollar Funds show a net negative alpha of -0.5%, combining a 3.2% positive alpha with a -3.8% negative alpha.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication analyzes market distortions and their implications for active managers, arguing that despite these headwinds, the fact that more than 50% of active managers in many categories have outperformed since 2014 is a positive sign for the long-term viability of active equity management. Six charts accompany this text to illustrate these structural market dynamics and the stark division between growth and value styles.

The first chart tracks the contribution of the top 5 and top 20 firms to the overall US market return from 1963 to 2018 during rolling 12-month periods when the overall market return was at least 10%. This scatter plot shows that the concentration of returns in the very largest firms has fluctuated significantly over the decades, with the top 5 firms sometimes representing a major share of total returns. 

The second chart displays average trailing 1-year pairwise correlations in the S&P 500 index from 1992 to 2018. It highlights that correlations spiked dramatically during periods of quantitative easing, labeled QE1, QE2, and QE3, where they rose to levels between 0.5 and 0.55. Since the end of these interventions, correlations have generally declined, hovering between 0.3 and 0.4 in the lead-up to 2019.

The third and fourth charts compare the cumulative net total returns of growth versus value stocks, indexing the ratio of growth to value. The US chart, indexed to January 2005, shows the growth-to-value ratio steadily rising, particularly after 2015, to reach nearly 1.5 by 2019. This demonstrates massive growth outperformance. A global perspective is offered in the next chart, indexed to January 2010, tracking Europe, Emerging Markets, Asia excluding Japan, and Japan. It shows a broad-based international trend where growth has outperformed value across all regions, with Europe and Emerging Markets showing the sharpest increases, peaking near 1.4 to 1.5 in 2019, while Japan lags but still displays a rising growth bias.

The fifth chart shows the ratio of P/E multiples of bond proxy stocks relative to Russell 1000 valuations from 1989 to 2019. While this ratio historically oscillated around 1.0, it spiked sharply starting around 2015, climbing to approximately 1.15 by 2019, which indicates that income-generating bond proxies have become highly valued relative to the broader market.

The final chart utilizes a log scale to show the cumulative excess return of the cheapest value stocks over the most expensive value stocks from 1926 to 2016, setting January 1926 equal to 100. This chart highlights that while cheap value stocks steadily outperformed expensive ones for nearly a century, the actual return line experienced an unprecedented break away from its long-term pre-2007 trend line after 2007, illustrating the deep and historic underperformance of the cheapest value equities.

This page from Michael Cembalest's Eye on the Market report presents Grade A manager outperformance charts across six distinct style categories. The central thesis of the page is identifying the investment styles where active managers have successfully outperformed their respective benchmark exchange-traded funds on a rolling one-year basis at or above a fifty percent average rate during the post-2014 period. Each of the six line charts plots monthly data from 1997 through mid-2019, showcasing a dotted horizontal line at fifty percent alongside average outperformance levels across three key historical periods: January 1996 to December 2009, January 2010 to June 2019, and January 2014 to June 2019. 

The first chart, focusing on Small Cap Growth, reveals that while active manager success is highly volatile, the average outperformance for all tracked periods, including the post-2014 timeframe, remains consistently above the fifty percent threshold. In the Small Cap Value category, manager outperformance has experienced wider swings, dipping as low as twenty percent in the late 1990s and late 2018, yet the post-2014 average remains strong at approximately fifty-five percent. The Global style category displays a similar long-term pattern, with the post-2014 average hovering just above the fifty percent baseline, recoverered from a deep dip down to twenty percent in the late 1990s.

The ACWI ex-US category illustrates a highly favorable environment for active managers, with the post-2014 average outperformance sitting near sixty percent. For the Europe category, active managers have maintained solid averages, with the post-2010 and post-2014 outperformance averages staying around fifty-five percent despite a notable plunge below forty percent in late 2018. Lastly, the Asia ex-Japan category showcases robust active manager performance, where the post-2010 and post-2014 averages both stand near sixty percent. Across all these categories, data sourced from eVestment and J.P. Morgan Asset Management indicates that active managers in these specific styles have maintained a net positive rate of outperformance against passive benchmarks.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, "Eye on the Market," examines how unorthodox central bank monetary policies, specifically quantitative easing, have created severe distortions in global markets that hinder the performance of active equity managers. Cembalest highlights several unprecedented market conditions, including negative real policy rates across the developed world, fourteen trillion dollars of European and Japanese government bonds with negative yields, and a general collapse in risk premia. 

To demonstrate the direct connection between central bank actions and active manager struggles, the page presents two side-by-side charts at the top. The left-hand chart, titled "Negative yielding debt as % of investment grade debt," plots the ratio of the negative yielding debt index to the global aggregate index from 2014 to 2019. This ratio surged from near zero percent in 2014 to a peak of roughly twenty-five percent in 2016, fluctuated around fifteen percent through 2017 and 2018, and then rose sharply to nearly thirty percent by mid-2019. The right-hand chart, titled "1 year manager outperformance, 3 year rolling average," shows the percentage of active managers outperforming their benchmark ETFs from 2000 through 2019, comparing "US style categories" against "Non-US style categories" with a shaded region denoting the "Quantitative easing era" from 2014 onward. The visual correlation is stark: as negative-yielding debt rose during the quantitative easing era, manager outperformance deteriorated significantly. US style manager outperformance fell from over fifty percent to around forty-one percent by 2018, while Non-US style outperformance tumbled from a 2017 peak of about sixty-seven percent to below fifty percent in 2019.

The analysis further attributes active managers' struggles to the historic length of the current US economic expansion. Active managers historically perform better during market downturns, a point illustrated by the bottom bar chart, "Managers generally outperform more in down markets." This chart plots the percentage of active managers outperforming their respective ETFs on a one-year basis using monthly data since January 1996 across twenty-three different style and regional categories. Across every single category—ranging from Large Cap Growth (LCG) and Mid Cap Value (MCV) to geographic regions like Europe, Japan, Canada, and Emerging Markets (EM)—the blue "Down market" bars are substantially higher than the gold "Up market" bars. In most categories, down-market outperformance easily clears the fifty percent mark, whereas up-market outperformance regularly falls below it. For example, in the USDF category, down-market outperformance nears seventy-five percent, while up-market outperformance sits around forty-five percent.

In the concluding commentary, Cembalest identifies additional structural hurdles for active stock-pickers. These include highly concentrated equity markets where a small handful of stocks drive the majority of market returns, and a rise in pairwise stock correlations that reduces differentiation between individual stock performances. Furthermore, the market has seen a prolonged outperformance of growth stocks since 2010 alongside strong gains for "bond proxy" stocks—defined in a footnote as the top decile of Russell 1000 large-cap stocks characterized by low equity beta, high negative beta to interest rates, high dividend yields, and high payout ratios. Finally, the author points to an anomalous, multi-year underperformance of value investing, which stands in sharp contrast to a seventy-year historical trend of positive value returns that serves as the foundation for most active management models.

This page analyzes investment management categories that receive a Grade C due to their weak post-2014 performance, specifically where the average share of active managers outperforming their respective benchmark ETF on a rolling one-year basis has fallen below forty-five percent. The page features five historical line charts tracking active manager outperformance from 1997 through 2019, using data sourced from eVestment and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. 

The first chart covers Large Cap Core managers, showing their rolling one-year outperformance rate peaking near eighty percent in the early 2000s before declining, with the post-2014 average represented by a red bar falling below forty-five percent. The second chart illustrates Large Cap Growth managers, revealing similar volatility with a post-2014 outperformance average also sitting below forty-five percent. The third chart focuses on All Cap Core managers, depicting a sharp decline in outperformance over the years, culminating in a post-2014 average well below the fifty percent mark. The fourth chart displays All Cap Value managers, showing robust outperformance in the early 2000s that has since degraded to a post-2014 average of roughly forty percent. The final chart covers US Dividend Focused managers, illustrating a highly volatile track record that similarly concludes with a post-2014 average outperformance rate stuck below forty-five percent. Together, these charts highlight the persistent challenges active managers face when trying to beat passive ETF benchmarks in these specific equity styles.

This page of the publication analyzes active management performance, designating a "Grade B" category for asset classes where the post-2014 average of active managers outperforming their respective ETFs sits between 45% and 50%. The analysis is supported by seven line charts tracking the percentage of managers outperforming their respective benchmarks on a rolling one-year basis from 1997 through 2019. 

Each chart features a volatile blue line showing historical rolling outperformance, a solid grey line representing the long-term historical average, a dotted line representing a 50% threshold, and a red horizontal line depicting the post-2014 average. The data across all charts is sourced from eVestment and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

The first chart, focusing on Large Cap Value managers, shows that outperformance peaked above 80% around 2000 and has since fluctuated, with the post-2014 average landing just below 50%. The Mid Cap Core chart displays a highly cyclical history, peaking near 80% around 2001 and 2009, but settling into a post-2014 average around 48%. The Mid Cap Growth chart shows similar cyclicality, with peaks near 80% in the early 2000s and late 2000s, followed by deeper drawdowns in the 2010s and a post-2014 average of approximately 47%. For Mid Cap Value, historical peaks also reached near 80%, but a downward trend in the latter half of the timeline brought the post-2014 average down to about 46%. 

The Small Cap Core chart reveals that while active small-cap managers frequently outperformed in the late 1990s and early 2000s, their success has moderated over time, resulting in a post-2014 average of roughly 48%. The All Cap Growth chart shows a steady decline in manager outperformance from peak levels near 80% in the early 2000s to a post-2014 average of around 46%. Finally, the chart for Australia equity managers presents an international perspective; it displays extreme volatility, including a sharp spike to 100% around 1999, followed by a protracted decline that bottomed out near 20% in 2019, yielding a post-2014 outperformance average of about 48%. Together, these charts illustrate that across these diverse equity styles and regions, active managers have struggled to consistently beat passive benchmarks in the post-financial crisis era, typically hovering just below a 50% success rate.

This page, titled Grade A (continued), is part of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market report by Michael Cembalest. It analyzes the performance of active equity managers across five global markets: Japan, EAFE (Europe, Australasia, and Far East), Canada, the United Kingdom, and Emerging Markets. The core focus is evaluating the percentage of active managers who outperform their respective benchmark exchange-traded funds (ETFs) on a rolling one-year basis from 1997 through 2019. Each of the five line charts displays historical rolling one-year outperformance percentages ranging from 0% to 100%. A horizontal dotted black line marks the 50% threshold, representing the point where half of the active managers outperform. Additional horizontal reference lines show historical averages for different multi-year periods. Across almost all regions, while active managers have historically averaged outperformance rates above the 50% line, there is a pronounced downward trend leading into 2019, with active manager success rates dropping significantly below their long-term averages.

The first chart focuses on Japan, where active manager outperformance has historically fluctuated between roughly 25% and 90%. After peaking around 85% in the mid-2010s, the percentage of outperforming Japanese managers plummeted sharply by 2019, approaching a near-historical low of around 25%. The second chart, representing EAFE equities, illustrates a similar pattern. After starting near 90% in 1997 and experiencing a severe dip to 25% around 1999, outperformance rates mostly consolidated between 45% and 80%. However, by 2019, the rate declined to approximately 35%, falling well below the historical median of around 60%. 

The third chart covers Canada, where outperformance peaked near 85% in 2015 but fell to around 35% in 2019, continuing a volatile trend that previously saw a deep trough of 20% around 2001. The fourth chart, tracking the United Kingdom, shows an extreme drop near 0% in the late 1990s, followed by a recovery that peaked above 80% in the early 2000s and mid-2010s. UK active managers faced a steep decline starting around 2016, dropping to roughly 20% before hovering around 35% by 2019. Finally, the Emerging Markets chart displays a volatile path, with a historical low of 20% around 2000, followed by a sustained period of majority outperformance peaking near 80%. By 2019, the percentage of outperforming managers in emerging markets fell to around 40%, breaking below both the 50% mark and the long-term historical average of approximately 60%. Collectively, these charts demonstrate that the headwinds facing active management are global, with active managers in international, developed, and emerging markets increasingly struggling to beat passive ETF alternatives by the end of the analyzed period.

This page serves as a section divider introducing Appendix II: Methodology for the J.P. Morgan Eye on the Market report. It outlines the methodological topics covered in the subsequent pages, which include the most frequently used manager benchmarks by style category, assets under management, the number of managers, benchmark/ETF availability, manager fee assumptions and sensitivity, and ETF tracking error by style category.

This page outlines several potential catalysts for a recovery in value investing, which is currently experiencing its deepest slump in over seventy years. The author argues that a value rebound could be triggered by investor exhaustion as the discount for value stocks vs. the broad market reaches historic extremes. 

To support this, the first two charts analyze valuation premiums from 1986 through late 2018. The first chart displays the forward P/E premium paid for momentum and low-volatility stocks over value stocks. It shows that the momentum premium has surged to around sixteen, approaching its historic dot-com bubble peak, while the low-volatility premium has risen steeply to approximately ten. The second chart depicts the broad market premium over value, measured by subtracting the value P/E from the S&P 500 P/E. This metric has risen to nearly seven, also nearing historic highs last seen around the year 2000.

Beyond simple market exhaustion, the author identifies a significant policy catalyst: a potential regulatory crackdown on high-performing growth and technology stocks. After a multi-decade decline in antitrust enforcement, House Democrats are prioritizing antitrust concerns within healthcare consolidation and major tech platforms. While major legislation is unlikely before the 2020 election, current Department of Justice investigations and proposed privacy laws could slow down the mergers and data-sharing that have fueled tech sector earnings. 

The historical context of this regulatory shift is illustrated in a stacked bar chart detailing the number of DOJ antitrust investigations initiated annually from 1970 to 2018, categorized by mergers, monopoly, and competition. The data highlights a collapse in enforcement activity, with annual investigations dropping from over five hundred in the 1970s and late 1990s to just around one hundred in 2018. 

Finally, a line chart illustrates the market concentration that is attracting this political and regulatory attention by tracking technology companies' share of industry sales from 2011 to 2019. This chart shows Google controlling roughly 70 percent of interactive media and services sales, while Amazon has grown its share of internet retailing to about 70 percent. Simultaneously, Apple’s share of tech hardware sales has climbed to around 25 percent, and Facebook’s share of interactive media and services has risen from near-zero to more than 20 percent. The author concludes that these dominant, high-momentum stocks are highly vulnerable to antitrust investigations at both the state and federal levels, which could ultimately serve as the catalyst for a market rotation back into value.

This page analyzes the potential for a market shift away from overbought "bond proxies" toward value laggards like the energy sector, driven by a normalization of US monetary policy and improved capital discipline. The author argues that while Europe and Japan show little inflation, the United States displays signs of exhausted spare capacity and persistent inflation that point to the "beginning of the end" of super-loose monetary policy, which should eventually favor value stocks. 

This argument is supported by two macroeconomic charts. The first, illustrating the US output gap as a measure of spare capacity from 1990 to 2018, tracks actual GDP relative to potential GDP. It shows that the deep output gap of nearly negative six percent during the financial crisis has steadily recovered, with post-crisis excess capacity now fully exhausted as the gap moves into positive territory by late 2018. The second chart shows US core CPI year-over-year from 2008 to 2019, highlighting that inflation has rebounded from its 2010 low of around one percent to consistently sit at or above two percent for over a year.

The discussion then shifts to the energy sector, historically one of the worst value laggards due to poor capital discipline and low investor returns on projects. To illustrate this, a chart indexes oil and gas production and sector performance from 2008 to 2018. It shows that while actual production soared to an index value of nearly 260 by 2018, the exploration and production sector's performance peaked around 2012 before crashing back to its 2008 baseline of 100, erasing a decade of investor gains. A third line on this chart estimates that production without external capital would have remained far lower, suggesting that massive capital inflows actually suppressed prices and profitability. 

However, the author points out that this trend is reversing as capital discipline returns to the sector. A final chart tracking energy sector capital raises from 2008 to 2019 displays the combined volume of US energy high-yield bond issuance and US E&P equity issuance in billions of dollars. Total capital raises peaked near eighty billion dollars annually in 2012 and 2013 but have since fallen dramatically to around thirty billion dollars in 2019. The author concludes that this sharp decline in debt and equity issuance signals a major shake-out and rationalization of the energy sector, which is likely to pave the way for better investment returns in the future.

This page focuses on the methodology of assessing investment manager performance by comparing their returns to their own stated preferred benchmarks rather than over-simplifying with a single benchmark for each equity style category. To illustrate this, the page features a comprehensive reference table detailing the top three most frequently used benchmarks across twenty-two distinct style categories, detailing the Assets Under Management (AUM) and the number of managers associated with each benchmark. 

The style categories represent domestic and international markets, capitalization tiers, and investment styles. Key domestic styles covered include Large Cap Core (LCC), Large Cap Growth (LCG), Large Cap Value (LCV), Mid Cap categories (MCC, MCG, MCV), Small Cap categories (SCC, SCG, SCV), All Cap categories (ACC, ACG, ACV), and US Defensive (USDF). International and regional categories include Global, ACWI ex US, Europe, Asia ex Japan, Japan, Australia, EAFE, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Emerging Markets (EM).

The data highlights several highly dominant benchmarks. For example, in the Large Cap Value (LCV) category, the Russell 1000 Value benchmark leads with 274 managers and 996,494 in AUM. In the Large Cap Growth (LCG) category, the Russell 1000 Growth benchmark is used by 226 managers, representing 722,351 in AUM. For the Global category, the MSCI World-ND is the top benchmark, employed by 303 managers with an AUM of 849,671. In Emerging Markets, the MSCI EM-ND dominates with 246 managers and 651,039 in AUM. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 is the most popular choice for Large Cap Core (LCC), utilized by 249 managers representing 555,350 in AUM. Other prominent local market benchmarks featured include TOPIX for Japan, the FTSE All Share for the UK, and the S&P/TSX Composite for Canada. The dataset is sourced from eVestment and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page analyzes the outlook for the US banking sector, arguing that while rate normalization and a steepening yield curve could provide modest catalysts, bank valuations are unlikely to return to their pre-financial crisis levels. The author points out that post-crisis regulatory capital requirements have permanently lowered the sector's return on equity, and the era of major interstate bank mergers is largely over, with current consolidation restricted to small- and mid-cap spaces. 

The analysis is supported by several charts and tables. Two line charts track S&P 500 banking metrics from 1990 to 2018 using Bloomberg data. The first, "S&P 500 banks return on common equity," shows that return on equity consistently hovered around 15% to 20% in the 1990s and early 2000s, crashed to below negative 15% during the 2008 financial crisis, and has only recovered to about 10% in recent years. The adjacent chart, "S&P 500 banks price to book value," displays a similar trajectory, with valuations peaking above 3.0x in the late 1990s and early 2000s before falling below 1.0x in 2009, and remaining depressed in the 1.0x to 1.3x range through 2018. 

An additional line chart, "Number of US commercial banks," uses FDIC data from 1934 to 2014 to show the long-term trend of industry consolidation. The total number of banks remained stable near 14,000 for decades before beginning a steep decline in the mid-1980s, falling below 6,000 by 2014. 

Finally, a table of US commercial banks from Q2 2019 FDIC data breaks down the sector by asset size. It reveals a highly concentrated industry where just 9 mega-banks with greater than $250 billion in assets control 53.23% of total banking assets, achieving a 12.66% return on equity and a 1.37 return on assets. In contrast, the smallest tier of 1,090 banks with less than $100 million in assets represents only 0.38% of total assets, yielding a much lower 6.75% return on equity and a 0.96 return on assets. Middle tiers range from $100 million to $250 billion in assets, illustrating the distribution of the remaining banks and assets.

This page, titled "Early signs of a value recovery?", examines whether the performance gap between growth and value investing is beginning to shrink. The author notes that in mid-September 2019, value stocks outperformed growth stocks within both the S&P 500 and Russell 1000 indexes by their widest margins since 2009. Additionally, Bloomberg's factor analysis revealed the second-largest weekly return of value versus growth since 2009. The author poses the open question of whether this nascent value recovery will continue and boost overall investment manager outperformance in the months ahead.

Four charts support this observation. The first chart tracks cumulative growth return minus cumulative value return from January to September 2019 for the S&P 500 and Russell 1000. It shows growth steadily outperforming value, peaking in mid-to-late summer 2019 at around 10% cumulative outperformance for the Russell 1000 and 5% for the S&P 500, before both lines drop sharply in September, signifying a sudden reversal where value outperformed.

The second chart displays the largest weekly S&P 500 value versus growth returns since 2009, measuring the weekly value index return minus the growth index return. The week of September 9–13, 2019, ranked as the fourth-largest weekly outperformance in a decade, with value beating growth by approximately 2.8%. This trailed only three notable weekly spikes from 2009, which peaked above 5.0% in March and May, and 3.3% in August.

The third chart illustrates the same metric for the Russell 1000 index. The week of September 9–13, 2019, again ranked as the fourth-highest weekly return spread since 2009, with value outperforming growth by about 3.1%. This relative performance came close to matching the August 2009 spread of 3.1% and stood behind the May 2009 high of 5.0% and the March 2009 high of 3.9%.

The final chart depicts the largest weekly value versus growth factor returns since 2009, using Bloomberg's factor analysis. For the week of September 9–13, 2019, the value factor outperformed the growth factor by about 2.0%, trailing only the week of November 7–11, 2016, which reached 2.1%. This makes the September 2019 move the second-largest factor reversal since 2009, significantly outpacing other major spikes from 2009, 2014, and late 2016.

This page serves as a reference guide defining key acronyms used throughout the publication. It outlines general financial terms such as assets under management, exchange-traded funds, price-to-earnings ratios, and quantitative easing. Additionally, it translates abbreviations for capitalization-weighted investment styles, spanning large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap, and all-cap categories across core, growth, and value strategies, including large cap core, large cap growth, large cap value, mid cap core, mid cap growth, mid cap value, small cap core, small cap growth, small cap value, all cap core, all cap growth, and all cap value. Finally, it lists regional and index-focused acronyms, which include U.S. dividend focused, All Country World Index, Europe, Australasia, and Far East, United Kingdom, and Emerging markets.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market report, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the availability of investable exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that correspond to the benchmarks used by active asset managers. By evaluating the eVestment database, which tracks managers reporting returns since 1996, the authors sought to match active managers' benchmarks with comparable, real-world ETFs. They argue that comparing active managers to ETFs rather than paper indices is a superior method because ETFs naturally incorporate the real-life constraints of management fees and tracking errors. Certain managers were excluded from the analysis, such as those with custom, blank, or benchmark-agnostic targets, as well as those failing to provide gross-of-fee or US-dollar-denominated performance data. These exclusions represented four percent of total assets and nine percent of all managers in the database. 

The primary visual component of the page is a comprehensive data table showing assets under management, manager counts, and benchmark/ETF availability across twenty-three different style categories. The table breaks down the availability of matching ETFs by percentage of total assets under management and by percentage of the number of managers. 

In aggregate, the database covers 6,707 managers representing nearly twelve trillion dollars in assets under management. Across all categories, seventy-six percent of assets and sixty-eight percent of managers have a corresponding ETF available, while twenty percent of assets and twenty-three percent of managers have no matching ETF available. 

Looking at specific style categories, Global equities represent the largest single category with nearly two point five trillion dollars in assets across 1,290 managers, showing sixty-six percent ETF availability by assets. Large Cap Value and Large Cap Growth also represent massive pools of capital, at one point two five trillion dollars and one point zero four trillion dollars respectively; Large Cap Growth has one hundred percent ETF availability by assets, and Large Cap Value has ninety-seven percent availability. Other large categories include EAFE with over one point zero five trillion dollars and sixty-eight percent ETF availability by assets, and Emerging Markets with nearly nine hundred and seventy billion dollars and seventy-one percent ETF availability. In contrast, All Cap Growth exhibits very low ETF availability, with eighty-two percent of its one hundred and twelve billion dollars in assets having no matching ETF. Regionally, Europe shows a notable portion of managers with no benchmark available at twenty-nine percent, while Canada shows twelve percent of its assets having no benchmark available.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication focuses on manager fee assumptions and sensitivity. The author explains that while the analysis of net manager returns utilizes a baseline of $50 million separate account fees, applying the higher fees associated with smaller $10 million separate accounts has a negligible impact on the overall manager outperformance statistics. 

To prove this point, the page features a comprehensive table titled "Manager fees (in bps) by category and by vehicle, and the outperformance impact of using higher fees." The table lists three separate account fee tiers ($10 million, $50 million, and $200 million in basis points) alongside the post-2010 outperformance percentage for both the $10 million and $50 million cases, concluding with the percentage-point difference between the two cases. 

The data spans twenty-two style categories, including US equity styles such as Large Cap Core—where fees range from 59 basis points at $10 million to 46 basis points at $200 million, resulting in a minimal post-2010 outperformance difference of 0.8% (42% versus 43%). For high-fee categories like Emerging Markets, fees are 90 basis points at $10 million and 88 basis points at $50 million, but the resulting outperformance remains identical at 65%, a difference of just 0.1%. Similarly, Asia ex Japan shows a 0.0% difference in outperformance, which remains at 62% under both fee cases. Other style categories detailed in the table include Mid Cap, Small Cap, All Cap, US Dividend Focused, Global, ACWI ex US, Europe, Japan, Australia, EAFE, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Across all categories, the difference in outperformance between the $50 million and $10 million fee cases never exceeds 0.8%, confirming the low sensitivity of these metrics to the specific fee assumption selected. The data is sourced from eVestment and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page is a professional biography profile for Michael Cembalest, the Chairman of Market and Investment Strategy for J.P. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management. The page features a headshot photo of Cembalest on the left alongside a detailed text summary of his career and educational background on the right. The profile highlights his responsibility for leading strategic market and investment insights across J.P. Morgan's Institutional, Funds, and Private Banking businesses, which manage two trillion dollars in client assets globally. It details his tenure as a member of the J.P. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management Investment Committee, his past service on the retirement plan investment committee, and his eight-year role as Chief Investment Officer for the Global Private Bank. His earlier experience at the firm includes serving as head of a fixed income division for Investment Management, head strategist for Emerging Markets Fixed Income at J.P. Morgan Securities, and joining the Corporate Finance division in 1987.
