This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market discusses the concept of ETF tracking error, which measures the degree to which an ETF's returns deviate from those of its benchmark index. Computed as the annualized standard deviation of monthly return differences, tracking error often arises because liquidity constraints prevent ETF creators from holding one hundred percent of a benchmark's constituent stocks. The author points out that some of these tracking errors are remarkably large, in some cases comparable to the tracking error budget of active managers seeking excess return.

To illustrate this, the page includes a comprehensive table titled ETF tracking error, which breaks down the assets under management weighted average annualized tracking error across various style categories and lists the top benchmarks used for the computations. US equity style categories display relatively tight tracking, generally staying under one percent. Specifically, Large Cap Value, Core, and Growth show tracking errors of 0.57 percent, 0.58 percent, and 0.65 percent, respectively, based on benchmarks such as the S&P 500, Russell 1000, and MSCI USA-ND. Mid Cap styles range from 0.47 percent for Mid Cap Value to 0.68 percent for Mid Cap Core, benchmarking against Russell MidCap and S&P 400 indices. Small Cap categories exhibit slightly higher tracking errors, with Small Cap Growth at 0.91 percent, Small Cap Core at 0.96 percent, and Small Cap Value at 1.01 percent, tied to Russell 2000 and S&P 600 indices. All Cap categories run between 0.58 percent and 0.81 percent, while US Dividend Focused stands at 0.59 percent.

In contrast, international and global categories display substantially higher tracking errors. Global ETFs have a tracking error of 2.02 percent based on MSCI World and ACWI benchmarks, while ACWI ex US reaches 3.01 percent. Individual countries and regions show considerable variation: the United Kingdom is at 1.39 percent, Canada at 1.75 percent, Australia at 1.80 percent, Japan at 2.39 percent, and the EAFE region at 2.98 percent. The most pronounced tracking errors are found in Asia ex Japan at 4.93 percent, followed by Europe and Emerging Markets, both of which experience tracking errors of 5.09 percent. The data for these calculations, sourced from eVestment and J.P. Morgan Asset Management, spans from the later of June 2004 or each ETF's inception through June 2019.

This page focuses on the performance of recent US technology initial public offerings (IPOs), distinguishing between highly successful "pure tech" companies and struggling "tangential tech" firms. The author argues that despite negative headlines, real technology IPOs are performing well, while marketplace, hardware, and hybrid business models are dragging down average returns. Many of these struggling companies fail the "rule of 40%" test, which combines revenue growth and free cash flow margins. For example, Uber, Arlo, Eventbrite, and Pivotal yield negative numbers under this test, while Zuora and Upwork score under 20%.

An accompanying bar chart displays the performance of 2018 and 2019 tech IPOs relative to their offering price, color-coded by business model. Pure tech companies—defined as cloud-based software-as-a-service (SaaS) business-to-business models with high returns to scale—dominate the top performers. Leading this group are Zscaler at positive 206 percent, Anaplan at positive 193 percent, and Smartsheet at positive 153 percent, followed closely by Zoom and CrowdStrike. Social media is represented by Pinterest, which also shows positive gains. In contrast, the negative-performing side of the chart is heavily populated by transactional marketplace companies like Upwork, Uber, and Lyft, as well as hardware-software blends like Peloton and Sonos, and pure hardware plays like Arlo. The chart also highlights several notable underperforming listings backed by the SoftBank Vision Fund, including Slack, Upwork, Uber, and Livongo.

The page also offers broader historical context on IPO investing, citing a Goldman Sachs study showing that diversified multi-sector IPO investing has underperformed since 2010. A strategy holding a portfolio of 200 IPOs performed flat relative to the market, while the median IPO performance under a two-year hold was 20 percent below the market. Average returns only managed to match the broader market because a tiny tier—just 2 percent of IPOs—delivered blockbuster returns exceeding 200 percent. The author identifies healthcare as the primary drag on these figures, noting it has been the largest issuing and worst-performing sector in the US IPO market since 2010. 

Finally, the text concludes with a brief commentary on physical limits in technology, noting that improvements in computer processing power under Moore’s law have slowed to just a few percent annually. Clock speed has seen no improvement since 2004 as microprocessors reach atomic dimensions, marking a physical barrier associated with the end of Dennard Scaling.

This page focuses on the growing global impact of the trade war, highlighting a stark divergence between resilient consumer activity and weakening corporate sentiment and manufacturing. Michael Cembalest argues that the gap between a strong consumer sector and a weakening corporate sector cannot be sustained indefinitely, warning that President Trump is playing with fire, though he ultimately expects modest growth and an earnings rebound to help the US avoid a recession. 

To illustrate these dynamics, the first chart, titled "Services holding up, manufacturing falling," plots the US service sector index against the US manufacturing index from 2000 to late 2019, where a level of 50 or above indicates expansion. The chart shows that while the US service sector index has remained comfortably in expansionary territory despite a recent tick downward, the US manufacturing index has fallen sharply below the critical 50 threshold. 

The second chart, titled "Consumer optimistic, CEOs retrenching," covers the period from 2000 to 2019 and compares US consumer confidence, measured on the left axis against a 1985 baseline of 100, with US CEO confidence on the right axis, where a reading above 50 represents a positive outlook. This chart reveals a massive divergence: US consumer confidence remains near historical highs above 130, whereas CEO confidence has collapsed, dropping well below 40 as corporate leaders retrench. 

The author also notes that export-reliant European business surveys are weaker than those in the US. In China, economic activity is cooling rapidly, as shown in the final chart, "China activity coincident tracker." This metric, which tracks year-over-year percentage growth from 2013 to 2019 by aggregating electricity production, fiscal revenue, real exports, port throughput, retail sales, financial services, and traffic data, shows a clear downward trend. Specifically, this one-year measure of Chinese coincident growth fell from 7% in January 2018 to just 4% in August 2019.

This page presents a progressive policy review, analyzing the policy proposals put forward primarily by Senator Elizabeth Warren across several major economic and social sectors. The author notes that while adopting many of these proposals would require a Democratic-controlled Senate, a cooperating Senate Majority Leader, and potentially ending the filibuster, some changes could alternatively be enacted through unilateral executive action and regulation, following precedents set by the Trump administration.

The core of the page is a detailed table mapping out the Progressive Democratic Agenda across six key categories: taxation, corporate governance, labor, healthcare, energy, and student debt. Under taxation, the proposals include doubling the capital gains tax for earners over one million dollars, eliminating the step-up in basis at death, taxing unrealized capital gains, taxing capital gains and dividends as ordinary income, levying a two percent wealth tax on assets over fifty million dollars, raising the top estate tax rate to seventy-seven percent, implementing a twelve point four percent payroll tax on income over two hundred and fifty thousand dollars, and removing corporate tax cuts while adding a surtax on profits over one hundred million dollars.

For the corporate sector, the table lists restrictions or bans on stock buybacks, breaking up large banks and reversing deregulation, breaking up big tech companies, requiring a federal charter for public companies with revenues over one billion dollars that mandates public and societal benefits, subjecting political expenditures to shareholder approval, and holding private equity firms responsible for the debt and pensions of acquired companies. Labor proposals include banning state "right to work" laws, eliminating secret ballots in union elections, establishing worker co-determination by allowing employees to elect over forty percent of corporate board members, and reducing the classification of independent contractors.

In healthcare, the table highlights Medicare for All with no deductibles or copays, banning private health insurance, capping drug prices, and allowing the government to manufacture generic drugs. Energy initiatives feature bans on hydraulic fracturing on both private and federal land, banning fossil fuel exports, halting new nuclear power plants, and spending one trillion dollars over ten years to transition to clean energy. Finally, under student debt, the proposed agenda aims to reduce student debt for ninety-five percent of Americans, entirely wipe out debt for seventy-five percent of borrowers, and institute universal free public college, with an estimated overall cost of nine hundred and fifty-five billion dollars.

Michael Cembalest discusses the state of the US-China trade war, arguing that US equity markets have become range-bound by the policies and unpredictability of Trumpism, with the S&P 500 capped at an upper limit of around 3,000. He details escalating tensions in Washington, noting bipartisan disillusionment with China nearly twenty years after its entry into the World Trade Organization. Specific legislative measures are highlighted, including Senator Marco Rubio’s proposals to delist Chinese companies that fail to comply with US auditing regulations, alongside proposals to ban Federal retirement accounts from investing in China-exposed products. Cembalest projects that the best near-term outcome is a narrow, agriculture-focused trade deal, which may be facilitated by China's need to import pork after domestic swine fever resulted in the loss of 100 million pigs.

Two charts support this analysis. The first, titled "So Long Yellow Brick Road: Trumpism shows its true colors to investors," plots the S&P 500 Index level from 2015 through late 2019. It marks the post-2016 election surge as a period where investors embraced the positive aspects of Trumpism, such as deregulation, tax cuts, and pro-business judicial appointments. This upward trajectory halts abruptly on January 22, 2018, when the trade war officially began with tariffs on washing machines and solar panels. Following this date, the S&P 500 enters a volatile "Trumpism trading range" bounded roughly between 2,400 and 3,000. 

The second chart, "China: the most mercantile country in the world," presents a Mercantilism Index where a score of zero represents the most mercantile state. China’s composite score is extremely low, sitting close to the zero mark. This index aggregates several protectionist behaviors, including public ownership of the private sector, inadequate protection of trade secrets and data, weak intellectual property enforcement, high levels of pirated software, severe barriers to market access, forced technology transfer, weak copyright protections, and low receptivity to foreign direct investment.

Additionally, the page addresses trade friction between the US and Europe. Cembalest notes that the World Trade Organization authorized the US to impose tariffs on up to $7.5 billion of European goods as recompense for unfair subsidies given to Airbus. He notes that the US Trade Representative plans to implement these tariffs starting October 18, 2019, applying a 10 percent duty on jetliners and a 25 percent duty on items like whiskies, wine, and cheese. While the total volume of targeted goods is relatively small, he warns that these measures risk provoking retaliatory tariffs from the European Union.

This page of Eye on the Market by Michael Cembalest, titled "Treat Wealth Like Wages," details a proposal by Senator Ron Wyden to tax existing and future unrealized capital gains on an annual basis. Cembalest notes that this plan could be adopted by Senator Elizabeth Warren's campaign as an alternative to her own wealth tax, which faces potential constitutional challenges. The Wyden proposal would tax all capital gains as ordinary income for taxpayers with income exceeding one million dollars or assets over ten million dollars in three consecutive years. It requires annual mark-to-market taxation on publicly tradable securities and a lookback tax on non-tradable assets like partnership interests, real estate, and collectibles. Tradable securities would establish a new basis each year based on year-end market values, while non-tradable assets would face a lookback charge upon sale to eliminate tax deferral benefits. Exemptions include the first two million dollars of primary and secondary residences, five million dollars of family farms, and three million dollars of retirement assets. This tax would retroactively apply to current unrealized gains, though transition rules would allow taxpayers to pay the initial liability over several years. Unlike Warren's proposal, Wyden's framework aligns with existing tax rules, citing precedents such as Sections 1256, 475, 877A, and 1291. Additionally, a footnote highlights a proposal from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy suggesting that local governments could use eminent domain to acquire real estate if taxpayers contest IRS assessments.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses redistribution, equity market sector risks, and a potential ban on stock buybacks in the context of progressive Democratic policy proposals. He argues that redistribution is not inherently positive or negative but warns that a broad agenda could harm the private sector. Drawing on a J.P. Morgan analysis of Nordic countries, he highlights that even the most progressive nations require a thriving private sector and rely on consumer and payroll taxes to fund entitlements. 

Cembalest identifies several sectors that face severe valuation risks under a potential Democratic sweep, including banks, biotech, chemicals, energy, independent power producers, megacap internet, and healthcare. While healthcare is already heavily discounted, further downside could occur if reforms target private sector rents. This risk is contextualized by a chart displaying the ratio of S&P 500 healthcare to S&P 500 valuations from 1990 to 2018, which highlights a sharp valuation drop to 0.6x during the Clinton healthcare reform proposal of the early 1990s compared to peaks above 1.4x in the early 2000s. 

Additionally, Cembalest addresses the possibility of buyback restrictions, pointing to a bar chart of quarterly buyback yields by S&P 500 sector based on a four-quarter average as of October 2019. The chart reveals that Financials and Info Tech are the most reliant on buybacks, with yields of around 1.3 percent and 1.2 percent of market cap repurchased, respectively, followed by Consumer Discretionary excluding Internet at 1.0 percent, whereas Real Estate is the least reliant at roughly 0.1 percent.

This page examines the rise of Senator Elizabeth Warren in the 2020 Democratic primary contest and contextualizes her progressive platform on the historical political spectrum. Author Michael Cembalest argues that Warren's policy proposals place her significantly further to the left than any twentieth-century Democratic president or major presidential nominee. 

Two small charts at the top of the page establish Warren's momentum as of late 2019 using data from Real Clear Politics. The first chart, depicting the 2020 Democratic presidential poll from January to September 2019, shows Joe Biden leading but declining from a peak near 40 percent in May to roughly 32 percent in September. Meanwhile, Warren rises steadily from approximately 5 percent to 25 percent, surpassing Bernie Sanders, who remains flat in the 15 to 20 percent range. The second chart shows betting odds for the nomination from March to October 2019, highlighting Warren's dramatic surge from under 10 percent to nearly 50 percent by October, leaving Biden at 20 percent and Sanders at 10 percent.

The main visual on the page is a comprehensive scatter plot charting the political ideology of presidential administrations and losing candidates from 1916 to 2020. Based on UCLA Voteview Liberal-Conservative scores derived from Congressional voting histories, the horizontal axis ranges from most liberal at negative 0.9 to most conservative at positive 0.9. Historical Democratic administrations—including Franklin D. Roosevelt/Harry Truman, John F. Kennedy/Lyndon B. Johnson, Jimmy Carter, Bill Clinton, and Barack Obama—consistently aggregate in a moderate-liberal range between negative 0.3 and negative 0.4. On the conservative side, administrations like Ronald Reagan/George H.W. Bush, George W. Bush, and Donald Trump score between positive 0.4 and positive 0.6. 

The chart maps the 2020 Democratic candidates against this historical backdrop, revealing a stark ideological divide. While Joe Biden and Amy Klobuchar align closely with traditional Democrats at around negative 0.35, Elizabeth Warren and Kamala Harris plot much further to the left at approximately negative 0.65. Bernie Sanders is positioned even further left, scoring near negative 0.4 before 2010 but shifting to nearly negative 0.8 in his post-2010 voting record. This visual historical comparison underscores the author's point that Warren and her progressive peers represent a substantial leftward departure from the historical mainstream of the Democratic Party.

This page analyzes the potential economic and market consequences of repealing the 2017 US corporate tax bill and introducing additional windfall corporate taxes. The author argues that before the 2017 reform, the US had the highest marginal effective corporate tax rate in the G-7 and the OECD, putting domestic corporations at a competitive disadvantage. Lowering these rates was historically a bipartisan goal, with President Obama’s 2010 Bipartisan Commission on Fiscal Reform proposing a switch to a territorial tax system to level the playing field. The author positions the current push toward higher corporate taxes as a fundamental shift in economic views within the Democratic Party.

The first chart on the page illustrates the marginal effective tax rate on new investment in manufacturing and services, showcasing GDP-weighted rates as of December 2017. It shows that prior to the tax cuts, the US had an effective rate of approximately 35%, significantly higher than Asia-Oceania at around 21%, Europe at 19%, Canada at 18%, and Mexico at 17%. The 2017 tax bill brought the current US rate down to a competitive 18%, while Africa sits at 15% and the Middle East and North Africa holds the lowest rate at roughly 11%. 

A second chart tracks US tax rates and corporate inversions from 1981 to 2015, showing the clear link between tax policy and expatriation. While the average statutory corporate tax rate for non-US OECD nations steadily declined from about 50% in 1981 to below 30% by 2015, the US statutory rate remained flat at nearly 40% after the late 1980s. This growing gap led to wave after wave of corporate inversions, peaking with several years in the mid-2000s and mid-2010s recording up to 10 inversions annually. The author warns that repealing the 2017 tax bill, which originally curbed these incentives, could trigger a renewed spike in US companies moving their headquarters abroad.

In terms of equity market impacts, the corporate tax cuts boosted S&P earnings by 8% to 10% in 2018. Consequently, the author calculates that a complete tax repeal could, in isolation, reduce the fair value of the S&P 500 by 8% to 10% assuming a 17.5x multiple. Key sectors benefiting most from the cuts—which would be most vulnerable to a repeal—include communication services, consumer discretionary, and financials. This baseline downside estimate does not account for additional progressive policies, such as Senator Elizabeth Warren’s proposal for a 7% windfall profit tax on corporate earnings exceeding $100 million to fund renewable energy initiatives. 

Footnotes clarify that a full reversal would hike rates back to 35% and narrow the tax base, though raising rates to 28% without expanding the tax base could have an identical economic impact. Additionally, the author references research on financial transactions taxes (FTTs), noting they are historically unsuccessful, generate less revenue than anticipated due to transaction relocation, and ultimately shift tax burdens onto everyday consumers and investors rather than the financial system.

This page contains legal disclaimers and regulatory disclosures for J.P. This page provides the methodological background and list of constituent politicians used to construct J.P. Morgan's "political spectrum pendulum chart." The author explains that each presidential administration’s score of liberalism or conservatism is based on selected politicians from both the Executive Branch and Congress who supported major legislative initiatives or defended the administration's core governing principles. These individual scores are derived from UCLA's Voteview database, a project initiated by Keith Poole and Howard Rosenthal that measures how frequently politicians voted with their respective party blocs. The author references a previous December 10, 2018 issue of "Eye on the Market" where they demonstrated how a decline in moderate politicians historically coincided with a decline in long-term US economic growth. 

To clarify who is factored into each administration's score, the page lists the selected politicians for eleven presidential eras. The Trump administration score includes Cotton, Graham, Hatch, McCarthy, Meadows, Paul, Perdue, Ryan, Scalise, and Sessions. The Obama era includes Biden, Durbin, H. Clinton, Kennedy, Kerry, Obama, Pelosi, Reid, and Waxman. For George W. Bush, the score utilizes Ashcroft, Blunt, Cheney, DeLay, Kyl, McConnell, and Santorum. The Clinton era lists Bentsen, Carper, Chiles, Gephardt, H. Ford, Nunn, and Robb. The Reagan and George H.W. Bush administrations combine Baker, Bush, Dole, Kemp, Latta, Laxalt, Lugar, and Michel. The Carter administration includes Bayh, Byrd, Hawkins, Mondale, O'Neill, and Wright. For Nixon and Ford, the figures are Ford, Lott, Percy, Rhodes, Sandman, Scott, and Wiggins. JFK and LBJ's era incorporates Bolling, Humphrey, JFK, Johnson, Mansfield, McCarthy, and McCormack. The Eisenhower administration utilizes Dirksen, Dulles, Flanders, Nixon, Saltonsall, Smith, and Taft. FDR and Truman's period includes Barkley, Black, Byrns, Garner, Guffey, McCormack, Robinson, Sabath, and Truman. Finally, the Coolidge and Hoover administrations are represented by Curtis, Hawley, Longworth, Moses, Tilson, and Watson.

At the bottom of the page, a reference list of "Acronyms of the Week" is provided to define common financial, regulatory, and policy terms. This includes business-to-business (B2B), Department of Justice (DoJ), Exploration and Production (E&P), European Union (EU), FAANG (Facebook, Amazon, Apple, Netflix, Google), Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Financial Transactions Tax (FTT), Foreign exchange (FX), Intellectual property (IP), Initial public offering (IPO), Individual Retirement Account (IRA), National Labor Relations Board (NLRB), Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), Value Added Tax (VAT), and World Trade Organization (WTO).

This page examines the growing political momentum behind antitrust investigations in the technology sector and analyzes the potential implications for investors. The author notes that after a 50-year decline in antitrust investigations, politicians are increasingly looking to curb the influence of tech giants. This shift presents a material risk to investors because the tech sector has significantly driven market returns over the past decade and relies heavily on acquiring smaller firms to sustain growth. Footnote commentary mentions the debate over a venture capital kill zone created by dominant firms like Facebook, Google, and Amazon, contrasting a 2018 Oliver Wyman study with critics who argue these giants stifle competing startup activity.

The historical context of antitrust enforcement is illustrated by a bar chart tracking the number of Department of Justice antitrust investigations initiated from 1970 to 2018. Broken down by mergers, monopoly, and competition, the chart shows a steep downward trend from peaks of nearly 600 annual investigations in the early 1970s to consistently fewer than 100 in the late 2010s. 

A companion bar chart details the rate of agency challenges by the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice, demonstrating that tech enforcement has been historically light compared to the broader economy. While the FTC challenges about 13 percent of cases across all sectors, its rate of challenge in the tech sector—defined as data processing, hosting, and related services—is 0 percent. Similarly, the DOJ challenges around 17 percent of cases across all sectors, but only about 6 percent in the tech sector.

The investment stakes are highlighted in a line chart comparing the S&P 500 Information Technology index against the S&P 500 ex-Information Technology index from 2010 to late 2019. Starting from a base of 100 in January 2010, the technology sector surged to an index level of approximately 450, nearly doubling the performance of the non-tech index, which reached only about 250 over the same period. 

The active acquisition strategy of major tech players is shown in a bar chart plotting big tech acquisitions from 1987 to 2018. Mergers and acquisitions were negligible until the late 1990s, after which they escalated rapidly, peaking at over 60 acquisitions in 2014 and 2015, and remaining elevated at over 40 in 2018.

At the bottom of the page, a comprehensive table tracks regulatory and antitrust actions across the technology sector, distinguishing between proposed and already implemented measures. Pending actions include multi-state and federal antitrust investigations into Google, Facebook, and Amazon, congressional requests for executive emails, and Elizabeth Warren's proposal to break up FAANG companies and treat major tech platforms as utilities. Already implemented measures, printed in red, include California's gig-economy worker reclassification law affecting Amazon, Uber, and Lyft; a 5 billion dollar FTC fine against Facebook for privacy practices; an antitrust ruling against Qualcomm; and new local tax collection requirements for platforms like Amazon, eBay, and Airbnb.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the post-2008 rise of "the Armageddonists"—pessimistic market forecasters and money managers whose apocalyptic predictions gained immense traction after the Global Financial Crisis. He attributes their popularity to investor trauma from two consecutive equity drawdowns of over 40% in 2001 and 2008, a devastating sequence not seen since the Great Depression. He notes that such mega-bearish commentary successfully exploits the human negativity bias, citing insights from Daniel Kahneman’s work on survival instincts and Stuart Soroka’s research on how negative headlines drive media consumption. Cembalest poses an open question regarding the financial consequences for investors who reacted to these dire, continuous warnings since 2010. 

To contextualize these market fears, the page features a line chart titled "A history of S&P 500 bear markets," which plots the percentage decline of the index from its prior peak from 1928 through late 2018. The vertical axis tracks drawdowns from 0% down to -90%. The chart highlights major historical drawdowns alongside their specific economic or geopolitical catalysts. Key events marked on the timeline include the Great Depression, which saw a catastrophic decline approaching -90%; the mid-1950s Suez Crisis and Soviet invasion of Hungary; JFK's clash with the corporate sector in the early 1960s; the tight money credit crunch of the mid-1960s; and the late 1960s Vietnam War spending that triggered the Great Inflation. It also highlights the mid-1970s stagflation period that caused an approximate -50% market decline, Paul Volcker's aggressive rate hikes to 20.5% in the early 1980s, the late-1980s portfolio insurance unwind, the U.S. Savings and Loan crisis, the tech collapse and corporate fraud of the early 2000s, the Global Financial Crisis, and finally, the late-2018 Federal Reserve tightening scare.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the critical role of hydraulic fracturing in the United States energy landscape and outlines the severe challenges that would arise from an immediate ban on the practice. Cembalest argues that because fracking accounts for 60 percent to 80 percent of domestic oil, natural gas, and natural gas liquid production, a sudden ban is highly impractical. The transition to renewable energy is not moving fast enough to replace these resources, particularly as the US seeks to retire aging coal and nuclear plants. Furthermore, natural gas remains an indispensable backup for intermittent renewables due to the lack of a nationwide electricity grid and cheap, large-scale energy storage. 

To support this argument, the page presents six charts. The first chart, showing the percentage of US oil and gas production derived from hydraulic fracturing from 1995 to 2019, illustrates the dramatic rise of unconventional extraction. By 2019, natural gas derived from fracking reached approximately 80 percent of total production, while crude oil and natural gas liquids both rose from negligible levels in the early 2000s to around 60 percent. 

The second chart demonstrates that hydraulic fracturing accounts for 40 percent of all US primary energy consumption. This stacked column chart breaks down total consumption, showing that fracked oil, gas, and natural gas liquids represent the single largest share of US energy, followed by conventional oil and gas, coal, nuclear, biomass, hydro, wind, and solar or geothermal sources.

The middle row of charts highlights the macroeconomic benefit of the shale revolution on the US trade balance. The third chart displays the US net energy deficit in dollar terms as a percentage of GDP from 1978 to 2018. This deficit peaked near 3.5 percent of GDP in the late 1970s and early 1980s, and again at nearly 3.4 percent around 2008, before plunging to nearly zero by 2018. The fourth chart displays this trend in physical energy terms, showing net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal in million tonnes of oil equivalent from 1972 to 2016. This deficit peaked at over 700 million tonnes in the mid-2000s before collapsing to under 100 million tonnes.

The fifth chart shows US sources of primary energy consumption from 1965 to 2015. Throughout this fifty-year period, oil and natural gas have remained the dominant sources, with oil hovering around 35 percent to 40 percent and natural gas near 30 percent. In contrast, modern renewables represent only a tiny fraction, ending the period at just a few percent of total consumption. 

The final chart underscores the massive hurdle facing grid decarbonization, showing that only 1 percent of US electricity generation is stored, while 99 percent is consumed immediately. Furthermore, of the small amount of electricity storage capacity that does exist, 94 percent is comprised of decades-old pumped hydro storage, while only 6 percent comes from other technologies such as thermal, battery, compressed air, and flywheels. This lack of storage capacity highlights why natural gas is currently a critical and irreplaceable complement to intermittent renewable energy.

This page analyzes the significant financial opportunity cost incurred by investors who followed the warnings of prominent bearish commentators, referred to as "Armageddonists," by shifting capital from equities to bonds between 2010 and 2019. The author argues that because the S&P 500 rose 175% since 2010—with 75% to 95% of this increase driven by solid earnings growth rather than multiple expansion—the penalty for avoiding equities was massive. 

The primary visual is a line chart titled "The consequences of listening to the Armageddonists, 2010-2019," which tracks the performance impact of shifting one dollar from the S&P 500 to the Barclay's Aggregate Bond Index on the week of a given commentator's bearish warning. The vertical axis measures performance impact from positive 5% down to negative 65% through November 2019. Every single tracked commentator's warning resulted in substantial underperformance. Following the warnings of Simon Johnson, Paul Krugman, David Levy, Carl Icahn, John Hussman, George Soros, Bob Janjuah, Peter Schiff, or Tom DeMark resulted in an opportunity loss of roughly 30% to 40%. The opportunity losses are even more severe, ranging from 45% to nearly 60%, for investors who acted on the warnings of David Stockman, Albert Edwards, Marc Faber, Laksham Achuthan, Robert Wiedemer, David Rosenberg, Jeff Gundlach, and Nouriel Roubini. 

Addressing the macroeconomic outlook, the author acknowledges several recessionary pressures, including the China-US Trade War, a plunge in CEO confidence, a US earnings recession, and a Duke CFO Survey indicating that 67% of respondents anticipate a recession by the end of 2020. However, the author predicts that a recession in 2020 will likely be avoided, pointing to a resilient US consumer, strong labor and housing markets, and a modest rebound in manufacturing. Quantitative recession models put the 12-to-24-month recession probability at approximately 25%. Additionally, the author notes that traditional yield curve inversion signals are currently distorted and less reliable due to downward pressure on long-term US yields from negative-yield policies in Europe and Japan, alongside a structural decline in the long-duration bond term premium since the 1980s. Ultimately, the author emphasizes that the next bear market will have to be exceptionally severe—requiring a sustained, multi-year decline of 35% to 45% from peak levels—just to recoup the performance sacrificed by exiting equities too early.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest assesses the potential severity of the next bear market, concluding that it will likely be less severe and shorter-lived than the previous two major downturns. He supports this view by highlighting several stabilizing factors, including reduced global economic imbalances, stronger capital levels and lower funding risks for US and European banks, healthier US household balance sheets, decreased vulnerability in Emerging Markets due to robust foreign exchange reserves, and a limited supply of new US equities resulting from five years of buybacks and mergers exceeding new stock issuances.

On the bearish side, Cembalest details several counterpoints, particularly highly elevated US equity valuations, which generally sit around the 90th percentile of historical expensiveness for metrics like price-to-book, price-to-earnings, and enterprise-value-to-sales. He qualifies this by noting that free cash flow yield is closer to its historical median, and the S&P earnings yield relative to US 10-year Treasuries sits at the 24th percentile. Other risks include deteriorating underwriting standards in leveraged loans, deficit-financed late-cycle growth, and potential US policy shifts after the 2020 election that could introduce heavy taxes and regulations across sectors such as technology, energy, healthcare, financials, biotech, wireless, and chemicals. Despite these concerns, Cembalest argues that diversified portfolio managers who remained exposed to risky assets since 2010 will likely be vindicated. He also reflects on the mechanics of market duration, pointing out that shorter-duration downturns, such as the late-2018 S&P 500 correction that recovered half of its 20 percent loss in 20 days, offer less dislocation than prolonged bear markets. 

Finally, a dedicated sidebar titled "Armageddonism: not just for financial markets" critiques overly pessimistic commodity forecasts. Cembalest highlights a 2012 Nature Magazine article by money manager Jeremy Grantham, which warned of global starvation due to an impending depletion of phosphorus and potassium fertilizers within 20 to 40 years. Cembalest debunks this claim using 2019 reports from the US Geological Survey and the United Nations, which show 140 to 420 years of economically viable reserves and over 1,000 years of technically recoverable resources for both potash and phosphates.

This page discusses the difference between a standard defensive investment posture—which typically involves modest ten percent risk reductions in a portfolio—and extreme "Armageddonist" commentary that calls for wholesale reductions in portfolio risk due to predictions of severe recessions, bear markets, and financial crises. The author explains that such catastrophic forecasts were highly prevalent during the post-Great Recession period of 2010 through 2016, though history showed them to be overly pessimistic or outright incorrect. To illustrate this point, the page presents a detailed chronological table containing seventeen alarmist predictions from prominent economists, fund managers, and commentators. 

The table begins in May 2010 with Nouriel Roubini warning of a double-dip recession on CBS. In June 2011, David Rosenberg declared he was ninety-nine percent sure of another recession by the end of 2012, followed in August 2011 by Jeff Gundlach describing stock-buying as suicidal, a sentiment Gundlach echoed in July 2016 with a call to sell everything. In early 2012, Lakshman Achuthan of the Economic Cycle Research Institute insisted a recession was inevitable by late summer, and Marc Faber gave one-hundred percent odds of a global recession by early 2013. The predictions grew even more extreme in late 2012, when Robert Wiedemer predicted fifty percent unemployment, a ninety percent stock market drop, and one-hundred percent annual inflation. 

Throughout 2013, commentators advised aggressive defensive moves. David Stockman urged investors to hide out in cash, while Albert Edwards predicted the S&P Composite would plunge seventy percent to bottom around 450. Peter Schiff expressed absolute confidence that a crisis worse than 2008 was imminent, suggesting President Barack Obama would not finish his second term before the bottom dropped out. Meanwhile, Tom DeMark claimed the Dow Jones was tracking the 1929 crash almost precisely, and Bob Janjuah predicted a global stock market sell-off of twenty-five to fifty percent. 

The warnings continued in July 2014 with David Levy predicting a global-led U.S. recession that would send home prices below their prior recession lows. In September 2015, Carl Icahn warned of a massive bubble and a non-systemic complete meltdown. Early 2016 brought warnings from George Soros regarding a crisis reminiscent of 2008 stemming from China's adjustment problems, alongside John Hussman stating a recession was the dominant likelihood. The table concludes in late 2016 with politically charged forecasts surrounding the U.S. presidential election. Simon Johnson warned that a Donald Trump presidency would crash the stock market and plunge the world into recession, comparing the threat to the United Kingdom's Brexit vote. Immediately following the election on November 9, 2016, Paul Krugman wrote that markets were plunging and a global recession with no end in sight was highly probable.

This page serves as an appendix outlining six potential economic and structural mitigants that could reduce the severity of the next bear market. Each of the six charts presents data showing how various financial buffers have strengthened compared to previous market cycles.

Chart 1, titled "A decline in global imbalances," tracks the absolute value of all country current account surpluses and deficits as a percentage of world GDP from 1980 to 2016. It shows that global imbalances peaked near 6% around 2006 to 2007, driven by Asian manufacturers, oil exporters, and Northern European finance funding housing booms in Anglo-Saxon nations and Spain/Portugal. By 2016, these imbalances had declined substantially to around 3.5%, reducing systemic global risks.

Chart 2 shows "Decreased risk in the financial system" by comparing key bank health metrics between 2007 and 2019. In the US, the bank risk-weighted-capital ratio increased from 8.5% to 13.7%, and in Europe, it rose from 8.0% to 15.6%. Bank liquid assets as a percentage of short-term liabilities grew from 41% to 45% in the US and from 35% to 41% in Europe. Meanwhile, bank loan-to-deposit ratios fell from 97% to 77% in the US and from 139% to 104% in Europe, signaling a far more resilient banking sector.

Chart 3, "Lowest household debt-service ratios in 40 years," displays US household debt payments as a percentage of disposable income from 1980 to 2019. The debt-service ratio, covering mortgage and consumer debt payments, reached its lowest level in four decades at approximately 10% in 2019, down from a peak of nearly 13% in 2007. The broader financial obligations ratio, which includes rent, auto leases, insurance, and property taxes, similarly declined from an 18% peak in 2007 to about 15% in 2019.

Charts 4 and 5 focus on emerging markets. Chart 4, "Emerging Markets foreign exchange reserves," indicates that the median level of country reserves as a percentage of GDP rose from under 10% in the 1980s and 1990s to a historically high level of approximately 18% in 2016, providing a significant cushion against external shocks. Chart 5, "Emerging Markets current account balances," compares country current accounts in 2018 against their worst historical levels since 1980. Across countries like Argentina, Brazil, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Turkey, and South Africa, the 2018 balances were substantially stronger than their historical worst-case deficits, with China and South Korea maintaining solid surpluses.

Finally, Chart 6, "Unprecedented low levels of net equity supply," illustrates the net supply of global equities in billions of US dollars based on the MSCI All Country World Equity Index from 1999 to 2019. Total net equity supply has fallen dramatically from peaks of roughly $1,200 billion in 2000 and 2007 to near-zero or slightly negative levels by 2019, driven by massive corporate share buybacks and limited initial public offerings, which supports equity prices by restricting supply.

This page analyzes the severe fiscal and economic challenges facing the state of Illinois, with the author suggesting the state may be heading toward a slow-moving fiscal crisis comparable to Detroit or Puerto Rico. The narrative highlights that the state’s population, labor force, and home prices are shrinking or stagnating in the wake of tax hikes, while pension obligations loom large. The author discusses the Pritzker tax plan, predicting it will create one of the most onerous business tax climates in the country, thereby accelerating the departure of businesses and households to neighboring states like Indiana, Michigan, Kentucky, Iowa, Wisconsin, and Missouri. A quote from former FDIC Chairman William Isaac is included, advocating for Chicago and Illinois to restructure their liabilities using Chapter 9 or tools similar to those Congress provided to Puerto Rico.

Six charts support these arguments, color-coding Illinois in red, neighboring states in gold, and other states in blue. The first chart, illustrating the percentage of state revenues required to fully repay pension and retiree healthcare obligations (assuming a 6% portfolio return and a 30-year amortization), shows Illinois at the extreme left of the distribution, requiring over 40% of its revenues—by far the highest in the country. 

The second chart, tracking the cumulative percentage change in population from 2010 to 2018, positions Illinois at the far right with a net population decline of roughly 1%, while most other states achieved positive growth. 

This trend is reinforced by the third and fourth charts on interstate migration. The third chart shows that Illinois experienced a population loss of nearly 1.0% due to interstate migration between 2017 and 2018, ranking among the worst nationwide. The fourth chart shows the percentage change in adjusted gross income due to interstate migration in 2016, with Illinois suffering a loss of about 1.3% of its adjusted gross income; a note indicates this is likely understated since more recent tax years are not yet reflected.

The fifth chart shows the one-year change in home prices as of the second quarter of 2019 using the FHFA purchase-only index. Illinois sits near the bottom of the list with a weak year-over-year increase of less than 2%. 

The final chart maps out how the Pritzker tax plan would affect the state's ranking on the Tax Foundation Business Tax Climate Index, where a rank of 1 is the best. An arrow shows Illinois plummeting from 36th place to 48th place, leaving it far behind its gold-coded neighboring states and almost all other states in tax competitiveness.

This page discusses the heavy burden placed on the Federal student loan system by for-profit, two-year, and non-selective colleges, noting that a lack of interest from private lenders has forced these students to rely almost entirely on public loans. 

The first line chart displays the percentage of undergraduates receiving Federal student loans by institution type from 1993 to 2015. It highlights that private, for-profit undergraduates have the highest reliance on federal loans, peaking at around 80% between 2009 and 2011, compared to private nonprofits (peaking near 65%) and public institutions (the lowest, ranging between 30% and 45%). 

Next, two stacked area charts track new first-time Federal borrowers and borrowers entering repayment from 1982 to 2014. Both charts show a massive surge in volume starting in the late 1990s and peaking around 2010. This rapid growth was driven predominantly by students at for-profit and two-year institutions. 

The final two bar charts compare the share of borrowers and the share of aggregate debt by institution type in 2014. The first of these shows that for-profit students constituted the single largest group of Federal borrowers at 25% of the total, followed by somewhat selective 4-year schools (22%), selective 4-year schools (19%), non-selective 4-year schools (15%), 2-year programs (14%), and graduate-only students (5%). Despite making up a quarter of all borrowers, the subsequent chart reveals that for-profit students only held 17% of aggregate federal student loan debt (amounting to roughly $190 billion). By comparison, somewhat selective 4-year schools held 24% of the debt, and selective 4-year schools held 23%. The author explains this discrepancy by noting that many students at for-profit colleges drop out early, preventing them from accumulating even higher debt balances but leaving them with unfinished degrees.

This page explores the dramatic expansion of the student loan borrower universe, showing how policy changes drove a rapid rise in borrowers—two to three times faster than college-age population growth—and examining the proliferation of for-profit and non-selective universities. 

The first line chart, "Number of students with outstanding federal loans" spanning 1985 to 2014, illustrates this overall growth. Outstanding federal loans for undergraduate students, measured on the left axis, rose from roughly 7 million in 1985 to approximately 40 million by 2012. Outstanding loans for graduate students, measured on the right axis, also grew steadily from around 0.5 million to over 2.0 million over the same period. 

A second line chart tracks the "Percentage of first time Federal borrowers at for-profit, 2 year, or nonselective 4 year institutions" from 1982 to 2014. This metric peaked at nearly 68% in the late 1980s, declined to a low of about 43% in the mid-1990s, and then climbed back up to approximately 60% around 2010 before declining slightly to 53% by 2014. 

The third chart, a stacked column comparison titled "Top 10 institutions at which students hold the most debt," shows a dramatic shift in debt concentration between 2000 and 2014. In 2000, the top ten list was dominated by selective four-year universities such as NYU, University of Minnesota, Temple University, Ohio State University, and Penn State, with the University of Phoenix being the only for-profit institution represented. By 2014, the profile inverted entirely, with the list composed almost exclusively of for-profit institutions including Ashford University, Argosy University, Kaplan University, Strayer University, Capella University, DeVry University, Walden University, and the University of Phoenix, leaving NYU as the sole remaining selective nonprofit institution on the list. 

The final chart, "Cumulative debt of bachelor's degree recipients, 2011-12," compares debt levels across different institution types. It highlights that graduates from for-profit colleges carry significantly higher debt loads than those from public or private nonprofit four-year universities. Specifically, over half of the bachelor's degree recipients at for-profit schools graduated with more than $40,000 in debt, and a negligible percentage finished with no debt. In contrast, nearly half of graduates from public and private nonprofit four-year schools graduated with either no debt or less than $20,000 of debt. 

The page notes that selectivity definitions, sourced from Brookings Institution researcher Adam Looney, classify institutions admitting more than 85% of applicants as non-selective, 75% to 85% as somewhat selective, and less than 75% as selective.

This page, titled "Appendix III: Should students be encouraged to choose majors based on outcomes?", addresses the mismatch between the skills of college graduates and the actual demands of employers. The author notes that this mismatch contributes to structural unemployment, reduced economic output, and high student loan default rates. To close this gap, the text suggests that loan availability and pricing could be structured to create incentives for higher-value majors, pointing out that other developed nations manage higher education through general tax revenues and competitive exams to align academic offerings with labor market demands. 

The analysis is supported by three charts. The first, "Average median earnings vs debt outstanding by major," shows that there is virtually no positive relationship between total outstanding student loan debt and post-graduation earnings. For example, Business majors accumulate the highest overall debt at nearly $6 billion despite moderate median earnings around $60,000, and Education and Psychology majors incur high debt (around $4 billion) for low median earnings (under $50,000). Meanwhile, higher-earning majors like Engineering and Computer Science, which command median salaries of $80,000 to $85,000, exhibit relatively lower total outstanding debt. 

The second chart, "Job offer rate by major, 2014," depicts the percentage of recent graduates with job offers at graduation. Accounting graduates lead the list with over a 60% offer rate, followed closely by Economics, Computer Science, and Engineering, which all exceed 50%. In contrast, liberal arts and social science majors, such as English and Sociology/Social Work, see the lowest offer rates at around 30%. 

The final chart, "STEM college degrees by country," measures STEM graduates as a percentage of total college graduates across various nations. It demonstrates that the United States is severely lagging, ranking near the bottom of the list at approximately 12%. This stands in stark contrast to top-performing countries like Korea, which leads at over 30%, followed by Germany, Sweden, and Finland, all of which maintain STEM graduation rates of 25% or higher.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s financial publication, authored by Michael Cembalest, argues that policy-driven increases in student attendance at for-profit and two-year colleges have led to highly adverse financial outcomes, specifically spiked default rates, low graduation rates, and weak labor market performance. The author highlights that the widely cited ten percent student loan delinquency rate requires nuance, as defaults are heavily concentrated within specific institution types rather than distributed evenly across higher education.

Four supporting charts visualize these trends using data from the Brookings Institution, the Bureau of Economic Analysis, and the National Center for Education Statistics. The first chart, tracking data from 1970 to 2010, demonstrates a tight correlation between the for-profit share of federal loans and two-year student loan default rates. This is highlighted by a dramatic spike in the late 1980s, when the for-profit loan share peaked near forty-five percent and two-year default rates surged in tandem to nearly forty-five percent before both sharply declined in the early 1990s. 

The second chart compares six-year graduation rates for bachelor's degree-seeking students who began their studies between 1996 and 2011. While nonprofit institutions maintained the highest graduation rates, rising from around fifty-eight percent to sixty-five percent, and public institutions followed closely behind, rising from fifty percent to nearly fifty-eight percent, for-profit institutions lagged significantly. Graduation rates at for-profits hovered between twenty-five and thirty percent before dropping to approximately twenty percent for the 2011 cohort.

The third chart illustrates the relationship between median earnings and unemployment rates for federal borrowers in their second year of repayment, categorized by school type. There is a clear linear trend showing that as school selectivity increases, student outcomes improve. For-profit graduates experience the worst outcomes, with median earnings of just twenty-two thousand dollars and an unemployment rate of twenty-two percent. In contrast, graduate-level borrowers earn over fifty-five thousand dollars with an unemployment rate of under eight percent.

The final chart details total outstanding borrowers in millions as of 2014 alongside five-year average default rates through 2011 across the same school categories. Two-year colleges represent the largest volume of borrowers at approximately eleven million, paired with a default rate of twenty percent. However, for-profit institutions exhibit the highest default rate at over thirty percent, despite having slightly fewer borrowers. Non-selective four-year schools also show a high default rate of nearly twenty-eight percent. These figures contrast sharply with selective four-year and graduate programs, where default rates drop to roughly eight percent and five percent, respectively. 

Additionally, a footnote emphasizes that graduates from for-profit institutions face further disadvantages, noting they are less likely to be invited for job interviews and tend to experience flatter wage trajectories over their careers.

This holiday edition of Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, titled "War of the Worlds: Life at home in 2019," serves as an introduction to a lighter holiday-themed piece about a typical evening in his household, while also previewing the upcoming 2020 market outlook. Cembalest highlights that 2019 was an excellent year for investors despite widespread recession anxiety, but he warns that the US equity rally was driven entirely by multiple expansion rather than earnings growth, making markets highly vulnerable to new tariffs. Looking ahead, he forecasts lower equity and fixed income returns in 2020, even as the global economy recovers, and asserts that a US recession is unlikely in 2020. The upcoming outlook is set to cover the ongoing trade war, the IPO market, China’s economic slowdown, the outperformance of US equities, negative interest rates in Europe, and potential market risks from a progressive overhaul of the US economy. 

To illustrate the strong market performance of 2019, the page features two bar charts representing year-to-date total returns in US dollars as of December 3, 2019. The first chart displays returns for major equity markets and regions. China onshore and the Nasdaq led global equity performance with outstanding returns of approximately 31% and 30%, respectively. US Large Cap also saw strong gains of about 25%, while Canada & Australia and the World ex-EM indices posted returns of roughly 22%. The All Country World Index rose by about 20%, followed closely by US Small Cap, Japan, the Eurozone, and Europe, which all clustered between 17% and 18%. Emerging markets trailed behind, with broad Emerging Markets yielding 12%, EM commodity exporters at 11%, China offshore at 10%, and EM ex-China manufacturing recording the lowest return at around 7%.

The second chart details year-to-date total returns for major fixed income markets. US Investment Grade corporate bonds was the top-performing sector at 14%. A footnote explains that this high return was propelled by a rally in ten-year Treasuries down to 1.7% alongside credit spreads tightening below 200 basis points—gains the author notes are unlikely to repeat in 2020. Other strong performers included US High Yield and External Emerging Market Debt, both returning approximately 12%. The US Barclays Aggregate and Domestic Emerging Market Debt both yielded around 9%, while US Treasuries Only and the Global Aggregate index returned about 7%. The Global Aggregate ex-US experienced the lowest positive return in this category at roughly 5%.

This appendix page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication analyzes the socio-economic profiles of student loan borrowers across different types of higher education institutions, emphasizing that borrowers at for-profit and two-year colleges face significantly greater financial and demographic disadvantages compared to those at selective four-year universities. 

The first chart shows that the median parental income of borrowers in 2011, measured in real 2014 dollars, rises steadily with school selectivity, starting at approximately $35,000 for for-profit students and increasing to roughly $80,000 for students at selective four-year institutions. Similarly, the second chart indicates that the percentage of borrowers who are dependents rises from about 35% at for-profit institutions to nearly 88% at selective four-year schools, showing that non-selective and for-profit borrowers are much more likely to be independent. 

The third chart demonstrates that local poverty rates of borrowers’ home areas are higher for those attending for-profit and nonselective four-year schools, both near 11%, compared to those at selective four-year schools, which average around 7%. This geographic disadvantage correlates with first-generation student status, depicted in the fourth chart, where first-generation borrowers make up nearly 57% of students at for-profit schools and 52% at two-year colleges, compared to only 25% at selective four-year universities. Additionally, the fifth chart shows that borrowers at for-profit and two-year schools enter college at older ages, with median entry ages of roughly 24.5 and 23 years respectively, while four-year selective college borrowers enter at a median age of around 19.

The final chart examines borrowers' credit scores by institution type in the year prior to entering repayment, using TransUnion data from 1998 to 2005. It reveals a stark divergence: approximately 57% of borrowers at for-profit schools and 47% at public two-year schools have low credit scores under 550, while only 17% and 24% respectively have high credit scores over 660. Conversely, at public and private nonprofit four-year institutions, about half of the borrowers have high credit scores, and only 22% to 24% fall into the low credit score range. Most charts on this page source their data from Adam Looney's 2014 Brookings Institution paper, "A crisis in student loans," while the credit score analysis is sourced from a 2015 study by Mezza and Sommer.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" analyzes the strength of US economic and market tailwinds heading into the 2020 presidential election, comparing them to historical data dating back to 1896. Cembalest argues that Donald Trump, as an incumbent, benefits from the strongest economic tailwinds on record. He suggests that if Trump is not removed from office through impeachment and goes on to lose the 2020 election, it could easily be described as the greatest presidential fumble of economic and market advantages in modern history. 

The primary visual is a column chart titled "2020: the strongest Presidential election tailwinds since 1896." This chart tracks the average percentile score of economic variables, including consumer and producer price inflation, unemployment levels and changes, US per capita GDP compared to other G10 nations, equity market returns and volatility, and home price appreciation, with a higher percentile score indicating more favorable conditions. The y-axis shows the percentile score from 0.00 to 0.80, while the x-axis lists election years from 1896 to 2019. The columns are color-coded to distinguish between years when an incumbent president ran for re-election (blue) and years with no incumbent running (gold). Individual bars are labeled "W" for a win or "L" for a loss. 

The chart highlights that the tailwind score for 2019, leading into the 2020 election, is the highest on record at over 0.75. Historically, with the exception of William Howard Taft in 1912, the only incumbent presidents who lost did so when this tailwind measure was below 0.50, namely Herbert Hoover in 1932, Gerald Ford in 1976, Jimmy Carter in 1980, and George H.W. Bush in 1992. 

In footnotes, Cembalest qualifies these findings by noting it is difficult to isolate how much of these favorable conditions are due to the Trump administration's policies versus cyclical improvements carried over from the Obama administration, easy Federal Reserve policy, and unsustainable fiscal deficits. Additionally, he observes that while House impeachment proceedings are likely intended to influence swing voters, they are highly unlikely to lead to Trump's removal by Senate Republicans and have not significantly altered public opinion.

This page consists entirely of legal disclosures, regulatory information, and jurisdictional disclaimers for the J.P. Morgan publication. It details the distribution and regulatory oversight of various J.P. Morgan entities across multiple global regions, including Europe, Asia, Australia, and Latin America. 

Specifically, the text outlines regulatory compliance and governing bodies for several jurisdictions, including BaFin in Germany, the Bank of Italy and CONSOB in Italy, the ACPR and AMF in France, and FINMA in Switzerland. For Asian markets, it defines the distribution roles and regulatory supervision of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Securities and Futures Commission of Hong Kong, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore. 

In Australia, the disclosure states that materials are intended solely for wholesale clients under the Corporations Act 2001, detailing regulatory exemptions and noting oversight by the Australian Securities and Investment Commission, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, FINRA, and the CFTC. Finally, the page addresses distribution restrictions in Latin America, noting that securities are offered on a private basis and referencing compliance requirements with the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission and Mexican financial platforms.

This page explores the dramatic contrast between state control and individual rights, centering on China’s unprecedented economic rise from 1981 to 2011 and its high societal and environmental costs. The author argues that while China engineered the largest leap in living standards in modern history, it did so by prioritizing the State over the individual, unlike Taiwan and Hong Kong, which achieved significant wealth gains while protecting individual rights.

The first chart, titled "China's economic transformation in context," measures the largest 30-year increase in real per capita GDP by country. China leads the list with an increase of nearly 1,400% between 1981 and 2011. This growth is followed closely by South Korea from 1965 to 1995 at approximately 1,300%, and other notable expansions like Oman, Japan, Greece, and Taiwan, which saw an increase of around 1,000% from 1946 to 1976. The author provides historical context for these growth periods, noting that while rebuilding efforts drove European and Japanese gains after World War II, China's surge followed Deng Xiaoping’s 1981 economic liberalization. In contrast, Venezuela’s earlier oil-driven growth has collapsed, with oil production falling from 3 million barrels per day in 2000 to just 830,000 by 2019.

The second chart, titled "The Rights of the Individual versus the State," evaluates countries on a scale from 40 to 95, where 100 represents the greatest protections of the individual. This index aggregates factors such as judicial independence, due process, press and religious freedoms, and property rights. Northern European nations like Finland and the Netherlands score at the top of the index, above 90, while the United States and Japan sit near 80. The chart highlights the divergence among Chinese-majority societies: Hong Kong and Taiwan score relatively high at approximately 81 and 76, respectively, reflecting strong individual protections. China, however, ranks near the absolute bottom with a score of roughly 45, placing it alongside nations like Haiti, Libya, and Chad. 

The author concludes by noting the environmental consequences of China's state-first model. Although wealthier nations generally enjoy better environmental conditions, China remains a stark outlier. According to Yale’s Environmental Performance Index, China has some of the worst environmental conditions in the world, with only a few poorer nations performing worse when adjusting for gross domestic product.

This page presents an analysis of news coverage from major left-leaning cable programs to explain why different political groups often talk past one another regarding the state of the nation. The author and his team compiled a tally of topics covered between September 2018 and September 2019 using transcripts from CNN and MSNBC. From an investment perspective, the author acknowledges that political governance and the president merit substantial coverage, noting that in J.P. Morgan’s global growth and policy model of 128 variables, the concepts of the rule of law and an uncorrupt government show the highest correlation to a nation’s per capita GDP. However, the author argues that these networks display a stark, almost total omission of positive economic news.

A horizontal stacked bar chart titled "The Medium is the Message: relative reporting of positive economic news on select cable programs" illustrates this media focus by tallying the number of times sixteen different topics were discussed in depth. The data is broken down across four popular shows: CNN's Cuomo Prime Time, CNN's Anderson Cooper 360, MSNBC's Rachel Maddow Show, and MSNBC's Last Word with Lawrence O'Donnell. The chart reveals that the "Mueller investigation / Russian interference" was by far the most discussed topic, totaling over 300 segments. Other highly covered topics include "Trump is inept/erratic/mendacious/biased" at roughly 210 segments, "Asylum and immigration" at nearly 180 segments, "Trump Administration corruption" at approximately 150 segments, and "Presidential politics" at about 140 segments. In stark contrast, "Positive economic news" lies at the very bottom of the chart, receiving almost zero deep discussions across all four shows combined. 

The author lists several examples of the positive economic developments that went virtually unmentioned during this period, including wages rising fastest for lowest-income workers, the highest rate of job vacancies in 20 years, and a sustained pickup in manufacturing dynamism. Additional ignored milestones include consumer confidence exceeding pre-crisis levels, the lowest household debt service to income obligations in 40 years, the lowest overall misery rate since the 1960s, a substantial rebound in prime-age labor force participation, and a return to pre-crisis levels of small business optimism.

The commentary concludes with historical and political reflections. To underscore the importance of resisting foreign interference, the author cites George Washington’s 1796 Farewell Address, noting the irony of Donald Trump reportedly considering a May Day parade invitation in Moscow. A final footnote highlights the shifting political consensus on foreign policy, mocking how Barack Obama and Joe Biden dismissed Mitt Romney’s 2012 assertion that Russia was the greatest geopolitical threat to the United States, only for political attitudes toward Russia to shift dramatically after the 2016 election.

This page presents the publication's annual cover theme, "Ghosts of Christmas Past," which uses historical figures and pop-culture symbols to illustrate economic and political trends heading into 2020. 

First, Franklin D. Roosevelt is portrayed celebrating Elizabeth Warren’s highly progressive policy proposals, recalling FDR's own historical shift of economic power toward Washington and his proposal of a 100 percent income tax. Next, Richard Nixon is shown alongside Donald Trump’s pressure on Fed Chair Jerome Powell, drawing a historical parallel to Nixon’s interference with Fed Chair Arthur Burns that resulted in near-zero real policy rates during a period of full employment. Henry VIII and Margaret Thatcher are paired to represent the momentum behind Brexit, drawing parallels to the 1533 Act in Restraint of Appeals and Thatcher's late-career criticisms of European dominance. The text notes that Boris Johnson’s December victory makes Brexit terms rigid, though EU agreement remains an open question at the end of 2020. 

Further down, Mao Zedong represents China's political shifts under Xi Jinping, who scrapped presidential term limits and invoked Mao's "long march" to signal a long-term strategic conflict with the US over mercantilist trade policies. Herbert Hoover is compared to Donald Trump in terms of high tariffs—which remain at 40-year highs even after the Phase I trade deal—and immigration enforcement, highlighting that Hoover's deportations occurred during a severe depression with 15 percent to 20 percent unemployment while Trump's occur at 3.5 percent unemployment. Charlemagne, as a symbol of European unity, looks on disapprovingly at the current Eurozone, which is weighed down by slow growth, trillions in negative-yielding sovereign debt, and political fragmentation. Finally, the Pets.com Sock Puppet serves as a metaphor for renewed market speculation, noting that unprofitable tech companies have reached their highest share of US market capitalization and spending since the late 1990s dot-com bubble, exemplified by SoftBank’s write-down of its investment in the dog-walking startup Wag, which it had once valued at over $600 million.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Holiday Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, presents a series of appendix charts designed to assess standard measures of economic growth and prosperity. In the introductory text, Cembalest addresses the debate on wealth and income inequality, pointing out that scholarship in this area is more art than science. He notes that researchers at the Joint Committee on Taxation, the US Treasury, and Columbia University have raised significant concerns regarding the widely shared inequality findings of economists Emmanuel Saez, Gabriel Zucman, and Thomas Piketty, which have been described as distorted and improbable. Cembalest highlights that alternative assessments indicate far more modest changes in wealth and income inequality over the last forty years.

Six distinct charts illustrate various positive indicators of US economic health up to late 2019. The first chart, tracking wage growth across all income levels from 1997 to 2019 using a twelve-month moving average of monthly median wage growth from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, shows a broad recovery since the Great Recession. Notably, the lowest income quartile has grown the fastest in the years leading up to 2019, reaching nearly 5% wage growth and outpacing the highest income quartile, which hovered near 3.5%.

The second chart displays the highest rate of job vacancies in twenty years, measured as a percentage of employment on a twelve-month average from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The vacancy rate across all sectors steadily rose from a low of about 2% in 2009 to a peak of 4.5% in 2019. Within the construction sector specifically, vacancies recovered even more dramatically, rising from under 1% in 2010 to approximately 4% in late 2019.

A third chart examines manufacturing job dynamism, illustrating the thousands of new hires, voluntary quits, and layoffs from 2001 to 2019. Although a note highlights that the start of the trade war coincided with a slight drop in manufacturing new hires from over 350,000 to around 300,000, the broader trend shows a sustained post-2009 pickup. Voluntary quits climbed steadily to over 200,000, while layoffs remained exceptionally low, hovering under 100,000.

Consumer confidence is analyzed in the fourth chart, which plots index levels from the Conference Board, the University of Michigan, and the Bloomberg weekly tracker from 2001 to 2019. All three indices reflect strong recoveries from their financial crisis lows; the Conference Board index surged from below 40 in 2009 to nearly 140 by late 2018, while the University of Michigan index neared 100.

The fifth chart illustrates that household debt service-to-income obligations in 2019 reached their lowest levels in forty years. The debt service ratio, which tracks mortgage and consumer debt payments as a percentage of disposable income, dropped below 10% in 2019, down from a peak of nearly 13% in 2007. Similarly, the broader financial obligations ratio, which includes rent, auto, homeowners' insurance, and property tax payments, declined from a peak of about 18% in 2007 to roughly 15% in 2019.

Finally, the sixth chart depicts the lowest misery rates since the 1960s, defined as the inflation rate plus the unemployment rate. From 1960 to late 2019, the misery rate for all groups collapsed to historic lows. The overall rate fell to around 6%, a level not seen since the late 1960s. Crucially, the misery rate for African Americans, which peaked near 28% in 1980 and above 20% in 2011, fell sharply to approximately 10% by late 2019, while the rate for women closely mirrored the overall population average of about 6%.

In this executive summary, the author shares a moderately improved outlook for the global economy, driven by the avoidance of worst-case trade war outcomes. However, the negative impact of recent tariffs is clear: they are estimated to have reduced 2019 S&P 500 earnings growth potential by 7% to 8% and to have dragged global economic growth from its 4.1% peak in early 2018 down to 2.9% by the third quarter of 2019. The commentary highlights that Europe and Japan bore the harshest brunt of the US-China trade war due to their reliance on exports and fragile initial growth trends. While a global GDP recession was avoided, an earnings recession did occur across the US, Europe, and Japan. Although earnings are projected to rebound, the author notes this expectation is already priced into most equity markets. Additionally, a key footnote warns of ongoing uncertainty regarding the enforcement of trade agreements, presenting a risk that trade conflicts could reignite.

Four charts illustrate these trends. The first, detailing regional manufacturing business surveys (PMI) from 2016 through late 2019, uses a threshold of 50 to differentiate contraction from expansion. The data shows Eurozone manufacturing activity peaking near 61 in early 2018 before plummeting into contraction territory, ending near 46 by late 2019. Japan's PMI also slid below 50, while the US experienced a less severe drop, and China remained relatively stable right around the 50 expansion line. 

The second chart displays global and US quarterly corporate earnings growth year-over-year, excluding buybacks, from 2012 to late 2019. It tracks a steep deceleration starting in late 2018; US earnings growth plummeted from over 20% to nearly flat, while global earnings excluding the US dipped into negative territory by late 2019, visually confirming the earnings recession.

The third chart tracks global capital spending growth as a quarter-over-quarter, seasonally adjusted annual rate from 2002 to 2018. It shows capital spending collapsing below negative 5% during the 2008 financial crisis, peaking near 15% during the recovery, and subsequently weakening into a highly volatile, low-growth pattern that sat nearly flat by 2018. 

The final chart shows trade volume growth on a six-month over six-month seasonally adjusted annual rate over the same 2002 to 2018 period. It illustrates a similar post-crisis collapse and recovery, followed by a steady downward trend that highlights trade stagnation, with growth rates dropping close to 0% by the end of the tracked period.

In this executive summary of J.P. Morgan's 2020 Outlook, Michael Cembalest argues that global growth and corporate profits are poised for a modest rebound in 2020, with the notable exception of Japan. This positive outlook is primarily underpinned by a coordinated surge in central bank easing. Emerging market central banks have significant room to maneuver due to historic lows in inflation, which has fallen to between 3.5% and 4.0% compared to 10% in the late 1990s and 6% over the last decade. For 2020, the author forecasts US corporate earnings growth of 5% to 7%, noting that this rate would be higher if not for headwinds in the energy sector and specific operational problems at Boeing. A similar earnings growth rate is projected for Europe, though the performance gap favoring US equities is expected to persist. In stark contrast to the global trend, Japan faces mounting recessionary risks; its economy is projected to shrink by 2.5% in the final quarter of 2019 following a sales tax hike that dragged October retail sales down by 7.1% year-over-year, while the Tankan manufacturing report has hit a six-and-a-half-year low.

To support the thesis of a central bank-led recovery, the page features three charts. The first is a dual-axis chart spanning 1998 through late 2019 that plots the global manufacturing survey against central bank rate cuts.
