This page analyzes the economic fallout of the COVID-19 pandemic on US GDP and corporate earnings, comparing the pessimistic expectations priced into contemporary markets against historical recovery timelines. Michael Cembalest highlights J.P. Morgan economists' forecast of an annualized 14% decline in US GDP for the second quarter of 2020, which would mark the largest quarterly contraction since 1947, surpassing the 10% drop in the first quarter of 1958. This baseline recovery model assumes US lockdown restrictions are gradually lifted in May, followed by a slow rebound, though the author acknowledges that more bearish outcomes are possible alongside upcoming Federal Reserve facilities and fiscal stimulus packages. 

To gauge market expectations, the author presents a line chart titled "US earnings per share level implied by dividend futures" as a percentage of the pre-virus level. This chart compares the optimistic market pricing from January 20, 2020—which anticipated steady earnings growth up to nearly 20% by 2030—with the severely depressed "Pricing today" from mid-March 2020. The updated market pricing implies a staggering 45% earnings decline that bottoms out by the end of 2022, followed by a sluggish recovery that fails to regain the pre-virus peak even by the end of the decade. 

The author argues that such a prolonged recovery would be highly anomalous compared to historical precedents. This point is supported by two historical charts. The first, "S&P 500 earnings drawdowns," plots the maximum peak-to-trough declines of reported and operating earnings from 1870 through 2010, illustrating major economic contractions. The second, "Peak-to-trough-to-peak analysis of large US earnings declines, years," looks at twelve historical earnings drawdowns exceeding 15% from 1876 to 2009. This bar chart breaks down the duration of each cycle into the years from peak to trough and the additional time required to regain the prior peak. The data shows that, apart from the Great Depression triggered in 1932 which took nearly 18 years to recover, post-World War II earnings cycles generally required less than four years—and often less than three—to regain their previous peaks.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest contextualizes the potential long-term economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic by comparing them to historically severe economic declines that required many years for GDP to recover. The author argues that deep, multi-year economic contractions typically stem from either the wartime destruction of physical capital or colossal government mismanagement. He posits that while the COVID-19 pandemic will certainly have an economic impact, its recovery timeframe is likely to be much shorter than these extreme twentieth-century crises. As additional examples of long-term economic recoveries, the text notes that it took Iran 15 years to regain its pre-1978 per capita GDP level following the Iranian Revolution, and it took Peru 13 years to recover its peak GDP during the conflict with the Shining Path movement.

To illustrate the impact of wartime destruction, a line chart shows real per capita GDP in thousands of 1990 dollars for Germany and Japan from 1930 to 1960. Both nations suffered severe economic collapses during World War II and took a full decade to recover to their prewar levels. Germany's per capita GDP peaked near 430 in 1944 before plummeting to a low of approximately 160 by 1946, only returning to its prewar peak around 1955. Similarly, Japan's per capita GDP crashed from roughly 240 in 1944 to a low near 130 in 1945, returning to its prewar peak around 1954. Supporting data highlights that by 1945, Germany lost 20% of its housing stock, saw food production halve compared to 1938 levels, and experienced a drop in daily caloric intake to just 1,250 calories. Japan lost 40% of its capital stock, a quarter of its housing, and sustained destruction across 180 square miles of 67 cities. Germany lost over 8% of its population to the war, while Japan lost 4%.

To illustrate the impact of economic mismanagement, a second chart plots the consequences of China's Great Leap Forward from 1955 to 1964. It maps a sharp decline in average daily caloric intake against a massive spike in the mortality rate. Caloric intake plummeted from about 2,100 calories per day in 1958 to a low of 1,550 in 1960, while the mortality rate surged from a baseline of roughly 11% to over 25% in 1960. The commentary attributes this catastrophic decline to forced collectivization, the abolition of private farming, the rejection of scientific agricultural practices, and industrial quotas that forced villagers to melt down household pots and pans to produce steel. This led to an estimated 30 to 60 million unnatural deaths between 1958 and 1961. Citing research by historian Frank Dikötter, the text highlights that a portion of this immense death toll was intentional under Mao Zediong's regime, driven by executions and torture rather than starvation alone.

This page demonstrates that forward-looking financial markets and asset prices consistently bottom out or peak before the actual real-world damage—such as defaults, bank failures, and delinquencies—fully manifests or begins to improve. This theme is illustrated across eight historical charts categorized into three rows. 

The first row analyzes high-yield credit spreads (spread-to-worst) against the number of cumulative corporate default issuers across three different economic crises. During the Savings and Loan Crisis from 1987 to 1993, credit spreads peaked when cumulative defaults were only at 55 percent of their ultimate total. During the tech collapse from 1999 to 2004, spreads peaked when cumulative defaults were at 76 percent. In the Global Financial Crisis from 2006 to 2013, high-yield spreads peaked when cumulative defaults were only at 30 percent of their ultimate cycle volume, showing how early credit markets anticipate recovery. 

The second row examines the relationship between stock indices and cumulative bank failures. During the Great Depression from 1929 to 1933, the Dow Jones Industrial Average bottomed out in mid-1932, when cumulative bank failures had only reached 48 percent of their cycle total. During the Savings and Loan Crisis from 1988 to 1994, the S&P 500 Bank Index bottomed out in late 1990 when cumulative bank failures were at 63 percent. In the Global Financial Crisis from 2008 to 2014, the S&P 500 Bank Index bottomed out in early 2009, notably marked near a highlighted red dot labeled SCA, when cumulative bank failures were at just 8 percent of the total crisis count.

The third row contrasts loan and commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) pricing and spreads against lagging default and delinquency rates. One chart compares the Leveraged Loan Price Index to the default rate over trailing 12 months from 2006 to 2011. The price index hit its bottom in late 2008, while trailing default rates did not peak until late 2009. The final chart displays AAA CMBS Spreads in basis points versus the 60-plus day delinquency rate from 2006 to 2014. Spreads peaked dramatically in late 2008 at over 1,400 basis points, whereas the 60-plus day delinquency rate did not top out until late 2012, peaking around 9 percent. These charts, using data sourced from J.P. Morgan Securities, FDIC, Bloomberg, Standard and Poor's, S&P/LSTA, and Trepp, collectively underscore the pattern of markets correcting and recovering well ahead of real-economy indicators.

Michael Cembalest discusses the resilience of economies during severe crises, arguing that economic rebounds can occur much faster than their preceding declines, even in the wake of catastrophic events like wars or pandemics. To illustrate this point, he references the US Civil War, highlighting that despite being the deadliest conflict in US history with six times the war dead as a percentage of the population compared to World War II and leaving the South in ruins with minimal federal assistance, agricultural recovery was remarkably swift. An accompanying line chart titled Post Civil War recovery in Confederate farm income, with an index base of 100 in 1859, shows that after farm income fell to its lowest point of approximately 85 around 1866, it rebounded dramatically. By 1869, the index surged back up past 104, demonstrating a rapid recovery that eventually reached approximately 106 by 1880. The chart sources data from Jack Hirshleifer's 1987 publication, Economic Behaviour in Adversity.

Cembalest connects this historical resilience to the COVID-19 pandemic. While acknowledging that the economic situation is likely to worsen in the near term, he predicts that the world will feel seventy to eighty percent back to normal within a year. His optimism is grounded in modern advancements, including twenty-first-century medical achievements, artificial intelligence, big data application in drug development, and the inherent adaptability of modern economies to severe demand and supply shocks. 

For investors, Cembalest advises that financial markets historically bottom out before crisis indicators, such as defaults or bank failures, actually show improvement, meaning markets can recover even as real-world indicators are still worsening. Therefore, investors should focus on monitoring the rate of COVID-19 infections and mortalities. A concluding footnote references a 2007 study by Hideki Toya and Mark Skidmore on the impacts of natural disasters, noting that countries with higher income, education, openness, robust financial systems, developed supply chains, and decentralized governments tend to experience fewer long-run losses during such systemic shocks.

This page evaluates the Federal Reserve's capacity to mitigate the credit and liquidity crunch in late March 2020 through a suite of newly launched credit facilities, including loans, asset purchases, and relaxed banking accounting standards. The author argues that credit spread increases are significantly smaller than those observed during the 2008 global financial crisis, reflecting a much healthier, better-capitalized banking sector. 

To support this argument, the page presents six charts tracing historical spreads from the mid-2000s through late March 2020, with current levels indicated by red dots. The first chart, tracking the spread between the 3-month LIBOR and the 3-month forward Fed Funds rate, shows a peak of over 350 basis points in 2008, compared to a current level of approximately 140 basis points. The second chart shows the US TED spread (3-month LIBOR minus the 3-month Treasury), which reached over 450 basis points in 2008 and is currently situated around 150 basis points. 

The third chart displays US commercial paper spreads over 3-month Treasuries for both financial and asset-backed commercial paper. In March 2020, financial commercial paper spreads spiked to about 260 basis points, while asset-backed commercial paper rose to around 200 basis points, representing elevated levels that are still below their historical extremes. The fourth chart illustrates AAA asset-backed securities spreads versus Treasuries for prime auto, credit cards, and commercial real estate from 1998 to 2020. During the 2008 financial crisis, prime auto spreads breached 600 basis points, whereas the current 2020 spikes for all three asset classes remain much lower, grouped between 100 and 200 basis points. 

The fifth chart plots US investment-grade corporate bond spreads using the JULI index versus Treasuries from 2000 to 2020. This spread peaked above 550 basis points in 2008, compared to a current level of roughly 310 basis points. The sixth and final chart displays the JULI index spread difference between financial and non-financial investment-grade bonds (banks versus non-banks) from 2005 to 2020. While this spread difference skyrocketed to over 300 basis points in 2008 due to intense banking sector distress, the current level is near zero. This final chart highlights that, unlike in 2008, bank debt spreads have barely widened relative to non-bank investment-grade corporate issuers, signaling stronger bank fundamentals.

This page of the publication, titled Man vs Nature: what the government can fix and what it can’t, explores the limitations of government intervention during a pandemic. The author distinguishes between issues the government can try to address, such as credit availability and income loss, and those it cannot control, like economic activity during a lockdown or the speed of medical advancements. To understand the early impacts, the report tracks high-frequency US manufacturing and consumer data alongside the historic surge in jobless claims. 

The first chart displays US jobless claims as a percentage of the active working population from 1970 through March 2020. The historical data shows that previous peaks in claims, such as those in the mid-1970s, early 1980s, and during the 2008 financial crisis, generally hovered between 0.4 percent and 0.6 percent. In stark contrast, March 2020 shows an unprecedented, nearly vertical spike that exceeds 2.0 percent. An accompanying commentary notes that a virus-led spike in jobless claims differs from a traditional demand-led recession because workers may quickly return to their jobs once lockdown measures are lifted. Additionally, provisions in the two trillion dollar fiscal stimulus bill incentivize companies to rehire workers by converting government loans into grants.

The page also features two dual-axis charts tracking economic activity alongside daily COVID-19 infections in thousands, which rose rapidly from zero in early March to nearly twenty thousand by March 25, 2020. The first of these charts, a US manufacturing tracker, plots the rolling four-week year-over-year percentage change for key industrial indicators, including lumber, steel, and coal production, electricity output, and railroad traffic. This index, measured on the left axis from negative three percent to negative eight percent, peaked at roughly negative three and a half percent in early February before plummeting to nearly negative eight percent by late March as daily infections surged. 

The second dual-axis chart, a US consumer tracker, highlights a stark divergence in retail behavior as daily infections climbed. Weekly year-over-year sales for discount stores, measured on a left axis spanning negative ten percent to positive twenty percent, spiked from around eight percent in late February to nearly twenty percent in mid-March, reflecting pandemic-driven stockpiling. Conversely, department store sales plummeted over the same period, dropping from zero percent growth to nearly negative ten percent by late March. This tracker utilizes data from Redbook Research and Johns Hopkins University to show how consumer behavior shifted rapidly in response to the public health crisis.

This J.P. Morgan appendix, authored by Michael Cembalest, outlines the global landscape of vaccine and antiviral development in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The author emphasizes that while the ultimate success of these treatments remains uncertain, the compilation illustrates the vast scale of global research underway. Countermeasures are broadly categorized into vaccines, immunomodulators, and direct viral inhibitors, the latter of which includes antivirals, antiretrovirals, prophylactic polypeptides, nanoviricides, cell therapies, and antibody-based therapies. The data in the table is current as of March 5, 2020.

Several therapies are already launched for other conditions and are being repurposed. Favipiravir, an antiviral by Fujifilm, Medivector, and Zhejiang Hisun Pharmaceutical originally approved for influenza and Ebola, entered clinical trials in China in February 2020. Bayer’s chloroquine phosphate, an immunomodulator approved for malaria, has shown signs of efficacy against COVID-19 related pneumonia in China. Genentech and Roche's immunomodulator Actemra was cleared by Chinese authorities for use in COVID-19 patients with serious lung damage. Rintatolimod, developed by Aim Immunotech, GP Pharm SA, and Goethe University for chronic fatigue syndrome, entered discovery for coronavirus.

In advanced clinical trials, ASC-09 combined with ritonavir by Ascletis Pharma was in Phase III trials in China, while Gilead's antiviral Remdesivir, originally developed for Ebola and Nipah virus, was also in Phase III trials. Regeneron and Sanofi's immunomodulator Kevzara entered Phase II/III trials in the United States. In Phase II, Beijing Defengrei's antibody BDB-1 received trial approval in China, and Innovation Pharmaceuticals was evaluating its antibody Brilacidin.

In the preclinical phase, various entities are developing vaccines and alternative treatments. Inovio, Beijing Advaccine Biotech, and GeneOne Life Science were preparing INO-4800, a DNA vaccine with plans for Phase I trials in the United States and China. Sorrento Therapeutics and Celularity were in discussions for fast-tracking CYNK-001 cell therapy in China. Other vaccine candidates in animal testing or preparing for clinical trials include projects by Chongqing Zhifei Biological, Novavax, Jenner Institute, and Wuhan Hamilton Biotechnology. Sichuan Kelun Pharmaceutical’s prophylactic polypeptide S-protein/ACE2 showed promising safety in primate studies.

Finally, a wide array of treatments are in the discovery phase. This includes vaccine candidates such as Moderna’s mRNA-1273 in collaboration with the National Institutes of Health, Curevac’s mRNA vaccine, Codagenix and the Serum Institute of India’s live-attenuated vaccine, Clover Biopharmaceuticals' recombinant vaccine utilizing GlaxoSmithKline's adjuvant, and Sanofi Pasteur's protein subunit vaccine. Antibody and other therapeutic programs in discovery include efforts by Regeneron, Vir Biotechnology in collaboration with Wuxi Biologics, Nanoviricides, and Immunoprecise Antibodies using the OmniAb platform.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest explores the historical relationship between stock market bottoms and peak unemployment rates, raising the question of whether the March 23 S&P 500 closing low of 2,237 will mark the bottom of the contemporary cycle. He argues that, historically, equity markets in the United States and Europe bottom well before unemployment levels begin to decline, noting that the tech collapse of the early 2000s was the only major exception where the market bottom and peak unemployment closely coincided. 

To support this thesis, the page presents six charts comparing equity market levels against unemployment rates during past economic crises. The first chart, focusing on the 1970s stagflation crisis, illustrates that the S&P 500 bottomed in late 1974 at around an index level of 70, just as the US unemployment rate was starting to rise toward its mid-1975 peak of 9.0%. The second chart, covering the 1980s inflation and housing crisis, shows the S&P 500 bottoming in mid-1982 at around 110, while the unemployment rate continued to rise, eventually peaking at nearly 11% in late 1982. The third chart shows the exception of the early 2000s tech collapse, where the S&P 500's bottom at around 800 in late 2002 and early 2003 closely aligned with a peak in the US unemployment rate at roughly 6.3%. The fourth chart, covering the 2008 global financial crisis, shows the S&P 500 bottoming in early 2009 at around 700, whereas the US unemployment rate continued its upward trajectory to peak at 10% in late 2009.

The analysis is further reinforced by international data. A fifth chart examining the United Kingdom in the 1970s demonstrates that the UK equity market bottomed in late 1974 at an index level near 60, while the UK unemployment rate was still under 2% and did not reach its peak of over 4% until late 1977. The final chart details European equities and Eurozone unemployment during the aftermath of the global financial crisis. It shows the STOXX European Broad equity index reaching its low point near 230 in late 2011, while the Eurozone unemployment rate continued to climb, ultimately peaking at over 12% in mid-2013. Together, these historical data points suggest that forward-looking stock markets routinely price in economic recoveries and rebound well ahead of improvements in the labor market.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market illustrates the severe financial market disruptions across various credit, mortgage, and emerging debt markets during the onset of the COVID-19 crisis in late March 2020, alongside a summary of Federal Reserve emergency lending facilities. Five charts plot historical spreads and asset prices to contextualize the scale of the shock compared to previous crises. 

The first chart shows that the spread between 30-year fixed-rate mortgages and 10-year Treasuries spiked sharply to approximately 320 basis points by late March 2020, matching the peak level seen during the 2008 financial crisis. Next, a chart tracking US high-yield corporate bond spreads shows they surged to around 1,000 basis points overall, while high-yield energy spreads skyrocketed to roughly 2,200 basis points—surpassing the overall peak of the 2008 financial crisis. 

For fixed-rate preferred securities, the option-adjusted spread rose to about 350 basis points, representing a notable spike though remaining far below the extreme peak of over 1,600 basis points in late 2008. Similarly, emerging markets dollar-denominated bond spreads versus US Treasuries jumped to approximately 600 basis points, reflecting heightened sovereign risk but stopping short of the 2002 and 2008 peaks of 950 and 850 basis points, respectively. In the leveraged loan market, the S&P 500 leveraged loan price index collapsed from near 97 down to approximately 82, indicating severe distress, though not quite reaching the nadir of 60 seen in late 2008.

To counter these widespread market strains, the page lists several Federal Reserve liquidity and purchase facilities deployed at the time. These emergency interventions include money market lending, purchases of US Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities, municipal and corporate commercial paper funding facilities, the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility, primary and secondary corporate credit funding facilities, and lending to the Exchange Stabilization Fund via the Main Street lending fund.

This page focuses on the chloroquine controversy during the early phase of the COVID-19 pandemic, examining the historical difficulties and rigorous requirements of antiviral drug development. Michael Cembalest argues that establishing the safety and efficacy of antiviral medications requires a lengthy, complex process of randomized trials and control groups. He warns that drawing concrete conclusions about COVID-19 treatments based on small, non-randomized studies of twenty or thirty people is premature. Highlighting the low historical success rate of drug candidates, he notes that of the thousands of antiviral inhibitors proposed in scientific literature between 1963 and 2016, only 90 were eventually approved. He cites the search for Ebola treatments as a cautionary example, where multiple tested therapies—such as chloroquine, favipiravir, brincidofovir, monoclonal antibodies, antisense RNA, and convalescent plasma—failed to prove safe or effective in randomized clinical trials.

The page features a line chart titled "History of antiviral drug development," which plots the cumulative number of approved drugs from 1960 to 2015 for nine different viral conditions. The chart demonstrates that drug discovery is highly uneven across diseases, with the vast majority of successes concentrated in HIV research. The curve for the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) begins a steep ascent in the late 1980s, culminating in 40 approved drugs by 2015. Hepatitis C (HCV) represents the next most successful category, climbing sharply after 2010 to reach 18 approved drugs by 2015. Other tracked diseases have seen far fewer successful treatments over the fifty-year period: Herpes simplex (HSV) reached approximately 11 approved drugs; Influenza and Hepatitis B (HBV) each reached about 8; Chickenpox (VZV) reached 5; and Human herpesvirus 5 (HCMV), RSV, and HPV all remained under 5 approved drugs. The chart's data is sourced from a June 2016 paper by De Clercq and Li in Clinical Microbiology Reviews.

This page addresses the scientific uncertainties and caution surrounding potential COVID-19 treatments in the early months of the pandemic, emphasizing the critical need for rigorous, randomized clinical trials over small, uncontrolled studies. The commentary highlights a paper from the Annals of Internal Medicine by Alfred Kim of the Washington University School of Medicine and Jeffrey Sparks of Harvard Medical School. They strongly discourage the off-label use of hydroxychloroquine as a prophylactic, warning that there is insufficient data to support it and that resulting shortages pose a real risk to patients with rheumatic diseases who rely on the drug for survival. 

The author also examines other pharmaceutical candidates, pointing out that a Lopinavir-Ritonavir trial of 199 patients in Wuhan showed no statistically meaningful difference in 28-day mortality rates, which were 19.2 percent for the treatment group and 25 percent for the placebo group. Meanwhile, an immunomodulator called tocilizumab, marketed under the brand name Actemra, showed positive early results in a small 20-patient study in China, prompting Genentech to expand it into a Phase III trial. 

Ultimately, the author argues that the medical community must stop relying on single-group studies of 20 to 50 patients without concurrent controls, as they cannot provide definitive answers on safety or efficacy. Instead, randomized clinical trials are presented as the only viable path forward. To support this, a quote from Andre Kalil of the University of Nebraska Medical Center praises the unprecedented speed with which randomized trials, such as the adaptive trial sponsored by the National Institutes of Health, have been initiated globally despite the ongoing pandemic. The page concludes with a list of scientific sources from February and March 2020 covering early clinical trials of remdesivir, chloroquine, and hydroxychloroquine.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication, detailing distribution compliance, licensing, and regulatory oversight across various jurisdictions including Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and countries in Latin America such as Brazil and Mexico.

This page from Michael Cembalest's publication analyzes the controversy surrounding early potential COVID-19 antiviral treatments, specifically Gilead's Remdesivir and Bayer AG's Chloroquine (including hydroxychloroquine). The author warns that initial positive findings were based on cell cultures in vitro rather than live trials, cautioning that many drugs that previously showed in vitro promise ultimately failed in clinical trials. 

To support this, the first chart on the top left, titled "Remdesivir (solid) and Chloroquine (dotted) test results" from the Wuhan Institute of Virology, plots the percentage of COVID-19 virus inhibition and cytotoxicity against dosage in micromoles on a logarithmic scale from 0.1 to 100. It demonstrates that both Remdesivir and Chloroquine successfully inhibited nearly 100% of the virus at higher dosages while maintaining very low cytotoxicity, or cell damage, close to 0%. 

The second chart, on the top right, illustrates the "Treatment results of patients with COVID-19" based on a highly-publicized French study by Gautret et al. It shows the percentage of patients testing positive over six days for three groups: a control group, which remains around 80% to 90% positive; a hydroxychloroquine-only group, which drops to about 50%; and a combination of hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin, which drops to 0% by day five. The author highlights that this chart went viral online but has since been discredited due to significant methodological flaws. These flaws include its non-randomized design with only 36 patients, the exclusion of six patients without discussion (some of whom died or required ventilation), unequal baseline viral loads, the imputation of over one-third of the control group's test results, and sourcing the treatment group from only a single medical center. 

To further muddy the outlook for Chloroquine, a third chart at the bottom presents the "Results of small 30-patient study using hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19" from the Shanghai Public Health Clinical Center. This bar chart compares a treatment group and a control group across three metrics: testing negative for COVID-19 nucleic acid on day seven, abnormal liver function, and radiological progression. The data shows no real benefit for the treatment group, as approximately 85% of the treatment group tested negative on day seven compared to about 90% of the control group. Furthermore, the treatment group suffered from higher rates of abnormal liver function, at nearly 30% versus 20% for the control group, though they did see slightly lower radiological progression at around 35% compared to 45% for the control group.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues that forecasting COVID-19 infection curves using mathematical models is highly unreliable because the parameters are often manually curve-fitted and fail to translate across different national contexts. He highlights the classic Kermack and McKendrick SIR (susceptible, infected, and removed) epidemic model, which relies on three primary inputs: infectiousness (beta), removal rates (gamma), and the exposed population ratio (Nper). Predicting cases is further complicated by large numbers of asymptomatic or unreported infections that models struggle to reconcile. 

To demonstrate the fragility of these models, the page features two comparative charts showing active infections in thousands over 100 days, utilizing data from Johns Hopkins and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The first chart, titled "A good fit for Korea in mid-February," shows how the model aligns almost perfectly with actual South Korean data using parameters of Beta 3.5, Gamma 1.74, and Nper 0.10 percent, with active infections peaking at approximately 8,000 cases near day 45. However, the second chart, titled "Korea parameters: a really, really bad fit for Italy," reveals the danger of using these exact same calibrated parameters to forecast Italy's outbreak. While the Italian model estimates a peak of only 9,000 active infections, actual infections in Italy surged exponentially, passing 62,000 cases by day 60. 

Cembalest explains that this massive estimation failure stems from the vastly different policy measures and behavioral dynamics between South Korea and Italy. The page concludes with a lighthearted footnote noting that the author’s son, Max, assisted with the python-based computational modeling for this section, prompting a humorous exchange regarding the extinction of Excel's Visual Basic (VBA) programming.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" discusses the limitations and "tail-chasing" nature of COVID-19 epidemiological forecasting models, focusing on the difficulty of calibrating these models to fit real-world data from Italy. Michael Cembalest argues that adjusting parameters to fit one country's data requires extreme, retroactive modifications—such as increasing a parameter tenfold—and yields results that are virtually useless for other countries. Furthermore, he demonstrates that multiple distinct sets of assumptions can fit historical data equally well while predicting wildly different future outcomes, making it impossible to know which curve is correct in real-time.

Two line charts illustrate this dilemma. The first chart, titled "The model, recalibrated for Italy: 10x higher infected population," plots active infections in thousands over a 200-day period. It shows actual historical data from Johns Hopkins showing cases rising to about 60,000 by day 60, mapped against an estimated projection curve. Using parameters of Beta (β) 3.6, Gamma (ϒ) 1.74, and Nper 1.0%, the model fits the historical data and projects a peak of 100,000 active infections around day 75 before declining. The second chart, titled "Which set of assumptions best predicts Italy? Still totally unclear," shows the same actual historical data plotted against three different projection curves. While all three curves fit the historical data up to day 60, they diverge significantly: one projection (3.8 β, 1.74 ϒ, 0.7% Nper) peaks near 90,000 cases; the middle projection peaks at 100,000 cases; and a more severe projection (2.7 β, 1.74 ϒ, 3% Nper) peaks much later, reaching approximately 160,000 cases around day 90. 

The author concludes that because infection prediction models require constant updates to fit observed data, what is learned from one country has almost no value in predicting the virus's evolution in another. Within any single country, predictions shift wildly based on testing levels and policy changes. Cembalest asserts that these models are most accurate only when infections have already peaked, at which point they become redundant. A footnote highlights that complex SIR models are not even necessary for fitting these trends, noting that the J.P. Morgan team replicated the South Korean infection curve with similar precision using a simple modified formula: $y = \exp(-x^2)$.

This page provides an overview of convalescent plasma as a potential treatment for COVID-19, noting that Houston Methodist Hospital was the first to receive FDA approval to use this approach. The process involves collecting serum from recovered patients containing virus-neutralizing antibodies and infusing it into active COVID-19 cases, a technique originating in the Victorian era and currently used against measles and mumps. The author points out that convalescent plasma requires clinical trials to prove efficacy, offers only temporary protection of a few weeks due to a thirty-day antibody half-life, and faces scalability and virus-transmission risks. Despite these drawbacks, it could serve as a critical tool for high-risk patients. Supporting background information from researcher Arturo Casadevall of the Johns Hopkins School of Public Health highlights past use cases, including a SARS study of eighty patients in Hong Kong where early treatment improved hospital discharge times, and the 2009 to 2010 H1N1 influenza pandemic where plasma therapy reduced viral load and mortality. Potential risks include serum sickness and accidental infection, which can be mitigated in principle through screening and donor blood-type matching.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest analyzes global COVID-19 infection data, advising investors not to over-extrapolate temporary trends or rely on simplistic classifications of countries as either accelerating or decelerating. He emphasizes that flattening the curve often results in a prolonged period of constant, high-level infection rates that continue to strain healthcare systems, rather than a rapid resolution. To illustrate this, the page categorizes various nations and territories into three distinct stages of the pandemic's progression using three charts, each plotting new daily infections per million people on a linear scale with a three-day trailing average against the number of days after total reported cases reached one hundred.

The first group, shown in the top-left chart, features regions that maintained minimal exposure early on, including Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, and Taiwan. While daily infections in these areas mostly remained extremely low, below four per million, Singapore experienced a minor late-stage uptick, rising to nearly fifteen infections per million around day thirty-eight. 

The second group, shown in the top-right chart, covers countries where infection rates peaked higher but have since convincingly rolled over, including Austria, Australia, and South Korea. Austria's infection rate peaked sharply near ninety per million around day twenty before falling to approximately thirty-five by day twenty-seven, while Australia and South Korea peaked much lower, between ten and fifteen per million, and successfully flattened their curves at low levels.

The third group, shown in the bottom chart, represents countries that have flattened their curves but at extremely high, stressful levels where the risk of reacceleration remains. This group includes Spain, Switzerland, and Italy. To accommodate their higher numbers, this chart uses a y-axis extending to two hundred infections per million. The data shows Spain peaking near one hundred eighty infections per million around day twenty-six before declining to roughly one hundred forty, Switzerland peaking near one hundred twenty and dropping to eighty, and Italy steadily rising to flatten out between eighty and ninety infections per million. 

Ultimately, the author uses these variations across different scales to caution against drawing broad, uniform conclusions about the trajectory of the virus and its immediate market implications. All charts utilize data compiled from Johns Hopkins University, the International Monetary Fund, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page examines the trajectory of COVID-19 infections across various US states and globally, offering the observation that most major US states, representing 70% of US GDP, are tracking on a lower infection curve than New York and New Jersey. The author notes that real-world infection curves are highly idiosyncratic and do not follow neat, exponential decay models found in scientific literature. For instance, while Italy has flattened its curve, it has struggled with a prolonged high rate of new daily infections. Globally, the pace of new cases continues to climb. While the author expects a sharp drop in new infections across the Developed World during April 2020, he stresses that this forecast must be proven by actual data.

These observations are supported by two charts. The first chart plots US new daily infections per one million people using a linear scale, three-day trailing average, aligned by the number of days after each state reached 100 total cases. It reveals that New York and New Jersey are extreme outliers; New Jersey's daily infections rise to around 450 per million by day 22, and New York's climb past 500 per million by day 28. In contrast, states like Massachusetts and Michigan peak or level off near 200 per million, while other major states like California, Texas, Washington, and Florida remain clustered below 100 infections per million.

The second chart tracks daily infections per million people globally, comparing China to the rest of the world over a 70-day period starting from when total cases hit 100. China's infection rate peaked early around day 23 at approximately 5 infections per million before dropping back to near zero. Conversely, the line representing the world excluding China shows a continuous upward trajectory, reaching nearly 14 infections per million people by day 67, highlighting that the global spread had not yet peaked.

This page of the publication analyzes the volatility of early COVID-19 infection trends and explores the divergence in infection rates between developed and emerging market nations. Michael Cembalest argues that simple trend-following models fail when initial downward trajectories turn out to be temporary "head-fakes" before infections rise again. 

This behavior is illustrated in two top charts tracking new daily infections per one million people on a linear scale with a three-day trailing average, plotted against the number of days after total cases reached 100. The top-left chart highlights France, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Germany, where temporary dips in daily cases—such as those seen in Germany and Belgium around day 25—ultimately reversed, with France's infection rate spiking sharply to approximately 180 per million by day 35. The top-right chart shows countries like the United States, Ireland, Great Britain, and Canada, where infections were either accelerating or displaying minor declines too early to project. For example, the United States climbed steadily to about 90 cases per million around day 32.

The analysis then transitions to the surprisingly low infection rates observed in emerging markets. Cembalest notes that by day 20 of their respective outbreaks, reported daily infection rates per million in these nations ranged from below 1 to 5. For comparison, day-20 figures were far higher in Western countries, reaching 73 in Spain, 40 in Italy, 36 in Germany, 25 in France, 22 in the US, and 17 in the UK. The bottom-left chart tracks these low rates for Brazil, the Philippines, Thailand, Pakistan, Indonesia, and India, where daily cases per million remained under 6, with Brazil peaking highest at around 5.5 cases by day 21. 

While acknowledging that poor data reliability or being early in the infection cycle could explain these low numbers, the author poses the open question of whether environmental and weather factors play a role. To support this hypothesis, he notes that 95% of reported infections have occurred between the latitudinal coordinates of 22.5°N and 57.5°N, where 59% of the world's population resides. Furthermore, 90% of infections from January to March took place in regions with temperatures between -5°C and 15°C and humidity levels of 0 to 8 grams per kilogram. This geographic concentration is visualized in the bottom-right chart, which plots infections and world population as a function of latitude. The chart reveals a dramatic divergence, with the percentage of global infections peaking near 17% around 40°N latitude, vastly exceeding the percentage of the world's population residing in that same narrow latitudinal band.

This J.P. Morgan report page analyzes how the COVID-19 lockdown in the United States compares to the Chinese version, examining both infection rates and high-frequency economic activity indicators. The author points out that even when adjusting for potential Chinese under-reporting, the gap in infection rates is substantial. This is illustrated in the first chart, which tracks total infections per one million people on a linear scale starting from the day total reported cases reached 100. Over a 35-day period, the US infection rate surges dramatically to over 1,000 cases per million, while China’s rate remains flat near the bottom of the axis, well under 100 per million.

To compare the economic suppression caused by each country's lockdown, the page presents energy-related data, noting that the Chinese lockdown was far more severe. A line chart titled "US electricity production vs Chinese coal consumption" shows both series as a percent of their 2019 levels from January 1 to March 31. While US electricity production remained steady between roughly 90% and 100% of the previous year's levels, China’s daily coal consumption plummeted to nearly 60% in late February before starting a gradual recovery. The text notes that US coal production is undergoing a secular shift to natural gas and renewables, whereas China expanded its coal capacity by 43 gigawatts from early 2018 to mid-2019, with another 121 gigawatts under construction.

Finally, a bar chart displays the regional changes in US electricity demand for the week ending March 25. This visual highlights that demand declines are modest outside of major hotspots. New York saw the deepest drop at around -7%, followed by small declines of 1% to 4% in regions like the Southeast, New England, California, the Northwest, PJM, SPP, and the Southwest. Meanwhile, electricity demand in MISO, Florida, and Ercot actually increased, with Ercot rising by about 4%. The page concludes with a footnote highlighting that US car sales dropped 35% in March 2020 compared to a massive 90% drop in China during February, serving as another indication of China's more extreme lockdown measures.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication argues that debating whether an economic recovery will be "U-shaped" or "V-shaped" is less important for investors than understanding that equity markets historically lead economic recoveries. The author, Michael Cembalest, emphasizes that equities typically reach their trough four to eight months before economic data bottoms out. Consequently, he suggests that a good time to search for value in equities is when the economic data starts showing signs of forming a bottom, specifically when the rate of decline begins to moderate.

To support this claim, the page presents four charts comparing the performance of the S&P 500 Index to US Real GDP across various historical downturns, drawing on data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis and Robert Shiller. In each chart, the S&P 500 index level is plotted against the left axis, and the US GDP, indexed to 2012, is plotted against the right axis.

The first chart examines the Eisenhower recession from May 1957 to December 1958. It shows the S&P 500 bottoming near an index level of 41 in late 1957, well ahead of the GDP bottoming at an index level of 18.0 in early 1958. 

The second chart covers the stagflation era from June 1973 to December 1976. During this period, the S&P 500 bottomed in late 1974 at around 65, leading the GDP trough which occurred in early 1975 at approximately 34.7. 

The third chart illustrates the 1980s double-dip recession from October 1980 to October 1983. In this scenario, the S&P 500 reached its low point around mid-1982 at an index level of roughly 105, which preceded the GDP trough of 42.1 in late 1982. 

The fourth chart displays the global financial crisis from May 2007 to May 2013. The chart highlights that the S&P 500 reached its lowest point in early 2009 at approximately 700 before beginning a strong upward trajectory, while the broader US economy did not see its GDP bottom out until mid-2009 at an index level of roughly 94. Across all four historical examples, the visual evidence demonstrates that equity markets consistently anticipate and lead the turnaround in economic growth.

This commentary discusses the significant uncertainties, limitations, and regulatory caveats surrounding COVID-19 serology testing while emphasizing its critical role in formulating "back to work" plans. The author highlights several sources of uncertainty in epidemiological models, including sensitivity to outbreak timing, potential false positives, non-representative sample populations, and individuals who recover without developing high levels of antibodies. A referenced study by Fudan University found that one-third of a 175-person recovered cohort had low antibody levels, suggesting their immune response relied on T-cells or cytokines, which leaves their long-term susceptibility unresolved.

Despite these caveats, the analysis notes that several countries are rapidly adopting serology tests. The United Kingdom has ordered 3.5 million tests, Germany is considering them for immunity certificates, and Singapore and China are utilizing them to determine more accurate infection rates. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration has allowed doctors to identify recovered patients to harvest antibodies for emergency treatments, and more than 50 private companies have registered intent to sell testing kits. Because these commercial kits are self-validated, the Food and Drug Administration mandates strict disclosures: the tests are not officially reviewed, negative results do not rule out infection, antibody tests cannot be the sole diagnostic basis, and positive results may cross-react with other non-SARS-CoV-2 coronaviruses. The author concludes that while these warnings are severe, nations focused on economic reopening are increasingly treating them as acceptable risks to facilitate a return to work by summer or fall.

This page analyzes how countries can transition back to normalcy after the initial COVID-19 infection wave subsides, highlighting early experiences in Asia and forthcoming decisions in Europe. To illustrate the differing scales of first-wave infection rates, two charts show new daily infections per one million people on a linear scale with a three-day trailing average, plotted by the number of days after total reported cases reached one hundred. 

The first chart covers East Asian nations and Australia, demonstrating relatively low overall peaks on a vertical axis capped at eighteen. In this group, South Korea peaked at roughly thirteen infections per million around day eleven, China peaked near twelve at day ten, and Australia reached its peak of approximately fourteen on day twenty-five before all three declined significantly. Hong Kong and Japan remained lower, though Japan showed a late, gradual tick upward to about four infections per million by day fifty. 

In contrast, the second chart uses a much larger vertical scale, up to one hundred twenty, to track Singapore, Austria, and Norway. Here, Austria peaked near ninety cases per million around day twenty, while Norway saw its highest peak near sixty around day twenty-five before both began declining toward twenty cases per million. Singapore remained low for the first thirty-five days but then experienced a worrisome, sharp upward spike, climbing toward forty daily infections per million by day forty-two.

The author outlines three main pathways for countries following the first wave, assuming travel restrictions remain in place to prevent importing new cases. The first approach is to keep flattening the curve and slowly return people to work as infections decline. However, the author warns that without a robust tracking system, a tiny number of active cases could easily reignite a second wave, which could be further complicated by seasonal changes or a fall resurgence. 

The second, and predicted most likely, scenario is to relax lockdowns and employ a targeted swat-team approach. This strategy relies on rapid contact tracing and the immediate quarantine of new clusters using tracking tools like credit card receipts, GPS, cell phones, and closed-circuit television. This method requires a highly organized healthcare system, a compliant population, and low enough daily infection rates to handle incoming cases. 

The final approach is serological testing to identify immune individuals with antibodies and allow them back to work, though its chief challenge is the necessity of herd immunity for maximum effectiveness.

This page of the report explores how cultural differences, specifically the societal dimension of collectivism versus individualism, correlate with the spread and containment of COVID-19. The discussion begins with a first-hand account of returning to Hong Kong, detailing the region's highly structured quarantine procedures, which include GPS phone tracking, mandatory electronic wristbands, immediate saliva testing, and randomized compliance phone calls. The author notes that developed Asian countries and China have successfully controlled the virus through these invasive methods, which also leverage credit card receipt tracking, close-circuit television monitoring, strict infectious disease laws, and machine learning-driven smartphone virus passports.

To illustrate how these policy choices reflect cultural norms, the page features a scatter plot titled "COVID-19 infections rates vs a measure of societal collectivism / individualism," which plots total infections per million people against the Hofstede dimension index of collectivism versus individualism. Based on data from Johns Hopkins University and the IMF as of April 17, 2020, a standard cluster analysis reveals an 82% cluster significance coefficient, separating the countries into two distinct groups represented by cluster centroids. 

The first cluster, representing more collectivist societies on the left, consists of countries such as China, Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, and Taiwan. These nations implemented rigorous tracking and quarantine protocols and kept infection rates extremely low, generally well under 500 cases per million. The second cluster, representing more individualist societies on the right, displays significantly higher infection rates. Notable data points in this group include Spain, which peaks near 4,000 infections per million; Switzerland and Belgium, both around 3,000; Italy and Ireland, near 2,700; the United States, at approximately 1,800; and the United Kingdom, at roughly 1,500. While individualist outliers like Australia and New Zealand maintained low infection rates near the bottom-right of the chart, the overarching cluster analysis demonstrates that collectivist social structures strongly correlate with more effective early-stage virus containment.

This page of the report analyzes early antibody serology test results in Europe and evaluates their implications for reaching herd immunity against COVID-19. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that random serological tests show actual exposure levels that are at least an order of magnitude higher than reported case numbers, indicating a large population of unreported, mild, or asymptomatic infections. 

A bar chart titled "How widespread is COVID-19? Serology test results vs reported cases as a % of population" compares the two metrics across three regions. In Denmark at Day 35, serology results showed 2.7% exposure compared to a reported case ratio of 0.1%. In Gangelt, Germany at Day 73, serology results indicated 14.0% exposure compared to a 3.4% reported ratio. In Scotland at Day 21, serology results showed 1.2% exposure compared to a 0.1% reported ratio. 

To determine how long it might take to reach herd immunity—defined as 60% population exposure—the report utilizes a Susceptible-Infected-Removed (SIR) epidemiological model. This is visualized in a second chart, "When might herd immunity occur, after which serology tests could have a greater 'return to work' impact?" which plots population percentages over 180 days. The chart features a declining curve for the susceptible population, an rising curve for the removed (recovered or deceased) population, and a low hump representing active infections. A horizontal dotted threshold line is set at 40% susceptibility, which represents the 60% exposure required for herd immunity. By plotting the actual Danish and German serology findings along the susceptible curve, the model projects that herd immunity is not a linear path and may arrive much sooner than expected. Specifically, the author estimates that much greater levels of immunity could be just one month away in Gangelt and two months away in Denmark.

This page examines when and how the United States might reopen its economy during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. The author argues that if the US has indeed entered a terminal infection decline phase, its recovery path can be modeled against other nations that have already passed their infection peaks. Because the US has not implemented broad quarantine or contact tracing measures comparable to China or South Korea, the author suggests that Germany and Austria represent more realistic paths for the US, while Italy serves as a slow-decline outlier.

The page features a dual-element graphic consisting of a chart and an associated data table. The chart plots the five-day average of US new daily infections, which peaked near 35,000 in early April 2020, and projects potential decline trajectories based on several international precedents. The accompanying table details these comparative decline rates. China is the fastest recovery path, showing a 98 percent decline from peak infection levels at a rapid daily decline pace of 35.1 percent. This is followed by South Korea at a 97 percent decline and an 8.4 percent daily pace, Australia at a 90 percent decline and a 7.2 percent daily pace, Thailand at a 76 percent decline and a 5.4 percent daily pace, Austria at an 85 percent decline and a 4.1 percent daily pace, and Germany at a 55 percent decline and a 2.9 percent daily pace. Italy marks the slowest trajectory, with a 43 percent decline from its peak and a daily decline pace of just 2.0 percent. 

The text outlines how reopening is likely to unfold, emphasizing that US state governments, rather than the federal government, will largely dictate the process. The author details the typical criteria proposed for "Phase I" reopening plans. These frameworks require a 14-day downward trajectory of documented cases or positive test percentages before lockdowns are lifted. They also demand that hospitals maintain sufficient capacity without resorting to crisis care, that adequate healthcare worker testing is available, and that states develop a sufficient workforce to conduct contact tracing for new infection clusters. Under these plans, non-essential travel remains restricted, though schools, churches, and low-margin businesses like restaurants and shops may reopen under strict social distancing guidelines. Lockdowns would persist for seniors and individuals with co-morbidities. 

Finally, the author warns that any significant resurgence in infections would trigger the reimposition of lockdowns, citing Singapore as an active example of this cycle. Because these transitional plans must be implemented in the absence of an effective anti-viral treatment, vaccine, or herd immunity, the author predicts that the economic recovery will be elongated rather than quick.

This page discusses the White House's general guidelines for identifying a reduction in COVID-19 infections, noting that the exact definition used by individual states remains uncertain. The author presents a table of possible litmus tests by U.S. state, evaluating whether states have met specific thresholds for meaningful declines over a two-week period. 

The extensive table evaluates every state across four main criteria: positive test percentage (targeting a 3% decline over two weeks), 3-day average of new cases (targeting a 10% decline), 3-day average of current hospitalizations (targeting a 10% decline), and 3-day average of current ICU patients (targeting a 10% decline). Each metric compares data from two weeks prior to the publication date against current figures, assigning a "PASS," "FAIL," or "no data" status.

A review of the data reveals that the vast majority of states fail to meet these thresholds. For test positivity decline, almost every state is marked as a "FAIL," including heavily populated states like California, Texas, and New York; rare exceptions that pass include Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Oklahoma. Performance on new cases is slightly more mixed, with states like New York, Florida, and Louisiana successfully passing the 10% decline threshold, while others like California, Illinois, and Texas fail. Hospitalization and ICU metrics suffer from widespread data gaps, but where data is available—such as in New York, California, Washington, and Minnesota—states almost universally fail to show the target 10% decline. The table underscores the author's assessment that very few states were meeting reasonable benchmarks for safely easing restrictions at this stage of the pandemic.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest analyzes the dramatic market rally following the March 23, 2020 low. He argues that while the market had initially priced in extreme pessimism, a combination of aggressive Federal Reserve interventions, crowded short positions, and a deceleration in the growth of COVID-19 infections sparked a sudden rebound. However, he warns that the market has now priced in too much optimism, with price-to-earnings multiples expanding from 13x to 16x 2021 consensus earnings. Because he expects 2021 earnings projections will ultimately be revised downward, he predicts future market gains will be slower and more volatile.

This analysis is supported by four charts. First, a chart of the S&P 500 index level from January 1 to April 10, 2020, shows the index falling from 3,400 to a low of approximately 2,200 on March 23, before climbing back to around 2,800. This trough is annotated as the intersection of three key catalysts: the peak of short interest, the Fed intervention, and a deceleration in infection growth. Second, a chart tracking the five-day percent change in new daily infections for New York City and Italy from March 10 to April 9 shows that by March 23, infection growth had peaked and was falling dramatically. Italy's rate declined from a peak near 200% down toward 0%, while NYC's rate plunged from an early March high of 1,600% down toward 200%. Third, a chart of the quantity-on-loan for the SPY US ETF as a percentage of outstanding shares shows short interest spiking to a multi-year peak of nearly 6% on March 23, creating a massive short squeeze. Finally, a chart of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet from 2008 to 2020 displays a vertical spike in assets from under $4 trillion to over $6 trillion in early 2020, representing the historic scale of the central bank's actions.

To explain this asset expansion, the page details the central bank's policy announcements from March 23. These emergency programs included the Primary Market Corporate Credit Facility for new bond and loan issuance, the Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facility to support liquidity in existing corporate bonds, and the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility to back consumer and small business loans. Additionally, the Fed expanded the Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility to include municipal variable rate demand notes and certificates of deposit, and expanded the Commercial Paper Funding Facility to include tax-exempt commercial paper.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication "Eye on the Market" by Michael Cembalest discusses early clinical data on the anti-viral drug Remdesivir and analyzes Sweden’s unique, non-lockdown strategy for managing COVID-19. 

The author first addresses a widely publicized report on Gilead’s Remdesivir, pointing out that the excitement was based on an uncontrolled, partial trial of just 125 patients who were selectively screened to exclude those with multi-organ failure or requiring ventilation. Conversely, a less publicized study on twelve rhesus macaque monkeys did include a control group and demonstrated positive outcomes—such as lower viral loads and reduced lung damage in the treated group—though the author cautions that approved human antivirals are still far off. 

The second half of the page evaluates Sweden's strategy of issuing voluntary recommendations rather than strict lockdowns. Unlike its neighbors, Sweden kept borders, schools for children under 16, gyms, and cinemas open, aiming for a faster path to herd immunity. Two line charts track the outcomes of this strategy up to 60 days after each region reached 100 total reported cases, comparing Sweden, Europe as a whole, Denmark, Finland, and Norway. 

The first chart, "New daily infections per mm people," measured on a linear scale with a 3-day trailing average, shows that Sweden’s infection rate climbed significantly higher than its Scandinavian neighbors, peaking near 70 daily infections per million people, closely mirroring the broader European trend. Meanwhile, Norway, Finland, and Denmark stayed mostly below 40 daily infections per million. 

The second chart, "Mortality: Case fatality rate," measured on a linear scale with a 1-day trailing average, shows that Sweden’s case fatality rate rose steeply to over 10% after 45 days, even exceeding the average European fatality rate of around 9% at that stage. In comparison, Denmark, Finland, and Norway maintained much flatter and lower fatality rates, all remaining below 4%. The author notes Sweden is betting that its neighbors will eventually experience comparable infection levels and worse economic damage once they lift lockdowns, though current data shows Sweden performing worse than its peers.

This page addresses the question of whether US equities bottomed in March 2020 during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that a March 23 bottom would be historically consistent because markets consistently rally substantially while broader economic crisis indicators, such as unemployment, GDP declines, bank failures, and defaults, are still actively worsening. 

To support this thesis, the page features a table titled "Market appreciation during times of ample economy-wide distress" that details historic market rallies from their lowest levels or widest spreads before key negative indicators reached their worst points. For example, during the Great Depression in 1932, the Dow Jones rallied 67% from its lowest level before bank failures reached 75% of their eventual total. Similarly, in 1957, 1974, 1982, and 2009, US equities bottomed and rallied by 4%, 25%, 26%, and 24%, respectively, before gross domestic product officially hit its bottom. 

Unemployment peaks also historically lag market bottoms. In 1974, 1983, 2003, 2009, and 2012, US and European equities rallied between 17% and 35% from their lowest levels before unemployment finally peaked. Additionally, the table outlines recovery trends in debt and bank markets. In 1990, 2002, and 2008, US High Yield spreads tightened by 350 basis points, 0 basis points, and 1177 basis points from their widest spreads before high-yield defaults reached 75% of their ultimate totals. Other data points include S&P Bank Index rallies in 1990 (90%) and 2009 (180%) before bank failures stabilized, and rallies in AAA CMBS (975 basis points) and leveraged loans (6%) in 2009 before delinquency and default rates crested. 

Ultimately, the author suggests that the potential bottoming of US equities on March 23, 2020, when COVID infections were only at 6% of their April levels, aligns with these historical patterns of anticipatory market recoveries.

It details distribution policies, regulatory oversight, and client restrictions across various jurisdictions, including Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America, along with standard copyright and personal use notices.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest contrasts recent disappointing news regarding antiviral treatments with highly ambitious and rapid vaccine development timelines. On the antiviral side, he notes setbacks with Gilead's Remdesivir, pointing to a prematurely terminated study and higher mortality rates in the treatment group than the control. In contrast, vaccine progress is moving faster than baseline expectations, led by two major initiatives. 

First, Oxford University’s Jenner Institute is testing a vaccine based on a modified chimpanzee virus to trigger SARS-CoV-2 antibodies; they have enrolled 1,100 volunteers in a randomized trial and target one million doses by the fall of 2020. Representing a significant commercial bet, the Serum Institute of India plans to manufacture 40 million doses of this Oxford vaccine before trials are even finished. Second, Johnson & Johnson is utilizing its established vaccine platform—previously used for Ebola, Zika, RSV, and HIV candidates—for a COVID-19 vaccine, aiming for Phase I trials in September 2020 and production by spring 2021. Cembalest also notes other long-term initiatives from companies like Sanofi/GlaxoSmithKline, CanSino, BioNTech/Pfizer, Sinovac/Dynavax, Moderna, and Inovio, but offers a cautionary reminder that several of these efforts rely on RNA, DNA, or viral vector technologies that have never previously been approved for communicable diseases.

This page critiques the hypothesis that the Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine, commonly administered to children for tuberculosis, is a key driver of regional differences in COVID-19 severity. The author details widespread skepticism across the medical, epidemiological, and mathematical biology communities. First, the World Health Organization has stated there is no medical evidence to support the BCG thesis. Second, because COVID-19 severity is strongly linked to age, differences in national age distributions—as noted by the Imperial College of London—are far more likely to explain cross-country variations, particularly since the BCG vaccine is used more widely in less developed countries with younger populations. Additionally, infection rates are rising in parts of the developing world that utilize the vaccine. Third, healthcare professionals in China observed no differences in infection or mortality rates based on BCG history, according to epidemiologist Salim Karim of Columbia University and Cornell University. Fourth, biologically, tuberculosis is bacterial while SARS-CoV-2 is viral, raising fundamental questions about the mechanism. Fifth, research supporting the BCG thesis has often ignored population heterogeneity, vaccination rates, and individual response differences, as noted by Dr. M. Noon of the University of Goettingen. Finally, the author stresses that many of these studies rely on quick, cross-country comparisons prone to ecological fallacy, where aggregate correlations are mistakenly assumed to apply to individuals. Madhukar Pai of McGill University is cited regarding the biases of these ecologic studies. This methodology is compared to the weak evidence that drove premature policy decisions regarding hydroxychloroquine. The author concludes by pointing readers to a chart on the subsequent page to further debunk the premise.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" discusses the timing and readiness of different global regions for lockdown relaxation and economic reawakening. The central argument is that Europe and Asia are structurally ready to begin reopening, whereas the United States, South America, and the Middle East are not yet in a safe position to do so. 

To support this argument, the page features five stacked area charts that monitor COVID-19 infection trends from February to late April 2020, with each region's data weighted by its GDP or, in the case of the United States, state-level GDP. A shared legend categorizes the share of regional GDP into infection status: red indicates infections rising faster than tests; orange represents infections rising slower than tests; shades of purple, dark blue, and light blue depict falling infections from peak levels at varying percentage thresholds; green marks infections falling below twenty-five percent of peak levels; and light grey represents areas with no infections or fewer than five cases per million.

The European monitor reveals a dramatic transition: in late March, nearly one hundred percent of European GDP was in the red zone, but by late April, this figure plummeted to below ten percent, with the rest of the chart dominated by purple, blue, and green bands showing sharp declines from peak infection levels. Conversely, the Asian monitor shows that outbreaks were never sustained at high levels, with the chart remaining almost entirely light grey throughout the period, except for brief, minor dips into red and orange. 

In contrast, the United States monitor shows a large red block starting in mid-March, which transitioned partially into a wide orange band by April, indicating that while infections are still rising, this trend is partly a by-product of increased testing. Only small pockets of purple and blue began to emerge by late April. The Middle East and South America monitors both demonstrate deteriorating situations. In both regions, initial periods of light grey gave way in late March to massive red bands that continued to dominate through the end of April, indicating that infections were rising faster than tests across the vast majority of their respective economic bases.

This page presents a critical analysis of the hypothesis that national BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) vaccine policies correlate with lower COVID-19 mortality rates, ultimately characterizing the theory as sloppy science. The analysis centers on a scatter plot titled "COVID-19 deaths per million people as a function of BCG vaccine policy," which maps 157 countries across six distinct vaccine policy groups using data from Johns Hopkins University and the BCG World Atlas as of April 23, 2020. The vertical axis measures COVID-19 deaths per million people ranging from 0 to 600. 

The author outlines three primary analytical reasons why the BCG thesis falls apart. First, the group of countries that never had a widespread BCG policy (Group 6) has an extremely small sample size of only six countries, yet its dispersion of death rates is very wide, ranging from near zero to over 500 deaths per million. Second, Group 3 consists of fifteen countries that terminated their BCG vaccine policies only after 1970, meaning anyone over the age of 50 in these nations received the vaccine; despite this, many of these countries (such as France and Spain) suffered from high COVID-19 death rates, with outliers marked on the chart by a red question-mark arrow pointing to rates well above 200 deaths per million. Third, Group 5 represents twenty-one countries that instituted BCG policies only after 1970 and currently show low COVID-19 death rates, also highlighted with a red question-mark arrow; the author questions how older, unvaccinated populations in these countries could be protected if the vaccine were indeed the driving factor. 

While Cembalest acknowledges that the complexity of the human immune system makes it impossible to predict whether clinical trials of the BCG vaccine will show efficacy against COVID-19, he argues that the current observational arguments used to support the thesis are analytically flawed.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest evaluates early COVID-19 antibody (serology) test results, cautioning that they must be interpreted carefully. He notes several major caveats, including a study from China where one-third of a 175-person recovered cohort lacked high levels of COVID-19 antibodies, leaving their long-term susceptibility to reinfection an open question. He also details concerns about test sensitivity and specificity, noting a UCSF and UC Berkeley study of twelve tests that found good to excellent sensitivity after three weeks of disease course, with specificity exceeding 95% for most tests and 99% for three of them. Other limitations include a lack of high-quality kits, minimal FDA quality control, small sample sizes, and demographic adjustments that can muddy findings. In a footnote, the author advises readers not to email him with assertions that false positives outnumber actual positives unless they can back it up with a disease prevalence estimate, a comparison of correct negatives to false positives, and a comparison with PCR testing accuracy. 

Despite these issues, Cembalest argues that serology markers remain highly informative for measuring actual infection and mortality rates compared to official reported cases. He provides a table titled "Serology test results to date," compiling data from J.P. Morgan Asset Management and Johns Hopkins University across eight global regions. The table details the time from the outbreak to the test day, the reported case-to-population ratio, the estimated percentage of the population with antibodies, the reported case fatality rate (CFR), the CFR based on serology estimates, and the study size. 

The data consistently demonstrates that antibody prevalence is much higher than reported case ratios, meaning serology-based CFRs are significantly lower than official CFRs. In Scotland, 21 days from the outbreak, the reported case ratio was 0.1% but antibody prevalence was estimated at 1.2%, reducing the CFR from 0.4% to 0.04% (study size 1,000). Denmark, tested at 35 days, had an estimated antibody prevalence of 2.7% and a serology CFR of 0.1% (study size 1,000). The Netherlands, at 49 days, showed a 3.0% antibody prevalence and a 0.8% serology CFR (study size 7,000). 

In NY State, tested at 52 days, the reported case ratio was 1.4% while estimated antibody prevalence was 13.9%, which reduced the CFR from 7.4% down to 0.7% (study size 3,000). Geneva, Switzerland, also at 52 days, showed a 5.5% antibody prevalence and a 0.8% serology CFR (study size 760). Santa Clara, tested at 64 days, showed an antibody prevalence of 3.3% and a serology CFR of 0.1% (study size 3,330). Gangelt, Germany, tested at 73 days, had a reported case ratio of 2.4% but an antibody prevalence estimate of 14.0%, lowering the CFR from 2.3% to 0.4% (study size 500). Finally, Los Angeles, tested at 76 days, showed a 4.2% antibody prevalence and a 0.1% serology CFR (study size 863).

This page presents a policy argument asserting that US states should have emergency access to Chapter 9 bankruptcy provisions to ensure the fair treatment of all creditors, balance discretionary spending on education and infrastructure, and prevent unconstitutional irrevocable obligations in times of dire fiscal distress. 

A side-by-side comparison table contrasts the Federalist argument on the left with the State's Rights argument on the right. The Federalist view leverages Article I, Section 8, Clause 4 of the US Constitution alongside Chapters 9 and 11 of the US Bankruptcy law to argue that Congress has the authority to establish uniform bankruptcy rules ensuring non-discriminatory, fair, and equitable creditor treatment. This perspective points out that 1930s Supreme Court rulings allowing municipal bankruptcy set a precedent that could logically apply to state-level bankruptcies without violating state sovereignty. In contrast, the State's Rights argument relies on the Tenth Amendment and state-level protections, citing Michigan's State Constitution as an example where retiree pensions are classified as contractual obligations that cannot be impaired. Under this view, a federal law allowing state bankruptcy would represent tortious interference with public sector contracts and state sovereignty.

The author aligns with the Federalist perspective, supporting former FDIC Chairman William Isaac’s 2016 assertion that the city of Chicago and the state of Illinois should utilize Chapter 9 or similar federal tools, such as those granted to Puerto Rico, to restructure their liabilities. The page also references academic support for state-level Chapter 9 access dating back to the 1990s from legal scholars at the University of Chicago, as well as ongoing advocacy by University of Pennsylvania Law Professor and bankruptcy expert David Skeel. A footnote highlights a contemporary paper by Skeel on flattening the corporate bankruptcy curve during the coronavirus pandemic, which suggests measures like prepackaged bankruptcies, government-provided debtor-in-possession financing, and an increase in temporary bankruptcy judges.

This page contains regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication, outlining distribution terms and compliance details for various jurisdictions including Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America.

This introductory page serves as an executive summary of the latest updates regarding the COVID-19 pandemic's economic and societal impacts. The author outlines key developments across public health, economic reopening, tracking indicators, medical therapies, fiscal policy, and corporate finance. 

On economic reopening, the text notes that while most of the US GDP is experiencing declining infection rates or rising rates driven strictly by expanded testing, the nation still maintains one of the highest infection rates per million people globally, trailing only Singapore. J.P.
