These sectors include primary metals excluding steel (requiring 1200 degrees Celsius, with 75% of fuel used for process heat), fabricated metal (requiring 430 to 680 degrees Celsius), machinery (requiring 730 degrees Celsius), secondary steel (requiring 1425 to 1540 degrees Celsius, with 87% used for process heat), wood products (requiring 180 degrees Celsius), vehicle parts drying (requiring 150 degrees Celsius), and plastics and rubber (requiring 260 degrees Celsius).

The page also explains the dual role of fossil fuels in industry, both as raw materials and as a source of high-temperature process heat. A flow diagram displays how metallurgical coke is used for smelting pig iron into steel, methane is used to synthesize ammonia for fertilizers, methane, naphtha, and ethane are used to synthesize plastics, and heavy petroleum products are used to produce carbon black for tires. 

Finally, a table details the historical and projected global production of the four industrial pillars: steel, cement, ammonia, and plastics. From 2000 to 2018, production grew rapidly, but growth is expected to slow through 2050. Steel production, which grew at a 4.3% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) from 848 million tonnes in 2000 to 1,817 million tonnes in 2018, is projected to grow at a slower 0.6% CAGR to reach 2,170 million tonnes by 2050. Cement is expected to rise from 4,100 million tonnes in 2018 to 4,682 million tonnes in 2050 (0.4% projected CAGR). Ammonia is forecasted to grow from 171 million tonnes in 2018 to 281 million tonnes in 2050 (1.6% projected CAGR). Plastics represent the fastest-growing category, projected to grow at a 2.6% CAGR from 359 million tonnes in 2018 to 818 million tonnes by 2050.

This page focuses on the environmental pressures of hydraulic fracturing, specifically examining the escalating water requirements and water intensity of shale oil and gas extraction compared to conventional drilling. The author points out that fractured wells require eight to ten times more water than conventional ones, driven both by the number of wells and a twenty to thirty percent increase in lateral well lengths from 2011 to 2016.

The relationship between well count and water volume is illustrated in two stacked bar charts covering select shale basins from 2012 to 2016. The first chart, showing total water use in millions of cubic meters, reveals that water consumption rose from roughly 150 million cubic meters in 2012 to a peak of nearly 220 million in 2014, experiencing only a modest decline to about 190 million by 2016. Meanwhile, the adjacent chart tracking the number of new wells drilled shows a much steeper decline after 2014, where well count peaked at approximately 13,000 before falling by more than half to around 6,000 in 2016. The resilience of high water demand despite fewer wells is attributed to the growing physical dimensions and intensity of individual wells.

To normalize these variables, the author looks at water intensity, measured in liters of water per gigajoule of energy produced during the first twelve months of well production from 2011 to 2016. Two line charts illustrate these trends for oil and gas basins. For shale oil, the median water intensity rose across all major basins; notably, the Permian basin climbed from about 21 liters per gigajoule in 2011 to roughly 45 in 2016, while Eagle Ford, Niobrara, and Bakken also experienced upward trends. For shale gas, the Permian basin showed an even more dramatic spike, surging from approximately 15 liters per gigajoule to over 50 by 2016. Eagle Ford gas wells also saw rising intensity, whereas Marcellus and Haynesville remained relatively low and stable.

The page concludes with a discussion of geographic and toxicological impacts. The author notes that approximately half of natural gas extraction occurs in water-stressed areas, though gas power generation is still far less water-intensive than coal power. Transitioning from coal to natural gas between 2013 and 2016 yielded a reduction of one cubic meter in water consumption and forty cubic meters in water withdrawal per megawatt-hour of electricity generated. However, when evaluating toxicity, the author describes the choice between produced water from fracturing and acidic drainage from unsealed, abandoned coal mines as a toss-up, with both posing severe risks of leaching heavy metals and toxic chemicals into groundwater.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" Eleventh Annual Energy Paper, written by Michael Cembalest, explores whether the "stranded asset" theory is currently the primary driver of oil and gas stock underperformance or if poor industry cash flow and a supply glut are better explanations. The debate hinges on future oil demand projections. Under BP’s base-case "evolving transition" model, global consumption remains flat near current levels until 2040, as growth in emerging countries offsets efficiency gains and electric vehicle penetration. A line chart illustrating global oil use from 1970 with BP projections to 2040 in million barrels per day shows historical demand rising from under 60 million barrels to nearly 100 million. From there, three paths diverge: a "Greater emerging country energy demand" scenario peaking near 130 million, the flat "Evolving transition" base case, and a "Rapid transition" falling to roughly 70 million barrels per day by 2040.

The text then details what would substantiate the stranded asset theory, pointing to the IEA's "Sustainable Development" scenario, which limits global warming to 1.8 degrees Celsius and reduces energy-related carbon dioxide emissions to zero by 2070. To contrast this, two tables compare stranded asset risks in different IEA scenarios, with figures shown in million tons of oil equivalent. Under the "Stated Policies" scenario, which reflects announced policy intentions, cumulative extraction from 2019 to 2070 is projected to exceed 2018 proven reserves for both oil (265,353 extracted versus 235,931 in reserves) and natural gas (228,266 extracted versus 169,334 in reserves), resulting in 0% stranded assets for oil and gas. Coal, however, faces a 67% stranded rate with 398,650 million tons left unextracted. 

Conversely, the "Sustainable Development" scenario shows significant stranded asset risks. In this projection, cumulative extraction falls short of reserves, leaving 42% of oil (98,454 million tons), 26% of natural gas (44,075 million tons), and 87% of coal (518,980 million tons) stranded by 2070. 

In terms of market behavior and investor actions, the page notes that high-profile moves, such as Berkshire Hathaway’s 10 billion dollar investment in Occidental Petroleum to support its acquisition of Anadarko, indicate that prominent investors believe oil and gas assets will not be stranded soon. Additionally, a footnote mentions that J.P. Morgan European Equity Research estimates that applying higher return thresholds and carbon-intensity considerations could reduce the estimates of viable proven reserves to about half of the levels reported by BP.

This page, titled "Maiming the Swamp: Trump and the Environment," provides a comprehensive grid outlining forty-two deregulatory actions taken or proposed by the Trump administration as of January 2020. The visual consists of a three-column table where white boxes denote rollbacks already implemented and shaded boxes represent those that were still pending at the time. The compilation illustrates a sweeping reduction in environmental, public safety, and health protections across multiple sectors, particularly energy, transportation, and agriculture. 

Key implemented rollbacks highlighted in the white boxes include the elimination of methane reporting requirements for oil and gas companies, the rescission of water pollution regulations for fracking on federal lands, the rejection of a proposed ban on pesticides linked to developmental problems in children, and the revocation of California’s authority to set its own vehicle emissions limits. Additionally, the administration lifted the ban on oil and gas drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, scaled back pollution protections for tributaries and wetlands, and reversed rules requiring train braking upgrades for hauling flammable liquids. 

The shaded, pending boxes list significant proposed actions. These include weaker fuel economy standards for cars and light trucks, eliminating the requirement for new coal plants to capture greenhouse gas emissions, weaker regulations regarding coal plant mercury emissions, and relaxing standards requiring more energy-efficient residential furnaces and commercial water heaters. The graphic also notes systemic changes, such as directing agencies to ignore the social cost of carbon, limiting community challenges to EPA-issued pollution permits, and limiting EPA studies that rely on confidential patient data. Sources for this data include environmental and climate deregulation trackers from Harvard Law School and Columbia Law School, the Brookings Institution, the Federal Register, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Department of the Interior.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market energy paper examines why primary steel production is highly carbon-intensive and highlights the steep challenges of decarbonizing the industry. The author explains that the two most carbon-intensive steps in steelmaking are the conversion of coking coal into coke at temperatures of 1,000°C in coke ovens and the iron-making process, which uses coke and limestone in a blast furnace to strip oxygen from iron ore. 

To illustrate these emissions, a table shows the breakdown of carbon dioxide emissions for integrated steel-making. Out of a total of 1,700 kilograms of carbon dioxide emitted per tonne of steel produced, coal and coking account for 990 kilograms, blast furnaces account for 610 kilograms, basic oxygen furnaces account for 85 kilograms, and iron ore sintering accounts for 15 kilograms. An adjacent area chart tracks energy usage and intensity for iron and steel production from 2000 to 2015. The chart reveals that energy intensity remained virtually stagnant, hovering between 20 and 22 gigajoules per tonne, while total energy usage in exajoules climbed dramatically over the fifteen-year period. This energy consumption is overwhelmingly dominated by coal, with gas, electricity, and other fuels comprising much smaller shares.

The author argues that true decarbonization requires eliminating coke and natural gas in favor of hydrogen-based direct reduction of iron ore. However, the author presents several reasons why rapid transition is unlikely, challenging optimistic projections. For instance, ArcelorMittal’s planned hydrogen demonstration plant has an initial output of 100,000 tonnes, representing a mere 0.01 percent of the 1.8 billion tonnes of global steel produced in 2018. Furthermore, the plant will initially rely on fossil-fuel steam methane reformation for hydrogen, delaying the transition to green hydrogen until sufficient quantities are available. 

Ultimately, the author critiques exponential growth forecasts by Bloomberg New Energy Finance, which estimated that half of global steel could be produced via green hydrogen by 2050. Citing steel industry experts, the author labels this forecast highly implausible, pointing out that blast furnace plants have useful lifespans exceeding 50 years and are rarely replaced early. Building hydrogen reduction plants from scratch will take decades; even Sweden, a leader in efficient steel production, is targeting 2045 for full operation of its own demonstration chemistry plant.

This page of the report analyzes the environmental impact of ride-hailing services, refuting the claim that they offer climate benefits. The text argues that ride-hailing actually causes a substantial net increase of 60% to 80% in greenhouse gas emissions and vehicle miles traveled compared to a world without these services. This rise is attributed to "dead-heading"—the time and distance drivers travel empty while waiting for fares—as well as the displacement of cleaner transportation modes like public transit, biking, and walking. To reverse this trend, Chicago and California have begun implementing regulatory penalties and incentives to promote electrification and rider pooling, though the sheer convenience of ride-hailing makes these patterns difficult to change. 

The analysis is supported by four charts. The first chart, a bar graph titled "US ride-hailing and taxi ridership," plots annual ridership in billions from 1990 to 2018. It shows traditional taxi ridership holding steady near 1.5 billion trips through 2012, after which the introduction of ride-hailing apps triggered an explosion in total demand, pushing combined ridership to nearly 4.0 billion by 2018, while traditional taxi volume shrank to a fraction of its former size. 

The second chart, an area graph titled "Volume of rides in New York City," shows millions of annual trips from 2010 to 2018, broken down by operator. Yellow Cab trips declined from roughly 170 million in 2013 to less than 100 million in 2018. Over the same period, total trips in the city swelled past 300 million due to the rise of ride-hailing services, with Uber representing the largest share, followed by Lyft, Via, and Juno.

The third chart, "Ride-hailing emissions," compares emissions per trip-mile in grams of CO2 equivalent. A typical ride-hailing trip produces approximately 650 grams of CO2 equivalent, which is 69% more than the 380 grams generated by a displaced trip. Conversely, an electric ride-hailing trip utilizing 50% passenger pooling emits only about 180 grams, achieving a 52% reduction compared to the displaced trip. 

The final horizontal bar chart, "Total vehicle miles traveled by ride-hailing services versus displaced choice of transportation," contrasts ride-hailing VMT against displaced VMT in millions of miles. Section A highlights where ride-hailing added significant new road miles, showing that ride-hailing generated over 800 million miles of travel to replace public transportation trips, and generated nearly 500 million miles for trips that otherwise would not have occurred at all. In contrast, Section B shows taxi and "get a ride" replacements, where ride-hailing VMT more directly substituted existing car travel.

This page consists entirely of legal disclaimers and regulatory disclosures for various jurisdictions—including Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin American countries—and contains no analytical content, charts, or financial commentary.

This page presents a comprehensive appendix table detailing key electricity and primary energy statistics by country and region, drawing on data from J.P. Morgan Asset Management and the US Energy Information Administration's 2019 International Energy Outlook. The statistics are categorized into three main sections: electricity, primary and delivered energy, and fossil fuels. These metrics are evaluated across twelve geographical regions: the World, US, OECD, OECD Europe, Japan, Canada, Non-OECD, China, India, Brazil, the Middle East, and Russia.

In the first section, dedicated to electricity, the table lists the primary energy used for electricity generation alongside actual electricity consumed, which is net of thermal conversion, power plant consumption, and transmission losses. Globally, out of 248.4 quadrillion BTUs of primary energy used for electricity, 80.3 quadrillion BTUs are consumed, showing that electricity accounts for a 13% share of primary energy and an 18% share of consumed energy. Renewables make up 31% of the primary energy used for global electricity. On a regional level, Canada and Brazil exhibit the highest renewable shares of primary energy used for electricity at 75% and 88%, respectively, while the Middle East shows the lowest at 9%. China leads in volume, utilizing 72.7 quadrillion BTUs of primary energy for electricity to yield 23.2 quadrillion BTUs of consumed electricity.

The second section, focused on primary and delivered energy, lists total primary energy, total consumed energy, sector-specific consumption for the industrial and transport sectors, and the overall renewable share of consumed energy, which includes renewable electricity and direct renewable use in buildings, transport, and industry. Globally, out of 627.0 quadrillion BTUs of total primary energy, 453.5 quadrillion BTUs are consumed, with the industrial sector taking 238.7 quadrillion BTUs and transport taking 122.4 quadrillion BTUs, resulting in an 11% renewable share of consumed energy. The United States accounts for 99.9 quadrillion BTUs of primary energy, with 75.1 quadrillion BTUs consumed and a 7% renewable share. China leads primary energy consumption at 152.7 quadrillion BTUs, with its industrial sector consuming 70.6 quadrillion BTUs and transport consuming 15.5 quadrillion BTUs, reflecting a 10% renewable share. Brazil stands out with a 36% renewable share of consumed energy.

The third section details fossil fuel metrics, including their share of electricity generation, their share of primary energy, and the percentage of total fossil fuels directed toward electricity. Globally, fossil fuels generate 57% of electricity and represent 80% of primary energy, with 29% of fossil fuels used specifically for electricity. OECD Europe shows lower fossil fuel reliance, with a 29% share of electricity generation and a 68% share of primary energy. In contrast, the Middle East relies almost entirely on fossil fuels, which represent 90% of its electricity generation and 97% of its primary energy. Brazil has the lowest fossil fuel share of electricity generation at just 9%, with fossil fuels accounting for 50% of its primary energy. Meanwhile, India and China show high fossil fuel dependency, with fossil fuels making up 75% and 65% of their electricity generation, respectively.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" discusses the resilience of the US economic recovery in the face of a severe surge in COVID-19 infections, noting that the United States has the third highest infection rate among the world's 50 largest economies by GDP. Michael Cembalest poses the critical question of whether this rising infection curve will ultimately derail economic recovery, observing that state-level counter-measures, such as closing bars, gyms, and indoor dining, have been relatively mild compared to earlier, more restrictive lockdowns. 

To contextualize this surge, the page presents two charts analyzing global infection data. The first chart displays infection levels for the 50 largest countries by GDP, sorted by their trailing seven-day average infection rate per million people. It plots both peak infection rates, represented by red markers, and latest infection rates, represented by blue markers, along with the percentage decline from the peak for each country. The data reveals that the US and Brazil have experienced virtually no decline from their peaks, with the US latest infection rate hovering near 175 cases per million people. In contrast, countries like Spain, Italy, Germany, and Ireland show dramatic declines of 93% to 99% from their peak infection levels, while China and Vietnam show a 100% reduction. A footnote adds that when looking at the largest countries by population rather than GDP, the US ranks second in infection rates, trailing only Brazil.

The second chart compares the trajectory of new daily infections per million people over time for highly infected countries against Europe and Hubei, China, using a seven-day trailing average. The horizontal axis measures the number of days after total reported cases reached 100, extending up to 180 days. This visual highlights a massive divergence in containment success. While Europe and Hubei flattened their curves to nearly zero cases per million people early in the timeline, highly infected nations show sustained, elevated waves. Brazil’s rate climbs past 180 infections per million people, the United States surges back upward toward 140, and South Africa shows a sharp, near-vertical spike past 140. Sweden peaked around 120 infections per million before beginning to decline, while Mexico shows a flatter but steadily elevated rate of around 40 infections per million.

This page analyzes the evolving dynamics of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, focusing on the relationship between rising infection rates, hospitalizations, and deaths. Author Michael Cembalest observes that while infections and hospitalizations were previously decoupling, hospitalizations are now starting to catch up with rising infections, even though deaths continue to fall. This lag in deaths may be due to improved medical treatments like anti-coagulants and corticosteroids, though time lags also play a role. He addresses the theory that rising infections are driven primarily by younger, less vulnerable people; while this is partially true, hospitalizations are rising regardless, and the long-term health consequences of the virus remain severe for all ages.

The analysis is supported by three charts. The first, "US infections, hospitalizations and deaths, 7 day avg," spans from mid-March to mid-July 2020. It plots current hospitalizations and new daily infections on the left-hand axis and daily deaths on the right-hand axis. The chart shows new daily infections surging past 50,000 and current hospitalizations rising to near 40,000, while daily deaths hover around 500, following a brief artificial spike in late June caused by New York and New Jersey adding probable deaths to their tallies. 

The second chart, "Hotspot infections, hospitalizations and deaths, 7 day avg," tracks the same metrics for a specific group of hotspot states, including North Carolina, Arkansas, Utah, California, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Nevada, and Louisiana. Here, new daily infections have skyrocketed past 35,000, with current hospitalizations climbing sharply in tandem, while daily deaths on the right-hand scale remain relatively flat, near 250. 

The third chart, "Recent Tennessee infections less risky, mostly due to lower age of newly infected persons, COVID Risk Index," uses data from the Vanderbilt School of Medicine up to June 1, 2020. It compares new cases to an age-adjusted Case Mix Index on a scale of 0.0 to 3.0. This visual shows that while new cases rebounded in May, the age-adjusted case mix index remained low, confirming that younger, lower-risk individuals drove the case expansion in Tennessee. 

The author cautions that most states do not report cumulative infection age distributions, making the "younger infection age" theory difficult to confirm nationwide. He concludes by emphasizing that survivors of all ages face debilitating lingering health risks from COVID-19, including lung scarring, cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, neurocognitive problems, and abnormal blood clotting.

This page discusses the rapid global economic recovery from the initial COVID-19 pandemic shock, noting that about half of the 17% contraction in global GDP from January to April has already been reversed. The recovery is supported by rebounding manufacturing and services surveys globally and strong US employment data, which showed nearly 5 million new jobs and a drop in the unemployment rate from a 16% peak to 11%. A particular area of focus is the recovery in leisure and hospitality, which is tracking closely with proprietary credit and debit card transaction data. Additionally, the author highlights the concept of operating leverage, showing how S&P 500 companies historically manage expenses aggressively during post-recession periods to generate profit growth well before sales recover.

The first chart, "Estimated virus impact on global GDP," traces the pandemic’s estimated impact from February 7 to June 26. The line drops precipitously from February through mid-April, bottoming out at approximately negative 17%, before steadily recovering to around negative 7% by late June.

The second chart, "Regional manufacturing & services business surveys," plots Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) levels from September to June for China, the Eurozone, the US, and Asia excluding China, where a reading above 50 indicates expansion. China reached its trough first in February at approximately 27 before recovering above 50. The other regions bottomed in April, with the Eurozone dipping the lowest to around 15, the US near 27, and Asia ex-China near 23. By June, all regions showed sharp V-shaped recoveries, with the US and Eurozone nearing or crossing back over the 50 mark.

The third chart, "Leisure and hospitality: changes in spending and employment," compares relative activity from March 1 to June 29. The blue line tracks restaurant, hotel, and travel/entertainment spending relative to 2019, which bottomed near negative 80% in late March and climbed back to around negative 45% by late June. The gold line shows leisure and hospitality employment relative to February 2020, which lagged spending slightly, bottoming at negative 50% in late April and rising to negative 35% by late June.

The final chart, "Contribution to S&P 500 profits from operating leverage after recessions and other market declines," examines quarterly year-over-year percentage changes in S&P 500 operating EPS growth. The data spans five historical post-crisis windows: the S&L crisis (1993), the LTCM crisis (1999), the Tech bubble (2002), the Global Financial Crisis (2010), and the Emerging Markets/oil collapse (2016–2017). Black diamonds indicate total operating EPS growth, which is decomposed into sales contribution (blue bars) and operating leverage contribution (tan bars). Across almost every recovery phase, such as the first quarter of 2010 where EPS growth approached 80%, the tan bars representing cost-cutting and operating leverage vastly outweigh the blue bars representing sales, proving that expense management dominates early post-recession earnings rebounds.

In this J.P. Morgan commentary, Michael Cembalest answers client questions following the publication of his tenth annual energy paper, addressing three specific topics: low energy nuclear reactors, renewable natural gas, and electric container ships. 

First, regarding low energy nuclear reactors, or LENR, Cembalest explains that he and co-author Vaclav Smil exclude technologies that have not yet reached early-stage commercialization, unlike Icelandic deep geothermal or utility-scale lithium-ion batteries. While space heating applications up to 200 degrees Celsius may emerge in the next five to ten years, there remains deep skepticism; a May 2019 study by researchers from MIT, the University of British Columbia, the University of Maryland, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and Google found no evidence of fusion or heat. 

Next, discussing renewable natural gas, or RNG, made from landfills and waste, he notes that while current US volumes are 200 to 300 million gallons annually, Platts and NREL estimate total potential at 2.9 billion to 4.8 billion gasoline gallon equivalents per year. Even at full potential, this would only offset about 2.5 percent of the 142 billion gallons of annual US gasoline demand, which is beneficial but not transformative. He also points out that Germany's waste-to-energy electricity generation is expensive, costing nearly 20 cents per kilowatt-hour compared to 9 cents for onshore wind, due to the energy-intensive process of collecting waste over large areas. 

Finally, addressing the electrification of container ships, Cembalest compares a small operational electric ship carrying 120 twenty-foot equivalent units to Maersk’s Triple-E class vessels. To match a Maersk ship's cargo capacity, speed, and range using state-of-the-art batteries with 300 watt-hours per kilogram of density, 40 percent of the ship's cargo space would have to be dedicated to batteries. For electric shipping to be economically competitive with diesel weight-wise, battery densities would need to improve tenfold, a daunting task given that commercial battery energy densities have not even quadrupled over the last 70 years.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, investigates the uniquely American surge in COVID-19 cases by exploring the nation’s systemic scientific trust gap. The author points out a stark paradox: although the United States leads the world in medical and biotechnology patents and claims over half of the top forty global clinical research universities, its citizens rank below most of the world on interest and trust in science. To explain this discrepancy, Cembalest notes that fifty-seven former government scientists and public health officials from both political parties have criticized the Trump administration for marginalizing scientific expertise. Furthermore, this lack of trust is exacerbated by America’s high score on the Geert-Hofstede index for individualism, which describes a cultural tendency to act on personal beliefs regardless of the impact on others. To illustrate the math behind this behavior, the text references pandemic visualizations by Grant Sanderson of 3Blue1Brown, which show how even a small share of scientifically skeptical, non-compliant individuals can disproportionately accelerate virus transmission.

The page features a bar chart titled "How Americans rank globally on trust in science, medicine and vaccines," which depicts the percentile rank of the United States among 144 countries using 2018 data from the Wellcome Trust and Gallup. Across all seven metrics, the United States consistently ranks in the bottom half of countries, generally sitting between the twentieth and fortieth percentiles. Specifically, Americans place in only the thirty-eighth percentile for wanting to know more about science. Trust indicators are even lower: the U.S. ranks in the twentieth percentile for trusting the national government a lot and around the twenty-first percentile for trusting medical and health advice from the government a lot. Trust in corporate scientists to benefit the public sits at approximately the thirty-second percentile. On vaccine-related queries, Americans place in the low thirties, ranking around the thirty-second percentile on whether vaccines are important for children, the thirty-third percentile on whether vaccines are safe, and the thirty-second percentile for whether their own children have actually received a vaccine. Cembalest argues that these cultural and scientific trust deficiencies explain why many Americans, politicians, and Wall Street strategists failed to understand how to control the pandemic in the spring of 2020.

In this page of Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, Eye on the Market, the author addresses the surge of COVID-19 infections in the United States and debunks common explanations such as increased testing or changes in public mobility. 

The first chart, US new daily infections per mm people, tracks daily infections against the number of days after total cases reached 100 using a seven-day trailing average. It shows that while New York and New Jersey saw an early peak of nearly 300 infections per million and a subsequent sharp decline, a group of hotspot states—including North Carolina, Arkansas, Utah, California, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Nevada, and Louisiana—experienced a severe second-wave surge, rising toward 250 infections per million. The adjacent chart, US daily tests per mm people, counters the argument that this surge is merely a result of increased testing. It illustrates that hotspot states and other states follow nearly identical testing trajectories, with both rising to around 1,500 to 2,000 daily tests per million by day 100, which is significantly lower than the peak testing levels of over 3,000 seen in New York and New Jersey.

The author further argues that mobility changes do not reliably predict infection trends. A line chart titled Country mobility changes do not predict infections compares retail, restaurant, transit, and workplace mobility declines from February to late June 2020. Despite having similar or even shallower peak mobility declines than the United States, nations like Japan, Germany, Thailand, and Italy maintained very low infection rates, ranging from 0.1 to 4.8 infections per million, while the United States skyrocketed to 146.5 infections per million. To look closer at the domestic situation, a scatter plot titled US mobility changes only partially explain infection rise compares peak declines in mobility against the change in recent infections per million versus a month prior. This chart reveals a wide variance: hotspot states like Georgia, Florida, Arizona, South Carolina, Nevada, and Louisiana saw massive spikes in infections, with Georgia approaching an increase of 500 infections per million, despite having similar peak mobility declines of roughly 50 to 55 percent compared to other states that saw virtually no rise in infections. 

Cembalest concludes that reopening dates, mobility changes, and other empirically measured behaviors do not lead to higher infections in any statistically consistent way. Looking ahead, he notes that if falling death rates remain the primary barometer for keeping state economies open, the US economy and equity markets may continue to rise gradually through the summer. He identifies the possible market consequences of a Democratic Sweep in the fall election as the next major litmus test for markets, while J.P. Morgan’s upcoming virus research will focus closely on tracking deaths relative to rising infections and hospitalizations.

This page analyzes COVID-19 testing trends and infection rates, comparing the successful testing strategies of Italy and New York and questioning the reported infection discrepancies in sub-Saharan Africa.

The first chart tracks Italy's virus progression from late February to late June 2020, displaying the positive testing rate on the left axis and total daily tests on the right axis. It shows that as daily tests ramped up from near zero to about 50,000 in late April before stabilizing around 30,000, the positive testing rate fell from a peak of approximately 25% in late March to under 2% by late June. 

The second chart displays a similar pattern for New York from early April to mid-July 2020. As New York increased its daily testing volume from around 20,000 to over 60,000, its positive testing rate fell sharply from a peak of about 45% to approximately 1%. The author highlights that both Italy and New York successfully adopted this aggressive testing approach and expresses the expectation that other US states will follow their lead.

The final chart tracks new daily infections per million people across several African nations—including South Africa, Ghana, Kenya, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Mozambique, Angola, and Tanzania—aligned by the number of days since each country reached 100 total cases. While most of these countries show flat infection trajectories near zero, South Africa's curve rises exponentially, exceeding 200 new daily infections per million people by day 100. The author poses an open question regarding this data, expressing doubt that South Africa's true infection rates differ so drastically from other sub-Saharan African countries and suggesting the discrepancy may be a function of data tracking or testing availability rather than actual viral spread.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures, legal disclaimers, and data privacy notifications for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication. It details the security and aggregation protocols used to protect confidential customer information when analyzing Chase credit and debit card transaction data, explicitly noting that all personally identifiable information is removed. The remainder of the page outlines standard investment risk warnings, local distribution restrictions, and lists the specific J.P. Morgan legal entities authorized to distribute the material across global jurisdictions, including the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Europe, the Asia-Pacific region, and Australia.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" by Michael Cembalest presents visual data and commentary on the course of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, highlighting emerging trends in hotspot states, international divergence, and national epidemiological metrics. 

The first chart, "Hotspots: rollover in infections and COVID symptoms," focuses on a group of critical US states, including South Carolina, Arkansas, Florida, North Carolina, Nevada, Utah, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia, and Idaho. Spanning from April 1 to late July 2020, the chart plots two trends. The percentage of doctor visits with COVID-like symptoms, shown in blue, peaked near 11 percent in early July and has since fallen sharply to roughly 7 percent. This decline is accompanied by a rollover in the absolute number of new daily infections, shown in gold, which peaked near 40,000 in mid-July and is starting to decline, signaling that further drops in infections are likely. 

Cembalest connects these public health outcomes to political dynamics, citing an anecdote where GOP Representatives called for the resignation of Representative Liz Cheney simply for publicly supporting NIAID director Dr. Anthony Fauci. He suggests this political polarization helps explain "The US infection gap" illustrated in the second chart. This chart compares the United States to peer nations—including Australia, France, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, and South Korea—by plotting new daily infections per million people on a seven-day average against the number of days since total cases reached 100. While the other developed nations successfully flattened their curves to near-zero infection rates by day 150, the United States diverged dramatically, spiking to over 200 new daily infections per million people around day 150.

Finally, the third chart displays the "US population share with positive epidemiological trajectory," utilizing a proprietary three-factor test designed by J.P. Morgan’s Technical Strategy group. To qualify, a state must have cumulative case growth under 3 percent, a testing positive rate under 10 percent, and an infection rate below 60 percent of its peak. The chart reveals that after plunging to 0 percent in March, the share of the US population living in states meeting this positive trajectory test peaked at nearly 50 percent in mid-June. However, that figure has since dropped, with only about 25 percent of the US population meeting the positive trajectory criteria by late July.

This page discusses the contrast in government policy responses to COVID-19 infections and reviews promising data from early-stage vaccine trials. Michael Cembalest first focuses on Hong Kong, which was experiencing a second wave of infections at the time. Despite having much lower transmission rates than Western nations, Hong Kong implemented severe mobility restrictions, including delayed school openings, a ban on indoor dining, strict gathering limits of four people, mandatory quarantine for arrivals, and steep fines for not wearing masks. Cembalest contrasts these measures with the much more modest restrictions in the United States, where infection rates were ten times higher. 

Two charts illustrate this disparity by tracking new daily infections per million people on a seven-day moving average, aligned by the number of days after total cases reached 100. The first chart, scaled from zero to 18 infections per million, shows Hong Kong and Australia experiencing matching surges near day 150, rising toward 14 to 16 cases per million, while Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan remain under six cases per million. The second chart puts this second wave into a broader context by expanding the vertical scale up to 250 infections per million. On this wider scale, Hong Kong's spike appears negligible at the bottom of the axis, whereas the United States and Israel are shown spiking aggressively toward 200 to 250 cases per million, with Costa Rica rising past 100 and Romania showing a moderate uptick.

The second half of the page details positive developments from Phase I clinical trials of the Oxford and AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. Cembalest explains that after trial participants received a second booster shot on Day 28, the vaccine successfully generated neutralizing antibody response levels comparable to those found in convalescent plasma samples. While this immunogenicity response justified advancing to Phase II and III trials, the author notes that it does not guarantee durable, long-term immunity. He also emphasizes that the wide variation in antibody levels across both vaccinated individuals and recovered patients highlights the underlying complexity of natural immune responses and the challenges of achieving herd immunity. 

This vaccine data is visualized in a final chart displaying neutralizing antibody response potencies on a logarithmic scale ranging from 16 to 16,384 across different intervals: day 0, day 28, day 35, and day 42. The data series compares Oxford COVID vaccine recipients to those who received a meningitis vaccine placebo. At day 0 and day 28, antibody levels remain low, but following the booster shot on day 28, the antibody levels measured on days 35 and 42 cluster tightly between 128 and 1,024, mirroring the distribution shown in the reference group of actual convalescent plasma samples.

This page analyzes the relationship between US COVID-19 hospitalizations and consumer spending, alongside a detailed look at mortality rates in hard-hit hotspot states. The author argues that US economic recovery, measured by consumer spending, is closely linked to the severity of the virus. When hospitalizations stopped declining, spending stopped recovering. 

The first chart demonstrates this correlation by plotting the seven-day average of current US hospitalizations against year-over-year in-person credit and debit card spending from March to July 2020. The data shows that around June 17, as hospitalizations hit a trough of approximately 30,000 and began to climb back toward 55,000, the year-over-year card spending recovery stalled, plateauing between 15% and 20% below the previous year's levels. 

The second chart focuses on a group of hotspot states, which include South Carolina, Arkansas, Florida, North Carolina, Nevada, Utah, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia, and Idaho. It compares new daily infections, current hospitalizations, and daily deaths from April to mid-July 2020. Daily infections and hospitalizations in these states rose dramatically starting in June, peaking near 40,000 in mid-July, which subsequently pushed daily deaths from around 100 to over 300. The author observes that infections appear to be rolling over, suggesting that hospitalizations and deaths may soon follow. 

The third chart compares mortality rates across different state categories, showing US daily deaths per million people over the number of days after total reported cases reached 100. While daily deaths in the hotspot states have risen to about three per million, this rate remains significantly lower than the April peak in New York and New Jersey, which reached roughly 16 deaths per million people. The author notes that other states peaked around five deaths per million earlier in the pandemic. The New York and New Jersey data also shows a sharp late spike due to a one-time addition of historical deaths that occurred over the course of the pandemic. While hotspot mortality is lower than the April surge, the author questions whether New York and New Jersey are the best benchmarks given how unprepared the country was at the start of the pandemic.

This page details COVID-19 infection trends across emerging markets and analyzes regulatory policies and scientific developments surrounding therapeutics and herd immunity. The author begins by highlighting Latin America as the emerging market region with the most severe outbreak, naming Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, and Peru as key contributors. A supporting line chart, titled "EM World infections," tracks new daily infections per million people on a seven-day average against the number of days after total reported cases reached 100. The visual reveals South America experiencing a massive, sustained spike, climbing near 180 daily infections per million people around day 150. In stark contrast, other emerging market regions—including Eastern Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Emerging Asia—all remain significantly lower, tracking well below 40 daily infections per million throughout the 200-day window.

The commentary transitions to US government "march-in" rights, which allow the federal government to directly produce medications in government labs or mandate third-party licensing if private patents were developed using federal funds. This mechanism applies to the government’s co-ownership of patents for Gilead's drug Remdesivir, though Gilead separately plans to allow generic suppliers to sell the drug in 127 low- and middle-income countries. Additionally, the author discusses 28 U.S.C. Section 1498, which enables the Department of Health and Human Services to seize control of patents, manufacturing, and distribution with just compensation. Historical precedents are cited, including the 2001 anthrax scare where Section 1498 was used to force down the price of generic Cipro to below one dollar, and a 2018 push to use the statute to break Gilead’s hepatitis C patents. 

Finally, the author addresses emerging research on COVID-19 herd immunity. While initial estimates suggested a threshold of 60% to 70%, newer models accounting for differences in human interaction intensity based on age and social networks suggest an aggregate national herd immunity level as low as 43%. However, the author cautions that this lower figure relies on younger, more active populations achieving immunity levels of 70% or higher, predicting that the 43% statistic will be widely misreported in the media without this crucial context.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" analysis examines the debate between President Donald Trump and Dr. Anthony Fauci regarding COVID-19 infection levels and testing rates in the United States. The author addresses President Trump's claim that the country's high reported virus levels are simply a result of doing more testing than other nations. While the author notes that the United States does indeed rank near the top globally in testing per capita, the underlying data reveals that the high case count is driven by a higher actual infection level and a significantly higher share of positive test results compared to peer countries.

The first visual, a bar chart titled "Total tests to date per million people for the largest 50 countries by GDP," tracks cumulative testing per capita across major global economies as of early August 2020. The chart shows the United Arab Emirates leading with nearly 300,000 tests per million people, followed by Denmark, Russia, and Israel. The United States ranks fifth, with roughly 160,000 tests per million people, placing it ahead of other major nations like the United Kingdom, Canada, Germany, and Italy. At the far right of the chart, nations like Japan, Mexico, and Indonesia show extremely low per capita testing rates, while China and Egypt report no available data.

The second visual, a line graph titled "Positive share of tests," measures the positive testing rate percentage over the number of days after total reported cases reached 100 in each country. This chart reveals that the United States maintains a persistently high positive testing rate, hovering around 8% past day 160. This is contrasted with Sweden, which peaked near 8% around day 120 before dropping to approximately 3.5%, and Switzerland, which tracks steadily lower. Japan shows a late rise toward 4%, while a large cluster of other developed nations—including France, Canada, Italy, Germany, South Korea, and the United Kingdom—all successfully brought their positive test rates down to 1% or lower by day 160. This high positive rate in the US supports the author's conclusion that the high volume of cases is a reflection of widespread infection, not just high testing rates.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s market analysis addresses the debate over whether the high COVID-19 infection rates in the United States relative to other countries are primarily a result of the US conducting more tests. Michael Cembalest argues that the higher US infection rate cannot be blamed solely on more testing. To demonstrate this, he presents an analysis where other countries' infection rates are adjusted by assuming they tested at the same high per-capita rate as the US. Even under this scenario, which likely represents an upper bound for infections, other countries still show significantly lower infection rates than the US. Cembalest attributes the discrepancy to behavioral differences, such as larger and more immediate mobility declines in Europe and stronger compliance with social distancing guidelines, as noted by Dr. Anthony Fauci and other experts.

The first visualization is a bar chart comparing actual 7-day average infection rates per million people against adjusted rates based on US testing levels. The countries analyzed include the US, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada, Australia, the UK, South Korea, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Sweden. The US actual infection rate stands exceptionally high, at approximately 175 cases per million. In comparison, other nations have much lower actual rates. Even when adjusted to US testing levels, their theoretical infection rates remain far lower than the US rate. For example, Japan’s adjusted rate rises to about 115 per million, Sweden's reaches approximately 75 per million, and Switzerland's adjusts to around 65 per million. France adjusts to roughly 40 per million, while Germany, Italy, Canada, Australia, the UK, South Korea, and the Netherlands all remain well below 40 per million even after adjustment.

The second visualization is a scatter plot illustrating that US mobility declines never reached European levels despite the countries experiencing similar infection rates prior to May 1. The horizontal axis measures the peak 7-day average of new daily infections per million people, ranging from 50 to 190, while the vertical axis tracks the peak decline in mobility (averaging retail, transit, and workplace activity) ranging from -50% to -95%. The US is a clear outlier, experiencing a peak infection rate of roughly 100 per million but only a 52% reduction in mobility. Conversely, European nations with comparable or higher infection rates saw much more dramatic drops in movement. Spain, with the highest peak infection rate near 175 per million, saw mobility drop by roughly 92%. Italy, with infections around 95 per million, and France, with infections around 125 per million, both saw mobility declines near 90%. Germany and the UK, with peak infections near 70 and 75 per million respectively, saw mobility contract by roughly 83% and 80%. Other European nations, including the Netherlands, Austria, Belgium, and Switzerland, all recorded mobility declines of 70% to 85%.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses COVID-19 news and political dynamics surrounding the 2020 election, specifically addressing the concept of plausible deniability and the controversy over expanding vote-by-mail policies. The author critiques a recent research note from Fundstrat Research that suggested herd immunity could be reached at fifteen to twenty percent infection levels, pointing out that using a question mark allowed them to float an unsubstantiated claim without taking responsibility. A similar parallel is drawn to President Trump's suggestion of postponing the election due to mail-in voting security concerns. 

To address the actual risks of voting by mail, the author references a paper by Charles Stewart at MIT. The study highlights that while approximately four percent of mail-in ballots were lost or miscounted during the 2016 presidential election, this rate is comparable to the four-to-six percent of in-person votes lost during the 2000 election due to administrative issues. Consequently, the research suggests that the net risks of a surge in mail-in voting for the 2020 election are negligible. 

The commentary is supported by a scatter plot chart showing public support for expanding vote-by-mail options, broken down by political party from 1996 to late May 2020. The chart tracks data from major polling organizations, including Pew, Gallup, Fox News, and ABC/Washington Post. In the pre-2020 period, support among both Democrats and Republicans was highly aligned and relatively low, generally hovering between twenty-five percent and forty-five percent. However, a dramatic partisan gap opened in the spring of 2020. While Republican support remained low, fluctuating between thirty percent and forty-five percent, Democratic support surged dramatically, rising from around forty percent in late 2018 to between seventy percent and nearly ninety percent across various polls conducted in April and May of 2020.

This page analyzes US corporate earnings, economic surprises, and COVID-19 infection trends in mid-2020. Michael Cembalest points out that although S&P 500 earnings for the second quarter are projected to fall by 35% to 40% year-over-year, actual results are significantly outperforming highly pessimistic expectations. Only three of twenty-four industries—healthcare equipment, utilities, and semiconductors—posted positive year-over-year results, but upside margin surprises have occurred across almost all sectors, paired with a massive jump in US economic data beating expectations. 

An accompanying dual-axis chart tracking S&P earnings beats and the Citi Economic Surprise Index from 2008 to 2020 illustrates these sudden positive deviations, showing S&P 500 earnings surprises spiking above 15% and the Citi Economic Surprise Index soaring to an unprecedented peak near 250 in mid-2020. The author cautions that these positive surprises are dependent on continued fiscal stimulus from Congress, which is expected to be extended in August. Looking ahead, Cembalest mentions preparing an upcoming analysis on what it will take to bring US debt levels back down to 80% of GDP.

The bottom half of the page focuses on a sharp decline in COVID-19 infections across several Southern US states, which is helping slow infection rates nationally. While US mortality was rising at the time of publication, the author predicts it will decline within two weeks based on downward trends in hospitalizations and infections. 

Two charts support this pandemic outlook. The first chart, tracking new daily infections per million people over a 150-day window following each state's 100th case, shows a clear peaking and downward turn for Florida, Arizona, South Carolina, and Texas. For instance, Florida's rate peaked near 500 cases per million before turning downward, while Arizona peaked close to 400. 

The second chart, tracking nationwide virus data from April to late July 2020, plots new daily infections and current hospitalizations on the left-hand scale against daily deaths on the right-hand scale. This national tracking chart shows that while new daily infections peaked near 70,000 in July and current hospitalizations flattened just below 60,000, daily deaths ticked up slightly to around 1,000 by late July but remained far below their April peak of over 2,000.

This J.P. Morgan analysis discusses the emergence of "mini-second waves" of COVID-19 infections in Australia and Europe, contrasting their aggressive containment policies and mortality outcomes with those of the United States. The author highlights that despite having infection levels far lower than the US, countries like Australia have implemented highly restrictive measures, such as Melbourne’s Stage 4 emergency restrictions, which include nighttime curfews and tight travel limits. While parts of Europe, particularly Spain and Belgium, are also experiencing mini-second waves, their mobility restrictions have remained relatively mild, and their mortality rates have not yet followed the upward trajectory seen in the US.

To support these observations, the page features two charts sourced from Johns Hopkins University, the IMF, and JPMAM, both of which track data based on the number of days after total reported cases in a region reached 100. 

The first chart, on the left, displays new daily infections per million people on a seven-day moving average. It shows a stark contrast between the US and other regions. While the US curve surges dramatically back upward to nearly 200 daily infections per million people by day 150, the curves for Spain, Belgium, Australia, and Hong Kong remain extremely low. Spain and Belgium show pronounced initial peaks of roughly 160 and 120 infections per million, respectively, followed by steep declines, while the line representing Australia and Hong Kong remains nearly flat along the bottom axis throughout the entire period.

The second chart, on the right, tracks daily deaths per million people on a seven-day moving average. This visualization highlights a clear divergence between the US and Europe. Europe experienced a much higher initial spike in mortality, peaking at nearly 9 deaths per million people around day 50 before falling sharply to near zero, where it has flattened out. Conversely, the US curve peaked at around 7 deaths per million and, after declining to about 2 deaths per million, has begun ticking upward again to approximately 3.5 deaths per million by day 150, illustrating the rising mortality per capita in the US that has not yet materialized in Europe.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" analysis evaluates the trajectory of COVID-19 in the United States, focusing on the relationship between infections, hospitalizations, and deaths, and how domestic mobility influences the spread. Michael Cembalest observes that while US infections and hospitalizations have recently rolled over, which should lead to a decline in mortality within a few weeks, overall US virus levels remain very high globally, with only a few Latin American countries exhibiting higher infection rates. 

A dual-axis line chart titled "United States virus tracking" illustrates these trends from early April to late July 2020 using seven-day averages. The left axis, measuring current hospitalizations and daily infections up to 70,000, shows new daily infections peaking at nearly 70,000 in mid-July before beginning to decline. Current hospitalizations follow a similar shape, peaking near 60,000 in late July, which matched the initial surge peak in mid-April. The right axis measures daily deaths up to 2,500, showing a peak of over 2,000 in late April, a drop to around 500 in early July, and a subsequent rise back to approximately 1,000 by late July. 

The author poses the question of why US infections are not declining more rapidly despite major drops in former hotspot states like California, Texas, Florida, and the Carolinas. He argues that because the United States does not have internal border controls, focusing purely on state-level data ignores the ease with which citizens cross borders. An accompanying map of the United States, captioned "Without border controls, Hotspots keep shifting," depicts current hotspot states in solid red. Bold black arrows trace the movement of the virus, demonstrating how infections have migrated from former hotspot states along the southern and western borders into new, often less-dense states across the West, Great Plains, Midwest, and Mid-Atlantic.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses COVID-19 transmission trends, exploring whether doctor visits with coronavirus-like symptoms can serve as a reliable leading indicator of infection, and examining the resurgence of cases in Western Europe.

In the first section, the author notes that while current infections in Arizona are falling, doctor visits for COVID-like symptoms have experienced a sharp spike, raising an open question about whether this indicator—collated by Carnegie Mellon University—is worth tracking. The accompanying chart, "Arizona virus tracking," covers the period from late March to early August 2020. It plots new daily infections per million on the left axis against the percentage of doctor visits with COVID-like symptoms on the right axis. The data shows daily infections peaking above 500 per million in early July before dropping below 200 by August, while the doctor visits metric, after falling to around 10% in mid-July, spiked back up to nearly 15% in early August.

The second section focuses on Western Europe, where infections are rising as schools, restaurants, and shops reopen. The author highlights that mobility in continental Europe has recovered significantly, showing only a 15% to 25% decline against a January baseline compared to the 50% to 80% drops seen in April and May. A second chart, "Western Europe infections," tracks the 7-day average of new daily infections per million people over the number of days since total reported cases reached 100. It covers Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands, France, Switzerland, Austria, Germany, and Italy. While Spain exhibits a notable second-wave surge rising toward 80 infections per million around day 150, Italy has experienced the smallest second wave among the depicted nations, remaining flat near the bottom of the scale.

This page addresses two distinct topics: state-level hospital capacity during the pandemic and the rapid normalization of e-commerce spending. 

First, the author examines hospital and ICU bed utilization rates using data from the US Health and Human Services Department. While current utilization levels are high, the commentary notes that most hospital systems are designed for 60% to 70% capacity in normal periods. A bar chart titled "Hotspot state hospital bed and ICU bed utilization rates" compares current utilization against 2018 baselines for several states, including Alabama, Georgia, Nevada, Oregon, Arkansas, Mississippi, North Dakota, Hawaii, Montana, Indiana, Missouri, Oklahoma, Illinois, and Virginia. The visualization reveals that states like Alabama, Arkansas, and Mississippi have seen utilization rates climb well above normal levels, with Alabama's ICU utilization rate reaching approximately 90%. 

Second, the page challenges the popular narrative of a permanent, massive shift toward e-commerce. The author notes that while online spending spiked during the initial April 2020 lockdowns, e-commerce market shares have dropped quickly even as COVID-19 infection levels remain elevated. The author projects that as infection levels continue to decline, e-commerce spending shares will likely end up much closer to their 2019 baselines than their April 2020 peaks. 

This trend is supported by a table detailing the "Evolution of e-commerce shares during the COVID pandemic," which uses internal Chase transaction data to track online spending shares across five sectors. For retail, the online share jumped from a 43% average in 2019 to 70% in April 2020, before cooling to 56% by July and August of 2020. Online healthcare and pharmacy spending rose from a 27% baseline to 45% in April, then fell back to 32%. Online restaurant spending experienced a dramatic spike from an 8% baseline in 2019 to 39% in April 2020, before declining to 25% in the summer. Wholesale and discount clubs saw online shares rise from 10% to 28%, settling at 21% by August. Supermarket online shares rose from 4% to 11% in April and remained flat at 11% through the summer.

This page consists entirely of standard legal disclaimers, regulatory disclosures, and data privacy notes for the J.P. Morgan publication. It outlines the target audience as institutional and professional investors, explains the security and anonymization protocols used for Chase credit and debit card transaction data, and provides jurisdiction-specific regulatory statements for various global markets including the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Europe, the Asia Pacific region, and Australia.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest examines the persistent outperformance of US and Emerging Market equities over European and Japanese markets in 2020, despite the US and EM being major epicenters of the COVID-19 pandemic. He attributes this resilience to the dominance of US megacap tech and internet stocks, contrasting their robust earnings outlooks with the weaker, cyclical sector compositions of Europe and Japan. He criticizes Europe's digital service taxes as protectionist tariffs born from a lack of competitive home-grown tech giants, while briefly referencing the failure of Wirecard AG.

To support this argument, a regional equity market barbell performance table shows a year-to-date US dollar barbell outperformance of 1.5 percent and a local currency barbell outperformance of 2.2 percent. The US, carrying a 62 percent baseline weight and a 72 percent revised weight, delivered a 5.1 percent return in both US dollar and local currency terms. Emerging Markets, with a 12 percent weight, returned negative 0.5 percent in US dollars but 3.8 percent in local currency. In contrast, Europe and Japan posted negative returns, with Europe returning negative 7.7 percent in US dollars and negative 10.7 percent in local currency, and Japan returning negative 5.5 percent in US dollars and negative 8.0 percent in local currency.

A line chart tracking the percentage change in forward 12-month earnings relative to January 2020 highlights the earnings divergence. The top five US firms—Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Facebook—remained remarkably resilient, holding forward earnings expectations steady or slightly positive. In contrast, the S&P 500 excluding these top five firms saw forward earnings expectations fall by roughly 25 percent, while small-cap companies in the Russell 2000 experienced an earnings collapse of nearly 80 percent by mid-year.

A final bar chart contrasts the index compositions of the US, Europe, and Japan, illustrating how high-growth tech drives US markets while older, cyclical sectors dominate elsewhere. In the US, technology represents approximately 34 percent of the total index market cap, while materials, energy, and industrials combine for only 12 percent. In Europe, this relationship is reversed, with technology accounting for just 7 percent of the index, whereas materials, energy, and industrials comprise 27 percent. Japan shows a similar pattern, with technology representing roughly 12 percent of the market cap and the three cyclical sectors accounting for 26 percent.

This page features commentary from Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan regarding the unprecedented international cooperation and funding driving COVID-19 vaccine development. While hopeful that a vaccine might be approved by the end of 2020 with distribution starting in early 2021, Cembalest cautions that this timeline is not an empirical forecast. Instead, it is a sentiment driven by early Phase I trial immunogenicity results and collective optimism. He emphasizes that many of the front-running candidates rely on novel RNA, DNA, or viral vector platforms that have never before been approved in developed countries. 

To clarify these approaches, a table outlines five methods for provoking an antibody response to SARS-CoV-2. Type one involves a live but weakened coronavirus to infect cells and prompt them to make viral proteins, though no select candidates are listed. Type two uses industrially produced coronavirus proteins that the blood recognizes as foreign, with GlaxoSmithKline, Sanofi, and Novavax listed as candidates. Type three utilizes a killed coronavirus, represented by Sinovac and Dynavax. Type four relies on a vector approach, where a different engineered virus, such as a human or ape adenovirus, codes for SARS-CoV-2 spike proteins. Candidates for this approach include CanSino, Oxford, J&J, and Merck/Themis. A footnote warns that no adenoviral vector vaccines had yet demonstrated disease prevention in humans, noting that J&J's Ebola vaccine was under European review and China's approved Ebola vaccine lacked Phase II proof of infection prevention. Finally, type five introduces DNA or RNA to prompt cells to manufacture coronavirus proteins, with Moderna, Innovio, and BioNTech/Pfizer listed as candidates. A corresponding footnote stresses that no DNA or RNA vaccines had ever been approved or tested in large-scale clinical trials prior to COVID-19.

This page from Michael Cembalest's Eye on the Market critiques a bullish August 2020 report by Goldman Sachs, which predicted that the FDA would approve at least one COVID-19 vaccine in 2020 and that large shares of the US and European populations would be vaccinated by mid-2021. Cembalest systematically dismantles Goldman's methodology, first dismissing their reliance on unnamed superforecasters from the Good Judgment project. He then strongly critiques their use of a linear estimation suggesting that 115 vaccine attempts would naturally yield 43 approvals. He argues that vaccine development is non-linear and context-dependent, highlighting that diseases like HIV and Hepatitis C have had zero vaccine approvals despite many attempts, whereas Hepatitis B and Rotavirus have success rates of 50 percent or higher. Furthermore, he cautions that because most COVID-19 vaccine candidates target the same coronavirus spike protein, there is a high risk of collective success or collective failure.

To offer a more rigorous historical perspective, the page includes a stacked bar chart titled Clinical trial outcomes for drug treatments entering Phase II, using 2018 data from Chi Heem Wong and colleagues at the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab. The chart illustrates the percentage of treatments that failed Phase 2, failed Phase 3, or ultimately gained approval across nine categories: Oncology, Central Nervous System, Autoimmune, Endocrinology, Genitourinary, Cardiovascular, Infectious Disease (all), Ophthalmology, and Infectious Disease (vaccines only). The visual data reveals that Oncology has the lowest final approval rate at roughly 15 percent, with about 71 percent failing in Phase 2. In contrast, the category for infectious disease vaccines has the highest approval rate, with approximately 48 percent of trials that enter Phase II successfully securing approval, while around 42 percent fail in Phase 2 and 10 percent fail in Phase 3. Cembalest concludes that while vaccines for infectious diseases historically perform better than other drug categories once they reach Phase II, observers should still wait for actual Phase II and III clinical trial results rather than relying on flawed linear forecasting models.

This page features a written commentary titled "Lost in translation: T-cells and financial industry co-conspirators in the war on science." Author Michael Cembalest discusses the critical scientific distinction between "cross-reactive immune memory" and true "immunity" concerning T-cell research for SARS-CoV-2. Referencing scientist Shane Crotty of the La Jolla Institute of Immunology, the author explains that T-cells typically limit disease severity rather than fully preventing infection or transmission, which makes preventative measures like mask-wearing still highly necessary. 

Cembalest strongly criticizes a financial research firm for spreading medical misinformation by quoting a discredited former ophthalmologist associated with the group "America’s Frontline Doctors." This individual falsely claimed that herd immunity could be reached at only 10% to 20% COVID-19 penetration and that lockdowns and masks were being pushed aggressively by pharmaceutical companies. Crotty himself publicly refuted these claims. Cembalest warns that such misinformation and the mindless reliance on unvetted sources by financial firms are contributing factors to why the United States has had a more difficult time flattening and lowering its virus curve compared to other developed and developing countries.

This page of the publication provides an update on the status of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States as of mid-August 2020, arguing that while infections are declining from their peak levels, the downward trend has flattened and remains gradual. The author highlights that daily mortality levels persist at roughly 1,000 deaths per day, and supporting indicators like the percentage of doctor visits for COVID-like symptoms suggest a slow contraction rather than a rapid drop. 

Two tracking charts illustrate these national trends from early April to mid-August 2020. The first chart, which tracks hospitalizations, daily infections, and daily deaths, shows that new daily infections peaked at nearly 70,000 and current hospitalizations peaked near 50,000 in July before starting a modest decline. Daily deaths, shown on the right axis, peaked above 2,000 in April, declined to around 500 in early July, and then climbed back to the 1,000 mark by mid-August. The adjacent chart compares new daily infections per million people on the left axis with the percentage of doctor visits for COVID-like symptoms on the right axis. Both curves track closely, with the percentage of doctor visits peaking around 7.5% in July and gradually declining to approximately 5.5% by mid-August, confirming a slow-moving retreat of the virus.

The bottom chart compares individual US states to European infection levels, showing that 46 out of 50 US states still have higher infection rates than the European benchmark of 30 infections per million people, indicated by a horizontal dotted line. This chart plots the peak infection rate alongside the latest infection rate for each state, sorted by their trailing seven-day average. The data shows that while most states have improved from their peaks—such as Florida dropping 53% from a peak of over 500 per million, and Texas dropping 30% from its peak—current infection rates in states like Georgia, Florida, Texas, and Nevada remain well above 200 per million. Only a few states, primarily in the Northeast, including New York, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Maine, and Vermont, have successfully pushed their infection rates below the European benchmark.

This page consists of a list of reference links under the heading "Sources (that were not hard to find)." The compiled URLs point to investigative and scientific articles addressing COVID-19 misinformation, specifically focusing on the group "America's Frontline Doctors" and the promotion of hydroxychloroquine as an unproven treatment. The listed sources include reporting from Snopes, MedPage Today, Rolling Stone, and ABC News, which track how hydroxychloroquine misinformation spread through media platforms like Breitbart and was amplified by Donald Trump. Additionally, a Twitter link from immunology researcher Professor Shane Crotty is included to provide scientific context on the virus and immunity.

This page analyzes the trajectory of COVID-19 infections in the United States and evaluates global progress toward herd immunity using antibody data. 

The first section addresses why US COVID-19 infections are not declining more rapidly, arguing that the lack of internal border controls allows the virus to easily spread across state lines. A map of the United States, titled "Without border controls, Hotspots keep shifting," illustrates this movement, with red-shaded states indicating current hotspots and arrows tracing how infections have spread from hotspot states of the previous month into new, often less dense, areas. 

The second section focuses on UK serology results, explaining that the latest antibody tests indicate populations are still far from achieving herd immunity. Large-scale testing from late June to mid-July 2020 revealed antibody rates of only 6% for England and 13% for London. This discussion is supported by a scatter plot titled "Estimated population with antibodies," which plots antibody prevalence on a vertical scale from 0% to 25% against a timeline from March to September 2020. The chart tracks twenty numbered data points corresponding to specific global cities, states, and countries. Aside from New York City, which peak-tested near 22% in June, and New York State and London, which hovered around 13% to 14%, nearly all other surveyed regions remain well below the 10% threshold. Notable reference points include Wuhan, China, near 9% in April; Spain around 5% in May; England at 6% in July; and Tokyo, Japan, showing minimal antibody presence near 1% in June. Other tracked locations include Santa Clara, Gangelt, Los Angeles, Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark, Geneva, Miami-Dade, San Miguel, Brazil, Oregon, Ontario, and Virginia, altogether reinforcing that herd immunity remains a distant milestone.

This page investigates whether the rise of work-from-home policies during the pandemic has accelerated housing demand shifts toward less dense areas with cheaper land. Utilizing data from the American Enterprise Institute, the author notes that while these shifts are occurring in some analyzed cities, they are not uniform across all of them. 

The accompanying chart, titled Post-COVID shift to lower land price locations, tracks the change in the share of mortgage rate locks by density quintile compared to 2019. The horizontal axis measures the land price for a median lot as a share of the median home price, ranging from ten percent to eighty percent. The vertical axis shows the percentage point change in rate locks, ranging from negative four percent to positive five percent. Each city’s data is plotted across five density quintiles, where one represents the lowest density and five represents the highest density.

The chart tracks five major metropolitan areas: Los Angeles-Long Beach, CA; Miami-Port St. Lucie-Fort Lauderdale, FL; New York-Newark, NY-NJ-CT-PA; Phoenix-Mesa, AZ; and Houston-The Woodlands, TX. In cities like Los Angeles and New York, there is a prominent downward trend from low-density quintiles to high-density ones. In Los Angeles, the lowest density quintile, where land accounts for roughly forty percent of the total home price, saw an increase in rate lock share of over three percent, whereas the highest density quintile, where land accounts for nearly seventy-five percent of the home price, saw a drop of over two percent. Similarly, New York's highest density quintile saw a drop of nearly four percent. This confirms that buyers are shifting to cheaper, less dense areas where they can spend more on the home itself rather than expensive land. 

Ultimately, the author highlights that while the economic incentive to move to cheaper, more remote locations has always existed, work-from-home flexibility has allowed buyers to act on it more than ever before. This is framed as an early read that J.P. Morgan will continue to monitor, along with other emerging trends like the cooling of e-commerce spending shares. Data sources cited include the AEI, Census, USDA, FHFA, Optimal Blue, and JPMAM.

This page consists entirely of legal disclaimers, regulatory disclosures, and informational notices regarding the J.P. Morgan Eye on the Market publication, including details on data privacy protocols for Chase credit and debit card transactions, distribution restrictions for non-retail qualified investors, and jurisdictional compliance statements.
