This page from the report argues that the monetary and fiscal policy response to the COVID-19 pandemic represents the largest debt monetization exercise in recorded history, dwarfing previous economic crises. Author Michael Cembalest discusses IMF projections indicating that advanced economies' fiscal deficits in 2021 will remain more than double their 2019 levels, driving overall debt-to-GDP ratios up from 105 percent to 132 percent. While such rapid balance-sheet expansion and ballooning deficits would typically trigger capital flight and a balance-of-payments crisis in emerging markets, developed nations are leveraging excess capacity to boost consumption and investment without immediate inflation. Cembalest aligns with the equity market's short-term bullish outlook, noting that while excessive monetization historically triggered the stagflation of the 1970s, it took years to materialize. For now, these policies effectively sustain private sector demand, benefiting both public and private entities.

To illustrate the unprecedented scale of this intervention, the page features a scatter plot titled "Debt monetization response to global virus crisis eclipses everything else." The chart plots the change in fiscal deficit against the change in central bank balance sheets, both measured as a percentage of GDP relative to pre-crisis levels. This visualization contrasts the 2020 Global Virus Crisis (GVC) with the 2008–2009 Global Financial Crisis (GFC), the 1930s Great Depression, World War II, and the 2012 Eurozone Balance of Payments Crisis. 

During the 2020 GVC, the United States saw a balance sheet expansion of roughly 13.5 percent of GDP coupled with a fiscal deficit increase of nearly 15 percent of GDP. Similarly, the United Kingdom experienced a 12 percent increase in its balance sheet and a 14 percent rise in its fiscal deficit, while Japan recorded a 17 percent balance sheet expansion alongside an 11 percent deficit increase. The Eurozone's response during the GVC was also substantial, with its balance sheet expanding by nearly 14.5 percent and its deficit rising by about 8 percent. 

By comparison, during the 2008–2009 GFC, the corresponding policy expansions were far more modest: the United States recorded a 10 percent balance sheet change and a 9 percent deficit increase, while the United United Kingdom, Japan, and the Eurozone plotted much lower, with Eurozone GFC metrics clustering near 4.5 percent for both axes. Even the policy responses to the Great Depression in the United States showed a more restrained 10 percent balance sheet change and 6 percent deficit increase. Only United States spending during World War II surpassed the GVC in fiscal deficit growth, surging to over 18 percent of GDP, though its corresponding central bank balance sheet expansion was much lower at under 6 percent of GDP.

This commentary discusses recent US political and regulatory developments concerning COVID-19 treatments, specifically focusing on the White House's controversial push for convalescent plasma. The author critiques President Trump's announcement of an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for the treatment, noting it lacked the rigorous, randomized controlled trial results that preceded the EUA for Remdesivir. While a Mayo Clinic observational study showed lower mortality rates for patients treated within three days of diagnosis compared to those treated later—with seven-day mortality at 8.7 percent versus 11.9 percent, and thirty-day mortality at 21.6 percent versus 26.7 percent—the author argues that without randomized trials, patient characteristics, dosages, and treatment settings remain uncontrolled, reminiscent of earlier premature hype around hydroxychloroquine. 

Key scientific figures, including Dr. Anthony Fauci and the director of the National Institutes of Health, discouraged the EUA due to weak data. The rollout was further marred by controversy when the FDA Commissioner admitted to misrepresenting the results, and the study's main authors rejected the White House's claim of a 35 percent mortality improvement. Additionally, the text quotes Derek Lowe from Translational Medicine, who warns that these politically motivated actions sow public doubt and harm the chances of an orderly, medically justified vaccine rollout. Looking ahead, the author notes that while a randomized trial is underway in the United Kingdom, progress is slow due to low hospitalization rates. Furthermore, because convalescent plasma is difficult to scale due to donor variability, scientists are increasingly focused on monoclonal antibodies manufactured in bioreactors as a more promising, scalable alternative.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market commentary addresses reports that the Trump Administration might bypass standard US regulatory processes to grant an Emergency Use Authorization for the Oxford/AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine before the 2020 presidential election. The author explains that this novel adenovirus vector vaccine utilizes a chimpanzee virus to instruct cells to produce spike proteins—a method never previously approved in the developed world. While AstraZeneca’s global Phase III trials span 50,000 participants across the UK, US, South Africa, and Brazil, the administration is reportedly considering approval based solely on the UK's 10,000-participant trial. This falls far short of the FDA's standard 30,000-participant minimum. The author emphasizes that because vaccines are administered to healthy populations to prevent a disease with a sub-one-percent mortality rate, safety and efficacy standards must remain exceptionally high. Bypassing these standards risks further damaging American vaccine confidence, which already ranks below the international median. The commentary concludes by citing sources such as the Financial Times and a New York Times piece critical of the federal government's scientific competency.

This page explores the puzzlingly high COVID-19 infection rates in Latin America compared to other emerging markets, alongside an analysis of the United States’ fitful economic reopening. 

The author begins by raising an open question, noting that there is no obvious explanation in terms of health systems, mobility, or behavioral dynamics to explain why Latin America has seen far higher infection levels than the rest of the developing world. To illustrate this, the first chart, "EM World infections," tracks new daily infections per million people on a 7-day average starting from the day total cases reached 100. It reveals that South America dramatically outpaced all other developing regions, surging past 160 cases per million by day 150, while Eastern Europe, the Middle East, Emerging Asia, and Africa all remained flat, well below 40 cases per million. A companion chart, "Latin America infections," breaks this down by country on a 14-day average. It shows Chile peaking early above 250 cases per million before declining, while Peru climbs back toward 250, and Brazil, Colombia, and Argentina all trend sharply upward between 150 and 200 cases per million by day 150. For context, the author notes that the contemporary US infection level stood at 125 per million, and Europe's at 40 per million.

The bottom half of the page shifts to US consumer behavior. A chart on national credit and debit card spending trends monitors year-over-year changes in "social distancing spending"—which includes in-person transactions at retail stores, hotels, restaurants, and amusement parks. This spending bottomed out near -70% in April, recovered steadily to about -30% by mid-June, and then plateaued through July as US infections spiked, before beginning to rise again toward -25% in August. 

A final chart compares airline credit and debit card spending against TSA checkpoint traveler volumes. Both metrics crashed by roughly 95% in April. However, by August, TSA traveler numbers recovered slightly faster, reaching about -70% year-over-year, while actual airline spending lagged behind at roughly -85%. The author infers from this divergence that the travel recovery is being driven by shorter trips, heavily discounted fares, and a persistent lack of lucrative business travel.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, "Eye on the Market," provides an analysis comparing the trajectory, societal mobility, and mortality rates of COVID-19 infections between the United States and Europe. The author notes that US infections are finally falling at a rate similar to what Europe experienced three months prior, though he cautions against expecting a linear decline due to the reopening of schools and businesses. Conversely, Europe's reopening has led to a modest rise in infections. 

A primary focus of the page is the distinction between first and second infection waves, specifically highlighting that the second waves are displaying much lower mortality rates. The author attributes this lower mortality to a younger average cohort of infected individuals and the introduction of better clinical treatments, such as anti-coagulants and steroids like Dexamethasone, which reduce vascular and pulmonary stress in hospitalized patients. 

The first chart, titled "US vs Europe infections," plots new daily infections per million people (7-day average) against the number of days after total reported cases reached 100. It shows that Europe’s initial wave peaked near 75 cases per million around day 50 before falling to low levels and showing a modest uptick past day 150. Meanwhile, the US experienced a primary peak of roughly 85 cases near day 50, followed by a massive secondary wave that spiked to over 200 cases per million around day 135, before collapsing back down to about 140 cases by day 170. 

The second chart, "Regional mobility data," tracks the percentage change from baseline activity for retail, restaurants, transit, and workplaces from February 12 to July 11, 2020. It illustrates a sharp drop in mobility for both regions during March, with Europe hitting a deeper trough of roughly -75% in mid-April compared to the US trough of about -50%. By mid-July, mobility in both regions had recovered to similarly situated levels of approximately -25% below baseline.

The final two dual-axis charts illustrate the divergence between infection rates and mortality. The chart for Europe compares infections per million on the left axis (ranging from 0 to 80) and deaths per million on the right axis (ranging from 0 to 10) between March and late July. In April, the European infection peak of about 75 per million corresponded with a peak of 8 deaths per million. By late July, infections rose to roughly 40 per million, yet deaths remained nearly flat, close to zero. The chart for the US uses a left axis of 0 to 250 infections per million and a right axis of 0 to 8 deaths per million over the same period. In the spring wave, US infections of about 100 per million peaked alongside deaths of approximately 6.5 per million. However, during the summer wave in July, while infections surged past 200 per million, the mortality rate peaked much lower, at roughly 3 deaths per million, demonstrating a significantly lower relative mortality rate.

This commentary examines the rapid pace of the US economic recovery following the initial COVID-19 pandemic shock, comparing it favorably to the much slower rebound after the 2008 financial crisis. The author highlights that while President Donald Trump's once-historically strong economic and market tailwinds have largely dissipated compared to late 2019, the economy is still bouncing back quickly. Q3 GDP growth is projected to reach an annualized rate of 35%, while the unemployment rate is forecast to decline to 7% by the end of 2020 and further to 5.5% by the end of 2021. Additional fiscal stimulus from Congress remains a toss-up due to a compressed legislative calendar ahead of the election. 

Four charts illustrate these economic developments. The first chart, depicting US manufacturing industrial production from 2006 to 2020 using an index where 2012 equals 100, shows a historic, near-vertical drop in early 2020 from about 103 down to approximately 83, followed by a sharp, incomplete V-shaped rebound to around 97. 

The second chart displays real retail sales in billions of 1982–1984 US dollars, showing that after a dramatic pandemic-induced plunge from over 200 billion down to around 163 billion, retail sales staged an almost complete recovery back above the 200 billion mark by mid-2020. A humorous footnote from the author attributes some of this retail rebound to personal quarantine purchases of DeWalt power tools for home projects.

The third chart combines unemployment and job openings from 2006 to August 2020 on a dual-axis graph. It shows that both the ratio of unemployed persons per job opening and the overall unemployment rate plummeted to near-record lows by late 2019, only to spike violently in early 2020, with the unemployment rate peaking near 15% before starting to trend downward. 

The final chart shows a high-frequency manufacturing tracker of weekly year-over-year percentage changes in 2020. This index, which aggregates lumber, steel, coal production, electricity output, and railroad traffic, reveals a deep contraction that bottomed out around negative 23% in late April before recovering to approximately negative 10% by late July. 

Key entities discussed on this page include Joe Biden, Donald Trump, Dwight Eisenhower, Bill Clinton, the US Congress, the Federal Reserve, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and China, specifically regarding its unfulfilled trade deal commitments.

This page discusses the potential negative tipping points for megacap technology stocks, focusing on the twin pressures of revived antitrust policy and market rotation driven by a potential COVID-19 vaccine. In terms of regulatory risks, the author notes that Attorney General Bill Barr has pushed to expedite an antitrust case against Google, which holds a ninety percent share of global web searches and a third of online advertising spend. Furthermore, a potential Biden administration is expected to step up antitrust enforcement via the Sherman and Clayton Acts and may look to revoke Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act to remove liability protections for platforms like Facebook, though a full breakup of big tech is deemed unlikely. An extensive footnote also addresses risks to Apple, explaining that a U.S. executive order targeting Chinese applications like WeChat and TikTok could severely harm Apple's business in China, where WeChat is central to the lives of nine hundred million citizens. 

A second risk to the outperformance of megacap growth stocks is the potential introduction of a COVID-19 vaccine, which would likely boost hard-hit value stocks by increasing mobility. This market dynamic is demonstrated in a bar chart titled "Growth stock correlation to volume of daily news flow" covering February through August 2020. Based on data from Empirical Research Partners' "Big Grower" universe, the chart shows that relative returns on growth stocks are positively correlated with news flow about the Federal Reserve (at approximately positive fourteen), inflation (around positive nine), and interest rates (near positive three). In contrast, growth stocks are negatively correlated with news stories on the election (around negative six), a vaccine (at negative ten), and fiscal stimulus (at negative sixteen). The author concludes that while vaccine benefits might take months to fully materialize, financial markets are likely to price these expectations in early, posing a near-term headwind for growth stocks.

This page discusses the unprecedented fiscal and monetary costs of the economic recovery from the 2020 global virus crisis (GVC), noting that the expansion of fiscal deficits and central bank balance sheets has eclipsed any prior crisis on record. The author references Modern Monetary Theory (MMT), whose proponents argue that debt monetization is sustainable when there is excess capacity and low inflation risk. Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell's Jackson Hole comments are noted as indicating a commitment to letting inflation rise above long-term targets, a policy stance that, combined with unconstrained fiscal deficits, has driven the US recovery. However, the author warns that US debt may exceed its World War II peak for the foreseeable future and raises the question of what would be required to reduce federal debt to its pre-virus level of 80% of GDP by the end of the decade.

Three charts support these arguments. The first scatter plot, "Debt monetization response to global virus crisis eclipses everything else," compares the change in government fiscal deficits against the change in central bank balance sheets, both as a percentage of GDP, relative to pre-crisis levels. It shows that the policy response to the GVC for the US, UK, Eurozone, and Japan far exceeds prior crises. For instance, the US GVC response shows a fiscal deficit increase of nearly 15% of GDP and a central bank balance sheet expansion of roughly 13% of GDP, while Japan’s central bank balance sheet expanded by over 20% of GDP. This is contrasted with historical episodes like the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), where expansions were much milder, and World War II, which saw a major deficit increase of about 17% of GDP but only a 5% change in the central bank balance sheet.

The second chart, "Gross federal debt held by the public," plots US public debt as a percentage of GDP from 1940 to 2020, with estimates for 2020 and 2021. The curve highlights a sharp spike in debt during World War II to over 100% of GDP, followed by a long decline into the 1970s, and a subsequent steady climb that accelerates sharply with the GVC, pushing debt estimates for 2020 and 2021 near the 100% mark once again. 

The final chart, "Fed projections vs actual Fed funds rate," details the Fed funds rate from 2012 to 2022. It plots the actual effective Fed funds rate as a solid black line against a series of grey lines representing median FOMC projections made at different points in time. The chart illustrates a persistent upward bias in the Fed's forecasts, which repeatedly projected rates climbing toward 3.0% or 3.5%, while the actual rate remained near zero for years, peaked briefly near 2.5% in 2019, and plummeted back to zero in 2020.

This page analyzes the fiscal implications of the proposed Biden policy agenda versus Trump-era policies, noting that while US Federal debt levels may rise further, Biden's tax and spending plans are not necessarily an a priori negative for economic growth. The author argues that a large part of Biden's spending targets areas with high growth multipliers, though the massive increase in corporate taxes could negatively impact short-term corporate profits and equity valuations.

To illustrate these points, the page features three charts. The first, a stacked bar chart titled "The Biden Agenda," details projected taxation and spending in trillions of dollars over a 10-year period. On the taxation side, revenue is raised through taxes on the wealthy, industry-specific taxes, corporate tax hikes and base broadening, and payroll taxes on incomes over $400,000, offset slightly by tax cuts for homebuyers and caregivers. On the spending side, investments are concentrated in healthcare, infrastructure and jobs, education, housing, and entitlement expansion, partially offset by drug price reforms.

The second chart, titled "CBO estimates of growth multipliers by policy," shows the range of change in economic output per dollar of fiscal policy across different tax cuts and spending categories. It highlights that spending policies have significantly higher multipliers than tax cuts. For example, federal government purchases of goods and services, federal transfers to states for infrastructure, and transfer payments to low-income individuals have some of the highest potential multipliers, ranging up to 2.5x. Conversely, corporate tax cuts and one-year tax cuts for higher-income earners have the lowest estimated multipliers, generally staying below 0.5x.

The third chart compares "Biden proposed corporate tax increase vs Trump corporate tax cuts" in trillions of dollars over 10 years, broken down by corporate entity tax and pass-through entity tax. This visual emphasizes that Biden's proposed tax increases of approximately $2.5 trillion are multiples higher than Trump's 2017 tax cuts, which reduced taxes by roughly $0.8 trillion. The author notes that even though Biden proposes removing only half of Trump's corporate tax rate cut, his additional base broadening and sector-specific tax proposals drive the large overall tax increase. 

Footnotes on the page address Biden's loose support for increasing the State and Local Tax (SALT) deduction from its current $10,000 cap, noting that without a full restoration of this deduction, taxes on the wealthy could rise by $2.5 trillion. They also attribute the multiplier data to a 2015 Congressional Budget Office paper by Charles Whalen and Felix Reichling.

In this J.P. Morgan publication, Michael Cembalest discusses the formidable policy actions required to reduce US Federal debt to its pre-pandemic level of 80% of GDP by 2030. The author argues that achieving this goal would require politically and economically unfeasible scenarios: either the largest tax hikes or spending cuts in US history, a GDP growth boom not seen in 50 years, or elevated but carefully managed inflation. Since these paths are highly unlikely, Cembalest asserts that the US will have to adapt to high levels of debt. While current deficit spending supports private sector demand, he warns that this unprecedented fiscal experiment could compromise future US flexibility to respond to geopolitical, climate, or other national emergencies. 

To provide context, the author notes that out of 52 historical cases where national debt-to-GDP exceeded 130%, 51 ended in default or severe inflation, with modern-day Japan being the sole exception. He references Stanford economist John Cochrane, noting that while the US grew out of its post-World War II debt through strong supply-side growth in a deregulated economy, those conditions do not characterize the modern world. In a detailed footnote, Cembalest draws a parallel between these high-debt experiments and other unprecedented endeavors, such as Florida's decision to release 750 million genetically modified mosquitoes, which critics fear could result in insecticide-resistant hybrid species.

The analysis is supported by four charts showing historical trends and future projections. The first chart, which examines raising tax revenues to record-high levels, tracks tax revenue as a percentage of GDP from 1935 to 2025. It shows that revenues historically hovered between 15% and 20%, but the projection indicates that a sharp spike to nearly 23% of GDP by 2025 would be required to meet the debt reduction goal. 

The second chart, focusing on cutting spending to pre-World War II levels, displays government spending as a percentage of GDP from 1930 to 2030. Following a spike of around 30% in 2020, the projection shows that government spending would need to fall drastically to approximately 15% by 2030 to match pre-World War II spending levels.

The third chart, illustrating the need to reproduce the 1960s growth boom, plots the five-year annualized percentage change in real GDP from 1936 to 2026. Highlighting a peak of over 6% GDP growth in the mid-1960s, the projection shows that real GDP growth would need to experience a dramatic recovery back to the 5% to 6% range by the mid-2020s.

The fourth chart, which looks at generating higher but controlled inflation, tracks the year-over-year percentage change in headline CPI from 1937 to 2027. The chart indicates that inflation would need to rise and stabilize at a steady 5% through the mid-2020s, a significant departure from the lower inflation environment observed over the previous decade. Data sources for these charts include the Office of Management and Budget, the Congressional Budget Office, the Bureau of Economic Analysis, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page, titled "Appendix I: COVID and The Fountainhead," discusses the relationship between COVID-19 infections and mortality rates in the late summer of 2020. The author, Michael Cembalest, observes that mortality rates collapsed relative to infections across the developed world. He attributes this positive trend to a younger cohort of recent infections, improved medical interventions like selective ventilation and the use of anticoagulants and steroids, and less overwhelmed healthcare systems. 

The author addresses arguments that COVID-19 data is skewed by overly sensitive PCR tests, misclassified hospitalizations, and misattributed deaths. While acknowledging that standardizing PCR equipment cycle thresholds could reduce exaggerated measures of infectiousness, he argues against dismissing the data entirely. He notes that PCR tests are crucial for monitoring community spread and strongly correlate with hospitalizations, with a median state correlation of 80 percent. Additionally, contacts at Johns Hopkins confirmed to the author that the national number of misclassified COVID hospitalizations is very small. In the footnotes, the author discusses how high-cycle PCR tests of 35 to 40 cycles can detect trace, non-contagious amounts of the virus, whereas 30 to 32 cycles might be more appropriate, though a United Kingdom study found that 8 percent of samples above 35 cycles were still infectious. He suggests a combination of PCR testing, antigen testing, and university-style dorm wastewater monitoring as a better path forward.

Two charts support these observations, plotting daily infections per million on the left-hand axis against deaths per million on the right-hand axis from March 1 to August 28, 2020, using data from Johns Hopkins University and Our World in Data. 

The first chart, focusing on the developed world excluding the United States, shows that infections peaked near 50 per million in early April, bottomed out near 10 in June, and rose back near 50 per million by late August. Despite this late-summer resurgence in infections, deaths collapsed from a peak of about 5.5 per million in mid-April to near zero by late August, illustrating a clear decoupling of the two metrics. 

The second chart displays the same metrics for the United States. US infections peaked around 75 per million in April, declined slightly, and then surged to a much higher second peak of over 200 per million in late July before dropping to around 150 per million by late August. US deaths peaked near 7 per million in late April and experienced only a moderate rise to around 3.5 per million in August before starting to trend downward again, showing that mortality remained significantly lower during the summer surge than during the spring wave. 

The author concludes by comparing dogmatic data skeptics to an Amtrak passenger he encountered reading Ayn Rand's "The Fountainhead," suggesting that an over-reliance on a single narrative prevents people from synthesizing contradictory information or understanding alternative viewpoints.

Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan argues against minimizing COVID-19 risks, urging observers to avoid debating mortality classifications by focusing on excess deaths. He points out that US weekly deaths consistently exceed the baseline threshold and that daily US COVID deaths remain 15 to 20 times higher per person than in Europe. Cembalest also cautions against overinterpreting a limited Swedish T-cell study, noting that only three participants recovered without antibodies, and points to Shane Crotty’s research at the La Jolla Institute of Immunology as the gold standard for understanding immunity. While acknowledging the immense stress of school closings, he emphasizes that safe reopening requires driving down infection rates so that contact-tracing and containment can function, warning that large gatherings present significant risks.

To illustrate reopening strategies, the page features a bar chart detailing Fall 2020 reopening plans for four-year colleges. It shows that public colleges leaned heavily into primarily online education at around 37% and hybrid models at 25%, while private colleges favored primarily in-person models at over 30%. Fully online plans were less common, accounting for roughly 3% of public and 8% of private colleges. 

A second chart displays K-12 school district reopening plans, showing that 46% of surveyed districts selected remote learning only, 28% opted for hybrid or partial reopening, 24% planned for a full in-person reopening, and less than 1% remained undecided. 

A chart tracking weekly US deaths from all causes shows total deaths from January through mid-August. The chart reveals a distinct surge of excess deaths rising well above the standard death threshold of approximately 55,000 to 58,000 weekly deaths. This surge peaked in mid-April near 80,000 total deaths and remained elevated through the summer. 

Lastly, a table estimates the probability that at least one COVID-19 positive individual is present at gatherings of different sizes in Texas's Dallas and Tarrant Counties. At a gathering size of 10, the chance was 26% in Dallas and 16% in Tarrant. These probabilities rose sharply to 52% and 36% for gatherings of 25; 78% and 59% for gatherings of 50; and 95% and 83% for gatherings of 100 people.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" addresses the dominance of technology and social media companies in US equity markets and the accompanying antitrust and valuation risks. Michael Cembalest points out that while S&P 500 earnings fell 33 percent year-over-year in the second quarter of 2020, profit margins declined only slightly and remained at the high end of their post-1950s range, with free cash flow at an all-time high when excluding financials, energy, and REITs. He highlights that pre-tax margins for technology and pharma/biotech companies were between 20 percent and 30 percent, more than double the margins of cyclical and consumer staple sectors. This strong performance of US tech and social media giants is identified as the primary driver of US equity outperformance over Europe and Japan. However, Cembalest warns that valuation is becoming a significant headwind, nearing levels seen in 1999, characterized by highly concentrated market-cap contributions from just a few large tech and social media firms.

Six charts support these assertions. The first chart, titled "S&P 500 ex-financials and REITs net profit margins," applies a three-month smoothing from 1952 to 2020 on a y-axis of 3 percent to 12 percent. It illustrates that the Q2 2020 net profit margin remained remarkably high, hovering near 9 percent, well above historical lows of around 4 percent seen in the 1980s. 

The second chart, "S&P 500 price/earnings," tracks the ratio of price to forward two-year earnings per share from 1990 to 2020 on an 8x to 26x scale. A red dot highlights that by late 2020, this multiple had climbed back up to over 22x, nearing the historic peak of 24x seen around the dot-com bubble in 2000. 

The third chart, "Contribution of top firms to overall US market cap" spanning 1990 to 2020, plots the percentage contribution on a y-axis from 10 percent to 45 percent. It compares the top 20 firms, which peaked above 40 percent in 2020, against the top 5 firms—specifically named as Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Facebook—which surged past 20 percent in 2020, representing the largest share of US market capitalization since 1990. 

The fourth chart, "S&P 500 megacap outperformance," shows the performance of market-cap weighted minus equal-weighted S&P 500 index from -30 to 60. It compares the 1997 to 2002 period, where outperformance peaked near 50 in 2000 before collapsing, with the 2017 to 2020 period, where the red line reached nearly 25 by 2020. 

The fifth chart displays the "Median free cash flow margin for 10 largest stocks within S&P 500 by market cap," showing the trailing 12-month free cash flow margin from 5 percent to 25 percent between 1991 and 2020. This metric shows a long-term upward trend, peaking near 23 percent in 2020, highlighting that these megacap firms are highly profitable compared to the non-profitable tech stars of the late 1990s. 

The sixth chart plots the "Top 10 companies in S&P 500 by market cap compared to bottom 100 companies by P/E" using the ratio of median forward P/E ratios on a 1.0x to 6.0x scale from 1995 to 2020. This ratio spiked to nearly 5.5x during the dot-com era, fell to below 1.5x, and has since steadily risen to approximately 3.0x by 2020. 

While noting that today's megacaps are vastly more profitable than their 1999 counterparts and the valuation gap with value stocks is less extreme, Cembalest cautions that this highly concentrated environment is unstable. He argues that a broader, more diversified earnings recovery will be essential to sustain the market and prevent frequent profit-taking or severe market corrections.

This page consists entirely of legal and regulatory disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication, detailing distribution conditions and regulatory oversight across various global jurisdictions. It provides specific licensing, compliance, and distribution statements for Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin American countries, including Brazil and Mexico. It notes that the material is intended for personal use and specifies the restrictions on public offerings and solicitations in these regions.

This appendix details the projected financial impacts of Joe Biden's proposed taxation and spending agenda, presented in two comprehensive tables compiled by J.P. Morgan Asset Management and Cornerstone Macro Research. 

The first table outlines the taxation agenda, listing eighteen tax proposals designed to generate a net total of 4,464 billion dollars in new revenue. The largest proposed revenue generator is a raise in the corporate tax rate to 28 percent, which is projected to yield 1,300 billion dollars by eliminating roughly half of the corporate tax cuts enacted under the Trump administration. The second largest item is the application of a 12.4 percent payroll tax on income above 400 thousand dollars, split between employers and employees, to generate 962 billion dollars; the commentary notes that this would likely require a Senate supermajority. Other significant revenue provisions include raising the top marginal income tax rate and limiting itemizations (520 billion dollars), increasing individual tax compliance and enforcement (481 billion dollars), and taxing capital gains as ordinary income for individuals with an adjusted gross income over 1 million dollars (448 billion dollars). These tax increases are offset by targeted tax credits, including a 300 billion dollar credit for first-time homebuyers, a 100 billion dollar expansion of the Child and Dependent Care Tax Credit, and a 98 billion dollar credit for informal caregivers.

The second table details the spending agenda, outlining eleven spending categories that sum to 7,412 billion dollars in total spending increases. The single largest spending proposal is healthcare, totaling 1,950 billion dollars, which involves expanding Affordable Care Act subsidies, establishing a public option, and automatically enrolling low-income individuals. This is followed closely by 1,700 billion dollars for infrastructure and clean energy programs, excluding housing, to rebuild transit networks, establish 5G and universal broadband, and transition to a carbon-pollution-free power sector. Education is also a major focus, with 750 billion dollars allocated to Pre-K and K-12 schooling, and another 750 billion dollars directed toward higher education, which includes providing debt-free community college and tuition-free public university for families earning less than 125 thousand dollars. Additional major spending includes 750 billion dollars for the "Made in America" federal procurement and job training plan, 547 billion dollars for guaranteed paid family and medical leave, and 450 billion dollars each for the Caring Economy Agenda and expanding Social Security benefits. These expenditures are partially offset by 400 billion dollars in savings achieved through proposed drug price reforms, which would allow the government to negotiate prices and cap price increases at inflation.

This page outlines the rules, deadlines, and legal procedures governing US presidential elections, specifically addressing concerns surrounding the legitimacy of mail-in voting. The author emphasizes that states have over a month—from election day on November 3 to the safe-harbor deadline on December 8—to count mail-in ballots and certify results before electors meet on December 14. To contextualize potential political friction, the text notes the party affiliations of Secretaries of State in key states, specifically listing Democratic election officials in Arizona, Colorado, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Wisconsin, alongside Republican officials in Florida, Iowa, and Ohio. 

The document details the constitutional process for Congressional objections to electoral results, noting that objections must be debated and agreed upon by both houses of the newly seated 117th Congress. If no candidate reaches the 270-vote majority by January 6, a constitutional default process is triggered, with the author postulating that unresolvable disputes over mail-in ballots amid the COVID-19 pandemic present the most likely risk of such an outcome. Finally, a detailed footnote addresses the historical risks of vote-by-mail systems, noting that while approximately 4% of mail-in ballots were lost or miscounted in 2016, this rate is comparable to the 4% to 6% of lost in-person votes in 2000. Citing election expert Charles Stewart from MIT, the author suggests that the net risk of a surge in mail-in voting on the election outcome is negligible.

This page analyzes the complex constitutional mechanisms of a potential U.S. contingent election alongside an update on Chinese compliance with the Phase One trade agreement. 

First, the author explains what occurs if no presidential candidate secures a 270 electoral vote majority. In this scenario, the decision shifts to the newly elected Congress. The House of Representatives selects the President, where each state delegation gets a single, equal vote regardless of population size. This means the sole representative from Alaska holds the same voting weight as the entire fifty-three-member California delegation. A simple majority of twenty-six states is required to win. Meanwhile, the Senate elects the Vice President, with each senator casting an individual vote to reach a simple majority of fifty-one votes. The author notes that a contingent election has not occurred since 1836, but if state delegations voted according to the party balance in the 116th Congress, Donald Trump would carry twenty-six states and Joe Biden would carry twenty-four. Under the Twentieth Amendment, if the House is deadlocked by January 20th, the newly selected Vice President serves as acting President, followed by the Speaker of the House as a final temporary stop-gap.

Second, the page assesses China’s progress on its Phase One trade deal purchase commitments through July 2020. During this period, China purchased only 30 percent of its total commitment, with supply disruptions from the pandemic in the United States slowing energy and manufacturing imports. An accompanying bar chart, titled Progress of US-China Phase 1 purchase agreement, illustrates these shortfalls across three major categories: agriculture, manufacturing, and energy. For agriculture, China’s imports reached 8 billion dollars against a 33 billion dollar target, representing 23 percent completion. In manufacturing, imports reached 28 billion dollars against an 83 billion dollar target, which is 34 percent of the goal. Energy lagged furthest behind, with imports of 4 billion dollars representing only 14 percent of the 26 billion dollar target. Despite the slow start, the author forecasts that agricultural purchases are poised to rebound in the latter half of the year due to a recovery in China's hog cycle following losses from African Swine Fever.

This page consists entirely of standard regulatory and legal disclosures for the publication, outlining compliance, distribution restrictions, and licensing details across several global jurisdictions. It covers specific regulatory frameworks and bodies in Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America. Key entities mentioned include the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Securities and Futures Commission of Hong Kong, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, and the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission. The page also defines restrictions concerning wholesale clients in Australia under the Corporations Act 2001 and private offering compliance in Latin American nations. No financial charts, market analyses, or investment forecasts are featured on this page.

In this edition of Eye on the Market, Michael Cembalest discusses the upcoming 2020 US presidential election, framing it as a referendum on the American economic and social system alongside the rising possibility of a contested transfer of power. Cembalest challenges a J.P. Morgan Investment Bank report that suggested investors position for a Trump re-election based on historical patterns from 1960 to 1972, which showed that the perception of violent protests boosted Republican vote shares by 2% to 8%. Cembalest argues that the modern context is fundamentally different. 

To illustrate this, two side-by-side line charts present historical data. The first chart, based on Pew Research data from 1958 to 2018, shows the percentage of the population that trusts the Federal government all or most of the time. This metric peaked above 70% in the early 1960s but has steadily declined over the decades, landing near 20% by 2018. The second chart, using FBI and Congressional Research Service data from 1960 to 2016, shows that the violent crime rate per 100,000 people was very low in 1960 at under 200, rose steadily to a peak of over 700 in the early 1990s, and subsequently declined to under 400 by 2016. Cembalest highlights that unlike the 1960s, current trust in the government is very low, and a September 2020 CNN/SSRS poll found that 58% of Americans considered the Trump administration's response to protests "more harmful" compared to 33% who found it "more helpful."

The text transitions to how the American system compares globally. Cembalest notes that the US ranks at the very top of World Bank high-income countries for equity investors and entrepreneurs due to low regulatory and tax burdens, easy hiring and firing, and an efficient legal system. This drives top-decile profit growth and equity returns, which is relevant to the 55% to 60% of US households that own equities. For workers, the US ranks above average on median income, housing costs, and the OECD's Better Life index. Finally, the author notes that financial markets are pricing in a substantial chance of a Democratic sweep, marked by the underperformance of tax-sensitive stocks and a record 25% valuation discount of healthcare stocks relative to the S&P 500.

This page from "Eye on the Market" focuses on the legal, procedural, and political uncertainties surrounding the 2020 US presidential election, specifically focusing on the post-election period starting November 3rd. Author Michael Cembalest outlines three baseline actions Congress will face on January 6th: confirming the Electoral College results, initiating a Contingent Election in the House if no candidate wins a simple majority, or designating the Speaker of the House as Acting President if a Contingent Election fails by January 20th. 

Cembalest details four critical, unresolved uncertainties that complicate this process. First, he questions whether the six-week window between election day and the Electoral College meeting on December 14th is sufficient to count and recount potentially massive volumes of mail-in and absentee ballots, which could exceed 30% to 40% in some states. Second, there is a risk that a state could submit multiple conflicting sets of electoral results—such as separate submissions from the Governor, Secretary of State, or State Legislature—leaving Congress and the Vice President to resolve the dispute. Third, a candidate could win with less than 270 electoral votes if some votes are rejected or delayed, which would lower the winning threshold to a simple majority of accepted votes. Finally, control of the newly seated 117th Congress, particularly the Senate, might remain unknown in early January due to close, unresolved races, further complicating the oversight and intervention process. The analysis references comments and analysis from legal experts such as Michael Morley, Donald Ayer, and Randall Eliason, alongside discussions regarding the position of President Trump and Attorney General William Barr on the mail-in voting process and the peaceful transfer of power.

This page outlines several potential election-related risks and "unknown unknowns" surrounding the 2020 US Presidential Election, focusing on technical and legal complications after the December 14 Electoral College deadline. Michael Cembalest discusses the ramifications of late reporting and incomplete reporting if states fail to finish counts or submit results after December 14. He raises questions about the impact of faithless electors shifting electoral outcomes, Congress potentially violating its own rules under the Electoral Count Act, and Congress overruling federal court decisions regarding election litigation. Additionally, he warns of a nightmare scenario featuring dueling inaugurations if a split Congress disagrees on the certified winner, drawing historical parallels to the disputed election of 1876.

Two appendix charts are featured at the bottom of the page. The first chart, titled Stocks sensitive to higher tax rates underperforming in 2020, illustrates the relative return of high-tax stocks versus low-tax stocks from 2017 through late September 2020, with a baseline index of 100 set in January 2017. The chart highlights the passage of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act in late 2017, which drove the index from under 100 to nearly 120 in 2018, followed by a steady decline in 2020 back down to approximately 110. The second chart, titled Healthcare sector valuation premium/(discount) vs S&P 500, tracks the percentage valuation premium or discount of the healthcare sector relative to the broader index from 1991 to late September 2020. The data shows significant volatility, with healthcare trading at a premium of over 40 percent around 2001, but dropping into steep discounts of around negative 25 percent in both the early 1990s and the early 2010s, with a final downward trend toward negative 20 percent in late 2020.

This page critiques the efficacy and equity of the United States' legal, economic, and social systems. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that while the US excels at creating a favorable environment for investors and entrepreneurs, it fails or underperforms peer nations on workers' security, basic public welfare, wealth distribution, and civil and criminal justice. He notes that these systemic issues have persisted for decades, but suggests that in 2020, voters may judge the incumbent presidential administration on whether these problems were mitigated or exacerbated.

The central visual is a comprehensive horizontal bar chart titled "How well does the US 'system' work, and for whom?" which ranks the United States against the World Bank's 34 high-income countries. On this index, a score of 100 represents the best rank among peers, while 0 represents the worst. 

The chart categorizes US performance into six thematic bands. First, the US ranks near the top, with scores between 90 and 100, on features that benefit investors and entrepreneurs, such as freedom from government regulation, corporate ability to challenge regulations, low tax burdens, equity market returns, ease of doing business, and corporate profit growth. Second, metrics for workers, including median income adjusted for purchasing power and the OECD Better Life Index, show rankings beginning to slip but remaining above average, with scores between 60 and 80.

The remaining four categories show significant declines. The US judicial and legal foundation shows clear cracks, ranking near or below the median with scores between 25 and 55 for judicial independence, integrity of the legal system, and perception of corruption. The author points out that the US corruption score fell by 6 points since 2017, a rare decline in a developed country that mirrors the drop seen in Hungary under Viktor Orban's administration. Furthermore, the US ranks well below the median, with scores between 20 and 40, on basic education, homelessness, healthcare quality, and COVID-19 mortality per million people. 

The lowest scores are reserved for inequality and justice. The US ranks poorly, with scores between 10 and 25, on intergenerational income mobility, the post-tax GINI coefficient, and poverty rates. At the very bottom of the chart, with scores under 15, the US ranks worst among its high-income peers on civil and criminal justice system discrimination, fundamental civil rights, and the overall access and affordability of civil justice.

This page contains standard regulatory disclosures, legal disclaimers, and jurisdictional distribution information for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication, covering compliance guidelines for Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America.

This page discusses the potential for significant delays in determining the winner of the 2020 US presidential election between Donald Trump and Joe Biden. Michael Cembalest argues that while a decisive victory for Biden in Florida or Texas could lead to an election-night projection, a close race that relies on Midwestern swing states like Pennsylvania and Wisconsin will likely take days or weeks to resolve. He attributes this to an "unholy trinity" affecting these key swing states: a lack of historical experience with large-scale mail-in voting, laws that prohibit processing ballots before election day, and their status as high-stakes swing states with many electoral votes.

A central bar chart, titled "Tracking potential electoral delays by state," illustrates the percentage of total voter turnout in the 2016 election that was cast via mail-in or absentee ballots across all US states, along with each state’s electoral votes. The chart shows that while historical mail-in voting was near 100% in states like Oregon and Washington, it was extremely low—around 5% to 10%—in critical swing states like Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Ohio, which are highlighted in gold. Red arrows on the chart point directly to Michigan, Ohio, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania as primary points of concern for election night delays. 

Beneath the chart, color-coded rows track state-by-state rules for both processing and counting absentee ballots. Processing rules are marked in red for states that wait until election day, yellow for states starting no earlier than five days before the election or with unspecified timing, and green for those starting earlier than five days before the election or upon receipt. Counting rules are coded red for counting that begins after polls close on election day, yellow for on election day, green for before election day, and gray for unclear. Both Wisconsin and Pennsylvania are flagged with red dots for processing, meaning they do not allow any pre-election day processing, and red or yellow dots for counting, ensuring a slow tabulation process.

The author notes that while 11 states—Alabama, Connecticut, Iowa, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, New York, Rhode Island, and South Carolina—modified their laws to allow earlier ballot processing, Republican-controlled legislatures in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania refused to do so. Additionally, Cembalest dismisses Michigan’s rule change, which allows processing only one day before the election, as mere window-dressing. By mid-October 2020, over 5.6 million absentee ballots had already been submitted nationwide compared to only 75,000 at the same point in 2016, highlighting the unprecedented scale of the challenge. A final section of the page details the highly demanding and time-consuming steps required to process absentee ballots, including verifying signatures and addresses, checking poll books, matching ward numbers, evaluating ballot irregularities, and feeding the physical papers into tabulators.

This page of the commentary focuses on the timing of a COVID-19 vaccine and its implications for virus-sensitive, small- to mid-sized businesses that are facing tight credit conditions. Pointing to survey data from Census, Verizon, and Goldman, the author notes that approximately seventy percent of small businesses could only survive three to six months before encountering severe cash flow shortfalls, making the timing of a vaccine crucial for restoring normal consumer behavior. 

The author outlines several critical caveats regarding vaccine development and public acceptance. First, a vaccine is not a foregone conclusion; Phase III results on efficacy and long-term immunity remain uncertain, as highlighted by clinical trial pauses from Johnson & Johnson and AstraZeneca. The author dismisses "superforecaster" predictions on timing and suggests that simpler vaccines based on coronavirus proteins are more likely to be approved than vector or mRNA vaccines. Furthermore, initial vaccines might only demonstrate fifty to sixty percent efficacy. 

Public trust presents another major hurdle, with the United States ranking in the bottom of the third quartile globally in vaccine trust. A USA Today poll indicates that only twenty-seven percent of Americans would take a vaccine immediately, while forty-four percent would wait, and the rest would decline it altogether. 

Because the US government funded these developments through Operation Warp Speed, it will control initial distribution based on CDC Advisory Committee prioritization. The distribution hierarchy targets twenty million healthcare workers first, followed by sixty million essential service workers, one hundred million high-risk individuals, fifty million people over sixty-five, and finally the general population. 

The author projects that if a vaccine is approved by the end of 2020, healthcare and essential workers will likely receive it in the first quarter of 2021, while the general population would be inoculated by the third quarter of 2021. He concludes that while financial markets are likely to price in vaccine benefits early, actual economic recovery and normal consumer behavior will not return until true herd immunity is established through a combination of vaccinations and natural recovery.

This page features a comparative analysis of COVID-19 infection rates, testing, age demographics, and the relationship between infections and mortality, focusing primarily on a stark comparison between neighboring regions in the United States and Canada. The analysis begins with a "COVID Rorschach test" comparing US "Big Sky" states—specifically Idaho, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Wisconsin, and Wyoming—to the adjacent Western Canadian provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba. Despite sharing similar population densities of 2.5 to 5.0 people per square kilometer and comparable testing rates, the two regions experienced dramatically different outbreak trajectories. 

This divergence is illustrated in the chart "What a difference a border makes," which shows new daily infections per million people over the 200 days after total cases reached 100. While Western Canada's infection rate remained flat and well below 50 daily infections per million, the US Big Sky states spiked sharply, surpassing 400 daily infections per million by day 200. The adjacent chart, "Testing: Western Canada vs 'Big Sky' US states," confirms that this gap is not due to a disparity in testing. Both regions tracked closely over time, steadily increasing their 7-day average of daily tests from near zero in March to between 2,000 and 3,000 per million by late September.

In addition to this regional comparison, the author notes several global trends, such as Northeastern US infections doubling from summer lows, Western European infections surpassing spring levels with lower mortality, Singapore bringing the virus under control, and Latin American infections rolling over outside of Argentina. 

A central question posed is how long it takes for rising infections in younger demographics to translate into infections and mortality in older populations. This shift in demographics is depicted in a chart showing the median age of individuals with positive PCR tests in the United States. Across all regions—the South, Northeast, West, and Midwest—the median age of infected individuals dropped steadily from between 43 and 51 years in May to the mid-to-high 30s by late August. 

The disconnect between rising infections and mortality is further analyzed in the chart "Spain daily infections vs mortality." During Spain's spring wave, infections per million on the left-hand axis peaked around 130 while daily deaths per million on the right-hand axis peaked at over 16. In contrast, during the late summer wave, Spain's infections surged past 220 per million, yet daily deaths remained very low, only creeping up to approximately 2 to 3 per million by late September.

This analysis evaluates the fiscal agendas of Donald Trump and Joe Biden ahead of the 2020 presidential election, emphasizing that both candidates' platforms point toward substantial deficit spending and continuous fiscal stimulus, which has been well-received by equity markets. 

The first chart, titled "The Biden Agenda," displays projected taxation and spending over a ten-year period in trillions of dollars. Taxation revenues, including taxes on the wealthy, corporate tax hikes, and payroll taxes for incomes over $400,000, sum to around $4 trillion, offset slightly by specific tax cuts. On the spending side, investments in healthcare, infrastructure, education, housing, and entitlement expansion total nearly $8 trillion, partially offset by drug price reforms, highlighting a multi-trillion-dollar funding gap. 

To compare the candidates directly, the second chart, "Deficit impact of Trump and Biden agendas," illustrates that their respective plans have surprisingly similar deficit outcomes over ten years. Under the central estimate, Trump’s plan would increase the deficit by approximately $5.0 trillion, compared to Biden’s $5.6 trillion. Under a high-cost estimate scenario, Trump's deficit impact could rise to roughly $6.8 trillion, while Biden's reaches about $8.1 trillion. 

The third chart, "Election prediction market probabilities vs S&P 500," plots betting market odds against the S&P 500 price level from January to October 2020. It tracks the probability of a Democrat winning the presidency, which rose from around 50% in early 2020 to over 60% by autumn, and Democrats winning the Senate, which rose from 30% to over 50%. Simultaneously, the S&P 500 recovered from its March crash of around 2,200 points to exceed 3,400 points by September. This co-movement suggests that rising odds of a Democratic sweep did not derail the stock market, as investors focused on the prospects of incoming fiscal support. 

Ultimately, the author notes that both candidates appear committed to keeping the fiscal stimulus tap flowing, regardless of long-term impacts on growth, taxes, and interest rates. This stance has been welcomed by equity markets due to limited near-term inflation risks and the Federal Reserve's perceived willingness to keep interest rates low even if debt markets revolt.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, offers several observations on how the upcoming U.S. presidential election is impacting equity markets. 

Cembalest first argues that as Joe Biden’s election prospects and Democratic Sweep projections rise, financial markets are pricing in a quicker resumption of global trade and lower trade tensions with China. This trend is demonstrated by two charts, both indexing performance to January 2018. The first chart measures the relative performance of companies with high exposure to the U.S.-China trade war against the S&P 500. After declining from 100 in early 2018 to nearly 80 in late 2019, this index has rebounded to roughly 93 by mid-2020. The second chart tracks the relative performance of companies with high exposure to international sales versus the S&P 500. This series experienced a dip below 90 in early 2020 before recovering to around 98 by the middle of the year, signaling that trade-sensitive equities are benefiting from shifting political expectations.

The commentary also highlights how markets are pricing in headwinds for mega-cap technology and social media stocks relative to the broader market. A third chart illustrates this by plotting the outperformance percentage of the market-capitalization-weighted S&P 500 against the equal-weighted S&P 500 from 2017 into late 2020. While the market-cap-weighted index rose to nearly 25 percent outperformance by mid-2020, the trend has been flat since July. Cembalest attributes this shift to potential antitrust scrutiny under a Biden administration and the anticipated stimulative impact of Democratic spending plans on the broader, non-tech economy.

Finally, Cembalest addresses concerns that higher capital gains tax rates under a new administration could trigger a market selloff as investors rush to realize gains at current lower rates. The fourth chart plots S&P 500 percentage returns from twelve weeks before to twelve weeks after the effective date of historical tax hikes, where week zero represents the effective date. Looking at the Tax Reform Act of 1986, which raised the top rate from 20 percent to 28 percent, and the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 combined with the Affordable Care Act, which raised the top rate from 15 percent to 25.1 percent, there is little historical evidence of a selloff. In both cases, the market rose after the effective date, with the S&P 500 up nearly 20 percent twelve weeks after the 1986 reform and up around 10 percent twelve weeks after the 2012 reform.

This page outlines the key issues in the United States Department of Justice antitrust case against Google. The author explains that, unlike European antitrust investigations that center on search or advertising dominance, the DoJ case focuses on Google's exclusivity agreements with distributors. Google pays billions of dollars annually to secure default status for its search engine from device manufacturers including Apple, Motorola, LG, and Samsung, wireless carriers like AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon, and browser developers such as Mozilla, Opera, and UC Web. Notably, the DoJ claims that 15% to 20% of Apple's worldwide annual income is derived from these default search engine payments.

The page highlights an legal standard cited by Assistant Attorney General Delrahim in 2019, which asserts that even a legitimately achieved monopoly cannot take actions designed solely to make it harder for competitors to catch up. Google has defended its arrangements by comparing its distributor payments to cereal companies paying for prime shelf space in supermarkets. However, the author notes that cereal consumption lacks the self-reinforcing network effects of search algorithms, which continually improve as they gather more user data. The allegations are compared to the Microsoft antitrust case from twenty years ago, where Microsoft restricted manufacturers to ensure the installation of Internet Explorer.

A complicating factor in the litigation is that the digital economy is characterized by duopolies rather than classic monopolies. Examples include Google and Facebook in digital advertising, Microsoft and Amazon in cloud computing, Amazon and Google in shopping searches, and Microsoft and Google in productivity software, which may provide the companies with a robust defense against monopoly charges. 

A specific callout box details a quote from the legal filing regarding Carrier Revshare Deals, revealing that Android devices distributed by carriers require Google Search exclusivity to prevent the pre-installation of competing search engines or browsers. The author concludes that while the judicial outcome remains an open question, the DoJ case increases regulatory risks for the big four technology and social media stocks that have driven a growing share of overall market returns.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for various global jurisdictions, including France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America, with no charts or financial market commentary.

This page discusses the House Judiciary Report on anti-competitive tech behavior issued on October 6, 2020. It details the accusations levied against major tech companies—specifically Facebook, Google, Amazon, and Apple—for stifling competition through "killer acquisitions," raising prices, misappropriating third-party data, stealing intellectual property, and acting as market gatekeepers. The report's conclusions discard the traditional consumer welfare standard that has guided antitrust enforcement for 40 years. Specifically, the report identifies Facebook as a social networking monopoly that preemptively copies or kills competitors, Google as an online search and advertising monopoly leveraging default software dominance, Amazon as a retail giant abusing its marketplace control to copy and undermine third-party sellers, and Apple as holding a gatekeeping monopoly over iOS software distribution.

The author notes that House Democrats support a wide range of remedies, including Glass-Steagall-style tech business breakups, rules against self-preferencing, and merger prohibitions. The GOP only favors a subset of these remedies, such as rules on data portability and interoperability, strengthening Section 2 of the Clayton Act, and restoring enforcement agencies to full strength. Cembalest forecasts that if Joe Biden wins the presidential election and the Senate filibuster is removed, these proposals could pass with a simple 51-vote majority, potentially leading to intense policy battles. Even without new laws, increased Congressional scrutiny and a rejuvenated Department of Justice are expected to maintain heavy antitrust pressure on the sector.

To illustrate the historical context of tech consolidations, the page includes a stacked bar chart displaying the number of acquisitions by year for Google, Apple, Facebook, and Amazon from 2000 through 2019. The chart reveals that acquisitions were minimal in the early 2000s, rarely exceeding five per year, but spiked dramatically starting in 2010. The peak occurred in 2014, with the four giants combined making over 50 acquisitions, heavily led by Google, which consistently represents the largest share of acquisitions throughout the two-decade period. Although total annual acquisitions tapered off slightly after 2014, they remained highly elevated through 2019, consistently hovering between 25 and 45 per year.

This page introduces a broader analysis of significant non-election market drivers, focusing primarily on the resurgence of antitrust enforcement against major U.S. technology companies. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that the looming threat of antitrust actions is a primary candidate for why the major tech firms—specifically Google, Amazon, Facebook, and Apple—and the broader market-capitalization-weighted S&P 500 index have ceased their significant outperformance relative to the equal-weighted S&P 500 index. 

To illustrate this trend, two charts compare performance trends from 2017 to late 2020. The first chart, S&P 500 megacap outperformance, tracks the percentage outperformance of the market-cap-weighted S&P 500 over the equal-weighted index. This trend peaked above 20% in mid-2020 before leveling off, marked by a label indicating performance has been flat since July of that year. The second chart, Antitrust target outperformance, tracks a custom index of the targeted firms—Facebook, Amazon, Apple, and Google—against the equal-weighted S&P 500. This index shows a dramatic rise to nearly 140% outperformance by mid-2020, which similarly plateaued and remained flat since July. 

A comprehensive table titled Market share overview for US markets details the combined market power of these tech giants and Microsoft across fifteen digital categories. The data highlights severe market concentration: Google and Apple combine for a 99% market share in phone operating systems, with Google at 52% and Apple at 47%. Google also commands a 91% share in internet search, including images, maps, and YouTube, alongside an 80% share in navigation applications. Amazon holds a commanding 73% share in video game streaming, 70% in eBooks, and 84% in e-Readers. Facebook holds a 51% share in social media and a 50% share in social media digital photos. Together, these four companies represent a dominant subtotal share in almost every listed category, such as 84% of web browsers, 75% of email, and 61% of digital advertising. 

The author points to the Department of Justice lawsuit against Google as a major catalyst for these discussions, while noting several other looming regulatory risks. These include independent filings by State Attorneys General, consumer class-action lawsuits regarding data privacy, the potential revocation or amendment of Section 230 liability protections, and a possible future DOJ antitrust lawsuit against Facebook. As an alternative explanation for the recent plateau in megacap performance, the author raises the possibility that progress toward a COVID-19 vaccine has intermittently revived investor interest in lagging sectors like financials and travel-related stocks.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the sharp rise in COVID-19 infections across Europe in the autumn of 2020 following the reopening of schools, bars, and restaurants, noting that current infection rates have surpassed those in the United States. Despite this steep rise, European mortality rates remain much lower than during the initial summer wave. The author attributes this divergence to a younger cohort of infected individuals, less strained hospital systems, and improved standards of care, such as the strategic use of steroids and blood thinners and a reduction in unnecessary mechanical ventilation. 

To explore whether this infection spike is merely an artifact of increased testing, the author analyzes positive testing rates across several nations. The argument presented is that flat positive testing rates indicate that increased testing is the primary driver of rising infections, whereas rapidly rising positive testing rates signal a genuine outbreak. 

The analytical points are supported by eight charts. The first chart, titled US vs Europe infections, plots new daily infections per million people (7-day average) against the number of days after total reported cases reached 100. It shows that by day 240, Europe's infection rate climbed steeply to approximately 250 cases per million, surpassing the US rate of around 200. The second chart, Europe daily infections vs mortality, displays infections per million on the left axis and deaths per million on the right axis from March to October. While spring deaths peaked at nearly 9.0 per million against only 60 infections per million, the October data shows infections soaring past 250 per million while deaths remained low at around 1.5 per million.

The remaining six charts analyze daily infections per million against positive testing rates from March 1 to October 27 for individual countries. Spain and Germany represent cases where testing is a major driver of case numbers; Spain's infections plateaued near 230 per million in October with the positive testing rate remaining relatively stable between 10% and 12%, while Germany's autumn infections rose to 60 per million but its positive testing rate stayed very flat and low at roughly 2% to 3%. 

In contrast, France, Italy, Belgium, and the Netherlands show clear signs of active outbreaks where positivity rates are rising quickly. In France, autumn infections surged to 400 per million, accompanied by a rapid rise in the positivity rate to around 9%. Italy's daily infections climbed toward 200 per million, with the positivity rate shooting up to nearly 15%. Belgium displays the most dramatic outbreak on the page, with daily infections skyrocketing to 900 per million and positive testing rates climbing sharply to 25%. Finally, the Netherlands saw autumn infections rise toward 500 per million, with the positive testing rate climbing back up to 15%. The author notes that the United Kingdom falls somewhere between these two groups of nations.

This page addresses two distinct topics: a comparison of US and Chinese debt levels in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, and an overview of the differences in accuracy between PCR and antigen testing. 

Regarding public finances, the author notes that looking solely at government debt suggests the pandemic was far more damaging to the US than to China. This is illustrated in a chart of general government debt as a percentage of GDP from 2003 to 2020. In this chart, US government debt climbs steadily after 2008, spiking dramatically to over 120% of GDP in 2020, while China's government debt remains low and relatively flat, hovering well under 40%. However, the author argues that because the line between public and private debt in China is blurred—largely due to state-owned enterprises acting at the behest of the government—a more accurate comparison includes both government and non-financial corporate debt. A second chart displaying this combined metric shows that the two nations are on much closer footing. In this view, both the US and China saw their combined debt-to-GDP ratios track closely together over the years, with both experiencing a sharp spike to approximately 210% of GDP in 2020.

The second section provides a primer on PCR versus antigen testing, focusing on their respective sensitivity and specificity rates. The author explains that sensitivity measures the ability to detect the virus in infected people, where failures result in false negatives, while specificity measures the ability to confirm a lack of infection in uninfected people, where failures result in false positives. While false positives present a productivity challenge by forcing healthy people to stay home, false negatives pose a severe public health risk by allowing infected individuals to unknowingly spread the virus. 

A data table sourced from the Johns Hopkins University Center for Health Security shows that PCR tests, which detect viral genetic material, have a sensitivity of 98.9% (with a range of 87.5% to 100%) and a specificity of 99.4% (with a range of 92.3% to 100%). In contrast, rapid antigen tests, which detect specific proteins on the virus surface, have a much lower sensitivity of 90.4% (with a range of 80% to 97.6%), though they maintain a high specificity of 99.2% (with a range of 96.6% to 100%). The author notes that because these tests have only received emergency use authorization from the FDA rather than full certification, individuals should remain aware of these error rates. A concluding footnote references a Cornell University study on COVID-19 misinformation, which identified President Trump as a prominent driver of the misinformation surrounding the pandemic.

This text-only commentary page, titled "Court Marshall: What happens next" and written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the immediate aftermath of the November 2020 US Presidential election. Cembalest observes that both political camps are preparing for extensive legal battles, reflecting a highly litigious American system. He outlines the shifting paths to victory, noting that overnight ballot counts in Green Bay, Milwaukee, and Kenosha shifted Wisconsin’s odds toward Joe Biden. With Biden favored in Arizona, Michigan, and Wisconsin, he would only need six more electoral votes from Nevada, Georgia, Pennsylvania, or North Carolina to win, though flexible state recount rules suggest a messy period ahead. 

If Donald Trump loses, Cembalest highlights that he would be the first incumbent in over a century to lose despite strong economic and market tailwinds, drawing a historical parallel to William H. Taft in 1912. Looking ahead to a potential Biden presidency with a Republican-controlled Senate, Cembalest argues this "split decision" will prevent the implementation of aggressive Keynesian tax-and-spend policies. Consequently, he advises investors to prepare for a partial reversal of "Blue Wave" portfolios and to focus on policies Biden can implement unilaterally via the Executive Branch, such as energy, healthcare, China trade, immigration, Iran, antitrust, and net neutrality. 

Although the page contains no physical charts, the text frequently references an external set of charts (labeled c1 through c11) supporting these arguments, and detailed footnotes track active election litigation across states like Texas, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Arizona, Tennessee, Ohio, Nevada, and Florida.

This page examines the historical swings of political ideology in US presidential administrations from the 1920s through 2020, illustrating the concept of a "political pendulum." The central visual is a line chart titled "Political ideology of US Presidents and their administrations," which plots UCLA Voteview Liberal-Conservative scores against a timeline from 1916 to 2020. The horizontal axis ranges from negative 0.8, representing the most liberal positions, to positive 0.8, representing the most conservative positions. 

The chart tracks an alternating shift between political extremes over the decades. The Coolidge and Hoover era sits on the conservative side at roughly 0.7. The pendulum then swings left for FDR and Truman to about negative 0.42, shifts back right for Eisenhower to 0.30, and moves left again for JFK and LBJ to negative 0.48. This pattern continues with Nixon and Ford at 0.31, Carter at negative 0.41, Reagan and Bush at 0.41, Clinton at negative 0.28, George W. Bush at 0.60, and Obama at negative 0.49. The Trump administration marks the most conservative peak on the timeline at approximately 0.72. Though the publication does not yet reflect the finalized 2020 election results, it plots potential markers for a prospective Biden administration, highlighting individual scores for Elizabeth Warren at approximately negative 0.70, Bernie Sanders at negative 0.58, and Joe Biden at negative 0.30, indicating a potential swing back toward the liberal side of the spectrum.
