An accompanying methodology section explains that each administration's ideological position is empirically derived from Congressional voting records using Nokken-Poole first-dimension Voteview data. The scores reflect how frequently key politicians voted within their legislative blocs. The page lists the specific political figures analyzed for each era to build these averages; for example, the proposed Biden administration score includes figures like Karen Bass, Joe Biden, James Clyburn, Chris Coons, Steny Hoyer, Nancy Pelosi, Cedric Richmond, Bernie Sanders, Chuck Schumer, and Elizabeth Warren, while the Trump administration includes figures such as Tom Cotton, Lindsey Graham, Orrin Hatch, Kevin McCarthy, Mark Meadows, Rand Paul, David Perdue, Paul Ryan, Steve Scalise, Jeff Sessions, Matt Gaetz, Mitch McConnell, and Jim Jordan.

This page examines the fiscal and market implications of the proposed Biden taxation and spending agenda compared to the policies of the Trump administration. The first section analyzes the long-term impact on the federal budget, illustrating how the Biden agenda would propel government spending and tax revenues to near post-war highs as a percentage of gross domestic product over a trailing 10-year average. Under current policy projections leading to 2040, federal spending is expected to hover around 22% of GDP while revenues remain near 17%. With the addition of Biden’s proposed policies, spending is projected to rise toward 24% of GDP and revenues are projected to climb to 20% of GDP, levels not seen since the mid-1940s. 

To fund this agenda, a companion chart details Biden’s proposed corporate tax increases compared to Donald Trump's corporate tax cuts, measured in trillions of US dollars over a 10-year period. While Trump’s tax cuts reduced corporate and pass-through entity taxes by roughly $0.6 trillion, Biden’s proposed plan would raise corporate taxes by over $2.0 trillion, consisting primarily of corporate entity taxes alongside a smaller share of pass-through entity taxes.

The second half of the page tracks the performance of thematic equity portfolios aligned with each candidate from January to late October 2020, based on an index where January 2020 equals 100. The Biden portfolio dramatically outperformed the Trump portfolio over this period, climbing to roughly 112 by late October, while the Trump portfolio fell sharply during the March market crash and struggled to recover, ending near 80. 

The composition of these thematic portfolios highlights differing sectoral priorities. The Biden portfolio is long on renewable energy, infrastructure (such as construction, engineering, and industrial machinery), China trade war stocks, companies with high international sales exposure, and healthcare equipment. It shorts large-cap pharma, diversified banks, antitrust targets like Facebook, Apple, Amazon, and Alphabet's Google, and labor-intensive companies sensitive to minimum wage increases, such as United Parcel Service, McDonald's, Uber, Walmart, and Starbucks. Conversely, the Trump portfolio is long on oil and gas, aerospace and defense, healthcare, diversified banks, and the primary beneficiaries of the 2017 corporate tax cuts, while shorting stocks exposed to the China trade war.

This page consists entirely of legal disclosures, regulatory notifications, and distribution disclaimers for J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" publication. It details the specific J.P. Morgan entities responsible for distributing the material in various jurisdictions, including Switzerland (J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA, regulated by FINMA), Hong Kong (JPMCB, regulated by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the Securities and Futures Commission), Singapore (JPMCB, regulated by the Monetary Authority of Singapore), Australia (JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., and JPMS, restricted to "wholesale clients" under the Corporations Act 2001), and countries across Latin America. Additionally, the page outlines regulatory exemptions, restrictions on public offerings of securities or funds without proper local registration (referencing the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission–CVM), and general terms regarding personal use and copyright restrictions.

This page analyzes key issues facing the healthcare sector, focusing on policy levers such as the Executive Branch's ability to run "demonstration" projects on Medicare drug price negotiations, alongside a comparison of US versus international drug pricing and the sector's market performance. 

The top-left chart examines the ratio of US discounted prices to average international prices per gram for top Medicare Part B drugs. It reveals a stark premium for US drug prices, with almost all of the twenty-seven analyzed therapies priced well above international levels. Treanda stands out at nearly eight times the international average, followed by Lucentis at over seven times, while other widely used treatments like Prolia, Neulasta, Cimzia, and Tysabri range between four to six times international prices. Even at the lower end of the spectrum, therapies like Soliris and Gammagard remain above parity. 

The top-right chart focuses on Medicare Part D drugs, showing that US discounted prices consistently exceed international benchmarks. A basket of seventy-nine drugs is priced between 3.2 times (the low estimate) and 3.6 times (the high estimate) the average international price. Individual blockbuster drugs also show significant premiums; Crestor, Lantus, Advair, and Januvia all trade at 3.3 to 3.7 times their international counterparts, while Humira has a relatively lower but still substantial premium of just over two times.

The bottom-left chart tracks the relative performance of large-cap pharmaceutical stocks against the S&P 500 throughout 2020. After rising in the spring to peak at roughly a 13% outperformance in April and May, the sector steadily lost ground, falling to an underperformance of approximately negative 8% by late October. 

The bottom-right chart contextualizes these dynamics within a longer-term trend, plotting the healthcare sector's valuation premium or discount relative to the S&P 500 from 1991 to late 2020. Historically, the sector enjoyed valuation premiums of 30% to over 40% in the early 1990s and around the turn of the millennium. However, for most of the decade following the 2008 financial crisis, the sector has traded at a discount. This discount bottomed near negative 25% around 2010 and remains in negative territory at roughly negative 18% in late 2020, reflecting ongoing regulatory and pricing pressures.

This page provides supplementary data and analysis for a J.P. Morgan "Eye on the Market" report. It features three distinct appendix exhibits focusing on international litigation metrics, election recount rules in key US swing states, and historical presidential tailwinds.

The first table, which details various measures of litigation per 100,000 people across select developed countries, demonstrates that the United States is uniquely litigious. Sourced from Harvard Law School, the data shows the US leads with 5,806 suits filed per 100,000 people, far ahead of the United Kingdom at 3,681, France at 2,416, Japan at 1,768, Australia at 1,542, and Canada at 1,450. To support this legal activity, the US has 10.8 judges and 391 lawyers per 100,000 people, which is notably higher than peer nations, with the exception of France's 12.5 judges and Australia's 357 lawyers. 

The second table outlines recount rules in key swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. The table details whether recounts are automatic, what the thresholds are, and if candidates or election officials have discretion to request them. For instance, Arizona, Michigan, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania have automatic recount laws under specific margins or circumstances, whereas Georgia and Wisconsin do not. Instead, Georgia allows candidates to request a recount if the margin of victory is within 0.50%, and Wisconsin allows it for a 1% difference.

The final visual is a bar chart tracking presidential tailwinds from 1896 to 2020 to evaluate whether the 2020 election will break a century-long trend of incumbents winning re-election when backed by strong market and economic tailwinds. The tracker scores economic conditions—derived from inflation, equities, employment, home prices, and per capita GDP—on a scale from 0.00 to 0.90. Historically, incumbent presidents facing highly favorable conditions (marked with a "W") almost always win, as seen with McKinley, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Eisenhower, Reagan, Clinton, George W. Bush, and Obama. Conversely, incumbents facing poor conditions (marked with an "L") tend to lose, such as Hoover, Carter, and George H.W. Bush. The author poses an open question for the 2020 election; while pre-COVID economic conditions in December 2019 were exceptionally strong with a score of approximately 0.85, the pandemic dragged the economic tailwind score down to around 0.60 by election time, leaving the ultimate outcome highly uncertain.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" focuses on key issues facing the energy sector, particularly US fossil fuel dependence, the hydraulic fracturing boom, transition policy disputes, and fuel efficiency standards. The author highlights several highly debated topics, including drilling on public lands, offshore drilling, development in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR), potential reversals of the Trump administration's softening of automobile Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, climate-related financial regulations, liquefied natural gas (LNG) export permits, and the trend of the US falling further behind Europe in decarbonization. 

Two charts illustrate the dramatic growth in US domestic energy production and its macroeconomic impact. The first chart plots the percentage of US oil and gas production derived from hydraulic fracturing through 2019. It shows that natural gas production from fracking grew from around 10% in 1995 to nearly 80% by 2019. Similarly, crude oil and natural gas liquids like ethane, propane, and butane, which were negligibly produced via fracking before the mid-2000s, both climbed to represent over 60% of total US production by 2019. The second chart measures the US net energy deficit, calculated as energy imports minus energy exports as a percentage of GDP, from 1978 to 2020. This deficit peaked at over 3.0% of GDP around 1980 and again in 2008, but the shale boom successfully eliminated this deficit, pushing the US into a net energy surplus (below 0.0% of GDP) by 2020.

The remaining two charts examine decarbonization and transport efficiency. A comparison of fossil fuel consumption between the US and Europe shows the percentage of primary energy consumption derived from coal, oil, and natural gas from 1965 to 2020. In 1965, both regions relied on fossil fuels for roughly 93% to 95% of their energy. Europe’s fossil fuel share fell sharply during its "nuclear adoption era" in the 1970s and 1980s, and declined further as the "solar/wind era" began in the mid-2000s, reaching roughly 74% by 2020. In contrast, the US decarbonized much more slowly, with fossil fuels still making up approximately 83% of its primary energy consumption in 2020. Finally, a chart on vehicle performance metrics shows the percentage change in fuel economy, horsepower, and weight relative to the 1975 model year baseline. While average vehicle weight decreased and remained 5% to 15% lighter than in 1975, both horsepower and fuel economy saw dramatic, concurrent improvements, with fuel economy increasing by nearly 90% and horsepower growing by about 80% by the 2020 model year.

This page consists entirely of standard regulatory disclosures and legal compliance information regarding the distribution of the publication across various global jurisdictions, including Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America, with specific mentions of Brazil and Mexico. It contains no investment analysis, charts, data, or forecasts.

This page analyzes two key policy areas: US immigration trends and geopolitical dynamics surrounding Iran. 

Under the topic of immigration, the report provides historical context on the US foreign-born population using data from the Brookings Institution. The first bar chart, depicting annual US foreign-born gains in millions of people from 2011 to 2019, shows that annual net gains peaked in 2014 at around 1.0 million people before declining sharply to approximately 0.2 million in both 2018 and 2019. A accompanying line chart tracks the foreign-born share of the US population from 1900 to 2019, illustrating a long-term U-shaped trend. The foreign-born share fell from nearly 15% in 1910 to a historic low of just under 5% around 1970, before steadily rising to a plateau of nearly 14% between 2017 and 2019.

The section on Iran examines the foreign policy challenge of how the US might re-engage with European allies while addressing perceived shortfalls in the original Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. Three charts illustrate the tangible impacts of the US withdrawal from the agreement in May 2018. The first line chart tracks the minimal breakout time in months needed for Iran to produce weapons-grade uranium from 2009 to 2020. This breakout time spiked dramatically above 12 months following the JCPOA implementation in January 2016 but plummeted back down to approximately three months by February 2020 following the US withdrawal. The second chart supports this by displaying Iran's stock of low-enriched uranium (less than 5% enrichment) in kilograms, which escalated rapidly from under 200 kg in May 2019 to over 1,000 kg by February 2020. The final chart displays Iranian oil exports in millions of barrels per day from 2016 to 2020, showing that while exports hovered between 2.0 and 2.5 million barrels per day during the JCPOA period, they collapsed to near-zero levels by 2020 following the re-imposition of US sanctions.

This page provides background on absentee ballot rules and recent court cases following the 2020 US presidential election. The author details the varying rules across key states, noting that Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin require absentee ballots to be received on or before Election Day, meaning any Republican legal challenges in these states cannot focus on receipt timing but must instead target procedural issues like signatures and envelopes. In contrast, Nevada allows ballots postmarked before Election Day to be counted up to seven days later, a long-standing rule that remains unchanged despite unsubstantiated claims of irregularities in Clark County. 

The discussion then focuses on North Carolina and Pennsylvania, which both extended their receipt deadlines due to the pandemic but did so through different mechanisms. In North Carolina, an appointed election commission extended the deadline to nine days, a change the US Supreme Court allowed to stand in a 5-3 ruling. In Pennsylvania, a state court mandated a three-day extension, which survived a challenge because the US Supreme Court tied 4-4, allowing the state ruling to remain in place. 

The author also highlights key legal battles in Wisconsin and Minnesota. In Wisconsin, the Supreme Court ruled 5-3 to block a lower court's extension, reinforcing the principle that federal courts should not alter state election rules near Election Day. In Minnesota, a Federal Appeals Court suspended a consent decree from the Secretary of State that would have allowed ballots to be accepted seven days late, ruling that the extension violated the US Constitution by bypassing the state legislature's exclusive authority to regulate federal elections. Lastly, a footnote explains that military and overseas voters are governed by special federal rules under the Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act, which accounted for over 650,000 votes in the 2016 election.

This commentary page provides an analysis of potential post-election litigation, absentee ballot rules, and the legal frameworks surrounding multiple slates of electors in the 2020 U.S. presidential election. The author singles out Pennsylvania as the primary target for GOP challenges, noting it is the only critical swing state that altered its absentee ballot deadline rules, appeared poised to go to Joe Biden, had its outcome depend heavily on absentee voting, and previously faced a split Supreme Court decision questioning the legitimacy of its deadline extension. A footnote highlights that Biden's early lead in the state was achieved solely through ballots received before Election Day under pre-existing rules, not including post-Election Day arrivals. 

The author poses several scenarios, noting that if late-arriving ballots determine the state's outcome and the state determines the national presidency, the Supreme Court—now with Justice Amy Coney Barrett seated—could re-litigate the deadline extension, though the author doubts they would invalidate already-cast votes. Additionally, the author addresses the possibility of the Pennsylvania legislature submitting a competing slate of electors. Under the Electoral Count Act, a split Congress—comprising a Democratic House and a Republican Senate—would trigger tie-breaking rules allowing Pennsylvania's Democratic Governor to select the final electors. While the state's legislature reportedly disavowed this action, the author cautions that this decision is non-binding and could still serve as a precedent for other states. Finally, the author notes that while wins in Georgia and Nevada would theoretically bypass Pennsylvania's role as the deciding state, potential recounts across Georgia, Nevada, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania mean the final national outcome could remain uncertain for several weeks.

This page examines the legal standing of potential Republican Party objections to counting late-received absentee ballots in the 2020 Presidential Election, focusing specifically on Pennsylvania. The author argues that Pennsylvania presents the GOP's strongest case because other key swing states either did not count late ballots (Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin), did not change their rules (Nevada), or had moot cases (North Carolina, where Trump appeared to win regardless). While the Supreme Court, with the seating of Justice Amy Coney Barrett, could potentially rule 5-4 that Pennsylvania's deadline extension was invalid, constitutional law experts consulted by the author suggest the Court would remain reluctant to invalidate already-cast votes due to due process concerns, the Purcell principle against late rule changes, and equitable factors like public interest. 

The analysis then addresses a "triple witching hour" scenario where Pennsylvania determines the election, leading to competing slates of electors being submitted to the Electoral College by the state's Democratic Governor and its Republican-controlled legislature. Under the Electoral Count Act of 1887, such a dispute would be resolved by Congress on January 6th. The author posits that in the event of a split Congress, the Democratic Governor would serve as the ultimate tie-breaker, ultimately favoring the Biden slate. A footnote highlights that Senate control on January 6th could depend on the outcome of two Senate runoff elections scheduled for January 5th, where the prevailing balance is estimated to be 50 Republicans and 48 Democrats. The commentary concludes with an acknowledgment of Florida State University Professor Michael Morley for his assistance on election law issues.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" by Michael Cembalest analyzes the ongoing US-China trade war, highlighting persistent concerns regarding Chinese mercantilism, human rights policies, and the eventual status of Trump-era tariffs. It also assesses China's compliance with the Phase 1 purchase agreement across the agricultural, manufacturing, and energy sectors.

The top left chart, "Points of dispute in the US-China trade war," evaluates China’s policy environment relative to the rest of the world on a scale of 0 to 100, where 100 is best and 0 is worst. China scores extremely low across all metrics. Its worst performance is on the Mercantilism Index—which covers forced local production, export subsidies, intellectual property theft, domestic favoritism, and currency manipulation—where it scores near 5. It also scores poorly on receptivity to foreign direct investment (around 15), copyright protections (around 20), barriers to market access and forced technology transfer (around 22), and the extent of pirated software (around 25). Its highest score, which remains weak, is in public ownership of the private sector, at approximately 45.

To the right, "The Rights of the Individual versus the State" ranks nations based on judicial independence, due process, press freedom, and freedom of association, where 100 represents the greatest protections. The chart displays a descending curve of global nations, with the United States positioned near the top of the range at approximately 80, while China is situated far down the curve with a score of roughly 45, reflecting minimal individual protections.

The middle section of the page assesses the trade war's impact on import shares. The chart on the left, tracking the six-month average share of US imports from 2015 to 2020, shows that China’s share peaked at roughly 22% in late 2018 before dropping sharply to about 18% in 2020. During this same period, Europe maintained the largest share of US imports, ending near 24%, while Mexico’s share rose to about 15%. Shares for Canada dropped slightly to 11%, Japan remained around 6%, and the combined share of South Korea, Vietnam, and Taiwan hovered near 5%. The adjacent chart shows US total monthly imports alongside imports from China. Total imports fluctuated between $175 billion and $230 billion, while monthly imports from China saw a severe drop starting in late 2018, hitting a low of around $22 billion in early 2020 before recovering to roughly $40 billion later in the year.

The bottom-left chart monitors the progress of the US-China Phase 1 purchase agreement using data through September 2020. It shows that China is falling significantly short of its 2020 targets across all three primary categories. In agriculture, actual US imports were $13 billion against a target of $33 billion (38% achieved). In manufacturing, imports reached $38 billion against an $83 billion target (45% achieved). In energy, imports stood at only $6 billion against a target of $26 billion (just 23% achieved).

Finally, the bottom-right chart tracks the relative stock performance of companies with high exposure to the US-China trade war versus the S&P 500, with January 2018 indexed to 100. This highly exposed group steadily underperformed the broader market, dropping to a low of approximately 77 in mid-2020 before recovering to a level of 92 by late October 2020.

This commentary examines how a divided US government limits President Biden's ability to pass large-scale tax and spending expansions while still leaving executive room to maneuver on energy, immigration, healthcare, trade, and antitrust. Michael Cembalest suggests that a divided government might favor a "purple" mix of both Biden and Trump portfolios. He recommends owning renewable energy, infrastructure, tax-cut beneficiaries, international exposure, and banks, while remaining cautious on China trade war stocks and large-cap pharma.

To illustrate market sentiment leading up to the election, a line chart plots the relative performance of the Biden portfolio against the Trump portfolio from January to November 2020, indexed to 100. Both portfolios dropped sharply during the March 2020 market crash, but starting in July 2020, the Biden portfolio steadily climbed, ending near 112 in November, while the Trump portfolio remained depressed, hovering around 83. The chart's sidebar defines the Biden portfolio as going long on renewable energy, infrastructure, and international sales while shorting big tech antitrust targets like Facebook, Apple, Amazon, and Google, as well as minimum-wage-sensitive stocks like United Parcel Service, McDonald's, Uber, Walmart, and Starbucks. In contrast, the Trump portfolio is long on tax-cut beneficiaries, oil and gas, aerospace, defense, and banks, while shorting China trade war stocks.

In terms of sector-specific forecasts, the author notes that while a comprehensive Green New Deal is unlikely, Biden can still use executive power to raise capital costs on oil and gas through stricter fracking rules on public lands, climate risk disclosures, and LNG permit limits. Infrastructure stands out as a strong candidate for a modest, bipartisan transportation and aerospace reinvestment bill in 2021. On trade, Biden is expected to proceed slowly with China, keeping Trump-era tariffs intact for at least 18 months due to low compliance with the Phase I trade deal and bipartisan support for anti-mercantilist policies. Finally, companies benefiting from the 2017 tax cuts and those with high international exposure are expected to thrive since a substantial corporate tax hike is unlikely under a split government.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market publication, detailing distribution rules and compliance guidelines for various jurisdictions including Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America.

This page discusses the outcome of the 2020 presidential election, noting that while a challenger successfully unseated an incumbent President for the first time in 100 years during positive economic and market tailwinds, the election was a referendum on Donald Trump himself rather than a mandate for Democratic policies. The commentary also references the concurrent Pfizer vaccine news and the implications of a possibly divided government. 

To demonstrate that a progressive wave did not materialize, the page features a chart tracking J.P. Morgan's Federal/State Partisan Balance Index from 1937 to 2021. The index measures the percentage control of key government bodies by political party, with the y-axis showing the percentage control from 20 percent to 80 percent, where Democratic control is depicted in blue and Republican control is in red. The index weights the U.S. Senate at 25 percent, the House of Representatives at 25 percent, Governorships at 25 percent, and state-level senates and houses at 12.5 percent each. 

The chart traces major party shifts over nearly a century, including the decline of the Democratic share after its Great Depression high, the dip during Dwight Eisenhower's presidency, peaks during the John F. Kennedy and Lyndon B. Johnson Great Society era, the Nixon impeachment era, the Republican resurgence following the Reagan Revolution, Newt Gingrich's 1994 Contract with America, the temporary Barack Obama wave in 2009, and the 2018 anti-Trump midterm reaction. Crucially, the post-election projection for 2021 shows that the Democratic tide actually receded compared to pre-election levels, dipping below the 50 percent mark on the index. 

For the 2021 index projection, J.P. Morgan assumes a 51-to-49 Republican majority in the Senate, predicting Republicans hold North Carolina and Alaska and win one of the two Georgia runoff elections. They also project a final House split of 223 Democrats to 212 Republicans once outstanding seats and vacancies are resolved. 

In footnotes, the author draws several historical and literary parallels. The title of the piece is a reference to Mikhail Sholokhov's epic novel on Cossack life, "And Quiet Flows the Don." Additionally, the commentary references political analyses that compare the Trump administration's populist appeal to historical figures such as Louisiana Senator Huey Long, Andrew Jackson, Joseph McCarthy, and George Wallace.

This page discusses post-election policy prospects, historical market performance under different political configurations, and the state of the US labor market recovery in late 2020. 

Regarding policy, the author notes that for large-cap pharmaceutical companies, a bipartisan prescription drug bill is a distinct possibility, and the Executive Branch may implement projects to lower Medicare Part D drug prices. For major antitrust targets like Facebook, Apple, Amazon, and Google, highly punitive measures—such as "Glass-Steagall" style tech legislation or merger prohibitions—are likely off the table, though active Justice Department cases against Google and Facebook remain.

To address investor questions, the author presents a table showing S&P 500 returns during various US political scenarios from 1945 to 2020. Over this 76-year period, the average annual return was 11.5%. Under a unified government (30 years), returns averaged 13.8%, with 13.1% under Democratic presidents and 15.6% under Republican presidents. During unified Congress periods (32 years), returns averaged 9.8%, showing a wide gap between Democratic presidents at 16.4% and Republican presidents at 6.9%. In times of a split Congress (14 years), returns averaged 10.5%, with Democratic presidents seeing 16.7% and Republican presidents seeing 8.1%. The author argues these party-affiliated return variations are largely random, reflecting the timing of recessions and Federal Reserve policies rather than presidential or congressional party control.

Instead, the author emphasizes the business cycle and projects that massive global monetary and fiscal stimulus will drive the economic recovery through 2021, forecasting a US unemployment rate of approximately 5% by the end of 2021. Two labor market charts support this positive outlook. The first chart tracks the total unemployment rate against permanent job losers as a percentage of the civilian labor force from 2008 to 2020. It shows that while total unemployment spiked to nearly 15% in 2020, the percentage of permanent job losers only rose slightly to around 3%, indicating that roughly half of the unemployment spike was temporary. The second chart displays the ratio of unemployed persons and job seekers per job opening from 2001 to 2020. This ratio peaked above 6 in the Great Recession and reached nearly 5 during the 2020 pandemic onset, but rapidly fell back toward 2. This lower ratio of job seekers to openings relative to previous recessions suggests that once the pandemic is under control, a strong and rapid recovery in employment and wages is likely.

This page outlines the critical challenges facing the United States in its battle against COVID-19 as infections, hospitalizations, and deaths surge, threatening to trigger further economic lockdowns. Michael Cembalest focuses on the complex path to herd immunity, which must overcome three distinct hurdles: vaccine approval, distribution, and public acceptance. 

While Pfizer’s announcement of 90% efficacy in its Phase III trials is a promising step toward emergency approval, the logistical challenge of vaccine distribution is massive. It requires ultra-cold storage at negative 94 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 70 degrees Celsius) and a booster shot 21 days after the initial dose. Furthermore, public acceptance remains a significant hurdle; the author highlights a September 2020 Pew Research poll revealing that only 51% of U.S. respondents would get a vaccine, alongside a USA Today poll indicating only 27% would take it immediately. Cembalest notes that the U.S. ranks in the lower third globally for vaccine acceptance and argues that greater adherence to scientific principles in Washington, including retaining Dr. Fauci, would bolster public trust.

To support these points, the page includes three visual exhibits. The first, a dual-axis line chart titled "United States virus tracking," plots current hospitalizations and new daily infections on the left axis and daily deaths on the right axis from March to November 2020. The chart shows a dramatic autumn surge, with daily infections skyrocketing past 100,000 by November, eclipsing the previous April and July waves. Hospitalizations are also shown climbing steeply toward 60,000, while daily deaths have begun to trend upward again, reaching roughly 1,000 per day. 

An accompanying text panel outlines the CDC's five vaccine priority groups to show the scale of the upcoming distribution effort. It details the target populations, starting with healthcare personnel (17 to 20 million people) and essential workers (60 to 80 million), followed by adults aged 65 or older (53 million), individuals with high-risk medical conditions like obesity or diabetes (over 100 million), and finally, the remaining general public, who make up about half of the population.

Lastly, a bar chart titled "Estimated COVID prevalence by state as of early August 2020" highlights how far the country remains from natural herd immunity. Based on CDC seroprevalence surveys, the chart shows that only New York has an estimated exposure rate above 20 percent, with New Jersey around 14 percent and Louisiana at roughly 11 percent. The vast majority of states show exposure rates below 5 percent, emphasizing that most of the country is still highly vulnerable.

This page features a critique by Michael Cembalest of various market prognosticators, referred to as "Armageddonists," who issued extremely pessimistic economic and stock market forecasts during the initial wave of the COVID-19 pandemic. 

The main visual is a line chart titled "Timing is everything," which tracks the S&P 500 index from January 1, 2020, through late October 2020. The chart’s vertical axis ranges from 2,000 to 3,800. It illustrates the index's steep drop in early 2020, followed by a steady, V-shaped recovery that eventually surpassed pre-pandemic highs, approaching 3,600 by the end of the period. Red dots plotted along the line mark the exact timing of bearish pronouncements by prominent figures, showing that these pessimistic forecasts occurred almost entirely near the market's absolute trough in March and April.

An accompanying table provides the specific dates, commentators, and quotes illustrated in the chart. On March 4, 2020, David Stockman predicted a 50% correction to 1,600 on the S&P 500 and a prolonged L-shaped bottom rather than a V-shaped rebound. On March 24, Nouriel Roubini warned of a "Greater Depression" worse than the 1930s. The next day, March 25, Peter Schiff described Federal Reserve interventions as highly bearish, predicting a brutal depression ravaged by inflation. On March 26, John Hussman stated he expected the S&P 500 to lose about two-thirds of its value. By March 31, Jeff Gundlach wagered that the March lows would be broken before finding an enduring bottom. On April 1, George Soros declared that the market was entering the worst bear market of his lifetime. Later in April, Albert Edwards dismissed the idea that central bank liquidity could lift equities as "ludicrous," arguing that profits would collapse and funds would flow into government bonds instead. Finally, on May 12, David Rosenberg insisted that the U.S. was in a full-scale economic depression, characterized by secular behavioral shifts and a wave of bankruptcies rather than a normal business-cycle recession. 

Together, the chart and table demonstrate the perils of market timing, illustrating how these dire forecasts were issued at the exact moment the market was poised for a historic recovery.

Michael Cembalest argues that the COVID-19 pandemic did not rescue bearish market commentators, whom he terms the Armageddonists, from their long-term underperformance purgatory. He explains that while these forecasters might have anticipated a disaster scenario, the sharp equity market selloff in March 2020 was reversed so quickly that it did not erase the massive opportunity losses they accumulated by being underinvested from 2009 through 2019. Consequently, with markets back at all-time highs by late 2020, their bearish stances remain deeply unprofitable. Cembalest suggests that the only near-term event that could temporarily rescue these commentators' positions is the potential for electoral illegitimacy and constitutional turmoil in the United States leading up to January 6, 2021.

To illustrate this ongoing underperformance, the page features a line chart titled "COVID did not rescue the Armageddonists from underperformance purgatory." This chart tracks the performance impact from 2010 to November 13, 2020, of shifting one dollar from the S&P 500 to the Barclays Aggregate Bond Index at the specific week each commentator made a notably bearish or apocalyptic warning. The y-axis measures the percentage return impact, ranging from positive 5% down to negative 65%. 

The chart plots individual performance lines for several prominent financial figures and academics, including Simon Johnson, Paul Krugman, David Levy, Carl Icahn, John Hussman, George Soros, Bob Janjuah, Peter Schiff, Tom DeMark, David Stockman, Albert Edwards, Marc Faber, Laksham Achuthan, Robert Wiedemer, David Rosenberg, Jeff Gundlach, and Nouriel Roubini. Every single plotted line ends deep in negative territory. The most resilient strategy, associated with Simon Johnson and Paul Krugman, still suffered a loss of roughly 30% to 35% compared to holding equities. At the bottom of the chart, the strategy following the advice of Nouriel Roubini resulted in the worst underperformance, ending between negative 60% and negative 65%. While the sudden market crash in early 2020 caused a visible upward spike for all these strategies as bonds temporarily outperformed stocks, the subsequent rapid market rebound quickly dragged every single line back down to near-historical lows, demonstrating that a highly precise and nearly instantaneous rebalancing would have been required to salvage any of these bearish positions.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" provides an in-depth analysis of the post-2020 election risks and the legal and political maneuvers being pursued to contest the presidential election results. Michael Cembalest discusses the breaking news surrounding the Wayne County Board of Canvassers in Michigan, where GOP members initially refused to certify, then certified, and subsequently sought to rescind that certification. He outlines how an old Michigan state law might allow the state legislature to intervene if results are contested, which would likely lead to a state Supreme Court battle or federal court involvement. Additionally, the author notes the remote risk of Attorney General William Barr directing the Department of Justice to seize or impound election records to investigate voter fraud, which could delay state certification past the December 14 Electoral College deadline and violate the department's forty-year-old Non-Interference Policy—a policy shift that prompted a senior DoJ official to step down. 

The piece also evaluates the status of recounts in Georgia, which showed no material changes, alongside potential recounts in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Nevada, concluding that historical margins make a reversal highly unlikely at these gaps. Ultimately, Cembalest emphasizes that while Donald Trump would need to successfully reverse or block results in three states to prevent Joe Biden from reaching 270 electoral votes, the likelihood of this succeeding is extremely low. He cites election law expert Ed Foley of Ohio State, who maintains that Biden will be sworn in on January 20 due to the high legal hurdles required to throw out certified results, despite Trump firing his top election security official and continuing to file campaign lawsuits.

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for the publication, outlining distribution restrictions, licensing, and regulatory oversight across various jurisdictions, including Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America.

This page analyzes the low-probability but high-impact market risk of US post-election constitutional instability surrounding the January 6th electoral certification. The author argues that financial markets could react very negatively if the United States, as the global reserve currency nation, is seen as sliding toward electoral illegitimacy. 

To illustrate this, a scatter plot compares equity market P/E ratios on the y-axis, from 0 to 30, against an index of constraints on government power on the x-axis, from 30 to 100, across 67 countries. The index measures factors such as limitations by the legislature and judiciary, independent auditing, sanctions for misconduct, and whether transitions of power are subject to the law. The chart shows a clear positive correlation where countries with more constraints on government power trade at higher valuations. The United States is plotted near an index score of 70 with a P/E multiple of approximately 18. The author warns that a modest decline in the rule of law could de-rate US equities by three to four multiple points.

The text evaluates several legal and political scenarios. It notes that while competing slates of electors are extremely rare, having occurred only once in the twentieth century in Hawaii in 1960, they would be resolved by the newly seated Congress under the Electoral Count Act of 1887. Under these rules, a split Congress would default to whichever slate was signed by the state's governor. This would favor Democrats in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Nevada, and Republicans in Georgia and Arizona. 

Additionally, the page addresses a nightmare scenario proposed by historian Graham Allison, in which Senate Republicans might declare the Electoral Count Act unconstitutional, allowing Vice President Mike Pence to cast a deciding vote to flip three states and declare Donald Trump the victor. This could lead to a refusal by Democrats to participate and the threat of dueling inaugurations. However, the author presents a counter-mathematics argument based on the projected January 6th Senate composition of 51 Republicans and 48 Democrats, noting that if just two Republican Senators respect the Electoral Count Act, the gubernatorial tie-breaker rules will remain intact, averting this systemic crisis.

This page presents four appendix charts addressing political and economic trends around the 2020 U.S. presidential election, detailing historical economic tailwinds for incumbents, Joe Biden’s proposed policy agenda, the rise of the Senate filibuster, and the unprecedented scale of global monetary and fiscal intervention during the pandemic. 

The first chart features a presidential tailwind tracker that measures market and economic conditions at each election from 1896 to 2020. Based on inflation, equities, employment, home prices, and per capita GDP, the index scores conditions on a scale of 0.00 to 0.90, where higher scores indicate more favorable environments. The data shows that for the first time in 100 years, an incumbent with strong tailwinds lost the presidency, as Donald Trump lost in 2020 despite a favorable score of approximately 0.65, down only slightly from the pre-COVID December 2019 peak of over 0.80. This stands in contrast to past incumbent losses—such as Herbert Hoover in 1932, Gerald Ford in 1976, Jimmy Carter in 1980, and George H.W. Bush in 1992—all of whom faced far weaker economic conditions. 

The second chart details Joe Biden's proposed fiscal agenda, outlining approximately $3 trillion in taxes and $8 trillion in spending over a ten-year period. On the taxation side, the major revenue drivers include corporate tax hikes and base broadening, payroll taxes on incomes over $400,000, industry-specific taxes, and increased taxes on the wealthy, which are partially offset by about $1 trillion in tax credits for caregivers, renters, homebuyers, and reshoring manufacturers. The $8 trillion in proposed spending is directed toward entitlement expansion, housing, education, infrastructure and jobs, and healthcare, with a small offset from drug price reforms. 

The third chart plots the number of cloture motions filed from the 65th Congress to the 116th Congress, spanning 1917 to 2017. Serving as a proxy for filibuster frequency, the graph reveals a dramatic upward surge from virtually zero motions in the mid-20th century to nearly 250 motions by 2017. The text emphasizes that between 1917 and 1996, the correlation between cloture motions and documented filibusters was incredibly strong at 0.94.

The final scatter plot compares the debt monetization response during the Global Virus Crisis to other historical economic disruptions. It plots the change in government fiscal deficits as a percentage of GDP on the y-axis against the change in central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP on the x-axis. The data illustrates that the response to the Global Virus Crisis eclipsed all prior historical crises, including the Global Financial Crisis, the Great Depression, and the European Balance of Payments Crisis. During the pandemic, nations like the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, and the Eurozone executed massive simultaneous expansions of both fiscal deficits and central bank balance sheets, with the U.S. deficit expanding by nearly 14% of GDP and Japan's central bank balance sheet expanding by over 20% of GDP relative to pre-crisis levels. This dual-pronged expansion vastly exceeded the response to the Global Financial Crisis and differed from World War II, which saw massive fiscal deficits in the U.S. but very little central bank balance sheet expansion.

This page analyzes why bearish, "Armageddonist-driven" portfolios have underperformed, pointing to massive fiscal and monetary stimulus, resilient corporate earnings, and a technical shortage of equity supply. Michael Cembalest notes that the US has experienced its longest period of negative real policy rates in recorded history outside of the Civil War, World War I, and World War II. The policy response to the COVID-19 pandemic was twice as large and four times faster than the response to the Global Financial Crisis. Furthermore, corporate earnings in the third quarter of 2020 significantly beat consensus expectations, contracting by only 8% compared to the anticipated 25% drop. Free cash flow remained resilient, and Cembalest forecasts that S&P 500 earnings per share will exceed pre-pandemic levels by the end of 2021. This recovery is expected to continue into 2021, supported by vaccine rollouts from companies like Pfizer, Moderna, NovaVax, Johnson & Johnson, and AstraZeneca, alongside an estimated $3 to $4 trillion in central bank asset purchases. A primary risk to this outlook is a potentially unlawful or unorthodox US transition of power, which could temporarily boost bearish portfolios. In the footnotes, Cembalest references high infection rates in Michigan and criticism of comments made by Trump coronavirus adviser Scott Atlas.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart shows the five-year average of real yields on cash (defined as the T-bill/Funds rate minus inflation) from 1830 to 2020. This visual highlights that negative real yields in 2020 reached levels seen only during major historical wartime periods: the Civil War, World War I, and World War II. 

The second chart compares the change in government fiscal deficits to the change in central bank balance sheets, both as a percentage of GDP relative to pre-crisis levels. It illustrates that the policy response to the Global Virus Crisis (GVC) in the US, UK, Japan, and Europe far exceeded the responses to the Global Financial Crisis, the Great Depression, and the Europe Balance of Payments Crisis. For example, Japan's central bank balance sheet expansion during the GVC reached nearly 30% of GDP, while the US GVC fiscal deficit expansion exceeded 12% of GDP, trailing only the fiscal deficit expansion seen during US participation in World War II.

The third chart tracks the net supply of US equities in billions of dollars from 1999 to 2020, based on the MSCI All Country World Equity Index. The data shows that net equity supply turned sharply negative starting in 2014 and remained deeply negative through 2020, dropping to between negative $200 billion and negative $300 billion annually. This structural deficit arose because stock buybacks and merger activity consistently outpaced new share issuances.

The fourth chart plots daily infections per million on the left axis against daily deaths per million on the right axis for developed regions from March to late November 2020. It shows that while daily infections surged to a new peak of over 350 per million in November—well above the spring peak of roughly 75 per million—the daily death rate, though rising to nearly 4.0 per million, remained below its spring peak of approximately 6.0 per million.

This page of the J.P. Morgan report examines the constitutional, legal, and political dynamics of the contested 2020 U.S. presidential election, particularly analyzing the role of the Supreme Court and the potential for a contingent election. The author argues that a contingent election is highly unlikely because most paths lead to a candidate securing 270 electoral votes; even if a state fails to submit its votes by the mid-December deadline, those votes would likely be omitted entirely, leaving the winner to be decided by a simple majority of the remaining votes. 

Regarding the Supreme Court, the author details two main scenarios. First, the Court is unlikely to alter the election outcome through state-level challenges, as many cases involving late absentee ballots in Pennsylvania or transparency complaints represent vote counts too small to shift results, and lower courts have already rejected most fraud claims. Second, the author posits that a constitutional challenge to the Electoral Count Act would fail due to a lack of legal standing under Article III, alongside the political question doctrine, which grants sole authority over electoral vote validation to Congress rather than federal courts.

To clarify the political control over election certifications, a table lists the party affiliations of key entities across six battleground states along with their certification deadlines. The table details Arizona (Republican Governor, Republican Legislature, Democratic Secretary of State, 11 electoral votes, November 30th deadline), Georgia (Republican Governor, Republican Legislature, Republican Secretary of State, 16 electoral votes, November 20th deadline), Michigan (Democratic Governor, Republican Legislature, Democratic Secretary of State, 16 electoral votes, November 23rd deadline), Nevada (Democratic Governor, Democratic Legislature, Republican Secretary of State, 6 electoral votes, November 24th deadline), Pennsylvania (Democratic Governor, Republican Legislature, Democratic Secretary of State, 20 electoral votes, November 23rd deadline), and Wisconsin (Democratic Governor, Republican Legislature, Democratic Secretary of State, 10 electoral votes, December 1st deadline).

The author includes a commentary box noting that Senate Republicans blocked several election security bills earlier in 2020 and references a fact-checking resource to debunk popular online conspiracy theories alleging that a supercomputer hacked and switched election votes. The analysis draws on insights from election law expert Michael Morley of Florida State University, as well as articles by Graham Allison in The National Interest and Edward B. Foley in the Washington Post.

This J.P. Morgan report page, authored by Michael Cembalest, introduces the upcoming 2021 Outlook while discussing the economic hurdles and recovery prospects associated with the COVID-19 pandemic. Cembalest notes that while the United States economy is experiencing speed bumps from rising hospitalizations and deaths, massive government stimulus and vaccine rollouts set the stage for a 2021 recovery, even if future generations bear the ultimate financial burden. He points out critical uncertainties, including vaccine hesitancy—potentially exacerbated by political pressures like White House Chief of Staff Mark Meadows' reported threats to the head of the FDA regarding the Pfizer vaccine—and whether vaccines block asymptomatic transmission. Additionally, citing CDC antibody tests showing exposure levels of twenty-two percent in New York and under ten percent in most other states, he warns that there is still a long path to herd immunity.

To illustrate consumer behavior during the pandemic, the page features two charts. The first chart, titled National Credit and Debit Card Spending Trends, tracks year-over-year transaction changes from March to November 2020 using Chase internal data. It shows that overall spending dropped to nearly negative thirty percent in April before recovering to fluctuations between zero and negative ten percent. Conversely, card-present transactions, representing in-person retail, fell much deeper to negative fifty percent in April and remained significantly depressed, fluctuating around negative fifteen to twenty percent through November. 

The second chart, titled Due to COVID, Potential Spending Exceeds Actual Consumption, plots year-over-year percentage changes from 1972 to 2020. It compares spending potential—modeled using taxable income, transfer payments, housing wealth, and financial wealth—against actual consumption growth. While these two lines historically moved in tandem, 2020 saw an unprecedented divergence. Spending potential spiked to around fifteen percent due to government stimulus and wealth growth, while actual consumption plunged below zero, reflecting a massive pool of pent-up demand ready to be unleashed as the economy eventually reopens.

This page of the publication focuses on the transition from the depths of the pandemic toward recovery, using the metaphor of the winter of our discontent giving way to summer. The author argues that despite currently overwhelmed hospital systems and elevated deaths, successful vaccine trials from Pfizer, Moderna, and AstraZeneca suggest that the crisis is nearing its end. The rapid development of these novel mRNA and vector-based vaccines contrasts with slow traditional vaccine development and past failures to find an AIDS vaccine. The author reiterates their March 2020 forecast that the world would be 70% to 80% back to normal by spring 2021, supported by historic fiscal and monetary stimulus rather than the multi-year depression predicted by pessimistic forecasters.

To illustrate how medical progress overcomes historical setbacks, a line chart tracks male life expectancy in France from 1740 to 2010. The data shows sharp, temporary drops in life expectancy during the Napoleonic wars, the War of 1870, World War I, and World War II, followed by a dramatic and sustained upward trajectory beginning after Alexander Fleming's invention of antibiotics, which pushed life expectancy from under 50 years to nearly 80 years.

An economic indicators table demonstrates that a rapid economic recovery is well underway. While total employment remains 6% below December 2019 levels (representing a 61% recovery from its peak decline), other areas have rebounded much faster. Leisure and hospitality employment has recovered 59% of its peak decline, and capacity utilization has recovered 66%. Consumer spending is nearly back to normal, down just 2% from December 2019 after recovering 89% of its peak losses, while housing starts have clawed back 91% of their decline. Crucially, several metrics have fully recovered and now exceed pre-pandemic levels: spending on consumer goods is up 9% compared to December 2019, retail sales are up 5%, core capital goods shipments are up 5%, and rail traffic of consumer goods is up 15%.

The page concludes with two charts highlighting the ongoing, immediate impact of the pandemic. The first is a bar chart showing the ten most overcrowded hospital systems as of late November 2020, ranked by the percentage of ICU patients in hospitals with ICU capacity rates above 90%. South Dakota leads this list at roughly 80%, followed closely by Texas, Minnesota, Oklahoma, and North Dakota. The final chart tracks weekly excess deaths from January 2019 through late 2020, plotting actual weekly deaths from all causes against the expected threshold for excess deaths. The visual shows substantial spikes in actual deaths far above the normal seasonal threshold, peaking near 80,000 deaths per week in the spring of 2020, which refutes arguments that recent mortality trends represent typical non-COVID causes of death.

This page contains standard legal and regulatory disclosures for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication. It outlines distribution guidelines, licensing information, and governing regulatory bodies across various international jurisdictions, including Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America. Additionally, the text details standard warnings regarding the private placement of financial instruments, currency risks, and local tax implications, alongside J.P. Morgan's copyright and personal usage restrictions.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s publication analyzes the turbulent political aftermath of the 2020 US Presidential Election, focusing on allegations of voter fraud, the legal system's response, and the structural factors of political polarization. The author highlights that despite intense legal challenges—including a lawsuit by the Texas Attorney General against Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Georgia—the judiciary consistently dismissed thirty to forty of Trump’s election lawsuits. Cembalest calls for objective academic research into how high rates of absentee voting impact polarized and gerrymandered districts, questioning why swing states like Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Wisconsin do not process absentee ballots before Election Day like most other states. He contextualizes fraud claims by citing their historical rarity, noting that the Brennan Center for Justice calculated a voter fraud rate of just 0.0025 percent, while the Heritage Foundation’s database documented only 1,300 proven cases since the year 2000. The text also notes that Senate Republicans blocked multiple election security bills in early 2020.

To illustrate the changing electoral landscape, the first chart displays the share of absentee and mail-in ballots as a percentage of total votes cast in 2016 versus 2020 across key swing states. The data shows dramatic surges in mail-in voting in 2020: Michigan leaped from roughly 20 percent to nearly 60 percent, Nevada rose from around 10 percent to over 50 percent, and both Pennsylvania and Wisconsin increased from near zero in 2016 to over 40 percent in 2020. Arizona saw the highest volume, growing from around 70 percent to more than 80 percent. The second chart presents a proxy for political polarization and gerrymandering by charting the number of competitive Congressional districts in presidential elections between 1997 and 2017, where competitive is defined as being within 5 percent of the party's national average. The line graph shows a steep, steady decline, with the number of competitive districts dropping from 163 in 1997 to just 73 out of 435 in 2017.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Holiday Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, addresses the post-election landscape of the 2020 US Presidential Election, contrasting popular conspiracy theories with the actual legal realities of the transition of power. 

The prominent visual is a highly convoluted, satirical flowchart presented as the output of a neural network model processing swing-state voting data, news stories, and Twitter feeds. The map connects disparate and absurd concepts to satirize the wild election conspiracy theories of the time. Key elements in the web of associations include Dominion Voting Systems linked to Minions and the Illuminati, the Deep State linked to Janet Jackson and Rhythm Nation, and the word FRAUD surrounded by references to Jack Dorsey, Twitter's disputed claim tags, and the play Rhinoceros. Additionally, the flowchart connects Hugo Chavez, vuvuzelas, and communism on one side, while linking Chris Krebs to Mr. Krabs and the Krusty Krab, and connecting affidavits to Michelangelo's Statue of David, oranges, and the Netflix documentary My Octopus Teacher. 

In the accompanying text, the author notes that while the chart is obviously satirical, there is a legitimate need for a post-mortem on absentee ballot handling and for the US Supreme Court to clarify the boundaries between state legislatures and state courts regarding election law changes. The author references the Ohio amicus brief, which denied Texas standing to sue other states but supported the need for judicial clarification. 

Looking forward, the author notes that all states have certified their results and electors are meeting to cast their votes, leading toward the January 6th Congressional joint session and the January 20th inauguration. He poses the question of whether Donald Trump has any remaining chance to stay in office, concluding that while technically possible, it is highly improbable. 

An extensive footnote provides legal context on the Trump campaign's challenges. It explains that the Supreme Court could eventually rule that only state legislatures, not state courts, can change election rules, referencing the dispute over Pennsylvania's three-day extension for absentee ballots. It also discusses pending equal protection cases regarding ballot-curing and voter identification requirements, noting a recent Wisconsin Supreme Court ruling against Trump and concluding that remedies such as decertifying state electors are highly unlikely to succeed.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management addresses the issue of growing political polarization in the United States, titled "The Purge." He argues that moderate politicians are becoming increasingly rare in both parties, which is contributing to a decline in long-term US economic growth. Cembalest observes that polarization has led voters to act out of antipathy toward the opposing party rather than support for their own, with many viewing the other side as "immoral." He highlights controversial proposals supported by most 2020 Democratic primary candidates—excluding Joe Biden—such as eliminating the Electoral College and ending the Senate filibuster, warning that these changes could disenfranchise resource-producing states and allow narrow, single-party majorities to push through major legislation without bipartisan input. In a historical footnote, Cembalest draws a parallel to the French Revolution, noting how the radical Jacobins eventually purged and executed the slightly less radical Girondins.

The page features a detailed bar chart titled "Partisanship gap for major US legislation," which plots the average difference in "yea" votes between parties in the House and Senate across major bills since the early 20th century. The vertical axis measures partisanship from 0% (least partisan) to 100% (most partisan). The chart illustrates a dramatic shift toward hyper-partisanship in recent decades. The most partisan bill in history is the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, with a gap of approximately 97%, followed closely by the Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 at over 90%, the Affordable Care Act of 2010 at about 86%, and the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Act of 2010 at roughly 83%. This modern polarization contrasts sharply with historic landmark legislation that enjoyed broad consensus, such as the Social Security Act of 1935 with a gap of roughly 40%, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 at about 30%, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 at around 25%. The least partisan bills highlighted include emergency measures and environmental protections, led by the Coronavirus CARES Act of 2020, the Clean Air Act of 1970, and the Environmental Policy Act of 1969, all of which register partisanship gaps under 10%.

This page analyzes the rising tide of political polarization and partisan extremism in the United States, evaluating its correlation with economic growth and tracking shifts in public sentiment. The author utilizes partisanship scores from UCLA's VoteView project, which defines moderates as politicians with voting scores between -0.25 and +0.25, and extremists as those below -0.6 or above +0.6. 

The first of six charts contrasts the share of moderates in the House and Senate against subsequent ten-year cumulative real GDP growth from 1950 to 2020. This visual reveals a parallel downward trend: congressional moderates plummeted from roughly 45% in the mid-20th century to nearly 10% by 2020, while subsequent ten-year cumulative real GDP growth slipped from over 50% to around 20%. 

The subsequent three charts detail the rise of extremists versus the decline of moderates in both congressional chambers from 1885 to 2020. In the House of Representatives, GOP moderates peaked near 55% in the mid-1900s before collapsing to under 10% by 2020, while GOP extremists rose sharply to nearly 30%. Democratic House moderates similarly peaked above 50% and fell to around 15%, though Democratic House extremists remained under 10%. In the Senate, GOP extremists spiked dramatically after 2005 to roughly 20% by 2020, while Democratic Senate extremists hovered near 5%.

The final two charts document growing animosity among the public. According to Pew Research data, the percentage of respondents who believe members of the opposing party are immoral rose significantly between 2016 and 2019; the Democratic view of Republicans rose from roughly 35% to 47%, and the Republican view of Democrats grew from 47% to 55%. This is reinforced by a longitudinal survey tracking feelings toward political parties on a scale from negative 50 degrees to positive 50 degrees. While voters' warmth toward their own party has remained consistently positive at around 20 to 25 degrees since 1976, their antipathy toward the opposing party has steadily deepened, dropping from a near-neutral negative 5 degrees in the late 1970s to nearly negative 30 degrees by 2020.

This page contains an appendix detailing the legal and constitutional rules governing the Joint Session of Congress on January 6th, specifically addressing the technical possibility of Donald Trump remaining President after the 2020 election. The analysis focuses on the Electoral Count Act of 1887, which was passed following the constitutional crisis of the 1876 Rutherford B. Hayes election to resolve electoral vote disputes. 

The author explains that if competing slates of electors are submitted, as suggested by White House Senior Advisor Stephen Miller, the House and Senate must vote separately on them. Democrats control the House, while the Senate has a narrow 51-to-48 Republican majority. Because it would only take two Republican Senators, such as Mitt Romney or Ben Sasse, to vote with Democrats to accept certified Biden electors, a Senate effort to accept competing Trump slates is highly unlikely to succeed. 

Furthermore, the author outlines the procedural rules under the Electoral Count Act. If the two chambers disagree on which slate to accept, the tie-breaker goes to the slate already approved by the state's governor. In the contested states of Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, Arizona, and Georgia, the governors have already approved the Biden slates. Therefore, the only way for Trump to win under the Act would be for both chambers to vote to accept three competing Trump slates that have not been signed by a governor, state legislature, or court. The author describes this scenario as preposterously implausible while still technically possible. 

The text also addresses objections to single slates in states without competing electors, noting that these are doomed to fail because both chambers must agree to discard a slate. Even if a slate were discarded, those electors would be removed from the overall count rather than transferred, meaning a candidate would still only need a majority of the remaining appointed electors to win. Finally, the author dismisses speculation about contingent elections under the 12th Amendment, clarifying that such an event would only occur in the highly unlikely scenario of an Electoral College tie, a massive faithless elector event, or the death of the winner before January 6th. Footnotes on the page elaborate on the academic debate over the constitutionality of the Electoral Count Act, the legal definition of a state's highest executive, and the rarity of faithless electors.

This page serves as an executive summary for J.P. Morgan’s 2021 market outlook, titled "The Hazmat Recovery." The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that while 2020 was dominated by the COVID-19 pandemic and a highly contested US presidential election, its defining characteristic for investors was the arrival of unprecedented monetary and fiscal "mega-stimulus." This massive, rapid policy response is expected to shape the investment landscape for 2021 and beyond. Although winter surges of the virus slowed US spending, vaccine rollouts are projected to bring the global economy close to pre-pandemic activity levels by late summer 2021. In the US, vaccine phases 1a through 1c—targeting healthcare workers, essential workers, and high-risk individuals—are expected to be completed by June. Developed nations overall are projected to secure enough vaccine capacity to cover 1.5 to 2.0 times their vulnerable populations, and half to 70% of their total populations, by the second quarter of 2021. 

To illustrate the sheer scale of the policy response, the first chart compares the fiscal and monetary stimulus of the "Global Virus Crisis" against past crises, plotting fiscal stimulus as a percentage of GDP on the vertical axis against monetary stimulus on the horizontal axis. The data shows that the current crisis dwarfs all historical equivalents, including the Global Financial Crisis. During the pandemic, Japan's monetary stimulus expanded its central bank balance sheet by over 32% of GDP, while the US, UK, and Europe all deployed combined fiscal and monetary packages in the double digits, with US fiscal stimulus near 13% and monetary stimulus near 15% of GDP. In comparison, stimulus during the Global Financial Crisis, the US Great Depression, and the European Balance of Payments Crisis was significantly smaller, rarely exceeding 10% of GDP on either axis. 

A second chart tracks the growth of the money supply (defined as M2 plus institutional money market fund balances) using an index starting at 100. During the Global Coronavirus Crisis starting in January 2020, this index shot up rapidly to nearly 125 by the end of the year. This stands in stark contrast to the Global Financial Crisis from August 2008 to September 2010, where the money supply index remained remarkably flat, barely reaching 105 over a similar multi-month timeline.

Economic activity trends are highlighted in a third chart displaying regional manufacturing and services business surveys (Markit PMI) from January 2020 to January 2021, where a reading above 50 indicates expansion. Following a dramatic plunge in early 2020 that dragged all major economies deep into contractionary territory, China and the US staged strong recoveries, climbing back into solid expansionary territory between 55 and 58 by late 2020. Conversely, the Eurozone experienced a secondary dip back below the 50 mark in late autumn, while Japan hovered just below expansionary territory. 

Finally, a fourth chart tracks current COVID-19 hospitalizations per million people as a 7-day average, plotted against the number of days after total cases reached 100. The chart illustrates a clear two-wave pattern for Italy, France, the US, and the UK. During the second wave, around 250 to 300 days into the local outbreaks, hospitalization rates spiked dramatically, with Italy and France peaking between 500 and 600 hospitalizations per million people, the UK surging past 550, and the US steadily rising to approximately 350 hospitalizations per million people.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market Executive Summary discusses the mixed signals in the US economy during the COVID pandemic, focusing on business inventory conditions, business creation, severe sectoral employment declines, and mortgage delinquency rates. 

Cembalest first argues that tight inventory conditions and elevated supplier delivery delays should support mid-year economic growth as businesses increase hiring and capital spending to meet demand. This trend is illustrated in the Business Inventory Tightening chart, which tracks the net percentage of businesses reporting inventories as too low versus too high. The data, sourced from the National Federation of Independent Business up to November 2020, shows a massive spike in late 2020 to nearly five percent, indicating highly depleted inventories. Surprisingly, despite widespread pandemic-related business closures, there was a massive spike in entrepreneurial activity. This is depicted in a chart showing weekly new business applications filed with the IRS in 2020 as a percentage of 2019 levels. Applications dipped to roughly seventy percent in April but surged dramatically to over two hundred and ten percent by July before leveling off to around one hundred and ninety percent by mid-December.

Conversely, the page notes that the employment decline in COVID-affected sectors has been catastrophic. To contextualize this, a scatter plot compares year-over-year changes in private sector employment against average weekly earnings across various industries, using BLS data from November 2020. The leisure and hospitality sector, which averages only about four hundred and fifty dollars in weekly earnings, suffered a devastating employment drop of approximately twenty percent. Cembalest highlights that in previous recessions, the peak employment decline was only four to six percent, which is roughly where better-positioned, higher-wage sectors like information services and financial activities sat in late 2020. 

Lastly, the author examines household financial resilience, noting that fiscal stimulus successfully restored spending for the lowest income cohorts to pre-pandemic levels by June. Regarding household mortgage health, the page explores a divergence in delinquency metrics shown in a final chart tracking rates from 2004 to 2020. The Mortgage Bankers Association delinquency rate, which counts loans in forbearance as delinquent, spiked sharply to over eight percent in 2020. Meanwhile, the Fed delinquency rate, which assumes borrowers in forbearance will eventually become current, remained much lower at around three percent. Cembalest concludes that because unpaid balances will ultimately be deferred to balloon payments at the end of the mortgage term, the actual state of household health is likely closer to the more optimistic Fed estimate.

In this page of J.P. Morgan's 2021 Outlook, Michael Cembalest argues that pandemic shocks differ fundamentally from traditional recessions, primarily because pandemic-driven economic cycles move much faster. This rapid pace is illustrated across employment, production, consumer spending, and capital spending. The author forecasts that the United States economic recovery will continue through 2021, expecting the US unemployment rate to end 2021 at approximately 5%. A central observation is that while unemployed individuals surged during the 2020 lockdowns, the actual number of active job seekers per job opening did not rise correspondingly, suggesting that most laid-off workers expected to return to their existing jobs once restrictions lifted.

This thesis is supported by six charts. The first chart, tracking national credit and debit card spending trends in 2020 versus 2019, shows that while card-present transactions plummeted by nearly 50% in April 2020, total spending across all transactions fell much less severely and staged a steady recovery, despite a minor spending speed bump around autumn. The second chart focuses on US unemployment and job openings from 2006 to 2022, displaying a dramatic spike in the unemployment rate to nearly 15% in early 2020, which is projected to fall to 5% by the end of 2021. This chart also shows that the ratio of unemployed persons per job opening spiked to around 5 in 2020, remaining lower than the peak of over 6 reached during the Great Recession. The third chart highlights the key labor market difference between 2009 and 2020, demonstrating that while the ratio of unemployed people per job opening spiked near 5 in 2020, the ratio of actual job seekers per job opening remained remarkably low, near 1, unlike in 2009 when both measures spiked in tandem to over 6.

The fourth chart presents US industrial production and manufacturing indexes from 2006 to 2020, showing a sharp, V-shaped collapse and partial rebound in 2020, which contrasts with the prolonged, multi-year contraction seen after 2008. The fifth chart, depicting capital spending expectations as the net percentage of companies planning to increase capex, illustrates a rapid recovery from a brief dip to around -10% in 2020, a much milder and shorter decline than the dip to around -20% recorded in 2009. Finally, the sixth chart plots US real retail sales in billions of 1982-1984 dollars, revealing an unprecedented V-shaped recovery in 2020, where retail sales rapidly plummeted to near 165 billion before surging to all-time highs above 210 billion, highlighting the unique nature of the pandemic shock compared to the sluggish recovery following the 2008 financial crisis.

This analysis from J.P. Morgan's Executive Summary addresses the rapid expansion of US federal debt, which is projected to reach levels not seen since World War II by the end of 2021. The author notes that the 2020 fiscal deficit hit 16 percent of GDP, the largest since 1945, and forecasts that the 2021 deficit will likely exceed 10 percent of GDP due to ongoing stimulus measures and growth adjustments. On top of these deficits, the proposed Biden administration tax and spending plans are estimated to introduce an additional 3 trillion dollars in taxes and 8 trillion dollars in spending over the next decade, driving national debt even higher. 

The visual layout supports these points with four key charts. The top-left chart tracks gross federal debt held by the public as a percentage of US GDP from 1940 to 2020, with estimates for 2021. It reveals a steep, post-WWII descent down to a low of approximately 25 percent in the mid-1970s, followed by a steady climb that accelerates dramatically after 2010, culminating in 2020 and 2021 estimates that nearly match the historical WWII peak of over 100 percent of GDP. To the right, a projection chart compares trailing ten-year averages of government spending and revenue as a percentage of GDP under "current policy" versus the "Biden agenda" up to 2040. While current policy keeps spending around 21 percent and revenues around 17 percent, the Biden agenda is projected to propel spending toward 24 percent and revenues toward 18 percent of GDP, representing post-war highs.

A major focus of the page is the impact of these changes on corporate taxation, which has been a primary driver of S&P 500 profit expansion since the 1980s. A chart on the bottom right depicts the steady decline in the median effective tax rate of large-cap stocks from roughly 50 percent in 1956 down to around 20 percent by 2020.
