Biden's proposal aims to raise 2.2 trillion dollars through corporate tax hikes, base broadening, and industry-specific taxes, a substantial shift compared to the 740 billion dollars in corporate tax cuts delivered by President Trump’s 2017 tax bill. The author estimates this plan could reduce S&P 500 earnings per share by roughly 10 percent, prior to factoring in any economic multiplier effects from increased government spending. 

The final chart on the bottom left details the composition of the proposed 3 trillion dollars in taxes and 8 trillion dollars in spending over ten years. The taxation bar shows that revenue will primarily be raised through payroll taxes on incomes over 400,000 dollars, corporate tax hikes, industry-specific taxes, and taxes on the wealthy, offset slightly by tax credits. The spending bar illustrates that the 8 trillion dollars will be distributed across healthcare, infrastructure and jobs, education, housing, and entitlement expansion, offset by savings achieved through drug price reforms.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, titled "Executive Summary," discusses the pervasive impact of zero interest rates on the broader investment landscape and their role in driving historically high equity valuations. 

To illustrate the unprecedented nature of current interest rates, the author presents two charts on developed market sovereign debt. The first chart, "Developed markets negative yielding government debt," tracks the percentage of total debt with negative yields from 2017 to 2020. By 2020, about a third of developed market sovereign debt yielded below zero in nominal terms, while roughly 75% carried negative real yields (after adjusting for inflation). The adjacent chart, tracking the five-year average of the lowest real yields on cash since 1830, shows that the last decade has experienced the longest sustained period of negative real policy rates in recorded US history, with the only exceptions being major wartime periods like the Civil War, World War I, and World War II.

This environment of depressed yields has pushed equity valuations to historical extremes, as detailed in an "Equity valuation percentiles" table. By late 2020, the median S&P 500 valuation metric reached the 93rd percentile of historical expensiveness, up from the 89th percentile in December 2019. Key metrics such as US market cap to GDP, Enterprise Value to Sales, and Enterprise Value to EBITDA all sat at the maximum 100th percentile, while the Forward P/E ratio was in the 97th percentile. The author notes that these high multiples are partially rationalized by the modern composition of the S&P 500. Today, 90% of the index's market capitalization is tied to intangible assets like software and intellectual property, compared to just 20% in 1975, 30% in 1985, and 80% by 2005. This less capital-intensive structure naturally justifies an upward drift in P/E ratios relative to the asset-heavy 1960–1980 era. 

Despite this structural shift, the author cautions that extreme investor optimism—with sentiment measures like the American Association of Individual Investors index at the 98th percentile, the NAAIM Active Managers Sentiment at the 99th percentile, and cash holdings of the top 20 US mutual funds at the 100th percentile of optimism—will likely limit S&P 500 gains to approximately 10% in 2021. This overly bullish consensus sets the stage for periodic market corrections and profit-taking.

For investors searching for cheaper opportunities, the page provides a table listing the S&P 500 industries that have not yet fully recovered from the pandemic's impact. The deepest 2020 declines were concentrated in energy equipment and services (down 37%), oil, gas, and consumable fuels (down 34%), and airlines (down 31%). Other lagging sectors include aerospace and defense (down 17%), banks (down 15%), gas utilities (down 15%), and real estate investment trusts (down 4%).

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market 2021 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, argues that while corporate earnings are poised for a strong rebound, much of this positive development is already reflected in market prices. Cembalest highlights the resilience of corporate earnings during the pandemic, noting that Q3 2020 S&P 500 earnings fell by only 8%, significantly beating the consensus expectation of a 25% drop. He points out that the earnings contraction was concentrated almost entirely in travel-related businesses and the energy sector; when excluding financials, REITs, and energy, core equity market free cash flow actually increased during the first three quarters of 2020. Cembalest predicts that S&P 500 earnings per share will exceed pre-pandemic levels by the end of 2021.

The analysis is supported by four charts. The first chart, showing the S&P 500 Q3 2020 consensus EPS expectations year-over-year percentage change from January to late October 2020, tracks how expectations plummeted from a positive 8% in January to a low of nearly negative 25% in May, before recovering to roughly negative 10% by the end of October. 

The second chart displays the contribution to S&P 500 profits from operating leverage after recessions and other market declines, measuring the year-over-year percentage change. It compares five historical recovery periods: post-S&L crisis, post-LTCM crisis, post-Tech bubble, post-GFC, and post-emerging markets/oil collapse. The data series show that in the quarters immediately following these crises, the contribution from operating leverage (represented by light orange bars) is the dominant driver of total operating EPS growth (represented by black diamonds), far exceeding the contribution from sales growth (represented by blue bars). Cembalest expects this operating leverage dynamic to repeat in 2021.

The second half of the page addresses the technical factors driving rapid bear market recoveries, specifically the shrinking supply of investible public equity in the United States. Since 2011, US buybacks and M&A activity have consistently outpaced primary and secondary equity issuances. Consequently, when institutional investors rebalance, supply constraints accelerate market gains. This phenomenon is illustrated by the two bottom charts, both measuring net equity supply in billions of US dollars from 1999 to 2020, based on the MSCI All Country World Equity Index. The left chart shows unprecedented low levels of net US equity supply, which turned deeply negative in 2007 and has remained consistently negative for nearly every year since 2011, bottoming near negative $300 billion in 2016. The right chart shows that outside the United States, net equity supply has continued to grow, staying consistently positive since 2003 and reaching over $400 billion in 2020, demonstrating that the equity shortage is uniquely a US phenomenon.

This page analyzes the policy and market implications of a narrow 51-50 Democratic Senate majority following Jon Ossoff’s election victory. The author argues that while Democrats could enact some tax and spending changes through budget reconciliation, they will face significant hurdles passing Joe Biden’s full legislative agenda or eliminating the Senate filibuster. Moderate Democrats, specifically Senator Joe Manchin, are expected to block progressive overhauls. A scatter plot of 2020 Senate polarization scores, ranging from 1.0 (most liberal) to -1.0 (most conservative), illustrates this dynamic, showing Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker, and Bernie Sanders at the liberal end, while Joe Manchin sits near 0.1, placing him closer to moderate Republicans Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski than to his own party's progressive wing.

Due to this polarization, eliminating the filibuster remains highly unlikely. This resistance is contextualized by a line chart showing the historical frequency of cloture motions—serving as a proxy for filibuster usage—which has climbed dramatically from near-zero in 1917 to over 200 in recent congressional sessions. Because the filibuster will likely remain, Democrats must rely on budget reconciliation, which is subject to strict rules. As detailed in the footnotes, reconciliation requires deficit neutrality after ten years and prohibits changes to payroll or social security taxes, which would block $870 billion of Biden’s proposed $3 trillion tax plan.

Consequently, the author anticipates a compromise tax bill that implements only about one-third of Biden’s original proposals. A waterfall chart illustrates how the original Biden tax plan would impact the 2022 S&P 500 EPS estimate, showing a drop from a baseline forecast of $195 down to a potential $176. This reduction is driven by an $8 hit from the statutory corporate rate hike (increasing from 21% to 28%), a $4 impact from the GILTI tax increase, a $3 headwind from Social Security payroll taxes on high earners, a $2 corporate minimum tax drag, and $2 in industry-specific taxes.

Instead of this full drag, a table summarizing policy expectations under a Democratic Senate predicts a moderate corporate tax hike of 25% rather than 28%, alongside an individual tax rate increase back to 39.6%. In other sectors, the publication predicts an expansion of the Affordable Care Act, drug price controls, a return to the Paris climate accord without a fracking ban, increased green energy subsidies, and a $1 trillion infrastructure deal funded via budget reconciliation. Beyond legislation, the administration is expected to reinstate Net Neutrality, expand DACA, and increase immigration agency staffing.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses market concentration, valuation, and antitrust risks among US equities. Michael Cembalest points out that since 2016, the top five megacap tech stocks—Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Facebook—have represented a disproportionate share of overall market capitalization and return contribution. While they are highly profitable and not as expensive relative to their late-1990s counterparts, he notes that J.P. Morgan is neutral on these stocks heading into 2021 due to domestic antitrust risks and digital service taxes abroad. As an alternative, he suggests looking at other secular high-growth stocks with strong fundamentals and lower antitrust profiles.

The analysis is supported by four charts and a table of stock ideas. The first chart, "Contribution of top firms to overall US market cap," tracks the market capitalization share of the top 5 and top 20 firms from 1990 through late 2020. The top five firms (Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Facebook) saw their share of the overall market cap surge after 2016 to over 20%, while the top 20 firms reached more than 40% of the total market cap by late 2020. The second chart, "S&P 500 megacap outperformance," compares the cumulative outperformance of the market-cap-weighted index over the equal-weighted index during two periods: 1997–2002 and 2017–2020. Megacap outperformance peaked near 50% in the dot-com bubble before collapsing, while the 2017–2020 trend peaked around 20% by late 2020, showing a more tempered run.

The third chart plots the trailing 12-month median free cash flow margin for the ten largest S&P 500 stocks by market cap from 1991 to late 2020. The data highlights a strong profitability trend, as the median margin climbed from under 10% in the early 1990s to over 20% by 2020. The fourth chart displays the ratio of the median forward P/E ratio of the top 10 S&P 500 companies to the bottom 100 companies from 1995 to late 2020. This ratio peaked above 5.5x in early 2000 and, despite rising to nearly 3.0x by late 2020, remained substantially below the dot-com era’s valuation peak.

The page concludes with a table listing "Secular growth stocks with strong fundamentals and lower antitrust risks." These companies represent S&P 500 firms with historical and projected sales growth exceeding 10%, free cash flow margins over 15%, and a share of GICS subindustry revenues under 33% to bypass antitrust concerns. Recommended holdings span multiple sectors, including TransDigm Group in Aerospace & Defense; Arista Networks in Communications Equipment; Align Technology in Health Care Supplies; Xilinx in Semiconductors; Adobe, Autodesk, ANSYS, Intuit, and Paycom Software in Application Software; Mastercard, PayPal, and Visa in Data Processing; Take-Two Interactive in Interactive Home Entertainment; Monster Beverage in Soft Drinks; Vertex Pharmaceuticals in Biotechnology; ABIOMED and Intuitive Surgical in Health Care Equipment; Etsy in Internet & Direct Marketing; and Fortinet and ServiceNow in Systems Software.

In this section of the J.P. Morgan 2021 Outlook, Michael Cembalest argues that high-yield bonds and leveraged loans have benefited significantly from financial repression. Driven by robust monetary and fiscal stimulus, the 2020 recession—despite being twice as deep as the 2009 downturn—witnessed default rates and corporate bankruptcy filings peaking at only half of their 2009 levels. However, Cembalest warns that aggressive underwriting and weakening covenant protections have led to declining recovery rates on defaulted debts. Regarding investment grade bonds, he expresses extreme caution, noting that the inflation-adjusted yield on the Barclays Investment Grade Corporate Bond Index is slightly negative, making them unappealing.

This point is supported by the first chart, which displays US high yield bond and leveraged loan default rates from 1999 to 2020 as a percentage of last twelve-month par-weighted default rates. High yield bonds and leveraged loans both peaked around 2009 (at approximately 14% and 11% respectively) and peaked in 2020 at much lower levels of roughly 6% and 4% respectively.

The second chart tracks US high yield corporate bond spreads measured in basis points against Treasuries from 1995 to early 2021 using the JPDFHYI index. Spreads spiked dramatically during the 2008 financial crisis, surpassing 1,200 basis points, and rose to nearly 1,000 basis points in early 2020 before sharply rallying down toward 400 basis points. A specific marker on the chart highlights the position of the high yield energy sector with a red dot at the end of 2020.

The third chart, which details US high yield and leveraged loan fund flows in billions of dollars from 2017 to 2020, displays how a massive flood of liquidity pushed investors into these assets. While leveraged loan fund flows experienced persistent outflows from late 2018 through 2020, high yield fund flows experienced a dramatic surge of inflows in mid-2020, with some months approaching 20 billion to 25 billion dollars.

The final chart illustrates US high yield bond and institutional loan recovery rates in cents on the dollar from 1990 to 2020. This visual confirms that aggressive underwriting has degraded investor recovery outcomes. First lien loans have fallen from historical levels of 70 to 80 cents on the dollar down to around 50 cents in 2020. Similarly, recovery rates for high yield bonds dropped to a historic low of around 20 cents on the dollar in 2020, a sharp decline from past peaks that hovered near 50 to 60 cents.

This executive summary page of the 2021 Outlook discusses the economic implications of post-pandemic vaccine rollouts, arguing that once COVID-19 risks are mitigated, a surge in pent-up consumer demand will be unleashed without immediate interference from the Federal Reserve. The author notes that while it may take three to four months for vaccinations to permanently lower hospitalization and mortality curves—complicated by logistical hurdles and a high rate of vaccine hesitancy in the United States, where 15% to 30% of surveyed citizens plan to refuse it—spending potential remains historic. After a decade of consistently overestimating inflation and recovery strength, the Federal Reserve is expected to keep interest rates low until significant inflation actually materializes. Other global central banks are anticipated to follow suit due to massive output gaps everywhere except China.

Four charts support these assertions. The top-left chart, titled "Due to COVID, potential spending exceeds actual consumption," displays year-over-year percentage changes from 1972 through 2020. It compares actual consumption growth against estimated spending potential, which is calculated based on taxable income, transfer payments, housing wealth, and financial wealth. In 2020, a dramatic divergence is visible: actual consumption growth plunged well below zero, while spending potential spiked upward, demonstrating a vast, unspent financial cushion.

The top-right chart, titled "Fed projections vs actual Fed funds rate," tracks the interest rate percentage from 2012 projected out to 2022. It plots the actual effective Federal Funds rate as a solid black line against a series of gray fan lines representing median FOMC projections over time. The visual shows a persistent pattern of the Fed forecasting aggressive rate hikes that never occurred, with the actual rate remaining near zero until 2016, peaking around 2.25% in late 2018, and crashing back to zero in 2020.

The bottom two charts track output gaps, which measure actual GDP relative to potential GDP as an indicator of spare economic capacity. The bottom-left chart looks at the period from 2006 to the present, while the bottom-right chart zooms in on 2019 to the present. Both charts track five regions: China, Emerging Asia, Developed World, Emerging Asia ex-China, and Latin America. The data shows a universal collapse in economic output relative to potential in early 2020. By late 2020, China had rebounded almost entirely, narrowing its output gap to near 0%. Conversely, the Developed World, Emerging Asia ex-China, and Latin America continued to suffer from severe output gaps, with Latin America remaining below negative 10% after bottoming out past negative 15% in mid-2020.

This page concludes the executive summary of the J.P. Morgan 2021 Outlook, presenting a forecast of approximately 10% US equity market gains in 2021, though with warnings of intermittent profit-taking and policy-driven volatility regarding tax policies and filibuster decisions. The author outlines key tactical market views for the year ahead, beginning with a recommendation to overweight US and Emerging Market equities while underweighting Europe and Japan. 

Regarding energy, the publication suggests waiting for more favorable entry points on renewable energy despite a suite of expected pro-climate actions from the Biden administration, such as tighter fracking rules, climate risk disclosures, and grid subsidies. This recommendation is supported by a chart titled "Global alternative vs traditional energy performance," which indexes performance from January 2016 to late 2020. The chart demonstrates that the MSCI Global Alternative Energy Index skyrocketed in late 2020 to reach an index level near 250, while the traditional MSCI All-Country World Energy Index lagged, dropping significantly during the 2020 pandemic downturn to end near 100. Consequently, the author finds deep value in traditional energy, noting that the S&P 500 oil and gas sector traded at half the market's book value—its lowest level since 1928—even after a 30% rally in November 2020. Furthermore, poor sector performance is attributed to a loss of capital discipline rather than stranded asset risks, and the author doubts the Biden administration will revive an Iran deal that would introduce an additional 1 million barrels per day to the market. 

For other sectors, the summary notes that infrastructure stocks could benefit from a bipartisan spending bill, whereas large-cap pharma faces headwinds from potential bipartisan prescription drug legislation and executive actions targeting Medicare Part D pricing. 

Finally, the author challenges the conventional wisdom that congressional gridlock is universally positive for markets, warning that extreme modern partisanship and the collapse of political moderates pose a long-term economic threat. This relationship is depicted in a chart titled "Moderates in Congress and GDP growth that followed," which spans from 1950 to 2020. The chart plots moderates as a percentage of the House and Senate, which steadily declined from over 40% in the mid-20th century to less than 10% by 2020. This decline closely mirrors a downward trend in subsequent 10-year cumulative real GDP growth, which fell from peak levels around 50% in the 1950s and 1960s to approximately 20% by the end of the historical series.

This page analyzes the consequences of the US-China trade war, focusing on bilateral foreign direct investment, semiconductor exports, and the operational strategies of US multinationals in China. The text argues that while the economic conflict has permanently lowered bilateral investment and prompted strict US semiconductor export bans, US multinational corporations are largely staying put in China because they operate there to serve the local Chinese and regional markets rather than exporting goods back to the United States.

A column chart titled "Decline in bilateral foreign direct investment may be permanent" tracks investment flows in billions of US dollars from 2004 through the second quarter of 2020. The chart shows that US foreign direct investment into China, depicted in gold, has remained relatively steady, fluctuating mostly between ten billion and fifteen billion dollars annually. In contrast, Chinese foreign direct investment into the US, shown in blue, surged dramatically to over forty-five billion dollars in 2016, but collapsed to negligible levels by 2020. This stark decline suggests a decoupling in direct investment due to tighter national security restrictions.

A line chart titled "US semiconductor exports to China" tracks monthly exports in billions of US dollars from 2015 to late 2020. The chart shows a long-term upward trend in exports, rising from around five hundred million dollars in 2015 to a peak of nearly one point two billion dollars in mid-2020. The chart highlights two key policy events: a May 16, 2019 restriction making US-produced technology out of reach for Huawei, and an August 17, 2020 restriction extending this ban to any technology based on US designs. Following the August 2020 restriction, exports dropped sharply back to around nine hundred million dollars. The accompanying text highlights that US companies hold a ninety to ninety-five percent global market share in advanced semiconductor equipment, meaning China’s self-sufficiency goals remain out of reach for the foreseeable future.

A 100% stacked bar chart titled "US multinationals in China planning to relocate manufacturing" presents AmCham China survey data from 2017 to 2019. It shows that the vast majority of surveyed companies—over eighty percent in all three years—have no plans to relocate their manufacturing operations. A minor fraction, representing less than ten percent, had actually moved, while around ten percent were considering a move, indicating very little actual flight of US manufacturing from China despite the tariff war.

Finally, a 100% stacked bar chart titled "US multinationals foreign affiliates' sales by country" explains why these companies are not leaving. Across four sectors—Manufacturers, Capital Goods, Computer and electronics, and Pharmaceuticals—the largest portion of sales (represented in red) is captured by the local host country, accounting for fifty to sixty percent of all sales. In contrast, sales back to the United States (represented in blue) make up only ten to fifteen percent of the total, with the remainder (represented in gold) going to other foreign countries. This demonstrates that US affiliates abroad are highly integrated into their host markets, making relocation impractical.

This page, titled "Executive Summary Appendix: The US, at war with itself," analyzes the deep political and social polarization in the United States around the time of the 2020 presidential election. The author highlights that the nation is politically split almost exactly 50/50 across federal and state levels, accompanied by rising distrust, animosity toward opposing political factions, and a corresponding surge in firearm sales.

Two charts at the top illustrate the extreme political division. The first, tracking the Federal/State Partisan Balance Index from 1937 to 2021, measures the percentage control of the House, Senate, Governorships, and state legislatures. It shows that control has converged to an almost equal split between Democratic and Republican control, a stark contrast to the dominant Democratic control seen from the late 1950s through the 1970s. The second chart details the historical majority margin in the House of Representatives since 1901. It shows that the Democratic majority in 2021 is one of the narrowest in over a century, pale in comparison to the massive House majorities held during the FDR era in 1937, the JFK era in 1961, or the LBJ era in 1965.

The middle portion of the page explores the psychological and cultural elements of this polarization. A chart summarizing GOP voter surveys from December 2020 shows that approximately two-thirds of Republican respondents believed the 2020 election was unfair and that mail-in voting led to fraud. Nearly half of those surveyed believed courts were biased against Donald Trump, and close to 40% believed Trump should not concede under any circumstances. This partisan distrust extends to personal judgments, as shown in a Pew Research Center chart tracking the percentage of respondents who believe members of the opposing party are "immoral." Between 2016 and 2019, the percentage of Democrats holding this view of Republicans rose from roughly 35% to 45%, while the share of Republicans viewing Democrats as immoral grew from about 47% to 55%.

The bottom of the page visualizes the escalation of personal animosity and physical preparation. A long-term chart from a Science Magazine study tracks respondents' feelings toward their own versus the opposing political party on a scale of -50 to 50 degrees, where 0 is neutral. It shows that while "warmth toward one's own party" has remained relatively flat between 20 and 25 degrees since 1976, "antipathy toward the opposing party" has plummeted from a mild -5 degrees in 1976 to below -30 degrees by 2020, meaning negative feelings toward rivals now far outweigh positive feelings for one's own side. This hostile climate coincides with a dramatic rise in domestic arms purchases, depicted in the final chart. This chart plots deviations from expected monthly firearm background checks from 2010 to 2020, revealing significant spikes in gun sales following events like the mass shootings at Sandy Hook, San Bernardino, and Parkland, culminating in a sustained, massive spike of over one million excess background checks during the combined COVID-19 pandemic and 2020 election cycle.

This page, titled "Trade War," outlines why the US-China economic conflict is likely to persist, even if the overall intensity of the rhetoric decreases under a Biden presidency. The author argues that domestic political pressures will prevent a rapid policy shift, citing research showing that Chinese import competition historically bolstered Republican vote shares in key swing states like Michigan, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania. Additionally, China has not fully complied with the Phase 1 trade deal purchase targets, and there is deep bipartisan concern regarding human rights issues, such as those addressed by the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act. A potential positive path forward could involve scrapping tariffs in exchange for China easing access to its domestic services industries, including finance, insurance, and healthcare.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, tracking the relative performance of companies with high exposure to the US-China trade war versus the S&P 500, shows that these exposed companies saw their relative performance drop from a high index level of over 100 in early 2018 to a low near 77 in mid-2020. They subsequently rebounded to about 93 by December 2020, reflecting market expectations of a potential Biden victory and reduced trade war volatility. 

The second chart illustrates China's shortfall in meeting its Phase 1 purchase agreements across three main categories as of late 2020. In agriculture, actual US imports were 22 billion dollars against a 33 billion dollar target, representing 67 percent compliance. Manufacturing imports reached only 48 billion dollars out of an 83 billion dollar target, or 57 percent compliance. Energy purchases fell the furthest short, with only 8 billion dollars imported out of a 26 billion dollar target, reflecting just 31 percent compliance. 

The third chart visualizes why China is considered the world's most mercantile country, comparing various regulatory and economic measures on a scale from 0 (worst) to 100 (best). Across all nine metrics—including public ownership of the private sector, IP enforcement, barriers to market access, and the overall Mercantilism Index—China's scores cluster far below 40, reflecting significant barriers, forced technology transfers, and favoritism of domestic companies.

The final chart measures individual protections versus state control on a scale where 100 represents the greatest protections of the individual. This index evaluates factors such as judicial system independence, due process, freedom of the press, and freedom of association. On a descending curve of international rankings, Hong Kong sits near 85 and the United States sits near 77, while China is located near the very bottom of the distribution with a score of roughly 44, underscoring the deep ideological rift that underlies the ongoing economic conflict.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2021 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the shifting military balance of power between the United States and China, with a particular focus on the geopolitical flashpoint of Taiwan. Cembalest argues that while rhetoric has deteriorated, the exceptionally deep economic linkages between the US and China make a Thucydides Trap style military conflict less inevitable than past historical precedents might suggest. However, Taiwan remains a major worry because global markets have become more reliant on semiconductors than on oil and gas, highlighted by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) overtaking Intel in market capitalization. Concurrently, the US's ability to militarily impose its will in the region has eroded as Chinese military spending has grown to near-parity with the US when adjusted for local costs, raising the open question of whether the US would be drawn into a conflict over Taiwan that it can no longer reliably win.

Four charts support this analysis. The first chart, titled "China and the US: much deeper economic linkages than actual and potential adversaries of the last 100 years," plots bilateral economic linkages as a percentage of combined GDP for various historical adversary pairs. The chart reveals that US-China linkages in 2014 stood at nearly 8% of combined GDP, dominated by bilateral annual trade and central bank holdings of government debt, with a small portion of foreign direct investment. In comparison, all other historical adversary pairs—including France and Germany in 1930, the US and Russia in 2014, and the US and Japan in 1940—remain below 2%, and often below 1% of combined GDP. 

The second chart, "Global energy vs semiconductor market capitalizations," tracks the MSCI AC World Energy Index against the MSCI AC World Semiconductor Index in trillions of US dollars from 2004 to 2020. The energy index peaked near $4.0 trillion in 2008 and again in 2014 before falling to roughly $2.5 trillion by late 2020. In contrast, the semiconductor index rose steadily from about $0.5 trillion in the mid-2000s to over $2.0 trillion in 2020, visually demonstrating the world's shifting reliance from fossil fuels to silicon.

The third chart, "US arms sales to Taiwan," tracks sales in billions of US dollars from 1990 to 2018. It shows highly volatile annual sales, with notable peaks of around $6 billion to $8 billion in the early 1990s and late 2000s, culminating in a historic record spike of over $10 billion around 2019. 

The final chart, titled "China and US military spending," demonstrates how adjustments for purchasing power parity (PPP) and wage differences change the comparison between the two powers. The chart shows that while China's reported defense budget is under $200 billion, adjusting its hardware and structures for PPP and its personnel costs for US wage levels increases its effective budget to over $500 billion. This brings China’s military purchasing power to approximately 90% of the reported US defense budget, which stands at around $600 billion. This adjustment explains why the regional balance of power has shifted so significantly, eroding the protective military umbrella the US historically provided to Taiwan.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, titled China Index Weight, discusses China's expanding role in global fixed income markets and analyzes its credit risk profile in comparison to other major global economies, particularly the United States. Cembalest notes that while foreign investors have added 2 trillion RMB to their Chinese government bond holdings since 2014, this still only represents about 2% of China’s total domestic fixed income market. China’s inclusion weight in the Barclays Global Aggregate index is currently 3% but is set to double to 6% upon full inclusion. Cembalest argues that China's bond market compares very favorably to other liquid global bond markets in terms of yield, volatility, and duration. 

The top left area chart, titled Foreign investment in Chinese stocks and bonds, tracks holdings in trillions of RMB from 2014 through 2020. It illustrates a steady climb in foreign holdings, rising from less than 1 trillion RMB to nearly 4.5 trillion RMB by 2020, with bonds making up a substantial and growing portion of the total alongside stocks. The top right scatter plot, titled Yield to worst vs volatility of aggregate bond indices, charts annualized volatility from 2013 to 2020 against the yield to worst. It positions China as an attractive outlier with a yield of approximately 3.2% and a low annualized volatility of around 3.0%. In contrast, the United States offers a lower yield of around 1.0% with higher volatility of over 4.0%, while other major regions like Germany, France, Spain, Italy, the United Kingdom, and Japan yield under 1.0% (with Germany in negative territory) despite suffering from much higher volatility levels ranging from 5.5% to nearly 10.0%.

The lower section of the page focuses on China's credit risk, noting that although the nation's overall debt levels are as high as those in the United States, Chinese debt is predominantly owed internally rather than externally. This distinction is supported by the bottom left line chart, titled General government and non-financial corporate debt as a percentage of GDP from 2003 to 2020. The chart shows that combined government and non-financial corporate debt for both China and the US has risen to similar levels, hovering between 200% and 220% of GDP by late 2020. However, China's explicit government debt makes up a small fraction of this, remaining around 40% to 45% of GDP, while the rest resides in the non-financial corporate sector, which includes state-owned enterprises. 

The bottom right bar chart, titled Net international investment position, displays the net stock of foreign assets less foreign claims as a percentage of trailing four-quarter GDP in the second quarter of 2020. It clearly divides countries into net creditors and net debtors. Net creditors include Switzerland, which leads at over 100% of GDP, followed by the Netherlands, Germany, Japan, Canada, Belgium, Russia, Sweden, and China, which sits at a positive position of around 15% of GDP. On the debtor side, Italy, India, the United Kingdom, France, Brazil, and the United States are shown with negative positions, with the United States exhibiting the deepest net debtor status at roughly negative 65% of GDP. Cembalest highlights that net external debt to GDP is 95% in the US compared to just 15% in China, leading to the conclusion that while China is typically treated as an emerging market by equity investors, its strong external balance sheet qualifies it as a developed market for fixed income investors.

In this page from the JP Morgan publication, Michael Cembalest discusses why the US equity market consistently outperforms Europe and Japan, dismissing contrarian recommendations to overweight those regions. He points out that since January 2010, US equities have generated a total return of 319 percent, far outpacing Japan at 124 percent, Europe at 87 percent, and Emerging Markets at 73 percent. The author argues that this outperformance is primarily driven by microeconomic factors, specifically the larger market weight of the high-growth technology sector in the US compared to Europe and Japan, alongside structurally superior profitability of US companies across all sectors. A footnote adds a macroeconomic projection, noting that the prime income population aged 30 to 49 in the US is expected to grow by 5 percent from 2020 to 2025, while Europe's is projected to decline by 3 percent.

Four visual elements illustrate these trends. The first chart, titled Overweight US, underweight Europe and Japan, displays the three-year rolling out- and under-performance of a portfolio overweight to the US and underweight to Europe and Japan versus the MSCI All World Index from 1991 to late 2018. It shows that this asset allocation strategy was consistently profitable, with the only sustained period of underperformance occurring between 2003 and 2009. The second chart, US outperforming Europe and Japan, tracks total returns in US dollars from January 2010 to late 2020, where the base is set to 100. By late 2020, the S&P 500 approaches a value of 400, whereas the MSCI Japan and MSCI Europe indexes lag significantly behind, ending near 200 and 180, respectively.

The third chart, High growth tech drives US markets, growth laggards drive Europe and Japan, compares the percentage of total index market capitalization for the technology sector versus a combined category of materials, energy, and industrials. In the US, technology makes up approximately 33 percent of the market cap, while materials, energy, and industrials account for only about 13 percent. In contrast, Europe and Japan are heavily weighted toward these growth laggards, with materials, energy, and industrials comprising roughly 27 percent in Europe and 26 percent in Japan, compared to technology weights of only about 7 percent in Europe and 14 percent in Japan.

Finally, two tables demonstrate that US companies achieve consistently higher profitability. The Return on Assets table shows the US leading in every sector listed, with a technology ROA of 9.9 compared to Europe's 5.4 and Japan's 3.9, and a consumer discretionary ROA of 4.1 compared to Europe's 0.6 and Japan's 1.7. Similarly, the Return on Equity table shows the US dominating with a technology ROE of 27.6 compared to Europe's 14.6 and Japan's 9.3, and a consumer staples ROE of 28.2 compared to Europe's 18.0 and Japan's 9.2. Across healthcare, communication services, and financials, the US similarly leads both regions in both ROA and ROE metrics.

This page analyzed by Michael Cembalest explores the detrimental impacts of negative interest rate policies on European banks, arguing that these policies have done "nothing good" for bank equity returns and valuations relative to their United States counterparts. 

To illustrate this disparity, the author presents two comparative line charts covering the period from 2009 to late 2020, both marking the mid-2014 start of the European Central Bank's negative interest rate era. The first chart, "US vs Europe: banks total return performance" (indexed to 100 in January 2009), shows a stark divergence following the 2014 policy shift; the S&P 500 banks index steadily climbed to peak near 300 by late 2019, while the Euro STOXX banks index languished, ending 2020 well below its 2009 baseline. The second chart, "US vs Europe: banks price to book," shows a similar valuation gap, with the S&P 500 banks price-to-book ratio maintaining a range of 1.0 to 1.4 after 2014, while the Euro STOXX banks ratio fell and remained depressed in the 0.4 to 0.6 range. 

The commentary notes that any recent uptick in European bank profits is not organic, but rather a reflection of reduced loan loss provisions. A third line chart, plotting European bank profitability in billions of euros from 2007 to 2019, supports this by showing that operating income remained flat around 500 billion euros and operating expenses hovered stably near negative 300 billion euros. Consequently, the slight positive turn in net profit/loss after 2015 was almost entirely mirrored by a corresponding reduction in loan provisions. 

Cembalest asserts that bank profitability is unlikely to recover as long as substantial portions of the European yield curve remain negative. A detailed table of the J.P. Morgan GBI Broad Index as of November 30, 2020, indicates that 64% of the total index traded with negative yields, including 100% of debt in the one-to-three and three-to-five-year maturity brackets. For core nations like Denmark, Finland, Germany, and the Netherlands, 100% of debt traded at negative yields across all maturities, even beyond ten years. Other nations like France and Belgium saw 100% negative yields up to ten years, and 45% negative yields even for maturities exceeding ten years. 

In conclusion, Cembalest strongly cautions against the United States adopting negative rate policies. He cites Princeton economist Markus Brunnermeier's concept of a "reversal rate," which is a critical threshold where further interest rate cuts do more harm to bank profitability and capital generation than good to the wider economy, ultimately rendering monetary easing contractionary by restricting banks' ability to make new loans.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan report argues that emerging markets present a compelling "trifecta of value" for investors due to improved current account deficits, undervalued currencies, and lower equity valuations compared to Europe. While recent years have been challenging for emerging market equity investors due to factors like slowing Chinese growth, commodity price collapses, US trade tensions, and COVID-19, the outlook is turning positive. Key drivers of this recovery include subsiding COVID risks, underway economic recoveries, low US real interest rates, a rapid Chinese recovery, and stimulative policies across many emerging market nations. Notably, despite record inflows in November, emerging market equities are still poised to post their largest yearly outflows on record for 2020.

Four charts support these assertions. The first chart, showing emerging market current account balances as a percentage of GDP in Q2 and Q3 of 2020, compares current balances to the worst levels recorded during the 2014 to 2016 period across several countries. For almost all represented nations—including Taiwan, Malaysia, Mexico, South Africa, Korea, India, the Philippines, Argentina, Russia, China, Brazil, Chile, Indonesia, Colombia, Turkey, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia—the current account balance has significantly improved. Taiwan leads with a surplus of around 14% of GDP, and nearly all others have moved well above their historical worsts, indicating a much lower risk of balance of payments adjustments.

The second chart traces the real trade-weighted emerging market currency basket from 2004 to late 2020, plotting percent deviations to identify overvalued or undervalued periods. In late 2020, the basket was significantly undervalued, hovering around negative four percent, which is close to historical lows last seen around 2004.

The third chart illustrates the MSCI Emerging Markets Price-to-Earnings discount or premium versus the Stoxx 600 based on forward earnings from 2006 to early 2021. Emerging market equities are currently trading at a discount of roughly fifteen percent relative to European equities, continuing a decade-long trend of trading at a discount, though up from its deepest discount of nearly thirty percent around 2015.

The fourth and final chart displays regional equity returns since December 2014, with total returns in US dollars indexed to one hundred. By late 2020, MSCI US and MSCI China led the pack, both reaching total returns close to two hundred. MSCI Emerging Markets trailed at around one hundred forty, while MSCI Europe lagged further behind, ending near one hundred twenty. This performance divergence underscores the valuation opportunity currently present in broader emerging markets.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, explores how investors can generate marginal returns in a high-valuation environment without taking on excessive risk. The analysis focuses on hybrid investments, which combine characteristics of bonds and equities to offer equity-like returns with potentially lower long-term wealth risk. The primary hybrids examined are high yield bonds, high yield loans, collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS), convertible bonds, equity REITs, mortgage REITs, preferred stock, and utility stocks. 

The first chart, a scatter plot, compares a traditional 60/40 portfolio (60% global equities and 40% local bonds) against a hybrid portfolio containing 40% hybrids, 40% global equities, and 20% local bonds. Plotting 10-year forward-looking annualized returns against historical annualized volatility from 1987 to 2019, the chart shows that the hybrid strategy shifts the portfolio's return expectations upward for all listed regions (United States, United Kingdom, Europe, and Japan). For example, the US traditional portfolio projects a return of approximately 2.8% with 5.7% volatility, whereas the US hybrid portfolio increases the projected return to 3.3% while holding volatility relatively steady around 5.6%. This illustrates that incorporating hybrids can project a modest return pickup in exchange for a minimal risk adjustment.

The author cautions, however, that these long-term annualized volatility measures can smooth over substantial short-term risks. To illustrate this, a comprehensive table tracks the performance and maximum drawdowns of nine hybrid asset classes during the Great Financial Crisis of 2008–2009 and the 2020 COVID-19 recession. While hybrids achieved a healthy average annualized return of 7.0% from 2011 to 2019—led by utility stocks at 12.3% and equity REITs at 11.0%—they also experienced severe drawdowns during market crises. In the 2008–2009 recession, hybrids suffered an average maximum daily drawdown of -51%, a monthly drawdown of -45%, and a quarterly drawdown of -37%. Mortgage REITs were particularly volatile, experiencing a -72% daily drawdown during the Great Financial Crisis and a -71% daily drawdown in the 2020 recession. Even high-performing utility stocks saw a -50% daily drawdown in 2008–2009. The author concludes that while drawdowns become less severe when viewed through monthly or quarterly lenses, investors must remain dedicated to a truly long-term horizon to successfully capture the benefits of diversified hybrid portfolios.

This page from the report focuses on the potential rebirth of antitrust enforcement targeting major US technology companies. The author argues that because the "Big 5" tech stocks represent an unprecedented concentration of market capitalization and returns, antitrust actions have become a key risk. Several ongoing developments are noted, including the Department of Justice's lawsuit against Google, distinct filings by State Attorneys General, class-action privacy lawsuits, potential changes to Section 230 immunity, and the Federal Trade Commission's lawsuit seeking to force Facebook to divest Instagram and WhatsApp. Additionally, the author references the October 2020 House Judiciary Report on antitrust as an indicator of political intent, though its legislative path remains uncertain due to slim Democratic majorities in Congress.

The text is supported by two charts and a detailed market share table. The first chart shows the number of Department of Justice antitrust investigations initiated from 1970 to 2018, broken down by Mergers, Monopoly, and Competition. The visual demonstrates a steep long-term decline in antitrust activity from its peak in the early 1970s, when total annual investigations neared 600, to around 100 or fewer by 2018, illustrating how postwar antitrust enforcement reached historic lows prior to the current wave of scrutiny.

The second chart demonstrates that US industry consolidation has returned to its historic 1969 peak. It measures the revenues of the 15 largest companies as a percentage of US GDP. In 1969, the top 15 industrial companies accounted for approximately 9% of GDP. This share dropped to 4% for tech and telecom companies during the 2000 dot-com peak but has surged back to nearly 9% in 2020, driven by the dominant tech, telecom, and e-commerce companies of today.

The comprehensive table at the bottom highlights the market share of major tech firms across various US digital categories as of September 2020. Phone operating systems are shared almost exclusively between Google at 52% and Apple at 47%. Google controls 91% of internet search (including images, maps, and YouTube) and 80% of navigation applications. Amazon dominates video game streaming at 73%, eBooks at 70%, and e-Readers at 84%. Web browsers are led by Google at 51% and Apple at 33%, combining for an 84% subtotal. In email, Apple holds 46% and Google holds 29%. Digital advertising is led by Google at 39% and Facebook at 20%. Amazon holds 54% of e-commerce, while Facebook holds 51% of social media and 50% of social media digital photos. The collective subtotal of Google, Apple, Facebook, and Amazon in almost every listed category exceeds 50%, and in many cases, reaches 80% to 99%, illustrating the high level of market concentration that has triggered the current wave of antitrust concern.

This page, titled Gold rally: modest so far, examines the historical context of gold price spikes and warns investors of the significant risks associated with timing gold investments. The author observes that while gold has surged about eighty percent from its post-financial crisis low, past bull runs suggest that when gold rallies, it can do so on a massive scale. 

The first chart, titled When gold prices rise, they usually rise by a lot, tracks gold prices in US dollars per Troy ounce on a log scale from 1900 to 2020. It identifies four historical gold spikes, highlighting the catalysts and percentage gains for each. The first is a sixty-eight percent rally during the Great Depression, when Japan, Germany, the United Kingdom, the United States, and France successively abandoned gold standards to combat deflation. The second is a stagflation-driven surge of two thousand three hundred thirty-three percent in the 1970s after President Nixon ended the gold standard, marking the beginning of the fiat money era. The third is a six hundred forty-four percent rally in the 2000s, sparked by the Federal Reserve utilizing negative real interest rates as a policy tool following the tech collapse and global financial crisis. The fourth, ongoing spike represents a seventy-nine percent gain driven by perpetual deficits and the COVID-19 policy response. 

The second chart, titled The infrequent outperformance of gold, illustrates the primary risk for investors: the extensive periods of underperformance that can occur between these rallies. It displays the five-year rolling out- or underperformance of gold against a balanced portfolio of sixty-five percent stocks, twenty-five percent bonds, and ten percent Treasury bills from 1932 to 2020. The chart shows that gold spent long stretches underperforming the balanced portfolio, depicted in red, notably before World War II and during a twenty-two-year drought between the 1970s rally and the early 2000s. Blue-shaded areas highlight gold's rare phases of superior performance, which peaked above three hundred percent in the late 1970s and reached over one hundred percent between 2002 and 2012, before entering another phase of underperformance.

In terms of market outlook, the author acknowledges that current conditions—such as unprecedented COVID-19 stimulus, a money supply expanding faster than gold production, and bipartisan political indifference to deficit reduction in the United States fueled by Modern Monetary Theory—suggest gold's outperformance could be just beginning. Although central banks briefly became net sellers in the third quarter of 2020 because financially strained countries like Turkey sold reserves to cope with the pandemic, the author predicts this is a temporary pause and that central banks will resume buying gold in 2021. However, the author cautions that because of the massive intervals between rallies, getting the timing wrong on a gold investment can take a generation or more to reverse.

This page consists entirely of legal and regulatory disclosures detailing the distribution terms of J.P. Morgan's financial materials across various jurisdictions, including Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Australia, and Latin America.

This analysis presents a four-part overview of the macroeconomic and historical factors driving gold markets, highlighting the effects of monetary policy, historical crises, and central bank behavior. 

The first chart examines economic recovery during the Great Depression, illustrating Barry Eichengreen’s finding that the sooner a country abandoned the gold standard, the quicker its economy rebounded. Indexed to 1929 levels, the chart tracks Japan, the United Kingdom, Germany, the United States, and France from 1929 to 1937. It marks each nation's exit year with a square: Japan and the UK exited early around 1931, showing rapid economic growth that reached index levels of roughly 175 and 135 respectively by 1937. In contrast, the US exited in 1933, and France delayed its departure until 1936, remaining economically depressed the longest and barely returning to an index level of 90 by 1937.

The second chart traces the five-year average of real yields on cash (calculated as the T-bill or Funds rate minus inflation) from 1830 to 2020. Historically, negative real yields were rare anomalies reserved for major conflicts, specifically the US Civil War, World War I, and World War II. However, the chart shows that following the dot-com crash and the 2008 financial crisis, the Federal Reserve initiated a peacetime strategy of negative real interest rates, with negative yields appearing once again in the years leading up to 2020. 

The third chart compares the growth in the US money supply to global gold production, plotting the ratio of the increase in M2 relative to the increase in gold production from 1966 through a 2020 estimate. Historically, surges in this ratio have preceded significant gold rallies, which are highlighted on the chart as shaded regions in the late 1960s to 1980 and the early 2000s to 2011. A massive projected spike in the ratio for 2020, reaching over 25x, points to a potential setup for another major gold rally.

The final chart details global central bank gold purchases and holdings from 2010 to 2020. It plots net purchases in tonnes on the left axis using blue bars, and total gold holdings as a percentage of total reserves on the right axis with a gold line. The data shows that after steady accumulation, central bank gold holdings as a percentage of reserves surged from under 10% around 2015 to nearly 14% by late 2020, marking the highest allocation level seen since 2002.

On this page, Michael Cembalest discusses the rising burden of US federal debt and its potential long-term threat to the US dollar's status as the global reserve currency. He argues that analyzing debt per working-age person in real terms is a critical metric because this demographic group generates the tax revenue needed to service the debt, thereby capturing the dual impact of rising debt and worsening demographics. He warns that these fiscal pressures could eventually lead to the end of the US dollar's reign as a reserve currency, drawing parallels to historical precedents.

The page features two charts illustrating US federal debt trends from 1940 to 2020, along with estimates for 2020 and 2021. The first chart displays gross federal debt held by the public as a percentage of US GDP. It shows a peak of over 100 percent in the mid-1940s following World War II, a steady decline to a low of nearly 20 percent in the mid-1970s, and a subsequent rise back up past 80 percent by 2020, with estimates for 2020 and 2021 approaching historical highs. The second chart presents gross federal debt per working-age person in constant 2012 dollars. This metric illustrates an even steeper and more alarming trend. While the post-World War II peak reached nearly 30,000 dollars per working-age person and fell below 10,000 dollars by 1980, it has since skyrocketed to over 70,000 dollars in recent years, heading toward 80,000 dollars in the 2020 and 2021 estimates.

To put these fiscal pressures into perspective, the page includes a historical timeline of reserve or dominant trade currencies. This timeline demonstrates that currency dominance has historically shifted every 100 to 300 years, transitioning from Rome, the Byzantine Empire, the Arabian Dinar, and Florence, to Portugal, the Iberian Union, the Netherlands, France, the United Kingdom, and finally to the United States, which has held the mantle since roughly 1920.

A final pie chart details the currency composition of global foreign exchange reserves as of the second quarter of 2020. This data shows that the US dollar remains the dominant global reserve currency, accounting for 61.3 percent of total allocated reserves. The Euro follows at 20.3 percent, with other holdings including the Japanese Yen at 5.7 percent, Pounds Sterling at 4.5 percent, the Chinese Renminbi at 2.0 percent, Canadian Dollars at 1.9 percent, Australian Dollars at 1.7 percent, Swiss Francs at 0.2 percent, and all other currencies making up the remaining 2.5 percent. This high level of reserves currently supports the US dollar, though the rising debt levels loom as a historical risk to this status.

This commentary page addresses the post-2020 election legal and political landscape, focusing on court challenges, executive orders, and the future of the Republican Party. Regarding court challenges, it is noted that while the US Supreme Court might eventually rule in favor of the Trump campaign on certain constitutional issues—such as asserting that only state legislatures, rather than state courts, have the authority to alter election rules—any such rulings would not impact the outcome of the 2020 election. The text cites Charles Geyh of Indiana Law School to describe the legal challenges as overzealous political arguments failing to meet hard judicial standards. Furthermore, a Wisconsin case involving voters who self-designated as indefinitely confined to bypass photo ID requirements is used to highlight the high hurdles of reversing election results after the fact, as courts ultimately rejected challenges due to the impossibility of proving how many voters took undue advantage of the rules. 

Addressing social media rumors, the commentary clarifies that Trump’s 2018 Executive Order 13848 deals exclusively with sanctions against foreign actors interfering in US elections and has no jurisdiction over the handling of domestic election results or challenges. Looking ahead to the future of the GOP, the author raises open questions about how Republican politicians will vote during the January 6 Joint Session in the face of threatened primary challenges from Trump supporters. Finally, the page outlines the broader political balance, noting that Democrats hold one of the smallest House majorities since 1900 and face historical headwinds in the 2022 midterms. The author concludes that instead of an expected Blue Wave, the firm's Partisan Balance Index of congressional, gubernatorial, and state legislative seats actually shifted more red after the election.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" features an analysis by Michael Cembalest outlining the legal and political mechanics of the upcoming January 6 joint session of Congress. Cembalest explains why the Electoral Count Act of 1887, rather than a Twelfth Amendment contingent election, will govern the certification process of the 2020 presidential election. He begins with historical context, referencing the bitter 1876 post-Civil War election dispute that led to Rutherford B. Hayes's presidency and the subsequent passage of the Electoral Count Act to prevent future constitutional crises. 

The analysis focuses on how the Electoral Count Act handles competing slates of electors, noting that each member of Congress votes individually rather than by state delegation. Given that Democrats hold a slim majority of approximately ten seats in the House, and the Senate sits at 51 Republicans to 48 Democrats, it would only take two Republican Senators voting with Democrats to accept the certified Biden slates. In the event of a split decision where the House and Senate disagree on competing slates, the Electoral Count Act dictates that the tie-breaker goes to the slate approved by the state's governor. Because the governors of Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, Arizona, and Georgia have already certified Biden's victory, Cembalest concludes that Vice President Mike Pence does not have the authority to unilaterally alter the outcome. Consequently, the only way Donald Trump could win would be if both chambers agreed to accept three or more uncertified Trump slates, a scenario deemed virtually impossible. 

Cembalest also dismisses objections to single slates of electors as doomed to fail, as rejecting a certified slate requires agreement from both the Democratic-controlled House and the Senate. Furthermore, he characterizes media discussions of a Twelfth Amendment contingent election—where each state delegation gets one vote—as highly misleading. Such an event would only occur under extreme and unlikely circumstances, such as an Electoral College tie, a third-party candidate preventing a 270-vote majority, faithless electors, or the death of a candidate. 

The analysis is supplemented by footnotes addressing critical legal nuances. One footnote describes the potential constitutional crisis if a chamber decides to ignore the Electoral Count Act, which some scholars believe is unconstitutional. In such an unprecedented situation, the nation would enter a political impasse where Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi could potentially resign her congressional seat to become Acting President on January 20 until Congress resolves the dispute. Other notes detail the historically narrow Democratic House majority, the limitations of court rulings on congressional counting authority, and the legal state-level variations governing faithless electors.

This page provides a primer on the legal and political landscape heading into the Joint Session of Congress scheduled for January 6 to certify the 2020 presidential election. The author, Michael Cembalest, outlines the background of COVID-induced changes to state election laws and the subsequent waves of lawsuits. While federal and state courts initially struck down some lower-court attempts to relax rules—such as in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Ohio, South Carolina, Georgia, and Arizona—the actual election saw a major surge in absentee ballot usage alongside a notable drop in ballot rejection rates. 

To illustrate these trends, the author includes two exhibits. The first is a bar chart showing the absentee and mail-in ballot share as a percentage of total votes cast, comparing 2016 to 2020 across key swing states: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and Iowa. In nearly all these states, the absentee ballot share grew dramatically in 2020; for example, Michigan's share rose from roughly 20% to over 50%, and Pennsylvania's increased from under 5% to over 40%. Alongside this surge, a companion table details the rejected absentee and mail-in ballot percentages for the same states in 2016, 2018, and 2020. The table highlights that rejection rates fell significantly in 2020 compared to prior years. For instance, Georgia’s rejection rate fell from 6.42% in 2016 to 0.60% in 2020, while Pennsylvania's dropped from 4.45% in 2018 to 0.28% in 2020. Rejection data for Arizona and Wisconsin in 2020 are noted as outstanding. 

Following the election, the Trump campaign and unaffiliated groups launched a flurry of unsuccessful lawsuits. The author cites a tally showing 36 defeats, 4 pending cases, and 0 wins, with bipartisan judges rejecting the cases due to unsubstantiated fraud claims, weak testimony, a high bar for proving dispositive fraud, lack of standing (such as the state of Texas trying to sue other states), and the legal principle of laches, which dictates that challenges to election procedures must be made in a timely manner rather than after the fact. Despite these court defeats, Cembalest notes that over 100 GOP House Representatives and at least 13 GOP Senators, led by Senator Josh Hawley, are poised to challenge the Electoral College results on January 6, forcing Congress to resolve competing slates of electors. The author poses an open question regarding whether Senator Hawley, a former clerk for Chief Justice Roberts, will address the attacks made by election lawyers against the Chief Justice's character. Finally, the page notes that Trump supporters are planning a caravan to Washington, D.C., to coincide with the January 6 congressional session.

This page introduces the J.P. Morgan report titled "Fear of Flying," authored by Michael Cembalest, which examines the concurrent surges in equity markets, COVID-19 cases, and corporate reactions to Congressional objectors following the January 6th Capitol riot. The report's forthcoming topics include a collapse in risk aversion among fully-invested market participants, headwinds for megacap stocks, rising COVID-19 mutations juxtaposed with slow vaccine rollouts, recovering oil consumption, and the underperformance of European equities. 

Cembalest outlines a positive yet cautious market outlook. While J.P. Morgan projects a global rebound in economic growth, corporate profits, and employment, the author warns investors to remain wary of one-directional markets. Given that many equity indexes rose by 90 percent to 130 percent on an annualized basis after April 2020, and considering lingering uncertainties around vaccine efficacy and virus mutations, Cembalest advises holding cash reserves. The primary forecast for the remainder of the year is characterized by generally rising markets interrupted by periods of sharp profit-taking.

The page features a line chart titled "All Systems Go," which plots the total return in U.S. dollars for various asset classes from January 2019 to mid-January 2021, indexed to 100 at the start. The visualization highlights the massive market rally following the March 2020 crash. Bitcoin dramatically outperforms all other assets, soaring off the primary chart scale to a value of 987. Below Bitcoin, MSCI Global Alternative Energy is the top-performing index, rising to nearly 300. The S&P 500 Semiconductors and FAANG stocks both track closely to finish around 230 and 225 respectively. The NASDAQ index follows at approximately 200, while the S&P 500 Consumer Discretionary index reaches about 190. The broader S&P 500 index finishes at roughly 160, slightly outperforming the MSCI Emerging Markets index, which concludes the period at approximately 145. 

Additionally, the page notes an upcoming webcast featuring Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel and includes a historical footnote explaining that the title "Fear of Flying" references Erica Jong’s prominent 1973 novel.

This commentary addresses the race between spreading COVID-19 mutations and the global vaccination rollout, while debunking misinformation about mortality rates. The author points out that even if new virus mutations are not inherently more deadly, their increased contagiousness drives up total infections and consequently absolute deaths. 

To illustrate this point, three charts display daily infections and mortality per million people from March 2020 to January 2021 in the United Kingdom, South Africa, and Ireland. In all three nations, the winter of 2020–2021 brought a massive spike in infections, which exceeded 800 per million in the UK, 300 in South Africa, and 1,200 in Ireland. This was accompanied by a rapid rise in daily deaths per million, climbing toward 15 in the UK and Ireland, and nearly 10 in South Africa.

Discussing vaccine efficacy, the text notes Pfizer's vaccine successfully fended off some highly contagious variants from Britain and South Africa in vitro using blood samples from 20 recipients. However, the E484 mutation from South Africa remains an open concern that could require new vaccine iterations if testing reveals low efficacy. Meanwhile, vaccine rollouts are slowed by bottlenecks and reluctance among healthcare workers, citing high resistance rates such as 60% among Ohio nursing home staff, 30% in New York City, 22% at Henry Ford Health System in Michigan, and 15% at Jackson Healthcare System in Miami. 

A chart tracking total vaccinations as a percentage of the population from mid-December 2020 to mid-January 2021 shows the United Kingdom leading the pace at nearly 6.0%, followed by the United States at roughly 4.0%, while Italy, Canada, Germany, and France lag behind, all remaining below 2.0%.

Finally, the author refutes the online fallacy that COVID-19 deaths merely replace other causes of death. A final chart plots total weekly US deaths from all causes against the expected baseline threshold for excess deaths from 2017 through early 2021. The data clearly shows weekly deaths surging far above normal historic seasonal thresholds starting in spring 2020 and peaking near 90,000 deaths per week in January 2021, confirming that overall mortality has risen dramatically due to the pandemic.

This page examines corporate political action committee funding for congressional candidates in the wake of the January 6 Capitol insurrection, noting that several prominent U.S. companies announced plans to halt donations to members of Congress who objected to the Electoral College certification. To provide context on where political candidates receive their money, the author presents data from the Center for Responsive Politics and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. 

A stacked bar chart illustrates average political funding sources from the 2014, 2016, and 2018 election cycles, split by party and chamber. Across both Democrats and Republicans in the House and Senate, funding is divided into political action committees, large individual contributions of more than two hundred dollars, small individual contributions of less than two hundred dollars, and self-financing or other sources. The chart highlights that PACs represent roughly twenty to forty percent of congressional funding, with House campaigns of both parties showing a higher reliance on PAC funds compared to Senate campaigns. 

An accompanying pie chart shows the breakdown of PAC funding received by the top fifty recipients in the 2020 election by type of PAC. This chart reveals that corporate PACs represent sixty-six percent of the total, followed by ideological PACs at twenty-five percent, and labor PACs at nine percent. Together, these charts emphasize that corporate PACs are a substantial source of capital for political campaigns.

The text also addresses who typically receives these corporate PAC donations. While there is a common perception that corporate money favors moderates, the author finds this is only partially true. Corporate PAC donations to Republican Senators align closely with their ideological spectrum without demonstrating a preference for moderates. For Democrats, however, corporate PAC funding is indeed skewed toward centrist Senators, with virtually no corporate PAC funding going to the most progressive members of the party. 

Footnotes on the page clarify procedural rules regarding the Electoral Count Act, citing constitutional law advisor Michael Morley, who explains that once electoral vote counting begins, establishing an electoral commission as suggested by Senator Ted Cruz is procedurally impossible. Additionally, the author notes that this PAC dataset excludes SuperPACs, which are prohibited from donating directly to candidates but saw two billion dollars in spending during the 2020 election cycle, split fifty-five percent conservative and forty-five percent liberal, with half of all individual SuperPAC donations coming from just twenty-five mega-donors.

This page analyzes the driving forces behind soaring equity markets, arguing that market participants are highly optimistic and fully invested. The author highlights that individual investors, mutual fund managers, and hedge funds have all dramatically increased their equity exposures, with hedge fund positioning rising faster than the market itself toward the end of 2020. 

To illustrate these trends, the author presents several charts. The first chart, titled "North America hedge fund exposures vs S&P 500," shows the percent change since January 2020 for net notional exposure, gross notional exposure, and the S&P 500 total return. After dropping sharply in March 2020, both net and gross hedge fund exposures staged a massive recovery, ending the year up over 50% and 40% respectively, significantly outpacing the S&P 500 total return, which finished up about 20%. A companion chart, "Hedge fund net exposure and S&P 500 returns," displays the six-month percent change of these metrics from 2015 to late 2020, demonstrating a close historical correlation and showing both indicators surging toward the 60% to 80% range in late 2020.

The page also details a painful short squeeze in the market. A chart titled "Short squeeze" tracks the index level of the 50 highest short interest names in the Russell 3000 from 2008 to early 2021. The index displays a vertical spike at the end of the timeline, rising from around 150 to nearly 300, indicating severe forced short covering. The author notes that 59 stocks have doubled in the prior three months while trading at over 10 times sales, a level of speculative activity not seen since 2000. Additionally, the "Equity put-call ratio" chart from 2000 to early 2021 reveals a collapse in the ratio of put-to-call options purchased to about 0.4, indicating a steep decline in risk aversion and demand for portfolio hedging.

Finally, the commentary shifts to the fixed income market, presenting a chart of "Investor demand at 30-year treasury auctions" as a percentage of total demand from 2006 to 2020. This metric includes direct bidders, such as pension funds and individuals, and indirect bidders, such as monetary authorities bidding through the Federal Reserve. Drawn in by a modest 20 basis point backup in yields, non-broker-dealer demand for 30-year U.S. Treasuries spiked to its highest level since 2006, approaching 80%. Looking forward, the author predicts that yields will rise further due to a projected 10% U.S. budget deficit in 2021. This deficit forecast does not account for future stimulus bills, such as President Joe Biden’s proposed $1.9 trillion spending package, which the author notes faces a long road in Congress.

This page of J.P. Morgan's publication, written by Michael Cembalest, argues that megacap technology stocks are experiencing an "Icarus Moment" as they face mounting headwinds. Cembalest highlights significant challenges confronting these massive companies, including antitrust actions, rising corporate tax rates, proposed taxes on low-tax jurisdictions, and digital service taxes. The commentary posits that the peak of megacap outperformance is likely behind us, drawing a historical parallel to the late 19th-century public backlash against concentrated corporate power that led to the passage of the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890. Additionally, the author addresses the content moderation challenges faced by tech platforms, citing the legal dispute between Amazon Web Services and Parler. A footnote notes reports that Parler may attempt to return online via an internet protocol address hosted by a firm in Rostov-on-Don, Russia.

The analysis is supported by a table and a line chart. The table, titled "Total returns since:", displays investment returns from three starting points—June 2020, September 2020, and January 2021—through mid-January 2021. It compares a basket of equal-weighted antitrust targets (Apple, Amazon, Facebook, and Google) against both the market-cap-weighted S&P 500 and the equal-weighted S&P 500. The data shows that since September 2020, the antitrust targets fell 4.7%, underperforming the market-cap-weighted S&P 500, which rose 8.3%, and significantly lagging the equal-weighted S&P 500, which gained 18.7%. 

Below the table, a line chart titled "S&P 500 megacap outperformance" illustrates the performance gap between the market-cap-weighted S&P 500 and the equal-weighted S&P 500. It overlays the historic dot-com era cycle from 1997 to 2002 with the contemporary cycle from 2017 to 2021. The historical blue line peaks near 50% outperformance around the year 2000 before sharply declining to roughly negative 20% by 2002. The red line representing the 2017 to 2021 period follows a highly similar upward trajectory, peaking at approximately 20% in late 2020 before showing initial signs of a reversal, supporting the author's projection that megacaps may have passed their peak outperformance phase.

This page discusses the debate surrounding corporate PAC funding for Congressional objectors following the events of January 6th. The author first presents two dual-axis charts to illustrate how corporate PAC donations generally correlate with political ideology, showing that the most extreme members of both parties receive very little corporate support. The first chart, "Senator political ideology vs corporate PAC funding," plots the number of senators as bars and 2020 corporate PAC donations in millions of dollars as a line, against an ideological spectrum from -1.0 (more liberal) to 1.0 (more conservative). It demonstrates that funding is highly concentrated among moderate-to-middle politicians, peaking at roughly $22 million for moderate conservatives and around $10 million for moderate liberals, while falling to near-zero at the ideological fringes. The second chart, "House Rep political ideology vs corporate PAC funding," reveals a matching distribution among House representatives, where funding peaks near $12 million for moderate liberals and $15 million for moderate conservatives, with negligible funding going to the most liberal and most conservative representatives.

In analyzing whether corporations should cease PAC donations to lawmakers who objected to the electoral vote certification, the author weighs both sides of the issue.
