First, staged selling utilizes a structured plan detailing share quantities, timeframes, and price levels to mitigate downward price pressure and timing risks; this section highlights 10b5-1 plans, which are pre-programmed selling formats used by U.S. corporate insiders. Second, block trades allow investors to sell large stakes quickly in the marketplace, though typically at a discount to the current market price. Third, covered call options allow investors to collect an upfront premium while setting a predetermined strike exit price. Fourth, target price selling strategies allow daily fractional sales at a target typically five to fifteen percent above market, incorporating a knock-out provision that halts sales if the stock declines below a certain price. Fifth, private company sales address concentrated holdings in non-public, venture-backed firms, noting that the global size of private, venture-backed companies is approaching two trillion dollars compared to just twenty-five billion dollars fifteen years ago. Finally, the page addresses the impact of taxes and the resulting tax drag on portfolio performance, noting that various planning options can help manage these liabilities without triggering immediate taxable events.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the retail-driven "Reddit meme stock" phenomenon of early 2021, examining the underlying business challenges that made these companies primary targets for hedge fund short-sellers in the first place. The commentary highlights that prior to the dramatic short squeeze of late January 2021, companies like GameStop, AMC Theaters, and Bed Bath & Beyond were struggling significantly due to structural disruptions from digital gaming, the dominance of online retail, and the COVID-19 pandemic. 

The analysis is supported by three historical stock charts using Bloomberg and FactSet data through December 2020. The first chart tracks GameStop's stock price from 2001 through early 2021, plotted on a vertical scale from $0 to $70. The visualization shows that the video game retailer peaked near $60 around 2007–2008 and had a secondary peak near $50 in late 2013, before steadily declining to single-digit valuations in 2019 and 2020, followed by a sharp uptick at the very end of the series. The accompanying caption humorously points out how long it had been since the average consumer last thought about visiting a physical GameStop store.

The second chart displays the stock price of AMC Theaters from 2014 to early 2021, with values ranging from $0 to $40. AMC’s stock consistently traded between $20 and $35 until 2017, after which it entered a steep downward trend, bottoming out near zero by late 2020. The author observes that the theater chain was on the verge of bankruptcy until it successfully raised capital during the late-stage retail frenzy, posing the open question of whether the company can ultimately recover. 

The third chart illustrates Bed Bath & Beyond's stock performance from 1999 through early 2021, on a scale from $0 to $90. The home goods retailer saw a multi-decade rise that peaked around $80 between 2013 and 2015, followed by a severe multi-year decline that dragged the stock below $10 in 2020. The caption criticizes the company for treating shareholders poorly and failing to modernize its unappealing store formats to compete with online retailers. The page concludes with the ongoing debate of whether the retail Reddit crowd or the short-selling hedge funds will eventually be proven correct in the long run.

This page begins a section on concentrated portfolio diversification and hedging strategies, addressing how investors can manage the risks of extreme wealth concentration. Despite the initial disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic, financial markets achieved rapid recoveries and all-time highs, coinciding with a historic renaissance in equity issuance. The success of emerging companies, including over five hundred private "Unicorns" valued at more than one billion dollars, has generated immense wealth but also led to highly concentrated portfolios. The author describes these wealth-holders as victims of success, noting that concentrated positions—whether from business sales, stock compensation, or long-term investments—expose portfolios to significant idiosyncratic risks. To help investors de-risk, access capital, and optimize for tax, legal, and personal goals, the section introduces five management categories: Sell, Monetize, Diversify, Give, and Hedge. 

A supporting column chart tracks global IPO value by announced date in billions of US dollars from 1994 to early 2021. The chart visualizes a historical peak in 2007 at nearly five hundred billion dollars, followed by a post-financial crisis recovery that peaked again in 2020 at approximately four hundred billion dollars. The year 2021, highlighted with a distinct gold bar for data through March 3, shows an extraordinarily strong start to the year, already reaching roughly one hundred fifty billion dollars.

This page analyzes the prolonged decline of brick-and-mortar retail since the mid-2010s, a trend the author terms "The Mall Rats." While noting that some aspects of the "retail apocalypse" narrative are exaggerated—highlighting that online sales only accounted for about 12 percent of total retail sales before the pandemic despite doubling their share—the author emphasizes that the weakest links in physical retail have suffered immensely. This distress has trickled down into the broader ecosystem, heavily impacting retail real estate and private-label credit card issuers. 

To demonstrate this structural decline, the author provides six stock charts of retail-adjacent companies spanning roughly the mid-2000s to 2020. The first chart details Men's Wearhouse, showing how its stock fell from a peak near $60 in 2015 to near zero by late 2020. This downfall is attributed to relaxed office dress codes, a hostile and ultimately ill-conceived merger with Jos. A Bank—which former CEO George Zimmer called a mistake—and the final blow of work-from-home policies. The second chart focuses on Signet Jewelers, whose stock rose to nearly $150 in late 2015 before falling below $20 by 2020 due to declining mall traffic and the price transparency brought by digital competitors. 

The third chart tracks the fashion retailer Express from 2010 to 2020. The stock regularly traded between $15 and $25 before collapsing to under $5 by 2020, driven down by inventory mismanagement, a shift toward fast-fashion competitors, and a failed private equity takeover. COTY Brands is depicted in the fourth chart, showing its stock peaking at over $30 in 2015 before steadily declining to under $5 by 2020. The author blames this decline on too much debt, high CEO turnover, and an overreliance on mergers and acquisitions to drive growth. 

The final two charts demonstrate how this pain spread beyond direct retailers. The fifth chart tracks the outlet mall landlord Tanger Outlets, whose stock climbed from about $10 in 2004 to around $40 in 2016, only to plunge back below $10 by 2020 as highway-adjacent outlet malls succumbed to secular retail trends. Lastly, the sixth chart displays Alliance Data Systems, a provider of private-label credit cards. Its stock soared from around $50 in 2004 to nearly $300 in 2015, but subsequently crashed back to approximately $50 by 2020. The firm struggled to pivot away from card partnerships with challenged retailers like J. Crew, Pier 1, and Pottery Barn, and was further weakened by a botched forced sale of its marketing services business.

This page provides a text-based overview of financial strategies designed to help clients manage, monetize, and diversify concentrated stock positions without triggering immediate tax liabilities or forced sales. 

Under the theme of position monetization, the text highlights four specific strategies that generate liquidity for lifestyle, charitable, or diversification goals. First, Principal Installment Stock Monetization (PrISM) combines a hedge with a non-recourse upfront cash advance, allowing the investor to de-risk the position, though they may forgo upside appreciation beyond a specified limit. Second, Charitable Remainder Trusts allow investors to pursue philanthropic goals by transferring shares to a trust in exchange for an annual income stream, after which the trust can sell the position tax-free to invest in a diversified portfolio. Third, security-based lines of credit let investors pledge their concentrated stock as collateral to access capital, though this increases overall portfolio risk and can lead to forced selling if the stock value drops below collateral requirements. Fourth, hedge and borrow strategies combine hedging tools like protective puts and collars with borrowing to stabilize collateral values, offering higher liquidity, lower costs, and a reduced risk of forced liquidation.

The text also explains how investors can diversify their holdings using an exchange fund. This method allows an investor to contribute concentrated shares directly into a diversified fund in exchange for fund units, bypassing the tax consequences of a traditional sale. After a seven-year period, the investor can redeem their units for a diversified basket of securities that retains the original cost basis of the contributed shares. Finally, the page mentions that some investors may choose to design and manage a custom "do-it-yourself" Personal Exchange Fund to maintain more direct control over their portfolio investments.

This page highlights the high risks and frequent failures associated with healthcare investing, emphasizing that while innovation offers strong long-term returns, ninety percent of drugs entering human clinical trials never reach the market. The author details these pitfalls—including lack of innovation, poorly executed merger and acquisition strategies, and regulatory or political headwinds—through five historical stock charts showing severe value destruction.

The first chart tracks Bluebird Bio from 2014 to 2021, showcasing how heavy analyst coverage fueled multiple hype cycles that ultimately yielded little value. The stock peaked around two hundred twenty dollars in late 2017 but fell below fifty dollars by early 2021, a decline capped by the company suspending trials for its sickle cell gene therapy treatment. Next, the Clovis Oncology chart from 2012 to 2020 illustrates the consequences of failing to develop a differentiated product and facing regulatory setbacks. The stock crashed from nearly one hundred dollars in late 2015 following a delayed FDA approval for a lung cancer drug, and despite a brief recovery driven by hype for its ovarian cancer drug Rubraca, it fell toward zero when management eventually guided to flat sales.

Two additional charts focus on the generic drug industry and aggressive M&A. The chart for Mylan spans 2005 to 2020, demonstrating how fifteen billion dollars spent on acquisitions—including Abbott Labs, Meda, and Renaissance—failed to boost cash flows against a backdrop of biosimilar competition. Mylan’s stock fell from over seventy dollars in 2015 to below twenty dollars by the time of its final merger with Pfizer's Upjohn generics business. Beside it, the Perrigo chart from 2005 to 2021 illustrates the sudden impact of political scrutiny. Perrigo’s stock peaked near two hundred dollars in 2015 but entered a structural decline down to forty dollars, a collapse triggered by a tweet from Hillary Clinton regarding drug prices and compounded by headwinds in generics and key management departures. 

Finally, a chart for Akorn Inc. from 2010 to 2020 details a highly chaotic decade for the ophthalmic pharmaceutical manufacturer. After peaking near fifty-five dollars in 2015, the company faced a series of compounding crises, including restated earnings, a hacked customer database, and a terminated premium acquisition agreement with Fresenius. Following subsequent litigation where Fresenius sought damages, the stock crashed completely, culminating in Akorn filing for bankruptcy in 2020.

This page, titled The Island of Misfit Toys, presents a collection of six stock price charts illustrating how various factors—such as digital shifts, regulatory actions, market fads, structural decline, and poor strategic decisions—can destroy shareholder value. 

The first chart tracks Mattel from 2005 to 2021, showing its stock price on a scale from zero to fifty dollars. The stock peaked near forty-eight dollars in late 2013 before tumbling to around ten dollars in 2019, reflecting a long-term decline as children increasingly shunned traditional physical toys in favor of digital video games.

The second chart focuses on Nu Skin from 2004 to 2020, with a price scale from zero to one hundred and sixty dollars. It demonstrates the risk of multi-level marketing companies running afoul of regulators. The stock surged to nearly one hundred and forty dollars in early 2014, but collapsed immediately after a Chinese newspaper published an article alleging that the company was operating a pyramid scheme. It eventually settled below sixty dollars by late 2020.

The third chart illustrates Tupperware’s performance from 2004 to 2020, on a scale of zero to one hundred dollars. The stock reached approximately ninety-five dollars in late 2013, followed by a protracted decline to under five dollars in early 2020. This downswing is attributed to an inability to generate free cash flow, high leverage, a failed sales model outside of the United States, and an unsuccessful pivot into cosmetics. The chart also shows a late-2020 rebound back to around thirty dollars.

The fourth chart displays WisdomTree’s stock price from 2005 to 2021, on a scale of zero to twenty-five dollars. The company suffered from extreme concentration, with sixty percent of its assets under management tied up in two hedged equity ETFs, DXJ and HEDJ, during the dollar surge of 2015. After peaking near twenty-five dollars in late 2015, the stock embarked on a multi-year decline, falling below five dollars by 2020.

The fifth chart shows Diebold Nixdorf from 1991 to 2021, on a scale of zero to sixty dollars. The long-term chart shows the stock frequently trading between thirty and fifty dollars for decades, before a massive collapse after 2017 to under ten dollars. This secular decline was driven by the global transition away from cash, which weakened the ATM market, compounded by Diebold's failure to successfully integrate its debt-financed acquisition of Wincor Nixdorf.

The final chart tracks Potbelly from its late 2013 debut to 2021, on a scale of zero to thirty-five dollars. Opening near thirty dollars, the stock fell rapidly and steadily declined to around five dollars. The author notes that this decline cannot be blamed on the COVID-19 pandemic, as it was set in motion years prior by weak marketing, poor sales, strained relationships with lenders and landlords, and stiff competition from stronger fast-casual competitors like Jimmy John's and Panera.

This page focuses on strategies for hedging concentrated stock positions, which allows investors to mitigate downside risk without selling their shares, thereby maintaining voting rights, continuing to receive dividends, and avoiding taxable events that create tax drag. The text details four primary hedging techniques. First, protective puts function as a form of insurance where an investor pays an upfront premium for the right to sell their stock at a specified strike price. Second, protective put spreads combine the purchase of a protective put with the sale of a lower strike put option to lower the strategy's overall cost, though this exposes the investor to losses below the lower strike price. The author notes that this spread strategy has become more popular due to option skew, a dynamic that has intensified since the Global Financial Crisis as financial regulations restricted market makers from selling deep out-of-the-money options. Third, collars are presented as the most widely used approach; they pair the purchase of a protective put with the sale of a covered call option, minimizing or eliminating upfront premium costs in exchange for capping potential future appreciation. Fourth, proxy hedges are suggested for insiders or affiliates who face regulatory restrictions on direct derivatives or wish to avoid creating selling pressure on their stock; these involve hedging with a highly correlated proxy asset, though they carry basis risk and cannot eliminate risk perfectly. Ultimately, the page emphasizes that managing concentrated positions requires balancing emotional and rational considerations, encouraging investors to work with J.P. Morgan teams to design customized diversification and hedging strategies that account for tax, legal, and personal financial goals.

This page of J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" outlines various estate planning and wealth transfer strategies for investors holding concentrated stock positions, focusing on the theme of "Give it away." The discussion highlights four primary vehicles for passing on wealth to loved ones or charitable organizations. 

First, direct gifts to family and friends allow an investor to transfer both the asset's current value and all future appreciation outside of their taxable estate, potentially utilizing the recipient's lower tax bracket to reduce capital gains impact upon sale. Second, Grantor Retained Annuity Trusts (GRATs) enable a grantor to transfer a concentrated position to an irrevocable trust, which pays back an annual annuity based on the IRS 7520 rate; any appreciation above this rate passes to beneficiaries free of transfer taxes, making high stock volatility a potential benefit for wealth transfer. Third, direct charitable contributions of appreciated stock allow investors to maximize their philanthropic impact by letting a tax-exempt charity sell the shares, effectively wiping out any embedded capital gains. Finally, Charitable Remainder Trusts (CRTs) offer a way to defer capital gains taxes by transferring shares to a trust in exchange for an annual income stream, allowing the trust to diversify the concentrated position before ultimately passing any remaining assets to a chosen charity.

This page consists entirely of legal disclosures and regulatory distribution notices for the J.P. Morgan publication across various international jurisdictions. It details the specific local J.P. Morgan entities, branches, and supervisory bodies responsible for financial compliance. 

For Europe, the text covers regulatory oversight in Spain by the CNMV; Germany by the CSSF, ECB, and BaFin; Italy by the Bank of Italy and CONSOB; the Netherlands by the DNB and AFM; Denmark by Finanstilsynet; Sweden by Finansinspektionen; France by the ACPR and AMF; and Switzerland by FINMA. In the Asia-Pacific region, the notice outlines operations in Hong Kong under the HKMA and SFC, and in Singapore under the MAS. 

For Latin American jurisdictions, it states that materials are offered on a private basis and notes the complete prohibition of unregistered public offerings under the Brazilian Securities and Exchange Commission (CVM). Finally, the disclosure covers Australia, indicating that services and materials provided by JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and J.P. Morgan Securities LLC are restricted to wholesale clients as defined under the Corporations Act 2001 and are overseen by the Australian Securities and Investment Commission (ASIC) and the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA).

This page consists entirely of regulatory disclosures and legal boilerplate detailing the distribution of J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication across various global jurisdictions, including European countries, Hong Kong, Singapore, Latin America, and Australia, with no financial market commentary, charts, or economic analysis.

This page discusses how high growth-stock valuations are increasingly vulnerable to rising interest rates and inflation expectations, particularly as massive fiscal stimulus and a rapid vaccine rollout threaten to overheat the economy. The author argues that growth stock outperformance has depended heavily on low interest rates and a negative term premium, making these equities highly sensitive to even minor shifts in inflation perceptions, regardless of when the Federal Reserve decides to act.

The first chart, titled "Equity multiples at risk as dormant bond market investors react to growth and stimulus," covers the period from 1990 to early 2021. On the left axis, measured in P/E points from -0.4 to 1.6, a blue line tracks the P/E ratio of large-cap stocks divided by five-year trailing revenue growth. This ratio has spiked sharply to over 1.2 by early 2021; when excluding the negative impact of COVID-19 on revenue growth, the adjusted ratio (indicated by a red dotted line) rises even higher toward 1.5. On the right axis, showing percentage premiums from -1% to 4%, a gold line displays the New York Fed’s yield curve term premium. This premium has steadily trended downward from around 2% to 3% in the 1990s and 2000s to negative territory below -1% by 2020, though it has recently begun to rise, signaling the end of an era of negative term premiums.

The narrative transitions to the impending economic reopening, noting that the combined total of vaccinated individuals and non-vaccinated COVID-19 survivors is projected to reach 70% by late May 2021. This milestone coincides with the distribution of $1.2 trillion from the newly enacted $1.9 trillion federal stimulus package, consisting of direct checks, small business aid, and state and local funding. The author warns that this unprecedented volume of stimulus could completely erase the U.S. output gap, which represents the economy's spare capacity. While the Federal Reserve plans a very gradual exit from its accommodative monetary policy—first tapering its monthly $120 billion bond purchases before slowly raising rates—the author questions whether long-term bond markets will tolerate such a slow timeline, especially since markets are already pricing in four rate hikes by January 2023.

Two smaller charts at the bottom of the page illustrate these trends. The chart on the left, titled "US vaccinated individuals and survivors," measures unique vaccinated individuals as a percentage of the U.S. population from January 1 to June 30, 2021, on a y-axis from 0% to 90%. A solid blue line shows the actual vaccination rate rising through mid-March. Multiple dashed projection lines (representing constant, 10%, 20%, and 30% weekly increases in vaccination rates) demonstrate that when accounting for non-vaccinated survivor antibodies, the population is on track to surpass the 70% threshold (marked by a solid horizontal line) between May and June.

The final chart on the bottom right, "US output gap (spare capacity measure)," tracks actual GDP relative to potential GDP from 1949 to 2029 on a scale from -12% to 8%. The solid blue line representing the historical actual output gap shows dramatic drops during major downturns, including a plunge toward -10% during the 2008 financial crisis and another sharp drop in 2020. The dashed blue line projects the recovery of this gap. Critically, two colored dashed lines model the impact of the $1.9 trillion stimulus bill on the 2021 output gap: assuming a conservative 0.5x fiscal multiplier (red line) pushes the output gap above 0% into positive territory, while a 0.75x multiplier (gold line) pushes it significantly higher to over 2%, suggesting the economy could quickly run out of spare capacity and trigger inflationary pressures.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication features commentary by Michael Cembalest on the threat of rising interest rates to the equity market. Cembalest argues that while interest rates remaining below two percent are highly positive for equities, the market is engaging in convoluted rationalizations—termed "interest rate pretzels"—to convince itself that rising rates are harmless. 

To visually depict this phenomenon, the page displays eight illustrated pretzel drawings, each paired with a popular market rationalization. These include claims that inflation is good for equities; that equity inflows increase alongside interest rates; that the Federal Reserve, foreign central banks, and sovereign wealth funds will intervene to buy bonds if rates rise too high; and that rising rates simply signal an improving economy. Other pretzel rationalizations suggest that massive money market fund balances will support stocks regardless of rates, that rising long rates do not matter while the Fed is on hold, and that rising real rates only pose a threat during late-cycle periods. The final pretzel humorously suggests that a steeper yield curve slope is simply "great for downhill skiing." In an accompanying footnote, Cembalest debunks the first pretzel, explaining that equity returns since 1975 have been highly dispersed and generally more negative than positive when inflation goes up, rendering mean and median outcomes meaningless. 

Looking ahead, Cembalest details the assumptions underpinning J.P. Morgan's 2021 Outlook, which forecasted roughly ten percent returns for US large-cap stocks. These assumptions included a surge in consumer and business activity, widespread vaccinations, a collapse in US unemployment to about four and a half percent by year-end, a $1.9 trillion fiscal stimulus, an autumn infrastructure bill, and antitrust risks for FAANG stocks. However, the author cautions that if ten-year Treasury rates hit two and a half percent or higher and stay there, his optimistic outlook for equities would significantly diminish. Additionally, the page includes a brief notice inviting readers to a webcast on SPAC returns sponsored by Tintin and Gritty the Flyers Mascot.

This page analyzes the potential "zoom shock" facing commercial and residential real estate due to the persistent shift toward working from home. While many facets of the US economy have recovered to near pre-pandemic levels, employee preferences for remote work remain highly disruptive. 

A bar chart detailing post-COVID employee preferences shows that among workers who can work from home, nearly twenty-eight percent prefer to do so five days a week. The next most popular options are two and three days per week, at roughly fifteen percent and fourteen percent respectively, while only about ten percent of remote-capable workers prefer to never work from home. 

An adjacent scatter plot tracks the percentage of paid days worked from home. From a pre-COVID level below ten percent, remote work peaked near sixty percent in May 2020 before trending down to around forty percent by late 2020. The chart reveals a significant post-COVID disconnect: employees prefer to work from home for nearly fifty percent of paid days, whereas employers only plan for about twenty percent. 

If a compromise is struck between these two positions, office owners face a "zoom shock"—a term coined by UK researchers to describe the geographic reallocation of economic activity as workers spend their workdays and money at their suburban residences rather than commercial centers. This dynamic is illustrated in a modeled net employment flow map of Greater London. The map reveals massive negative employment flows in central London, with many areas losing more than five thousand workers, contrasted against positive employment inflows of over twelve hundred workers in the outer residential suburbs. This model, based on job-sector remote work potential developed by Jonathan Dingel and Brent Neiman, is noted by the author as a strong proof of concept for actual observed remote work activity.

This page analyzes how the rise of work-from-home arrangements is starting to reshape both residential and commercial property values across major U.S. metropolitan areas. Grounded in research by Nicholas Bloom of Stanford and Lukas Althoff of Princeton, the author presents the concept of the donut effect, where higher-density cities and zip codes with a high concentration of jobs that can be done from home are experiencing downward pressure on real estate values as families relocate. 

To illustrate the residential impact, a scatter plot charts the share of jobs that can be done from home against the year-over-year percentage change in residential property values across approximately 2,400 zip codes. The data reveals a clear downward trend: zip codes where only 34% of jobs can be done from home enjoyed property price gains of around 8%, whereas zip codes with a high work-from-home capacity of 54% saw property price appreciation muted at under 4%. Simultaneously, commercial real estate has suffered unevenly based on urban density. A line chart tracking commercial office price indices from January 2018 through July 2020 shows that after March 1, 2020, high-density metros experienced a sharp drop in their price index from 100 down to roughly 85. Meanwhile, low-density metros saw their commercial price index rise slightly, ending near 102.

The analysis also positions public transit usage as a critical indicator for return-to-office trends. A scatter plot compares the percentage of workers who commute via public transport against office utilization rates. Metros with high public transit reliance, such as New York and San Francisco, exhibit very low office utilization rates of around 15% to 18%. Conversely, Texas cities like Dallas, Austin, and Houston, which have less than 5% public transit usage, show the highest office utilization rates, though still constrained to between 35% and 40%. This trend is detailed further in a timeline chart of office utilization rates based on Kastle keycard data from February 2020 to February 2021. Following a near-simultaneous drop from 100% to under 20% in March 2020, office utilization rates staged only a weak recovery, with Texas cities topping out near 40% and coastal cities like New York and San Francisco remaining flatlined below 20%.

Ultimately, the author urges investors to prepare for the long-term, structural consequences of these virtual work trends. Open questions remain regarding the solvency of public transit systems, declining municipal tax bases, municipal bond risks, and the commercial viability of urban service industries that depend on daily commuters. A key unresolved legal question highlighted is whether high-tax jurisdictions like New York City can legally tax remote workers who no longer physically enter the state but remain employed by firms incorporated there.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the strong performance of value sectors, specifically financials, industrials/basic materials, and energy. He highlights that since the beginning of 2021, the cheapest value stocks have recovered nearly half of their valuation discount compared to expensive growth stocks. Reaffirming a bullish call on oil and gas first made in June 2020, he argues that the sector's historical struggles were driven by shale supply shocks and poor management decisions rather than structural threats like peak oil demand, stranded assets, or the rise of renewable energy. He points out that despite recent gains, the energy sector remains heavily shorted compared to historical averages, indicating persistent investor skepticism. He also previews topics for an upcoming mid-May 2021 energy paper, including the electric vehicle transition, industrial decarbonization, transmission project challenges, carbon capture infrastructure, President Biden’s energy policies, China’s rare earth metals diplomacy, green hydrogen, and the Texas power grid outage.

Four charts support these insights. The first, "Growth sectors vs S&P 500," tracks cumulative total returns relative to the benchmark index from 2015 to early 2021. It shows a massive outperformance by an equal-weighted "Antitrust basket" consisting of Apple, Amazon, Facebook, and Google, which peaked between 350% and 400% above the S&P 500 in late 2020, alongside strong performances from the Information Technology, Consumer Discretionary, and Healthcare sectors. 

In contrast, the second chart, "Financials, cyclicals and small caps vs S&P 500," shows how cyclical sectors dramatically underperformed over the same 2015 to 2021 period. The S&P 500 Energy sector experienced the steepest decline, bottoming out near negative 140% relative to the S&P 500 in late 2020 before starting a sharp upward recovery. The Russell 2000, S&P 500 Financials, and S&P 500 Industrials also lagged the broader index but began to rebound in late 2020 and early 2021.

The third chart, "Shale revolution: a revolution in supply, not profit," details cash flow measures for 24 shale companies in billions of US dollars from 2010 to 2020. It illustrates that while operating cash flow remained consistently positive, capital expenditures were so high—peaking near negative $80 billion in 2014—that free cash flow remained negative for almost the entire decade, only crossing into positive territory in 2020 as capital spending declined.

The final chart, "The shale and renewable rallies relative to the S&P," displays the cumulative total return index from January 2013 to early 2021, comparing the S&P 500 to a renewable energy portfolio and the 24-company shale revolution portfolio. Highlighting returns since June 2020, the chart shows that the renewable energy portfolio surged by 128%, the shale revolution portfolio rebounded by 67%, and the S&P 500 grew by 31%, reflecting a broad-based rally across both green and fossil-fuel energy sectors.

In this appendix focused on employment, supply shortages, and Federal Reserve policy, the author addresses the Fed's stance that the post-reopening inflation surge will be transitory. The author expresses skepticism, suggesting that even a minor increase in wage or price inflation could quickly misalign current monetary policy with the actual economic recovery. 

To support this view, the author presents several charts illustrating current labor market anomalies and historical policy missteps. The first chart contrasts the ratio of unemployed people per job opening against actual job seekers per job opening from 2006 through late 2020. Unlike the financial crisis of 2009 when both ratios spiked in tandem, 2020 saw a sharp divergence where the ratio of unemployed people per opening shot up to nearly five, while actual active job seekers per opening remained low at around 1.5 because most workers expected to get their previous jobs back. 

A breakdown of the year-over-year change in people not in the labor force from March 2020 to February 2021 reveals that the vast majority of those staying out of the workforce do so for personal reasons—specifically categorized as "don't want a job" or "unable to work"—rather than economic reasons like being discouraged or failing to search for a job. 

Additionally, two indicators point to significant supply-side pressures reaching multi-decade highs. The percentage of small businesses reporting "hard to fill" job openings in the NFIB survey surged toward 40% in early 2021, near historical highs. At the same time, the ISM Manufacturing Supplier Deliveries Index spiked to nearly 70, signaling some of the slowest delivery times and most intense supply shortages since the inflationary periods of the 1970s and early 1980s.

Lastly, the page highlights a history of inaccurate policy projections with a chart of Fed projections versus the actual Fed funds rate from 2012 to 2022. The black line representing the actual effective Fed funds rate sits far below a series of gray fan-like projection lines, illustrating how the Federal Open Market Committee consistently overestimated growth and inflation for nearly a decade, leading to repeated, incorrect forecasts of policy tightening.

This page provides a comprehensive global COVID-19 update focusing on the race between vaccination campaigns and rising viral variants, highlighting the diverging paths of the United States, Continental Europe, and Latin America, specifically Brazil. 

In the United States, the situation is improving rapidly. The author projects that the US could reach 50% vaccination plus 20% natural immunity among non-vaccinated survivors by mid-May, potentially winning the race against contagious variants like the UK B117 variant, which represents only 8.8% of US exposure. This improvement is illustrated across three charts. The first, tracking US daily vaccinations as a 7-day average, shows daily doses climbing past 2.2 million by mid-March 2021, distinguishing between partial first doses, completed second doses, and the newly introduced single-dose Johnson & Johnson vaccine. The second chart tracks US daily infections, hospitalizations, and deaths, showing a dramatic collapse from winter peaks where daily infections exceeded 250,000 and daily deaths neared 4,000. The third chart examines the eight states with the highest hospitalization rates, showing that while hospitalizations per million in states like New York, New Jersey, and Georgia remain somewhat elevated between 200 and 300 per million, they are generally declining from their winter highs.

In contrast, Continental Europe is paying a price for its slower vaccine rollout, with the UK variant now causing over 50% of new infections in France, Italy, and the Netherlands. This is exacerbated by the temporary suspension of the AstraZeneca vaccine in Germany, France, Italy, and Norway due to blood clot concerns. Three charts depict these dynamics. The West Europe chart shows daily infections per million rising back toward 300 to 400 in Italy, France, and the Netherlands. Conversely, the United Kingdom chart shows infections, hospitalizations, and deaths plummeting from winter peaks, where infections had reached nearly 1,000 per million. The vaccination disparity is made clear in the unique people vaccinated chart, which shows the UK leading near 40% of its population and the US near 30%, while Denmark, Germany, Italy, France, and Canada lag far behind at under 10%.

Finally, the report addresses Latin America, where Brazil's deteriorating mortality situation is driving the region's overall worsening metrics. Brazil has vaccinated only 3.8% of its population, resulting in high mortality rates. Although the severe mortality spike in the Amazonas state—which peaked at over 35 deaths per million in early 2021—is rolling over, deaths are now rising in larger states like Sao Paulo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, and Bahia. Three final charts support these observations. The regional daily deaths chart shows Latin America's daily deaths rising back toward 8 per million as Europe and the US decline. The Brazil states chart illustrates the dramatic spike and decline in Amazonas alongside rising death rates in other populous states. Lastly, the Latin American country comparison chart reveals Brazil's daily deaths spiking sharply toward 10 per million, diverging from other nations in the region like Mexico, Colombia, and Argentina, which are seeing stable or declining death rates.
This page contains only legal disclosures, regulatory notices, and distribution information for various jurisdictions, with no market analysis, charts, or commentary.

This page from Eye on the Market discusses the rapid economic liftoff occurring in the United States as COVID-19 vaccinations approach 30 percent. Author Michael Cembalest highlights sharp recoveries in heavily impacted sectors like lodging, dining, and travel, alongside an exceptionally strong housing market characterized by record-low inventories and surging lumber prices. An interesting market disconnect is noted: while lumber prices are soaring, timber owners are not reaping the rewards because a tree-planting glut in Texas and the Southeast has depressed raw timber prices to multi-decade lows. Cembalest observes that it could take years to work through this excess timber supply, despite high demand from sawmills operating near capacity.

Six charts support these observations on US economic activity and housing market dynamics. The first chart tracks card-present transactions for social distancing sectors, showing that spending, which crashed to nearly 70 percent below 2019 levels in early 2020, recovered to roughly 10 percent below baseline by March 2021. The second chart focuses on lodging spending, illustrating a recovery from a low of over 100 percent below 2019 baselines to roughly 20 percent below baseline by early spring 2021. The third chart shows that airline spending, which also fell below negative 100 percent in the initial lockdowns, has clawed its way back to approximately 50 percent below 2019 levels. 

Broad economic health is captured by the US activity tracker index, which fell to a low near 10 in April 2020 and recovered to over 70 by April 2021, reflecting gains in manufacturing, rail traffic, department store sales, and job postings. The housing sector's tight supply is illustrated by a chart of existing single-family home inventory, which shows months of supply collapsing to an all-time low of about two months by early 2021, far below the historical average of six to eight months. Lastly, a historical chart of lumber prices from 2000 to early 2021 shows prices exploding past $1,000 per 1,000 board feet, eclipsing any previous cyclical peak in the past two decades.

This page evaluates the fiscal and market implications of proposed Biden infrastructure spending and corporate tax hikes under a backdrop of already elevated US deficit and debt levels. The author points out that getting enough Democratic support via reconciliation could take months, and the final bills may change. To frame the discussion on debt, two historical charts from 1930/1940 to 2021 are presented. The first chart shows the US fiscal deficit as a percent of GDP, which plummeted to nearly negative 30% during World War II and is estimated at roughly negative 15% for 2021. The second chart details gross federal debt held by the public as a percent of GDP, which peaked post-WWII at over 100%, bottomed around 25% in the mid-1970s, and is estimated to rise back up to near 100% in 2021. 

Regarding the market impact, a static analysis of Biden's corporate tax plan suggests a potential 8% to 9% drag on S&P 500 earnings per share, with the Tech, Healthcare, and Communications sectors bearing the largest effective tax rate increases. The author contrasts static estimates with a dynamic analysis, noting that corporate tax hikes hit immediately, while physical infrastructure spending takes longer to trickle down unless paired with broader "human" infrastructure. To determine the effectiveness of various policies, a horizontal bar chart shows estimated fiscal multiplier ranges from the Congressional Budget Office. It compares tax cuts, which have lower multipliers—such as corporate tax cuts at 0.0x to 0.4x and middle-income tax cuts at 0.3x to 1.5x—with spending programs, which offer higher multipliers, such as direct infrastructure at 0.4x to 2.2x and federal government purchases of goods and services at 0.5x to 2.5x. This supports the argument that direct government purchases yield the highest growth multipliers.

This page from the publication discusses how global equity markets are keeping pace with improving global business surveys, shrugging off concerns about COVID-19 variants and European lockdowns in favor of rising business activity. This economic optimism is illustrated in the first chart, titled Global Equities vs Global Business Surveys, which tracks the year-over-year percentage change of MSCI World Equities on the left axis against the year-over-year difference in the Global PMI Business Survey on the right axis from 2011 to 2021. The chart shows a strong historical correlation, with both indexes rebounding sharply in early 2021 after a steep decline in 2020. This trend is reinforced by the second chart, Industrial metal prices, which plots a price index from 2000 to early 2021. The index has surged from around 200 in 2020 to over 400 in 2021, signaling robust global industrial demand.

While developed world equity markets are expected to maintain their gains as economies gradually reopen and European vaccinations rise despite some restrictions on AstraZeneca in Germany, Scandinavia, and Canada, the author maintains that a 10% gain for the S&P 500 in 2021 remains the right target. This target is based on the premise that much of the recovery's good news is already priced in, as highlighted by two indicators of highly stretched market valuations. 

The third chart, Market cap of high P/E (>40x) or unprofitable firms, shows that the share of these speculative companies has reached nearly 40% of the total US market capitalization, a level not seen since the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s when it peaked near 50%. This metric includes a dashed line projecting forward twelve-month earnings. Complementing this, the fourth chart plots the Number of years for US corporate debt and equity holders to be paid back from 1900 to 2021, using data from Bridgewater. This measure, which reflects high P/E ratios and corporate leverage, has climbed close to 25 years, matching historic valuation peaks seen in 1929, the late 1990s, and the late 2010s.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s financial publication explores how extremely slim voting margins in swing counties—coined by the author as the Smalligarchy—could lead to some of the largest tax and spending increases in post-World War II history. The author points out that Joe Biden’s physical and human infrastructure plans represent a massive shift in economic policy, funded by proposed tax increases that fall roughly two-thirds on corporations and one-third on high-income individuals.

The first chart on the page, titled Revenue impact of major tax bills, measures annual tax increases as a percentage of GDP, utilizing a two-year average for historical comparison. The chart reveals that the proposed Biden physical and human infrastructure bills of 2021 would represent the second-largest tax increase since World War II at approximately 1.3 percent of GDP, surpassed only by the Revenue Act of 1951, which reached nearly 2.0 percent of GDP. This proposal ranks ahead of other significant historical tax changes, such as the Revenue and Expenditure Control Act of 1968 and the Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act of 1982. A footnote clarifies the underlying assumptions of the Biden plans: the physical infrastructure proposal involves 1.6 trillion dollars in new taxes and 2.3 trillion dollars in spending, while the human infrastructure proposal includes 1.0 trillion dollars in new taxes and 1.5 trillion dollars in spending.

The second chart, Effective corporate tax rate on new investment, illustrates how the proposed tax changes would affect the competitiveness of the United States on the global stage. It highlights that the 2017 Trump corporate tax cuts dropped the US effective rate from 34 percent in 2016 down to 19 percent in 2020. However, the proposed Biden plan would raise this rate back to around 32 percent by 2028, almost entirely reversing the previous tax cuts. This increase would leave the United States with one of the highest effective corporate tax rates among developed nations, trailing only Japan at 38 percent, and landing well above the OECD average of 23 percent, the European average of 17 percent, and low-tax jurisdictions like Switzerland at 7 percent.

To explain why simple comparisons of corporate tax revenue to GDP can be misleading over time, the author provides a third chart titled The rise of pass-through entities subject to personal (and not corporate) tax. This line chart tracks the number of tax returns in millions from 1980 to 2016. It shows that while traditional C Corporations steadily declined from 2.2 million to 1.6 million, pass-through entities surged. S Corporations grew dramatically from 0.5 million to 4.5 million, and Partnerships increased from 1.3 million to approximately 3.8 million. The author notes that this shift, initiated by US adoption of pass-through tax rules in the 1980s, means that much of the country's business income is now taxed under individual rather than corporate tax codes, muddying long-term comparisons of corporate tax burdens.

This page discusses the market pricing of Biden's proposed infrastructure bill, valuations in clean energy and other infrastructure-related sectors, and what markets are currently focused on, namely the massive buildup of US spending potential and an unprecedented expansion of the money supply. 

The author argues that Biden's infrastructure plan is largely priced in, as shown by the outperformance of industrials and the PAVE ETF relative to the S&P 500—gaining 10% and 24% respectively since the election. Valuations in digital, broadband, and traditional infrastructure sectors remain near five-year averages. Clean energy, however, has experienced a very large three-year run-up despite a correction from its January highs. Corporate tax hikes are not yet being priced in, likely due to high levels of policy uncertainty. Instead, equity markets are focusing on lift-off as accumulated consumer spending potential starts to deploy alongside significant growth in the money supply.

The top bar chart compares the 2019–2021 renewable stock price surge with historical sector or country stock price gains of over 200% within three years, showing what happened three years after each bubble. Renewable sectors include electric vehicles, solar, hydrogen, and battery technologies, all showing extreme run-ups compared to historical episodes. To account for Tesla's outsized impact, electric vehicles are shown as both market-weighted, which peaked near 1400% in January 2021, and equal-weighted, which peaked near 1000%. Historical comparisons like the Nikkei index (1985–1989), Nasdaq 100 (1997–2000), commodities (2005–2008), and agriculture (2003–2006) all eventually collapsed. Conversely, interactive home entertainment (2012–2015) and healthcare facilities (2009–2012) continued to rise, while FANG stocks (2017–2021) remain unknown.

The bottom-left line chart plots excess spending potential piled up by year-end, defined as rolling four-quarter spending potential in excess of consumption in trillions of dollars. From 1972 through late 2019, this metric fluctuated near zero, ranging between negative $0.5 trillion and positive $0.5 trillion. By late 2020, it spiked vertically to nearly $2.5 trillion, representing a massive, unprecedented build-up of unspent funds. 

The bottom-right line chart displays index growth in the money supply, combining M2 and institutional money market fund balances, indexed to 100. It contrasts the Global Coronavirus Crisis starting in January 2020 with the Global Financial Crisis from August 2008 to September 2010. During the Global Financial Crisis, the money supply grew slowly, peaking near 110 before drifting down. In contrast, the Global Coronavirus Crisis witnessed explosive growth, soaring to 125 by mid-2020 and approaching an index level of nearly 130 by early 2021, pointing to a dramatically faster and larger expansion of liquidity.

This page discusses two distinct themes: modest macroeconomic headwinds paired with financial market excesses, followed by an analysis of the declining Atlantic striped bass population. 

The author begins by outlining headwinds such as rising inflation expectations and declining globalization. The first chart, showing the ten-year breakeven inflation rate from 2000 to early 2021, depicts a sharp recovery toward 2.5% in early 2021 after a dramatic plunge in 2020. Concurrently, a globalization index tracking global trade, portfolio flows, and foreign direct investment as a percentage of global GDP (indexed to 2010 = 100) shows that globalization peaked near 120 around 2007 before falling in a volatile downward trend to approximately 80 by 2020. Meanwhile, U.S. equity markets have kept pace with rising margin debt. A chart comparing the year-over-year change in margin account debit balances against the S&P 500 year-over-year percentage change from 1998 to 2021 shows a massive, record-breaking spike in margin debt in early 2021, representing the largest increase since FINRA records began in 1998. The final financial chart tracks the percentage of outstanding pre-announcement Special Purpose Acquisition Companies (SPACs) trading below their issue price from January 2019 to March 2021. After a euphoric January 2021 where almost no pre-announcement SPACs traded below issue price, the metric spiked vertically to over 80% by late March, presenting a potential opportunity for SPAC arbitrageurs. 

The second half of the page shifts to ecological concerns as fishing season approaches, examining the declining mortality of the Atlantic striped bass. The author explains that this decline is not due to conservation successes or reduced fishing activity, but rather because there are simply fewer fish left to catch. This is supported by a stacked bar chart of Atlantic striped bass mortality from 1982 to 2018, which decomposes mortality into recreational release mortality, recreational retention, and commercial retention and discards. Total mortality peaked near 10 million fish in 2006 and has since dropped to around 6 million. The final line chart of Atlantic striped bass biomass over the same period confirms a steep ecological decline; biomass peaked at roughly 250 million pounds around 2003–2004 and has since steadily fallen to about 130 million pounds in 2018. The author notes that new slot limits and mandated circle hooks are being deployed to reverse these worrying biomass trends.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest discusses the Biden administration's aggressive fiscal policy, characterized as a "go for broke on growth" strategy, and its unusual market implications. He argues that the economic recovery of 2021 is fundamentally different from prior downturns in 1991, 2000, and 2008. Historically, the federal government increased fiscal deficits to offset shortfalls in private sector demand, meaning private investment and fiscal deficits moved in opposite directions. In 2021, however, massive fiscal stimulus is occurring at the same time private sector investment is sharply recovering. This unprecedented combination has fueled substantial equity market momentum, with global equity funds drawing nearly $570 billion in inflows over a five-month span, exceeding the cumulative inflows of the prior twelve years combined, which totaled $450 billion.

To illustrate this contrast, the page features four comparative line charts plotting private sector investment as a percentage of GDP on the left axis against the fiscal deficit as an inverted 12-month average percentage of GDP on the right axis. The charts for 1991, 2000, and 2008 demonstrate the traditional counter-cyclical relationship: as private sector investment fell, the fiscal deficit widened (moving upward on the inverted right axis). For example, during the Great Recession of 2008, private investment plunged from roughly 19.5% to 13% of GDP, while the fiscal deficit widened to nearly 10% of GDP. In contrast, the chart for 2020, which includes 2021 projections, shows both lines moving in the same upward direction. Following a brief drop in 2020, private investment is projected to rebound to around 18% of GDP in 2021 and 2022, while the fiscal deficit remains exceptionally wide, projected to hover between 14% and 16% of GDP.

Cembalest notes that this dual economic push has driven several coincident and leading indicators close to all-time highs. While some indicators are positive, others raise concerns, such as rising federal debt and deficits, high equity valuations, margin debt, and widespread supply shortages. A strong rebound in pre-tax corporate earnings provides a bullish signal, but it is partially offset by rising inflation expectations, increasing input costs, and the prospect of higher corporate taxes. The author points out that a recent rollover in cyclical, low-quality, and small-cap stocks suggests these positive factors are already partially priced into the market. With the S&P 500 up 11% year-to-date, driven by surging value stocks, Cembalest projects a slow upward grind for equities in the coming months, identifying a further rise in inflation expectations as the primary risk to this outlook. 

The page also includes a lighthearted footnote explaining a cultural reference to Sesame Street's Ernie and Bert. The author cites legal analyst Dahlia Lithwick's categorization of public figures as either impulsive "chaos muppets" (such as Supreme Court Justices Breyer and Scalia) or regimented "order muppets" (such as Justice John Roberts), serving as a metaphor for the contrasting policy environments.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the state of value stocks following a significant market rally. The author notes that while value benchmarks in both US and non-US markets have rebounded above pre-COVID-19 levels, the recovery has been uneven. Price-to-earnings ratios for US value stocks recovered from 11.5 during the April 2020 selloff to 17, compared to 15 in December 2019. Despite this rebound, about half of financial, energy, and industrial stock prices within the All County World Index remain below pre-pandemic levels. Additionally, value stocks have recaptured very little of their long-term underperformance relative to growth stocks over the prior decade. The author notes that value stocks outperformed from 2000 to 2007, but growth stocks dominated from 2008 to 2020. A footnote adds that while value rallies usually benefit European equities due to their high allocation to value sectors, the MSCI Europe index has underperformed the US in 2021 in both local currency and dollar terms.

The page features four charts based on MSCI and Bloomberg data tracing trends from 1997 to 2021. The first chart, titled US value performance, tracks the total return index starting at a base of 100 in December 1996. It shows the US value index steadily climbing over the long term despite notable pullbacks, ending above 500 in 2021. The second chart, All Country World ex-US value performance, measures the total return index on the same December 1996 baseline. It illustrates a more volatile path, peaking near 300 in 2007, dropping during the financial crisis, and eventually rising to around 400 by 2021. 

The third chart, US value vs growth performance, displays the ratio of the value index to the growth index on a scale from 0.4x to 1.2x. This ratio highlights a clear shift in market leadership: value outperformed growth from 2000 to 2007, peaking near 1.2x, before steadily declining to around 0.5x in late 2020, with only a marginal tick upward by early 2021. The fourth chart, All Country World ex-US value vs growth performance, shows a similar dynamic for non-US markets with a ratio scale ranging from 0.6x to 1.6x. The non-US value-to-growth ratio rose from around 1.0x in 2000 to nearly 1.6x in 2007, before trending downward to below 1.0x in late 2020, followed by a slight recovery in early 2021.

This J.P. Morgan analysis discusses the challenges of achieving textbook sterilizing herd immunity for COVID-19. Michael Cembalest argues that due to vaccine hesitancy, the emergence of new variants like those in South Africa and Brazil, delayed vaccinations for children, and low vaccination rates in emerging nations, COVID-19 will likely become an endemic disease similar to the flu. However, a return to normalcy remains possible if seroprevalence—the combination of antibodies from vaccinations and prior infections—can drive down severe health outcomes. 

To evaluate this transition, a line chart titled "Infections vs vaccinations" plots new daily infections per million on a seven-day average (ranging from 0 to 1,200) against the percentage of unique people vaccinated in the population (ranging from 0% to 65%). The chart tracks several geographies, including Uruguay, Michigan, Sweden, France, New Jersey, Chile, Minnesota, New Hampshire, Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Israel. 

The analysis reveals distinct regional patterns. While the United Kingdom's infections fell quickly as vaccinations began, this trend is difficult to isolate from the country's highly restrictive lockdown. Israel did not see a sustained decline in infections until its vaccination rate hit 60%. Given Israel's estimated 10% survivor population prior to vaccination, the author suggests herd immunity may begin to appear around a combined seroprevalence level of 65%. Meanwhile, infections continue to rise at vaccination levels around 35% in Minnesota, Chile, New Hampshire, and Michigan. Michigan’s rise is especially notable because, when combined with an 18% survivor antibody rate measured by the CDC at the end of 2020, its total seroprevalence is likely over 40%. Lastly, Uruguay's surge at a 25% vaccination level represents a concern that is likely linked to imported cases from Brazil.

This page analyzes why value stocks underperformed growth stocks for an extended period and explores whether a structural shift is underway. The author explains that value’s initial underperformance was driven by slower earnings growth, but later transformed into a massive expansion of growth stock multiples. From 2010 to 2017, investors paid a fair premium for faster growth-stock earnings, keeping relative price-to-earnings (P/E) multiples stable. However, after 2017, discipline broke down: while value P/E multiples rose modestly from 15.7 to 17.2, growth stock multiples surged from 19.5 to a towering 33.7. This divergence was heavily driven by the high weighting of strong-performing tech companies alongside struggling banks and energy companies in key benchmarks. Tech sustained high margins, whereas banks never recovered their pre-financial crisis valuations, and shale overexpansion pushed energy valuations to 90-year relative lows. Despite this, the S&P 500 energy sector has recently shown strength, rising 37% from June 2020 to April 2021, and gaining 28% year-to-date compared to 11% for the S&P 500.

Four charts visually support this valuation narrative. The first chart, depicting US value versus growth P/E ratios from 2004 to 2020, compares the relative 12-month forward P/E ratios of Value to Growth and Financials to Info Tech. Both ratios peaked around 0.9x to 1.0x in the late 2000s and early 2010s before steadily collapsing to historic lows of approximately 0.5x by late 2020. The second chart shows All Country World ex-US value versus growth P/E ratios over the same period, demonstrating that this collapse is a global trend. The relative global multiple peaked at nearly 0.8x in late 2008 and plummeted to roughly 0.5x by late 2020. 

The bottom two charts highlight the sector-specific drags of financials and energy. The third chart displays the price-to-book ratios for US and European banks from 1999 to 2019. It illustrates how the S&P 500 banks index and the Euro STOXX banks index plummeted after the 2008 financial crisis; US banks stabilized around 1.0x to 1.5x, while European banks continuously deteriorated, falling below 0.5x. The final chart plots energy sector valuations from 1928 to 2016, specifically measuring energy stocks' price-to-book ratios divided by the overall market's price-to-book ratio. Despite a historical average near 1.0, the ratio plummeted to all-time lows of roughly 0.5 near 2020, underscoring just how deeply discounted the energy sector has become relative to its nearly century-long average.

This page presents a collection of twelve financial and economic charts illustrating that a wide array of indicators are currently at or close to all-time highs, reflecting a highly stimulative and supply-constrained environment in early 2021. 

Beginning with consumer and market demand, the excess spending potential—defined as consumer spending potential less actual consumption in rolling four-quarter trillions of dollars—has spiked unprecedentedly to over $2.0 trillion. This surge in unspent cash coincides with a historic tightness in the housing market, where the ratio of monthly home sales to inventory has jumped to an all-time high of nearly 60%. Consequently, business inventories have become exceptionally lean, with the net percentage of businesses reporting inventories as "too low" versus "too high" rising sharply toward 5%.

Global economic activity is expanding robustly, as shown by both the global services survey index and the global manufacturing survey index surging deep into expansionary territory well above the neutral 50-point mark. This rapid expansion has strained supply chains, resulting in a dramatic, vertical spike in Chinese shipping rates to an index level exceeding 2,000. 

Labor market indicators also show extreme tightening. US job openings as a percentage of the adult labor force have climbed rapidly toward 4.5%. At the same time, the percentage of small businesses with job openings they find "hard to fill" has reached an all-time high of approximately 40%. 

In financial markets, investor optimism and leverage are extremely elevated. Bullish investor sentiment over the next six months has spiked, while year-over-year debit balances in margin accounts have surged by nearly $150 billion in inflation-adjusted 1998 dollars. Reflecting these conditions, market valuations have stretched, with the enterprise value to cash flow ratio climbing toward 23x, close to its previous historical peaks. 

Finally, government balance sheets reflect unprecedented fiscal expansion. Federal debt held by the public has risen to approximately 100% of US GDP, a level not seen since the aftermath of World War II. This massive debt accumulation is driven by a fiscal deficit that has ballooned to around 15% of US GDP, as shown in 2021 estimates from the Congressional Budget Office and the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.

This page discusses the impact of COVID-19 vaccines on mortality and hospitalizations, noting that while vaccines have successfully driven down both metrics by approximately 70% in the United States, several notable exceptions exist. In regions like Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, Chile, and Uruguay, mortality and hospitalizations remain flat or are rising after initial declines. The author asserts that Israel is the only country currently close to COVID normalcy, with a total seroprevalence probably exceeding 65%. He rejects low herd immunity estimates, such as a 10% to 20% projection from Fundstrat Research which he heavily criticizes in a footnote as being based on discredited sources, and argues herd immunity almost certainly requires a seroprevalence above 40%. Consequently, governments will need to work harder to overcome vaccine resistance, a task complicated by emerging concerns about thrombosis risks linked to vector vaccines.

To support these observations, the page features two charts. The first chart, titled Mortality vs vaccinations, plots the 14-day average of daily deaths per million against the percentage of unique people vaccinated across twelve regions: Uruguay, Chile, France, Michigan, New Jersey, the United States, Sweden, Minnesota, New Hampshire, Israel, Canada, and the United Kingdom. This chart illustrates a distinct downward trend for countries with high vaccination rates, such as the United Kingdom, where daily deaths peak near 18 per million around a 10% vaccination rate but fall to near zero as vaccinations approach 50%. Israel shows a similar low-mortality profile as its vaccination rate crosses 60%. In contrast, Uruguay's daily deaths spike sharply to around 14 per million at roughly 25% vaccination, and Chile shows an upward tick in deaths near the 40% vaccination mark.

The second chart, titled Hospitalizations vs vaccinations, compares the 7-day average of current hospitalizations per million against the percentage of unique people vaccinated for the same locations. Similar to the mortality chart, the United Kingdom and Israel show significant declines in hospitalizations as vaccination rates rise, with both dropping below 100 hospitalizations per million at higher vaccination levels. However, several regions show concerning rebounds or persistently high rates. For instance, Michigan's hospitalizations rise sharply from roughly 100 to nearly 300 per million as vaccination progresses toward 35%. Similarly, Chile shows rising hospitalizations past 250 per million as vaccinations approach 40%, and France shows a high plateau of over 400 hospitalizations per million around a 20% vaccination rate.

Michael Cembalest addresses the efficacy of value investing, distinguishing between traditional sector allocation and using value as a stock selection tool within individual sectors. Portfolio managers using a sector-neutral, or structured equity, approach evaluate companies within each sector—such as technology, healthcare, banking, and energy—and buy the cheapest stocks based on metrics like price-to-book or price-to-free cash flow. This approach typically results in small sector deviations compared to the broader market, showing a performance trend that differs markedly from traditional value versus growth indices.

To support this distinction, the page displays two charts. The first chart, titled "Russell 1000 value vs growth: performance," tracks performance from 1990 to 2020 using Bloomberg and J.P. Morgan Asset Management data. It compares the traditional value vs growth index ratio (plotted in gold) with a sector-neutral value strategy using price to free cash flow (plotted in blue). While the traditional ratio peaked in 2006 and steadily fell thereafter, the sector-neutral strategy climbed consistently to a peak near 1.5x around 2017, before suffering a sharp decline. The second chart, titled "S&P 500 value vs growth: performance," covers 1997 to 2021 using Bloomberg and Goldman Sachs data. It exhibits a highly similar contour, showing that the Goldman Sachs sector-neutral value strategy peaked above 1.3x in 2017/2018 before falling, but shows a sharper recent rebound in late 2020 and early 2021 compared to the traditional gold line, which remains near historical lows.

Cembalest observes that while traditional value has only recovered a small fraction of its underperformance, value as a stock selection tool in sector-neutral portfolios has recovered much more rapidly over the three to four months prior to publication. Looking ahead, Cembalest states he has low conviction that value-heavy sectors like banks and energy will close their performance gap with technology. Consequently, traditional value vs growth index comparisons may look cheap for some time. However, he predicts that asset managers utilizing value as a stock selection tool within sector-neutral portfolios will continue to recover much of the ground they lost after 2017.

This page consists entirely of legal and regulatory disclosures regarding the international distribution of the publication. It details compliance information, regulatory bodies, and legal entities responsible for the material in various countries and regions, including Spain, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Latin America, and Australia. There are no charts, tables, financial market discussions, or economic forecasts on this page.

This page analyzes the emerging thrombosis risks associated with adenovirus vector COVID-19 vaccines, specifically those from Johnson & Johnson and AstraZeneca, and evaluates how safety-related pauses and age restrictions might impact global inoculation timelines. 

An area chart titled "US vaccinations by type" plots the percentage of the US population vaccinated from January 1 to April 9, 2021. The chart shows total vaccinations rising steadily to nearly 40% of the population. The data is divided into two series, revealing that Pfizer and Moderna mRNA vaccines represent almost the entirety of the vaccinated share, with the Johnson & Johnson vector vaccine appearing only as a tiny sliver at the very top. 

Because mRNA vaccines already provide the bulk of the vaccination coverage, the author predicts that timelines to reach 50% population vaccination will remain broadly unchanged. These timelines are projected for mid-May in the US, early May in the UK, late May in Canada, July in Europe, and September in both Japan and Australia. Given that adverse clotting events are extremely rare—occurring at a rate of one in 170,000 in Europe and one in one million in the US—the author expects J&J vaccinations to eventually resume in the US for older populations. Furthermore, the US is likely to experience declining overall vaccine demand before J&J availability issues become a major constraint. The maximum projected impact of these vector vaccine disruptions is a minor 3% to 5% decline in the vaccinated population across the developed world by late June.

The background text explains that vector vaccines like AstraZeneca and J&J use an unrelated virus to deliver genetic instructions, unlike mRNA vaccines. The primary concern is thrombosis, specifically cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) and splanchnic vein thrombosis (SVT), which can lead to pulmonary embolisms. Out of 34 million AstraZeneca doses administered in Europe, there were 169 cases of CVST and 53 cases of SVT. The European Medicines Agency suggests this stems from an autoimmune response similar to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Studies in Europe and Norway identified this rare clotting disorder with low platelets as vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT), which has led to several deaths, primarily among young, otherwise healthy women. 

In response, major health organizations like the World Health Organization and Britain's MHRA maintain that the vaccine's benefits outweigh its risks. Nevertheless, numerous countries have imposed restrictions: Germany and the Netherlands restrict AstraZeneca to individuals over 60, France limits it to those over 55, Britain advises alternative vaccines for people under 30, and Norway halted its rollout entirely. In the United States, out of more than 6 million J&J doses administered, six cases of CVST and thrombocytopenia occurred in women between 18 and 48 years old, resulting in one death and leading the CDC and FDA to recommend a temporary pause on the J&J vaccine.

This introductory page of Michael Cembalest’s eleventh annual energy paper for J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market outlines the challenges of the fourth great energy transition, asking why the transition to renewable energy is taking so long despite aggressive decarbonization plans. Cembalest argues that prior forecasts for renewable adoption have been overly ambitious because they ignored the complex realities of incumbent energy systems, energy density, and intermittency. He introduces the report's topics, which include an update on oil and gas, President Biden’s energy agenda, China’s rare earth metals diplomacy, US distributed solar power, the Texas power outage, and client inquiries on sustainable aviation fuels, electrified shipping, hydrogen, and carbon accounting. Cembalest acknowledges his technical advisor, Vaclav Smil, who has guided his energy work for over a decade.

The page features a line chart titled Overly ambitious forecasts of the 4th great energy transition, which plots the renewable share of US primary energy consumption from 1960 to 2030. The y-axis shows percentages from 0% to 50%. The chart contrasts the actual historical share of renewable energy—including wind, solar, hydropower, geothermal, biomass, wood, and waste—which remained flat at around 5% to 7% for decades before ticking up to just over 10% by 2020, with several overly optimistic historical forecasts. 

These forecasts include a 1970s prediction by physicist Bent Sorensen that renewables would reach nearly 45% of US primary energy by 2000, and a projection by Amory Lovins of the Rocky Mountain Institute predicting over 30% by 2000. Other overly aggressive forecasts shown include the Carter Administration's solar-only goal of 20% by 2000, a Clinton Presidential Advisory Panel forecast aiming for 50% by 2030, an Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change forecast pointing to roughly 35% by 2030, the Google 2030 Clean Energy Plan target of 35%, and a National Renewable Energy Laboratory forecast targeting 30% by 2030. A text note adds that in 2020, Stanford researcher Mark Jacobson forecast an even more extreme target of 80% by 2030.

This page discusses the critical need for massive transmission grid updates to achieve deep decarbonization, focusing on an MIT study analyzing electricity optimization and trade between Canada and New England. 

A bar chart titled "New England capacity mix by energy source" displays capacity in gigawatts across three scenarios: 2019 actuals, a 2050 scenario with 80% decarbonization, and a 2050 scenario with 80% decarbonization plus 4 gigawatts of new transmission capacity. In 2019, capacity is just over 35 gigawatts, heavily dominated by natural gas. In both 2050 projections, overall capacity rises to nearly 45 gigawatts, with natural gas dramatically reduced and replaced primarily by wind and solar power, alongside a steady base of nuclear and hydro capacity. 

Below this, two area charts compare modeled hourly New England generation in gigawatt hours over a two-week period in October 2050. The chart on the left illustrates the generation mix using the 2050 capacity plan with existing transmission lines, where cross-border trade is constrained. Under this setup, New England's annual carbon dioxide emissions would drop from 27.5 million metric tons today to 6.7 million metric tons in 2050, showing relatively minor imports shown in red and exports shown below the axis in green. The chart on the right models the same period but assumes an additional 4 gigawatts of transmission capacity, allowing New England to double its electricity imports and exports. This additional transmission enables a much higher volume of imports and exports, reducing New England's annual emissions to just 2.0 million metric tons. 

The author points out that MIT's analysis shows the financial cost of building this new transmission would be entirely offset by the lower cost of imported Canadian hydropower, representing a clear economic and environmental win. However, the author poses a cautionary note, warning that while these plans look promising on paper, they face major real-world implementation challenges from local regulatory bodies, such as the New Hampshire siting committee.

Michael Cembalest assesses the status of the global energy transition, arguing that despite rapid cost declines for wind and solar, transitioning away from fossil fuels is a slow, capital-intensive process. He notes that the aggregate impact of nuclear, hydro, and wind/solar generation only reduced global reliance on fossil fuels from approximately 95 percent of primary energy in 1975 to roughly 85 percent in 2020. Although the International Energy Agency expects a faster transition going forward—boosted by lower capital costs for wind and solar (3 to 5 percent) relative to natural gas (10 to 15 percent) and oil projects (up to 20 percent)—the agency still forecasts that fossil fuels will supply 70 to 75 percent of global primary energy in 2040. The primary bottleneck is that renewables are mostly used for electricity generation, which accounts for only 18 percent of final global energy consumption, while direct fossil fuel use remains dominant.
