It illustrates that Britain led the world in major inventions during the late 18th and early 19th centuries, but was vastly overtaken by an exponential surge in technological innovations from the United States in the late 19th century, which spiked to nearly 300 major inventions by 1900.

This page, titled "Food Fight: 2021 private equity update," presents a structured debate between Steve Kaplan of the University of Chicago and Ludovic Phalippou of the University of Oxford regarding whether private equity outperforms public equity net of fees. The discussion is framed around the Public Market Equivalent measure, where a value greater than 1.00 signifies that private equity has outperformed.

The debate is structured as an alternating dialogue of highlighted blocks. First, Phalippou asserts that private equity underperformed public equity, citing a private equity public market equivalent of 0.99 from 2006 to 2015 when benchmarked against the S&P 500. Kaplan counters that while this is true for that specific timeframe, all other contiguous periods from 1996 to 2015 show private equity outperforming with a public market equivalent above 1.00. Kaplan further argues that Phalippou's definition of private equity is too broad because it includes real assets, real estate, infrastructure, and energy. If the definition is restricted to buyout, growth equity, and venture capital, the public market equivalent for the 2006 to 2015 period rises to 1.05.

Phalippou raises a counterpoint, questioning whether underperforming real assets like oil and gas should also be removed from the S&P 500 benchmark if they are removed from the private equity universe. The text notes that while the energy sector did underperform the S&P 500 from 2006 to 2017, the index's modest 5% to 15% energy weight means an ex-energy benchmark would only be 25 to 30 basis points higher on an annualized basis.

The debate then shifts to the choice of small- and mid-cap benchmarks. Kaplan questions Phalippou's use of the S&P 600, pointing out that approximately 90% of small-cap managers use the Russell 2000 as the industry standard. He notes that for buyout, growth equity, and venture capital from 2006 to 2015, the private equity public market equivalent is 1.05 using either the S&P 500 or S&P 600, but rises to 1.11 using the Russell 2000. Phalippou defends his choice by stating that managers prefer the Russell 2000 because it has significantly underperformed the S&P 600 since the year 2000. He attributes this underperformance to the Russell 2000's lack of an IPO seasoning requirement, its lack of profitability tests, its smaller float requirements, and the trading pressures from ETF inflows and outflows during index rebalancing.

A footnote details an additional dispute from 2020. Phalippou had claimed that private equity managers would need to grow earnings by 50% over a typical four-year holding period to outperform public equity. Kaplan disputed this, arguing that Phalippou failed to account for debt paydown, which acts similarly to dividends in total return calculations. When debt paydown is factored in, Kaplan asserts that private equity earnings only need to grow by 10% rather than 50% to achieve outperformance.

This page serves as an introduction and table of contents for the J.P. Morgan biennial private equity review. Michael Cembalest explains that measuring private equity performance historically involved debates over data sources, noting that most modern analyses now utilize data sourced from limited partners rather than databases suffering from voluntary reporting and stale information. To maintain objectivity, the publication relies on analyses from Steven Kaplan and finance professors at Vanderbilt, the University of Virginia, and Duke. Key parameters for the review include focusing on vintage years through 2017 to allow sufficient time for distributions, reporting buyout and venture performance net of all fees, and using size-weighted averages based on fund commitments and distributions. 

The detailed table of contents outlines sections on absolute and relative buyout performance, benchmark selection, manager dispersion, performance drivers, secondary private equity funds, and venture capital performance. It also lists topics such as the split of gains between venture capital and post-IPO investors, buyout versus venture capital comparisons, co-investments, fundraising pace, fees, and relevant academic papers. Finally, four appendices are listed, covering alternative industry data, transaction return dispersion within commingled funds, sources for manager performance, and technical explanations of internal rate of return, Direct Alpha, cash flow timing, and subscription lines.

In this J.P. Morgan publication, Michael Cembalest, Chairman of Market and Investment Strategy, discusses the dynamics of private and public equity markets alongside current global COVID-19 developments. Cembalest begins by noting that while private equity continues to outperform public equity, this outperformance has narrowed due to widespread market stimulus and rising private equity acquisition multiples. Transitioning to public equities, he explains that the slowing pace of gains since April reflects a robust recovery in earnings and capital spending that is nevertheless complicated by a tight labor supply, high valuations, and the Federal Reserve's transition toward normalizing monetary policy. He cautions that future equity gains will need to be driven solely by earnings rather than valuation expansion, with pending domestic and international tax changes representing the next major policy hurdle. 

The economic and market backdrop is illustrated by two financial charts. The first, tracking year-to-date S&P 500 performance total return index from January to June, displays how S&P 500 Value consistently outperformed both the broader S&P 500 and S&P 500 Growth for most of the period, peaking near 120 before a late June convergence when Growth rallied. The second chart focuses on US leading indicators for capital spending, comparing actual Capex growth with demand-based estimates across several sectors. It highlights robust expected capital expenditures, with demand-based estimates for vehicles exceeding 50% and industrial machinery near 30%, whereas structures actual capex remains negative at roughly -10%, and technology equipment shows actual capex growth near 30%.

Cembalest also addresses the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting that while infections and mortality are dropping across most of the developed world, regional hotspots and localized risks remain. He warns that the United States is being eclipsed in vaccination rates by Europe, Canada, and China, leaving unvaccinated pockets highly vulnerable. To demonstrate this risk, the chart on COVID-19 hospitalizations per million people compares reported rates with the rates calculated specifically for the unvaccinated population across various regions, such as Washington, DC, Missouri, and Nevada. In every state shown, the hospitalization rate among the unvaccinated is two to three times higher than the reported overall rate; for instance, in DC, the reported rate is around 110 per million, whereas the unvaccinated rate spikes to over 300 per million. 

Lastly, a scatter plot mapping the latest COVID-19 trends in developing countries tracks log-scale mortality per million people against log-scale infections per million people across South America, Central America, the Middle East, Eastern Europe, Emerging Asia, and Africa. The chart visualizes a clear upward trend, pointing to South America as a severe, unrelenting hotspot with many countries clustered in the top-right quadrant of high infections and high mortality, contrasting with lower levels observed in Africa and parts of Emerging Asia.

This page of the report evaluates absolute buyout performance, examining how multiples of invested capital (MOIC) and internal rates of return (IRR) have historically behaved. The author argues that while average and median MOICs and IRRs moved in tandem prior to 2009, they have since diverged: MOICs have been declining while IRRs have been rising. This decoupling is attributed to the growing use of subscription lines, where fund managers finance investments with bank loans to delay capital calls to limited partners (LPs), thereby artificially boosting the time-weighted IRR at the expense of a slightly lower MOIC due to interest costs. 

Two line charts illustrate this divergence using data from Steve Kaplan of Chicago Booth and Burgiss. The first chart, tracking US buyout MOICs by vintage year from 1991 to 2016, shows that MOICs peaked near 3.0 in 1991, fell to around 1.5 by 1997, and experienced subsequent cyclical peaks near 2.0 in 2001 and 2009 before embarking on a steady decline toward 1.5 by 2016. In contrast, the second chart, showing US buyout IRRs by vintage year over the same period, shows IRRs peaking above 30% in 1991, bottoming near 5% in the late 1990s, and then rising steadily from 2009 onward to reach between 20% and 25% by 2016. Both charts show a very tight gap between the average and median performance lines.

The text goes on to discuss the quantified impacts and market adoption of subscription lines. The author notes that estimates of IRR inflation vary, citing a Cambridge Associates projection of a 3% annual boost and a Carnegie Mellon study finding a 2.6% increase, contrasted against a Notre Dame study suggesting a less material impact and the Institutional Limited Partners Association finding a median impact of no more than 0.45%. To demonstrate the potential magnitude of impact drivers, a hypothetical case is presented where using subscription lines for 100% of invested capital throughout the investment period increases IRR by 7%, lifting it from 15% to 22%. Lastly, the page highlights an industry "arms race" in subscription line adoption, citing Mercer research showing credit line usage has grown six-fold since 2010, with over 90% of funds now utilizing them, and a poll indicating 87% of private equity respondents use or plan to use subscription lines.

This page addresses the relative performance of buyout private equity versus public equity, examining why relative buyout returns have declined since the 2008–2009 financial crisis. The author explains that because traditional metrics like the multiple on invested capital and the internal rate of return do not measure performance against public equity, analysts rely on the Public Market Equivalent ratio and Direct Alpha. The central argument is that central bank "maximum accommodation" policies post-crisis drove up public equity valuations, while a "food fight" over private companies—fueled further by the SPAC boom—pushed buyout acquisition multiples higher. These dual factors of higher buyout purchase prices and strong public equity performance have reduced excess returns. The author poses an open question for investors: are the post-2009 annualized excess returns of 1% to 5% over public equity high enough to justify the illiquidity of private equity?

Four charts support this analysis. The first chart, "US buyout PMEs by vintage year," plots the PME ratio versus the S&P 500 from 1991 to 2018, showing both average and median series. The ratios peaked near 1.5 for vintages around 2001 before falling to hover just above the 1.0 parity line for vintages post-2009. The second chart, "US buyout direct alpha by vintage year," shows annualized outperformance versus the S&P 500 over the same period. Direct alpha reached approximately 15% for the 2001 vintage but has remained compressed in a 1% to 5% range for vintages since 2009. 

The remaining two charts illustrate the rising costs of both public and private assets. The third chart, "S&P 500 price / earnings ratio," tracks the price divided by forward two-year earnings per share from 1990 through late 2020. It shows public valuations climbing steadily from a post-crisis trough of around 9x in 2011 to approximately 20x by late 2020. The final chart, "Buyout purchase price multiples," presents a stacked bar chart of the average EBITDA purchase price multiples for US LBO transactions from 2003 through the first quarter of 2021. The multiples are broken down by senior debt, subordinated debt, equity, and other contributions relative to EBITDA. This visual highlights that total purchase multiples have risen from roughly 7x to 8x in the 2003–2005 period to over 11x in 2019, 2020, and early 2021, with equity representing a larger share of the purchase price over time.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" examines performance dispersion among private equity buyout managers, highlighting that picking a below-average manager has become less risky. The author notes that average and median managers consistently outperform, but since 2010, the gap between top and bottom-quartile managers has narrowed, and underperformance for the bottom quartile remains modest. 

This trend is illustrated in two top charts using data from Steve Kaplan and Burgiss. The first chart plots US buyout public market equivalent (PME) quartiles versus the S&P 500 by vintage year from 1991 to 2016. It shows that the median manager (in blue) consistently stays above a 1.0 PME ratio, and while the top quartile (in gold) has historically reached ratios near 1.8, the bottom quartile (in red) has converged closer to the 1.0 mark post-2010, showing narrower overall dispersion. The second chart tracks US buyout direct annualized alpha versus the S&P 500 over the same period. For vintage years after 2010, the bottom-quartile direct alpha remains stable, hovering just below 0%, while the median and top quartiles show tighter, less volatile dispersion compared to the wide swings seen in the late 1990s and early 2000s.

The bottom chart, sourced from Hamilton Lane using 2010–2019 vintage years, visualizes absolute performance dispersion across four distinct strategies by mapping the percentage of funds against their trailing 10-year annualized returns. The curves show that different asset classes exhibit highly distinct risk-return distributions. Private credit has the tightest dispersion, peaking sharply around an 8% return. Real estate is also relatively narrow, with a peak near 10%. Buyouts demonstrate moderate dispersion, forming a broader curve that peaks between 13% and 15%. In contrast, venture capital displays the widest dispersion of all, featuring a flatter, highly distributed curve that spans from low single digits to well over 30% annualized returns.

This page examines the underlying drivers of private equity buyout performance by decomposing changes in enterprise value into three sources: operating cash flow (EBITDA) growth, changes in valuation multiples, and changes in debt levels. Analyzing data from J.P. Morgan Private Bank for three consecutive buyout funds managed by a major manager, the author argues that operating cash flow improvements at target companies consistently accounted for more than half of the total change in enterprise value, outperforming the impact of multiple expansion. 

The analysis is presented through three pairs of charts, each featuring a detailed breakdown of individual investments on the left and aggregate enterprise-value-weighted results on the right. The first set of charts analyzes a Pre-GFC fund, where individual investments are sorted by cumulative enterprise value growth. In the aggregate results for this Pre-GFC fund, overall enterprise value growth is around 80%, with EBITDA growth contributing approximately 65%, multiple expansion contributing about 18%, and changes in debt reducing the total by about 8%. 

The second set of charts focuses on Post-GFC fund I. For this fund, aggregate enterprise value growth reaches roughly 160%. This total is driven by about 98% from EBITDA growth, 44% from multiple expansion, and 23% from changes in debt. 

The third set of charts covers Post-GFC fund II, showing a more modest overall enterprise value growth of about 52% in aggregate. Here, EBITDA growth accounts for roughly 26%, multiple expansion represents about 18%, and changes in debt contribute approximately 8%. 

Across all three successive funds, the data illustrates that operating cash flow improvements are the primary driver of enterprise value growth. While the author notes this specific manager's data is not necessarily indicative of the private equity industry as a whole, it highlights how operational value creation can play a central role in generating investment returns.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the debate surrounding the appropriate benchmark for evaluating US buyout funds. Many analysts argue that the large-cap S&P 500 is an unsuitable benchmark because buyout managers typically invest in smaller companies. While US buyout deal sizes have been rising, the average US buyout is still relatively small at $2.5 billion, compared to a median S&P 500 market cap of $21 billion and a median Russell 2000 market cap of $1.1 billion. 

To illustrate these dynamics, the page features four charts. The first chart displays the distribution of US leverage buyout deal sizes as a percentage of total deal value from 2001 to 2020. It demonstrates a clear shift over the two decades: while deals under $100 million and those between $100 million and $250 million dominated in the early 2000s, mega-deals of $1 billion or more grew to represent the largest share of total deal value by 2020. 

The second chart compares the US buyout average Public Market Equivalent ratios from 1991 to 2016, comparing buyout performance against the Russell 2000 and the S&P 500. A PME ratio above 1.0 indicates that buyouts outperformed the respective public index. The data shows that buyouts consistently outperformed both benchmarks for nearly all vintage years, though the outperformance relative to the Russell 2000 was highly volatile, peaking at around 1.5 in the early 2000s.

The third and fourth charts analyze the underlying performance of these public indices. A chart of major index returns from 2000 to 2020, set to a base of 100 in January 2000, reveals that the S&P 600 significantly outperformed other indexes, rising to nearly 900 by late 2020. In contrast, the Russell 2000, S&P 500, and Russell 2000 Growth clustered much lower, ending between 400 and 600. Because of this divergence, the final chart shows that the Russell 2000 has trailed the S&P 600 on a rolling three-year basis for almost the entirety of the last two decades, with underperformance frequently hovering between 5% and 15% and dipping as low as 25% in the early 2000s, before briefly showing modest outperformance around 2020.

This page analyzes the secondary private equity market, distinguishing between traditional limited partner (LP)-led transactions and the more recent growth of general partner (GP)-led transactions. The author explains that LP-led transactions involve purchasing limited partner units for liquidity or asset allocation purposes, while GP-led transactions, which emerged around 2014, allow managers to roll remaining portfolio companies into a new vehicle to extend their investment lifespan. Although early GP-led deals sometimes involved underperforming "zombie" managers seeking more management fees, the author notes that the quality of these funds has generally improved, even if empirical proof remains elusive.

Three charts illustrate the market's dynamics. The first chart, showing secondary market volume in billions of US dollars from 2010 to 2020 based on Credit Suisse data, depicts a market that expanded from around $20 billion in 2010 to a peak of approximately $80 billion in 2019, before dipping slightly to around $70 billion in 2020. This volume is broken down into other secondaries, GP-led secondaries, and single-asset continuation funds, showing that GP-led and single-asset vehicles have captured a significant portion of the market since 2014.

The second chart, based on Coller Capital data, displays the average secondary market pricing for private equity LP positions as a percentage of net asset value (NAV) from 2005 to 2021. Buyout positions, represented by a dashed line, and venture capital positions, represented by a solid line, both bottomed out near 60% of NAV during the 2008 financial crisis. Since 2010, buyout pricing recovered to fluctuate between 85% and 100% of NAV, while venture capital has priced lower, between 75% and 85% of NAV. By 2021, buyouts stood near 90% and venture capital rebounded strongly to about 85% of NAV.

The third chart plots alternative investment performance by asset class for the 1999 to 2018 vintage years, comparing the median total value to paid-in capital (TVPI) on the horizontal axis against the median internal rate of return (IRR) on the vertical axis. According to self-reported Cambridge Associates data, secondary funds achieved the highest median IRR at approximately 13%, with a TVPI of about 1.38. This compares to buyouts at roughly 12.3% IRR and 1.55 TVPI, growth equity at 11.5% IRR and 1.46 TVPI, fund of funds at 10% IRR and 1.57 TVPI, private credit at 9% IRR and 1.28 TVPI, real estate at 8.8% IRR and 1.33 TVPI, venture capital at 8.5% IRR and 1.41 TVPI, and infrastructure at 7.5% IRR and 1.32 TVPI. 

The author concludes with a cautionary note regarding secondary performance. Aside from relying on self-reported data, some GP-led secondary funds layer 30% to 50% leverage at the fund level on top of the debt already held by the underlying portfolio companies, which the author warns is a highly risky amount of leverage to carry into an economic downturn.

This page analyzes absolute and relative venture capital performance, focusing on the period from 2004 to 2016. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that venture capital performance discussion should start in 2004 because the late 1990s boom and bust are too distorted to be relevant today. To illustrate this distortion, a footnote details that the peak 1996 vintage reached a massive 7.0x multiple on invested capital and a 120% internal rate of return, whereas the 1999 bust vintage ended up with a 1.0x multiple on invested capital and a negative 1% internal rate of return. A major theme of the page is the substantial gap between average and median manager performance, which indicates that a small number of high-performing managers or very large funds skew the averages upward. Additionally, the author notes that after 2012, subscription lines and faster distributions drove internal rates of return higher even as multiples on invested capital declined.

These observations are supported by four charts using data from Steve Kaplan of Chicago Booth and Burgiss. The first chart, showing US venture capital multiples on invested capital by vintage year, tracks the average and median performance from 2004 to 2016. The average multiple on invested capital peaks at approximately 3.7x for the 2012 vintage before falling to about 2.3x by 2016, while the median multiple on invested capital peaks lower at 2.6x in 2010 and declines to 1.6x by 2016, highlighting the persistent performance gap. The second chart tracks US venture capital internal rates of return by vintage year. In this chart, the average internal rate of return rises from about 26% for the 2012 vintage to nearly 37% by 2017, while the median internal rate of return rises more modestly from 18% to 21% over the same period.

The remaining two charts examine performance relative to the S&P 500. The third chart shows US venture capital public market equivalents by vintage year, using a baseline ratio of 1.0 where any value above 1.0 represents outperformance of the S&P 500. While the average manager ratio remains consistently above 1.0 and peaks at 1.8 in 2012, the median manager ratio falls well below the 1.0 line for vintage years 2004 to 2008, bottoming out at 0.7 in 2006. The fourth chart displays annualized US venture capital direct alphas relative to the S&P 500. Mirroring the public market equivalent data, the average direct alpha rises steadily to peak near 18%, whereas the median direct alpha is negative for the 2004 to 2008 vintages, hitting a low of nearly negative 7.5% in 2006, before averaging a modest positive alpha of 3% to 5% for later vintages.

This page examines the division of value creation between pre-IPO venture capital investors and post-IPO public market investors for US tech, internet retailing, and interactive media IPOs from 2010 to 2019. The author argues that, contrary to the belief that venture capitalists capture all the upside and leave public investors with worthless assets, post-IPO investor gains have actually been substantial over the last decade. 

To demonstrate this, the page features a detailed chart titled "Value creation in pre-IPO and post-IPO markets" analyzing 165 IPOs. The chart’s left y-axis shows the percentage of value created post-IPO, ranging from negative 50 percent to 150 percent, while the right y-axis inversely maps the percentage of value created pre-IPO. The chart is divided into three colored zones representing distinct outcomes. 

The pink-shaded lower-left region represents companies where pre-IPO investors pocketed virtually all value, leaving public market investors with losses or zero gains; notable companies in this group include Blue Apron, Green Sky, Groupon, Quotient, Rocket Fuel, SolarWinds, Sabre, Eventbrite, and The RealReal. 

The yellow-shaded middle region indicates where pre-IPO and post-IPO investors shared the total value creation, featuring companies like Dropbox, Switch, SurveyMonkey, Yelp, Twitter, DataDog, and Pinterest. 

Finally, the blue-shaded upper-right region covers companies where post-IPO investors captured the vast majority of value creation. This dominant category contains high-performing stocks such as LinkedIn, Chewy, Cloudflare, Zoom, CrowdStrike, Snap, DocuSign, Facebook, Square, and First Data. 

The analysis defines total value creation as market capitalization minus pre-IPO paid-in capital and primary or secondary issuance, counting the post-IPO lockup period toward pre-IPO performance. Ultimately, the data shows that the vast majority of these 165 analyzed IPOs generated significant, shared, or majority value for public market equity investors, despite a few painful, loss-making exceptions.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, written by Michael Cembalest, explores the performance benefits and downside risk mitigation associated with private equity co-investments. Co-investments occur when sponsors seek additional capital from limited partners to complete acquisitions, offering a way to access deals with lower fees and strong security selection. The author notes that historically, buyout and growth co-investment funds have outperformed the broader industry. Specifically, 80% of co-investment funds from the 2009 to 2016 vintages outperformed primary private equity funds, while 60% did so over the longer 1998 to 2016 period. Additionally, the net median IRR for co-investment funds was 18.9% for 2009 to 2016 vintages, compared to 14.6% for primary private equity funds.

To illustrate downside risk mitigation, the page features two charts utilizing Capital Dynamics data from 2020. The first chart compares primary private equity funds to co-investment funds using Net Total Value to Paid-In capital (TVPI) to measure downside performance. For primary private equity, the lower quartile TVPI stands at 1.20x and the lower decile falls to a loss-generating 0.93x. In contrast, co-investment funds demonstrate stronger downside protection, with a lower quartile TVPI of 1.27x and a lower decile that remains profitable at 1.09x. 

The second chart displays the proportion of loss-generating funds, defined as those with a TVPI of less than 1.0x, across two vintage periods. For the 1998 to 2016 vintages, roughly 12% of primary private equity funds generated losses compared to only about 8% of co-investment funds. For the 2009 to 2016 vintages, this gap widened, with primary private equity funds showing a loss rate of approximately 11.5%, while the loss rate for co-investment funds dropped significantly to around 3.5%. This visual data underscores the argument that co-investment structures provide limited partners with substantial downside protection alongside their potential for outperformance.

This page focuses on venture capital performance benchmarking and manager dispersion. Michael Cembalest argues that the S&P 500 may not be the most appropriate benchmark for venture capital due to significantly smaller average deal sizes. Because the S&P 500 has outperformed other US equity benchmarks like the Russell 2000 and the Russell Microcap Index since 2010, benchmarking venture capital against these smaller-cap indices would make venture outperformance look even larger. He also observes that since 2010, the performance gap between top and bottom-quartile venture capital managers has narrowed, with bottom-quartile managers showing surprisingly modest underperformance against public equities.

The analysis is supported by four charts. The first chart, showing US venture capital average Public Market Equivalent (PME) ratios from 2004 to 2016, compares performance against the Russell Microcap, Russell 2000, and S&P 500. Average PMEs peaked around the 2012 vintage, reaching approximately 2.2 against the Russell Microcap and 1.8 against the S&P 500, with all three benchmarks remaining above a PME of 1.0 throughout the period. The second chart presents median PMEs over the same period, showing a similar shape but at lower levels; the median PME against the S&P 500 dipped to around 0.8 in 2009 before peaking near 1.2 in 2013 and ending just under 1.1 in 2016, while comparisons to the Russell indices consistently showed higher median outperformance.

The third chart tracks US venture capital PME quartiles versus the S&P 500 by vintage year. It demonstrates that while top-quartile PMEs remained high and volatile, ranging between 1.4 and 1.8, bottom-quartile manager performance steadily improved from a PME of 0.5 in 2004 to nearly 0.8 by 2016, narrowing the dispersion gap. The fourth chart displays US venture capital deals by size as a percentage of total deal value from 2006 to 2021. This visual highlights a dramatic structural shift: deals larger than $50 million grew from less than 20% of total deal value in 2006 to accounting for nearly 60% of total value by 2021, while smaller deal brackets, particularly those under $10 million, saw their share of total deal value shrink significantly over the fifteen-year period.

This page analyzes private equity and venture capital fundraising relative to US stock market capitalization. The central argument is that while absolute dollar commitments to buyouts and venture capital have been rising sharply toward historical highs, these levels appear much less alarming when measured as a percentage of total stock market capitalization. 

The analysis is supported by four charts spanning 1980 to 2020, based on data from Steve Kaplan of Chicago Booth and Burgiss. The first chart displays commitments to US private equity and leveraged buyout partnerships in billions of dollars. This series shows clear cyclical peaks: first rising to nearly $100 billion in 2000, spiking to over $200 billion in 2007, and, after a sharp post-financial-crisis decline, climbing steadily to a peak near $350 billion in the late 2010s. The second chart measures these same private equity and LBO commitments as a percentage of all-cap stock market capitalization. Through this lens, the recent peak of approximately 1.0% is notably lower than the pre-crisis peak in 2007, which exceeded 1.2%.

The third and fourth charts focus on venture capital. The third chart shows absolute commitments to US venture capital partnerships in billions of dollars, highlighting the massive spike during the dot-com bubble when commitments surpassed $70 billion in 2000. After collapsing to around $10 billion, fundraising slowly rebuilt and surged back up toward $70 billion by 2020. The final chart scales these VC commitments against all-cap stock market capitalization. It reveals that while absolute funding is nearing dot-com era heights, as a share of the total stock market, recent commitments hover around 0.20%, which is less than half of the bubble-era peak that exceeded 0.40% in 2000.

This page analyzes the performance of buyout funds versus venture capital (VC) funds, arguing that while venture capital has outperformed buyout since 2010, the gap is much narrower for the median manager than it is for the average manager. The author contends that median results offer a more realistic reflection of the opportunity set available to an individual limited partner. Data throughout the page is sourced from Steve Kaplan of Chicago Booth and Burgiss, covering 2020.

Four line charts compare median performance metrics by vintage year from 2004 to 2016. The first chart displays US buyout versus VC median Multiple on Invested Capital (MOIC). Buyout MOICs remain relatively steady between 1.5 and 2.0, while VC MOICs start low at around 1.1 in 2004, spike to a peak of roughly 2.7 in 2009, and gradually decline to meet buyout near 1.5 by 2016. The second chart tracks median Internal Rates of Return (IRRs), showing that both strategies have followed a similar trajectory since 2008, hovering between 15% and 20% in the later vintage years, though VC started significantly lower in 2004 near 0%. The third chart compares median Public Market Equivalent (PME) ratios against the S&P 500. Buyout PMEs start strong above 1.2 in 2004 and settle near 1.1, while VC PMEs rise from a low of 0.6 in 2004 to peak at over 1.2 in 2012 before declining back to around 1.1. The fourth chart illustrates median annualized direct alphas relative to the S&P 500, showing that buyout alphas generally remained positive between 0% and 5%, whereas VC alphas were deeply negative at around negative 8% in 2004 but rose to match or slightly exceed buyout levels after 2010.

Two tables at the bottom of the page contrast the performance of median versus average managers for the 2004–2017 vintage years. For the median manager, venture capital slightly leads in MOIC at 1.8 versus 1.7 for buyout, but buyout outperforms in IRR at 15.3% versus 14.3%, in PME at 1.1 versus 1.0, and in direct alpha at 2.4% versus 0.3%. In contrast, the average manager table shows venture capital dominating across all metrics, with an average MOIC of 2.6 compared to buyout's 1.7, an IRR of 21.4% compared to buyout's 16.1%, a PME of 1.3 compared to 1.1, and a direct alpha of 6.7% compared to 3.2%.

This page of the report focuses on the dynamics of private equity fundraising and the lagging pace of investment, which has led to a major accumulation of global "dry powder." Michael Cembalest observes that global dry powder has surged from $2 trillion to approximately $3 trillion. However, he notes that this figure includes all private equity categories; for buyout and venture capital specifically, dry powder is closer to $1 trillion. Furthermore, the rising use of subscription lines—estimated at $500 billion outstanding—inflates the perceived amount of real undrawn and committed capital, making up a significant portion of the dry powder growth since 2012. Because of elevated valuations in both public and private markets, exits and distributions are currently outstripping capital calls, particularly in the United States. Since many 2020 exits occurred through initial public offerings (IPOs) and special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs), much of that value remains public but undistributed, leading to the author's prediction that distributions will remain high through 2021.

Four charts illustrate these points. The first, a stacked bar chart titled "Global private equity capital raised by year" (measured in trillions of US dollars from 2003 to 2020), shows annual fundraising climbing from around $0.2 trillion in 2003 to a peak of nearly $1.1 trillion in 2019 and 2020. The categories shown include buyout, venture capital, real estate, infrastructure, and other segments like secondary, growth, distressed, SPACs, and natural resources. The second stacked bar chart, "Global dry powder by category" (also in trillions of US dollars from 2003 to 2020), demonstrates a massive accumulation of uninvested capital, rising from roughly $1.0 trillion in 2012 to nearly $3.0 trillion in 2020, with the "other" category and buyout segments representing the largest shares. Both of these charts are sourced from the 2021 Bain Global Private Equity Report.

The final two line charts compare capital calls and distributions as a percentage of fund size from 2000 through 2020, using data from Burgiss. The chart for US private equity capital calls and distributions shows that distributions (represented by a dashed blue line) spiked to roughly 4.5% of fund size by the end of 2020, while capital calls (represented by a solid gold line) sat much lower at around 2.5%. The adjacent chart, depicting global private equity capital calls and distributions, shows a highly synchronized pattern where global distributions rose to nearly 4% of fund size by the end of 2020, while global capital calls hovered near 2.5% to 3%.

This page contains standard regulatory disclosures and legal disclaimers for J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publication. It details the distribution, licensing, and oversight of various J.P. Morgan entities and branches across global jurisdictions, including Spain, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Latin American countries, and Australia. The text specifies which local financial regulatory bodies oversee these branches—such as the SEC, FINRA, CFTC, and various European and Asian authorities—and outlines restrictions on offerings and services, particularly regarding private placements in Latin America and services intended solely for wholesale clients in Australia. There are no charts, tables, market forecasts, or analytical observations presented on this page.

This appendix page discusses the evolution and reliability of data sources used to track private equity manager performance relative to the public equity market. The author explains that older data aggregators, such as Venture Economics, suffered from severe data limitations and survivorship bias. Specifically, a 2013 Oxford University study by Rudiger Stucke revealed that over forty percent of active funds in the database stopped updating, and incomplete funds missed over sixty percent of cash distributions, creating a significant downward bias. Re-engineering these historical findings reversed an estimated private equity underperformance of three to six percent against the S&P 500 into an outperformance of four percent per annum. To address these historical inaccuracies and avoid self-reported performance data, the author relies on the Burgiss database, which sources net-of-fee cash flow data directly from limited partners. The Burgiss investor universe includes three hundred state and corporate pension funds, endowments, and foundations investing across fourteen hundred private equity funds, covering at least seventy percent of all private equity funds ever raised according to a 2018 study by Steve Kaplan.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market analyzes the structure and dynamics of private equity fees, dividing them into three categories using estimated earnings from 2008 to 2020 for major public firms such as Carlyle, KKR, Blackstone, and Apollo. 

The first category, carried interest, generated thirty billion dollars. While academic literature generally indicates that higher fee levels correlate with superior performance rather than worse net-of-fee returns, it identifies an agency conflict where general partners accelerate asset realizations during the "waterfall quarter" immediately following the payment of the limited partner's preferred return. This behavior sacrifices potential limited partner upside to guarantee the general partner's catch-up return. 

The second category is management fees, which totaled twenty-six billion dollars and are typically charged on committed rather than invested capital. 

The third category is net monitoring and transaction fees, also known as company fees, which totaled four point six billion dollars. Paid directly by portfolio companies whose boards are controlled by general partners, these fees are controversial and have historically drawn regulatory scrutiny from the SEC. While not detailed in Limited Partnership Agreements, they are specified in Management Services Agreements, with rebate rates back to limited partners commonly landing between eighty and eighty-five percent from 2011 to 2014.

Two charts illustrate these dynamics. The first chart, depicting the private equity management fee approach by manager type, shows the proportion of fees charged on committed versus invested capital using March 2021 Preqin data. It reveals that buyout, growth, and venture capital managers heavily favor charging on committed capital, with buyout managers doing so at a ninety percent rate. Conversely, debt and real asset strategies, such as direct lending, mezzanine, and real estate, utilize invested capital structures far more frequently, with real estate managers charging on invested capital about forty percent of the time. 

The second chart demonstrates how managers cluster realizations around the waterfall quarter, showing excess realizations as a percentage of original committed capital compared to an average quarter. Drawing on academic research from Robinson and Sensoy, the chart shows that excess realizations spike to nearly forty percent for buyout managers and climb past sixty percent for venture capital managers during the waterfall quarter, visually confirming the tendency of managers to accelerate realizations to lock in their catch-up returns.

This page summarizes key insights from recent academic papers on private equity, focusing on performance persistence, maturity-related volatility, scaling challenges, timing, and post-IPO holding periods. 

The first insight concerns performance persistence, noting that while top-quartile performance tends to persist in subsequent venture capital and buyout funds, interim performance is a poor indicator of final performance for buyouts. In contrast, partial performance information is useful for venture capital investors, where the average public market equivalent for funds with top-quartile interim performance is 0.8x higher than those in the bottom quartile. 

The second topic addresses volatility in the secondary market, illustrating that investors should expect a wider dispersion in fund performance as a fund matures. This is depicted in a line chart titled "Dispersion of remaining buyout fund performance over fund life, Remaining direct alpha." The chart, which tracks remaining direct alpha across fifteen years of fund age, shows that percentiles begin to diverge significantly around years seven and eight. By year fifteen, the 90th percentile reaches approximately 60% alpha while the 10th percentile drops to nearly -70%, signaling substantial risk for secondary private equity funds purchasing mature assets with a diminishing number of remaining deals.

The commentary also highlights that private equity firms often struggle with subsequent fund raises. After strong performance, firms frequently increase fund sizes, but these later funds historically experience performance declines due to scaling difficulties or reversion to the mean. Furthermore, attempting to time private equity commitments yields only modest benefits because general partners naturally adapt their fundraisings to market cycles and valuations.

Finally, the page examines post-IPO manager decision-making. Private equity funds tend to hold companies for an average of three years post-IPO, which typically does not add value and forces investors to continue paying management fees. A bar chart titled "Faster exits post-IPO improve fund performance" plots the net IRR of the median deal across various exit strategies. The fastest exits in the top quartile generate a net IRR of approximately 38%, compared to an actual median deal net IRR of 26%. Spacing share sales equally over three years would yield a net IRR of roughly 31%, while the slowest exits in the bottom quartile yield only about 14%. The text notes that faster disposition of IPOs could have reduced overall management fees by 7%. Specific academic researchers cited on this page include Harris from the University of Virginia, Rossi from the University of Arizona, Jenkinson from Oxford, and Brown from the University of North Carolina.

This page of Michael Cembalest’s publication, titled "COVID and Thy Brother’s Keeper," examines the impact of the Delta variant on public health policies, societal expectations, and financial markets. Cembalest argues that despite a rise in Delta variant infections, developed world equity markets should remain resilient. He asserts that the US reopening is irreversible because governments are unlikely to reimpose business and mobility restrictions to protect unvaccinated individuals who chose not to receive a vaccine. He details a contrast between the United Kingdom, where a 96% vaccination rate among people over age 50 has decoupled rising infection rates from hospitalizations and deaths, and the United States, where only about 75% of those over age 50 are vaccinated. This lower vaccination rate in the US, particularly in rural areas and hotspot states like Arkansas, Florida, Louisiana, Missouri, Nevada, and Wyoming, means hospitalizations are rising more sharply than in the UK, but political will for renewed lockdowns remains very low.

Two charts illustrate these trends. The first chart, titled "United Kingdom," tracks daily infection levels, current hospitalizations (both measured on the left axis from 0 to 70,000), and daily deaths (measured on the right axis from 0 to 1,400) from February 2020 through June 2021. It visualizes the decoupling effect: while the daily infection line spikes dramatically toward 40,000 cases in mid-2021, the hospitalization and death lines remain flat near the bottom of the chart, showcasing the efficacy of the UK's high vaccination rate in preventing severe outcomes.

The second chart, titled "Lockdown stringency index: US, UK and Europe," measures the strictness of government response on an index from 0 to 100, where 100 represents the highest level of lockdown strictness, from February 2020 through July 2021. It tracks three series: the US (blue line), the UK (gold line), and a combined group of France, Germany, Italy, and Spain (red line). The index shows that after peaking in early 2020 and late 2020 near 80 to 90, lockdown stringency has steadily declined. By mid-2021, the US stringency level is the lowest of the groups, hovering near 40, which supports the author's argument that the US reopening has "left the station" and is unlikely to reverse.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the return dispersion of individual buyout and venture capital transactions within commingled private equity funds. Cembalest argues that because individual private equity investments exhibit a very wide range of performance, investors should prioritize diversified private equity funds. This dispersion is especially pronounced in venture capital, where a majority of transactions lose money but overall fund returns remain positive due to a small number of exceptional winners.

A performance table titled "Deal specific performance data (mid 1990's to 2018)" quantifies these differences using Total Value to Paid-in Capital and Public Market Equivalent metrics. For buyout transactions, the value-weighted mean TVPI is 1.9, the equal-weighted mean is 2.1, and the standard deviation is 2.8. Its 25th percentile TVPI is 1.0, the 50th percentile is 1.6, and the 75th percentile is 2.7, with 27% of transactions yielding a TVPI of less than 1.0x and 21% yielding under 0.5x. In contrast, venture capital transactions show a value-weighted mean TVPI of 2.2, an equal-weighted mean of 2.1, and a much larger standard deviation of 6.9. The 25th percentile for venture capital TVPI is just 0.1, the 50th percentile is 1.0, and the 75th percentile is 2.0. Crucially, 61% of venture capital transactions lose money with a TVPI under 1.0x, and 54% return less than half their capital with a TVPI under 0.5x.

An accompanying line chart titled "VC and buyout reliance on a subset of transactions" illustrates the cumulative percentage of value creation on the vertical axis against the cumulative percentage of all transactions on the horizontal axis. A diagonal reference line shows what the distribution would look like if each deal contributed equally to the fund's return. The buyout curve demonstrates a moderate skew, but the venture capital curve remains nearly flat at zero value creation until reaching about 80% of all transactions, where it rises sharply to 100%. This visualizes the striking reality that venture capital managers rely on approximately the top 20% of their transactions to drive almost all overall fund returns. Both the table and chart are based on transaction data from the mid-1990s to 2018, compiled in a 2020 study by researchers Brown, Harris, Hu, Jenkinson, Kaplan, and Robinson using Burgiss holdings data.

This appendix page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the sensitivity of Internal Rate of Return (IRR) and Direct Alpha to cash flow timing and the usage of subscription lines. The analysis utilizes a hypothetical 2010 fund with a four-year investment period ending in 2014, a seven-year harvesting period, and a total distribution of two times the committed capital, using the S&P 500 Index as the benchmark. The extreme subscription line scenario assumes that all called capital is funded by the line and not repaid until the end of the investment period in 2014.

An illustrative net cash flows line chart shows net cash flows as a percentage of committed capital from 2010 to 2020 across three distribution profiles: Base Case, Front Loaded, and Back Loaded. The Front Loaded scenario peaks earlier around 2015, while the Back Loaded scenario peaks later around 2019, demonstrating how cash distributions are shifted in time.

Four tables quantify these sensitivities across various combinations of commitment and distribution schedules (Base Case, Front Loaded, and Back Loaded). Without a subscription line, IRR ranges from a low of 9% (Back Loaded distribution with Front Loaded commitment) to a high of 26% (Front Loaded distribution with Back Loaded commitment), while the Base Case/Base Case combination yields a 15% IRR. Direct Alpha without a subscription line ranges from -4% to 10%, with the Base Case/Base Case at 2%. 

The introduction of a subscription line significantly inflates these return metrics, though the impact is highly uneven. For IRR with a subscription line, the Front Loaded distribution/Back Loaded commitment scenario surges to 43% (up from 26%), whereas the Back Loaded distribution/Back Loaded commitment scenario only improves slightly to 13% (up from 12%). Similarly, Direct Alpha with a subscription line spikes to 32% for the Front Loaded distribution/Back Loaded commitment scenario, but only reaches 1% for the Back Loaded distribution/Back Loaded commitment scenario. The author concludes that subscription lines have a dramatically larger positive impact on reported performance metrics when fund distributions are front-loaded compared to when they are back-loaded.

This page serves as a data appendix focusing on private markets, buyout trends, venture capital exits, and institutional asset allocation. The overarching analysis suggests that private equity and private markets have seen massive expansion, which may pose risks similar to the historical proliferation of hedge funds, though recent macroeconomic backstops, such as rapid central bank actions during COVID-19, have shielded buyouts from severe losses.

The first chart, "Global active private capital firms by asset class," tracks the number of active firms from 1990 to 2020. It illustrates a dramatic surge in private markets overall, rising toward nearly 11,000 firms by 2020. Notably, the number of private equity firms has steadily climbed and recently surpassed the number of hedge funds, which peaked around 2008 and has since plateaued. Other asset classes pictured include Real Estate, Natural Resources, Private debt, and Infrastructure, all of which remain relatively flat at much lower levels.

To the right, "Distribution of US LBOs by type" displays the percentage share of overall transaction volume from 2002 to the first quarter of 2021. It tracks four deal types: sponsor-to-sponsor, public-to-private, corporate division divestitures, and other. The chart visualizes a declining trend in sponsor-to-sponsor buyouts relative to corporate division divestitures and public-to-private transactions since their peak share around 2014.

Two side-by-side charts cover US venture capital exits by type from 2006 to 2021. The first chart, showing the absolute number of exits, indicates that acquisitions consistently make up the vast majority of transactions by volume, representing 65% of the total in 2021, with public listings and buyouts making up much smaller fractions. Conversely, the adjacent chart, measuring exit value in billions of US dollars, shows the opposite dynamic: public listings account for 90% of total exit value in 2021, driving the massive value spikes in 2020 and 2021 where total exit value neared $300 billion.

The next chart, "Institutional investors' portfolio allocation," spans 2008 to 2019 and outlines the slow drift of institutional capital. It demonstrates how public equities have shrunk as a percentage of portfolios over the decade, while allocations to bonds, private equity, infrastructure, and other alternative assets have incrementally expanded.

Finally, the bottom right chart, titled "Impact of rapid central bank response," plots the percentage loss rate for buyout deals by year of exit from 2005 to 2020. During the 2008–2009 Financial Crisis, loss rates spiked to nearly 30%. In contrast, during the 2020 COVID-19 crisis, the loss rate was kept remarkably low at around 10%. The text attributes this resilience directly to rapid and aggressive central bank intervention.

In this commentary, the author characterizes the Federal Reserve as acting simultaneously as a firefighter and an arsonist, stimulating private sector demand while eroding market and underwriting discipline through unprecedented monetary easing and a symbiotic relationship with the US Treasury. 

To illustrate these conditions, the page features four charts. The first chart, tracking the five-year average of real yields on cash (the Treasury bill or Funds rate minus inflation) from 1830 through 2020, shows that real yields have dipped into deeply negative territory, marking the lowest real yields on cash since 1830 outside of major wartime periods such as the Civil War, World War I, and World War II. The second chart details Federal Treasury purchases covering net issuance in trillions of US dollars on a three-month average from 2003 to 2021. It highlights a massive spike during 2020 and 2021, showing that Federal Reserve purchases of Treasuries have essentially absorbed the entirety of net Treasury issuance. 

The remaining two charts focus on highly elevated equity valuations. The S&P 500 forward price-to-earnings ratio chart, mapping price against forward two-year earnings per share from 1990 to mid-2021, shows the ratio climbing near 20x in July 2021. The final chart presents the S&P 500 cyclically adjusted P/E ratio, or CAPE ratio, based on trailing ten-year average inflation-adjusted earnings from 1880 to 2021. This metric shows valuations reaching an extreme of 37x on July 8, 2021—one of the highest levels on record, contrasted against the historical low of 6x recorded on July 8, 1932.

Looking ahead, the author notes that while markets are pricing in a significant amount of optimism, the underlying US and global economies are set for a strong recovery supported by pent-up demand and US household debt service ratios that are near forty-year lows. As the global economy transitions closer to trend growth in 2022, the author forecasts modestly higher inflation. Under these conditions, reflation sectors such as industrials, energy, and financials are expected to outperform, and the author predicts that future equity market returns will be driven by corporate earnings growth rather than continued valuation expansion.

This page consists entirely of legal disclosures and regulatory disclaimers regarding the distribution of J.P. Morgan materials across various global jurisdictions. It lists the specific J.P. Morgan entities, branches, and licensing details responsible for distributing the publication, along with their supervising regulatory authorities, in Spain, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, France, Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, Latin America, and Australia. Key regulatory bodies mentioned include the Spanish Securities Market Commission, the European Central Bank, Germany's BaFin, the Bank of Italy, the Danish Financial Supervisory Authority, the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority, France's ACPR and AMF, Switzerland's FINMA, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, and the Australian Securities and Investment Commission. The text also details specific compliance requirements and restrictions, such as the limitation of materials to wholesale clients in Australia and private placement rules in Latin American jurisdictions.

This page analyzes the policy risks facing Chinese equities, arguing that domestic regulatory actions from Beijing pose a far greater threat to Chinese tech stocks and American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) than the numerous hostile policies enacted by the US Biden administration. The text details a wide array of US initiatives, including the Holding Foreign Companies Accountable Act, the CHIPS Act, and the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, but notes these mostly aim to boost US competitiveness or impact smaller firms. Instead, the primary headwinds stem from China’s own regulators cracking down on monopolies, data privacy, and foreign listings—such as requiring cybersecurity reviews for companies with over one million users seeking to list abroad, a policy that directly impacted the ride-hailing app Didi. The author suggests that because of these domestic hurdles, Chinese tech stocks should trade at a discount compared to their US peers, though they have recently traded at similar levels.

Two charts support this analysis. The first chart, a bar graph titled "YTD total return for China equity indices," displays year-to-date returns in US dollars as of July 8, 2021. It shows a stark divergence between onshore indices and tech-heavy offshore listings. While domestic indices like the MSCI China B Shares and the Shenzhen Composite posted positive returns of approximately 12% and 8% respectively, tech-heavy indices suffered deep losses. Specifically, the Hang Seng Tech index dropped by about 11%, the FTSE China Tech index fell roughly 12%, and China ADRs (which consist of 70% tech and consumer services) plummeted by about 14%. 

The second chart, a line graph titled "US and China tech valuations," tracks the price-to-forward-two-year-earnings multiples of US and Chinese technology sectors from 2017 to mid-2021. The data shows that Chinese tech valuations have historically been highly volatile, frequently trading at a premium to US tech, with peaks near 32x in early 2018 and over 35x in early 2021. However, following the regulatory crackdowns, Chinese tech valuations experienced a sharp contraction, falling to converge with US technology valuations at around 24x to 26x by mid-2021. The converging lines illustrate the author's point that Chinese tech has lost its historical premium and now faces headwinds that should arguably push its valuation below that of US tech.

This page examines the concept of a US-China "economic divorce," a narrative resurfaced by a 25% drop in Didi’s stock. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that despite this headline, substantial economic normalcy remains intact between the US and China across most channels, with bilateral foreign direct investment (FDI) being the only major casualty of national security policy shifts.

The trade war's impact on import counterparties is illustrated in the first chart, tracking the six-month average share of US imports from 2015 to 2021. It reveals that China's share of US imports, though down from its peak of over 20% in late 2017, has rebounded to around 18% in 2021, remaining only modestly below pre-trade war levels, while Europe maintains the highest share at over 20%. 

The second chart tracks the relative performance of US companies with high exposure to the US-China trade war compared to the S&P 500, indexed to 100 in January 2018. This index dropped to a low of about 72 during the pandemic sell-off in early 2020 but rebounded strongly to roughly 95 by mid-2021, indicating that exposed US stocks are holding up well. 

The third chart plots US semiconductor exports to China in billions of dollars from 2015 to 2021, noting key US policy restrictions on technology reaching Huawei in May 2019 and August 2020. Despite these barriers, exports rose from around $0.8 billion in late 2020 to reach a record high of approximately $1.3 billion in early 2021. 

The fourth chart highlights US holdings of Chinese stocks and bonds from 2012 to 2020, showing a steady accumulation of Chinese assets from $100 billion in 2012 to nearly $300 billion in late 2020, driven almost entirely by equity investments. 

The fifth chart compares US Treasury ownership by China and Russia from 1995 to 2020 in trillions of dollars. While Russia liquidated its holdings down to near zero after 2018, China's holdings have remained highly stable, hovering around $1.0 to $1.1 trillion since 2010.

The final chart shows bilateral FDI between the US and China in billions of dollars from 2004 to 2020. While US FDI into China remained steady, averaging between $10 billion and $15 billion per year, Chinese FDI into the US collapsed from a peak of nearly $50 billion in 2016 to under $5 billion in 2020, representing a potentially permanent downward trend.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication argues that the Federal Reserve's expansionary monetary policies have fostered severe excesses across financial markets, characterized by a collapse in high-yield bond spreads, a flood of unprofitable companies issuing equity, escalating home prices, and a dramatic erosion of credit standards. The author cautions that while these vulnerabilities are easily overlooked during expansions, they will present major risks when the business cycle inevitably turns downward.

Six charts illustrate these developments. The first chart, showing the US corporate high-yield bond index spread over the 10-year Treasury from 2001 to 2021, depicts spreads collapsing to near-historical lows of roughly 3% by mid-2021, a stark drop from the 2008 financial crisis peak of nearly 18% and the early 2020 spike of around 9%. 

An adjacent chart illustrates how unprofitable companies have flooded the market by plotting net secondary offerings as a percentage of the US stock market. This metric, which subtracts the secondary offerings of unprofitable firms from those of profitable ones, plunged into negative territory at around negative 0.1% in mid-2021. This indicates that unprofitable firms are issuing secondary offerings at a rate exceeding profitable firms, a trend last seen during the dot-com bubble.

A third chart follows the market capitalization of young unprofitable companies—defined as companies with negative net income in two of the last three years, less than five years since their IPO, and annual revenue growth exceeding 15%—as a share of the total market capitalization from 1990 to 2020. This share surged to over 4% in late 2020, representing the highest level since the dot-com bubble peak of approximately 5.5% in 2000.

In housing, a chart showing the year-over-year change in the US home price appreciation index from 2013 to 2021 highlights a sudden, vertical surge in 2021. The medium-to-high price tier skyrocketed by approximately 25% year-over-year, while the low-to-medium price tier increased by roughly 15%.

The final two charts document a severe decline in underwriting discipline. A timeline of Moody's loan covenant quality score from 2012 to 2021, where a score of 5 represents the weakest protections, shows the score steadily rising from 3.2 in 2012 to nearly 4.5 by 2021. A concluding bar chart compares these scores across specific credit protection categories between 2007 and the 2019–2020 period. Across every single dimension—including overall score, financial covenants, subordination, restricted payments, debt incurrence, risky investments, asset sales, and voting rights—the 2019–2020 scores are substantially higher than those from the notorious credit bubble of 2007. The overall quality score deteriorated from under 3.0 in 2007 to over 4.0 in 2019–2020, demonstrating that modern lenders have discarded traditional credit disciplines.

This page of the publication analyzes the trajectory of the US economy, globalization, and inflation, arguing that while President Biden's China policies are unlikely to derail China's economy, a decline in globalization and increased US national security enforcement will likely push inflation slightly higher in the coming years. Despite some unusually high transitory inflation readings, the author maintains that the US economy is experiencing a robust boom supported by capital spending and hiring tailwinds.

Six charts support these arguments. The first, illustrating a globalization index based on global trade, portfolio flows, and foreign direct investment as a percentage of global GDP from 1970 to 2020, shows globalization peaking near an index value of 130 in the late 2000s before falling in a volatile downward trend to around 85 by 2020. Alongside this decline, a chart on the US Committee on Foreign Investment (CFIUS) actions shows rising national security enforcement. The total number of annual CFIUS notices and investigations rose from under 100 in 2010 to over 200 by 2017 through 2019, with manufacturing comprising the largest sector and China-specific cases peaking in 2017 and 2018 before declining.

To illustrate the domestic economic boom, the middle section displays two charts on capital spending and employment. A chart of US leading indicators compares actual capex growth with demand-based estimates across various sectors, showing that while actual structures and resource equipment capex contracted, demand-based estimates for resource equipment, vehicles, and industrial machinery are highly positive, and tech equipment capex growth is already strong at over 20%. Meanwhile, the US CEO hiring plans index, where a reading above 50 indicates increased hiring expectations, shows that after a steep drop during the 2020 pandemic downturn, hiring expectations surged to a near-record level of over 100 by mid-2021.

The final two charts address inflation. The core consumer price index chart, tracking year-over-year percentage changes from 2001 to 2021, demonstrates that inflation stayed largely between 1% and 3% for two decades before spiking sharply toward 4% in 2021. To put this spike in perspective, the used car prices index, which had remained relatively stable between 80 and 100 for years, shows an unprecedented vertical spike to over 110 in 2021, representing the kind of extreme, isolated price pressure that professional forecasters expect the market to eventually look past.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" focuses on the debate surrounding inflation, with author Michael Cembalest expressing skepticism about the assumption that wage inflation will easily cool. While he agrees that overall goods, services, and commodity price inflation will prove transitory and return to the Federal Reserve’s comfort zone by 2022, he argues that wage inflation has strong structural momentum that will persist even after federal COVID unemployment benefits expire in the fall of 2021. To support this view, he presents six charts detailing labor market tightness, rising wages, and worker sentiment.

The first chart, "Workers losing federal unemployment benefits," projects the total number of people losing various forms of federal aid from May through September 2021. It shows a steep cliff in September, when roughly 14 million people are expected to lose benefits across Pandemic Unemployment Assistance, PEUC extended benefits, regular extended benefits, and regular state programs. Despite this impending drop in benefits, the second chart, "Total private employment vs wages," shows that total wages have risen much faster than actual employment. Indexed to February 2020, total wages climbed to nearly 104 by mid-2021, while the employment index remained depressed around 95.

Further evidence of business pricing and labor pressure is shown in the third chart, "Small businesses planning to raise worker compensation and prices." Both series spiked dramatically in 2021 to levels not seen since the mid-1980s, with around 40% of small businesses planning to raise prices and roughly 25% to 30% planning to raise worker compensation. The fourth chart, "Not in labor force: want a job vs don't want a job," illustrates shifts in the labor supply. The percentage of the population aged 16 and older who are not in the labor force and do not want a job has risen steadily over two decades to about 36% in 2021. Conversely, those who are out of the labor force but want a job spiked briefly during the pandemic's onset but quickly declined back down toward 2.5%.

The final two charts underscore how difficult it has become for employers to recruit. "Small businesses with 'hard to fill' job openings" indicates that nearly 48% of small businesses reported unfilled openings in 2021, marking an all-time high in a data series stretching back to 1985. Lastly, the "'Reservation wage'" chart tracks the lowest wage respondents are willing to accept for a new job, indexed to late 2019. It reveals a stark divergence based on income: the reservation wage for lower-income workers making under $60k spiked dramatically, with its index crossing 125 in 2021, whereas the reservation wage index for workers earning over $60k actually declined to around 95. This page utilizes data from Goldman Sachs, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, J.P. Morgan Asset Management, Bloomberg, the National Federation of Independent Business, and the Federal Reserve Bank.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s analysis discusses the long-term, systemic impacts of China’s entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001 on the US economy, the labor market, and domestic social issues, ultimately shaping current Federal Reserve policy expectations. The author argues that rising US wages are positive, but they present a challenge for the Fed's zero-rate policy. To trace this relationship, the author outlines a sequence of events beginning with China's 2001 WTO entry, which was followed by unprecedented Chinese currency interventions to boost exports. This fueled the greatest economic boom in post-war history, suppressing US import prices but causing severe US manufacturing job losses and a sharp decline in the labor share of gross profits. This economic displacement is directly linked to domestic social crises, such as the opioid epidemic. Looking forward, the author posits that because the US labor share of profits is finally rising back toward its post-war average, the Fed will be highly reluctant to interfere with wage growth. Consequently, the Fed is expected to tolerate initial wage pressures, supporting a portfolio pivot toward reflation strategies in 2022 and beyond.

To illustrate this narrative, the page features four charts. The first chart displays the ten-year percentage change in US manufacturing job losses alongside Chinese foreign exchange intervention as a percentage of GDP on an inverted scale. Following China's WTO entry in 2001, Chinese FX intervention surged to nearly forty percent of GDP, coinciding with an acceleration of US manufacturing job losses that reached a peak ten-year decline of nearly forty percent in the late 2000s. The second chart links this same manufacturing job loss trend to the labor share of non-financial gross profits. After 2001, the labor share of corporate profits plummeted from historically stable levels of around sixty-two to sixty-four percent down to a low of approximately fifty-seven percent around 2012, highlighting how corporate capital captured a larger share of profits at the expense of workers. The third chart correlates these manufacturing losses with the rise of the domestic opioid epidemic, plotting US manufacturing job losses against per capita opioid prescriptions measured in morphine milligram equivalents. As manufacturing jobs declined, opioid prescriptions rose dramatically from negligible levels in 2000 to peak at nearly eight hundred milligram equivalents per capita in the 2010s. Finally, the fourth chart puts China's economic rise into a global, historical perspective by comparing the largest thirty-year increases in real per capita GDP across different countries. China's growth from 1981 to 2011 represents an unprecedented expansion of roughly fourteen hundred percent, far exceeding other notable historical booms such as South Korea from 1965 to 1995 at approximately eight hundred percent, Oman from 1955 to 1985 at around seven hundred percent, and mid-century expansions in Japan, Greece, and Taiwan.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, explores the strong correlation between political ideology in the United States and COVID-19 vaccine resistance during the rise of the Delta variant. The author notes that while vaccine resistance exists across the political spectrum, conservative ideology is strongly linked to lower vaccination rates. Despite the highly contagious Delta variant causing 95% to 99% of hospitalizations among the unvaccinated, an Associated Press poll revealed that 80% of unvaccinated Americans definitely or probably will not get vaccinated, highlighting deep political polarization. 

The first chart illustrates this relationship by plotting district-level vaccination rates against the ideological voting scores of Congressional Representatives, which range from negative one for most liberal to positive one for most conservative. The y-axis shows the percentage of fully vaccinated people in a district, spanning from 20% to 70%. The scatter plot displays two distinct clusters: liberal representatives (blue dots) correspond to districts with higher vaccination rates, generally between 35% and 70%, whereas conservative representatives (red dots) are associated with lower vaccination rates, mostly between 25% and 55%. The Georgia 14th district is specifically labeled near the highly conservative, low-vaccination corner of the chart, with a vaccination rate of approximately 25%.

The second chart corroborates this political trend at the local level by mapping the percentage of fully vaccinated people as a share of county population against the share of the county's population that voted for Donald Trump in the 2020 presidential election. The x-axis spans from 0% to 100% of Trump voters, and the y-axis ranges from 0% to 80% vaccinated. The scatter plot shows a clear downward trend, demonstrating that as the share of Trump voters in a county increases, the county’s vaccination rate steadily decreases. Counties with high support for Trump (80% or greater) frequently show vaccination rates below 30%, while counties with low Trump voting shares commonly exhibit rates exceeding 50% or 60%.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the risk-reward ratio of COVID-19 vaccines and evaluates whether the rising prevalence of the Delta variant warrants new lockdowns. He argues that reimposing lockdowns is likely futile given how widespread the Delta variant has already become, while also asserting that vaccines are demonstrably effective and present an overwhelmingly positive risk-reward profile.

To support this view, the page features five distinct charts. The first chart, COVID variant reproductive number estimates, plots the estimated number of people infected by a single infected person across different virus lineages. The reproductive number ranges from roughly 1.5 to 3 for the original variant, climbs to between 4 and 5 for the Alpha variant, and spikes significantly to between 6 and 8 for the Delta variant. The second chart, Delta variant prevalence, shows that the Delta variant represents a dominant share of cases across many countries, exceeding 90 percent in the United Kingdom, Singapore, Denmark, and Australia, reaching about 80 percent in the United States, and remaining above 50 percent even in countries with lower prevalence like Sweden.

The next two charts visually weigh the benefits of vaccination against the risk of rare, severe side effects. The first of these compares the foregone COVID-19 risks to expected negative outcomes from the Johnson and Johnson vaccine, normalized per 6 million doses. The data shows that the vaccine prevents over 13,000 long-haul COVID cases and over 2,000 deaths, whereas the expected severe adverse reaction of Guillain-Barre syndrome is represented by a virtually imperceptible bar of just 50 to 60 cases. Similarly, the chart for mRNA vaccines, normalized per 4 million doses, illustrates that vaccination prevents over 5,000 long-haul cases and around 1,000 deaths, compared to only 50 to 60 cases of myocarditis, which is noted as generally treatable.

Finally, the bottom scatter plot, US county infections vs vaccinations, plots daily infections per million against the percentage of fully vaccinated residents across United States counties. The plot demonstrates a clear downward trend, showing that counties with vaccination rates below 40 percent experience highly elevated daily infection spikes of up to 1,000 or more per million. Conversely, in counties where vaccination rates exceed 60 percent or 80 percent, daily infection rates remain consistently low, clustering tightly near zero, which Cembalest notes is proof that the vaccines are working. The page also references and provides links to detailed CDC reports for further reading on these vaccine safety metrics.

This page features a detailed analysis of the relationship between COVID-19 vaccination rates and subsequent hospitalization and mortality trends, focusing on the United Kingdom and various US states. Author Michael Cembalest highlights a promising trend in the United Kingdom, where a high vaccination rate of over 95% among individuals aged 65 and older has resulted in a very low rate of infection passing through to hospitalizations and deaths. He contrasts this positive decoupling with the United States, where elder vaccination rates are 10% to 15% lower.
