Conversely, older vintages all recorded negative net absorption, with the 1980–1990 era suffering the steepest decline at nearly negative 37 million square feet, followed by pre-1960 buildings at roughly negative 22 million square feet. Based on these trends, the author advises real estate investors to focus portfolios on modern office assets in growth nodes rather than generic central business district offices.

This page, authored by Michael Cembalest, focuses on timber investing as a source of steady, modest yields with potential upside for investors seeking carbon sequestration. Cembalest traces the history of timber return analysis back to German forester Martin Faustmann in 1850 and observes that US timber returns have been lower since the 2008 housing crisis. This underperformance is due to a collapse in demand and a surplus of Southern Pine in the US Southeast. J.P. Morgan's timber managers project that while sawlog prices could start rising in two to four years, it may take another eight to ten years for structural demand to fully restore the Southern Pine supply/demand balance. Cembalest also cautions that the tracked NCREIF indexes represent unleveraged property returns, whereas most managed real asset products carry leverage, such as the NCREIF ODCE index, which uses approximately 25% leverage. 

To compare timber against other real assets, the page presents two tables detailing annualized returns, standard deviations, and Sharpe ratios based on Bloomberg and NCREIF data. For the period from 1991 to 2021, farmland led all assets with a 10.6% annualized return, followed by industrial properties at 9.9%, timberland at 8.9% with a 0.91 Sharpe ratio, apartment properties at 8.7%, retail properties at 7.5%, and office properties at 6.9%. For the period from 2000 to 2021, farmland again performed best with an 11.6% annualized return, while industrial properties returned 10.9%, retail properties and apartments both returned 8.5%, office properties returned 7.6%, timberland dropped to 5.6% with a 0.95 Sharpe ratio, and hotel properties returned 4.6%. 

An accompanying line chart plots the growth of these unleveraged real asset returns since 2000, indexing performance to 100 in the fourth quarter of 1999. Farmland is the top-performing index line, showing a 12% annualized return. It is followed by industrial properties at 11%, retail and apartments at 9%, office properties at 8%, timberland at 6%, and hotel properties at 5%.

Finally, Cembalest references an October 2018 Wall Street Journal article regarding losses incurred by a large institutional investor's timber portfolio in Texas and Mississippi. He highlights that these losses were not representative of the broader asset class, but rather the result of purchasing at peak 2008 valuations, over-leveraging, lack of regional diversification, and being locked into below-market lease pricing and escalation clauses.

This page examines the structural decline of office space within institutional and REIT investment portfolios, alongside low post-pandemic office occupancy levels across major U.S. metropolitan areas. The author argues that office fundamentals are facing long-term headwinds as investors shift their capital toward industrial, life sciences, and specialty property sectors. 

To support this observation, the page features a line chart tracking property type allocations within the MSCI commercial real estate core index from 2000 to 2020. The chart illustrates a gradual decline in office allocations, which fell from a peak of nearly 40% in the early 2000s to approximately 25% by 2020. Meanwhile, industrial property allocations rose dramatically over the same period, converging with office and apartment allocations near the 25% mark. Other categories like retail saw declines, while medical, lab, and life science properties established a small but growing footprint.

The shifting landscape is further demonstrated by a stacked bar chart detailing the sector breakdown of U.S. REITs by percentage of market capitalization. Comparing the Wilshire US Real Estate Index in 2015 and 2021 alongside the MSCI US IMI Real Estate Index in 2021, the data reveals a significant contraction in traditional core sectors like offices, malls, and shopping centers. Conversely, specialty sectors—defined to include data centers, single-family rentals, land, and cell towers—surged from a 6% share of market capitalization in 2015 to 17% in 2021 on the Wilshire index, and commanded a substantial 39% share of the MSCI index in 2021. Expanded core sectors, including self-storage, hotels, senior housing, medical offices, student housing, and manufactured homes, made up 20% to 29% of the market capitalization across these indices.

The lower half of the page presents two charts illustrating measures of office utilization across ten major metropolitan areas: Austin, Houston, Dallas, Philadelphia, New York City, Los Angeles, Washington D.C., Chicago, San Jose, and San Francisco. The first chart, based on Kastle keycard and fob data through mid-December 2021, displays utilization rates relative to pre-pandemic baselines. Following a near-total collapse in March 2020 to around 10% to 15%, office occupancy experienced a very slow and geographically unequal recovery. By late 2021, Texas metros led the recovery, with Austin and Houston reaching nearly 50% to 60% utilization, while major coastal and tech hubs like New York, San Jose, and San Francisco lagged significantly behind, hovering between 20% and 30%. 

The second chart corroborates these patterns using Google workplace mobility trends, measuring smartphone geolocation activity relative to a January 2020 baseline through late December 2021. Workplace mobility fell sharply in March 2020 to levels between 30% and 50% of the baseline. Though mobility gradually recovered to between 60% and 80% by late 2021, the geographic disparity persisted, with Houston and Dallas recording the highest return-to-work activity, and San Francisco, San Jose, and New York City remaining at the bottom of the spectrum.

This page of the publication analyzes non-US timber investments, pointing out that while international timber portfolios often carry higher risks, they also offer the potential for higher returns than US-only holdings. To illustrate this, the author shares data from a 2020 paper published in Forest Policy and Economics that details the Internal Rate of Return (IRR) for various timber species across multiple countries. The author notes that these IRR calculations assume pre-existing land ownership and exclude land costs, which, if factored in, would typically reduce the reported figures by three to eight percentage points. The main takeaway remains that international timber investments can achieve yields far superior to those in the United States.

A comprehensive table titled "Timber investment rates of return excluding land costs" lists rates of return for various species in North America, South America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania. In the United States, timber returns are relatively modest, ranging from 3% for Mixed Hardwoods to 7% for high-yield Pinus taeda and high-site Pseudotsuga menziesii. European nations also show lower rates of return, such as Finland's Picea abies at 4% and Poland's Pinus sylvestris in state forests at a mere 1%. 

In contrast, several emerging markets boast remarkably high IRRs. For instance, China's Eucalyptus shows a 29% return, and Vietnam's Acacia Smallholder stands at 26%. In Laos, Eucalyptus outgrower operations show the highest listed rate on the table at 32%, while industrial Eucalyptus sits at 21%. Latin American nations also demonstrate strong yields, with Eucalyptus grandis reaching 21% in both Argentina and Mexico, and Eucalyptus clones in Paraguay delivering a 22% return. Not all Latin American options are high-yielding, however, as Colombia's Pinus patula pulpwood shows a 0% return.

The text concludes with a qualitative assessment of these regional differences. Northern Hemisphere native temperate forests grow much more slowly than exotic plantations located in subtropical and equatorial Southern Hemisphere zones. South American forests, utilizing genetically improved pine from North America and eucalypt from Australia, benefit from intensive management on highly productive sites. Brazil, in particular, achieves some of the world's highest growth rates—up to 40 cubic meters per hectare per year for pine and 50 for eucalypt—though these operations require higher establishment costs. Lastly, the author warns that timber investing in Asia presents unique challenges, as the region suffers from land scarcity, poor infrastructure, weak institutions, and elevated biological and political risks.

This page from "Eye on the Market" discusses the balance of factors influencing the Chinese economy and its stock markets at the start of 2022. Michael Cembalest argues that despite a regulatory purge and stalling growth in late 2021, the positives are likely to outweigh the negatives for onshore Chinese stocks, though he advises caution regarding offshore internet stocks. On the positive side, J.P. Morgan expects a modest stimulus, a 50-basis-point cut in bank reserve requirements, and pro-growth policies targeting local governments and small businesses to support a 19% earnings growth, 4.7% real GDP growth, and 2% inflation in 2022. On the negative side, tough antitrust and internet regulation, lack of federal help for defaulting property developers, ongoing zero-COVID policies, and anti-pollution measures ahead of the Winter Olympics continue to drag on growth. A footnote explains that China's recent power problems were caused by a global surge in demand, lower hydropower output, coal production slowdowns due to climate policies, and restrictive utility price controls.

The page includes five charts to illustrate these dynamics. The first three charts index various Chinese economic indicators to 100 starting in January 2018. The "China economy: positive signs" chart shows that exports surged dramatically, reaching index levels above 140 by late 2021, while A-share corporate earnings remained stable and positive. The "stable signs" chart displays indicators like electricity consumption, industrial production, retail sales, and construction and real estate GDP, which recovered from 2020 lows to stabilize around the 110 to 130 level. The "negative signs" chart highlights a sharp downturn in late 2021, with crude steel production dropping back to the base index level of 100, and residential and commercial construction starts falling down to index levels of 80 and 60, respectively.

The remaining two charts cover corporate earnings and monetary policy. The chart showing MSCI China consensus earnings expectations tracks the year-over-year percentage change during 2021. It shows that expectations for both 2021 and 2022 earnings per share fell continuously throughout the year. EPS expectations for 2021 fell from 18% in January to under 13% by November, while 2022 expectations dropped to 15%. However, J.P. Morgan's own forecasts are more optimistic, positioning 2022 EPS growth at approximately 19%. Finally, a chart on China's lending rates and reserve requirements from 2012 to 2023 shows a general easing cycle. The 1-year loan prime rate, 1-year medium-term lending facility, and open market operations yields on the left-hand axis have all trended downward. Simultaneously, the reserve requirement ratio on the right-hand axis shows a steady decline from peak levels of 20% in 2012 to roughly 11.5% following a cut on December 15, 2021.

This page analyzes emerging market portfolio inflows, focusing on the changing dynamics of the MSCI Emerging Markets (EM) equity index and the investment outlook for China despite its 2021 regulatory purge. The author argues that the MSCI EM index has lost geographic diversity, as China, South Korea, and Taiwan now collectively account for two-thirds of the entire index. Money managers tend to track these benchmarks closely, and the author suggests that China's index weight could eventually rise from 35% to 45% as more of its onshore market cap is included. Despite regulatory headwinds, the author asserts that the long-run opportunity in China is highly compelling due to strong venture capital inflows and the dramatic expansion of its middle class. 

Four charts support these arguments. The first chart, "Emerging markets country weights," displays the percentage weight in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index from 2000 to 2021. It visualizes the shrinking footprint of Latin America and other countries as Taiwan, South Korea, and especially China expand their dominant shares of the index. 

The second chart, "China VC investments by US dollar denominated funds," tracks venture capital inflows from 2010 through year-to-date December 2021 in billions of US dollars. The data shows VC investments peaking at over $120 billion in 2018, dropping in 2019, and then rebounding to a record level of nearly $140 billion in 2021, illustrating robust investor confidence in Chinese private enterprises. 

The third chart, "Private equity performance versus public equity in Asia," compares 10-year annualized returns through Q2 2020. It demonstrates that private equity and venture capital have substantially outperformed public markets, with Asia EM PE and VC returning nearly 13% and Asia DM PE and VC returning roughly 11%, compared to returns of about 6% for both the MSCI EM Asia and MSCI Pacific public equity indexes. 

The fourth chart, "Middle class consumption in 2020," measures consumption in trillions of US dollars using 2011 purchasing power across major global economies. China leads the world at more than $7 trillion, followed by the United States at approximately $5 trillion, India at over $3 trillion, and smaller shares for Japan, Russia, Germany, Indonesia, the United Kingdom, Brazil, and France. 

A footnote adds historical context to regional performance, noting that from 2000 to 2020, MSCI EM Asia and MSCI EM Latin America generated cumulative returns of 377% and 300%, respectively. Over a ten-year horizon, the performance gap widened significantly, with MSCI EM Latin America posting a negative 28% return compared to a 95% gain for MSCI EM Asia, though both regional indices underperformed the S&P 500's return of 267%. Sources cited on this page include Bloomberg, Preqin, Cambridge Associates, J.P. Morgan Equity Research, the Brookings Institution, and Gavekal Research.

This page provides an early assessment of Brexit's impact on the United Kingdom, specifically looking at banking, housing, and international trade, while noting that the analysis is complicated by the short time since the UK's formal exit and the disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic. 

The author begins by addressing the pessimistic outlooks of British economists, noting that their own interests in financial institutions and London real estate were highly vulnerable to Brexit. This is illustrated in the first two charts. The chart comparing UK banks to Eurozone banks, indexed to 100 in June 2016, shows that UK banks have consistently lagged behind their European peers since the referendum, with their index level falling significantly before recovering to around 100 by the end of 2021, while Eurozone banks climbed higher. Meanwhile, the London home prices chart, indexed to 100 in Q2 2016, shows that local property prices dipped and plateaued after the 2016 vote, dropping to an index level of around 95, before rising alongside global home prices to reach nearly 110 by 2021.

The commentary then shifts to trade, explaining that while Brexit proponents hoped non-EU trade would offset losses with the European Union, the actual data shows a different trend. Trade with the EU did not decline immediately but began to fall in 2019 and collapsed further during the pandemic. However, a 15 percent depreciation in the British Pound since the referendum helped stabilize the overall balance of trade, keeping the current account deficit at 3.3 percent in the third quarter of 2021, which is in line with the nation's 20-year average. 

Two final charts, which index trade volumes to June 2016 using a 12-month moving average, visualize these dynamics. The chart for UK trade volumes with the European Union shows that both UK exports to the EU and EU exports to the UK peaked around 2019 near an index level of 105, then declined sharply, with EU exports to the UK bottoming out around 90 in late 2021. The final chart on UK trade volumes with non-EU countries illustrates that while UK exports to non-EU nations remained depressed at an index level of roughly 95, non-EU exports to the UK surged dramatically, climbing to an index level of approximately 110 by late 2021. The author concludes that while the trade outlook is not positive, it remains too heavily obscured by pandemic-related demand shocks to draw definitive conclusions.

This page analyzes the financial characteristics, performance, and risks of timberland investments, contrasting private timberland indices with public timber Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs). The author begins by noting that while harvesting income is steady, capital returns are highly variable due to monetary policy, long-term interest rates, housing policies, and changes in land use. Furthermore, timberland returns are shown to have a strong positive correlation with inflation, and US tax policy offers favorable capital gains treatment for harvesting income.

A bar chart titled "Timberland performance: income vs capital return" displays year-end total returns from 2000 to 2020 based on the NCREIF U.S. Timberland Property Index. The data shows that the income return component (represented by gold bars) is remarkably stable, consistently contributing positive returns of approximately 2.5% to 4% annually. In contrast, the capital return component (represented by blue bars) is highly volatile, peaking near 15% in 2005 and falling into negative territory during economic downturns in 2001 and 2009–2010.

An accompanying table, "Returns vs inflation (1991 - Q3 2021, 5 yr ann)," highlights timberland's role as an inflation hedge. Among the analyzed real assets, timberland shows the strongest connection to inflation with a 54% correlation and an R-squared of 30%. This is significantly higher than other property sectors over the same period: apartment properties (31% correlation, 9% R-squared), office properties (27% correlation, 7% R-squared), retail properties (19% correlation, 4% R-squared), farmland (13% correlation, 2% R-squared), and industrial properties (3% correlation, 0% R-squared).

The discussion then compares public timber REITs to private timberland investments. To maintain steady distributions, public REITs generally harvest timber every year regardless of market prices, whereas private timberland managers have the flexibility to time harvests to align with favorable log prices. A line chart titled "NCREIF Timberland vs Timber REITs" plots annual total returns from 2011 to 2021 to illustrate this difference. The FTSE NAREIT Timber REITs Index exhibits severe volatility, plunging to nearly -30% in 2019 before rebounding to over 40% in 2020, while the private NCREIF Timberland Index shows a much smoother, consistently positive return profile.

Several structural factors explain these differing return profiles. Public timber REITs use leverage, whereas the NCREIF index is unleveraged. Additionally, public REITs often own downstream operations like sawmills; for example, Weyerhaeuser frequently generates as much, and sometimes three times more, income from manufactured wood products than from raw timber harvesting. REITs can also hold international assets, such as Rayonier, which derives half of its net income from New Zealand forest holdings and other non-forest interests. Finally, public REITs trade daily and reflect broader economic recessions immediately, while private timberland valuations rely on infrequent, appraisal-based pricing.

The bottom of the page addresses physical investment risks, drawing on research from Fred Cubbage at North Carolina State University. Biological risks from insects and diseases are rare in managed forests, causing less than 0.2% mortality per year. Fire losses have historically remained below 1% annually across all US forestland. While fires are predominantly a public land issue—such as in Oregon, where the US Forest Service owns 60% of the forestland but has sustained 86% of the burned acreage over the last decade—anomalous wind events in 2020 led to high private-land losses, with private and industrial lands accounting for 40% of the 1 million burned acres in Oregon. Recovering from such fires is costly, with soil rehabilitation and replanting seedlings reaching up to $1,500 per acre for mature forests. Lastly, the page notes that severe weather events like hurricanes and storms impact a minimal portion of US timberland, affecting only 0.2% to 0.5% of holdings per year.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan argues that Brexit has had a distinctly negative impact on the United Kingdom's economy, particularly visible in business investment, construction output, and real disposable household income. He contends that the UK's performance in these categories has lagged significantly behind peers like the United States, the Euro Area, and Japan since the 2016 EU referendum.

The argument is supported by four charts. The first, "UK business investment relative to developed markets," indexes investment to the second quarter of 2016. It shows that while UK capital spending was rising in line with its 2011–2016 trend, it plummeted relative to other developed markets post-referendum, falling to roughly 15% below trend before COVID-19, and dropping to nearly 30% below trend by 2021. The second chart, "Real business investment," indexes US, Euro Area, Japan, and UK investment to June 2016. While the US and Euro Area indexes grew to roughly 120 and 110 respectively by late 2021, the UK's index flatlined around 100, plunged to 80 during the COVID-19 shock, and remained depressed below 90 in 2021. 

Cembalest then analyzes the construction sector, presenting a chart titled "Construction sector output," also indexed to June 2016. This visual shows a widening gap between the US and Euro Area—which climbed to index levels near 115 and 105—and the UK, which plummeted to an index level of nearly 60 during the pandemic before recovering to around 95, well below its peers. 

Lastly, the author examines consumer impacts with a chart titled "US vs UK real disposable household income" (indexed to June 2016). This chart shows a dramatic divergence: while US disposable income steadily climbed, peaking near 140 during pandemic-related stimulus programs and settling around 120, UK disposable income stagnated, barely remaining above the 100 baseline. Cembalest highlights a London School of Economics estimate that the 2016 depreciation of the British Pound increased consumer prices by 2.9%, resulting in a £870 annual cost-of-living increase for the average UK household. 

Cembalest concludes by noting that while cross-country economic relationships are multidimensional and influenced by many factors, the timing of these widening gaps is inextricably linked to the Brexit referendum. He leaves open the question of whether the structural deficiencies created by Brexit will permanently hamper the UK's ability to rebound from COVID-19 as quickly as other regions, identifying this as a key trend to watch.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, written by Michael Cembalest, focuses on the massive wave of venture capital pouring into cryptocurrency and blockchain investments leading up to late 2021. Cembalest observes that while the sheer mobilization of capital is accelerating and drawing top Silicon Valley talent, the long-term viability of the sector depends on its eventual returns rather than just the initial influx of cash. He breaks down the destination of these venture capital investments, noting that about 40 percent goes to trading, investing, and lending businesses, 20 percent to Web 3.0 applications and non-fungible tokens, 10 percent to custody services, and the remainder to compliance, mining, and data security. 

To support these observations, the page features four charts utilizing data from Pitchbook and Galaxy Digital Research up to January 2022. The first chart, depicting venture capital investments by sector in billions of dollars from 2017 to 2021, reveals that while fintech and artificial intelligence still drew the largest total dollars in 2021—at over 100 billion dollars and roughly 60 billion dollars respectively—crypto investments surged dramatically to approximately 30 billion dollars. 

The second chart, which details venture capital investments in crypto and blockchain on a quarterly basis, illustrates that both money invested and deal counts skyrocketed in 2021, with quarterly funding peaking near 10 billion dollars and quarterly deal counts climbing over 500. 

A third chart examines the same investment volumes by funding stage, showing that the 2021 boom was heavily dominated by later-stage and Series A rounds, whereas earlier years were characterized by much smaller pre-seed and seed-stage investments. 

Finally, the fourth chart compares pre-money valuations of crypto and blockchain startups against all venture capital from 2016 through 2021. It reveals that the average pre-money valuation for crypto and blockchain companies surged to over 70 million dollars in late 2021, which was more than double the average valuation of approximately 30 million dollars seen across the broader venture capital landscape during the same quarter.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, focuses on rising cryptocurrency adoption trends and shifting investor attitudes across different regions and investor types. The text highlights that while institutional ownership has historically been low, it is currently growing, citing a Bridgewater estimate that institutional investors hold approximately one million Bitcoin, representing about five percent of the total issued supply, via custodial intermediaries. Notable corporate anecdotes illustrate this trend: Square and Tesla combined have invested nearly two billion dollars in Bitcoin, while retail customers on Square and PayPal reportedly purchase a volume of Bitcoin equivalent to the majority of the new daily supply. 

The analysis is supported by four charts utilizing data from the September 2021 Fidelity Institutional Digital Assets Survey. The first chart, showing crypto adoption by region from 2019 to 2021, illustrates a steady upward trajectory in the percentage of investors with digital asset allocations. US investor allocations rose from roughly 22 percent in 2019 to 33 percent in 2021, while European allocations grew from 45 percent in 2020 to 56 percent in 2021. Asia, for which data was only available in 2021, led all regions with 71 percent of surveyed investors holding digital assets. 

The second chart examines crypto adoption by investor type, revealing that ownership is highly concentrated among certain categories. Financial advisors and high-net-worth individuals show the strongest adoption rates, particularly in Asia and Europe, where rates exceed 70 percent and approach nearly 100 percent for Asian financial advisors. US family offices show relatively robust adoption at 50 percent, but traditional institutional segments like pensions and endowments remain very slow to adopt; pension fund ownership stands at only about four percent in both the US and Europe, though it reaches 15 percent in Asia. 

The third chart tracks ownership by specific digital asset across regions. Bitcoin remains the dominant asset across the board, owned by over 40 percent of investors in Europe and Asia and over 20 percent in the US. Ethereum is the second most widely held asset, with ownership rates of 27 percent in Europe, 22 percent in Asia, and 12 percent in the US. Minor cryptocurrencies, including Litecoin, XRP, Bitcoin Cash, and Binance Coin, generally see ownership rates below 15 percent, with European and Asian investors consistently outpacing US investors in altcoin ownership. 

Finally, the fourth chart illustrates the future purchase intent of digital assets, showing a clear upward trend. In the US, future purchase intent grew from 50 percent of investors in 2019 to 60 percent in 2021. European future purchase intent reached 75 percent in 2021, while Asian purchase intent topped the chart at over 80 percent, signaling robust forward-looking demand for digital assets globally.

This page examines the "store of value" thesis for Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies, placing the rise of digital currencies within the context of a historical confidence void in fiat currencies. The author argues that the developed world has accumulated debt and printed fiat money at an unprecedented pace, surpassing even the extraordinary measures of the 2008 financial crisis. 

To illustrate the current cryptocurrency landscape, a bar chart displays the market capitalization of the top 20 cryptocurrencies by segment. As of late January 2022, Bitcoin dominates as a "Currency" with a market cap of approximately $700 billion, followed by Ethereum, a "Platform" valued at around $300 billion. The remaining top assets include stablecoins like Tether and USD Coin, exchange tokens like Binance Coin, and various DeFi, platform, and meme coins. 

The structural drivers behind the interest in fixed-supply currencies are illustrated through several macroeconomic charts. One chart tracks developed-world government debt and central bank balance sheets, showing that government debt has climbed from around 90% of GDP in 2009 to over 130% by 2021, while central bank balance sheets expanded dramatically from under $5 trillion to over $25 trillion. Another chart compares the US money supply expansion (M2 plus institutional money market funds) during recent crises, showing that during the Global Coronavirus Crisis, the money supply index rapidly shot up from 100 to over 140 in two years, a far steeper and faster trajectory than the modest increase to around 110 seen during the Global Financial Crisis of 2008–2010. 

A chart on global debt as a percentage of GDP highlights that total debt—comprising public, household, and non-financial corporate debt—has risen from roughly 100% in 1970 to nearly 250% by 2020, with public debt showing the sharpest acceleration. Finally, a timeline of major reserve currencies since 1250 AD traces the lifespans of dominant historical currencies, such as the Florentine Florin, Venetian Ducat, Spanish Real, and British Sterling. The visual serves to demonstrate that world reserve currencies historically experience periods of dominance followed by eventual decline, suggesting that the US Dollar and Eurodollar are subject to these same long-term historical cycles.

This page discusses the potential for a coming fiat currency reckoning and evaluates whether Bitcoin can serve as a viable store of value to complement gold. The author argues that by 2030, US Federal tax revenues will be entirely consumed by mandatory outlays on entitlements and interest, leaving non-defense discretionary spending to be funded entirely by deficit spending. 

This warning is illustrated in a chart titled "Crossover point is coming in the next decade," which plots various components of US government spending and revenue as a percentage of GDP from 1970 with projections to 2030. The chart shows Federal revenues historically fluctuating between 15% and 20% of GDP. By 2030, the line for entitlements, other mandatory outlays, and interest rises to cross above the revenue line at approximately 18% of GDP, while non-defense discretionary spending steadily declines to just over 2% of GDP. To highlight the limited options for stable fiat currencies, an adjacent table lists the short number of countries that have never defaulted, imposed exchange controls, or confiscated assets. This table, based on historical research by Carmen Reinhart and Ken Rogoff, shows that many of these safe-haven nations have extremely high national debt-to-GDP ratios, led by Singapore at 150%, the United States at 128%, Canada at 114%, and Belgium at 113%.

The author addresses skepticism regarding digital currencies becoming a store of value as quickly as gold did. Disagreeing with critics, the author asserts that rapid post-war behavioral shifts make a digital store of value highly possible, provided three proof points are met: growing adoption, stabilized volatility, and resilience during systemic crises. The page notes that Bitcoin is already capturing a larger portion of store-of-value investments relative to gold. This comparison is detailed in a bar chart of Bitcoin versus gold market capitalization from 2010 to 2022, measured in trillions of dollars. While gold excluding jewelry dominates the comparison—fluctuating between roughly $3.0 trillion and $6.5 trillion—Bitcoin shows rapid growth starting in 2020, peaking at approximately $1.0 trillion in 2021 before a slight decline in 2022. Finally, a line chart of the Bitcoin price in thousands of dollars from 2017 to early 2022 illustrates its extreme volatility, showing a massive run-up from near-zero levels to peaks near $65,000 in 2021, followed by a correction down to around the $40,000 range by early 2022.

Michael Cembalest argues against the thesis that Bitcoin serves as a reliable store of value, pointing to its extremely high and equity-correlated volatility. He attributes this instability to concentrated ownership, noting that just 2% of Bitcoin holders own 72% of its total value—a much higher concentration than United States household wealth, where it takes 10% of households to reach 70% of total wealth. Furthermore, Cembalest expresses skepticism regarding cryptocurrency valuation models, particularly Metcalfe’s Law, which links network value to the square of its users. While he acknowledges the law is useful for relative pricing among digital assets, he argues it fails to predict absolute valuation levels, such as whether Bitcoin is cheap or expensive at fifty thousand dollars.

Four charts illustrate these arguments. The first, titled "Bitcoin volatility vs S&P 500, gold and US dollar," displays rolling three-month annualized daily volatility from 2015 to early 2022. The data shows Bitcoin’s volatility is consistently extreme, regularly fluctuating between 50% and over 125%, whereas the S&P 500, gold, and the US dollar remain comparatively stable, generally staying well below 25%. 

The second chart, "Gold vs Bitcoin drawdowns," maps declines from prior peaks from 1960 to 2020. It demonstrates that while gold suffered a long-term drawdown bottoming out near 70% in the late twentieth century, Bitcoin has endured multiple rapid drawdowns approaching 80% to 90% during its much shorter history. 

The third chart, "S&P 500 vs Bitcoin drawdowns," focuses on the period from 2011 to 2021. It reveals that Bitcoin repeatedly plummeted between 50% and over 80% below its prior peaks, while the S&P 500’s drawdowns rarely exceeded 20% to 30% over the same decade. 

The fourth chart, sourced from Goldman Sachs and titled "Metcalfe's Law: Valuation vs network size," plots cryptocurrency market caps against active addresses using log scales. The visual demonstrates a clear linear relationship between user network size and valuation, placing Bitcoin and Ethereum at the top right with the highest market caps and active addresses, followed in descending order by Cardano, Ripple, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Ethereum Classic, Dash, and Zcash.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes whether gold serves as a reliable inflation hedge. The author argues that while gold functioned well as an inflation hedge from 1790 to 1900, its real price has fluctuated dramatically since then, particularly after the abandonment of the gold standard, making it a poor hedge for both inflation and currency. Instead, Cembalest suggests that gold behaves more as a hedge against the fear of inflation or financial instability, which is closely tied to rising government deficits.

The page features three charts to support these arguments. The first chart, titled "Real price of gold since 1790," plots the ratio of the gold price to the US Consumer Price Index from 1790 to late 2021. It shows that for over a century, the real price ratio remained exceptionally stable, mostly hovering between 1x and 2.5x. However, starting around 1970, the ratio began to swing wildly, spiking near 8x in 1980, falling back, and then rising sharply again after 2000. 

The second chart, "Real price of gold since the advent of US futures trading," narrows the time frame to 1970 through 2020. This chart highlights the extreme volatility of gold's real price ratio in the modern era, showing a peak near 8x in 1980, a steady decline to around 1.5x by 2000, a rapid ascent back to around 8x by 2011, and another steep rise toward 8x leading into 2020. 

The third chart, "Gold prices vs developed markets deficit," compares the gold spot price in dollars per ounce to the G10 countries' fiscal deficit as a percentage of GDP on a trailing four-quarter average from 1970 to early 2022. The data series reveal a strong correlation between the two; major increases in G10 fiscal deficits correspond with surges in gold prices. Notably, when G10 deficits spiked during the global financial crisis around 2010 and surged past 12% during the 2020 pandemic, gold spot prices experienced parallel climbs, peaking near $1,800 and $2,000 per ounce respectively.

The commentary references research from Claude Erb and Campbell Harvey's May 2013 NBER paper, "The Golden Dilemma," to support the assertion that changes in Emerging Market Central Bank gold reserves may be a more influential determinant of gold prices than traditional hedging metrics.

This page analyzes the potential for cryptocurrency and stablecoins to disrupt the traditional cross-border remittance market, which currently processes between $500 billion and $600 billion annually. The author, Michael Cembalest, notes that while traditional remittance costs have been declining, they remain high compared to emerging digital options. He questions whether families will shift to sending remittances via crypto to save money, noting that while only about 1% of remittances are currently sent via crypto according to Moneygram, the use of stablecoins is poised to rise. However, a major hurdle is that recipients in destination countries require bank accounts to convert crypto back into local fiat currency. The author predicts that this shift will be deflationary for traditional remittance providers like Western Union but will not drive speculative crypto valuations upward, as stablecoins are the primary tool used for these transfers.

The page features three charts and one table supporting this analysis. The first line chart, titled World personal remittances received, tracks total global remittances from 2008 to 2020 in billions of U.S. dollars, showing a steady rise from approximately $400 billion in 2008 to a peak near $650 billion in 2019, followed by a slight decline in 2020. 

The second chart, titled Personal remittances and bank account ownership, shows total received remittances alongside 2017 bank account penetration rates for major recipient countries. India is the largest recipient at around $80 billion (with 80% of its population holding bank accounts), followed by Mexico at around $40 billion (37% bank account ownership), the Philippines at roughly $35 billion (35% ownership), Egypt at over $30 billion (33% ownership), and Pakistan (21% ownership). Other notable countries include China with an 80% bank account ownership rate and France with 94%.

The third chart, Global remittance costs, tracks the declining cost of transfers as a percentage of the remittance amount from 2009 to 2021. The global average cost decreased from nearly 10% to about 6.3%, while the global weighted average (weighted by flow size) fell from around 8% to approximately 4.5% over the same period.

A final table, titled Select stablecoin off-ramp costs to fiat, illustrates how cheap it is to convert stablecoins into local currencies using regional crypto exchanges. In India, the total fee is 0.2% via CoinDCX; in South Africa, it is 0.2% via Luno; in Mexico, it is 0.1% via Bitso; in Brazil, it is 0.7% via Mercado Bitcoin; and in the Philippines, it is 2.1% via PDAX. Even the highest stablecoin off-ramp fee, which is in the Philippines, remains well below the weighted global average cost of traditional wire transfers.

This page from the publication analyzes the viability of cryptocurrency and stablecoins for cross-border remittances, highlighting the technological and structural challenges currently facing unbanked individuals. The author observes that crypto transaction costs remain prohibitively high for those without bank accounts due to a severe shortage of Bitcoin-to-fiat ATMs, citing Coin ATM Radar data showing only two such ATMs in India, 11 in Mexico, and 13 in the Philippines. These machines typically levy high conversion fees of five percent from Bitcoin to fiat and ten percent for the reverse. To address these hurdles, MoneyGram is collaborating on a project to reduce Bitcoin-to-fiat conversion fees to four percent and has partnered with the Stellar Development Foundation to facilitate conversions between stablecoins and physical cash. 

The discussion then transitions to stablecoins, which are pegged to external reserve assets to eliminate typical cryptocurrency volatility. While stablecoins theoretically redeem close to par value, the author cautions that their opaque backing compositions carry risks reminiscent of the structured investment vehicles from the 2008 financial crisis. For example, Tether’s early disclosures revealed that forty-nine percent of its reserves were backed by unspecified commercial paper, and the coin temporarily dropped to ninety-two cents on the dollar in 2017 when Wells Fargo withdrew its banking support. 

Two charts illustrate these stablecoin trends. The first chart displays the market capitalization of select stablecoins in billions of US dollars from January 2020 to January 2022. This stacked area chart shows a massive surge in total market cap, growing from nearly zero to roughly one hundred and sixty billion dollars by early 2022. Tether represents the largest share, followed by USD Coin, with smaller contributions from Binance USD, Dai, HUSD, and Paxos. The second chart tracks the prices of USD Coin and Tether from 2016 to 2022 to demonstrate how increased market participation has successfully suppressed price volatility. Although Tether experienced sharp fluctuations in its early years, spiking toward one dollar and eight cents and dropping to ninety-two cents, both stablecoins have traded virtually flat at their one-dollar peg since late 2020. 

Finally, the page concludes with an update on a January 2022 report from the US Federal Reserve regarding digital money and payment systems. The Federal Reserve is actively evaluating the potential benefits and risks of establishing a central bank-backed US dollar stablecoin. Such an official digital currency would eliminate the liquidity and reserve vulnerabilities inherent in private stablecoins, potentially establishing a more secure foundation for future digital payment systems.

This page features a commentary by Michael Cembalest of JP Morgan Asset Management, using the 1941 classic film The Maltese Falcon as an allegory for his personal investment stance on cryptocurrency. He summarizes the movie's plot, highlighting the characters played by Mary Astor, Sydney Greenstreet, and Humphrey Bogart, who chase a legendary jeweled statue that ultimately turns out to be a fake. Cembalest quotes Bogart's refusal to play the sap for Astor despite his feelings for her, drawing a direct parallel to his own financial discipline. He explains that he refuses to buy cryptocurrency now, despite the psychological temptation to do so, because he believes current crypto holders rely on that exact behavior from others to sustain the market. While he notes he might reconsider if crypto valuations and related companies plummeted to deeply distressed levels, he currently views the popular use cases and high valuations of cryptocurrencies as the stuff that dreams are made of. Accompanying the text is a black-and-white archival film still depicting Humphrey Bogart inspecting the falcon statue with a cigarette in hand.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues that blockchain adoption is distinct from cryptocurrency valuations. He highlights J.P. Morgan's own permissioned, private blockchain repo system, which has cleared over $200 billion in transactions. Because it is a closed system based on trust rather than mining rewards and uses an internal J.P. Morgan Coin of fixed value to enable intraday repo transactions, its adoption does not increase the value of any external token. 

Cembalest notes that other non-financial giants like Walmart, for food supply chain safety, and Alibaba, for tracking e-commerce orders, utilize blockchain to validate practical enterprise use cases rather than public crypto use cases. He states that any economic value from these cost-saving, private networks will accrue to corporate shareholders or enterprise technology vendors like IBM, Oracle, and Microsoft, rather than public token holders. 

The author contextualizes blockchain as merely the latest productivity and communication tool in a lineage that includes carrier pigeons, telegraphs, telephones, faxes, and the internet. To illustrate this technological transition, a line chart titled "The life cycle of the Telegraph" displays the millions of messages handled per year in the United States from 1860 to 1980. The volume grew from near zero in 1860 to a peak of approximately 230 million messages in the mid-1940s before sharply declining to under 100 million by 1970 as newer technologies took over. Alongside this chart, a historical photograph depicts British soldiers in August 1940 training a carrier pigeon in the south of England, demonstrating how older communication methods survived into the era of the telegraph and telephone during World War II. Ultimately, the author suggests that while incumbent technology providers often disappear during these evolutionary cycles, incumbent users like J.P. Morgan, Walmart, and Alibaba successfully adapt by transitioning to the next dominant tool.

This page analyzes the current state and competitive landscape of programmable public blockchains, focusing on Ethereum’s limitations regarding high transaction fees and slow processing speeds, which have allowed competitors to gain significant market share. 

The first line chart, titled "Ethereum average daily transaction costs" measured in Gwei, displays highly volatile transaction fees (or "gas" fees paid to miners) from February 2021 to February 2022, with spikes occasionally exceeding 350 Gwei and remaining consistently elevated. The neighboring bar chart, "Ethereum vs Ethereum competitors market cap" in billions of US dollars, shows that while Ethereum’s market cap grew from near-zero in early 2020 to approximately $450 billion by the fourth quarter of 2021, its competitors grew even faster in relative terms, rising to roughly $250 billion by late 2021. 

To explain why these competitors are gaining ground, the author provides a table titled "Processing speeds of financial infrastructures." This table shows that traditional financial networks are vastly faster than legacy blockchains: Bitcoin processes only 7 transactions per second and Ethereum processes 15, compared to Ripple at 1,500, EOS at 8,000, Visa at 45,000, and Paypal at 56,000 transactions per second. The text highlights competitors like Solana, which claims 50,000 transactions per second, as well as Cardano, Polkadot, Avalanche, Hedera, and Algorand, noting that identifying the few long-term survivors in this venture capital landscape will be highly rewarding. 

Finally, a timeline diagram titled "Ethereum's projected upgrade path" details the network's planned transition from a Proof-of-Work model to a Proof-of-Stake model to address scalability, speed, and energy efficiency. Key milestones depicted include the deposit contract deployment in October 2020, the Beacon chain launch in December 2020, the London & EIP-1559 upgrade in August 2021, "The Merge" in early 2022, and planned data sharding for 2022 to 2023. The author notes that "zero-knowledge proof" Layer-2 offerings are already demonstrating 100x to 1000x improvements in transaction costs and latency, while humorously pointing out the prevalence of obtuse jargon among blockchain professionals.

This page, titled Appendix C: Improvements in the Metaverse, presents five charts that detail the rapid technological advancements enabling the infrastructure of the metaverse, specifically focusing on computing power, storage costs, artificial intelligence capabilities, and wireless network speeds. 

The first chart illustrates CPU improvement rates from 1980 to 2020 as a multiple of their 1979 value on a logarithmic scale. It shows that transistor density and overall efficiency have both increased dramatically, approaching a million-fold improvement by 2020, while CPU speed has also grown by nearly one hundred thousand times. Directly adjacent is a chart showing the collapsing cost of information storage. Measured as the US dollar cost of hard drive storage per gigabyte on a log scale, the price plummeted from around one million dollars in 1980 to less than one cent by 2020. 

The next pair of charts highlights the accelerating capabilities of artificial intelligence. One chart plots the time required to train an AI model to classify images, demonstrating a massive decline from over ten hours and forty-one minutes in September 2017 to just one minute and twenty-eight seconds by August 2019. Next to this, a chart compares computer image identification accuracy against a human baseline. While the human benchmark remains flat near seventy-eight percent, computer accuracy rose steadily from about fifty-three percent in 2016 to approximately seventy-four percent by late 2019, rapidly closing the performance gap.

Finally, a horizontal bar chart compares average download speeds in megabits per second between 5G and 4G networks across ten major global telecommunications carriers, reflecting data from April 2020. The carriers include T-Mobile, AT&T, Sprint, Vodafone, EE, Telstra, KT, SK telecom, LG U+, and Verizon. Across all companies, 5G speeds dwarf legacy 4G speeds. Verizon recorded the fastest average 5G download speed, exceeding five hundred megabits per second, followed by LG U+ at over two hundred megabits per second, while average 4G speeds for all listed carriers remained consistently low, well under fifty megabits per second.

This page serves as an introduction to a J.P. Morgan market analysis focusing on the rapid accumulation of global risk factors in early 2022. The author highlights three primary concerns weighing on global markets: persistent inflation that has debunked the transitory theory, Europe’s severe energy dependence on Russia amid the threat of an invasion of Ukraine, and slower-than-expected resolution of US supply chain bottlenecks. Due to these headwinds, global equity indices fell 3% to 10% year-to-date, while global fixed income indices fell 3% to 4%. 

To illustrate the swift shift in monetary policy expectations, the page features a line chart tracking market-implied Federal Reserve rate hikes over the next 12 months, derived from the futures market. The chart shows that expectations for 25-basis-point interest rate hikes surged from under one hike in August 2021 to between six and seven expected hikes by February 2022. 

A second line chart compares US and European electricity prices in US dollars per megawatt-hour on a 30-day average from 2015 to early 2022. While US prices remained stable, ending the period at $51, prices in Germany, Spain, and France spiked dramatically in late 2021 and early 2022, reaching $218. This visual underscores Europe's unique energy vulnerability, which is reinforced by footnotes explaining that Europe imports roughly the same amount of oil and gas from Russia as it produces for itself. 

The author also touches on cryptocurrency trends, referencing a J.P. Morgan publication titled Maltese Falcoin. The commentary argues that blockchain use cases may eventually be satisfied by central bank-issued stablecoins and private, permissioned blockchains, which would have little positive impact on public crypto valuations. To support this cautious stance, the author cites reports of the SEC negotiating a $100 million fine with DeFi lender BlockFi for selling unregistered securities and notes emerging trends where NFT buyers are starting to transact in fiat currency rather than Ethereum.

This page examines the geopolitical tensions surrounding Russia and Ukraine, arguing that comprehensive Western sanctions could trigger Russian retaliation in energy supplies, which energy-dependent Europe is ill-equipped to withstand. The author reflects on John Mearsheimer's 2014 Foreign Affairs essay attributing the crisis to Western liberal delusions and NATO expansion. The commentary outlines the history of NATO enlargement since the Clinton administration, noting George Kennan's 1998 warning that expanding the alliance was a tragic mistake. Despite Russian warnings, Western leaders announced in 2008 that Georgia and Ukraine would eventually join NATO. The text contrasts the foreign policy schools of Liberalism and Realism, suggesting Realists may be proven correct as the West has made clear it will not militarily defend Ukraine, with Mearsheimer proposing a Finlandization of Ukraine as the optimal compromise. A footnote highlights the limitations of the Budapest Memorandum, noting it offered security assurances rather than a legally binding defense treaty when Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons.

An accompanying map of Europe illustrates the stages of NATO enlargement. Original members from 1949 are colored black, while subsequent additions from 1950 to 1980 are shown in brown. Eastern European expansion is depicted with purple representing members joining between 1999 and 2004, and red showing members joining between 2009 and 2020. Ukraine itself is highlighted in orange to signify its status in the intensified NATO dialogue, while neighboring areas with a NATO Membership Action Plan are shown in blue, and non-NATO countries are shaded in gray. The map visually demonstrates the extensive eastward advance of the alliance toward Russia's borders.

This page, titled Appendix B: Tracking creative destruction, argues that the optimal time to sell legacy technology, media, and retail companies is when they are still at their peak, just as the disruptive forces that will replace them—such as personal computers, digital advertising, massive household data consumption, and e-commerce—are in their infancy. 

To frame this pattern of obsolescence, the first chart plots the cumulative number of companies removed from the S&P 500 due to distress from 1980 to 2019. This line rises steadily and almost linearly from zero in 1980 to nearly 400 by 2019, illustrating the relentless, long-term impact of creative destruction on the index.

The second chart focuses on Wang Labs and the demise of data processing equipment from 1980 to 1994. It shows that as the percentage of households with at least one computer rose from roughly 5% to nearly 30%, the stock price of Wang Labs collapsed from its peak of over $40 in the early 1980s to near zero by the early 1990s, demonstrating how the rise of the PC destroyed the dedicated word processor market.

The third chart illustrates the decline of newspaper advertising revenue and its impact on stock performance from 1999 to 2020. As the newspaper share of total ad revenue plummeted from roughly 35% in 1999 to below 5% in 2020, a newspaper stock index composed of TRB, NYT, KRI, and MNI peaked around 2004 before collapsing to near-zero. This index dramatically underperformed the broader S&P 500, which grew to over 350 on a December 1998 base index of 100.

The fourth chart examines electronics retailers from 1999 to 2020. As the e-commerce share of electronics sales grew from about 5% to over 35%, an electronics retailers index comprising CC, CPU, ODP, and RSH spiked briefly around 2006 before falling to near-zero. During the same period, the benchmark S&P 500 rose to approximately 600 relative to its December 1998 base.

The final chart details wireline telecom stocks from 2010 to 2022. It reveals a stark divergence: while monthly household data use rose dramatically from under 50 gigabytes to over 350 gigabytes, a Telecom/DSL stock index composed of LUMN, FTR, and WIN steadily declined from its December 2009 base of 100 to near-zero. Meanwhile, the benchmark S&P 500 rose to over 500, showing that massive growth in data demand did not translate to value for legacy telecom providers.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the challenges of accurately tracking COVID-19 mortality, noting that over one hundred countries fail to collect or timely release reliable death statistics. To counter this, demographers estimate true COVID-19 deaths by examining excess mortality—the difference between all-cause deaths and historical trends. The author argues that developing countries and emerging markets massively underreport their pandemic death tolls, even though their younger average populations should theoretically lower their mortality rates. 

A scatter plot illustrates this underreporting by comparing excess total mortality against reported COVID-19 mortality per million people from February to December 2020. A diagonal reference line indicates where excess deaths equal reported COVID-19 deaths. Countries plotted far above this line represent places where true excess mortality greatly exceeded official reports. Major outliers in this upper region include Peru, Ecuador, Russia, Lithuania, Bolivia, Bulgaria, and Mexico. Meanwhile, several countries such as New Zealand, Japan, Australia, South Korea, and Taiwan cluster near the bottom left, showing negligible or even negative excess mortality. 

Beneath this scatter plot, three line charts track estimated excess deaths against reported COVID-19 deaths per million from 2020 through early 2022, divided by country income levels. In high-income countries, the two metrics track relatively close to one another, with excess deaths approaching 2,000 per million and reported deaths near 1,500 per million by 2022. In upper-middle-income countries, a significant gap emerges as estimated excess deaths climb past 2,000 per million while reported deaths remain below 1,000. This disparity is most pronounced in lower-middle-income countries, where estimated excess deaths surge toward 3,000 per million by early 2022, while officially reported COVID-19 deaths barely register above 500 per million. The author concludes that claiming the emerging market world has inherently lower death rates despite lower vaccination rates represents a fundamental misunderstanding of pandemic research. The data is sourced from studies in Nature, JAMA Network Global Health, and The Economist.

This page analyzes the European energy crisis in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, focusing on the limitations of liquefied natural gas imports to substitute for Russian pipeline gas. The author argues that because liquefied natural gas exporters generally price their gas near European pipeline spot prices, it would take an massive influx of imports to drive down surging European gas and electricity prices. Infrastructure constraints present major bottlenecks, as European liquefied natural gas terminals with excess capacity are poorly integrated into the broader continent-wide grid, and existing regasification and exporter liquefaction facilities are operating at very high utilization rates. The author points out that even if the Netherlands lifted its drilling moratorium on the Groningen gas fields—currently in place due to earthquake risks—there is still not enough overall import capacity to fill the gap if Russian energy flows were to be cut in half. Consequently, European Union governments are contemplating emergency plans for gas rationing, which would curtail supplies to industrial users like steel, aluminum, silicon, chemical, and fertilizer manufacturers to preserve household heating. In fact, companies like the silicon producer Ferroglobe have already shut down furnaces in Spain due to high costs.

Four charts support this analysis. The first, tracking weekly European natural gas imports from 2015 to early 2022 in billions of cubic meters, shows that Russian pipeline gas has historically dominated, typically ranging between 2.0 and 3.5 billion cubic meters per week. While total liquefied natural gas imports have climbed and United States imports have entered the mix, they remain volatile and insufficient to fully replace pipeline flows. The second chart, tracking natural gas prices in dollars per million British thermal units from 2019 to early 2022, highlights how European natural gas and Asian liquefied natural gas prices spiked from under $10 to nearly $60, while the United States Henry Hub price remained relatively flat and cheap below $10. The third chart illustrates the compounding impact on European electricity and natural gas prices in dollars per megawatt-hour from 2015 to early 2022, showing that both hovered well under $50 for years before skyrocketing to recent daily peaks of $225 for electricity and $140 for natural gas. Finally, a pie chart breaks down the annual capacity of European Union natural gas imports in terawatt-hours, comparing pipeline imports with liquefied natural gas import facilities. It emphasizes Europe’s massive dependence on pipeline imports, led by Russia at 2,800 terawatt-hours, Norway at 1,100, and North Africa at 800. In comparison, total liquefied natural gas import capacities are highly fragmented and concentrated in countries like Spain with 700 terawatt-hours, France with 440, and Italy with 200, with much smaller capacities distributed among other European nations.

Michael Cembalest discusses the state of financial market risk unwinding, arguing that while the unwind of investor credit overweights has barely begun, the repricing of equities is much further along. He notes that the Federal Reserve's long run of negative real interest rates since the 1860s drove massive credit overweights that will take time to unpack. However, speculative equity sectors have already seen dramatic corrections. He suggests that a potential 50 basis point Fed rate hike in March 2022, alongside further market capitulation, could create an attractive entry point for equity investors.

The first chart, titled Implied investor credit overweight, shows credit overweighting as a percentage from 2005 to early 2022. Driven by central bank policy, this metric climbed from post-financial crisis lows of under 4% to a peak of nearly 18% in late 2020, showing only a slight decline to around 15% by early 2022. 

The second chart, Retail favorites performance, tracks an index of retail investor-favored stocks against the S&P 500 from January 2020 to early 2022. The retail favorite index surged to a peak of around 220 in early 2021 before tumbling back down to approximately 160 by early 2022, converging toward the S&P 500's steadier path which sat around 140.

The third chart, S&P 500 valuation vs real rates, plots the index's forward price-to-earnings ratio against 10-year US real yields from 2016 to early 2022. It illustrates how the S&P 500 forward P/E peaked near 24x as real yields sank to negative 1.0% in late 2020. By early 2022, the forward P/E moderated toward 20x as real yields rose back up toward negative 0.5%.

The fourth chart, Drawdowns of individual NASDAQ stocks from their respective peaks, provides a histogram of drawdowns for 2,915 NASDAQ stocks. It reveals that the average NASDAQ stock has fallen 42% from its peak, with substantial clusters of stocks experiencing drawdowns of 50%, 70%, or greater, even as only a small fraction of stocks remained at or near their peaks.

The final chart, Weak links crumbling, tracks the total return index of speculative sectors from August 2020 to February 2022, comparing the IPO Index, SPAC Index, S&P Renewable & Clean Tech, and Solactive Fintech Index. All four indices peaked near early 2021—with the SPAC index topping out near 200—before suffering severe de-ratings that brought all of them back down to near or below their baseline level of 100 by early 2022.

This page provides an appendix of charts assessing global supply chain conditions, illustrating that while conditions remain very tight, there are modest signs of improvement from recent peak levels. 

The first chart illustrates the container freight rate between Los Angeles and Shanghai from 2012 to early 2022. It highlights a massive divergence between shipping routes, as the rate for Shanghai to Los Angeles skyrocketed to over $12,000 per 40-foot box in late 2021, while the return rate from Los Angeles to Shanghai remained flat and cheap at under $2,000. 

A second chart compares container freight rates against the number of anchored containerships in Los Angeles and Long Beach from January 2019 to February 2022. Freightos China to West Coast rates surged toward $20,000, and WCI Shanghai to Los Angeles rates climbed past $10,000. This rate surge occurred alongside a dramatic spike in anchored containerships, which peaked at over 100 vessels waiting off the coast in late 2021 and early 2022. 

Global manufacturing delivery times are shown using an index from 1998 to early 2022. Lower index values indicate longer lead times, and the index plunged to near-unprecedented depths around 35 in late 2021, reflecting severe shipping delays, before showing a very slight upward tick in early 2022. 

The fourth chart tracks annual auto production in millions of units across the United States, Japan, and Germany from 2000 through early 2022. Production in all three regions fell sharply during the pandemic, with the US hovering around 10 million units, Japan dropping toward 8 million, and Germany falling below 4 million, demonstrating the impact of parts shortages on the automotive sector. 

Domestic logistics challenges are illustrated by the truckstop market demand index, which measures the ratio of truck demand to truck supply from January 2019 to January 2022. The index spiked from near zero in early 2020 to a peak above 200 in mid-2021, remaining extremely elevated around 150 to 180 in early 2022. 

Average air freight rates also experienced significant inflation, rising from approximately $3 per kilogram in 2019 to nearly $8 per kilogram by late 2021. 

Finally, a chart on shipping rates compares container freight rates with the Baltic Dry Index from 2018 to early 2022. Both surged dramatically in tandem during 2021, but by early 2022, the Baltic Dry Index had dropped sharply from its peak of over 5,000 down to around 2,000, while container freight rates also showed signs of topping out but remained near historical highs.

This page of the publication, written during the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine crisis, reflects on the historical debate between Liberalism and Realism in Western foreign policy. The author, Michael Cembalest, reviews John Mearsheimer's 2014 essay arguing that the West's expansion of NATO provoked Vladimir Putin. He traces this back to the Clinton administration's NATO enlargement in the 1990s, which added more territory than the combined landmass of France, Germany, and Italy. The narrative cites George Kennan's 1998 warning that expansion was a tragic mistake and notes the crossing of Russian red lines when NATO announced in 2008 that Georgia and Ukraine would eventually join. Cembalest critiques past liberal optimism regarding Ukraine joining Europe, asserting that those predictions have aged poorly. He suggests that because the West has made clear it will not defend Ukraine militarily, the Realist school of thought may be proven correct, pointing to Mearsheimer's proposal of a Finlandization of Ukraine as a more realistic outcome. Footnotes add context regarding the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, clarifying that it was not a binding defense treaty. 

An accompanying map of Europe details the chronological stages of NATO enlargement. It visually tracks original members from 1949 in black, expansions from 1950 to 1980 in brown, the major eastward expansion from 1999 to 2004 in purple, and further additions from 2009 to 2020 in red. Countries with a NATO Membership Action Plan are shown in blue, and Ukraine is highlighted in orange as participating in an intensified NATO dialogue, illustrating its geographic position between the expanded NATO territories in Eastern Europe and Russia, which is shown in gray alongside other non-NATO nations.

This page critiques the International Energy Agency's ambitious "shock treatment" plans designed to rapidly wean Europe off of Russian energy, arguing that Europe's reliance is far too deep to reduce quickly. The author systemically deconstructs four proposed strategies. First, diversifying gas suppliers will likely narrow supply and raise prices rather than curb global demand, especially since eighty percent of US liquefied natural gas is already bound for Europe and new US export capacity won't come online until 2025. Second, accelerating wind and solar is hindered by a historically slow one percent annual growth rate since 2000 and severe transmission bottlenecks. Third, scaling up residential heat pumps faces slow adoption rates, which remain largely flat at twenty-five percent since 2013 outside of Scandinavia. Lastly, maximizing nuclear power is unrealistic given that European reactors already operate at an eighty percent capacity factor, with remaining capacity offline for necessary maintenance. 

Four supporting charts illustrate these structural dependencies and the resulting price shocks. A pie chart of OECD Europe's final energy consumption shows that electricity accounts for only nineteen percent of energy use, while industry and transport dominate at thirty-five percent and twenty-seven percent, respectively, with residential heating at thirteen percent and commercial heating at six percent. This underscores how grid decarbonization alone cannot solve Europe's reliance on fossil fuels for heavy industry and heating. 

A line chart tracking European reliance on Russian energy from 1980 to 2020 reveals a steady decline in domestic oil and gas production, which fell to around four million barrels of oil equivalent per day by 2020, while imports from Russia rose to approximately six million barrels of oil equivalent per day. Other imports remained high, hovering around ten million barrels. 

Two final charts compare wholesale energy prices between Europe and the United States to highlight the stark economic divergence. The wholesale electricity price chart shows European prices skyrocketing in early 2022, reaching peaks of $571 per megawatt-hour in Germany, Spain, and France, and $522 in the United Kingdom, compared to a flat $34 in the United States. Similarly, the wholesale natural gas price chart shows European and UK prices peaking at $87 per million British thermal units in early 2022, while the US Henry Hub price remained extremely low at just $5. Ultimately, the author projects that European energy costs will only decline with a resolution of the Ukraine conflict, the natural seasonal demand drop in spring, or a halt in strategic reserve buying.

This page examines the geopolitical context surrounding the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, posing the open question of whether alternative diplomatic paths might have prevented the conflict and highlighting historical warnings against NATO's eastward expansion. The author traces Russian authoritarianism back to the geopolitical vulnerabilities of the 1990s when Russia suffered a sovereign debt default, a collapse in oil prices to ten dollars per barrel, and a depletion of financial reserves. This period triggered a domestic desire for authoritarian stability, a shift predicted in a 1999 NATO report and warned against by numerous US foreign policy experts—including George Kennan, Bill Bradley, Sam Nunn, and Robert McNamara—who opposed NATO's expansion. The text notes that alternative strategies, such as the "Finlandization" of Ukraine or a structured path to NATO membership with immediate military protection, were bypassed. Instead, the November 2021 US-Ukraine Charter on Strategic Partnership offered symbolic support with no actual defense guarantees. The author connects this modern tragedy to Stalin's Holodomor terror-famine, which killed four million Ukrainians ninety years prior.

Two line charts illustrate Russia's macroeconomic recovery since its late-1990s low point. The first chart, displaying Russia's foreign exchange reserves in billions of US dollars from 1998 to 2022, shows reserves rising from near zero to more than six hundred billion dollars by the start of 2022. The second chart, detailing Russia's current account balance as a percentage of GDP from 1996 to 2021, shows a dip below zero in the late 1990s, a dramatic peak above fifteen percent around 2000, and subsequent volatility that hovered around five percent by 2021.

Two tables compare starkly uneven military matchups, drawing a historical parallel to frame Ukraine's defensive struggle. The first table outlines the asymmetric 2022 military balance between Russia and Ukraine, showing Russia’s overwhelming superiority in every metric, including 850,000 ground forces to Ukraine's 200,000, 4,173 aircraft to 318, 12,420 tanks to 2,596, and 544 attack helicopters to just 34. The second table provides historical context by detailing the lopsided military balance between Britain and the United States during the Revolutionary War, where Britain held 270 naval ships in 1776 against the colonies' 27, and field forces of 194,000 soldiers against a peak American force of 30,000. By comparing Ukraine's situation to the American Revolution, the author implies that Ukraine's survival, much like that of the early United States, may ultimately depend on extraordinary resilience and favorable external intervention.

This page analyzes China’s current economic activity, global and Chinese year-to-date equity performance, and the mounting pressure on the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in early 2022. The author notes that China’s newly announced 5.5% GDP growth target is 1% lower than targets from recent years and will likely require additional fiscal stimulus to achieve. This is particularly true given the Chinese government’s continued regulatory pressure on the real estate sector under its stance that housing is for living in, not speculation. 

To illustrate China’s diverging economic trends, the author presents three charts indexing activity from January 2018 to early 2022. The positive signs chart shows that exports, electricity consumption, and crude steel production have recovered strongly, with exports indexing well above 120. The stable signs chart shows that industrial production, construction and real estate GDP, retail sales, and corporate earnings for onshore A shares are holding relatively steady, generally tracking between index levels of 100 and 120. In contrast, the negative signs chart shows a stark contraction in residential and commercial construction starts, which have fallen steeply to index levels of roughly 60 and 80, respectively. 

The middle of the page focuses on equity market performance, noting that Chinese equities have sold off in 2022 alongside major global regions despite stabilizing domestic economic data. A bar chart of year-to-date total returns across major global regions shows negative performance across the board as of March 4, 2022. While Canada and Australia held up best with losses of around 2%, the Eurozone, Europe, and Nasdaq fell the furthest, posting declines between 12% and 15%. A neighboring chart of Chinese equity indices shows double-digit negative returns across all tracked benchmarks. The steepest declines occurred in offshore and tech sectors, with the Hang Seng Tech index, China ADRs, and the five largest Chinese tech stocks falling between 15% and nearly 20%, while onshore indices like the CSI 300 fell around 10%. 

The bottom portion of the page explains that these global equity declines are largely driven by market expectations of substantial Fed tightening. A line chart tracking market-implied Fed hikes shows that the number of expected 25-basis-point interest rate hikes over the subsequent 12 months rose dramatically from near zero in August 2021 to over six hikes by February 2022. This rapid shift is contextualized by a final chart showing the required Fed Funds rate from 2008 through 2022 under various economic policy rules. Models such as the Taylor Rule and the Balanced Approach suggest that inflation and economic conditions in early 2022 demand a Fed Funds rate of 5% or higher, reflecting intense structural pressure on the central bank to act. Ultimately, the author cautions that markets have likely not yet experienced the worst of the geopolitical conflict or the bottom of the stock market selloff.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes geopolitical and energy vulnerabilities facing Europe and global markets. The author highlights issues surrounding LNG contracts, European reliance on Russia for oil and gas, tightening agricultural grain supplies, and the behavior of cryptocurrency as a market beta exposure rather than a safe-haven asset.

Addressing the assumption that long-term US LNG contracts are universally cheaper than spot markets, the author uses Asian market history to show that long-term oil-linked LNG contracts actually traded at a premium to spot prices in 2018 and 2019. Although spot prices have surged above long-term contracts since 2020, securing long-term LNG contracts for Europe would lock countries into 5-to-15-year terms at prices significantly higher than normalized pipeline levels. Geopolitical risks are also underscored by the fact that 30% of Europe's energy imports transit through pipelines in Ukrainian territory, exposing them to conflict risks. Furthermore, Europe depends on Russia for 27% of its 2021 oil imports, occurring at a time when OECD oil inventories are at their lowest levels in 15 years and global capital expenditure in oil and gas has plummeted.

The first chart, titled "Global fossil fuel use vs energy capital spending," illustrates this investment deficit. Plotted from 2005 to 2021, it compares global primary energy fossil fuel use in exajoules on the right axis against capital spending by S&P Global 1200 energy companies in US billions on the left axis. While global fossil fuel consumption steadily climbed from approximately 350 exajoules in 2005 to nearly 500 exajoules in 2019—experiencing only a brief COVID-19 decline in 2020—capital spending peaked near $400 billion in 2013 and plummeted to about $150 billion by 2021.
