The second chart, "Cereal prices rising as supply remains tight," tracks the stocks-to-use ratio of major exporters against a cereal prices index from 2014 through J.P. Morgan forecasts for 2023. The stocks-to-use ratio has steadily fallen from a peak of nearly 17% in 2018 to below 12% by late 2021, causing cereal prices to surge toward an index value of 140. Accompanying forecast dots for wheat and corn indicate that tight supplies and elevated prices are expected to persist into 2022 and 2023.

In a brief section titled "Before I forget," Cembalest critiques cryptocurrency's role as a store of value. The chart "Bitcoin vs relative performance of high Beta stocks" shows a near-identical correlation from July 2019 to January 2022 between the price of Bitcoin (on a logarithmic scale from $4,000 to $80,000) and the performance ratio of the S&P 500 High Beta Index relative to the S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF. The visual alignment suggests that Bitcoin trades primarily as high-beta market exposure rather than an uncorrelated hedge.

The final chart, "Asia long-term and spot vs US LNG contracts," displays prices in dollars per MMBTU from 2018 through late 2021 for the JKM LNG spot price, JCC long-term oil-linked LNG contracts, and the US Henry Hub. While the US Henry Hub price remained flat and low, below $5, the JKM spot price spiked dramatically from under $5 in late 2020 to nearly $35 in late 2021. The chart visually supports the text's assertion that in 2018 and 2019, JCC long-term contracts, which hovered around $10, were priced higher than the JKM spot market.

This page focuses on the historical context and geopolitical implications of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, highlighting Russia’s declining global economic significance and its energy relationships with Europe and China. The author argues that Russia’s actions in Ukraine have a brutal historical precedent, specifically pointing to the Holodomor famine of the 1930s. To illustrate this, the first chart compares the Ukraine Holodomor terror famine (1930–1935) to other major global famines. Measured in death rate per 1,000 people over a five-year horizon, the Holodomor peaked catastrophically in year three at nearly 130 deaths per 1,000. This peak dramatically dwarfs other historic famines—such as those in Ireland (1845–1850), North Korea (1993–1998), Bengal (1940–1945), and China (1957–1962)—none of which exceeded 40 deaths per 1,000 people on this scale.

The commentary then addresses Russia’s long-term economic trajectory. A second chart traces the Russia/USSR share of world GDP since 1820. It shows how imperial expansion and Soviet annexations of Eastern Europe pushed the region's share of global GDP to a peak of nearly 16% in the mid-20th century. However, following the dissolution of the USSR, this share collapsed, leaving the modern Russian Federation representing less than 3% of global GDP. The author suggests that if Europe manages to sharply reduce its reliance on Russian energy through LNG expansion, renewables, and nuclear power, Russia's share of world GDP will shrink even further, potentially turning the nation into an energy vassal state for China. This is compounded by the lopsided trade relationship where China is Russia's largest trading partner, yet Russia accounts for only 2% of Chinese exports.

To contextualize these energy dynamics, a final chart displays energy dependence and independence from 1980 to 2020, measuring net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal in million tonnes of oil equivalent. The data highlights Europe as a massive, consistent net importer of energy, hovering near 800 million tonnes. China has also rapidly risen as a net importer, climbing from near-zero in the 1990s to over 600 million tonnes by 2020. Conversely, the United States successfully transitioned from a major net importer to a net exporter by 2020. Russia has steadily grown its position as a dominant net exporter, reaching nearly 800 million tonnes of oil equivalent exported by 2020, underscoring the deep global dependencies at stake.

This J.P. Morgan report page, titled "How bad is the selloff? Tracking opportunities for bottom fishing investors," written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the state of the US equity market selloff as of March 2022. The author argues that if the US avoids a recession—which he believes it will, despite headwinds like rising energy prices, credit spreads, wages, supply shortages, and Federal Reserve interest rate hikes—the March 8th market low likely represented a bottom. 

The first chart, "March 8 a likely bottom if no US recession occurs," plots the percentage decline of average stocks from their prior peaks across various indices, comparing the March 8 low against historic recession averages and other large sell-off averages. It shows that for indices like the Russell 2000 and Nasdaq Composite, the March 8 decline (near 35% and 40% respectively) was much closer to non-recession sell-off averages than to recessionary bottoms, which typically exceed 50% to 60%. 

The second chart, "The average stock fell a lot more than the index it's in," compares the index decline, median stock decline, and average stock decline from their 52-week highs as of March 8. It demonstrates that individual stocks suffered far worse than the broader indices; for instance, while the S&P 500 index fell roughly 12%, its average stock fell nearly 20%, and while the Nasdaq Composite index fell about 20%, its average stock collapsed by over 40%. 

The third chart, "P/E ratio of top 25 stocks vs the market," traces the forward price-to-earnings ratios from 1986 to early 2022, comparing the 25 largest stocks in the S&P 500 to the rest of the index. This visual highlights that the forward P/E ratio of the top 25 stocks, led by Apple, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Tesla, remains historically elevated at nearly 27x, while the rest of the S&P 500 is valued closer to 17x, reflecting strong investor confidence in mega-cap earnings resilience. 

The final chart, "Hedge fund gross leverage," tracks leverage percentages from January 2020 to January 2022. It reveals that gross leverage, which peaked near 206% in early 2021, has moderated to approximately 187% by early 2022, indicating a risk reduction that is still less severe than typical recessionary capitulations. Additionally, the author notes that while long-only institutional futures positions in major indices are approaching their 2018 and 2020 lows, small-cap futures positions have plummeted to their lowest levels since the 2008 financial crisis.

This page from the publication analyzes global credit spreads and the deep selloff in Chinese equities, arguing that while credit spreads have widened, they do not yet signal a recession. This observation is supported by two historical charts spanning 1987 to 2022 with shaded recession bands. The first chart, tracking US and emerging market high yield credit spreads, shows that both the emerging market high yield sovereign spread and the US high yield spread have ticked up slightly but remain around the 5 percent level, far below the spikes of 15 percent to over 20 percent seen in past recessions. Similarly, the second chart, showing US investment grade credit spreads, indicates that current levels are under 2 percent, which is well below historical recessionary peaks that reached over 6 percent in 2008.

In contrast, the author observes that Chinese equities, particularly in the internet sector, are pricing in severe adverse news. Investors face the likely elimination of Chinese American Depositary Receipts, higher capital costs, and strict lockdowns in Shenzhen and Shanghai. Despite these headwinds, the author predicts that the Chinese government will deploy its substantial fiscal and monetary stimulus ammunition to meet the Communist Party leadership's 5.5 percent annual growth target. 

This dramatic market action in China is illustrated in two additional charts. The first, comparing China internet stocks since September 2019 to the NASDAQ from 1999 to 2004, indexes both series to a peak of 100. The comparison reveals that the China Internet Index has closely tracked the post-bubble NASDAQ crash trajectory, falling to a low point near 30. The final chart displays MSCI China equity index drawdowns as a percentage decline from prior peaks from 2007 to early 2022. It highlights that the latest drawdown reached negative 45 percent, which, while severe, remains less extreme than the peak drawdown of over 70 percent experienced during the 2008 financial crisis.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest assesses the deteriorating economic growth outlook for Europe, arguing that a recession appears inevitable due to an unprecedented commodity and producer price shock that overwhelms the region's structural energy efficiency. This crisis is compared to the OPEC oil embargoes of the 1970s, with a broad basket of energy, metals, agriculture, and livestock up approximately 80% since the fall of 2019. 

To contextualize Europe's baseline vulnerability, the first chart, titled "Europe: generally lower energy intensity of growth," plots primary energy consumption in exajoules per trillion US dollars of real GDP across major nations using 2020 data. It highlights that European nations such as Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Italy, Germany, Spain, and France are highly efficient, consuming fewer than two exajoules per trillion dollars of GDP, whereas the United States consumes around 3.5 exajoules, and Russia and Canada exceed seven exajoules. 

Despite this efficiency, Europe is facing an extraordinary producer price shock. The second chart, "Unprecedented surge in European producer prices vs consumer prices," tracks the percentage difference between producer price inflation and consumer price inflation from 1970 to early 2022. While the United States has maintained a relatively stable spread that has historically fluctuated between negative 5% and positive 5%, Europe has experienced an unprecedented spike, with producer price inflation exceeding consumer inflation by nearly 30% in early 2022. Cembalest notes that this extreme gap must eventually be absorbed by companies through lower margins and reduced capital spending, or passed on to consumers, triggering tighter central bank policy.

The bottom two charts illustrate the specific utility spikes driving this shock. The wholesale electricity price chart, measuring the seven-day average in US dollars per megawatt-hour from 2015 to early 2022, reveals a stark regional divergence. While US electricity remains low at $33, prices in Germany, Spain, and France have surged to $258, and prices in the United Kingdom have reached $261. Similarly, the wholesale natural gas price chart in US dollars per million British thermal units shows that between 2019 and early 2022, the US Henry Hub benchmark remained flat near $5, while European and UK natural gas prices spiked dramatically to around $30. 

Consequently, the author warns that European corporate earnings, currently projected to be flat in 2022 with equities trading at 13 times earnings, could drop by 25% with price-to-earnings ratios falling below 10 during an impending recession. He concludes that European equities do not offer good value unless the Russian invasion of Ukraine comes to an unexpectedly swift conclusion.

This page analyzes how rising metals prices since early 2020 might impact electric vehicle prices, focusing on the differences between battery chemistries. The author argues that while Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries have seen manageable metal cost increases of about $500, Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt and Lithium Nickel Cobalt Aluminum batteries have seen estimated cost increases of around $1,500. This could lead to sticker shock for nickel- and cobalt-reliant EVs, potentially creating adoption headwinds in the United States that may require more generous federal subsidies. An additional $500 cost increase could also affect all EVs due to non-battery copper and aluminum requirements.

The analysis is supported by several charts and a table. A line chart tracking the metals cost per 60 kWh EV battery from January 2020 to January 2022 shows NMC and NCA battery metal costs rising in tandem from roughly $1,400 to nearly $2,500, while LFP metal costs rise far more moderately, ending just below $1,000. A stacked bar chart breaking down these costs shows that nickel and cobalt are the primary cost drivers for NMC and NCA chemistries, while lithium is the dominant cost for LFP batteries, with copper and aluminum making up most of the remainder. 

A metal prices index chart set to a December 2019 baseline of 100 shows that by early 2022, lithium prices had skyrocketed to an index value of 597. Cobalt and nickel also experienced major spikes, reaching index values of 257 and 228, respectively, while manganese, aluminum, copper, iron, and steel rose to index values between 146 and 222. 

An automaker battery chemistry table reveals which manufacturers are most vulnerable to these cost spikes. It shows that Audi, BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, Ford, and high-end Volkswagen models utilize NMC batteries. Tesla uses NCA for long-range vehicles and LFP for short-range vehicles. Other users of LFP batteries include Chinese manufacturers like BYD and Hongguang, entry-level Volkswagen passenger cars, and Rivian for both its passenger trucks and delivery vans.

Despite upfront price concerns, a footnote highlights that EV owners still stand to save approximately $1,250 per year in fuel expenses over gasoline cars, assuming 11,000 miles driven annually at $4 per gallon for gasoline and 14 cents per kWh for electricity. This annual savings rate helps determine the payback period for the incremental upfront cost of an EV.

This page from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" by Michael Cembalest examines why growth equity mutual funds have struggled to outperform their benchmarks, identifying regulatory diversification constraints as a major headwind. 

The core of the argument is that active growth mutual fund managers have underperformed because they are legally restricted from keeping pace with the highly concentrated nature of growth indices. Under Section 5-b-1 of the 1940 Investment Company Act, diversified funds must limit positions that represent over 5% of the portfolio to a collective maximum of 25% of the fund. Many Defined Contribution plans demand adherence to this rule. However, by March 2022, the four largest stocks in the Russell 1000 Growth Index—Apple (AAPL) at 12.5%, Microsoft (MSFT) at 10.8%, Amazon (AMZN) at 6.6%, and Alphabet (GOOG) at 6.4%—collectively comprised 36% of the index. Similarly, they represented 41% of the S&P 500 Growth Index. Complying with the 25% regulatory threshold forces active managers to remain structurally underweight in these dominant market leaders.

To illustrate this trend, a bar chart analyzes the relative performance of 138 Russell 1000 Growth benchmarked mutual funds from January 2017 to February 2022. The chart plots the number of mutual funds against their relative cumulative performance bins, revealing that a substantial majority of the funds underperformed the benchmark, with a heavy concentration of funds falling in the negative 10%, 20%, and 30% performance categories relative to the index. 

A corresponding line chart tracks the performance of these four mega-cap stocks (Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet) against the broader S&P 500 Growth and Russell 1000 Growth indices from 2017 through early 2022, indexed to 100 in January 2017. While the broader growth indices peaked at just under 300, the top four stock group soared to nearly 600, showing that their performance more than doubled that of the growth indices.

Finally, a line chart illustrates the impact of this diversification constraint on growth investors by plotting the percentage of cumulative outperformance an unconstrained portfolio would achieve over a constrained portfolio (assuming constrained managers remain at a combined 23% weight across the four largest stocks). The cumulative cost of the constraint rose steadily after 2019, creating an estimated 14% to 15% performance drag on constrained managers by 2022.

This page analyzes the performance of technology long-short hedge funds and growth-oriented "Tiger Cub" hedge funds using PivotalPath data from January 2017 to February 2022. The author highlights the challenge of data limitations, noting that only 27 out of 104 technology funds and 12 out of 29 Tiger Cub funds had consistent monthly reporting over this entire timeframe. 

The first section evaluates the performance of the 27 technology hedge funds. A line chart indexes their cumulative performance alongside a Russell 1000 Growth benchmark adjusted to 45% net exposure. The accompanying table shows that the performance distribution of these technology funds looks normal. The 75th percentile manager outperformed the benchmark, achieving a 90% cumulative return and a 13% annualized return with 13% volatility (a 1.0x return-to-risk ratio). The median, or 50th percentile, manager achieved a 63% cumulative return and generated a high risk-adjusted return with a 1.6x return-to-risk ratio and low volatility of 6%. The 25th percentile manager underperformed with a 37% cumulative return, a 6% annualized return, and a 0.7x return-to-risk ratio.

The second section shifts focus to the 12 generalist growth-oriented Tiger Cub funds, which are descendants of the original Tiger fund. A line chart and performance table illustrate that these funds struggled relative to the benchmark, particularly during a market correction in early 2022. Only the 75th percentile Tiger Cub fund kept pace with the Russell 1000 Growth benchmark, matching its 60% cumulative return (10% annualized return with a 1.0x return-to-risk ratio). The median Tiger Cub manager fell well below the benchmark, experiencing a sharp drawdown to end with a 37% cumulative return, a 6% annualized return, and a 0.6x return-to-risk ratio. The 25th percentile manager recorded weak results with a cumulative return of just 14% (3% annualized) and high volatility of 12%, resulting in a low 0.2x return-to-risk ratio and a current-value-to-peak ratio of 82%. The author notes that some highly volatile Tiger Cub funds experienced even more severe drawdowns, with one fund seeing a 37% peak-to-trough drop by February 2022 and further reported losses in March despite a broader recovery in growth stocks.

This analysis examines whether allocating portfolio assets to growth stocks between January 2017 and February 2022 generated substantial excess returns compared to other equity benchmarks. The author chooses January 2017 as a starting point, reflecting when the market began focusing on the higher revenue growth and stronger profit margins of technology and healthcare companies in a slower-growth world. The main finding is that while growth generated significantly higher returns than value and international alternatives with comparable levels of volatility, nearly half of this outperformance was driven by only four mega-cap stocks: Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Google. Additionally, the author notes that only the top quartile of equity mutual funds and hedge funds managed to outperform their growth benchmarks.

The first line chart, titled "Equity benchmark performance," tracks total return indexes starting at 100 in January 2017 through February 2022. It illustrates that the Russell 1000 Growth and NASDAQ indexes substantially outperformed the S&P 500, MSCI World Small Cap, Russell 1000 Value, Russell 2000 Small Cap, MSCI Emerging Markets, and MSCI Europe. By late February 2022, these growth and technology indexes remained far ahead of all other cohorts, despite experiencing a market selloff.

The second line chart, "Closer look at the Russell 1000," isolates the impact of the four largest mega-caps on performance. By comparing the standard Russell 1000 Growth Index to a custom version that excludes the four largest stocks, the chart visually demonstrates how a significant portion of the growth index's rise above the broader Russell 1000 Index and the Russell 1000 Value Index was driven exclusively by Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and Google.

A performance table, titled "Growth equity vs other equity benchmarks, January 2017 - February 2022," presents key performance indicators across eight benchmarks. The Russell 1000 Growth Index achieved a 171% cumulative return and a 21% annualized return, matching the NASDAQ's 168% cumulative return and 21% annualized return. Both indexes registered a high return-to-risk ratio of 1.2x and standard deviations of 17% and 18%, respectively. In comparison, the S&P 500 generated a 115% cumulative return (16% annualized, 1.0x return/risk), while the Russell 1000 Value Index produced a 64% cumulative return (10% annualized, 0.6x return/risk). Mid-period drawdowns left the growth and NASDAQ indexes at 88% of their peak values by February 2022, while the value index retained 97% of its peak value. International benchmarks lagged significantly, with MSCI Europe posting a 50% cumulative return and MSCI Emerging Markets posting a 52% cumulative return.

This page analyzes hedge fund performance using two separate databases, Hedge Fund Research (HFR) and eVestment, to evaluate how long-short equity managers perform relative to a beta-adjusted benchmark. The overarching observation across both datasets is that the median manager closely tracks a passive, beta-adjusted benchmark—specifically, the Russell 1000 Growth Index modeled at a 45% net exposure—while top-quartile managers outperform by a larger margin than bottom-quartile managers underperform.

The first section focuses on HFR technology and healthcare long-short hedge funds across a sample of 55 funds from January 2017 through early 2022. A line chart reveals that the 75th percentile far outpaces the rest, ending above 240, while the 50th percentile and the 45% net exposure Russell 1000 Growth benchmark trend closely together. The accompanying table details these outcomes, showing that the 75th percentile achieved a cumulative return of 126% and an annualized return of 17%, compared to 65% cumulative and 10% annualized for the 50th percentile, and 60% cumulative and 9% annualized for the benchmark. However, the benchmark demonstrated superior efficiency, with a return-to-risk ratio of 1.2x compared to just 0.7x for the top-quartile funds, driven by the index's low annualized volatility of 8% versus 24% for the 75th percentile.

The second section replicates this analysis using the eVestment database of 231 high-beta hedge funds that exhibited a beta to the S&P 500 Growth Index of at least 0.45. While the author notes that eVestment has a lower rate of missing performance data than HFR, the trends are nearly identical. The eVestment line chart similarly shows the 75th percentile diverging upward while the median and the benchmark remain closely aligned. According to the eVestment performance table, cumulative returns were 103% for the 75th percentile, 66% for the 50th percentile, and 38% for the 25th percentile. As with the HFR dataset, the benchmark's return-to-risk ratio of 1.2x outperformed all fund quartiles due to the lower volatility of the passive index.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication analyzes the performance of growth-focused investment strategies, equity mutual funds, and hedge funds from January 2017 through February 2022. The central thesis is that while growth allocations delivered substantial returns over this period despite a selloff in early 2022, only the top-quartile managers in equity and hedge funds managed to deliver excess returns compared to growth benchmarks. For equity mutual funds, underperformance against the Russell 1000 Growth Index was common, largely driven by managers underweighting the four largest stocks, which collectively outperformed the rest of the market by 300% during this timeframe.

Hedge fund performance is illustrated through three line charts tracking index returns from a January 2017 baseline of 100 through early 2022, comparing five series: eVestment high beta, PivotalPath Tech, HFR Tech/Healthcare, the Tiger Cub manager pool, and a customized benchmark represented by the Russell 1000 Growth Index at 45% exposure. The first chart, depicting the 50th percentile or median managers, shows that most tracked the beta-adjusted benchmark closely, ending between 140 and 150, with the notable exception of the median Tiger Cub manager, which trailed the benchmark after a sharp drop in late 2021 to around 130. The second chart focuses on 25th percentile underperforming managers, showing that all categories lagged the benchmark, with index values ending between 110 and 130, while also exhibiting 1% to 5% higher volatility. The third chart shows 75th percentile outperforming managers, utilizing a larger vertical scale up to 280. In this top quartile, the HFR Tech/Healthcare and eVestment high beta categories significantly outperformed, peaking near 260 to 280, while the 75th percentile Tiger Cub manager lagged its peers, peaking around 180 before falling to around 160 and failing to beat the benchmark.

The author notes that while some hedge funds suffered severe drawdowns in early 2022, their high prior returns kept long-term investors ahead of benchmarks—a point often ignored in press reports, such as a March 2022 Financial Times piece on Tiger Cub funds. However, the author cautions that risk may still be understated for funds with large private exposures. The commentary concludes by highlighting research limitations, including the simplicity of standard beta-adjusted benchmarks, selective reporting, survivorship bias, and substantial missing data, noting that less than half of the managers in the PivotalPath dataset could be analyzed.

This page functions as the executive summary of the annual energy paper, arguing that the global transition away from fossil fuels is progressing much slower than falling renewable energy prices would suggest. While wind and solar power purchase agreements have plummeted over the last decade, fossil fuels still account for the vast majority of global energy consumption. The author, Michael Cembalest, attributes this slow transition to two factors. First, levelized cost comparisons are misleading because they ignore critical integration costs like transmission expansion, thermal backup power, and battery storage. Second, overall electrification remains very low in the heavy industrial and transport sectors, meaning grid decarbonization only addresses a small fraction of total energy use.

The first chart, titled "The world uses fossil fuels for approximately 83 percent of its energy," tracks the percentage of global primary energy consumption derived from coal, oil, and natural gas from 1965 to 2050. It delineates eras of energy transition, highlighting a plateau around 94 percent during the pre-existing hydropower era, a decline to roughly 86 percent during the nuclear adoption era, and a slow downward slope during the solar and wind era. Looking to the future, the chart presents two International Energy Agency projections for 2050: the Stated Policies Scenario, which projects fossil fuel reliance will only drop to 66 percent, and the Announced Pledges Scenario, which targets a deeper drop to around 48 percent.

The second chart displays average power purchase agreements by year of operation from 2010 to 2020 in real 2020 dollars per megawatt-hour. This visual illustrates the dramatic cost declines for solar and wind power, noting that these agreements reflect benefits from subsidies like the US Investment Tax Credit. Global solar photovoltaic prices plummeted from about 200 dollars per megawatt-hour in 2010 to roughly 45 dollars in 2020, while US solar photovoltaic dropped from around 160 dollars to under 40 dollars. Over the same period, global wind fell from approximately 90 dollars to 40 dollars, and US wind dropped from about 60 dollars to 20 dollars. A footnote warns that these costs are now rising again due to inflation, higher interest rates, and pricing pressures facing turbine manufacturers such as GE and Siemens.

The third chart illustrates low levels of electrification in global industry and transport, measuring final energy consumed by sector in quadrillion BTUs. The industrial sector consumes by far the most energy at over 225 quads, but it is dominated by direct fossil fuels and direct renewables, with electrification representing only about 40 quads. Transport is the next largest at approximately 140 quads and is almost entirely powered by direct fossil fuels. Residential and commercial buildings consume far less total energy but show much higher shares of electrification.

The final chart breaks down US electricity uses in quadrillion BTUs across residential, commercial, and industrial sectors. It reveals that in the residential and commercial sectors, the vast majority of electricity is used for space cooling, lighting, ventilation, refrigeration, computers, and other electronics. In contrast, heavy-duty applications like space heating, water heating, motors, and industrial process heat make up only a small fraction of electricity use, underscoring the challenge of decarbonizing thermal energy needs.

This page highlights the growing energy divide between the developed and developing world, arguing that the developed world has outsourced its carbon-intensive manufacturing to emerging economies. While the developed nations are projected to reduce their energy consumption in the coming decades, energy use in the developing world will continue to rise, heavily reliant on coal and other fossil fuels. 

To illustrate the shift in carbon-intensive production, the first chart displays the share of global production for manufacturing, ammonia, steel, cement, and plastic between developed and emerging economies from the mid-1990s to 2020 or 2021. Across every category, the emerging world’s share has grown dramatically; for instance, developed economies’ share of steel production dropped from around 40% in 1998 to roughly 15% in 2020, while their share of cement fell to nearly single digits. 

The second chart, based on the International Energy Agency's Stated Policies Scenario, projects changes in primary energy consumption in exajoules from 2020 to 2050 compared to historical changes from 2010 to 2020. Developed regions like the European Union, Japan, and the United States are projected to see negative energy consumption growth. In contrast, emerging regions like India, Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia are expected to see significant positive growth. Notably, China is the only emerging market projected to slow its primary energy consumption growth, with its projected 2020–2050 increase of around 10 exajoules being far smaller than its massive historical increase of over 30 exajoules between 2010 and 2020. 

The third chart tracks the share of primary energy derived from wind, solar, hydro, and other renewables from 1965 to 2025. It shows that both the OECD and China have increased their total renewable share to around 14% by 2021, with wind and solar alone rising sharply to around 5% to 7%. Meanwhile, non-OECD countries excluding China lag behind, with total renewables at roughly 10% and wind and solar comprising only about 2% of their primary energy.

The fourth chart illustrates the persistent reliance on coal, plotting the coal share of primary energy consumption from 1990 to 2020 across various countries. Coal remains a dominant energy source in South Africa at over 70%, and in China and India at roughly 55%. Furthermore, coal shares have actually risen over the last decade in developing nations like Vietnam (approaching 50%) and Indonesia, while declining steadily in Western countries such as the United States, Germany, and Poland. 

Finally, the bottom chart illustrates a critical paradox: while global CO2 intensity per thousand dollars of GDP has steadily declined from over 0.50 in 1965 to around 0.25 in 2020, total absolute CO2 emissions have more than tripled over the same period, rising from roughly 11 billion tonnes to over 33 billion tonnes. The author concludes that because emissions continue to rise despite year-over-year gains in energy efficiency, effective decarbonization must rely on the outright replacement of fossil fuels rather than just reducing per-capita consumption.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market argues that Europe is paying a steep price for its reliance on Russian energy, having miscalculated by rapidly cutting its own fossil fuel production without a matching reduction in consumption. The author warns that the ramifications of this dependence include a likely recession, high energy costs displacing non-energy consumption, diminished competitiveness of energy-intensive exports, and potential curtailments of industrial production in sectors like steel, fertilizer, and cement. He notes that Russia recently halted natural gas shipments to Poland and Bulgaria for refusing to pay in rubles, and recalls Mitt Romney's ignored 2012 warnings about Russia.

Six charts support these assertions. The first chart, illustrating European oil and gas production alongside imports from 1980 to 2020 in thousand barrels per day of oil equivalent, shows domestic production peaking around 2000 at roughly 7,000 thousand barrels before falling to nearly 3,500 thousand by 2020. Over this same period, European oil and gas imports from Russia remained steady, hovering around 5,000 to 6,000 thousand barrels per day. The second chart measures energy dependence and independence via net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal in million tonnes of oil equivalent. It highlights Europe’s status as a major net importer peaking near 900 million tonnes, and China's rapid rise to a net importer of over 600 million tonnes, contrasting sharply with the United States, which transitioned into a net exporter by 2020, and Russia, which grew into a massive net exporter of over 600 million tonnes.

The next two charts highlight the resulting pricing disadvantages for Europe. The wholesale electricity price chart shows a massive US-Europe gap, with the United States averaging $50 per megawatt-hour while the United Kingdom stands at $209 and Germany, Spain, and France hover at $235, having spiked from historical averages near $50. Similarly, the wholesale natural gas price gap reveals US Henry Hub prices at just $8 per MMBTU compared to $21 in the United Kingdom and $32 in Europe. 

The final two charts detail European gas import capacity and supply routes. A pie chart on annual gas import capacity for the EU 27 shows that Russian pipeline imports dominate at 2,800 TWh, followed by Norway at 1,100 TWh, North Africa at 800 TWh, and Azerbaijan at 130 TWh. Liquefied natural gas import facility capacity is fragmented, led by Spain at 700 TWh and France at 440 TWh, followed by smaller allocations in Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Greece, Portugal, Poland, Lithuania, and Croatia. Lastly, a stacked area chart tracks Russian natural gas exports to Europe from 2019 to early 2022. It reveals a clear downward trend in overall volume, showing declining shipments through the Yamal pipeline via Poland and transit routes through Ukraine, while Nord Stream 1 and LNG volumes remained relatively steady.

This page examines the immense logistical and economic hurdles facing Europe as it attempts to rapidly diversify away from Russian energy, alongside the broader global challenge of declining energy capital expenditures amid persistent fossil fuel demand. The author notes that replacing 2.6 million barrels per day of Russian crude oil imports will require increased supply from the US, Canada, Norway, the UK, and Denmark, with any remaining gap potentially requiring a deal with Iran. Substituting natural gas is even more challenging due to Europe's high reliance on Russian gas—amounting to 174 billion cubic meters per year—and limited liquefied natural gas regasification and pipeline infrastructure. Furthermore, alternative options like wind, solar, nuclear, and electrification face severe constraints, high costs, and regulatory delays.

Four supporting charts and tables illustrate these dynamics. The first line chart compares global primary energy fossil fuel use against the capital spending of S&P Global 1200 Energy companies from 2005 to 2021. While fossil fuel consumption has remained steady and high, averaging near 500 exajoules despite a brief decline in 2020, energy company capital expenditure has collapsed from a peak of nearly 400 billion dollars in 2013 to just over 100 billion dollars in 2021. This trend is mirrored in a bar chart showing the expected 2022 investment levels versus their 10-year averages across various sectors. While non-energy sectors like media and insurance show modest investment growth, capital-intensive sectors have experienced sharp declines: steel is down nearly 30 percent, marine shipping is down 35 percent, mining and metals are down 38 percent, and oil and gas producers have experienced the steepest decline at nearly 45 percent.

The third element is a twin table listing the nations with the largest proven reserves of natural gas and oil. Russia and Iran lead natural gas reserves with 1,320 and 1,134 trillion cubic feet, respectively, while the US sits in fifth with 446 trillion cubic feet. For oil, Venezuela holds 304 billion barrels and Saudi Arabia holds 298 billion barrels to top the list, followed by Canada, Iran, Iraq, and Russia, while the US holds 69 billion barrels. Finally, a table highlighting global market share in renewable energy production demonstrates China's overwhelming dominance. In 2019, China held a 63 percent market share in solar PV module shipments and a 46 percent share in the wind capacity order book. Furthermore, as of 2021, China controlled 79 percent of lithium-ion battery manufacturing capacity, 79 percent of electric vehicle mineral processing and refining, and 85 percent of electric vehicle cathode and anode production. In contrast, the US and EU maintain single-digit market shares across nearly all of these critical transition sectors, with the sole exception of the EU holding a 40 percent share in the wind capacity order book. The author concludes that achieving a faster renewable transition requires policymakers to tackle regulatory bottlenecks and establish carbon pricing rather than relying on fossil fuel divestment, while noting that a potential revival of the US Build Back Better bill could provide a modest boost.

This page presents J.P. Morgan's executive summary exhibits comparing energy consumption by country, end-use sector, and fuel type for the United States, OECD Europe, and China, alongside a comprehensive glossary of energy acronyms. 

The first section details energy consumption in the United States, displaying a stacked bar chart of final energy consumed in quadrillion BTUs across industrial, transport, residential, and commercial sectors. The chart categorizes fuel types by oil, coal, natural gas, renewable, and nuclear, with dotted segments representing electricity consumed. The transport sector is dominated by oil, while the residential sector relies heavily on electricity. Accompanying key statistics show the US consumes 93.3 quads of primary energy and 70.1 quads of final energy. Fossil fuels account for 79% of primary energy, while coal represents only 10%, giving a coal-to-natural-gas ratio of 0.3. Electricity makes up 18% of total energy consumed, including 44% of residential energy. Renewables provide 20% of electricity generation, while low-carbon sources account for 43% of electricity and 21% of primary energy.

The second section provides identical metrics for OECD Europe. The corresponding bar chart shows a similar sectoral distribution but with lower overall consumption. Key stats reveal primary energy consumption is 76.8 quads, with final consumption at 56.7 quads. Fossil fuels represent a smaller share at 69% of primary energy, and coal accounts for 10% with a coal-to-gas ratio of 0.4. Electricity is 19% of consumed energy, with low-carbon generation standing at a substantial 69% and renewables making up 44% of electricity generation. 

The third section focuses on China, where the profile differs dramatically. China's primary energy consumption is massive at 160.2 quads, with 109.6 quads of final energy. The industrial sector is by far the largest energy consumer, heavily dominated by coal. Fossil fuels represent 84% of primary energy, with coal alone accounting for 59%, resulting in a high coal-to-natural-gas ratio of 7.9. Electricity constitutes 20% of energy consumed. Renewables account for 25% of electricity generation, with hydropower making up 57% of that renewable generation. Low carbon sources represent 30% of electricity generation and 16% of primary energy.

The bottom of the page features an acronym reference guide defining common industry terms including billion cubic meters, barrels per day, British thermal units, carbon capture and storage, US Energy Information Agency, exajoules, enhanced oil recovery, Environmental Protection Agency, greenhouse gases, gigawatts, hydrogen, International Energy Agency, independent system operators, kilowatt hours, liquefied natural gas, cubic meters, megajoules, million metric tons, metric tons, million tonnes of oil equivalent, megawatt hours, power purchase agreements, quadrillion BTUs, and terawatt hours.

This page of the publication focuses on the severe backlogs and low completion rates plaguing the United States electrical transmission interconnection queues, taking the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) region as a primary case study. The author notes that across major regional grids including CAISO, ISO-NE, MISO, NYISO, and PJM combined, only 24% of projects in queues reached commercial operation between 2010 and 2020. This rate was even lower for wind at 19% and solar at 16%, while queue times nearly doubled from an average of 2 years between 2000 and 2010 to 3.7 years between 2011 and 2021.

Four distinct charts illustrate the scale of this problem. The first chart, titled "The clogged MISO interconnection queue," displays requested gigawatts in the queue from 2000 to 2020 by generation type. It shows a dramatic transformation in the queue's makeup, transitioning from predominantly gas and wind requests in the early 2000s to a massive surge of solar, storage, and hybrid projects in 2019 and 2020, with total requests approaching 55 gigawatts in the final year.

The second chart, "Less than 50% of MISO queue projects are completed," pairs MISO's requested gigawatts (ranging from 0 to 60 gigawatts) with the historical percentage of completed interconnection agreements from 2000 to 2020. It illustrates that while requested gigawatts spiked dramatically post-2015, the percentage of completed agreements plummeted from historically high levels of around 40% to 60% down to virtually 0% for the most recent years.

The third chart, "Renewable capacity in interconnection queues dwarfs existing capacity" from December 2021, compares capacity in the queue to currently operating capacity. For solar, the capacity in the queue exceeds 600 gigawatts compared to less than 100 gigawatts of existing capacity. Storage capacity in the queue stands at roughly 430 gigawatts against almost negligible existing capacity. Wind queue capacity is around 240 gigawatts compared to 130 gigawatts existing, whereas natural gas is the inverse, with about 500 gigawatts of existing capacity dwarfed by a minimal queue.

The final chart, "US interconnection queue by fuel type," tracks national requested gigawatts from 2014 to 2021. It documents an explosive rise in total national queue volume from approximately 400 gigawatts in 2014 to over 1,400 gigawatts in 2021, driven almost entirely by the rapid expansion of solar and storage project requests. The author emphasizes that these backlogged projects represent multiples of existing clean energy capacity, but their completion timelines remain highly uncertain.

This J.P. Morgan report page discusses the stagnant state of the United States power transmission grid and how it presents a massive bottleneck for transitioning to renewable energy. The author argues that despite grand plans to electrify households and commercial energy, actual grid growth is far too slow to support deep decarbonization goals. 

Two charts support this argument. The first chart, titled "US transmission grid growing at just 2% per year since 1978," displays grid capacity in thousands of gigawatt-miles from 1978 to a projected 2048. It highlights that the historical trend of 2% annual growth leads to an estimated capacity of around 300 thousand gigawatt-miles by 2031. However, this is vastly insufficient compared to the Princeton Net Zero requirement for 2050, which is marked as a red dot at over 1,100 thousand gigawatt-miles, illustrating a massive deployment gap. The second chart, titled "Most recent growth has been just 1% per year," breaks down the miles of transmission lines added annually from 2013 to 2020 by region, including Non-RTO/ISO, SPP, PJM, New York, New England, MISO, ERCOT, and CAISO. The total miles added annually peaked near 2,500 miles in 2013 and 2016 but dropped to just over 1,000 miles by 2020, proving that recent growth is even slower than the historical average.

The commentary shifts to examine the regulatory, legal, and local hurdles blocking expansion, specifically targeting NIMBYism and environmental groups opposing the physical infrastructure needed for electrification. The defunct Northern Pass project, intended to bring Canadian hydropower to Massachusetts, was blocked by New Hampshire, while Maine voters approved a referendum by 59 percent to 41 percent to block the New England Clean Energy Connect, despite Avangrid and Iberdrola already spending 350 million dollars on the project. Other state-level blockages include Iowa passing a law preventing the use of eminent domain for transmission lines—shelving projects meant to export Iowa's abundant wind energy to Illinois and Wisconsin—along with Arkansas blocking wind energy from Oklahoma, Missouri blocking Kansas wind power, and Colorado blocking Wyoming wind power from reaching Western states. Additionally, California's state environmental laws are frequently used to delay solar farms and transit projects, whereas Florida presents an unusual counterexample where Governor DeSantis and the legislature passed laws preventing local entities from blocking solar and renewable natural gas projects. Finally, the text notes that 39 gigawatts of coal, gas, and nuclear capacity have retired since 2013, with another 27 gigawatts slated for retirement by 2028, intensifying the grid's capacity issues.

This J.P. Morgan report page introduces introductory comments on the global push for the electrification of energy use, expressing skepticism about deep decarbonization plans that rely on rapid, widespread electrification. The author argues that over the past twenty years, electricity's share of primary energy consumption in most countries has risen by a mere two to three percentage points. While small, resource-rich nations like Iceland and Norway have reached electrification rates of twenty-five to thirty percent due to abundant hydroelectric and geothermal power, larger countries still rely on electricity for less than twenty percent of their energy needs. The author emphasizes that many energy blueprints lack real-world proof of concept.

A bar chart titled "The slow advance of electrification, 2000 to 2020" measures the electricity share of primary energy consumption from zero to thirty-five percent for various countries, comparing data from 2000 and 2020. It shows that Iceland and Norway lead the world, reaching roughly thirty-three percent and twenty-eight percent respectively by 2020. In contrast, major global economies remain heavily reliant on non-electric energy sources; the United States sits around seventeen percent, China is at approximately sixteen percent (up from less than ten percent in 2000), and Germany, India, and Brazil all remain below twenty percent.

The text goes on to discuss the immense physical scale and vulnerability of the US electricity grid, which consists of seven thousand seven hundred power plants, three thousand three hundred utilities, and two point seven million miles of power lines. Ensuring the stability of this massive network is a primary challenge for policymakers, especially as some utilities are already struggling with rising grid outages.

This instability is illustrated in a stacked bar chart titled "US reported electric disturbances by season" from 2002 to 2021. The chart shows a steep upward trend in total disturbances, which historically remained under one hundred per year prior to 2008 but surged to over three hundred and fifty occurrences annually by 2020 and 2021. These seasonal disturbances are color-coded by spring, summer, autumn, and winter, with summer and winter typically representing the largest portions of the annual totals during peak stress years.

To further detail grid performance, a scatter plot titled "System average interruption duration index (SAIDI)" maps outage minutes (annual average per customer) on the vertical axis, from zero to eight thousand, against electricity sales per utility in terawatt-hours on the horizontal axis, from zero to sixty. The data shows that while larger utilities with sales exceeding ten terawatt-hours generally keep customer outages below one thousand minutes per year, numerous smaller utilities with sales under ten terawatt-hours experienced severe, prolonged outages in 2020, with several reaching between four thousand and nearly eight thousand minutes of average outage time.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Annual Energy Paper, written by Michael Cembalest, addresses the challenges of transition to electric vehicles (EVs) in the United States and globally, specifically focusing on the slow rate of fleet replacement and the American preference for large, low-efficiency vehicles. The author argues that while global EV sales surged to nearly 9% of total vehicle sales in 2021, they still account for only 1.5% of the total existing global vehicle fleet. This discrepancy is highlighted in the first chart, "Global electric vehicle market share," which plots the sharp upward trajectory of annual EV sales share from 2010 to 2021 alongside the flat, near-zero line representing the actual EV share of the existing global fleet. 

A major barrier to rapid EV adoption is the increasing lifespan of modern automobiles. The second chart, "Cars last a lot longer than they used to," shows that the average age of US light vehicles in operation has risen steadily from under 6 years in the early 1970s to approximately 12 years by 2020. This longer useful life limits how quickly newer electric options can replace internal combustion engines on the road unless aggressive subsidies are introduced.

The US market faces additional hurdles, which Cembalest notes include low gasoline prices, high vehicle ownership, long average driving distances, and low public transit usage. The third chart, "Electric vehicle market shares in 2021," reveals that US EV sales trailed many other regions at just 4.5% of annual vehicle sales, compared to nearly 80% in Norway, over 40% in Sweden, and a global average of 9%. 

Furthermore, US consumer behavior heavily favors light trucks and SUVs over smaller, more fuel-efficient cars or EVs. The final chart, "US: top 20 vehicles sold in 2021," lists the top twenty vehicles sold by unit volume, categorizing them into SUVs/light trucks, passenger cars, and electric vehicles, while displaying each vehicle's combined city/highway mileage. The top three best-selling vehicles are all large trucks: the Ford F-Series (selling over 700,000 units with 24 mpg), the Ram Pickup (21 mpg), and the Chevrolet Silverado (20 mpg). Out of the top twenty, only one electric vehicle makes the list—the Tesla Model Y at 129 MPGe, selling fewer than 200,000 units—while the vast majority of the top sellers are low-mpg SUVs and light trucks. 

To illustrate the challenging economics of EV ownership for certain drivers, Cembalest shares a personal anecdote in a footnote about his own 2022 Jeep Wrangler hybrid. Because he only drives it about 2,000 miles per year for local fishing trips, he calculates that his payback period is 13 years, even with the assistance of a federal subsidy.

This page from the publication analyzes the impact of local objections and interconnection queue delays on the energy transition, focusing on the underutilization of wind and solar resources and the challenges of meeting electricity demands in Massachusetts and New York. The author argues that there is a severe disconnect between the transmission grid assumptions in Net Zero plans and the reality on the ground, leaving states dependent on electricity imports and fossil fuels.

The first section features two scatter plots examining resource potential versus actual generation. The first chart, titled Wind resource vs generation, plots wind megawatt-hours (MWh) per capita in 2020 on the y-axis (from 0 to 18) against the wind capacity factor for projects built from 2015 to 2019 on the x-axis (from 38% to 48%). While North Dakota leads with around 17 MWh per capita at an approximately 48% capacity factor, a highlighted red box at the bottom-left shows states like Illinois, Vermont, and Wisconsin generating under 2 MWh per capita despite capacity factors exceeding 38%. The adjacent chart, Solar resource vs generation, tracks solar MWh per capita in 2020 (from 0.0 to 1.0) against the solar capacity factor (from 26% to 32%). Nevada leads at around 0.9 MWh per capita, but a red box highlights Colorado, Texas, Idaho, and Washington, which generate virtually zero solar MWh per capita despite having capacity factors of 26% to 27%. 

The text details the consequences of these delays in the Northeast. Since Maine and New Hampshire blocked access to low-cost Canadian hydropower, Massachusetts has increasingly relied on electricity imports. The state plans to rely heavily on offshore wind, which represents nearly 50% of its long-term policy commitments. However, the author warns of potential consumer sticker shock, noting that procurement prices for offshore wind projects expected by 2025 range from $70 to $100 per MWh, compared to last year's average wholesale price of $50 per MWh. In New York, the shutdown of the Indian Point Nuclear Plant has forced the state to close its electricity gap with coal- and gas-powered imports from the PJM grid. Although construction is starting on a 339-mile high-voltage transmission line for Canadian hydro, it has taken 17 years to reach this stage and will not be completed until 2025. 

The bottom of the page features two line charts illustrating electricity generation by source in terawatt-hours (TWh) from 1990 to 2020. The chart for Massachusetts shows imports rising dramatically from under 5 TWh in 1990 to nearly 30 TWh in 2020, becoming the dominant source as nuclear and coal generation fell to zero, and natural gas declined to around 15 TWh. Wind and solar remain negligible, below 5 TWh. The chart for New York shows natural gas rising to nearly 50 TWh by 2020, while nuclear power declined to around 30 TWh. New York’s imports rose to nearly 20 TWh, hydro remained steady at around 30 TWh, and wind and solar made up a very small portion of the mix, staying well below 10 TWh.

This page from J.P. Morgan's publication addresses the critical challenge of US gasoline super-users, defined as the top ten percent of gasoline consumers who collectively account for nearly one-third of all US gasoline consumption. An accompanying bar chart titled "The US gasoline super-users" illustrates annual gasoline consumption in billions of gallons across deciles of the driver population, using July 2021 data from Coltura. The chart shows that the first decile—the top ten percent of drivers—consumes nearly forty-four billion gallons of gasoline, representing thirty-two percent of total consumption. This is more than the bottom sixty percent of drivers (deciles five through ten) combined. The text highlights that these super-users drive three times more miles than the average driver, are more likely to drive pickup trucks and SUVs, and are more likely to live in rural areas. Although they have similar income and education levels to the general population, they spend eight to thirteen percent of their income on gasoline, which is more than twice the share spent by the average driver.

The fundamental hurdle for decarbonizing US passenger travel is demonstrated through two side-by-side maps of the United States, also sourced from Coltura. The left map, showing the superusers' share of state gasoline consumption, highlights a heavy concentration of super-users in the Great Plains, South, and Rocky Mountain regions, where they account for over thirty-five percent of state gasoline consumption. Conversely, the right map, detailing EV registrations by state, reveals that electric vehicle adoption is heavily concentrated in coastal regions, particularly California, where registrations reach up to one point four percent. The central and southern states where super-users are most prevalent exhibit the lowest rates of EV registration, often at or below zero point two percent. The author points out that the EV registration map is nearly the inverse of the super-user map, highlighting a geographic disconnect between where EV adoption is occurring and where gasoline consumption is most heavily concentrated.

This page analyzes the impact of surging metal prices on electric vehicle battery costs, focusing on a hypothetical 60 kilowatt-hour battery across three chemistries: Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC), Lithium Nickel Cobalt Aluminum (NCA), and Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP). The author argues that falling inventories of key metals have driven dramatic price increases that could trigger vehicle sticker shock. While LFP batteries have risen in cost by about $500 since January 2020 due to copper prices, NMC and NCA batteries have surged by approximately $1,500 over the same period, driven by spiking nickel and cobalt costs. An additional $500 increase could affect all EVs due to copper and aluminum used for non-battery purposes. The author cautions that EV battery supply chain pressures could soon dwarf the semiconductor shortage, citing Rivian’s CEO who estimated that up to 95% of the battery supply chain needed in ten years does not yet exist. Fuel savings, estimated at about $1,250 annually under certain baseline driving conditions, can only partially offset these upfront capital premiums.

Four visual elements illustrate these points. A line chart depicting estimated metals costs per 60 kilowatt-hour battery from January 2020 to early 2022 shows NMC and NCA tracking closely together, rising from roughly $1,000 to nearly $2,500. LFP battery costs track much lower, rising from $500 to around $1,000. 

A stacked bar chart breaks down current EV battery costs, illustrating that nickel and cobalt represent the vast majority of the roughly $2,500 cost for NMC and NCA batteries. For LFP batteries, which total around $1,000, lithium carbonate and copper are the largest cost contributors, while iron and steel shares are too small to be visible. 

A bar chart showing EV metals price increases relative to a December 2019 baseline indexed at 100 reveals that lithium carbonate has skyrocketed to an index value near 600. Cobalt, nickel, aluminum, iron, copper, manganese, and steel have all risen by 50% or more, with cobalt index values nearing 300 and nickel surpassing 200. 

Lastly, a table categorizes auto manufacturers by battery chemistry. It shows that major traditional passenger EV lines—including Audi, BMW, GM, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, Ford, and high-end Volkswagen lines—predominantly use NMC. LFP batteries are favored for short-range Tesla models, entry-level Volkswagen lines, BYD, Hongguang, and Rivian’s electric trucks, SUVs, and delivery vans. NCA batteries are notably used for long-range Tesla models.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s annual energy paper evaluates the technical and economic feasibility of transitioning US residential heating to heat pumps, focusing on the role of backup systems on extremely cold days and the economic incentives for homeowners to switch. 

The author begins by evaluating whether non-electric backup thermal power is a viable solution to avoid massive electricity grid peak load increases during cold spells. Table 3 presents four scenarios based on research from Columbia University. In the current scenario, space heating is split between 20% electric resistance, 6% heat pumps, and 69% fossil fuels, resulting in 589 million metric tons of CO2 emissions. If all residences transitioned to electric resistance heating, peak load would increase in 100% of census tracts by an average of 135%. If all residences transitioned to heat pumps with no backup thermal power, 63% of tracts would see peak load increases, averaging 109%. However, if all residences use heat pumps but keep backup thermal power in place, peak load increases are completely eliminated (0% in all tracts) while residential emissions drop to 281 million metric tons of CO2. The author questions whether it is economically viable for the natural gas industry to maintain pipelines and residential infrastructure solely for backup purposes.

The discussion then shifts to the economic incentives for individual homeowners to make this transition. A second table shows that economic incentives vary dramatically by the current heating fuel type. Natural gas accounts for the largest share of the US housing stock at 56%, but only 8% of these homeowners have a financial incentive to switch to heat pumps. In contrast, homeowners using electric resistance (20% share of housing stock), fuel oil (8% share), and propane (6% share) have much higher incentives to switch, at 48%, 40%, and 79% respectively. 

The primary driver behind these low incentives for natural gas users is illustrated in a line chart comparing residential fuel prices in US dollars per million BTU from 2000 through 2020. The chart tracks three series: heating oil, propane, and natural gas. Throughout this twenty-year period, natural gas prices remained consistently lower than the other two fuels, generally staying between $10 and $15 per million BTU. In comparison, propane and heating oil prices experienced high volatility, frequently spiking into the $25 to $35 range. This price disparity makes natural gas a far cheaper heating option, suppressing the economic motivation to adopt electric heat pumps. Finally, the page includes details on the assumed upfront costs of heat pump adoption, noting equipment costs ranging from $3,300 to $4,800, plus installation and potential ductwork costs that can add up to $6,000.

This page examines the challenges and realistic timeline of the hydrogen economy, contrasting market excitement with the reality of its current fossil-fuel dependency. The author argues that hydrogen's viable use cases are much narrower than advertised and its development timeline will be long, despite being promoted as a key option for Europe to reduce its reliance on Russian energy. 

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, "The performance of hydrogen linked equities," plots several financial instruments from January 2019 to January 2022, including the Solactive Hydrogen Economy Index along with hydrogen ETFs from Direxion, VanEck, Global X, and Defiance. It reveals that hydrogen equities quadrupled by early 2021 before experiencing a sharp 35% to 40% decline. 

The second chart, "Hydrogen demand by sector," shows that total demand in million metric tons grew from about 60 million tons in 2000 to 90 million tons in 2020. This demand is almost entirely divided between refining for desulfurization and chemicals for ammonia fertilizer, with a negligible amount used in iron and steel. 

The third visual, a pie chart titled "Energy sources used to create hydrogen," breaks down the 90 million metric tons of annual hydrogen production. It shows that 59% comes from natural gas without carbon capture and storage (CCS), 21% is a by-product of naphtha reformation, 19% comes from coal, 0.6% from oil, and only 0.7% from fossil fuels with CCS. This emphasizes that almost all hydrogen is currently "grey" hydrogen, with less than 1% created via renewable-powered electrolysis. 

The fourth chart, "Share of global primary energy used to create hydrogen," tracks this metric from 1975 to 2020. It shows that the share rose from about 1.1% in 1975 to around 2.0% in 2000, and has remained largely unchanged at approximately 2% through 2020. 

Ultimately, the author stresses that hydrogen is not a native energy source but an energy carrier. Footnotes cite major hydrogen publications by the International Energy Agency, Goldman Sachs, Barclays, J.P. Morgan, and IRENA, illustrating the intense volume of research surrounding the topic.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication analyzes electric vehicle (EV) penetration by looking at both its share of new sales and its share of the total fleet size on the road. The author outlines how standard EV analyses define electric vehicles, typically including battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) because they use electric motors as their primary mover. Conversely, hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) and mild hybrids (MHEVs) are usually excluded because they rely primarily on internal combustion engines. 

The first chart illustrates electric vehicle battery capacity by type in kilowatt-hours (kWh), sorted in descending order of capacity. The y-axis ranges from 0 to 120 kWh. It shows that BEVs, represented by blue dots, have the largest batteries. Vehicles like the Tesla Model X and Tesla Model S sit near the top of the chart around 100 kWh, followed closely by the Audi e-tron, Porsche Taycan Turbo, Jaguar I-PACE, and Polestar 2, with the Tesla Model 3 and Nissan LEAF situated further down the BEV list between 40 and 60 kWh. Plug-in hybrids, shown in gold dots, have much smaller capacities, ranging from about 10 to 30 kWh, and include models like the Chevy Volt, Chrysler Pacifica, BMW i8, and Toyota Prius Prime. Hybrids and mild hybrids, shown in red and dark blue dots respectively, have negligible battery capacities of only a few kilowatt-hours or less; examples include the Toyota Prius Hybrid, Honda Insight Hybrid, and Dodge Ram 1500 eTorque. This capacity data is sourced from Car and Driver, Automotive World, and manufacturers as of February 2021.

The remainder of the page features four separate charts showcasing 2021 global forecasts from BloombergNEF (BNEF). These charts model the lag between EV new vehicle sales and the actual accumulation of EVs on the road across four classes of vehicles: passenger, light-duty (under 3.5 tons), medium-duty (3.5 to 15 tons), and heavy-duty (over 15 tons). The author notes that while BNEF's forecasts may be overly optimistic, the modeling successfully demonstrates how slowly fleet turnover occurs. 

In the passenger vehicles chart, which spans from 2015 to 2040, the EV share of new vehicle sales is projected to rise steeply to around 65% by 2040, whereas the EV share of vehicles actually on the road lags significantly, reaching only about 38% by the same year. For light-duty vehicles, shown from 2020 to 2040, the EV share of new sales climbs to approximately 55% by 2040, while the share on the road only reaches about 30%. In the medium-duty sector, new sales share is modeled to reach roughly 32% by 2040, but the fleet share on the road remains low at around 12%. Finally, for heavy-duty vehicles, the EV share of new sales is forecast to reach 27% by 2040, while the corresponding share of heavy-duty vehicles on the road rises to only about 14%.

In this section of the J.P. Morgan annual energy paper, Michael Cembalest engages in a dialogue addressing the limitations and environmental challenges of blue hydrogen and carbon capture and storage. Cembalest argues against the environmental benefits of blue hydrogen, pointing to research by Robert Howarth of Cornell University that estimates its greenhouse gas impact is over twenty percent higher than simply burning natural gas or coal directly. This elevated impact stems from the energy intensity of grey hydrogen production, carbon capture rates falling well below one hundred percent, and the substantial energy demands required to run carbon capture systems. Cembalest also addresses potential commercial solutions for utilizing captured carbon dioxide, dismissing the viability of enhanced oil recovery, which currently utilizes carbon dioxide in only two and a half percent of United States crude oil production and accounted for just zero point two percent of global emissions in 2019. Furthermore, he casts doubt on optimistic projections, such as a McKinsey forecast of over ten billion metric tons of carbon dioxide demand by 2030, and characterizes ideas of repurposing the United States natural gas pipeline network for carbon transport as highly unrealistic.

Two charts support these arguments. The first chart, which illustrates global carbon capture and storage capacity as a percentage of global carbon dioxide emissions from 2010 to 2021, categorizes capacity into early development, advanced development, construction, and operational phases. Throughout the eleven-year period, total capacity never exceeded zero point five percent of global emissions, peaking in 2011 near zero point forty-five percent, falling to around zero point two percent in 2016, and rising back to nearly zero point four percent by 2021. Most notably, actual operational capacity stayed stagnant and extremely low, consistently remaining well below zero point one percent of global emissions. 

The second chart compares the greenhouse gas emissions of blue hydrogen against direct fossil fuel combustion, measured in grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule of energy and split between methane and carbon dioxide emissions. The data shows grey hydrogen with the highest emissions at approximately one hundred fifty-five grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule. Blue hydrogen, which combines grey hydrogen with carbon capture and storage, still results in approximately one hundred thirty-five grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule due to a massive methane emission footprint of about ninety-five grams. This makes blue hydrogen significantly dirtier than direct combustion of natural gas at one hundred ten grams, coal at one hundred ten grams, and diesel oil at eighty-five grams.

This page analyzes the viability and progress of heat pump adoption in cold climates, focusing on the strong success seen in Scandinavia and the structural challenges of replicating this success in the United States and the rest of Europe. The author argues that while heat pump adoption without backup thermal power is highly successful in Scandinavia, it cannot easily serve as a template for larger, denser regions. Scandinavian homes are significantly more energy-efficient than American homes, which consume about twice as much energy and would struggle to heat safely without backup systems. Furthermore, the author highlights that Norway’s unique environment—characterized by a small population, low density, high carbon and fossil fuel taxes of approximately 130 dollars per metric ton, and a grid that is 97 percent powered by cheap hydropower—makes its model difficult to duplicate. In contrast, the rest of Europe must manage massive electricity surges on very cold days, which can reach up to four times normal peak loads. Consequently, only six percent of Europe's 240 million residences currently utilize heat pumps.

The page features two charts illustrating these dynamics. The first chart, titled "Heat pump adoption highest in Scandinavia," displays the number of heat pumps per 10,000 people across various countries using 2020 data. Norway leads significantly with approximately 2,300 heat pumps per 10,000 people, followed by Finland at roughly 1,900, Sweden at 1,800, and Estonia at 1,500. The United States sits further down the list with around 400 heat pumps per 10,000 people, while major European countries like Germany, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom have very low adoption rates, well under 200 per 10,000 people. 

The second chart, titled "Europe heat pump types," details the percent of stock across different heat pump technologies using 2018 data for ten European nations. It reveals that "Reversible air-air" heat pumps dominate the market in Scandinavia, accounting for nearly 90 percent of the stock in Norway and roughly 80 percent in Finland, Sweden, and Estonia. Conversely, central and southern European nations show different preferences; Switzerland, Austria, and Denmark rely heavily on "H-air/water" (hybrid air-to-water) systems, which make up over 70 percent of Switzerland's installations. Other categories shown in the mix include ground/water systems, sanitary hot air, other reversible types, exhaust air systems, and hybrid fossil fuel systems.

Finally, the page details Europe's ambitious policy roadmap to phase out fossil fuels for residential heating by 2040. Under the International Energy Agency's ten-point plan to reduce reliance on Russian energy, 40 percent of residential and 65 percent of commercial buildings must be electrified by 2030, requiring the deployment of 35 million new heat pumps. The author lists several expanding national combustion bans driving this momentum, including Denmark’s 2013 ban on oil and gas boilers in new buildings, the Netherlands’ 2018 ban on new gas grid connections, Austria and Norway's respective 2020 bans on oil-based heating, France’s 2022 CO2 emission standards that effectively ban mono-fuel fossil systems in new construction, Belgium's Flemish region banning fuel oil boiler installations starting in 2022, and Germany's upcoming 2026 ban on mono-fuel oil and coal boilers.

This page analyzes the viability of hydrogen fuel cells versus electric batteries for ground transportation, focusing primarily on long-haul trucking. The author notes that while hydrogen offers faster refueling and potentially longer range—making it a theoretically strong candidate for heavy-duty trucking—its massive energy conversion losses make it unappealing for passenger cars compared to electric vehicles. For instance, a comparison between class 8 freight trucks reveals that Freightliner’s pending eCascadia electric vehicle truck weighs 82,000 pounds with a range of 250 miles, whereas Hyzon’s pending hydrogen fuel cell truck claims a much longer range of 375 to 500 miles on 50 to 70 kilograms of hydrogen. However, the author cautions that hydrogen trucking technology is still in its infancy with limited track records, referencing the SEC fraud investigation of Nikola Motors as a cautionary tale. Cummins Engine forecasts that hydrogen will capture only a 2.5% share in long-haul heavy-duty trucking by 2030, placing the adoption timeline in the medium term. 

To contextualize the sector's environmental impact, a horizontal bar chart shows the breakdown of global carbon dioxide emissions from transport using 2020 data from Our World in Data. Road passenger transport (cars, motorcycles, buses, and taxis) accounts for the largest share at 45%, followed closely by road freight (trucks and lorries) at 29%. Aviation makes up 12% of transport emissions, shipping accounts for 11%, rail represents 1%, and other sources comprise 2%. 

A second diagram from the Center for Sustainable Road Freight in the United Kingdom details the compound round-trip efficiency of hydrogen in vehicles, starting with 1 kilowatt-hour of renewable AC electricity. The energy degrades step-by-step through several phases: AC to DC conversion (95% efficient, leaving 95% of the starting energy), electrolysis (75% efficient, leaving 71% energy), hydrogen compression (90% efficient, leaving 64% energy), transport and transfer (80% efficient, leaving 51% energy), and finally the fuel cell itself (50% efficient). This final conversion leaves only 26% of the initial energy to power the vehicle, a stark contrast to the 69% final round-trip efficiency reported for electric vehicle batteries.

This page presents a cautious analysis of the future "hydrogen economy," concluding that while a very long energy transition journey has begun, many proposed paths are likely to be dead ends. Michael Cembalest argues that the transition depends not only on reducing the production costs of green hydrogen but also on the massive time and cost required to build out electrolyzers, storage, and distribution networks, alongside redesigning engines to use hydrogen. While investors may find opportunities in specific pockets of modest demand over the next decade—such as natural gas pipeline blending, shipping, trucking, steel, and back-up power—future growth is unlikely to match the explosive "hockey-stick" forecasts popularized in current renewable energy literature. To illustrate that hydrogen hype has historically run ahead of reality, the author lists prominent articles from publications like Science in 1972 and 1973, the New York Times in 1988, the International Journal of Hydrogen and Grist in 1999, and author Jeremy Rifkin in 2003, all of which promised that a hydrogen-fueled future was just around the corner.

A central component of the page is a table detailing summary statistics for the hydrogen economy, showcasing significant energy conversion and transportation losses. According to the data, global carbon capture and storage (CCS) represented only 0.1% of global emissions in 2021, and the emissions potential of projects under development in the US and Europe sits at just 1% to 2% of regional emissions. In terms of energy loss, converting natural gas to hydrogen via steam methane reformation incurs a 30% loss, while alkaline and PEM electrolysis lose 25% to 35% of the energy value. Downstream efficiencies are similarly low, with fuel cell efficiency in converting hydrogen to electricity at 50% to 60%, and round-trip efficiency in transportation dropping to 25%. When liquefaction, shipping, and regasification are required for transportation, round-trip efficiency falls to 15% to 30%, with 30% to 40% of the energy lost during the liquefaction of gaseous hydrogen alone. Shipping using liquid ammonia produced from green hydrogen fares even worse, with a round-trip efficiency of just 11% to 19%. 

Finally, the page defines the hydrogen color spectrum using a color-coded visual reference. Green hydrogen is produced via electrolysis using renewable electricity, yielding zero emissions, while pink, purple, or red hydrogen uses nuclear-powered electrolysis. Yellow hydrogen relies on grid electricity, and white hydrogen is a byproduct of industrial processes like fracking. On the fossil-fuel side, turquoise hydrogen is produced by the thermal splitting of methane, yielding solid carbon instead of gaseous carbon dioxide. Black or gray hydrogen is extracted from natural gas via steam-methane reforming, whereas blue hydrogen is gray or brown hydrogen with its carbon dioxide sequestered or repurposed. Brown hydrogen is extracted from fossil fuels, typically coal, using gasification.
