This page of the J.P. Morgan report, titled Hydrogen Economy, addresses the potential for hydrogen to replace diesel fuel in non-electrified passenger and freight rail. While hydrogen-powered trains have established proof of concept in places like China, Germany, and the United Kingdom, and companies like Alstom have active order books, the authors argue that the overall global addressable market is small and adoption will be a very long-term process. This is because rail accounts for a mere one percent of global transport emissions, and seventy percent of global passenger rail kilometers traveled were already electrified by 2016.

To illustrate passenger rail trends, a stacked bar chart shows global passenger rail transport activity by fuel type from 1995 to 2016 in trillion passenger-kilometers. Total activity grew from around 2.2 trillion passenger-kilometers in 1995 to about 4.2 trillion in 2016. Over this period, conventional diesel remained flat, while electrified options like conventional electric, urban electric, and high-speed electric captured almost all of the growth.

The primary potential for hydrogen in rail lies in replacing diesel-powered freight, particularly in North America. Another bar chart tracks rail energy consumption in million tonnes of oil equivalent (Mtoe) across key regions, indicating the share of energy from diesel. North America consumes nearly 15 Mtoe, with a ninety-six percent share of diesel, primarily freight diesel. In contrast, other major regions have lower diesel shares, with India at fifty-three percent, Russia at thirty-three percent, China at thirty-one percent, Europe at twenty-seven percent, and Japan at just four percent. Although North America represents the largest opportunity, the author notes that there is currently very little movement toward hydrogen freight in the United States due to potential competition from battery-electric pathways, which offer a cost-effective alternative for existing diesel-electric trains. Aside from a small passenger rail project in San Bernardino scheduled for 2024, United States activity remains limited.

The page includes a horizontal bar chart depicting the breakdown of global carbon dioxide emissions from transport. Road passenger vehicles make up the largest share at forty-five percent, followed by road freight at twenty-nine percent, aviation at twelve percent, shipping at eleven percent, rail at only one percent, and other sources at two percent. This breakdown reinforces why decarbonizing rail is a relatively low priority for global emissions reduction. Finally, footnotes discuss catenary infrastructure, referencing a 2017 SINTEF analysis that estimated expansion costs at 55 million Euros per year, making overhead lines roughly 2.5 times more expensive than hydrogen fuel cell or battery-powered trains, despite Germany testing electric road systems for trucks.

This page argues that China's ambitious long-term deep decarbonization plans are built on extremely aggressive assumptions, given the country's immense industrial energy consumption and its profound, ongoing reliance on coal. The author positions China as the primary challenge in global energy transition efforts, pointing out that its industrial sector alone consumes four times more energy than its transportation sector and more than the combined industrial sectors of the United States, Europe, and Japan. 

To illustrate this scale, a bar chart titled "The elephant in the room: China's industrial sector" compares final energy consumption in quadrillion BTUs. It shows that China's industrial sector consumes roughly 75 quadrillion BTUs, dwarfing China's transportation sector at around 15 quadrillion BTUs and the combined industrial output of the US (about 25 quadrillion BTUs), Europe (about 18 quadrillion BTUs), and Japan (about 10 quadrillion BTUs). 

A second, dual-axis line chart titled "China & coal: declining shares vs declining consumption" highlights the divergence between relative energy share and actual consumption from 1990 to 2020. While coal's share of China’s primary energy has steadily declined from approximately 75% to under 60%, its absolute consumption in exajoules has skyrocketed from about 20 exajoules in 1990 to more than 80 exajoules by 2020. This trend is reinforced by data showing that in 2020 and 2021, China built 67 gigawatts of new coal plants—nearly double the 35 gigawatts built by the rest of the world combined—resulting in net capacity growth of 52 gigawatts while the rest of the world's net capacity declined by 23 gigawatts.

The global impact of this expansion is visualized in a stacked bar chart titled "The impact of China on global coal capacity" from 2000 to 2020. The chart demonstrates that China’s net additions consistently drive global coal capacity growth, easily outpacing retirements in the US and Europe. A fourth chart, "China coal production," tracks monthly coal output in million tonnes from 2005 to 2021, showing a volatile but clear upward trajectory from around 150 million tonnes to over 350 million tonnes. 

The author also addresses China's plans to scale up nuclear power from 50 gigawatts to 130 gigawatts by 2030. Although this is a significant expansion compared to the retreating nuclear sectors of the developed world, the text notes that these new plants will only represent about 6% of China's 2030 electricity generation and 3% of its primary energy, meaning nuclear power is not a self-sufficient solution. The bottom line of the analysis emphasizes that before evaluating long-term decarbonization plans, observers must recognize that China remains highly coal-dependent, with coal supplying roughly 60% of its primary energy compared to just 10% in Europe and the United States.

This page from Michael Cembalest's Annual Energy Paper analyzes the International Energy Agency’s September 2021 report, "An Energy Sector Roadmap to Carbon Neutrality in China." The author examines two pathways outlined by the IEA: the Stated Policies Scenario, or STEPS, which incorporates China’s explicit commitments for 2030, and the Announced Pledges Scenario, or APS, which aligns with Chairman Xi Jinping's goals of peaking emissions before 2030 and reaching carbon neutrality by 2060. The author argues that while the STEPS scenario is plausible, the rapid decarbonization modeled in the APS scenario relies on highly aggressive, potentially unrealistic assumptions. These assumptions include a major projected decline in Chinese primary energy demand, heavy reliance on prototype and demonstration-stage energy technologies, and the simultaneous electrification and decarbonization of the entire energy system.

To illustrate these scenarios, a stacked bar chart titled "China primary energy demand by fuel by scenario" measures energy consumption in exajoules from 2020 to 2060. In 2020, China's primary energy demand stands at around 145 exajoules, dominated heavily by coal and oil. Under the STEPS scenario, energy demand grows to nearly 160 exajoules in 2030 and remains at that level through 2060, with coal consumption shrinking but remaining a substantial source of power alongside expanding solar, wind, and nuclear energy. Under the APS scenario, the demand also reaches nearly 160 exajoules in 2030 but is projected to drop sharply to roughly 120 exajoules by 2060. In this 2060 APS projection, coal is almost entirely phased out, replaced primarily by wind, solar, bioenergy, and nuclear.

A second chart, a scatter plot titled "China energy-related CO2 emissions by scenario," details carbon dioxide emissions in billions of tonnes from 2015 to 2060. Historical emissions hovered around 10 billion tonnes by 2020. Under the STEPS scenario, represented by red data points, emissions peak around 10.5 billion tonnes in 2030 before steadily declining to about 6.5 billion tonnes by 2060. Under the APS scenario, represented by gold data points, emissions decline rapidly after peaking around 2025, falling steeply to near-zero levels—around 1 billion tonnes—by 2060. This comparison highlights the extreme speed of the decarbonization curve assumed in the APS scenario versus the more gradual path of current stated policies.

This page, titled "Electrification and decarbonization of everything," focuses on China's decarbonization pathway. Author Michael Cembalest expresses strong skepticism toward the International Energy Agency's (IEA) Announced Pledges Scenario (APS) for China. He argues that a simultaneous transition across electricity production, transmission, industrial production, heavy-duty trucking, and shipping is highly unrealistic, warning readers to follow actual trends rather than unrealistic projections. He notes that this projected shift would represent a massive U-turn for China, which remains the global epicenter of coal consumption.

Four charts illustrate these ambitious IEA projections. The first chart, "Electricity generation share by fuel in the APS," shows the percentage breakdown for 2020, 2030, and 2060. It depicts a dramatic decline in fossil fuels without carbon capture and storage (CCS) from over 60% in 2020 to near zero in 2060, while renewables and nuclear energy expand to dominate electricity generation.

The second chart, "China industrial final energy consumption in the APS," displays total energy use in Exajoules from 2020 to 2060 in five-year increments. Under this scenario, total industrial energy consumption peaks around 2025 at approximately 65 Exajoules and declines to under 60 Exajoules by 2060. Concurrently, the share of electricity, bioenergy, and hydrogen increases steadily from 32% in 2020 to 70% in 2060, while the consumption of traditional fossil fuels like coal, oil, and natural gas drastically shrinks.

The third chart, "Heavy-duty truck activity in the APS," measures shipping activity in tonne-kilometres for 2020, 2030, and 2060. It forecasts a virtual eradication of internal combustion engine (ICE) trucks, which account for nearly all activity in 2020 and 2030, to be replaced by 2060 almost entirely by battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and fuel-cell electric vehicles (FEVs).

The fourth chart, "China shipping energy in the APS," shows fuel consumption in Exajoules for the years 2020, 2030, and 2060. It models a wholesale transition from a sector completely dominated by oil in 2020 and 2030 to a diversified fuel mix in 2060. By 2060, total shipping energy falls to about 1.3 Exajoules, with ammonia, hydrogen, and biofuels representing the vast majority of the fuel supply, and oil relegated to a minor fraction.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, "Eye on the Market," evaluates China’s progress and challenges regarding decarbonization. The author acknowledges China's substantial achievements, noting that it has met or exceeded all carbon reduction targets in its 12th and 13th Five-Year Plans. China accounts for approximately 40 percent of global photovoltaic solar and wind capacity, half of the global electric vehicle stock, and 70 percent of global solar thermal capacity. Large-scale infrastructure projects are highlighted, such as the 16-gigawatt Baihetan hydroelectric station currently under construction and the 22-gigawatt Three Gorges Dam. The footnote notes that China has 15 operational hydroelectric dams of at least 3 gigawatts, whereas the United States has only two, including the Grand Coulee Dam at 6.8 gigawatts and the Bath County Virginia Dam at 3 gigawatts.

A detailed data table tracks China's Five-Year Plan targets and actual attainment across the 12th, 13th, and 14th cycles. For the 12th plan (2011–2015), China targetted a 17 percent reduction in carbon dioxide intensity per unit of GDP and achieved a 20 percent reduction, while solar capacity reached 43 gigawatts against a 21-gigawatt target, and wind capacity reached 131 gigawatts against a 100-gigawatt target. In the 13th plan (2016–2020), carbon dioxide intensity was reduced by 19 percent, beating the 18 percent target, while solar capacity surged to 253 gigawatts, far exceeding the 110-gigawatt target. For the 14th plan (2021–2025), China targets an 18 percent decrease in carbon intensity, a 14 percent decrease in energy intensity, and a non-fossil fuel share of primary energy of approximately 20 percent. 

Despite these successes, the author argues that China's decarbonization path will become significantly more difficult. The early successes represent the easiest phase of integrating intermittent wind and solar into the grid, whereas future deep decarbonization is built on highly aggressive assumptions. 

This challenge is illustrated by two charts. The first chart, depicting regional carbon dioxide emissions in 2020, plots the carbon intensity of primary energy against per capita emissions, with bubble size indicating total emissions. China stands out with a massive bubble representing the largest total emissions globally. Its carbon intensity is high at nearly 70 million tonnes of carbon dioxide per exajoule, and its per capita emissions sit around 7 tonnes. By comparison, India has higher carbon intensity but lower per capita emissions, while the United States and Canada have lower carbon intensity but much higher per capita emissions, at around 14 and 15 tonnes, respectively.

The second chart displays China’s primary energy consumption by fuel from 2000 to 2020. Total consumption exploded from around 45 exajoules in 2000 to over 140 exajoules in 2020. The stacked area chart clearly shows that coal is the overwhelmingly dominant source of energy throughout this period, followed by oil, natural gas, and hydropower. Although wind and solar energy have grown, they still represent a relatively small fraction of China’s total primary energy consumption, underscoring the scale of the transition that lies ahead.

This page analyzed by Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan argues that the economic slowdown caused by central bank tightening is only in its infancy, urging investors to remain patient before adding risk to their portfolios. While many Wall Street research teams and the IMF claim that inflation is peaking, Cembalest contends that we have not yet reached the peak. He supports this view by pointing to persistent supply chain pressures, an unprecedentedly tight US labor market, and an emerging wage-price spiral. 

To demonstrate the fragility of inflation forecasts, a set of three charts titled "IMF projects headline inflation to peak this summer" tracks US, European, and Emerging Market projections from July 2021 to July 2023. Comparing forecasts from October 2021, January 2022, and April 2022 against the actual current levels shows that inflation has continually outpaced expectations. For Europe, the current actual inflation rate is plotted well above the peak projected by the IMF just a month prior. 

Further evidence of domestic inflation pressure is shown in a chart titled "Evidence of a wage-price spiral in low wage industries," which displays year-over-year percentage changes from 1991 to late 2021. It shows a tight correlation between wage growth in low-wage sectors and price increases by companies employing those workers; both metrics historically hovered between 2% and 4% but spiked in tandem in 2021, climbing past 8% as companies passed substantial wage hikes on to consumers. 

This spiral is exacerbated by the tightest post-war US labor market in history, as depicted in the chart "Largest worker shortage in the post war era." By plotting job openings plus employment as a percentage of the labor force from 1951 to 2021, the chart illustrates a dramatic surge into positive territory, indicating a historic imbalance where there are far more jobs than workers. 

Additionally, supply chain blockages remain unresolved, as shown in the chart "Time required for producers to acquire raw materials and intermediate inputs." From 2000 to early 2022, the average supplier delivery time skyrocketed from its typical range of 50 to 60 days to nearly 100 days. 

Cembalest concludes that with rising food and energy costs feeding into cyclical services like airlines, restaurants, and lodging—which are experiencing 10% inflation, a level not seen since the Volcker era of the early 1980s—the Federal Reserve has a long way to go before it can halt its monetary tightening.

This page discusses how rising inflation, central bank tightening, and shifting real interest rates are driving down S&P 500 P/E multiples and stalling economic growth. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that the current market correction is primarily about overpriced multiples normalizing as real Treasury yields transition back into positive territory. He counsels patience for investors looking to add risk, noting that while the S&P 500’s 18% selloff from its peak represents about 70% of the average drawdown seen in the prior 11 recessions, US equity markets are not yet fully pricing in a recession. To support this, he cites a Goldman Sachs analysis showing that cyclical versus defensive stock pricing implies an ISM reading of 49 and flat GDP growth of 0% to 1%.

Four charts illustrate these valuation and macroeconomic shifts. The first chart, tracking S&P 500 forward P/E multiples against 10-year US real yields (based on TIPS, plotted on an inverted right axis) from 2016 to 2022, shows a strong historical correlation. When real yields fell deep into negative territory in 2020, S&P forward P/Es shot above 20x. As real yields climbed back toward positive territory in 2022, the P/E multiple contracted to around 17x. 

The second chart tracks the P/E ratio spread between growth and value stocks from 1994 to 2022 to show that investors are still paying a high premium for growth. Although this spread has fallen from its pandemic-era peak of over 10x, it remains highly elevated by historical standards, sitting around 7x to 8x compared to the near-zero spreads seen between 2010 and 2016.

The third chart presents a global manufacturing PMI leading indicator model from 2007 through early 2024. This model—which incorporates short rates, global bond yields, Brent oil prices, and the US dollar—projects a sharp decline in global manufacturing activity, forecasting a bottom of 46.6% in January 2023. 

The final chart shows year-over-year percentage changes in real values for US retail sales and retail inventories (excluding motor vehicle dealers) from 1993 to 2022. This data demonstrates that the lean inventory conditions of 2021 have vanished, as rapidly falling retail sales have converged with sharply rising inventory levels. The author warns that this combination of bloated inventories and declining manufacturing activity historically precedes significant corporate earnings declines.

This page of the publication argues that the 2022 market downturn is a valuation-driven correction similar to 1987 and 2001, potentially accompanied by a shallow recession, rather than a credit-led crisis like 2008 or 1991. Because the primary issues do not involve banking insolvency or housing crashes, the damage is concentrated in equities rather than credit markets. 

To illustrate this, the first pair of charts focuses on valuation contraction using 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios from 2006 to 2022. The first chart shows that the "Megacap 8" stocks—defined as Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Netflix, Nvidia, and Tesla—saw their collective forward P/E surge toward 45 before collapsing back down toward 25. Meanwhile, the Russell 1000 Growth, Russell 1000, and Russell 1000 Value indices experienced more modest compressions, with Value remaining the lowest around 15. The second valuation chart covers the S&P 500, S&P Midcap 400, S&P Small Cap 600, and the EURO STOXX Index, demonstrating broad-based multiple compression across capitalization sizes and European equities.

The next set of charts highlights the severity of the equity sell-off compared to the stability of the credit markets. A chart detailing stock drawdowns from their peaks shows that half of NASDAQ stocks have experienced drawdowns of at least 45%, and one-third of NASDAQ stocks are down at least 70%, with Russell 1000 Growth stocks tracking a similarly painful path. Conversely, a chart tracking the option-adjusted spread of fixed-rate preferred securities shows that spreads remain quiet. The spread, represented by the P0P1 index, sits near 200 basis points, which is dramatically lower than the 1,400 basis point spikes seen during the 2008 financial crisis. 

The final two charts focus on Chinese equities. One chart compares the China Internet Index from September 2019 onward to the historical NASDAQ composite from 1999 to 2004. The comparison reveals that the recent boom and bust in Chinese internet stocks has almost perfectly mirrored the trajectory of the classic dot-com bubble. Finally, a historical chart tracking drawdowns of the MSCI China equity index from 2007 to 2022 shows that the Chinese market has suffered a massive decline, reaching a drawdown of 49% from its prior peak.

This page serves as a diagnostic dashboard monitoring fixed-income metrics as "bear market barometers" to assess the severity of market stress in mid-2022. Across six charts, the data collectively indicates that while credit spreads and yields are rising, systemic stress remains far below the levels observed during prior recessions. 

The first chart tracks US and emerging market high-yield credit spreads from 1987 to 2022. Both the US high-yield spread (CSI BARC Index) and the EM high-yield sovereign spread (JPBYHYSW Index) have ticked upward in 2022, but they remain well below the dramatic spikes seen during previous US recessions, such as in 2000, 2008, and 2020. Similarly, the second chart shows that US investment-grade credit spreads—measured by the corporate BAA 10-year spread—have risen to 2.1% as of May 13, 2022. While this is an increase from recent years, it is notably lower than the peaks of over 3% in 2002 and over 6% during the Great Financial Crisis.

The third chart illustrates the S&P 500 leveraged loan price index from 2000 through mid-2022. The index shows a recent moderate decline, dipping to around 95 to 97, which is a mild correction compared to the precipitous drops to near 60 in 2008 and approximately 80 during the 2020 pandemic onset. The fourth chart displays US 10-year municipal bond yields from 1990 to 2022, showing a sharp spike at the far right of the timeline. The yield to worst has climbed back above 3%, while the tax-equivalent yield, assuming the top federal tax rate, has surged toward 5%, reaching levels not seen since the mid-2010s.

The final two charts focus on short-term and structured funding markets. The fifth chart details the US commercial paper spread versus the 3-month Treasury in basis points, separating financial commercial paper from asset-backed commercial paper. Despite minor upticks, both series remain extremely low and close to 0 basis points, showing none of the severe funding stress that drove spreads above 400 basis points in 2008 or 200 basis points in 2020. Finally, the sixth chart evaluates AAA asset-backed securities spreads versus Treasuries for prime auto, credit cards, and commercial real estate from 1998 to 2022. While all three categories show slight upticks at the tail end of the data, they remain tightly clustered well below 100 basis points, far beneath their historic peaks during the 2008 financial crisis when prime auto spreads alone peaked near 600 basis points.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest addresses J.P. Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon’s warning of an impending economic hurricane. Dimon’s warning is driven by the end of massive fiscal and monetary experiments, alongside the disruptive impact of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on global food and energy prices. Cembalest praises Dimon’s candid, straight-talking leadership style, drawing a parallel to Lew Preston, the J.P. Morgan CEO in the 1980s. While Cembalest agrees with the macroeconomic thesis that strong US employment, wages, and consumption cannot sustain the Federal Reserve’s interest rate unwinding and the withdrawal of fiscal stimulus, he introduces a critical timing caveat for investors. He argues that in major downturns, equity markets historically anticipate economic weakness, meaning they decline first and bottom out while the broader economy is still getting worse.

To prove this historical pattern, the page includes four charts comparing the S&P 500 index level to US GDP, where GDP is represented as an index indexed to 100 in 2012. The first chart, depicting the Eisenhower recession from May 1957 to December 1958, plots the S&P 500 on the left axis from 40 to 50 and US GDP on the right axis from 18.0 to 19.0. It shows the stock market bottoming in late 1957, well ahead of the GDP bottoming in mid-1958. The second chart, covering the stagflation era of the 1970s from June 1973 to December 1976, maps the S&P 500 on the left axis from 60 to 110 and US GDP on the right axis from 34.5 to 38.0. Here, the S&P 500 reached its low point in late 1974, whereas GDP did not bottom until mid-1975.

The third chart illustrates the 1980s double-dip recession from October 1980 to October 1983, with the S&P 500 on the left axis from 100 to 170 and US GDP on the right axis from 42.2 to 44.0. During this period, the stock market hit its trough in mid-1982, while the GDP bottomed several months later in late 1982. Finally, the fourth chart analyzes the Savings and Loan crisis of the 1990s from June 1989 to November 1991, plotting the S&P 500 on the left axis from 300 to 425 and US GDP on the right axis from 57.0 to 59.0. The S&P 500 bottomed in late 1990, preceding the GDP bottom in early 1991. Together, these charts show that in every post-war business cycle downturn, equity markets led the economic recovery, a phenomenon Cembalest suggests may be repeating in the current environment.

This page, titled "Independence Days" from Michael Cembalest's "Eye on the Market," explores the critical importance of food and energy self-reliance in an era of rising global resource nationalism. Highlighting how recent events—like Europe's energy crisis, China's trade disputes with Australia, and export restrictions on wheat and palm oil in India and Indonesia—underscore the national security risks of import reliance, the author notes that the United States enjoys a uniquely high degree of independence in food and energy relative to other nations. 

To visualize this dynamic, the page features a cartogram titled "An energy, mineral, and food weighted map of the United States." In this map, states are sized based on their 2021 production value of energy, food, and non-fuel mining, and colored based on their production relative to their population. States with the largest output surplus are colored blue, while those with the largest deficit are colored red. Consequently, Texas and the mid-Western and mid-Atlantic states swell dramatically and dominate the map in blue, while the Northeast, Southeast, and Pacific Northwest shrink into small red slivers. The map's categories define energy to include fossil fuels, nuclear, and major renewables; non-fuel mining to encompass metals and construction aggregates; and food to cover gross farm receipts. 

The author links this geographical production disparity to the Biden administration's struggle to contain historic inflation through policies like summertime ethanol increases, gas tax holidays, and potential refined product export bans. In the footnotes, the author provides two critical warnings. First, an export ban on refined products could counterintuitively raise domestic gasoline prices; refiners burdened with excess, non-exportable diesel might cut refinery runs altogether rather than store it at a loss, unless a gasoline-only export ban is implemented instead. Second, the author warns that a future transition to renewable energy could actually erode US energy independence, given China's overwhelming dominance in the production of solar modules, wind turbines, lithium-ion batteries, and EV mineral processing.

In this commentary titled "A COVID apology," Michael Cembalest reflects on the social strain of vaccine disagreements and issues a personal apology for previously disparaging a long-time acquaintance's views on vaccine efficacy. Emphasizing the value of preserving relationships over ideological disputes, he presents a bar chart from South Dakota State University showing the "Impact of COVID-19 disagreements on relationships." According to the survey, approximately 36% of respondents experienced relationship stress, 35% stopped socializing, 29% suffered damaged family relationships, and 26% lost their temper due to COVID-related disagreements. 

Despite these interpersonal conflicts, Cembalest notes that public health data strongly confirm the massive benefits of vaccines. A pair of scatter plots displays "Vaccinated vs unvaccinated total hospitalizations and deaths from November 2021 to April 2022" in Virginia, Utah, California, and Minnesota. In terms of hospital admissions per million, unvaccinated populations experienced dramatically higher rates, peaking above 12,000 in Minnesota, while partially, fully, and boosted vaccinated cohorts remained clustered far lower, mostly under 2,000. Similarly, deaths per million among the unvaccinated climbed above 2,500 in Minnesota and 1,500 in Utah, contrasted with extremely low rates among vaccinated groups. A footnote adds that in New York City, the unvaccinated hospitalization rate was 16 times higher than the vaccinated rate from February to April.

An "Omicron variant update" table compiled from Scripps Research outlines the evolution of the virus from BA.1 to BA.2, BA.2.12.1, and BA.4/BA.5. Transmissibility has consistently risen, with BA.2 representing a 30% increase over BA.1, BA.2.12.1 rising 25% over BA.2, and BA.4/BA.5 increasing about 10% over BA.2. Immune escape and resistance to monoclonal antibodies have both strengthened significantly (indicated as +++) for BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 compared to BA.1. Cross-immunity with BA.1 is reduced for these newer variants, which are dominant in US regions like New York and New Jersey (BA.2.12.1) and South Africa (BA.4 and BA.5). While 3-shot efficacy against hospitalization was 81% for BA.1 and 83% for BA.2, efficacy data for the newer subvariants is still to be determined. 

In terms of future outlook, a footnote mentions that Pfizer has tested a vaccine booster based on BA.1, with results expected by the end of June 2022 to help guide FDA recommendations for the fall. However, Cembalest raises an open question regarding the utility of these new Omicron-specific vaccines, noting that the rapid evolution of the virus may prevent strain-specific vaccines from keeping pace.

In this section of the publication, Michael Cembalest argues that equity markets have not yet hit bottom for the current cycle. He predicts another leg down in stock prices, possibly during the summer of 2022, as the consequences of fiscal and monetary policy withdrawal become clearer, alongside declines in corporate earnings and capital expenditures. Cembalest observes the first signs of 1970s-style stagflation, noting that this risk is not yet fully priced in, given that nearly two-thirds of the NASDAQ by market capitalization still trades at a price-to-sales ratio above four times. While some regional monthly PCE measures suggest core inflation may be cooling, tight supplies in the oil and gas sectors present a continuous risk of inflation spikes and recession. He cautions investors that selling now with the goal of buying back lower is a risky strategy requiring near-perfect timing, and points to the PMI and other leading indicators as the key metrics to monitor for signs of a true market bottom.

To support his analysis, the page features two charts and an accompanying classical artwork. The first chart, titled "Equity markets gag on the YUCs," tracks "young unprofitable companies" as a percentage of overall equity market capitalization from 1990 to 2022. These companies are defined as having negative net income in two of the last three years, being less than five years past their initial public offering, and showing annual revenue growth of over 15 percent. The data series shows that these companies peaked at over 4 percent of market capitalization during the 2000 dot-com bubble, fell to around 1 percent or lower for over a decade, and then surged to nearly 3 percent around 2021 before starting to decline. 

The second chart, titled "The end of the Gargantua era," spans from 1975 to projections for 2025, illustrating the massive scale of monetary and fiscal intervention that is now being rolled back. The chart plots three key metrics: the Federal Reserve's balance sheet as a percentage of GDP on a standard 0 percent to 40 percent axis, inverted real policy rates on an axis from 10 percent to negative 6 percent, and the inverted fiscal deficit as a percentage of GDP on an axis from 4 percent to negative 16 percent. The Fed balance sheet, which hovered well below 10 percent of GDP from 1975 to 2008, spiked to roughly 25 percent post-Great Financial Crisis and climbed to nearly 40 percent during the COVID-19 pandemic. Simultaneously, inverted real policy rates hit record-low negative levels of around negative 6 percent, while the inverted fiscal deficit plunged to an extreme historical low of nearly negative 15 percent of GDP. 

To visually represent this massive era of government intervention, the page includes Gustave Doré’s 1875 watercolor scene from "Gargantua," depicting a colossal giant laying on the ground surrounded by tiny people. This artwork reinforces the author's message that the giant era of fiscal and monetary support is ending, leaving investors to navigate the markets without the safety net of extraordinary stimulus.

This page presents a collection of four economic charts demonstrating that global inflation is peaking while economic growth and corporate profit indicators are declining, alongside significant pressures and regional divergences in global energy prices.

The first chart illustrates a leading indicator of global manufacturing, plotting the Global Manufacturing PMI Survey from 2007 through early 2022 and providing a projected trend through 2024. This projection, based on short rates, ten-year developed market and emerging market bond yields, Brent crude oil, and the US dollar, forecasts a sharp drawdown in global manufacturing. The model projects the PMI to drop well below the expansion threshold of fifty, hitting a contractionary trough of 46.6% by January 2023.

The second chart provides evidence of a wage-price spiral in low-wage industries, comparing year-over-year percentage changes from 1991 to mid-2022. The two highly correlated trends tracked are wage growth in low-wage sectors and price increases by companies employing low-wage workers. Both series spiked dramatically following the pandemic recovery, with wage growth climbing toward 10% and price increases tracking closely behind, indicating that rising labor costs are being rapidly passed on to consumers.

The remaining two charts focus on energy market pressures. The third chart shows the historical path of US wholesale oil prices from 2005 to mid-2022 in US dollars per barrel. After hitting historical lows during the initial stage of the pandemic in 2020, US wholesale oil prices experienced a sharp, sustained recovery, climbing back toward $120 per barrel by June 2022.

The fourth chart highlights the severe price divergence in global natural gas markets from 2019 to June 2022, measured in US dollars per million British thermal units. While US Henry Hub natural gas remained relatively cheap at $9 per MMBTU, European and United Kingdom wholesale prices spiked astronomically. By mid-2022, UK natural gas sat at $20 per MMBTU and European natural gas was at $26 per MMBTU, after both briefly spiked past $40 per MMBTU earlier in the year, highlighting a massive transatlantic energy cost gap.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest discusses the rising risks of a US recession and explains why waiting for lagging economic indicators like GDP and employment to recover before investing in equities carries a heavy opportunity cost. He argues that equity markets historically bottom well before a recession ends, meaning investors need to rely on leading indicators like Manufacturing PMI and long-term Treasury yields to identify turning points.

To illustrate this, a table titled "Waiting for Godot: the opportunity cost of waiting for economic recovery before investing" details six historical recession cycles from 1957 to 2020. The table lists the dates of equity market bottoms and GDP bottoms, showing that the gap between the two ranged from 61 days in 1982 to 182 days in 1974. By the time GDP actually bottomed, the equity market had already posted significant positive returns, ranging from 5% in 1957-1958 to 31% in 1974-1975. By the time GDP started rising again, cumulative equity returns were even higher, reaching up to 50% in the 1974 cycle and 44% in the 2009 cycle. 

To help investors spot turning points, the author introduces two charts. The first chart, "Bond yields peak prior to equity market bottoms," plots the percentage yield of the 10-year Treasury from 1950 to 2020, with vertical shaded bars representing S&P 500 Index bottoms. It demonstrates that during the secular rising-rate environment from 1950 to 1982, Treasury yields peaked precisely at the equity bottom. In the three cycles after 1982, yields began falling well before the equity bottom. 

The second chart, "Looking for turning points in leading indicators and yields," is a dual-axis chart spanning 2018 to 2022. It plots the 10-year Treasury yield on the left axis (ranging from 0.0% to 4.0%) and the Manufacturing PMI index on the right axis (ranging from 40 to 65, where 50+ indicates expansion). This chart shows that by mid-2022, the 10-year Treasury yield had spiked to over 3.0%, while the Manufacturing PMI was on a downward trajectory from its 2021 peak of over 60. The author suggests that a peak in Treasury yields coupled with a bottoming out of the Manufacturing PMI would serve as a strong sign for investors to step back into equities, even if broader economic data continue to deteriorate.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest argues that Russia’s reduction of natural gas exports to Europe is driving up German inflation and indirectly triggering a sovereign debt crisis in Italy, forcing another European Central Bank rescue program. Because Russia cut Nord Stream 1 gas flows by sixty percent, European headline inflation is projected to reach nine percent later in 2022, which is about two percentage points higher than previous European Central Bank forecasts. This energy squeeze impacts food prices as well, because natural gas accounts for seventy to ninety percent of nitrogenous fertilizer costs. 

To support this, the first chart, titled "Russian natural gas exports to Europe plummeting," tracks exports in millions of cubic meters per day on a seven-day average from January 2019 to July 2022. It shows a severe overall decline in flows across Nord Stream 1, Yamal, Ukrainian routes, and LNG, with annotations showing mid-2022 Ukrainian transit falling to forty-one million cubic meters and Nord Stream 1 down to sixty-two million cubic meters. Next to this, the chart "German inflation since 1980" plots the year-over-year percentage change for both consumer and producer prices. While German consumer price inflation remains in the single digits, the Producer Price Index has skyrocketed to over thirty percent in 2022, marking the fastest rate of growth since 1980.

This inflationary environment is creating severe problems for Italy, one of the world’s most indebted countries. Historically, Italy has relied on low interest rates to manage its sovereign debt. Cembalest points out that whenever Italy’s ten-year government bond yields drift above its nominal economic growth rate, its debt ratio rises. The chart "Italy 10 year government bond yields vs GDP" compares these two indicators from 1992 to 2022, highlighting historical periods like the Euro accession monetary tightening of the mid-1990s and the Eurozone balance of payments crisis around 2012. The adjacent chart, "Italy debt to GDP ratio," tracks Italy's debt-to-GDP percentage over the same period, showing how the ratio has escalated from roughly ninety percent in 1992 to nearly one hundred and sixty percent following COVID-19 stimulus programs. 

As yields rise and economic growth falls, Italian ten-year yields recently hit a threshold of four percent, about two and a half percentage points over German yields. In response, Cembalest predicts that the European Central Bank will announce a new rescue program, likely in July. He forecasts that the bank will attempt to sterilize its purchases of Italian debt by soaking up money supply through European bank deposits, much like the Federal Reserve’s repo programs. Ultimately, Cembalest asserts that these actions signal Italy has become a permanent financial ward of the Eurozone, which effectively deprives German savers of their own economic independence.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest evaluates mixed market signals regarding investor capitulation and examines the winding down of what has been described as the millennial lifestyle subsidy. The author begins by discussing market capitulation, noting that while some indicators suggest investors are throwing in the towel on growth investments, retail investors remain stubbornly optimistic. 

To illustrate this mixed picture, the top-left chart, titled "Signs of capitulation: stocks trading underwater," tracks the percentage of all-cap companies trading below the value of their cash and short-term investments from 1990 to 2022. This metric has recently spiked to nearly 11% in 2022, a level reminiscent of previous market bottoms in 2002 and 2008, signaling significant capitulation among growth-stock investors. Conversely, the top-right chart, "Consumer sentiment vs investor positioning," contrasts the University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment index against the American Association of Individual Investors equity asset allocation percentage from 1990 to 2022. This chart reveals a glaring divergence: while consumer sentiment has plummeted to historical lows near the 50 level, retail investor equity allocation remains highly elevated at around 65% to 70%. Although this gap indicates retail optimism, the author argues that broader capitulation is indeed occurring when considering that average stocks in the NASDAQ, Russell 1000 Growth, and Russell 2000 Small Cap indexes have fallen 40% to 50% from their peaks alongside declining hedge fund leverage.

The discussion then turns to the end of the "Millennial lifestyle subsidy," a term coined to describe how overly optimistic equity investors have effectively subsidized everyday services for millennial consumers. The author lists a prototypical millennial portfolio consisting of Casper, Peloton, Uber, WeWork, DoorDash, Lyft, Blue Apron, Snap, and Beyond Meat. The bottom-left chart, "Millennial portfolio: free cash flow," aggregates the total annual free cash flow for these nine companies from 2018 to 2021. The chart shows that this portfolio ran massive annual deficits, peaking at over $10 billion in 2019 and still exceeding $3 billion in 2021. The author notes that as investor patience wears thin, these companies will be forced to transition to profitability, which will likely result in higher prices for consumers. 

To show how these firms are trying to adjust, the bottom-right chart, "WeWork free cash flow detail," provides a case study of WeWork’s financial metrics from 2019 to 2021. The chart plots revenue, capital expenditures, cash from operations, and free cash flow in billions of US dollars. It shows that WeWork's free cash flow deficit narrowed from negative $3.8 billion in 2019 to negative $2.2 billion in 2021. However, this improvement was not driven by operational strength; operating cash flow actually worsened, and revenues declined from over $3 billion to around $2.5 billion. Instead, the deficit was narrowed almost entirely by slashing capital expenditures from nearly $3 billion to almost zero, representing a retraction of the company's footprint rather than sustainable growth. The author concludes with the observation that only two major firms, Mizuho Securities and Piper Sandler, still have research analysts covering WeWork.

This page presents a tongue-in-cheek commentary linking the volatile price history of Bitcoin to famous quotes from William Shakespeare. A primary chart, titled The Annotated Shakespeare's Guide to Bitcoin, plots Bitcoin's price from February 2017 to July 2022, tracing its rise from near zero to peaks near sixty thousand dollars in early 2021 and close to seventy thousand dollars in late 2021, followed by a sharp drop back down toward twenty thousand dollars by mid-2022. Thirteen numbered annotations on the price curve correspond to a table of literary quotes. For example, during Bitcoin’s initial ascent near twenty thousand dollars in late 2020, Malvolio's "Be not afraid of greatness" is referenced, while the first peak is marked by Prospero's "We are such stuff as dreams are made on." The late 2021 peak is matched with Julius Caesar's declaration of being "constant as the northern star," which is quickly followed by downward slides labeled with Richard the Third's "winter of our discontent" and finally Claudio's desperate "The miserable have no other medicine, but only hope" as the price plunges below twenty thousand dollars in July 2022.

In addition to this literary analogy, the page addresses the serious structural issues undergirding the cryptocurrency market, specifically focusing on the collapse of the Decentralized Finance (DeFi) lending market. The author reiterates a warning from earlier in the year that DeFi lending, which is largely comprised of over-collateralized crypto loans used to buy more crypto or extract tax-free liquidity, cannot survive a sustained decline in asset prices. Describing the DeFi market as a house of cards, the author notes that lending volumes have collapsed at the same rate as Ethereum and other token prices, leading to major failures among prominent platforms, including Celsius, Anchor Protocol, Babel Finance, BlockFi, Vauld, and Voyager.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication features commentary by Michael Cembalest assessing the Manchin-Schumer bill and the broader economic challenges of the energy transition. Cembalest argues that while the bill will accelerate the renewable transition and benefit subsidized business models, it carries a high cost and risks grid instability by prematurely reducing dispatchable power, such as natural gas. He raises open questions about the assumed energy efficiency improvements for 2030, noting that while US energy intensity per unit of GDP has fallen by nearly 30 percent since 2005, overall energy consumption has remained flat due to rising demand. He expresses deep skepticism that advanced nuclear or direct air carbon capture will materially impact greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, dismissing carbon capture as an expensive distraction despite some tech companies paying up to $1,200 per ton. Additionally, he warns that provisions increasing wind and solar subsidies tenfold—from $0.03 to $0.31 per kilowatt-hour for meeting prevailing wage and domestic content requirements—could trigger substantial inflation. 

The text is supported by two line charts illustrating the stark divergence in energy costs between the United States and Europe. The first chart, titled "The US-Europe natural gas gap," displays wholesale natural gas prices in US dollars per MMBTU from 2019 to 2022. It reveals that while the US Henry Hub price remained low at $8, UK prices spiked to $44 and European prices surged to $58. The second chart, "The US-Europe electricity gap," tracks the seven-day average wholesale electricity price in US dollars per megawatt-hour from 2015 to 2023. It shows US electricity prices remaining flat at $71, whereas UK electricity spiked to $330, and prices across Germany, Spain, and France reached $309. Cembalest uses these data points to highlight a terrifying economic and political crisis in Europe, emphasizing that European natural gas and electricity prices have risen to levels five to seven times higher than those in the United States.

This page examines energy and food independence alongside the drivers of food price inflation, contrasting the domestic resource security of the United States with that of the European Union. The author observes that while the United States has finally achieved independence in both food and energy, the European Union remains a net food exporter but continues to rely heavily on energy imports. In response to supply constraints, US farmers have requested that the USDA relax Conservation Reserve Program rules to allow planting on idle land, though the USDA has only permitted minor adjustments for contracts expiring in 2022. Additionally, US corn prices are climbing due to increased summer ethanol blending, soaring natural gas prices that drive up nitrogenous fertilizer costs, and a twenty-five percent drop in Russian fertilizer exports. Rather than lowering import tariffs, the US administration has introduced a grant program to encourage domestic fertilizer production.

Six charts support these arguments. The first two show US and EU food and energy independence as a percentage of GDP. The US chart, spanning 1975 to 2022, shows agriculture consistently maintaining a positive net exporter position of under one percent of GDP, while the energy sector recovered from a deep deficit of over negative three percent of GDP in the mid-2000s to achieve positive net exporter status around 2020. In contrast, the EU chart from 2000 to 2022 shows that while agricultural net exports remain marginally positive, the energy sector remains a substantial net importer, fluctuating between negative one point five percent and negative four percent of GDP.

The third chart tracks year-over-year percentage changes in the consumer price index for food in the US and the EU from 1970 to 2022. It highlights a dramatic dual spike in 2022, with both regions experiencing food price inflation approaching ten percent, a rate not seen in the US since the early 1980s. The fourth chart displays US corn prices in dollars per bushel from 1992 to 2022, showing a steep climb toward eight dollars per bushel in 2022, nearly matching the historical highs of 2012. 

The fifth chart shows the North America fertilizer price index, which is set to a baseline of one hundred in January 2002. By early 2022, this index skyrocketed past twelve hundred, significantly eclipsing its previous peak of approximately nine hundred in 2008. The final bar chart illustrates the combined share of global exports held by Russia and Ukraine in 2021, showing their massive dominance in sunflower seed oil at nearly seventy percent, alongside significant export shares of fifteen to twenty percent for barley, wheat, potassic fertilizer, rapeseed, nitrogen fertilizer, maize, and phosphorous fertilizer, illustrating the severe global vulnerability to disruptions in these two nations.

This page addresses US refining capacity, gasoline prices, and the challenges associated with a tight refined products market. The author argues that while US petroleum product consumption has recovered to pre-COVID levels, domestic refining capacity has fallen significantly. Refinery shutdowns have risen due to high maintenance and repair costs, declining bank lending and institutional investor interest in the oil and gas sector, widespread opposition to refinery expansion, and conversions to biofuels by companies such as Marathon, Phillips 66, and HollyFrontier. Because refinery shutdowns are costly and nearly impossible to reverse, US refineries are operating near historical capacity limits, and options for importing refined products are unfavorable, particularly as sanctions affect Russia, the world's second-largest exporter of refined products.

Several charts support this analysis. A chart comparing US refining capacity against petroleum product consumption from 1985 to 2025 shows refining capacity peaking near 19 million barrels per day around 2020 before falling sharply, while petroleum product consumption rebounded to around 20 million barrels per day. This capacity decline is detailed in a bar chart showing permanent US refinery shutdowns from 1990 to 2022, highlighted by massive spikes in 2020 and 2021 of nearly 600,000 and 500,000 barrels per day of shut-down capacity, respectively, alongside an estimated shutdown of nearly 300,000 barrels per day in 2022 for Lyondell.

Consequently, remaining refineries are running at high utilization rates. A chart tracking the utilization rate of US refineries from 1990 to 2022 shows that after a deep pandemic-era drop, the utilization rate rebounded to 93.7% as of June 10, 2022. Finding external sources for refined products is also difficult, as shown by a chart on the top exporters of petroleum products in 2021. The United States leads net exports at approximately 130 million tonnes per annum, followed closely by Russia at around 120 million tonnes, with other countries like Saudi Arabia, Korea, India, and Kuwait exporting significantly less. 

The resulting supply crunch has driven up prices and refining margins. A comparison of crude oil versus gasoline prices from 1997 to 2022 shows both retail gasoline prices and refiner oil acquisition costs spiking in 2022, with gasoline climbing past $3.50 per gallon. Finally, a chart of the US crack spread—defined as refined product prices minus refiner oil acquisition costs—from 1997 to 2022 illustrates that refining margins have reached an unprecedented peak of over $1.20 per gallon in 2022, far surpassing historical highs of around $0.75 per gallon.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest critiques optimistic projections surrounding the Inflation Reduction Act, specifically challenging the popular narrative that the climate bill is guaranteed to achieve a forty percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared to 2005 levels. He argues that the underlying models from institutions like the Princeton REPEAT project, Energy Innovation, and the Rhodium Group assume perfectly optimal human and market behavior. In reality, these projections ignore crucial bottlenecks, such as domestic content rules for electric vehicle subsidies, critical mineral supply chain constraints, transmission interconnection delays, and political gridlock surrounding federal permitting reform. Cembalest warns that overestimating these emission declines could lead policymakers to prematurely restrict the domestic natural gas industry, risking a severe energy crisis similar to the one experienced in Europe.

To illustrate these points, the page features four charts. The top-left chart displays estimates of greenhouse gas emissions declines from 2005 through 2030. While historical emissions hovered near six billion metric tons of carbon dioxide and current policies are projected to yield a twenty-seven to thirty-one percent reduction by 2030, the three modeling groups project aggressive declines ranging from thirty-seven to forty-four percent. The top-right chart puts these projections into historical context, mapping the rolling ten-year annualized rate of decarbonization. Historically, the actual rate of decarbonization has fluctuated between negative one and negative two percent, but the annual reduction assumed in the Inflation Reduction Act forecasts jumps to over negative four percent, implying a near quadrupling of the historical pace of decarbonization. 

The bottom half of the page serves as a cautionary tale using European data. The bottom-left chart shows the dramatic surge in European wholesale energy prices between 2019 and August 2022, with wholesale natural gas prices spiking toward one hundred dollars per MMBTU and wholesale electricity prices soaring to nearly four hundred and fifty dollars per megawatt-hour. The bottom-right chart details the natural gas supply-demand balance in Germany for the winter of 2022–2023. This chart demonstrates that under average demand scenarios, even with normal imports, Germany would run out of gas reserves in late winter. If Russian imports cease entirely, Germany depletes its reserves by December or January. The model shows that Germany can only successfully navigate the winter without running out of gas if it maintains a strict fifteen percent reduction in natural gas demand.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market commentary focuses on equity markets, inflation, and the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy pathway. Michael Cembalest discusses the summer 2022 market rally, noting that while equity markets had experienced a severe correction earlier in the year—with half of NASDAQ stocks down 45 percent and a third down 70 percent by May—the subsequent bounce from June lows was broader than expected. He attributes part of this bounce to short covering, noting that the S&P 500 rose 12 percent from its June lows while an index of the most shorted stocks surged 35 percent. Despite this rally, he expresses skepticism about sustained expansion in equity multiples, arguing that terminal interest rates remain highly uncertain as the Federal Reserve attempts to combat sticky, less cyclical service and housing inflation alongside elevated wage growth. 

Cembalest outlines two primary potential outcomes for the economy. While a recession remains a distinct risk due to declining new orders, high inventories, a weak housing market, and a historically strong U.S. dollar, he predicts that any downturn would be mild compared to the severe contractions of 2009 or 2020. This relative stability is supported by high private sector savings and more resilient macroeconomic cycle indicators.

Two charts illustrate these dynamics. The first chart, titled Implied Fed funds target rate: Fed vs market expectations, plots percentages on the vertical axis from 2.0 percent to 4.0 percent against a timeline extending from August 2022 through late 2024 and into the longer term. It compares market expectations derived from overnight indexed swaps against the Federal Open Market Committee's median June 2022 projections. The market curve shows expectations peaking near 4.0 percent in April 2023 before steadily declining to about 3.0 percent by the end of 2024. In contrast, the FOMC's median projections plot at roughly 3.4 percent for late 2022, peaking near 3.8 percent in 2023, falling to 3.4 percent in 2024, and settling at 2.5 percent over the longer term. 

The second chart, S&P 500 P/E closely tracking real interest rates, covers the years 2016 through 2022. It maps the S&P 500 price-to-earnings multiple based on 12-month forward earnings, ranging from 13 to 24 on the left axis, against the inverted U.S. real yield, ranging from negative 1.5 percent to positive 1.5 percent on the right axis. The real yield is represented by the 10-year Treasury yield minus TIPS-calculated inflation. This chart demonstrates a tight correlation between the two metrics, illustrating how the sharp contraction in S&P 500 valuation multiples throughout 2022 directly mirrored the rapid rise in real yields.

In a concluding footnote, Cembalest references a report released by Senator Rob Portman regarding a long-running campaign by the Chinese government to target Federal Reserve employees to acquire monetary policy secrets. Cembalest poses a rhetorical question, suggesting that the Federal Reserve's historically poor track record in forecasting inflation and policy rates might make its secrets far less valuable than foreign actors assume.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the feasibility of the Inflation Reduction Act's plan to allocate $45 billion for new IRS tax enforcement agents. Michael Cembalest questions whether the Congressional Budget Office's initial projection of $203 billion in additional revenue—which was later revised down to $180 billion—is achievable if agents follow the directive from Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and IRS Commissioner Charles Rettig to only target taxpayers earning over $400,000. 

The author notes that individual tax return audit rates dropped from 0.90% in 2010 to 0.25% in 2019 due to funding cuts and agent attrition. The first chart, titled "Audit rates by income for the 2019 tax year," displays audit percentages across different income brackets. It shows that audit rates are heavily skewed toward the wealthiest taxpayers: the rate for the lowest bracket of $1 to under $25,000 is roughly 0.4%, middle-income brackets such as $200,000 to under $500,000 dip to about 0.1%, while the rate spikes to roughly 1.1% for those earning $1 million to under $5 million, and to nearly 2.4% for those earning $5 million or more. 

Crucially, the second chart, "Estimated additional tax revenue from audit by income level," tracking the years 2010 through 2021 in billions of US dollars, reveals that the vast majority of incremental revenue from audits historically comes from lower earners. Across the decade, total additional revenue from audits fell from nearly $8 billion to roughly $4.5 billion. Throughout this timeline, the two largest stacked revenue segments consistently come from individuals earning less than $25,000 and those earning between $25,000 and $200,000, whereas higher-income brackets yield far less. Additionally, wealthier taxpayers had the highest rate of "no change to taxes owed" after an audit. 

If audit rates for those earning over $400,000 were to return to 2010 levels, which represents a seven-fold increase, J.P. Morgan estimates it would raise only $8 billion to $10 billion per year by 2031, falling far short of the CBO's annual projections. Finally, the author challenges the Treasury's estimated annual tax gap of $300 billion to $600 billion. Citing analysts at the Brookings Tax Policy Center, the text argues this gap is heavily overestimated because only 63% of recommended additional taxes from 2015 to 2019 were actually assessed after administrative appeals, and the IRS's "detection controlled estimations" methodology artificially inflates the individual underreporting gap by scaling up compliance studies using the largest upward adjustments.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, authored by Michael Cembalest, compares J.P. Morgan's 2030 energy transition assumptions with those of Group X, a modeling group that analyzed the US energy bill on behalf of the Senate. Cembalest emphasizes that assumptions regarding the natural gas share of primary energy represent a critical policy issue because they dictate decisions surrounding pipelines, electricity transmission, energy storage, export policies (especially with European demand for liquefied natural gas expected to rise 2.5 times by 2030), winter heating regulations, and decommissioning policies for coal and nuclear power.

The detailed table compares historical 2021 baseline data with 2030 forecasts from J.P. Morgan and Group X, color-coded to highlight the greatest differences, where red signals very different projections, yellow signals moderate differences, and green indicates similar outlooks. 

In the energy consumption sector, J.P. Morgan projects flat delivered energy growth and a modest 4 percent growth in electricity consumption by 2030, whereas Group X assumes a much higher 25 percent growth in electricity consumption. Electrification of final energy and industrial energy use are projected similarly by both groups. 

For fossil fuels, major disagreements emerge. J.P. Morgan assumes natural gas will command a 32 percent share of primary energy consumption and a 31 percent share of electricity consumption in 2030. In contrast, Group X models a much lower 20 percent share of primary energy and a 15 percent share of electricity consumption. Group X also projects a far more aggressive decline in gasoline and diesel consumption of negative 28 percent compared to J.P. Morgan's assumption of negative 12 percent. Both groups agree that coal's share of primary energy will decline to around 4 percent or 5 percent.

Regarding wind and solar, Group X models highly optimistic additions, projecting 302 annual average watts per capita of new solar and wind capacity from 2022 to 2030, which is far higher than the historical US peak of 197 watts per capita achieved in 2002. J.P. Morgan models a more conservative 162 watts per capita. Group X also models solar capacity additions at 6.9 times the 2019 to 2021 pace, compared to J.P. Morgan's 3.4 times pace. 

Electric vehicle assumptions highlight another stark divide. Group X models that electric vehicles will reach a 100 percent share of passenger car sales by 2030, making up 23 percent of the total fleet. J.P. Morgan projects a more moderate 25 percent to 40 percent share of sales and a 10 percent to 15 percent share of the fleet, pointing out that domestic and allied sourcing requirements for critical minerals will restrict access to the 7,500 dollar subsidies. Discrepancies are also wide for medium and heavy-duty truck sales, where Group X expects EV shares of sales to reach 88 percent and 92 percent, respectively, compared to J.P. Morgan's 28 percent assumption for both.

Among other assumptions, Group X models a massive 37 percent cumulative transmission grid growth by 2030, compared to J.P. Morgan's 10 percent, which is highly dependent on federal and state siting policies and eminent domain. Both groups align closely on nuclear energy's share of electricity at 15 percent to 17 percent, supported by Inflation Reduction Act production tax credits. On carbon sequestration, Group X projects 200 million metric tons per year while J.P. Morgan projects 150 million metric tons, noting that even 200 million metric tons represents just 3 percent to 5 percent of US carbon dioxide emissions despite 45Q tax credits.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan commentary focuses on rising interest rates, tightening financial conditions, and potential stress in the corporate credit markets. The author argues that equity markets are beginning to digest a much higher path of future policy rates. He points to additional global headwinds, including Europe’s energy crisis and China’s real estate collapse, where the bad debt ratio is at thirty percent and rising. While the author does not envision a deep US recession because consumer balance sheets remain strong, he notes that better entry points for equities likely lie ahead. 

To highlight credit market vulnerability, the author discusses the Citrix buyout deal as a potential canary in the coal mine, noting that its senior notes priced at ten percent compared to initial underwriting levels of six and a half percent. This indicates tightening credit conditions that could heavily impact other pending, lower-rated corporate buyouts, including Twitter, Nielsen, Tegna, and Tenneco. 

Three charts support these arguments. The first, titled "Fed funds target rate: current vs prior market expectations," charts expected interest rates through December 2024. It demonstrates a massive upward shift in expectations, showing the current curve peaking near four and a half percent in early 2023 before gently declining to around four percent by late 2024. This stands in stark contrast to previous curves, such as the flat September 2021 expectation of around one percent, the May 2022 peak of three and a quarter percent, and the August 2022 peak of three and a half percent. 

The second chart, "Gap between asset yields and short rates is finally closing," covers the years 1960 through 2020. It plots developed world asset yields against developed world short rates adjusted for quantitative easing. The chart illustrates how the historically wide gap that characterized the post-financial crisis decade of cheap money is rapidly closing, a shift that the author notes will force lower valuations on nearly all asset classes. 

The third chart, titled "Credit pricing," displays historical credit spreads from 1988 to September 2022. It plots the US high yield spread against the leveraged loan price index. The high yield spread is currently around six percent, and the leveraged loan index is near ninety-three. The chart shows that while credit markets have begun to soften, they are still far from the severe distress levels seen during previous downturns like the 2008 global financial crisis or the 2020 pandemic crash.

This page examines why the Federal Reserve is tightening monetary policy into a weakening global economy, arguing that the threat of a wage-price spiral is their primary concern. The author raises the critical question of whether the US labor supply can expand sufficiently without triggering a deep recession. To support this, several labor market indicators are noted: a collapsed monthly job fill rate, a record-high ratio of employment plus job openings to the labor force, a significant wage premium for job switchers, and a National Bureau of Economic Research paper that estimates the non-inflationary rate of unemployment, or NAIRU, at a historically high six percent. Additionally, about two and a half percent of the US workforce has been lost to excess retirement, COVID-related issues, childcare shortages, and lower immigration. 

Four key charts illustrate these dynamics. The first chart, showing the lowest job fill rate since the year 2000, plots jobs filled as a percentage of outstanding job openings from 2001 through July 2022. It shows a dramatic collapse in this rate, dropping below sixty percent by 2022, which is significantly lower than previous cyclical troughs. The second chart depicts the largest worker shortage in the post-war era, plotting job openings plus employment as a percentage of the labor force from 1951 through July 2022. The data exhibits a massive spike in 2021 and 2022, climbing well above the zero percent baseline to nearly five percent, indicating far more jobs than available workers. The third chart shows the Atlanta Fed Wage Tracker from 1998 to August 2022, comparing year-over-year wage growth for job switchers and job stayers on a three-month rolling average. Both series spiked dramatically after 2020, with job switchers earning a premium of around eight percent compared to job stayers who received roughly five to six percent. The fourth chart presents US consumer price inflation measures from 1985 through August 2022, comparing the Cleveland Fed median CPI, the Cleveland Fed trimmed mean CPI, and the Atlanta Fed sticky CPI. All three underlying measures synchronized in a sharp upward trajectory starting in 2021, with each measure rising into the six to eight percent range by late 2022.

The author notes that increasing the labor supply remains difficult due to stagnant birth rates, slow-to-recover immigration, and the difficulty of luring retired individuals back to work. While labor force participation has returned to normal levels for prime-age workers aged twenty-five to fifty-four, it remains depressed for those over fifty-four. Consequently, the author identifies individuals with criminal arrest records who were never convicted of serious crimes or incarcerated as one of the few remaining pools of underutilized labor.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s financial publication presents six charts, labeled Exhibits 6 through 11, that analyze macroeconomic indicators, labor market dynamics, earnings expectations, equity valuations, and historical market behavior around Federal Reserve policy shifts. 

The analysis begins with Exhibit 6, which tracks leading indicators using the ISM Manufacturing PMI new orders less production index from 2015 to 2022. The chart reveals a steep drop in this index to approximately negative four in 2022, signaling a sharp loss in demand momentum. This trend is paired with Exhibit 7, which plots the ISM Manufacturing PMI inventories index from 1980 to 2022. This index has climbed to nearly 55, indicating expanding inventories and suggesting that businesses are facing oversupply issues as demand cools.

Exhibit 8 examines the post-pandemic labor force participation rate. It splits the labor force into prime-age workers aged 25 to 54, plotted on the right axis from 79.5% to 83.5%, and older workers over 54 years old, plotted on the left axis from 38.0% to 41.0%. The data shows that prime-age participation has nearly recovered to its pre-pandemic levels, rising back to around 82.5%. Conversely, participation among workers over 54 remains deeply depressed, languishing around 38.5% compared to its pre-pandemic peak of over 40.5%, indicating structural labor shortages among older demographics.

Exhibit 9 focuses on corporate profits, presenting a leading earnings indicator model from Morgan Stanley US Equity Strategy against actual trailing year-over-year earnings growth from 2001 to 2022. The model forecasts modest downside ahead for corporate profits, as the leading indicator has plunged to negative territory at around negative 10%, suggesting actual trailing earnings growth will likely follow it downward.

Exhibit 10 displays 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios from 2006 to 2022 for the Russell 1000 Index, Russell 1000 Growth Index, Russell 1000 Value Index, and a "Megacap 8" basket consisting of Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Netflix, Nvidia, and Tesla. While valuations have compressed significantly from their late 2020 peaks—with the Megacap 8 forward PE collapsing from roughly 40 down to the mid-20s—they still remain elevated compared to the historical averages seen between 2010 and 2015.

Finally, Exhibit 11 contextualizes the current monetary tightening cycle by plotting the S&P 500 return index before and after the last Federal Reserve interest rate hike of previous cycles, indexed to 100 at the month of the final hike. Looking at the cycles of 1995, 1997, 2000, 2006, 2015, and 2018, the chart shows that in five of the six historical cases, equities performed positively over the 18 months following the final hike. The sole exception was the 2000 dot-com bust, where the S&P 500 steadily declined to an index level near 85, serving as a warning that positive post-hike performance is not guaranteed, particularly when preceded by high valuations.

This page of exhibits analyzes current US inflation trends, housing costs, wage expectations, and the historical relationship between Federal Reserve rate-hiking cycles, food and energy price shocks, and recessions. 

The first exhibit provides a table breaking down the contributions to Consumer Price Index inflation across six major categories. It reveals that while goods categories like food and energy, autos and parts, and other goods are expected to see falling forward inflation estimates due to dropping commodity prices and recovering supply chains, service sectors remain sticky. Most notably, housing, which carries the largest CPI weight at 31 percent, is projected to see its inflation contribution rise from a latest value of 3.90 percent to a forward estimate of 4.10 percent as higher market rents gradually filter through to existing tenants.

This lag in official housing metrics is illustrated in the second exhibit, a line chart indexing US home prices, observed rents, and housing CPI from 2018 through mid-2022. While the official housing CPI grew slowly to an index level of roughly 110, actual home prices and observed rents surged to index levels of around 145 and 135, respectively, signaling that substantial housing inflation pressure has yet to be reflected in government metrics.

Wages present another primary driver of persistent inflation, as shown in the third and fourth exhibits. The third exhibit charts US Business Leaders Survey Wage Expectations from 2005 to 2022, demonstrating that wage expectations spiked dramatically to near-historical highs around an index value of 65 in late 2021 and 2022. This trend is mirrored in the fourth exhibit, which compares the year-over-year percentage change of the US employment cost index and core Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation from 1980 to 2022. Both metrics have historically moved together and have recently spiked upward, with the employment cost index reaching approximately 5 percent.

The final exhibit is a historical table evaluating recessions following Fed rate hikes and food and energy price spikes from 1965 to the present. The table highlights that the US has only successfully avoided a recession during a Fed rate-hike cycle when food and energy inflation remained low, typically at or below 5 percent, as occurred in the mid-1960s, mid-1980s, mid-1990s, and late 2010s. Conversely, when peak food and energy inflation spiked to double digits, such as during the 1971–1974 cycle (22 percent inflation) and the 1976–1981 cycle (20 percent inflation), a recession always followed. For the cycle starting in February 2022, peak food and energy inflation stands at 22 percent, matching historical recessionary periods and casting doubt on the likelihood of a soft landing.

This appendix page presents a collection of charts and data tables detailing US immigration visa issuance, US arrest statistics, and international male labor force participation rates. Together, these visualizations outline trends in immigration, crime enforcement, and labor dynamics across major economies.

The first chart, located at the top left, displays US Immigrant Visa issuance from 2000 through mid-2022, indexed to December 2016. The index generally fluctuated between 60 and 100 during the two decades preceding 2020, peaking close to 110 in 2016. However, it experienced a precipitous drop to near zero in 2020, coinciding with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent border restrictions, before staging a sharp recovery back to approximately 90 by 2022. 

To the right, a line chart illustrates the share of US drug offense arrests by type from 1994 to 2015. It highlights a growing divergence: arrests for drug possession steadily rose from under 70% of all drug arrests in 1994 to over 80% by 2015, while arrests for drug manufacturing declined from roughly 25% to around 15% over the same period. 

Supporting this crime data, a detailed table in the center of the page breaks down US arrests by type and their share of total arrests between 2014 and 2016. Drug abuse represents the single largest individual arrest category listed at 12.0%, followed closely by property crime at 11.3%, larceny at 8.9%, other assaults at 8.4%, and driving under the influence (DUI) at 8.4%. When aggregated into subtotals, property crime categories make up 24.9% of arrests, violent crimes account for 17.5%, DUIs and related liquor/disorderly categories comprise 16.9%, and drug/vandalism categories make up 14.3%, with other unspecified offenses accounting for the remaining 26.4%.

The bottom half of the page focuses on labor demographics. The bottom-left line chart tracks male labor force participation rates for prime-age workers (ages 25-54) from 1970 to 2020 across several major nations, including Japan, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Spain, Canada, South Korea, the United States, and Italy. Nearly all these countries have seen a long-term decline in prime-age male labor participation over the last fifty years.
