Japan maintains one of the highest rates, remaining above 95% in 2020, whereas the United States and Italy have fallen toward the bottom of the group, hovering around 88% to 89% in 2020. 

The final bar chart at the bottom right contextualizes this by comparing the broader OECD male labor force participation rate (ages 15-64) across dozens of countries in 2021. Iceland boasts the highest participation rate, approaching 88%, followed closely by Switzerland, the Netherlands, and Japan. The United States is highlighted in red, sitting in the lower third of the ranked countries with a participation rate of approximately 73%. This puts the US behind the overall OECD average and well below peers like Canada and the United Kingdom, though still ahead of countries at the far right of the chart like France, Belgium, and Italy, the latter of which sits near the bottom at roughly 67%.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market," authored by Michael Cembalest, argues that despite prevailing bearish sentiments and a "litany of gloom" regarding valuations, inflation, monetary policy, and other economic headwinds, historical patterns show that equities consistently bottom several months before other economic indicators—such as corporate earnings, GDP, and payrolls—reach their nadir during recessions. 

To illustrate this trend, the author presents four historical charts comparing the S&P 500, GDP, S&P 500 earnings (represented as a rolling four-quarter average), and payrolls across different recessionary periods, with each metric indexed to 100 at the start of the tracked period. 

The first chart, titled "Eisenhower recession" (indexed to June 1957 and spanning June 1957 to June 1959), shows the S&P 500 bottoming in December 1957 at an index level of around 88. In contrast, GDP and payrolls did not begin to recover until mid-1958, and corporate earnings did not bottom until late 1958, nearly a year after equities. 

The second chart focuses on the "Stagflation era of the 1970's" (indexed to June 1973 and tracking data through December 1976). Here, the S&P 500 plummeted to its bottom around December 1974 at an index value near 65, while GDP and payrolls lagged to their lowest points in mid-1975, and corporate earnings did not bottom until mid-1976. 

The third chart examines the "1980's double-dip recession" (indexed to December 1980 and tracking data through January 1985). In this cycle, the S&P 500 hit its bottom in mid-1982 at around 83, whereas GDP and payrolls did not turn around until late 1982 and early 1983, respectively, and earnings lagged further, bottoming in late 1983. 

Finally, the fourth chart illustrates the "S&L crisis of the 1990's" (indexed to December 1989 and running through January 1993). The S&P 500 bottomed near October 1990 at approximately 90, whereas GDP, payrolls, and earnings all lagged, bottoming roughly a year later between late 1991 and early 1992. 

All charts utilize data sourced from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, Bloomberg, Robert J. Shiller, S&P Dow Jones, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management to reinforce the author's point that equities are a leading indicator that bottoms well ahead of fundamental economic data.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest critiques the media tendency to hold up small, high-renewable-energy nations as sustainability models for the rest of the world, a phenomenon he labels the Pitcairn Problem. Referencing a New York Times article praising Uruguay, he argues that the unique conditions enabling these tiny nations to achieve high renewable shares do not translate to larger, developed, or developing economies. These small countries generally benefit from small shares of global GDP, low population densities that ease wind and solar siting, and small land areas that minimize transmission investment. Furthermore, they often have lower economic complexity, abundant pre-existing hydroelectric resources, unique geothermal assets, or high-energy-return biomass. He also notes that countries like Uruguay and Denmark rely on biomass for backup and benefit from proximity to large neighbors, such as Brazil and Germany, for grid stabilization. 

To support this argument, a comprehensive Energy Profiles table compares three cohorts: high renewable share countries, large developed countries, and large developing countries. The data demonstrates a stark contrast in renewable electricity generation. While the high renewable group boasts total renewable electricity shares of 80% to 100%—including Uruguay at 94%, Iceland and Costa Rica at 100%, and Norway at 98%—large developed nations lag far behind, with the United States and Japan at 20% and Germany at 45%. Large developing countries show similarly low renewable electricity shares, such as China at 28%, India at 18%, and South Korea at 6%, with Brazil as a major hydro-heavy exception at 84%. 

The table also highlights structural discrepancies in scale and economic demand. The high renewable nations represent miniscule shares of global GDP, mostly 0.5% or lower, and have small populations, with Uruguay at 3 million and Norway at 5 million. In contrast, the United States represents 24% of global GDP with a population of 337 million, and China represents 18% of global GDP with 1.4 billion people. Additionally, highly industrialized economies show much higher economic complexity scores, such as Japan at 100 and the US at 92, compared to renewable leaders like Uruguay at 52 or Mozambique at 13. Cembalest concludes that larger, industrialized nations must pursue a renewable future that depends heavily on wind and solar, creating distinct challenges around raw materials, transmission, and thermal backup power, which he promises to address in the next annual energy paper.

This J.P. Morgan report page analyzes historical market cycles to project when the S&P 500 might bottom during the late 2022 bear market. Michael Cembalest argues that the current economic downturn—labeled as the "Negative real rate experiment implodes as inflation returns"—will likely follow historical precedents where equity markets bottom out well before economic indicators like corporate profits, GDP, and payrolls stop deteriorating. The dot-com collapse is highlighted as the key historical outlier because earnings declines actually preceded the equity market decline. For the current cycle, Cembalest suggests that the ISM manufacturing survey bottom will roughly coincide with the equity market bottom, pointing to an S&P 500 range of 3200 to 3300 as a highly attractive entry point for long-term investors if reached during the fall or winter of 2022.

The analysis is supported by four charts comparing the trajectories of the S&P 500, GDP, Payrolls, and Earnings (as represented by rolling four-quarter average S&P 500 earnings per share), with each cycle indexed to 100 at its start. The first chart, depicting the Global Financial Crisis starting in March 2007, shows the S&P 500 index bottoming sharply in early 2009 at around 60, followed by a GDP bottom in mid-2009, and trailing bottoms in corporate earnings and payrolls that extended into late 2009 and early 2010. The second chart focuses on the Global COVID pandemic starting in December 2019, illustrating a sharp V-shaped crash where equities bottomed in April 2020, followed immediately by GDP and payrolls, while earnings continued to decline before finally bottoming at an index level of 87 in late 2020. The third chart highlights the Dot-com bubble recession starting in December 1999, showing that corporate earnings fell significantly before the equity market peak, and equities did not bottom until late 2002, long after the mild recession and the ISM bottom had passed. The fourth chart illustrates the current cycle from June 2021 through October 2022, displaying a sharp decline in the S&P 500 to an index level near 85, while payrolls and earnings remain historically elevated, suggesting the lag in the real economy has yet to play out.

A supporting table compares the historical timing of equity market bottoms to ISM manufacturing bottoms across seven major recessions. In the Eisenhower recession, the equity market bottomed on December 31, 1957, one month before the ISM bottom on January 31, 1958. During the 1970s stagflation era, the equity bottom on September 30, 1974, preceded the ISM bottom on January 31, 1975, by four months. In the 1980s double-dip recession, the equity bottom occurred on July 31, 1982, two months after the ISM bottom on May 31, 1982. During the Savings and Loan crisis of the 1990s, the equity bottom on October 31, 1990, led the ISM bottom on January 31, 1991, by three months. For the Dot-com bubble, the equity bottom on September 30, 2002, lagged the ISM bottom on October 31, 2001, by eleven months. In the Global Financial Crisis, the equity bottom on February 28, 2009, lagged the ISM bottom on December 31, 2008, by two months. Finally, during the Global COVID pandemic, the equity market bottomed on March 31, 2020, just one month before the ISM bottom on April 30, 2020.

This page presents six appendix charts illustrating that US financial and economic indicators are generally downbeat, characterized by aggressive monetary tightening, elevated inflation, deteriorating affordability, and a historically tight labor market. 

The first chart tracks the year-over-year percentage change in the US dollar from 1990 to 2022, demonstrating that the current dollar surge of nearly 20% matches levels historically associated with major global crises. Notable past crises highlighted on the chart include the Mexican debt crisis, Russian default, the tech bubble recession, the housing bubble peak, the Great Financial Crisis, the sovereign debt crisis, and the Chinese devaluation. 

The second chart displays various US consumer price inflation measures from 1985 to 2022, plotting year-over-year percentage changes. The Cleveland Fed median CPI, the Cleveland Fed trimmed mean CPI, and the Atlanta Fed sticky CPI have all surged in tandem to between 6% and 7% by late 2022, reaching their highest levels since the late 1980s and early 1990s.

The third chart focuses on corporate earnings, comparing actual year-over-year trailing earnings growth to two leading indicator models. While actual trailing earnings growth remained positive at the time of publication, both J.P. Morgan leading indicator models are pointing sharply downward, projecting a contraction into negative territory for the near future.

The fourth chart contextualizes the Federal Reserve's current monetary policy by comparing the 2022 tightening cycle to previous historical cycles since 1958. Measuring the change in basis points against the number of months since the first tightening action, the chart shows that the 2022 cycle is exceptionally steep, spiking over 300 basis points in under a year. Market expectations derived from Overnight Interest Swaps suggest this aggressive path will plateau and slightly decline over the subsequent 36 months.

The fifth chart shows the US housing affordability index from 1970 to 2022. The index has collapsed from its high point near 200 down to approximately 100, indicating that US housing is less affordable than at any point since the late 1980s. 

The final chart measures the US worker shortage from 1951 to 2022 by calculating job openings plus employment as a percentage of the labor force. The metric has surged well above the 0% equilibrium line to nearly 3%, marking the largest post-war worker shortage in history, where available jobs vastly outnumber available workers.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market, written by Michael Cembalest, provides a preliminary assessment of the 2022 midterm election results, titled Little Red Wagon. The author argues that while midterm losses for the President's party are often expected during weak economic times, history shows that voter behavior is frequently driven by non-economic factors. Historical examples include the 1922 midterms under President Warren G. Harding where prohibition backlash led to a loss of 77 Republican seats despite good market conditions; the 1942 midterms where FDR's Democrats lost 45 seats due to early World War II frustrations and wage/price controls; and the 1966 midterms when Vietnam War concerns and New Deal backlash cost Democrats 47 seats despite favorable economic trends. 

The accompanying bubble chart is titled Midterm White House party losses since 1910 adjusted for economic & market conditions. The vertical axis represents an economic index of employment, wages, and inflation, ranging from 0 (worst) to 100 (best). The horizontal axis shows market performance, measured by the trailing two-year real return on equities, home prices, and government bonds, ranging from minus 30 percent to positive 30 percent. Each bubble's color represents the incumbent president's party—blue for Democrats and red for Republicans—while the bubble size and label indicate the year and the number of House seats lost. For instance, in the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 seats (R-41) despite strong market and economic conditions. 

The 2022 forecast, indicated by a blue bubble labeled D-11, is based on the New York Times needle forecast as of November 9, 2022. It shows a projected loss of only 11 seats for the Democrats, which sits in the lower-left quadrant representing poor economic conditions (an index value of about 35) and negative market returns (around minus 15 percent). Cembalest notes that if this projected loss holds, the President’s party will have performed significantly better than historically expected given the adverse economic climate. 

Regarding predictions and market outlook, the author states that the projected seat changes would lead to the GOP regaining control of the House by a very narrow margin, comparable to the slim governing margin Democrats held previously. Cembalest asserts that the market consequences of the midterms will likely be negligible due to broader business cycle dynamics already at play. At the time of writing, the Senate remained a toss-up, and final conclusions were pending the outcomes of five unresolved races. Data sources cited for the chart include Robert Shiller, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Christina Romer, John Pencavel, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management, excluding the midterm years of 1934, 1998, and 2002 when the President's party gained seats.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" by Michael Cembalest focuses on the dramatic repricing of highly speculative and unprofitable companies during 2022, drawing direct parallels to the post-2000 dot-com market crash. The author introduces the topic with a satirical cartoon of a bored ape holding a burning dollar bill, labeled as an "APE Innovation ETF" non-fungible token, pointing out that virtual real estate trading volumes and prices have collapsed by 98% and 88% from their peaks despite a McKinsey estimate that $120 billion has been invested in the Metaverse. Cembalest argues that the 2019–2022 cycle was particularly irrational because market participants ignored the clear historical precedent of the dot-com bubble, noting that roughly 60% to 70% of the recent market surge has now been reversed.

Three charts support this analysis. The first chart, titled "Dumb and Dumber," plots index values from 2019 to 2022 against the historical NASDAQ 100 trajectory from 1998 to 2003. The chart illustrates an extraordinarily close correlation: the index of profitless innovations—including Metaverse, Hydrogen, Fintech, SPACs, crypto, software, e-commerce, and biotech—peaked at over 450 in early 2021 before crashing down toward 150 by late 2022, mimicking the rise and fall of the NASDAQ 100 two decades prior.

The second chart, "The YUCs: Young Unprofitable Companies," measures these companies as a percentage of total equity market capitalization from 1990 through late 2022. Defined as businesses with less than five years since their IPO, annual revenue growth above 15%, and negative net income in two of the last three years, YUCs peaked at roughly 4.5% of market cap during the 2000 dot-com peak. This metric rose again to over 3% during the recent pandemic-era bubble before falling sharply back toward 1.5%.

The final chart, "The MUCs: Megavalued (P/E >50x) or Unprofitable Companies," measures their share of total US market capitalization. This series peaked at over 40% in 2000, declined to a low of approximately 10% around 2010, and surged again to nearly 35% in late 2020 and 2021. By late November 2022, the MUC share had fallen back to roughly 18%, illustrating the massive scale of the recent market correction.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, authored by Michael Cembalest, highlights the high efficacy of mRNA vaccines in reducing COVID-19 mortality risk, even as vaccine immunity wanes and new variants like BQ.1.1 and XBB show resistance to monoclonal antibody treatments such as Bebtelovimab and Evusheld. Cembalest points out that bivalent booster uptake in the United States is quite low, ranging from 12% to 15%, which ranks the US 73rd globally. He calls for the development of nasal delivery vaccines and pan-coronavirus vaccines to better prevent transmission and infection. 

To support the argument that vaccines save lives, the page presents four charts. The top-left chart displays US COVID-19 deaths per 100,000 people aged six months and older from April 2021 to July 2022. It demonstrates a massive gap between the unvaccinated population, whose death rate peaked near 27 deaths per 100,000 around January 2022, and the vaccinated population, whose death rate consistently hovered close to zero. 

The top-right chart focuses on US COVID-19 deaths per 100,000 people aged 50 and older from April 2022 to August 2022, illustrating a clear gradient of protection. Unvaccinated individuals in this older demographic suffered a death rate that peaked near 11 per 100,000, while those with a primary series only, primary series plus one booster, and primary series plus two or more boosters saw progressively lower mortality rates, with the doubly-boosted group keeping death rates near 1 per 100,000.

The bottom-left chart shows cumulative preventable US COVID-19 deaths among adults aged 18 and older from January 2021 to April 2022. It compares the actual cumulative deaths of 641,305 against an estimated 322,324 deaths that would have occurred if 100% of adults had been fully vaccinated, indicating that nearly half of these deaths were preventable. 

The bottom-right chart tracks age-adjusted all-cause excess death rates by registered political party from January 2018 to January 2022. While the excess death rates of registered Republicans and Democrats tracked closely prior to the wide availability of vaccines, they diverged significantly after mid-2021. During the late 2021 and early 2022 wave, the excess death rate for Republicans spiked to nearly 40%, whereas the rate for Democrats peaked at roughly 15%. 

Finally, a detailed footnote explains that reported COVID-19 death statistics are often unreliable due to poor data collection, particularly in developing nations. The author suggests using all-cause mortality instead, noting that true excess death rates are estimated to be 1.3 times higher than reported COVID-19 death rates in high-income countries, 3 times higher in middle-income countries, and 6 times higher in lower-income countries.

This J.P. Morgan report examines the passage of the US CHIPS and Science Act of 2022, analyzing its relative bipartisanship, the high costs of semiconductor self-sufficiency, and China's extreme reliance on Taiwan for advanced microchips. 

The first chart, titled "Semiconductor bill spending and estimated amounts required for US self-sufficiency," contrasts the funding of the US CHIPs bill, which allocates less than one hundred billion dollars, against the estimated amount needed for full US semiconductor self-sufficiency, which sits between four hundred billion and five hundred billion dollars. This indicates that the federal bill, while significant, is only a fraction of what is required for total domestic independence.

The second chart, titled "Partisanship gap for major US legislation," displays the average difference in "yea" votes between parties in the House and Senate for major bills passed since 2001. The data shows a stark rise in political polarization over the last two decades. While the Patriot Act of 2001 and the Coronavirus CARES Act of 2020 had very low partisan gaps, recent landmark bills like the 2021 American Rescue Plan and the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act recorded a maximum one hundred percent partisanship gap, meaning they passed without a single opposition party vote. In contrast, the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 registers a much lower partisanship gap of around sixty-eight percent, highlighting its rare status as a highly bipartisan achievement supported by seventeen Republican Senators and twenty-four Republican House members.

The report also addresses global supply chain vulnerabilities, specifically focusing on China's massive reliance on Taiwan. China accounts for sixty percent of global semiconductor demand, yet only ten percent of this demand is satisfied by Chinese domestic production. Taiwan accounts for seventy percent of China's chip consumption, with TSMC producing ten percent inside China and exporting sixty percent directly from Taiwan. This seventy percent reliance is unprecedented for a high-value import, far exceeding Europe's pre-war reliance on Russian energy, which stood at twenty-five percent in 2021.

A third chart, "TSMC semiconductor capabilities," tracks the rapid progression of chip miniaturization in nanometers from 1987 to 2022. The line shows TSMC shrinking its fabrication capabilities from three thousand nanometers in 1987 down to one hundred thirty nanometers in 2002, twenty-eight nanometers in 2012, and ultimately reaching five nanometers in 2022. While most Chinese foundries are currently limited to producing fourteen to twenty-eight nanometer chips, global leaders like TSMC are already fabricating at five to seven nanometers. 

The author outlines the severe technical barriers to catching up in this space, noting that advanced chips at ten nanometers and below can only be produced using specialized extreme ultraviolet photolithography machines made by the Dutch company ASML. ASML only produces forty-five to fifty-five of these complex machines per year. Furthermore, the manufacturing process requires specialized clean rooms that are ten thousand times cleaner than hospital surgical rooms, involves up to seven hundred separate fabrication steps over several weeks, and depends on global logistics networks spanning thousands of miles to transport exotic chemicals, gasses, and rare metals.

This page analyzes the market's ongoing rotation from speculative digital and "innovation" assets back into physical and old-economy assets, driven by the normalization of monetary and fiscal policy after a long period of negative real interest rates and high fiscal deficits. The author observes that real-world traditional energy, pipeline, and agricultural sectors are outperforming renewable energy and highly valued speculative tech stocks. 

This trend is illustrated in the first chart, "The Tortoise and the Hare," which tracks performance indexed to December 2016. It shows the ARK Innovation ETF peaking near an index level of 800 in early 2021 before tumbling to below 200 by late 2022. In contrast, an "old economy basket" composed of farm equipment, industrial REITs, and office cleaning supplies and uniforms rose steadily, eventually overtaking the ARK ETF in late 2022 at an index level of over 400. 

A second chart, titled "Reports of my death were greatly exaggerated," displays the annual returns of traditional energy versus renewables in 2021 and 2022. In 2021, the MSCI World Energy Index, representing oil, gas, and pipelines, returned nearly 40% while a composite of major clean energy indices, including the NASDAQ Clean Edge, Wilderhill Clean Energy, and others, fell roughly 13%. This gap widened in 2022, with traditional energy surging over 50% and the renewables composite falling another 12%.

The author argues that investors and politicians critically underestimated Russia’s energy importance by focusing too much on its historically low share of world GDP, which currently sits at just 3%. This miscalculation was tied to a broader underappreciation of thermal energy and fertilizer relative to wind and solar. To illustrate this historical context, a line chart titled "Russia/USSR share of World GDP since 1820" shows Russia's global GDP share starting at around 5% in 1820 as it added Georgia, Dagestan, Azerbaijan, and Armenia. It rose to around 8% by 1913, fell during the creation of the USSR, and peaked at nearly 16% following postwar Soviet annexations of Eastern Europe before plummeting to its current 3% level after the 1991 dissolution. 

This geopolitical realignment is further detailed in a chart showing "Cross-border syndicated loans to Russia" in billions of US dollars from 2010 to 2022. Following Russia's invasion of Crimea in 2014, Western nations, including France, Germany, Italy, Great Britain, the United States, and Japan, sharply curtailed their syndicated lending to Russia, with most dropping well below $12 billion. Conversely, China’s syndicated loans to Russia rose dramatically from around $24 billion in 2014 to nearly $50 billion by 2022. 

Looking forward, the author notes that European nations are pivoting back toward energy security, with Germany building floating liquefied natural gas regasification units and France planning a substantial nuclear renaissance, while China imports record amounts of Russian coal and gas. Despite Russia’s ongoing attacks on Ukraine's power grid, the author suggests a future ceasefire could be partially driven by Europe’s pragmatic need to regain access to Russian land-based oil and natural gas pipelines, given the physical damage to the Nord Stream pipelines. The page ends with a transition to three core rules for investors navigating the year ahead.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest presents a sharp critique of the cryptocurrency industry and its political supporters in the wake of the FTX collapse. He argues that accusing the Securities and Exchange Commission and Commissioner Gary Gensler of failing to regulate the sector is hypocritical. To demonstrate this, he outlines the Gensler Rule, a set of criteria that critics must meet to have a valid grievance. These conditions include acknowledging that most cryptocurrencies are securities under the classic Howey test, supporting the SEC's numerous enforcement actions against firms like Grayscale, LBRY, and Coinbase, and admitting that US investors use offshore exchanges—such as FTX's offshore unit, which handled about sixty percent of US crypto derivative trades—to evade domestic rules rather than because of a lack of regulatory clarity. 

Cembalest highlights the political and corporate lobbying that historically pushed back against SEC oversight, pointing out that several members of Congress who criticized the SEC had previously received campaign contributions from major crypto and venture capital firms like Coinbase, Ripple, and Andreessen Horowitz, or had formally complained that SEC inquiries into FTX were too burdensome. He emphasizes that the crypto industry has consistently litigated against anti-fraud reporting requirements, such as those in the 2021 Infrastructure Act. 

To the right of the text is a visual showing the cover of a J.P. Morgan report from February 2022 titled "The Maltese Falcoin: On cryptocurrencies and blockchains." The black-and-white, film-noir style illustration depicts a nervous man in a suit clutching a physical Bitcoin coin as if it were the titular Maltese Falcon treasure, while a classic detective in a trench coat and fedora looms behind him in the shadows. Cembalest concludes by urging readers to compare this skeptical perspective with Sequoia Capital's highly laudatory, archived profile of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried to see two vastly different views of the crypto market.

Michael Cembalest introduces the J.P. Morgan Asset Management 2023 Outlook, titled "The End of the Affair," by arguing that the major catalysts of the previous decade's bull market—such as Federal Reserve quantitative easing, Modern Monetary Theory, profitless innovation, negative real rates, and unregulated cryptocurrency—are coming to an end. He warns of an impending growth slowdown in both the United States and Europe but cautions investors against becoming overly bearish as markets decline. Based on historical recessionary trends, Cembalest asserts that equity markets typically bottom well before lagging economic indicators like GDP, payrolls, S&P 500 earnings, and housing starts hit their respective lows. He specifically forecasts that equity markets will find a bottom in the first half of 2023, that the October 2022 lows will hold, and that US inflation will cool sufficiently to allow the Federal Reserve to pause its rate hikes at 5% in the spring of 2023.

Supporting this outlook is a multi-era line chart titled "When recessions occur, the ISM survey has been the best coincident indicator of a bottom in equities." The chart's vertical axis displays the S&P 500 index, normalized to 100 at the start of each recessionary period, while the horizontal axis tracks timeline intervals across seven historical downturns: the Eisenhower recession (1957–1959), Stagflation (1973–1976), the Double dip recession (1981–1983), the S&L recession (1990–1992), the DotCom collapse (2000–2003), the Great Financial Crisis or GFC (2007–2011), and the COVID-19 recession (2020). Colored markers on the S&P 500 trend line plot exactly when various key economic indicators bottomed relative to the stock index. These series include the ISM survey (represented by a dark blue circle), GDP (gold circle), payrolls (white square), S&P earnings (red circle), housing starts (light blue triangle), and real estate delinquencies (yellow circle).

The visual data demonstrates that with the sole exception of the 2001 dot-com collapse, the equity market consistently bottoms far earlier than hard economic measures. Crucially, the ISM survey marker aligns almost perfectly with the absolute troughs of the S&P 500 line across nearly every cycle. In contrast, indicators such as S&P Earnings, GDP, and real estate delinquencies lag considerably, often bottoming months or even years after the stock market has begun its recovery. This lag is especially stark in the stagflation era of the mid-1970s and the GFC, where S&P earnings bottomed near the absolute end of the charted periods, well after equities turned upward. In the brief COVID-19 recession of 2020, the ISM, payrolls, and housing starts all bottomed simultaneously at the nadir of the sharp market downturn. The chart reinforces the author's primary argument that monitoring the ISM survey, rather than backward-looking employment or GDP data, is the most reliable way to identify when equity markets have reached a bottom.

In this J.P. Morgan publication, Michael Cembalest argues that declining leading indicators point to a significant economic slowdown across both the United States and Europe, which is poised to drag corporate profits down regardless of whether a technical recession occurs. He expects manufacturing surveys to bottom out in the first half of 2023 at levels higher than the lows seen in 2008 and 2020, suggesting a milder downturn than the previous two recessions, alongside an anticipated 10% to 15% year-over-year decline in S&P 500 earnings for 2023. In Europe, soaring energy costs are crowding out consumer spending, and despite government efforts to cushion these impacts, households face substantial bill increases. Meanwhile, core inflation in Europe remains high at 5%, prompting the European Central Bank to tighten monetary policy amidst economic weakness.

The page features four charts illustrating these macro trends. The first, titled "US new orders less inventories predicting ISM downturn," spans 1983 to 2023 and compares the ISM manufacturing PMI composite index against a three-month leading indicator of new orders minus inventories. The sharp drop in the leading indicator points to an impending contraction in the ISM index below the 50-expansion threshold. The second chart, "EU new orders less inventories predicting PMI downturn," shows a parallel trend for Europe from 1997 to 2022, where the leading indicator has plummeted, signaling a deep downturn for the EU manufacturing PMI.

The third chart, "Leading earnings indicators point to S&P 500 earnings decline," covers 2001 to 2022 and maps trailing year-over-year S&P 500 earnings, which stood at 14% in late 2022, against two predictive models. Model one incorporates manufacturing PMI, business surveys, credit spreads, and housing starts, while model two analyzes business surveys, supplier deliveries, wage trackers, inflation, and a cyclical GDP indicator. Both models dive sharply below zero, indicating that S&P 500 earnings growth is headed for a steep contraction.

The final chart, "Europe's energy bill goes off the rails," displays net exports of energy products as a percentage of GDP from 1978 to 2022. This chart highlights a stark divergence between the US and the EU: while the US has risen to become a net energy exporter at roughly 0.5% of GDP, the EU's net energy imports have plummeted to a historic low of nearly negative 5% of GDP, underscoring the severe energy headwinds impacting European employment, housing, and production.

In this analysis of the banking system, the author argues that the financial sector is in a much stronger position today than during the 2008 crisis, though rising interest rates present a new challenge. To support the argument of improved resilience, the text highlights that US bank tier 1 capital ratios have risen substantially, risky lending has largely migrated to capital markets and private credit, wholesale funding has dropped to 7.5% of liabilities from 17.5% in 2000, and loan-to-deposit ratios are near historic lows of 0.65x compared to 1.00x in 2008. 

Supporting these historical trends, two line charts trace the banking sector’s structural improvements. The chart for US bank tier 1 capital ratios, measuring capital as a percentage of risk-weighted assets from 1991 to Q3 2022, shows capital rising from around 10.5% in 2008 to over 14% by 2021, indicating a much healthier buffer. The chart for the US loan-to-deposit ratio across all commercial banks from 1973 to late 2022 illustrates a sharp decline from the 1.00x peak in 2008 down to historical lows near 0.60x in 2021, demonstrating the highest liquidity levels seen since the 1970s.

However, the author introduces a critical caveat: rising interest rates have caused high-quality bonds held by banks to trade below par. A bar chart of FDIC Q3 unrealized bank losses on investment securities from 2008 to 2022 shows that these unrealized losses—divided between Available-for-Sale (AFS) and Held-to-Maturity (HTM) securities—have ballooned to an unprecedented negative $700 billion in 2022, a stark contrast to the near-zero levels maintained over the previous decade.

Because of these paper losses, the author evaluates individual bank vulnerability using a scatter plot that compares loan-to-deposit ratios (adjusted to include securities) against the "stickier" retail share of total deposits as of Q3 2022. On this chart, the vertical axis measures the retail deposits share (from 0% to 80%), and the horizontal axis measures loans plus securities as a percentage of deposits (from 70% to 120%). Banks with lower-risk deposit bases sit in the upper left, while higher-risk profiles sit in the bottom right. JPMorgan Chase (JPM) occupies a low-risk position with high retail deposits and a low loans-plus-securities ratio of about 73%. In contrast, Citigroup (C) is positioned in a higher-risk area with a low retail deposit share of around 13% and loans-plus-securities close to 90%. Other major regional and national banks, including Bank of America (BAC), Wells Fargo (WFC), PNC, KeyCorp (KEY), and Truist (TFC), are plotted across the middle of the spectrum. 

Finally, a chart on Fed assets and liabilities tracks US dollar trillions from January 2022 with projections through July 2023. It details a contraction in the Federal Reserve's balance sheet, showing Fed assets declining from nearly $9.0 trillion to an estimated $8.0 trillion. Concurrently, bank reserves are projected to decline from roughly $3.8 trillion down toward $1.8 trillion, while overnight reverse repos are depicted peaking over $2.0 trillion before beginning a downward trend.

This page of the publication argues that Chinese equities and bonds reached deep value pricing in late 2022, suggesting that even minor improvements in macro conditions or policy could spark a significant asset price recovery. Author Michael Cembalest suggests that if China successfully navigates its intense COVID wave, a US-emerging markets equity barbell strategy could outperform in the coming year. This view is supported by massive cash reserves held by Chinese households, whose deposits have increased by 60 percent compared to pre-pandemic levels, alongside mortgage rates that have fallen back to 2017 levels. Additionally, policy support such as central bank relending programs and loosened restrictions on shadow finance and equity fundraising could aid the real estate market.

Four charts illustrate these extreme valuation levels. The first chart, titled Equity index drawdowns: China vs World, tracks percentage declines from prior peaks from 2005 through late 2022. It highlights a massive divergence, showing that while the MSCI World index suffered an 18 percent drawdown, the MSCI China index fell by a dramatic 49 percent. The second chart, China earnings yields, displays the 12-month forward earnings yield for the Hang Seng Index and MSCI China from 2006 to late 2022. Yields recently peaked between 11 percent and 12 percent—levels close to those seen during the Global Financial Crisis—before settling near 9 percent for the Hang Seng and 8 percent for MSCI China. 

The third chart, Chinese bank valuations, plots the average price-to-book ratio from 2010 to 2022 for four major institutions: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, China Construction Bank, Agricultural Bank of China, and Bank of China. This ratio has steadily deteriorated over more than a decade, falling from nearly 2.0x in 2010 to less than 0.5x by late 2022. The fourth chart, China property high-yield bond price distribution, maps the bond price as a percentage of par value against the cumulative percentage of notional outstanding as of November 10, 2022. Categorizing bonds into defaulted, exchanged, and undefaulted/unexchanged buckets, the data shows that only 5 percent to 10 percent of China’s high-yield property bond universe trades above 60 percent of par value. Conversely, an astonishing 85 percent of the universe trades or was exchanged at less than 20 percent of par value. Cembalest notes that throughout his career in emerging markets since 1987, he has never seen a default or restructuring episode of this severity across an entire sector.

This page analyzes the deep economic, demographic, and political headwinds facing Chinese equities. Michael Cembalest discusses how stringent pandemic restrictions, sluggish consumer spending, and a collapsing property market have severely impacted China, leading to expectations that other Asian economies will outpace China's growth for the first time in three decades. He notes political roadblocks to China's pandemic response, including a refusal to license highly effective Western mRNA vaccines from Moderna or Pfizer due to intellectual property disputes, which left a third of China's elderly population without a third vaccine dose by late 2022. Cembalest suggests that China's abrupt reopening, despite the associated health risks, was likely accelerated by a severe demographic crisis.

The page features four charts illustrating these demographic and market trends. The first chart, showing China's total births from 1950 to 2022, reveals a dramatic decline from a peak of over 30 million births per year in the late 1960s to a historic low of around 10 million in 2022. 

The second chart displays projections for China's working-age population (ages 15 to 64) through 2090. It highlights a massive downward revision between the United Nations' 2019 and 2022 estimates. While both projection series show the working-age population peaking near 1 billion people around 2015, the 2022 estimate projects a far steeper collapse, bottoming out at approximately 400 million people by 2090, compared to the 2019 projection of nearly 600 million.

The third chart tracks China's index weight, performance, and policy changes from 2005 to late 2022. It plots China's weight in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index alongside the rolling three-year performance of Chinese equities versus world equities. Following years of market-friendly policies, China's weight in the index peaked at 40% in 2020. However, the launch of President Xi Jinping's "progressive authoritarianism" campaign in late 2020 marked a stark turning point, ushering in a historic underperformance of Chinese equities versus world equities that reached negative 50% by late 2022.

The final chart shows the historical performance of J.P. Morgan’s long-standing equity barbell strategy—which maintains a 10% overweight to the US, a 10% underweight to Europe, a 5% overweight to Emerging Markets, and a 5% underweight to Japan—measured as a three-year rolling outperformance against the MSCI All World Index from 1991 to late 2022. Despite China’s steep downturn, this barbell strategy has remained resilient, consistently generating positive relative performance throughout most of the last thirty years.

This page addresses the growing risk in the leveraged loan and private credit markets as the economy faces a potential recession. Michael Cembalest argues that a decade of declining investor protections and rising leverage has not yet been properly reflected in loan repricing. He attributes this "lender surrender" in part to financial repression by the Federal Reserve, which pushed investors to relax underwriting standards. Many of these issues also apply to the private credit market, which, at $1.2 trillion, is now the same size as the US high-yield market. A key contributor to this deterioration is the practice of EBITDA adjustments, with S&P data showing that EBITDA add-backs increased from 10% of deals to approximately 30% by 2019.

To illustrate these trends, the page features four distinct charts. The first line chart, titled "Loan investors waving the white flag," tracks Moody's loan covenant quality score from 2012 to 2021, where a score of 5 represents the weakest covenant quality. The score steadily climbs from a relatively stronger 3.3 in 2012 to nearly 4.5 by 2021, demonstrating a significant erosion of investor protections. 

The second visual, "Loan covenant quality scores: 2007 vs 2019-2020," compares covenant categories between the two eras. In every single category—including financial covenants, subordination, restricted payments, debt incurrence, risky investments, asset sales, and voting assignments—the scores from 2019–2020 are substantially higher (and therefore weaker) than those in 2007. For example, the overall covenant quality score rose from approximately 2.5 in 2007 to nearly 4.0 in the 2019–2020 period.

The third chart, "Leveraged loan issuance by debt-to-EBITDA ratio," displays the composition of loan issuance from 2008 to 2022. It highlights a dramatic shift away from higher credit quality. The share of issuance with debt-to-EBITDA ratios under 4x fell from over 50% in 2010 to under 20% in 2022. Meanwhile, higher-risk loans with ratios between 5x and 6.9x, as well as those exceeding 7x, have grown to dominate the marketplace. 

The final chart, "Risky credit not pricing in recession," plots the US high-yield spread alongside the leveraged loan price index from 1988 through late 2022. It demonstrates that during previous downturns, such as the 2008 financial crisis, high-yield spreads spiked above 20% and loan prices bottomed near 60. By contrast, current markets show the leveraged loan price index remaining relatively stable above 90 and the US high-yield spread hovering around a modest 5% to 6%, suggesting that risky credit assets have not yet priced in a coming recession. Additionally, a footnote highlights the practice of "sponsor-designated counsel," where financial sponsors influence which law firms banks use during transactions, further eroding protections.

This page discusses the global repricing of financial assets driven by the closing of the extraordinary gap between asset yields and policy rates. Michael Cembalest argues that this narrowing gap triggered the sell-off in speculative, profitless innovation sectors before spreading to the broader equity market. He predicts a modest valuation correction early in 2023 to bring assets closer to long-term averages as economic growth slows. He also anticipates a continuation of key trends: physical assets outperforming digital ones, traditional energy outperforming renewables, and fintech returning all of its post-2019 outperformance compared to traditional banks. 

A series of six charts supports these arguments. The first chart, "Gap between asset yields and short rates is finally closing," plots developed world asset yields against developed world short rates adjusted for quantitative easing from 1960 to late 2022. It illustrates how the historically unprecedented gap that opened post-2008 and widened during the pandemic is rapidly shrinking as adjusted short rates rise toward asset yields.

The second chart, titled "Dumb and Dumber," indexes performance to January 2019 to compare the 2019–2022 bubble in "profitless innovation" (including metaverse, hydrogen, fintech, SPACs, crypto, software, e-commerce, and biotech) with the historic 1998–2003 bubble of the NASDAQ 100. The trajectories are nearly identical, with the modern basket peaking above an index level of 450 in 2021 before plunging back to near 150 by late 2022, mirroring the Dot-com crash.

The third chart, "Forward PE ratios: Russell 1000, growth & value," shows the price-to-consensus 12-month forward earnings per share from 2006 to 2022. It highlights a massive valuation compression among major tech firms. The "Megacap 8" basket—consisting of Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Netflix, Nvidia, and Tesla—saw its forward PE ratio spike near 45 in late 2020 before falling to around 25 by late 2022. The broader Russell 1000 Growth Index compressed similarly to around 21, while the Russell 1000 Value Index remained relatively flat, ending near 15.

The fourth chart, "S&P 500 price to earnings ratio," tracks the index’s forward P/E from 1990 to late 2022. The chart emphasizes that the S&P 500's post-COVID valuation peak of roughly 24x has corrected back down to its long-term average of 16.7x.

The fifth chart, "The Tortoise and the Hare," tracks index performance from December 2016 to late 2022. It compares the ARK Innovation ETF to an "old economy" basket containing farm equipment, industrial REITs, and office cleaning supplies or uniforms. The high-flying ARK ETF soared to an index value of over 800 in early 2021 before plummeting back to approximately 200, where it was overtaken by the steady rise of the old economy basket, which climbed to nearly 300 by late 2022.

The final chart, titled "'Reports of my death were greatly exaggerated,'" tracks clean energy versus traditional fossil fuels from late 2018 to late 2022. It compares an equal-weighted renewables composite (comprising the NASDAQ Clean Edge, Wilderhill Clean Energy, FTSE Renew/Alt Energy, S&P Global Clean Energy, and MAC Global Solar indices) against the MSCI World Energy Index for oil, gas, and pipelines. While the renewables composite peaked above an index level of 400 in early 2021 and declined to around 250 by late 2022, traditional energy rebounded dramatically from a low of nearly 50 in 2020 to reach roughly 150, showcasing the strong resurgence of traditional fossil fuel and pipeline companies.

In this section, Michael Cembalest discusses the outlook for inflation and Federal Reserve policy in 2023, presenting the argument that inflation pressures will subside enough to allow the Fed to pause its tightening cycle at 5% and keep the 10-year US Treasury yield below 4%. While inflation expectations have receded to 2.25% from a 3% peak, Cembalest notes that the expected rapid cooling of inflation would be historically anomalous. The primary obstacle for the Fed remains wage pressure driven by the tightest post-war US labor market on record, although some wage growth indicators are beginning to roll over.

To illustrate these trends, the page features four charts. The first chart, "Fed tightening cycles, 1958-2022," plots the basis points change since the start of tightening cycles against the number of months since the first policy action, ranging from 36 months before to 36 months after the initial hike. The 2022 cycle stands out as an exceptionally steep blue line, climbing aggressively to around 400 basis points within nine months of its start, far outpacing the trajectories of all historical cycles since 1958. 

The second chart, "Developed market inflation episodes since 1970," displays the year-over-year percent change in inflation against the number of months since inflation rose above 8%. It contrasts historical trends—such as the historic median, first quartile, and third quartile—with the current US and Eurozone cycles, which are extended via dotted lines representing Bloomberg consensus forecasts. These consensus forecasts project an unusually rapid drop in inflation, with both regions expected to fall toward 2% to 3% within 20 months of crossing the 8% threshold, a trajectory far swifter than the historic median or even the historic first quartile.

The third chart, "Largest worker shortage in the post-war era," plots job openings plus employment as a percentage of the labor force from 1951 to 2022. It highlights a massive spike above the 0% equilibrium threshold in the post-pandemic era, visually demonstrating that the US has entered an era of "more jobs than workers" that is unprecedented in the post-war period. 

The final chart, "Wage growth measures," covers the period from 2008 to 2022 and tracks three key metrics: the Atlanta Fed Tracker (year-over-year change, 3-month average on the left-hand scale), the quarterly annualized Employment Cost Index (on the left-hand scale), and a monthly wage survey average (on the right-hand scale). These measures all peaked dramatically in 2022, with the Atlanta Fed Tracker approaching 7% and the monthly wage survey index climbing above 60. However, the chart shows that these metrics have begun to roll over, signaling the initial stages of a wage slowdown. An accompanying footnote explains that these alternative wage measures are preferred over Average Hourly Earnings to avoid distortions caused by pandemic-era shifts in the composition of the labor force.

This page analyzes the emerging global divide between the US and China/Russia spheres of influence, linking public opinion allegiances to actual financial and energy flows. The author highlights how these alignments support the "no-limits" partnership announced by Russia and China, which has mitigated the impact of Western financial and energy embargoes on Russia.

The primary visual is a scatter plot illustrating the structure of global public allegiances across 137 countries. The horizontal axis measures the percentage of the population with a positive view of the United States, and the vertical axis measures the average positive view of China and Russia. The data points demonstrate an inverse relationship, with countries migrating away from the middle and toward distinct poles. On one end, countries like Russia, China, Laos, Serbia, and Iran show high positive views of China and Russia (above 80%) and low positive views of the United States (under 30%). On the opposite end, the United States, Japan, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Sweden, Poland, and major European nations cluster with high favorability toward the US (70% to 90%) and low favorability toward China and Russia (under 25%). Numerous other countries, including Brazil, India, Kenya, and Colombia, populate the intermediate space.

To demonstrate how these political alignments translate into economic support, the bottom-left chart tracks cross-border syndicated loans to Russia in billions of US dollars from 2010 to 2022. A vertical line marks the 2014 Russian invasion of Crimea. Following this event, syndicated lending from Western nations collapsed, with French lending dropping from over twenty billion dollars to near zero, and similar sharp declines seen for Germany, Italy, Great Britain, and the United States. Conversely, Chinese syndicated loans to Russia surged, rising from under twenty billion dollars before 2014 to over forty billion dollars by 2022, effectively replacing Western capital.

The bottom-right chart tracks the shift in Russian energy exports by plotting Chinese versus European purchases from 2019 through late 2022. European purchases of Russian energy, measured in million tonnes of oil equivalent per day on the right axis, fell dramatically from a peak of around 0.8 in late 2021 to below 0.4 by late 2022. Meanwhile, Chinese purchases of Russian energy, measured in billions of US dollars on the left axis, spiked from a baseline of two to three billion dollars in 2021 to over seven billion dollars by late 2022. Together, these charts show how China’s financial and energy trade has acted as a critical safety valve for Russia against Western sanctions.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication focuses on the geopolitical vulnerability and technological complexity of the global semiconductor supply chain, specifically highlighting China's massive reliance on Taiwan. Only ten percent of Chinese semiconductor demand is met through domestic production, while Taiwan accounts for seventy percent of China’s chip consumption. TSMC produces ten percent of this demand in its factories located in Nanjing and Shanghai, exporting the remaining sixty percent from Taiwan. 

The extreme nature of this dependency is illustrated in a bar chart titled "Regional reliance for critical goods." The chart plots percent values to compare Chinese semiconductor consumption sourced from Taiwan, which stands at seventy percent, against pre-war European reliance on Russian energy, which is much lower at twenty percent. The comparison emphasizes that there is likely no other global precedent of one nation being so reliant on another for a specific high-value import. Although China’s National Integrated Circuit Investment Fund has backed successful domestic champions like SMIC (producing seven-nanometer chips), YMTC, San’an Optoelectronics, AMEC, and JCET, other state-supported ventures have gone bankrupt. Consequently, domestic Chinese foundries remain behind, mostly working on older fourteen to twenty-eight nanometer chips. 

A line chart titled "TSMC semiconductor capabilities" plots the chronological shrinking of semiconductor sizes from 1987 to 2022. The curve shows manufacturing capabilities starting at 1,500 nanometers in 1987, dropping to 130 nanometers by 2002, reaching 28 nanometers in 2012, and finally bottoming out at five nanometers by 2022. 

The commentary concludes by describing advanced semiconductors as the "Faberge eggs of industrial complexity." The most profitable chips—ranging from ten down to three nanometers—are incredibly difficult and costly to fabricate. They can only be produced using extreme ultraviolet photolithography machines designed and built by the Dutch company ASML, which produces just forty-five to fifty-five of these machines per year. Furthermore, advanced foundries require clean rooms ten thousand times cleaner than hospital surgical rooms. The chip-etching process itself requires operating twenty-four hours a day for weeks, navigating seven hundred separate steps, and moving materials across multiple air flights over thousands of miles to access global sites with specialized capabilities. The entire ecosystem is highly globalized, relying on exotic chemicals, rare metals, and components sourced from thousands of companies across dozens of countries.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s market outlook focuses on housing as the critical factor that will drive down US inflation in 2023, ultimately allowing the Federal Reserve to pause its interest rate hikes at five percent. The author argues that because housing costs in official consumer price index data are heavily lagged, the dramatic price increases of recent years are only now showing up in official reports. However, real-time indicators reveal a sharp collapse in housing demand and rental growth that will soon dampen overall inflation.

To support this outlook, the page features six charts. The first chart, depicting US new rents, shows that while the official CPI rent of primary residence (measured on the left axis as an annualized quarterly percentage change) continued its upward climb toward eight percent in late 2022, real-time measures have plummeted. Specifically, quarterly annualized asking rents from Apartment List (measured on the right axis) crashed from a peak of nearly thirty-five percent in late 2021 to near zero percent by late 2022, while monthly asking rents from RealPage experienced a similar drop. This rental slowdown is exacerbated by a surge in supply, as illustrated in the second chart, which shows multifamily units under construction relative to rental stock reaching two percent in 2022, the highest level of new supply coming online since the mid-1970s.

The collapse in housing demand is driven by historically poor affordability and surging mortgage rates. The third chart shows annual mortgage cost as a percentage of household income spiking to forty-five percent in late 2022, a level not seen since the late 1970s and early 1980s. As a result, existing home sales have dropped precipitously. The fourth chart indexes existing home sales over a sixteen-month period across various historical periods, showing that the current housing activity decline is faster than the decline during the Global Financial Crisis and is closely mirroring the double-dip recession of the early 1980s, falling below an index value of seventy.

Lastly, the author examines monetary policy, noting that quantitative tightening is making financial conditions tighter than the headline policy rate indicates. The fifth chart compares the Federal funds rate to the San Francisco Fed’s proxy funds rate, which accounts for balance sheet shrinkage. In late 2022, this proxy rate rose above six percent, exceeding the actual Federal funds rate by the widest margin on record. The final chart displays various US consumer price inflation measures, including the Cleveland Fed median CPI, the Atlanta Fed sticky CPI, and the Cleveland Fed trimmed mean CPI, all of which hovered between six and eight percent on a three-month annualized basis in late 2022, showing the broad inflation pressures that these housing and monetary headwinds are expected to cool.

This page discusses the divergent energy inflation dynamics in Europe and California, emphasizing the structural vulnerabilities and policy choices driving dramatic price spikes in both regions. In Europe, the primary driver is a marginal pricing mechanism where fossil fuel power plants set the market price for all electricity generation, regardless of whether it is produced by cheaper solar, wind, hydro, or nuclear sources. 

A table titled "How marginal electricity prices are set in Europe" supports this by showing the percentage of all hours that different sources set marginal prices across various nations. Fossil fuels dictate prices for 91% of hours in Germany, 89% in Spain, 86% in Italy, and 84% in the UK, while France is a major outlier with non-fossil sources setting the price for 93% of hours. To mitigate the resulting price shocks, European governments have introduced subsidies and electricity price caps on non-gas producers, ranging from €67 per MWh in Italy and Spain to €150 in Germany and €245 in the UK, compared to uncapped December 2022 prices that ranged between €100 and €350 per MWh. Infrastructure challenges exacerbate the situation; Germany’s first of five LNG import regasification facilities saw its cost triple to $10 billion, and France’s nuclear power industry has been running at only 50% capacity, threatening exports to surrounding countries.

Concurrently, California is experiencing severe price spikes of its own. The author attributes these spikes to a combination of policy and logistical headwinds, including shutting down PG&E natural gas storage, closing nuclear power plants, urban outmigration to rural and suburban areas with higher per capita energy demand, pipeline maintenance delays, and future export competition from Canada and Mexico.

The page features three charts illustrating these trends. A line chart of "Euro Area energy inflation" showing year-over-year percentage changes from 1997 to late 2022 highlights an unprecedented vertical surge in 2022, peaking near 45%, which vastly exceeds any historical level over the past quarter-century. 

Two comparative charts at the bottom illustrate the regional gaps in gas and power markets from January 2021 to January 2023. "The US-Europe natural gas gap" compares wholesale natural gas prices in US dollars per MMBTU. While the US Henry Hub remained stable around $5, the European TTF benchmark experienced extreme volatility, peaking near $85 in mid-2022 before retreating to $26. Meanwhile, California natural gas prices experienced a massive local spike, ending the period at $38, significantly higher than both the US benchmark and the European TTF price at that moment. 

Finally, "The US-Europe electricity gap" shows wholesale electricity prices in US dollars per MWh on a 7-day average. The average price for Germany, Spain, and France spiked repeatedly, peaking above $450 in mid-2022. While the US PJM market stayed flat and low, California electricity prices spiked sharply in late 2022, reaching nearly $300 per MWh, mirroring the localized natural gas supply crunch.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s market outlook discusses the gradual decline of globalization, arguing that while globalization is not in a total collapse, it has receded from its peak and is undergoing a major structural shift. The author explains that global trade and foreign direct investment rebounded after the COVID-19 pandemic, noting that the decline in traded goods values since peak levels is partly due to falling commodity prices between 2011 and 2020 rather than a true decline in trade volumes. In fact, only about forty percent of the decline in traded goods values is estimated to be the result of reshoring international supply chains. 

To track these broad trends, the top of the page features three line charts spanning 1970 to 2020 or 2022. The first chart displays global exports of goods and services as a percent of world GDP up to the 2021 fiscal year. It shows that goods exports peaked near twenty-five percent around 2008 and fluctuated down to around twenty-two percent by 2021, while services exports rose steadily from roughly three percent in 1970 to around six percent in 2021. The second chart shows global foreign direct investment flows as a percent of world GDP, demonstrating high volatility with peaks around five to six percent in 2000 and 2007, dropping back below two percent by early 2022. The third chart, mapping global portfolio equity flows as a percent of world GDP, also shows high volatility, peaking near two percent in the late 1990s and late 2000s and ending just over one percent in 2021.

The commentary shifts to argue that what is actually collapsing is the Western conceit of change through trade or constructive engagement, particularly with Russia and China. This is illustrated by Europe’s financial and energy embargo on Russia following the failure of its Ostpolitik approach. Regarding China, the author details declining import shares, a collapse in OECD direct investments, rising CFIUS investigations, and declining portfolio flows. The text notes that the United States has placed severe restrictions on AI chip, equipment, and component exports, expanding its restricted list to five hundred Chinese companies, including China’s flagship flash memory producer. These actions are further reinforced by the US Foreign Direct Product Rule. Consequently, rising US-China tensions have become the top concern for US companies in China, according to AmCham’s 2022 survey. Looking forward, the author predicts impending US restrictions on outbound FDI into China, referencing comments by US Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo on protecting national security in critical technologies like advanced semiconductors.

Two charts at the bottom of the page illustrate the tangible impacts of these geopolitical tensions. The first chart plots the trade war's impact on US import counterparties as a six-month average from 2015 to 2022. It reveals that China's share of US imports fell from a peak of around twenty-two percent in 2017 to approximately seventeen percent in 2022. During this same period, Europe maintained the largest share at around twenty-four percent, while Mexico rose to fourteen percent, Canada held near thirteen percent, and the combined share of Korea, Vietnam, and Taiwan grew to about ten percent. The second chart tracks OECD greenfield capital spending indexed to one hundred in January 2012. It depicts a dramatic retreat from China, with OECD investments into China falling from an index level near one hundred and fifty in 2018 down to approximately thirty-five by late 2022. In contrast, OECD investments into the European Union and the United States rose to index levels of roughly two hundred and ten and one hundred and seventy, respectively, in 2022.

This page from Michael Cembalest's Eye on the Market Outlook explores how the post-2009 era of central bank financial repression challenged active investment managers. The author argues that falling risk premia, low valuation spreads, and extensive central bank liquidity—such as the European Central Bank purchasing near-junk bonds—artificially sustained insolvent "zombie" companies. Citing data from the Bank for International Settlements, the text notes that these zombie companies in the developed world rose from just 1% of market cap in 1990 to 12% by 2018. This climate made it difficult for active equity and hedge fund managers to outperform the S&P 500. However, the author suggests that if the financial system returns to a world of positive real interest rates, value-oriented portfolio managers may face more favorable stock-picking and bond-picking conditions.

The page features four charts that track active manager performance from 1990 through late 2022. The top-left chart compares active equity manager performance against real policy rates. It plots the average US large-cap core manager versus the S&P 500 (indexed to 100 in January 1990) against the Fed funds rate less core CPI (measured as a five-year average of the year-over-year percentage change). The chart shows a steep decline in the active manager index from a peak near 105 in the mid-1990s down to approximately 86 by 2022, closely mimicking the downward trajectory of real policy rates into negative territory. The top-right chart compares the same active equity manager index against consumer price inflation, showing how the suppressed inflation environment of the 2010s coincided with underperformance.

The bottom row of charts focuses on hedge funds, utilizing the HFRI Equity Hedge Funds index compared to the S&P 500, indexed to 100 in December 1989. The bottom-left chart compares hedge fund performance against real policy rates, showing the HFRI outperformance index peaking at nearly 240 around 2009 before steadily collapsing to around 80 by 2022 as real rates went negative. The bottom-right chart compares this HFRI index to consumer price inflation, demonstrating a similar downward trend in relative hedge fund performance during the post-2009 period of low inflation. Data for the charts is sourced from Bloomberg, Lipper, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page from the report analyzes global fixed income opportunities for yield-oriented investors at the beginning of 2023. The author argues that while fixed income spreads have widened, they remain far below the crisis levels of 2009, reflecting that current systemic risks and financial solvency concerns are not comparable to that period. However, the author warns that exceptionally low market depth and liquidity could trigger flash crash volatility in 2023, exacerbated by the Federal Reserve shrinking its balance sheet or potential disruptions from a debt limit standoff between a Republican House and a Democratic President, which Congress must resolve by the fall.

To support this analysis, the page features eight historical charts detailing various fixed income segments. The first chart shows US Municipal yields from 2000 to late 2022, demonstrating a sharp rise at the end of the period, with long-duration munis approaching five percent and short-to-medium-term municipals rising toward four percent. The second chart focuses on ten-year sovereign bond yields for Europe and China, showing that European yields reversed their negative trend to reach nearly three percent by late 2022, while Chinese yields stabilized around three percent. The third chart displays the spread between thirty-year mortgages and ten-year Treasuries, which surged dramatically in late 2022 to nearly 275 basis points, approaching levels last seen during the global financial crisis.

The fourth chart traces AAA asset-backed securities spreads against Treasuries for commercial real estate, auto, and credit card debt from 1998 through 2022. It highlights that current spreads remain low, sitting well below 150 basis points, in stark contrast to the 2008 peak when auto and commercial real estate spreads exceeded 600 basis points. The fifth chart tracks ten-year sovereign bond yields for South Africa and Mexico, showing both emerging markets experiencing rising yields in late 2022, with South Africa climbing toward eleven percent and Mexico near ten percent. The sixth chart displays USD floating-rate instruments, showing that yields on US investment-grade corporate floating-rate notes and AA bank commercial paper both surged from near-zero in 2021 to around five to six percent by late 2022.

The final two charts address preferred securities. The preferred option-adjusted spread chart shows that spreads for US investment-grade preferred stock ended late 2022 at roughly 300 basis points, compared to a spike of nearly 1,600 basis points in 2009. The preferred yields chart tracks three categories: European Contingent Capital, US High Yield Preferred, and US High Grade Preferred. European Contingent Capital yielded the most, rising toward nine percent, followed by US High Yield Preferreds at around eight percent and US High Grade Preferreds near 6.5 percent. A brief note explains that European Contingent Capital, or CoCo securities, typically yield more than US preferred stocks because of lower overall credit ratings, explicit write-down or payment triggers linked to capital ratios, and a ten to fifteen percent exposure to emerging market bank securities.

This page discusses how rising US government entitlement spending is crowding out non-defense discretionary spending, which is crucial for productivity and future economic growth. To frame the discussion, the page provides a detailed breakdown of what falls under non-defense discretionary spending, including transportation infrastructure, education and training, science and energy, law enforcement, and healthcare initiatives such as vaccine development and disease control programs.

The central chart, titled "What does the Federal government spend money on?", tracks spending as a percentage of GDP from 1970 with projections out to 2030, using data from the Congressional Budget Office and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The chart illustrates a widening gap between entitlement spending and non-defense discretionary spending. In 1970, shortly after Medicare and Medicaid were created, the ratio of entitlement to non-defense discretionary spending was equal at 1.0x. This ratio climbed to 2.0x in 1990, reached 3.2x in 2015, dipped slightly to 2.8x in 2021, and is projected to reach 4.0x by 2032. At that point, entitlement payments plus interest are expected to permanently consume all Federal revenue, leaving virtually nothing for discretionary spending.

To address this fiscal challenge, the author highlights a sidebar of partial solutions, including tax proposals from Senator Bernie Sanders to raise income and capital gains taxes on incomes over $250,000, and Senator Elizabeth Warren's wealth tax on fortunes over $20 million. Other listed options include converting Social Security into a pure entitlement program by eliminating the income tax cap without raising benefits, implementing further means-testing for Medicare and Social Security, raising the retirement eligibility age, and cutting defense spending, which currently stands at 3.5% of GDP.

In the footnotes, the author contextualizes the history of entitlement politics, noting that programs like Social Security and Medicare were historically decried as socialist or communist plots by political figures like Alf Landon, Republican Senators, William Randolph Hearst, and Ronald Reagan. Finally, the author poses an open question about whether a single-payer healthcare system could lower entitlement spending. He concludes that while a single-payer system would offer the government more leverage to control Medicare and Medicaid costs, it does not guarantee a cheaper system overall, especially given that entitlement program costs have historically far exceeded initial projections.

This page of the J.P. Morgan report argues that several key fixed-income categories are currently unappealing because their spreads and yields are too tight relative to the macroeconomic outlook and do not adequately compensate for the inherent risk. While the author does not expect major systemic issues for high-grade corporate bonds, they view a 150 basis point spread as poor value and express separate concerns about the leveraged loan market. 

Five historical charts, tracking data up to late December 2022, illustrate this tightness. The first chart shows US investment grade corporate spreads (using the JULI index versus US Treasuries) from 2000 to 2022, highlighting that the current spread is tight at approximately 150 basis points. The second chart details Emerging Markets dollar bond spreads over US Treasuries from 2002 to 2022, showing the current spread hovering around 400 basis points. The third chart illustrates US high yield bond spreads (using the JPDFHYI index) from 1995 to 2022, where the current spread sits at roughly 450 basis points, noting high yield energy within this segment. The fourth chart displays US leveraged loan prices via the SPBDALB index from 2000 to 2022, showing that prices have declined to around 92, which is lower than historical norms but well above the sharp drops of 2008 and 2020. The fifth chart tracks Pan European high yield percent yields from 2000 to 2022, revealing a current yield of around 6%, which is up from recent years but low relative to historic highs. 

The second section of the page shifts focus to Brazil, stating that the portfolio management team is cautious and waiting for clarity on the new Lula administration's fiscal framework before increasing exposure to local bonds. Key catalysts to watch include tax reform and plans for state-owned enterprises. While Brazil currently offers one of the highest risk premiums among EM local bonds, the team is maintaining a tactical stance rather than initiating long-term positions. An accompanying chart tracks Brazil's 10-year sovereign bond local currency yields from 2006 to late 2022. Yields have risen to about 13% at the end of 2022, up from a low near 6% in 2020 but below the 2015 peak of over 16%. The chart is annotated to reflect caution until Lula's spending plans are clarified, though a possible upgrade is noted.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication, titled Topic #7: Just the Vax and nothing but the Vax, features Michael Cembalest’s analysis of mRNA COVID-19 vaccine efficacy, particularly among older populations. Cembalest cites CDC data showing that bivalent mRNA vaccine efficacy ranges from 73% to 84% against hospitalization for immunocompetent people over 65 years old. He notes that unvaccinated individuals experienced approximately 14 times higher COVID mortality compared to fully vaccinated individuals between April and September 2022. However, he highlights a critical adoption gap: while 94% of Americans over 65 completed their original vaccination series, only 36% received the updated bivalent booster, which likely explains why seniors represent the largest share of recent hospitalizations. 

The text addresses political opposition to vaccines, noting that Florida Governor Ron DeSantis recommended investigating vaccine manufacturers for fraud. Cembalest finds this position counterproductive given that Florida has the second-oldest population in the United States. He compares vaccine skepticism to belief in a faked moon landing, which is reportedly held by one in ten Americans. This point is punctuated by a photograph of astronaut Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin Jr. on the moon in July 1969, taken by Neil Armstrong. 

The page includes a line chart titled "The XBB variant Reproductive rate," which plots the reproductive rate on the vertical axis from 1.0 to 2.0 against time on the horizontal axis from 0 to 90 days. The chart, sourced from Trevor Bedford and JP Weiland in December 2022, compares several COVID-19 variants, including BA.2, BA.4, BA.5, BA.2.12.1, BQ.1, XBB, and XBB.1.5. It illustrates that while most variants see their reproductive rates drop significantly toward 1.0 within 40 to 60 days, the recombinant variant XBB.1.5 maintains a highly elevated and flat reproductive rate of around 1.7 to 1.8 across the entire 90-day period. This visual demonstrates why XBB.1.5 is outcompeting other variants in the Northeast United States, posing a new challenge for vaccine-induced and acquired immunity.

In this concluding commentary, Michael Cembalest warns that failure to address long-term US debt and spending sustainability risks inviting chaotic intervention, metaphorically comparing fiscal brinkmanship to the Visigoths sacking Rome. While he expects the current year's immediate crisis to be resolved, he cautions that the underlying day of reckoning remains a looming threat. 

The page features a dramatic historical painting by Joseph-Noël Sylvestre from 1890 showing the Visigoths plundering Rome in 410 AD under Alaric I.
