Substantial weakness is predicted for the ISM manufacturing index in twelve months—driven by changes in Treasury yields, global short rates, emerging market bond yields, and prices paid—and for economy-wide profits in eight months, driven by the Fed Funds Rate, corporate tax rates, unemployment, and productivity. Modest weakness is projected for corporate bankruptcies, non-residential capex, construction activity, bank lending, and S&P profits. Slight weakness is anticipated for S&P revenue growth, sales growth, and corporate wage expenses. Despite these warning signs, the overall pulse of these seventeen indicators points to modestly weaker US conditions in six to nine months rather than a severe contraction. Furthermore, the "new orders less inventories" metric has improved for three consecutive months, offering a positive leading signal for the PMI index.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s Eye on the Market addresses the extremely narrow leadership driving year-to-date US equity returns, noting that rising valuations in just a few mega-cap stocks have heavily boosted performance despite mostly flat earnings projections. The author observes that market cap concentration is at its highest level since the early 1970s—even narrower than during the 2000 technology, media, and telecom bubble—and that growth factor crowding has reached the 97th percentile. Six massive tech stocks, specifically Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia, and Salesforce, explain 51% of the S&P 500's year-to-date performance and 54% of the Nasdaq 100's performance. Historically, such steep rises in market concentration have reversed, leading to the S&P 500 equal-weighted index outperforming its market-cap-weighted counterpart.

Three charts visually support these assertions. The first chart, titled "Market cap of largest 7 companies," tracks their share of the total large-cap market cap from 1990 through mid-2023. It reveals that the concentration of these top seven firms spiked rapidly after 2015, climbing past its previous peak of roughly 18% during the dot-com bubble in 2000 to nearly 25% in 2023. 

The second chart, titled "World equity returns vs US Fed Funds rate, 1970-2023," is a scatter plot comparing the MSCI World equity return through July of each year against the trailing 12-month change in the Federal Funds rate. The data point for 2023 is circled to highlight that global equity returns have remained highly positive, climbing toward 20%, despite a substantial trailing rate hike of around 3% to 4%. This sits in contrast to typical historical periods where aggressive interest rate hikes constrained equity returns.

The third chart, "Mega-cap stock earnings expectations for 2023," indices consensus earnings expectations from December 2022 to August 2023. It illustrates a stark divergence among the market leaders. Nvidia's index surged to nearly 170 by August 2023, and Meta's rose to approximately 120. In contrast, earnings expectations for Google, Microsoft, Apple, and Amazon remained flat near the baseline of 100, while Tesla's expectations collapsed to around 60. The author notes the irony that despite these flat or falling earnings projections, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Apple rose 40% to 60% year-to-date, and Tesla rose over 100%.

This page analyzes the stagnation of China’s post-pandemic economic reopening, arguing that the primary headwind is a severe real estate overhang rather than excess industrial capacity. The author notes that China’s homeownership rate is roughly 90%, with 20% of households owning multiple properties, and vacant units representing more than two years of sales. Consequently, China’s housing situation has led to slower economic growth and equity markets trading at discounted multiples of 10 to 12 times earnings, though the Chinese Politburo has hinted at potential, yet unspecified, stimulus. 

Four visuals support this analysis. The first chart, tracking real economic activity using a weighted average of ten monthly indicators, shows that after a dramatic spike in early 2021 following the pandemic downturn, activity has fallen back to historically weak levels near 5 on the index by mid-2023. The second chart illustrates a severe drag on the housing market, showing that year-over-year state-owned land transfer revenues and residential floor space starts both crashed into deep negative territory after 2021. By 2023, land transfer revenues were down nearly 30% year-over-year, while new residential floor space starts plummeted to around 40% below prior-year levels. 

A third chart shows that Chinese consumer confidence, which had consistently remained above an index level of 120 during the late 2010s, suffered a massive and unprecedented collapse in 2022, dropping to historic lows near 85 and remaining highly depressed into 2023. Finally, a comparative table contrasts the housing markets of China and the United States, illustrating the outsized role real estate plays in the Chinese economy. The value of China's housing stock is 6.0 times personal consumption expenditures, compared to 2.2 times in the US. Direct real estate activities account for 18% of Chinese GDP, triple the US share of 6%. Additionally, home price-to-income ratios in tier-1 Chinese cities like Shanghai and Beijing reach approximately 40 times income, compared to roughly 10 times in major US metropolitan areas like New York and San Francisco, and the overall homeownership rate stands at 90% in China versus 66% in the US.

This page analyzes why rising interest rates are taking longer than usual to impact corporate profit margins and household balance sheets. The author explains that, unlike some US banks that mismanaged duration risk, many US and European companies successfully extended their liability duration when interest rates were at historic lows. Consequently, corporate interest expense is falling for the first time on record during a Federal Reserve rate-hiking cycle. 

This trend is illustrated in the first chart, which displays US nonfinancial corporate net interest costs at a 60-year low. It plots corporate net interest payments as a percentage of after-tax NIPA profits alongside the Federal Reserve funds rate from 1970 to 2023. Even as the Fed funds rate has spiked, net interest payments as a share of profits have remained remarkably low, hovering around 20%. 

A similar buffering effect is occurring on household balance sheets, as shown in the second chart tracking US household debt from 1980 to 2023. This chart displays the debt service to disposable income ratio alongside the average rate on outstanding mortgages. While market mortgage rates have spiked to around 7%, the average outstanding mortgage rate remains insulated at approximately 3.5%, keeping the overall debt service ratio near historical lows of 6%. 

The housing market is also defying typical cyclical downturns due to a severe supply shortage, which is detailed in the third chart showing the months' supply of existing single-family homes from 1982 to 2023. This metric has fallen to extremely low levels, between two and three months, which has mitigated home price declines and caused new home prices to align with existing home prices for the first time since the late 1960s. 

Tight labor markets and stable consumer spending on services and automobiles have further delayed the anticipated economic downturn. The final chart displays the timing and magnitude of the expected consumer slowdown by comparing Blue Chip Financial forecasts for quarter-over-quarter real personal consumption expenditures from January 2023 and July 2023. The January report forecasted a sharp drop in consumption growth to nearly 0% by mid-2023. By contrast, the July report shows a much shallower and delayed slowdown, with consumption growth bottoming out at around 0.5% in early 2024 before recovering. 

The page concludes with commentary on the US banking system post-Silicon Valley Bank collapse. Despite a massive yield gap—with deposit rates averaging 0.5% compared to 1-year CDs at 1.8% to 2.6% and money market rates near 5.0%—deposit outflows have slowed due to implicit FDIC guarantees on uninsured deposits and Fed borrowing facilities. The next development to watch is the proposed Basel III regulations, which could raise capital requirements for major banks by 1.5% to 2.0%, potentially driving more lending activity into private markets and fintech firms.

This page analyzes the resilient US economic outlook and the inflationary pressures from rising oil prices. The author argues that fiscal deficits, industrial policies, and strong balance sheets cushion the economic slowdown, while higher energy prices have forced futures markets to abandon expectations for early interest rate cuts. 

Four charts support these observations. The first displays estimated OPEC spare capacity from 2000 to 2023, showing that non-recession spare capacity is currently at historically high levels of around 4 to 6 million barrels per day. The second chart compares rising global fossil fuel consumption, which is nearing 500 exajoules, against a sharp drop in capital spending intensity for S&P Global 1200 energy companies down to roughly 0.3x of operating cash flow. The third chart illustrates the shift in market expectations for the Fed funds target rate, showing a transition from projected rate cuts in early 2024 to a "higher-for-longer" path peaking near 5.4%. The final chart plots the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which has plummeted to its lowest level since 1983 at roughly 350 million barrels.

This page discusses whether the intense optimism and market surge surrounding artificial intelligence are fully justified. Michael Cembalest notes that while AI-linked stocks have been the primary catalyst for US equity markets this year, their momentum has cooled since July. 

To illustrate the financial impact of the AI trend, the page features two charts based on J.P. Morgan’s internal analysis of a representative AI ETF's constituents. The first chart, showing the forward P/E ratio for the XYZ Generative AI ETF, depicts valuations starting around 24x forward earnings in January 2023, peaking near 32.5x in July, and retreating to roughly 28x by mid-September. The second chart compares year-to-date returns through September 20, 2023, showing that the XYZ AI ETF gained nearly 60%, vastly outperforming the broader S&P 500, which rose about 16%. Crucially, the S&P 500 excluding the AI ETF's constituents returned only about 5%, highlighting how concentrated the market gains have been.

The text transitions into an assessment of generative AI's real-world capabilities, presenting three images generated by Bing, Starry AI, and Dall-E. The models were prompted to depict two workers looking nervously at a robot labeled "Strategy Team Trainee." The results highlight a mix of impressive imagery and bizarre errors: Bing added an eerie third person resembling a horror movie character, Starry AI omitted one of the requested workers, and Dall-E splattered gibberish letters spelling "STAAT TRATGY" across the table instead of the correct label. 

Based on these mixed results and an exercise where the author graded GPT-4 on 71 questions from the "Eye on the Market," the author concludes that generative AI is a superior technology compared to recent short-lived investment fads. However, he cautions that it is unlikely to deliver the transformational productivity shock that its most vocal proponents predict for equity markets over the long run.

This page presents a post-COVID forensic analysis comparing New York City to 21 other major US cities. Author Michael Cembalest advises clients to treat New York City like a megacap stock in a diversified portfolio, suggesting they avoid holding an overweight position due to mounting concentration risks. 

While the city boasts immense scale, dominant financial services, and a solid post-pandemic recovery in jobs, dining, and airport use, it faces profound structural hurdles. Key headwinds include a persistent mass transit deficit with utilization at only 73 percent of 2019 levels, historically high office vacancies of 18 percent, and a high rate of remote work where approximately 35 percent of workdays are still done from home. The author outlines further challenges such as potential budget cuts or tax hikes to counter operating deficits, restrictive zoning, severe home unaffordability, high municipal debt, and financial strain from an asylum-seeker crisis. Furthermore, electricity prices remain high, exacerbated by the closure of the Indian Point nuclear plant and low regional renewable capacity, which has driven significant outmigration, ranking New York State next to last nationally in taxpayer outmigration between 2011 and 2021.

To contextualize these issues, a comparative heat map table ranks the 22 cities across several weighted categories, where higher scores indicate stronger performance. New York City ranks relatively well in the Urban Recovery category with a score of 63, trailing leaders like Boise at 82 and Miami at 78, but far ahead of San Francisco at 26. However, New York City falls short in other categories, scoring a low 31 in Economy and Demographics since 2019, 38 in Business Conditions, and 39 in Fiscal Health. Ultimately, New York City’s equal-weighted composite score of 43 places it near the bottom of the list, ahead of only Chicago at 38, Detroit at 36, and San Francisco at 34, while Boise tops the overall composite rankings at 73.

This page explores the potential implications of generative artificial intelligence on employment, drawing on academic research from MIT to challenge the widely held view that technology-driven productivity gains always create enough new jobs to offset losses. Author Michael Cembalest presents three charts based on a 2019 study by Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo that analyze historical job creation and displacement effects. The first chart, looking at services and manufacturing from 1947 to 1987 (indexed to 1947), shows a balanced trend where job displacement effects, which fell to around negative 17, were almost identically offset by job creation effects, which rose to around 17. The second chart reveals that this balance broke down from 1987 to 2017; during this latter period, job creation effects only rose to about 12, while job displacement effects sank to nearly negative 20. The third chart isolates manufacturing from 1987 to 2017, illustrating an even more severe impact on workers: job creation effects rose to only about 7, while job displacement effects plummeted to roughly negative 32. 

To further support this argument, the page references a 2022 study by David Autor and co-authors, which found that innovation shifted in the 1980s away from worker augmentation and toward worker replacement. This shift is detailed in two tables tracking employment and wages as functions of exposure to augmentation and automation. The first table shows that from 1940 to 1980, employment gains from augmentation exposure (1.85) roughly balanced losses from automation exposure (negative 1.52). However, from 1980 to 2018, augmentation exposure fell to 1.31 while automation exposure worsened significantly to negative 3.99. The second table displays a corresponding trend for wages: between 1940 and 1980, wage augmentation (2.05) outpaced wage displacement (negative 1.68), but from 1980 to 2018, wage augmentation dropped to 1.34 while wage displacement worsened to negative 3.93. Collectively, these findings suggest that the historical equilibrium between job destruction and creation has decoupled, leaving automation-exposed occupations more vulnerable to erosion in both employment and wages.

This introductory page of the publication argues that geopolitical events rarely act as primary drivers for equity market returns because conflict zones typically represent a very small fraction of global economic and financial activity. Michael Cembalest points out that of roughly twenty post-World War II geopolitical events, only the 1973 Arab-Israeli War significantly drove equity markets over the subsequent six to nine months, primarily due to the associated oil embargo, wage and price controls, and stagflation. 

A detailed table, titled Conflict zone countries as a percent of total world, supports this assertion by comparing sixteen global economic, trade, and financial metrics across a group of over twenty conflict-afflicted nations, presenting figures both excluding and including Russia. The conflict list includes nations such as Afghanistan, Iraq, Israel, Ukraine, and Venezuela. Excluding Russia, these conflict-zone countries account for only 1.3 percent of global GDP, 1.5 percent of trade, 1.5 percent of imports, 0.1 percent of equity market capitalization, and 0.2 percent of interbank claims and portfolio investment inflows. Even when Russia is included, their share of global GDP is only 3.6 percent, and equity market capitalization is 0.3 percent. Russia's inclusion does, however, significantly impact energy metrics, shifting the group's share of global oil production from 7.3 percent to 19.2 percent and natural gas production from 2.3 percent to 17.5 percent. 

The page concludes with a table of contents outlining six central questions addressed in the document, which focus on whether the Middle East war will trigger a 1970s-style economic collapse, the relationship between Europe's Pillar II international tax system and NATO defenses, the historical precedents and primary ballot risks of the Trump and Biden 2024 election match-up, Taiwan's military viability against China, the necessary fiscal policies to stabilize the US Federal debt, and Thanksgiving reflections on the American experiment.

This page examines the historically unprecedented ages of Joe Biden and Donald Trump as potential 2024 presidential nominees and analyzes the legal and political procedures that would unfold if either candidate had to drop out during the primary process or the general election. 

A line chart at the top of the page, titled "2024 election, assuming Biden vs Trump," plots the average age of both major-party presidential candidates as a percentage of prevailing non-infant male life expectancy from 1790 to 2030. The data points show that the proposed 2024 Biden vs. Trump matchup represents an average candidate age that is more than 100 percent of the average male life expectancy, peaking at roughly 1.05 on the chart's index. This makes them the second-oldest pairing in U.S. history relative to life expectancy, trailing only the 1848 matchup of Zachary Taylor and Lewis Cass, which reached nearly 1.1 on the index. The chart lists several historical matchups along this timeline, showing a general decline in relative candidate age during the mid-20th century before rising sharply with recent elections, including Trump vs. Clinton in 2016 and Biden vs. Trump in 2020. 

Because of these age dynamics, the author raises the question of what would happen if a candidate withdrew for health reasons. Using Joe Biden as the nominee and California Governor Gavin Newsom as a hypothetical replacement, the text outlines four procedural scenarios based on legal guidance from Florida State University election law professor Michael Morley. 

In the first scenario, if a candidate drops out well before the primary ballot eligibility deadline, the replacement candidate would need to submit the required signatures to secure a spot on the ballot. In the second scenario, if the withdrawal happens just before the ballot deadline, no primary would be held, leaving the state's delegates unbound for the convention. In the third scenario, if a candidate drops out after the final June primary but before the August national convention, all delegates would become unbound, and party officials would use convention rules or floor votes to put the replacement nominee forward. In the final scenario, if a candidate drops out after the August convention but before the November general election, the national committee would name a replacement. Under this last scenario, some states would allow ballots to be updated with the new nominee, while others might still display the original candidate's name, requiring the party to clarify to voters that a vote for the original candidate would transfer to the replacement.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s "Eye on the Market" by Michael Cembalest assesses whether the Middle East conflict will trigger 1970s-style oil price surges, high inflation, and equity market collapses. Cembalest argues that contemporary energy risks to the United States are generally much lower than they were in the 1970s, though he highlights a few critical caveats regarding domestic production trends and depleted reserves. 

To support the argument that risks are lower today, the author notes that the United States has transitioned into a net energy exporter, with net crude imports down 75 percent from their 2005 peak, and net refined product imports flipping from 4 million barrels per day of imports to 4 million barrels per day of exports. Furthermore, the oil intensity of US GDP growth is 65 percent lower than in the 1970s, and annual global oil consumption growth has plummeted from 8 to 10 percent down to just 0 to 2 percent today. Geopolitically, an OPEC oil embargo carries less leverage now because 75 percent of Saudi Arabian oil exports go to Asia, while the United States secures most of its imported oil from Canada, Mexico, and non-OPEC sources. Saudi Arabia also maintains spare capacity to deploy if necessary. 

However, the analysis presents two primary warning signs. First, record-high US oil production is driven primarily by bringing drilled but uncompleted wells online rather than starting new projects, as capital spending on new projects by public energy companies has declined. Second, the Biden Administration chose not to refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve before the current conflict erupted, leaving the reserve down roughly 50 percent from its peak and at its lowest level since 1983.

Four charts illustrate these shifting dynamics. The first chart, depicting US energy dependence and independence from 1970 to 2020, shows net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal as a share of total primary energy consumption peaking near 30 percent in 2005 before plunging below zero percent around 2020, marking the transition to a net exporter. The second chart tracks US oil intensity alongside global five-year rolling oil demand growth from 1965 to 2015. It reveals that US oil intensity steadily declined from nearly 6 megajoules per US dollar of GDP to under 2, while global demand growth cooled from around 8 percent to nearly 0 percent. The third chart shows estimated OPEC spare capacity from 2000 to 2021, tracking volatile cycles between 2 million and over 10 million barrels per day across estimates from Bloomberg, J.P. Morgan, and Bridgewater. Finally, the fourth chart contrasts rising global fossil fuel consumption, which is nearing 500 exajoules, with a sharp drop in capital spending intensity among S&P Global 1200 Energy companies, which fell from over 1.0x operating cash flow in 2014 to roughly 0.4x in 2022. This divergence underscores the structural underinvestment that could keep energy prices elevated outside of economic recessions.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest examines Europe's global initiative for multinational tax reform under "Pillar II," focusing on the controversial implications of its third component, the Undertaxed Profits Rule (UTPR). The author frames the UTPR as an aggressive "bounty-hunting rule" because it allows a third-party nation to collect taxes from a multinational company's local subsidiary if it deems that the parent company or its other foreign subsidiaries paid too little tax under standardized Pillar II rules. This occurs even when all entities are fully compliant with their local tax laws, representing an intervention into foreign tax policies where the taxing country has no legal nexus. Cembalest argues this framework undermines U.S. tax sovereignty and hamstrings Congress's ability to design independent domestic policies. Although the Biden Administration has proposed aligning U.S. tax laws with these rules—including a UTPR, a 15% corporate Alternative Minimum Tax, and higher tax rates—the U.S. has not officially adopted Pillar II or Pillar I.

A detailed four-row table breaks down the principles of Pillar II. The first two components, the Qualifying Domestic Minimum Top-Up Tax (QDMTT) and the Income Inclusion Rule (IIR), are categorized as consistent with existing tax policy. For instance, if a Turkish subsidiary of a UK parent company pays an effective tax rate below 15%, Turkey can apply a QDMTT, or the UK can enforce its IIR to collect the top-up tax. In contrast, the table designates the UTPR as "bounty hunting with no nexus." In one scenario, if neither Turkey nor the UK collects the tax, an unrelated country where the parent has another subsidiary, such as Italy, can collect the underpaid Turkish taxes from the Italian subsidiary. In another scenario, if a U.S. parent company's effective tax rate falls below 15% due to its domestic R&D credits, France could tax the French subsidiary of that U.S. company to make up the difference.

Footnotes further highlight technical contentions, such as how Pillar II rules count non-refundable U.S. R&D credits as tax reductions while counting refundable European R&D credits as income. Cembalest also addresses the stalled "Pillar I" initiative on Digital Service Taxes, noting that unilateral actions like France taxing Google's ad revenues act as extraterritorial service sector tariffs that disrupt traditional standards of taxable nexus and transfer pricing.

This page addresses the intersection of European tax policy and international defense spending, arguing that discussions over Europe’s proposed tax policies, specifically Pillar II and GloBE rules, must also account for Europe's defense spending deficit and reliance on the United States. Michael Cembalest contends that Europe's new tax policies collide with US fiscal and economic sovereignty by taxing US subsidiaries based on parent income. Consequently, he suggests the US should raise political sovereignty and defense shortfalls as part of the discussion, particularly in light of heightened security risks following Russia's invasion of Ukraine and threats made against Polish statehood by former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev. 

To illustrate the gap in military funding, a line chart on the left compares US vs. European defense spending as a percent of GDP from 1968 to 2023. While US defense spending has consistently remained well above the 2% NATO agreement target—ranging from a peak of around 9% in the late 1960s to roughly 3.5% in recent years—spending by NATO members excluding the US has trended downwards, dipping below the 2% target in the early 1990s and remaining below it ever since. 

An accompanying table on the right quantifies this gap, detailing the "Shortfall in NATO defense spending by country vs 2% of GDP defense spending target" in billions of 2022 US dollars across three historical intervals: since the 1983 Reagan "evil empire" speech, since Vladimir Putin came to power in 1999, and since the 2006 NATO defense spending agreement. The table tracks ten countries: the United Kingdom, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Denmark, Portugal, Belgium, Norway, Germany, and Spain. Summing these figures, the total cumulative unpaid defense debt for these nations reaches $2.041 trillion since 1983, $1.785 trillion since 1999, and $1.43 trillion since 2006. Germany accounts for the largest share of this deficit by far, with shortfalls of $896 billion, $770 billion, and $590 billion across the three periods, respectively. Italy also shows substantial deficits of $365 billion since 1983, $287 billion since 1999, and $236 billion since 2006. In contrast, the United Kingdom and France have nearly met their targets, showing relatively minor shortfalls of $5 billion and $53 billion, respectively, across all three periods. 

Ultimately, the author advises that US Presidents should refrain from supporting Pillar II unless all facets of national sovereignty are negotiated, and should consider retaliating against European nations if they proceed with rules that disadvantage US multinationals, particularly regarding research and development credits.

This page, titled "Anything else to add on the US at Thanksgiving?" and authored by Michael Cembalest of JP Morgan Asset Management, explores the enduring appeal of the United States to immigrants. Despite various domestic challenges, the author argues that the US remains a global beacon of opportunity, where migrants can integrate and construct a new American identity.

To support this observation, the page features three charts. The first is a bar chart titled "US remains a beacon that few people leave," which plots the ratio of arriving migrants to departing emigrants based on the 2022 UN International Migration Stock Database. The United States leads the world by a wide margin with a ratio of approximately 16 migrants for every emigrant. Australia is second with a ratio of around 12, followed by Canada at 6, while other nations like Sweden, Spain, Jordan, Germany, France, Japan, and Argentina show much lower ratios, mostly sitting between 1 and 4.

The other two visual aids use data from the 2021 DHS Yearbook of Immigration Statistics to analyze lawful personal resident status in the US by country of origin from 1820 through the early 2000s. The first of these area charts tracks the absolute volume of incoming residents in millions of people. It highlights two distinct historical peaks: a turn-of-the-twentieth-century surge that reached nearly 9 million people (dominated by European nations like Italy, Russia, and Austria-Hungary) and a late-twentieth-century surge that peaked near 10 million people (dominated by Mexico, Central America, China, India, the Philippines, and other parts of Asia). 

The final area chart scales this same raw volume of incoming residents as a percentage of the total US population. This comparison shows that while the absolute volume of immigrants was highest in the late 20th century, the demographic impact of immigration was far greater in previous eras. Historical immigration waves in the mid-1850s (led by the United Kingdom, Germany, and Ireland) and the early 1900s both exceeded 10% of the total US population, whereas the modern peak around the year 2000 represented under 3% of the population.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication argues that recent private equity gains, particularly for vintage years 2016 through 2019, remain largely unrealized or "on paper." The author notes that for these vintage years, more than half of the total value in private equity funds is still tied up in existing, unsold positions, meaning their ultimate performance remains highly sensitive to market conditions. Highlighting the scale of this issue, Bain & Company estimates that buyout firms are holding roughly $2.8 trillion in unsold investments. Furthermore, very little dry powder remains for these specific vintage cohorts. 

The core of the page is a data table titled "US buyout: average manager stats by vintage year," sourcing peer-group median data from Burgiss and J.P. Morgan Asset Management as of Q2 2023. It tracks metrics from vintage years 2005 through 2022. For the critical 2016 to 2019 vintages, the paid-in capital to capital committed ranges from 0.90x to 1.00x, demonstrating how little committed capital is left uncalled. Crucially, the remaining value as a percentage of total fund value plus distributions climbs significantly for these cohorts, registering at 52% for 2016, 58% for 2017, 77% for 2018, and 84% for 2019. These cohorts also show solid, though on-paper, average Public Market Equivalent ratios against the S&P 500, ranging from 1.17 for the 2018 vintage to 1.30 for the 2017 vintage. 

In a critical footnote, the author cautions that while a remaining value percentage of 54% to 65% is typical for vintages around 6.5 years old, the macroeconomic environment has changed. Unlike past cycles, these pending, unsold investments must now navigate a dramatically altered, higher interest rate regime. The page also includes methodological details about the Burgiss database, which aggregates cash flow data from 300 limited partners across 1,400 funds, contrasting its robust dataset with Venture Economics data, which academic research has shown suffered from downward bias due to incomplete reporting.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest examines why private equity outperformance improved for recent vintage years, arguing that private equity investors owe a debt of gratitude to public market IPO and SPAC investors. Thanks to Federal Reserve and Treasury stimulus boosting investor risk appetite, the 2020–2021 market boom allowed private equity firms to offload companies at highly inflated valuations. This exit windfall occurred despite PE managers paying higher entry multiples—with a median enterprise value to EBITDA ratio of around 11x for 2017–2019 vintages compared to 8x in 2010—and leveraging their acquisitions more heavily, shown by a median debt to EBITDA ratio rising from 4.5x in 2010 to 5.5x in the 2017–2019 period. The author poses an open question: given these highly favorable selling conditions, why didn’t private equity managers sell even more of their holdings?

To support this narrative, the page presents four charts. The first, "US public listing proceeds by type, $ billions," tracks proceeds from 2010 through 2022, distinguishing between traditional IPOs and SPACs. It illustrates a massive surge in listings in 2020 and 2021, with total proceeds peaking well above $300 billion in 2021—heavily driven by a spike in SPAC activity—before plummeting back to near-zero levels in 2022. 

The second chart, "Average IPO/SPAC net returns by sector for vintage years 2020 and 2021," shows the subsequent two-year relative performance of these new listings against the Small Cap Growth Index across four key sectors: Healthcare, Technology, Consumer, and Diversified. Across all sectors, both IPOs and SPACs vastly underperformed the benchmark. For instance, healthcare IPOs underperformed by roughly 35% and healthcare SPACs by over 60%, while consumer SPACs underperformed by more than 60%, and diversified SPACs fared the worst, lagging the index by nearly 70%.

The third visual, "US private equity exit activity," charts quarterly exit values in billions of dollars alongside the total number of exits from 2012 to mid-2023. It reveals that US private equity exits peaked sharply in late 2021, with quarterly exit values approaching $300 billion and the exit count spiking above 600, aligning perfectly with the public listing boom before dropping off precipitously in 2022 and 2023. 

Finally, the fourth chart, "Global private equity cash flows by year," displays annual distributions and contributions in billions of dollars from 2014 to 2023 year-to-date. This visual demonstrates that the exit surge of 2021 directly powered record-breaking distributions back to investors, topping out near $700 billion and comfortably exceeding capital contributions for that year, before both distributions and contributions declined through 2022 and 2023.

This page presents an analysis of how geopolitical events and military conflicts historically impact equity markets six to nine months after their onset. The central argument is that while geopolitical events can cause short-term market anxiety, they rarely trigger prolonged equity selloffs on their own. The author points out that the 1973 Arab-Israeli War is the primary exception to this rule. Other notable selloffs during geopolitical crises, such as those in 2001 and 2022, were actually driven by underlying macroeconomic trends, specifically the dot-com tech bust in 2001 and the initiation of Federal Reserve rate hikes following a decade of negative real interest rates in 2022. 

To support this observation, the page features four line charts tracking the price returns of the S&P 500 Index from twelve months before to twenty-four months after a conflict begins. In all charts, the index value is normalized to 100 at the start of the conflict (Month 0).

The first chart examines military invasions and conflicts from 1950 to 1968. It shows that after the start of the Korean War in June 1950, the S&P 500 rose dramatically, reaching an index level near 140 after twenty-four months. The Six-Day War in June 1967 also saw post-conflict gains, climbing to around 115. The Soviet invasion of Hungary in November 1956 and the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968 experienced milder fluctuations, generally stabilizing or recovering near the 100 mark.

The second chart covers the period from 1973 to 1983 and highlights the Arab-Israeli War of October 1973 as the standout exception, where the market plummeted to index levels below 70 within a year of the war's start. In contrast, other events from this period, including the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979, the declaration of martial law in Poland in December 1981, the Falklands War in April 1982, and the United States invasion of Grenada in October 1983, all saw the S&P 500 trend upward after the initial event, with several lines reaching index levels between 110 and 130 by Month 24.

The third chart traces events from 1991 to 2010. Following the U.S. invasion of Kuwait in February 1991, the index rose from below 80 before the conflict to over 110 after. A similar positive trajectory followed the Serbian entry into Kosovo in February 1998 and the U.S. invasion of Iraq in March 2003, with the Kosovo period peaking near 140. Conversely, the market’s performance around the September 11 attacks and the subsequent U.S. invasion of Afghanistan in 2001 illustrates a steady decline from an index value of 130 down to 90, reflecting the contemporaneous dot-com market crash. The chart also plots the market's resilient response to North Korea sinking a South Korean navy vessel in March 2010.

The final chart tracks conflicts from 2014 to the publication date. It shows that the S&P 500 gained ground following both the Russian invasion of Crimea in February 2014 and President Trump's withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal in May 2018, with the index rising to around 115. However, the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 is associated with a sharp drop in the S&P 500 from roughly 115 to below 85, a downturn the author attributes to the onset of aggressive Fed rate hikes.

This page examines the subjective nature of evaluating hedge fund performance, specifically addressing how institutional constraints can inadvertently limit portfolio volatility to cash- or bond-like levels, leading to inappropriate benchmarking and perceptions of underperformance. To analyze actual performance through recent periods of stress, such as the pandemic-era drawdowns, the analysis filters a database of over six thousand funds down to 644 US-domiciled, monthly reporting hedge funds across four core strategies: relative value, equity hedge, event-driven, and macro. 

The primary visual is a scatter plot comparing these 644 individual hedge funds to 300 randomly constructed 20-fund portfolios from January 2018 to September 2023. The chart plots annualized excess return over T-bills on the vertical axis, ranging from negative 10 percent to 40 percent, against annualized excess return volatility on the horizontal axis, ranging from 0 percent to 50 percent. Individual hedge funds, represented by blue dots, show a wide dispersion, with returns ranging from negative 10 percent to over 30 percent and volatilities stretching across the entire horizontal scale up to 50 percent. In contrast, the 20-fund composites, represented by gold dots, are tightly clustered, demonstrating the powerful impact of diversification. These portfolios exhibit much lower, controlled volatilities clustered mainly between 5 percent and 15 percent, alongside steady annualized excess returns concentrated between 2 percent and 10 percent. 

The author notes that this pre-tax analysis is most relevant for non-taxable, diversified institutional investors, as after-tax performance evaluation is highly complex due to differing treatments of gains and income alongside fund-specific tax loss carryforwards.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication focuses on what the author terms paper moon effects, arguing that recent venture capital vintage years are exceptionally sensitive to market conditions compared to private equity. Specifically, the author notes that for venture capital vintages from 2013 to 2019, more than 50 percent of the total fund value remains unmonetized and reliant on existing, marked positions that have yet to be sold. This indicates that venture capital investors face greater market exposure than buyout investors.

The first visual is a comprehensive table titled US venture capital: average manager stats by vintage year, which covers vintages from 2005 through 2022 using data from Burgiss and J.P. Morgan Asset Management as of the second quarter of 2023. The table tracks metrics including paid in capital to capital committed, total value to paid in capital, distributions to paid in capital, remaining value to paid in capital, remaining value as a percentage of fund value plus distributions, and the average Public Market Equivalent ratio versus the S&P 500. This data highlights a clear trend of dwindling liquidity in younger funds. For instance, the 2012 vintage achieved distributions of 1.62x and has 43 percent of its value remaining. In contrast, the 2016 vintage has distributed only 0.34x and has 85 percent of its value remaining, while vintages from 2019 through 2022 have distributed 0.00x, meaning 100 percent of their fund value is still locked up as remaining value. The average Public Market Equivalent ratio remains above 1.00 for all reported years, peaking at 1.61 for the 2011 vintage and ending at 1.23 for the 2019 vintage.

The second visual is a bar chart titled Greater share of VC investments have yet to be monetized, which plots the remaining value as a percentage of fund value plus distributions for venture capital and buyout funds from vintage years 2010 to 2022. The chart reveals that venture capital consistently holds a much higher proportion of unmonetized value than buyout funds for every single vintage year shown. For example, in the 2014 vintage year, venture capital has 62 percent of its value remaining compared to buyout's much lower share of roughly 30 percent. By the 2018 vintage, the gap persists with venture capital at 96 percent remaining value compared to roughly 70 percent for buyouts. Both fund types converge to 100 percent remaining value by the 2021 and 2022 vintages, but the historical lag in venture capital distribution highlights the segment's prolonged market exposure.

This report by Michael Cembalest from J.P. Morgan examines the future of the private equity sector in a landscape of higher interest rates. The central argument is that a major disconnect exists between buyer and seller expectations, leading to a severe drop in deal and exit activity. The author highlights how private equity exit activity has fallen to its lowest level since 2012. As a case study, he points to Carlyle's failed acquisition of the healthcare software firm Cotiviti, where debt financing yields of roughly 12 percent ruined the transaction's economics, causing the seller to walk away when Carlyle tried to renegotiate the valuation downward. To maintain distributions to limited partners, some private equity firms are controversial, borrowing against net asset value or using payment-in-kind financing, which the author warns obscures the underlying health of the funds. 

Furthermore, the 2016 to 2019 vintage years face refinancing headwinds. Triple-C rated bond and loan issuance has collapsed by approximately 80 percent from the prior year, and B/B- loan issuance is down 70 percent from 2021 levels. Citing data from Moody's, the author notes that more than half of all B- loan market borrowers will not generate sufficient cash flow to cover capital expenditures and debt service by the end of 2023. This strain has driven "amend and extend" activity to its fastest pace since 2009, alongside an uptick in pre-emptive selective defaults for companies like Bausch Health, Carvana, AMC Entertainment, and US Renal Care. Lenders are also tightening terms by reducing their tolerance for artificial EBITDA adjustments.

Four charts visually support these observations. The first chart, titled US private equity exit activity, tracks the total exit value in billions of US dollars on the left axis and the number of exits on the right axis from 2012 to the third quarter of 2023. It illustrates a stark contraction from the peak in 2021, showing that both exit values and volumes have plummeted back to levels last seen a decade prior. 

The second chart, US LBOs: purchase price multiples, breaks down the equity and debt components of purchase multiples relative to trailing EBITDA from 2004 to 2022. This stacked bar chart highlights that purchase multiples climbed steadily over the last decade, peaking near 11x to 12x in 2021 and 2022, which is significantly higher than the historical average of roughly 8.5x recorded between 2004 and 2018.

The third chart, Interest coverage for B- rated issuers in the US loan market, depicts the percentage of borrowers falling into three interest coverage ratio categories from January 2022 to December 2023. The data reveals a dramatic deterioration in credit quality: the share of issuers with interest coverage below 1.0x surged from under 20 percent to half of the market by late 2023, while the healthiest tier of issuers with coverage above 1.5x shrank from over 50 percent to less than a third. 

The fourth chart, US leveraged loans amendments and extensions, plots the annual count of loan amendments from 2009 through year-to-date November 2023. The bar chart shows that these restructurings spiked to nearly 400 cases in 2023, representing the highest volume of amend-and-extend activity since the aftermath of the financial crisis in 2009.

This page explores the validity of current valuations for private equity assets, asking how realistic current private equity marks actually are by evaluating them through secondary market transactions. The author points out that although secondary buyout pricing in the first half of 2023 was only 10% below Net Asset Value, this pricing was recorded when the 10-year Treasury rate was still under 4%. This raises an open question of what year-end discounts will reveal. Additionally, the author warns that the secondary market lacks depth, meaning even modest transaction volumes could alter these pricing estimates substantially. 

The first chart on the page, titled "Secondary market pricing," displays the percent of Net Asset Value from 2017 through the first half of 2023 for buyout, credit, real estate, and venture funds, using data from Jefferies. Buyout pricing peaked in 2021 at around 96% of Net Asset Value, fell to roughly 83% in the second half of 2022, and recovered to 90% by the first half of 2023. Venture capital marks fared worse, dropping from a peak of nearly 88% in 2021 to around 70% in both the second half of 2022 and the first half of 2023. Real estate and credit tracked at roughly 73% and 76% of Net Asset Value, respectively, in the first half of 2023.

As another, albeit imperfect, measure of valuations, the author examines secondary market discounts in UK-listed investment companies investing in alternative investments. This lens suggests valuation discounts for buyout funds are closer to 30%, which represents the steepest discount since 2003 outside of the Global Financial Crisis, when discounts reached 50%. The second chart, titled "UK-listed investment companies discount to NAV," presents percent discounts as of November 2023 across eleven distinct asset classes, displaying market-cap weighted averages, medians, and equal-weighted averages alongside the number of funds and total market value in billions of pounds. 

According to this JP Morgan research, funds investing in growth capital (with five funds totaling 2.8 billion pounds) exhibit the widest discounts, clustered between negative 55% and negative 60%. Funds of private equity funds (with six funds totaling 5.1 billion pounds) trade at discounts of around negative 40% to negative 45%. Funds investing directly in private equity (with eight funds totaling 25.9 billion pounds) show discounts spanning from a negative 25% market-cap weighted average to a negative 35% median. Renewable energy, private credit, CLOs, and infrastructure funds exhibit discounts roughly between negative 15% and negative 25%. Traded credit funds (with ten funds totaling 1.1 billion pounds) trade closest to par, with discounts of only negative 2% to negative 5%. The chart highlights an anomaly in leasing funds for private shipping and aircraft, where a highly concentrated fund holding 70% of its Net Asset Value in a single investment trades at a positive premium of roughly 4% over Net Asset Value, pulling the market-cap weighted average for the category up to negative 20% while the median sits at negative 35%.

This analysis explores the shifting venture capital landscape, which is experiencing a correction after the highly liquid, easy financial conditions of 2020 and 2021. The author notes that tightening financial conditions have led to longer gaps between funding rounds, a surge in startup bankruptcies, a rise in down rounds, and steep drops in post-money valuations. 

To support this narrative, the page includes several charts using data from Carta and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The first chart shows that the median time between venture rounds has lengthened considerably from the first quarter of 2020 to the third quarter of 2023. Specifically, the median duration from a priced seed round to Series A grew from about 530 days to 710 days, Series A to Series B grew from 650 to 715 days, and Series B to Series C jumped from 680 days to approximately 840 days. 

This funding delay coincides with a dramatic rise in startup failures, as shown in a stacked bar chart mapping quarterly startup shutdowns due to bankruptcy or dissolution from 2019 through Q3 2023. Quarterly shutdowns remained largely below 75 from 2019 through mid-2022 but began climbing rapidly in late 2022, peaking at more than 200 shutdowns by the third quarter of 2023. This increase is heavily driven by startups that had previously raised a priced round, indicating that even more mature, funded companies are struggling to survive.

Finally, a dual horizontal bar chart illustrates the dramatic jump in both the prevalence and severity of down rounds between 2022 and 2023 across Series A through E. In terms of frequency, Series D startups saw the highest percentage of down rounds in 2023, jumping from roughly 10 percent in 2022 to over 30 percent in 2023, while Series C and E also experienced notable increases to approximately 18 percent and 25 percent, respectively. When down rounds did occur, the post-money valuation declines were severe. For instance, the median decline in post-money valuation for Series C down rounds worsened from under 20 percent in 2022 to a stark 50 percent drop in 2023, while Series E down rounds averaged declines of more than 50 percent. Overall, the text notes that the general incidence of down rounds rose from 8 percent to nearly 20 percent between the two years, signaling a broad-based valuation hangover for the startup sector.

This page addresses the issue of survivorship bias, which tends to artificially inflate reported hedge fund performance because underperforming funds that stop reporting are typically excluded from historical averages. To evaluate the impact of these dead or dying funds, the analysis incorporates Pivotal Path data from December 2017 onward, allowing 20-fund composites to randomly include 432 partially reporting funds alongside the 470 fully reporting ones, provided they have at least 24 consecutive months of performance data. After a fund stops reporting, its remaining position is assumed to be redeemed for cash, earning the prevailing monthly Treasury bill rate. 

A scatter plot visualizes these 20-fund composites against risk-adjusted benchmarks of S&P 500 and Barclays Aggregate index mixes, ranging from 20/80 to 80/20. The chart plots annualized excess return volatility on the horizontal axis (from 4% to 18%) against the annualized return versus Treasury bills since January 2018 on the vertical axis (from 0% to 10%). Although incorporating the partially reporting funds shifts the cluster of gold hedge fund composite dots downward, the vast majority of these random composites still outperform the benchmark combinations, which trend diagonally upward from a 20/80 mix near a 1% excess return up to an 80/20 mix near an 8% excess return. 

The author notes a major caveat: this model does not fully capture the real-world impact of survivorship bias because it ignores the losses incurred when a failing fund liquidates its most illiquid positions. To provide context, an accompanying table lists academic estimates of survivorship bias, defined as the decline in average annual hedge fund returns once dead funds are factored in. Every cited study shows a positive bias, meaning excluding dead funds consistently overstates performance. The estimates range from minor impacts, such as Ackerman’s 0.16% estimate in 1999 and Yuen’s 0.54% estimate in 2018, to mid-range findings between 2.00% and 3.50% from researchers such as Amin, Horst, Liang, Brown, Edwards, and Fung. The most pronounced estimates of survivorship bias come from Malkiel in 2005 at 4.50% and Aggarwal in 2010 at 5.00%.

This page examines whether randomly constructed hedge fund portfolios can outperform a risk-adjusted benchmark, which is defined as the efficient frontier of various stock and bond combinations using the S&P 500 and the Barclays Aggregate Index. Michael Cembalest analyzes performance over a five-year period starting in January 2018, emphasizing how crucial diversification is to achieving consistent outperformance. 

The first scatter plot, titled "20-fund composites vs benchmarks [HFR]," displays annualized excess return over Treasury bills on the vertical axis, ranging from 0% to 10%, against annualized excess return volatility on the horizontal axis, ranging from 4% to 18%. It plots three hundred randomly generated 20-fund portfolios from the HFR database as a cluster of gold dots alongside benchmark stock/bond combinations from 20/80 to 80/20, which are plotted as black squares. In this HFR-based analysis, 78% of the hedge fund portfolios outperformed their corresponding risk-adjusted benchmark, with the gold cluster showing generally higher returns and lower volatility compared to the stock/bond frontier. 

To demonstrate the impact of diversification, a corresponding bar chart shows that the outperformance of hedge fund portfolios declines as the number of funds included in each portfolio decreases. The chart's vertical axis tracks the percentage of portfolios that beat the benchmark, ranging from 50% to 80%, while the horizontal axis displays the number of randomly selected hedge funds in the portfolios, categorized into groups of 20, 15, 10, and 5. While a 20-fund portfolio yields a 78% outperformance rate, this rate falls to approximately 72% for 15 funds, 64% for 10 funds, and drops to about 55% for a 5-fund portfolio, representing a near-even 55/45 chance of beating the stock/bond benchmark.

The final scatter plot, "20-fund composites vs benchmarks [PivotalPath]," replicates the first analysis using the Pivotal Path database. The axes and benchmark points remain identical to the HFR chart, but the gold dots represent 20-fund portfolios constructed from the alternative database. Under these parameters, the results are even stronger, with nearly every single randomly selected 20-fund portfolio outperforming the risk-adjusted benchmark frontier. 

A footnote explains the Pivotal Path inclusion methodology, which started with a database of 2,200 funds and applied a series of exclusions. The process eliminated 716 non-US domiciled funds, 59 funds outside of the four core strategy types, 327 funds launched after 2018, 567 funds that did not report for the entire period, and 61 funds that had not yet reported data for August and September of 2023, leaving a remainder of 470 funds for the analysis.

In this page of the 2024 Outlook titled "Pillow Talk," Michael Cembalest discusses the rising expectations of a soft landing for the United States economy, driven by falling inflation and the prospects of easier Federal Reserve policy. While leading indicators suggest slowing growth and rising delinquency rates in real estate, corporate, and household sectors, the author argues these are lagging indicators for investors. He suggests that any potential recession in 2024 is likely to be mild, aided by back-door liquidity from the Federal Reserve. However, challenges persist, including mega-deficits, fully priced-in markets, and high market concentration. For context, in 2023, S&P 500 earnings were flat overall, with a thirty-three percent increase for the seven largest megacap stocks offsetting a five percent decline for the remaining S&P 500. Consequently, Cembalest forecasts slowing gross domestic product growth, single-digit earnings growth, and single-digit returns for the median S&P 500 stock in 2024. He recommends a diversified portfolio of cash, long-duration government bonds, high-quality corporate bonds, and equities, with specific interest in the industrial and energy sectors due to US industrial policies, as well as Japan.

The page features a scatter plot titled "Equities tend to bottom first during recessions" that maps the number of months since the beginning of a recession—ranging from minus eight to thirty-two months—against several historical recession periods, including the COVID recession, the Global Financial Crisis, the Dot-Com bust, the 1990s Savings and Loan crisis, the 1980s double dip, the 1970s stagflation, and the Eisenhower era. The chart plots the "time of worst reading" for various indicators: equities, the ISM manufacturing survey, gross domestic product, payrolls, S&P earnings, housing starts, high-yield default rates, real estate delinquencies, and the official end of the recession. Across almost all tracked recessions, equities (represented by red diamonds) bottomed early, typically within four to twelve months from the start of the recession, and well before lagging indicators like S&P earnings or real estate delinquencies reached their worst levels. The Dot-Com cycle is explicitly labeled as the sole exception to this rule, where the equity bottom occurred approximately nineteen months after the recession's start, far later than usual.

This page of the publication focuses on the current state of commercial real estate, specifically analyzing the challenges facing the office sector, CMBS delinquency trends, and the financial feasibility of office-to-residential conversions. The author highlights that the decline in office allocations within private portfolios began in 2015, long before the pandemic, with office exposure now comprising less than 20% of these portfolios according to MSCI estimates. This reduction helps shield investors from the ongoing headwind of work-from-home trends, which remain elevated at 30% to 35% of paid days in large urban areas, compared to a pre-pandemic baseline of just 3% nationally. 

Four distinct charts illustrate these developments. The first chart details MSCI commercial real estate core index property type allocations from 2000 through Q3 2023. It shows that office allocations peaked around 40% in the early 2000s and have steadily declined to under 20%, while allocations for apartments and industrial properties have grown substantially, with industrial experiencing a sharp upward trajectory around 2020. The second chart tracks the percentage of full paid days worked from home across major metropolitan areas from October 2020 to October 2023. It underscores that the Bay Area is a significant outlier with 45.5% of days worked from home, followed by New York City at 36.8%, Los Angeles at 36.7%, Miami at 34.6%, Washington D.C. at 34.1%, Dallas at 34%, Atlanta at 32.5%, Houston at 31.5%, and Chicago at 25.6%.

The third chart illustrates CMBS delinquencies by property type from 2001 to September 2023. Aside from regional malls, which remain heavily distressed with delinquency rates near 20%, and a recent uptick in office delinquencies, most other property types—such as hotels, multifamily, and industrial—have shown flat or improving delinquency trends. The fourth chart displays special servicing rates for office versus non-office CMBS loans from 2002 to September 2023. While historically aligned, the two series have diverged dramatically in 2023; office special servicing rates have spiked to over 8%, while non-office CMBS special servicing rates remain lower, at around 5% to 6%.

A dedicated analysis at the bottom of the page addresses the challenging financial model of office-to-residential conversions. Focusing on a sample pre-war Class B office building in New York City with current office rents of $3.50 per square foot per month, the author outlines the rigorous math required for a viable conversion. Assuming conversion costs of $320 per square foot, an additional $40 per square foot for green efficiency, a 15% loss in rentable space post-conversion, and premium residential rents at the 90th percentile ($96 per square foot annually for a 1-bedroom apartment), a buyer would still need to negotiate an acquisition price of just $175 per square foot to generate a 15% to 18% return. This acquisition price represents a steep 60% discount from pre-pandemic valuations, posing an open question as to whether sellers will be willing to transact at such heavily discounted levels.

This page explores why the aggressive Federal Reserve policy rate hikes have not yet triggered a US recession. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that while monetary policy is tighter, real interest rates remain below the painful levels that catalyzed prior recessions. Additionally, corporate cash flows are healthy rather than in deficit, and corporations strategically lengthened their debt maturities before rates spiked, shielding themselves from immediate interest rate shocks. Although the risk of a recession appears to be receding, the author cautions that recessions historically lag the initial Fed rate hike by at least seven quarters, which is precisely the timeline the US economy entered at the start of 2024. 

To support these observations, the page presents five charts and one historical table. The first chart, "Real cost of money," tracks real interest rates defined as Fed Funds minus Core CPI from 1957 to late 2023. It shows that current real interest rates of roughly 1% to 2% are significantly lower than the historical peaks of 6% to 8% that triggered prior economic downturns. The second chart, "US corporate sector financial balance," measures net savings as a percentage of corporate gross value added. It reveals that previous recessions were preceded by deep corporate deficits of negative 2% to negative 4%, whereas the current balance is stable, hovering near 0%. 

The third chart, "Corporate net interest costs stable despite rising funds rate," overlays the Fed funds rate against corporate net interest payments as a percentage of after-tax NIPA profits from 1970 to 2023. Despite the steep climb in the Fed funds rate, corporate net interest payments as a share of profits remain near historical lows at roughly 5%, a stark contrast to the 15% to 20% spikes seen in previous cycles. The fourth chart, "US private non-financial credit creation as a % of GDP," shows that credit creation remains normalized at around 5% of GDP, indicating healthy private-sector credit flow. 

Looking forward, the fifth chart, "US liquidity conditions set to improve in 2024," plots a liquidity proxy in trillions of US dollars. After declining from over $7.0 trillion in 2022 to a low of approximately $5.5 trillion in late 2023, liquidity is projected to rebound toward $6.5 trillion in 2024, bolstered by the Bank Term Funding Facility, the Overnight Reverse Repo Facility, and the Treasury General Account. 

Lastly, a historical table titled "Recessions usually take place at least 7 quarters after the initial Fed hike" lists eight tightening cycles since 1958. It illustrates that the time elapsed between the first Fed rate hike and the onset of a recession ranges from 4 quarters to 16 quarters, with most cycles taking 8 to 14 quarters. This historical lag underscores that while a recession has not yet materialized, it is still too early to completely rule one out.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2024 Outlook, authored by Michael Cembalest, argues that while leading indicators point to weaker US economic growth, they do not suggest a sharp recession. However, the author warns that investors must prepare for the risk of a hard landing in corporate profits even if the broader economy achieves a soft landing, drawing a parallel to the cycle in 2001. 

To support this view, the page presents six charts. The first chart, titled "US new orders less inventories," tracks the ISM manufacturing PMI composite index on the left axis, scaled from 30 to 70, alongside the ISM new orders less inventories index with a three-month lead on the right axis, scaled from -20 to 30, from 1983 to 2023. This chart illustrates that the author’s preferred leading indicator is improving marginally, hovering near the expansion threshold of 50. In contrast, the second chart, "Small business expectations," shows the net percentage of NFIB Optimism Survey respondents from 1986 to 2022. It reveals that small business expectations for both sales and profits are deeply depressed, with profit expectations falling to around negative thirty percent, mirroring levels seen during major past downturns.

The second row of charts highlights specific sector-level leading indicators. The chart "US bank lending standards => US non-residential capex" compares year-over-year non-residential capital expenditures on the left axis, scaled from -20% to 25%, against inverted bank lending standards with a nine-month lead on the right axis, scaled from -50% to 90% net tightening, between 1992 and 2022. It shows that significant net tightening in bank lending standards is signaling an impending decline in non-residential capex. Next, "Leading economic indicator => construction activity" plots year-over-year construction activity on the left axis, scaled from -25% to 25%, against the Conference Board's LEI Index with an 18-month lead on the right axis, scaled from -20% to 16%, from 1998 to 2023. This LEI leading indicator has dropped sharply to around negative ten percent, pointing to a severe contraction in construction activity ahead.

The final row of charts focuses on broader macroeconomic trends and corporate earnings. "Coincident and leading economic indicators" plots year-over-year coincident indicators on the left axis, scaled from -10% to 10%, against leading indicators on the right axis, scaled from -20% to 20%, from 1970 to 2020, demonstrating how the current decline in leading indicators historically signals a subsequent drop in coincident economic health. Lastly, the chart titled "Fed funds, effective corporate tax rate, unemployment, productivity growth => Corporate profits" displays corporate profits on a year-over-year percentage scale from -30% to 60% alongside a leading indicator model with an 18-month lead, compiled by Piper Sandler using the macroeconomic factors listed in the title. This model forecasts a steep decline in corporate profit growth to negative ten percent or lower by late 2023 and 2024, reinforcing the author's cautionary outlook on corporate earnings.

This page discusses the outlook for wage inflation alongside long-term inflation risks driven by US energy and industrial policies. The author argues that wage inflation is poised to decline, pointing to several leading indicators such as drops in temporary help, manufacturing, overtime hours, and voluntary quits, as well as rising female labor force participation. While union-negotiated pay raises remain at peak levels, unionized workers represent only seven percent of the workforce, a fraction of the twenty to thirty percent range seen in the 1970s. 

To illustrate this trend, the top-left chart, titled Wage Inflation Measures, tracks three metrics from 1985 through late 2023: negotiated first-year raises in union contracts, the Atlanta Fed Wage Tracker, and the year-over-year Employment Cost Index for wages. While union raises spike sharply at the end of the timeline, the other two broader indices show a distinct downward turn. This projected decline is further supported by the top-right chart, Wages in Job Postings => Wages, which overlays the Atlanta Fed Wage Growth Tracker with the average growth in wages advertised in job postings plotted with a four-month lead. This chart shows a steep drop in advertised wage growth from a peak of nearly ten percent down to around four percent by late 2023, indicating a imminent decline in broader wage growth.

The author next warns that long-term inflation risks tilt higher due to massive US fiscal deficits and energy policies that require duplicating power generation capacity. Focusing on the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, or MISO, which stretches from Minnesota to Louisiana, the author argues that expanding renewable generation does not allow for a one-to-one retirement of fossil-fuel backup power. The bottom-left chart, MISO: Wind, Solar and Gas Capacity as a Function of Wind/Solar Share of Load, maps capacity in megawatts against the wind and solar share of load ranging from eight percent to forty-four percent. The chart shows that while wind and solar capacity rises dramatically from roughly fourteen thousand megawatts to eighty thousand megawatts, natural gas capacity declines only modestly from ninety-four thousand to eighty thousand megawatts. This redundant capacity will increase capital investment and raise the ultimate cost of power.

Finally, the page addresses semiconductor policy and TSMC's construction of two fabrication plants in Arizona, totaling forty billion dollars. Citing TSMC's CFO, the author notes that these US fabs cost four to five times more than equivalent facilities in Taiwan due to higher capital and labor costs. While onshore semiconductor manufacturing addresses geopolitical risks, it will inevitably raise supply chain costs for key sectors. This secular trend is highlighted in the bottom-right chart, Global Semiconductor Market Value, which shows the industry growing from around six hundred billion dollars in 2021 to over one trillion dollars by 2030. The chart segments this market value across several categories, with computing and data storage, wireless communication, and automotive electronics representing the largest share of the projected trillion-dollar market.

This page of the report argues that the global fight against inflation is mostly accomplished, which is paving the way for central banks to pause or reverse their interest rate hikes. The author notes that the Federal Reserve is gaining much-needed breathing room due to resolving supply chain pressures, rising automobile inventories, falling used car values, and cooling residential rent inflation. However, the author cautions that futures markets pricing in 1.4% of Fed easing by the end of 2024 may be too aggressive, warning that easing too much and too quickly could reignite inflation and harm the Fed's credibility.

To support this outlook, the page features six charts. The first, titled "Developed world core inflation declines," tracks the three-month annualized percent change in core inflation across various nations, comparing their cycle peaks to their latest values as of late 2023. It demonstrates stark declines across Sweden (dropping from around 11% to roughly 2%), the UK, Norway, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, the Euro Area, the US (PCE measure), and Switzerland, all of which have seen inflation fall near or below 4%. The second chart, "US consumer price inflation measures," plots three-month annualized changes from 1985 through late 2023 for the Cleveland Fed median CPI, the Atlanta Fed sticky CPI, and the Cleveland Fed trimmed mean CPI. All three measures show a steep post-pandemic spike that peaked near 7% to 8% but have since retreated significantly to the 3% to 4% range.

The third chart, "Supply chain pressures subside," illustrates the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's Global Supply Chain Pressure Index from 2018 to 2023. The index peaked dramatically above 4 during pandemic-era bottlenecks but has plummeted back below its historical average, landing near zero. The fourth chart, "US used vehicle prices fall and auto inventory recovering," utilizes a dual-axis format to track the Manheim US Index alongside auto inventories as a percent of their 2019 average from 2019 to early 2024. This visual shows that as inventories plummeted to a low of nearly 10% in 2021, used vehicle values spiked to over 245. As inventories have steadily recovered toward 40% of their baseline, used vehicle values have declined back toward 200.

The final two charts focus on the housing sector. "Timely residential rent measures vs CPI rent" compares the annualized six-month change of the Zillow rent index against official CPI Rent from 2016 through 2023. The leading Zillow index peaked above 15% in late 2021 before plummeting to nearly 0%, while the lagging CPI Rent peaked later at around 9% and is now in a clear downward trend. Finally, the "Housing supply under construction" chart displays multi-family and single-family units under construction as a percentage of owner-occupied housing stock from 2000 to 2024. It reveals that multi-family construction surged to a historic peak near 1.4% before ticking downward, while single-family construction continues to rise toward 1.2%, indicating a massive wave of housing supply coming online that will help further depress shelter inflation.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan 2024 Outlook, titled "Leviathans: US equity markets and the domination of megacap stocks," analyzes the unique conditions facing the US stock market, specifically the convergence of asset yields and the valuation divergence driven by megacap companies. Cembalest argues that because yields on equities, high-grade bonds, T-bills, and REITs have converged for the first time in two decades, cash offers strong risk-adjusted value. Furthermore, underlying corporate fundamentals are weaker than headline figures suggest, with flat real revenues, flat operating earnings, and flat free cash flow since early 2022 when excluding the seven largest megacap stocks. Looking ahead to 2024, he forecasts single-digit earnings growth and returns for the median US stock, with megacaps continuing to lead and the market already pricing in a soft landing.

A line chart titled "Convergence of yields across assets" displays yields from 2000 through late 2023 for four asset classes: the S&P 500 12-month forward earnings yield, US corporate investment-grade bonds yield to maturity (YTM), the US three-month Treasury rate YTM, and All Equity REITs implied unlevered cap rate. By late 2023, these four series tightly converge within the 5% to 6% range, illustrating why cash has become an attractive relative play. 

A second line chart, "S&P 500 valuations," tracks forward P/E multiples from 1995 to late 2023, comparing the market-cap-weighted S&P 500 against the equal-weighted version. It shows a stark divergence: the market-cap-weighted S&P 500 sits at a high 19x forward P/E, near the upper end of its historical range, whereas the equal-weighted S&P 500 is much closer to its historical median at 16x.

Beyond technology, Cembalest identifies industrials and energy as compelling sectors. A line chart titled "Industrial valuations vs the market" plots the ratio of the industrial sector's forward P/E to the S&P 500 from 1996 to late 2023. The ratio hovers around 1.00 to 1.05, indicating industrials are inexpensive relative to the broader market and well-positioned to benefit from legislative support for energy, semiconductors, and infrastructure. 

Lastly, a heatmap table titled "Percentile rank of energy sector valuations relative to S&P 1500" shows valuation ranks from historical inception to November 2023. Across sub-sectors like Drilling, Equipment & Services, Integrated Oil & Gas, Exploration & Production, Refining & Marketing, and Storage & Transport, energy is exceptionally cheap. On a last-and-next 12-month basis, the overall energy sector ranks in the 4th percentile for enterprise value to EBITDA (lower is cheaper) and the 87th to 88th percentile for free cash flow yield (higher is cheaper). Although stranded asset concerns may cap valuation multiple expansion, the author argues the energy sector remains a highly attractive source of earnings yield, dividends, and stock buybacks.

This page analyzes the relative paths of European and Japanese equities, highlighting the long-term success of the author's "barbell" investment strategy, which overweights the United States and Emerging Markets while underweighting Europe and Japan. Despite European equities trading at a near-record valuation discount, they underperformed the US by 7% in 2023. An accompanying chart illustrating the barbell strategy's three-year rolling outperformance versus the MSCI All World Index from 1991 to 2021 shows that this strategy has outperformed in 84% of all three-year rolling periods, yielding an average positive return of 3.0% compared to a negative 1.2% return when it does not work. A second chart tracks the European price-to-earnings discount relative to the US from 2006 to late 2023 based on forward earnings from Bloomberg and Datastream. This visual demonstrates a steadily widening gap that plunged to nearly a negative 40% discount by late 2022 and 2023.

Turning to Japan, the author argues that corporate governance reforms and macro policies are creating a stronger foundation for equity investing, making cash less attractive as real short-term interest rates sit at negative 2%. Key structural shifts include the Tokyo Stock Exchange threatening to delist companies trading below book value, the emergence of over 50 activist funds, and the share of companies with over 50% independent external directors doubling from 30% to 60%. Additionally, new tax incentives and pressure on pensions to align with the Government Pension Investment Fund are driving households and institutions to increase equity allocations. 

A comparative table detailing the room for Japan to "equitize" contrast Japan with the United States across several financial metrics. Japan’s 10-year dividend payout ratio is 30% compared to the US's 70%, cash as a percentage of market capitalization is 21% in Japan compared to 7% in the US, and a massive 50% of Japanese companies trade below book value versus only 4% in the US.
