Additionally, corporate buybacks represent 0.7% to 1.4% of market capitalization in Japan versus 2.0% to 3.5% in the US, household equity allocation is only 11% compared to 40% in the US, and household cash allocation is a high 55% in Japan compared to 15% in the US. A final chart tracking Japan's Consumer Price Index excluding fresh food and energy from 1980 to 2023 shows that after decades of near-zero or negative inflation, Japan has finally exited deflation with core inflation rising sharply to approximately 4% year-over-year.

This publication analyzes how Japan transitioned into a compelling value investment in 2023, recapturing the attention of international investors despite substantial long-term economic challenges. While Japan faces structural headwinds, including unfavorable demographics that limit its potential growth rate to less than one percent, negative real wage growth, and being eclipsed by China as the world's largest auto exporter, a one-time exit from deflation paired with corporate governance reforms has bolstered its near-term appeal. The author notes that while these changes offer a tailwind, they may not serve as a multi-year investment rationale. 

Four exhibits support this analysis. The first chart, illustrating year-to-date cumulative overseas investor inflows into Japan in trillions of Yen, shows that while inflows in 2023 did not match the historic 2013 peak of nearly fifteen trillion Yen, they represents a significant recovery compared to prior years like 2017 and 2019, climbing past six trillion Yen by mid-year. 

A comparative table of major equity factor returns for 2023 year-to-date highlights the strength of Japan's value factors. Japan's price-to-earnings factor return stood at thirty-three percent, and its price-to-book factor return reached thirty percent. This vastly outperformed the United States, which saw returns of minus eight percent and minus four percent for those factors respectively, and Europe, which recorded two percent and minus three percent. Japan also led with a thirteen percent return on equity compared to negative fourteen percent in the United States and zero percent in Europe. 

The third chart tracks global investor underweighting to Japanese stocks from 2003 to 2023 by comparing the MSCI All World Global Equity Index Japan weight with actual portfolio weightings. Although global investors have chronically underweight Japanese equities for twenty years, the gap has narrowed to a modest underweight of approximately one percent, with the actual weight hovering around four and a half percent against the index weight of roughly five and a half percent. 

The final chart shows Japan's real broad effective exchange rate index from 1994 to late 2023. The exchange rate has experienced a massive secular decline, falling from an index peak of nearly one hundred ninety in the mid-1990s to below eighty by late 2023, emphasizing the historical cheapness of the Yen as a major tailwind for foreign buyers.

Michael Cembalest discusses how the extreme concentration and valuation of the market's largest megacap stocks—collectively known as the "Magnificent 7," consisting of Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla—are fundamentally supported by their superior profit margins and free cash flow. Absent any major antitrust actions, these dominant firms continue to grow stronger. However, this has led to a highly crowded market position where almost all investors seem aligned on the same trade. 

To demonstrate this market dominance, the first chart, titled "Market cap of largest 7 companies in S&P 500," shows the percent of total index market cap from 1996 to late 2023. This concentration reached an all-time high of nearly 28% in 2023, surpassing the previous dot-com bubble peak of approximately 21% in 2000. This concentration is driven by massive performance differences, as illustrated in the next chart, "Magnificent 7 stocks led S&P 500 in 2023." Here, the Year-to-Date return for the Magnificent 7 is shown at approximately 75%, compared to about 25% for the overall S&P 500 and only 12% for the S&P 500 excluding these seven companies.

Cembalest argues that these valuations are justified by fundamental superiority, as shown in two subsequent charts comparing the Magnificent 7 to the rest of the S&P 500. The chart on "Magnificent 7 growth in free cash flow vs rest of S&P 500" uses an index starting in 2018 to show that the free cash flow index for the megacaps surged to over 210 by late 2023, while the rest of the S&P 500 languished around 145. At the same time, the chart "Magnificent 7 profit margin vs rest of S&P 500" shows the megacaps maintaining profit margins near 21% in late 2023, compared to just 9% for the rest of the S&P 500.

Addressing valuation concerns, the chart "Valuations of Magnificent 7 vs median S&P 500 stock" plots two lines from 2013 to 2023. While the standard relative P/E ratio is high at 1.7x, the relative P/E ratio adjusted for long-term earnings growth expectations is actually quite reasonable at 0.9x, suggesting that these megacaps are not as overpriced as they initially appear. However, the final chart, "Nasdaq 100 positioning: asset managers & leveraged funds," highlights a potential risk. Plotting the net number of contracts from 2010 to 2024, the data shows that net long positions spiked sharply in late 2023 to nearly 100,000 contracts, revealing that the market has become extremely crowded around this single thesis.

This page analyzes the primary sources of credit stress in the United States, focusing on regional malls and offices within commercial real estate, subprime auto loans and credit cards in the household sector, and falling interest coverage and rising restructurings within the leveraged loan market. Notably, the author points out that delinquency rates remain remarkably low in other sectors, such as hotels, non-mall retail, multifamily, and industrial properties.

The first chart displays commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) delinquencies by property type from 2001 through late 2023. It highlights that regional malls experienced a massive spike in delinquencies starting in 2020, peaking near 25% and remaining highly elevated through 2023. While hotel delinquencies also spiked sharply during the pandemic, they have since normalized back to low single digits, while multifamily and industrial delinquencies remain negligible, hovering near 0%. 

The second chart traces special servicing rates for office and non-office CMBS loans from 2002 to late 2023. It reveals a sharp divergence: while non-office special servicing rates have declined from their 2020 peak of around 12% down to approximately 6%, office special servicing rates are climbing steeply, approaching 9% by late 2023.

Focusing on the corporate sector, the third chart illustrates interest coverage for B- rated issuers in the US loan market between January 2022 and December 2023. It shows a severe deterioration in debt service capacity, as the percentage of issuers with interest coverage below 1.0x skyrocketed from roughly 20% to over 60%. Concurrently, issuers with interest coverage above 1.5x shrank from over half of the market to around 15%. 

This corporate stress is further illustrated in the fourth chart, which counts US leveraged loan amendments and extensions from 2009 through November 2023. The chart shows that amendments and extensions surged to nearly 450 in 2023, representing the highest level of restructuring activity seen since the aftermath of the global financial crisis in 2009, when the count peaked above 500.

Finally, the fifth chart tracks US 90+ days loan delinquency transition rates from 2004 to mid-2023 across various consumer loan types. It demonstrates that household credit stress is concentrated in subprime auto loans, which have risen sharply to over 4%, and credit cards, which are approaching 4%. In contrast, prime auto loans, first mortgages, and second mortgages remain highly stable and near historical lows of 1% or less.

This page analyzes the state of US fixed income, focusing on the resilience of large-cap corporate debt and the end of an unprecedented era of negative real interest rates. The author argues that rising interest rates have had a minimal impact on US large-cap companies because their debt structures are highly insulated. This is illustrated by a pie chart of S&P 500 debt composition showing that 76% of the debt is long-term fixed, while only 10% is short-term fixed, 8% is long-term floating, and 6% is short-term floating. Consequently, interest coverage ratios remain robust despite high overall leverage. The investment grade market is further aided by credit upgrades exceeding downgrades, as shown in a bar chart tracking rating changes from 2010 to 2023 where the net change line has remained firmly positive in recent years.

For high yield bonds, maturities have fallen to an all-time low. A line chart tracking the weighted average maturity of US corporate high yield debt from 1987 to 2023 shows a steady decline from over 10 years in the late 1980s to just over 5 years today. While this shorter maturity increases exposure to higher rates, the author notes that high yield bonds benefit from much stronger fundamentals than in prior cycles. A table comparing the current historical percentile rank of US investment grade and high yield debt across various leverage, profitability, and liquidity metrics supports this. US high yield stands at a very favorable 92nd percentile for interest coverage and a safe 19th percentile for interest expense to debt. Meanwhile, US investment grade sits in a historically highly leveraged 100th percentile for total debt to assets, yet still maintains a solid 69th percentile for interest coverage. 

Finally, the author places the recent macroeconomic environment into historical context. A bar chart spanning 1830 to the present plots the five-year average of the T-bill/Funds rate less inflation. The data reveals that the recent era of financial repression was the longest peacetime period of negative real rates on record, comparable only to the eras of the Civil War, World War I, and World War II. However, with the one-year policy rate finally turning positive, the author declares that this long period of peacetime financial repression has finally ended, bringing relief to fixed income investors.

This page presents a comprehensive fixed income monitor, focusing on whether 10-year US Treasury yields will trend toward 3.5% or 5.5%. The author, Michael Cembalest, forecasts that 10-year Treasuries will fluctuate between 4.0% and 5.0% in 2024, though he suggests a breakout would more likely push yields up to 5.5% rather than down. He notes that yields above 4.5% offer appealing value to long-term investors. 

The analysis is supported by nine historical charts tracking yields, spreads, and different fixed-income sectors through late 2023. The first chart, tracking US Treasury yields, compares the 3-month US Treasury bill against the 10-year Treasury from 2000 to late 2023, showing the dramatic rise of both yields to around 5% before a slight cooling-off period. Next, the US Municipal yields chart shows a similar trend for 1-17 year municipals and long-duration (20+ year) municipals, both spiking and then easing slightly at the end of 2023. A sovereign bond chart for Europe and China shows Europe's 10-year yield surging from negative territory up to nearly 3%, while China's 10-year yield has steadily trended downward to around 2.5%.

The second row of charts examines spreads and emerging market sovereigns. The chart tracking the spread between the 30-year mortgage rate and the 10-year Treasury shows a historical spike, peaking near 300 basis points in late 2023. The AAA asset-backed securities spreads chart compares commercial real estate (CRE), auto, and credit card spreads against Treasuries from 1998 to late 2023; while auto and credit card spreads remain low, CRE spreads saw a distinct uptick toward 150 basis points. The second sovereign bond chart highlights emerging markets, showing South Africa's 10-year local currency yield climbing toward 12% and Mexico's rising to approximately 9% by late 2023.

The final row of charts details floating rate and preferred markets. The floating rate instruments chart shows US investment-grade corporate floating rate notes and AA bank commercial paper climbing rapidly from near-zero in 2021 to around 6% in 2023. The preferred option-adjusted spread chart shows US investment-grade preferred stock spreads versus US Treasuries; while these spreads reached over 700 basis points in 2008 and 400 basis points in 2020, they sat near a more modest 200 basis points in late 2023. Lastly, the US preferred yields chart shows that both high yield and high grade preferred yields to worst rose sharply from 2021 to late 2023, peaking near 8% and 7% respectively.

This page from the publication presents a comprehensive dashboard of credit spreads, yields, and debt prices across global fixed-income sectors as of late December 2023. The collective visual data underscores a market environment where broad corporate credit and high-yield spreads have compressed significantly toward historical lows, contrasting sharply with intense, localized distress in commercial real estate, specifically office debt.

Starting with investment-grade corporate bonds, the US investment-grade corporate spreads chart, tracking the JULI index against US Treasuries, shows that spreads have compressed to approximately 100 basis points, well below historical peaks seen in 2002, 2008, and 2020. Similarly, emerging markets dollar bond spreads over US Treasuries have settled around 350 basis points. In US high-yield debt, broad JPDFHYI index spreads vs. US Treasuries hover tight at around 350 to 400 basis points. This tightness is even more pronounced in the US high-yield energy sector, where spreads have collapsed to roughly 250 to 300 basis points, a stark contrast to the dramatic spikes above 1,500 basis points in 2016 and 2,000 basis points in 2020. US leveraged loan prices, tracked via the SPBDALB index, reflect this high credit demand, trading near the upper end of their historical range at roughly 96 to 97. 

In Europe, the Pan-European high-yield index yield sits at approximately 7% to 8%, down significantly from its 2008 peak of over 18%. The analysis also compares European Contingent Capital, or "CoCo" preferreds, using two series for yield to worst: one from ICE/Bank of America and another from JP Morgan. The ICE/BofA series, which includes emerging market issuers and subordinated Tier 2 debt, sits at a yield to worst of roughly 8.5%, while the JPM series, focusing strictly on European AT1 capital preferreds, is slightly lower at around 7.5%. In sovereign debt markets, the chart for Brazil's 10-year local currency sovereign bond yield displays a current level of approximately 10% to 11%, down from its 2015 peak of over 16% but up from its 2020 lows of under 7%.

The final chart, illustrating single-asset single-borrower commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) for offices, provides a dramatic contrast to the tight conditions in corporate credit. Spreads versus US Treasuries have widened severely across all tranches since late 2022. As of December 2023, Office BBB spreads have surged to over 700 basis points, Office A spreads stand near 550 basis points, Office AA spreads are at roughly 450 basis points, and even the highest-rated Office AAA spreads have widened to approximately 300 basis points. This visual emphasizes that while broader credit markets display calm and tight pricing, the commercial office real estate sector continues to face extreme market-implied risk.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2024 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, walks through five key exhibits analyzing the trajectory of the U.S. Federal debt, rising interest expenses, and deteriorating budget deficits. The author's primary argument focuses on the anticipated fiscal strain of the public debt, noting the unusual presence of a large budget deficit during a period of full employment, and exploring downside scenarios that could worsen the primary deficit.

The first chart, titled Debt Held by the Public, plots public debt as a percentage of GDP from 1970 to 2030. Historically, public debt rose from around thirty-five percent in the 1970s, stabilized in the 1990s, and then spiked dramatically following the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. The chart compares the January 2020 CBO projection with the May 2023 CBO projection, illustrating a significant upward revision where public debt is now expected to exceed one hundred ten percent of GDP and approach one hundred twenty percent by 2030.

The second chart, Interest Expense, tracks gross and net interest as a percentage of GDP from 1962 to 2032. Gross interest expense peaked near five percent in the late 1980s and early 1990s before declining, but has started to surge again. Looking forward, projections from the November 2023 J.P. Morgan forecast and the May 2023 CBO forecast show net interest expense rising sharply from under two percent to approximately three point five percent of GDP by 2032. The author highlights that these forecasts show net interest expense potentially reaching new post-war highs and exceeding defense spending for the first time since the 1990s.

The third chart, Budget Deficit, displays the budget deficit as a percentage of GDP from 1970 to 2030. Historical data shows massive deficit spikes during the Global Financial Crisis and COVID-19. The May 2023 CBO projection shows the deficit deteriorating and remaining persistently elevated around six percent of GDP through 2030.

The fourth chart, US Budget Balance vs Unemployment Rate, overlays the budget balance as a percentage of GDP against an inverted unemployment rate from 1969 to 2019. Historically, the budget balance and unemployment rate tracked each other closely, but after 2015, they diverged sharply. While the unemployment rate fell to historic lows, the budget deficit widened, demonstrating how unusual it is to run a large fiscal deficit during a period of full employment.

The final chart, Primary Budget Balance, shows the primary budget balance excluding interest as a percentage of GDP from 1985 to 2025. It compares the May 2023 CBO projection, which shows the primary deficit flatlining near negative three percent, against J.P. Morgan's November 2023 downside projection, which dips lower to around negative five percent. The author lists three primary catalysts that could trigger this downside trajectory: lower tax revenues than CBO projections even after the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act cuts expire, discretionary spending rising above CBO projections to grow in line with inflation due to defense needs, and more frequent federal disaster funding.

This page from the report analyzes the durability of the US dollar's global reserve currency status despite deteriorating fiscal metrics, while debunking the popular narrative that China is rapidly divesting from US dollar-denominated assets. 

The first chart, titled Government debt / GDP vs average credit rating, illustrates that the United States is a significant fiscal outlier. Plotting average credit ratings on the horizontal axis against government debt-to-GDP ratios on the vertical axis, the chart reveals that the US holds an AA+ rating despite a debt-to-GDP ratio of approximately 120 percent. This ratio is far higher than other nations with comparable ratings, such as Canada, Germany, and Australia, and sits well above the general trendline. Other heavily indebted nations, like Spain and Portugal, carry much lower BBB-tier ratings, while Japan is an extreme outlier with a 260 percent debt-to-GDP ratio and an A rating. Accompanying this chart is a historical timeline of dominant reserve currencies, ranging from the Roman Empire to the British Pound, illustrating that every major currency's dominance eventually ends. The US dollar has held this mantle since approximately 1920, raising the open question of how long its good fortune will last.

The second portion of the page addresses the warning sign of China's apparently falling allocation to US dollars in its foreign exchange reserves. To investigate this, a chart titled Estimating China's dollar assets displays four data series from 2008 to 2022 in billions of US dollars. While headline figures show that China's directly custodied US Treasuries have steadily declined from about 1.25 trillion dollars in 2013 to roughly 800 billion dollars in 2022, research by Brad Setser at the Council on Foreign Relations reveals a far more stable reality. After adjusting for US Treasuries held by offshore custodians, such as Belgium's Euroclear, and apparent reallocations into US Agency bonds, China's estimated US dollar assets have actually remained stable since 2015, hovering between 1.75 trillion and 2.0 trillion dollars. This adjusted metric aligns closely with another estimate of China's dollar holdings derived from IMF COFER shares, which has remained above 2.0 trillion dollars. This evidence suggests that China's total dollar exposure is not in steep decline.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2024 Outlook, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the strength of the US consumer, arguing that while spending remained strong in 2023, it is poised to slow as excess pandemic-era savings are depleted. The author highlights strong holiday retail indicators, such as Black Friday online sales growing by 7.5 percent and Cyber Monday sales by 9.5 percent in November 2023. However, this spending, driven by tight labor markets, a wealth effect from rising home and equity prices, and the drawdown of excess savings, is facing headwinds as those savings run out.

Four charts support this analysis by comparing the United States with the Eurozone, Japan, and the United Kingdom. The first chart, plotting real personal consumer spending indexed to the fourth quarter of 2019, shows the United States leading other regions significantly, rising to an index level of nearly 110 by late 2023, while the Eurozone sits around 102, Japan near 100, and the United Kingdom remains depressed below 100 at around 97. The second chart, tracking wealth relative to pre-pandemic levels indexed to the fourth quarter of 2019, displays a similar trend of US outperformance. US wealth reached an index level above 130 by late 2023, compared to roughly 124 for the United Kingdom, 120 for the Eurozone, and 112 for Japan.

The third chart demonstrates how this spending is funded, showing the saving rate deviation from pre-pandemic levels as a percentage-point deviation from the 2019 average. The US saving rate has dropped sharply to about negative 3 percent to 4 percent, whereas savings rates in Japan and the Eurozone remain positive relative to their pre-pandemic averages, at around 5 percent and 2 percent respectively, and the United Kingdom hovers near zero deviation. Finally, the fourth chart shows estimates of US household excess savings in billions of US dollars from various J.P. Morgan divisions. These savings peaked at nearly 2.5 trillion dollars in 2021. Both J.P. Morgan Economics and J.P. Morgan Private Bank project these savings will dwindle to approximately 500 billion dollars by early 2024, while J.P. Morgan Investment Bank predicts a complete exhaustion of excess savings, dipping into negative territory below zero by early 2024. These projections are compared against a San Francisco Fed estimate suggesting exhaustion will occur sometime in the first half of 2024, after which consumer spending is highly likely to slow down.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication focuses on the international role and enduring dominance of the US dollar, drawing on data from an April 2023 analysis. The core observation is that despite ongoing discussions surrounding de-dollarization, the US dollar remains the overwhelmingly dominant currency in global trade, reserves, and transaction volumes, far outstripping the actual size of the United States economy.

The first chart, titled Foreign Exchange Turnover by Currency, illustrates the percentage share of different currencies in global turnover from 2001 to 2022. Because every foreign exchange transaction involves two currencies, the total percentage sums to 200 percent. The data reveals that the US dollar has maintained a nearly flat, dominant share of around 85 to 90 percent over the two-decade period. The Euro consistently occupies the second position, followed by the Japanese Yen, British Pound, other minor currencies, and a very small, recently visible share for the Chinese Renminbi.

A second visual, titled Dollar Still Dominates FX Transactions, uses a donut chart to break down world transactions by currency pair based on April 2022 data. It shows that US dollar transactions account for 89 percent of the global total, leaving non-US dollar transactions with just an 11 percent share. The largest single category is the US dollar paired with all other currencies at 43 percent, followed by the US dollar/Euro pair at 23 percent, the US dollar/Yen at 14 percent, and the US dollar/British pound at 10 percent. Transactions not involving the dollar are small, with the Euro/all other pair at 8 percent and all other currency pairs combined at 4 percent.

The third chart, a horizontal bar chart titled The International Role of the US Dollar, contrasts the actual global economic footprint of the United States with the global footprint of its currency. While the United States accounts for only about 25 percent of global GDP and roughly 10 percent of world trade, the US dollar’s share of global markets is disproportionately vast. The dollar accounts for about 40 percent of SWIFT payments, 50 percent of trade invoicing, 60 percent of official foreign exchange reserves, nearly 90 percent of FX transaction volume, and roughly 50 percent of both international debt securities and cross-border loans, with a substantial portion of the latter two categories being held offshore.

The final visual is an area chart tracking the Share of Global Foreign Exchange Reserves by Currency from 1973 through 2023. This chart demonstrates the long-term stability of the dollar as the world's primary reserve currency. Although its share of global reserves has fluctuated—falling from over 80 percent in the 1970s to a low of nearly 50 percent in 1990, rebounding to over 70 percent in the early 2000s, and gradually declining to just under 60 percent by 2023—it remains far ahead of any competitor. The Euro has held a stable second-place share of around 20 percent since its creation, while other currencies such as the Japanese Yen, British Pound, Canadian Dollar, Australian Dollar, Swiss Franc, and Renminbi make up only minor fractions of global foreign exchange reserves.

This page of the publication analyzes the health of US household balance sheets, focusing on loan delinquencies, interest costs, and debt service levels. The author observes that while delinquencies are rising for riskier categories like subprime auto loans and credit cards, overall household interest costs remain low. This financial resilience is largely due to US consumers locking in very low mortgage rates below four percent prior to the recent cycle of rate hikes.

A chart on the top left displays US ninety-plus days loan delinquency transition rates as a percentage from 2004 to 2024. It tracks five categories: subprime auto loans, credit cards, standard auto loans, first mortgages, and second mortgages. The data reveals that subprime auto loan delinquencies have surged to a new all-time high of approximately five percent, surpassing their financial crisis peak. Credit card delinquencies are also rising, hovering near four and a half percent, though they remain below historical highs. Meanwhile, standard auto loans, first mortgages, and second mortgages remain stable and historically low, with mortgages sitting near zero percent. 

To the right, another chart tracks annualized ninety-plus days delinquency transition rates as a percentage of current balances over the same twenty-year period for credit cards, auto loans, and mortgages. This visualization emphasizes a sharp post-pandemic surge in credit card delinquencies, which rose from around four percent to six percent by late 2023. Annualized auto loan delinquencies saw a more moderate rise to two percent, while annualized mortgage delinquencies remained flat and near zero.

The bottom left chart evaluates household interest costs as a percent of disposable personal income from 1977 to 2023. It divides these costs into mortgage interest and consumer interest. Mortgage interest costs have dramatically declined from their late-1980s and mid-2000s peaks of over six percent down to under three percent. Consumer interest costs have remained remarkably stable for decades, hovering between two and three percent, showing only a slight upward tick at the end of the series. 

The final chart on the bottom right examines US household debt from 1980 to 2023. It plots the debt service ratio as a percentage of disposable income on the left axis against the average rate on outstanding mortgages on the right axis. The average mortgage rate shows a long-term downward trend from nearly eleven percent in the early 1980s to historical lows of under four percent by 2021. Consequently, the household debt service ratio, which peaked at nearly thirteen and a half percent in 2007, dropped to a historic low of nine percent during the pandemic and has only ticked back up slightly to around ten percent, highlighting the insulated state of the broader US consumer.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2024 Outlook examines the structural economic challenges facing China, particularly its severe housing market contraction, weak consumer confidence, and a historic downturn in foreign investment. The author notes that while some indicators are beginning to improve from very low levels, the Conference Board still expects China’s GDP growth to slow from 5% in 2023 to 4% in 2024. This slowdown is primarily attributed to misallocated investment in real estate rather than excess industrial capacity.

To illustrate these trends, the page features four charts and one comparative table. The first chart shows that foreign direct investment into China, measured in billions of US dollars from 1998 through 2023, has fallen into negative territory for the first time, dragging net FDI below zero. The second chart tracks China's real economic activity using a weighted index of ten monthly indicators, including real estate investment, vehicle exports, electricity production, and enterprise output. This index reveals that after a brief post-pandemic rebound in 2020–2021, real economic activity has remained weak, hovering just above zero through 2023.

Two additional charts detail the domestic downturn. The chart on China's housing drag from 2017 to 2023 shows a sharp contraction in state-owned land use right transfer revenue and a steep drop in the floor space of newly started residential houses, which fell past negative 40% year-over-year before showing a minor bottoming-out pattern. Mirroring this real estate weakness, the China consumer confidence index, which benchmarks 100 to 1997 levels, collapsed in 2022 from historical highs of around 120 down to historic lows below 90, where it remained through late 2023.

A comparative table contrasts China’s housing market at its peak with that of the United States to underscore the scale of China’s real estate exposure. The value of China's housing stock relative to personal consumption expenditures reached 6.0x at its peak, compared to 2.2x in the US. Direct real estate-related activities accounted for 18% of China's GDP at its peak, three times the US level of 6%. Mid-2023 home price-to-income ratios in premier Chinese cities like Shanghai and Beijing stood at approximately 40x, compared to 10x in high-cost US markets like New York and San Francisco. Additionally, China's homeownership rate peaked at 90% (with 20% of households owning more than one home) compared to 66% in the US. China's housing stock of 430 square feet per capita is double the levels found in Europe or Japan.

The page concludes with a discussion of policy responses to these deflationary pressures and banking system weaknesses, noting that China's net interest margins are just 1.75% compared to 3.25% in the US. For 2024, J.P. Morgan China economists project a slightly higher budget deficit, modest cuts to interest rates and bank reserve requirements, and targeted programs to mitigate local government financial stress.

This page introduces a section titled "The Fats Dominoes," analyzing the impact of glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1) weight loss and diabetes drugs on equity markets. The author explains that GLP-1 drugs show substantial efficacy in treating diabetes and obesity, and early data suggests they may also address related co-morbidities and addictive behaviors such as alcoholism. Equity markets have already begun pricing in these behavioral shifts, negatively impacting stock prices for insulin manufacturers, snack food makers, and alcoholic or sugary beverage producers. 

With more than 100 weight loss agents currently in development, researchers expect global GLP-1 drug sales to exceed $100 billion by 2030, even if market penetration among eligible obese populations remains in the single digits. Highlighting the intense interest from major pharmaceutical companies, the text notes that Roche acquired Carmot for $2.7 billion in December, and suggests that other giants—including Pfizer, Bristol, Merck, AstraZeneca, GlaxoSmithKline, Sanofi, and Takeda—will likely pursue acquisitions of venture-backed firms to secure a foothold. Key open questions remain regarding the durability of weight loss once treatment stops, who will cover the high cost of these drugs, and the true extent of co-morbidity reductions. The section outlines seven primary investor issues to be addressed, including funding sources, side effects, clinical trials, delivery methods (injectable versus oral), and consumer behavior impacts.

An accompanying line chart illustrates the historic and projected US average monthly total GLP-1 prescriptions in millions from 2008 to 2030. The timeline highlights key FDA milestones, including the approvals of Victoza in 2010; Trulicity and Saxenda in 2014; Ozempic in 2017; Wegovy in 2021; Mounjaro in 2022; and Zepbound for obesity in 2023. Projections starting in 2023 show rapid growth from both J.P. Morgan and TD Cowen. Type II Diabetes prescriptions are forecast to climb from around 3 million in 2023 to between 11 million (Cowen) and nearly 12 million (J.P. Morgan) by 2030. Obesity-specific prescriptions are projected to grow from under 1 million to roughly 4 million under Cowen’s forecast, or up to nearly 10 million under J.P. Morgan's forecast by 2030. Next to the chart, an AI-generated Dall-E illustration depicts a round, cartoonish character constructed from gaming dice sitting in a dimly lit piano bar, serving as a playful visual pun on the "Fats Dominoes" section title.

This page of the publication evaluates the efficacy, sustainability, and side effects of GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs for weight loss. Michael Cembalest explains that while weight loss from these treatments is significant—averaging about 10% at 20 weeks and 15% at 40 weeks before flatlining—it falls short of the 25% to 30% weight loss typically achieved through bariatric surgery. Furthermore, weight loss is rarely permanent; patients tend to regain most of the lost weight, and their cardiometabolic markers like blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, and hemoglobin levels regress to baseline once treatments like Wegovy or Zepbound are stopped. 

The first visual, a bar chart titled "Weight loss observed in clinical trials," displays the percentage of body weight lost across various drugs, color-coded by development stage: Approved, Phase 3, and Phase 1/2. Eli Lilly's Retatrutide demonstrates the highest weight loss at nearly 24%, followed by Zepbound (also Eli Lilly) at roughly 21%. Novo Nordisk's Wegovy and CagriSema show weight losses of about 15% to 16%. A wide range of other pipeline drugs from companies like Amgen, AstraZeneca, Pfizer, and Zeiss are shown with lesser weight loss percentages, mostly clustered between 5% and 15%. 

The second visual, a line chart titled "Change in body weight during and after treatment," traces the weight trajectory of patients on Wegovy versus a placebo over 120 weeks. The Wegovy group steadily loses weight, bottoming out at approximately 16% weight loss around week 68. At this point, indicated by a vertical line, treatment is discontinued. Following discontinuation, patients experience rapid weight regain, recovering to only about a 5% weight loss by week 120. Meanwhile, the placebo group remains relatively stable, hovering around a 2% weight loss before returning to baseline.

Beyond weight regain, the author outlines several physical and psychiatric side effects of GLPs. Nausea and vomiting are the most common, affecting up to 45% and 30% of clinical trial participants, respectively. Rarer but serious adverse risks include pancreatitis, loss of muscle mass, and reduced bone density, highlighting an open research need for effective weaning and discontinuation strategies. Cembalest also notes the rising threat of overdoses linked to non-FDA-tested, compounded GLPs sold at drugstores that require manual syringe filling. Finally, the text addresses "anhedonia"—a condition linked to depression caused by the mitigation of dopamine rewards—though notes that Phase III obesity trials for semaglutide showed no clinical difference in psychiatric effects compared to placebo groups.

This page from Michael Cembalest's J.P. Morgan 2024 Outlook explores whether glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists can be used to treat addictive behaviors such as alcoholism and smoking. Because GLPs mitigate dopamine activity in the brain's reward circuitry, researchers are examining their potential to curb compulsive actions. Preliminary evidence in animal studies indicates that GLPs alter reward pathways, reducing dopamine rushes from substances like alcohol, cocaine, nicotine, and oxycodone. 

Specifically, a bar chart titled "Consumption of sweet alcohol by mice taking GLPs" illustrates a dramatic, dose-dependent decrease in alcohol intake in mice treated with semaglutide. While the placebo group consumed over 6 grams of alcohol per kilogram of body weight, the consumption fell steadily with higher doses, dropping to under 1 gram per kilogram at a dose of 0.03 milligrams per kilogram of body weight before leveling off slightly above 1 gram at the 0.1 milligram dose. 

The text also outlines early human studies. In a trial of 127 patients with alcohol use disorder, heavy drinking days and total alcohol intake were significantly reduced, though notably only within the subgroup of patients who were also obese. These patients also showed reduced activation of brain reward centers when shown images of alcohol, while less overweight cohorts saw no reduction in drinking. Additionally, a study by researchers at the University of Texas found that 46 percent of patients combining nicotine patches with GLP injections successfully stopped smoking, compared to only 27 percent of those relying on nicotine patches alone. Accompanying the text is a stylized illustration depicting a round, white, mascot-like figure in a fedora playing the piano in a cozy bar called Danny's, symbolically bridging the concepts of weight management, alcohol consumption, and behavior.

This page examines how glucagon-like peptide (GLP) drugs work and highlights ongoing clinical trials that could dramatically expand their addressable market. The author argues that while direct Medicare coverage for obesity is currently hindered by legislation, successful clinical trials could allow GLPs to be reclassified as cardiovascular or other treatments that are already covered by Medicare. Reflecting this potential, Goldman Sachs forecasts double the monthly GLP users compared to estimates from Cowen and JP Morgan. 

A central visual element is a grid titled "Ongoing Trials," which lists six molecular compounds and shows which indications are currently being tested by their respective manufacturers. Eli Lilly’s orfoglipron is in trials for cardiovascular conditions, while its compound tirzepatide is being evaluated for cardiovascular diseases, obstructive sleep apnea, chronic kidney disease, advanced liver disease, and heart failure (HFpEF). Lilly is also trialing retatrutide for knee osteoarthritis. Boehringer, partnering with Zealand Pharma, has ongoing trials for survodutide in cardiovascular and advanced liver disease. Novo Nordisk has trials for CagriSema targeting cardiovascular disease, and is testing semaglutide for chronic kidney disease, peripheral arterial disease, heart failure (HFpEF), and Alzheimer's disease, the latter using an oral formulation.

The text also highlights research by Daniel Drucker at the University of Toronto, who discovered that GLPs work through brain pathways to reduce inflammation. This finding points to potential applications for treating inflammatory and neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. Furthermore, Drucker notes that major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) benefits begin before patients experience significant weight loss, suggesting weight loss is not the sole driver of these health improvements. 

Finally, the author describes how GLPs benefit various organs throughout the body. In the stomach, they decrease gastric emptying and gastrointestinal motility. In the liver, they decrease gluconeogenesis and liver fat accumulation, or steatosis. In the brain, they decrease food intake stimuli and reward behavior, while in the muscles, they increase insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake. In the pancreas, GLPs increase insulin secretion and synthesis, decrease glucagon secretion, and promote beta-cell survival.

This page explores how glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, commonly used as anti-obesity medications, affect household consumer behavior and purchasing patterns. The author presents two distinct datasets to analyze these behavioral shifts: actual receipt-based household spending data compiled by J.P. Morgan Equity Research and a self-reported survey from Morgan Stanley AlphaWise. Both sources align directionally, demonstrating a pronounced reduction in the consumption of unhealthy foods, sugary beverages, and snacks once individuals begin taking GLPs.

The first visual is a table titled "Year-on-year change in projected units of consumption by household," which compares GLP-1 users against the total U.S. population across various food categories. The data shows that GLP users significantly cut back on high-calorie, processed snacks. For instance, meat snacks saw a 27% decline for GLP users compared to a 2% decline for the total U.S. population, representing a 26% difference. Similar stark differences are noted in snack seeds, nuts, and trail mixes (a 25% difference), popcorn (a 24% difference), crackers (a 23% difference), and chips (an 18% difference). Soft drinks also experienced a notable drop, with consumption among GLP users declining by 15% compared to a 4% decline in the total U.S. population. 

An accompanying whimsical illustration depicts a blue, round cartoon character with musical notes, representing the lifestyle shift associated with these dietary changes. 

The second visual is a horizontal bar chart detailing the "Change in food category consumption since starting anti-obesity medication," based on a survey of 311 GLP patients. The chart lists the percentage of respondents who are consuming more, about the same, or less of various food groups, alongside a net percentage calculation. The data reveals a strong pivot toward healthier foods. Fruits and vegetables recorded the highest net increase at positive 46%, followed by weight-loss management foods at positive 31%, and poultry and fish at positive 23%. On the opposite end of the spectrum, indulgent and processed categories suffered massive declines. Confections recorded the largest net drop at negative 66%, followed closely by carbonated and sugary drinks at negative 65%, cookies and baked products at negative 65%, alcohol at negative 62%, and salty snacks at negative 61%. Even staples like red meat and grains saw net declines of 25% and 35%, respectively. Together, these data points suggest a transformative shift in grocery and beverage markets as anti-obesity medications gain broader adoption.

This page discusses the equity market impacts of increased GLP-1 penetration, triggered in part by Novo Nordisk's Wegovy trial results in the summer of 2023. Michael Cembalest observes how the market initially priced in clear winners and losers, with major gains for GLP-1 manufacturers and sharp losses for sectors like insulin pump makers, alcoholic beverages, and calorie-rich food distributors, including Dollar Tree, Dollar General, and BJ’s Wholesale. Many of these hard-hit sectors recovered later in the year, reflecting either general rising equity markets or investor caution regarding the actual speed of GLP-1 adoption and its impact on other medical conditions. 

The author highlights a divergence in forecasts for US GLP-1 penetration by 2030. TD Cowen projects 33% penetration for diabetes and only 3% for obesity, while J.P. Morgan Research projects 35% for diabetes and a much higher 15% for obesity. Based on TD Cowen’s lower obesity forecast, the analysis suggests that adjacent healthcare sectors are unlikely to see massive negative impacts. For example, even if GLPs were perfectly curative for cardiovascular disease, a 3% obesity penetration rate would translate to only 400,000 treated people, representing a mere 0.5% reduction in the overall pool of people suffering cardiovascular events.

A line chart titled "The GLP-1 effect on equity sectors and industries" tracks performance from January to November 2023. It shows GLP-1 manufacturers spiking to cumulative gains of around 40% to 60%, while insulin pumps plummeted to nearly negative 50% in the autumn before recovering to around negative 20%. Other categories tracking relative losses and partial recoveries include calorie-rich/fast food, beverages (beer, sugary, and spirits), orthopedic devices, and exposed food retail.

An adjacent bar chart depicts the year-to-date relative return of large-cap stocks to the S&P 500 by sector. It illustrates underperformance across the board, led by the Food sector at roughly negative 37%, followed by Pharma excluding Eli Lilly at negative 27%, Managed Care at negative 25%, Biotech at negative 20%, Life Sciences and Medical Devices at roughly negative 18%, and Beverages at negative 12%.

Finally, a table outlines the "Projected pool reductions due to obese patients taking GLPs by 2030" using TD Cowen data. It lists co-morbidities alongside their average rate of co-morbidity with obesity, prevalence reduction in millions, and the resulting percentage reduction in the total patient pool. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which has a 72% co-morbidity rate, sees a 2.1 million patient reduction but only a 1.0% reduction in the total pool. Obstructive sleep apnea sees a 1.1% total pool reduction. Chronic kidney disease, osteoarthritis, Type 2 diabetes or prediabetes, and cardiovascular disease all see estimated total pool reductions of 0.5% or less. This data suggests that sharp declines in the share prices of companies treating adjacent conditions may be premature.

Michael Cembalest introduces a list of potential top ten surprises for 2024, written in honor of the late market strategist Byron Wien, known for his annual non-consensus predictions. 

The first surprise predicts that the US dollar will remain stable, ending 2024 within seven percent of its starting value and retaining its roughly fifty percent share of global trade invoicing. This outlook is supported by two charts. The first chart, showing the US Fed trade-weighted nominal broad dollar index from 1980 to late 2023 with a base of 100 in January 1980, shows a long-term upward trend peaking near 400 by 2023. The second chart, detailing the international role of the US dollar, demonstrates the currency's dominance across global markets. It shows the US dollar accounting for nearly eighty-eight percent of foreign exchange transaction volume, about sixty percent of official foreign exchange reserves, fifty-five percent of trade invoicing, and over fifty percent of cross-border loans and international debt securities, even though the US share of global gross domestic product is only around twenty-five percent and its share of world trade is near ten percent.

The second surprise is that the Department of Justice or the Federal Trade Commission will win a major antitrust case against Google, Amazon, Meta, or T-Mobile, ending a decades-long drought in major antitrust victories since the 2001 Microsoft case. 

The third surprise forecasts that President Joe Biden will withdraw from the presidential race between Super Tuesday and the November election due to health concerns, passing the torch to a Democratic National Committee replacement candidate. This prediction is framed by two political and economic charts. A scatter plot of presidential popularity and job creation 1,051 days after inauguration shows Biden as an extreme outlier, holding a low approval rating of around thirty-eight percent despite a high payroll growth of roughly ten percent since his inauguration. For comparison, other past presidents like Eisenhower, JFK, and Truman achieved higher approval ratings with lower or similar job growth rates. The final chart, illustrating nonfarm payrolls from 2018 to late 2023, shows the dramatic drop in employment during the 2020 pandemic and the subsequent recovery. It marks Biden's inauguration at around one hundred forty-three million employees, which climbed to nearly one hundred fifty-five million by late 2023, highlighting that his strong job creation numbers are largely a function of the post-pandemic economic reopening.

This page of the publication focuses on two primary geopolitical and economic arguments: the predicted failure of Argentine dollarization and the continuation of the Russian invasion of Ukraine into 2024. 

Addressing Argentina, the author argues that President Javier Milei’s dollarization plans will fail even if implemented, rapidly yielding to de-dollarization. The author points out that currency convertibility requires high productivity, central bank backing like the European Central Bank, or substantial commodity-related foreign exchange reserves, none of which Argentina possesses. To illustrate this, a chart titled "Institutions, labor market flexibility, business freedoms and business dynamism" rates countries on a scale of 0 to 100. While the United States scores over 80 and successful peggers like Hong Kong score near 80, Argentina sits at the bottom of the chart with a score below 50. The page lists Milei’s ambitious proposals, which include cutting $20 billion in public spending, halving the number of ministries, privatizing major utilities, and legalizing cryptocurrency for contracts, but the author remains skeptical that Milei can successfully dismantle the country's Peronist legacy.

Turning to the conflict in Ukraine, the author predicts the war will drag on through 2024 without a ceasefire despite severe Russian military losses, including two-thirds of its tanks and 87 percent of its prewar active troops. The author anticipates that US financial aid to Ukraine will continue, facilitated by a political compromise where Democrats agree to fund US border security. This compromise is contextualized by a chart titled "Total US Customs and Border Protection Enforcement Actions," which depicts a steep rise in enforcement actions from roughly 0.5 million in 2017 to over 3.0 million in fiscal year 2023. 

Lastly, the author forecasts that the war will push European nations to finally meet the 2 percent GDP defense spending target agreed to in the 2006 NATO agreement. According to calculations, Europe has underspent on its defense by $2.0 trillion since 1983 by relying on US expenditures. This dynamic is illustrated in the chart "US vs European defense spending," which tracks defense spending as a percentage of GDP from 1968 to 2023. The data shows US defense spending consistently remaining well above the 2 percent NATO target—peaking near 9 percent in the late 1960s and currently sitting around 3.5 percent—while non-US NATO defense spending has remained below the 2 percent target since the early 1990s, averaging around 1.5 percent in recent years.

This J.P. Morgan commentary page argues that multiple complex, negative societal realities can coexist, focusing on the long-term impacts of Covid-19 lockdowns, FDA regulatory oversight, and the pharmaceutical industry's reputational decline. First, the author asserts that US lockdown costs will linger for decades, arguing that school closures harmed 50 million children to protect older demographics, erasing two decades of math and reading progress. The text cites Stanford estimates showing national chronic absenteeism rose from 15% pre-pandemic to over 25% in 2021–2022, and doubled in states like California by 2022–2023. Lockdowns are also linked to lower lifetime earnings, a drag on economic growth, rising domestic violence, loneliness, depression, anxiety, and increased alcohol dependency. 

The center of the page features a side-by-side comparison table illustrating that substantial drug risks are often discovered after FDA approval, leading to recalls or black box warnings. For recalls, key examples include Pfizer's Bextra in 2005 (recalled for heart attacks and strokes), Merck's Vioxx in 2004 (coronary heart disease), Bayer's Baycol in 2001 (rhabdomyolysis), and Wyeth-Ayerst's Fen-Phen in 1997 (heart disease). Under black box warnings, the table highlights Merck's Singulair in 2020 (mental health side effects), Pfizer's Tygacil in 2013 (increased all-cause mortality), Glaxo's Lamictal in 2010 (skin and organ disorders), Janssen Biotech's Remicade in 2009 (infection risk), Takeda Pharma's Actos in 2007 (heart failure), Abbott Labs' Depakote in 2006 (birth defects), and Eli Lilly and Pfizer's Prozac and Zoloft in 2004 (mental health side effects).

Lastly, the page details how unlawful drug company behavior has eroded public trust, dragging the pharmaceutical industry's Gallup net rating down to -31 in 2019—the very bottom of the poll, below even the federal government, law firms, and oil and gas—and further down to a -42 net rating today. It lists major historical settlements, including Purdue's ongoing $6 billion Oxycontin settlement, which is under Supreme Court review with a ruling expected in spring. Other examples include GlaxoSmithKline's $3 billion payment in 2012 for illegal promotion of Paxil and Wellbutrin, Johnson & Johnson's $2.2 billion settlement in 2013 regarding Risperdal, Invega, and Natrecor, and Pfizer's $2.3 billion fine in 2009 for off-label marketing of Bextra. The author notes that this deep distrust may explain recent declines in medication adherence, clinical trial enrollment, and vaccine acceptance.

This commentary highlights the historic success of vaccines in dramatically reducing preventable diseases globally, while warning of the public health risks associated with recently declining immunization rates. The author argues that vaccines represent one of the greatest achievements in public health, despite skepticism found in popular media. 

To support this, the page presents two tables. The first table details vaccine-preventable diseases in the United States, comparing pre-vaccine annual statistics to post-vaccine figures (using 2006 case data and 2004 death data). It shows a 100% decline in cases for diphtheria, measles, polio, rubella, and smallpox. Significant declines are also recorded for mumps (96%), pertussis (92%), hepatitis A (87%), and tetanus (93%). The second table details similar success in China, showing that by the 1980s, cases of measles had declined by 80%, pertussis by 83%, diphtheria by 81%, and polio by 75%. By the 2010s, China also saw declines in rubella (83%), hepatitis A (66%), meningitis (78%), and encephalitis (65%).

The author addresses safety concerns, noting that serious vaccine safety incidents are extremely rare. Only three major safety-related recalls or withdrawals have occurred since the 1950s: a polio vaccine incident in 1955, a swine flu vaccine in 1976 linked to Guillain-Barre syndrome, and a rotavirus vaccine in 1998–1999 linked to infant bowel obstruction. The text also mentions CDC-funded research investigating aluminum adjuvants and childhood asthma, noting that experts do not believe current empirical associations provide strong evidence to question vaccine safety, though research remains ongoing.

Lastly, the text details a concerning decline in US childhood vaccination rates, which fell from 95% pre-Covid to 93% for the 2021–2022 school year, leaving an estimated 250,000 children unprotected against measles. This decline has already led to local measles outbreaks, including 85 cases in Columbus, Ohio in late 2022 and 71 cases in Clark County, Washington in 2018–2019, with the vast majority of infected children being unvaccinated. A Kaiser Survey found that 28% of US adults now oppose mandatory school vaccinations, up from 16% in 2019, and 36 states currently fall below the 95% vaccination threshold required to maintain herd immunity against measles.

This page focuses on the effectiveness and waning protection of original COVID-19 vaccines and Omicron boosters over time, highlighting that while rapid virus mutation has eroded initial vaccine-specific efficacy, broader population-wide immunity is successfully keeping hospitalization rates low. The author notes that the Commonwealth Fund estimated vaccines prevented over 18 million hospitalizations by December 2022. However, because the SARS-CoV-2 virus accumulates mutations 2.5 times faster than influenza A and 7 times faster than other coronaviruses, protection declined. Although protection from original vaccines and early boosters eventually became similar to that of unvaccinated individuals with previous infections, overall population immunity remains robust, with 99 percent of people having some combination of vaccination and prior infection.

A detailed data table tracks vaccine and booster efficacy across various studies, doses, and demographics from 2020 through 2023. Early studies by Fisman and Stoliaroff-Pepin demonstrate initial hospitalization protection rates between 77 percent and 93 percent. However, multiple sources document rapid waning; for instance, a Bermingham study shows that three-dose hospitalization protection declined from 78 percent to 68 percent after three months, while a Link-Gelles study published in JAMA showed a decline from 68 percent to 36 percent after six months. Booster data from Bacon and the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control show similar patterns of declining efficacy against hospitalization and mortality over four to six months, with a Link-Gelles CDC study noting booster efficacy against hospitalization dropping to 24 percent after four months.

Two line charts illustrate how these immunity dynamics translate to real-world outcomes, plotting weekly US COVID-19 hospitalizations per 100,000 people from March 2020 to late 2023 using CDC and J.P. Morgan Asset Management data. The first chart, tracking cohorts aged 40 and older, shows that the oldest group of 75-plus years saw dramatic hospitalization peaks near 150 per 100,000 in early 2021 and early 2022, but successive peaks in late 2022 and 2023 remained well below 60. The second chart, focusing on the 30 to 64 age range, shows that the 50-64 age group peaked above 40 hospitalizations per 100,000 in early 2022, but subsequent waves remained near or below 10 per 100,000. Taken together, these trends demonstrate that despite waning vaccine efficacy, the combination of vaccine-induced and acquired immunity is holding up well, keeping serious illness rates substantially lower than in prior infection waves.

This page begins with brief commentary on improving January US manufacturing surveys, noting a rise in new orders alongside warning signs of tight labor markets and rising inflation. The primary focus of the page is an analysis of the "Magnificent 7" technology stocks, arguing that their massive rally has been fundamentally driven by earnings rather than the speculative multiple expansion seen during the 2000–2001 dot-com bubble. Specifically, of the group’s 28% return since 2019, 21% is attributable to sales growth, 6% to margin expansion, and only 1% to multiple expansion. 

To support this, a comparative table contrasts the Magnificent 7 against the other 493 stocks in the S&P 500. It shows that for Q4 2023, the Magnificent 7 achieved 14% sales growth, a 7.5% increase in profit margins, and a 23% overall profit margin, whereas the S&P 493 saw only 2% sales growth, a 1.1% decline in margins, and a 9% overall profit margin. While the Magnificent 7 holds a 29% share of the S&P 500 market capitalization and accounts for 22% of its consensus net income, it trades at a higher price-to-earnings multiple of 30x (compared to 18x for the S&P 493) but carries a stronger three-year forward earnings-per-share growth projection of 15% versus 12%. 

Despite these strong fundamentals, the author highlights risks identified by J.P. Morgan strategists Marko Kolanovic and Dubravko Lakos-Bujas. First, market concentration has reached its highest level since 1972, making it difficult for active managers to outperform. In 2023, only 23% of Russell 1000 large-cap managers beat their benchmarks, down from 66% in 2022. This extreme concentration is illustrated in a line chart tracking the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) concentration measure from 1964 to 2024. The HHI has spiked to nearly 180, a level significantly higher than the tech bubble peak of approximately 120, and the chart's shaded recession bars indicate that such spikes historically precede or coincide with economic downturns. 

The author points to antitrust regulation as the primary threat that could disrupt these dominant companies. While most of the giants continue to thrive, Tesla is noted as an exception, facing pricing pressures and lower volumes. Tesla's Q4 2023 earnings were heavily assisted by a one-time, $5.9 billion non-cash tax valuation allowance adjustment. This divergence is visualized in a final line chart tracking the annual earnings per share of individual Magnificent 7 members from 2018 to 2024. The chart shows Meta and NVIDIA experiencing vertical earnings spikes toward $19 and $16 respectively, Microsoft and Apple maintaining solid upward trajectories, and Amazon recovering from its 2022 dip, while Tesla's earnings curve remains flat and depressed.

This page analyzes the underlying structural issues facing the Chinese economy and its equity valuations, focusing on the massively overbuilt domestic real estate sector and the vulnerabilities in the shadow banking system. 

At the top, a bar chart titled "Cheapest equity market valuations" shows forward price-to-earnings ratios across various global markets and indices. Valuations range from under 2x for Russia and Pakistan to between 4x and 6x for various Chinese equity segments, such as China H shares, Red Chips, and All Shares on the Hong Kong Exchange. This compares to valuations around 10x to 11x for S&P 500 Energy and the FTSE 100. A sidebar titled "China’s equity alphabet soup" defines the complex terminology of Chinese share classes, explaining the differences between A, H, and B shares, Red Chips, P Chips, and ADRs.

To illustrate the scale of China’s housing bubble, a comparative table titled "China / US housing comparison" contrasts Chinese peak metrics with the United States. The value of China's housing stock relative to personal consumption expenditures peaked at 6.0x, compared to 2.2x in the US. Direct real estate activities accounted for 18% of China's GDP, three times the US level of 6%. Additionally, mid-2023 home price-to-income ratios in major Chinese tier-one cities reached roughly 40x, compared to about 10x in major US cities, while China's homeownership rate stood at 90% versus 66% in the US.

Author Michael Cembalest argues that this housing crisis has direct, negative consequences for the banking and shadow banking systems. He points to the December 2023 failure of Zhongzhi Enterprises—which went bankrupt with $30 billion in assets and $60 billion in liabilities—and the default of Zhongrong Enterprises as key indicators of shadow banking fragility. Although shadow banking comprises only 5% of China's regular banking system assets, regular commercial banks provide nearly half of its funding. Consequently, squeezing the shadow banks inevitably stresses the entire banking system. 

Looking forward, Cembalest compares China's current situation to the US response during the 2008 financial crisis, referencing an IMF paper on systemic banking crises. He argues that short-term technical rallies may occur, especially after the dismissal of regulatory heads, but that a sustainable recovery requires the direct government recapitalization of both regular and shadow banks, similar to the direct purchase of bank liabilities and equities under TARP. He concludes that trying to manage the markets by targeting short sellers or forcing state-owned entities to buy equities is unlikely to succeed long-term, particularly as bipartisan US congressional support for tariffs and trade restrictions remains strong ahead of the US 2024 presidential election.

This page, titled Armageddonist update, is a critique by Michael Cembalest of ultra-bearish market pundits, whom he terms Armageddonists or the Legion of Doom. Cembalest argues that the media frequently highlights these commentators because of human negativity bias, citing Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman's research, political scientist Stuart Soroka's work on magazine covers, and a German newspaper experiment to demonstrate that negative news drives media engagement. 

To support his critique, Cembalest presents a bar chart titled "The consequences of Armageddonism, 2010-2019," which calculates the underperformance of shifting one dollar from the S&P 500 to the Barclay’s Aggregate Bond Index on the dates of various bearish predictions made between 2010 and 2016. Every single prediction, ranging from Nouriel Roubini in May 2010 to Paul Krugman in November 2016, resulted in subsequent investment underperformance of 30% to 60% by the end of 2019. Specific commentators analyzed include David Rosenberg, Jeff Gundlach, Peter Schiff, Carl Icahn, George Soros, and John Hussman.

The analysis then shifts to the 2020 pandemic period. A line chart titled "Timing is everything" tracks the S&P 500 index from 2020 through early 2024, demonstrating that the index almost doubled from its March 2020 lows to nearly 5,000 by early 2024. The chart points out that major Armageddonist warnings were clustered precisely at the market’s lowest point in early 2020. An accompanying table details these specific quotes. For instance, on March 4, 2020, David Stockman predicted a 50% correction and an L-shaped recovery. On March 24, Roubini warned of a Greater Depression worse than the 1930s, and on March 26, Hussman expected the S&P 500 to lose two-thirds of its value. Additional warnings came from Peter Schiff, Jeff Gundlach, George Soros, Albert Edwards, and David Rosenberg, who claimed on May 12, 2020, that the country was in a prolonged economic depression. 

In terms of future outlook, Cembalest notes that current investor sentiment is highly bullish, leverage is elevated, and markets are pricing in substantial good news. Consequently, he states he would not be surprised to see a market correction later in the year. However, he warns investors that the Armageddonists will likely use that inevitable correction to falsely signal that a much worse collapse is on the horizon.

This page from the report explores the highly positive impacts of artificial intelligence on biomedicine, highlighting major breakthrough developments in protein mapping, antibiotic discovery, and medical diagnostics. 

The author first focuses on protein structure prediction, highlighting Google’s AI-driven AlphaFold program. A visual on the left side of the page demonstrates the accuracy of this technology by overlaying the insanely complex actual shape of a DNA replication enzyme in green with its blue AI-predicted shape, showing a nearly perfect match. While traditional methods like MRI and x-ray crystallography took years and millions of dollars—resulting in only twenty percent of proteins being mapped by 2021—AlphaFold can complete the task in hours at minimal cost. Consequently, ninety-nine percent of proteins are now mapped according to the Institute for Cancer Research.

The second section details the discovery of the first new class of antibiotics in decades, led by Jim Collins of MIT and Harvard alongside Felix Wong at Integrated Biosciences. To address MRSA, a staph infection responsible for seventy thousand severe illnesses and seven thousand deaths annually, researchers trained an AI model on thirty-nine thousand molecular compounds to predict antibacterial inhibition and human toxicity. They then applied neural networks and Monte Carlo tree search to screen a database of twelve million commercially available compounds. This process, further detailed in a December 2023 Nature paper, narrowed down ten thousand promising molecules to a cohort of two hundred and eighty, ultimately identifying two highly effective compounds currently undergoing promising trials in mice. A cluster diagram visualizes this search, using distance and color to map antibacterial activity and non-toxicity. Dark green and black dots represent high-scoring novel compounds without unfavorable substructures, while two distinct purple dots mark the top-performing compounds in laboratory testing.

The author also highlights research from McMaster University, where scientists used a generative AI model to screen billions of molecules against the highly drug-resistant bacterium Acinetobacter baumannii. This effort led to the synthesis of thirteen thousand five hundred molecules, yielding six promising novel antibacterial candidates, as detailed in a March 2024 Nature Machine Intelligence publication. Finally, the page addresses AI-driven diagnostics for diabetic retinopathy, the leading cause of adult blindness. By using retinal cameras paired with AI, clinicians with minimal training can deliver immediate diagnostic results, expanding medical coverage and facilitating early treatment.

This page discusses the 2024 US Presidential election, featuring a qualitative 360-degree performance review of the presumptive GOP nominee, Donald Trump, alongside two hypothetical constitutional crisis scenarios. 

The primary visual is a horizontal bar chart titled "Trump 360 review by former Trump Cabinet members and other senior positions," which categorizes 43 individuals who served in senior roles during the Trump administration from 2016 to 2020. To be included, individuals must have served at least nine months in key positions, such as Vice President, Cabinet department heads, White House Chiefs of Staff, or major congressional leadership roles. The chart divides these officials into three columns based on J.P. Morgan’s interpretation of their public statements. The largest group, with eighteen individuals, consists of "Repudiations/disavowals," which includes high-profile figures such as Mike Pence, Nikki Haley, Rex Tillerson, Jim Mattis, William Barr, John Bolton, and John Kelly. The second group contains fourteen individuals who have given "2024 endorsements," featuring names like Mike Pompeo, Mitch McConnell, Steven Mnuchin, and Ben Carson. The third group consists of eleven individuals categorized under "No public comment," which includes Chris Wray, Kirstjen Nielsen, and Alex Azar, with the author noting that some in this group hold roles that legally or professionally prevent public political commentary.

The text also details two "triple witching hour" constitutional election scenarios. In the first scenario, "Insurrection redux," Trump wins the general election, but Democrats capture both houses of Congress. Upon being seated, the Democratic-majority Congress votes during the January 6th Joint Session to declare Trump ineligible under Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment, citing insurrection. This would trigger a Contingent Election in the House of Representatives where Joe Biden would be the only eligible candidate. A footnote supports this scenario by explaining that Trump's 2021 Senate acquittal does not trigger double jeopardy protections, as the impeachment trial was civil rather than criminal. In the second scenario, third-party candidates from the No Labels movement or Robert F. Kennedy Jr. secure enough electoral votes to prevent either major candidate from obtaining the required 270 electors. This triggers a Contingent Election in the House, where votes are cast by state congressional delegations, which are currently controlled by a narrow Republican majority.

This page addresses the structural, economic, and environmental hurdles facing investors looking to "bottom fish" in China. It highlights that despite improvements in coastal waters since 2015, China's inland water systems remain heavily polluted, with roughly 70% of rivers and lakes unsafe for human use according to Nanjing University, and a clear link identified by the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences between elevated surface water pollution and cancer. 

Beyond these environmental issues, the page compiles several charts detailing China's deteriorating economic health, marked by rising debt, worsening credit intensity, a shrinking shadow banking system, real estate struggles, and capital flight. 

A chart tracking the credit intensity of GDP shows that the increase in credit required to generate one unit of GDP growth, measured as a three-year moving average, has risen dramatically from around 1 in 2004 to nearly 7 by 2022, signaling severely declining capital efficiency. At the same time, a chart plotting total government, household, and corporate debt to the non-financial sector shows that China's total debt has climbed steadily from 250% of GDP in 2018 to over 300% in 2023. This level surpasses the leverage ratios of the United States, the United Kingdom, and Germany, though it remains below Japan's level of roughly 420%.

Meanwhile, core shadow banking activities, measured in trillions of Yuan, have gradually shrunk from a peak of around 23 trillion Yuan in 2019 to roughly 18 trillion Yuan in late 2023, driven primarily by declines in trust loans and undiscounted bankers' acceptances, while entrusted loans remained relatively flat around 10 trillion Yuan. The China real activity monitor, an index weighting ten monthly indicators such as real estate investment, clean energy production, and enterprise output, shows a volatile path over the last decade. A massive expansion spike near index value 25 in 2021 was followed by a crash to below -5 during pandemic-era lockdowns, leaving only a modest, flat recovery around 3 to 5 by late 2023.

The housing market continues to act as a significant drag on the economy. A chart tracking the year-over-year percentage change of state-owned land use right transfer revenue and residential floor space starts shows both metrics deeply depressed. Newly started housing floor space has contracted heavily since 2021, hovering between -30% and -40% year-over-year, while land transfer revenues have also fallen into negative territory. Finally, the China FDI monitor, measuring inward and outward foreign direct investment in billions of US dollars, illustrates that net foreign direct investment has plummeted into negative territory, dropping below -$40 billion by late 2023 as inward foreign investment collapsed.

This page analyzes the immense energy requirements of artificial intelligence and the challenges that technology companies face in securing reliable power. 

The author begins by illustrating the hidden energy costs of AI benchmarks, pointing to a chart comparing Gemini Ultra and GPT-4 accuracy on Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) tests. While Google’s Gemini Ultra achieved approximately 90% accuracy (surpassing GPT-4's 86.5% and human expert performance of around 89%) under a "Chain of Thought: 32x + 5-shot + Greedy sampling" approach, this method required running through the prompt 32 times, consuming 32 times the compute time and energy of a typical prompt. 

This growing AI energy demand is directly translating to massive grid projections. A chart showing the progression of power demand forecasts in gigawatts for Dominion Resources, prepared by PJM, reveals that while forecasts from 2019 to 2022 remained mostly flat between 20 and 24 gigawatts, the 2023 forecast skyrocketed, projecting demand to rise to over 40 gigawatts by 2039. The sole driver is increased data center activity. In addition, the author cites McKinsey, BCG, and S&P Global predictions that US power demand will grow by 13% to 15% annually until 2030. At the same time, grid supply chains are constrained; a chart detailing core goods producer price index (PPI) component inflation shows that out of 47 categories, "Transformers & Power Regulators" experienced the sharpest price jump since 2018, rising nearly 75%.

The author then addresses where AI providers will secure energy, referencing Amazon's purchase of up to 40% of the output from Talen Energy’s Susquehanna nuclear plant at a 50% premium. However, the author cautions that such deals may not be widely replicable because state regulators in vertically integrated utility frameworks—which cover roughly 50% of US nuclear generation—will likely block data centers from taking existing baseload nuclear power offline. 

Consequently, data centers might need to build their own nuclear generation, which has historically suffered from massive delays and cost overruns. To illustrate this, a final bar chart compares the levelized cost of four modern nuclear plants against a wind-solar-gas system in US dollars per megawatt-hour. The levelized cost of the nuclear plants is extraordinarily high, with the UK's Hinkley Point near $225/MWh, Georgia's Vogtle around $180/MWh, France's Flamanville near $175/MWh, and Finland's Olkiluoto around $125/MWh. By contrast, a high-renewable system combining wind, solar, and natural gas backup is far cheaper, costing only about $60/MWh (with gas priced at $3.45/mmbtu) to $65/MWh (with gas at $6.90/mmbtu). The author concludes that these levelized nuclear costs are 2x to 4x higher than alternative baseload-equivalent systems.

In this publication, Michael Cembalest argues that the prospects of a rare US disinflationary boom are fading as inflation measures experience a U-turn, pushing 10-year Treasury yields back up toward 4.7%.
