Despite resilient economic growth, the rise in the Consumer Price Index (CPI), particularly driven by non-discretionary items like medical care, childcare, car insurance, and electricity, has dashed hopes for aggressive interest rate cuts, with futures markets now pricing in only one to two federal funds rate cuts by the end of 2024. An accompanying footnote highlights inflationary pressures linked to the energy transition, noting that transformer equipment prices have surged 71% since 2019—the highest increase among all 47 core goods categories in the Producer Price Index—and that electricity prices have risen faster than food, commodities, and core CPI.

An extensive leading indicators table compares 18 different economic signals from April 2024 against August 2023, spanning categories such as bankruptcy, capex, construction, the broader economy, employment, lending, production, profits, sales, wages, and equities. This table demonstrates that while many economic and profit leading indicators have improved since late 2023—moving from yellow and orange zones indicating slight to modest weakness to green zones indicating strength—some areas remain under pressure. For instance, the leading indicators for bank lending, non-residential capex, and corporate bankruptcy filings still signal slight-to-modest weakness, while the leading indicator for economy-wide profits based on federal funds, corporate tax rates, unemployment, and productivity remains flagged in red for substantial weakness.

To visualize the recent reversal in inflation, two charts are provided. The first chart plots year-over-year percentages for CPI core services from 2016 through early 2024, tracking two specific series. The series for core services excluding shelter fell from a peak of over 6% in late 2022 down to about 3.5% in late 2023, only to spike sharply back above 5% in early 2024. Similarly, the series excluding both shelter and transportation dipped to around 2% in late 2023 before reversing upward to approximately 3.5% in 2024. 

The second chart illustrates a longer-term perspective of US consumer price inflation measures using a three-month annualized change from 1985 to early 2024. It displays three key series: the Cleveland Fed median CPI, the Atlanta Fed sticky CPI, and the Cleveland Fed trimmed mean CPI. All three measures show a dramatic spike in 2021 and 2022, reaching the 6% to 8% range, followed by a steady decline through 2023, and a clear, coordinated U-turn in early 2024 that has pushed these annualized rates back up toward 4% to 5%.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s commentary explores the contrasting forces currently impacting the economy, highlighting lingering consumer financial pressure from rising interest rates alongside supportive market dynamics that could cushion equity selloffs. 

The first section focuses on consumer stress. While existing obligations like mortgages are insulated from rising rates, new credit card balances are not, which has driven credit card delinquencies up faster than other loan types. Two side-by-side charts illustrate this trend. The first chart, "Credit card interest rates and delinquencies," tracks data from 2003 to 2024. It shows that the equal-weighted financing rate on accounts assessed interest has risen sharply to nearly 23%, pushing 90-day delinquencies up from their post-pandemic low of roughly 3% to nearly 5% by early 2024. The second chart, "Consumer financial stress," spans 2012 to 2024 and tracks revolving credit card balances alongside the percentage of accounts making only minimum payments. Revolving balances have surged to nearly $650 billion, while the share of accounts making only minimum payments has spiked to about 11%, signaling that high interest rates are placing direct pressure on household balance sheets.

The second section argues that despite Federal Reserve policy uncertainty, systemic indicators remain supportive of equities. The chart titled "US commercial bank recovery" focuses on the period from January 2023 to early 2024, plotting the relative performance of S&P 500 banks alongside total US commercial bank deposits. Following the March 2023 regional banking crisis, bank deposits stabilized at approximately $17.5 trillion, and relative bank returns recovered from their deep troughs, indicating that systemic financial risks have successfully settled. The final chart, "Net equity supply globally," displays annual data from 1999 to 2023, categorized by US, non-US, and US/non-US SPAC issuances. It shows that global net equity supply has been negative for three consecutive years through 2023, settling near negative $200 billion. This indicates that corporate buybacks are significantly outstripping new primary and secondary equity issuances, creating a tight supply environment that traditionally supports resilient market returns.

The page concludes with a playful graphic of a cicada rock band, complete with tiny drums and guitars, titled "In-A-Cicada-Da-Vida"—a whimsical nod to the classic rock song and the major cicada emergence of 2024.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, "Eye on the Market," discusses the potential impact of Elon Musk’s political commentary on Tesla’s stock performance, suggesting that his rhetoric may be alienating Democratic buyers who make up the core demographic for electric vehicles. Strategic Vision research estimates that the proportion of Democrats buying Tesla vehicles fell by over 60% in the fall of 2023 before rebounding slightly in March, with many opting instead for competitors like the Cadillac Lyriq, Hyundai Ioniq, or Mercedes EQE SUV. J.P. Morgan notes that Tesla's overall market share has declined from 80% in 2020 to 55% in 2023.

The critical reliance of the EV industry on Democratic buyers is illustrated in a chart titled "EV adoption vs county-level political ideology," which plots the EV share of all new vehicles registered from 2012 to 2022 against the Democrat vote share in Presidential elections. The chart shows two data series—one without income controls and one controlling for income—both displaying an upward curve. EV adoption is virtually nonexistent in counties with low Democratic vote shares but rises steadily to nearly 1.6% in counties with an 80% Democratic vote share, highlighting a strong direct relationship regardless of income levels. This is further supported by UC Berkeley research indicating that half of all EVs went to the 10% most Democratic counties in the United States.

The page also addresses how Musk's acquisition of Twitter has coincided with a rise in climate denialism and misinformation on the platform. This is depicted in a bar chart titled "Misinformation/disinformation hit rate," which measures the percentage of content returned from sensitive searches across major social media platforms according to an EU Commission report from September 2023. Twitter has the highest frequency of disinformation at over 40%, followed by Facebook at roughly 33%, Instagram at approximately 23%, TikTok at 19%, and LinkedIn and YouTube at approximately 10% and 8% respectively. 

The author details several of Musk's controversial online statements in the footnotes, including his promotion of conspiracy theories, attacks on political and public figures, and highly partisan statements such as warning of doom if a "red wave" does not occur in the November election. The analysis concludes that these viewpoints are highly inconsistent with the political leanings of typical EV buyers, raising open questions about the long-term impact on Tesla's sales that J.P. Morgan plans to monitor closely.

This page of J.P. Morgan’s report, authored by Michael Cembalest, argues that the US economy is showing limited signs of the profit or capital spending declines that typically precede recessions, supporting a "Pillow Talk" soft-landing thesis. While yield curve inversions historically preceded downturns because they coincided with deeply negative corporate cash flows and rising interest burdens, the current cycle is different: the corporate sector is in surplus and interest expenses remain highly stable. 

To support this, the first chart, "US economy-wide profits and S&P 500 operating profits," tracks US national corporate profit after tax and S&P 500 operating profits from 1995 to 2023 on a log-scale index where January 1995 equals 100. It shows that despite temporary dips during recessions, both profit measures have rebounded strongly and remain near historic highs. 

The second chart, "US corporate sector financial balance," measures gross savings less capital transfers, capital expenditures, and foreign profits retained abroad as a percentage of corporate gross value added from 1960 to 2023. While past recessions were consistently preceded by deep deficits reaching negative 4% to 6%, the current corporate financial balance remains historically healthy and hovering near a surplus state of 0%. 

The third chart, "Corporate net interest costs stable despite rising funds rate," displays the Federal Funds rate on a 0% to 20% right axis and corporate net interest payments as a percentage of after-tax NIPA profits on a 0% to 120% left axis from 1970 to 2023. It reveals that despite the Federal Reserve's aggressive recent interest rate hikes, corporate net interest costs remain remarkably flat and stable at roughly 20% of profits, contrasting sharply with past rate-hiking cycles when interest expenses surged. 

The final chart, "Ratio of cash yields to S&P 500 dividend yields," covers 1934 to 2023 and shows that the ratio of cash yields to dividend yields has spiked close to 4x. This is the highest level on record other than a major spike during the 2000 dot-com bubble, explaining why investors may hold onto more excess cash. 

Looking forward, Cembalest anticipates high single-digit equity returns for the remainder of 2024, though tech stock P/E multiples face risks as disinflationary boom prospects fade. Post-election, the market faces two distinct policy paths outlined by Don Schneider at Piper Sandler Research. A unified Republican government under Trump could enact a 60% tariff on Chinese goods, repeal the corporate alternative minimum tax and buyback tax, increase defense spending, fully extend the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, and execute mass deportations that could restrict labor growth and fuel wage inflation. Conversely, a unified Democratic government under Biden could pursue $2 trillion in tax increases evenly split between corporations and high-net-worth individuals to support a $2 trillion safety net expansion, posing a risk of a wider deficit if spending underperforms estimates, echoing the rising costs of the Inflation Reduction Act.

This page features J.P. Morgan commentary on artificial intelligence developments and social media valuations. The first section discusses the rapid evolution of open-source large language models, highlighted by Meta’s planned release of a 400-billion-parameter version of Llama 3. This advancement is expected to make the choice to build custom models more appealing to enterprises than buying access to proprietary APIs, particularly for highly specialized fields like finance. Additionally, local hosting offers superior security by keeping data in-house rather than sending it to providers like OpenAI. Meta’s efficiency gains are highlighted by the Llama 3-8B model, which matches the performance of the older Llama 2-70B model despite a 90 percent reduction in parameter size, making fast, high-quality AI accessible on more affordable hardware. Although Meta is investing billions of dollars in training these models without a clear revenue path, open-weight models are closing the performance gap with proprietary models. 

An accompanying chart, titled "Closed-source vs open-weight model performance," plots Arena ELO scores against model release dates from March 2023 to March 2024. While top-tier closed-source models like GPT-4 Turbo and Claude 3 Opus maintain the lead with ELO scores near 1250, open-weight models like Command R+, Qwen1.5-72B, and DBRX-Instruct have rapidly climbed to scores around 1150 to 1200, narrowing the performance gap to a lag of just six to ten months.

The second half of the page addresses the highly inflated market valuation of Truth Social. A bar chart titled "Social media market cap per active user" compares public and private social media platforms based on their market capitalization divided by monthly active users. Truth Social is valued at an exceptional $890 per active user, after peaking at $1,794 at its second-day close. This valuation dramatically exceeds established peers: TikTok (US) is valued at an estimated $588, Meta at $408, Discord at $100, Twitter (X) at $47, Pinterest at $45, Snap at $24, and Reddit at a mere $8 per monthly active user.

On this page, Michael Cembalest discusses the surprising resurgence of the Japanese equity market and structural reforms, highlighting that the Nikkei 225 Index finally returned to its 1989 peak after a 34.5-year drought. By comparison, it took the S&P 500 25 years to recover from the 1929 crash and the NASDAQ 15 years to recover after the 1999 tech bubble. From 1991 to 2022, the Nikkei returned just 1.6% annually, underperforming US Treasury bills at 2.5% and US equities at 9.6%. Despite this history, Japanese corporate governance and M&A are experiencing a major rebirth.

This transformation is detailed across four charts. The first chart, titled Corporate Finance Activity in Japan, shows data from 2012 to 2023. It tracks the number of deals on the left axis and the aggregate deal value in billions of US dollars on the right axis. The chart displays a clear upward trend, with deal volume climbing from well under 50 in 2012 to over 250 by 2023, while aggregate deal values rose to nearly 50 billion dollars in recent years, spanning buyouts, corporate carve-outs, and restructuring. The second chart, Japanese Deal Making Accelerates, displays Japan’s share of total deal volumes in Asia from 2005 to 2023. After fluctuating historically between 12% and 30%, Japan's share surged dramatically from its 2022 lows to finish near 30% in 2023. 

The third chart, Free Cash Flow Yield, plots the MSCI Japan and MSCI US yields from 2000 to 2024. The yield curves track closely, mostly fluctuating between 2% and 6%. This demonstrates that Japanese companies have long generated free cash flow comparable to US firms, but historically accumulated it rather than using it to enhance shareholder value. The fourth chart, Japan Performance vs 50/50 Europe and Emerging Markets, details the percent excess return from 1988 to 2024. While Japan has faced deep periods of underperformance, it has recently experienced a strong spike in outperformance over the last 18 months, even when factoring in a weak Yen. 

Ultimately, Cembalest notes that while investors are re-embracing Japan, the market is no longer cheap. Price-to-earnings multiples have expanded from 12.2 times in September 2022 to 17.0 times by early 2024, meaning future gains will rely heavily on continued structural changes and successful M&A integration.

This page examines public market equity investments in crop agriculture, focusing on seven large-cap US stocks across three sectors: farm machinery, represented by Deere; fertilizer, seed, and chemistry, including Mosaic, CF Industries, FMC Corp, and Corteva; and agricultural products, represented by Archer Daniels Midland and Bunge Global. Note that this analysis excludes meat and packaged food companies such as Tyson Foods, Pilgrim’s Pride, Hormel Foods, and BRF SA. 

The author observes that an equal-weighted basket of these US agricultural industries has outperformed the S&P 500 ex-tech index since 2015, a trend driven heavily by a surge in Deere stock in 2021. However, agricultural valuations have compressed. According to the chart displaying forward P/E ratios from 2015 to 2024, agricultural industries currently trade at lower multiples than the S&P 500 ex-tech index, which hovers around 17.5x. Fertilizer, seed, chemistry, and agricultural products currently trade at forward P/Es closer to 10x to 15x. 

This valuation compression is attributed to mounting cyclical pressures. A chart tracking the monthly inventory of unsold US farm equipment shows that unsold tractor inventories have risen sharply from a low in 2022 to nearly 28,000 by early 2024, while combine inventories have similarly climbed from a low of 4,000 to nearly 8,000 over the same period. 

Looking to the medium term, the author outlines several drivers and drags. Positive drivers include increased crop demand for renewable diesel and aviation fuels, alongside growing US agricultural exports. Conversely, significant drags include cost premiums for green fertilizers, transition costs associated with electrifying farm machinery, and rising ESG reporting standards. The author highlights a February 2024 estimate by the Buckeye Institute warning that compliance with net-zero decarbonization goals could raise corn farm operating expenses by up to 34%. Additionally, the potential impact of weight loss drugs on the consumption of cereals, sugar, and other crops remains an open question.

Finally, the analysis evaluates whether investors can gain superior agricultural exposure through non-US equities, farmland REITs, or commodity futures. A comparative chart indexing returns from 2015 to 2024 shows that the equal-weighted US agricultural stocks basket significantly outperformed all alternative vehicles, reaching a peak index value of 479 in late 2022. In contrast, Gladstone Land Corp, Farmland Partners Inc, the FTSE MFC global agriculture index, and the JPM Agriculture and Livestock futures total return index delivered vastly lower returns, remaining flatter and mostly below the 200 level.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication focuses on the resilience of global agricultural markets and the stabilization of prices, contrasted against the severe local environmental devastation in Ukraine. The overarching argument is that global supply chains have normalized, with other nations stepping up production to offset the shortfalls caused by the war in Ukraine and supply restrictions from Russia and China. 

The first section examines fertilizer markets. A line chart titled "Global prices for fertilizers" tracks five key fertilizer components in US dollars per metric ton from January 2021 to April 2024. It shows that prices spiked dramatically in mid-2022—with potassium chloride peaking near twelve hundred dollars and urea near one thousand dollars—before returning to early 2021 levels of around four hundred to six hundred dollars per metric ton. This trend of normalization is also observed in diammonium phosphate, triple superphosphate, and phosphate rock. An adjacent stacked bar chart, "Global fertilizer exports," measures annual export volumes in millions of tons for nitrogen, phosphate, and potash from 2021 to 2023. Total exports fell from one hundred million tons in 2021 to eighty million tons in 2022, but recovered to ninety million tons in 2023, reversing about half of the previous decline as global producers increased output to offset Russian and Chinese shortfalls.

The second section analyzes grain production using two charts indexing wheat and corn output from 2008 to 2024, with 2008 serving as the base year of one hundred. The "Production of wheat" chart highlights that while Ukraine’s indexed wheat production fell sharply from roughly one hundred twenty in 2021 to eighty in 2022, global wheat production remained highly stable, maintaining an index value around one hundred fifteen as Canada, Russia, Brazil, and Kazakhstan increased their output. The "Production of corn" chart shows a similar story: Ukrainian corn production plummeted from an index peak above three hundred fifty down to two hundred in 2022. Global corn production dipped in 2022 to an index of about one hundred thirty-five, but rebounded to nearly one hundred fifty in 2023, supported by increased output from China, the United States, Brazil, and Argentina. 

Despite global supply chain resilience, the author details the catastrophic toll on Ukraine's domestic agricultural base. Roughly one-third of Ukraine’s territory is now contaminated with toxic elements like lead, cadmium, arsenic, and mercury leaching from weaponry into the soil. Additionally, nine thousand three hundred acres of forest have been burned, local waterways have been heavily polluted, and land mines are now scattered across sixty-seven thousand square miles. The author notes that this damage is poised to worsen, citing a Wall Street Journal report that Ukraine’s air defense missile interception rate has fallen to thirty percent from eighty-three percent a year prior.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication highlights positive governance changes and economic developments in Japan, focusing on its potential to equitize and its exit from long-term deflation, which makes the country's equities highly attractive to global investors despite ongoing demographic and structural headwinds. Michael Cembalest argues that there is substantial room for Japan to align more with global equity standards, supported by several corporate governance shifts, including threats from the Tokyo Stock Exchange to delist companies trading below book value, a drop in poison pills among Nikkei 225 companies from 65 in 2012 to just 8 as of April 2024, and active prodding from over 50 activist funds. 

The analysis is anchored by a comparative table titled Room for Japan to Equitize, which contrasts corporate and financial metrics between the United States and Japan using December 2023 data. The data reveals stark differences: Japan's 10-year dividend payout ratio is 30% compared to 70% in the US, and cash as a percentage of market capitalization stands at 21% in Japan versus 7% in the US. Furthermore, 50% of Japanese companies trade below book value compared to just 4% in the US, and corporate buybacks are significantly lower in Japan, ranging from 0.7% to 1.4% of market capitalization compared to 2.0% to 3.5% in the US. On the allocation side, Japanese households hold 55% of their assets in cash and only 11% in equities, whereas US households hold 15% in cash and 40% in equities. Similarly, Japanese pensions allocate 25% to equities compared to 40% in the US, pointing to substantial untapped demand for equity investment.

These allocation pressures are supported by an exit from deflation, as shown in the chart Japan finally exits deflation. Tracking Japan’s consumer price index excluding fresh food and energy on a year-over-year basis from 1980 to early 2024, the chart illustrates decades of near-zero or negative inflation since the late 1990s. This trend has reversed sharply, with inflation climbing to nearly 4% by 2024, which lowers the appeal of holding cash. Consequently, aggregate demand is rising, as represented in the chart Japan bank loans as a percent of GDP. This chart tracks bank loans from 1980 through late 2023, showing that credit demand peaked in the early 1990s at around 110% of GDP, bottomed out near 82% around 2010, and has recently rebounded strongly to about 108% of GDP.

Despite this positive momentum, global investors remain historically underweight. The chart titled Global investor underweight to Japanese stocks tracks portfolio weights from 2003 through 2023. It compares the MSCI All World Global Equity Index weighting for Japan, which declined from roughly 10% in 2005 to around 5.5% in 2023, against the actual weighting of Japan in global investor portfolios. The actual weighting has consistently lagged the benchmark, bottoming out around 4% before rising slightly to 5% by late 2023, demonstrating a persistent but narrowing underweight gap.

Cembalest cushions this positive outlook with a note of caution regarding Japan’s structural limitations. The country remains a slow-growing economy with a potential growth rate below 1% due to unfavorable demographics, with 28% of its population aged 65 or older. Additionally, domestic consumption remains weak, with 2023 growth driven largely by exports, while China has eclipsed Japan as the world's leading auto exporter. High government debt relative to GDP also poses a threat if domestic interest rates rise alongside a weakening Yen. Nonetheless, the momentum of escaping deflation and the comparatively attractive valuations lead J.P. Morgan to view Japanese equities favorably relative to European and emerging market counterparts.

This page explores the growing intersection of private equity and the sports industry, focusing on the specific categories PE funds plan to invest in or lend to following the decision by US sports leagues to permit private equity ownership. The author argues that constructing a diversified sports portfolio is far more feasible in private markets than in public ones. While some franchises like the Atlanta Braves, Manchester United, and the New York Knicks and Rangers are publicly traded, actual voting control is heavily concentrated. For instance, John Malone controls approximately 50% of the voting power of the Braves, the Glazer family controls 69% of Manchester United, and the Dolan family controls 71% of the Knicks and Rangers through Class B shares carrying ten times the voting power of public Class A shares. Furthermore, major sports media properties exist as subsidiaries of giant conglomerates—such as Disney's ESPN, Warner Bros. Discovery's TNT Sports, Paramount's CBS Sports, Fox Corporation's FOX Sports, and Comcast's NBC Sports—making them inaccessible as pure-play public investments. 

The author outlines several regulatory and conflict-of-interest hurdles facing private equity, noting that firms are generally barred from acquiring minority team stakes if they hold investments in sports gambling or player representation. Additionally, a PE firm cannot invest in a league if one of its principals is already a control owner within that league. An open question posed at the end is whether the traditional private equity holding period of five to seven years is actually practical for sports investments.

To illustrate the vast sports ecosystem available to private investors, the page features a detailed table categorizing potential investment and lending targets across ten key sectors. Under Teams, funds look at minority and majority ownership, though majority PE ownership is currently prohibited in the four largest US sport leagues. Collectibles covers trading cards, memorabilia, NFTs, and apparel. Players and Talent includes performance services like training and physical rehabilitation, analytics software, agencies, and contract underwriting. Real Estate encompasses stadium financing, arenas, adjacent property developments, and fitness franchises. Media covers streaming rights, fan engagement platforms, and sports media outlets. Operations includes venue management, equipment, and third-party ticketing apps. Leagues spans emerging leagues, youth academies, and summer camps. Betting covers fantasy sports, betting apps, and live sportsbooks. Finally, Video Games covers e-sports and sports gaming.

This page introduces professional sports league ownership and related businesses as an emerging investment class for institutional and private equity investors. Michael Cembalest explains that sports team ownership was historically restricted to extremely wealthy individuals. This point is illustrated by a log-scale chart titled "Net worth of major league sports team control owners," which plots the estimated net worth of owners in the NBA, NFL, MLB, and NHL from under $1 billion to nearly $100 billion. The chart shows that the vast majority of current control owners possess a net worth concentrated between $1 billion and $10 billion, indicating that team ownership has historically been out of reach for average or diversified institutional investors. 

However, ownership rules have begun to change, with most major North American sports leagues now permitting select private equity funds to purchase minority stakes. Cembalest highlights that minority investments accounted for 45% of global sports deals in 2023 and approximately 60% of deals within the four major US sports. Footnote data points out that there are currently 138 minority owners in the NBA, 90 in the NFL, and 24 in the MLB. 

A detailed table titled "North American leagues' private equity rules" outlines these shifting regulations. Major League Baseball (MLB) was the first to allow private equity in 2019, permitting a maximum aggregate private equity ownership of 30% per team, a 15% limit for any single fund, and allowing a single fund to own stakes in an unlimited number of teams; sovereign wealth funds are not permitted. Major League Soccer (MLS) followed in 2020, setting limits of 30% across firms, 20% for a single fund, and a maximum of 4 teams per fund, with sovereign wealth funds also restricted. The National Basketball Association (NBA) and National Hockey League (NHL) both adopted rules in 2021, setting a 30% limit across firms, a 20% single-fund limit, and a maximum of 5 teams per fund. Unlike MLB and MLS, both the NBA and NHL permit investments from sovereign wealth funds. All rules for the National Football League (NFL) are listed as pending. 

The author concludes by noting that sports investing goes beyond team ownership to encompass real estate, media, operations, collectibles, personal fitness, player management, and sports betting. He previews that this special issue of "Eye on the Market" will analyze team valuations, operating margins, league parity mechanisms like salary caps and revenue sharing, broadcasting revenues, ticket prices, comparisons to European soccer, emerging leagues, stadium subsidies, and the esports market.

This page offers an analysis of sports franchise ownership, outlining key factors such as valuations, debt caps, cross-ownership trends, real estate development, tax benefits, and portfolio integration. The author notes that fifty to seventy percent of NBA and NFL revenues are tied to long-term contracts, which can allow for alternative valuation models that discount these contractual flows at investment-grade rates. On the topic of debt, both the NFL and NBA enforce strict leverage caps: the NFL caps debt at 1.4 billion dollars for new acquisitions and 700 million dollars for existing owners, while the NBA caps it at 325 million dollars. A line chart titled "Debt to valuation for major sports teams" plots teams sorted in descending order of debt-to-valuation ratio across the NHL, NFL, MLB, and NBA, showing that leverage is generally very low across all four leagues. The chart highlights three key high-leverage exceptions: the Arizona Coyotes at sixty-two percent, which is the lowest-valued NHL franchise and was recently sold for relocation to Utah; the LA Rams at forty-six percent, due to an NFL-approved debt waiver for constructing SoFi Stadium; and the Miami Marlins at forty-five percent, reflecting high acquisition debt from 2017. Beyond these exceptions, the curves for all leagues drop off rapidly, falling well below twenty percent for the majority of teams.

The author also details the growing trend of cross-ownership, citing major conglomerates like Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, Harris Blitzer Sports, Monumental, and Fenway Sports Group, alongside eleven MLS owners with cross-holdings. In terms of physical development, franchises are increasingly revitalizing the areas surrounding their venues, as seen in projects like Camden Yards in Baltimore, The Battery at Truist Park in Atlanta, the Wrigley Field area, the district surrounding DC's Capital One Arena, and the new urban district at SoFi Stadium. Furthermore, sports ownership offers substantial tax advantages; active owners can depreciate assets such as player contracts, ticket lists, stadium leases, and broadcast deals against active income, while passive limited partners can leverage depreciation within partnerships to offset passive income. Finally, the author cautions against claims that sports team ownership improves portfolio risk-adjusted returns, arguing that such studies rely on infrequent appraisals that fail to capture true risk within a mean-variance framework, advising instead that sports assets be evaluated against public equities using time-weighted return comparisons.

This page analyzes the valuations, transactions, debt levels, and operating margins of the four major US sports leagues—the NFL, NBA, MLB, and NHL. The author explains that professional sports franchises benefit from three distinct revenue streams: league-wide revenue-sharing, local brand-building within protected marketing areas, and ancillary stadium or media businesses. Operating essentially as lightly regulated monopolies under the Sherman Act, these franchises have seen their valuations rise dramatically, with actual sale prices closely matching Forbes' pre-sale appraisals.

A chart titled "NBA, NFL, NHL, and MLB sale values since 2014" illustrates transaction prices in billions of US dollars, showing actual sales as colored bars and Forbes' pre-sale appraisals as black dots. Notable high-value transactions include the NFL's Washington Commanders selling for nearly $6 billion in 2023 and the Denver Broncos selling for over $4 billion in 2022. In the NBA, significant sales include the Phoenix Suns and Dallas Mavericks in 2023, both clearing the $3 billion mark. The data demonstrates how closely actual transaction values track Forbes’ estimated appraisals. 

An accompanying table detailing "Actual sales transactions, 2022-2024" lists valuation-to-revenue multiples. NBA teams commanded some of the highest multiples, led by the Suns in 2023 at 13.2x, followed by the Hornets at 11.2x, the Bucks at 9.7x, and the Mavericks at 8.9x. The NFL’s Commanders and Broncos transacted at multiples of 11.1x and 9.4x, respectively. Meanwhile, the NHL’s Coyotes (2024) and Senators (2023) traded at 8.3x and 6.1x, and the MLB’s Orioles traded at 6.5x in 2024.

Two additional charts compare sports franchise valuations to public equity markets. The first, "Sport team valuations vs equity markets," indexes valuations from a base of 100 in 2005. By 2024, all four sports leagues have vastly outperformed the S&P 500, which sits at an index level of roughly 350. The NBA index leads the pack, surging past 1,200, followed by the NHL near 900, the MLB near 800, and the NFL near 600. The second chart, "Valuation to revenues for major sports teams vs S&P 500 price to sales," plots individual team multiples sorted in descending order. Most sports franchises are valued between 5x and 12x revenue, far exceeding the S&P 500's average multiple of approximately 3x. NBA franchises maintain the highest multiples, hovering between 9x and 12x, followed closely by the NFL, while NHL and MLB teams display a wider distribution that descends toward 4x.

The author notes that the valuation gap between the most and least valuable teams within a league varies significantly. The NFL and NHL have the narrowest gap at roughly 2.5x, and the NBA is at 3.2x. In contrast, the MLB has a much wider valuation gap of 7.6x, driven by weaker revenue-sharing mechanisms, the lack of a salary cap, and greater reliance on local media rights.

This page analyzes the financial operating margins of major professional sports leagues, arguing that teams in the NFL, NHL, and NBA benefit significantly from rising broadcast revenues, salary caps, and revenue socialization. Over the past 20 years, operating margins in these three leagues have generally improved as player salaries have declined as a share of overall revenues. In contrast, Major League Baseball lacks a salary cap and strict fiscal discipline, resulting in lower and sometimes deeply negative operating margins. 

The author notes that the median NHL operating margin has tripled since the 2018-2019 season following lucrative seven-year broadcast deals signed in 2021 with Disney and Turner Sports, which average 635 million dollars annually. Additionally, teams in low-tax jurisdictions like Texas, Florida, and Nevada hold a recruiting advantage under the cumulative 2.4 percent salary cap increase since 2020, representing 11 of the 20 teams that made the conference finals in that span. A footnote highlights this tax disparity, noting that on a 3 million dollar contract, an NHL player pays zero dollars in state taxes in Texas compared to 371,000 dollars in California. The author cautions that operating income is not a direct proxy for positive cash flow, as it excludes debt interest, taxes, and capital expenditures.

The analysis is supported by three visual charts. The first chart, titled "Operating income margin by team and league," plots individual teams ranked by their operating margin. The data shows that NFL, NBA, and NHL teams consistently maintain positive operating margins, mostly clustered between 10 percent and 40 percent. The MLB series shows a steeper downward trend, with several teams falling into negative territory, including the Athletics, Rockies, White Sox, Blue Jays, Padres, and the Mets, whose operating margin drops precipitously to nearly negative 80 percent. Labeled underperforming NBA teams include the Nets, Clippers, and Bucks.

The second chart, titled "League revenue by type," displays the percentage breakdown of total revenue for each league. The NFL relies overwhelmingly on national revenue, which makes up over 60 percent of its total, with seating and suites accounting for about 25 percent. The NBA features a more balanced mix, with national revenue at roughly 30 percent, followed by seating, team sponsorships, and local media. MLB is highly dependent on local media and seating, each accounting for about 25 percent of revenue. The NHL relies most heavily on seating and suites at approximately 35 percent of its total revenue, with national revenue making up only about 20 percent.

The third chart, "Player expenses as a percentage of revenue," tracks the historical trend from 2006 through 2020. Across the board, player expenses have generally declined from their mid-2000s levels. In 2006, NFL and NHL player expenses hovered around 60 percent to 63 percent, but fell to around 45 percent to 48 percent by the late 2010s. The chart also captures a sharp, volatile spike around 2020 across all leagues, particularly for the MLB, NFL, and NHL, driven by the dramatic drop in total league revenues during the COVID-19 pandemic.

This page analyzes how salary caps influence competitive parity and prevent financial arms races by comparing major US sports leagues with European soccer leagues. The author argues that hard salary caps, such as those in the NFL and NHL, effectively flatten the payroll curve across teams. The NBA’s soft cap, which allows for exceptions, shows slightly more slippage, while the MLB’s lack of a cap results in a much steeper curve where spending depends on owner wealth and luxury tax tolerances. Additionally, the NFL, NBA, and NHL caps adjust dynamically with aggregate league revenue, a stabilizing feature that MLB lacks.

The first chart illustrates payroll parity in US sports leagues by plotting each team’s 2023 payroll divided by the league's median payroll. The curves for the NFL, NHL, and NBA remain flat and clustered near the 1.0 median line. In contrast, the MLB curve is highly skewed. High-spending outliers like the New York Mets exceed 2.0 times the median payroll, followed closely by the New York Yankees, San Diego Padres, Philadelphia Phillies, and Los Angeles Dodgers. On the opposite end, low-spending MLB teams like the Oakland Athletics, Baltimore Orioles, Pittsburgh Pirates, Tampa Bay Rays, Cincinnati Reds, Cleveland Guardians, and Kansas City Royals drop below 0.5 times the median.

The second chart compares MLB's payroll distribution to the English Premier League (EPL) and Spain's La Liga, utilizing a vertical axis that extends up to 9.0 times the median payroll. This visual highlights extreme spending disparity in European soccer. La Liga represents an extreme "arms race," with Real Madrid’s payroll approaching 9.0 times the league median, FC Barcelona exceeding 7.0 times, and Atletico Madrid near 5.0 times. The EPL curve is also steeper than MLB's, with top teams spending over 2.5 times the median, though the author notes that the EPL plans to introduce a salary cap in the near future to address this disparity.

This page focuses on the landscape of the streaming wars and the parallel decline of regional sports networks, highlighting the soaring demand and massive financial value of broadcast and streaming media rights for professional sports leagues. The author argues that broadcasting rights have become the primary lifeblood of professional leagues, accounting for 50 percent to 70 percent of total revenues for the NFL, NBA, and MLB, and 30 percent for the NHL. This marks a massive historical shift from a few decades ago when franchise value was driven almost entirely by gate attendance; for example, in 1946, media contracts comprised a mere 3 percent of MLB revenue. Highlighting this rapid expansion, global sports media contracts have risen from $24.5 billion in 2011 to more than $62.4 billion today. This trend is exemplified by a pending 11-year NBA deal with NBC, Amazon, and ESPN valued at $76 billion, representing a 2.6-fold annual increase over the preceding 2016 to 2025 deal.

A detailed table lists media contract value increases at their start dates for various leagues. It shows that MLB's 2022 to 2028 deal with Fox, TBS, and ESPN increased contract value by 1.3 times. The NFL's 2023 to 2033 deal with CBS, Fox, NBC, and ESPN rose 1.8 times. The NHL's 2021 to 2028 contract with ABC, ESPN, and TNT grew 2.1 times. The NBA's media contracts saw a 2.9 times increase for the 2016 to 2025 cycle and are projected to grow 2.6 times for the 2025 to 2036 cycle. 

Several charts illustrate these dynamics of consumer and advertiser demand. A line chart tracking the price of a 30-second Super Bowl commercial in real 2023 dollars shows a relentless climb from under $1 million before 1975 to over $7 million by 2025, with the cost doubling since 2005. A bar chart tracking the estimated number of adult scripted original series shows the rise of "Peak TV," with the number of series growing from under 200 in 2002 to a peak of around 600 in 2021 and 2022, before dropping sharply to roughly 400 in 2023. Adjacent to this, a bar chart of US sports media rights payments shows steady upward growth from approximately $15 billion in 2015 to projected levels exceeding $30 billion by 2026.

The text concludes with further evidence of robust consumer demand for live sports. Over 30 percent of adults in both the United States and the United Kingdom purchased at least one pay-per-view sports event over the previous 12 months, primarily UFC and boxing matches, which account for four of the top five most-watched pay-per-view events of all time. Additionally, the NFL’s dominance of live television has grown; in 2023, NFL games accounted for 93 of the 100 most-watched TV broadcasts, up from 82 in 2022 and 61 in 2018. Within the top 50 most-viewed broadcasts, 48 were NFL games, alongside only the State of the Union address and the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Finally, eight of the top ten most-watched events in US television history were Super Bowls.

This page addresses the ongoing economic controversy surrounding public subsidies for professional sports stadiums in the United States. Citing an April 2022 meta-study by Bradbury et al., the text explains that the economic justification for funding these facilities is highly weak. An analysis of 130 individual studies shows that stadium subsidies typically far exceed the local economic benefits they create, primarily because stadium-related spending represents a shift in existing local consumer spending rather than net-new economic activity. Consequently, these subsidies function primarily as wealth transfers from local taxpayers to sports team owners.

To support this conclusion, the page includes two horizontal bar charts demonstrating a strong consensus among economists. The first chart, which surveys American Economic Association members, shows that nearly 60% of respondents strongly agree and approximately 27% agree that local and state governments should eliminate subsidies to professional sports franchises. The second chart, surveying an IGM panel of economic experts on whether stadium subsidies cost taxpayers more than the generated local economic benefits, shows that over 60% agree and around 12% strongly agree. In both surveys, the shares of economists who disagree or strongly disagree are extremely small, remaining in the single digits.

Despite this evidence, the author observes that stadium subsidies continue to persist, posing an upcoming challenge for local jurisdictions. This issue is set to intensify because a massive wave of stadium construction is imminent. The median age of existing venues across major leagues is 24 years, bringing them close to the typical 30-year replacement cycle. By the year 2030, roughly 25% of all stadiums—representing 30 facilities—will be at least 30 years old.

The page concludes with a line chart titled "Stadium ages by league," which displays the age or time since renovation (up to 40 years) for venues across the MLB, NHL, NBA, and NFL, ranking teams from oldest to newest. The chart highlights that MLB venues trend the oldest, with the top facilities exceeding 35 years. Across all four sports leagues, a significant volume of stadiums is clustered between 20 and 30 years of age, visually illustrating the looming demand for a new generation of stadium replacements and the accompanying political pressure for public subsidies.

This page analyzes the financial dynamics of European soccer, specifically focusing on the English Premier League (EPL) and comparing its structure to the US Major League Soccer (MLS). The author addresses the severe financial risks of relegation and the intense pressure that escalating player salaries place on club profitability. 

A detailed table displays team revenues for the EPL and the lower-tier EFL Championship during the 2019–20 season, illustrating a massive financial gulf depending on league standing. Teams finishing in positions one through four (qualifying for the UEFA Champions League) brought in £444 million in total revenue, driven by £200 million in commercial and £178 million in broadcast revenue. In contrast, middle-tier EPL teams in positions 9 to 17 generated £141 million, while relegated teams in positions 18 to 20 earned £112 million. The financial cliff of relegation is clear in the next tier: EFL Championship teams receiving "parachute payments" to cushion the transition managed £52 million in total revenue, while those without parachute payments brought in just £20 million—representing an 82% drop from the EPL's bottom tier. A case study box on the Luton Town Hatters illustrates this volatility, showing how the team's revenue rose dramatically from £17.6 million in the EFL in 2021 to over £200 million in 2023 upon promotion back to the EPL.

An accompanying stacked bar chart details cumulative revenues for the "Big Five" European leagues during the 2021–2022 season. The EPL dominates the landscape with approximately £6 billion in cumulative revenue, followed by Spain's La Liga at about £3.3 billion, Germany's Bundesliga at £3.1 billion, Italy's Serie A at £2.2 billion, and France's Ligue 1 at £2.1 billion. Across all leagues, broadcasting and commercial revenues represent the vast majority of income, while matchday revenues remain a minor contributor.

The text explains that despite these massive revenues, the European model presents major challenges for team owners. Due to the absence of salary caps and rookie contracts, EPL player salaries grew 36-fold between 1992 and 2021, outstripping the 27-fold growth in league revenues over the same period. Total wages consume 73% of revenue for the average EPL team, rising to 87% for teams outside the top six. Consequently, only seven EPL teams reported a profit during the 2021–2022 season. In contrast, the US MLS employs a highly structured parity model characterized by heavy revenue-sharing, pooled national broadcast and sponsor funds, and a 2024 salary budget cap of $5.5 million per team (with a designated player rule allowing only three exceptions). This approach has successfully fostered parity, with average MLS team values rising 17% over five years and individual team valuations tightly clustered around the league average.

Michael Cembalest discusses the highly controversial practice of using public subsidies to fund sports stadiums and arenas, arguing that these taxpayer contributions represent a substantial transfer of value to franchise owners. While the percentage of public financing for these projects has generally declined over time, the absolute dollar amounts have ballooned as sports facilities have become increasingly advanced and expensive. 

This trend is illustrated in the first chart, "Stadium and arena median construction costs by decade," which tracks median costs in inflation-adjusted 2020 dollars from the 1970s to the 2020s. The chart reveals a dramatic surge in total stadium costs, which have grown from a median of under $200 million in the 1970s to nearly $2 billion in the 2020s. Although the public cost share represents a smaller percentage of the total in recent decades, the absolute volume of public dollars spent has escalated alongside the overall cost explosion. 

The second chart, "Public funding share of total stadium construction costs," illustrates the distribution of public funding across venues built since 1990. While there is a notable peak of over 20 venues that received zero public funding, the overall median public funding share stands at 61%, with many facilities cluster-funded at 70% to 90% by taxpayers. This bimodal reality is contextualized in a footnote noting that the most expensive sports stadium ever built, SoFi Stadium, cost $5.5 billion and was entirely privately financed, whereas other communities are beginning to push back, such as Kansas City voters rejecting a sales tax renewal in April 2024 to subsidize a stadium for the Royals.

The value of these subsidies to team owners is explored in the third chart, "Stadium costs as a share of team valuation," which plots 2023 stadium construction costs as a percentage of total team value for select venues built since 2000 that received more than 70% public funding. This ratio peaks with the Miami Marlins, whose stadium cost represents roughly 80% of the team's entire valuation, and runs down to around 20% for the Oklahoma City Thunder, proving that public subsidies often construct assets worth a massive portion of the underlying franchise. 

The direct impact of these stadium deals on owner wealth is underscored by the final chart, "Valuation of the Raiders," which plots the team's estimated franchise value from 1997 to 2024. Prior to 2015, the team was among the NFL's least valuable franchises, hovering around a $1 billion valuation. However, following the 2015 approval of plans for a new Las Vegas stadium supported by $750 million in taxpayer funding, the franchise’s valuation skyrocketed from $1.4 billion to more than $6 billion by 2024.

This page analyzes adjacent businesses in the sports industry, focusing on apparel, name, image, and likeness (NIL) licensing, and player management. 

The author first highlights apparel giant Fanatics, which achieved a $31 billion valuation in 2022 after raising $700 million. Fanatics possesses data on 94 million sports fans and exclusive rights for branded fan apparel, alongside strategic acquisitions like Topps and clothing brands partnered with Kevin Durant and LeBron James. Despite estimated revenues of $5 billion to $8 billion, the firm faces growing pains; S&P affirmed its BB- rating but revised its outlook to negative due to elevated leverage, production delays that slowed revenue growth, a 5.5 percent decline in EBITDA margins in the second quarter of 2023, guaranteed minimum royalty commitments, and antitrust litigation with the NFL. 

Next, the text addresses NIL licensing through OneTeam Partners, which manages group licensing for major professional unions—including the NFL, MLB, MLS, WNBA, and the US Women’s National Soccer Team—and is expanding internationally. OneTeam has partnered with Fanatics for college athletic jersey production across over 100 schools, spanning sports such as football, soccer, volleyball, and basketball, though the business faces the operational challenge of unpredictable demand requiring on-demand production. 

Finally, the page looks at player management, which is driven by an aggregate payroll of approximately $20 billion across the four major US sports leagues. A detailed table lists the top fifteen sports agencies by commissions, contracts, and investors. Creative Artists Agency (CAA) leads the industry with $971 million in commissions and $18.0 billion in contracts, backed by investors like TPG, CMC, Temasek, Pinault, and Taiwan Mobile. Wasserman ranks second with $733 million in commissions and $9.0 billion in contracts, followed by WME Sports with $588 million in commissions and $6.0 billion in contracts. Excel Sports Management holds fourth place with $499 million in commissions and $6.0 billion in contracts, while Octagon, Boras Corporation, and Roc Nation Sports all report commissions just over $200 million. Other agencies in the top fifteen include Athletes First, Klutch Sports Group, You First, GSE Worldwide, Newport Sports Management, Rep 1 Sports, Priority Sports & Entertainment, and Independent Sports & Entertainment.

This page provides a comprehensive financial overview of National Football League franchises, focusing on valuations, revenues, debt, and operating margins using data compiled from Forbes and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. 

A detailed table outlines the financial metrics of all 32 NFL teams, sorted in descending order of total valuation. The Dallas Cowboys rank as the most valuable franchise at $9.0 billion, yielding the highest revenue at $1.14 billion, the highest operating income at $504 million, and a league-leading operating margin of 44%. The New England Patriots follow as the second most valuable team at $7.0 billion, while the Cincinnati Bengals rank at the bottom of the list with a valuation of $3.5 billion. Among other notable team statistics, the Chicago Bears carry the highest valuation-to-revenue multiple at 11.3x, the Las Vegas Raiders lead the league in five-year annualized revenue growth at 15%, and the Los Angeles Rams stand out with a exceptionally high debt-to-valuation ratio of 46%, compared to a league where most teams hold less than 15% debt. The lowest operating margins in the league are tied at 10% for both the Detroit Lions and the Las Vegas Raiders.

Below the table, two charts illustrate the historical financial trends of the league from 1998 to 2022. The first chart, showing the NFL median valuation-to-revenue multiple, demonstrates a significant long-term expansion in team valuations relative to their sales. The median multiple hovered between 3x and 4x for nearly fifteen years before beginning a steady climb around 2012. This growth accelerated dramatically after 2018, with the median multiple peaking near 9x in 2021 and closing out 2022 at approximately 8.5x. 

The second chart tracks the volatile trajectory of the NFL's median operating margin over the same period. The margin fluctuated widely, dropping from 15% to 10% in 2000, peaking near 24% in 2003, and falling back to 10% by 2006. After stabilizing around 20% between 2015 and 2019, the median operating margin collapsed to below 5% in 2020—undoubtedly due to pandemic stadium restrictions—before staging a rapid recovery to a historic high of 25% in 2021, eventually settling at nearly 20% in 2022.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market discusses the rapid rise of sports parlay betting and the regulatory arbitrage surrounding Daily Fantasy Sports (DFS). The author explains that parlays, which combine multiple wagers for higher payout odds, are increasingly popular and highly lucrative for sportsbooks due to their superior profit margins. Citing data from Illinois, the text notes that the average profit margin on parlays is 18%, compared to just 5% on straight bets, a profitability boost that is only partially offset by the fact that straight bets are typically five to six times larger in dollar size. 

The first chart, "Increase in parlay bets: Parlay bet share of total bets placed," tracks the growing share of parlays from 2020 to 2023 across major operators. FanDuel leads the pack, seeing its parlay share rise from approximately 50% in 2020 to over 70% in 2023. DraftKings saw its share rise from about 30% to over 50%, while other platforms like PointsBet, BetRivers, BetMGM, Caesars, and Barstool also exhibited steep upward trajectories. The second chart, "Size and profitability: straight bet vs parlay bet," illustrates this dynamic by comparing average bet sizes and profit margins. It shows that average straight bet sizes are quite high, ranging from around $60 for FanDuel to $150 for Caesars, but carry low profit margins of around 5%. Conversely, average parlay bet sizes are small, generally between $10 and $20, but boast parlay profit margins that range from 14% up to nearly 25% for FanDuel.

The second half of the page covers the regulatory arbitrage of fantasy sports. DFS companies operate under legal exemptions in many states, allowing them to offer products with a very similar look and feel to parlay bets without being regulated as traditional sportsbooks. This has fueled rapid growth, as shown in the chart "Sports-gambling app downloads (July 2022-June 2023)." During this period, the daily fantasy platform PrizePicks was the third most downloaded sports gambling app overall with about 4.5 million downloads, trailing only FanDuel Sportsbook at over 8 million and DraftKings Sportsbook at around 7.5 million. Other notable apps in the download rankings include DraftKings Fantasy at 3 million, BetMGM at 2.5 million, and Underdog at 1.5 million.

The analysis concludes by detailing the daily fantasy sports loophole. States representing 33% of the U.S. population—including California, Alabama, Georgia, Minnesota, Missouri, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Utah, and Texas—do not allow traditional sportsbooks like DraftKings and FanDuel to operate. Yet, major states within this group, such as California and Texas, permit DFS companies like PrizePicks to operate because of how their bets are legally structured. In California, these DFS companies remain unregulated and do not pay taxes. Adding to the regulatory patchwork, some states that do permit traditional sportsbooks choose to ban DFS companies entirely.

This page analyzes the financial valuations, revenues, operating income, and overall financial health of NBA franchises, highlighting a massive increase in team values over the last decade. A comprehensive table details the thirty NBA teams, topped by the Golden State Warriors with a valuation of $7.7 billion on $765 million in revenue and a 10.1x valuation-to-revenue multiple. The New York Knicks and Los Angeles Lakers follow closely with valuations of $6.6 billion and $6.4 billion respectively, with the Knicks boasting a high 34% operating margin and a 13.1x valuation-to-revenue multiple. At the bottom of the list, the Memphis Grizzlies have the lowest valuation at $2.4 billion. The table also shows that while most teams are highly profitable, some are operating at a loss, such as the Milwaukee Bucks with an operating margin of negative 11%, the Los Angeles Clippers at negative 3%, and the Brooklyn Nets at negative 1%. 

Two historical line charts at the bottom of the page track league-wide trends from 1998 through 2022. The first chart, titled NBA median valuation to revenue, displays how the median multiple remained steady between 2x and 3x from 1998 until 2011, after which it began a dramatic upward ascent, exceeding 10x by 2022. The second chart, titled NBA median operating margin, illustrates the volatility of league profitability over the same period. Median operating margins rose from 5% in 1998 to a peak of 15% in the mid-2000s, before plunging below 0% around 2010. Following this dip, operating margins rebounded strongly, reaching nearly 30% around 2022 before settling back slightly above 20%. The dataset for both the table and charts is sourced from Forbes and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page presents detailed financial metrics and historical trends for Major League Baseball teams, utilizing data compiled by Forbes and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The main focus is a comprehensive table detailing the latest valuations, revenues, debt levels, and operating incomes for thirty franchises. 

The table ranks teams by their total valuation in billions of US dollars. The New York Yankees lead the league with a valuation of $7.6 billion and $679 million in revenue, though they report a slim operating income of $2 million, representing a 0.3% operating margin. They are followed by the Los Angeles Dodgers, valued at $5.5 billion, and the Boston Red Sox, valued at $4.5 billion. At the bottom of the list are the Miami Marlins, valued at $1.0 billion with $295 million in revenue and a high debt-to-valuation ratio of 45%. The table highlights significant operational losses for several franchises, most notably the New York Mets, who posted a massive operating loss of -$292 million, resulting in a -74% operating margin. The San Diego Padres also registered a substantial operating loss of -$116 million.

Two historical line charts at the bottom of the page track MLB median financial trends from 1998 through 2022. The first chart displays the median valuation-to-revenue multiple, showing that the ratio stayed consistently between 2x and 3x from 1998 until around 2014. After 2014, the median multiple rose steadily, culminating in a dramatic peak of over 12x around 2021, before correcting back down to approximately 5x to 6x in 2022. 

The second chart traces the median operating margin for MLB teams. Over the twenty-four-year period, median margins typically fluctuated between 0% and 10%, with notable cyclical peaks. However, the median operating margin suffered a severe contraction during the pandemic years of 2020 and 2021, plunging below -5%. By 2022, median operating margins rebounded sharply, returning to a healthy level of around 10%.

This page discusses methods for tracking the political ideology of United States Supreme Court justices and Court of Appeals judges. 

The first visualization is a detailed line chart tracking the ideological leanings of Supreme Court justices from 1930 to 2030 based on Martin-Quinn scores. The vertical axis ranges from negative five (most liberal) to positive five (most conservative). The chart plots the trajectory of dozens of individual justices over their tenures, demonstrating how their ideological positions shift. For example, William O. Douglas is noted at an extreme liberal score of negative eight by 1975, while William Rehnquist and Clarence Thomas peak near the top of the conservative scale at positive four to five. Current justices like Sonia Sotomayor sit near negative four, while John Roberts and Brett Kavanaugh are positioned closer to the center, and Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito remain more solidly conservative.

The second visualization, a bar chart on the bottom left, measures the "bridging alliance score" of the court’s current conservative justices with their liberal colleagues, reflecting how often they vote together. Neil Gorsuch has the highest score at approximately 3.5, frequently aligning with liberals on criminal and indigenous law. John Roberts and Brett Kavanaugh follow with scores of 2.5, Amy Coney Barrett sits at roughly 2.2, and Clarence Thomas is at 1.8. Samuel Alito has the lowest score at 1.0, making him the only current conservative justice who has never joined all of the liberal justices in a five-to-four decision.

The third visualization, a bar chart on the bottom right, shows the percentage of US Court of Appeals judges appointed by a Republican president from 1981 to 2024. The proportion peaks in 1993 at nearly 65%, bottoms out near 40% in 2001 and 2017, and stands at just over 50% in 2024.

This page presents a detailed financial analysis of National Hockey League (NHL) franchises, focusing on latest team valuations, revenues, operating income, valuation multiples, debt levels, and profit margins. 

A central table displays these metrics for thirty-two NHL teams, sorted from highest to lowest valuation. The Toronto Maple Leafs lead the league with a valuation of 2.8 billion dollars, 281 million dollars in revenue, 127 million dollars in operating income, and a high valuation-to-revenue multiple of 10.0x. This is closely followed by the New York Rangers, valued at 2.7 billion dollars with a 10.0x multiple, and the Montreal Canadiens at 2.3 billion dollars. On the other end of the spectrum, the Arizona Coyotes represent the lowest-valued franchise at 0.5 billion dollars, carrying a valuation-to-revenue multiple of 4.2x and a high debt-to-valuation ratio of 62 percent, compared to the single-digit debt levels of many top franchises. The table also indicates that the Edmonton Oilers registered the strongest five-year annualized revenue growth at 13 percent, while the Toronto Maple Leafs achieved the highest operating margin at 45 percent.

Below the table, two historical line charts illustrate median league-wide trends from 1998 through 2022. The chart on the left, tracking the NHL median valuation-to-revenue multiple, shows that the league median hovered near 2.0x from 1998 to 2012 before climbing upward, spiking dramatically to over 8.0x around 2021, and then settling back to approximately 5.5x in 2022. The chart on the right depicts the NHL median operating margin, showing historical volatility generally between negative 5 percent and positive 8 percent. This margin dipped deeply below negative 10 percent during the pandemic period around 2020 and 2021 before surging to an unprecedented high of nearly 25 percent in 2022. Data across the page is sourced from Forbes and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page of the publication examines "the Ronaldo effect" of superstar player departures on both sports team valuations and athletic performance. It argues that while a legendary player's departure can devastate a team's brand value and stock price, as seen with European soccer clubs, the financial structures of US sports leagues—such as revenue sharing—largely shield US team owners from the worst of these financial shocks, even when team winning percentages plummet on the field. 

To illustrate the financial impact in European soccer, a line chart plots the share price of Juventus in Euros against the Prospect global interest index from 2014 to 2024. During Cristiano Ronaldo's tenure with the club, highlighted between late 2018 and 2021, both metrics surged. The Juventus share price spiked from under two Euros to nearly ten Euros, while the global interest index jumped from two percent to three and a half percent. Once Ronaldo departed, both metrics precipitously crashed back to their pre-arrival baselines, even though the team's on-field performance only experienced a modest decline. 

The second chart looks at the on-field impact of superstar departures in US sports leagues, tracking the change in winning percentages when key players join or depart a franchise. It presents eight high-profile examples across baseball, basketball, and football, focusing on Julius Erving, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Reggie Jackson, Barry Bonds, Shaquille O'Neal, Manny Ramirez, LeBron James, and Michael Jordan. In almost every case, the team joined, shown in blue, saw its winning percentage rise, while the team departed, shown in red, saw its winning percentage fall. The most dramatic examples include LeBron James's departure from the Cleveland Cavaliers to the Miami Heat, where Cleveland's winning percentage plummeted from over seventy percent to under thirty percent, and Michael Jordan's second retirement from the Chicago Bulls, which sent Chicago's winning percentage crashing from over eighty percent to approximately twenty percent.

This page from the publication analyzes the persistent underperformance of US small-cap stocks and introduces the concept of the "unholy trinity," which comprises three major lagging portfolio strategies since 2010: small cap stocks, large cap value versus growth, and non-US stocks versus US stocks. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that while asset allocators in 2010 reasonably expected US small caps to outperform based on the historical "small cap anomaly" that existed from 1930 to 2010, they have instead experienced severe underperformance driven fundamentally by weaker earnings growth compared to US large-cap growth stocks.

The first chart, titled "Small cap vs large cap index returns," illustrates the three-year rolling outperformance or underperformance of small-cap versus large-cap stocks from 1930 to 2024. The data shows that while small caps historically enjoyed six distinct eras of substantial outperformance—frequently reaching rolling outperformance levels of 50% to over 100%—the period since 2010 has been dominated by large-cap outperformance, with the trend line spending most of its time in negative territory.

Below this, two side-by-side charts detail "The Big Three" underperforming strategies. The first, "The Big Three: relative underperformance," tracks five-year cumulative relative performance from 1990 to 2022. It shows a steep, prolonged decline for all three strategies starting around 2010: Russell 2000 and S&P 600 versus S&P 500 (underperforming by roughly 50%), Russell 1000 value versus growth (also underperforming by about 50%), and MSCI World ex-US versus S&P 500, which has suffered the worst cumulative underperformance, dropping below negative 100%. The companion chart, "The Big Three: relative valuations," displays the relative price-to-earnings premium or discount from 1995 to 2025. It reveals that all three strategies are trading at their deepest valuation discounts in twenty years, with forward and last-twelve-month discounts ranging between 25% and over 50%.

The bottom-left chart, "Earnings growth," indexes corporate earnings to 100 starting on December 31, 2010, and traces them through late 2023. This chart highlights the divergence that explains the valuation gap: Russell 1000 growth surged to an index level near 350, and the S&P 500 rose past 250, while the Russell 2000 and Russell 1000 value lagged behind. Most notably, the MSCI World ex-US indexes for both developed and developed-plus-emerging markets flatlined near 100 to 125. 

In his concluding commentary on "American exceptionalism," Cembalest characterizes non-US stocks as an "earnings wasteland" over the past decade. Looking forward, he expresses a preference among the three out-of-favor strategies, stating that he sees better future prospects for US small caps than for large-cap value or non-US equities. The page concludes with a thematic reference to the 1968 film "The Lion in Winter," starring Peter O’Toole as Henry II of England, serving as a metaphor for familial conflict and succession struggles.

In this J.P. Morgan publication, Michael Cembalest analyzes the relative valuation of US small cap equities compared to large caps, arguing that small caps are currently at the very cheap end of their 20-year valuation range across multiple measures, potentially offering an attractive entry point for investors. He presents two primary methodological frameworks to support this observation.

The first method utilizes forward price-to-earnings ratio comparisons. A chart titled "Relative valuation: small vs large cap forward P/E ratio" displays data from 1995 to 2025, tracking the relative forward P/E premium or discount for the Russell 2000 versus the S&P 500 and the S&P 600 versus the S&P 500. This chart highlights that the S&P 600 is trading at a steep discount of nearly 35% relative to the S&P 500, which is close to historical lows. Cembalest notes a statistical anomaly in Bloomberg’s historical Russell 2000 data during the early 2000s when positive P/E ratios were reported despite negative index earnings. To address data quality, a second chart from Empirical Research titled "Small cap vs large cap forward P/E for highest quality stocks" looks at the top quintile of free cash flow margins from 1976 to 2024. This high-quality relative forward P/E has plummeted to around 0.6x, hovering near record lows last seen in the late 1970s and the dot-com bubble crash of the early 2000s. 

The second method evaluates relative valuations using earnings yield, which is the inverse of the P/E ratio, meaning a higher relative yield indicates cheaper valuations. Two charts from J.P. Morgan's Structured Equity Group depict these relationships using winsorized data from Compustat and Factset to eliminate outliers. The first of these charts, tracking the difference in trailing earnings yield from 1990 to 2025, shows that the S&P 600 versus the S&P 500 is trading at a trailing yield premium of over 1%, while the Russell 2000 versus the S&P 500 sits around negative 3%, both pointing to relative cheapness. The final chart displays the difference in forward earnings yield over the same period. In this visual, the S&P 600 vs the S&P 500 forward earnings yield premium is elevated near 4% to 5%, and the Russell 2000 vs the S&P 500 is trading near a negative 1% difference, confirming that US small caps are remarkably cheap compared to large caps on both a trailing and forward basis.

This page argues that US small-cap stocks suffer from significantly lower profitability and higher exposure to interest rate risks than large-cap stocks. To support this thesis, the author points to several depressing metrics, including lower free cash flow margins, a larger share of companies with negative earnings, lower return on invested capital (ROIC), higher debt-to-cash flow ratios, a larger proportion of floating-rate debt, and a shorter debt maturity profile where roughly 70% of small-cap debt matures within the next five years compared to only 45% for large-cap debt.

Six charts illustrate these points in detail. The first chart shows the free cash flow margins of the S&P 500, S&P 600, and Russell 2000 from 1996 through 2023. S&P 500 large caps consistently lead with a smoothed margin of about 10% by late 2023, whereas the small-cap S&P 600 sits near 5% and the Russell 2000 lags at around 2%. The second chart tracks the percentage of companies with negative last-twelve-month earnings from 1990 to 2024. While the share of unprofitable large-cap companies remains stable near 10%, the share for small-cap companies has dramatically increased to over 40% in recent years. 

The third chart depicts aggregate ROIC from 1990 to 2023, revealing that large-cap ROIC has held steady around 10% to 12%, while small-cap ROIC has steadily deteriorated over the decades, landing near 4% in 2023. The fourth chart illustrates the breakdown of fixed versus floating rate debt for non-financial companies as of July 2024. While S&P 500 companies have successfully locked in fixed rates for about 85% of their debt, both the Russell 2000 and S&P 600 are heavily exposed, with floating-rate debt comprising roughly 45% of their total debt portfolios. 

The fifth chart shows the 90-day trailing moving average of net debt to EBITDA from 2000 to 2024. Leverage for the S&P 500 has consistently hovered under 2x, whereas Russell 2000 leverage peaked near 8x during the pandemic and remains elevated above 4x, with S&P 600 leverage also high at over 3x. Finally, the sixth chart plots total debt to equity over the same 2000 to 2024 period. This metric highlights that large-cap S&P 500 companies have significantly deleveraged from a peak ratio of over 2.0x in the mid-2000s down to approximately 1.0x by 2024, bringing them in line with the Russell 2000 and just slightly above the S&P 600, which both hover near 0.8x to 1.0x.

This analysis by Michael Cembalest discusses the long-term underperformance of US small-cap stocks relative to large-caps on a cumulative and rolling basis since late 2010. The author highlights that small-cap stocks are a shrinking portion of the US market, currently representing only 2.5% of the S&P 1500, down from a peak of 4.5%. 

To explore this space, the analysis compares the two primary small-cap benchmarks, the S&P 600 and the Russell 2000. The S&P 600 is characterized as a higher-quality, quarterly-rebalanced index because it requires positive earnings for inclusion. In contrast, the Russell 2000 rebalances annually based purely on market capitalization without earnings requirements. This structural difference results in the Russell 2000 having a much higher share of unprofitable companies (42% vs. 23% for the S&P 600), a lower median market cap ($925 million vs. $1.8 billion), and more expensive valuations, despite similar index volatility and high constituent turnover.

Four charts visually support this comparison. The first chart, titled "Large and small cap performance since 2011," plots total return indices starting at a base of 100 in January 2011. It illustrates massive outperformance by the cap-weighted S&P 500, which rose to nearly 600 by mid-2024, followed by the S&P 500 Equal Weighted, the S&P 600, and finally the Russell 2000, which lagged considerably at around 300 to 350. Beside it, the chart titled "Rolling small cap performance vs large cap" plots the relative three-year rolling returns of both small-cap indices against the S&P 500. This visual demonstrates persistent underperformance, with rolling relative returns frequently falling below zero and plunging as low as negative 30% to 40% in the post-2020 period. 

The third chart, "Earnings growth," displays indexed earnings starting at 100 in December 2010. It shows that the S&P 600 generated far stronger earnings growth, surging to over 500 by 2022 before a moderate decline, whereas the Russell 2000 struggled to exceed 250 over the same timeframe. Finally, the scatter plot titled "Analyst coverage vs market capitalization" maps the number of analysts covering individual stocks against company market capitalization on a log scale from $0.1 billion to over $100 billion. The data reveals that small-cap stocks in the S&P 600 and Russell 2000 typically receive far less analyst attention—usually fewer than 10 to 15 analysts, and often fewer than five for companies under $1 billion—compared to S&P 500 companies, where analyst coverage frequently ranges from 15 to nearly 40 analysts per stock.

This page of Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication focuses on small-cap equity performance and valuations, exploring how small-caps compare to large-caps domestically and how US small-caps stack up against international markets. The author argues that US small-cap equities are cheap relative to their historical performance against large-caps across a variety of valuation metrics. A line chart titled "Small cap valuation measures" illustrates this by plotting the historical premium or discount of the S&P 600 versus the S&P 500 from 2000 through mid-2024.
