Across five distinct valuation metrics—Forward P/E, EV/EBITDA, Trailing P/E, Price to Cash Flow, and Price to Book—small caps have steadily declined from peak premiums of 40% to 80% in the mid-2000s and early 2010s to substantial discounts today. Specifically, by mid-2024, all five metrics show a deep discount ranging roughly from -20% to nearly -60%, confirming that US small caps are historically cheap relative to large caps.

Despite lagging behind US large-caps, US small-cap stocks have significantly outperformed international equity markets since 2010. This is visualized in a line chart titled "US small cap performance vs international indices," which tracks cumulative returns from December 2010 through mid-2024 with an initial index value of 100 in US dollar terms. A blend of US small-caps, consisting of the S&P 600 and Russell 2000, peaked near 350 to 400 by late 2021 and remains near those highs in 2024. In comparison, international indices like the MSCI Europe, MSCI Japan, and MSCI Emerging Markets have struggled to keep pace. While MSCI Europe and MSCI Japan rose modestly to settle between 200 and 250 by 2024, MSCI Emerging Markets underperformed significantly, barely rising above 125. This demonstrates that non-US equities have suffered the worst relative performance among underperforming asset classes during this multi-decade period.

The final section of the page explains that recent small-cap underperformance is primarily a developed market phenomenon rather than an emerging market one. A bar chart titled "Small cap vs large cap returns by geography" displays the annualized trailing out- or underperformance of small-cap indices relative to large-cap counterparts over three, five, and seven-year horizons ending June 30, 2024. In Emerging Markets and India, small-caps actually outperformed large-caps, with India showing annualized outperformance of roughly 3% to 8% across all three timeframes. Conversely, developed markets show pervasive underperformance. Japan, Europe, US core, and Japan growth all show negative annualized relative returns, with small-cap underperformance worsening as one moves toward US growth. US growth small-caps experienced the most severe relative lag, underperforming large-caps by roughly 12% to nearly 16% on an annualized basis over the 3, 5, and 7-year periods. Details in the footnotes identify the exact index pairings used for each region, such as the Russell 2000 versus the S&P 500 for the US core, and the NSE Nifty Small Cap 250 versus the MSCI India for India.

This page analyzes whether the outperformance of active small-cap managers can generate enough alpha to offset the recent underperformance of small-cap stocks relative to large-cap stocks. The analysis reveals mixed results across global regions. For US small-cap core and growth, median active manager alpha is positive but only offsets 30% or less of the small-cap underperformance gap, potentially because 80% of the small- and mid-cap universe is thinly covered or entirely uncovered by research analysts. However, US small-cap value managers have performed much better, with median manager alpha closing most of the performance gap and top-quartile managers closing virtually all of it. In Europe and Japan, active small-cap core managers struggled, with median alphas that were negative or only slightly positive, offsetting a mere 15% to 20% of the gap. Conversely, India and broader Emerging Markets small-cap benchmarks actually outperformed their large-cap counterparts; in India, active managers additionally achieved positive median alpha, whereas active emerging market managers posted negative median alpha.

These points are supported by a detailed table adjusted for ETF fees and tracking error, which breaks down performance over three-year, five-year, and seven-year horizons. The table measures the performance gap between small-cap and large-cap indexes alongside active manager alpha at the 25th, 50th (median), and 75th percentiles. For US small-cap blend over the three-year horizon, small-caps underperformed large-caps by 12.6%, while the median manager generated 3.5% alpha. Over seven years, this underperformance was 7.4%, with a median manager alpha of 0.9%. For US small-cap value over five years, the underperformance gap was narrow at negative 1.9%, while the median manager alpha was 2.0%, demonstrating that active value managers successfully overcame the gap. In Europe, small-caps underperformed by 9.8% over three years, with a negative median manager alpha of 2.9%. India small-cap displayed strong outperformance, beating large-caps by 5.1% over three years and 5.9% over five years, while median manager alpha reached 5.0% and 5.1% over those respective periods. Emerging Markets small-cap also beat large-cap by 7.9% over three years, though active managers lagged with a median alpha of negative 1.1%. 

The methodology section explains that the analysis utilizes Morningstar data for active managers, excluding those with more than 35% exposure to large-cap stocks. To ensure a fair comparison, the lowest-fee institutional share class was analyzed for each manager, noting that retail share classes would have dragged down performance by 75 to 100 basis points. Crucially, the author applies an ETF adjustment to correct for the fact that indices are uninvestible; this adjusts benchmarks downward to reflect the real-world tracking error and fees of corresponding ETFs. While this adjustment is negligible for US benchmarks, it is highly significant for India. For example, over the trailing five-year period, the India Small Cap Index returned 132% while the corresponding investible ETF returned 97%, resulting in a substantial 3.8% annualized adjustment that improves the calculated alpha of active Indian managers.

This page concludes J.P. Morgan's analysis of US small-cap equities, focusing on historical performance data sources and small-cap behavior around recessions. The author argues that small-cap stocks function as a strong early-cycle asset class but a poor late-cycle one. Following recessions, small caps have historically outperformed large caps in 15 out of 16 instances. This performance is tied to the cyclicality of the asset class, with the S&P 600 possessing a 55% cyclical sector share compared to only 28% for the S&P 500. In contrast, during the run-up to recessions, small-cap relative performance is highly dispersed with no clear directional signal. 

The page contains five charts detailing these dynamics. The first chart, titled "Small cap vs large cap index returns," displays the three-year rolling outperformance or underperformance of small caps versus large caps from 1930 to 2020. The chart tracks four historical data series: Ibbotson small versus large cap, Fama-French small minus big, Russell 2000 versus S&P 500, and S&P 600 versus S&P 500. It demonstrates that the different data sources generally tell the same story, with a notable exception in the late 1940s when Ibbotson and Fama-French data diverged.

Below this, a pair of charts tracks the cumulative small-cap premium around recession inflection points. The chart "Small cap premium following end of recession" tracks the cumulative percentage premium from month zero to month 12 after a recession ends. It shows a highly consistent upward trend across cycles, reaching a median outperformance of 16% after one year, with a massive outlier from March 1933 reaching 198%. Conversely, the chart "Small cap premium prior to onset of recession" tracks the cumulative premium in the 12 months leading up to a recession. This chart shows wide, mixed dispersion across historical cycles, finishing with a median cumulative underperformance of negative 4% at the onset of the recession. In both charts, recent recessions are highlighted in dark gray.

The bottom of the page addresses corporate lifecycles and the IPO market. The chart "Age of companies going public" presents the median age of companies at the time of their IPO from 1980 to 2020, comparing all IPOs to technology IPOs. Both series show that companies are waiting longer to list, with the median age of all IPOs rising from roughly six years in 1980 to around 11 years in 2020, having peaked near 14 years in the prior decade. Finally, the stacked bar chart "Tech IPOs by market cap at time of issuance" illustrates the percentage share of tech IPOs from 2010 to 2021 across four categories: large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap, and micro-cap. The chart reveals a structural shift over the decade; small-cap tech IPOs, which represented the largest share of issuance in 2010 and 2011, shrank significantly by 2021 as mid-cap and large-cap tech companies came to dominate the share of new public offerings.

This page analyzes the sudden unwinding of the Japanese Yen carry trade, which triggered a significant global stock market correction in mid-2024. The author explains how years of negative interest rates in Japan prompted a massive, estimated twenty-trillion-dollar carry trade, wherein institutional and retail investors funded investments in higher-yielding foreign assets using low-cost Yen. This trade accelerated when the Federal Reserve began hiking rates in 2022, pushing the Yen to its weakest levels since 1986. However, rising inflation and wage growth in Japan forced the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates just as the Federal Reserve was poised to ease, causing a dramatic fourteen percent rally in the Yen and leading to a global equity correction. J.P. Morgan FX traders warn that more carry trade unwinds could lie ahead. 

Four charts illustrate these dynamics. The first chart, tracking examples of the Yen carry trade indexed to January 1, 2020, compares the returns of the S&P 500 in JPY and Mexican fixed income in JPY against Japanese fixed income in JPY. It demonstrates that while Japanese domestic fixed income remained flat to slightly negative from 2020 to mid-2024, the S&P 500 and Mexican fixed income in JPY soared to index values between 150 and 175, illustrating the massive nominal profits generated by foreign investments before the reversal. 

The second chart displays the correlation between the Federal Funds rate and the USD-JPY exchange rate from 2020 to mid-2024. As the Fed aggressively raised its target rate from near zero percent to over five percent, the exchange rate weakened from approximately 100 Yen per USD to peak around 160 Yen per USD in 2024, showing how widening rate differentials drove the Yen's collapse. 

The third chart plots the Bank of Japan's policy rate, Japan's core CPI, and the Japan Spring Wage Negotiation increase rate from 2020 to 2024. While the central bank kept its policy rate negative for years, core CPI spiked above four percent in late 2022, and spring wage negotiations secured wage increases exceeding five percent in 2024, prompting the Bank of Japan to finally raise its policy rate above zero. 

The fourth and final chart tracks rolling twenty-three-day percentage changes in the Yen's value against the US dollar from 1971 to 2024. A distinct red dot highlights the recent spike of roughly thirteen to fourteen percent, confirming that the mid-2024 Yen rally ranks among the most rapid and extreme currency appreciation events in the last fifty years.

This page analyzes the complex state of the commercial office real estate market, highlighting marginal fundamental improvements alongside severe, lingering distress in financing. 

The author begins by pointing out several positive indicators at the margin, which he describes as second and third derivative improvements. First, the rate at which major tenants are downsizing has eased; firms are currently giving back 10% to 12% of their leased space upon maturity, compared to 13% to 15% during 2021 and 2022. This shift is illustrated in the "Downsizing rate for major tenants (25,000+ square feet)" chart, which depicts the percentage of space cut recovering from its low point near -17% in late 2021 to around -11.5% in 2024. Additionally, net office absorption has stabilized, as shown in the "Office net absorption" chart. This metric plummeted to between -40 million and -45 million square feet in 2020 and 2021 according to JLL and CoStar, but has returned close to zero in 2024, with CoStar showing a small positive figure and JLL registering a minor negative. Only 12.5% of buildings saw vacancy increases in the most recent quarter, marking the lowest share since late 2017. Supply-side dynamics are also supporting fundamentals, with construction starts hitting their lowest levels since 2000. The active pipeline has shrunk nearly 70% since 2019 to 46 million square feet, with 65% of that space preleased, meaning very few new completions will arrive in 2025 and 2026.

In contrast to these fundamental glimmers of hope, the financing landscape for commercial real estate continues to deteriorate, closely mimicking the patterns observed during the 2008-2009 financial crisis. The "Office CMBS distress tracker" chart traces various indicators of distress—such as special servicing, modifications, delinquencies, and foreclosures—from 2002 to 2024. These metrics have spiked sharply in the last two years, with special servicing approaching 10%, a level not seen since the aftermath of the Great Recession. The author notes that CMBS trusts, banks, and insurers face a massive wave of loan modifications to prevent distressed property sales, driven by $320 billion in total office loan maturities scheduled between 2024 and 2027. This maturity wall is detailed in the "Office loan maturities by lender group" chart, which shows that maturities peak in 2024 at over $110 billion and remain high in 2025 at nearly $95 billion, before tapering to around $60 billion annually in 2026 and 2027. Banks and securitized debt represent the largest shares of these maturing loans, followed by insurance companies and debt funds.

Michael Cembalest discusses the persistence of the work-from-home trend and its ongoing negative impact on the commercial office real estate market. Although modest improvements exist in office markets, work-from-home rates have plateaued at roughly 30%. Consequently, distressed office buildings require steep discounts of 60% or more compared to their 2019 values to lure new investors. Cembalest points out that some potential bottoming activity is appearing, including a collapse in new office construction, rising conversions or demolitions, and accelerating foreclosures. However, he cautions that a major looming question remains: how banks and securitized office loan trusts will manage the impending wave of office loan maturities, pointing out that current delinquency and foreclosure patterns closely resemble those of the 2008 financial crisis. 

To demonstrate that the work-from-home trend has firmly plateaued, the author analyzes three contemporaneous datasets: mass transit ridership, Stanford professor Nicholas Bloom's work-from-home surveys, and Kastle key fob swipe data. 

The first visual is a table showing the post-Covid recovery in mass transit ridership, comparing transit volume from Q2 2019 to Q1 2024 and Q2 2023. With a median recovery of 70%, the data displays significant regional variation. Miami leads the recovery at 111% of pre-Covid levels in early 2024 (an 11% increase from mid-2023), followed by Houston at 97% and Salt Lake City at 93%. Conversely, Raleigh is at the bottom with just a 30% recovery, while other major metro areas like Detroit, Atlanta, and San Francisco struggle at 50%, 54%, and 57%, respectively. New York City transit recovery remains flat at 73% across both periods.

Below this table, a line chart illustrates the percentage of full paid days worked from home in large metropolitan cities from October 2020 to April 2024. Based on survey data from Bloom, Barrero, and Davis of workers aged 20 to 64 earning over $10,000 to $20,000, it shows that the percentage of work-from-home days peaked above 40% in late 2020 and has since stabilized. By early 2024, most major cities like New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago are clustered around the 30% mark, though San Francisco remains on the higher end of the spectrum and Houston sits near the bottom.

The final line chart displays commercial property utilization rates based on Kastle key fob swipes relative to February 2020 levels, tracking several major US cities from 2020 through July 2024. Swipe rates cratered to nearly 10% during the initial lockdowns and have clawed back, but have clearly plateaued. By mid-2024, office utilization rates fluctuate between 40% and 60% of pre-pandemic levels. Texas markets like Austin and Houston lead with utilization rates approaching 60%, while San Francisco, San Jose, and Philadelphia linger near the bottom around 40% to 45%.

This page analyzes whether commercial banks will become major sellers of office loans and foreclosed properties, presenting two contrasting views on commercial real estate market health. According to J.P. Morgan Research, bank loan loss reserves typically sit at 8% to 12% of office loans, with some reaching 14%. These levels imply a 20% default rate and a 50% recovery rate. Although these assumptions might seem optimistic given weak office fundamentals, conservative loan-to-value ratios at origination—averaging 50% to 60% for banks, 50% to 70% for commercial mortgage-backed securities, and 39% for insurers—suggest banks might not be far off in their risk assumptions. Conversely, distressed office investment firms present a more bearish outlook, estimating that over 90% of office loans maturing by 2025 will have re-underwritten loan-to-value ratios exceeding 80%, indicating a much higher potential default rate and a surge in distressed sales.

To track this distress, a detailed table lists twenty-four discounted office building sales across major U.S. cities, comparing their current sales prices to their original purchase values. The data reveals steep discounts, frequently exceeding 60% of pre-COVID levels, largely driven by the high capital expenditures needed for building renovations or residential conversions. The steepest discounts are found in Chicago, where 300 W Adams sold at a 92% discount ($16 per square foot compared to an original $202 in 2012), and San Francisco, where 995 Market sold at a 90% discount ($72 per square foot compared to an original $685 in 2016). Notable residential conversion candidates in New York City also show dramatic drops, with 222 Broadway and 1740 Broadway suffering discounts of 70% and 69% respectively. Other transactions listed span Denver, San Jose, Washington D.C., Philadelphia, Houston, and Miami, with the smallest discount on the list belonging to Miami’s 100 SE 2nd St at 26%.

The author notes that experienced distressed investors buy well before delinquency rates peak. This investment principle is illustrated in a dual-axis line chart titled "Bottom fishing during the global financial crisis: real estate delinquencies vs REIT returns." Plotting data from 2006 to 2011, the chart tracks the residential delinquency rate and commercial delinquency rate on the left axis (0% to 14%) against an indicative REIT Index on the right axis (300 to 1200). The visual data reveals that the REIT index hit its absolute bottom of around 350 in early 2009, well before residential delinquencies peaked near 11% in early 2010 and commercial delinquencies peaked above 8% in late 2010. By the time these delinquency rates actually peaked, 70% of the recovery gains in the REIT index had already occurred. 

The page concludes with a personal sign-off from Michael Cembalest, who mentions his recent travels to cities including Tallahassee, Columbia, Charlotte, Atlanta, Baltimore, Washington D.C., Sonoma, and Dallas. He shares plans for a late-August tarpon fishing trip to Trinidad with clients and closes with a cautious forecast that the upcoming fall season may be highly turbulent.

Michael Cembalest argues that NVIDIA and its GPU customers—specifically the "Magnificent 7" cohort consisting of Amazon, Apple, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla—have become dominant drivers of equity market returns, earnings growth, earnings revisions, industrial production, and capital spending. He highlights that the capital spending of these seven companies now exceeds that of the entire energy sector, underscoring the massive impact of AI-related investments.

This market concentration is illustrated in the first line chart, titled "Magnificent 7 domination," which tracks these companies' share of the total large-cap market cap from 1990 to 2025. After fluctuating between 10% and 18% for decades, their collective market share spiked dramatically after 2020, climbing to nearly 30% by mid-2024. 

The second chart, a bar chart titled "Top quintile of stocks are driving earnings revisions and market returns," reinforces this concentration by segmenting the S&P 500 into quintiles. It compares trailing 12-month performance against the change in 2024 earnings estimates since June 2023. The top 20 stocks in the S&P 500 significantly outpaced all other cohorts, posting trailing 12-month performance of over 40% and receiving positive earnings estimate revisions of approximately 15%. In contrast, all other cohorts (S&P 21-100 down to S&P 301-500) saw negative earnings estimate revisions and progressively lower trailing performance.

The third chart, "US industrial production of high tech industries," indexes production to January 2020 to show how high-tech manufacturing is outperforming the broader economy. While the index for all industries excluding high tech has remained flat at around 100 through 2024, communication equipment has surged past an index level of 150, with computer equipment and semiconductors also climbing to around 130.

The final chart, "Capex + R&D, Magnificent 7 vs rest of market," indexes capital expenditure and research and development spending to January 2020. It shows an extreme divergence: while the Bloomberg US Large Cap ex-Magnificent 7 Index remains nearly flat, hovering just above 100, the Bloomberg Magnificent 7 Index has climbed exponentially and is projected to reach an index level of nearly 600 by 2026.

This page argues that Nvidia’s exceptional financials make it the antithesis of dot-com bubble companies like Cisco. Michael Cembalest asserts that Nvidia's rising operating margins, surging revenues, and robust earnings justify its high valuation, unlike dot-com era leaders whose stock prices soared without corresponding profit growth. Additionally, analysts project that Nvidia will maintain a 90% or greater market share in artificial intelligence chips over the next two years, even in the face of potential delays to its next-generation Blackwell chips and rising competition.

To support this argument, the page features several charts comparing Nvidia to its peers and historical equivalents. A bar chart comparing the operating margins of the Magnificent Seven tech companies as of July 2024 highlights that Nvidia leads the pack with an operating margin exceeding 60%, significantly outperforming Microsoft at around 45%, Meta at 40%, Alphabet at 35%, Apple at 30%, Amazon at 12%, and Tesla at around 8%. This is paired with a historical line chart tracking Nvidia’s net income margins from 2009 through 2023, which shows a dramatic rise from negative levels in 2009 to nearly 60% by the end of 2023.

Nvidia's revenue trajectory is depicted in a chart displaying actual sales and estimate revisions in billions of US dollars. Comparing projections from March 2023 to August 2024, the data shows an enormous step-change upward. While March 2023 estimates anticipated moderate growth peaking around 24% in 2024, the August 2024 projections show actual and projected year-over-year revenue growth skyrocketing to 126% in 2023 and 104% in 2024, before tapering to a still-strong 42% in 2025 and 16% in 2026, with total annual sales projected to surpass 200 billion dollars.

The final charts contrast Nvidia's current market position with Cisco's dot-com era trajectory. A chart of forward P/E ratios compares Cisco from 1996 to 2002 against Nvidia from 2018 to 2024; while Cisco's forward P/E peaked near 130x in 2000, Nvidia's forward P/E peaked below 80x and has since fallen to around 40x. This contrast is further emphasized by two indexed charts tracking share price against one-year forward earnings per share. Nvidia’s chart from 2018 to 2024 reveals that its share price and forward EPS have risen closely in tandem, reflecting that the stock's growth is driven by actual earnings. In stark contrast, Cisco’s index from 1996 to 2002 shows its share price exploding past 1,600 while its forward EPS remained nearly flat below 400, illustrating the speculative bubble that Nvidia has so far avoided.

This page, titled Appendix II: The fate of prior equity market leaders, examines the historical trajectory of companies that have held the title of the largest company in the S&P 500. The topic is framed by Nvidia briefly achieving the largest S&P 500 market capitalization of $3.33 trillion in June 2024, momentarily surpassing Microsoft. The author observes that most historical market leaders eventually hit an inflection point, after which their share of the total market capitalization declined significantly. This pattern of decline is illustrated through nine individual charts tracking each company's end-of-quarter share of total market cap over time, with gray bars highlighting the periods when they were the single largest stock in the index. 

Six of the charts show former giants whose market share ultimately deteriorated. General Motors peaked at over 10% of total S&P 500 market cap in the late 1950s and 1960s before falling below 1% by 2015. IBM declined from nearly 3.0% in 1990 to under 0.5% by 2025. Altria similarly fell from a peak near 2.5% in the early 1990s to below 0.5%. Cisco spiked dramatically to nearly 4.0% in 2000 during the dot-com boom before falling and stabilizing below 1%. General Electric saw multiple periods as the top stock, peaking around 4.5% in 2000, but has since declined to near 0.5%. Exxon Mobil reached a share of over 4.0% in the late 2000s but steadily declined to around 1% by 2025. 

In contrast, Apple and Microsoft are highlighted as the only exceptions that have continued to thrive. Apple's market cap share climbed from near 0% in the 1990s to nearly 8% by 2024, while Microsoft peaked near 4.5% in 2000, experienced a multi-year decline, and then surged back to nearly 8% in the 2020s. A final chart for Nvidia shows its sudden, near-vertical rise starting around 2020 to reach roughly 6% of the total S&P 500 market capitalization by mid-2024, raising the open question of whether it will follow the path of past tech giants like Cisco or continue to thrive like Microsoft and Apple.

This page provides a comprehensive overview of the commercial real estate sector, focusing on office properties, mortgage ownership, and market performance metrics across six distinct charts. 

The first chart, titled "Banks hold over half of the overall stock of CRE loans," tracks the percentage ownership of commercial mortgages from 1980 to the first quarter of 2024. It reveals that banks have consistently held a dominant share of more than fifty percent of the total market. Since 2010, this bank ownership is split to show that small banks account for a substantial and rising portion of the bank-held stock compared to large banks. Other notable categories of mortgage holders include insurance companies, commercial mortgage-backed securities, government and agency bodies, real estate investment trusts and finance companies, and pension funds. 

The second chart, "Vacancies by property type," tracks quarterly vacancy rates from 2005 through 2023 for office, retail, apartment, and industrial properties. It highlights a stark divergence within the sector. While apartment, retail, and industrial vacancies remain relatively low—with industrial vacancies hovering around five percent and retail at approximately seven and a half percent—office vacancies have surged dramatically since 2020, reaching a near-twenty-year peak of seventeen and a half percent by late 2023.

The third chart, "CMBS loan-to-value ratios by vintage year," presents a stacked bar chart illustrating the distribution of loan-to-value ratios from 2003 to 2022. It contrasts lax pre-Great Financial Crisis lending standards with modern risk discipline. Between 2004 and 2007, a massive portion of CMBS loans had loan-to-value ratios exceeding seventy percent. In contrast, loans issued between 2018 and 2022 demonstrate much safer underwriting, with only a tiny fraction carrying an LTV above seventy percent, while the vast majority fall comfortably between fifty and seventy percent, or even under fifty percent.

The fourth chart, "CMBS credit enhancement by vintage year and rating," displays the subordination percentages beneath three key tranches from 2004 to 2022. The chart demonstrates that structural protection for investors has expanded significantly since the financial crisis. Subordination for the lowest-rated BBB- tranche rose from around three percent in 2004 to nearly ten percent by 2022, while the AA tranche increased from roughly ten percent to approximately eighteen percent, and the Mezz AAA tranche maintained high subordination near twenty percent.

The fifth chart, "Recovery in transit ridership vs office price growth," is a scatter plot comparing transit ridership recovery from the second quarter of 2019 to the first quarter of 2024 against three-year trailing growth in price per square foot across major United States cities. A clear positive correlation indicates that cities with stronger public transit ridership recovery also experience more resilient office price performance. San Francisco marks the negative extreme of this trend, showing transit ridership recovery of around forty-five percent and a steep decline in office prices of approximately seventy percent. Meanwhile, Miami represents the positive outlier, showing transit ridership recovery above one hundred and ten percent and positive price growth of roughly twenty-five percent. Other major metropolitan areas plotted include Houston, Austin, New York, Dallas, Boston, Chicago, Detroit, and Raleigh.

The final chart, "Office groundbreakings fall to all time low," tracks quarterly office construction starts in millions of square feet from 2000 to the second quarter of 2024. The data displays a dramatic drop-off in new developments, plunging from historical heights that frequently ranged between fifteen million and twenty-five million square feet down to near-zero levels by mid-2024, signaling an unprecedented freeze in new office supply.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest assesses the current state of corporate AI adoption, highlighting a mix of highly positive trends and cautious, mixed signals regarding actual production and labor market impact. While CEO surveys indicate that generative AI is a top priority with significant planned spending, actual enterprise data suggests that AI adoption is still largely concentrated in pilot stages, and job penetration remains low compared to prior technology waves.

A chart titled "Census: AI adoption rates by sector and date" displays the share of firms using AI across fifteen industries, comparing data from October 2023, August 2024, and projections for the next six months. The data shows that the information sector leads in adoption, rising from about 12% in late 2023 to nearly 18% in August 2024, with expectations to exceed 20% in the near term. Professional, scientific, and technical services follow closely, while sectors like construction, transportation, and accommodation and food services show the lowest penetration, remaining under 5%. 

The second chart, "Bain: generative AI adoption rates by stage and sector, Oct 2023 vs Feb 2024," breaks down adoption into development/pilot stages and actual production use. The visual emphasizes that across all business functions—including software, customer service, marketing, knowledge workers, operations, IT, finance, sales, HR, and legal—AI is primarily stuck in the pilot phase. For example, while total software AI adoption exceeds 50%, only about 20% represents actual production use, and legal functions show less than 15% total adoption with negligible production deployment.

The third chart, "Fed: technology penetration in job openings," tracks the percentage of urban areas with a significant job presence for various technologies from 2007 through 2023. It reveals that AI job skill penetration is currently flat and extremely low, closely mirroring the slow adoption curve of 3D printing rather than the rapid, widespread adoption paths previously experienced by cloud computing and smart devices.

The final chart, "US private employment," tracks employment trends from 2021 to 2024. It compares private industries excluding information services on the left axis against information services on the right axis. While broader private employment has risen steadily from roughly 117 million to over 131 million, information services employment peaked at approximately 3.1 million in late 2022 and has since steadily declined to around 3.0 million in 2024.

Cembalest poses the open question of whether this decline in tech sector employment during a period of overall job growth indicates that AI is successfully reducing tech labor intensity. He notes the correlation is currently modest. Drawing historical parallels, he remarks that while e-commerce took 20 years to capture 20% of addressable retail and Uber took eight years post-iPhone to reach massive scale, AI adoption appears comparatively faster. He concludes that the clearest current winners are consulting firms, noting that Boston Consulting Group (BCG) already generates 20% of its revenue by advising companies on generative AI.

This page addresses political polarization and leadership, highlighting the highly unusual situation where a large number of senior officials from Donald Trump's first presidential term now actively oppose his 2024 campaign. The author reflects on how political acrimony has reached unprecedented levels compared to the debates of the Gore, Bush, Obama, and Romney eras. He also offers a critique of corporate standards, advising banks and companies against inviting guest speakers, such as Elon Musk, whose public social media behavior would violate standard employee conduct policies.

The central visual is a bar chart titled "Former Trump Cabinet members and other senior positions: their positions on Trump 2024." It tracks forty-three senior officials who served between 2016 and 2020 for at least nine months, including the Vice President, Cabinet heads, National Security Advisors, and congressional leaders. The data is divided into three groups. The first group, "Repudiations/disavowals," comprises sixteen individuals shown in red, including Mike Pence, Rex Tillerson, Jim Mattis, Mark Esper, John Kelly, John Bolton, and Mick Mulvaney. The second group, "2024 endorsements," also totals sixteen individuals shown in green, which includes Bill Barr, Nikki Haley, Mitch McConnell, Mike Pompeo, and Jeff Sessions. The final group, "No public comment," contains eleven individuals shown in gold, including Chris Wray, Alex Azar, Kirstjen Nielsen, and Sonny Perdue. A footnote adds context, noting that beyond these Cabinet-level figures, over seven00 former national security and military officials signed a September 2024 open letter criticizing Trump as impulsive and ill-informed.

The page also serves as an introductory table of contents for the publication, outlining subsequent sections on fiscal policy, tariffs and trade, energy, immigration, inflation and price controls, NATO, the regulatory state, the Electoral College, and the implications of China's recent economic stimulus package.

This page, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes US fiscal policy and the long-term outlook of federal debt. Cembalest argues that neither presidential candidate has addressed the critical crossover point projected for the early 2030s, when federal spending on entitlements, mandatory outlays, and net interest will begin to exceed total federal revenues. He positions specific campaign proposals as marginal issues compared to this looming structural challenge. 

A line chart illustrating this trend displays entitlement spending, mandatory outlays, and net interest payments alongside federal revenues as a percentage of GDP from 1965 to 2035. Using data from the Congressional Budget Office, the chart shows that while revenues have historically fluctuated between 15% and 19% of GDP, spending on entitlements and interest has steadily climbed since the 1960s. The two lines are projected to cross in the early 2030s, where spending will permanently surpass revenues at roughly 18% to 19% of GDP.

An accompanying sidebar compares federal debt accumulation under the Trump and Biden administrations, citing research from Marc Goldwein at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. It notes that if nominal GDP had followed pre-pandemic projections, debt-to-GDP would have grown by 15% under Donald Trump and 16% under Joe Biden. When excluding major COVID-19 relief legislation like the CARES Act and the American Rescue Plan, Trump approved approximately $4.8 trillion of borrowing, whereas Biden approved about $2.2 trillion.

The page also details Kamala Harris’s fiscal proposals as a proxy for a policy of economic redistribution. A comprehensive table tracks her deficit-increasing spending proposals against her revenue-raising policies over a ten-year horizon, using data from PSC and Don Schneider. Her spending initiatives total $6.004 trillion, dominated by extending the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act for individuals making under $400,000 at a cost of $2.6 trillion, making the expanded Child Tax Credit permanent at a cost of $1.1 trillion, and child care programs costing $600 billion. On the revenue side, her deficit-decreasing proposals total $4.727 trillion. This revenue is driven by her specific proposal to raise the corporate tax rate to 28% (generating $978 billion) and taxing unrealized capital gains for ultra-high-net-worth individuals (generating $503 billion). She also endorses provisions from Biden's budget, including raising the ACA Net Investment Income Tax to 5% for high earners (generating $404 billion) and applying it to active business income (generating $393 billion). Cembalest notes that even with a Democratic sweep, these proposals would likely be scaled back, and the remaining $1.3 trillion deficit gap would be financed through borrowing.

In this analysis, Michael Cembalest provides historical context on corporate taxes, focusing on the potential consequences of Kamala Harris's proposals to raise them. Cembalest argues that the US corporate tax rate was historically uncompetitive, leading to a rise in corporate inversions where companies reincorporated overseas. Although the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act temporarily resolved this issue by lowering rates and halting tax-driven inversions, the proposed Harris policies could drive US corporate taxes to their highest level as a share of GDP since 1980, potentially prompting a new wave of inversions. 

This historical trend is illustrated in the first chart, which tracks corporate income tax rates and the number of US inversions from 1981 to 2015. As the average tax rate for non-US OECD nations steadily declined from nearly 47% to around 25%, the US rate remained flat near 35% to 40%. This divergence triggered a spike in corporate departures, peaking with 10 inversions in 2014 and 2015. 

The second chart compares the marginal effective corporate tax rate on new investment across major economies. While the current US effective rate sits at a competitive level of around 23%, the Harris 2025 proposal would elevate it to roughly 31%, and the Harris 2028 proposal would push it further to approximately 32.5%. This shift would make the US rate higher than those of Germany (31%), France (30%), the Netherlands (25%), the United Kingdom (20%), and Canada (17%), leaving the US behind only Italy and Japan. 

The third chart visualizes US corporate income tax receipts as a share of GDP from 1980 to 2030. Historically, receipts have fluctuated between 1.0% and 2.5% of GDP. Under the projected Harris policies, receipts are forecast to rise and plateau at approximately 2.3% of GDP by 2030, approaching the upper bound of historical levels. 

Finally, the fourth chart documents the shifting structure of US business entities from 1980 to 2016, showing the rise of pass-through entities subject to personal rather than corporate tax. During this period, the number of C corporations fell from 2.2 million to 1.6 million, while S corporations surged from under 0.5 million to over 4.0 million, and partnerships grew to 3.5 million. This structural shift highlights why the US corporate tax-to-GDP ratio is not directly comparable to other countries, as a large portion of US business income is taxed through personal returns rather than corporate filings.

This page of the commentary focuses on tariffs and trade policy, specifically examining Donald Trump’s proposals for a 60% tariff on Chinese imports and a 10% universal tariff on all imported goods. The author highlights that despite campaign assertions that foreign nations pay these tariffs, the economic consensus overwhelmingly concludes that US consumers bear the cost. Goldman Sachs estimates that a 10% across-the-board tariff would increase US inflation by 1% and decrease GDP growth by 0.5% on a one-time basis, while Barclays estimates a larger GDP hit of negative 1.4%. Despite these economic costs, US voters appear increasingly willing to accept globalization rollbacks due to the severe domestic impacts felt after China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001. This domestic discontent spans the political spectrum, with both Donald Trump and Kamala Harris supporting the termination of the De Minimis exemption for Chinese imports. 

Four charts are presented to illustrate the domestic consequences of China's rise and its mercantile economic model. The first chart plots the 10-year percentage change in US manufacturing job losses against Chinese foreign exchange intervention, measured as FX reserves as a percentage of GDP on an inverted scale. This visual shows that immediately following China's accession to the WTO, its FX intervention surged alongside an acceleration in US manufacturing job losses, which reached a 10-year decline of nearly 40% by the late 2000s. The second chart demonstrates that this decline coincided with a sharp drop in the US labor share of non-financial gross profits, which fell from roughly 64% in 2000 to under 58% by 2010. The third chart connects these economic hardships to public health, showing a dramatic rise in US opioid prescriptions per capita—surging from near zero to a peak of roughly 800 morphine milligram equivalents—directly mirroring the timeline of manufacturing job losses. Finally, a bar chart details China’s Mercantilism Index compared to the rest of the world, where a score of 100 is best and 0 is worst. China scores extremely poorly, frequently below 20, across key indicators such as public ownership of the private sector, protection of trade secrets, intellectual property enforcement, barriers to market access, and receptivity to foreign direct investment. This final chart underscores why isolating China has become one of the most bipartisan policy positions in the US Congress.

In this commentary, the author discusses the Electoral College, addressing the common criticism that it disproportionately allocates voting power to smaller states, such as Wyoming having only 144,000 people per electoral vote compared to California's 472,000. The author counters this critique by observing that the production of food, energy, and minerals is also highly concentrated in these less-populated areas. Because the domestic content of US food and energy is about 80 percent—much higher than other manufactured goods—the author argues that granting political power in excess of population to these key resource-producing states is logical for national security and resource independence. 

To illustrate this point, the page features an energy, mineral, and food-weighted cartogram of the United States based on 2022 production values. In this map, states are resized by their total production value and colored by their per capita surplus (green) or deficit (red). Heavily populated, resource-consuming states like New York, California, and Florida shrink significantly, while Texas, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, and the heartland states expand dramatically. The production calculations include crude oil, coal, natural gas, electricity generation (including wind, solar, nuclear, hydro, geothermal, and biomass), agricultural outputs, precious and industrial metals, natural aggregates, and non-fuel minerals. 

Additionally, the page contains a map of Pennsylvania from the 2020 presidential election, overlaying voting results (red for Republican and blue for Democratic) with the state's oil and gas fields. This visual demonstrates how Republican-leaning counties correlate closely with regions containing shallow oil fields, shallow gas fields, deep gas fields, and gas storage areas, highlighting the political divide between resource-producing and resource-consuming regions.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" analyzes US energy policy, focusing on domestic production realities, the rising costs of energy transition incentives, and the political and economic significance of hydraulic fracturing. The author notes that US production of oil, gas, and natural gas liquids has reached all-time highs under the Biden administration. Rather than direct restraint, the current policy approach relies on substantial subsidies for renewable energy, hydrogen, battery storage, and electric vehicles, with costs projected to reach between $1 trillion and $3 trillion by the end of the decade. These transition dynamics coincide with rising domestic residential electricity prices and supply chain bottlenecks, particularly in the power grid sector. The page also touches on the political importance of fracking in swing states like Pennsylvania, noting that Vice President Harris has shifted away from her previous opposition to fracking and her support for a firm 2035 zero-emissions vehicle deadline. 

Four charts illustrate these arguments. The first chart plots monthly US production of crude oil, natural gas, and natural gas liquids in trillions of BTUs from 2000 to mid-2024. It shows a massive upward trajectory starting around 2010, with total monthly production rising from roughly 3,000 trillion BTUs to nearly 8,000 trillion BTUs by 2024, driven by major gains in natural gas and natural gas liquids. 

The second chart tracks residential electricity prices from 2016 to 2024 in California, New York, Pennsylvania, and Texas, expressed as a multiple of the average price in China and India. California's multiple rose most sharply, climbing from approximately 2.4 times the China-India average in 2016 to nearly 4.0 times by 2024. New York's multiple grew to about 3.4 times, while Pennsylvania and Texas reached roughly 2.5 times and 2.0 times, respectively. 

The third chart focuses on core goods Producer Price Index component inflation, displaying the percentage price increase since 2018 for forty-seven core goods categories. The category for transformers and power regulators experienced the highest inflation, surging over 70% by July 2024. 

The fourth chart is a stacked bar depicting the components of US primary energy consumption in 2023. It reveals that unconventional oil, gas, and natural gas liquids requiring hydraulic fracturing accounted for 61% of all US primary energy consumption. Conventional fossil fuel sources accounted for the next largest share, followed by coal, nuclear, biomass/geothermal, wind, hydro, and solar, demonstrating the ongoing US reliance on fracking.

This page of the report addresses NATO defense spending and the expansion of the US regulatory state. In the section on NATO, the author contextualizes Donald Trump’s controversial comments regarding allies who fall short of their financial obligations by analyzing the actual spending gap between the United States and European members. A line chart displaying US versus European defense spending as a percentage of GDP from 1968 to 2023 shows that the United States has consistently remained far above the 2% target. In contrast, non-US NATO members collective spending fell below the 2% target around 1990 and remained there until very recently, despite a formal agreement in 2006 requiring each country to spend at least 2% of GDP on defense. 

An accompanying table calculates the individual and total shortfalls in NATO defense spending relative to this 2% target since the 2006 pact, measured in billions of 2023 US dollars. The cumulative unpaid amount across the ten listed nations from 2006 to 2023 totals 1.54 trillion dollars. Germany represents the largest shortfall at 634 billion dollars, followed by Italy at 255 billion dollars, Spain at 212 billion dollars, and the Netherlands at 141 billion dollars. Belgium also shows a significant gap of 112 billion dollars, while France stands at 55 billion dollars and the United Kingdom has the smallest shortfall at just 5 billion dollars.

The second half of the page shifts to the regulatory state, contrasting the approaches of Donald Trump and Kamala Harris, with the Biden administration serving as a proxy for Harris. Regardless of the upcoming election outcome, the author points to four recent Supreme Court decisions that could curtail federal agencies: the end of Chevron deference, the expansion of the Major Questions Doctrine, adjusting the statute of limitations to start at the time of injury rather than the passage of a regulation, and granting the right to a jury trial for civil fines levied by federal agencies. 

A line chart showing the cumulative number of economically significant rules by month 40 of each presidency visualizes the stark contrast in regulatory activity. The Biden administration leads with the highest volume of rules, approaching nearly 270 by month 40, followed by the Obama administration at roughly 200 and the Trump administration at approximately 140. Prior administrations like those of Clinton, George W. Bush, and George H.W. Bush hover near 125, while the Reagan administration enacted the fewest at around 35. Finally, a historical chart tracking the annual number of new pages in the Federal Register using a four-year moving average from 1961 to 2021 illustrates the long-term growth of federal regulation. This regulatory barometer shows page counts rising from just 10,000 in 1961 to a peak of over 70,000 in the late 1970s, before dipping and climbing back up to near-record levels of 85,000 pages by 2021.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication analyzes the competing fiscal agendas of Donald Trump and Kamala Harris, arguing that a Trump victory and potential Republican sweep would likely cause US budget deficits to rise significantly more than under a Harris administration. The author, Michael Cembalest, outlines the volatility of Trump’s fiscal plans, which include extending all Tax Cuts and Jobs Act tax cuts, lifting the state and local tax deduction cap, exempting tips from income tax, lowering corporate income tax to 15% for domestic manufacturers, and ending taxes on Social Security benefits. He contends that Trump's proposed spending cuts, mainly targeting green energy provisions like electric vehicle tax credits, along with highly uncertain revenues from universal 10% tariffs and 60% China tariffs, would not offset these vast tax cuts. Citing research by economists and an op-ed by Jason Furman, Cembalest asserts that Harris’s proposals present a smaller primary deficit impact and constitute a safer economic choice.

Four charts illustrate these deficit projections. The first chart, showing nominal budget deficit estimates for Trump's proposals as a percentage of GDP from 2024 to 2030, contrasts the CBO baseline against private forecasts. While the CBO baseline projects the nominal deficit to narrow from 6.0% of GDP in 2024 to roughly 5.3% by 2030, independent estimates from Bridgewater and Suttle Economics show the nominal deficit widening dramatically to near 6.7% over the same period. The second chart focuses on primary budget deficit estimates for Trump's proposals, where the CBO baseline narrows from 2.5% of GDP to 1.6% by 2030. In contrast, private forecasts from Goldman Sachs, Piper Sandler, and Wharton all anticipate larger primary deficits, with the combination of Wharton's model and a SALT cap removal pushing the primary deficit close to 3.0% of GDP by 2030.

The final two horizontal bar charts contrast the 10-year budget deficit effects, in trillions of US dollars, of both candidates' proposed policies as of September 2024. Under Harris’s proposed policies, revenue-raising corporate tax hikes of over 2.0 trillion dollars and wealth taxes of roughly 1.0 trillion dollars largely counter spending policies, which are dominated by a 1.8 trillion dollar extension of tax cuts for individuals making under 400,000 dollars in adjusted gross income. This leaves Harris with a net 10-year deficit effect of approximately negative 1.4 trillion dollars. Under Trump's proposed policies, projected revenue gains from a universal 10% tariff of 1.8 trillion dollars, a 60% China tariff of 400 billion dollars, and the repeal of clean energy subsidies are overwhelmed by tax cuts. These include extending individual tax cuts costing 2.8 trillion dollars, eliminating Social Security benefit taxes costing 1.2 trillion dollars, and repealing the SALT cap costing 900 billion dollars. Consequently, Trump’s policies result in a much larger net 10-year deficit increase of nearly 3.7 trillion dollars.

This page examines the complex economic and social impacts of immigration on the United States. While immigration is noted to boost overall economic growth, reduce the pressure on the Federal Reserve to tighten policy rates, and expand the workforce during a period of low domestic birth rates, the author highlights that unmanaged immigration and surging migrant inflows create substantial budgetary strain for US cities, putting credit ratings at risk, forcing budget cuts, and worsening housing shortages. 

A series of six charts supports this analysis. The first line chart, displaying annual net immigration in millions of people from 2000 to 2025, shows that net immigration historically fluctuated between 0.5 million and 1.5 million annually before plummeting during the pandemic. Following this, it experienced a massive spike, reaching an unprecedented high of roughly 3.3 million people between October 2023 and September 2024. 

This historic influx is mirrored in the second chart, a bar chart tracking pending immigration cases in millions from 1998 to 2024. The volume of pending cases has grown almost exponentially over the last decade, rising from under 0.5 million in 2012 to more than 2.0 million cases by 2024. 

The third chart tracks permanent immigrant visa issuances at an annual rate in millions from January 2018 to January 2024, along with its six-month moving average. This data reveals a steep drop in visa issuances to nearly zero in mid-2020, followed by a steady post-pandemic recovery that peaked near an annual rate of 0.8 million by late 2023.

The fourth chart presents monthly Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) removals from 2002 to 2024, broken down by presidential administration. Removals rose during the George W. Bush presidency, peaked during the Obama administration at around 40,000 monthly removals, declined during the Trump presidency, and then dropped precipitously to historic lows under the Biden administration—falling below 5,000 monthly removals before climbing back toward 20,000 by mid-2024. 

The regional distribution of court workloads is shown in a bar chart tracking new proceedings filed in immigration courts from 2020 to 2023 across four selected states: Colorado, Illinois, New York, and Texas. Court filings rose drastically across all four states, with Texas seeing filings grow from under 50,000 in 2020 to more than 300,000 in 2023, while New York experienced a similar surge to approximately 200,000 over the same period. 

Finally, a pie chart breaks down foreign-born population estimates from 2022, illustrating that prior to the recent migrant surge, unauthorized immigrants made up 23% (11.0 million) of the US foreign-born population. The remaining 77% (36.9 million) consisted of lawful immigrants, broken down into naturalized citizens at 49% (23.4 million), lawful permanent residents at 24% (11.5 million), and temporary lawful residents at 4% (2.0 million).

This page outlines the severe economic headwinds facing China and details the comprehensive policy stimulus package introduced in response. The page opens by noting falling commercial and residential property prices, capital fleeing the country via foreign direct investment, historically low consumer confidence, and a contraction in real-time economic tracking surveys, which have also seen five consecutive quarters of deflation and falling year-on-year wage growth. 

Four charts illustrate these economic challenges. The first chart tracking China's commercial and residential property prices shows year-over-year percentage change from 2010 to mid-2024, revealing that property prices have plunged deep into negative territory, hovering around negative four percent to negative five percent growth. The second chart, a foreign direct investment monitor measuring USD in billions, reveals that net FDI has collapsed from positive levels of around fifty billion dollars down to nearly negative seventy-five billion dollars in 2024, driven by a surge in outward FDI and a drop in inward investment. The third chart shows China's consumer confidence index, which has collapsed from above one hundred and twenty in late 2021 to historically depressed levels between eighty-five and ninety, where it remains through 2024. The fourth chart plots Bloomberg’s China economic activity monitor, showing that year-over-year growth across key real economy sectors—including exports, coal and electricity consumption, steel production, real estate investment, and private enterprise output—declined from over nine percent in early 2022 to below three percent in 2024.

In response to these conditions, the page provides a detailed breakdown of China's stimulus package, categorizing measures by their primary target and lever. To support the broader economy, the government deployed monetary, fiscal, and macro levers. Monetary actions include a fifty-basis-point cut to the reserve ratio requirement, a twenty-basis-point cut to the short-term policy rate (PBoC seven-day repo), and a thirty-basis-point cut to the mid-term policy rate. The fiscal lever consists of a one-off cash transfer to people living in poverty. Macroeconomic housing interventions feature an approximate fifty-basis-point interest rate cut on existing mortgages, expanded loan guarantees for state-owned enterprises to purchase vacant homes for social housing conversion, a reduction in the down payment requirement on second home purchases to fifteen percent from twenty-five percent, and expanded availability of loan extensions to businesses. To support financial markets, the package utilizes monetary levers to establish swap facilities for securities, funds, and insurance companies to fund equity purchases, alongside a new relending program for stock repurchases. Additionally, market regulation levers are being used to attract mid- to long-term capital, encourage mergers and acquisitions, and request listed companies to actively manage their market value through buybacks.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication examines the immediate equity market impact of China's September 2024 economic stimulus package and addresses whether the country represents a short-term tactical trade or a long-term portfolio investment. The author notes that while previous piecemeal stabilization attempts over the past two years failed, the sheer breadth of this new package and the commitment to further action set it apart. He highlights the People’s Bank of China’s new lending facilities, which offer up to RMB 2.4 trillion in potential support. This includes a swap facility allowing financial institutions to exchange bond and ETF holdings for highly liquid central bank bills to fund stock purchases, alongside a relending facility where the central bank lends to commercial banks at 1.75% so they can in turn provide loans to listed companies at 2.25% specifically for share buybacks.

The author presents four main visual elements to support his analysis. The first chart, showing China equity returns in US dollars since the package was announced on September 23, 2024, depicts a massive rally. Returns range from around 10% on the lower end for indices like MSCI China B Shares to over 30% for the CSI Onshore IT Services index. This swift move is shown in the second chart to have pushed most Chinese equity sectors into positive year-to-date territory, with the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index and MSCI P Chips leading the year-to-date returns at around 35%, though a few sectors like CSI Onshore IT Services remained slightly negative. 

The third chart traces China's equity valuations from 2014 to 2024 using the forward price-to-earnings ratio for China A-Shares and the MSCI China Index. Despite the recent sharp rally, forward valuations remain near the bottom of their historical ten-year range, hovering between roughly 10x and 12x forward earnings, well below the peaks of over 20x seen in 2015 and early 2021. 

The core of the author's argument—that China is a tactical trade rather than a structural investment—is supported by a table detailing the pass-through of nominal GDP growth to corporate earnings and market returns across major global economies from 2010 to 2024. China ranks dead last on both measures. Its earnings growth was only 0.4 times its nominal GDP growth, and its equity market return was a mere 0.3 times its nominal GDP growth. This stands in stark contrast to the United States, where the NASDAQ saw earnings growth at 3.0 times and market returns at 4.7 times nominal GDP growth, and the S&P 500 achieved ratios of 1.4 and 2.3, respectively. Other regions like France, Taiwan, Canada, the Eurozone, the United Kingdom, Australia, India, Brazil, and South Korea all outperformed China on these metrics, underscoring the author's point that nominal economic expansion does not automatically translate into wealth for equity investors.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest argues that geopolitical risk is a highly overrated signal for US equity investors, challenging the common narrative that international friction heavily dictates market performance. He critiques a 2017 forecast by the Eurasia Group that warned of a volatile political environment comparable to the 2008 financial crisis, pointing out that global equity markets actually rose 23% that year with record-low daily annualized volatility of 5.6%. 

To demonstrate which signals actually drive markets, the page features a table detailing the net predictive return benefit by indicator from December 1998 through June 2023, over a 12-month investment horizon. The data shows that hard economic indicators possess the highest predictive power for S&P 500 monthly returns. Payroll growth and the industrial production diffusion index lead the list, each providing a 0.5% net monthly return benefit. The Bureau of Labor Statistics percentage of businesses with rising employment, the Leading Indicator Index, and the National Financial Conditions Index follow closely, each offering a 0.4% net benefit. 

In contrast, the Geopolitical Risk Index yields a negative return benefit of negative 0.1%, indicating that using it as an investment signal would have been counterproductive. Other sentiment-driven metrics also perform poorly, with the Small Business Optimism Index, the Economic Policy Uncertainty Index, and Consumer Confidence showing negative net benefits of negative 0.3%, negative 0.7%, and negative 0.8% respectively. 

The author points out that historically, only the 1973 Arab-Israeli war had a lasting impact on global markets, largely due to the OPEC oil embargo, US energy dependence, and President Nixon’s wage and price controls. Furthermore, he explains that the S&P 500 is fundamentally more aligned with production than consumption, noting that two-thirds of S&P 500 profits come from manufacturing, whereas two-thirds of consumption in US GDP is comprised of services.

Michael Cembalest discusses the prevalence of high-profile Chinese espionage cases against United States entities and warns investors about geopolitical risks capping the upside of Chinese equities. Citing data from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, he notes that while actual espionage numbers are likely much higher, open-source data reveals a persistent trend of intellectual property and national security targeting. He advises investors to take profits on any rebound in the Chinese equity market and take the money and run. This warning is reinforced by potential market implications from China's October 2024 military exercises around Taiwan, which involved a record 125 aircraft and the Liaoning aircraft carrier simulating a blockade of key ports.

The page features a line chart plotting the annual number of publicly reported Chinese espionage incidents from 2000 through approximately 2023. The vertical axis measures the number of cases from zero to 30, and the horizontal axis tracks the timeline. The trend begins near zero in 2000, with Lucent listed as an early target, before rising to a minor peak of about eight cases around 2006, targeting sensitive entities like the Pentagon, Oak Ridge Labs, and Los Alamos. After a subsequent rise to around 12 cases in 2013 targeting gas pipelines and NASA, the chart displays a sharp drop to around five cases in 2015. This dip followed a bilateral agreement between President Obama and President Xi Jinping to restrict commercial espionage, though the decline quickly reversed within a year. By 2020 and 2021, the number of incidents spiked dramatically to a peak of over 25 cases, targeting high-profile entities such as the National Institutes of Health, General Electric, Microsoft, Verizon, and the United States Navy, before declining to around 17 cases toward 2023. Other notable targets annotated across the timeline include Apple, Coca-Cola, Google, Boeing, Lockheed Martin, and Dow.

In this J.P. Morgan publication, Michael Cembalest evaluates China's equity market following recent monetary, fiscal, and regulatory reforms. While the announcements triggered a sharp rally, Cembalest advises viewing Chinese equities as a tactical trade rather than a long-term investment. He argues that China suffers from exceptionally weak conversion of GDP growth to corporate profits and faces a geopolitical valuation ceiling, which he terms a Thucydides Cap.

This argument is first supported by a chart detailing China equity valuations from 2014 through October 2024. The chart tracks the forward price-to-earnings ratios of China A Shares and MSCI China, showing that A Shares have historically commanded a premium. After peaking above 20x around 2021, multiples for both indices bottomed near 10x to 12x in 2024. Although recent policy stimulus triggered a sudden spike to a post-stimulus peak of around 15x to 16x for A Shares, the current valuation has already retreated slightly. 

To demonstrate why long-term investing in China is challenging, a table compares the pass-through from nominal GDP growth to corporate earnings and equity market returns from 2010 to 2024. China ranks last among all listed major global economies, with earnings growth at just 0.4 times nominal GDP growth and market returns at a mere 0.3 times nominal GDP growth. For comparison, the US NASDAQ leads the pack with an earnings growth multiple of 3.0 and a market return multiple of 4.7, while the US S&P 500 shows multiples of 1.4 and 2.3 respectively. 

Cembalest then addresses the geopolitical risk by referencing Graham Allison’s book on the Thucydides Trap, which notes that most historical instances of a rising power challenging a dominant state ended in conflict. While Cembalest previously argued that deep financial integration would stave off conflict, he admits that ongoing tensions are eroding this optimism, prompting US investors to secure quick returns and exit. This historical comparison is visualized in a final bar chart displaying bilateral economic linkages between major adversaries over the last century as a percentage of their combined GDP. In 2014, the US and China stood highly integrated at over 7% of combined GDP, driven largely by bilateral trade and central bank holdings of each other's government debt. This level of economic interdependence is vastly larger than past rivalries, such as France and Germany in 1930, the UK and Germany in 1930, or the US and Russia in 2014, none of which exceeded 2% of combined GDP. Nevertheless, the author concludes that these deep economic ties are no longer enough to ease geopolitical anxieties for investors.

This page analyzes the political and financial risks of unmanaged immigration in the United States, arguing that while immigration is necessary for economic growth due to low native birth rates, its current chaotic nature poses severe challenges. The author highlights the discrepancy between official municipal projections and realistic costs, pointing to New York City and New York State as primary examples of mounting fiscal strain.

To illustrate these financial pressures, a chart on the components of New York City Comptroller estimated budget revisions for 2023 through 2027 shows that projected expenditures are more than twenty billion dollars higher than the official Office of Management and Budget figures. This gap is driven primarily by an underestimated ten billion dollars in asylum seeker expenses, alongside smaller unbudgeted costs for education, rental assistance, and overtime, which far outweigh a modest three to four billion dollar surplus in projected property tax and other revenues. A secondary chart on New York State spending on asylum seekers by agency shows total outlays rising sharply from under four hundred million dollars in June 2023 to nearly one point four billion dollars by September 2024, with the Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance bearing the vast majority of these costs.

On the enforcement and policy front, a chart displays monthly Immigration and Customs Enforcement removals from 2002 through mid-2024, categorized by presidential administration. The data reveals that monthly deportations peaked under the Obama administration at nearly forty thousand, hovered between fifteen thousand and twenty-five thousand during the Trump administration before dropping sharply during the pandemic, and bottomed out at under five thousand under the Biden administration before rising back to around twenty thousand by 2024. 

Finally, a chart on US labor force growth indexed to December 2009 demonstrates the economic reliance on immigration. The native-born labor force index grew very slowly over fifteen years, reaching only about one hundred and five by 2024. In contrast, the foreign-born labor force index surged to nearly one hundred and forty over the same period, illustrating that foreign-born workers have driven almost all recent US labor force expansion.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, Eye on the Market, analyzes why the Republican Party’s messaging on inflation resonated with voters, focusing on the Biden-Harris administration's populist fiscal policies and the subsequent crisis in housing affordability. Cembalest argues that the administration adopted a high-spending fiscal strategy aimed at rapid full employment, influenced by a 2020 Hewlett Foundation memo that incorrectly assumed there was substantial "headroom for spending without causing undue inflation." He asserts that this policy led to the worst inflation spike since the late 1970s and the worst housing affordability on record.

To support this, the author provides four charts. The first, titled "US core and food inflation," tracks year-over-year percentage changes in Food CPI and Core CPI from 1970 through mid-2024. The data illustrates a steep, historic climb starting around 2020, with food inflation peaking above 12% and core inflation exceeding 6%, which is the highest surge since the late 1970s. Alongside this, the "Home price to income ratio" chart reveals that the ratio of home prices to income skyrocketed from a baseline of around 7.0–8.0 in previous decades to an unprecedented peak above 10.0 in 2024, indicating the worst housing affordability ever recorded. 

Cembalest critiques Kamala Harris’s campaign proposals for homebuyer stimulus, arguing that more demand-side stimulus would worsen inflation. Instead, he attributes the housing affordability crisis to supply-side issues, specifically restrictive zoning and land-use regulations that have stifled the construction of entry-level housing. This dynamic is illustrated in the third chart, "Land use regulation vs starter homes," which spans 1974 to 2024. This dual-axis chart shows a clear inverse relationship: as state supreme and appellate land-use court cases per million people rose from around 1.0 to a peak near 3.0, the share of new homes sold that were under 1,400 square feet plummeted from approximately 35% in the late 1970s to a mere 5% by 2024.

Finally, the author expresses skepticism that a Harris administration would deliver the necessary nationwide deregulation to solve this housing supply crisis, given the administration's record. This point is visualized in the final chart, "Cumulative # of economically significant rules by month 40 of each presidency." The chart compares modern U.S. presidents from Reagan to Biden. Biden's trajectory is the steepest by far, enacting nearly 300 economically significant rules by month 40 of his presidency. This volume of regulation far outpaces that of his predecessors, with Obama coming in second at around 180 rules, followed by Trump, Clinton, George W. Bush, George H.W. Bush, and Reagan, the latter of whom enacted fewer than 50 such rules by month 40.

This publication from J.P. Morgan, written by Michael Cembalest, centers on the controversial nomination of Matt Gaetz as US Attorney General by Donald Trump. Cembalest frames this pick as highly unorthodox, illustrating that Gaetz’s qualifications are at the extreme low end of the historical range. The central argument is that Gaetz lacks any prior service in the Department of Justice, a US Attorney’s office, or a State Attorney General’s office. He has no prosecutorial experience at either the federal or state level, nor does he possess executive leadership experience at any major US or state agency. Instead, his legal career is limited to service on the House Judiciary Committee and time spent at a small Florida law firm, much of which overlapped with his tenure in the Florida State Legislature.

To support this claim, the page features a detailed stacked bar chart titled "100 years of US Attorney General appointments: prior years of experience," which displays the years of pre-AG experience per position from 1924 to 2024. The vertical axis measures years of experience from zero to 45, while the horizontal axis chronologically lists appointed Attorneys General from Harlan Stone under President Coolidge to Matt Gaetz under President Trump. The chart employs a multi-colored legend representing sixteen distinct professional roles, such as serving as a US Attorney, working in the Department of Justice, acting as a Federal Judge, or serving in the US House of Representatives. 

The visual contrast is stark: most historic Attorneys General possess substantial columns reflecting decades of judicial, prosecutorial, or federal agency experience. For instance, nominees like William Barr, Michael Mukasey, Eric Holder, and Merrick Garland show between 25 and over 40 years of combined legal experience, characterized heavily by dark blue segments representing US Attorney and Department of Justice service. In contrast, Matt Gaetz’s column is one of the shortest on the chart, totaling only about 13 years of experience. His bar is colored entirely in light pink for law firm practice and peach for the US House of Representatives, emphasizing his lack of traditional prosecutorial and executive credentials. The chart also contains brief annotations above several historical bars identifying key law firms and educational institutions associated with past nominees.

The author provides historical context for controversial nominations through a detailed footnote regarding the appointment of Robert F. Kennedy by his brother, John F. Kennedy. At the time, RFK’s nomination was heavily criticized by major publications due to his lack of state or federal court experience. The footnote reveals that JFK was initially reluctant to nominate his brother, but was overruled by his father, Joseph Kennedy Sr. RFK was ultimately confirmed through a voice vote coordinated by LBJ advisor Bobby Baker and Senator Richard Russell Jr., a maneuver believed to be necessary because RFK likely would not have secured even 40 votes in a standard Senate roll-call.

This page discusses the risks surrounding private credit, focusing on the prevalence of "phantom" Paid-In-Kind (PIK) income within Business Development Corporations (BDCs), a market that has tripled in size over the last five years. The author explains that PIK income adds principal to the borrower's outstanding balance instead of paying cash, posing a potential threat to actual dividend coverage. 

To illustrate this, a line chart tracks PIK income as a percentage of total investment income from 2019 through mid-2024 for both the Fitch and Moody's BDC universes. The Fitch universe shows a rise from a low of nearly 3.5% in 2020 to approximately 9% in 2024, while Moody’s universe tracks a similar climb from around 5% in 2021 to roughly 7.5% in 2024. A adjacent bar chart breaks down Q2 2024 PIK income as a percentage of net investment income (net of cash expenses) across major BDCs, showing wide variation: Prospect tops the list at nearly 38%, followed by Blue Owl and New Mountain, while other firms like Ares, Blackstone, and Apollo sit much lower, with Apollo near 0%.

The growth of this sector is framed by a third chart plotting outstanding US private debt against commercial and industrial (C&I) loans from 2010 to 2024 in billions of US dollars. While C&I loans remain larger at roughly $2.7 trillion in 2024, private debt has experienced explosive growth, rising from negligible levels in 2010 to over $1.5 trillion in 2024.

Despite the rise in PIK income, the author highlights research demonstrating that bank lending to BDCs offers a vastly superior return on equity proposition compared to lending directly to middle-market companies. A detailed financial table compares these two lending channels.
