This page of the publication critiques financial analyst Meredith Whitney’s famous late-2010 prediction on a CBS News *60 Minutes* broadcast warning of an impending wave of massive municipal bond defaults. Although Detroit did default in 2013 in the largest Chapter 9 municipal default in U.S. history, the author argues that Detroit was a unique, idiosyncratic outlier rather than a harbinger of systemic municipal failure. Ultimately, the author's skepticism was vindicated, as the average five-year municipal default rate since 2012 has been a mere 0.1%, and an indicative intermediate-duration tax-free municipal bond fund generated 7.5 times the return of a municipal money market fund between 2011 and 2021. 

The top line chart, "Municipal bonds, cash and 60 Minutes," displays the total return index from September 2010 to July 2011, indexed to 100 on December 19, 2010. It shows a representative intermediate-duration tax-free municipal bond fund dropping briefly following Whitney’s interview on that date, hitting a low near 100 in January 2011, before embarking on a steady recovery to nearly 106 by July 2011. In contrast, a representative municipal money market fund flatlines at 100 throughout the period, demonstrating how quickly the market shook off the default fears. 

Two bottom charts show why Detroit's economic situation was uniquely dire compared to other municipal issuers, placing it below the 5th percentile of other U.S. cities. The bottom-left chart, "Growth in Gross Metropolitan Product" from 2001 to 2011, indexes performance to 100 in 2001. While other municipal regions experienced growth, with even the 5th percentile ending above 110, Detroit's economy contracted sharply after 2007, tracking far below the 5th percentile and ending back near 100 in 2011. The bottom-right chart, "Labor force growth (employed + unemployed)" from 2000 to 2012, indexes the labor force to 100 in January 2000. It demonstrates that while the broader U.S. municipal landscape saw positive labor force growth, Detroit's labor force steadily declined to approximately 85 by 2012, languishing deep below the 5th percentile line.

This page from Eye on the Market features a single chart and commentary arguing that equities almost always bottom before other major economic and market indicators during U.S. recessions. The chart, titled "Equities tend to bottom first during recessions," plots the number of months since the beginning of a recession on the horizontal axis, ranging from negative eight months to thirty-two months, against seven historical recession periods on the vertical axis: Eisenhower, the 1970s stagflation, the 1980s double dip, the 1990s Savings and Loan crisis, the DotCom crash, the Great Financial Crisis, and the COVID-19 pandemic. 

The chart tracks the timing of the worst readings for ten distinct indicators, including equities, the ISM manufacturing survey, GDP, industrial production, payrolls, S&P earnings, housing starts, high yield default rates, real estate delinquencies, and the official end of the recession. Across nearly all of these historical episodes, the red diamond representing equities is among the first symbols to appear, indicating that stock markets bottomed well before lagging metrics like payrolls, real estate delinquencies, or high-yield defaults. The ISM manufacturing survey is identified as the indicator most closely associated with the equity bottom. The prominent exception to this rule is the DotCom recession of 2001 and 2002, labeled on the chart as "the exception," where equities bottomed last, roughly nineteen months after the recession began. Based on these historical patterns, the author advises investors that economic and market news will likely still be highly negative when financial assets reach their lowest, most opportunistic prices. Data for the chart is sourced from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, the Census Bureau, the National Association of Realtors, Shiller, Bloomberg, S&P/Dow Jones, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page argues that geopolitical events are generally poor indicators for equity investors, as most major military conflicts in the post-World War II era did not lead to lasting market declines. The author points out that only two key events over the last several decades preceded substantial S&P 500 downturns a year later: the September 11, 2001 attacks, which coincided with the dot-com collapse, and the Arab-Israeli War of 1973, which triggered a severe US energy crisis, an oil embargo, and recession-inducing inflation. 

A chart in the upper left displays the trajectory of the S&P 500 Index over the twelve months following various conflicts, indexed to 100 at the start of the conflict. The visual highlights the resilient market paths after the 2023 Israel-Gaza War, which rose to around 130, and the 2022 Russia-Ukraine War, which hovered around 100. In contrast, the market fell to approximately 80 following the September 11 attacks and dropped sharply to nearly 60 following the 1973 Arab-Israeli War. An adjacent table lists nineteen historical military invasions and conflicts spanning from the 1950 Korean War to the 2023 Israel-Gaza War.

To identify what signals actually matter, a table at the bottom analyzes S&P 500 monthly returns from January 1985 to August 2017 based on whether various indicators are above or below average. The data confirms that economic growth, employment, profits, and confidence are the most powerful market signals. The Leading Indicator Index proves most valuable, showing a 1.2% monthly excess S&P return when above average (1.6% vs 0.4%). This is followed closely by the CEO Confidence Index at 1.1% excess return and payroll growth at 0.9% excess return. Meanwhile, political and geopolitical metrics have almost no predictive value; the Economic Policy Uncertainty Index and the Geopolitical Risk Index show negligible monthly excess returns of negative 0.2% and negative 0.1%, respectively. Shaded indicators like the National Financial Conditions Index imply negative outcomes when levels rise, posting a negative 0.5% excess return.

This page analyzes the timing of market pricing relative to fundamental credit distress during historical downturns, showing that credit spreads peak and asset prices bottom well before actual defaults and delinquency rates reach their apex. 

The first chart, titled "Savings and Loan Crisis," tracks the period from 1987 to 1993, comparing High Yield credit spreads (spread-to-worst, on a left axis from 0 to 1,200) with cumulative defaults measured by the number of issuers (on a right axis from 0 to 300). It highlights that during the 1990 Savings and Loan crisis, high yield credit spreads peaked when only 55% of eventual corporate defaults had actually occurred. 

The second chart, "Financial crisis," focuses on the 2008 downturn from 2006 to 2013. It plots the same metrics: High Yield credit spreads (spread-to-worst, left axis from 0 to 2,500) and cumulative defaults by number of issuers (right axis from 0 to 250). This chart demonstrates that high yield spreads peaked in late 2008 when only 30% of the eventual corporate defaults had taken place. 

The third chart, "CMBS spreads vs. delinquency rates: 2006 to 2014," demonstrates a similar phenomenon in the commercial real estate market. It plots the AAA CMBS Spread in basis points (left axis from 0 to 1,600) against the 60+ day delinquency rate (right axis from 0% to 9%). Spreads peaked dramatically at over 1,400 basis points in late 2008, when the delinquency rate was still only 0.5%. Deliquencies did not peak until 2012, reaching 8.5% long after spreads had returned to lower levels. 

The final chart, "Leveraged Loan prices vs. defaults: 2006 to 2011," details the corporate loan market by plotting the Leveraged Loan Price Index (left axis from 60 to 105) against trailing 12-month default rates (right axis from 0% to 9%). The price index bottomed near 65 in late 2008 when the default rate was 4.5%. By the time the default rate peaked at 8% in 2010, the leveraged loan price index had already recovered back above 90. 

Collectively, these charts support the observation that financial markets act as forward-looking indicators, pricing in distress and recovering long before physical defaults peak in the broader economy. Data is sourced from J.P. Morgan Securities, Trepp, Standard & Poor's, and the S&P/LSTA Leveraged Loan Index.

This page from the publication presents a retrospective analysis titled "History of Bottom-Feeding," originally published in 2014, which details how equity markets historically bottom well before underlying fundamental economic crises peak or resolve. The author outlines three core lessons from financial history: during the Great Depression, the Dow Jones Index bottomed when only half of eventual bank failures had occurred; during the 2008 financial crisis, bank stocks bottomed when only a tiny fraction of failures had materialized; and during the 2011 European sovereign debt crisis, European equities bottomed long before unemployment or capital flight peaked.

The first chart, titled "The Great Depression: Equity market vs. bank failures," plots the Dow Jones Industrial Average index level on the left axis (ranging from 0 to 400) against cumulative bank failures on the right axis (ranging from 0 to 10,000 institutions) from January 1929 to December 1933. It illustrates that while cumulative bank failures steadily climbed to around 10,000 by late 1933, the Dow Jones Industrial Average reached its absolute bottom in mid-1932. A prominent data label highlights that at this equity bottom, only 48% of the ultimate cumulative bank failures had actually taken place.

The second chart, titled "Financial crisis: Bank stocks vs. bank failures," covers the period from January 2008 to January 2014. It plots the S&P 500 Bank Index on the left axis (0 to 300) against the total number of cumulative bank failures on the right axis (0 to 500 institutions). The S&P 500 Bank Index hit its low point in early 2009, marked by a red dot denoting the release of the Supervisory Capital Assessment Program (SCAP) bank stress test results. At this exact trough, only 8% of the eventual 500 bank failures of the crisis era had occurred.

The third chart, titled "European equities bottomed almost 2 years before unemployment stopped rising," compares the STOXX European Broad equity index level (left axis, 225 to 350) with the Eurozone unemployment rate (right axis, 9.5% to 12.5%) from 2010 to 2014. The STOXX European Broad equity index bottomed in late 2011 near the 225 level, whereas the Eurozone unemployment rate continued to climb for nearly two more years, finally peaking above 12% in mid-2013.

The fourth chart, titled "Equity recovery preceded capital flight reversal...", compares the same STOXX European Broad equity index (left axis, 225 to 350) to cumulative capital outflows from the periphery to the core, measured by the Periphery Target 2 balance in billions of euros (right axis, 0 to 1,000 billion EUR) from 2010 to 2014. The chart demonstrates that the STOXX European equity index began its sustained recovery in late 2011, preceding the peak and subsequent reversal of peripheral capital flight, which reached nearly 1,000 billion euros in late 2012. 

A concluding text box at the bottom summarizes that the full 2014 analysis also examines different countries and cycles to show how Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) data is typically the variable most closely aligned with equity market bottoms. It additionally notes that in emerging markets, currency devaluations often coincide with bottoms in local equity markets.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication highlights the persistent risks of concentrated stock portfolios and the historical performance benefits of hedge fund diversification. Michael Cembalest begins by examining distress-based business failures to show why stock concentration is highly risky over the long term. Under the heading of S&P 500 distress removals, two charts analyze "negative index removals" between 1980 and 2013, which exclude benign removals like mergers or premium acquisitions. The first chart, a bar graph tracking the number of distressed company removals by year, demonstrates that while removals spike during economic downturns—reaching a peak of over 25 companies in 2001 and more than 20 in 2008—there is a constant pulse of corporate failure across the entire business cycle. The adjacent line chart tracks the cumulative total of these distressed removals, showing a steady climb from zero in 1980 to approximately 320 by 2013. The text notes that these failures were concentrated in the consumer discretionary, technology, and financial sectors. Furthermore, an analysis of the Russell 3000 Index since 1980 reveals that many failures occurred due to external factors outside of management’s control, including changes in government policy, commodity price risks, rapid technological obsolescence, competitor expansion, and patent infringement.

The second half of the page argues that a diversified, portfolio-based approach to hedge funds can significantly improve investor outcomes relative to traditional fixed income. Two scatter plots analyze the performance of randomly generated four-fund portfolios from 2012 to 2014 against the Barclays Aggregate Index, plotting annualized return against annualized volatility. The first scatter plot, focusing on relative value hedge funds, shows that 84% of the random portfolios outperformed the Barclays Aggregate Index with equal or lower volatility, while 97% outperformed the index overall. The second plot, focusing on market-neutral and other low-volatility long-short equity hedge funds, shows that 79% of random portfolios outperformed the Barclays Aggregate Index with equal or lower volatility, and 95% outperformed the index overall. To show this trend is persistent, Cembalest references a 2023 update using HFRI and Pivotal Path data from 2018 to 2023, which found that 78% to 95% of randomly generated 20-fund portfolios outperformed comparable stock-bond benchmarks at equivalent volatility levels.

This page examines the growing fiscal pressures facing the United States federal government, specifically how rising entitlement spending is crowding out critical non-defense discretionary spending and driving the nation toward a permanent crossover point where mandatory outlays and interest payments exceed total revenues. 

A chart on the top left, titled "What does the Federal government spend money on?", tracks entitlement spending and non-defense discretionary spending as a percentage of GDP from 1970 through CBO projections up to 2025. It highlights the shifting ratio between these two spending categories: starting at an equal 1.0x ratio in 1970, the ratio of entitlement to non-defense discretionary spending rose to 2.0x in 1990, 3.3x in 2015, and is projected to reach 5.1x by 2025. Over this period, entitlement spending climbs from approximately 4% to over 12% of GDP, while non-defense discretionary spending drifts downward toward 3%. 

A companion chart on the top right, "Permanent crossover point is coming in the next decade," displays historical data and projections from 1965 to 2035. It shows that while federal revenues historically hover around 17% to 18% of GDP, the combined total of entitlements, other mandatory outlays, and net interest is on a steep upward trajectory, projected to reach roughly 22% of GDP by 2035. The permanent crossover point where these mandatory costs exceed total revenues is forecast to occur in the early 2030s.

The main text outlines how the US entitlement system, originally created to alleviate widespread elderly poverty in the mid-20th century, lacks mechanism controls to calibrate spending relative to national income. This unchecked growth now threatens vital discretionary investments in infrastructure, job retraining, disease control, and education. To address potential solutions, the author presents a table of fifteen select revenue-raising options compiled by Piper Sandler in September 2024, showing their projected 10-year revenue increases in billions of dollars. The largest revenue generators listed include raising the corporate tax rate from 21% to 28% ($978 billion), implementing an unrealized capital gains tax on ultra-high-net-worth individuals ($503 billion), increasing the ACA Net Investment Income Tax to 5% for incomes over $400,000 ($404 billion), and applying that same tax to active business income ($393 billion).

Finally, a dedicated callout box addresses the viability of a wealth tax. It discusses a March 2021 CBO scoring of a proposal from Senator Elizabeth Warren, which was projected to raise $2.1 trillion over ten years. This proposal assumed a 2% tax on net worth above $50 million and a 3% tax on net worth above $1 billion, alongside a $100 billion IRS investment to ensure a 30% audit rate. However, the author cautions that international precedents show wealth taxes often under-deliver due to tax evasion and avoidance, and notes that any such US policy would face complex constitutional challenges requiring Supreme Court adjudication. Footnotes add historical context on the political opposition faced during the creation of Social Security and Medicare, referencing figures like Ronald Reagan, Harry Truman, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Alf Landon, and William Randolph Hearst.

This page presents a retrospective analysis of J.P. Morgan's early 2021 warning about an impending wave of post-COVID inflation, arguing that the unprecedented scale of monetary and fiscal stimulus made a severe inflation spike virtually inevitable. 

The top-left scatter plot, titled "Stimulus response to COVID sets a new bar," compares fiscal stimulus as a percentage of GDP on the vertical axis against monetary stimulus via central bank balance sheets as a percentage of GDP on the horizontal axis. This visual contrasts the massive policy response of the Global Virus Crisis with past crises, demonstrating how COVID-era interventions dwarfed those of the 2008 Global Financial Crisis and the 2011 Europe Balance of Payments Crisis. During the pandemic, Japan’s monetary stimulus exceeded 30% of GDP, while the UK and the United States implemented substantial fiscal packages of approximately 14% and 11% of GDP, respectively, alongside 15% monetary stimulus. 

The top-right line chart, titled "Faster growth in the money supply this time around," indexes the M2 money supply plus institutional money market fund balances starting from the onset of both the 2008 and 2020 crises. It shows that money supply growth during the Global Coronavirus Crisis was vastly faster and larger than during the Global Financial Crisis, with the index peaking near 127 within a year and a half, compared to a peak of only about 108 in the post-2008 period. 

The bottom-left chart, "US core CPI since 2017," tracks year-over-year core inflation, marking the exact moment in early 2021 when core inflation was hovering around 1.5% and J.P. Morgan published its warning. From there, inflation rapidly escalated to a peak of 6.6% in 2022 before gradually declining to 3.3% by late 2024. The bottom-right chart, "US core CPI since 1960," places this recent spike in a long-term historical context, showing that the 6.6% peak was a jolting level last seen in 1982, though still below the double-digit inflation peaks of the 1970s and early 1980s. 

In the commentary, the author notes that J.P. Morgan's early 2021 anxieties were mirrored two weeks later by economist Larry Summers in a Washington Post op-ed, which similarly argued that a combination of rapid labor market healing, pent-up savings, herd immunity, and massive deficits would reignite inflation. Ultimately, the author observes that even though core inflation halved from its peak to 3.3% by the time of the 2024 election, the dramatic surge remained a major political vulnerability for the Biden/Harris reelection campaign.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s publication outlines the dramatic rise and subsequent collapse of Special Purpose Acquisition Companies (SPACs), reinforcing the author's long-standing view that the structure was primarily designed to benefit sponsors while delivering dismal results to retail and institutional investors. The commentary notes that during the peak in February 2021, SPACs represented nearly half of all new US issue activity despite bringing highly risky, unprofitable companies to market. 

To illustrate this lack of quality, the first chart, titled "Poor profitability of companies brought public via SPACs since 2019," examines a sample of 85 companies as of February 1, 2021. It reveals that only a tiny fraction, roughly 15 companies, achieved positive net income and free cash flow, while the vast majority (about 70 companies) recorded negative figures for both metrics. Adjacent to this chart is a stylized circular diagram titled "SPAC wealth transfers," illustrating how value systematically flows away from retail, PIPE, and post-merger buy-and-hold investors directly into the hands of the SPAC sponsor and the selling company.

This wealth transfer is quantified in a table evaluating cumulative returns for SPAC companies brought public or liquidated from January 1, 2019, to January 22, 2021. The table tracks average and median performance metrics across March 2021 and August 2021. It highlights that while SPAC sponsors enjoyed median returns of 682% in March 2021 (retaining 418% even after concessions, forfeiture, and vesting), buy-and-hold investors suffered severe losses. By August 2021, the median post-merger buy-and-hold investor experienced a negative 15% gross return, which translated to underperforming the IPO index by negative 68% and underperforming the Russell 2000 by negative 51%. 

The final chart comparing two-year average net returns for 2020 and 2021 vintages demonstrates that SPACs underperformed traditional IPOs across every major industry. In the healthcare sector, traditional IPOs fell about 38% while SPACs dropped 64%. In technology, IPOs declined 30% compared to a 60% drop for SPACs. In the consumer space, traditional IPOs fell 48% while SPACs lost 63%. The widest gap occurred in the diversified sector, where traditional IPOs fell 20% while SPACs collapsed by nearly 68%. 

The author concludes that by 2023, SPAC investors had suffered losses two to three times worse than those in traditional IPOs. While pronouncing the trend dead, the author highlights a open question regarding a potential, regulatory-driven revival, citing a May 2025 New York Times report detailing a renewed flurry of SPAC transactions linked to Howard Lutnick’s Cantor Fitzgerald under an SEC regulatory environment that is reportedly becoming more permissive.

This page argues that the commercial and technical case for hydrogen as a green transition fuel continues to deteriorate, urging investors and policymakers not to believe the hype. The author points to fundamental physical limitations, extreme economic costs, poor financial performance, and rising rates of project abandonment to support this skeptical view. 

A central table lists the summary statistics of the hydrogen economy's low round-trip efficiencies. Notable figures include 30% conversion losses from steam methane reformation, 25% to 35% conversion losses from alkaline and proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolysis, and fuel cell efficiencies of 50% to 60%. Ultimately, the round-trip efficiency of fuel cells in transportation is only 25%, dropping to between 15% and 30% when liquefaction, shipping, and regasification are required. For liquid ammonia produced from green hydrogen for shipping, the efficiency drops to an even lower 11% to 19%, while liquefying gaseous hydrogen into liquid hydrogen consumes 30% to 40% of the energy.

To illustrate the economic challenges, a bar chart depicts the carbon abatement cost of green hydrogen by sector in US dollars per ton of carbon dioxide, drawing from a 2024 Harvard study by Roxana Shafiee and Daniel Schrag. The cost ranges from a low of around $500 to $600 per ton for ammonia and refining to upwards of $1,000 to $1,250 per ton for power and industrial heat. The author notes that these figures in some cases exceed the high cost of direct air carbon capture.

A line chart shows the performance of hydrogen equity indices from June 2021 through June 2025 relative to the broader market, indexed to 100 in June 2021. While the MSCI World Equity Index steadily climbed to nearly 140, both the WilderHill Hydrogen Economy Index and the Solactive Global Hydrogen Index cratered, with the Solactive index losing roughly 80% of its value to end near 15. The chart highlights the publication date of the author's original 2022 "Whydrogen?" report, which marked the beginning of this prolonged decline. 

The difficulties facing the sector are further emphasized by a final line chart tracking quarterly mentions of hydrogen project delays or cancellations in news or company disclosures from 2020 through early 2025. This metric has risen exponentially, climbing from fewer than 200 quarterly mentions in 2020 to nearly 1,300 by the first quarter of 2025, signaling widespread commercial challenges for hydrogen developers globally.

This page addresses the growing public health risks associated with a decline in public trust in vaccines, focusing particularly on the MMR vaccine and the potential re-emergence of measles in the United States. The author argues that disputes over COVID-19 vaccine safety and efficacy have had substantial negative social consequences, causing widespread interpersonal conflict and eroding trust in medical science. 

To illustrate the social toll, a bar chart displays the impact of COVID-19 disagreements on relationships among respondents to a September 2021 South Dakota State University survey. It shows that approximately 36% of respondents reported relationship stress, about 34% stopped socializing, roughly 29% experienced damaged family relationships, and around 26% lost their temper. 

To contrast this friction with the historical benefits of immunization, a table lists the massive declines in vaccine-preventable diseases in the US following vaccine adoption, citing data from a 2007 JAMA study. It shows 100% declines in both cases and deaths for diphtheria (vaccine adopted in the 1940s), measles (1960s), acute polio (1950s), rubella (1960s), and smallpox (1790s). Mumps and pertussis also saw case declines of 96% and 92% alongside near-total death declines of 100% and 99%, respectively. Hepatitis A and tetanus similarly saw massive declines in both cases and mortality.

The narrative shifts to the specific threat of measles, explaining that US adults immunized between 1963 and 1967 received an inactivated version of the MMR vaccine, which offers lower long-term immunity, leaving only 25% of recipients with detectable antibodies after just one year. This historical vulnerability is compounded by falling current vaccination rates. Because measles is highly contagious—with an infectiousness measure of 12 to 18, compared to just 1 to 2 for COVID and the flu—a 95% vaccination rate is required to achieve herd immunity. However, the median US MMR vaccination rate fell from 95% in 2013 to 92% in 2023, with Georgia, Colorado, Wisconsin, Alaska, and Idaho all falling below the 90% threshold. 

The author highlights Gaines County, Texas, as a specific area of concern where a measles outbreak occurred; the county's MMR vaccination rate sits at 82%, with one school district dropping below 50% and nearly one in five kindergarten students opting out of at least one vaccine. The page concludes with warnings from medical experts. University of Texas pediatrics professor JB Cantey cautions that measles is the "canary in the coal mine" for other vaccine-preventable diseases, while a Stanford University study warns that measles could become endemic again in the United States within two decades, with international travelers acting as "matches" to spark outbreaks in under-vaccinated populations.

This page presents a detailed defense of the effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines and boosters, while also addressing skepticism regarding pandemic mortality statistics. The author argues that several critical interventions went right, highlighting that original vaccines and bivalent boosters prevented massive numbers of hospitalizations and severe illnesses. According to referenced estimates from the Commonwealth Fund, vaccines prevented over 18 million hospitalizations by December 2022. Additionally, the text notes that the XBB booster from late 2023 reduced hospitalization risk by 68% in the United States and approximately 70% in the Netherlands. The author also emphasizes the threat of Long COVID, which is shown to cause severe cognitive deficits equivalent to 20 years of aging, noting that risk is substantially mitigated by vaccination, with three or more doses reducing the risk by 73%. Lastly, the author contrasts the extremely low risk of vaccine-induced blood clots—about 1.4 per million—with the much higher risk of contracting blood clots from COVID-19 itself, which affected over 12,000 per million infected individuals.

To support these assertions, the page features two charts. The first visual on the left, titled "Vaccinated vs unvaccinated total hospitalizations and deaths from November 2021 to April 2022," presents state-level data from Virginia, Utah, California, and Minnesota. It is split into two scatter plots. The left plot measures hospital admissions per million, with a vertical scale from 0 to 14,000. It shows unvaccinated individuals in Minnesota peaking near 13,000, California near 10,000, Utah near 9,000, and Virginia near 4,000, while the corresponding dots for fully vaccinated and boosted individuals in all four states cluster near the bottom, well under 1,000 admissions. The right plot measures deaths per million, with a scale from 0 to 3,000. Here, unvaccinated deaths reach nearly 2,700 in Minnesota and 2,100 in California, whereas vaccinated and boosted cohorts stay extremely low, mostly under 500 deaths.

The second visual on the right, titled "Excess US deaths from all causes," tracks weekly deaths in the United States from 2017 through late 2021. The chart plots actual deaths from all causes as a blue line against a gold baseline threshold for excess deaths. Prior to the onset of the pandemic in early 2020, actual weekly deaths tracked closely with the threshold, fluctuating seasonally between roughly 50,000 and 65,000. Once the COVID-19 pandemic began, actual deaths spiked dramatically above the threshold, reaching a peak near 80,000 in early 2020 and a secondary peak exceeding 85,000 in early 2021. The author presents this visual to counter the argument that people merely died "with" COVID rather than "from" it, showing that overall mortality rose far above normal historical baseline levels.

This page explores whether the strong economic ties between the United States and China can prevent them from falling into "Thucydides’ Trap," a concept popularized by political scientist Graham Allison, who noted that twelve of sixteen historical rivalries between rising and dominant states over the last 500 years ended in war. Initially, in 2018, the author was optimistic because bilateral economic linkages between the US and China—consisting of bilateral trade, foreign direct investment, and central bank holdings of government debt—totaled about 7.3% of their combined GDP in 2014. This was vastly higher than any comparable historical rivalry over the last century, such as France and Germany in 1930, the UK and Germany in 1930, or the US and the Soviet Union in 1983. However, this optimism has faded as these linkages have since declined to approximately 4% of combined GDP due to stagnating Chinese holdings of US debt, falling FDI, and an ongoing trade war. Furthermore, China remains highly mercantilist, preferring the operations of US subsidiaries within its borders—which facilitates technology transfer—over direct bilateral imports.

Four distinct charts support this analysis. The first chart, in the top left, displays the bilateral economic linkages of various historical and potential adversaries over the last 100 years as a percentage of their combined GDP in a specified year. It highlights that the US and China in 2014 possessed unique and unprecedentedly deep integration compared to all historical parallels, where most rivalries saw combined economic linkages of less than 3% of GDP. 

The top-right chart illustrates key points of dispute in the US-China trade war, ranking China against developed and emerging economies on a scale from 0 to 100, where 0 is the worst. China scores extremely poorly across almost all measures, registering near zero on the Mercantilism Index, which tracks forced local production, IP theft, and domestic favoritism. It also scores under 20 on protections for trade secrets, IP enforcement, software piracy, and barriers to market access.

The bottom-left chart addresses the common narrative that China is shedding its US dollar reserves. It plots China’s dollar assets in billions of US dollars from 2008 to 2022, comparing the declining custody of US-held Treasuries—which dropped from over $1.25 trillion around 2012 to roughly $800 billion in 2022—against broader estimates. Once adjusting for holdings by offshore custodians like Belgium's Euroclear and reallocations into US Agency debt, China’s total estimated US dollar assets have remained remarkably stable since 2015, hovering between $2 trillion and $2.25 trillion. This stability is supported by Brad Setser's analysis of both IMF COFER data and US Treasury International Capital plus agency data.

Finally, the bottom-right chart highlights the nature of American business in China, showing that the US trade relationship is highly dependent on in-country subsidiaries rather than direct exports. While the reported US-China trade deficit worsened to over -$400 billion around 2018 before ending near -$280 billion in 2023, the deficit is far shallower when factoring in the sales of US subsidiaries operating directly inside China. When including these subsidiary sales, the combined balance has stayed much closer to even, fluctuating between -$50 billion and -$150 billion over the last two decades. This confirms that while bilateral trade is heavily skewed in China's favor, American companies remain highly active in the Chinese market through local production.

This page discusses the changing nature of US bank failures, highlighting how the banking crisis of 2023 introduced a new failure catalyst: interest rate risk rather than traditional credit risk. Historically, bank failures resulted from bad credit underwriting leading to rising non-performing loans and declining income ahead of a recession. 

This historical context is illustrated in the first chart, titled Rate of bank failures in the US from 1865-2023, which tracks failed banks as a share of total banks. The chart shows national banks from 1865 onward and FDIC member banks from the 1930s onward. Significant spikes in bank failure rates coincide with historical panics, such as the Panics of 1873, 1884, 1893, and 1907, the Recession of 1920-1921, and most dramatically, the Great Depression, where national bank failures peaked near six percent of all banks. Subsequent periods, including the Savings and Loan Crisis and the Global Financial Crisis, saw much lower failure rates.

The author notes that Silicon Valley Bank (SIVB) departed from this credit-driven pattern; it had a pristine credit book but failed due to interest rate risk. Flooded with deposits during the 2020-2022 stimulus period, SIVB purchased long-duration government securities at cyclical lows in interest rates. When interest rates subsequently surged, SIVB's equity was wiped out. SIVB relied heavily on corporate and venture capital funding, with 152 billion dollars of its 173 billion dollars in customer deposits uninsured at the end of 2022. Furthermore, its hold-to-maturity securities portfolio grew dramatically from 14 billion dollars in 2019 to 99 billion dollars in 2022, while its available-for-sale book grew from 14 billion dollars to 27 billion dollars.

To demonstrate the vulnerability of SIVB and other institutions, the second chart, Impact of unrealized securities and loan losses on capital, plots various US banks' capital ratios as of the fourth quarter of 2022. It displays three metrics: the baseline Common Equity Tier 1 Capital Ratio, the ratio adjusted for unrealized losses on securities, and the ratio adjusted for unrealized losses on both securities and loans. For SIVB, adjusting for these unrealized losses plunges its capital ratio from a baseline of over twelve percent down into negative territory, around negative four percent. Other institutions like First Republic Bank (FRC), Signature Bank (SBNY), and PacWest (PACW) also show severe capital depletion under these adjustments, with FRC's adjusted ratio falling below zero percent.

Looking forward, the author warns that the banking sector's unrealized loss issue has not disappeared. As of June 2025, US banks still held approximately 500 billion dollars in unrealized losses across available-for-sale and hold-to-maturity portfolios. While this is down from the peak of 700 billion dollars in 2022 and 2023, it remains exceptionally high compared to the period from 2008 to 2021, when the largest unrealized loss was less than 100 billion dollars and the sector typically enjoyed small unrealized gains.

This page analyzes the structural drivers behind the outperformance of US equities compared to European equities since 2009, challenging the simplistic narrative that the performance gap is merely a function of lower price-to-earnings multiples in Europe. The author attributes this divergence to fundamental performance factors, currency movements, and sector weights, while noting that the long-running trend of US outperformance began to reverse in 2025 due to shifts in trade policy.

At the top of the page, a chart decomposes the total return index of US versus European equities from December 2009 to May 2023. Starting at a baseline of 100, the MSCI US index rose to over 500, vastly outperforming the MSCI Europe index in US dollars, which ended near 200. The chart attributes this performance gap to five key layers: the outperformance of the US dollar against the euro; sector weight differences, specifically the US being overweight in technology and Europe being overweight in financials, industrials, and staples; and within-sector outperformance, where US technology, consumer discretionary, and financials all beat their European counterparts.

To explain this within-sector outperformance, a table on the bottom left displays sector-by-sector data on Return on Assets (ROA) and Return on Equity (ROE) as of December 2024. Except for the healthcare sector, where Europe leads with an ROA of 6.3 percent and ROE of 15.1 percent compared to the US's 4.4 percent ROA and 12.7 percent ROE, US sectors show dominant efficiency across the board. For example, in technology, the US boasts an ROA of 12.6 percent and ROE of 28.9 percent, compared to Europe's 5.8 percent ROA and 11.4 percent ROE. Similar patterns of US dominance are visible in consumer discretionary, with a 30.0 percent ROE versus Europe's 11.8 percent, and communication services, with a 17.8 percent ROE versus Europe's 6.9 percent.

Finally, a line chart on the bottom right tracks the total return index for both markets from 2010 through June 3, 2025, revealing that the onset of the Trump trade wars in 2025 finally dented this long-term trend of US outperformance. The performance difference between the MSCI US and MSCI Europe peaked in November 2024 when Trump was elected, at which point the US index approached 700 while Europe's sat near 220. By June 2025, trade tensions began to erode this gap, bringing US outperformance since 2010 down to 88 percent of its peak level.

This page addresses the argument that US equities are overvalued compared to international equities by analyzing valuation in the context of corporate profitability. The author notes that while simple relative price-to-earnings or price-to-book multiples make the US appear expensive, this premium is justified because US companies are generally more profitable than their non-US counterparts. 

To illustrate this, the page features a scatter plot titled "S&P 500 vs developed world ex US" which maps the price-to-book ratio (ranging from 0 to 12 on the vertical axis) against consensus forward return on equity (ROE, ranging from 0% to 35% on the horizontal axis) for ten major economic sectors. The chart distinguishes between S&P 500 sectors, represented by blue dots, and MSCI World ex US sectors, represented by red dots. 

The data reveals a strong positive correlation, showing that the market is willing to pay higher book multiples for sectors that deliver higher returns. The S&P 500 sectors stretch upward and to the right, led by US Information Technology (IT) with a price-to-book ratio above 11 and a consensus forward ROE of approximately 32%. In contrast, the international IT sector sits much lower, with a price-to-book ratio of around 4 and an ROE of about 12%. Similarly, US Consumer Discretionary (CD) exhibits a price-to-book ratio near 8.5 and an ROE around 25%, whereas its international counterpart sits below a price-to-book of 2 with an ROE of approximately 10%. Other prominent US sectors like Consumer Staples (CS), Industrials (IN), and Health Care (HC) trade at elevated price-to-book multiples that align with their strong ROE values. Meanwhile, almost all MSCI World ex US sectors—including Energy (EN), Financials (FN), Materials (MT), Utilities (UT), and Communication Services (TC)—remain tightly clustered in the lower-left quadrant, generally featuring ROEs below 15% and price-to-book ratios under 4. Ultimately, the visual evidence suggests that the higher valuation multiples of US sectors are in line with their superior earnings power.

This page focuses on two core topics: the extraordinary financial dominance of the United States technology sector relative to Europe, and the persistent global hegemony of the United States dollar despite ongoing predictions of its decline.

The top portion of the page highlights the unmatched profitability of US technology and interactive media companies. A line chart tracing S&P 500 free cash flow margins from 1977 through 2025 shows that while the rest of the S&P 500 has maintained relatively flat margins fluctuating between 5% and 10%, the technology and interactive media sector has seen its margins soar from around 5% in the late 1970s to nearly 25% in recent years. Today, these high-performing tech stocks account for 35% of market-wide earnings, up significantly from 19% a decade ago. This domestic success is mirrored in a cumulative market capitalization chart tracking new public companies created in the 21st century, a visual inspired by a report by Mario Draghi on European competitiveness. This chart reveals an immense divergence: the United States has generated nearly 18 trillion dollars in cumulative market cap from around 200 new companies, led by massive players like Alphabet, Meta, Tesla, Visa, Mastercard, Netflix, Salesforce, T-Mobile, ServiceNow, and Accenture. In stark contrast, the European Union's curve remains nearly flat, barely reaching 2 trillion dollars in market cap from companies such as Industria de Diseno Textil, Airbus, Equinor, Porsche, and Adyen.

The bottom half of the page refutes claims that the US dollar is losing its global reserve currency status. A horizontal bar chart illustrates the international role of the dollar, demonstrating that its share of global financial markets is vastly disproportionate to the US share of world trade, which is roughly 10%, and global GDP, which is about 25%. A corresponding table tracks the US dollar share of global markets between 2022 and the latest available data up to mid-2025, revealing that the greenback's dominance has actually strengthened in several areas. Specifically, the dollar's share of cross-border loans rose from 50% in 2022 to 52% in the fourth quarter of 2024, and its share of international debt securities increased from 49% to 53% over the same period. SWIFT payments denominated in dollars experienced a significant jump from 42% in 2022 to 49% in October 2024. Meanwhile, FX transaction volume held steady at 88%, while official FX reserves saw a minor decline from 60% to 58%, and trade invoicing fell from 50% to 42%. Ultimately, the data indicates that despite deteriorating US fiscal dynamics, there are very few signs of the dollar losing its pre-eminent global position.

This page discusses the grading and performance of various generative artificial intelligence models when tested on historical finance and economics questions. Michael Cembalest evaluates how OpenAI’s GPT-4 and subsequent models handle 71 questions from the Eye on the Market archives covering markets, economics, politics, and energy. He highlights common flaws in language models, such as hallucinating numbers, incorrectly executing correct problem-solving steps, misreading data files, failing to exclude subtotals from calculations, and using incorrect constants for energy conversions. 

The evaluation is supported by four tables. The first table, titled Chat GPT-4 grading from September 2023, shows the distribution of grades for the initial 71 questions, which resulted in 26 A grades, 5 A- minus grades, 3 B grades, 3 B- minus grades, 2 C+ plus grades, 7 C grades, 2 C- minus grades, 13 D grades, 2 D- minus grades, and 8 F grades. The second table displays GPT-4's GPA by subject from the same period, showing a GPA of 2.62 for Economics, 2.31 for Markets, 2.70 for Energy, and 2.06 for Politics, leading to an overall GPA of 2.47. 

The third table, from May 2025, grades GPT-4o's performance specifically on the 23 questions that the original GPT-4 flunked with D or F grades. GPT-4o showed significant improvement, scoring 8 A grades, 2 A- minus grades, 1 B+ plus grade, 3 B grades, 1 B- minus grade, 1 C+ plus grade, 1 C grade, 1 C- minus grade, 1 D+ plus grade, 2 D grades, 2 D- minus grades, and no F grades. 

The fourth table, from June 2025, displays results from a "Best of AI" model grading approach on those same 23 questions. This approach routed the poorest-performing questions to alternative models, including Gemini 2.5, Claude Opus 4, and OpenAI o3, to select the best answer. This method further improved results, yielding 10 A grades, 2 A- minus grades, 3 B+ plus grades, 3 B grades, 2 B- minus grades, 1 C+ plus grade, 1 C grade, 1 D grade, and no other failing marks. 

Cembalest observes that while the best-of-model approach raised the overall GPA across all 71 questions to a 3.36, or a B+ grade, the process is too labor-intensive to justify for his daily work. He concludes that, for his purposes, the primary value of large language models remains finding sources and defining simple concepts.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses the resilience of the United States economy in 2023 and 2024 despite an aggressively inverted yield curve, drawing a parallel to the legend of Grigori Rasputin's survival skills. The author argues that while market commentators in 2023 were obsessed with the inverted yield curve as a recession predictor, the underlying macroeconomic context differed profoundly from past cycles, meaning no recession materialized. 

The analysis is supported by four charts. The first chart, titled Yield Curve Inversion Preceded All Recessions, plots the 10-year minus 3-month yield spread in basis points with 30-day smoothing from 1967 to 2022. It shows that although the spread historically dipped below zero before every recession, dropping past negative 100 basis points heading into 2023, the inversion alone was insufficient to trigger a downturn this time. 

The second chart, titled But Were Caused by a Higher Real Cost of Money, tracks real interest rates from 1957 to 2022, defined as the Federal Funds rate minus Core CPI with 21-day smoothing. It reveals that prior yield curve inversions were accompanied by high real interest rates that often peaked between 4 percent and 8 percent. In contrast, during the 2023 cycle, the Federal Reserve had barely brought real interest rates above 0 percent, meaning the real cost of money remained historically low.

The third chart, titled US Nonfinancial Corporate Net Interest Costs at 60 Year Low, spans from 1970 to past 2020 and compares the Federal Funds rate with corporate net interest payments as a percentage of after-tax NIPA profits. While the Fed funds rate spiked dramatically, corporate net interest payments as a share of profits actually fell to a near-record low of around 4 percent, demonstrating that the corporate sector had immunized itself against rising rates by extending its debt duration during the preceding decade of low interest rates.

The fourth chart, titled US Corporate Sector Financial Balance, tracks corporate financial balance as a percentage of corporate gross value added on a four-quarter average from 1960 to past 2020. This measure, representing gross savings less capital transfers, capital expenditures, and retained foreign profits, serves as a proxy for corporate cash flow. It shows that in prior recessions, corporate cash flows were deeply negative, dipping to negative 4 percent or negative 6 percent, which forced companies to slash spending. In 2023, however, the corporate sector was in a healthy cash-flow surplus, hovering above 0 percent. 

The author concludes that because corporations maintained strong cash flows and low interest burdens, the predicted recession of 2023 and 2024 never occurred, leaving recession indicators very benign heading into 2025 before the initiation of subsequent trade wars.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" addresses the decline of political moderates in the U.S. Congress and argues that this deep political polarization has contributed to falling economic growth and less effective, highly volatile policymaking. While demographic shifts like declining birthrates and rising longevity explain some of the post-war U.S. growth slowdown, the author asserts that the erosion of the political center has created a gridlocked, grandstanding legislative environment where major policies are repeatedly enacted and then repealed as party control shifts. 

To support this, a line chart displays the percentage of moderates in the House of Representatives from 1950 to 2010 alongside subsequent ten-year cumulative real GDP growth. The share of moderates—defined by a Voteview score between negative 0.25 and positive 0.25—remained robust near 40% through the 1970s before steadily collapsing to under 10% by 2010. This decline mirrors a long-term downward trend in subsequent ten-year cumulative real GDP growth, which fell from highs near 50% in the post-war decades to roughly 20% by the end of the timeline. 

This decline in legislative functionality is further detailed in a table showing congressional problem-solving metrics across three eras. Between the 92nd Congress (1971–1973) and the 111th Congress (2009–2011), the average number of witnesses testifying at congressional hearings dropped from fifteen to six. Simultaneously, the share of hearings dedicated to proposing solutions to complex national problems collapsed from 65% to a mere 20%, highlighting a shift away from rigorous policymaking toward partisan grandstanding.

A final, comprehensive chart tracks the partisanship of major U.S. legislation from 1913 to 2022, measuring partisanship as the level of support from the legislating party minus the support from the opposition party. The chart illustrates that historic mid-century legislation, such as the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, enjoyed broad bipartisan consensus with partisanship scores of 20% or lower. In stark contrast, modern landmark bills are passed with virtually no opposition support; legislation such as the Affordable Care Act, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, the American Rescue Plan Act, and the Inflation Reduction Act show partisanship scores spiking between 80% and nearly 100%. The author concludes that U.S. legislative partisanship has returned to extreme levels not seen in almost a century.

This page of the publication, authored by Michael Cembalest, discusses the pace and structural challenges of the global energy transition, arguing that decarbonization behaves as a slow, linear industrial transition rather than an accelerating one. Reflecting on his years working with technical consultant Vaclav Smil, the author contrasts the current renewable transition with past rapid industrial shifts and highlights key bottlenecks in electrification and mineral supply chains.

The top-left line chart, titled "Decarbonization is a linear industrial transition," plots the renewable share of final energy consumption from 1990 to 2025 across Europe, China, the US, and Asia excluding Japan and China. It demonstrates that progress is linear and slow, with leading Europe rising at only about 0.6% per year to reach approximately 14% by 2023, while the US and China hover below 10%. To contrast this, the top-right chart, titled "Rapid energy-saving steel transition of the 1960s/1970s," traces global steel production shares from 1920 to 2020. This chart shows how open hearth production plummeted from nearly 80% in 1960 to near zero by 2000, rapidly replaced by basic oxygen steelmaking, which surged to over 60% by 1980, and electric arc furnaces, which rose to around 30% by 2020. The author notes this historical transition was remarkably fast because basic oxygen technology reduced energy use and production times by 80% to 90%, allowing the shift to pay for itself. In contrast, today’s renewable transition has required nine trillion US dollars in global spending since 2010 just to maintain its slow linear pace, meaning that human prosperity will remain reliant on natural gas for many years.

The bottom-left chart, titled "US grid decarbonization outpaces electrification of energy use," compares the electricity share of final energy consumption with the renewable share of electricity generation in the US from 1990 to 2025. While the renewable share of electricity generation has risen steadily from around 10% in 2010 to nearly 25% by 2024, the overall electricity share of final energy consumption has remained stagnant at around 30% since 2000. The author points out that until final energy uses are electrified, the decarbonization of the power grid cannot translate to broad decarbonization. Finally, the bottom-right bar chart, titled "Share of refined material production by country, 2024," illustrates China's overwhelming dominance in critical minerals essential for the transition. Based on IEA data, China controls roughly 90% of refined production for graphite and rare earths, around 75% for cobalt, 65% for lithium, 45% for copper, and 35% for nickel, highlighting the deep geopolitical concentration of the green energy supply chain.

This page from the publication addresses the massive scale and economic risks of capital spending on artificial intelligence, highlighting how the current boom compares to historical technological revolutions. The author argues that we are witnessing the "bet of the century," driven by major technology firms spending immense capital to build AI infrastructure. 

To support this, the page features three charts and one comparison table. The first chart, "AI capital spending in context," shows NVIDIA's data center revenues as a share of market-wide capital spending from 2020 through 2026 estimates, juxtaposed with historical benchmarks. While NVIDIA's share was near 1% in 2020, it is projected to approach 14% by 2026. This trajectory puts it in the company of historical peaks, such as IBM's mainframe peak revenue share of approximately 17% in 1969 and the combined peak of Cisco, Lucent, and Nortel at around 13% in 2000 during the dot-com boom.

The second chart, "Hyperscaler capex and R&D as a share of revenues," tracks spending from 2017 to 2025 for Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon. It illustrates that capital outlays are climbing, with Meta leading the volatility. Meta’s spending spiked to nearly 65% of revenue during its metaverse investment phase in late 2022, plummeted, and is rising again toward 60% by 2025. Microsoft and Alphabet show a steadier but clear upward trend, rising from historical bands around 20% to 25% toward 35% by 2025. Combined, spending from these four companies is projected to grow 35% from $440 billion in 2024 to $596 billion in 2025.

The third chart, "Hyperscaler free cash flow margins," tracks the underlying profitability of these same four companies over the same period. It demonstrates highly volatile free cash flow margins, with Amazon dropping below -10% in late 2022 before recovering, and Meta showing a steep dip in late 2022. The chart emphasizes that these companies' cash generation is highly sensitive to their massive spending cycles.

Finally, a comparison table titled "Magnificent 7 stocks vs S&P 493" highlights the divergence and future outlook of these market leaders. Over the last five years, the Magnificent 7 achieved an annualized sales growth of 31% and price returns of 39%, compared to just 6% sales growth and 11% price returns for the S&P 493. The Magnificent 7 also boast a superior free cash flow margin of 26% and net profit margin of 24%, compared to 16% and 9% respectively for the S&P 493. Crucially, the table reveals a dramatic expected slowdown: while the Magnificent 7's annualized operating earnings growth was 43% over the last five years, the two-year forward consensus operating earnings growth is projected to slow to just 11%, barely ahead of the S&P 493's projected 9%. This expected deceleration, the author notes, is partly a consequence of depreciating the immense, newly built AI infrastructure. Ultimately, while corporate surveys indicate growing interest in AI, the central open question is whether companies will generate enough actual revenue to justify the massive, risky capital outlays of the hyperscalers.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Eye on the Market discusses how the policies of Donald Trump draw from various historical precedents established by past American presidents. The author notes that these presidential portraits and descriptions have been used in client presentations since February 2025 to frame modern policy proposals through a historical lens. 

The page features painted portraits of seven former U.S. presidents, organized into two rows, each captioned with the specific policy themes they represent. In the top row, Andrew Jackson is associated with establishing a new political order and waging battles against the deep state; James Polk is linked to the concept of Manifest Destiny within the Western Hemisphere; and William McKinley represents a precedent of tariffs and economic protectionism. In the bottom row, Woodrow Wilson is paired with prewar isolationism; Calvin Coolidge represents small-government, pro-business policies; Dwight Eisenhower is connected to lower corporate taxes, large-scale deportation efforts, and infrastructure investments; and Richard Nixon is associated with political enemies lists, personal vendettas, and aspirations for national energy independence.

This page from the publication addresses the public messaging and notable "surges" of the Biden-Harris administration, questioning whether Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen was an effective public advocate compared to her predecessors. To illustrate her low public profile, a Google Trends chart tracks the search index for the Treasury Secretary by month of presidency on a scale from 0 to 100. The data shows that Donald Trump's Treasury Secretary, Steven Mnuchin, maintained a much larger digital footprint, with major spikes peaking near 100 around month 43. In contrast, Janet Yellen’s search index remained extremely low, mostly staying below 20 after an initial spike to 40 at the beginning of her tenure. The author notes that this muted media presence occurred despite positive economic talking points she could have championed, such as near-record labor force participation, a surge in manufacturing reshoring driven by the CHIPS Act, and exceptional year-to-date equity gains.

The focus then shifts to what the author calls the "Biden surges," which include inflation, troop deployments in Eastern Europe, federal regulations, and immigration. A chart on the left illustrates the cumulative number of economically significant rules enacted by month of presidency, comparing administrations from Ronald Reagan through Joe Biden. The Biden administration clearly outpaces its predecessors, cumulative rules rising sharply to over 300 by month 45. For comparison, the Trump administration ended its comparable period near 250 rules after a flat period during COVID-19, while the Reagan administration issued the fewest, ending at approximately 50. 

A companion chart on the right depicts net immigration from 2001 through 2024, measuring both monthly rates (up to 400,000) and equivalent annual rates (up to 4.8 million). The chart distinguishes between authorized immigrants (lawful permanent residents and students, shaded in blue) and unauthorized immigrants (illegal entrants and refugees, shaded in red). It highlights a massive and unprecedented spike in unauthorized immigration beginning in 2021, which peaked near an annual rate of 4.2 million (or 350,000 monthly) in late 2023, a surge that heavily impacted major city budgets. 

The page concludes by highlighting "Prediction #3" from the author's Top Ten Surprises list for 2024, published on January 1, 2024, which forecasted that President Biden would withdraw from the presidential race between Super Tuesday and the general election due to health reasons.

This page explores the escalating legal battles and systemic challenges surrounding the Trump Administration’s executive orders, detailing the surge in executive actions and subsequent lawsuits, the history of nationwide injunctions, and specific judicial setbacks regarding executive orders targeted at law firms. 

The first chart, titled "Executive Orders and Federal lawsuits in first 100 days," compares executive order counts against lawsuits filed against the president across several administrations. In his second term, President Trump’s executive orders reached nearly 140, accompanied by a nearly equal volume of approximately 130 lawsuits. This represents a significant escalation from Trump’s first term, which saw around 30 executive orders but over 70 lawsuits in the first 100 days. By comparison, the Biden administration had about 40 executive orders and roughly 20 lawsuits, while Obama 2, Obama 1, and Bush 2 registered even lower counts of early-term litigation. 

To the right, a second chart titled "A history of nationwide injunctions by Federal judges" illustrates the dramatic rise in judicial blocks of presidential policies. While the entire 20th century saw only 27 nationwide injunctions, they surged during Trump’s first term, reaching 86 according to Congressional Research Service (CRS) data, 64 according to Harvard data, and 55 according to Department of Justice (DoJ) data. In the first 100 days of Trump's second term, federal judges had already issued 25 nationwide injunctions, compared to 14 throughout the entire Biden administration. The text notes that while nationwide injunctions have been a primary tool for Democrats to counter administration policies, a June 2025 Supreme Court ruling restricted relief solely to the specific plaintiffs bringing a lawsuit. This decision makes "jurisdiction-shopping" by political parties far more difficult, even as plaintiffs attempt to pivot by converting their challenges into class-action lawsuits.

At the bottom of the page, a detailed table titled "DC District Courts issued permanent injunctions and declaratory judgments suspending the following Executive Orders" highlights a "0 for 4" track record for the administration's "law firm executive orders." The table documents challenges by major law firms Jenner & Block, WilmerHale, Susman Godfrey, and Perkins Coie against Executive Orders 14246, 14250, 14263, and 14230, respectively. In each instance, the court permanently enjoined every single provision, including suspending security clearances, ending agency representation, canceling contracts, barring firm personnel from federal buildings, and banning the government from hiring firm personnel. The rulings were handed down by Judges Bates, Leon, AliKhan, and Howell, who were appointed by presidents George W. Bush, Biden, and Obama. One judge described the administration's actions as "an unconstitutional act of retaliation" meant to chill legal representation. The text concludes by noting that these judicial defeats, alongside rulings against Trump’s reciprocal and fentanyl tariffs, have reportedly triggered a public split between President Trump and the conservative Federalist Society due to Republican-appointed judges ruling against the administration.

This page features a personal reflection from Michael Cembalest on his early career at J.P. Morgan, which he joined in 1987, alongside two supporting charts that illustrate the shifting social and technological trends of the era. Cembalest recounts meeting his wife Rachel, a more senior colleague running Latin American Capital Markets, and gaining her attention by building a three-dimensional surface plot using Lotus 1-2-3 macros. He reflects on how much has changed since then regarding workplace dating rules and technological dominance. He shares an anecdote about being transferred from the Emerging Markets trading floor to Asset Management under Nick Rohatyn after the couple was spotted sharing candy in the lunchroom, as well as a humorous story about being excluded from a Managing Director dinner hosted by his wife at their home in 1997 because he was still only a Vice President, which fueled his drive for promotion.

The narrative is paired with two line charts. The first chart, titled "How heterosexual couples meet, 1940-2019," tracks the percentage of couples meeting through various avenues. It highlights the dramatic rise of meeting "Online," which surged from near 0% in the mid-1990s to nearly 40% by 2019, becoming the most common meeting method. In contrast, traditional methods like meeting "Via friends" declined from a peak of nearly 40% in 1990 to around 20% in 2019, while meeting "As coworkers" peaked near 20% in the late 1980s and 1990s before steadily falling. Other categories such as meeting "Via family," "Church," and "Neighbors" show long-term declines over the depicted period.

The second chart, titled "Revenue share of spreadsheet market, 1988-1997," visualizes the rapid displacement of Lotus 1-2-3 by Microsoft Excel. In 1988, Lotus 1-2-3 dominated the market with a revenue share of around 70%, while Excel held roughly 10%. By 1997, this dynamic had completely reversed, with Excel capturing nearly 90% of the market share and Lotus 1-2-3 plummeting to about 10%. The third competitor shown, Quattro, remained stable but low, never exceeding 15% market share during the decade.

This page highlights medical breakthroughs made possible by machine learning, focusing on two primary areas: protein folding and the discovery of a new class of antibiotics. 

The author begins by detailing how Google and DeepMind’s AlphaFold algorithm has revolutionized protein mapping. Traditionally, determining the three-dimensional shapes of enzymes and proteins required years of work and millions of dollars using MRI and x-ray crystallography; consequently, only 20% of proteins were mapped as of 2021. Today, AlphaFold can perform this task in hours at minimal cost, resulting in 99% of proteins being mapped. The first graphic on the page illustrates this capability, showing the complex, winding shape of a DNA replication enzyme with the actual structural design in green perfectly aligned with AlphaFold’s predicted design in blue. 

The text then shifts to the discovery of a potential new class of antibiotics to treat MRSA, a staph infection responsible for 70,000 severe illnesses and 7,000 deaths each year. Researchers Jim Collins of MIT/Harvard and Felix Wong of Integrated Biosciences trained an AI model on 39,000 molecular compounds to understand their antibacterial properties and toxicity. Using neural networks, they screened 12 million commercially available compounds, narrowing the list down to 10,000 potential candidates, then to 280 candidates based on toxicity and structural uniqueness, and ultimately finding two highly promising compounds currently being tested on mice. This process is illustrated by the second visual on the page: a dense, circular cluster map where distance and color represent antibacterial activity and non-toxicity. Dark green and black dots indicate the highest-scoring novel compounds with no unfavorable substructures, while two purple dots point directly to the best-performing candidates in lab testing, labeled "Compounds 1 and 2."

Lastly, the author references similar AI-driven breakthroughs, including work at McMaster University where researchers screened billions of molecules to identify six promising candidates to combat the antibiotic-resistant bacterium *Acinetobacter baumannii*. Additionally, the page notes that AI diagnostics are being used with retinal cameras to allow low-trained clinicians to immediately detect early signs of diabetic retinopathy.

This page is a visual compilation consisting of a twelve-panel grid of colorful and stylized editorial illustrations from J.P. Morgan's "Eye on the Market" publications. The images depict various economic, environmental, and financial themes covered in the reports. 

The illustrations include:
- A tropical beach covered in signposts with economic indicators such as gross national debt, real GDP growth, and stimulus measures.
- A dark, industrial scene of workers processing heavy crates representing taxpayers, state pensions, and the IRS.
- A person bundled up on a snow-covered park bench surrounded by floating coronavirus particles.
- A boat on the water under a night sky where constellations list emerging green technologies like nuclear fusion, quantum glass batteries, and carbon-neutral liquid fuels.

Collectively, these panels represent key themes of climate change, technology, monetary policy, and market trends analyzed by Michael Cembalest.

This page evaluates the real-world implications of relaxing certain US bank capital regulations, specifically the Supplementary Leverage Ratio, for the eight domestic systemically important banks. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that the impact of the Federal Reserve's proposal to reduce the supplementary leverage ratio from five percent to a range of three point five to four point five percent would be far less significant than expected. This is because banks are constrained by multiple capital ratios, and if one is relaxed, another quickly becomes the binding limit. 

This dynamic is illustrated in two scatter charts at the top of the page. Both charts measure excess Tier 1 capital by ratio, comparing current capital minus the minimum required capital as a percentage of current capital across JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, BNY Mellon, and State Street. The first chart, showing current rules, plots four ratios: Tier 1 Leverage, Tier 1 Capital-Advanced, Tier 1 Capital-Standard, and the Supplementary Leverage Ratio. It shows that the supplementary leverage ratio is only the most binding constraint—represented by the lowest dot—for Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, BNY Mellon, and State Street, with other ratios closely behind. The second chart shows that under revised rules, while the supplementary leverage ratio dots shift upward, other ratios immediately become the active binding constraint for almost all eight banks. 

Consequently, a bar chart on the bottom left demonstrates that excess Tier 1 capital across these eight institutions would only increase by a marginal six billion dollars in total, rising from one hundred twenty-four billion to one hundred thirty billion dollars. The visual shows that individual banks like JPMorgan, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America see virtually no change in their excess capital, which severely limits the potential for new stock buybacks or expanded risky asset lending.

However, a major change would occur on paper regarding the banks' theoretical capacity to purchase zero-risk-weight assets, such as US Treasury bonds. A final bar chart on the bottom right shows that under revised rules, treasury buying capacity would increase sharply across all eight banks. In aggregate, this capacity would jump from two point seven trillion dollars under current rules to approximately eight trillion dollars. For example, Bank of America's buying capacity would rise from around zero point five trillion to nearly two trillion dollars, and Wells Fargo's would increase from around zero point eight trillion to over one point five trillion dollars. Despite this massive theoretical expansion, the author poses an open question as to whether these banks would actually step in to buy Treasuries during a sudden demand collapse, noting that they currently hold ample unused capacity that they have chosen not to utilize.

In this page of Eye on the Market, Michael Cembalest addresses three distinct topics: J.P. Morgan's blockchain initiatives, AI voice cloning fraud risks, and his upcoming personal fishing trips. 

First, he evaluates whether J.P. Morgan's blockchain projects, such as its new intraday repo settlement system called Kinexys, suggest investors should build positions in Ethereum. Cembalest argues they do not yet support this, noting that Kinexys was built on a fork of Ethereum with no direct connection or tolling revenues back to the Ethereum network. He highlights that Kinexys handles just 2 billion dollars in daily volume compared to J.P. Morgan's 10 trillion dollars in traditional daily payments. However, he notes that future public blockchain products from the firm could leverage Ethereum, its Layer 2 chains, or competitors like Solana. He also mentions JPMD, a permissioned stablecoin-like deposit token offered on Base, which is a Coinbase Layer 2 on Ethereum, which could eventually provide incidental benefits to Ethereum holders. 

Second, Cembalest discusses Sam Altman’s warning from a Federal Reserve conference regarding an impending fraud crisis caused by AI voice cloning. With cloning tools requiring as little as three seconds of audio, traditional voice authentication is at risk. He outlines various defensive tools used by banks, including AI deepfake detectors like Reality Defender, in-app push notifications, digital payment verification via mobile apps, SIM-swap and call-forwarding detection services, and behavioral pattern recognition for unusual payment characteristics. 

Finally, Cembalest shares his upcoming fishing schedule, which includes catching sturgeon in British Columbia in late August and tarpon at Bocas del Dragon in Trinidad in November. The page features two photos from prior trips showing a fisherman in a yellow Hobie Mirage Outback kayak proudly displaying a very large sturgeon in one image and a silver tarpon in the other.

This page examines the latest developments in US tariffs and their potential unforeseen consequences. Although a US-EU trade deal has somewhat softened the outlook compared to a month prior, projected US tariff rates are still expected to reach their highest levels since before World War II. The author highlights several critical, unresolved questions, such as the actual compliance rate of US trade with Mexico and Canada under the USMCA, the scale of import substitution away from China, pending Section 232 investigations on pharmaceuticals and semiconductors, and the potential impact of ongoing legal appeals in the DC Circuit and Federal Circuit courts. While Yale's Budget Lab estimates that current tariffs could raise up to $230 billion annually in revenue, the author warns that protecting a small number of upstream steel and aluminum workers could negatively impact roughly fifty times as many workers in downstream industries. Furthermore, rising costs for raw materials and intermediate capital goods could complicate US efforts to build out artificial intelligence and energy infrastructure, even as firms like Piper Sandler project an domestic capital spending boom due to onshoring.

To illustrate these trends, the page features a series of charts and a detailed data table. A line chart showing the average tariff rate on all US imports from 1900 to 2025 reveals a sharp upward spike in the 2020s, climbing toward the 15% to 20% range after decades of holding below 5%. This dramatic spike is driven by a combination of active and contested tariffs, a 25% global auto tariff, 50% steel and aluminum tariffs, a 10% reciprocal tariff, and targeted fentanyl tariffs on China, Canada, and Mexico. 

An accompanying table details the estimated final destination tariff rates by exporting country as of July 2025. It highlights major partners like Mexico, with $506 billion in imports, seeing its tariff rate rise from 0.2% in 2024 to an estimated 7.7% in 2025; China, with $439 billion in imports, facing a massive surge from 10.7% to 43.2%; and Canada, with $413 billion in imports, rising from 0.1% to 2.5%. Other notable projected tariff jumps include Vietnam rising to 18.6%, South Korea to 21.1%, Germany to 16.0%, and Thailand to 24.4%.

Two bar charts at the bottom of the page analyze the domestic fallout of these policies. The first compares the number of steel and aluminum manufacturing employees in 2022, contrasting a very small "upstream" workforce—such as the 3,848 workers in aluminum refining—with the millions of "downstream" employees working in fabricated metal, machinery, and transportation equipment manufacturing who rely on these metals as raw materials. The second bar chart plots the effective tariff rate on the largest categories of US capital and intermediate goods imports. It reveals high tariff barriers for critical high-tech and energy infrastructure components, including pending tariffs near 35% on semiconductor manufacturing machinery, over 20% on microchips and semi devices, and roughly 25% to 30% on batteries, transformers, and power converters, while raw resources like crude oil and refined fuel remain near 0%.

In this commentary, Michael Cembalest addresses the assertion by Charles Gave of Gavekal that the US dollar has lost its status as the world's reserve currency. Cembalest counters this claim, arguing that while the dollar declined five to ten percent in 2025, it did so from highly elevated levels. To support this, a chart of the Fed Trade Weighted Real Dollar, Fed Trade Weighted Nominal Dollar, and Spot Dollar Index from 1973 to 2025 demonstrates that the dollar's recent pullback is minor when viewed against its long-term historical strength. 

Further evidence is presented in a table tracking the US dollar’s share of global markets, comparing 2022 to the latest available data through mid-2025.
