Other critical minerals with high US import reliance from China include Yttrium (one hundred percent US reliance, ninety-three percent from China for jet engine coatings and radar), Dysprosium (eighty percent US reliance, seventy percent from China for F-35 jet magnets and wind turbines), Samarium, Gadolinium, Lutetium, Scandium, Thulium, Ytterbium, Europium, Tungsten, Bismuth, and Indium. 

To illustrate why US tariff threats may have limited efficacy, a horizontal bar chart on the right displays revenue exposure for Chinese industries, demonstrating that very few Chinese sectors depend on exports to the US. Across categories such as consumer electronics, electrical equipment, toys, automobiles, and general machinery, the vast majority of revenue is generated domestically, with other non-US export revenues forming a smaller share and direct US export revenues representing a tiny fraction of the total. 

Finally, a comparative table at the bottom highlights how China has mirrored the US national security toolkit, showing Chinese analogs to US policies. For instance, China uses rare earths and magnets to counter US controls on lithography and semiconductors. China's Unreliable Entity List matches US Commerce and Treasury lists; its anti-foreign sanctions laws mirror the IEEPA and Magnitsky Act; cybersecurity, antitrust, and data transfer reviews mirror CFIUS, ICTS, and FCC reviews; and port fees on US vessels mirror Section 301, 232, and 122 tariffs.

This page of the publication, written by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the disruptive impact of generative AI on the entertainment industry's content creation moat. The author argues that while the prior decade was defined by disruption in content distribution, the next decade will be defined by disruption in content creation, creating substantial opportunities and risks for legacy media companies. Historically protected by high distribution and infrastructure costs, legacy entertainment saw its distribution moat fall with the rise of unbundled streaming. Consequently, combined video-related profits of major media companies—including CBS, Discovery, Disney, Fox, NBC Universal, Viacom, and Warner Media—fell 38% between 2018 and 2023, before rebounding slightly to a 27% decline through 2024.

Four charts illustrate these shifting dynamics. The first line chart, titled "Streaming earnings," plots net income and losses in billions of dollars from 2019 to 2023. It shows Netflix net income rising steadily from approximately $2 billion to over $5 billion. In contrast, the major studios—including Disney, NBCU, Warner Bros Discovery, and Paramount—saw their direct-to-consumer losses widen from negative $2 billion in 2019 to a bottom of nearly negative $10 billion in 2022, before recovering slightly to around negative $7 billion in 2023. 

The second chart, "Viewing time of top 100 streaming titles, 2023," shows monthly percentages of viewing time across different categories. Although Netflix's share from original content declined from 34% in January to 20% in December, its overall share remained stable between 50% and 55% due to legacy studios licensing their popular content, shown by large shares of Netflix exclusive and nonexclusive acquisitions compared to other non-Netflix platforms.

The third visual, an area chart titled "Share of US TV viewing time" from January 2023 to July 2025, highlights the decline of traditional television. Legacy broadcast and cable fell from 57.4% to 42.3%, while Netflix grew from 7.5% to 8.6%, and all other streaming platforms (such as YouTube) expanded from 24.8% to 37.7%. 

The final stacked bar chart, "US video revenue, traditional vs new," displays revenue from 2011 to 2024. It demonstrates that total industry revenue is virtually flat compared to 2018, remaining just above $200 billion. The growth of streaming revenue has merely offset the steady decline of traditional TV, box office, and home entertainment, proving that the overall revenue pie is barely growing. 

The page concludes with a notice for an upcoming biennial Alternative Investments Review covering buyouts, venture capital, hedge funds, private credit, real estate, and secondary funds.

This page explores whether AI generative video models are learning physical laws or simply predicting pixels, centering on Google DeepMind’s Physics-IQ benchmark. A bar chart displaying Physics-IQ scores reveals that physical understanding remains low across all evaluated models; VideoPoet (multiframe) scores the highest at approximately 28%, followed by Lumiere and Runway Gen 3, while OpenAI's Sora 1 scores around 14%. DeepMind researchers express optimism that scaling training datasets will continue to improve physical comprehension over time. The page also features a visual comparison illustrating the rapid progress of Midjourney’s text-to-image capabilities from February 2022 (V1) to July 2024 (V6.1), demonstrating a massive leap in rendering realism.

This page analyzes the structural headwinds facing the legacy film and television industries, specifically pointing to a sharp decline in cable TV viewership among younger cohorts and a sluggish post-pandemic box office recovery compared to other hospitality and leisure sectors. The author argues that while the traditional distribution moat has weakened, the cost of high-end content creation remains incredibly high, even as new, low-cost digital platforms compete for consumer attention. 

To support this argument, the first chart measures legacy TV viewing time (excluding sports) compared to 2015 levels. It reveals a dramatic generational split: while the 50+ demographic has retained nearly 90% of its viewing time, the overall index has slid to roughly 60%, dragged down by a drop in the 18-49 demographic to around 35%, and a near-total collapse of the 2-17 demographic to roughly 10% to 15% of 2015 levels by 2023. 

The struggle is mirrored in the theatrical market, as shown in a chart detailing annual US domestic box office results from 1995 to 2025. Annual ticket sales peaked at over 1.4 billion in the early 2000s and held near 1.2 billion until the pandemic. By 2025, annualized ticket sales had recovered to only about 700 million, while total box office receipts hovered near $8 billion, down from their pre-pandemic peak of over $11 billion. 

A comparison of recovery rates relative to 2019 levels across various sectors highlights how far behind the film industry lags. While US restaurant revenues, average daily hotel rates, and airline passengers have rebounded to 110% to 130% of pre-pandemic levels, film industry box office receipts and tickets sold sit at the bottom of the recovery list, lagging between 60% and 75%—even underperforming the 10-city back-to-work office recovery rate. 

These trends have driven divergent performances for major media stocks in an index starting in January 2022. Streaming giant Netflix has massively outperformed, climbing past an index level of 200 by late 2025. Fox also showed resilience, rising to nearly 150. However, legacy media companies like Disney, Warner Brothers Discovery, Comcast, and Paramount have severely underperformed both the broader S&P 500 (ex-Mag 7 and ex-info tech indices) and their 2022 baselines, with several languishing between 50 and 75 index points.

Finally, the author notes that while legacy distribution is fading, the barrier to entry for content creation remains steep. A chart tracking the median budgets of top-grossing films at the domestic box office shows that median budgets for top-10 films remain high at around $150 million, top-20 films cost around $130 million, and top-50 films average around $75 million. Highly popular television series like Wandavision, Hawkeye, The Rings of Power, and Stranger Things regularly exceed $25 million per episode. This high-budget environment creates a daunting content moat for traditional competitors, though the author poses an open warning that newer, fast-growing platforms competing for viewer attention do not require these massive capital investments.

This page explores the rapid advancement and decreasing costs of AI text-to-video generation tools. The author highlights that benchmarks like VBench show open-source options, such as HPC-AI's Open-Sora 2.0, can create videos of comparable quality to proprietary models like OpenAI's Sora 1.0 at just ten percent of the training cost, or around two hundred thousand dollars. Although these open-source videos are currently limited to five seconds in length, the technology is progressing so quickly that AI-generated digital actresses, like Particle6's Tilly Norwood, are already seeking talent representation. The author emphasizes that newer programs like OpenAI's Sora 2.0, LTX, and Google's VEO 3.1 are rapidly eclipsing models that were state-of-the-art only months ago.

The page features two charts comparing video model capabilities and a leaderboard table. The first visual is a polar chart titled "VBench evaluation of video generation models," which maps the capabilities of OpenAI Sora 1.0 alongside three Chinese programs—Hunyuan, CogVideoX-1.5, and Kling 1.6—across multiple categories such as human anatomy, camera motion, complex plots, and physical mechanics. To its right, a bar chart displays "Video generation model VBench scores," comparing total, quality, and semantic scores on a scale of 70 to 86. The data series include OpenAI Sora 1, HPC-AI Open-Sora 2.0, HunyuanVideo, CogVideo, and HPC-AI Open-Sora 1.2, showing that the lower-cost Open-Sora 2.0 closely rivals OpenAI Sora 1 across all metrics. At the bottom of the page, the "LMArena text-to-video leaderboard" ranks twenty models based on user preference. Google dominates the top of the list, with Google veo-3.1-audio ranking first with a preliminary score of 1404, followed closely by Google veo-3.1-fast-audio at 1395 and OpenAI sora-2-pro at 1365. Other competitive entries on the leaderboard are fielded by companies like KlingAI, MiniMax, Bytedance, Alibaba, Luma AI, Pika, and Genmo AI.

This page examines the democratization of high-quality content creation, arguing that the combination of generative AI tools and shifting consumer standards is disrupting traditional media. AI text-to-video tools like Pika, Runway, Stable Diffusion, and Sora are making it cheaper and easier for new creators to produce appealing digital and television content. Highlighting the scale of this disruption, the text notes that Hollywood produced roughly 15,000 hours of TV and film in 2023, compared to 300 million hours uploaded to YouTube. If viewers find just 0.01% of YouTube's content as interesting as traditional programming, it would double Hollywood's annual output. This shift is mirrored in the music industry, where the independent and creator share of Spotify music streams grew from 13% to 29% between 2017 and 2024. Ultimately, consumers are becoming more comfortable with lower-fidelity, user-generated content alongside polished, high-production values, a trend comparable to how low-bitrate MP3s previously replaced CDs.

Four charts support these observations on shifting media consumption. The first chart, depicting the media company share of television screen time as of August 2025, shows YouTube leading all distributors with roughly 12% of total broadcast, cable, and streaming watch time. This puts YouTube ahead of traditional media giants and streaming services, including Disney at nearly 10%, Netflix at around 8%, and NBCUniversal at 7.5%. The second chart, illustrating US weekly news consumption by source from 2013 to 2025, shows that social and video networks have steadily risen to over 50%, overtaking traditional television, which fell below 50% over the same period. Print media experienced a sharp decline to under 15% by 2025, while newer options like news podcasts, radio, and AI news hovered between 10% and 20% at the end of the period.

The third chart tracks global media revenue between 2019 and 2023, comparing corporate media with the creator economy. The creator share of the total media economy, indicated by a rising red line, nearly doubled from about 7% in 2019 to approximately 14% in 2023, while the total creator media economy grew to roughly $200 billion out of a nearly $1.6 trillion total market. The final chart contrasts the percentage of US video gamers with Roblox's daily active users from 2018 to 2025. It reveals that while the overall share of US gamers has remained stagnant, fluctuating around 70% to 75% of the population, Roblox's daily active users have climbed dramatically from about 3 million in 2018 to over 20 million by 2025, underscoring the strong consumer pull toward lower-fidelity, user-generated platforms.

This page argues that technological developments, particularly virtual production and generative AI, present notable cost-saving opportunities for legacy film studios rather than just competitive threats. Citing a 2023 analysis by Bain & Company, the text explains that virtual production can significantly reduce production times and costs, particularly for higher-budget movies, family films, sci-fi sequels, and animation. Savings are driven by technological innovations such as post-production colorization, markerless motion capture, automated rotoscoping and background removal, and the real-time rendering of physical set elements against LED volume backgrounds. The author positions generative AI as the next logical step in a long lineage of cinema innovations, spanning from King Kong's stop-motion in 1933 to the underwater motion capture of Avatar II in 2023.

A column chart illustrates the projected percentage range of time and cost savings from adopting virtual production methods across different film categories. For a fifty-million-dollar comedy, both time and cost savings are expected to range from five percent to ten percent. For a one-hundred-million-dollar family film, time savings rise to twenty percent, while cost savings range between fifteen and twenty percent. At the high end, a two-hundred-million-dollar sci-fi film is projected to experience time savings of twenty-five percent and cost savings between fifteen and twenty percent. 

The page also features a table listing notable startup AI animation studios that are actively seeking to disrupt the industry. Animaj, backed by HarbourView, has developed the AI-assisted work Pocoyo, which generates one billion views per month on YouTube. AiMation, supported by private equity, is working on Where the Robots Grow, while Animated Co has pre-seed funding for The Myth. Asteria, backed by Moonvalley, has worked on titles like Uncanny Valley, Love Letter to LA, and Odd Birds. Invisible Universe, which boasts backing from SevenSevenSix, SV Angel, Initialized Capital, Serena Williams, and Jennifer Aniston, produces Qai-Qai. Native Foreign works independently on Critterz, and Promise, backed by North Road, Andreessen Horowitz, Google AI, Crossbeam, Saga, and Kivu, has projects in development. Finally, Toonstar, backed by Founders Fund, Snap, and Greycroft, has produced StEvEn & Parker, which has accumulated eight billion views. 

The thematic undercurrent of these disruptions is captured in an illustration titled "Richard III sitting on top of a crumbling content moat." The image depicts a dejected, crowned king sitting atop a decaying, stone wall with a distant castle in the background, symbolizing how the traditional "content moats" of major studios are being eroded by emerging AI and virtual production technologies.

Michael Cembalest reflects on the survival of traditional film studios, expressing a hope that their "content moat" persists in an increasingly complex media landscape. Utilizing data from his personal Letterboxd account, where he has rated over 400 films, he presents a table listing 29 of his top-ranked 21st-century films, excluding documentaries, that received a score of either 4.5 or 5.0 out of a maximum of 5.0. Cembalest notes that while the ratio of worldwide box office receipts to production budgets remains a useful rough indicator of a film's success, these multiples have become less accurate in the streaming era due to opaque licensing fees, direct-to-streaming models, and alternative screening outlets like Patreon. 

The accompanying table lists these top-rated films chronologically from 2000 to 2025, detailing the release year, Cembalest’s ranking, the producing studios, and the box office-to-budget ratio. The data reveals highly lucrative theatrical releases, led by *Lost in Translation* (2003) with a remarkable box office multiple of 29.3, followed by *Three Billboards* (2017) at 13.4, *Last King of Scotland* (2006) at 8.2, and *The Artist* (2011) at 8.0. In contrast, several highly ranked films reflect the changing dynamics of modern distribution with ratios of 0.0, including Netflix's *Mank* (2020) and A24's *The Tragedy of Macbeth* (2021). Other featured films include recent releases like *The Ballad of Wallis Island* (2025, ratio of 4.0), *All of Us Strangers* (2023, ratio of 4.4), and *Anatomy of a Fall* (2023, ratio of 7.4), alongside older favorites such as *Memento* (2000, ratio of 7.9) and *In Bruges* (2008, ratio of 2.3). 

A concluding footnote lists several of Cembalest's favorite documentary subjects, highlighting films focused on Jeff Buckley, Luther Vandross, Robert Downey Sr., Louis Kahn, Robert Evans, Glen Campbell, Humphrey Bogart, Sam Harkness, and the documentary *My Octopus Teacher*.

This page argues that legacy content creators hold a distinct advantage over user-generated content due to the enduring value of professional storytelling, particularly as manifested in deep movie and TV episode libraries. The text notes that smaller studios have increasingly taken over the storytelling mantle as larger studios exhibit capital discipline. It cites major industry deals to illustrate the massive premium placed on libraries, such as Amazon valuing MGM’s catalog at $3.4 billion, Disney’s $87 billion in acquisitions (including Pixar, Marvel, Lucasfilm, and Fox), and Netflix’s rumored interest in acquiring Warner Bros' studio and streaming assets (which include Harry Potter, DC Comics, and Game of Thrones).

Four visual exhibits support this thesis. The first chart, "Nationwide movie releases by year," tracks film releases from 1995 to 2025. It shows that releases from the "Major 6" studios (Warner Bros, Disney, Fox, Paramount, and Universal) have trended downward from around 120 annually in the late 1990s to about 70 in 2025. Conversely, releases from "Other studios" have risen dramatically, particularly after a pandemic-era dip, spiking to over 100 releases by 2025.

The second chart, "Platform catalog share of industry content," displays horizontal bars representing content share as of the first quarter of 2024, split between series and movies. Netflix leads the industry with a total content share of roughly 27%, followed by Amazon Prime Video at about 23%. Hulu, Max, Peacock, Paramount, and Disney+ follow, ranging down to about 10% share. For nearly all platforms, series make up the vast majority of the catalog compared to movies.

The third chart, "Movie share of streaming revenue," highlights that despite movies representing a smaller share of overall catalog content, their share of streaming revenue grew substantially between 2022 and 2024. Disney+ saw its movie revenue share rise from roughly 53% to about 70%. Amazon Prime Video saw a dramatic increase from approximately 28% to nearly 60%, while Netflix grew to over 40% and Warner Bros reached about 36%. 

The final exhibit is a table listing the top streaming programs, divided into US viewership for the first half of 2025 (in billions of minutes viewed) and global viewership for the second half of 2024 (in millions of hours viewed). In the US, the animated series "Bluey" leads with 25.1 billion minutes, followed closely by long-running dramas like "Grey's Anatomy" at 22.6 billion minutes and "NCIS" at 19.1 billion minutes. The table also underscores the long-tail value of legacy television, with classic western "Gunsmoke" ranking 18th with 11.0 billion minutes viewed. Globally, "Grey's Anatomy" dominates with 1,000 million hours viewed, followed by "Prison Break" at 788 million hours and "Lost" at 700 million hours, demonstrating the immense global demand for deep television archives.

This page marks J.P. Morgan's 2025 Alternative Investments Review, authored by Michael Cembalest, which examines performance, underwriting standards, and portfolio risks across buyout, venture capital, hedge funds, private credit, and real estate. Cembalest observes that while top-quartile buyout and venture funds continue to outperform public markets, and private credit continues to deliver higher returns than syndicated loans, alternative asset managers are increasingly operating in risky territory. Buyout and venture portfolios remain heavily burdened with unmonetized companies from the mid-2010s, hedge funds suffer from unprecedented concentration and crowding, and private credit has suffered from loosened underwriting standards due to a deluge of committed capital. 

Visually supporting the review's title, "The Deep End," is an alternative cover illustration featuring the cartoon horse BoJack Horseman wading in a swimming pool while looking out at the ocean. Beside this illustration, three key charts detail the rapid expansion and systemic integration of alternative investments. 

The first chart shows global alternative assets under management from 2014 to 2024 in trillions of US dollars. Total alternative assets have grown steadily from roughly 7 trillion dollars in 2014 to nearly 20 trillion dollars in 2024. This growth is categorized into private equity, hedge funds, venture capital, real estate, private debt, infrastructure, and natural resources, with private equity consistently representing the largest individual sector. 

The second chart tracks private equity and venture capital assets under management as a percentage of MSCI World market capitalization from 2014 to 2024. This share has doubled over the decade, rising from approximately 7 percent in 2014 to a peak of just over 16 percent in 2022, before settling at around 13 percent in 2024. 

The third chart illustrates bank loan exposure to private credit and private equity intermediaries as a percentage of legal entity Tier 1 bank capital as of March 31, 2025. This chart highlights significant bank exposure, led by First Citizens at 207 percent, followed by Morgan Stanley at 119 percent, Goldman Sachs at 98 percent, Wells Fargo at 88 percent, Truist at 68 percent, BMO at 63 percent, PNC at 60 percent, State Street at 52 percent, US Bancorp at 50 percent, J.P. Morgan at 35 percent, Capital One at 34 percent, Bank of America at 29 percent, and Citigroup at 18 percent. The exposure is divided into private equity exposure and private credit exposure, demonstrating how heavily banking institutions have funded the growth of these alternative asset classes. Finally, the author notes that the report concludes with an analysis of the litigation risks tied to the retail democratization of alternative assets alongside a summary of recent academic research.

This page examines the structural shifts in media consumption as traditional TV viewership transitions to digital and social platforms, leading to deflationary pressures on media monetization. The author argues that while video production studios may cut costs by ten to fifteen percent using generative artificial intelligence, they face severe competition from alternative content types. Additionally, technology giants like Apple and Amazon treat video as a loss leader to attract users to their broader ecosystems, with AppleTV+ originally projecting fifteen to twenty billion dollars in losses over its first five years. The page also includes an anecdotal footnote from the author about receiving dog rescue video feeds on TikTok and donating to them.

Two charts on the page track adult viewing habits in the United States. The first chart, showing the average daily time spent by U.S. adults from 2021 to 2025, reveals that digital video consumption surpassed traditional TV; digital video rose from around 2.9 hours to roughly 3.7 hours, while traditional TV fell from 3.4 hours to about 2.7 hours. The second chart details video consumption by type in 2024, showing total daily viewing time of approximately 8.0 hours, led by legacy TV at about 3.3 hours, followed by subscription video on demand and social video at 2.2 hours each, and free ad-supported streaming TV at around 0.3 hours.

Two tables further detail the audience dynamics and monetization challenges of new media. The first table compares TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts. Instagram Reels has the most monthly active users at 2.0 billion, followed by YouTube Shorts at 1.5 billion and TikTok at 1.2 billion. TikTok holds a stronger appeal for younger audiences with 42.9 percent Gen Z users and a dominant engagement rate of 8.9 percent, compared to Reels at 2.0 percent and Shorts at 0.6 percent. However, YouTube Shorts enjoys the largest ad reach of 2.6 billion users, or 32.4 percent of the total population, versus TikTok at 884.9 million and Reels at 675.3 million. The final table highlights the deflationary nature of digital content by listing monetization rates per hour of play. For video, traditional linear TV monetizes at fifty-four cents per hour, compared to thirty-seven cents for Netflix and nineteen cents for YouTube. In music, CD monetization stands at sixty-seven cents per hour while Spotify brings in only six cents. In gaming, console play monetizes at eleven cents per hour, with PC and mobile both bringing in six cents per hour.

This page from the report analyzed by Michael Cembalest discusses the shifting dynamics of global private equity and venture capital, highlighting that, except for the anomalous boom of 2021, global private equity distributions have remained relatively flat despite growing assets under management. To illustrate this trend and its consequences, the page features six charts that track cash flows, exit activity, holding periods, and alternative liquidity sources. 

The first chart, tracking global private equity cash flows by year in billions of US dollars from 2014 to annualized 2025, shows that annual distributions have generally fluctuated between 300 billion and 400 billion dollars, with the sole exception of 2021 when they peaked near 700 billion dollars. Annual contributions have closely tracked or exceeded distributions in most years, with annualized 2025 contributions nearing 400 billion dollars while distributions remained closer to 350 billion dollars. 

The decline in exit options is detailed in the second chart, which illustrates US private equity and venture capital exit activity in terms of the quarterly number of exits from 2013 to 2025. Following a dramatic spike in 2021 where quarterly private equity exits peaked around 650 and venture capital exits peaked near 550, both metrics have fallen significantly. By 2025, private equity exits plummeted to below 200 per quarter, while venture capital quarterly exits hovered near 300. This slowdown is further contextualized by the third chart, showing global buyout exits as a share of global buyout assets under management. This ratio has experienced a long-term downward trend, falling from over 30 percent in 2014 to a bottom of roughly 7 percent in 2023, before recovering slightly to around 10 percent in 2024. 

With exits harder to come by, sponsors are holding onto assets longer. The fourth chart tracks the global buyout median holding period in years from 2000 to 2025. The median holding period has risen from a low of approximately 3 years in the early 2000s to over 6 years in 2024, showing only a minor downtick in 2025. 

To address the lack of traditional distributions, fund managers have turned to alternative liquidity structures. The fifth chart demonstrates the growing prominence of continuation vehicles, showing their share of global private equity exits rising from around 5 percent in 2020 and 2021 to approximately 14 percent in 2024, and surging further to nearly 18 percent in 2025. Finally, the sixth chart highlights the expansion of global secondary assets under management from 2014 to 2024. Total secondary assets under management grew steadily from around 200 billion dollars in 2014 to over 500 billion dollars by 2024. While the secondary market's share of overall private equity assets declined from a peak of over 4.5 percent in 2014 down to roughly 3.7 percent in 2021, it has since sharply rebounded to approach 4.75 percent by 2024.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Alternative Investments Review analyzes whether the current pace of private equity and venture capital fund monetization is slower than in past cycles. The author, Michael Cembalest, argues that the current cycle ending in 2025 shows the slowest median monetization speed on record for both buyout and venture funds when looking at funds that are 6 to 9 years old. 

To support this observation, the page features two line charts sourced from Steve Kaplan of the University of Chicago, MSCI/Burgiss, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The first chart, titled "The speed of monetization in buyout funds," plots the median remaining value as a percentage of total value on the y-axis (ranging from 10% to 70%) against the fund age in years on the x-axis, tracking ages from 9 down to 6. It compares six different vintage eras: 2016–2019 (evaluated in 2025), 2010–2013 (in 2019), 2005–2008 (in 2014), 2000–2003 (in 2009), 1995–1998 (in 2004), and 1990–1993 (in 1999). The data shows that the 2016–2019 vintage has the slowest pace of monetization, with approximately 35% of total value remaining unmonetized at age 9, rising to about 45% at age 8, 60% at age 7, and 68% at age 6. This is significantly higher than the fastest-monetizing cycle of 1990–1993, which had only about 21% of value remaining at age 9.

The second chart, titled "The speed of monetization in venture funds," uses the same format with a y-axis extending to 90% to illustrate that venture capital funds are experiencing even more severe monetization delays. For the 2016–2019 vintage evaluated in 2025, the unsold portion of total value remains remarkably high, sitting at approximately 62% at age 9, 61% at age 8, 79% at age 7, and 88% at age 6. This represents a stark contrast to the historic 1995–1998 vintage cycle evaluated in 2004, where the median remaining value was just 11% by age 9. The author highlights that for the 2017 vintage at age 8, the median venture fund has over 60% of its value still unsold, compared to a still-high 45% for the median buyout fund.

This page from the 2025 Alternative Investments Review by J.P. Morgan assesses the absolute performance of private equity buyouts and venture capital, comparing multiples of invested capital and internal rates of return across median, 75th percentile, and 25th percentile managers. 

For buyouts, the author highlights a period of relative stability from 1999 to 2019, during which the median manager's multiple on invested capital hovered around 2.0x, and internal rates of return remained steady between 15% and 20%. Two charts illustrate this performance using data from Steve Kaplan at the University of Chicago, MSCI/Burgiss, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The first chart shows US buyout multiple on invested capital by vintage year from 1999 to 2022. The 75th percentile peaked near 2.5x around 2016 before falling sharply, the median remained near 2.0x for most of the period before declining to around 1.2x by 2022, and the 25th percentile hovered between 1.2x and 1.6x before sliding to 1.0x by 2022. The second chart, displaying North American median buyout internal rates of return, shows similar trends, with the median manager's return dropping to approximately 8% for 2022 vintages and the 25th percentile falling close to 0%. The author notes that because recent 2021 and 2022 vintage funds are still in their original commitment periods and hold most investments near cost, it remains an open question whether the recent performance decline is a structural issue or simply a temporary J-curve effect. A footnote clarifies that while some managers use temporary credit lines to delay capital calls, the differences between multiple on invested capital and total value paid in multiples are very small for median managers.

In contrast, venture capital performance has been far more volatile. Following the dot-com bust, median venture funds generated almost no positive absolute returns. While post-financial crisis vintages from 2009 to 2018 improved—delivering median multiples of 2.0x to 2.5x and internal rates of return between 13% and 15%—performance began declining again in 2019. The author argues this downturn is not merely a J-curve issue but represents real capital destruction from the Metaverse and special purpose acquisition company investment cycles. Because the median 2019 vintage venture fund still holds 80% of its assets, future markdowns on eventual dispositions could depress performance further. This volatility is captured in the final two charts. The US venture capital multiple on invested capital chart illustrates a dramatic spike for the 75th percentile manager, peaking near 5.0x around the 2011 vintage before plummeting below 1.5x by 2022, while the median multiple slid toward 1.2x. The North American venture capital internal rate of return chart shows median performance hovering near 0% after the dot-com crash, peaking around 15% in 2010, and dropping back toward 3% by 2022, while the bottom 25th percentile dipped back into negative territory at around negative 2%.

This page from the report discusses the timely recovery of capital markets and M&A activity, which provides a critical liquidity pathway for private equity and venture capital managers. This broad trend is analyzed across six charts tracking IPOs, secondary offerings, merger and acquisition volumes, M&A-related debt issuance, and sponsor-backed block trades. 

The first chart tracks US IPO activity on a three-month rolling average from 2018 through 2025, plotting both deal value and offering count. After peaking dramatically in late 2020 and 2021—when monthly deal values surged past $20 billion and offering counts exceeded 90—activity collapsed to near-zero in late 2022 and 2023. By 2025, a visible recovery is underway, with deal values climbing back toward the $5 billion to $8 billion range and offering counts steadily rising. This trend is complemented by the second chart, which illustrates the US average IPO return on the first trading day for transactions greater than $25 million from 1995 to 2025. First-day returns peaked at around 70% in 1999 and 60% in 2000 during the dot-com era, against a long-term median of approximately 16%. In 2025, first-day returns have rebounded to roughly 30%, indicating renewed investor appetite and strong pricing momentum.

The third chart depicts US secondary offering activity on a three-month rolling average. Similar to IPOs, secondary activity peaked in late 2020 and 2021, with quarterly deal values exceeding $30 billion and offering counts near 175. Following a steep decline through 2022, secondary offerings have steadily rebounded through 2024 and 2025, with deal values recovering to nearly $20 billion and offering counts rising above 100. Additionally, the fourth chart examines quarterly announced M&A volumes from 2018 through the third quarter of 2025, breaking down deals by strategic versus sponsor-led acquisitions. Quarterly volumes peaked above $1.5 trillion in late 2021 before bottoming near $600 billion in late 2022 and 2023. A robust recovery is apparent through 2024 and 2025, with total announced volumes in the third quarter of 2025 climbing back to nearly $1.3 trillion, supported by strong showings from both strategic corporate buyers and financial sponsors.

The final two charts focus on the financing and exit mechanisms facilitating this market turn. The fifth chart details leveraged loan and high yield issuance used specifically for M&A proceeds from 2020 to annualized 2025. Funding peaked at nearly $375 billion in 2021, dominated heavily by leveraged loans, before dropping to a low of approximately $110 billion in 2023. By annualized 2025, M&A debt funding has recovered to roughly $240 billion, indicating that debt capital markets are open and supportive of transaction activity. Lastly, the sixth chart looks at block trade volumes linked to financial sponsors in registered blocks from 2015 to annualized 2025. This exit pathway saw volume plummet from historical averages to less than $5 billion in 2022. However, block trades have staged a major comeback, reaching $28 billion in 2024 and an annualized level of around $23 billion in 2025, showing that financial sponsors are once again able to successfully sell down their equity positions.

This page analyzes the role of leverage in private equity buyouts and how it complicates performance benchmarking compared to public equities. The author examines whether leveraged buyout (LBO) funds are overleveraged and how adjusting benchmarks for leverage affects measured outperformance. 

The first chart, titled "US buyout vs comparable public equity debt ratios," plots net debt to EBITDA from 2008 through roughly 2021 for US buyouts compared to the Russell 3000. It shows a large and widening leverage gap: while the average Russell 3000 company saw its net debt to EBITDA drop from around 3.5x in 2008 to under 2.0x by 2021, average US buyout leverage rose from about 5.0x to well over 6.0x during the same period. 

To address academic arguments that private equity benchmarks should be leveraged to account for this risk difference, the author models a pro-forma sample private equity fund with a 12.7% IRR and a 1.9x multiple on invested capital. The second chart, "Pro-forma excess returns on a sample private equity fund based on start year," shows the Public Market Equivalent (PME) ratio for this fund across vintage start years from 1993 to 2014. It compares performance against both an unleveraged S&P 500 and a 2.5x leveraged S&P 500. While comparing the fund to the leveraged benchmark generally results in a lower PME ratio (dropping, for instance, from 0.8 to 0.4 for a 1993 start), the leveraged benchmark occasionally yields higher relative performance during specific vintage spikes, such as in 1998 and 2005. The author highlights a crucial risk mitigation factor: buyout leverage is deal-specific and lacks cross-default provisions, meaning investors only risk losing their specific equity contribution rather than exposing an entire portfolio to margin-call risk. 

Finally, the author addresses whether buyouts are structurally overleveraged by citing a Federal Reserve analysis. The study found that current LBO leverage levels align closely with theoretically optimal corporate finance levels. The Fed researchers justify these higher debt loads because private equity sponsors often step in with capital during downturns to reduce distress costs, LBO targets typically exhibit lower sales volatility than public companies, and the underlying assets of value buyout targets are inherently less volatile than public equity counterparts.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication by Michael Cembalest argues that traditional metrics of risk-adjusted returns cannot be reliably applied to buyout, venture capital, real estate, and most other alternative investments. The author contends that private equity valuations are structurally smoothed, which creates artificially high autocorrelation of returns and hides true underlying volatility—a practice referred to by hedge fund manager Cliff Asness as volatility laundering. 

To illustrate this, the page presents two line charts and a table of statistics. The first chart, titled Lincoln Private Market Index vs public markets, 3Q21-1Q25, indexes valuations from Q3 2021 at 10,000. It demonstrates that the Lincoln Private Market Index rises smoothly and steadily to over 13,000 by late 2024, completely bypassing the dramatic decline and subsequent recovery seen in public equities, which are represented by the volatile curves of the S&P 500 enterprise value and the S&P 500 excluding the Magnificent 7. The second chart, titled Lincoln Private Market Index by company size, 1Q14-1Q25, indexes valuations from Q1 2014 at 10,000 and shows that larger private companies with EBITDA between 50 million and 250 million dollars outperformed smaller cohorts, climbing to near 24,000 by 2025. By comparison, mid-sized companies with EBITDA between 20 million and 50 million dollars reached roughly 21,000, and the smallest tier with EBITDA between negative 5 million and 20 million dollars finished lowest, near 19,000.

The structural smoothing of private valuations is quantified in the table, Autocorrelation rates by index, quarterly data, 2001 to 2025, using a one period lag. Highly smoothed private asset classes show elevated autocorrelation, led by venture capital at 0.76, real estate at 0.70, buyouts at 0.64, and secondaries at 0.60. In contrast, public markets show virtually no autocorrelation, with the S&P 500 at negative 0.01, Russell 3000 at negative 0.02, and Russell 2000 at negative 0.08. Cembalest cites academic research from a 2022 paper by Baz et al. to show that when this smoothing is mathematically stripped away, private equity's true economic volatility is close to 30 percent rather than the headline 10 percent, and its true maximum expected drawdown is 40 percent rather than the smoothed headline figure of 12 percent.

This page from the J.P. Morgan 2025 Alternative Investments Review, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes the performance of buyout funds relative to public equity markets. Cembalest observes that from the early 1990s to 2020, the median buyout fund consistently outperformed the S&P 500, with very little difference between average and median fund performances. However, manager selection remains critical: top-quartile managers performed significantly better than the median, while fourth-quartile managers almost always underperformed public equities. Post-2020, relative buyout performance has declined. Cembalest attributes this to the soaring US stock market, which has been driven by a few megastocks that differ from typical buyout targets, alongside the normal J-curve process. Consequently, he cautions that post-2020 data does not yet provide a definitive signal.

The page features three charts to support this analysis. The first chart, on the upper left, displays US buyout performance from 1992 to post-2020 using the Public Market Equivalent ratio against the S&P 500. It plots two highly correlated lines for average and median funds. Both series peak around 1.4 to 1.5 in the early 2000s, experience a decline around 2004, recover slightly, and then drop below the 1.0 threshold after 2020. The upper right chart displays the same historical PME data but breaks it down by percentiles. The 75th percentile line consistently hovers well above the 1.0 mark, peaking near 1.8 in the early 2000s, whereas the 25th percentile line regularly dips below 1.0, bottoming out near 0.7. Both top charts cite data from Steve Kaplan of the University of Chicago, MSCI/Burgiss, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

The bottom half of the page explains the methodology of the PME ratio, which compares private equity capital calls and distributions to public market investments over identical periods, and notes that PME can be converted into direct alpha to measure annual percentage outperformance. A scatter plot illustrates the relationship between PME and Direct Alpha for a hypothetical fund based on its inception year. The hypothetical fund model assumes LP commitments of $25 million in periods 1, 5, 9, 13, and 17, and LP distributions of $40 million in periods 21, 25, 29, 33, 37, and 41. 

In this scatter plot, the horizontal axis measures the PME ratio against the S&P 500 from 0.75 to 2.00, while the vertical axis represents Direct Alpha from -4% to 14%. The chart demonstrates a clear positive correlation: inception years from the late 1990s and early 2000s, such as 1998, 1999, and 2004, cluster in the upper right, showing high PME ratios between 1.50 and 1.80 and direct alphas between 10% and 13%. Conversely, inception years from the early 2010s, such as 2012 and 2013, as well as 2008 and 2009, cluster in the lower left, where PME ratios fall below 1.00 and direct alpha drops to near zero or into negative territory, reaching a low of nearly -4% for the 1993 vintage. Cembalest notes that when a fund is assumed to begin in the early 2010s, both PME and direct alpha are at their lowest due to the exceptionally high subsequent returns of public equities during that decade.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Alternative Investments Review addresses the subjective nature of evaluating hedge fund performance, arguing that standard equity-biased benchmarks like a 70-30 stock/bond mix might be inappropriate due to fundamental differences in volatility. The author discusses how a large state defined benefit plan terminated its hedge fund platform based on perceived underperformance, likely because they failed to use a benchmark that reflected the lower, cash-and-bond-like volatility of their constrained managers. 

To analyze five-year hedge fund performance from September 2020 to August 2025, the author examines US-based hedge funds reporting monthly to Hedge Fund Research across relative value, equity hedge, event-driven, and macro strategies. This analysis is visualized in two charts. 

The first chart, titled "Individual hedge funds and 20-fund composites [HFR]," plots annualized excess return over T-bills on the y-axis, ranging from negative 10 percent to 40 percent, against annualized excess return volatility on the x-axis, ranging from 0 percent to 50 percent. Individual funds, represented by blue dots, display highly dispersed returns and volatilities. In contrast, randomized portfolios containing twenty diversified funds—specifically six long-short, four event-driven, four macro, and six relative value funds—are shown as gold dots. This gold cluster is highly concentrated, demonstrating how diversification benefits compress volatility, keeping most composite portfolios within a 5 percent to 10 percent volatility range and a 5 percent to 10 percent return range, driven by a low average fund correlation of 0.25.

The second chart, titled "20-fund composites vs 70/30 benchmark [HFR]," zooms in on these 20-fund composites relative to a common benchmark consisting of 70 percent S&P 500 and 30 percent Barclays US Agg 1-5, marked by a black square. The y-axis shows annualized excess return from 0 percent to 12 percent, while the x-axis shows annualized excess return volatility from 4 percent to 14 percent. The chart illustrates that only about one-third of the randomized hedge fund composites outperformed the 70-30 benchmark on an absolute return basis. However, the 70-30 benchmark exhibited volatility of nearly 12 percent, which is higher than almost all the randomized hedge fund composites. The author concludes by questioning the validity of the 70-30 portfolio as a fair benchmark given this pronounced difference in risk profiles.

This page analyzes private equity and venture capital dynamics, focusing on buyout multiples, uninvested capital (dry powder), and venture capital demand-to-supply ratios. The main argument is that buyout multiples are expected to remain high due to massive amounts of dry powder waiting to be deployed, despite these measures being in absolute dollar terms rather than relative to market opportunities. At the same time, substantial venture capital dry powder has driven down the demand-to-supply ratio for VC funding.

The analysis of buyout multiples is illustrated through two line charts tracking the median total enterprise value to EBITDA ratio from 2004 to 2024 for North America and Western Europe. In North America, buyout multiples rose from a post-financial crisis low of under 7x in 2009 to a peak of over 12x around 2021, ending 2024 at approximately 11.5x. Western European multiples followed a highly similar trajectory, rising from 6x in 2009 to roughly 11.5x in 2024. This persistent elevation in valuations is supported by a stacked bar chart showing global buyout dry powder by years since capital was raised. This pool of uninvested capital has steadily climbed from about $0.8 trillion in 2017 to roughly $1.25 trillion in 2024. The overwhelming majority of this capital is fresh, having been raised less than three years prior, while older vintages of four to five years or more than five years constitute only a small fraction.

Turning to venture capital, a line chart tracking US venture capital dry powder from 2014 to 2024 shows that capital reserves exploded from under $100 billion to a peak exceeding $300 billion in 2023, before settling slightly below $300 billion in 2024. An inset pie chart reveals that the dry powder remaining in 2024 is dominated by the 2022 and 2023 vintage years, with smaller portions held in 2024, 2021, and pre-2021 vintages. 

Finally, a line chart illustrates the US venture capital demand-to-supply ratio from 2020 through early 2025 across three stages: early stage, late stage, and venture growth stage. All three indices spiked dramatically starting in late 2021 and peaked around mid-2023. The venture growth stage index saw the most extreme surge, peaking at 4.0x, while the late stage index peaked near 3.3x and the early stage index reached approximately 2.8x. Since then, ratios have steadily declined, indicating easing competition for capital. By early 2025, the late stage index fell to around 2.7x, the venture growth stage index dropped to roughly 2.3x, and the early stage index declined to about 1.7x.

This page, titled "Wrapping up" within a broader report on alternative investments, argues that the trend toward democratizing alternative assets could trigger a massive wave of retail litigation if a sharp economic recession and liquidity crunch occur simultaneously. The author warns that documentation firewalls designed to shield fund managers will likely face intense legal scrutiny, drawing parallels to previous waves of financial litigation. To support this thesis, the page features four charts and explanatory footnotes detailing past and current legal disputes in the financial sector.

The first chart, "401k excessive fee litigation settlements," displays the annual number of settlements alongside their total dollar value in millions of US dollars from 2020 to 2023. The number of settlements grew steadily from roughly 12 in 2020 to 41 in 2023. Meanwhile, total settlement values peaked at nearly $300 million in 2021, fell to around $180 million in 2022, and then surged to over $350 million in 2023. An adjacent chart, "401k excessive fee and performance lawsuits by year," tracks the total number of filed lawsuits from 2016 to 2023, showing a major spike in 2020 with 100 lawsuits, followed by 60 in 2021, 85 in 2022, and 45 in 2023. Accompanying footnotes explain that these lawsuits typically target plan sponsors for fiduciary breaches, such as concentrating portfolios in higher-fee, underperforming funds instead of cheaper passive alternatives.

The third chart, "Percentage of failed auction rate security auctions in 2008," details the sudden systemic collapse of the auction rate security market between late 2007 and mid-2008. It tracks two definitions of failed auctions: one where the auction reset rate hit the maximum auction rate, which peaked at over 40% in early 2008, and another where buy orders by new investors fell short of sell orders by existing bondholders, which spiked dramatically to nearly 60% in February 2008 and remained elevated. The footnotes highlight that the SEC received over 1,000 complaints in 2008 alone, leading to a massive 2009 settlement where major financial institutions made approximately $50 billion available to repurchase securities from misled investors.

The final chart, "Summary of trend cases," tracks core federal filings across several modern legal flashpoints—cybersecurity, cryptocurrency, cannabis, COVID-19, SPACs, and the 2023 banking turbulence—from 2019 through the first half of 2023. Notable trends include a peak in crypto-related filings in 2022 with over 20 cases, and a dramatic surge in SPAC litigation, which peaked in 2021 with over 30 core filings and stayed high in 2022 with over 20 filings. A footnote adds that approximately two-thirds of SPAC class-action suits filed in 2021 and 2022 targeted the directors and officers of the SPAC entities.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s 2025 Alternative Investments Review, published by J.P. Morgan, focuses on evaluating hedge fund performance through calibrated, risk-adjusted benchmarks rather than pre-selected fixed mixes. Under this ex-post approach, rather than choosing a benchmark mix beforehand, investors wait until the returns and volatilities of the portfolios are known and then measure each fund against a stock-bond mix of equivalent volatility. The benchmarks are composed of various weighted combinations of the S&P 500 and the Barclays US Aggregate 1-5 Index. The author argues that this method is crucial for investors who prioritize risk-adjusted returns over absolute returns and are comfortable utilizing ex-post benchmarks to judge performance.

To support this argument, the page features four scatter plots tracking annualized excess returns versus Treasury bills on the y-axis (from 0 percent to 12 percent) against annualized excess return volatility on the x-axis. The data spans from September 2020 to August 2025. 

The top two charts use HFR data to compare randomized hedge fund composites against risk-adjusted benchmark lines, represented by black squares denoting stock-bond allocations ranging from 30/70 to 80/20. The top-left chart shows that for 20-fund composites, a vast majority of 98 percent of the randomized hedge fund portfolios outperformed their corresponding interpolated benchmarks, as most gold dots lie above the benchmark line. The top-right chart repeats this analysis with smaller, 10-fund randomized portfolios; despite greater dispersion, the outperformance rate remains very high at 91 percent.

The bottom two charts demonstrate that these findings are consistent when using the Pivotal Path hedge fund universe instead of HFR data. The bottom-left chart compares 20-fund composites against a single, fixed 70/30 stock-bond benchmark. Under this rigid absolute lens, only 30 percent of the funds outperform. However, the bottom-right chart applies the risk-adjusted benchmark curve to these same Pivotal Path composites. By shifting to this risk-adjusted lens, practically all of the hedge fund composites show outperformance, illustrating how high correlation benefits dramatically lower their overall volatility relative to equivalent stock-bond mixes.

This page analyzes the explosive growth of the global private credit market, which has risen from $250 billion in 2007 to $2.5 trillion, and argues that the next recession will create a stark performance dispersion between strong and weak underwriters. The author emphasizes that this growth does not reflect a massive expansion of overall US risky credit, but rather a structural market-share shift. 

This shift is illustrated in a stacked area chart tracking US risky credit market shares as a percentage of US GDP from 2000 to 2025. While the overall risky credit volume has remained relatively stable at around 18% to 20% of GDP, private credit has steadily taken share from traditional bank loans to small and medium-sized enterprises and high-yield bonds. A second chart, a stacked bar chart detailing US middle-market leveraged buyout loan issuance from 2014 to 2024, shows that direct lending expanded its share from less than 40% to a dominant 90%, almost entirely displacing syndicated bank debt.

To explain this transition, a comparative table outlines the financial metrics of bank lending. It shows that lending to a middle-market company has a 100% risk weight, a 4.00% assumed default rate, and an 18% return on equity. Conversely, a bank loan to a Business Development Company (BDC) carries only a 20% risk weight, a 0.25% assumed default rate, a 95% assumed recovery rate, and yields a far higher 46% return on equity, giving banks a significant regulatory capital incentive to lend to BDCs instead of directly to businesses.

Finally, the page addresses systemic risk concerns using a stacked area chart showing indexed revolving-credit liabilities of BDCs from 2015 to 2024. Total liabilities expanded roughly ninefold over this period, with undrawn revolving credit lines growing to represent about half of the total volume. While this massive pool of undrawn credit poses questions about potential drawdown risks during a downturn, the author notes that a May 2025 Federal Reserve study found US banks sufficiently capitalized to absorb these risks. This stability is bolstered by the average BDC’s stressed capital ratio of 30%, which compares favorably to the 10% average for US banks. Additional footnote data from Preqin, the IMF, and the Federal Reserve highlights that US BDC and private credit assets under management grew from around $250–$300 billion in 2010 to $1.4 trillion in 2024.

This page from J.P. Morgan's 2025 Alternative Investments Review, authored by Michael Cembalest, examines the risk-return profile and performance of private credit relative to broadly syndicated loans, high-yield bonds, and leveraged loans. The central argument is that while private credit has delivered strong excess returns, it carries higher structural risks, and its outperformance may be partially attributed to hidden equity-like exposures. 

To support the risk comparison, a top-right table compares the collateral quality of collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) for broadly syndicated loans versus small and medium-sized enterprise private credit. It shows that private credit portfolios are significantly riskier: exposure to assets rated B- or below by S&P is 87% for private credit compared to 30% for broadly syndicated loans. Similarly, S&P CCC exposure is 13% versus 6%, Moody's Caa exposure is 12% versus 5%, and the weighted average rating factor is 3,734 for private credit versus 2,804 for broadly syndicated loans. Additionally, Moody's weighted average recovery rate estimate is slightly lower for private credit at 44% compared to 47% for broadly syndicated loans. The text highlights a 2025 IMF estimate finding that roughly 40% of direct-lender borrowers had negative free operating cash flow.

A top-left line chart plots yield to maturity from 2020 through 2025 for private credit, broadly syndicated loans, and high-yield bonds. It tracks four series: the Houlihan Lokey Private Performing Credit Index, JPM Securities private credit at transaction close, the JPM Loan Index, and the BAML High Yield Bond Index. Private credit yields peaked near 12% to 13% during late 2023 and 2024 before easing slightly in 2025, consistently maintaining a premium over traditional loan and high-yield indices. The commentary notes that private credit spreads versus loans narrowed from 200 to 250 basis points in early 2023 to 150 to 175 basis points in September 2025 due to an influx of new capital.

Performance is detailed in two bottom bar charts measuring annual total returns from 2014 to 2025. The bottom-left chart compares a private credit composite (made up of Cliffwater, Preqin, and PitchBook indexes) to the JPM Leveraged Loan Index. It demonstrates steady private credit outperformance, particularly during down market years like 2022, with the annualized return for the 2014–2025 period reaching approximately 9% for the private credit composite compared to roughly 5.5% for the leveraged loan index. The bottom-right chart compares the individual private credit indexes—Cliffwater Direct Lending, Preqin Private Debt, and PitchBook Private Debt—illustrating that there are no major performance differences among them, as all three converged on an annualized return of roughly 9% over the 2014–2025 period. Finally, the author cautions that ~20% of private credit holdings have equity-like exposure on a value-weighted basis; adjusting for this exposure, the historical outperformance of private credit would be closer to zero.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication, written by Michael Cembalest, argues that performance dispersion will eventually impact the private credit market, just as it has other alternative asset classes. Cembalest observes that private credit managers' performances have been tightly bunched since 2014 because of the absence of a lasting recession. To support this, a line chart titled "COVID was not a typical recession" plots high-yield credit spreads and default rates from 1987 to 2025. It illustrates that while there was a recession during the COVID pandemic, high-yield default rates peaked at much lower levels than in the three prior recessions, and both the peak level and duration of credit spreads were muted due to aggressive fiscal and monetary policies. 

Cembalest predicts that the next recession will trigger significant manager dispersion in private credit, drawing parallels to other alternative asset classes. To demonstrate this historical dispersion, he provides several charts. A chart on US buyout performance plots the multiple on invested capital (MOIC) by vintage year from 1999 to 2020. It shows a clear gap between the 75th percentile—which often stays above 2.0x—and the 25th percentile, which frequently hovers between 1.2x and 1.6x. This gap is even wider in a matching chart on US venture capital performance, where the 75th percentile for the 2011 vintage peaks near 5.0x MOIC, while the 25th percentile sits below 2.0x. 

Manager dispersion is also shown for hedge funds in a scatter plot comparing top and bottom quartile annualized excess returns against annualized excess return volatility from September 2020 to August 2025. Top quartile funds show significantly higher excess returns, reaching up to 30%, whereas bottom quartile funds cluster near or below 0% return across similar volatility levels. Furthermore, a chart showing the distribution of absolute returns from activist events between 1994 and 2014 demonstrates a highly unequal, long-tailed outcome for individual activist campaigns, where a small number of campaigns generated massive returns, including 43 campaigns yielding 210% to 500%, 12 yielding 510% to 800%, and 11 exceeding 800%.

Ultimately, Cembalest asserts that the key determinant of private credit manager success in the next downturn will be underwriting discipline and covenant strength. A final horizontal bar chart highlights how the broadly syndicated loan (BSL) market is far less protective than private credit. While approximately 75% of BSL deals allow inside maturities and about 65% allow the conversion of unused restricted payments into debt, private credit deals exhibit 0% allowance for these borrower-friendly features, alongside 0% allowance for automatic debt increases per dollar of new equity or asset sale repayments of less than 100%. Private credit also completely blocks the "J Crew" intellectual property transfer loophole. This strict underwriting discipline is expected to protect private credit portfolios when economic conditions deteriorate.

This page from the report analyzed middle-market private credit valuations, arguing that Business Development Company (BDC) loan prices are often held at par for as long as possible, masking deterioration until it is too large to ignore. To support this, the author presents four main exhibits showcasing price declines, valuation staleness, pricing discrepancies across different managers, and a case study of a complete write-off.

The first chart, titled "Price declines on select middle market securities," plots prices in cents on the dollar from January 2025 through September 2025. It reveals dramatic, abrupt collapses for Tricolor 2025-2A E (ABS) and First Brands TLB 2027 (loan), both of which fell from par to near-zero and below thirty cents, respectively, following reported collateral fraud. NFE 12% 2029 and Saks 11% 2029 senior secured bonds also declined steadily over this period to around thirty to forty cents on the dollar. The author cites investor Howard Marks’s "Cockroaches in the Coal Mine" note, which detailed clear red flags for First Brands, including factored receivables not remitted directly to banks, opaque structures concealing high debt, an unprofiled CEO with prior misconduct allegations, and abnormally high profit margins.

The second chart, "Accounting fair value of BDC first-lien loans," indexes prices from 2014 to 2024 to demonstrate BDC pricing staleness. While the market prices of BB-rated and B-rated liquid leveraged loans fluctuated significantly—dropping sharply during the late 2015 commodity downturn and the 2020 Covid-19 crash—the accounting fair value of BDC loans remained exceptionally stable near par, highlighting how private credit managers lag in marking down assets during periods of market stress.

To illustrate valuation inconsistencies, a table titled "Fair value assigned to Medallia's private credit loan" tracks the valuation in cents on the dollar from Q2 2024 to Q3 2025 across several prominent BDCs. By Q3 2025, the marks for the exact same loan varied significantly: Apollo marked it lowest at 77 cents, Blackstone marked it at 82 cents, Monroe marked it at 84 cents, and FS KKR and Onex marked it highest at 91 cents. 

The final chart, "BlackRock TCP BDC loans to Renovo," presents a case study of a sudden, total write-off for a direct-to-consumer home remodeling platform. The chart tracks both cost and fair value in millions of dollars alongside the loan marks in cents per dollar from Q4 2022 to Q4 2025. The position was held near par (95 to 98 cents) through early 2024 before entering payment-in-kind (PIK) mode, causing the mark to fall to 53 cents by Q4 2024. Following a recapitalization in 2025 where a portion of the debt was written off in exchange for preferred stock, the remaining debt was initially marked back near par (94 to 97 cents) before abruptly crashing to zero in Q4 2025 due to a full write-off and Chapter 7 liquidation. The author notes that for asset-light businesses, salvage value in liquidation can quickly become zero.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Alternative Investments Review analyzes the financial health of private credit borrowers by evaluating their cash flow growth, covenant defaults, and actual payment default rates across different company sizes and industries. The overarching narrative highlights a clear divergence: larger private credit borrowers continue to demonstrate strong cash flow growth and lower default risks, while smaller companies remain financially challenged, resulting in higher covenant defaults.

The first chart, depicting year-over-year EBITDA growth for private companies based on data from Lincoln International through Q2 2025, shows that companies with more than $100 million in EBITDA have consistently achieved the strongest growth, hovering between 9% and 11% from Q3 2024 to Q2 2025. In contrast, middle-market firms with $50 to $100 million in EBITDA grew at a more moderate pace of 5% to 8%, while the smallest category, those with less than $50 million in EBITDA, experienced sluggish growth of only 2% to 4% over the same period.

This weaker cash flow performance for smaller entities directly correlates with the second chart, which illustrates private company covenant default rates. For companies with less than $10 million in EBITDA, covenant default rates peaked at over 30% in Q1 2025 before settling slightly below 30% in Q2 2025. This stands in sharp contrast to the largest cohort of companies with more than $100 million in EBITDA, whose covenant default rates remained negligible, barely registering above 1% in Q2 2025.

While covenant defaults are highest for the smallest entities, actual payment default rates tell a slightly different story, as shown in the third chart using Proskauer data through Q3 2025. Here, actual credit defaults have been most acute for mid-sized borrowers with $25 to $50 million in EBITDA, peaking at nearly 5% in Q4 2024 and declining to approximately 3.2% by Q3 2025. Meanwhile, companies with less than $25 million in EBITDA saw default rates fluctuate steadily between 1.5% and 2.0%, and the largest tier of over $50 million in EBITDA recorded the lowest overall defaults, falling below 1% in Q2 2025 before rising slightly in Q3 2025.

Finally, the fourth chart displays actual private credit default rates across five key industries. The author notes that sector-specific trends are largely unremarkable except for periodic stresses in manufacturing and consumer retail. Manufacturing defaults spiked to 8% in Q1 2025, while the consumer sector peaked at over 6.5% in the same quarter. Software and technology also experienced a temporary rise in defaults, reaching around 5.5% in Q1 2025 before falling below 2% by Q3 2025. Healthcare defaults showed a gradual decline from their Q4 2024 high of nearly 5% down to under 2% in late 2025, while business services maintained the most stable profile, with default rates consistently remaining below 1%.

This page from the report analyzed by Michael Cembalest highlights that there are currently very few signs of private credit distress, with the aggregate market showing stability reflective of a broader economic expansion. Downgrade-to-upgrade ratios for private credit declined significantly through late 2024 before a minor uptick in the third quarter of 2025, and overall default rates remain low. The author notes that non-performing exposures for both broadly syndicated and middle market loans remain well below one percent. This resilience is partially attributed to implied support from financial sponsors; while sponsor-backed loans make up only ten percent of loans to middle market companies by count, they account for roughly eighty percent when measured in dollar volume. Additionally, despite widespread market concern regarding payment-in-kind interest allowances, data shows that the payment-in-kind share of gross business development company investment income has barely risen between 2023 and the second quarter of 2025.

Several charts and tables support these observations. The first chart, showing the ratio of downgrades-to-upgrades from 2021 to 2025 across direct lending, private credit, and broadly syndicated loans, demonstrates that private credit and direct lending ratios peaked near five-times in late 2023 and early 2024 before dropping below two-times. The second chart traces default rates with and without selective defaults from 2017 to 2024. It shows that while private credit default rates including selective defaults peaked near eight percent in 2020 and saw a secondary peak near six percent in 2023, they have since trended downward, while default rates excluding selective defaults remain extremely low at around one percent. The third chart shows that nonperforming loans as a share of total loans for both broadly syndicated and middle market loans have hovered safely below one percent since late 2021, a marked improvement from the pandemic-era peak of nearly one and a half percent.

The remaining visual data focuses on the payment-in-kind interest share of gross investment income. A bar chart comparing publicly traded business development companies to non-traded perpetual business development companies reveals that publicly traded peers carry a significantly higher payment-in-kind share, hovering around twelve to thirteen percent, whereas non-traded perpetual peers stay near five percent. 

Two detailed tables break this down by specific entity. For publicly traded business development companies, the asset-weighted average payment-in-kind interest share went from 11.9% in 2023 to 12.8% in 2024, before settling at 12.5% in the twelve months ending in the second quarter of 2025. Individual performance in this category includes Blue Owl Technology Finance Corporation, which decreased its share from 22.0% in 2023 to 17.6% in the second quarter of 2025, and Ares Capital Corporation, which rose from 13.9% to 16.3%. Other tracked entities include Blackstone Secured Lending Fund, Blue Owl Capital Corporation, Golub Capital, Main Street Capital Corporation, Prospect Capital Corporation, and Sixth Street Specialty Lending. 

For non-traded perpetual business development companies, the asset-weighted average was much lower, moving from 4.9% in 2023 to 5.4% in 2024, and ending at 5.1% in the second quarter of 2025. Within this group, Apollo Debt Solutions remained very low at 1.5% in the second quarter of 2025, while Blue Owl Capital Corporation II was the highest at 13.5%. Additional entities in this category include Ares Strategic Income Fund, Blackstone Private Credit Fund, Blue Owl Credit Income Corporation, Golub Capital Private Credit Fund, HPS Corporate Lending Fund, and Sixth Street Lending Partners.

In this page from the 2025 Alternative Investments Review, Michael Cembalest argues that real estate fundamentals remain weak across multiple sectors. He notes that office delinquencies are soaring, multifamily delinquencies have exceeded 10% in certain Texas and Florida cities, and industrial vacancy rates have doubled since 2022. Additionally, the hotel sector faces pressure, with CBRE projecting a revenue per available room decline of 0.1% for 2025 due to labor challenges, rising operating costs, and increased competition from short-term rentals. 

To illustrate these trends, the page features six charts. The first line chart tracks CMBS delinquencies by property type from 2001 to 2025, showing a dramatic spike in office delinquencies toward 15% and persistently elevated delinquency rates for regional malls near 20%. A second line chart compares CMBS special servicing rates between office and non-office loans from 2002 to 2026. This chart highlights that office special servicing rates have spiked to nearly 15%, exceeding their Great Financial Crisis peak, while non-office special servicing rates have plateaued at around 7%. 

Residential vacancy trends are explored through a long-term line chart showing the US residential vacancy rate from 1965 to 2025. The national vacancy rate has ticked up to around 7% after bottoming near 6% around 2022. A companion bar chart of the 25 largest metropolitan statistical areas as of Q2 2025 reveals stark regional variations, with Sunbelt cities like Orlando, Austin, Houston, and Dallas experiencing vacancy rates above 11%, while Boston, Baltimore, and Riverside remain tight at roughly 3% or lower. 

The final two charts address the industrial sector. A historical line chart of the US industrial vacancy rate shows a rapid rise from a record low of under 4% in 2022 to over 7% in 2025. A corresponding bar chart of industrial vacancy rates for select US cities in Q3 2025 highlights Austin as the highest at nearly 14%, followed by San Francisco and Phoenix, while Detroit and Washington D.C. maintain the lowest vacancy rates in the sample at around 4% to 5%.

This page analyses the commercial real estate (CRE) capital markets, highlighting nascent signs of life in debt origination alongside severe structural headwinds from looming loan maturities. The author observes that while CRE debt origination volumes are starting to recover across several lending types and regions—including a notable rebound in Manhattan office lending—a massive wave of distress is building. Between 10% and 50% of securitized loans maturing by 2027 face insolvency, and many others suffer from a debt service coverage ratio below 1.25x.

The first chart on the page tracks quarterly commercial real estate debt origination volume in billions of US dollars from the first quarter of 2015 through the first quarter of 2025. It shows that quarterly volumes peaked in late 2021 at nearly $275 billion before plunging to a low of approximately $100 billion in 2023. By early 2025, volumes had recovered to nearly $200 billion. 

The second chart illustrates the rolling 12-month total of CRE debt origination value by lender type from 2002 to 2026. Banks have historically been the dominant originators, peaking at over $400 billion in 2022, declining sharply, and recovering to around $250 billion in 2025. Government agencies represent the second-largest lending source, peaking near $200 billion in 2021 and showing a renewed uptick toward the end of the period. CMBS, which experienced an all-time peak of approximately $250 billion in 2007 before collapsing, is also showing a modest recovery alongside financial and other lending categories.

The third chart displays real estate loan volume for the top 15 markets by property type, measured in billions of US dollars. Manhattan is by far the largest market, nearing $28 billion in volume, and is unique for its large concentration of office lending. Other leading markets, such as Los Angeles and the NYC boroughs, register significantly lower volumes—between $15 billion and $20 billion—and are dominated by apartment, industrial, and retail loans, with very little office lending activity. 

The fourth chart plots the distressed share of total CRE volume as a percentage from 2005 to 2025. Distressed volume peaked at roughly 18% in 2010 in the aftermath of the global financial crisis and remained near historic lows of 1% to 2% for nearly a decade. In 2024 and 2025, this metric began a gradual upward trend, reaching approximately 4%, which the author characterizes as a healthy sign of market-clearing.

The final chart details the debt service coverage ratio of outstanding securitized CRE debt maturing before 2027, categorized by sector: overall, multifamily, industrial, office, retail, and hotel. It highlights the vast scale of potential insolvencies, defined as a ratio under 1.0x. This insolvency risk is most acute in multifamily, where over 50% of maturing debt is insolvent, followed closely by the office sector at approximately 40% insolvent and an additional 30% categorized as higher risk. Retail has the lowest insolvency profile at around 10%. Across all sectors, approximately 30% of maturing securitized CRE debt is insolvent, and another 15% is classified as high-risk with a coverage ratio below 1.25x.

This page from the report details a profound structural transition in commercial real estate: the dramatic shift of institutional investor allocations away from office properties in favor of industrial space. The author highlights that investors who made this pivot in 2015 captured massive returns, with industrial NCREIF returns yielding 250% compared to just 20% for office properties. However, the analysis suggests the worst of the office downturn is subsiding. Indicators such as stabilizing net absorption, a sharply declining construction pipeline, and decreasing sublease availability point to a bottoming process. Looking ahead, future office deliveries are projected by JLL to drop to just one million square feet annually between 2027 and 2030, with 70% of that supply already preleased. Furthermore, the distress in the office sector is not uniform; demand remains highly concentrated in newer properties built since 2015, while vacancy is overwhelmingly concentrated in older, obsolete "zombie" buildings.
