The page features six charts that support this thesis. The first chart displays MSCI commercial real estate property type allocations from 2000 to 2025. It shows office allocations steadily declining from approximately 35% in 2000 to roughly 15% in 2025, while industrial allocations surged from around 10% to over 30% over the same period, overtaking apartments to become the largest asset class in the index.

The second chart tracks US office net absorption and deliveries in millions of square feet from 2020 to 2025. It illustrates that net absorption, which was deeply negative during the pandemic years—bottoming near negative 40 million square feet—has steadily climbed back toward zero by mid-2025, while new deliveries have consistently trended downward. 

The third chart depicts the US office construction pipeline from 2019 to 2025. Total square footage under construction has collapsed from a peak of nearly 160 million square feet in late 2020 to around 30 million square feet in 2025, indicating that future supply pressure will be minimal.

The fourth chart compares the US office vacancy rate against sublease availability. While the vacancy rate has risen continuously from under 10% in 2019 to nearly 14.5% in 2025, sublease availability peaked in late 2023 at over 230 million square feet and has since steadily declined to approximately 200 million square feet in 2025, which represents a leading indicator of stabilizing demand.

The fifth chart shows cumulative net absorption since Q2 2020 broken down by the year a building was constructed. It reveals a stark bifurcation: buildings constructed from 2015 to the present have enjoyed over 150 million square feet of positive net absorption, whereas every other vintage has experienced negative net absorption. Properties built in the 1980s have fared the worst, suffering cumulative net losses of roughly 130 million square feet.

The final chart illustrates office vacancy concentration by plotting the share of vacant space against the share of total office inventory. The data shows an extreme concentration of distress: a tiny portion of the inventory accounts for over 40% of all vacant space, while 40% of all office assets have virtually no vacant space at all.

This page provides a professional biography and portrait photograph of Michael Cembalest, the author of the publication and the Chairman of Market and Investment Strategy for J.P. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management. The text highlights his role in leading strategic market and investment insights across the firm’s Institutional, Funds, and Private Banking businesses, which oversee six trillion dollars in client assets. It details his extensive career at J.P. Morgan since joining in 1987, including his previous tenures as Chief Investment Officer for the Global Private Bank, head of a fixed income division, and Head Strategist for Emerging Markets Fixed Income. Additionally, the biography notes his academic background, which includes a Master of Arts from the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs and a Bachelor of Arts from Tufts University.

This page from the 2025 Alternative Investments Review provides an analysis of the characteristics and performance of evergreen funds, comparing them to traditional closed-end drawdown funds. The introductory text defines evergreen funds as hybrid, open-ended structures with no end date that continuously accept new capital, offering investors faster access to diversified portfolios alongside some liquidity, though this is tempered by redemption caps and gates. Based on a sampling of the three largest evergreen and drawdown funds across private credit, private equity, and real estate, the author notes that evergreen funds tend to carry higher vehicle-level leverage but lower deal-level leverage, maintain high cash and credit facility levels of 20 percent to 25 percent, and exhibit greater diversification.

The visual analysis begins with a stacked bar chart illustrating the growth in the number of evergreen funds by asset class from 2015 to 2025. The total number of funds grew from roughly 100 in 2015 to nearly 600 in 2025. Private debt and real estate consistently represent the largest shares of these funds, with private equity and infrastructure showing more modest expansion. A corresponding pie chart displays 2024 evergreen launches by vehicle type, showing a diverse mix that includes European long-term investment funds, interval funds, tender offers, private BDCs, and non-traded REITs, with European long-term investment funds and interval funds representing substantial portions of the total.

Four comparative bar charts contrast the structural metrics of evergreen funds against drawdown funds across private equity, private credit, and private real estate. The first of these charts, analyzing vehicle-level leverage proxy, shows that evergreen funds utilize significantly more vehicle leverage in private credit (around 40 percent versus 22 percent for drawdown) and private real estate (roughly 53 percent versus 13 percent for drawdown), while drawdown funds lead in private equity leverage (about 20 percent versus 5 percent). Conversely, the chart on deal-level loan-to-value leverage shows that drawdown funds hold slightly higher deal leverage, with private credit at approximately 52 percent for drawdown versus 44 percent for evergreen, and real estate at 60 percent for drawdown versus 50 percent for evergreen. 

Liquidity practices are compared in a chart detailing cash levels as a percentage of the fund. Evergreen funds maintain substantial total liquidity cushion—combining evergreen cash and credit facilities—to manage redemptions, totaling approximately 22 percent for private equity, 25 percent for private credit, and 24 percent for real estate. In contrast, drawdown funds hold very little cash, typically under 5 percent. Finally, a chart comparing the number of investments highlights the superior diversification of evergreen funds, which hold roughly 510 investments in private equity (compared to 40 for drawdown), 500 in private credit (compared to 90 for drawdown), and 180 in real estate (compared to 90 for drawdown).

This page from the J.P. Morgan Alternative Investments Review analyzes the capital health of Business Development Companies (BDCs) and the financial incentives for banks lending to them, drawing on research by Chernenko et al. from March 2025. The core argument is that BDCs are highly well-capitalized compared to traditional bank regulatory frameworks, making bank lending to these private credit funds highly lucrative and safe. 

The first chart, titled "Distribution of BDC risk weighted capital ratios," plots the number of BDCs against their risk-weighted capital ratios. It reveals that BDCs possess median risk-based capital ratios of approximately 36%, well above the Federal Reserve's stress testing requirement for banks, which sits around the 10% mark. The second chart, "Distribution of BDC stressed capital ratios," displays a multi-peaked distribution of BDCs across stressed capital ratios up to 60%. The average stressed BDC capital ratio stands at 30.4%, with only a single BDC falling below 4.5%. In comparison, the average bank stressed capital ratio in the 2024 stress tests was just 9.9%.

The author explains that these strong capital positions make lending to private credit funds highly attractive for banks. This dynamic is detailed in a comparative table titled "The RoE on bank lending to small companies," which contrasts a direct bank loan to a middle-market company with a bank loan to a BDC. While direct middle-market lending offers a higher spread of 6.25% compared to the BDC loan's 2.00% spread (against a matching 5.30% SOFR overnight rate), the structural advantages of lending to BDCs are overwhelming. The BDC loan benefits from an assumed default rate of just 0.25% compared to 4.00% for the middle-market company, and an assumed recovery rate of 95% versus 60%, resulting in an expected loss of only 0.01% compared to 1.60%. Furthermore, BDC loans incur significantly lower operating expenses at 0.10% versus 2.00% and enjoy a favorable risk weight of 20% compared to 100% for direct corporate lending. This lower risk weight reduces the required capital from 12.00% of assets down to 2.40%, ultimately driving the bank's Return on Equity on BDC loans to an impressive 46%, compared to only 18% for direct middle-market loans.

This page from the publication discusses the viability of office-to-residential conversions as a solution for excess office supply, followed by positive trends in retail leasing and the booming data center sector. 

The author begins by illustrating the financial difficulties of office-to-residential conversions. Using a hypothetical prewar Class B office building, the analysis shows that even with high-end residential rents at the 90th percentile ($96 per square foot annually) and a 15% decline in post-conversion rentable space, a buyer would need to purchase the building at a 60% discount from pre-pandemic levels—specifically $175 per square foot—to achieve a 15% to 18% return. This is due to high conversion costs of $320 per square foot, plus an additional $40 per square foot for green efficiency. Citing an August 2025 Reuters article, the author highlights that while 100 million to 150 million square feet of office space are slated for conversion across the United States, these projects face significant hurdles, including zoning laws, structural floor plate mismatches, expensive utility retrofits, and reduced tax incentives for luxury conversions. JLL data shows that actual office supply reductions average only about 35 million square feet per year, a small fraction of the 430 million square feet of vacant space added since 2019.

Two charts illustrate these office supply dynamics. The first chart, "Office conversions by status & estimated completion year," tracks the number of projects and total square footage from 2018 through 2027 and beyond. While completed projects peaked in 2024, a massive surge of planned or announced projects is slated for 2027 and later, which is projected to push total square footage from around 10 million square feet in 2025 to over 60 million square feet in the outer years. The second chart, "Office conversions & demolitions vs new supply deliveries," shows that in 2025, the combined total of demolitions and conversions (projected at roughly 20 million square feet) is set to exceed new supply deliveries (projected at around 13 million square feet) for the first time since 2018.

The discussion then shifts to positive news in retail and data centers. In retail, strip center real estate investment trusts (REITs) are experiencing a recovery in blended re-leasing spreads. The chart "Strip center REIT blended re-leasing spreads" shows that these spreads—measuring the rent change between expiring and new leases—recovered from a post-pandemic low of about 4% in 2020 to nearly 13% by 2024, approaching levels not seen since before the Great Financial Crisis. 

Data centers are experiencing even stronger demand, with vacancy rates remaining below 3% and pre-leasing rates near 75%. Data centers have grown to command 31% of fundraising in 2025, up from just 2%, with artificial intelligence workloads estimated to account for half of all data center square footage. The final chart, "US data center vacancy rates and pre-leasing," visualizes this trend from 2020 through 2025. The colocation vacancy rate plummeted from nearly 10% in 2020 to approximately 2.5% in 2025, while the pre-leased share of megawatts under construction rose from about 50% in 2020 to hover between 75% and 80% from 2023 to 2025. Data sources for these analyses include CBRE Research, CBRE Econometric Advisors, JLL Research, Green Street, and J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

This page examines the structural shift in office real estate fundamentals, driven by a persistent work-from-home trend. The author argues that despite return-to-office initiatives, work-from-home employment continues to hover between 30% and 35%, a stark contrast to the pre-pandemic level of less than 5%. To substantiate this, three separate metrics are analyzed: survey-based work-from-home levels, security badge swipe data, and mass transit recovery. 

The first chart on the left illustrates the percentage of full paid days worked from home in large metropolitan areas from October 2020 to October 2025, focusing on employed U.S. residents aged 20 to 64 earning over $10,000 to $20,000. Tracking cities like Los Angeles, Miami, Washington D.C., Chicago, New York, Atlanta, San Francisco, Houston, and Dallas, the data shows that work-from-home rates peaked between 35% and 45% in late 2020 and have since stabilized in a range of roughly 25% to 35% by late 2025. San Francisco consistently represents the higher end of work-from-home prevalence, while Dallas sits near the lower end.

The second chart on the right tracks commercial property utilization rates through security card key fob swipes compared to February 2020 baselines. Following a sharp plunge to nearly 10% in early 2020, utilization rates gradually rebounded in a jagged, upward trajectory, plateauing between 40% and 65% by late 2025. The data reveals a regional divergence, where Texas metro areas like Austin, Dallas, and Houston lead the recovery near the 60% to 65% range, while coastal and tech hubs like San Francisco, Philadelphia, and San Jose remain at the bottom, struggling to surpass 40% to 45% utilization.

The bottom table details post-COVID mass transit ridership recovery by comparing Q1 2025 to a Q2 2019 baseline across twenty-two cities. The median recovery across all tracked transit authorities stands at 71%, up only 4% over a two-year period. Only Miami has exceeded its pre-pandemic baseline, showing a 105% recovery, followed closely by Salt Lake City at 97%. Major transit systems in New York, Washington D.C., and Los Angeles sit at 80% recovery. Meanwhile, major commercial hubs like San Jose, San Francisco, and Chicago show weaker ridership returns at 62%, 60%, and 60% respectively, with Boise registering the lowest recovery at just 22%. Collectively, these data points suggest a permanent structural shift in urban transit and office utilization rather than a temporary disruption.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s Alternative Investments Review, authored by Michael Cembalest, analyzes LP-led versus GP-led secondary transaction markets and compares the performance and dispersion of secondary funds against direct buyout funds. The author explains that LP-led secondaries, where limited partners sell positions to secondary funds, typically trade at discounts of 5% to 15% for buyout, private credit, and infrastructure, but experience wider discounts in venture and real estate. Conversely, GP-led transactions, which have grown to a larger share of the secondary market over the last ten years, generally see smaller discounts. 

The first chart on the page tracks LP-led secondary transaction prices as a percentage of reference date NAV from 2013 through the first half of 2025. It illustrates that infrastructure, private credit, and buyout prices remain relatively high, mostly ranging from 85% to 100% of NAV. In contrast, venture/growth and real estate prices plummeted to lows of 60% and 65% in 2022 and 2023, before staging a modest recovery to around 70% to 75% by the first half of 2025. The adjacent chart displays secondary market transaction volume in billions of US dollars, highlighting that total transaction volume peaked near $140 billion in 2021, fell during 2022 and 2023, and rose back toward $140 billion in 2024. This chart also shows how GP-led transaction volume has expanded over the decade, consistently representing a substantial portion of overall activity.

The second half of the page addresses the performance trade-offs of secondary funds. While median global secondary funds have underperformed their buyout counterparts in every vintage year since 2010, the author notes that secondaries offer a compelling value proposition by providing quicker exposure to shorter-duration portfolios with less uncertainty and lower dispersion. To illustrate, the chart on median TVPI (total value to paid-in capital) by vintage year from 2010 to 2022 shows global buyouts starting around 1.9x for 2010 vintages and slowly declining to meet secondaries at roughly 1.35x by 2021. Meanwhile, global secondaries maintain a flatter trajectory, generally hovering between 1.4x and 1.6x. 

Finally, the chart on IRR dispersion, defined as the top quartile fund IRR minus the bottom quartile, shows that global buyout funds experience a much wider performance dispersion, ranging from approximately 9% to 15%. In contrast, global secondaries display a significantly narrower and more stable dispersion, mostly tracking between 4% and 9%. This tighter band of outcomes represents a lower-risk profile, which many investors find worth the trade-off of modestly lower median returns, such as the median buyout IRR of 15.4% compared to the median secondary fund IRR of 13.5% for vintages 2010 to 2021.

This page from the J.P. Morgan Alternative Investments Review analyzes multifamily housing supply, hotel industry performance divergence, and Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust (BREIT) redemption trends. 

The author begins by addressing multifamily housing, noting that recent high vacancy rates stem from a major surge in supply over the past two to three years. A line chart titled "Housing supply under construction" shows multi-family and single-family supply as a percentage of owner-occupied housing stock from 2000 to 2024. While single-family supply peaked before the financial crisis in 2006 at roughly 1.5%, the multi-family pipeline reached its highest level in the 21st century, peaking at over 1.3% of stock around 2023. A complementary chart, "Historical and projected US multifamily supply," displays units in thousands alongside their share of inventory from 2014 through projections to 2028. This visual shows new supply peaking in 2024 at nearly 600,000 units, representing a 3.0% share of inventory, but forecasts a steep drop over the subsequent years down to approximately 200,000 units and a 1.0% share of inventory by 2028 as the market absorbs the supply.

Turning to the lodging sector, the page highlights a stark performance divergence between luxury hotels and the rest of the market, which the author attributes to a strong stock market paired with a sluggish broader economy. This is detailed in a bar chart titled "Hotel performance by class, YTD through Q2 2025," which tracks Average Daily Rate (ADR) and Revenue Per Available Room (RevPAR) across six segments: Luxury, Upper upscale, Upscale, Upper midscale, Midscale, and Economy. Positive growth is concentrated in the Luxury segment, where both ADR and RevPAR rose by about 2.5%, and to a lesser extent Upper upscale. In contrast, all lower-tier segments from Upscale to Economy suffered negative growth, with Economy RevPAR falling by nearly 2.0%. 

Lastly, the page provides an update on BREIT. The author notes that redemption requests have normalized back to historical levels of 1% to 2% of NAV, down from a peak of 8% of NAV in early 2023 when fulfillment rates collapsed to 5%. This normalization is unsurprising given BREIT's low 3% exposure to the office sector. The accompanying dual-axis chart, "BREIT investor redemptions and fulfillments" from October 2022 to June 2025, displays monthly requests as a percentage of NAV on the left-hand scale and monthly fulfillments as a percentage of total requests on the right-hand scale. It visualizes the peak in requests in early 2023 when fulfillments dipped below 20%, followed by a steady recovery starting in early 2024 where monthly fulfillments returned to 100% of requests and monthly requests fell back below 2%.

In this publication, Michael Cembalest of J.P. Morgan Asset Management presents a market outlook focused on how the generative AI investment theme has dominated—or "smothered"—the rest of the US equity market since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022. He argues that 65% to 75% of the S&P 500’s returns, profits, and capital spending since then have been driven by just 42 AI-linked companies, noting that without them, the S&P 500 would have underperformed European, Japanese, and Chinese markets. To support this, he points out that tech sector capital spending contributed 40% to 45% of US GDP growth over the last three quarters of 2025, a dramatic increase from less than 5% in early 2023.

This theme of extreme concentration is detailed in a performance table comparing AI-related categories against global benchmarks since November 2022. The 42 "Total AI" stocks, which are categorized into direct AI, AI utilities, and AI capital equipment, generated a massive 190% price return, 153% earnings growth, and 68% capex/R&D growth. By comparison, the S&P 500 ex-AI benchmark saw only a 26% price return, 19% earnings growth, and 19% capex/R&D growth, while regional indices like MSCI Europe, Japan, and China underperformed the AI block significantly. Furthermore, the table reveals that these 42 AI stocks accounted for 78% of all S&P 500 price returns, 66% of its earnings growth, and 71% of its capex/R&D growth over this multi-year period.

To illustrate the sheer scale of this investment boom, Cembalest includes a bar chart comparing 2025 tech capital spending against historic US infrastructure and science initiatives as a peak annual percentage of GDP. The chart shows that tech capex in 2025 reached nearly 1.8% of US GDP. This spending vastly eclipses the peak spending of major historical projects like the Manhattan Project in 1944, the Apollo Project in 1964, the Interstate highway system in 1966, and the entire 1930s public works program (which built the Hoover Dam, the Golden Gate Bridge, and LaGuardia Airport, among others)—all of which peaked at around 0.3% to 0.4% of GDP. Even the telecom-era broadband capex boom of 2000 peaked near 1.1%, illustrating the historically unprecedented nature of the current tech spending phase.

Looking forward, Cembalest raises four major "moat risks" that investors should consider: US power generation constraints, China's capacity to scale its own technology independently, China's geopolitical approach to Taiwan, and the ultimate return on investment for the $1.3 trillion spent on hyperscaler capex and R&D since 2022. For his market outlook, he predicts a year characterized by a 10% to 15% correction driven by profit-taking and a growth scare, but ultimately forecasts that equity markets will end the year higher than they began.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s "Eye on the Market" report addresses the massive market dominance of artificial intelligence and semiconductor firms, questioning whether the largest technological "moat" in market history is indestructible. The foundation of this moat is built on NVIDIA chip designs, TSMC manufacturing, and ASML lithography. The report illustrates this dominance through two charts tracking the eight largest hyperscalers (Meta, Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft) and "semiscalers" (AMD, ASML, TSMC, NVIDIA) from 2018 to late 2025. The first chart, showing absolute market capitalization in trillions of dollars, depicts their combined market value expanding from $3 trillion to $18 trillion. The second chart displays this growth as a percentage of global market capitalization, showing that these eight stocks now constitute approximately 20% of the MSCI World index and roughly 16% of the MSCI All Country World Index, which includes emerging markets. 

The author transitions to trade dynamics, asserting that the AI revolution relies heavily on imported technology. Despite new trade barriers, the U.S. semiconductor ecosystem has largely been spared from Donald Trump’s tariffs. A line chart tracking monthly annualized U.S. imports of technology components from 2015 to late 2025 demonstrates this heavy reliance, showing a massive spike in large computer imports—specifically GPU and CPU rack servers—which surged past $200 billion in late 2025. Meanwhile, imports of standalone semiconductors and computer parts remained steadier, hovering around $75 billion and $50 billion respectively. 

To explain why these imports have continued to flow, a horizontal bar chart details the percentage of 2024 U.S. product imports excluded from Trump tariffs. The data reveals that the semiconductor ecosystem enjoys some of the highest exemption rates, with computer parts, computers, and semiconductors receiving between 70% and 85% tariff exclusions. This ranks them just below energy and pharma, and far above consumer-facing categories like apparel, footwear, and cosmetics, which receive almost no exemptions. Looking forward, the author notes that an ongoing Section 232 investigation on semiconductors is an open question, though it may eventually offer substantial exemptions to companies that commit to manufacturing within the United States. 

The page concludes with two key reference points. A footnote highlights the critical role of Dutch manufacturer ASML, the largest technology company in Europe with a market cap over $300 billion, whose extreme ultraviolet lithography machines are essential for etching sub-10 nanometer features onto silicon wafers. Finally, the author defines J.P. Morgan’s "S&P 500 AI universe," which is composed of 42 stocks split into three buckets: 28 "Direct AI" companies (spanning giants like NVIDIA, Microsoft, Apple, and Tesla), 8 "AI utilities" providing power (such as Vistra and NextEra), and 6 "AI capital equipment" firms (including Eaton and GE Vernova).

This page of the report examines the rising adoption rates of generative artificial intelligence across various sectors and user groups, while posing the critical caveat that these adoption surveys do not indicate how much users are willing to pay or how much can be monetized via advertising. The author cites a December 2025 OpenAI report noting that ChatGPT message volume grew eight-fold and API reasoning token consumption per organization surged 320 times year-over-year, indicating a substantial increase in both the breadth and intensity of enterprise AI usage. 

To illustrate these trends, the author presents four charts. The first chart, titled "AI adoption rate by sector," shows the share of US businesses with paid subscriptions to AI models, platforms, and tools from January 2023 to September 2025, using data from Ramp. Information technology leads the pack, rising from under 20 percent to nearly 70 percent, closely followed by Finance and Insurance, which climbs to around 60 percent. Sectors like Educational Services, Manufacturing, and Retail also show strong upward trends, while the US government estimate remains flat at the bottom, under 10 percent. 

The second chart, "Census: AI adoption rates by sector and date," draws from a US Census Bureau survey of 200,000 businesses to illustrate the share of firms using AI across three periods: August 2024, October 2025, and a projection for the next six months. It highlights that the Information sector is projected to lead with nearly 40 percent adoption, with Professional, Scientific, and Technical services close behind at around 38 percent. Other sectors like Finance and Insurance and Educational Services show steady gains, whereas Accommodation and Food Services remains at the very bottom, below 5 percent.

The third chart, "Generative AI adoption survey" from the St. Louis Fed, tracks the percentage of 25,000 adult respondents using generative AI from August 2024 to August 2025. The overall usage rises from roughly 45 percent to over 50 percent, driven primarily by non-work usage, which increases from roughly 37 percent to around 47 percent, whereas work-related usage inches up more modestly from around 33 percent to 38 percent. 

The final chart, titled "Depth of AI usage across organizations," is sourced from Anthropic and the Stanford AI Index Report. It plots the fraction of occupations against the minimum fraction of tasks utilizing AI, based on a sample of one million Claude conversations. The curve illustrates that while many occupations have a small percentage of tasks executed by AI, 36 percent of occupations use AI on at least 25 percent of their tasks, demonstrating that AI is deeply integrating into a significant portion of daily workflows.

Michael Cembalest addresses the common investor concern that high valuations represent the primary risk to the current artificial intelligence cycle. He argues that US equity market valuations are internally consistent because higher valuation metrics, such as price-to-book ratios, align closely with superior profitability, measured by return on equity. To illustrate this relationship, the page presents two scatter plots of consensus forward price-to-book ratios against consensus forward return on equity as of December 2025. The first plot shows S&P 500 sectors following a clear upward-sloping trend, where the Information Technology sector sits at the highest end with a return on equity of roughly 34 percent and a price-to-book ratio of 12, while value sectors like Utilities, Energy, and Financials cluster at the bottom left with return on equity figures between 10 percent and 15 percent and price-to-book ratios of 2 to 3. 

The second scatter plot expands this comparison by including individual high-growth technology and semiconductor companies, showing they fall along the same upward-sloping valuation-to-profitability curve. On this expanded scale, NVIDIA stands out at the far right with an exceptional return on equity of around 85 percent and a price-to-book ratio of approximately 28. ASML is positioned at a return on equity of roughly 65 percent and a price-to-book ratio of 17, while other major tech companies like Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, Amazon, Advanced Micro Devices, and Taiwan Semiconductor are also plotted to show how their valuations are justified by high profitability. 

A historical line chart from 1976 through late 2025 compares S&P 500 free cash flow margins of the tech and interactive media sector against the rest of the market, excluding financials and real estate investment trusts. This chart shows a dramatic divergence over the last two decades. While the rest of the market has seen its free cash flow margins hover relatively flat between 5 percent and 10 percent, the tech and interactive media sector's margins have climbed steadily from around 5 percent in the early 2000s to about 25 percent by late 2025, highlighting the sector's extraordinary cash-generating power.

Lastly, a chart tracking PEG ratios from 1995 to late 2025 compares the forward price-to-earnings ratio divided by year-two forward earnings-per-share growth for the MSCI All World Equity Info Tech Index against the broader MSCI All World Equity Index. This visual shows that despite high absolute valuations, the tech sector's growth-adjusted valuation is in line with the broader market. By late 2025, both indexes have PEG ratios of approximately 1.3 to 1.4, which is far below the peak of the dot-com bubble in 2000, when the tech index's PEG ratio spiked to 2.5 compared to the broader market's 1.75. Cembalest concludes by noting that S&P 500 forward price-to-earnings multiples only rose by about 3 percent in 2025, meaning that the vast majority of the market's 18 percent year-to-date gain was driven by actual earnings growth rather than multiple expansion.

This page of the J.P. Morgan report examines the dramatic but uneven progress of generative artificial intelligence models across several data science benchmarks. While the author cautions that these benchmarks can sometimes be gamed through trial and error, the advances remain undeniable. Today's AI models can match or exceed human capabilities in areas such as image recognition, visual reasoning, and competition-level math. Notable achievements include OpenAI's o3 model, which performed better than 99% of human competitors on Codeforces coding challenges, and Otto-SR, a medical research synthesis model that reproduced a systematic review in just two days—a feat that would typically require twelve human work-years. However, the author notes that AI still struggles in domains where models are not explicitly trained, showing mixed results in hallucination rates and genuine reasoning abilities.

The first visualization on the page is the AI Model Performance Tracker, which plots the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v3.0 from September 2022 to September 2025. This index averages performance across ten distinct evaluations, including GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro. The chart reveals a steep upward trajectory for both US and Chinese models, though US models consistently lead. The US performance line, topped by Gemini 3 Pro Preview (high), rises from an index score of around 10 in late 2022 to nearly 80 by late 2025. China’s line, represented by models like Kimi K2 Thinking, begins its climb later in late 2023 but finishes strong, rising from under 10 to nearly 60 by September 2025.

To the right, another line graph details the ability of these models to solve real-world GitHub issues from the second quarter of 2024 through the fourth quarter of 2025. Using the SWE-bench framework, the chart plots the percent of issues resolved by the highest-scoring model per developer, including Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, Alibaba, DeepSeek, xAI, and Meta AI. Both verified and bash-only test series demonstrate steep improvements; top developers like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic saw their resolution rates jump from around 30% to 40% in mid-2024 to peak levels between 70% and 80% by the end of 2025. 

The bottom-left bar chart tackles the persistent problem of AI hallucinations, defining the hallucination rate as the share of incorrect responses out of all questions asked. The results vary widely by developer and model. Anthropic's Claude 4.5 series, including Haiku, Opus, and Sonnet, displays the lowest rates of incorrect answers, hovering between 15% and 20%. In contrast, several open-source and alternative models struggle significantly; for example, the gpt-oss-20B (high) and gpt-oss-120B (high) models suffer from hallucination rates that approach 50%.

The final chart, in the bottom right, serves as a proxy for opaque reasoning ability, measuring how long it takes a human to solve the math problems that AI models can solve in a single pass without using chain-of-thought reasoning. The vertical axis runs from zero to four minutes, with a higher time indicating stronger pre-trained reasoning capabilities. Models are plotted by their release dates from January 2023 to July 2025. The chart shows a clear upward curve over time: older models like GPT-4 and GPT-4o score well under one minute, while newer iterations like Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Gemini 3 Pro show massive gains, with Gemini 3 Pro and Opus 4.5 reaching the top of the chart near the four-minute mark. This suggests that some leading developers are successfully improving the underlying reasoning capabilities of their models through pretraining, rather than simply relying on increased computing power during inference.

In this J.P. Morgan Executive Summary, Michael Cembalest argues that while the four dominant hyperscalers are aggressively ramping up capital expenditures and R&D for the artificial intelligence arms race, this spending boom is fundamentally healthier than historical precursors because it is largely self-funded rather than debt-driven. The universe of twenty-eight direct AI stocks represents half of the S&P 500 market capitalization but accounts for only five percent of its net debt. However, credit markets are beginning to react to a very recent uptick in debt-financed spending, with Oracle serving as a cautionary tale as its stock fell about thirty-five percent and its credit spreads widened by ninety basis points following rising leverage. 

Four charts illustrate these dynamics in detail. The first chart, tracking hyperscaler capex and R&D as a share of revenues from 2017 through late 2025, shows Meta leading the surge, with its combined spending hitting a record high of seventy percent. This dwarfs peers like Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft, which cluster between thirty and forty percent, and stands in stark contrast to the S&P 500 Info Tech median of around twenty percent and the broader S&P 500 median of ten percent. 

The second chart compares historical capex financing cycles from 1996 to 2026. It plots capex to sales against the share of capex and dividends financed with debt rather than internally generated cash flow. During the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, capex to sales peaked above forty percent and debt financing topped fifteen percent. By contrast, in late 2025, capex to sales has only ticked up to around nine percent, and the share of debt-financed capex remains historically low at around five percent, emphasizing the organic strength of the current cycle.

The third chart displays net debt to EBITDA ratios for direct AI stocks as of the third and fourth quarters of 2025. It reveals that the vast majority of AI leaders—including NVIDIA, Microsoft, Apple, Google, Meta, Tesla, and Amazon—register at zero, meaning their cash and marketable securities exceed their total debt. A few companies show moderate leverage, but Oracle stands out with its leverage multiple surging to over six times EBITDA by the fourth quarter of 2025. 

The final chart shows free cash flow to revenue ratios for these same AI companies. Most of them dramatically outperform the S&P 500 median of roughly five percent and the tech median of eighteen percent. NVIDIA, Broadcom, and Adobe lead the group with free cash flow margins exceeding forty percent, while Intel and Oracle are the key underperformers with negative margins of roughly negative twenty percent and negative twelve percent, respectively.

Adding a sharp personal note, a prominent footnote details Cembalest's frustration with Meta for failing to police fraudulent WhatsApp stock scams that use his name. Citing a bipartisan press release from Senators Hawley and Blumenthal, the footnote notes that Meta reportedly generates up to sixteen billion dollars annually hosting fraudulent advertisements, displaying fifteen billion high-risk ads daily, and playing an unprecedented, central role in facilitating consumer scams.

This page, titled Metaverse moment, analyzes the impact of artificial intelligence on labor productivity, specifically highlighting findings from Goldman Sachs research. Author Michael Cembalest discusses how generative AI applications appear to already be boosting productivity, particularly in coding, customer service, and consulting. Goldman Sachs projects that AI adoption will eventually spread to other sectors, potentially leading to a fifteen percent boost to US productivity and an eight trillion dollar net present value gain. The text frames this potential AI productivity surge as a critical counterbalance to upcoming economic challenges, including slowing US labor force growth driven by an aging population, low birth rates, and Trump immigration policies, as well as inflation risks from tariffs, a weaker dollar, and high budget deficits.

Two bar charts at the top of the page illustrate the estimated productivity boosts from AI. The left chart displays company-specific estimates, showing Anthropic at the high end with an estimated productivity increase of around eighty percent, followed by Autodesk and UC San Diego at approximately sixty percent, Adobe at fifty percent, and other firms like Deloitte, Tencent, and Ally Financial in the thirty to forty percent range, tapering down to Klarna at roughly ten percent. The right chart displays academic estimates from various research studies, showing the highest productivity boost in the Ju Aral 2025 study at over seventy percent, followed by Peng et al. 2023 and Gambacorta et al. 2024 at over fifty percent, with several other studies estimating gains of between ten and forty percent. 

Two tables at the bottom compare annualized productivity gains from the pre-COVID era (Q1 2016 to Q1 2020) with the post-GPT eras (Q4 2022 to Q2 2025 and Q3 2023 to Q2 2025). The first table, utilizing the Real GDP method, shows non-financial corporate productivity gains rising from 1.1 percent pre-COVID to 3.1 percent and 3.9 percent in the post-GPT periods. In the Information sector, annualized gains increased from 5.0 percent pre-COVID to 8.9 percent and 6.0 percent post-GPT, while Data processing gains rose from 8.0 percent to 12.1 percent and 9.9 percent. The second table, utilizing the Real gross output method, reveals a similar upward shift. Non-financial corporate gains rose from 1.1 percent to 3.1 percent and 3.9 percent. Information sector gains increased from 3.7 percent pre-COVID to 7.3 percent and 5.7 percent post-GPT, and Data processing gains went from 7.8 percent to 10.2 percent and 10.6 percent over the same periods.

In this page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, the author evaluates the progress of artificial intelligence capabilities in performing economically valuable, real-world tasks. Using findings from an OpenAI study on the GDPval benchmark, which assesses models across 44 professions, Cembalest notes that while human experts are still generally preferred overall, AI models are rapidly approaching parity, especially in software engineering. When humans partner with AI, efficiency in both speed and cost improves by about 1.5 times. 

The first chart, titled AI model overall performance on realistic work tasks, plots the percentage of time an AI work product is preferred over a human expert's work across several models. The y-axis ranges from 0 percent to 60 percent, with a dashed line at 50 percent indicating parity. None of the models cross this parity threshold for general tasks. GPT-4o performs lowest at just over 10 percent, followed by Grok 4 at about 20 percent, Gemini 2.5 Pro at around 22 percent, o4-mini high at roughly 26 percent, o3 high at 32 percent, GPT-5 high at 38 percent, and Claude Opus 4.1 performing best at approximately 45 percent.

The second chart, AI model performance on software developer work, uses the same axis and models but shows a much higher preference rate for AI. On software tasks, several advanced models surpass the 50 percent parity threshold, meaning judges prefer the AI’s work over human experts. While GPT-4o, Grok 4, and Gemini 2.5 Pro remain below parity, o4-mini high reaches roughly 63 percent preference, GPT-5 high reaches about 64 percent, and both o3 high and Claude Opus 4.1 reach approximately 68 percent preference.

The third chart, Efficiency gains from AI assistance to human experts, is a scatter plot comparing cost improvements on the vertical axis against speed improvements on the horizontal axis, with an unassisted baseline set at 1.00x. While using GPT-4o actually degrades performance to around 0.60x for both metrics, more advanced models show clear gains. Assisted by o4-mini, experts achieve roughly 1.15x speed and 1.25x cost improvements. Assisted by o3, they reach about 1.25x speed and 1.45x cost improvements, and with GPT-5, they achieve approximately 1.50x speed and 1.55x cost improvements.

The fourth chart, AI software engineering task complexity, measures complexity by the hours a human takes to complete tasks that AI models can solve with 50 percent accuracy. Plotted against large language model release dates from 2019 to 2025, this complexity displays an exponential upward curve. Early models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 scored near zero hours. By late 2025, Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview and GPT-4o solved tasks taking humans 0.5 to 0.6 hours. The newest models show dramatic growth, with o4-mini at roughly 1.1 hours, o3 at 1.4 hours, Claude Opus 4.1 at 1.6 hours, Grok 4 at 1.8 hours, and GPT-5 handling complex tasks that take humans about 2.2 hours.

Finally, the page poses the question of whether AI models will soon run out of training data. Pointing to Stanford’s 2025 AI Index Report, the author concludes that a data shortage is unlikely before 2030. The text details massive reserves of available tokens, including a median of 130 trillion tokens in Common Crawl, 510 trillion in the indexed web, and roughly 3,100 trillion across the entire web, supplemented by 300 trillion tokens in images and 1,350 trillion in video.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication, titled Metaverse Moment, examines the revenues, free cash flow margins, cash balances, and general AI commentary of major tech hyperscalers. The central argument is that despite massive capital expenditure on generative AI, tracking actual profitability remains difficult because only Microsoft systematically discloses AI-specific revenue. The author warns that with declining free cash flow margins and falling cash balances, hyperscalers will need to demonstrate a clearer path to AI profitability in 2026 to justify their current valuations, a path further obscured by questions about GPU and networking equipment depreciation. A footnote highlights that NVIDIA sought to downplay vendor financing concerns by noting that its 2025 private company investments of 4.7 billion dollars represented only 3 percent of its revenues, with these companies primarily raising capital from third parties and maintaining a stable days sales outstanding of 53 days.

Earnings call commentary summarized on the page suggests robust top-line AI momentum. Microsoft reported that its inference business reached a 10 billion dollar revenue run rate faster than any line of business in its history, though constrained by compute capacity. Amazon reported billions in annualized revenue for its AWS AI business, while pointing out that infrastructure must be built out well ahead of customer monetization, and noted its Rufus shopping assistant was on track to deliver 10 billion dollars in incremental annualized sales. Google reported a 200 percent year-over-year revenue increase in products built on generative AI models, with its AI Max for Search serving as its fastest-growing AI-powered search ads product.

Four charts support these observations with historical data up to late 2025 and projections into 2026. The first chart, showing quarterly cloud service revenues in billions of US dollars, tracks steady growth across major providers from 2021 through 2025. Amazon Web Services remains the leader, rising from 15 billion dollars to approximately 35 billion dollars, followed by Microsoft Azure rising from 10 billion to roughly 25 billion dollars. Google Cloud shows more moderate but steady growth from 5 billion to about 15 billion dollars, while Oracle Cloud and IBM Cloud trail at lower levels.

The second chart displays hyperscaler free cash flow margins net of capital expenditures as a percentage of trailing 12-month revenues. This visual demonstrates a broad downward trend toward the end of the period. Microsoft’s margins declined from over 30 percent in 2021 to around 25 percent by 2026. Alphabet’s margins fell from nearly 30 percent to around 17 percent, while Meta's margins peaked near 35 percent in late 2024 before dropping toward 28 percent. Amazon’s margins dipped below zero in 2022, recovered to around 10 percent, and then began falling again, keeping several hyperscalers close to or below the S&P 500 median free cash flow margin of approximately 13 percent. 

The third chart illustrates hyperscaler cash and cash equivalents as a share of total assets from 2019 to 2026. This metric shows a severe draw-down in liquidity across the industry. Alphabet’s cash ratio plummeted from nearly 50 percent in 2019 to around 17 percent by 2026. Microsoft experienced a similar drop from 45 percent to around 15 percent, and Meta declined from 40 percent to about 15 percent, while Amazon fluctuated at lower levels, ending near 13 percent. 

The final chart tracks annualized revenue from AI in billions of US dollars from January 2024 through December 2025. This chart shows Microsoft Azure leading with a steep growth curve from roughly 3 billion dollars to nearly 19 billion dollars in annualized revenue. OpenAI follows with annualized revenues climbing to around 13 billion dollars by mid-2025. Anthropic, CoreWeave, xAI, and Nebius represent smaller but growing shares, with Anthropic approaching 8 billion dollars, CoreWeave near 6 billion dollars, and xAI and Nebius hovering at lower annualized thresholds.

This page analyzes the potential financial impact on major hyperscalers if they are forced to shorten the depreciation lifespans of their graphics processing units and networking equipment back to historical standards. Since 2020, major technology firms have extended the depreciable lives of these assets from three or four years up to five or six years, under the assumption that older chips remain highly utilized. However, declining hourly rental rates for graphics processors suggest that real-world depreciation may be faster than these accounting changes reflect. 

A table tracking Nvidia GPU hourly rental rates from November 2024 to December 2025 reveals that rental costs have generally slid by 20% to 26%. For instance, H100 rental rates at Neoclouds dropped 26% from $2.70 to $2.00, and AWS H100 rates fell 24% from $4.50 to $3.40. Bucking this downward trend, A100 rates for hyperscalers rose 15% to $3.60, and AWS H200 rates climbed 11% to $3.30. This broader downward rate pressure coincides with a drop of more than 50% in CoreWeave stock from its June 2025 peak. Another table tracking historical depreciation assumptions shows how systematically companies have extended asset lives from 2020 to 2025: Meta went from 3.0 to 5.5 years, Google from 3.0 to 6.0 years, Oracle from 5.0 to 6.0 years, Microsoft from 3.0 to 6.0 years, and Amazon from 4.0 to 5.0 years.

A third table models the estimated impact on corporate income statements if these five giants revert to a stricter three-year depreciation assumption for GPU and networking capital expenditures added since January 2023. Under this scenario, estimated depreciation would surge, causing operating margins and earnings per share to compress. For Google, estimated depreciation would double from $8,667 million to $17,335 million, pushing its operating margin down by 2.2 percentage points and shaving 6% off pro-forma EPS. Oracle would suffer the most severe impact, with its operating margin dropping by 4.3 percentage points and its pro-forma EPS falling 17%. Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon would each see their pro-forma EPS decline by 7%. 

The author poses several open questions regarding what could force this shift, including high annual GPU failure rates of roughly 9%, rapid data center refurbishment that discards older chips, or customers insisting on newer Blackwell GPUs even for simple inference tasks. Conversely, the analysis notes that the Trump administration's policy allowing Nvidia H200 chips to be exported to China could support the secondary market value of older hardware, potentially defending the hyperscalers' current longer-term depreciation schedules.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s outlook examines the massive potential gap between future AI workload compute supply and demand, specifically focusing on consumer inference. It features a main analysis based on estimates from SemiAnalysis, showing that Western AI workload compute is expected to rise sharply to approximately 36,000 exaflops at FP8 precision in 2026, up from 11,500 exaflops in 2025. A key supporting detail in the footnotes reveals that while there are 125 gigawatts of global data center capacity, only 10 to 13 gigawatts are currently capable of supporting AI workloads. 

Assuming a 50 percent utilization rate, the projected 2026 compute translates to about 1.7 billion exaflops per day, which is well below the estimated 7.2 billion exaflops needed to satisfy consumer inference demand. Under a wider GPU utilization spectrum of 33 percent to 75 percent, the 2026 AI compute supply would only cover 14 percent to 66 percent of consumer inference needs. Crucially, this projection is calculated before even adding demand from enterprise applications, national defense, or low-latency inference fields like robotics, autonomous driving, and commercial drones.

A central table evaluates hyperscaler compute as a share of future consumer inference demand for 5 billion users across different scenarios of token intensity and GPU utilization. If consumer token demand is 800,000 cloud tokens per day, the compute meets 66 percent of demand at 75 percent GPU utilization, falling to 29 percent at 33 percent utilization. If token demand scales to 1,600,000 per day, those shares drop significantly to 33 percent at the highest utilization and just 14 percent at the lowest.

To illustrate what might shift these dynamics, the author enlists J.P. Morgan AI professionals to outline drivers that could increase or decrease cloud compute demand. Upward pressures include the rise of reasoning models that use 20 to 40 times more tokens than standard models, the scaling of early-stage finance and legal models, highly token-intensive creative and ad agency applications, continuous dev-ops monitoring by autonomous agents, and the migration of fraud detection to transformer architectures. Conversely, demand could be mitigated by the use of specialized accelerators, mixture-of-experts model architectures, post-trained smaller purpose-built models, and a shift of AI workloads directly to edge devices, PCs, and mobile devices where cheap accelerators can run inference locally.

Finally, a lighthearted sidebar titled "On flops and floppers" contrasts floating-point operations per second (flops) used to measure GPU power with soccer players famous for diving or "flopping." It cites a 2018 Bleacher Report rating of the worst floppers based on frequency, success, and difficulty, listing Angel di Maria, Sergio Busquets, Cristiano Ronaldo, Arjen Robben, Neymar, and an honorable mention for Jurgen Klinsmann.

This page, titled "WCGW #2: US power generation constraints," examines the growing risk that US power grid capacity will struggle to support the massive energy demands of artificial intelligence and data centers. The author opens with a quote from Sam Altman's May 2025 Senate testimony asserting that the availability of AI will ultimately be limited by the abundance of energy, alongside a PJM Independent Market Monitor quote attribute nearly all peak load forecast increases for 2026 and 2027 to data center additions. Although data centers currently consume only 4% to 8% of US power, they are projected to account for two-thirds of future load growth, even after factoring in a 40% annual improvement in chip efficiency. To underscore the desperation for reliable baseload power, the text highlights Microsoft and Constellation Energy's agreement to restart a decommissioned nuclear reactor at Three Mile Island at an expensive rate of $110 to $130 per MWh for 20 years, which is about double the national average for long-term power purchase agreements.

The first chart on the page tracks the power required to train frontier AI models from 2018 projected out to 2026. This metric has grown at an estimated 2.2x per year, rising from below 0.1 megawatts for early models to roughly 10 megawatts for GPT-4 and Llama 3.1-405, and heading toward 1,000 megawatts for massive models like Grok-3. 

The second chart displays US construction spending from 2014 to 2025 in seasonally adjusted billions of dollars. It shows a dramatic surge in electric power infrastructure spending, which has risen above $100 billion, while spending on data centers steadily climbs toward $40 billion, surpassing the declining spending on traditional office buildings. 

The third chart depicts soaring capacity prices in the PJM competitive power market, which covers "data center alley" across Virginia, Pennsylvania, Maryland, and Ohio. Base Residual Auction rates for both the Mid-Atlantic Area Council and the broader Regional Transmission Organization have historically fluctuated below $150 per MW but are shown spiking violently to approximately $350 per MW for the 2025/2026 and 2027/2028 delivery years, with a note indicating that uncapped rates would have hit $530 per MW. 

The fourth and most critical chart compares annual US electricity generation and storage capacity additions from 1950 through the mid-2020s. While raw nameplate capacity additions have recently surged to over 60 gigawatts, nameplate capacity adjusted by effective load carrying capability factors—which account for the intermittency and reliability of solar, wind, and hydro—remains remarkably low and flat, sitting near 20 gigawatts. This stark divergence shows that reliable grid additions are growing far more gradually than nominal numbers suggest. Footnotes elaborate that PJM leads with 67 GW of existing and planned data center capacity, followed by ERCOT in Texas with 20 GW, and CAISO in California and Nevada with 8 GW.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan publication, titled "Metaverse moment," analyzes the massive growth projections of OpenAI and the severe energy and corporate bottlenecks that threaten their realization. The central argument is that while OpenAI remains significantly ahead of its AI competitors in user growth, monetization, and capabilities, its ambitious expansion presents a profound physical grid constraint and an unprecedented corporate risk. The author notes that OpenAI is currently on track to make between $10 billion and $20 billion in revenue, yet it has committed $1.4 trillion to its corporate partners while relying heavily on subscription fees rather than search, advertising, or cloud revenues. Additionally, its own chief economist disclosed that 72% of GPT queries are non-business related.

To highlight OpenAI's rapidly expanding targets, a table titled "OpenAI forecasts keep rising" compares the company's 2027 outlook made in mid-2025 with an updated forecast from October 31, 2025. Over just a three-month span, the projected 2027 revenue was revised upward by 50%, jumping from $60 billion to $90 billion, while projected inference compute costs rose 43% to $30 billion. Weekly average users increased from 1.4 billion to 1.8 billion, and paid subscribers grew 31% to 76 million, with the average revenue per paid user increasing to $880.

A second table, "Current and future GPU and power requirements," details the physical hardware and electrical grid capacity needed to sustain this growth. The data shows that the equivalent of new B200 GPUs added annually for inference is projected to surge from 72,098 in 2024 to nearly 2 million by 2030, while GPUs added for training will scale from 120,163 to over 2.2 million. To power these GPUs, the cumulative capacity required is forecasted to rise from 0.5 gigawatts in 2024 to 30.2 gigawatts by 2030. Cembalest marks this 30-gigawatt demand as a major bottleneck, pointing out that the entire United States only added 25 gigawatts of reliable capacity in 2024. He warns that turbine delays, grid bottlenecks, overly optimistic timelines for small modular reactors, and limited nuclear recommissioning options will make this energy requirement very difficult to fulfill.

Finally, a column chart titled "OpenAI projected compute budget" outlines the company's projected spending on inference versus training compute in billions of dollars from 2024 through 2030. The chart demonstrates that OpenAI expects training compute to remain more expensive than inference compute throughout the decade. In 2024, inference cost was $2 billion and training was $3 billion. Training costs are projected to peak in 2028 at $81 billion compared to $30 billion for inference. By 2030, the spending gap narrows slightly, with inference compute costs rising to $49 billion and training compute costs projected at $56 billion.

This page analyzes the severe power grid and supply chain constraints facing the United States as data center electricity demand surges. The author argues that while utilities are introducing higher, specialized tariffs for data centers, these rates remain insufficient to cover the capital costs of constructing new generation capacity. 

A bar chart titled "Specialized data center power rates still trail cost of new generation" illustrates this shortfall across various utilities, such as Idaho Power, Florida Power & Light, Duke Energy, and Dominion. While specialized rates increase the cost per megawatt-hour to between roughly $30 and $55, they still fall short of the cost thresholds for new generation assets. Specifically, these rates lag behind the cost of subsidized solar and storage, unsubsidized solar and storage at approximately $72 per megawatt-hour, and combined cycle gas turbines at around $95 per megawatt-hour. Footnotes highlight that proposals in states like California, Georgia, Indiana, Maryland, Michigan, Ohio, and Oregon are attempting to force data centers to shoulder more of these grid-addition costs.

Compounding this pricing mismatch is a critical shortage of physical infrastructure, particularly gas turbines. A sidebar details how combined cycle turbine costs have doubled over the last 24 months, rising from approximately $1,200 per kilowatt to $2,500 per kilowatt, with delivery lead times stretching to three to seven years. Single cycle turbine costs have similarly escalated from $800 to $1,500 per kilowatt. This supply bottleneck is visualized in a chart of "Global gas turbine orders," which shows projected orders for 2025 through 2028 soaring far above the current production limit of approximately 56 gigawatts, peaking near 100 gigawatts. This shortage directly collides with massive regional demand projections, as shown in the "ERCOT large load interconnection requests" chart. Interconnection requests in Texas are projected to grow exponentially from virtually nothing in 2022 to over 200 gigawatts by 2030, though the vast majority of this capacity remains unstudied, under review, or approved but not yet operational. 

Finally, the author points out a regulatory headwind: unlike the semiconductor sector, the power generation supply chain does not benefit from substantial tariff exemptions. A chart comparing "Power generation vs semiconductor tariff exclusions" shows that while 80 percent or more of imported computer parts and computers are excluded from tariffs, key electrical equipment such as transformers, electrical switches, solar panels, and batteries see exclusion rates below 30 percent, with batteries and electric boards near zero. Despite these tariff barriers, the final chart shows that US power generation imports have surged dramatically to meet domestic needs, climbing from a monthly annualized rate of roughly $110 billion in 2021 to over $200 billion by late 2025.

This page of the J.P. Morgan publication examines the escalating power constraints facing data centers, focusing on the projected rise in natural gas demand and the growing momentum behind onsite power generation, often referred to as "bring your own generation." 

The author starts by citing BloombergNEF projections showing that data centers could boost US natural gas demand by 3 to 4 billion cubic feet per day by 2030. This is a substantial addition given that total US dry natural gas production sat at approximately 107 billion cubic feet per day in 2025. An accompanying stacked bar chart of data center natural gas demand by 2030 indicates total demand could approach 5 billion cubic feet per day, split between current grid demand, new grid-based demand, and new behind-the-meter demand. A second chart illustrating the incremental grid-connected data center fuel mix from 2025 to 2030 shows that natural gas will dominate the mix, holding steady at approximately 60 percent, while coal's share shrinks and wind and solar make up the remainder.

The shift toward onsite generation is largely driven by severe grid connection delays. A line chart detailing the months elapsed from an interconnection request to a commercial operation date shows that wait times have risen dramatically between 2000 and 2024. The median delay climbed from around 20 months to 50 months, while the 75th percentile surged to over 70 months by 2024. Consequently, a survey by Bloom Energy reveals that while only 1 percent of data centers currently use onsite power, 38 percent expect to rely on it partially by 2030, and 27 percent expect to rely on it entirely. High-profile examples of current and proposed onsite power projects include xAI's Colossus 1 and 2, OpenAI and Oracle's Stargate, Microsoft's Three Mile Island project, Equinix, CoreWeave, and Meta's Socrates South. 

To meet this demand, new competitors are entering the gas-fired power generation market, challenging traditional giants like GE Vernova, Mitsubishi, and Siemens. These new entrants include South Korea's Doosan Enerbility, Finland's Wartsila, and US companies Boom Supersonic and Caterpillar. 

Finally, a detailed technical table from SemiAnalysis compares seven onsite generation options across physical and financial metrics. The table highlights trade-offs in scale, cost, and speed. For instance, aeroderivative gas turbines provide 30 to 60 megawatts per unit, have an 18-to-36-month lead time, and an estimated levelized cost of energy of $80 to $130 per megawatt-hour. In comparison, fuel cells offer rapid deployment with a lead time of just 3 to 4 months but come with high capital expenditures of $3,000 to $4,000 per kilowatt and a levelized cost of energy between $100 and $200 per megawatt-hour. Meanwhile, large-scale H-Class combined-cycle gas turbines offer massive capacities of 600 to 1,000 megawatts but require the longest lead times of 36 to 60 months.

This page analyzes power constraints for data centers, focusing on fuel availability and alternative power sources as artificial intelligence infrastructure demands scale. Michael Cembalest discusses the potential for a looming global LNG supply glut, which may leave more domestic gas for US consumption and counteract BloombergNEF’s prediction that data center gas demand could flip the US into a supply deficit by 2030. The first chart, "Global LNG capacity utilization," displays LNG export capacity, imports, and utilization from 2005 to 2035. It shows that while global LNG export capacity and imports are projected to rise steadily toward 1,000 billion cubic meters, utilization is expected to plunge to a low of roughly 84% around 2029–2030, illustrating the projected glut before recovering slightly by 2035.

Next, the author assesses whether behind-the-meter solar and battery configurations can act as baseload substitutes for gas turbines. He argues that solar and storage configurations remain significantly more expensive per megawatt-hour than combined-cycle gas turbines, even when incorporating a 40% investment tax credit. This is illustrated in the second chart, "Data center behind the meter configuration, $ per MWh," which models a 1-gigawatt data center in Las Vegas. The unsubsidized cost of energy rises sharply from roughly $60 per megawatt-hour for a 100% natural gas configuration to nearly $180 per megawatt-hour (or $150 with a 40% tax credit) for a system with 6.0 gigawatts of photovoltaics and 17 gigawatt-hours of battery storage. Despite these high costs, less price-sensitive developers may deploy solar and storage to bypass grid connection delays and avoid billions in lost AI infrastructure revenue, highlighting Google’s December 2025 acquisition of Intersect Power as a key transaction to watch.

The page then addresses nuclear power, noting that only two to three decommissioned plants in the US—Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania, Palisades in Michigan, and Duane Arnold in Iowa—are viable candidates for restart. Cembalest expresses skepticism toward small modular reactors (SMRs), describing them as a "reverse learning curve in motion." The third chart, "The original learning curve led to larger nuclear plant sizes," tracks the average capacity of global nuclear plants by construction start year from 1950 to 2025. It shows that average capacities rose from under 200 megawatts in the 1950s to around 1,000 to 1,200 megawatts by the late 20th century to spread high fixed capital costs. The author argues that SMRs lack evidence of cost-effectiveness unless they can achieve costs of $4 to $6 million per megawatt, or less than twice the cost of grid power. Finally, the author briefly notes that quantum computing is several years away from being a viable, energy-efficient replacement for GPUs in handling complex mathematical operations.

Under the theme "China scales the moat," this page argues that China is rapidly ascending the global innovation food chain, suggesting that its mastery of proprietary lithography and semiconductor technology is a matter of "when, not if." The author supports this premise with five line charts showing China outpacing the West in innovation, export complexity, patents, and scientific research, alongside a commentary on how Western regulatory actions are inadvertently aiding Chinese competitors.

The first chart, "China breaks into top 10 most innovative economies," tracks rankings in the Global Innovation Index from 2012 to 2026. It highlights China’s rapid climb from 34th place in 2012 to the cusp of the top ten by 2024, converging toward the United States, which has remained steady near the top five. The second chart, "US and China export complexity," displays country rankings from 1998 to 2023, demonstrating a clear convergence. While the United States saw its rank slide from near the top ten down to 14th, China’s rank climbed dramatically from 33rd to 16th, representing a massive shift toward more complex exported products.

Three subsequent charts illustrate China's dominance in clean energy, artificial intelligence, and nuclear research. The chart depicting "Annual clean energy patent applications by country" in thousands from 2000 to 2020 shows China's applications growing exponentially after 2015 to exceed 250,000, while the rest of the world, the United States, and the European Union remained flat, with each under 50,000 applications. The chart for "AI patents by geographic area" shows the percent of world total AI patents from 2010 to 2022. During this period, China's share of global AI patents surged from roughly 12% to over 60%, while the shares of the United States and the rest of the world both declined from roughly 40% to approximately 15% each. The final chart, "Nuclear science and engineering research by country," measures the count of publications in the top 10% of most-cited publications from 2008 to 2022. While the European Union and the United States saw their publication counts trend downward from around 600 and 500 respectively to the mid-400s, China's count rose from 100 to over 300, far outpacing France and South Korea, which remained flat at low levels.

The page concludes with a narrative box titled "China’s willing innovation partners: US and European antitrust regulators." The author criticizes Western regulators, specifically pointing to European Union regulators and the Federal Trade Commission under Lina Khan, for blocking Amazon's acquisition of the consumer robotics company iRobot. Following the termination of the acquisition, iRobot laid off half its staff and filed for bankruptcy, potentially leaving a Chinese supplier in control of the company. The text contrasts this regulatory environment with China's heavily subsidized robotics sector, noting that Chinese robotics hubs receive 20 to 40 times more government funding than their United States counterparts, directly positioning subsidized Chinese rivals Ecovacs and Roborock to benefit from iRobot's decline.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s 2026 Outlook, titled China scales the moat, examines China’s aggressive expansion of power generation, rapid electrification of energy consumption, and dominant industrial policies supported by massive government subsidies. It also analyzes the stark differences in how the United States approaches industrial policy, contrasting its support for critical minerals producer MP Materials with its approach to semiconductor manufacturer Intel.

A stacked area chart titled China electricity generation by source measures output in terawatt-hours from 2000 to 2024, demonstrating that while coal remains the largest source of electricity, China’s total power generation has skyrocketed toward 10,000 TWh. This growth is supplemented by rising shares of hydro, wind, solar, and nuclear. Since 2019, China added 2,500 TWh of power generation, compared to an increase of only 221 TWh in the US and a decline of 110 TWh in Europe.

Next to this, a line chart titled Electrification: China and Japan power ahead shows the electricity share of useful final energy from 1990 to 2025. It reveals that China and Japan are leading global electrification, with China's share rising sharply from around 10% in 1990 to nearly 38% in 2025, while regions like Europe and the United States lag behind in the 20% to 28% range.

A stacked bar chart titled Industrial policy spending in key economies ranks nations by spending as a percentage of GDP. China ranks first, spending roughly 1.7% of its GDP on industrial policies—utilizing tools such as state investment funds, below-market credit, R&D tax incentives, and direct subsidies—far outpacing South Korea at roughly 1.0% and the United States at around 0.4%.

A companion horizontal bar chart titled China direct subsidies for listed firms by subsector illustrates that from 2017 to 2020, government subsidies accounted for an extraordinary share of profits for listed Chinese companies. This includes about 34% of profits for software and services, 30% for technology hardware and automobiles, and roughly 24% for semiconductors.

Finally, a callout box compares two different strategies of US industrial policy, looking at MP Materials versus Intel. The author notes that US support for MP Materials, a critical minerals firm, provides a solid anchor of demand through ten years of guaranteed price support for neodymium and praseodymium at $110 per kilogram, plus a Department of Defense commitment to purchase 100% of the output from its upcoming magnet facility. In contrast, the US approach to Intel lacks a demand anchor. Of the $12 billion in grants and subsidies allocated to Intel under the CHIPS Act, only $3 billion was actually deployed, with the remaining $9 billion converted by the Trump Administration into a cash investment with stock warrants. This structure assumes Intel's primary obstacle is capital liquidity, ignoring deeper issues like manufacturing quality that led to defects in its 13th and 14th Gen Core CPUs. Although companies like NVIDIA and Softbank pledged capital, they did not commit to using Intel's foundries. The author poses an open question: will the US government eventually feel compelled to force major American tech companies like Apple, NVIDIA, Qualcomm, and Broadcom to manufacture their chips at Intel's facilities?

This page, titled "WCGW #4: China and Taiwan" from the J.P. Morgan 2026 Outlook, analyzes the critical global and United States reliance on Taiwanese semiconductor chips and artificial intelligence hardware. The author argues that this reliance dwarfs past European dependence on Russian energy prior to the invasion of Ukraine. 

Four charts illustrate these supply chain dynamics. The first, "Regional reliance for critical goods," compares the roughly 20% European reliance on Russian primary energy consumption in 2021 to a global semiconductor reliance on Taiwan of approximately 65% overall, rising to nearly 90% for advanced chips. The second chart, "US semiconductor reliance on Taiwan," breaks down this exposure, showing that while direct Taiwan imports account for roughly 18% of US semiconductor imports by value, US exposure rises to about 24% for memory chips and 45% for logic chips when accounting for indirect flows through third-party intermediaries. The third chart displays monthly annualized US semiconductor-related imports from 2021 through 2025 across multiple nations, noting that the reported Taiwan figure of around $10 billion to $15 billion is understated due to USITC data tracking limitations that ignore final packaging and assembly flows. The fourth chart, "US AI related computer imports," tracks annualized imports of large computers, GPUs, and parts, showing a massive spike in imports from Taiwan beginning in late 2024 and peaking near $160 billion in mid-2025, dwarfing imports from other major suppliers like Mexico, Vietnam, and Malaysia.

The final section of the page, titled "Biden’s Taiwan moment, predictions and the 2024 election," reflects on the geopolitics of "strategic ambiguity" established after the US recognized the People’s Republic of China in 1979. The text contrasts Joe Biden’s repeated public assertions that the US would militarily defend Taiwan with past presidents, noting that when George W. Bush made similar comments in 2001, the White House immediately walked them back. In contrast, Biden's repeated departures from strategic ambiguity left National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan to repeatedly clarify US policy. The author connects these repeated rhetorical departures to their previous prediction, published in January 2024, that Biden would withdraw from the 2024 presidential race prior to the Democratic convention.

This page from the report, titled China Scales the Moat, examines how China is aggressively reducing its reliance on Western semiconductor technology, particularly NVIDIA's artificial intelligence chips and lithography machines from ASML. The author highlights that China has banned ByteDance and other domestic firms from using NVIDIA chips in newly built, state-funded data centers for inference tasks. This policy shift is occurring alongside a massive domestic stockpiling effort and rapid quality improvements by Chinese chipmakers, whose latest products now outscore NVIDIA's export-compliant H20 chips in performance. As a key indicator of this decoupling, ASML has forecast that its revenue share from China will decline from a peak of 25% to 40% in 2024 and 2025 down to approximately 20% by 2026. The key open question posed is how quickly Chinese firms will transition to domestic alternatives like those made by Cambricon, a competitor backed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Four charts support these observations. The first chart, depicting a large surplus of inference chips in China in exaflops from 2025 to 2030, shows a massive and widening gap between supply and demand. By 2030, supply is projected to rise dramatically to nearly 11,000 exaflops, while demand is expected to reach only about 5,000 exaflops, leaving a significant oversupply. 

The second chart is a scatter plot mapping AI chip performance, comparing total processing performance on the y-axis against memory bandwidth on the x-axis. While the US permits the sale of NVIDIA's H20 and H200 chips to China, it restricts higher-performing models like the H100, B100, B200, and B300. The plot highlights that Huawei's Ascend 910B and 910C chips are closing the gap, with the Ascend 910C achieving a processing performance score close to NVIDIA's restricted H100, though with lower memory bandwidth than the allowed H20 model. 

The third chart tracks ASML’s revenue share by country as a percentage of total net sales from 2018 to 2026.
