Lastly, although a sixth chart shows a positive trend where air-source heat pump shipments overtook gas furnaces around 2020—reaching 4.1 million units compared to 3.1 million gas furnaces in 2025—the author notes that the overall impact on winter heating systems remains slow. This is because existing furnaces and boilers have long operational lifespans, and new home construction adds only about 1% annually to the housing stock in both the US and Europe.

This page of J.P. Morgan's Annual Eye on the Market Energy Paper analyzes the persistent growth of global fossil fuel primary energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, alongside a pending global liquefied natural gas glut and the decoupling of absolute and relative coal trends in China. The author argues that tracking primary energy is crucial for understanding why emissions continue to rise, noting that since 2010, other emerging countries besides China account for about half of the emission increases, with oil, coal, and gas consumption all rising. 

Two charts illustrate these global trends using historical data. The first, detailing global fossil fuel primary energy consumption in exajoules from 1965 to 2025, shows that oil (climbing to nearly 210 exajoules), coal (climbing to approximately 160 exajoules), and natural gas (rising steadily to about 150 exajoules) all continue to rise. Beside it, the chart for global carbon dioxide equivalent emissions from energy, processes, methane, and flaring shows a near-uninterrupted climb from 24 billion tons in 1990 to around 40 billion tons by 2025, with only a brief decline around the 2020 pandemic.

The next section details a pending glut in liquefied natural gas. The chart for global LNG capacity utilization tracks and projects capacity, imports, and utilization rates from 2005 to 2035. It predicts that a massive wave of new LNG export capacity will outpace import growth, dragging capacity utilization down from historical norms of 90 percent to 98 percent down to a record low of approximately 84 percent by 2030. The companion chart, tracking the cumulative change in LNG export capacity from 2025 to 2031, highlights that North America and the Middle East are the primary drivers of this supply surge, pushing cumulative capacity additions to nearly 400 billion cubic meters by 2031, with minor additions from Russia, Sub-Saharan Africa, and other regions.

Finally, the page explores global and domestic coal trends. A chart of coal useful final energy by country from 1965 to 2025 depicts the dramatic shift in coal consumption. While the United States and Europe have steadily reduced their coal use, China and India have expanded rapidly, with China dominating total global consumption, which approaches 60 exajoules. To explore this dynamic further, the China coal tracker from 2000 to 2025 compares absolute consumption to relative share. It shows that while coal's share of power generation has fallen below 60 percent for the first time (dropping to around 57 percent in 2024) and coal's share of useful final energy has declined to around 53 percent, absolute coal consumption for both power and useful final energy continues to rise, highlighting a scenario where relative decarbonization masks absolute emission increases. Sources cited across the visuals include the Energy Institute, J.P. Morgan Asset Management, the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, the International Energy Agency, and the Global Energy Monitor.

This page from Michael Cembalest's energy paper focuses on the critical role of hydraulic fracturing in US energy production, the rising estimates of domestic natural gas supply, and the stability of petroleum demand alongside rising exports. The author highlights that 68% to 87% of US crude oil, natural gas liquids, and natural gas were derived from fracking in 2024, collectively accounting for 62% of total US primary energy consumption. Domestic gas reserve estimates are expanding because of resources in the Haynesville and Deep Bossier Shale in the Gulf Coast, a fresh assessment of Alaskan gas, and new offshore resources in Alaska and the US Atlantic East Coast. Despite widespread analyst predictions of a peak in US oil consumption, demand remained stable through the end of 2025, and liquefied natural gas exports have risen to 10% of total domestic production.

Six charts support these observations. The first chart, showing the percentage of US oil and gas production derived from hydraulic fracturing through year-end 2024, tracks the share of crude oil, natural gas, and natural gas liquids from 1995 to 2024. Natural gas shows a steady rise from about 30% in the late 1990s to nearly 90% by 2024, while crude oil and natural gas liquids experienced a dramatic upward trend starting around 2008, both reaching approximately 70% to 80% by the end of the period. The second chart visually reinforces this dominance by illustrating that hydraulic fracturing accounted for 62% of all US primary energy consumption in 2024, using a stacked column where the unconventional fracked oil, gas, and natural gas liquids segment easily dwarfs all other components combined, including conventional fossil fuels, coal, nuclear, biomass, hydro, wind, and solar.

The middle row of charts details the scale of US natural gas resources. The chart on the left, measuring estimates of US natural gas supply in trillion cubic feet from 1988 to 2024, shows a massive expansion in total potential resources and proved reserves, growing from roughly 1,000 trillion cubic feet in 1988 to over 4,000 trillion cubic feet by 2024. The adjacent chart decomposes these resources by component from 1988 to 2023, stacking cumulative production, proved reserves, and traditional potential resources—consisting of probable, possible, and speculative resources, along with coalbed gas—which collectively approach 7,000 trillion cubic feet by 2023.

The bottom row addresses demand and export trends. The chart showing US demand for crude oil and petroleum products, measured in millions of barrels per day on a 12-month trailing average from 1965 to 2025, reveals that demand climbed from around 11 million barrels per day in the mid-1960s to a peak of over 20 million in the mid-2000s, and despite subsequent dips, has recovered and stabilized near that peak level through 2025. Finally, the chart tracking US monthly LNG exports as a share of gas production shows a rapid, volatile ascent from under 2% in 2017 to approximately 10% by late 2025, marking the growing integration of US gas production with global markets.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication focuses on essential charts for US fossil fuels, emphasizing the necessity of ongoing investment in tight oil and shale gas, the advanced age of the nation's power fleets, and shifting global dynamics in natural gas and liquefied natural gas utilization. 

An initial chart highlights the steep natural decline rates of unconventional US energy production by modeling what would occur if all investment ceased on January 1, 2026. Under this scenario, US shale gas production would plunge from its late-2025 peak of approximately 850 billion cubic meters to about 200 billion cubic meters by 2035. Concurrently, tight oil production would collapse from nearly 9 million barrels per day in 2025 down to approximately 2 million barrels per day by 2035, underscoring the short productive lives of these wells. 

Another chart depicts the capacity-weighted average fleet age for US electricity generation as of September 2022, revealing a highly mature conventional power infrastructure. Hydroelectric plants represent the oldest fleet at nearly 60 years of age, followed by coal at roughly 43 years, oil at 42 years, and nuclear at 41 years. Biomass and geothermal fleets average 36 and 32 years, respectively, while gas generation facilities average 26 years. Modern renewable sources remain much younger, with wind averaging 7 years and solar averaging just 4 years of age.

The publication also presents a forecast for US LNG export capacity utilization from 2017 through 2035. After maintaining high utilization rates that peaked near 95% around 2024 and 2025, utilization is projected to drop precipitously to a low of approximately 61% by 2031 due to a projected global glut in LNG capacity, before rising back to around 75% by 2035.

Finally, the rise of natural gas relative to oil is traced from 1990 to 2025 by dividing natural gas consumption by oil consumption on a unit of fuel equivalent basis across various regions. The US leads this transition, with gas consumption rising from about 100% of oil consumption in 1990 to nearly 150% by 2025. Globally, this ratio has climbed from approximately 75% to slightly over 100% during the same timeframe. Meanwhile, China has seen steady growth from less than 20% in 1990 to around 60% in 2025. Europe’s ratio peaked near 130% around 2010 before declining to roughly 90% by 2025, while Japan and Asia excluding Japan and China hover between 65% and 70% in the final years of the series.

This page, titled "New US liquids and gas pipeline projects: some progress off a low base," analyzes the state of US midstream infrastructure, highlighting a significant construction slowdown that began in 2022. While growth in liquids pipeline additions remains subdued, natural gas pipeline completions experienced a notable uptick in 2024. Major recent gas additions include the Matterhorn Express Pipeline carrying 2.5 billion cubic feet per day from the Permian Basin to Houston, the Mountain Valley Pipeline transporting 2.0 billion cubic feet per day of Appalachian Basin gas from West Virginia to Virginia, and the ADCC Pipeline carrying 1.7 billion cubic feet per day to the Corpus Christi Stage 3 LNG export facility. According to the Energy Information Administration, pending natural gas pipeline projects represent 29 billion cubic feet per day of new capacity, which would increase existing end-2024 capacity by approximately fifteen percent. In particular, twelve projects in Texas, Oklahoma, and Louisiana set to complete in 2026 represent the largest pipeline buildout in nearly two decades, driven by growing demand for US liquefied natural gas. Notable upcoming projects include NextDecade’s Rio Bravo Pipeline and the Blackcomb Pipeline out of the Permian Basin. 

The text addresses a critical regional bottleneck in the Permian Basin, where natural gas is produced as a byproduct of oil drilling. Due to a lack of takeaway capacity, regional gas prices at the Waha Hub in Pecos County, Texas, frequently fell below zero in 2025, forcing producers to pay customers to take the gas. To alleviate this glut, new infrastructure like Energy Transfer’s Hugh Brinson Pipeline is being built to route gas from West Texas to Dallas-Fort Worth, from where it can access LNG export facilities and growing power demand from data centers.

Four charts illustrate these trends. The first chart displays annual US liquid pipeline capacity added from 2013 to 2024 in million barrels per day, categorized by crude oil and condensate, hydrocarbon gas liquids, and petroleum products. It highlights a massive decline from a peak of over seven million barrels per day in 2019 to nearly negligible levels by 2022 and 2023. The second chart tracks annual US natural gas pipeline capacity additions from 2013 through 2027 in billion cubic feet per day, separating interstate and intrastate gas and projecting future additions currently under construction. This chart shows a projected capacity addition rebound peaking at around sixteen billion cubic feet per day in 2026. The third chart shows the annual miles of pipelines added from 2013 to 2024, showing a decline from a peak of nearly twelve thousand miles in 2015 down to under two thousand miles in recent years. Finally, a daily line chart for Waha Hub gas prices from December 2024 to December 2025 shows extreme price volatility, with prices regularly dipping below zero and hitting a low of nearly negative eight dollars per million British thermal units in mid-2025.

This page of J.P. Morgan's annual energy paper explores global energy independence, highlighting how the United States has achieved net exporter status for the first time in four decades while Europe and China must compete for global energy resources. 

The first chart, tracking energy dependence and independence via net imports of oil, natural gas, and coal in million tonnes of oil equivalent, shows that Russia remains a massive net exporter, reaching nearly 600 million tonnes by 2020. The United States transitioned from importing around 400 million tonnes in the early 2000s to becoming a net exporter of nearly 200 million tonnes. Meanwhile, Europe has remained a consistent net importer of roughly 800 to 900 million tonnes, and China's net imports have dramatically surged from near zero in 2000 to match Europe's levels by 2020. 

The second chart expresses these net imports as a percentage of primary energy consumption. It reveals that while China's raw import volume is similar to Europe's, its imports account for only about 20% of its total consumption, whereas Europe relies on imports for over 40% of its energy needs. The United States has crossed below the 0% line, cementing its status as a net exporter relative to its own consumption.

The third chart illustrates a structural shift in energy-intensive manufacturing from developed to emerging economies, comparing data from the mid-1990s or mid-2000s to 2023 or 2024. Across every sector analyzed—including overall manufacturing, ammonia, steel, cement, and plastics—the share of global production belonging to developed economies has shrunk significantly. For instance, the developed world’s share of steel production dropped from nearly 50% in 1998 to under 20% in 2024, and cement fell from roughly 30% to about 10%.

The fourth chart identifies countries with the highest degree of import dependence on fossil fuels. Singapore and Hong Kong top the list, relying on imports for nearly 100% of their primary energy consumption, with Taiwan, Morocco, Cyprus, the Philippines, Belarus, Japan, and South Korea all showing import dependencies well over 70%.

The final segment evaluates Europe’s plan to phase out Russian natural gas by 2028. A line chart tracks the Russian gas share of EU gas demand from 2000 to 2030, marking key events such as the 2006 and 2009 supply cuts through Ukraine, the 2014 annexation of Crimea, and the peak of EU reliance at roughly 45% during the 2021 "artificial scarcity" period. Following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the implementation of the REPowerEU initiative, the share is projected to drop to near 0% by 2028. However, the author poses a counter-prediction, arguing that a resumption of European purchases remains a highly likely outcome. Because the pipelines Russia is currently constructing toward China will only be able to carry half of the volume that Europe imported in 2019, Russia faces immense economic pressure to settle hostilities and restore gas flows to its highly lucrative European market.

This page from the publication focuses on the global transition of nuclear energy development from Western, developed nations to China and the broader developing world. The central argument is that while the West struggles with soaring costs and prolonged construction timelines, China and other emerging markets are leading the modern expansion of nuclear power.

A chart on global nuclear power plants by year of completion shows that global installations peaked in the mid-1980s at nearly 35 gross gigawatts before declining sharply. A modest projected recovery leading up to 2030 is driven almost entirely by emerging markets, which represent ninety-five percent of the projected capacity. This shift is further illustrated by a chart showing the market share of global megawatt nuclear starts. Developed nations held nearly one hundred percent of the market in the 1960s, but during the 1980s, development shifted rapidly. By the 2020s, developing countries accounted for the vast majority of global nuclear construction starts.

Looking forward, a chart on nuclear plants under development with estimated grid connection dates between 2025 and 2030 shows China dominating the pipeline with nearly 38 gigawatts of capacity. Other developing countries like Russia, India, Turkey, and Egypt follow with smaller but notable pipelines, while developed nations like the United Kingdom and South Korea have only minimal capacity scheduled to connect. 

The divergence in completion times and costs explains this geographic shift. A scatter plot of average completion times shows that while developing countries consistently finish plants in under ten years, developed nations have seen timelines balloon, highlighted by Olkiluoto-3 in Finland taking nearly eighteen years and Vogtle 3 and 4 in the United States taking over a decade. 

In terms of actual generation, the United States remains the largest absolute producer of nuclear power, plateauing near 800 Terawatt-hours. However, China has experienced exponential growth since 2000, rising to around 450 Terawatt-hours and overtaking France, while Germany has phased out its nuclear generation entirely. 

Finally, a chart on construction costs reveals a stark financial contrast. US overnight construction costs have risen dramatically over the decades, with Vogtle 3 and 4 approaching 15 million dollars per megawatt, and France's Flamanville 3 nearing 10 million dollars per megawatt. Meanwhile, China has kept its overnight construction costs remarkably flat and low, consistently tracking between 2 million and 3 million dollars per megawatt over the last several decades.

In this section of the J.P. Morgan Energy Paper, titled "Whydrogen? More like ‘Bye-drogen!’", Michael Cembalest argues that the outlook for green hydrogen production is increasingly bleak, a view corroborated by rising project cancellations. Citing Wood Mackenzie, he notes that green hydrogen project cancellations since 2020 are four times higher than the current clean hydrogen capacity of one million tons per year. The transportation sector was particularly hard-hit in 2025, with French taxi firm Hype shifting to battery electric vehicles, fuel cell car sales collapsing outside of Korea's subsidy programs, and major refueling network closures in Europe, North America, and China by companies like Shell and BP. Furthermore, automotive and industrial giants such as Daimler, Stellantis, GM, Honda, and MAN withdrew from hydrogen truck programs, while developers like Nikola, Hyzon, and Quantron went bankrupt. Other entities, including Cummins, the city of Dijon, Germany's rail projects, Fortescue, Airbus, and ZeroAvia, also scaled back or abandoned various hydrogen transportation initiatives in favor of cheaper, more reliable battery electric options.

Cembalest highlights key economic conclusions from a December 2025 article in The Chemical Engineer, illustrating them with four sensitivity charts showing the levelized cost of green hydrogen in US dollars per kilogram. The first chart, illustrating utilization rate sensitivity, shows that low utilization is highly uneconomical; the levelized cost drops sharply from around thirteen dollars and fifty cents per kilogram at a ten percent utilization rate down to about five dollars at an eighty percent utilization rate. The second chart explores capital expenditure sensitivity, demonstrating a linear increase in levelized cost from roughly six dollars and fifty cents per kilogram at an eight-hundred-dollar per megawatt capex level up to eleven dollars and fifty cents per kilogram at twenty-two hundred dollars per megawatt. 

The third chart focuses on electrolyzer efficiency sensitivity, showing that improving efficiency from sixty-five percent to eighty-five percent yields only a minor cost decrease from about nine dollars and ten cents to eight dollars and ten cents per kilogram. The final chart presents electricity price sensitivity, revealing a steep, linear relationship where completely free electricity still results in a levelized cost of five dollars per kilogram, which escalates to twelve dollars and fifty cents per kilogram when power prices reach one hundred sixty dollars per megawatt-hour. Cembalest emphasizes that because electricity represents sixty to seventy percent of total levelized costs, even completely free power would leave green hydrogen three to four times more expensive than traditional steam methane reforming or coal gasification.

This page from the J.P. Morgan publication "Eye on the Market" argues that sustainable aviation and motor fuels are failing to gain meaningful traction, remaining "stuck in neutral" due to high production costs, policy shifts, and technical limitations. 

The first section focuses on sustainable aviation fuels (SAF). A chart titled "Renewable jet fuel cost estimates," measured in US dollars per gallon, compares the production costs of various SAF pathways—including HEFA (food oils), Alcohol-to-jet fuel, Power-to-liquids, and Gasification—using both NREL and third-party estimates. Every single alternative pathway is dramatically more expensive than traditional fossil jet fuel, which sits near the bottom of the chart at around two dollars per gallon. Power-to-liquids is the most expensive, with some estimates exceeding twenty-two dollars per gallon. Consequently, a second chart, "Global sustainable aviation fuel usage" (measuring sustainable fuel as a percentage of commercial aviation fuel consumption), shows that actual global usage has flatlined near zero percent from 2020 through 2025, severely lagging behind the airline industry's target of reaching ten percent by 2030.

The second section shifts to sustainable motor fuels in the United States, contrasting renewable diesel—a drop-in chemical equivalent to traditional diesel—with biodiesel, which tends to gel and must be blended in ratios of two to twenty percent. Renewable diesel is produced via hydrotreating and requires about eight pounds of feedstock per gallon, while biodiesel is produced via transesterification and requires about seven and a half pounds. The chart titled "Sustainable share of US diesel consumption" illustrates that the combined share of biodiesel and renewable diesel rose steadily to a peak of over ten percent in late 2024, only to fall back sharply to approximately six percent in 2025. This decline was driven by a US tax credit policy change that limited incentives to domestically produced fuels, excluding imports. 

The final chart, "Sustainable share of US motor fuel consumption," tracks the percentage of all US motor fuels from 2011 to 2025. It reveals that the overall sustainable share has remained flat, hovering between six and seven percent for more than a decade. This total share is dominated by a steady baseline of ethanol at about four to five percent of the fuel mix, with biodiesel and renewable diesel making up only minor fractions. Ultimately, the author demonstrates that despite industry ambitions, alternative fuels have made little progress in displacing fossil fuels in either aviation or road transport.

This page analyzes the slow progress of carbon capture and storage (CCS) technology, characterizing its development as advancing at a snail's pace. The author argues that the academic citation-to-actual deployment ratio for CCS is the highest in the history of science. Despite global CCS capacity growing from 51 million tons per annum in 2024 to 64 million tons per annum in 2025, this capacity represents a mere 0.168% of global fossil fuel emissions, up from 0.135% the previous year. The author poses a highly skeptical open question regarding whether this figure will ever reach even 3%.

Five charts support this argument. The first chart illustrates the ratio of carbon capture research citations per year divided by million tons of annual global operational CCS capacity. The ratio has risen dramatically from around 2,500 in 2015 to over 4,750 by 2023, emphasizing that academic interest vastly outpaces practical implementation. The second chart shows the global CO2 capture capacity commercial facility pipeline from 2010 to 2025. Total capacity has grown slowly, projected to reach just over 100 million tons per annum by 2025, split between roughly 60 million tons of operational capacity and 40 million tons under construction.

The third and fourth charts detail the technical hurdles facing CCS. The third chart displays annual US greenhouse gas emissions from the industrial sector, showing that the largest sources are coal power plants at nearly 800 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent and natural gas power plants at 600 million tonnes. The fourth chart displays the percent of CO2 concentration by volume in various flue gas and by-product streams, illustrating that the highest-emitting sources have the lowest CO2 concentrations; natural gas power plants and coal-fired plants have concentrations below 15%, while highly concentrated streams near 100%, such as ethanol biomass fermentation and ethylene oxide, represent much smaller total emissions. This low concentration drastically increases the cost and complexity of capturing emissions from the largest polluters.

The final chart shows that real-world CO2 capture rates for existing projects are generally well below original design targets. For coal plants, the Petra Nova project captures only 35% of emissions from flue gas and 15% when including the project's own power source, while Boundary Dam captures 40%. In natural gas processing, capture rates vary widely, with the Shute Creek and Gorgon facilities capturing only 30% to 35% of emissions, while the Century plant sits near 10%. Hydrogen production facilities like Quest and Air Products capture between 45% and 78%, and steel initiatives like Emirates Steel/Al Reyadah capture only about 15%. This operational performance data demonstrates that even deployed CCS projects consistently fall short of their theoretical emissions reduction potential.

This page outlines the methodology and assumptions used to calculate "useful final energy" (UFE). The author explains that while typical Sankey energy flow diagrams adjust only for heat loss during combustion in power generation, J.P. Morgan's useful final energy measure goes further. It attempts to quantify the energy actually consumed by end-users in the industrial, transport, commercial, and residential sectors. To do this, the methodology accounts for waste heat lost during energy-to-electricity conversion, transport, and thermal heat, alongside energy losses occurring during the extraction, refining, and distribution of all forms of energy. 

The page presents these assumptions across several detailed tables. The first section covers internal combustion engines and transport efficiency. It lists the share of fossil fuel transport and tank-to-wheel efficiency for passenger cars (45% share, 18% efficiency), trucks (28% share, 43% efficiency), aviation (12% share, 33% efficiency), maritime (10% share, 47% efficiency), buses (4% share, 14% efficiency), and rail (1% share, 35% efficiency). This results in a weighted average transport tank-to-wheel efficiency of 30%. When factored alongside an 82% oil-well-to-pump efficiency, the final well-to-wheel efficiency is calculated at 24%.

The second section addresses electricity generation via combustion turbines. Coal plants are modeled at 40% efficiency and oil plants at 30% efficiency. For gas plants, the U.S. fleet is assumed to be 60% combined cycle plants (with 60% efficiency) and 40% simple cycle plants (with 38% efficiency), which yields a blended gas plant efficiency of 51%. 

The third section details furnaces and boilers used for industrial, commercial, and residential heat. Gas furnaces have a 90% efficiency, oil furnaces have 85%, and coal furnaces have 75%. When incorporating extraction, refining, distribution, and compression losses, the well/mine-to-furnace efficiency is 85% for gas, 82% for oil, and 92% for coal. Ultimately, this leads to a final well-to-heat efficiency of 77% for gas, 70% for oil, and 69% for coal. 

The final section details the electricity grid and balance of plant functions, assigning a 5% loss to transmission and distribution, and a 5% energy consumption penalty for nuclear balance of plant functions. The data points throughout the page are attributed to various peer-reviewed and industry sources, including Rystad Energy, the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, the International Council on Clean Transportation, the National Academies, the Energy Information Administration, and energy analyst Vaclav Smil.

This page presents an analysis arguing that a modern conflict designated as Gulf War III, starting in 2026, could lead to the most severe oil market imbalance seen since World War II. The argument is supported by a table titled approximate oil disruptions and global spare capacity, which compares historical energy crises against the current situation by looking at the percentage of world oil supply disrupted versus the percentage of global spare capacity available. 

Historically, major crises had significant spare capacity buffers to cushion energy shocks. For example, during the Suez Crisis of 1956-57, a 10% supply disruption was cushioned by 35% spare capacity. The Arab Oil Embargo of 1973 saw a 7% supply disruption against 8% spare capacity, and the Iranian Revolution of 1978-79 saw 5% disrupted against 5% spare capacity. Even more modern crises, such as Gulf War II from 2003-11 and the Abqaiq drone strikes of 2019, retained 1% spare capacity against disruptions of 7% and 5%, respectively. 

In stark contrast, the projection for the ongoing Gulf War III estimates a massive 20% global oil supply disruption with absolutely no remaining global spare capacity to offset the loss. This severe deficit highlights an unprecedented vulnerability in global energy security, based on data sourced from the Rapidan Energy Group, the Energy Information Administration, BP, the St. Louis Fed, and the US Senate.

This page from J.P. Morgan's Eye on the Market asks the question, "What is citrine?" The slide explains that most citrine is not naturally occurring but is instead anthropogenically melted quartz. To illustrate this, the page features an image collage labeled "CITRINE" containing four visual examples: a pale yellow-green natural quartz crystal cluster on the far left, a bright orange-yellow cluster in the middle, and two faceted gemstones on the right, including a brilliant triangular reddish-orange cut and a golden-brown cushion-cut gem showing intricate patterns of light reflection. The page contains no financial data, charts, or forecasts, serving as a brief informational slide on the gemstone.

In this entry of the energy paper, Michael Cembalest argues that sustainable shipping fuels remain stuck in neutral, currently accounting for less than one percent of global maritime fuel consumption despite the availability of flexible-engine vessels. The primary obstacle is cost, which Cembalest illustrates using two charts based on Covalent-IQ data from January 2026. 

The first chart, titled "2026 levelized cost of shipping fuels," measures costs in US dollars per metric ton of very low sulfur fuel oil (VLSFO) equivalent. Traditional benchmark fuels, including VLSFO, liquefied natural gas (LNG), and their equivalents adjusting for the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), all cost well under one thousand dollars per metric ton. Blue ammonia utilizing auto-thermal reforming (ATR) is the cheapest alternative, costing between one thousand and fifteen hundred dollars. However, the costs for e-fuels rise dramatically: E-ammonia produced via alkaline electrolysis (AEL), proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolysis, or solid oxide electrolyzer cells (SOEC) ranges from fifteen hundred to over four thousand dollars. E-methanol utilizing point source carbon dioxide ranges from two thousand to five thousand dollars, while E-methanol utilizing direct air capture (DAC) reaches extreme highs of twenty-five hundred to nearly six thousand dollars per metric ton.

To explain why these costs are unlikely to decline quickly, the second chart, "2026 levelized cost of shipping fuels breakdown, base case," breaks down these expenses. It reveals that capital expenditure (capex) represents less than half of the levelized cost for most pathways. Instead, the cost profiles are dominated by operating electricity and carbon dioxide transport and storage. Because capex is such a small portion of the overall cost, Cembalest predicts that learning-curve-driven declines in equipment costs will be insufficient to achieve parity, and he notes that carbon taxes are unlikely to bridge these immense gaps. 

Lastly, the page discusses the severe safety and environmental hurdles of using ammonia as a marine fuel. Cembalest distinguishes between transporting ammonia safely as cargo and using it actively within an open ship engine system, quoting chemical engineer Paul Martin of Spitfire Research, who asserts that using ammonia as a fuel fails the primary principle of safety in design due to its highly toxic and corrosive nature. The page relies on data and publications from the Renewable Fuels Association, the International Energy Agency, Covalent-IQ, and Spitfire Research.

This page examines the historical relationship between major spikes in crude oil prices and subsequent declines in the equity market, illustrating that a doubling of oil prices has consistently coincided with material S&P 500 selloffs. 

The analysis is anchored by two stacked, vertically aligned timeline charts covering the period from 1970 through 2025. The top chart plots the year-over-year percentage change of the S&P 500, with values ranging from roughly negative forty percent to positive sixty percent. Directly below, the second chart tracks the year-over-year percentage change of West Texas Intermediate crude oil prices, peaking as high as two hundred fifty percent, with a horizontal red dashed line marking the one hundred percent threshold—signaling a doubling of prices. Vertical dashed lines connect several major historical oil price shocks to concurrent downturns in the S&P 500. These marked events include the Yom Kippur War, the Iranian Revolution, an OPEC production cut, the first Gulf War, a commodities bull market around the turn of the century, the second Gulf War, the Chinese demand surge of 2008, and the post-pandemic inflation surge. 

An accompanying table titled Length of WTI Crude Oil Price Spikes outlines the peak dates of these surges and details their reversal timelines to pre-spike levels. The data shows that some historical spikes resulted in permanent structural price shifts rather than temporary shocks, recorded as no reversal, price shift for the peaks in January 1974, April 1980, January 2003, and February 2010. Conversely, other oil spikes reversed relatively quickly, such as the full reversals within six months following the September 1990 and June 2008 peaks, and a swift three-month full reversal following the February 2017 peak. Other periods, such as October 2000 and June 2022, saw a two-thirds reversal over twelve and nine months, respectively. Together, the visuals demonstrate that while the duration of oil price spikes varies, their rapid onset historically correlates with significant equity market contractions.

This page from Michael Cembalest’s J.P. Morgan Energy Paper analyzes the geopolitical and commodity market aftershocks of conflict, focusing particularly on the divergence between oil and gas futures. A featured chart titled "Oil & gas futures curves" plots Dutch TTF natural gas in US dollars per MMBtu on the left axis and Brent crude oil in US dollars per barrel on the right axis from 2026 through 2030. The chart demonstrates that futures markets expect a rapid, steep decline in Brent crude oil prices from over one hundred dollars per barrel in early 2026 to near seventy dollars by late 2026, stabilizing just above the prewar average level of approximately sixty-six dollars. In contrast, European natural gas futures are projected to decline much more slowly, dropping from nearly twenty dollars per MMBtu to around fourteen dollars in late 2026, and lingering near the prewar average price level of ten to eleven dollars through 2030. An accompanying illustration titled "Pandora’s Box" depicts a glowing chest releasing dark smoke over a barren landscape, symbolizing the chaotic geopolitical consequences of these market disruptions.

The text outlines the broader report's scope, which covers commodity developments, oil shocks, regional gas markets, equity impacts, the negligible benefit of global Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases, impacts on agriculture, and the depletion rate of US munitions. Cembalest highlights the prominent role Iran plays in the American military psyche, citing a historian's list of the five worst US military defeats. This list ranks the failed 1980 Desert One hostage rescue mission in Iran at number one, ahead of Task Force Smith in 1950, Kasserine Pass in 1943, Little Big Horn in 1876, and the Battle of Long Island in 1776. 

Drawing historical parallels, Cembalest compares Donald Trump’s isolationist campaign promises to Woodrow Wilson's 1916 campaign neutrality pledge, noting that both presidents found themselves bogged down in foreign conflicts within a year of election. However, he contrasts the two by noting that Trump is acting unilaterally without Congress, NATO allies, or a broad coalition to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The author argues that Trump’s previous actions tariffing and mocking NATO allies have left them unwilling to provide military assistance, leaving the US to deal with this latest crisis largely on its own. A footnote highlights the extreme geopolitical friction of the era, citing reports of Danish soldiers preparing explosives and medical supplies to defend Greenland against a potential US attack.

This page of the publication argues that natural gas pricing is highly localized due to market fragmentation, making countries with high consumption of imported gas particularly vulnerable to energy shocks. To illustrate this, a pie chart of global natural gas production shows that out of 11.3 billion cubic meters per day, the vast majority—73 percent—is consumed directly by the producing countries. Pipelines account for 13 percent, non-Hormuz LNG accounts for 11 percent, and LNG flowing through the Strait of Hormuz represents just 3 percent of global production, although this is about 20 percent of the global LNG market. 

A corresponding line chart tracks regional natural gas prices from 2020 through early 2026 in US dollars per MMBtu. It highlights a massive divergence: while European Dutch TTF and Japan/Korea LNG prices are spiking back up toward the twenty-dollar range in early 2026, domestic prices at the US Henry Hub, in Canada, and in Australia remain flat and cheap under five dollars. 

The text then shifts to the severe downstream impacts on petrochemicals, which are essential building blocks for manufactured goods. Due to the ongoing conflict, 40 percent of the world's methanol supply from the Gulf Region is stranded. A line chart tracking the methanol price index from January 1 to mid-March 2026 shows that prices in Rotterdam, Netherlands, and Zhengzhou, China, have skyrocketed by roughly 50 percent. 

The global breadth of this commodity shock is detailed in a table showing year-to-date price changes for major primary petrochemicals across key regions as of March 13, 2026. Propylene, representing 21 percent of global consumption, has seen prices jump 64 percent in the United States, 78 percent in Europe, 53 percent in Japan, and 56 percent in Korea. Ethylene, which accounts for 31 percent of global consumption, has risen 42 percent in the US, 59 percent in Europe, and 63 percent in both Japan and Korea. Other significant price jumps include butadiene rising 118 percent in Korea, toluene rising 50 percent in Europe and 70 percent in Korea, and benzene rising between 35 percent and 60 percent globally. Methanol, which represents 15 percent of global consumption, shows year-to-date price increases of 27 percent in the US, 53 percent in Europe, and roughly 60 percent across Japan, Korea, and India.

This page assesses global energy vulnerability by analyzing various countries' sensitivity and insulation to spikes in international oil and gas prices. The core concept introduced is the "Total insulation factor," defined as the share of useful final energy that is less exposed to global oil and gas shocks because it is derived from domestically produced gas, domestically produced coal, nuclear energy, or renewable energy. Notably, domestically produced oil is excluded from this insulation metric since oil and oil products remain heavily tied to volatile global market prices regardless of where they are extracted.

The top table details energy metrics for a subset of countries ranked 36 through 52 by their useful final energy. The table breaks down sensitivity to price spikes, oil and gas crisis insulation factors, transition opportunities, and year-to-date equity market returns. For example, Romania has a high total insulation factor of 64% due to its 37% share of domestically produced gas and 14% renewables, leaving it with a relatively low 40% oil and imported gas share of primary energy. In contrast, Greece exhibits high vulnerability with a 20% total insulation factor, as oil and imported gas make up 75% of its primary energy. Other countries, such as China Hong Kong and Morocco, show critical vulnerability with insulation factors of just 1% and 8%, respectively.

The bottom stacked bar chart visualizes the total insulation factor across dozens of global economies, ranking them from most insulated to least insulated. South Africa, Indonesia, China, Uzbekistan, and the United States lead the rankings with insulation factors ranging from approximately 65% to nearly 80%. South Africa and China rely heavily on domestically produced coal for their insulation, whereas countries like Sweden, France, and Switzerland rely more on nuclear and renewable energy. At the far right of the chart, highly vulnerable nations such as Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Belarus, Morocco, Taiwan, and Singapore register extremely low insulation factors, highlighting their near-total exposure to external energy price shocks.

In this analysis of oil and refined products, Michael Cembalest discusses the sharp rise in global oil prices and the even more dramatic price spikes seen in refined products like jet fuel, shipping fuel, and gasoline. The commentary emphasizes that although the United States has achieved net exporter status, it remains highly vulnerable to global energy shocks because crude oil is priced in a globalized market. To combat these rising costs, the author notes that various US policy measures have been implemented or considered alongside Strategic Petroleum Reserve releases, including increasing ethanol blending from 10 percent to 15 percent, issuing vapor pressure waivers for summer gasoline sales, banning refined product exports, temporarily suspending the Jones Act, and waiving federal taxes on oil and gas.

The page features six charts that visually detail these energy trends. The first chart, depicting crude oil prices in US dollars per barrel from 2019 to 2026, shows a steep upward trajectory in early 2026. Oman and Dubai crude grades, which are priced for immediate delivery, lead this surge by spiking to between $150 and $170 per barrel, while Brent and WTI crude lag slightly but still sit at elevated levels of around $140 and $120 respectively. 

Refined product charts, indexed to January 1, 2026, demonstrate how derivative fuels have outpaced crude oil gains. The second chart shows jet fuel prices by region through mid-March 2026; Singapore and Northwest Europe jet fuels surged dramatically to index levels near 280, far exceeding Brent crude's index rise to roughly 180. Similarly, the third chart highlights shipping fuel prices, where Singapore bunker fuel spiked to over 260, while Rotterdam and Houston bunker fuels rose to index values between 180 and 200, all outpacing Brent's index performance. 

Wholesale gasoline prices, shown in the fourth chart, also reflect this regional shock. By mid-March 2026, wholesale gasoline prices in Japan, India, and Singapore jumped to an index level of 210 to 220, while the US and Northwest Europe experienced slightly lower but still severe rises to around 180. The fifth chart contrasts US retail gasoline and diesel prices against WTI crude, showing that US retail gasoline prices leaped to an index level near 170, surpassing US diesel at 150 and WTI crude at 145. 

Finally, the sixth chart provides long-term historical context from 1980 to 2020 regarding global oil dependence and independence, measured in net imports in million tonnes. It tracks the dramatic rise of China as a net importer, climbing from zero in 1990 to nearly 600 million tonnes by 2020, alongside Europe, which remains a massive net importer at around 500 million tonnes. Meanwhile, India’s net imports have risen steadily toward 200 million tonnes, and Japan's have gradually declined to around 150 million tonnes. In stark contrast, the United States transitioned from a peak importer of nearly 600 million tonnes in the mid-2000s to a net exporter by 2020, diving below the zero line to approximately negative 100 million tonnes.

This page from J.P. Morgan’s 2026 Energy Paper analyzes the massive disruptions in the global oil market caused by the conflict referred to as Gulf War III and explores its potential consequences for global equity markets. The author argues that with an estimated 20 percent of global oil markets disrupted, this crisis represents the largest disruption in terms of volume and loss of spare capacity since World War II. 

To support this argument, a table titled Approximate Oil Disruptions and Global Spare Capacity compares the current conflict with nine historical energy crises dating back to the 1956 Suez Crisis. While previous crises like the Arab Oil Embargo or the Iranian Revolution occurred alongside some buffer of global spare capacity—ranging from 1 percent to 35 percent—the current Gulf War III shows a 20 percent global supply disruption paired with 0 percent available spare capacity. A detailed footnote explains the mechanics of this supply shock, noting that prior to the war, approximately 21 million barrels per day (mbd) of crude and refined products flowed through the Strait of Hormuz. Currently, with only 1.8 mbd from Iran continuing to flow and 4 to 5 mbd rerouted, 14 to 15 mbd of crude is stranded. When combined with 5 mbd of stranded petrochemical feedstocks like LPG and ethane, the total liquids disruption reaches 19 to 20 mbd, or roughly 18 percent of the global supply.

An intraday price chart for Brent crude oil from March 4 to March 12 shows prices climbing from about $83 per barrel to a peak near $118 on March 9. The chart highlights the coordinated IEA oil stock release announcement on March 10, which brought only temporary relief before prices climbed back over $100 per barrel. The author explains that the market largely ignored this intervention because the 400 million barrels of strategic reserves can only be released at a rate of 2 mbd. This volume covers only 45 days of imports for IEA members and depletes 20 percent of the global strategic petroleum reserve, a stark contrast to the 1991 Gulf War when Brent and WTI crude prices fell by 40 percent following reserve releases.

Finally, a dual-panel line chart compares year-over-year percentage changes in the S&P 500 and WTI crude oil prices from 1970 to 2025. It demonstrates that when year-over-year oil prices spike above 100 percent, the S&P 500 typically undergoes a major correction, dropping deep into negative territory. This correlation is highlighted across several historical periods marked on the chart, including the Yom Kippur War, the Iranian Revolution, and the post-pandemic surge. While WTI has risen 50 percent during the current conflict, other global grades are up over 100 percent. Citing J.P. Morgan Equity Strategy and Quantitative Research, the author warns that if $120 oil is sustained for six months, annual S&P 500 earnings per share estimates would fall by $12.70, marking a 4 percent decline from the current consensus EPS of $317.

This page presents a comprehensive "Oil & Gas Sensitivity Heat Map" analyzing 35 countries' exposure to energy shocks, transition readiness, and market performance. The table ranks countries by their Useful Final Energy (UFE) consumption in exajoules (EJ). China and the United States lead global consumption, accounting for 29.2% (87.7 EJ) and 14.8% (44.5 EJ) of global UFE, respectively, followed by India at 6.7% (20.0 EJ). 

The heat map evaluates countries across three core dimensions. First, under "Sensitivity to spikes in oil & gas prices," key risks include reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, where South Korea (33% of primary energy), Thailand (27%), Taiwan (27%), and Pakistan (25%) show the highest import exposure. In terms of overall import shares, Singapore is highly vulnerable with an 86% oil import share and a combined oil consumption and imported gas share of primary energy at 99%. Conversely, net exporters of oil and gas display negative percentages, such as Colombia (oil import share of -38%), Australia (gas import share of -68%), and Brazil (oil import share of -19%). 

Second, the "Oil & Gas crisis insulation factors" column aggregates domestically produced gas, coal, nuclear, and renewable energy to calculate a "Total insulation factor." Ukraine leads with an 81% insulation factor, followed closely by South Africa at 79% (heavily reliant on domestically produced coal at 75%), Indonesia at 77%, China at 76% (backed by 54% domestic coal), and the United States at 70% (underpinned by 47% domestic gas). At the opposite extreme, countries like Singapore (1% insulation), Taiwan (6%), Belarus (8%), and South Korea and Japan (each at 13%) show minimal domestic energy insulation.

Lastly, the heat map correlates these energy dynamics with year-to-date equity market returns, which are generally negative across the board.
